units.la: apientissime, ut alia omnia, dictum est à Salomone: Librorum multorum faciendorum non esse finem & multam meditationem fatigare corpus Eccl. XII. 22: Quibus tamen verbis non prohibet ille omnem librorum scriptionem, sicut nec omnem meditationem vult esse sublatam. Ex opposito præcepto Scopus & mens Regis Sapientissimi facile cognoscitur. Timorem Dei commendat præ omnibus, quo si careant, sive meditatione multâ fatigantes corpus, sive scriptione multorum librorum se macerantes, vana sunt eorum opera & frustranea omnia. Sed si accuratius attendamus ad omnia, non aliud videtur Ecclesiastes voluisse indicare, quàm, si quis de singulis rebus, quæ humano generi cognitu sunt utilia, plenè & accuratè scribere velit, nullum eorum finem esse futurum, cùm filum vitæ incidatur prius, quam omnia absolveris; compendium verò horum omnium in timore Domini vult contineri, cui propterea omnem operam navandam esse monet. Neque enim videtur, ipsis temporibus adeo excrevisse librorum copiam, ut eo nomine conquerendum fuerit Regi. Is quippe ægrè non fert, libros sacros θεοπνεύστως esse auctos, præter quos an alii fuerint scripti privatâ industriâ & labore, non nisi merâ conjecturâ potest firmari. Insana tamen post illa tempora invaluit scribendi consuetudo, de quâ jam olim Iuvenalis lib. II. Sat. 7. vers 51. — tenet insanabile multos Scribendi cacoëthes, & ægro in corde senescit. Id nunc his temporibus in immensum est auctum, ut omnem medelam superasse videatur, nec alio modo possit coërceri, quam si plures divulges libros; quam rationem agendi forte paradoxam aliquis dixerit, optimam tamen nemo jure negaverit. De multitudine librorum utilium immenso numero non est quod jure conqueraмur, qui non facile nimis augentur. Quamvis enim de rebus iisdem scribunt plures, modo illa sint cognitu digna gnæ, nullum id nocumentum veritati videtur inferre, quæ sic ad plures sibi viam pandit, cùm lectorum alii his potius, quàm illis scriptoribus delectentur, quamvis de eodem argumento commentatis. Quod rectè observavit Augustinus lib. I. de Trinitate cap. 3. Neque enim omnia, quæ ab omnibus conscribuntur, in omnium manus veniunt. Et fieri potest, ut nonnulli, qui etiam hæc nostra intelligere valent, illos planiores non inveniant libros, & in istos saltem incidant. Ideoque utile est, plures à pluribus fieri diverso stylo, non diversâ fide, etiam de quæstionibus eisdem, ut ad plurimos res ipsa perveniat, ad alios sic, ad alios autem sic. Quâ ratione inutiles libri sensim eliminantur, ut alii postea non sint usui, quàm ut piperi & thuri involvendo inserviant. Nec errores noxii melius tolli ex hominum animis, nec libri pestilentes commodius ex manibus excuti possunt, quam per ejusmodi commentarios, qui errores detegunt & refutant. Quid me ad Consensum Veritatis ante plures annos edendum impulerit, & quam justam ejus scribendi habuerim causam, ex Præfatione sequenti, quæ primæ editioni antea fuerat præfixa, & nunc hic est repetita, cognoscere potest Lector. Hoc meo scopo non visus fui plane excidisse, cùm multi relius de veritatibus illis, quæ ibi tractantur, caperint judijudicare. Iam à multis annis desiderata exemplaria secundam editionem flagitabant, quæ in publicis librorum auctionibus iniquo pretio vendebantur. Itaque undique omnes petere, rogare, instare, ne sibi in hac parte desim; in quo tamen difficiliorem me experti sunt, fateor, quàm speraverant; anni enim viginti & tres inter hanc & primam editionem intercesserunt; donec tandem cùm animadverterem, vel me invito Typographum aliquem Secundam Editionem multis forte mendis deturpatam protrusurum, malui hunc laborem in me suscipere, ut menda Typographica, quæ in primam editionem irrepserant, tollerem, quæ verò ad uberiorem intellectum veritatum demonstratarum facere viderentur, variis in locis adjungerem, ne sine novo ornatu hæc editio prodiret. Adversariorum, quantum sciam, nemo refutationem hujus opusculi aggressus fuit; & quamvis alii hinc & inde quædam carpserint, quia nihil tamen attulerunt, quod vel à veritatis defensoribus non fuerit refutatum, vel quod nullâ operâ à quovis attento lectore mei Consensus, falsitatis posset convinci, operæ pretium non videbatur inutili repetitione eorum, quæ sæpius in eo fuerunt dicta, Lectorem onerare. Ex adversariis Cl. Herbinius, cujus majorem præ aliis modestiam antehâc laudavi, veritati cessit, scriptis ad me Anno MDCLXIV a.d. x. Dec. humanissimis Trajecto
units.tr: Most wisely, as with everything else, Solomon has said: "Of making many books there is no end, and much study is a weariness of the flesh" Eccl. XII. 22: Yet by these words he does not forbid every writing of books, just as he does not wish all meditation to be abolished. The aim and mind of the most wise King is easily recognised from the opposite precept. He commends the fear of God above all things, and if men lack this, whether wearing out their bodies with much meditation or wasting themselves with the writing of many books, their works are vain and all their labours fruitless. But if we attend more carefully to the whole, Ecclesiastes seems to intend nothing other than this: if anyone wishes to write fully and accurately about each of the things that are useful for the human race to know, there will be no end to them, since the thread of life is cut off before you have finished everything; the summary of all these things, however, he wills to be contained in the fear of the Lord, and therefore he admonishes that all effort be devoted to it. For it does not seem that in those times the abundance of books had grown so great that the King had cause to complain on that account. Indeed, he is not displeased that the sacred books were written by divine inspiration, and whether others were written by private industry and labour can be established only by mere conjecture. Yet after those times a mad custom of writing took hold, of which Juvenal long ago spoke in Satire 2, line 51 (as printed): "Many are held by an incurable itch of writing, and it grows old in a sick heart." This has now increased so immensely in our times that it seems to have overcome every remedy, nor can it be restrained in any other way than by publishing more books; someone may perhaps call this method of acting paradoxical, yet no one could rightly deny that it is the best. Concerning the multitude of useful books, in such an immense number, there is no reason for us to complain justly, since they do not increase too easily. For although several write about the same things, provided those things are worth knowing, this seems to bring no harm to the truth, which by this means opens a way to more people, since some readers take more delight in these writers than in those, even though they treat the same subject. Augustine rightly observed this in Book I of On the Trinity, chapter 3: "For not all the things that are written by all men come into the hands of all." And it may happen that some who are able to understand even these things of ours do not find the plainer books, and fall in at least with these. Therefore it is useful that many be made by many, in a different style but not with a different faith, even on the same questions, so that the matter itself may reach many people in this way and others in that. By this method useless books are gradually eliminated, so that afterwards they are of no use except to serve for wrapping pepper and incense. Nor can harmful errors be better removed from men's minds, nor pestilent books more conveniently shaken out of their hands, than by commentaries of this kind, which expose and refute errors. What moved me to publish the Consensus Veritatis several years ago, and what just cause I had for writing it, the Reader may learn from the following Preface, which was formerly prefixed to the first edition and is now repeated here. I did not seem to have wholly missed my aim, since many have begun to judge rightly concerning those truths that are treated there. For many years copies that were wanted had been calling for a second edition, which were being sold at unfair prices in public book auctions. So everyone sought, asked, and pressed me from every side not to fail them in this matter; in this, I confess, they found me more difficult than they had hoped, for twenty-three years passed between this and the first edition. At last, when I perceived that some printer, even against my will, might put out a second edition perhaps disfigured by many errors, I preferred to take this labour upon myself, so as to remove the typographical errors that had crept into the first edition, and to add in various places whatever seemed to make for a fuller understanding of the truths demonstrated, so that this edition should not appear without new ornament. As far as I know, no one of the opponents has undertaken a refutation of this little work; and although others here and there have picked at certain points, since they nevertheless brought forward nothing that had not been refuted either by the defenders of the truth, or that could be shown by any attentive reader to be false in my Consensus without any effort, it did not seem worth burdening the reader with the useless repetition of things that have been said over and over in it. Among the opponents, the distinguished Herbinius, whose modesty I have praised above others before now, has yielded to the truth, writing to me in the year MDCLXIV, a.d. x. Dec., in the most courteous terms, from Trajectum [Utrecht].

units.la: Ělo ad Rhenum, literis, in quibus, inter alia be-nevolentiæ & amicitiæ signa, hæc lego: Gaudeo magnopere mihique palam de Te tantæ Virtutis adversario gratulor, responsionibus tuis contentus sum. Contuli tecum & cum aliis Magnis Viris sententiam meam communicavi: ad quam quia modestissimè reposuisti, cùm non tanti sit momenti, scribere ultra atque disputare de eâ supersedeo. Contentus sum, & gratias tuæ Claritati ago pro tam amicâ animi sententiæque suæ mecum collatione, meque Tibi ac tuorum servituti pro hâcce benevolentiâ, quoad vixero, addictum fore scito. Utinam verò similis esset aliorum omnium animus! utinam nemo nisi ea mente ad scribendum se accingeret, ut veritatibus sibi revelatis alios imbueret! quod profecto nunquam obtineri potest per convitia, per calumnias, per detorsiones verborum alienorum in aliam planè mentem, per sannas, per sarcasmos, quibus potius animus à veritate indagandâ avertitur; sed per placidam veritatis demonstrationem ad conscientiam, & ut scriptum pro Veritate propagandâ adornatum spiret amorem erga proximum, & studium illum juvandi quævis pagina loquatur. Sic ἀληθεύοντες ἀγάπην vere & sincerè, si charitatem non ore, quávis occasione, verborum vaniloquentiâ jactemus, sed corde geramus & ipso opere.
units.tr: From Elo on the Rhine, in a letter in which, among other signs of goodwill and friendship, I read this: I rejoice greatly and openly congratulate myself on you, a formidable opponent, and I am content with your replies. I have compared views with you and have shared my opinion with other great men. Since you replied to it most modestly, and since the matter is not of such great importance, I refrain from writing further or disputing about it. I am content, and I thank Your Clarity for so friendly a comparison of your mind and opinion with mine. You may know that, for as long as I live, I shall be devoted to your service and that of your family for this goodwill. I wish indeed that everyone else had the same spirit! I wish that no one would set about writing except with the purpose of imbuing others with the truths revealed to himself! This can certainly never be achieved through insults, slanders, twisting the words of others into an entirely different meaning, sneers, and sarcasm, which turn the mind away from seeking the truth; rather, it is achieved through a calm demonstration of the truth to the conscience, and so that every page of a writing composed to spread the truth breathes love towards one's neighbour and speaks of a desire to help him. Thus, "speaking the truth in love" [ἀληθεύοντες ἀγάπην], truly and sincerely, if we display charity not merely with our mouths, on any occasion, through empty chatter of words, but bear it in our hearts and in our deeds.

Sic in iis, ad quæ omnes pervenimus, eadem ambulantes regulâ, idem sentiremus, & spe magnâ armati confidere possemus, Deum reliquas veritates nostrâ operâ interveniente etiam aliis revelaturum. Id quod saxit Deus benignissimus, gratiâ & efficaciâ Spiritus Sancti nos ducens in omnem veritatem. Amen.
units.tr: We may demonstrate it by our works. In this way, in those matters which we have all reached, walking by the same rule, we would think alike, and armed with great hope we could trust that God, by means of our labour, will also reveal the remaining truths to others. May the most gracious God grant this, guiding us by the grace and power of the Holy Spirit into all truth. Amen.
