units.la: Haud raro contingit, ut remedia discordiis civilibus exstinguendis apta nata, culpâ eorum, quibus turbida læta & tutiora, magis illas excitent & incendant. Idem aliquando fatum dissensionibus eorum, quibus literarum studia sunt cordi, ut, dum moderata ingenia iis tollendis, dextrâ & sanâ mentis suæ sinceræ interpretatione, intentorumque criminum purgatione, omnem navant operam, magis exardescant, enixe id agentibus calumniarum reis, ne, veritate in lucem protractâ omnium oculis expositâ, ipsi in crimine deprehendantur. Quam primùm Philosophia Nobilissimi Cartesii caput suum extulit, quamvis non intenta sententiis aliorum oppugnandis, pervulgata inter Philosophos hujus & aliquot præcedentium seculorum consuetudine, intra sua se munimenta contineret, soli veritati investigandæ dedita, non defuerunt, qui eam tùm voce tùm scriptis vehementer aggrederentur, neque tàm justis armis quàm veneno calumniarum & tinctis maledicentiæ felle spiculis peterent, & quoad potuerunt confossum irent; hac via sibi certiorem de ea victoriam promittentes. Igitur necessitas imposita iis, qui per eam se profecisse profitebantur, illiusque beneficio multa, quæ ignara adhuc, quamvis multum quæsita, protulisse in apricum, nisi profungis & ceritis, qui omnes anteirent stultitia, vel, quod gravius, pro atheis & devotis habeii vellent; ut, expositis sententiis, quibus non sua & nativa facie, sed sub horrenda larva, quam imposuerat ambitiosa ignorantia aut maligna eruditio, productis invidia quærebatur, seque & eam, quam merito probabant Philosophiam propugnarent, & propulsata calumniantium iniquitate indignò reatui eriperent. Herbornæ quietè & qua debui modestia unà cum Clarissimo Claubergio ex munere nostro studiosam juventutem instruebam, rarioremque illam philosophandi rationem, quæ à præjudiciis veritati percipiendæ nimium quàm obstantibus defæcatam mentem in veritatis penepenetralia deduxit, commendabam, cum ab invidis & æmulis livido oculo nostri successus aspiciuntur, & quæ tunc calumniandi materies, sententiæ incond.tæ & inficetæ, impiæ imo nefariæ, & quæ sanctam Dei aut verbi divini majestatem violarent, nobis affinguntur, & quas ipsi agnoscebamus, malevolis rumoribus & scriptis differebantur. Cartesius & Cartesiani odii & probri erant vocabula. Tum Cyriaco Lentulo Eloquentiæ & Historiarum Professori (ad quem nihil attinebat Philosophia, sed putabat suis luminibus à nobis offici) dum munia Professionis suæ obeunda, placuit invectiva in Cartesium & nos insurgere, qua ut Sceptici, Athei, impii, novarum rerum cupientes, aliisque indignis nominibus traducebamur. In vulgus rumores audiebantur, quibus nos tum aliorum horrendorum dogmatum, tum quod negaremus Resurrectionem mortuorum insimul abamur. Sententi imprimis Cartesii, quæ vicissitudinem diei & noctis non Solis circa Terram rotationi, sed Telluris circa suum axem volutationi acceptam refert, tanquam lymphatorum delirium pipulo disseri, & tanquam Dei oraculis manifestissimè contraria incusari, exsibilari. Ostentabantur varia Jacobi Revii scripta, interque ea Statera Philosophiæ Cartesianæ, quibus calumniæ memoratæ tanquam tibicinibus innitebantur: nobisque, his scriptis injuriam fieri Philosophiæ innoxiæ & immeritissimè præcepta illius, detorta scilicet & mala fide deformata atque ita propósita lacerari, testantibus dictirabatur, etiam ab iis qui amicitiam nostri præ se ferebant; non itaque debuisse tamdiu inulta ferri, sed, si causa nostra potior, de gradu dejici & calumniarum convinci. Tandem patientia nostra audacior factus, scriptisque Revii tanquam tibicine nixus Lentulus properavit, si stylum excipias, scriptum ineptissimum, titulo: Nova Renati des Cartes Sapientia, in quo ace bius & iniquius in Cartesium à Revio jacta iterantur & inculcantur, n visque calumniis detortæ sententiæ Cartesii proscinduntur. Igitur his injuriis quasi vi quâdam pertracti & necessitate constricti sumus (quod quivis æquus judex existimabat) ad nos & nostri modeste defendendum, atque innocentiæ demonstratione sententiarumque Cartesii dextrâ expositione, ceu scuto objecto, tela adversariorum tàm confertim ad nos obruendos conjecta repellendum. Tunc Clarissimus Claubergius editâ Defensione Cartesianâ contra Revium & Lentulum in varia Cartesii dogmata commentari orsus est: ego peculiarem materiam de Volutatione Telluris circa suum axem, maximæ invidiæ nullâ causâ obnoxiam defensitare, nec adversus sacras literas infesto incurrere agmine, demonstrare. Editæ itaque à me Dissertationes duæ, quarum prior de S. Scriptura in rebus Philosophicis abusu, altera altera de vera quiete & vero motu Terra; utraque destinata restinguendo incendio, quod alii conflaverant. Ad loca scriptuiæ Gyrationi Terræ, ut videntur, contraria, eoque opponi solita, responderam, loquendi ratione à Copernicanis frequentatâ, scripturam ita in locis loqui secundùm opinionem vulgi, non secundùm accuratam veritatem; quam nullo modo putabam, tanquam labefactantem & evertentem eam, quæ sacris divinisque literis tribuenda est Auctoritas & Veritas omnium verè Christianorum consensu, acceptum iri, cum, si hæc mea mens fuisset, compendiosiore viâ potuerim ista scripturæ loca, tanquam Auctoritate & Veritate destituta rejicere. Ego vero e contrario fueram testatus, me scripturæ auctoritatem summa cum reverentia suscipere, & testimoniis adductis variorum Theologorum, qui eodem illo loquendi modo in locorum scripturæ interpretatione utuntur, quorum nubem lector videre non neglegat cap. 31. hujus libri, satis tutus videtur, minimeque reus criminis, quo arguor, quasi istis verbis utendo Auctoritatem & Veritatem scripturæ lederem, imo convellerem; nisi quis forte eadem opera ejusdem criminis postulare tot orthodoxos Theologos sustineret. Ceterum longe alius ac speraveram scripti hujus fuit eventus, & quod defendendæ & liberandæ opinioni Cartesii à profana temeritate & impietate, concilandæque cum sacris literis erat comparatum, hominum malevolorum opera impietatis & profanæ temeritatis accusatum, & tanquam Auctoritati & Veritati scripturæ evertendæ adornatum, fuit traductum. Primus impetus contra illud factus ex Academia Ultrajectina per Disputationes sub titulo: De Auctoritate, Veritate & Infallibili Fide sacra Scriptura in rebus Philosophicis, auctoribus iis (nam librorum titulis fides deroganda non est) qui respondendi navaverunt operam, quibus insimulatus fui, quod studuerim infringere Auctoritatem & accuratam Veritatem S. Scripturæ in rebus Philosophicis. Quibus, omissis Respondentibus, unâ Disputatione Duisburgi habita ita respondi, ut & sententiam meam clarius explicarem, & adversarii mecum consensum, dum concedit: Scripturam fuisse usitam formulis receptis, etsi innitterentur opinionibus erroneis, docerem, caque Disputatio deinde sub titulo: Consideratio Theologica de Stylo Scripturæ Anno LVI. publici juris fuit facta. Quantumvis autem postea iidem Respondentes Vindicias singuli pro suis Disputationibus edi fuerint, quando tamen Præses earum infra se exiliimaverit, ut alio modo quam per Respondentes in scenam productos mecum congrederetur, nec in ipsis Disputationibus quicquam sit, speciem veri habens, quod, repetitum ab aliis adversariis, in hoc tractatu à me non sit dilutum, nec in Vindiciis crimen calumniarum Præsidi di impactum sit purgatum (conferat tantum Lector meam accusationem in Consideratione cum Vindiciis), nemo mihi vitio vertet, si ulterius contentionis serram cum Respondentibus recipiscari dedigner. Attigeram quaedam contra hanc sententiam objecta à Dn. Jacobo du Bois in Dialogo Theologico Astronomico, eaque modeste inter alias objectiones refutaveram, qua re bilis ipsi adeo mota, ut tractatu virulento, cujus inscriptio: Veritas & Auctoritas sacra in Naturalibus & Astronomicis, me censuerit adoriendum & lacerandum. Dn. Revius reliquis, quae ad ipsum pertinebant, praetermissis, quaestionem, quae in priori opere per occasionem erat tractata, de Indefinito Mundo, solam sibi sumsit ventilandam, composito ad id libello, cui titulum fecit tractatui parum convenientem AntiWittichius, cum non nisi paucissima mei libri tangat, statumque Controversiae, de Infinitate Mundi à me nullibi asserta, praeter meam mentem constituat. Ac ne quid deesset oppositionum, accesserunt praeterea, tum Dn. Petri van Maeltricht Vindicia, quas vocat, Auctoritatis & Veritatis Scripturae, tum Dn. Johannis Herbinii Examen Theologico-Philosophicum famosa de Solis vel Telluris motu controversia, quo inter alios adversarios etiam me sibi sumsit invadendum, ut ita Oppositionum & adversariorum multitudine tantum non viderer obruendus. Hi omnes uno ore à me Auctoritatem & Veritatem scripturae oppugnatam asserebant, quam etiam in titulis librorum contra me defensuros polliceabantur, eorumque scripta, ut fiab iis, qui quam semel imbiberunt animo sententiam, nunquam vel examinare volunt, sola volvebantur. Nec defuerunt alii, qui quavis occasione & loco, in Cathedris Scholasticis, Ecclesiasticis, Classibus, Synodis, scriptum meum tanquam profanum & inimicum sacris literis traducerent, & ut in summam adduceretur invidiam, omni ope & opera niterentur. Accessit ad gravandam meam causam, quod à non paucis, ineptissimis scilicet judicibus, tum ex frontispicio libri, e quo, si animum nolis advertere ad explicationem à me in ipso libro adhibitam, non impossibile est dirius quid colligere, judicium ferebatur; tum nimium habebatur fidei cuidam Suetonio Tranquillo, qui verba mea excerpta, tanquam membra aliqua à corpore suo divulsa propositu, quo separata ab antecedentium & consequentium connexione atque illustratione deteriora viderentur. Quae occulta perversitas scribendi & judicandi si obtineat, nihil quicquam erit, in quo damnatoria sententia non possit ferri. His causis simul concurrentibus factum est, ut Synodi & Classes commota, nescio quod malum Ecclesiae à Philosophia Cartesiana proximum putaverint, atque Auctoritatem & Veritatem Scripturae ea nimium quantum infirmatum iri metuerint. Quapropter, ut & quæ offensionem concitavisse ex scriptis adversariorum didici, dextra explicatione vel substitutione clariorum tollam, & ab illo metu quoscunque liberem, dummodò non velint sponte tuta timere, & meæ Defensioni post adversariorum accusationem alteram aurem apertam præbeant; vel, si ne nunc quidem id obtinere queam, posteritas aliquando iniquitatem istiusmodi judicum cognoscat & miretur, iteratam hanc scriptionem necessarium habui suscipere. Est ea Dissertationum secunda Editio, dispositione commodiori & alio titulo. Post explicatam differentiam, quæ inter Cognitionem humanam Communem omnibus hominibus, atque eò Vulgarem dictam, & Philosophicam, ac propterea Accuratam appellatam, demonstro argumentis, Philosophicæ istius Cognitionis Principium non esse Sacram Scripturam, quam ostendo, non datam esse à Spiritu Sancto, ut Philosophos & sapientes mundi efficiat, verùm eo fine Deum hominibus largitum esse lumen rationis, quo, si bene utantur, atque legitimæ viæ tramite incedant, ad multarum abscondITarum veritatum cognitionem pervenire possunt, exemplo Cartesii, cujus progressuum tali methodo factorum aliquot specimina adduco; qui sic cognovit, tum Mundi Extensionem Indefinitam, quam declaro, probo & defendo, tum legitimum situm & Ordinem præcipuorum Mundi corporum inter se, qua occasione determinatur; num vicissitudo dierum & noctium à Solis circa Terram Motu, an à volutatione Telluris circa suum axem dependeat? His adjicio, quòd quamvis Cartesius ex lumine tantùm naturæ Philosophicam rerum cognitionem hauserit, tantam tamen semper deferat (quod & ego facio) scripturæ Auctoritatem, ut, si eam cognoscat aliquid revelare, quod cum lumine rationis pugnet, potius velit Auctoritati divinæ, quàm proprio suo judicio fidem adhibere, qua occasione evinco, etiamsi statuatur, scriptutam sacram de rebus naturalibus loquentem stylo uti vulgari iisque formulis, quæ, nullam quidem docentes falsitatem, veritatem tantùm generalem, relatam ad homines, & præjudiciis quoad modum enunciandi involutam, significent, nihil quicquam asseri, quod Auctoritatem & Veritatem scripturæ evertat; simul speciatim arguo, per opinionem de Gyratione Telluris nihil quicquam Auctoritati & Veritati scripturæ adversum doceri, atque loca scripturæ, quæ ei videntur contradicere, eodem concilio. Mutatus prioris Editionis titulus, ne porrò offenderentur, qui solis è titulis, ipsis interim libris non inspectis, toto de librorum argumento, quod ne opera quidem perfunctoria lustrarunt, judicium ferre consueverunt. Etiam hoc dedi infirmiorum teneræ Conscientiæ, ut modo dum illum loquendi, scripturam saepe de rebus naturalibus loqui secundum opinionem vulgi, non secundum accuratam veritatem, quo antea eram usus, isti lapidi offensionis removendo, mutaverim; alia commodiore formula substituta; qui vero arbitrantur, se offensos phraseos istius usu, mihi unà cum Theologis plurimis Orthodoxis, quibus idem dicendi genus usitatum, ignoscant peto. Simul rogo, ne iterum offendantur, si dicam cum adversario Ultrajectino: Scripturam uti formulis receptis etsi prajudiciis innitantur; vel, Scripturam uti talibus loquendi modis, qui veritatem aliquam, sed generalem tantum atque relatam ad homines & prajudiciis quoad verba involutam significent. Idem enim his verbis quamvis diversis significatur, meaque verba eandem referunt sententiam, ac est Clarissimi Dn. Velthusii, (quod & ipse observavit pag. 42. in libello Belgico, Nieder Beryjs, dat noch de leere van der Sonne stilstandt &c. noch de gronden van de Philosophie van Renatus des Cartes strijdigh zijn met Godts Woort; & Irenæi Philalethii pag. 62. in tractatu Belgico: Bedenckingen op den staat des geschils over de Cartesiaensche Philosophie. Cavi, quantum potui, in hac secunda Editione, ne verba excīderent, in quibus quisquam meritò offenderetur, ideoque pacis studio omisi locutiones, quas vidi in sequiorem sensum facilè detorqueri, atque ita materia n scandali esse posse; &, si, præter spem, ejusmodi quid non animadversum huic editioni adhuc inst (quis enim immunitatem ab omni defectu etiam in verbis sibi tribuere audet) id, perspecta sana mea sententia, per alia mea verba clariora ut exp natur, precor. Locupletata est altera hæc Editio accessione Instantiarum, quæ contra primam à Dn. du Bois, Revio, Heidanio & Maestricht fuerunt motæ, & Responsionum, quibus illæ retundunt. r. Ex his itaque, sed lectis & accuratè perpensis judicate, quicunque estis, Doctores, Pastores, Synodi, Classes, num mercatur Cartesianæ Philosophiæ laudatorum causa cum Arminianorum comparari, & num similes tubæ Cartesianorum dictorum operæ & culpa metuendæ? quo metu simpliciores quosdam & rei ignaros corripi fertur. Nos utique, præterquam quòd Verbi divini Auctoritati libenter omnes nostros sensus & opiniones subjicimus, nihil quicquam innovamus in Confessionibus receptis, nihil reprehendimus, sed eas tanquam communis fidei Reformatorum testes as recipimus, atque subscribendo probavimus, & ex animo etiamnum probamus. Non fidem spectant, non Theologiam Revelatam Controversias, quas excitare placuit Sophistis. Philosophia Cartesiana quieta est, & tantum in mente amatorum sui veritate instruendā, non aliorum opinionibus & falsitate evertenda occupatur. Spectant vel mentem Cartesii, quam Sophistæ Sophistæ conantur pervertere, vel res naturali lumine cognoscendas, quas is optime intelligere dicendus, qui rectissime isto lumine utitur. Ac, nisi ab antagonistis scriptura in partes fuisset vocata, atque pro illorum sententia adducta, nulla controversia circa eam ruisset exorta. Quæ tamen non est de ejus Veritate & Auctoritate, cui, si non plus, saltem non minus deferunt Cartesiani, atque isti, qui eâ male intellectâ suos errores conantur palliare, sed de ejus Sensu, adversariis ei, quod nolis suis pueri, affingentibus sensum opinionibus suis convenientem. Non quæritur: An Scriptura sit credendum? An Scriptura falsum loquatur? An Scriptura multis falsitatibus scateat? quod adversarii petulantissime mihi affingunt, mihi tamen nunquam in mentem venit asserere. Sed quæstio est: An non Scriptura utatur sermone e trivio desumto & phrasibus, quæ ex præjudiciis habent ortum, non tamen illa ipsa præjudicia docendo, sed veritatem generalem talibus verbis quasi involutam? ubi ego affirmantium sententiam sequor. Quis enim negabit, quin sermo quavis in lingua multis præjudiciis sit involutus? Quis dicet, novi sermonis inventorem esse scripturam sacram, & non potius inter homines recepto, quamvis non satis accuratè respondente rebus, earumque naturam non accuratè exprimente, uti? Atque hic eos, cum quibus mihi est negotium, etsi contra meam sententiam varia objiciant, veritatis vi coactos mecum consentire oportet. Sic enim Dn. Herbinius pag 248. de Chananja loquens, qui in scriptura Propheta vocatur inquit: Spiritus Sanctus mutuatus est hic verbum opinionis sive nomen a populo, non verò opinionem; quæ pr. facto ipsissima mea est sententia. Et Dn. Maestricht pag. 115 inquit: Si fixere, si statuamus Cordis vocabulum ea vere significare, quæ Sp. S. co nobis significare intendit, sive ea vera significatio errorem aliquem N B auctorum illius phraseologia suppenat, sive non. Ergo Spiritus Sanctus potest uti phraseologia, cujus vera significatio erroris aliquem auctorum ejus supponit, quod tamen à me dictum tanquam adversans Veritati verbi divini impugnatur. Atque cum Dn. du Bois sæpius repetat: A proprio verborum sensu sit recedendum, debere esse cogentes rationes, vide pag. 19, 72, & 127, quæstione prius dicta insuper habita, inter me & adversarios tantum disceptandum impositum: An sint claræ rationes, quæ nos jubeant à proprietate verborum recedere circa textus contra volutationem Telluris adductos? vel potius: An in laudatis textibus non sint tales formulæ loquendi, quæ ex præjudiciis habentes ortum, non nisi veritatem aliquam generalem, nihil contra gyrationem Telluris facientem, doceant? quod ego tucor contra adversarios id negantes. Neque est, quod dicatur: Clara esse ista loca contra Terræ gyrationem adducta, & proinde in iis doceri Terræ quietem & Solis motum: Sic enim dicere etiam potuerunt, qui terram aquis innatare persuasi fuerunt & Antipodes negârunt, clarè id docere Psal. xxiv. 2. Nam ipse super maria fundavit Terram & super flumina stabilivit illam, & Psal. cxxxvi. 6. Qui expandit Terram super aquas, quia in seculum est benignitas ejus; cùm tamen homo liber à præjudicio id inde non colligat. Non ergo ex nostris præjudiciis scriptura exponenda, sed iis prius depositis videndum, ex consideratione scopi & circumstantiarum textus, quid Sp.S. quovis in loco nobis velit testari. Proin non convelluntur fundamenta Theologiæ per Philosophiam Cartesianam, quod multis est persuasum. Quærit tamen Dn. du Bois pag. 140. quanam sit ratio tam vehementis querimonia, quæ in prioris editionis præfatione habetur, si Controversiæ hæ fundamentum salutis non tangant, & neutri errores obsint saluti? Verba mea super quibus hanc quæstionem fundat in Præfatione prioris Editionis sunt: quòd Veritas Diaboli omnis Veritatis osoris instinctu gravissimis calumniis impetatur, oneretur & prematur; item, quòd dolosus Cacodæmon nihil potuerit invenire aptius ad majorem ejus cursui remoram injiciendam, quàm si larvis mendaciorum & absurditatum dedecoratam mundo exhiberet, ut sic odiosam & invidiosam redderet; quæ justæ querelæ rationem habere possunt, etiamsi non omnis Veritas pertineat ad fundamentum salutis, vel non spectet Fidem & Theologiam Revelatam. Cùm enim omnis Veritas mentem perfectione ornet, eique jucunda & grata accidat vera multarum rerum & causarum naturalium cognitio, non potest non menti veritatis cupidæ esse molestum, quòd propter istas calumniarum & mendaciorum nebulas sibi aditum ad eam videat esse factum difficilem, aliis etiam, eas non sentientibus, & propterea nec discutere conantibus, impervium. Dubitatio Cartesiana, neque ad res fidei neque ad usum vitæ se extendens, eumque respiciens, qui philosophari incipit, nihil aliud denotat, quàm serium examen omnium opinionum, quas quis ab infantiâ hausit, ut nulla admittatur, nisi quæ fundamentis solidis insistat; quod non tantùm licitum, sed etiam necessarium esse ei, qui certam & indubitatam quærit scientiam, quis non videat? Quidni etiam, dùm Fide firmiter teneas Dei existentiam, liceat inquirere, num eadem ex lumine naturæ possit cognosci & demonstrari? Verùm lucernam in meridie accenderem, si pluribus de his agere conarer, cùm Dubitatio Cartesiana integro tractatu à Dn. Claubergio sit explicata, & ab omnibus incommodis libera facta. Qui ea legere dedignatur, & tamen desistere ab hac Dubitatione accusandâ detractat, ejus improbitas nec nostrâ scriptione poterit coerceri. Senten-tia tia Cartesii de Libero Arbitrio eadem planè est, quæ nostrorum Theologorum omnium, quod ex Meditatione quartâ cuilibet potest esse manifestum. Neque enim, inquit, opus est, me in utramque partem ferri posse, ut sim liber, sed contra, quò magis in unam propendeo, sive quia rationem veri & boni in eâ evidenter intelligo, sive quia Deus intima cogitationis meæ ita dispo- nit, tantò liberius eam eligo; nec sanè divina gratia nec naturalis cognitio un- quam imminuunt libertatem, sed potius augent & corroborant. Indifferentia autem illa, quam experior, cùm nulla me ratio in unam partem magis quàm in alteram impellit, est infimus gradus libertatis, & nullam in ea perfectio- nem, sed tantummodò in cognitione defectum sive negationem quandam testatur; quæ verba ad Cartesii consensum cum nostris Theologis probandum à solidissimæ eruditionis Theologo Johanne Coccejo in tractatu de Fœdere Dei art. 99. laudantur. Dominium quod ei assignat non est absolutum, sed dependens à Deo, nihilque hic est diversitatis inter Cartesium & Theologos nostros. Vide Claubergii Defensionem Cartesianam cap. 20. De Omnipræsentia Dei quæ sit Cartesii sententia, eadem cum sententia multorum Theologorum, consistens in accuratiori Omnipræsentiæ explicatione Philosophicâ, videre licet hujus mei tractatus art. CCI. An bestiæ ita sentiant, ut homines? est quæstio Philosophica, ubi negativam Cartesius non sine magnâ ratione tuetur, bestiis denegans cogitationem & rationem. Plures posse esse mundos negat Cartesius, quia implicat contradictionem, atque eo ipso divinam Omnipotentiam non evertit, non negans, quòd Deus plures possit creaturas sive corporeas sive incorporeas condere. Sed hoc facto, ex non no- vam aliquam Universitatem corporum, si sint corporeæ; nec novam ali- quam Universitatem creaturarum, adeoque non novum mundum essent constituturæ. Vide art. CLIV. hujus tractatus & Claubergii Defensionem Cartesianam p. 487. & seqq. In his ergo & similibus vel detorquetur mens Cartesii, &, quod non est controversum pro controverso habetur; vel quæstio est potius de nomine quàm de re; vel ad summum Philosophica, non ad Fidem, sed ad explicationem quandam ex lumine naturæ pertinens. Rogatos itaque volo & monitos quoscunque, qui huiusque clamoribus iniquis adversariorum in transversum acti, zelo forte Dei, sed non secundum scientiam judicârunt, sententias, quas Cartesianas vocant, adversâ fronte cum sacris literis concurrere, vel in fundamenta Religionis arietare, ut æquo animo citra affectus expensis juxta nostris defensionibus ac adversariorum accusationibus, mitius de nobis judicent, certoque sibi persuasum habeant, nihil nos innovatum in religione & receptis fidei symbolis, Confessionibus Reformatorum, velle. Distinguant obsecro inter quæstiones de Veritate sententiarum & illarum Pondere, &c, si Cartesianas sententias minus veras existimant, fruantur suo judicio, sed & permittant nos frui nostro, habeantque has quæstiones saltem eo loco, circa quas salvo Religionis Reformatæ vinculo liceat modeste dissentire, prout tales multas ipsa etiam in Theologia dari omnes Theologi agnoscunt. Sin è contra io sententias vobis vix auditas, nisi vocabulo Cartesianas, vel ex adversariorum accusationibus tantùm cognitas, nunquam verò libratas trutinâ incorrupti judicii, tanquam adversas Verbo divino cæco jud cio placet condemnare, eoque fine judicia, verè præjudicia, Academiarum vel Synodorum & Classium emendicare, sciatis nos parum istis iri motum; vos autem ita vestra opera implicitum iri crimine neglectæ charitatis, posterosque habituros, in quo vestram injustitiam accusent. Reprehenditis Pontificiorum iniquitatem, quòd à lectione librorum à nostris pro defensione Religionis scriptorum, tanquam condemnatorum abstineant, & sic in errore permaneant; cavete itaque, ne eandem merearnini notam, atque eadem judicii temeraria iniquitate pervertamini. Vos nunc compello, quibus prætet meum meritum in me acerbius invehi, & contra meas Dissertationes placuit vehementius insurgere. Caussam Dei agere contra me arbitramini, atque defendere Auctoritatem & veritatem ejus verborum, quam tamen juxta vobiscum indubitatam & infallibilem agnosco. Etiam illi putabant amici Job, pervertentes ejus verba, contra quos tamen Deus pronuntiavit sententiam. Si vestra causa bona, quid tanta virulentia opus est? cui bono contumeliæ & criminationes? Si par pari voluissem reponderre, quoties mihi subministratis materiam, ut vos potuissem aceto perfundere, & sale multo perfricare! Sed vobis condono, & ipse mihi in refutatione vestrarum objectionum occasionem præscindo, dum prætermissis reliquis, ea tantum, quæ ad caussam faciunt, cito & refuto. Velim tantum, ut ex multis sequentia vestra verba expendatis, eorumque iniquitatem agnoscatis. Tu imprimis Dn. du Bois consídera serio, an conveniant cum tuo munere sacro, quæ passim in tuo tractatu comparent. Tota tua Præfatio tuba est belli excitandi contra eos, qui Cartesii Philosophiam probant, à quibus malum Ecclesiæ gravius portendis, quàm à Remonstrantissimo Initio tractatus hoc argumentum proponis: Quod sacra litera claris & distinctis verbis testantur esse verum, id etiam ut verum a nobis habendum & credendum est: Atqui Solem circa Terram moveri sacra litera claris & distinctis verbis testantur: Ergo, atque inquis: Concedi a nobis Majorem rem in materiis fidei, sed negari in rebus naturalibus, Physicis, Astronomicis. A quonam vero istam responsionem didicisti? Id vel ostende vel calumniam agnosce. Non Majorem, sed Minorem negamus, quam salsissimam esse sumus persuasi, neque magis asseri à sacris literis, quàm eædem docent, Terram aquis innatare, & proinde nullos dari Antipodes. Pag. 25. me accusas contortarum expositionum scripturæ, novitatum in Theologiâ & heterodoxarum opinionum, de quo te injuriæ postulo. Quoties vero studio & opera data mea verba pervertis? Sic p. 85. ex eo, quòd dixeram: Ne videamur tantum niti præsumtionibus, mihi tribuis, quòd mea argumenta habeam tantùm pro præsumtionibus. Juvenilis audacia & temeritas, puerilis responsio, ingenium novaturiens, me nimis citò pulverem scholasticum excussisse, & similia ubique tuas paginas exornant. Nos vilia mancipia Cartesii, qui credamus & omnibus viribus defendamus, quod ab ipso didicimus, quia αὐτὸς ἔφα pag. 213. Cùm tamen non auctoritate, sed rationibus à Cartesio monstratis, & à nobis rectè perceptis ducamur, nemoque minus auctoritatibus humanis in scientiarum studio tribuat, quàm dicti Cartesiani, satis exploratum habentes, scientiam non nisi demonstrationibus & rationibus indubitatis generari. Deum in nobis non obscura lineamenta proponere Philosophorum, qui postquam tramitem verbi divini deseruerunt, justo Dei judicio prolabuntur in ματκιολογίαν, inquis pag. 266. Scomma in Cartesium acerbum est: Damnum illud esse deplorandum, quòd hoc demùm seculo in lucem è Jesuitarum scholis prodierit tantus doctor, qui si tempore Josuæ vixisset, virum illum secundum veritatem loqui docuisset pag. 152. Hæc & similia innumera, quæ passim conspiciuntur in tuo libello, causam tuam nulli modesto & pacis amanti lectori probabunt. Itaque impositorum à talibus ut abstineas hortor, &, si huic meæ Defensioni quid opponere velis, id fiat citra calumniam & contumelias. Meminisseris tamen, tibi prius satisfaciendum Dn. Velthusio, cujus tractatui sub titulo: Naeder Bewys, dat noch de Leere van der Sonne stilstandt en des aerdtrÿcks beweging &c. strÿdigh zÿn met Godes Woordt tegens I. du Bois, responsum adhuc debes, ut & Irenæi Philalethii scripto: De verstrickte Astronomus Jacobus du Bois. Hos si accuratè refutaveris, satis maturè ad mihi respondendum te accinges. Tu vero Dn. Maestricht perpende, num ad sacri Ministerii functionem acerbo tuo & virulento scripto rectè te præparaveris? Præfat. pag. 3. inquis: Satanam operâ Renati des Cartes enervatis genuinis fidei Christianæ principiis in Scepticismum primò, post in Atheismum Ecclesiam proturbare conatum esse. Item, Cartesium imitatum exemplum Iulii Vaninii Atheismum propagare volentis. Pag. 5. Satanam ad expugnandum scripturam proposuisse sententiam de Terræ motu, quibus nihil contumeliosius & iniquius in Cartesium dici potuit. Pag. 8. tibi sum novitius & novaturiens Theologus. pag. 11. incurro πολυπεραγμοσύνης notam. pag. 12. non vereor in arenam cum scriptura sacra consistendere. Sic in ipso tractatu p. 39. dicor, locutionibus Sp. S. falsitatis dicam scribere pag. 61. Veracitatem scripturæ nefario ausu in dubium adducere. pag. 232. ea tantum ex adversariis meis, te sic volente, excerpsi, quæ meis exceptionibus & cavillationibus maximè judicaverim expositu. Quibus si te audacter & impudenter calumniari & convitiari dixero, quod res est pronuntiavero. Pag. 206. mihi tribuis: Conceptus scripturæ de Deo ejusque attributis exigendos esse ad limam rationis humanæ eaque corrigendos, cum non de conceptibus scripturæ, sed de conceptibus vulgi fuerim locutus. pag. 210. verba mea pervertis, id quod dixeram; Nulla blasphemia in Sp. S. committitur, sic exponendo: dicendo ipsum deserta accuratâ veritate ad errorem deflexisse, cum hic eorum sit sensus: Nulla blasphemia in Sp. S. committitur, si dicamus, ipsum relictis accuratis locutionibus ad populares deflexisse erroribus innitentes. Pag. 218. calumniatorie admodum agis, dum inquis, me dicere: Scripturam aliquatenus esse verbum Dei non purum, idque more dolosi generaliter proponis, & postea impietatis accusas; cum si verba mea, quæ respicis, recte considerentur, nihil quicquam sit, quod temetipsum concedere non oporteat. Quæro enim, si per purum Dei verbum intelligatur tale verbum, in quo nulla sit locutio humana à Deo adoptata, & suam originem referens ad aliquod præjudicium, an cofensu Scripturam audeas asserere purum Dei verbum? Revera ergo fluctus in simpulo moves, quando hic ita paratragœdias. Tandem, ut infinita alia omittam, consIDera, num à calumniâ excusare possis, quòd p. 257, dum tractatum concludis, ais: me ne nimis honorifice de sacrâ scripturâ sentirem, eam erroribus vulgi scatere asserere non vereri. Hæc & alia tibi opinor ostendent, non fuisse Zelum Dei, quo agitatus contra charitatem tot aliena à meâ sententiâ mihi tribuisti. Ad te nunc me converto Dn. Herbini, qui ceteris modestior & doctior, styloque elegantiori usus, tamen non potuisti cavere, quin quædam duriora in me dicta tibi excident, qualium specimina sunt, (ne dicam de Epistolâ Dedicatoriâ, in quâ acerbissimè adversarios tuos generatim perstringis) p. 93. me ex hypothesi Copernicaa S. Spiritui in sua materia loquenti audacter præscribere non dubitasse. pag. 94. me dedisse rationibus meis Deum, Deo ne reverentiam quidem; me temere & indigne tractavisse sacras literas. pag. 113. Estne Christiani hominis taceo Theologia Doctoris tremenda Majestatis taliter tractare oracula & p. 193. Taliter philosophari illos decet; qui qui praeconceptam ad furorem usque deperientes hypothesin, omnino omni atque adeo & supra rationem veneratione dignissimis contradicunt literis. p. 194. inquis: demirari te non posse satis superque D Wittichii Spiritum, qui ex solita Spiritui S. contradicendi, ejusque oracula ad hypothesin suam retorquendi libidine, quid non tandem de Deo statuit? Ego vero hujusmodi dictis injuriam mihi fieri, & sententiam attribui, quae nunquam mihi venit in mentem, protestor. Spero fore & opto, ut his perpensis & mea sententia clare latis nunc saltem cap. 20. hujus tractatus propositā agnoscatis, vos vel errasse in mente mea percipienda, vel, si eam antehac agnovisslis, gravium calumniarum crimine vos obligasse, ac proinde serió earum veniam à Deo petendam, & imposterum à similibus abstinendum. Dn. Revius, dum Defensio mea sub prælo est, satis concessit; itaque quamvis non mitius mecum egerit quàm alii, à recensendis durioribus ejus dictis abstineo. Quod superest, Deum veneror, ut fratribus de rebus leviorībus dissentientibus tales inspiret mentes, ut linguas & calamos suos non convertant in gladios, sed invicem amice conferant, & leviorem dissensum patienter ferant, spiritu lenitatis alter alterum instituentes, donec quoque Deus ea, quae ignorant, aliis revelet. Amen.
units.tr: Hardly ever does it happen that remedies, fitted and intended to put out civil discords, are made to stir up and inflame them more, through the fault of those who turn them to their own advantage and safety. Sometimes the same fate befalls disputes among those who are devoted to literary studies. While moderate minds labour with all their might to end such quarrels, by a fair and sound interpretation of their own sincere meaning and by clearing away the crimes laid against them, the disputes only blaze up the more, because those who are accused of slander do their utmost to prevent the truth from being brought into the light and laid open to everyone's eyes, lest they themselves be caught in the crime. As soon as the philosophy of the most noble Descartes raised its head, it did not aim at refuting the opinions of others. It kept within its own defences, devoted only to the search for truth, in keeping with the custom, common among philosophers of this and some earlier centuries. Yet there were those who attacked it vehemently, by voice and in writing. They did not assail it with fair weapons but with the poison of slander and with darts dipped in the gall of abuse, and they went on stabbing it as far as they could, promising themselves a surer victory by this means. Hence those who professed to have made progress through it were compelled, unless they wished to be thought fools or, worse, atheists and devotees, to bring into the open many things which, though sought long and hard, had until then been unknown. They would defend both themselves and the philosophy they rightly approved, and by repelling the injustice of the slanderers they would snatch themselves from an unworthy charge. Together with the most distinguished Claubergius, I taught the studious young men at Herborn quietly and with the modesty I owed, in my post there. I commended that rarer method of philosophizing which, freed from prejudices that greatly hinder the perception of truth, leads the mind into the innermost sanctuary of truth. But our success was viewed with an envious and jealous eye. Then there was material for slander: opinions were invented against us, unbecoming and absurd, even impious and abominable, opinions that would violate the holy majesty of God or of the divine word. We did not recognise these as our own, but they were spread by malicious rumours and writings. "Cartesius" and "Cartesian" became words of hatred and reproach. Then Cyriacus Lentulus, Professor of Eloquence and History, to whom philosophy meant nothing, but who thought he should be aided by our light while he discharged the duties of his profession, decided to rise against Descartes and against us with an invective. In it we were labelled sceptics, atheists, impious men, lovers of novelties, and by other unworthy names. Rumours were heard among the common people that we taught other horrible doctrines, and also that we denied the resurrection of the dead. Above all, the views of Descartes were cried down and hissed at as the ravings of madmen, and condemned as plainly contrary to the oracles of God. These views were that the alternation of day and night is due not to the motion of the Sun around the Earth but to the turning of the Earth about its own axis. Various writings of Jacob Revius were paraded, among them The Balance of Cartesian Philosophy, on which these slanders leaned as on props. We were told, and those who pretended friendship with us repeated it, that injury was being done to an innocent philosophy by these writings, and that its precepts, plainly twisted and falsely distorted in bad faith and so set forth, were being torn to pieces. It was not right, therefore, that such things should be suffered unpunished for so long; if our cause were the stronger, our opponents should be thrown from their place and convicted of slander. At last, growing bolder from our patience, and leaning on Revius's writings as on a prop, Lentulus hurried to produce a most silly piece of writing, if one excepts its style, under the title The New Wisdom of René Descartes. In it the more bitter and unjust charges that Revius had levelled against Descartes were repeated and hammered in, and the opinions of Descartes, twisted by slanders, were torn apart. Therefore we were, as every fair judge admitted, driven by these injuries as if by some force, and bound by necessity, to defend ourselves and our friends modestly, and to repel the missiles of our adversaries, hurled so thickly to overwhelm us. We did this by demonstrating our innocence and by an honest exposition of the opinions of Descartes, holding them up as a shield. Then the most distinguished Claubergius, publishing his Cartesian Defence against Revius and Lentulus, began to comment on the various doctrines of Descartes. I undertook to defend a particular matter, the rotation of the Earth about its own axis, which was exposed to no great hatred, and to show that it does not run with hostile column against the holy Scriptures. And so I published my Two Dissertations, the first on the abuse of Holy Scripture in philosophical matters, the second on the true rest and true motion of the Earth. Both were intended to quench a fire which others had kindled. To the passages of Scripture which seemed to be contrary to the rotation of the Earth, and were usually brought against it, I had replied with the manner of speaking used by the Copernicans, that Scripture in such places speaks according to the opinion of the common people, not according to exact truth. I did not think that this would be received by any means as weakening and overturning that authority and truth which all truly Christian people agree must be ascribed to the sacred and divine writings. For if this had been my mind, I could have rejected those passages of Scripture more quickly, as destitute of authority and truth. On the contrary, I had declared that I receive the authority of Scripture with the greatest reverence. And by the testimony of various theologians who use that same way of speaking in interpreting such passages of Scripture, whose number the reader will not neglect to see in chapter 31 of this book, I seem safe enough and far from guilty of the crime with which I am charged, as if by using these words I were injuring, indeed overthrowing, the authority and truth of Scripture. Unless, perhaps, someone should at the same time dare to bring that same charge against so many orthodox theologians. But the outcome of this writing was quite other than I had hoped. What had been prepared to defend and free the opinion of Descartes from profane rashness and impiety, and to reconcile it with the sacred writings, was turned by malicious men into an accusation of impiety and profane rashness, and was represented as if it had been devised to overthrow the authority and truth of Scripture. The first assault against it was made from the Academy of Utrecht, through disputations under the title On the Authority, Truth and Infallible Faith of Holy Scripture in Philosophical Matters. Their authors (for faith should not be given to book titles) were those who took the trouble to reply, and by them I was accused of having aimed to undermine the authority and exact truth of Holy Scripture in philosophical matters. I answered these disputations, leaving aside the respondents, in one disputation held at Duisburg. In it I both explained my opinion more clearly and showed that my opponent agreed with me, since he conceded that Scripture used the formulas in common use, even though these rested on erroneous opinions. This disputation was then published under the title Theological Consideration on the Style of Scripture in the year 1656. However, although these same respondents afterwards each published a Vindication of his own disputations, the president of these disputations thought it beneath him to engage me otherwise than through the respondents brought onto the stage. Nor is there anything in the disputations themselves that has the look of truth which, when repeated by other opponents, has not been refuted by me in this treatise. Nor has the charge of slander brought against the president been cleared in the Vindications; the reader need only compare my accusation in the Consideration with the Vindications. So no one will blame me if I refuse to take up the saw of dispute again with the respondents. I had touched on some objections against this opinion made by Mr. Jacob du Bois in his Theological-Astronomical Dialogue, and had modestly refuted them among other objections. For this his bile was so stirred up that he chose to attack and tear me apart in a virulent treatise whose title is The Sacred Truth and Authority in Natural and Astronomical Matters. Mr. Revius, leaving aside the other things that concerned him, took upon himself alone the question that had been treated by occasion in my earlier work, that of the Indefinite World. For this he composed a little book, which he titled AntiWittichius, a title ill suited to the treatise, since it touches on very little of my book and sets up a state of controversy about the infinity of the world, which I nowhere asserted, beyond my intention. And lest there be any lack of opposition, there also came the Vindication, as he calls it, of the Authority and Truth of Scripture by Mr. Peter van Maestricht, and the Theological-Philosophical Examination of the notorious controversy on the motion of the Sun or Earth by Mr. John Herbinius. In it, among other opponents, he took it upon himself to attack me too, so that I might seem almost overwhelmed by the multitude of objections and adversaries. All of them with one voice asserted that I had attacked the authority and truth of Scripture, and they promised to defend this against me in the titles of their books. Their writings were read over and over only by those who, once they have drunk in an opinion, never want to examine it. Nor were there lacking others who, on every occasion and in every place, in academic chairs, churches, classes and synods, denounced my writing as profane and hostile to the sacred letters, and made every effort, with every means, to bring it into the greatest odium. It also added weight to my cause that many, namely the most inept judges, pronounced judgment on the strength of the book's title page, from which, unless one is willing to pay attention to the explanation I give in the book itself, one can gather something rather harsh. Too much trust was placed in a certain Suetonius Tranquillus, who picked out my words and set them forth like limbs torn from a body, so that, separated from the connection and illumination of what comes before and after, they appeared worse. If this hidden perversity of writing and judging prevails, there will be nothing in which a condemning verdict cannot be pronounced. With these causes concurring together, it came about that the Synods and Classes were stirred up, and imagined some evil, I know not what, akin to the Cartesian philosophy, and feared that the authority and truth of Scripture would be weakened by it to an excessive degree. Therefore, in order both to remove by a fair explanation or by clearer substitution whatever I have learned from my opponents' writings to have caused offence, and to free from that fear whoever is willing not to fear without cause, and who after the accusation of my adversaries will lend an open ear to my defence, or else, should I not be able to obtain even this now, so that posterity may one day recognise and marvel at the iniquity of such judges, I thought it necessary to undertake this rewriting. It is the Second Edition of the Dissertations, with a more convenient arrangement and another title. After explaining the difference between human knowledge common to all men, called therefore vulgar, and philosophical knowledge, called accurate for that reason, I show by arguments that the principle of this philosophical knowledge is not Holy Scripture. I show that Scripture was not given by the Holy Spirit to make men philosophers and wise men of the world. Rather, God granted men the light of reason for this purpose: if they use it well and walk along the path of the right way, they can attain knowledge of many hidden truths. As an example I bring some specimens of the progress made by Descartes by such a method. In this way he came to know both the Indefinite Extension of the World, which I declare, prove and defend, and the legitimate position and order of the principal bodies of the world with respect to one another, by which occasion it is determined whether the alternation of days and nights depends on the motion of the Sun around the Earth or on the turning of the Earth about its own axis. To these I add that, although Descartes drew his philosophical knowledge of things from the light of nature alone, he has always given such authority to Scripture (as I also do) that, if he knows it to reveal anything that fights with the light of reason, he would rather give faith to divine authority than to his own judgment. On this occasion I show that, even if it is laid down that Scripture, when it speaks of natural things, uses a common style and such formulas which, though teaching no falsehood, signify only a general truth related to men and involved in prejudices as to the manner of expression, nothing is asserted that overturns the authority and truth of Scripture. At the same time I argue in particular that through the opinion about the rotation of the Earth nothing is taught contrary to the authority and truth of Scripture, and that the passages of Scripture which seem to contradict it are to be reconciled by the same method. The title of the earlier edition has been changed, so that those will not be offended any further who are accustomed to pass judgment from the titles alone, without having looked at the books themselves, and on the whole subject of the books, which they have not even glanced at in a cursory way. I have also made this concession to the tender consciences of the weaker sort: I have changed the phrase I used before, Scripture often speaks of natural things according to the opinion of the common people, not according to exact truth, in order to remove that stone of offence, and I have put in a more convenient formula. But I ask pardon of those who think they are offended by the use of that phrase. It was customary for me, together with many orthodox theologians, to use this kind of speech. I ask them likewise not to be offended again if I say, with my Utrecht opponent, that Scripture uses the formulas in common use, even though they rest on prejudices, or, that Scripture uses such ways of speaking as signify some truth, but only a general one, related to men and involved in prejudices as regards words. For these words, though different, signify the same thing, and my words express the same opinion as that of the most distinguished Mr. Velthuysen. (He himself noticed this on page 42 of his Dutch pamphlet, Nieder Beryjs, dat noch de leere van der Sonne stilstandt &c. noch de gronden van de Philosophie van Renatus des Cartes strijdigh zijn met Godts Woort; and Irenaeus Philalethius on page 62 of his Dutch treatise Bedenckingen op den staat des geschils over de Cartesiaensche Philosophie.) In this second edition I have taken care, as far as I could, that no words should be left in which anyone might rightly be offended. And so, for the sake of peace, I have omitted expressions which I saw could easily be twisted into a worse sense, so that they might become a material of scandal. And if, beyond my hope, anything of that kind has not been noticed and still remains in this edition (for who dares claim for himself immunity from every fault, even in words?), I ask that, once my sound opinion is seen, it be explained by my other, clearer words. This second edition has also been enriched by the addition of the Objections which were raised against the first by Mr. du Bois, Revius, Heidanus and Maestricht, and of the Replies by which I beat them back. So judge these things, you Doctors, Pastors, Synods, Classes, whoever you are, after reading them and weighing them carefully: is the cause of the Cartesian philosophy, praised by some, really to be compared with that of the Arminians? And are the trumpets of the so-called Cartesians to be feared, through their work and fault? It is with this fear that the simpler sort and those ignorant of the matter are said to be stirred up. For our part, apart from the fact that we gladly subject all our senses and opinions to the authority of the divine Word, we introduce nothing new into the received Confessions. We find nothing to reprehend in them. Rather, we accept them as witnesses of the common faith of the Reformed, and we have approved them by subscribing, and still approve them from our hearts. They do not concern the faith, nor revealed theology; they are controversies which the Sophists have chosen to stir up. The Cartesian philosophy is quiet and occupied only in instructing in the truth the minds of those who love it, not in overthrowing the opinions of others with falsehood. They concern either the mind of Descartes, which the Sophists try to pervert, or things to be known by the natural light, of which he is rightly said to understand best who uses that light most correctly. And unless Scripture had been dragged into the fray by our antagonists and brought forward in support of their opinion, no controversy would have arisen about it. Yet the controversy is not about its truth and authority, which the Cartesians (and those who try to cover their errors by misunderstanding it) grant to it no less, if not more, than these men do. It is about its sense, which our adversaries, like boys who do not know what they are doing, ascribe to it in accordance with their own opinions. The question is not: Is Scripture to be believed? Does Scripture speak falsely? Does Scripture abound in many falsehoods? These things my adversaries most shamelessly ascribe to me, though it never once entered my mind to assert them. The question is this: Does not Scripture use common speech, taken from the crossroads, and phrases which have their origin in prejudices, not by teaching those prejudices themselves, but by wrapping up a general truth, as it were, in such words? Here I follow the opinion of those who affirm it. For who will deny that speech in any language is wrapped up in many prejudices? Who will say that Holy Scripture is the inventor of a new kind of speech, and does not rather use the speech received among men, though it does not answer very exactly to things and does not express their nature with precision? Here those with whom I have to deal, though they bring many objections against my opinion, must by the force of truth agree with me. For Mr. Herbinius, speaking on page 248 of Chananiah, who is called a prophet in Scripture, says: The Holy Spirit here borrowed from the people the word or name of opinion, not the opinion itself; which is precisely my own opinion. And Mr. Maestricht says on page 115: If we establish, if we hold that the word heart truly signifies those things which the Holy Spirit intends to signify to us, whether that true signification presupposes some error of its authors' phraseology or not. So the Holy Spirit can use a phraseology whose true signification presupposes some error of its authors. Yet when I said this, it is attacked as opposed to the truth of the divine Word. And since Mr. du Bois often repeats, one must depart from the proper sense of words only when there are compelling reasons (see pages 19, 72 and 127), and sets aside the question previously stated, the dispute imposed between me and my adversaries is only this: Are there clear reasons which bid us depart from the proper meaning of words in the texts adduced against the rotation of the Earth? Or rather: Are there not in the praised texts such forms of speech which, having their origin in prejudices, teach nothing but some general truth which does nothing against the rotation of the Earth? This I defend against adversaries who deny it. Nor is there cause for anyone to say: the passages brought against the Earth's rotation are clear, and therefore the rest of the Earth and the motion of the Sun are plainly taught in them. For those who were persuaded that the Earth floats on the waters and denied the Antipodes could say the same, that Psalm 24:2 clearly teaches it: For he hath founded it upon the seas, and established it upon the floods, and Psalm 136:6: To him that stretched out the earth above the waters: for his mercy endureth for ever. Yet a man free from prejudice does not infer this from them. Therefore Scripture must not be explained according to our prejudices, but, once these have been laid aside, we must see from a consideration of the aim and circumstances of the text what the Holy Spirit wishes to testify to us in each place. Therefore the foundations of theology are not overturned by the Cartesian philosophy, as many have been persuaded. Yet Mr. du Bois asks on page 140: What is the reason for the so vehement complaint which is found in the preface to the first edition, if these controversies do not touch the foundation of salvation, and neither error hinders salvation? The words of mine on which he bases this question in the preface to the first edition are: that the Truth is attacked, burdened and oppressed with the most grievous calumnies at the instigation of the Devil, the hater of all truth; and also, that the crafty Cacodaemon could find nothing more apt for placing a greater obstacle in the way of its course than to present it to the world disfigured by the masks of lies and absurdities, so as to make it hateful and odious. These are complaints which can have a just basis, even if not all truth pertains to the foundation of salvation, or concerns faith and revealed theology. For since all truth adorns the mind with perfection, and the true knowledge of many things and natural causes is pleasant and welcome to it, it cannot but be troubling to a mind desirous of truth to see that, because of these clouds of slanders and lies, access to it has been made difficult for it, and blocked to others too, who do not perceive these clouds and therefore do not try to disperse them. The Cartesian doubt, which extends neither to matters of faith nor to the practice of life, and which concerns the person who begins to philosophize, means nothing other than a serious examination of all the opinions that one has drunk in from infancy, so that none is admitted except those which rest on solid foundations. Who does not see that this is not only lawful but even necessary for one who seeks certain and indubitable knowledge? Why should it not also be permitted, while you firmly hold the existence of God by faith, to inquire whether the same can be known and demonstrated from the light of nature? But I would be lighting a lamp at noon if I tried to say more about these matters, since the Cartesian doubt has been explained in a whole treatise by Mr. Claubergius and has been freed from every inconvenience. Whoever disdains to read that and yet shrinks from accusing this doubt, his wickedness cannot be restrained even by my writing. The opinion of Descartes on free will is plainly the same as that of all our theologians, as anyone can see from his Fourth Meditation. For there is no need, he says, for me to be carried in both directions in order to be free; on the contrary, the more I lean toward one, whether because I clearly understand in it the reason of the true and the good, or because God so disposes the inmost thoughts of my mind, the more freely I choose it. Certainly neither divine grace nor natural knowledge ever diminishes freedom; rather they increase and strengthen it. But that indifference which I experience, when no reason impels me toward one side more than the other, is the lowest degree of freedom, and bears witness to no perfection in it, but only to a certain defect or negation in knowledge. These words are praised by the most learned theologian John Coccejus in his treatise On the Covenant of God, art. 99, to prove Descartes's agreement with our theologians. The dominion which he assigns to the will is not absolute but dependent on God, and here there is no difference between Descartes and our theologians. See Claubergius's Cartesian Defence, chapter 20. As to what Descartes's view of the omnipresence of God is, it is the same as the view of many theologians, consisting in a more exact philosophical explanation of omnipresence. This can be seen in art. 201 of my treatise. Whether beasts feel as men do is a philosophical question, where Descartes defends the negative side not without great reason, denying thought and reason to beasts. Descartes denies that there can be several worlds, because it implies a contradiction, and in that way he does not overthrow divine omnipotence, not denying that God could create several creatures, whether corporeal or incorporeal. But by doing so they would not constitute a new universe of bodies, if they were corporeal, nor a new universe of creatures, and so not a new world. See art. 154 of this treatise and Claubergius's Cartesian Defence, p. 487 and following. In these and similar cases either the mind of Descartes is twisted, and what is not in controversy is treated as controversial; or the question is about a name rather than a thing; or at most it is philosophical, not concerning faith but some explanation pertaining to the light of nature. I therefore beg and admonish all those who, hitherto driven aside by the unjust clamours of the adversaries, perhaps out of zeal for God but not according to knowledge, have judged that the opinions they call Cartesian clash head-on with the sacred letters, or batter against the foundations of religion, that they weigh our defences and the accusations of our adversaries with an even mind, free from passion, and judge us more gently. Let them be firmly persuaded that we desire nothing new in religion and the received creeds of faith, or in the Confessions of the Reformed. Please, let them distinguish between questions about the truth of opinions and about their weight. If they think the Cartesian opinions less true, let them enjoy their own judgment; but let them also permit us to enjoy ours. Let them consider these questions at least as belonging to that class in which, without breaking the bond of the Reformed religion, it is lawful to dissent modestly, as all theologians acknowledge that there are many such questions even in theology itself. But if, on the other hand, you condemn with blind judgment, as adverse to the divine Word, opinions which you have scarcely heard, except under the name Cartesian, or known only from the accusations of our adversaries, and never weighed on the balance of an uncorrupted judgment, and if you seek for that purpose the judgments, truly prejudices, of Academies, Synods and Classes, know that we shall be little moved by this, and that you will thus be entangled by your own work in the crime of neglected charity, and that posterity will have a charge against you for your injustice. You rebuke the iniquity of the Papists, who keep from reading the books written by our side in defence of religion, as if they were condemned, and so remain in error. Take care, then, lest you incur the same mark and be overturned by the same rash injustice of judgment. I now address you, to whom it has pleased to rail more bitterly against me, and to rise up more vehemently against my Dissertations. You think you are pleading the cause of God against me, and defending the authority and truth of his words, which I nevertheless acknowledge, as you do, to be indubitable and infallible. The friends of Job also thought so, perverting his words; yet God pronounced sentence against them. If your cause is good, why is such virulence needed? To what good are insults and accusations? If I had wished to answer tit for tat, how often you supply me with material, so that I could have drenched you with vinegar and rubbed you with plenty of salt! But I forgive you, and I cut off for myself the occasion for refuting your objections, since I set aside the rest and quickly refute only those which bear on the cause. I only wish that from many things you would weigh your own following words and recognise their injustice. You, above all, Mr. du Bois, seriously consider whether the things that appear everywhere in your treatise agree with your sacred office. Your whole Preface is a trumpet to stir up war against those who approve the philosophy of Descartes, and you foretell from them a greater evil to the Church. In the very beginning of your treatise you propose this argument: What the sacred letters testify to be true in clear and distinct words, that too we must hold and believe as true. But the sacred letters testify in clear and distinct words that the Sun moves around the Earth. Therefore. And you say: We grant the major premise in matters of faith, but deny it in natural, physical and astronomical things. From whom, then, did you learn this reply? Show it, or acknowledge your slander. We do not deny the major but the minor, which we are persuaded is most false. Nor are the sacred letters more plainly asserting this than they teach that the Earth floats on the waters, and therefore that there are no Antipodes. On page 25 you accuse me of distorted expositions of Scripture, novelties in theology and heterodox opinions; for this I demand that you make amends. But how often do you pervert my words deliberately and with intent? So on page 85, from my saying: lest we seem to rest only on presumptions, you attribute to me that I hold my arguments only as presumptions. Youthful audacity and rashness, a boyish reply, a mind eager for novelties, having shaken off the scholastic dust too quickly, and similar expressions adorn your pages everywhere. You call us vile slaves of Descartes, who believe and defend with all their strength what they have learned from him, because "he himself said it" (autos epha) (p. 213). Yet we are led not by authority but by reasons shown by Descartes and rightly perceived by us. No one attributes less to human authorities in the study of the sciences than the Cartesians do, being well assured that science is generated only by demonstrations and indubitable reasons. You say on page 266 that God sets before us no obscure outlines of the philosophers, who, after they have abandoned the path of the divine Word, fall by the just judgment of God into idle talk (matalogia). Your scornful taunt against Descartes is this: It is to be lamented that so great a doctor should have come forth to the light only in this age from the schools of the Jesuits, who, if he had lived in the time of Joshua, would have taught that man to speak according to truth (p. 152). These and countless similar things, which appear everywhere in your little book, will not commend your cause to any modest reader who loves peace. So I urge you to abstain from such things as these, and if you wish to oppose anything to this defence of mine, let it be done without slander and insult. Remember, however, that you still owe an answer to Mr. Velthuysen, whose treatise, under the title Nader Bewys, dat noch de Leere van der Sonne stilstandt en des aerdtrÿcks beweging &c. strÿdigh zÿn met Godes Woordt, tegens I. du Bois, you have not yet answered, and likewise to the writing of Irenaeus Philalethius, De verstrickte Astronomus Jacobus du Bois. If you refute these accurately, you will get ready to answer me soon enough. As for you, Mr. Maestricht, consider whether you have prepared yourself rightly for the office of the sacred ministry by your bitter and virulent writing. In your Preface, page 3, you say: Satan, by the work of René Descartes, has tried to undermine the genuine principles of the Christian faith, to drive the Church first into scepticism and then into atheism. Likewise: Descartes, imitating the example of Julius Vanini, who wanted to propagate atheism. On page 5: Satan proposed the opinion about the motion of the Earth in order to attack Scripture; nothing more insulting and unjust could be said against Descartes. On page 8 you call me a novice and innovating theologian. On page 11 I incur the mark of busybodiness (polypragmosyne). On page 12 you say: I do not fear to contend in the arena with Holy Scripture. So in the treatise itself, p. 39, I am said to write that the utterances of the Holy Spirit are falsehood; p. 61: I rashly call the veracity of Scripture into doubt; p. 232: I have excerpted from my adversaries only those things, as you wish, which I thought most deserving of my exceptions and cavils. If I say that you are slandering and reviling audaciously and impudently, I am only saying what is true. On page 206 you attribute to me: The conceptions of Scripture about God and his attributes must be brought to the file of human reason and corrected by it, though I was speaking not of the conceptions of Scripture but of the conceptions of the common people. On page 210 you pervert my words, which said: No blasphemy is committed against the Holy Spirit, by explaining them as: by saying that he has turned away from exact truth to error, though their sense is: No blasphemy is committed against the Holy Spirit if we say that he, leaving exact expressions, has turned to popular ways of speaking that rest on errors. On page 218 you act very slanderously when you say that I assert that Scripture is in some measure not the pure word of God, and you propose this in general terms, after the manner of a deceiver, and then accuse me of impiety. Yet if my words which you refer to are rightly considered, there is nothing that you yourself ought not to concede. For I ask: if by the pure word of God is meant a word in which no human speech is adopted by God and which does not refer its origin to some prejudice, will you dare to assert on your conscience that Scripture is the pure word of God? In truth, then, you stir up a storm in a teacup when you make such mock-tragedies. Finally, to omit countless other things, consider whether you can excuse yourself from calumny for your words on page 257, where, concluding your treatise, you say: Lest I think too highly of Holy Scripture, I do not hesitate to assert that it abounds in the errors of the common people. These and other things, I think, will show you that it was not zeal for God that moved you, when, against charity, you attributed to me so many things alien to my opinion. Now I turn to you, Mr. Herbinius, who, more moderate and learned than the rest, and using a more elegant style, nevertheless could not avoid letting fall some harsher things against me. Examples are: (not to speak of the Dedicatory Epistle, in which you harshly rebuke your adversaries in general) page 93: that I did not hesitate to prescribe boldly to the Holy Spirit, speaking in his own matter, from the Copernican hypothesis. Page 94: that I gave my reasons precedence over God, and showed God no reverence; that I rashly and unworthily handled the sacred letters. Page 113: Is it the theology of a Christian man, I say nothing of a doctor, to treat the oracles of the tremendous Majesty in such a manner? And page 193: It befits them to philosophize in such a way, who, burning to the point of madness with a preconceived hypothesis, contradict letters most worthy of veneration, even above reason. Page 194: You say: you cannot sufficiently marvel at the spirit of Mr. Wittich, who, by his habitual lust to contradict the Holy Spirit and twist his oracles to his own hypothesis, has at last decided what not about God? I, for my part, protest that injury is done to me by such sayings, and that an opinion is attributed to me which never entered my mind. I hope and wish that, having weighed these things, and now at least having recognised my opinion clearly stated in chapter 20 of this treatise, you will see either that you have erred in perceiving my mind, or, if you recognised it before, that you have bound yourselves to the guilt of grave calumnies, and that therefore you must seriously seek pardon for them from God, and abstain from such things in future. Mr. Revius, while my Defence was in the press, has conceded enough. And so, although he has not treated me more gently than the others, I refrain from listing his harsher sayings. For the rest, I pray to God that he may inspire the minds of brethren who dissent in lesser matters, so that they do not turn their tongues and pens into swords, but confer with one another in a friendly way and bear the lesser dissent patiently, instructing one another in a spirit of gentleness, until God also reveals to others the things they do not know. Amen.

units.la: Caeterum adhuc te monitum velim, Amice lector, me in citandis adversariorum meorum scriptis compendio fuisse usum, quod ne tibi ea cum nostris conferre volenti obstaculo sit, notas istas compendiarias hic explicare lubet.
units.tr: Furthermore, I would have you know, friendly reader, that in citing the writings of my opponents I have used abbreviations; so that they may not be an obstacle to you when you wish to compare them with ours, I think it worthwhile to explain these shorthand marks here.

units.la: Littera B. designat tractatum Jacobi du Bois, titulo: Veritas & Auctoritas sacra in Naturalibus & Astronomicis &c.
units.tr: The letter B. designates the treatise of Jacobus du Bois, entitled: Veritas & Auctoritas sacra in Naturalibus & Astronomicis &c.

units.la: B. Dial. vel B. D. significat ejusdem Jac. du Bois Dialogum Theologico-Astronomicum.
units.tr: B. Dial. or B. D. signifies the same Jacobus du Bois's Theologico-Astronomical Dialogue.

units.la: H. significat Joh. Herbinii famosa de Solis vel Telluris motu Controversia Examen Theologico-Philosophicum &c.

units.la: CAPUT I. Cognitio humana duplex, Vulgaris & Accurata, sive Com- munis & Philosophica.
units.tr: CHAPTER I. Human knowledge is twofold: ordinary and exact, or common and philosophical.

units.la: I. [O woodcut initial] mnis homo, eo ipso quòd homo est, animâ nempe rationali praeditus, habet facultatem percipiendi & intelligendi varia Objecta, quorum quaedam, prout perfectus est, clarè & distinctè percipit, ita ut menti ejus sint praesentia & aperta, nihilque iis sit admixtum, quod non sit planum & perspicuum; alia vero, prout participat de nihilo atque aliquam imperfectionem sibi habet admixtam, obscurè & confusè intelligit, ita ut vel planè mentis acie penetrare nequeat, vel si ex parte perspiciat, multa tamen iis maneant admixta, quae ipsius intellectionem effugiunt.
units.tr: I. Every man, simply because he is a man, that is, endowed with a rational soul, has the faculty of perceiving and understanding various objects. He perceives some of them clearly and distinctly, to the extent that he is perfect, so that they are present and open to his mind, with nothing mixed in that is not plain and evident. Others he understands obscurely and confusedly, to the extent that he partakes of nothingness and has some imperfection mixed into him. So either he cannot penetrate them at all with the sharpness of his mind, or, if he sees them in part, many things remain mixed in with them that escape his understanding.

units.la: II. Sed & eidem competit tum Facultas judicandi de illis ipsis objectis, eaque vel ad mentem, vel ad se invicem in mente, vel ad res extra intellectum referendi, tum facultas prosequendi quaedam, aliafugiendi, cui utrique Libertas est conjuncta, quâ ad id quod ab intellectu proponitur affirmandum aut negandum, sive prosequendum vel fugiendum ita fertur, ut à nullâ vi externâ se ad id determinari sentiat.
units.tr: II. But the same man also has the faculty of judging about those very objects, and of referring them either to the mind, or to one another within the mind, or to things outside the intellect. He also has the faculty of pursuing some things and fleeing others, and to both of these liberty is joined. By this liberty he is carried to affirm or deny what the intellect puts before him, or to pursue or flee it, in such a way that he feels himself determined to this by no external force.

units.la: III. Ac quando Intellectus quidem aliquid clarè & distinctè affirmandum vel negandum, sive prosequendum vel fugiendum propositum, non potest fieri, quin illud affirmemus vel negemus, prosequamur vel sugiamus quamdiu ad id attendimus; sed cùm ab eodem aliquid confuse & obscure est perceptum, quamvis fieri possit, ut ad illud affirmandum vel negandum, prosequendum vel fugiendum feramur, tamen etiam contingere potest, ut non feramur, sed suspensi maneamus. Posterius si faciamus, non erramus, nec prave agimus, nexum illum, qui inter Perceptionem & judicium, ita ut illa praecedat hoc sequatur, esse debet, non violantes; si prius, vel erramus & peccamus, dum nempe affirmamus ea quae sunt neganda & contra, & prosequimur ea quae sunt fugienda & contra, vel casu tantùm incidimus in verum aut bonum, adeoque nec verum scire, nec bonum appetere sumus dicendi.
units.tr: III. When the intellect proposes something to be clearly and distinctly affirmed or denied, or pursued or fled, it is impossible that we should not affirm or deny it, pursue or flee it, for as long as we attend to it. But when the intellect has perceived something confusedly and obscurely, although it may happen that we are carried to affirm or deny it, pursue or flee it, it may also happen that we are not carried, but remain in suspense. If we do the latter, we neither err nor act wrongly, since we do not violate the bond which ought to exist between perception and judgment, so that the one precedes and the other follows. If we do the former, we either err and sin, namely when we affirm what ought to be denied, and the reverse, and pursue what ought to be fled, and the reverse; or we stumble upon the true or the good only by chance, and so we cannot be said to know the truth or to desire the good.

units.la: IV. Communis ergò Regula esse debet omnis Certitudinis humanae, næ, ut nihil admittamus tanquam verum, nisi quod clare & distincte cognovi- mus, & percepimus verum, quâ observatâ ab erroribus nobis cavebimus; & ut omne quod clare & distincte percepimus, verum esse judicemus, qua ratione veritatem assequemur. Atque hanc regulam nemo sanus in dubium revocare poterit, nisi eo ipso omnem certam cognitionem & scientiam è rebus humanis velit sublatam, atque ad scepticissimum palàm defectionem paret.
units.tr: IV. The common rule of all human certainty must therefore be this: that we admit nothing as true except what we have clearly and distinctly known and perceived as true; by observing this we shall guard ourselves against errors. And that we judge to be true whatever we have clearly and distinctly perceived; by this rule we shall attain the truth. No sane man will be able to call this rule into doubt, unless by that very act he wishes all certain knowledge and science to be removed from human affairs, and prepares an open lapse into the most extreme skepticism.

units.la: V. Neque isti Regulæ obstat, quòd fide multa sint admittenda, quæ clare & distincte non fuerunt percepta: est enim per se manifestum, illam spectare cognitionem naturalem, quam homo per naturam acquirere potest. At in Fide loco istius claræ & distinctæ perceptionis rei credendæ est revelatio divina, cui fides innititur, cùm sit assensus & judicium, quo aliquid affirmatur vel negatur propter testimonium divinum. In quo tamen ipso clarà & distinctâ opus est perceptione, in tantum, ut nihil divinâ fide admittamus, nisi de quo constiterit, illud à Deo credendum esse propositum, quodque Deum testatum esse clarè & distinctè cognoverimus.
units.tr: V. Nor does this rule stand in the way of the fact that by faith many things are to be admitted which have not been clearly and distinctly perceived. For it is self-evident that this rule concerns natural knowledge, which man can acquire by nature. But in faith, in place of that clear and distinct perception, the thing to be believed rests on divine revelation, since faith is an assent and judgment by which something is affirmed or denied on the strength of divine testimony. Yet even here clear and distinct perception is required, to such an extent that we admit nothing by divine faith unless it is established that it has been proposed by God to be believed, and we have clearly and distinctly known that God has given testimony to it.

units.la: VI. His facultatibus dum rectè homo utitur, innotescunt ei, Primò, Notiones quædam communes, quæ sunt tam claræ ex se ipsis, ut earum cognitio possit sine meditatione acquiri, quales sunt: Totum est majus suâ parte. Impossibile idem simul esse & non esse &c.
units.tr: VI. When man uses these faculties rightly, there become known to him, first, certain common notions, which are so clear in themselves that their knowledge can be acquired without meditation. Such are: The whole is greater than its part; it is impossible for the same thing to be and not to be at the same time, etc.

units.la: VII. Deinde, per easdem addiscimus omne id, quod experientia sensuum docet, qualia sunt 1. nos habere corpus arctissimè nobis junctum & quasi permixtum, ut unum quid nostra anima cum illo componat.
units.tr: VII. Next, through these same faculties we learn everything that the experience of the senses teaches, such as: 1. that we have a body most closely joined to us and, as it were, mixed with us, so that our soul composes one thing with it.

units.la: VIII. 2. Varia corpora circa nos existere, quæ nos commodis vel incommodis afficere possunt, eaque pro re natâ vel prosequenda vel fugienda, talia sunt: Ignem urere, aquam madefacere; cultrum scindere, gravia decidentia contundere &c.
units.tr: VIII. 2. That various bodies exist around us, which can affect us with benefits or harms, and which, as the case may be, are to be pursued or fled. Such are: fire burns, water wets; a knife cuts, heavy things falling crush, etc.

units.la: IX. 3. Sic variæ qualitates sensibiles, quales calor & frigus, humiditas & siccitas, varii sapores, odores grati & ingrati, soni acuti & obtusi, lumen & colores varii &c. ita percipiuntur, ut inde concludere possis, aliquas esse in corporibus, à quibus variæ istæ sensuum perceptiones adveniunt, varietates iis suo modo respondentes, quæ etiam per istam ad sensuum perceptionem relationem distinguuntur, ut hinc corpora lucida, calida, colorata, sonora &c. denominentur.
units.tr: IX. 3. Likewise, various sensible qualities are perceived, such as heat and cold, moisture and dryness, various tastes, pleasant and unpleasant odours, sharp and dull sounds, light and various colours, etc. They are perceived in such a way that from them you can conclude that there are in bodies some things from which these various sense perceptions come, with varieties corresponding to them in their own way. These are also distinguished by this relation to sense perception, so that bodies are called luminous, warm, coloured, sonorous, etc.

units.la: X, 4.
