Extendit etiam se ista per sensus cognitio ad varias corporum magnitudines, varias figuras, varium situm, motum & quietem rectè distinguenda, flinguenda, ut & ad perceptionem substantiarum quarundam extensarum, quibus haec omnia insint, quae etiam per haec à se invicem distinguantur, unde & oritur, ut quilibet communem his naturam animo abstrahere & contemplari possit.
units.tr: X. 4. This knowledge through the senses also extends to the correct distinguishing of the various magnitudes of bodies, their various figures, their various position, motion and rest, and to the perception of certain extended substances in which all these things inhere, and which are distinguished from one another by these. Hence it comes about that anyone can abstract the common nature of these things in his mind and contemplate it.

units.la: XI. 5. Notandum insuper sensuum imprimis visus adminiculo varias corporum actiones, vel unius in aliud, ut cum ignis comburit corpora, & resolvit in cineres, aqua fervida carnes coquit, securis signum secat: vel alterius cujusvis Corporis in nostrum insignem inducentis mutationem, quemadmodum in medicamentorum usu experimur.
units.tr: XI. 5. It must further be noted that, chiefly with the aid of sight, we observe various actions of bodies, either of one upon another, as when fire burns bodies and reduces them to ashes, hot water cooks flesh, an axe cuts wood; or the remarkable change which another body brings about in ours, as we experience in the use of medicines.

units.la: XII. Dum autem ita per sensusnon paucarum rerum cognitionem homo acquirit, impressae imagines à memoriâ conservantur, quae Phantasia postea contemplatur; atque ita licet menti haec sensuum Objecta inter se conferre, ut inde agnoscatur, saepius unum esse alterius antecedens vel consequens, causam vel effectum, unde unius notitiâ alterius cognitionem insigniter promoveri percipi-mus. Sic elevationem vaporum causam pluviae cognoscimus, auroram antecedens esse ortus solis, & si-milia.
units.tr: XII. Now while man thus acquires knowledge of many things through the senses, the impressed images are preserved by the memory, and the imagination afterwards contemplates them. And so, although the mind can compare these sensory objects with one another, from which it is recognised that one is more often the antecedent or consequent, the cause or effect, of another. Thus we perceive that the knowledge of one notably advances the knowledge of another. So we know that the rising of vapours is the cause of rain, that dawn is the antecedent of sunrise, and similar things.

units.la: XIII. Sed & haec cognitio efficit, ut quia ex communi instituto & consuetudine res una alteram significat ac notam facit, per praesentiam unius non tantum provehamur ad recordationem alterius, sicut ex vocibus & sermone, picturis & variis characterum generibus, gestibus item & scripturâ apparet; sed etiam propter similitudinem variam aliarum rerum cognitionem consequamur.
units.tr: XIII. But this knowledge also has the effect that, since by common institution and custom one thing signifies and makes known another, by the presence of one we are led not only to the recollection of another, as appears from voices and speech, pictures and various kinds of characters, and likewise from gestures and writing; but also, by a varied similarity, we arrive at the knowledge of other things.

units.la: XIV. Ex his ita per sensum notatis, Memoriae mandatis, & interveniente Phantasiâ inter se invicem collatis per Discursum plurima alia fuere inventa, quae Anatomiae, Arti Medendi, Mechanicis variis artificiis, Geographiae ipsi speciali & aliis ortum dederunt.
units.tr: XIV. From these things thus noted through the senses, committed to the memory, and compared with one another through the imagination by means of discourse, very many other things have been discovered, which have given rise to anatomy, the art of healing, various mechanical arts, and to geography itself in particular, and others.

units.la: XV. Atque haec est notitia Communis, omnibus hominibus communibus adminiculis acquirenda concessa, in quâ tamen etiam alii aliis ulterius progrediuntur, quae collata cum cognitione Philosophica rerum naturalium, deprehenditur imprimis in his duobus ab eâ superari, nimirum, 1. quòd ubscurae admodùm sint & confusae qualitatum sensibilium perceptiones. Quamvis enim quilibet minùs attendendo sibi facilè persuadeat, se clarissimè videre lucem, colorem &c. percipere calorem, frigus &c. verè etiam unum ab altero per sensus rite dispositos distinguat, si tamen quidnam sit examinet, quod iste calor vel color repraesentat, omninò fatebitur, se id ignorare, praesertim si conferat cum magnitudinis, figurae, situs, motus, quietis longe evidentiori cognitione. Quòd si verò per sensus earum qualitatum natura percipieretur, nonne quo sensus firmiores, tanto etiam evidentior earum cognitio esse deberet, & quandoquidem, secundùm vulgatum versiculum Nos aper auditu præcellit, aranea tactu, Vultur odoratu, lynx visu, simia gustu,
units.tr: XV. This is common knowledge, which is granted to be acquired by all men through the common means available; yet in it some advance further than others. When it is compared with the philosophical knowledge of natural things, it is found to be surpassed by it chiefly in these two respects: first, because the perceptions of sensible qualities are very obscure and confused. For although anyone, by attending less, easily persuades himself that he sees light and colour most clearly, and perceives heat, cold, etc., and indeed distinguishes one from another rightly through the properly disposed senses, if he examines what this heat or colour represents, he will fully confess that he does not know it, especially if he compares it with the far more evident knowledge of magnitude, figure, position, motion and rest. But if the nature of those qualities were perceived through the senses, would not the knowledge of them have to be the clearer the firmer the senses are? And since, according to the common verse, the boar surpasses us in hearing, the spider in touch, the vulture in smell, the lynx in sight, the monkey in taste, must we not judge that those beasts also have a clearer knowledge of these qualities?

units.la: nonne etiam bestias istas clariorem habere harum qualitatum cognitionem erit censendum?
units.tr: Must we not also judge that these beasts have a clearer knowledge of these qualities?

units.la: XVI. 2. Quod pauca sint comparate ad Philosophicam cognitionem, quæ hoc modo percipiuntur. Nulla enim substantiæ intima natura per hanc notitiam nobis innotescit; unde non tantum vulgus, sed etiam philosophi multi, qui aliis non utuntur cognitionis subsidiis, fateri coguntur, se cum vulpeculâ Æsopi vas vitreum lambere, pultem non attingere, cum omnium rerum formæ substantiales, exceptâ solâ animâ rationali, ignotæ illis dicantur. Multa etiam corpora suâ subtilitate & exiguitate sensus nostros plane effugiunt, ut vel ex acari membris subtilissimis, item ex spiritmeans quorundam Chymicorum subtilitate vasa vitrea penetrantium &c: patet. Ut non dicam de hujus adminiculi tenuitate circa ea, quæ pluribus sensibus usurpare non possumus, præsertim, quæ à nobis valde sunt remota, circa quæ nonnisi pauca & valde generalia sensus nos docent.
units.tr: XVI. 2. It is because these are few compared with philosophical knowledge, which is gained in this way. For the inner nature of a substance is never made known to us by this kind of knowledge. Hence not only the common people but also many philosophers, who have no other aids to knowledge, are forced to admit that they are like Aesop's little fox, licking a glass vessel but unable to reach the porridge, since the substantial forms of all things, except the rational soul alone, are said to be unknown to them. Many bodies, too, escape our senses altogether by their subtlety and smallness, as is clear from the very fine parts of a mite, and likewise from the subtle spirits of certain chemists, which penetrate glass vessels, and so on. I say nothing of the feebleness of this aid with regard to things that we cannot grasp by several senses, especially things that are very remote from us, concerning which the senses teach us only a few very general points.

units.la: XVII. Verùm enim vero, quoniam facultatibus à Deo concessis homo non raro abutitur, judicium ultra perceptionem extendens, & ordinem ab ipso Deo constitutum infringens; fit, ut in istâ cognitione multa Præjudicia, nec pauci errores reperiantur, quibus veritas, quæ per notitiam communem & vulgarem retegitur, est involuta. Horum hic exempla plurima afferri possent, nisi id jam ab aliis nominatim à Clarisf. Dn. Clauberg io in fine Defens. Cartes. sequente præeuntem Cartesium, esset factum, attamen in gratiam Lectorum quædam hic attingemus. Ortum ea communem debent non tam ipsis sensibus, ut sunt à Deo dati, quàm quod ultra eorum perceptionem sese judicium in primâ infantiâ extendit, plus judicat rebusque adscribit, quàm unquam in iis percepit, quibus præjudiciis tam firmiter adhæret in posterum, ut ea, ne examinari qui dem libenter patiatur, quemadmodum exemplum hujus rei manifestum in adversariis exiit.
units.tr: XVII. But since man often misuses the faculties granted him by God, extending his judgment beyond perception and breaking the order established by God himself, it comes about that many prejudices and not a few errors are found in this knowledge, by which the truth that is disclosed through common and ordinary knowledge is obscured. Very many examples of these could be brought forward here, had not others already done so by name, following Descartes, who went before them, especially the most distinguished Mr. Clauberg at the end of his Defence of Descartes. Yet, for the sake of the readers, we shall touch on some of them here. These common errors arise not so much from the senses themselves, as God gave them, but from the fact that judgment, in earliest infancy, extends beyond their perception. It judges more and attributes more to things than it ever perceived in them, and it clings so firmly to these prejudices afterwards that it does not willingly allow them even to be examined, as a clear example of this has appeared among our opponents.

units.la: XVIII. Et cùm visus omnium sensuum sit communissimus, & quàm latissimè se extendat, fit etiam, ut Præjudiciorum segetem amplior em præbeat reliquis. Hoc modo decepti ab ineunte ætate existimamus, terram esse planam, quod ob magnitudinem ejus gibbositas obtuta oculi cognosci non possit; & contra plana ejus figura oculis insinuare se apertè videatur, qui error non potuit corrigi citius in vulgo, quam navigationes circa totum orbem terrarum & historiæ fide dignæ aliter homines edocuissent. Quo Præjudicio non minus est suâ natura, quod ab infantiâ judicemus, Cœlum Terræ incumbere, ubi oculorum nostrorum acumen sistitur, quamvis facilius deponatur, quod cuivis per experi-menta contraria illum errorem liceat emendare. Tale est, quòd cuilibet è vulgo persuasum, Lunam post Solem reliqaas stellas & luce & magnitudine in tantum superare, quantum nobis apparet, quod & firmiter retinetur à multis, qui nomen Eruditorum sibi vendicant, sed ab Astronomiæ studiis alieni exstiunt. Sic existimamus, ex visus indicio, Solem suâ luce & magnitudine tantum superare stellas, quantum nobis apparet; cum tamen sola nimia stellarum remotio causa istius diversæ apparentiæ esse possit: ipsas etiam stellas fixas tantoperè inter se differre magnitudine, ut aliæ sint primæ, secundæ, tertiæ &c. magnitudinis, cum diversæ earum distantiæ à nobis sine variatione magnitudinis hoc phænomenon tan quam causæ adscribi possit. Esse enim omnes in unicâ sphæricâ superficie creditum quidem fuit vulgo, sed hactenus à nemine demonstratum, imò contrarium ejus facile evinci posset: ut nunc de aliis non dicam. Qui vero omnia Præjudicia sensuum pro nugis habent ea agnoscere nolentes, satis ostendunt, quantis ipsi adhuc sint Præjudiciis obruti.
units.tr: XVIII. And since sight is the most common of all the senses, and extends as widely as it can, it also happens that it provides a richer crop of prejudices than the other senses. Deceived in this way from an early age, we think that the earth is flat, because its curvature cannot be perceived by the eye on account of its size; and on the contrary its flat shape seems plainly to present itself to the eyes. This error could not be corrected among the common people any sooner than voyages around the whole globe and trustworthy histories taught men otherwise. No less by its nature is the prejudice, which we form from infancy, that the heavens rest upon the earth, at the point where the keenness of our eyes comes to a stop. Yet this is more easily laid aside, since anyone may correct that error by contrary experiments. Such is the belief, persuaded in every common person, that the Moon surpasses the other stars after the Sun in both light and size by as much as it appears to us. This is firmly held by many who claim the name of learned men, yet are strangers to the study of astronomy. So we judge, from the evidence of sight, that the Sun surpasses the stars in its light and size by as much as it appears to us, although the great remoteness of the stars alone can be the cause of this different appearance. Likewise, the fixed stars themselves are thought to differ so greatly in magnitude that some are of the first, others of the second, third and so on magnitude, although their different distances from us, without any variation in size, could be assigned as the cause of this phenomenon. It was indeed commonly believed that all of them lie on one spherical surface, but this has never been demonstrated, and indeed the contrary could easily be proved; I say nothing now of other matters. Those who regard all the prejudices of the senses as trifles, yet refuse to acknowledge them, sufficiently show how deeply they are still overwhelmed by prejudices.

units.la: XIX. His observatis apparet, umbratilem esse Objectionem B. p. 27. sensus nimirum non fallere in naturali suâ dispositione constitutos, sed judicium Intellectus errare posse, & sæpissime errare circa ea quæ à sensibus percipiuntur.
units.tr: XIX. Having noted these points, it appears that the objection of B., p. 27, is a shadow: namely, that the senses do not deceive when they are constituted in their natural disposition, but that the judgment of the intellect can err, and very often errs, concerning those things that are perceived by the senses.

units.la: Sed à Deo optimo & perfectissimo Creatore, cujus opera omnia valde sint bona, Gen. I. 31. nobis esse increatos, ut eorum adminiculo ad cognitionem rerum, quæ extra nos sunt, perveniremus, & aptos esse creatos ad attingendum eum finem in quem nobis sunt inditi, qui sit Objecta externa taliter sensui Communi & per eum Intellectui deferre, qualiter se exhibent, & in eo nec errare, nec decipere &c. Vanissima ergo esse quæ de errore sensuum circa propria Objecta docet Philosophia Cartesiana. Nam 1. nec Philosophia Cartesiana docet, sensus oppositè ad Intellectum nos fallere, cùm sic non aliter, quàm ut motus quidam corporei possint spectari, excitati à corporibus extra nos positis. 2. Ne quidem in illis ideis, quatenus à sensibus oblatæ solo intellectu percipiuntur, ulla est falsitas, si nullum judicium intercedat, sed in eo est error, quando judicium sese ultra perceptionem extendit, & de illis Ideis, quas per sensus accepit, plus judicat quam in iis percepit. Vide Cartef. Medit. quartam & sextam. 3. per Intellectum est cognoscendum, an sensus sint in suâ naturali dispositione constituti, ut appareat, quid in Ideis per sensus oblatis revera percipiamus. 4. si sensus propterea non sunt fallaces, quia à Deo Opt. Max. nobis sunt increati, Ergo nec judicium, quod dicit, Intellectus, propter eandem rationem; itaque distinguendum ipsum judicium, in quo nullus error, ab abusu ejusdem, qui causa erroris exstitit.
units.tr: But God, the best and most perfect Creator, whose works are all very good (Gen. 1:31), made us so that by their aid we might arrive at knowledge of the things that are outside us, and made us fit to attain that end for which they were implanted in us, which is to convey external objects to the common sense, and through it to the intellect, just as they present themselves, and to neither err nor deceive in this. Therefore the things which Cartesian philosophy teaches about the error of the senses concerning their proper objects are most empty. For, first, Cartesian philosophy does not teach that the senses deceive us in opposition to the intellect, since they can be regarded in no other way than as certain bodily motions, excited by bodies placed outside us. Second, there is no falsehood at all in those ideas, insofar as they are presented by the senses and perceived by the intellect alone, if no judgment intervenes; but the error lies in this, that when judgment extends itself beyond perception, it judges more about those ideas that it has received through the senses than it perceived in them. See Descartes, Meditations 4 and 6. Third, it is by the intellect that we must know whether the senses are constituted in their natural disposition, so that it may appear what we truly perceive in the ideas presented by the senses. Fourth, if the senses are not deceptive for this reason, that they were granted to us by God, the Best and Greatest, then neither is the judgment which the intellect pronounces, for the same reason. Therefore one must distinguish the judgment itself, in which there is no error, from its misuse, which has been the cause of error.

units.la: XX. Sic dicta Notitia Communis distinguitur à Notitiâ Accuratâ, quæ istius imbecillitates tollit & errores emendat. Hæc Notitia Communis appellatur à Salomonem Eccl. III. 18. דברת בני האדם juxta quam dixit se cogitasse olim : אמרתי אני בלבי על דברת האדם Dixi ego in animo meo juxta rationem filiorum hominum, h. e. juxta ductum, quem homines in cogitando sequi solent ex sensibus & iis, quæ extrinsecus apparent, judicantes. Quamdiu talia cogitent homines ostendit in seqq. לברם האלהים ולראות שהם בהמה להם donec discernat eos Deus & videre faciat, quod illi sint bestia sibi ipsis, h. e. donec Deus lumine Sp. Sancti eos illustret iisque demonstret, quod dum hanc sequuntur viam ratiocinandi, in his rebus externis ut ἄλογα ζῷα corrumpantur. Hic ergo Notitiam istam Communem emendat notitia illa, quam Sp. Sanctus per verbum divinum hominibus suggerit; quòd circa ea, quæ spectant ad statum futuræ vitæ Ratio & Notitia Philosophica homini non multum suppeditare possit, quod facit ad Notitiæ istius Communis emendationem. Quid jam Salomon juxta istam notitiam communem judicaverit ostendit vers. 19. & seqq. quòd idem eventus sit homini & bestiæ, quod æque moriatur homo ac bestia, quod unus Spiritus sit omnibus illis, quod excellentia hominis præ bestia nulla deprehendatur, quia omnes sint vanitas &c. Hæc notitia emendatur à Sp. Sancto juxta dicta, quo referri potest Eccl. xii. 7. ubi docetur, pulverem redire in terram, sicut ille fuit, sed spiritum redire ad Deum, qui dedit eum. In cæteris, quæ captum Rationis non superant, emendat Ratio & supplet ea, quæ Notitia communis vel non attingit, vel perperam collegit, & Præjudiciis imprimis sensuum remedium affert.
units.tr: Thus named, the Common Notion is distinguished from the Accurate Notion, which removes its weaknesses and corrects its errors. This Common Notion is called up by Solomon in Eccl. III. 18: [דברת בני האדם], according to which he says that he once thought in his heart [אמרתי אני בלבי על דברת האדם], "I said in my heart, concerning the reasoning of the sons of men," that is, according to the course which men are accustomed to follow in thinking, judging from the senses and from what appears externally. He shows in what follows how long men think in such a way: [לברם האלהים ולראות שהם בהמה להם], "that God may separate them and make them see that they are beasts to themselves," that is, until God, by the light of the Holy Spirit, enlightens them and shows them that while they follow this way of reasoning, they are corrupted in these external matters like irrational creatures [ἄλογα ζῷα]. Here, then, that notion which the Holy Spirit suggests to men through the divine Word emends this Common Notion. Reason and philosophical knowledge can supply man with little concerning the state of the life to come, and this helps to correct the Common Notion. What Solomon judged by this common notion he shows in verse 19 and following: that the same outcome befalls man and beast, that man dies just as the beast does, that all have one spirit, that no excellence of man over beast is discovered, since all things are vanity, and so on. This notion is corrected by the Holy Spirit according to what is said in Eccl. XII. 7, where it is taught that the dust returns to the earth as it was, but the spirit returns to God who gave it. In other matters, which do not exceed the grasp of Reason, Reason corrects and supplies what the Common Notion either does not reach or has gathered wrongly, and above all it brings a remedy for the prejudices of the senses.

units.la: XXI. De cætero cum Præjudicia hominibus adsint, antequam sermone uti possint, hinc factum est, ut sermo ordinarius super iis fuerit fundatus, qui etiam post Præjudicia depsita debuit retineri, ut homines se mutuò intelligetent; unde Astronomi etiam post detectos errores phrases consuetas usurparunt, ut apparet, quando solem oriri dicunt & occidere, Lunam varias subire phases, nunc corniculatam, nunc plenam, nunc semiplenam esse. Hinc est locus astri verus, qui etiam vocatur apparens, Eclipsis Solis, quæ Soli tamen non convenit, sed potius visui nostro. Inde orta est formula loquendi apud Ptolemaicos, ut Cœlum dicatur moveri ab Oriente in Occidentem, quod non nisi respectu nostri Horizontis est intelligendum: nam ab altera parte movetur ab Occidente in Orientem. Videatur Clavius in sphær. de sacro Bosco p. 40. Manifestum itidem talis locutionis exemplum, quando apud Astronomos dicitur, stellas fixas ingredi solis radios, item ex iis emergere, cum tamen nec secundum Copernicum, neque secundum Ptolomæum, id Stellarum, sed vel Terræ, vel Solis motui convenit. Videsis Kepl. Epit. Astron. Copern. lib. 6. parte 1. ab init. Atque is sermo super præjudiciis fundatus non tantum est proprius, sed etiam sæpe Metaphoricus, ita ut Metaphoræ ratio ab aliquo Præjudicio sit desumta, à Poëtis imprimis frequentatus. Eæ autem locutiones à nemine reprehenduntur, nec Astronomi mendacii & deceptionis propter eas accusantur (sicut antagonistæ scripturam accusandam putant, si eodem modo phrases consuetas usurparet.) Imo tota Astronomia cum in Phænomenis, hoc est, apparentiis explicandis versetur, etiam phrases apparentiis convenientes debuit retinere.
units.tr: XXI. Since prejudices are present in human beings even before they can use speech, it came about that ordinary speech was founded on them, and it had to be retained even after the prejudices were laid aside, so that people could understand one another. Hence astronomers too, even after the errors were discovered, kept up their customary phrases, as appears when they say that the sun rises and sets, that the moon undergoes various phases, now horned, now full, now half-full. Hence the "true place" of a star, which is also called the "apparent" place, and the "eclipse of the sun," which does not belong to the sun but rather to our sight. From this arose the manner of speaking among the Ptolemaics, that the heaven is said to move from east to west, which must be understood only with respect to our horizon, for on the other side it moves from west to east. See Clavius on the Sphere, on the Sacrobosco, p. 40. There is also a plain example of such speech when astronomers say that the fixed stars enter the rays of the sun, and likewise emerge from them, although this belongs neither according to Copernicus nor according to Ptolemy to the motion of the stars, but to the motion of either the earth or the sun. See Kepler, Epitome of the Copernican Astronomy, book 6, part 1, at the beginning. And this speech, founded on prejudices, is not only proper but often metaphorical as well, so that the basis of a metaphor is taken from some prejudice, and it is especially frequent among the poets. Yet no one finds fault with such expressions, nor are astronomers accused of lying or deceiving on their account (although our opponents think Scripture ought to be accused if it used customary phrases in the same way). Indeed, since the whole of astronomy is concerned with explaining phenomena, that is, appearances, it ought to retain phrases that agree with appearances.

units.la: XXII. Atque hic est crassus stylus, hoc est loqui πηχυλῶς & ἐξωπείκως, quando usurpas phrases, quæ quidem veritatem aliquam, sed ad nos relatam & generalem, confuse etiam perceptam & præjudiciis involutam, significant. Hic autem usus sermonis in multis præjudicia confirmat, qui suos conceptus verbis alligantes, posthac non nisi ad ea Præjudicia attendere solent, dum phrasibus vulgatis utuntur; unde etiam per totam ætatem ea non deponunt. Nec enim est, quod Præjudiciorum depositionem facilem cum Adversariis putemus; vel ipsum illud Præjudicium de Cœli extremitatibus, quamvis inter populos cultiores sit depositum ab hominibus adultæ ætatis, qui vel propria experientiâ contrarium didicerunt, vel ex aliorum conversatione, tamen apud populos incultiores, infantes, simpliciores, quibus forte nec propria experientia, nec cum aliis conversatio illud ademit, manet. XXIII. Cum ergo hæc Præjudicia sint firmiter radicata, ut homines ab ineunte ætate putent, se à naturâ de iis edoctos, adeoque quicquid iis repugnat, nisi certo ordine & Methodo clarè fuerit demonstratum, pro commento soleant habere; etiam scriptura loquens de rebus naturalibus censenda est retinuisse sermonem receptum, ne difficultatem non necessariam objiceret idiotis. Pone enim, solicitè cavisse scriptores sacros, ut ubi formula usitata alicui Præjudicio inniteretur, eam mutarent in accuratam, quæ nudam veritatem exprimeret, annon inde magna confusio fuisset exorta, multumque de intelligentiâ & perspicuitate sacrarum litera-rum periisset; ad cujus mentem percipiendam opus fuisset accuratâ rerum istarum cognitione, quæ per formulam accuratam fuerint expres-sæ?
units.tr: XXII. This is the coarse style, that is, to speak "in the common manner" and "in the popular way," when one uses phrases which indeed signify some truth, but one related to us and general, perceived confusedly and enveloped in prejudices. Yet this use of speech confirms prejudices in many people, who, binding their concepts to words, afterwards tend to attend only to those prejudices while they use the common phrases; hence they do not lay them aside throughout their whole life. Nor should we think that the laying aside of prejudices is easy with our adversaries. Even that prejudice about the extremities of the heavens, although it has been laid aside among the more cultivated peoples by adults who learned the contrary either by their own experience or from the conversation of others, remains among less cultivated peoples, infants and simpler folk, from whom perhaps neither their own experience nor conversation with others has taken it away. XXIII. Since therefore these prejudices are firmly rooted, so that from early age people think they have been taught them by nature, and so they are wont to regard as a fiction whatever contradicts them, unless it has been clearly demonstrated in a certain order and method, it must be judged that Scripture too, when it speaks of natural things, kept the accepted language, so as not to raise an unnecessary difficulty for the unlearned. For suppose the sacred writers had carefully taken care that wherever a customary phrase rested on some prejudice they would change it into an exact one that expressed the bare truth: would not great confusion have arisen from this, and much of the understanding and clarity of the sacred letters have been lost? For to grasp their meaning there would have been need of an exact knowledge of those things, which had been expressed through an exact formula.

units.la: XXIV. Propter ista Præjudicia & errores fit, ut Philosophica rerum cognitio non tantùm in eo vulgarem superet, quod multa, quæ per communem cognosci nequeunt, detegat, quæ obscure & confuse tantum fuerunt percepta, clare & distincte explicet, prout suprà dictum; sed etiam, quod ista Præjudicia & errores tollit & emendat veritate retecta. Hæc cognitionem rerum naturalium deducit à primis earum Principiis & Causis, iisque tam claris & evidentibus, ut ingenium humanum non possit dubitare de eorum veritate, quando se cum attentione ad illa consideranda applicat. Atque eam deductionem sic instituit, ut nihil sit in totâ istius deductionis consequentia, quod non sit valde manifestum. Sic aperiuntur interiora rerum naturalium, earumque abditæ eruuntur causæ, sic cognoscuntur minutissimarû partium structuræ, nexus, intervalla, latentesque motus notantur; sic earum veræ formæ & intima constitutio declarantur, totumque naturæ artificium retegitur. Per Cognitionem Philosophicam rationes formales & causæ qualitatum sensibilium, vulgò confuse cognitarum, explicantur, & quomodo tam diversas in sen'u affectiones excitent, distincte ostenditur. Hæc in effectuum causis reddendis, non in generali & confusa causæ redditione consistit, cum vulgo dicens, hanc esse rerum naturam, talesque iis inditas potentias, ut opera quæ præstari videmus præstent, sed harum ipsarum potentiarum & hujus talis naturæ causas investigat. Et quoniam omnia à primis principiis manifestâ deductionis consequentiâ derivat, nihil admittens, nisi quod vel per se sit clarè & distinctè perceptum, vel ex claris notionibus per apertam & perspicuam Consequentiam deductum, Præ-judicia Infantiæ & sensuum errores vulgari notitiâ haustos sponte sua cadere oportet.
units.tr: XXIV. Because of these prejudices and errors it comes about that philosophical knowledge of things surpasses common knowledge not only in this, that it discovers many things which cannot be known by the common understanding, things which were perceived only obscurely and confusedly, and explains them clearly and distinctly, as said above; but also in that it removes and corrects these prejudices and errors by bringing the truth to light. It deduces the knowledge of natural things from their first principles and causes, and these are so clear and evident that the human mind cannot doubt their truth when it applies itself with attention to considering them. And it institutes this deduction in such a way that there is nothing in the whole sequence of the deduction which is not most manifest. Thus the inner parts of natural things are laid open, their hidden causes are drawn out, thus the structures, connections and intervals of the smallest parts are known, and their hidden motions are noted; thus their true forms and inner constitution are declared, and the whole art of nature is uncovered. Through philosophical knowledge the formal reasons and causes of sensible qualities, commonly known only confusedly, are explained, and it is clearly shown how they excite such diverse affections in the senses. This consists in giving the causes of effects, not in a general and confused giving of a cause, as when the common man says that this is the nature of things and that such powers have been put into them that they perform the works we see them performing; rather it investigates the causes of these very powers and of this kind of nature. And since it derives all things from first principles by a manifest sequence of deduction, admitting nothing except what is either clearly and distinctly perceived in itself or deduced from clear notions by an open and perspicuous consequence, it must follow that the prejudices of infancy and the errors of the senses, drawn in from common knowledge, fall away of their own accord.

units.la: CAPUT II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: Cognitionem accuratam & Philosophicam rerum natura- lium ex sacris literis hauriri non posse hic constituitur in sequentibus demonstrandum.
units.tr: That an accurate and philosophical knowledge of natural things cannot be drawn from the Holy Scriptures is here set out to be demonstrated in what follows.

units.la: XXV. Ex dictis apparet, quid observandum, quibusque principiis initendum ei, qui accuratam & philosophicam rerum naturalium cognitionem acquirere cupit, oportere nempe, ut à principiis lumine naturali evidenter cognitis, manifesta consequentia quævis particularia deducantur, eorumque causæ distincte & clare explicentur. Hæcque si conferat Lector cum iis quæ M. c. i. de Principiis cognitionis humanæ disserit sufficientem iis paratam refutationem videbit: neque enim tanti sunt, ut particularem mereantur responsionem.
units.tr: XXV. From what has been said it is clear what must be observed, and on what principles the one must proceed who wishes to acquire an accurate and philosophical knowledge of natural things: namely, that from principles evidently known by the natural light, any particular matters be deduced by manifest consequence, and their causes be explained distinctly and clearly. If the Reader compares this with what M. in chapter 1 discusses concerning the principles of human knowledge, he will see that a sufficient refutation of them is ready to hand; for they are not of such weight as to deserve a particular reply.

units.la: XXVI. Hoc tantum ad M. p. 4. & 5. annotamus, 1. Rectam rationem consistere in omnium hominum mentibus originaliter, sed non ab omnibus recte adhiberi. Quòd si enim eò usque sit corrupta ratio, ut nullus nisi regenitus ea recte possit uti in naturalibus & civilibus, nonne hoc modo omnem certitudinem è rebus humanis ibis sublatum? 2. Lumen Rationis & scripturæ esse diversa lumina formaliter, cuivis per se esse notum, etiamsi in eo conveniant, quod utrumque à Patre Luminum veritatem docente sit derivatum.
units.tr: XXVI. We note only this on M. pp. 4 and 5: (1) Right reason exists originally in the minds of all men, but it is not rightly employed by all. For if reason were so corrupted that no one except the regenerate could use it rightly in natural and civil affairs, would not all certainty be thereby removed from human affairs? (2) The light of Reason and the light of Scripture are formally different lights, as is known to everyone in itself, even though they agree in this, that both are derived from the Father of Lights who teaches truth.

units.la: XXVII. Ex eodem præcedente capite manifestum evadit, quid de scriptura sacra censeamus ratione scientiæ & cognitionis Philosophicæ, nimirum, 1. cognitionem Philosophicam rerum naturalium non posse ex sacris literis hauriri. 2. ex scriptura non debere nec posse systemata Physica concinnari. Utrumque statuimus contra eos, qui nobis Physicas Mosaicas, sacras, Christianas &c. voluerunt procudere, quales Casmannus, Valesius, Danæus & alii, ita tamen, ut argumenta nostra ad primum directe inferendum instituamus, cum posterius ex priori asserto tanquam corollarium sponte fluat. Frustra ergo quærit M. p. 222. contra quem disputem, cum hoc satis & ex hac & priori editione fuerit manifestum.
units.tr: XXVII. From the preceding chapter it becomes plain what we think of Holy Scripture with respect to science and philosophical knowledge, namely: (1) that philosophical knowledge of natural things cannot be drawn from the Holy Scriptures; (2) that from Scripture physical systems ought not and cannot be constructed. We maintain both against those who wished to forge for us Mosaic, sacred, Christian physics and the like, such as Casmannus, Vallesius, Daneus and others; yet we set out our arguments so as to infer the first directly, since the second flows spontaneously from the first as a corollary. Therefore he seeks in vain on M. p. 222 whom I am disputing against, since this has been made sufficiently plain both from this and from the earlier edition.

units.la: XXVIII. Huic sententiæ meæ videntur consonare ea verba (H. p. 259.) Dixerunt multi, dico & ego, scripturam posse hominem in Physicis reddere materialiter, confuse & certo modo scientem atque in particulari doctum, & p. 261. scripturam non loqui, quomodo Philosophus debeat loqui, explicare, philosophari formaliter, quæ tamen postea p. 262. his verbis evertuntur, Accurate & philosophice loqui est rem secundum formalem essentiam & nativam suam significationem proponere & considerare, hoc est, sicuti in se & sua est natura, idque facere Sp. S. non in paucis. Non enim haec inter se invicem conciliare possum: scripturam non loqui, quomodo Philosophus debet loqui, explicare, philosophari formaliter, & tamen rem secundum formalem suam essentiam &c. proponere. Saltem plane mecum consensit Cl. Coccejus in Gen. I. p. 83. Neque Dei propositum fuit, neque esse debuit rerum essentias explicare.
units.tr: XXVIII. My view seems to be in harmony with those words (H. p. 259): "Many have said, I too say, that Scripture can make a man learned in physics materially, confusedly, and in a certain manner knowing and learned in particulars," and (p. 261) "that Scripture does not speak as a philosopher ought to speak, to explain and philosophise formally"; which nevertheless are afterwards overturned on p. 262 by these words: "To speak accurately and philosophically is to set forth and consider a thing according to its formal essence and native signification, that is, as it is in itself and by its nature; and this the Holy Spirit does not do in a few cases." For I cannot reconcile these with one another: "Scripture does not speak, as a philosopher ought to speak, to explain and philosophise formally, and yet sets forth a thing according to its formal essence, etc." At least the distinguished Coccejus agreed plainly with me in Gen. 1, p. 83: "Neither was it God's purpose, nor ought it to have been, to explain the essences of things."

units.la: XXIX.
units.tr: XXIX.

units.la: Quod autem dicitur (H. p. 259.) Neminem dixisse, scripturam posse hominem reddere in Physicis distincte & formaliter eruditum, id falsum comperitur, si quis systemata illa Physica Danaei, Vallesii &c. inspiciat, quae ostendunt, mentem istorum auctorum directe oppositam fuisse meae sententiae prout patet ex statu Controversiae, quem supra constitui; falsum etiam ostenditur per verba antea ex p. 262. citata.
units.tr: But as to what is said (H. p. 259), that "no one has said that Scripture can make a man distinctly and formally learned in physics," this is found to be false if anyone looks into those physical systems of Daneus, Vallesius and others, which show that the minds of those authors were directly opposed to my opinion, as appears from the state of the controversy which I set out above; it is also shown to be false by the words cited before from p. 262.

units.la: XXX. Quod si vero forte per τὸ Philosophari formaliter intelligas cum ordinem & modum observare, quem Philosophi in systematibus vulgaribus observant per Definitiones & Theoremata, facile concedo neminem dicere, scripturam ita philosophari; neque vero ratio ita Philosophandum docet; sed & tibi concedendum, me hoc nomine nemini ullam litem movisse. Manet ergo status Controversiae, An Cognitio Philosophica, prout explicata cap. praeced. possit ex sacris literis hauriri, & an ex scriptura possint debeantve systemata Physica concinnari? ubi ego negativam teneo & defendo.
units.tr: XXX. But if perhaps by "to philosophise formally" you mean to observe that order and method which philosophers observe in the common systems through definitions and theorems, I readily concede that no one says Scripture philosophises in that way; nor does reason teach that one should so philosophise. Yet you too must concede that I have raised no quarrel with anyone on this head. The state of the controversy therefore remains: "Whether philosophical knowledge, as explained in the preceding chapter, can be drawn from the Holy Scriptures, and whether physical systems can or ought to be constructed from Scripture?" Here I hold and defend the negative.

units.la: XXXI. Quamvis autem negem, scripturam debere haberi pro Principio Cognitionis Philosophicae, nihil tamen ejus Auctoritati vel Infallibilitati etiam in rebus Philosophicis detraho. Nam pro certo & indubitato teneo, & a quo Christiano tenendum censeo: Omne illud quod scriptura testatur & docet; de quacunque re id fuerit, etiamsi illud ratione nostra assequi non valeamus, imo etiamsi illud pugnare videatur cum ratione, pro certo & indubitato esse habendum, idque propter ejus Auctoritatem divinam, quae ei fidem divinam & infallibilem conciliat.
units.tr: XXXI. Although I deny that Scripture ought to be held as a principle of philosophical knowledge, I nevertheless take nothing away from its authority or infallibility, even in philosophical matters. For I hold as certain and indubitable, and I judge that every Christian ought to hold: whatever Scripture witnesses and teaches, concerning whatever matter it may be, even if we cannot grasp it by our reason, and even if it seems to clash with reason, is to be held as certain and indubitable, and this on account of its divine authority, which gives it divine and infallible credit.

units.la: XXXII. Verum sciendum, illud omne, quod ita suscipitur propter auctoritatem divinam, non scientifice & philosophice cognosci, sed Fide Divina definita cap. praec. art. 5. quod non tantum intelligendum de ipsis illis, quae αὐτολεξεὶ in sacris literis habentur, sed etiam de iis, quae exinde per manifestam & certam consequentiam eliciuntur. Omnis enim conclusio a Principio suo, ex quo deducitur, naturam & nomen suum mutuatur. XXXIII. Quicquid autem sit, quod scriptura de rebus naturalibus docet & testatur, aliam quàm cognitionem vulgarem & Communem in nobis ex eâ formari posse, nego, quod ex sequentibus evadet manifestum.
units.tr: XXXII. Yet it must be understood that everything which is received in this way on account of divine authority is not known scientifically and philosophically, but by divine faith, as defined in the preceding chapter, article 5; and this is to be understood not only of those things which are found word for word in the Holy Scriptures, but also of those which are drawn from them by manifest and certain consequence. For every conclusion borrows its nature and name from the principle from which it is deduced. XXXIII. Whatever it is that Scripture teaches and witnesses about natural things, I deny that any other knowledge than ordinary and common knowledge can be formed in us from it, as will become manifest from what follows.

units.la: CAPUT III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: Argumentum pro eâ sententiâ proponitur primum à for- mulis loquendi Scripturæ usitatis, & secundum à Scripturæ finibus.
units.tr: The argument for this view is put forward first from the forms of speech customary in Scripture, and second from the ends of Scripture.

units.la: XXXIV. Argumentum primum pro nostra sententia à formulis loquendi, quibus scriptura utitur, hoc modo formamus: Si Scriptura loquens de rebus naturalibus promiscuè utitur formulis receptis, sive eæ veritatem nudam exprimant, sive talem, quæ ad hominum sensus sit relata & præjudiciis atque erroribus involuta: E. non potest cognitio Philosophica rerum naturalium ex Scripturâ peti: sed verum est prius: E. Maj. manifesta fiet ei qui Cap. I. attente consideraverit. Min. probamus Cap. 21. & seq.
units.tr: XXXIV. We frame the first argument for our view, from the forms of speech Scripture uses, as follows. If Scripture, when speaking of natural things, uses received expressions indiscriminately, whether these express the bare truth or a truth related to human perception and wrapped up in prejudices and errors, then philosophical knowledge of natural things cannot be drawn from Scripture. But the first claim is true. Therefore the second follows. The major premise will be clear to anyone who has carefully considered Chapter I. We prove the minor in Chapters 21 and following.

units.la: XXXV. Secundum Argumentum pro nostra sententia petimus à Fine scripturæ. Hoc argumento utitur Cl. Coccejus in Gen. I. ubi §. 17. sic loquitur: Qui scopum Scripturæ novimus esse eum ut credamus Deo, quippe in quo habeamus justitiam & vitam; quæ Scriptura non tantùm pro Sapientibus, sed etiam pro insipientibus facta est; neque Dei propositum sit, neque esse debuerit, rerum essentias nobis explicare: satis habemus, quod noscimus, Deum initio fecisse discrimen inter diem & noctem, quanquam dies esset sine sole & nox sine lunâ & sideribus: quanquam etiam nullus esset adhuc oculus, qui luce illuminari posset. Fines scripturæ in ipsa scriptura nobis recensentur 2 Tim. III. 16, 17. Tota scriptura divinitus est inspirata, & utilis ad doctrinam, ad redargutionem, ad correctionem, ad Disciplinam in justitia: ut perfectus sit homo Dei, ad omne opus bonum perfecte instructus. Deut. vi. 1, 2. Hoc est præceptum, statuta, judiciaque illa, quae præcepit Jehova Deus vester, ut doceam vos, ut exerceatis ea in terra: ut timeas Jehovam Deum tuum, observando omnia statuta ejus & præcepta ejus, quae ego præcipio tibi. Rom. xv. 4. Quæcunque ante scripta sunt, ad nostram doctrinam ante scripta sunt, ut per tolerantiam & consolationem scripturarum spem habeamus. Joh. xx. 31. Hæc autem scripta sunt ut credatis, Jesum esse Christum illum filium Dei, & ut credentes vitam habeatis per nomen ejus. Omnes autem Fines scripturæ secundum ductum loci 2 Tim. III. referri possunt ad hos quatuor, ad doctrinam, ad redargutionem, gutionem, ad correctionem, ad disciplinam in Justitia. Utilis autem est scriptura ad doctrinam non quamvis, sed, explicantibus Belgis, quæ est de capitibus Christianæ religionis, ad redargutionem errorum in fide, ad correctionem vitæ & morum pravorum, ad disciplinam in justitia, ostendendo, quid justum & injustum, honestum & turpe sit. Nullibi autem invenimus finem Scripturæ esse instructionem in cognitione Philosophiæ naturalis. Neque etiam Theologi quando fines scripturæ recensent, unquam inter eos referunt cognitionem & sapientiam philosophicam. Cum autem finis medii præscribat ordinem & mensuram, æquum est, ut hæc illi sint adæquata, non latiora nec angustiora. Ergo existimandum est, à scriptura etiam non alia præscribi media, quam quæ ad cognitionem salutarem sint appropriata, & sine quibus illa obtineri non possit. Verum enim vero tantum abest, ut æstimemus, sine explicatione naturæ rerum scopum suum in scripturam obtinere non posse, ut certum sit, potius sufficere πως χυλω & crassiorem rerum naturalium explicationem, qualis per sensus & experientiam haberi potest. Non male Cl. Gassendus de util. Phil. ad Theologiam p. 31: Quis enim est hodieque, qui cælum instar metalli esse conflatum; tellurem basi tanquam tibicine niti, sibi tuendum sumat, & sexcenta sunt alia hujusmodi nota, quæ brevitatis causa prætermitto. Et paulo post: Quod Physica in scripturis tractantur, id sit illustrationis causâ tantum, cum non quod maximè verum est, sed quod maximè verum esse plebi videtur, auctores sacri edisserant. Sufficit, si Scriptura nos sapientes reddat ad Salutem 2 Tim. III. 15. etsi non sapientes in rebus Physicis: sufficit, si per eam perfectus redditur homo Dei, satagens rerum divinarum, etsi homo mundi vel Philosophus inde parum de rebus naturalibus cognoscat. Ex quibus tale constitui poterit argumentum: Quidquid non est necessarium, ut scriptura omnes suos fines obtineat, illud non quærendum in scriptura: At Explicatio Philosophica rerum naturalium non est ad id necessaria. E Min. probatur: Ad fines supra recensitos non est necessaria, quoniam hi sine illa possunt obtineri, neque alius quis indicatur finis scripturæ. Quod, si hic inter alios esset finis scripturæ, ut nobis enuclearet interiorem rerum naturalium essentiam, futurum esset, ut si non de omnibus rebus naturalibus in specie ageret, saltem fundamenta talia jaceret & principia poneret, ex quibus opera artificum omnia erui possent, quod fieri nullibi videmus.
units.tr: XXXV. We take the second argument for our view from the end (purpose) of Scripture. The celebrated Coccejus uses this argument on Genesis 1, where at §17 he speaks thus: We know that the aim of Scripture is that we should believe God, since in him we have righteousness and life; and this Scripture has been given not only for the wise but also for the unwise. Nor is it God's purpose, nor ought it to be, to explain to us the essences of things. It is enough that we know God at the beginning made a distinction between day and night, although the day was without the sun and the night without the moon and stars, and although there was not yet any eye that could be illuminated by the light. The ends of Scripture are listed for us in Scripture itself, 2 Tim. III. 16, 17: All Scripture is divinely inspired and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for discipline in righteousness, that the man of God may be perfect, thoroughly equipped for every good work. Deut. vi. 1, 2: These are the commandments, statutes and judgments which Jehovah your God commanded, that I might teach you, that you might do them in the land; that you may fear Jehovah your God, by keeping all his statutes and his commandments, which I command you. Rom. xv. 4: Whatever was written before was written for our instruction, that through the patience and comfort of the Scriptures we might have hope. John xx. 31: But these things are written that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life through his name. Now all the ends of Scripture, following the drift of the passage in 2 Tim. III, can be referred to these four: to teaching, to refutation, to correction, and to discipline in righteousness. Scripture is profitable for teaching not in any way whatever, but, as the Dutch explain it, concerning the heads of the Christian religion; for refutation of errors in faith; for correction of life and of wicked morals; for discipline in righteousness, by showing what is just and unjust, honourable and shameful. Nowhere, however, do we find that the end of Scripture is instruction in the knowledge of natural philosophy. Nor do theologians, when they list the ends of Scripture, ever include philosophical knowledge and wisdom among them. Since the end of a means prescribes its order and measure, it is fair that the two be commensurate, neither wider nor narrower. Therefore we must judge that Scripture prescribes no means other than those suited to saving knowledge and without which that knowledge cannot be obtained. Indeed, we are so far from thinking that its purpose cannot be attained in Scripture without an explanation of the nature of things, that it is certain a rough and cruder explanation of natural things, such as can be had through the senses and experience, is rather sufficient [πως χυλω]. Gassendi, not badly, in his work on the usefulness of philosophy for theology, p. 31: For who is there even today who would undertake to defend the heaven as if it were cast like a metal, the earth resting on its base like a pillar, and there are six hundred other such familiar things, which I pass over for the sake of brevity. And a little later: That physics is treated in the Scriptures is only for the sake of illustration, since the sacred authors set forth not what is most true, but what seems most true to the common people. It is enough if Scripture makes us wise unto salvation, 2 Tim. III. 15, even if we are not wise in physical matters. It is enough if through it the man of God is made perfect, busy with divine things, even if the man of the world or the philosopher learns little from it about natural things. From these a argument can be constructed: Whatever is not necessary for Scripture to attain all its ends is not to be sought in Scripture; but a philosophical explanation of natural things is not necessary for this. The minor is proved thus: it is not necessary for the ends listed above, since these can be attained without it, and no other end of Scripture is indicated. But if this were among the ends of Scripture, that it should unfold to us the inner essence of natural things, it would follow that, even if it did not treat all natural things in particular, it would at least lay such foundations and set down such principles from which all the works of craftsmen could be drawn out. This we nowhere see done.

units.la: XXXVI. Exc. 1. (R. St. p. 321.)
units.tr: XXXVI. Exc. 1. (R. St. p. 321.)

units.la: Hoc argumentum præsupponit, vel de natura nihil agi in Scriptura, quod falsum est, vel quæ in ea de rebus naturalibus, non pertinere ad doctrinam &c. quod iidem falsum est, vide Psal.
units.tr: This argument presupposes either that nothing is treated in Scripture concerning nature, which is false, or that what it says about natural things does not pertain to doctrine, etc., which is likewise false. See Psalm

units.la: VIII, XIX. CIV. Rom. I. & infinita alia loca quae contrarium evincunt.
units.tr: VIII, XIX. CIV. Rom. I. and countless other passages that prove the contrary.

units.la: Resp. 1. quo tendat hoc argumentum, liquet satis ex praecedentibus, eo nimirum, ut ex mediorum ad Finem propositione manifestum fiat, non quaerendam in scriptura rerum Physicarum naturam accurate explicatam, sed ei, cui curae sint haec sacra, aliis principiis innitendum. Non autem negamus de natura vel rebus naturalibus agi in scriptura, & sic pertinere ad doctrinam, dummodo nobis concedatur, id fieri tantum incidenter, indirecte & propter aliud, non ex instituto & propter se, πραγυλῶς non ἀκριβῶς, ut concernat cognitionem vulgarem & communem, non accuratam & Philosophicam. 2. quando scriptura inter alios finem suum esse doctrinam docet, intelligit utique doctrinam non quamvis, sed salutarem, sed illam quae est de articulis fidei, uti superius ex Belgis interpretibus didicimus; unde bene inferimus, cum nullius alterius finis mentio fiat, quam istorum quatuor, de quibus 2 Tim. III. ejus ergo finem non esse doctrinam Physicam; quamvis autem faciles largiamur cognitionem rerum naturalium catenus ad doctrinam salutarem prodesse, quatenus ex iis cognoscuntur Existentia Dei, Sapientia, Potentia, Bonitas &c. ad id tamen sufficit cognitio qualiscunque, qualem etiam vulgus obtinet, cum liber naturae pateat plebejis juxta ac eruditis, quamvis fatear multo uberiora exempla cognoscendae divinae Potentiae, Sapientiae & Bonitatis &c. reperiri in rerum natura ab iis, qui per lumen naturae eam habent accuratius cognitam, quam ab illis, qui ultra vulgarem cognitionem non ascenderunt. Hic autem commodum notanda verba Riveti in Isagoge ad Scripturam Sacram p. 49. Dum scriptura versatur circa ea praecipue, quae gratiam & gloriam aeternam spectant, cognitionem omnem Philosophicam sibi ipsa substernit, eque rerum naturis tantum sumit, quantum opus est ad fabricandum speculum, per quod divina oculis nostris quadantenus representantur. 3
units.tr: Reply 1. The purpose of this argument is clear enough from what has gone before: namely, that from the proposal of the means to the end it should become evident that one should not look in Scripture for an exact explanation of the nature of physical things, but that those who are concerned with these sacred matters should rely on other principles. We do not, however, deny that Scripture treats of nature or natural things, and so pertains to doctrine, provided it is granted to us that this happens only incidentally, indirectly and for the sake of something else, not by design and for its own sake, crudely [παχυλῶς] and not accurately [ἀκριβῶς], so that it concerns ordinary and common knowledge, not exact and philosophical knowledge. 2. When Scripture teaches that its own end is doctrine, it certainly means not any doctrine whatever, but saving doctrine, namely that which concerns the articles of faith, as we have learned above from the Belgic interpreters. Hence we rightly infer that, since no other end is mentioned than those four of which 2 Tim. III speaks, its end is not physical doctrine. Although we readily grant that a knowledge of natural things serves saving doctrine insofar as from them are known the existence of God, his wisdom, power, goodness, and so on, nevertheless any kind of knowledge suffices for this, such as the common people possess, since the book of nature lies open to the plain folk as well as to the learned. I admit that far richer examples of knowing the divine power, wisdom and goodness are found in the nature of things by those who have a more accurate knowledge of it through the light of nature than by those who have not risen above common knowledge. Here it is worth noting the words of Rivet in his Isagoge to Holy Scripture, p. 49: While Scripture is occupied chiefly with those things that concern grace and eternal glory, it lays aside all philosophical knowledge and takes from the natures of things only as much as is needed to make a mirror through which divine things are represented to our eyes to some degree. 3

units.la: XXXVII. Inst. 1. (M. p. 224.) Dato, non concesso, hunc non esse finem scriptura, nihilominus ista, de quibus Sp. S. incidenter agit, multo sunt certiora, quam omnes vestrae demonstrationes, adeoque Physica ex illis multo certior construitur, quam ex omnibus demonstrationibus vestris.
units.tr: XXXVII. Inst. 1. (M. p. 224.) Granted, though not conceded, that this is not the end of Scripture, nevertheless those things which the Holy Spirit treats incidentally are far more certain than all your demonstrations; and so a physics built from them is far more certain than one built from all your demonstrations.

units.la: Resp. illa quae in scripturis de rebus naturalibus dicuntur, docenturque, sunt certissima, sed cum tantum pertineant ad notitiam communem, non potest ex illis Physica constitui secundum antea dicta.
units.tr: Reply: The things said and taught in Scripture about natural things are most certain, but since they pertain only to common knowledge, a physics cannot be constructed from them according to what has been said before.

units.la: XXXVIII. Inst. 2. (M. p. 225.) Inter fines scripturae non comparent quoque historica & Chronologica, quae hinc concludet, Historiam quoque & Chronologiam non posse construi ex scriptura? Resp. Ea tamen necessaria sunt ad finem aliquem scripturæ, nempe ad cognitionem Christi nativitatis, vel ad cognitionem status Ecclesiæ Iudaicæ &c. Ergò ut media traduntur in sacris literis ; & sic historiæ quoddam & Chronologiæ systema exinde potest constitui. 2. Res historicæ & Chronologicæ pertinent ad vulgarem notitiam tantùm & ad τὸ ὅτι, non ad τὸ διότι.
units.tr: XXXVIII. Inst. 2. (M. p. 225.) Do not historical and chronological matters also fail to appear among the ends of Scripture? From this you will conclude that history and chronology also cannot be constructed from Scripture? Reply: Nevertheless they are necessary for some end of Scripture, namely for knowledge of the birth of Christ, or for knowledge of the state of the Jewish Church, and so on. Therefore they are handed down in the sacred letters as means, and so a certain system of history and chronology can be constructed from them. 2. Historical and chronological matters pertain only to common knowledge and to that [τὸ ὅτι], not to why [τὸ διότι].

units.la: XXXIX. Inst. 3. (M. p. 225.) Omnia quæ in scripturis traduntur, sive sint naturalia sive supernaturalia, pertinent eò ut credamus &c. Act. XXIV. 14. Ergò absque ratione negatur rerum naturalium expositionem facere ad doctrinam.
units.tr: XXXIX. Inst. 3. (M. p. 225.) Everything that is handed down in the Scriptures, whether natural or supernatural, tends to make us believe, etc. Acts XXIV. 14. Therefore it is without reason denied that an exposition of natural things serves doctrine.

units.la: Resp. Quæ traduntur in scripturis, eò facere ut credamus concedo; Verum ego hoc modo arguo, quod cum Accurata & Philosophica rerum naturalium cognitio non sit necessaria, ut scriptura omnes suos fines obtineat, sed sufficiat Vulgaris, non censendum sit illam in sacris literis reperiri.
units.tr: Reply: I concede that what is handed down in the Scriptures tends to make us believe. But I argue thus: since an accurate and philosophical knowledge of natural things is not necessary for Scripture to attain all its ends, but ordinary knowledge suffices, it should not be thought to be found in the sacred letters.

units.la: XL. Inst. 4. (M. p. 225.) Si scriptura finis non sit tradere res naturales, (intellige Philosophice) sequitur, cum certum sit vel ex ipsa Adversariorum Confessione: eam saltem agere de aliquibus rebus naturalibus, ut Ecclesiast. 1. de fluminum ortu, sequetur, inquam, Sp. S. agere hoc absque fine, adeoque temere & irrationabiliter.
units.tr: XL. Inst. 4. (M. p. 225.) If it is not the end of Scripture to hand down natural things (understood philosophically), it follows, since it is certain, even from the confession of our opponents themselves, that it at least treats of some natural things, as in Ecclesiastes 1 concerning the rising of rivers, it follows, I say, that the Holy Spirit does this without end, and so rashly and irrationally.

units.la: Resp. quod tradit Sp. S. de rebus naturalibus, illud eo ipso quo tradit facit ad finem ipsius; sed nego, quod id notitiam communem ex cedat, qualis vulgaribus cognoscendi mediis haberi potest. 2. etsi igitur concedatur, scripturam docere quædam de rebus naturalibus eo modo quo explicatum est, tamen non sequitur, quod illa doctrina sit scripturæ finis, sed ad summum erit medium, cùm non propter se, sed propter alia expetatur.
units.tr: Reply: What the Holy Spirit hands down about natural things, by the very fact that it hands it down, serves its end. But I deny that this yields common knowledge, such as can be had by ordinary means of knowing. 2. Even if it is granted, therefore, that Scripture teaches certain things about natural things in the way explained, it does not follow that this doctrine is the end of Scripture. At most it will be a means, since it is sought not for its own sake but for the sake of other things.

units.la: XLI. Inst. 5. (M. p. 226.) Quò ego tendam hoc meo argumento apertum quidem; sed quo ipsum meum argumentum tendat, id necesse habuisse mihi monstrari.
units.tr: XLI. Inst. 5. (M. p. 226.) Where my argument tends is indeed clear; but where your own argument tends, you ought to have shown me.

units.la: Resp. At ostendi, non eò tendere argumentum, ut exin colligi possit, vel in eo præsupponendum, de natura nihil agi in scripturis, vel quæ in ipsa de rebus naturalibus leguntur, nihil facere ad doctrinam: neutrum enim ex argumento sequitur: sed tantum non nisi cognitionem vulgarem rerum naturalium in sacris literis tradi, quam ad doctrinam facere non nego; nec quærendam in iis cognitionem Philosophicam.
units.tr: Reply: But I have shown that the argument does not tend toward this, that it could be inferred from it either that one must presuppose that nothing is treated in the Scriptures concerning nature, or that what is read in them about natural things has nothing to do with doctrine. For neither follows from the argument. It only means that the Scriptures hand down nothing but common knowledge of natural things, which I do not deny serves doctrine, and that philosophical knowledge is not to be sought in them.

units.la: XLII. Inst. 6. (M. p. 227.) Si non negetu, scripturam agere de natura & rebus naturalibus, non negabitis quoque, scripturam id agere in hunc finem, ut ut nos erudiamur de natura & rebus naturalibus, adeoque id agere ad doctri-nam nostram.
units.tr: XLII. Inst. 6. (M. p. 227.) If you do not deny that Scripture treats of nature and natural things, you will not deny either that Scripture does this for the purpose that we may be instructed about nature and natural things, and so does this for our doctrine.

units.la: Responsio ad illud jam sæpius est sufficiens data.
units.tr: A reply to this has already been given sufficiently many times.

units.la: XLIII. Inst. 7. (M. p. 227.) Id vobis libenter largiemur, scripturam aliquando de natura & rebus naturalibus agere πανυλῶς, dummodo vos nobis concedatis, ubicunque scriptura de rebus naturalibus agit, nunquam tamen aberrare à stricta rei veritate.
units.tr: XLIII. Inst. 7. (M. p. 227.) We will gladly grant you this, that Scripture sometimes treats of nature and natural things crudely [πανυλῶς, i.e. παχυλῶς], provided you concede to us that wherever Scripture treats of natural things, it never nevertheless strays from the strict truth of the matter.

units.la: Resp. Id vero utraque manu largimur; neque enim unquam (Deum sancte testor) mihi venit in mentem, quod unanimiter mihi adversarii affin-gunt, Sp. S. in sacris literis cum vulgo errare. At demonstratum hic existimo, non tantum scripturam aliquando παχυλῶς loqui, sed in universum cognitionem Philosophicam & accuratam rerum naturalium ex sacris literis non posse hauriri. Essent vero & alia, quæ loco Instantiarum ex M. p. 228. ad 232. possent afferri: verùm Lectori & tempori parcendum censeo, cùm ea omnia ex dictis satis possint refutari. Si cui tamen tanti videantur, is responsionum loco hæc quatuor annotet.
units.tr: Reply: We grant this with both hands. For never (I solemnly call God to witness) has it come into my mind what our opponents unanimously attribute to us, that the Holy Spirit in the sacred letters errs along with the common people. But I think it has been demonstrated here that Scripture not only sometimes speaks crudely [παχυλῶς], but that in general a philosophical and accurate knowledge of natural things cannot be drawn from the sacred letters. There would indeed be others which could be cited in place of instances from pp. 228 to 232 of the Mutual Opponent: but I think the reader and time should be spared, since all of these can be sufficiently refuted from what has been said. If any of these nevertheless seem important to someone, let him note these four points as replies.

units.la: 1. Nos non negare cognitionem rerum naturalium facere ad doctrinam salutarem, sed huic rei sufficere existimamus cognitionem communem.
units.tr: 1. We do not deny that a knowledge of natural things serves saving doctrine, but we judge that common knowledge suffices for this purpose.

units.la: 2. Etiam agnoscimus, ea quæ dicuntur & traduntur de rebus naturalibus facere ad doctrinam simpliciter, sive, ut hactenus instituamur in rebus naturalibus, ut notitia communis confirmetur: in quo tamen non acquiescit scriptura, sed illam institutionem ad aliquid aliud ordinat: unde inter fines scripturæ hæc cognitio referri nequit.
units.tr: 2. We also acknowledge that the things said and handed down about natural things serve doctrine simply, or, so that we may be instructed thus far in natural things, so that common knowledge may be confirmed. Scripture, however, does not rest in this instruction, but orders that instruction to something else. Hence this knowledge cannot be counted among the ends of Scripture.

units.la: 3. Concedimus, ex instituto hactenus agere scripturam de rebus naturalibus, quatenus dirigit illam doctrinam qualemcunque ad istum finem, nempe doctrinam salutarem; sed non ex instituto agit, quatenus rerum naturalium Essentiam & constitutionem interiorem non explicat.
units.tr: 3. We concede that Scripture so far treats of natural things by design, insofar as it directs that doctrine, of whatever kind, to that end, namely saving doctrine; but it does not treat them by design insofar as it does not explain the essence and inner constitution of natural things.

units.la: 4. Ignorationem Elenchi esse vel calumniam, quando mihi tribuitur, falsum esse aut exprimere (sive significare) vulgi opinionem erroneam, quod Spir. Sanctus in Scriptura tradit.
units.tr: 4. That the charge of ignoratio elenchi, or even of calumny, applies when it is attributed to me that I say, or express (or mean), that the common erroneous opinion, which the Holy Spirit hands down in Scripture, is false.

units.la: XLIV. Inst. 8. (H. p. 260.) me tamen in responsione secunda concedere, finem Scripturæ secundarium esse reddere hominem Eruditum in Physicis.
units.tr: XLIV. Inst. 8. (H. p. 260.) Yet in my second answer I concede that the secondary end of Scripture is to make a man learned in physics.

units.la: Resp. Nequaquam hoc concessi: nam non is potest dici Eruditus in Physicis, qui notitiam habet vulgarem & communem rerum naturalium, sed is, qui novit rerum causas interiores, formas & constitutionem, quod nemo ex scripturis potest discere.
units.tr: Reply. I by no means conceded this. For a man cannot be called learned in physics who has a common and popular knowledge of natural things, but only one who knows their inner causes, forms and constitution, which no one can learn from Scripture.

units.la: XLV. Inst.
units.tr: XLV. Inst.

units.la: XLV. Inst. 9. (H. p. 262.) Ecel 1. 7. explicat philosophice & accurate, fluminum ortum, quem dicit ex mari esse, item cur mare non redundet, & superfluat, cum tot & tam vasta flumina in illud influant? hanc reddit rationem, quia ex eo aquae sese subducunt ut iterum influant. Ergo scriptura accurate & philosophice aliquam rem naturalem explicat.
units.tr: XLV. Inst. 9. (H. p. 262.) Ecclesiastes 1:7 explains philosophically and accurately the origin of rivers, which it says come from the sea. It also explains why the sea does not overflow and rise above its bounds, although so many vast rivers flow into it. The reason given is that the waters are drawn up from it so that they may flow in again. Therefore Scripture explains a natural thing accurately and philosophically.

units.la: Resp. Hanc quidem veram esse explicationem ortus fluminum, sed qualis per communem notitiam haberi potest, non philosophicam, quae proximas & interiores rei causas scrutatur (vide Claub. Defensi. Cartes. c. 31. de fontium origine & aquis) nam eo ipso, quo (concedente H. ibid.) Ecclesiastes modum refluendi per canales & Terrae colationem non ostendit, sed nobis meditandum reliquit, cum haec demum sit philosophica & accurata explicatio, largitur illud ipsum quod petebam.
units.tr: Resp. This is indeed a true explanation of the origin of rivers, but it is the kind that can be reached through common knowledge, not a philosophical one, which investigates the nearer and inner causes of the thing (see Clauberg, Defensio Cartesii, ch. 31, on the origin of springs and waters). For by the very fact that Ecclesiastes (as H. concedes, ibid.) does not show the way the water flows back through channels and the filtering of the earth, but leaves it for us to think about, this explanation is in the end not philosophical and accurate. So he grants the very point I was asking for.

units.la: XLVI. Inst. 10. (H.p.263.) Sp. S. philosophice res naturales distinguit, Ergo Philosophice etiam agit & loquitur. prob. antec. quia Psal. CXLVIII. 1. incipit ab excelsis coelis, pergit v. 7. ad Elementorum systema, descendit postea ad corpora animata v. 10. definit in homine v. 11. &
units.tr: XLVI. Inst. 10. (H. p. 263.) The Holy Spirit distinguishes natural things philosophically. Therefore he also speaks and acts philosophically. I prove the antecedent: because Psalm 148:1 begins with the high heavens, goes on at verse 7 to the system of the elements, descends afterwards to living bodies at verse 10, and ends with man at verse 11, and

units.la: Resp. Talis est illa distinctio, qualis per notitiam communem facile haberi potest, ut quis a coelo supremo & iis quae in eo sunt, ordine, quem per sensus facile cognoscere potest, progrediatur ad terram & ea quae super ea reperiuntur. Si autem Psalmes Philosophicam distinctionem ex mente Adversarii observare voluisset, debuissent forte praeponi stellae fixae Soli & Lunae, quia his sunt superiores. 2. debuisset meteora conjunctim tradere, cum tamen v. 4. agat de aquis quae supra in coelo sunt, quae sunt nubes; & postea, interpositis versu 7. terrestribus, iterum v. 8. de meteoris agat grandine & nive. Inspiciatur totus ille Psalmus, & apparebit, non tam sollicitum & scrupulosum fuisse in ordine, qualem forte Philosophus quis praescribere vel sequi voluisset, observando, ita ut hoc argumentum exigui admodum sit momenti. Verum ille auctor videtur existimasse, mihi rerum naturalium explicationem non philosophicam & accuratam eandem esse cum falsa, quae cum satis distinxerim saepius, cadunt reliqua omnia, quae contra me, ex iis quae habet p. 264. & 265. forte dirigi possent: quae si ita videatur, lector cum meis poterit conferre.
units.tr: Resp. That distinction is only of the kind that can easily be gained by common knowledge: one proceeds from the highest heaven and the things in it, in an order that can easily be recognized by the senses, down to the earth and the things found upon it. But if the Psalmist had wished to observe a philosophical distinction in the sense of my opponent, he should perhaps have placed the fixed stars before the Sun and Moon, since these are higher. Second, he should have set out the meteors together, whereas at verse 4 he speaks of the waters that are above in the heavens, which are the clouds, and afterwards, after the earthly things of verse 7 have intervened, he again at verse 8 speaks of meteors, hail and snow. Let the whole Psalm be examined, and it will appear that the writer was not so anxious and scrupulous about order as some philosopher might wish to prescribe or follow; so this argument is of very little weight. But that author seems to have thought that for me a non-philosophical and inaccurate explanation of natural things is the same as a false one. Since I have distinguished these often enough, everything else that could perhaps be directed against me from what he has on pages 264 and 265 falls away. If this seems right, the reader can compare it with my own words.

units.la: XLVII. Except. 2. (S. p. 405.) Quamvis non diffitendum sit, primarium scripturae sacrae scopum esse, ut nobis viam monstret ad vitam aeternam; hic tamen principalis finis non excludit alios minus principales. Cum enim haec ipsa variis in locis res naturales, earumque seriam meditationem nobis proponat,
units.tr: XLVII. Except. 2. (S. p. 405.) Although it must not be denied that the primary aim of Holy Scripture is to show us the way to eternal life, this principal end does not exclude other, less principal ends. For since Scripture itself sets before us, in various places, natural things and their orderly consideration,

units.la: E ut objectivè nos excitent ad Deum laudandum, quis dubitare ausit, quin de iis ipsis rebus veras assertiones proponat, quarum subsidio rerum naturalium cognitionem acquirere queamus. Item p. 406. Vera explicatio rerum naturalium à Spiritu S. in scriptura propositä nequaquam avertit fideles à primario scriptura scopo, sed illa eos ipsos convenienter ad eundem scopum dirigere potest.
units.tr: so that they objectively stir us up to praise God, who would dare to doubt that it sets forth true assertions about those very things, by whose help we may acquire knowledge of natural things? Likewise on page 406: a true explanation of natural things set forth in Scripture by the Holy Spirit by no means turns believers away from the primary aim of Scripture, but can rather direct them suitably to that same aim.

units.la: Resp. 1. Nec primarium, nec secundarium scripturæ finem esse reddere hominem Eruditum in Physicis ostensum. 2. etsi scriptura per res naturales velit nos excitari ad Deum laudandum, tamen non propterea cognitio accurata rerum naturalium inter fines scripturæ reponenda est; & ad id sufficit cognitio vulgaris, aut si quis velit plura argumenta habere Dei laudandi, illi accuratiorem rerum naturalium cognitionem è libro naturæ petere licebit. 3. non dicimus, quod ipsa vera explicatio rerum naturalium homines fideles avertat à primario scripturæ scopo per se & naturâ suâ, sed tamen existimamus, facilè fieri potuisse, ut rudiores turbarentur, si in scripturâ de rebus naturalibus tam subtilia reperissent captum suum excedentia, vel etiamsensuum præjudiciis contraria.
units.tr: Resp. 1. It has been shown that neither the primary nor the secondary aim of Scripture is to make a man learned in physics. 2. Even if Scripture wishes us to be stirred up by natural things to praise God, it does not follow that accurate knowledge of natural things must be counted among the aims of Scripture. Common knowledge is enough for that. And if someone wants more arguments for praising God, he may seek a more accurate knowledge of natural things from the book of nature. 3. We do not say that a true explanation of natural things turns believers away from the primary aim of Scripture by its own nature and in itself, but we do think it could easily happen that the less educated would be disturbed if they found in Scripture such subtle matters about natural things, beyond their grasp, or even contrary to the prejudices of the senses.

units.la: XLVIII. Exc. 3. Danæus part. 1. c. 33. Nonne ab iisdem isti Theologia & Ethica Philosophiæ pars toto genere discernuntur? Et tamen quis eorum tam temerarius erit, qui Ethicem, eamque verissimam & universam Sacræ Scripturæ tradi negare audeat? Ergo distincti artium & tractationum fines non obstant, quò minus eadem Sacra Scriptura iisdemque literis & Physica illa Universalis, & Theologia sit comprehensa, quia & ipsa Physica quodammodo Theologiæ pars est, illique subservit.
units.tr: XLVIII. Exc. 3. Danaeus, part 1, ch. 33. Are not Theology and Ethics as a whole distinguished from the philosophy of these same things? And yet who would be so rash as to dare deny that Ethics, and that the most true and universal ethics, is taught in Holy Scripture? Therefore the distinct ends of the arts and disciplines do not stand in the way of Holy Scripture, and of that same Universal Physics, being comprehended in the same Scripture and the same writings as Theology. For Physics itself is in some way a part of Theology and serves it.

units.la: Resp. 1. Ita quidem vulgò obtinet, ut Ethica diversa tradatur à Theologiâ Practicâ, quod an rectè fiat non est hujus loci prolixius disputare. Amesius tamen lib. 2. Medullæ Theol. c. 2. ab illâ vulgatâ sententiâ recedit, statuens, non aliam debere dari virtutum disciplinam, quam ipsam Theologiam. Nec ab ejus sententia ratio abludit. Certum quippe est, non nisi gradibus differre virtutes morales ita dictas à virtutibus Christianis: at gradus non mutat speciem, uti fert vulgata sententia. Et annon absurdum, disciplinarum distinctionem ex modo tradendi aliquid perfectè vel imperfectè eruere? quis unquam audivit, Physicam aliquam imperfectè explicatam esse aliam speciem disciplinam à Physicâ perfectè explicatâ? quin ergò hic lux major extinguit minorem, gradus perfectior absorbet imperfectiorem, & quemadmodum in vitâ æternâ Fides mutabitur in Visionem; ita exortâ Euangelii luce, id quod imperfectum ex lacunis Ethnicorum de virtutibus moralibus est haustum, per illud perfectum absumitur, inque illud transmutatur.
