Ita que sic Danæi exceptio sponte sua collabascit; unde & diversitatis ratio apparet inter Physicam & Ethicam, quod scripturæ finis sit mores nostros secundum normam legis divinæ informare, unde moralia præcepta perfectissima tradit, non vero rerum naturalium essentiam enodare, uti ostensum. 2. qui vero volunt, distinctas esse Ethicam & Theologiam practicam disciplinas, illi à diversitate Principiorum limites iis ponunt, nimirum, ut Ethica tantùm tradat illas Regulas morum, quæ è reliquiis luminis naturalis possunt eruì, sed Theologia practica eas, quas divina revelatio præscribit; Ergo secundum hanc sententiam scriptura non traderet Ethicam, sed Theologiam Practicam tantum, adeoque nec hâc ex parte allata Exceptio nobis obcrit.
units.tr: Resp. 1. It is indeed the common view that Ethics is taught as a different subject from practical Theology. Whether this is rightly done is not a matter to be argued at length here. Amesius, however, in book 2 of his Medulla Theologiae, ch. 2, departs from that common opinion, holding that there ought to be no other discipline of the virtues than Theology itself. Nor does the reasoning disagree with his view. For it is certain that the so-called moral virtues differ from Christian virtues only in degree, and degree does not change the kind, as the common view holds. And is it not absurd to make a distinction of disciplines depend on the manner of teaching something perfectly or imperfectly? Who has ever heard that Physics explained imperfectly is a different kind of discipline from Physics explained perfectly? Rather, the greater light extinguishes the lesser, and the more perfect degree absorbs the less perfect. Just as in eternal life faith will be changed into vision, so with the rising of the light of the Gospel, what was imperfect, drawn from the gaps in the heathens' knowledge of moral virtues, is swallowed up by what is perfect and transformed into it. Thus Danaeus' exception collapses of its own accord. From this also appears the reason for the difference between Physics and Ethics: the aim of Scripture is to shape our conduct according to the rule of divine law, so it delivers the most perfect moral precepts, but it does not unfold the essence of natural things, as has been shown. 2. Those who want Ethics and practical Theology to be distinct disciplines set their limits by the difference of principles: Ethics should teach only those rules of conduct that can be drawn from the remnants of the natural light, but practical Theology those that divine revelation prescribes. According to this view, then, Scripture would not teach Ethics but only practical Theology, and so the exception brought forward in this respect does not harm us.

units.la: XLIX. Objicit (M. p. 232.) ad me nihil facere hanc exceptionem, cum auctor ibi videatur agere ad hominem, sive ex hypothesi eorum, qui Ethicam & Theologiam diversas esse disciplinas admittebant &c.
units.tr: XLIX. He objects (M. p. 232.) that this exception does nothing against me, since the author there seems to argue ad hominem, that is, on the hypothesis of those who admitted that Ethics and Theology are different disciplines, etc.

units.la: Resp. Contra me omninò facit hæc exceptio, quoniam Major mei argumenti si in formâ proferatur, talis erat. Quicquid non est necessarium, ut scriptura omnes suos fines, qualcs recensiti sunt 1 Tim. III. obtineat, illud non est quærendum in sacrâ scripturâ, cujus fundamentum in eo consistit, quod distincti sint artium fines, qui etiam faciunt, ut distincta media adhibeantur: quod omnino evertere Danæus conatur, dum dicit, distinctos artium fines non obstare, quò minus eâdem Sacrâ Scriptura iisdemque literis & Physica illa Universalis & Theologia sit comprehensa, idque probat exemplo Theologiæ & Ethicæ, ad quæ sic respondeo. 1. Ita quidem vulgò &c. Vid. art. XLVIII. adeoque nego Danæi Minorem. *2, nego etiam Majorem propositionem, ut ex dictis manifestum.
units.tr: Resp. This exception works entirely against me, since the major premise of my argument, if put in form, was this: whatever is not necessary for Scripture to attain all its ends, such as are listed in 1 Timothy 3, is not to be sought in Holy Scripture. Its foundation lies in the fact that the ends of the arts are distinct, which also means that distinct means are used for them. Danaeus tries entirely to overturn this when he says that distinct ends of the arts do not stand in the way of the same Holy Scripture and the same writings comprehending both that Universal Physics and Theology. He proves this by the example of Theology and Ethics, to which I reply thus: 1. It is indeed the common view, etc. See art. XLVIII. So I deny Danaeus' minor premise. *2. I also deny the major premise, as is clear from what has been said.

units.la: L. Except. 4. (B. Dial. p. 9. & 10.) Apostolus ibi agit de rebus creditu & actu necessariis ad salutem, & de fundamento fidei salvifica; ad quæ sa-cram Scripturam sufficientissimam esse nemo orthodoxus negat; sed non negat Apostolus, textum Biblicum habere usum praeter illa necessaria. Quid? annon habemus multa Historica, Chronologica, Physica, aliaque, quæ citra salutis dispendium ignorari possunt: an ergò propterea poterunt illa floccifieri, vel argumenta inde deducta rejici? Verum Christianum decet, testimonia sacra in omni materiâ arripere, ut verissima, & doctrinam suam ad ea formare.
units.tr: L. Except. 4. (B. Dial. p. 9. & 10.) The apostle there treats of things that must be believed and done for salvation, and of the foundation of saving faith. No orthodox person denies that Holy Scripture is wholly sufficient for these. But the apostle does not deny that the biblical text has uses beyond these necessary things. What then? Do we not have many historical, chronological and physical matters, which can be left unknown without loss to salvation? Can these therefore be held in contempt, or arguments drawn from them be rejected? Rather, a Christian ought to seize upon the sacred testimonies in every subject, as wholly true, and shape his doctrine accordingly.

units.la: Resp. Apostolus ibi docet, hos esse Scripturæ sines non alios, ex quibus de mediis judicandum existimo: Ergo non est, quod in ea quæramus rerum naturalium explicationem accuratam, quemadmodum superiùs recte intulimus; Adversario vero ostendendum fuisset, vel Scripturae finem esse accuratam rerum naturalium doctrinam, vel eam esse medium necessarium ad obtinendum aliquem ejus finium, ita ut nisi adhiberetur, aliquis etiam finis obtineri non posset, quorum neutrum quamdiu praestatur ab adversario, nihil obtinetur. 2. Non negamus, etiam scripturam agere de historicis & chronologicis, sed illa quamvis non pertineant ad Essentiam Fidei, tamen necessaria sunt ad ejus amplitudinem, defensionem & explicationem. Quod autem incidenter agens de rebus naturalibus formulas adhibeat non accuratam & nudam veritatem exprimentes, inde existit, quod homines per sensus varia praejudicia de iis hauserint, quae habent pro natura notis: at non ita est comparatum cum rebus historicis, ubi, si homines forte falsi aliquid habeant praeconceptum, id fundatum est in auctoritate humana, cui cum vident opponi auctoritatem divinam, facile possunt ab eo deflectere. Imo amplius dicam: si aliquid in historicis fuerit, quod communiter ab hominibus fuisset receptum pro vero, & firmiter radicatum, dummodo illud non pugnet cum fide, etiam hic Sp. S. pro sua sapientia se hominibus errantibus, formulas receptas adhibendo, non vero errando cum errantibus, accommodaturum fuisse, si non potuisset sine magna turbatione simpliciorum contrarium doceri; simili modo, quo ostendemus postea, Apostolos condescendisse hominibus in usurpanda versione minus correcta.
units.tr: Answer. The apostle there teaches that these are the ends of Scripture and no others, and from these I judge that the means must be decided. Therefore we need not seek in it an accurate explanation of natural things, as we rightly inferred above. But the opponent should have shown either that the accurate teaching of natural things is an end of Scripture, or that it is a necessary means to obtaining one of its ends, so that unless it were employed, some end could not be obtained. As long as the opponent does not establish either of these, nothing is gained. 2. We do not deny that Scripture also deals with historical and chronological matters. But although these do not belong to the essence of faith, they are nevertheless necessary for its enlargement, defence and explanation. That Scripture, when dealing incidentally with natural things, uses forms of speech that do not express the accurate and bare truth, arises from this: men have drawn various prejudices about such things from their senses, which they hold as known by nature. But it is not so with historical matters. There, if men happen to have some false preconception, it is founded on human authority, and when they see divine authority set against it, they can easily turn away from it. Indeed I will say more: if there were something in historical matters that had been commonly received by men as true and firmly rooted, provided it does not conflict with faith, the Holy Spirit, in his wisdom, would have accommodated himself to erring men by employing the received forms, not by erring with them, if the contrary could not have been taught without great disturbance to the simple. In the same way we will show later that the apostles condescended to men in using a less correct translation.

units.la: LI. Inst. 1. (M. p. 233.) me hic non recte concludere, sed hoc modo debuisse conclusionem formare. Ergo non est quod in Scriptura quaeramus rerum naturalium cognitionem, to vero accuratam gratis annectli.
units.tr: LI. Inst. 1. (M. p. 233.) I do not here conclude rightly; he says I ought to have formed the conclusion in this way: Therefore it is not that we should seek in Scripture the knowledge of natural things, which however is gratuitously annexed to the accurate.

units.la: Resp. Imo rectissime, cum mens mea sit demonstrare, non esse quaerendam in scripturis Physicam, hoc est, scientiam qualis debet esse Physica, quae utique debet tradere explicationem rerum naturalium accuratam.
units.tr: Answer. Quite rightly, indeed, since my intention is to show that Physics is not to be sought in the Scriptures, that is, a science such as Physics ought to be, which surely ought to deliver an accurate explanation of natural things.

units.la: LII. Inst. 2. (M. p. 234.) Potuisse Sp. S. ex superabundanti gratia alia quoque ad salutem praecise & per se non ita necessaria rebus fidei gratiose auxiliii loco adjicere vel admiscere.
units.tr: LII. Inst. 2. (M. p. 234.) The Holy Spirit could, out of overflowing grace, have added or mixed in with the things of faith, as a helpful supplement, other things that are not strictly and in themselves so necessary for salvation.

units.la: Resp. Quae Deus tractat in sacris literis, ea etsi omnia non sint praecise ad salutem necessaria, attamen necessaria sunt ad amplitudinem & explicationem fidei defensionemque, atque ita etiam de rebus naturalibus Scriptura agit, ad quod ut saepius dixi, cognitio communis abunde est sufficiens.
units.tr: Answer. Those things that God treats of in the sacred writings, even if not all are strictly necessary for salvation, are nevertheless necessary for the enlargement, explanation and defence of faith. And so Scripture also treats of natural things, and for this, as I have often said, common knowledge is more than sufficient.

units.la: LIII. Inst. 3 loco sit id quod (M. p. 235.) arguitur, a tractatione rerum Chronologicarum & historicarum, ad tractationem rerum naturalium accuratam. Resp. Verum id non procedit, propter hanc differentiam, quia tractatio rerum naturalium accurata non est necessaria ad amplitudinem, defensionem & explicationem fidei, sed sufficit cognitio vulgaris; At tractatio historica & Chronologica est necessaria ad aliquod ex dictis.
units.tr: LIII. Inst. 3. (M. p. 235.) What is argued is this: from the treatment of chronological and historical matters to the accurate treatment of natural things. Answer. This does not follow, for this reason: an accurate treatment of natural things is not necessary for the enlargement, defence and explanation of faith, since ordinary knowledge suffices; but a historical and chronological treatment is necessary for one of the purposes mentioned.

units.la: LIV. Inst. 4. (M. p. 237.) Quod si istud praejudicium per oppositas a Cartesio rationes e me & similibus tolli potuerit, quidni persuasio Auctoritatis & Infallibilitatis divinae aeque vulgum retrahere potuisset a praejudicio aliquo physico, atque eundem retrahit a praejudicio Historico & Chronologico.
units.tr: LIV. Inst. 4. (M. p. 237.) If that prejudice could be removed from me and people like me by the reasons Descartes set against it, why could not the persuasion of divine authority and infallibility have drawn the common people back from some physical prejudice just as it draws them back from a historical and chronological prejudice?

units.la: Resp. Differentiam jam dedimus, nempe non ita firmiter radicatum esse id, quod suscipitur propter auctoritatem humanam adeoque facilius posse relinqui, posita auctoritate divina contraria, ac id quod susceptum est propter sensuum praejudicia, ac habetur tanquam si natura notum esset.
units.tr: Answer. We have already given the difference: namely, that what is accepted on account of human authority is not so firmly rooted, and so can more easily be given up when divine authority to the contrary is set against it, than what is accepted on account of the prejudices of the senses and is held as if known by nature.

units.la: CAPUT IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: Argumentum tertium ex eo desumtum, quòd Scriptura in se non quaerendam doceat sapientiam Philosophi- cam, proponitur & defenditur.
units.tr: The third argument, drawn from the fact that Scripture teaches that philosophical wisdom is not to be sought in itself, is set forth and defended.

units.la: LV. Sequitur nostrum Argumentum tertium. Sed non tantum non docet Scriptura, finem suum esse doctrinam rerum naturalium, verum ita etiam in solidum doctrinam salutis sibi vendicat, ut non quaerendam in se dicat sapientiam humanam sive Philosophicam. Considerentur ea quae Paulus habet 1 Cor. I. 22,23. Quandoquidem & Judaei signum petunt, & Graeci Sapientiam quaerunt. Nos autem praedicamus Christum Crucifixum, Judaeis quidem offendiculum, Graecis vero stultitiam. Item 1 Cor. II. 6, 7. Sapientiam vero loquimur inter adultos: sapientiam autem non seculi hujus neque principum seculi hujus, qui abolentur: sed loquimur sapientiam Dei in mysterio. Et verf. 12. Nos vero non spiritum mundi accepimus, sed spiritum, qui est ex Deo, ut sciamus quae Deus est nobis gratificatus. Sapientiam mundi vocat eam, qua homines seculi naturali perspicacia in rebus mundanis theoreticis & practicis excellere possunt, cujusmodi sapientes Graecia praesertim jactabat Thaletem, Solonem, Socratem &c. Verba sunt Parei in hunc locum. Illam sapientiam quaerebant Graeci, utpote apud quos il is temporibus studium Philosophiae florebat. Illa per spiritum mundi, hoc est, rationem naturalem sive spiritum naturalis intelligentiae, qui communiter hominibus est concessus, poterat reperiri. Hanc sapientiam dicit se non tradere, Graecos eam apud se vel in suis dictis non reperire, ideoque frustrà ibi quaesi-turos; negat, se sapientiam mundi docere, sed eam quae est in mysterio, quam mundus naturali indagatione indagare non potest. Hinc est, quod omnia quae in scripturis, ad Christum referantur. Quemadmodum testatur Augustinus super Psalmum 71, ita dicens: Ad illum (scil. Christum) omnia, quae divinitus scripta sunt, referuntur. Cum itaque expresse testetur Scriptura, se non docere sapientiam humanam, sapientiam mundi, sed Christum crucifixum, omniaque ad ipsum referri, quis non videt, multum falli eos, qui contra mentem & protestationem Scripturae, ex eâ sapientiam humanam, Philosophiam naturalem volunt educere?
units.tr: LV. Here follows our third argument. But Scripture not only does not teach that its purpose is the doctrine of natural things; it so claims for itself the whole doctrine of salvation that it says human or philosophical wisdom is not to be sought in it. Let us consider what Paul says in 1 Cor. 1.22–23: "For the Jews ask for a sign, and the Greeks seek wisdom; but we preach Christ crucified, to the Jews indeed a stumbling-block, and to the Greeks foolishness." Likewise 1 Cor. 2.6–7: "Yet we speak wisdom among the mature; but not the wisdom of this age, nor of the rulers of this age, who are brought to nothing; but we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery." And at verse 12: "Now we have received not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit which is from God, that we may know the things that have been freely given us by God." He calls "the wisdom of the world" that wisdom in which the men of this age can excel in worldly theoretical and practical matters by their natural acuteness; the wise men whom Greece especially boasted of, such as Thales, Solon, Socrates and others, were of this kind. These are the words of Pareus on this passage. The Greeks sought that wisdom, since among them the study of philosophy was then flourishing. It could be found by "the spirit of the world," that is, by natural reason, or the spirit of natural understanding, which is commonly granted to men. Paul says that he does not hand down this wisdom, since the Greeks do not find it among themselves or in their sayings, and so they will seek it there in vain; he denies that he teaches "the wisdom of the world," but the wisdom that lies in the "mystery," which the world cannot search out by natural inquiry. Hence it is that all things in the Scriptures are referred to Christ. As Augustine testifies on Psalm 71, saying: "To him (namely Christ) all things that have been divinely written are referred." Since Scripture therefore expressly testifies that it does not teach human wisdom, the wisdom of the world, but Christ crucified, and that all things are referred to him, who does not see how greatly those are mistaken who, against the mind and declaration of Scripture, want to draw human wisdom and natural philosophy out of it?

units.la: LVI. Exc. 1. Eâtenus saltem doceri, quatenus ad Christi cognitionem juvant.
units.tr: LVI. Objection 1. It is taught only so far as it helps the knowledge of Christ.

units.la: Resp. Juvant ad cognitionem existentiae Dei & Attributorum divinorum, sed parum admodum ad Christi Servatoris & Mediatoris notitiam, & sufficit ad illud cognitio crassior & minus accurata, ut saepius jam dictum.
units.tr: Answer. It helps toward the knowledge of the existence of God and of the divine attributes, but very little toward the knowledge of Christ the Savior and Mediator, and for that a cruder and less exact knowledge is sufficient, as has often been said already.

units.la: LVII. Exc. 2. (M. p. 240.) Me ipsum concedere res Physicas, Historicas, & Chronologicas in sacris literis tradi, & Mosen, Davidem, librum Jobi, Salomonis, si non concedam, mihi facile os obstructuros.
units.tr: LVII. Objection 2 (M. p. 240). That I myself concede that physical, historical and chronological matters are handed down in the sacred writings, and that if I do not concede that Moses, David, the book of Job and Solomon would easily stop my mouth.

units.la: Resp. 1. De historicis & Chronologicis non est quaestio. 2. nullibi concessi, res Physicas secundum interiorem Essentiam & naturam, secundum causas proximas in sacris literis tradi, nec contrarium ex Mose, Davide, libro Jobi & Salomonis potest ostendi.
units.tr: Answer. 1. There is no question about historical and chronological matters. 2. I nowhere conceded that physical things are handed down in the sacred writings according to their inner essence and nature, or according to their proximate causes, nor can the contrary be shown from Moses, David, the book of Job and Solomon.

units.la: LVIII. Exc. 3. M. p. 240. per σοφίαν, veram & sanam non inte- lligi locis citatis, sed eam quam Col. 11. Apostolus vocat κενὴν απάτην &c.
units.tr: LVIII. Objection 3 (M. p. 240). By σοφία, true and sound wisdom is not understood in the passages cited, but that which the Apostle in Col. 2 calls empty deceit [κενὴν ἀπάτην], etc.

units.la: Resp. Ego verò probavi sapientiam veram & sanam intelligi his verbis: Illam sapientiam quaerebant &c. qua mea probatio fuisset refutanda.
units.tr: Answer. But I have shown that true and sound wisdom is understood in these words: They sought that wisdom, etc. My proof would have had to be refuted by this.

units.la: LIX. Exc. 4 M p. 240. agitur hic de huiusmodi σοφίᾳ, quae 1. apta est κενὴν τῆς σαρκὸς & Χριστῷ 1 Cor. 1. 17. 2. quae judicabat Christum & salutarem de eo Theologiam esse μωρίαν v. 18, 21, 23. esse vanam & inutilem. 3. Cui Deus, utpote rei in se malae, extremum minatur exitium v. 19. 4. Quae Christiana Theologia opponitur ut inimicissime cum ea pugnans. E. non etiam de sapientiâ verâ agitur. Resp. Neg. ista majoris Connexio, quoniam de omni sapientiâ quam Graeci quaerebant, & quae per spiritum mundi hoc est rationem naturalem indagatur, agitur, eaque rejicitur; At Graeci non tantum vana quaerebant vel inveniebant, sed etiam vera & solida Graecorum sapientia consistebat in cognitione naturae habente vera falsis admixta, in Eloquentiâ probâ, cum vanitate tamen conjunctâ: utramque rejicit: Abusum & vanitatem propter eas rationes, quæ in Exceptione allata; veram etiam & solidam non esse sufficientem ad salutem docet. Expresse enim dicit Apostolus 1 Cor. I. 21. quoniam mundus per suam sapientiam Deum in sua sapientia non agnoverit, propterea Deo placuisse per stultam concionem salvare eos qui credunt.
units.tr: LIX. Objection 4 (M. p. 240). Here it is a matter of that kind of wisdom which 1. is suited to make the cross of Christ void [κενωθῇ] (1 Cor. 1:17); 2. which judged Christ and the saving theology concerning him to be foolishness, vv. 18, 21, 23, to be vain and useless; 3. to which God, since it is evil in itself, threatens extreme destruction, v. 19; 4. which is set against Christian theology as most hostile to it. Therefore it is not also a matter of true wisdom. Answer. I deny the connection of this major premise, since the discussion concerns all the wisdom that the Greeks sought, and that which is pursued through the spirit of the world, that is, through natural reason, and this is rejected. But the Greeks not only sought or found vain things; their wisdom also consisted of true and solid knowledge of nature, mixed with falsehoods, and of a sound eloquence, yet joined with vanity. The Apostle rejects both: the abuse and vanity, for the reasons given in the objection; and he teaches that the true and solid wisdom is also not sufficient for salvation. For the Apostle says expressly in 1 Cor. 1:21: Since the world, through its own wisdom, did not know God in his wisdom, it pleased God through the foolishness of the preaching to save those who believe.

units.la: LX. Exc. 5. M. p. 241. per spiritum mundi intelligitur hujus sapientia Auctor, Satanas, qui Eph. II. 2. appellatur ab hoc effectu τὸ πνεῦμα ἐνεργοῦν ἐν τοῖς υἱοῖς τῆς ἀπειθείας, sana v. Philosophia nullibi appellatur τὸ πνεῦμα ξ κόσμου.
units.tr: LX. Objection 5 (M. p. 241). By the spirit of the world is understood the author of this wisdom, Satan, who from this effect is called in Eph. 2:2 the spirit that now works in the sons of disobedience [τὸ πνεῦμα ἐνεργοῦν ἐν τοῖς υἱοῖς τῆς ἀπειθείας]; sound philosophy is nowhere called the spirit of the world [τὸ πνεῦμα τοῦ κόσμου].

units.la: Resp. Per πνεῦμα τοῦ κόσμου intelligi debet naturalis perspicacia secundum Paræum, spiritus naturalis intelligentiæ, qui communiter hominibus est concessus; Eodemque modo spiritum mundi alii Interpretes intelligunt. Sic Martyr, Spiritus mundi, inquit, est consueta vis animi, quâ homines ad agendum & cognoscendum incitantur secundum rationem & facultatem sua natura &c. quæ vide apud ipsum. Gualtherus, spiritum mundi hic dicit; non malum illum & impurum, per quem Diabolus in Impiis agit, sed mentem sive rationem, qua homines naturaliter intelligunt, sapiunt, cogitant, ea denique faciunt, quæ naturali illa anima facultate perfici possunt. Musculus. Et quid vocat spiritum mundi? Dixit, neminem scire quæ Dei sunt, nisi spiritum Dei, ut nec quæ hominis sunt nisi spiritum hominis, ita nunc dat mundo, hoc est, mundanis hominibus suum spiritum, veluti homini cuipiam, per quam intelligit eam partem, quâ constat rerum cognitio, sapientia & intellectus (hoc enim loco de sapientia Dei & humana loquitur) ut spiritus mundi sit sapientia & intellectus mundi. Atque hæc interpretatio textui, si is inspiciatur, convenientissima.
units.tr: Answer. By the spirit of the world [πνεῦμα τοῦ κόσμου] one must understand, according to Paraeus, natural sharpness of mind, the spirit of natural understanding, which is granted in common to men; and other interpreters understand the spirit of the world in the same way. So Martyr: The spirit of the world, he says, is the usual force of the mind by which men are stirred to act and to know according to the reason and faculty of their nature, etc., which see there in his own words. Gualther says: Here he speaks of the spirit of the world, not that evil and impure spirit through which the Devil works in the impious, but the mind or reason by which men naturally understand, have sense, think, and finally do those things which can be brought to completion by that natural faculty of the soul. Musculus: And what does he call the spirit of the world? He said that no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God, just as no one knows the things of a man except the spirit of man; so now he gives to the world, that is, to worldly men, their own spirit, as it were to some man, through which he understands that part by which knowledge of things, wisdom and understanding consist (for in this place he speaks of the wisdom of God and of human wisdom), so that the spirit of the world is the wisdom and understanding of the world. And this interpretation is most fitting to the text, if it is examined.

units.la: LXI. Exc.6. M. p. 241. Interpretationem Parai hïs Exceptionibus non adversari.
units.tr: LXI. Objection 6 (M. p. 241). Paraeus's interpretation does not conflict with these objections.

units.la: Resp. Contrarium patet ex collatione, Paræus intelligit talem sapientiam, quam homines seculi naturali perspicacia consequuntur; at superior interpretatio vanam & inanem, quæ non naturali perspicacia, sed sophisticatione acquiritur.
units.tr: Answer. The contrary is clear from comparison. Paraeus understands such wisdom as men of this age attain by natural sharpness of mind, but the earlier interpretation understands vain and empty wisdom, which is acquired not by natural sharpness but by sophistry.

units.la: LXII. Exc. 7. M. p. 242. At potest intelligi hic per σοφίαν, ὑπερχῆ λέγει ἡ σοφία.
units.tr: LXII. Objection 7 (M. p. 242). But it can be understood here by σοφία, what wisdom says [ὑπερχῆ λέγει ἡ σοφία].

units.la: Resp. Quid debeat intelligi superius à me est ostensum.
units.tr: Answer. What must be understood has been shown by me above.

units.la: LXIII. Exc. 8. M. p. 242. Si omnia ad Christum referuntur, ut paulo ante cum Augustino referebas, quomodo ergo hoc loco asseris, res naturales parum admodum facere ad Christi Mediatoris & Salvatoris notitiam.
units.tr: LXIII. Objection 8 (M. p. 242). If all things are referred to Christ, as you a little earlier referred with Augustine, how then do you assert in this passage that natural things contribute very little to the knowledge of Christ the Mediator and Savior?

units.la: Resp. Id quod hic dico ex mente omnium Reformatorum dico, qui ad Obj. Arminianorum ex cap. 1. &c. ad Rom. pro vocatione Universali desumtas, respondent, hanc vocationem quae fit per creaturas, earumque consideratione non ducere ad Deum Redemtorem, sed ad Deum Creatorem, Ergo parum admodum per se, & quatenus tales, juvant ad Christi Mediatoris quatenus talis notitiam, quamvis remote & per singularem directionem divinam ad Christum referantur, in quibus nulla plane est contradictio.
units.tr: Answer. What I say here I say in the mind of all the Reformed, who, in answer to the objection of the Arminians drawn from Rom. 1 and elsewhere in favor of universal calling, reply that this calling, which takes place through creatures and their consideration, leads not to God the Redeemer but to God the Creator. Therefore, in themselves and as such, they contribute very little to the knowledge of Christ as Mediator, although remotely, and through a special divine direction, they are referred to Christ; and in this there is plainly no contradiction.

units.la: Reliqua quae hic objiciuntur (M. p. 243.) de <bl>ἀποφία</bl> quam Apostolus docuit, item, quod non tantum incidenter egerit scriptura de rebus naturalibus, ut & de cognitione erronea, sunt meri coccysmi, de quibus saepe est dictum.
units.tr: The remaining points raised here (M. p. 243) about perplexity [ἀπορία] which the Apostle taught, and likewise that Scripture has not only incidentally treated of natural things, as also of erroneous knowledge, are mere jeers, of which it has often been spoken.

units.la: CAPUT V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: Quartum argumentum cujus Summa, quod Deus ab iis, quos sapientia Philosophica ornaverat, nihil ad eam faciens voluerit conscribi, proponitur & vindicatur.
units.tr: The fourth argument is set out and defended, its summary being that God willed that nothing bearing on this matter should be written down by those whom he had endowed with Philosophical wisdom.

units.la: LXIV. Quartum argumentum inde petimus, quod Deus ab illis, quos ornaverat sapientia humana & cognitione Philosophica, nihil voluerit ad hanc rem spectans consignari. Patet id 1. Exemplo Mosis, de quo legimus Act. VII. 22. Et eruditus fuit Moses omni sapientia Aegyptiorum. Erant ii tunc temporis Philosophiae Antistites, unde & in Graeciam est translata. Quare nullum dubium esse potest, quin Moses insignem habuerit rerum naturalium cognitionem. Is tamen cum Creationis opus describit, ubi occasio erat de iis Creaturis & operibus Dei subtiliter differendi, earumque interiores naturas & essentias explicandi, breviter tantum recenset earum praecipuas species, omnia uno capite absolvens, omittens etiam ea, quae sensibus non erant obvia; unde factum, ut Angelorum Creationis distinctis verbis non meminerit, nec etiam Metallorum, Gemmarum & aliorum in visceribus terrae reconditorum mentionem ullam fecerit, abunde se suo scopo satisfecisse statuens, & omnia illa, quae in oculos hominum incurrunt, ostenderit, a Deo creata & producta fuisse: contra vero quam prolixus est in iis, quae ad Ecclesiam ejusque administrationem spectabant, describendis. Ibi non unum caput
units.tr: LXIV. We take the fourth argument from the fact that God willed nothing bearing on this matter to be recorded by those whom he had endowed with human wisdom and Philosophical knowledge. This is clear, first, from the example of Moses, of whom we read in Acts 7:22: And Moses was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians. At that time they were the leaders of philosophy, whence it was also transferred to Greece. Therefore there can be no doubt that Moses had a notable knowledge of natural things. Yet when he describes the work of Creation, where there was an opportunity to discuss those creatures and works of God in detail and to explain their inner natures and essences, he only briefly recounts their chief kinds, finishing everything in one chapter. He also omits what was not obvious to the senses; hence it is that he makes no distinct mention of the creation of the Angels, nor of any mention of metals, gems and other things hidden in the depths of the earth. He judged that he had sufficiently met his purpose, and he showed that all those things which fall under human eyes were created and produced by God. On the other hand, how full he is in describing those things which pertained to the Church and its administration! There it is not one chapter

units.la: { } Catchword: caput sufficit, sed fere omnia capita Exodi posteriora, à 25. ad 40. inclusive, exceptis 32, 33, 34. eò collimant, ut tabernaculi constructio & cultus Levitici administratio plenè quoad omnes partes explicentur. Tota Genesis absolvitur in fatis Ecclesiæ ab initio mundi usque ad sua tempora describendis; succenturiantur ei reliqui quatuor Mosis libri, qui in formandâ & describendâ Ecclesiâ Israelitica toti occupantur. Aliorum scriptorum sacrorum simbillis est ratio. Unde vel cœco patere potest, non quærendam in S. Scriptura Physicam vel Philosophiam, quæ præcipuè à Mose in his sacris erudito, occasione tàm egregiâ data, per operum Creationis descriptionem, debuisset explicari, si Deus librum scripturæ huic rei voluisset destinatum. Sententiæ meæ accinit Paræus in Gen. cap. 1. v. 1. jam supra visus c. 4. art. 35. Is, ubi inquirit, cur Moses Angelorum non expresse meminerit Creationis, rejectis causis ab aliis allatis, inquit: Simplicior est ratio Chrysostomi homilia 2. in Genesin, quam & Basilius attingit Hom. 1. in Hexaem. Mosen historiam suam traditi Judæorum attemperâsse. Erant enim homines terreni, tantum sensibilia sapientes, tantum igitur sensibilium Dei operum descriptionem Moses aperte prosequi voluit, quorum contemplatione ac sensu ad intellectum sublimiorum rerum, & ad ipsius invisibilis Dei conditoris agnitionem populus quasi infans eveheretur, omissa doctrina de cœlestium spiritduum formatione, quæ captum ejus longe superatura videbatur, & quam satis ei fuit obscure per nomina Cœli & cœlorum exercitus quasi per transennam ostendi. Consentit Calvinus, qui Comment. in Genes. cap. 1. verf. 14. Tenendum est illud, Mosen non acute philosophari de occultis mysteriis, sed referre quæ etiam rudibus nota sunt, & posita in vulgari usu. Et ad v. 16. Moses populariter scripsit, quæ sine DOCTRINA & LITERIS omnes idiotæ COMMUNI SENSU percipiunt; & paulo post. Nec Moses sane ab eo studio (puta Astronomico) retrahere nos voluit, cùm omisit, quæ sunt artis propria, sed quia non minus indoctis & rudibus, quàm doctis ordinarium erat Magister, non aliter partes suas potuit implere, quam si se demitteret ad crassam ejus rationem. Si de rebus vulgò ignotis locutus foret, causari potuerant Idiotæ altiora hæc esse capta suo. Denique cum hic spiritus Dei promiscuam omnibus scholam aperiat, non mirum est si ea maxime deligat, quæ possunt ab omnibus intelligi.
units.tr: { } Catchword: a chapter suffices, but nearly all the later chapters of Exodus, from 25 to 40 inclusive, except 32, 33 and 34, aim at this: that the construction of the tabernacle and the administration of the Levitical worship are explained fully in all their parts. The whole of Genesis is taken up with describing the fates of the Church from the beginning of the world down to his own times; the remaining four books of Moses are added to it, which are wholly occupied with forming and describing the Israelite Church. The case is similar with the other sacred writers. Whence it can be plain even to a blind man that Physics or Philosophy is not to be sought in Holy Scripture. If God had wished a book to be devoted to this matter, then, with so fine an occasion given by the description of the works of Creation, these things, especially as Moses was taught in these sacred matters, ought to have been explained. Paraeus agrees with my view on Genesis chapter 1 verse 1, already cited above in chapter 4 article 35. When he inquires why Moses did not expressly mention the creation of the Angels, he rejects the reasons given by others and says: The explanation of Chrysostom in his second homily on Genesis, which Basil also touches on in his first homily on the Hexaemeron, is simpler: that Moses adapted his history to the Jews' capacity. For they were earthly men, wise only in sensible things. Therefore Moses chose to set out openly only the description of God's sensible works, by whose contemplation and perception the people, like infants, might be raised to the understanding of higher things and to the knowledge of the invisible God the Creator himself. The doctrine of the formation of the heavenly spirits was omitted, since it seemed to surpass their grasp by far, and it was enough for them that it was shown to them obscurely, as through a chink, by the names of Heaven and the host of heaven. Calvin agrees, who in his Commentary on Genesis chapter 1 verse 14 says: It must be held that Moses does not philosophize sharply about hidden mysteries, but relates what is known even to the unlearned and is in common use. And on verse 16: Moses wrote in a popular way, setting out what all unlearned people perceive by COMMON SENSE without DOCTRINE and LETTERS; and a little later: Certainly Moses did not wish to draw us away from that study (namely astronomy) when he left out what is proper to the art; but because the teacher was no less ordinary for the untaught and rude than for the learned, he could not fulfil his part otherwise than by stooping to their crude reasoning. If he had spoken of things commonly unknown, the unlearned could have complained that these things were beyond their grasp. Finally, since this school of the Spirit of God is open in common to all, it is no wonder if it chooses above all those things which can be understood by all.

units.la: LXV. Exc. 1. M. p. 244. Negatur minor, quam refutarunt Zanchius, Vallesius, Danæus & alii, nec illi tantum, sed & ipsa sacra pagina Gen. 1. Psal. VIII. Item IX. Item CIV. &c. liber Jobi &c. diserte huic commento reclamant.
units.tr: LXV. Exception 1, M. p. 244. The minor premise is denied, which Zanchius, Vallesius, Danaeus and others have refuted; and not only they, but the sacred page itself, Genesis 1, Psalm 8, likewise Psalm 9, likewise Psalm 104, etc., the book of Job, etc., expressly cries out against this fiction.

units.la: Resp. Ego vero ostendi, ea quæ Vallesius & Danæus habent ex scriptura de rebus naturalibus, non esse talia quæ Physicam cognitionem generare possint, atque similis ratio est Zanchii & aliorum. De interiori natura rerum naturalium, an ex scriptura possit haberi talis rerum naturalium cognitio, quæ scientifica queat dici quæritur? quod nego. Afferant vero adversarii legitimas demonstrationes ex scriptura, quibus hæc vel illa proprietas & operatio rerum naturalium ex proximis causis demonstretur, & victores eos prædicabimus. Quin Gen. I. Psal. VIII. & alibi mentio fiat rerum naturarum nos non negamus, sed de scientifica & philosophica est quæstio.
units.tr: Reply: I have indeed shown that what Vallesius and Danaeus draw from Scripture about natural things is not of such a kind as can generate Physical knowledge, and Zanchius and others argue in a similar way. The question is whether from Scripture a knowledge of natural things can be had of their inner nature, such as might be called scientific. I deny it. But if our opponents bring forward legitimate demonstrations from Scripture by which this or that property and operation of natural things is demonstrated from their proximate causes, we shall proclaim them victors. Indeed, we do not deny that mention is made of natural things in Genesis 1, Psalm 8 and elsewhere; but the question concerns what is scientific and philosophical.

units.la: Ut autem causæ redderentur (à M. p. 245. & seq.) brevitatis, quare à Mose præcipuæ rerum naturalium species tantum tractentur, non erat opus, cum manifestum sit ita breviter tractari, ut tantum illæ species recenseantur & referantur ad causam primam, earum vero interioris constitutionis nulla fiat mentio. Itaque non scientifice res naturales tractantur, quod est illud de quo hic quæritur. Chrysostomum & Calvinum habeo consentientes, qui statuunt expresse, Deum se ruditati Judæorum attemperasse, non subtiliter disseruisse, sed retulisse ea quæ rudibus etiam nota sunt, (quibus verbis notitia communis significatur). Per quam observationem nostram cadunt & aliæ objectiones (confer si placet M p. 245 & 246.)
units.tr: But as for the reasons given (from M. p. 245 and following) why Moses treats only the chief kinds of natural things briefly, there was no need for them, since it is manifest that they are treated so briefly that only those kinds are enumerated and referred to the first cause, and no mention is made of their inner constitution. Thus natural things are not treated scientifically, and that is what is at issue here. I have Chrysostom and Calvin agreeing with me, who expressly hold that God adapted himself to the rudeness of the Jews, not that he discoursed subtly, but that he related those things which are known even to the unlearned (by which words common knowledge is signified). By this observation of ours the other objections also fall (please compare M. pp. 245 and 246).

units.la: LXVI. Exc. 2. Danæi, simpliciter quidem Moses, sed vere; nude, sed recte: populariter sed sincere tradit, quæ sunt nobis de mundo, ejus partibus præcipuis, rerum causis & effectis credenda & tenenda & docenda inter homines. Ingenue etiam fateor, ad nostri sensum captum Mosen se attemperasse, nego tamen quod illi ajunt, propterea ad rei veritatem illum nec collimasse nec attendisse; fuit enim illi propositum facile, nude & vere illa scribere.
units.tr: LXVI. Exception 2, of Danaeus: Moses indeed speaks simply, but truly; plainly, but rightly; popularly, but sincerely. He hands down what we must believe, hold and teach among men about the world, its chief parts, and the causes and effects of things. I frankly admit too that Moses adapted himself to our capacity of understanding; yet I deny what they say, that for this reason he neither aimed at nor attended to the truth of the matter. For it was easy for him to write those things plainly, simply and truly.

units.la: Resp. Facilis est ad illa responsio. Nam 1. quod dicit, sincere tradidisse, quæ sunt nobis de mundo, ejus partibus præcipuis, rerum causis & effectis credenda &c. admittimus, sed inde colligimus, quia de præcipuis: Ergo non de omnibus. Et quia de rerum causis externis tantum, nempe de Deo agit: E. non de interiori earum formatione, textura & constitutione; adeoque quærenda in scriptura rerum omnium causa Prima, Universalis & Remota, sed non ideo causa Secunda, Particularis & Proxima omnium rerum naturalium proprietatum & effectuum; Atque ita manet nostrum Argumentum firmum & immotum. 2. Et nos concedimus, Mosen ad rei veritatem generalem collimasse, per formulas præjudiciis & sensuum apparentiis innitentes ab ipso usurpatas, sed negamus, omnibus & singulis verbis speciale quid, quale homines præjudiciis occupati talibus verbis significarent, fuisse testatum. Vide infra specialiter dicenda de formulis scripturæ, quas adhibet, cum de rebus naturalibus loquitur.
units.tr: Reply: The answer to this is easy. For, first, when he says that he sincerely handed down what we must believe, hold and teach about the world, its chief parts, and the causes and effects of things, we admit this, but we conclude from it that it is about the chief things, and therefore not about all things. And since he treats only of external causes, namely God, therefore not of their inner formation, structure and constitution. Hence the First, Universal and Remote cause of all things is to be sought in Scripture, but not on that account the Second, Particular and Proximate cause of all the properties and effects of natural things. And so our argument remains firm and unshaken. Second, we concede that Moses aimed at the general truth of the matter, relying on the forms of speech used by himself, which rest on prejudices and appearances to the senses; but we deny that in every single word there was testified something special, such as men occupied with prejudices would signify by such words. See below what is to be said specifically about the forms of Scripture which he uses when he speaks of natural things.

units.la: LXVII. Inst. 1. M. p. 247. Si concedis, Moßen de mundo & præcipuis ejus partibus &c. egisse, qua fronte ergo supra dixisti, eum nihil consignasse ad rem Philosophicam spectans. quo pacto negaveris, ex præcipuis (quales sunt Essentiales) mundi partibus, ex præcipuis rerum causis, præcipuis earum effectis Physicam aliquam essentialiter totam concinnari posse ?
units.tr: LXVII. Objection 1, M. p. 247. If you concede that Moses treated of the world and its chief parts, etc., then with what face did you say above that he recorded nothing bearing on a philosophical matter? By what means could you deny that from the chief parts of the world (such as the essential ones), from the chief causes of things, and from their chief effects, some Physics could be essentially put together in full?

units.la: Resp. Nihil consignavit Moses ad rem Philosophicam præcisè quatenus talem, oppositè ad notitiam vulgarem, spectans, qui tantum effecta refert, & Primam atque Universalem causam, non vero interiorem naturam & proprietates scientificè explicavit & demonstravit. 2. Præcipuæ mundi partes (de quibus agit scriptura) sunt Cœlum & Terra, & præcipua rerum Causa est Deus; At quoniam hæ sunt partes & causæ nimis generales, cum in Physica requiratur proximarum causarum & specialium partium explicatio, recte dicitur, ex his Physicam concinnari non posse. Nec, præcipua tradi (eo sensu quo concessi) in scriptura, sufficit ad Physicam cognitionem inde deducendam, quia ea tradi oportebat, quæ scientiam generare queant.
units.tr: Reply: Moses wrote nothing that bears on natural philosophy strictly as such, as opposed to common knowledge; he only reports effects and explains the First and Universal Cause, but does not explain and demonstrate scientifically the inner nature and properties of things. 2. The principal parts of the world (which Scripture treats) are heaven and earth, and the principal cause of things is God. But since these are parts and causes that are far too general, whereas physics requires an explanation of proximate causes and particular parts, it is rightly said that physics cannot be built from these. Nor is it enough, for deriving physical knowledge from them, that the principal things (in the sense I conceded) are taught in Scripture, because it would have had to teach those things which can generate knowledge.

units.la: LXVIII. Inst. 2. (M. p. 248.) At Moses agit de omnium rerum materia, quæ est causa rei interna, item multarum rerum formas tradit. E. non tantum de causis rerum externis tractat.
units.tr: LXVIII. Objection 2 (M. p. 248). But Moses treats of the matter of all things, which is the internal cause of a thing; he also hands down the forms of many things. Therefore he does not treat only of external causes of things.

units.la: Resp. Non sufficit generalis materiæ cognitio omnium rerum, sed requiritur specialis cujusque corporis materia, atque ad demonstrationes Physicas, & inde ortam scientiam (de quâ agitur) opus est cognitione causarum efficientium proximarum. 2. Mirum est, quod si Moses tradat multas rerum formas, hactenus Scholastici professi sint, se nullius rei formam substantialem nosse, præterquam solius hominis, & quod hic nulla nobis forma substantialis ex Mose monstretur.
units.tr: Reply: A general knowledge of the matter of all things is not sufficient; what is required is the specific matter of each body, and for physical demonstrations, and the science that arises from them (which is the point at issue), knowledge of the proximate efficient causes is needed. 2. It is remarkable that, if Moses hands down many forms of things, the Scholastics have hitherto professed that they know the substantial form of nothing except man alone, and that no substantial form of any other thing is shown to us from Moses.

units.la: LXIX. Inst. 3. M. p. 248. Non sequitur, si Moses tantum tractat de omnium rerum causa prima externa, Universali, remota &c. E. non est quærenda in tota Scriptura causa rerum secunda particularis & proxima.
units.tr: LXIX. Objection 3 (M. p. 248). It does not follow that, if Moses treats only of the external, universal, remote first cause of all things, therefore the secondary, particular and proximate cause of things is not to be sought in the whole of Scripture.

units.la: Resp. 1. Argumentum meum tale est: Si Deus voluisset Physicam scientiam in Scripturis tradi, curasset eam procul dubio à Mose & Daniele, quos singulariter ea sapientia instruxerat, designari; At neuter ex his eam habet. Non Moses, quod hic demonstratum. Nec Daniel, quod mox probabitur. Ergo. Cui argumento, si quid respondendum, negandæ sunt Prop. Maj. ejusque probatio retorquenda, & dein afferendi alii scriptoscriptores sacri, atque ex iis demonstrationes Physicæ assignandæ.
units.tr: Reply: 1. My argument is this: If God had wished physical science to be handed down in the Scriptures, he would without doubt have arranged for it to be designated through Moses and Daniel, whom he had endowed with that wisdom in a special way; but neither of them has it. Not Moses, which has been demonstrated here; nor Daniel, which will be shown presently. Therefore... If anything is to be answered to this argument, the major premise must be denied and its proof turned back, and then other sacred writers must be brought forward, and physical demonstrations assigned from them.

units.la: 2. Non nego, quod Moses & Prophetæ subsequentes Judæos in artibus ingenuis instruxerint, verùm quod hoc in Scripturâ fecerint pernego.
units.tr: 2. I do not deny that Moses and the later Prophets instructed the Jews in the liberal arts; but that they did this in Scripture I flatly deny.

units.la: LXX. Inst. 4. M. p. 249. Philosophus ipse omnium rerum naturalium omnes proprietates, omnium effectuum omnes causæ non explicuit, E. inique hoc à scriptura exigitur.
units.tr: LXX. Objection 4 (M. p. 249). The philosopher himself did not explain all the properties of all natural things nor all the causes of all effects; therefore it is unjust to demand this of Scripture.

units.la: Resp. Philosophus Principia scripsit rerum naturalium eaque fundamenta, ex quibus rerum variarum interior natura e. g. magnetis, ignis, vitri &c. ab ipso scientificè explicata, pluresque alii effectus possunt similiter explicari. Inde nomine Physicæ ejus tractatus rectè potest venire, licet obstante vi majori tractatum de homine, de plantis &c. non potuerit absolvere. Ac in Scriptura talis scientifica explicatio non habetur, nec ab ea exigitur, ab iis qui statuunt, non esse hunc ejus scopum, ut instruat in cognitione scientifica rerum naturalium: sed ab adversa parte convenienter suis principiis non tantum exigenda, sed etiam ostendenda.
units.tr: Reply: The philosopher wrote the principles of natural things and those foundations from which the inner nature of various things, e.g. the magnet, fire, glass, etc., was scientifically explained by him, and several other effects can similarly be explained. Hence his treatise can rightly bear the name Physics, although, being overcome by greater difficulty, he could not complete the treatise on man, on plants, etc. But in Scripture such a scientific explanation is not found, nor is it demanded of it, by those who maintain that its purpose is not to instruct in the scientific knowledge of natural things; rather, it should not only be demanded but also shown by the opposing side, in keeping with its own principles.

units.la: LXXI. Patet 2. Minoris Propositionis præcedentis argumenti veritas ex Daniele, de quo legimus Dan. I. 17. quod Deus illi dederit notitiam & intelligentiam in omnibus litteris & sapientia, & v. 4. quod fuerit institutus literis & lingua Chaldæorum. Noluit tamen is in libro Prophetiæ suæ istius sapientiæ Chaldaicæ, quæ in cognitione Philosophiæ præcipuam partem constitebat, specimina edere, neque de rerum naturalium interiori Constitutione & Essentia differere, ut offenderet, hæc ex disciplina humana non divina hauriri.
units.tr: LXXI. The truth of the minor premise of the preceding argument is clear from Daniel, of whom we read (Dan. 1:17) that God gave him knowledge and understanding in all letters and wisdom, and (v. 4) that he was instructed in letters and the language of the Chaldeans. Yet he was unwilling, in the book of his Prophecy, to set out specimens of that Chaldean wisdom, which constituted the chief part of knowledge of philosophy, nor to discourse on the inner constitution and essence of natural things, lest he give offence by implying that these things are drawn from human and not divine learning.

units.la: LXXII. Exc. 1. M. p. 251. Nullam esse in hoc argumento consequentiam: non enim sequi: Daniel in Philosophia naturali egregie exercitatus noluit specimen ejus in libello Prophetiæ suæ extare: E. Spiritus Sanctus noluit quicquam res Philosophicas spectans in tota Scriptura exstare.
units.tr: LXXII. Objection 1 (M. p. 251). There is no consequence in this argument: for it does not follow that, because Daniel, thoroughly trained in natural philosophy, was unwilling for a specimen of it to exist in the little book of his Prophecy, therefore the Holy Spirit was unwilling for anything bearing on philosophical matters to exist in the whole of Scripture.

units.la: Resp. Hoc non est meum argumentum, ut patet ex articulo 64. & 69. cujus etiam consequentia per rationes articulo 64. est stabilita.
units.tr: Reply: This is not my argument, as is clear from article 64 and 69, whose consequence is also established by the reasons given in article 64.

units.la: LXXIII. Exc. 2. M. p. 249, 251. Moßis & Danielis erat specialis ratio: Moses noluit hoc agere, quia hæc non convenie bant ruditati Judæorum servitiis Ægyptiacis usque adeo emancipatorum, ut rerum naturalium & Philosophicarum contemplationi vacare plane non potuerint. p. 246, 249. Daniel ne scilicet ansam præberet Judæis pauxillum illud tempus, quod exercitiis fidei & pietatis, inter quæ meditatio verbi divini concedebatur, speculationibus philosophicis impendendi. p. 251.
units.tr: LXXIII. Objection 2 (M. p. 249, 251). Moses and Daniel had a special reason: Moses was unwilling to do this, because these things did not suit the rudeness of the Jews, so thoroughly emancipated from Egyptian servitude that they could not at all devote themselves to the contemplation of natural and philosophical things. (p. 246, 249.) Daniel, namely, so as not to give the Jews an occasion of spending that little time, which was granted to the exercises of faith and piety, among which meditation on the divine Word was included, on philosophical speculations. (p. 251.)

units.la: Resp. Quasi vero in deserto per integros annos quadraginta non potuissent rerum Philosophicarum contemplationi incumbere, quando non amplius servitute Ægyptiaca distinebantur, si Moses voluisset eos in Pentateucho de rebus Philosophicis informare. 2. si Jobi & Psalmorum meditatio, in quibus adversarius vult Philosophica contineri, non avocavit Judæos ab exercitiis fidei & pietatis. E etiamsi Deus à Daniele scribi philosophica voluisset, non tamen per ea fuisset Judæos ab istis exercitiis avocaturus.
units.tr: Reply: As if indeed in the desert, for a full forty years, they could not have applied themselves to the contemplation of philosophical things, when they were no longer held back by Egyptian servitude, if Moses had wished to inform them about philosophical matters in the Pentateuch. 2. If the meditation on Job and the Psalms, in which the adversary wants philosophical matters to be contained, did not call the Jews away from the exercises of faith and piety, then even if God had wished philosophical matters to be written by Daniel, he would not have called the Jews away from those exercises through them.

units.la: LXXIV. Exc. 3. H. p. 298. Illa quæ Moses & Daniel naturalia suis scriptis inseruerunt, non tantum Ægyptiaca & Chaldaica fuerunt institutionis, sed divini quoque spiritus.
units.tr: LXXIV. Objection 3 (H. p. 298). Those natural things which Moses and Daniel inserted in their writings were not only of Egyptian and Chaldean instruction, but also of the divine Spirit.

units.la: Resp. Ego vero non nego, quod si fuissent Moses, Daniel &c. de rebus naturalibus scripturi, ex immediatâ Inspiratione fuissent acturi, quamvis Chaldaicam sapientiam haberent cognitam, eodem modo, quo ea, quæ Apostoli ipsi viderant de Christo, ita Deus libris Evangelistarum inseri curavit, ut infallibiliter & ex dictamine Spiritus Sancti ea retulerint; sed nego, quod in eorum libris Philosophica rerum naturalium explicatio reperiatur.
units.tr: Reply: Indeed I do not deny that, if Moses, Daniel, etc. had been going to write about natural things, they would have treated them from immediate Inspiration, although they had known Chaldean wisdom; just as God arranged that those things which the Apostles themselves had seen concerning Christ should be inserted into the books of the Evangelists, so that they related them infallibly and from the dictation of the Holy Spirit. But I deny that a philosophical explanation of natural things is to be found in their books.

units.la: CAPUT VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: Quintum Argumentum ab amissione eorum, quæ Salomon de rebus naturalibus consignaverat, cum vindiciis.
units.tr: The fifth argument, from the loss of what Solomon wrote about natural things, with its defence.

units.la: LXXV. Mosen itaque & Danielem, ut sapientiæ suæ Philosophicæ specimina in sacris literis ederent, Deum noluisse vidimus. At quid de Salomone dicemus, quem Scriptura à sapientiâ præ omnibus hominibus 1 Reg. commendat? Hic vero ne quidem voluit Deus, ut ea quæ de rebus naturalibus disseruerat, proculdubio egregia & rerum naturam accuratius explicantia, quàm ab aliis factum fuerat, conservarentur, sed ea intercidere est passus. Ita enim legimus 1 Reg. iv. 33. Locutus est etiam de plantis, à cedro quæ in Libano usque ad hyssopum, quæ prodit à pariete: denique locutus est de jumentis, & de volucribus, & de reptilibus, & de piscibus. Nec tamen vel vestigium eorum invenitur, cum contrà Providentia Dei in conservandis iis, quæ ad salutem nobis sunt necessaria, ubivis elucet. Nonne ergo hoc facto tacitè quasi Deus significare voluit, naturæ lumine nos in harum rerum indagatione contentos esse debere, & frustra agerc agere, si naturas rerum ex scriptura cognoscere velimus, cum ea, quae de his optime nos potuisse instruxisse, Deus permiserit interire. Unde tale argumentum in forma potest constitui: Si Deus voluisset Physicam scientiam in sacris literis tradere, tum proculdubio conservaturus fuisset praecipua, quae ad eam fecerunt, qualia Salomonis fuerunt, vel saltem ea alibi fuisset suppleturus. At hoc non fecit: E. Mss. quoniam qui vult finem vult etiam media ad finem imprimis facientia.
units.tr: LXXV. We have seen that God was unwilling for Moses and Daniel to publish specimens of their philosophical wisdom in the sacred writings. But what shall we say of Solomon, whom Scripture, 1 Reg., commends for wisdom above all men? Here God was not even willing that what Solomon had set out about natural things, doubtless excellent and explaining the nature of things more accurately than others had done, should be preserved; instead he allowed them to perish. For we read at 1 Reg. iv. 33: He spoke also of plants, from the cedar that is in Lebanon even unto the hyssop that springeth out of the wall: he spake also of beasts, and of fowl, and of creeping things, and of fishes. Yet not even a trace of them is found, whereas God's providence in preserving what is necessary for our salvation shines out everywhere. Does not God, by this act, seem to signal in a tacit way that we ought to be content with the light of nature in investigating these things, and that it is vain to labour to know the natures of things from Scripture, since God has allowed to perish those writings which could have best instructed us about them? Hence the argument can be framed in form thus: If God had wished to deliver natural science in the sacred writings, he would doubtless have preserved the chief works bearing on it, such as those of Solomon, or at least would have supplied them elsewhere. But he has not done this. Therefore (he did not wish to deliver it). For whoever wills the end also wills the means most conducive to the end.

units.la: LXXVI. Exc. 1. (M. p. 252.) Deus passus est Salomonis de rebus naturalibus scripta interire, quia judicavit reliqua sufficere ad scopum suum.
units.tr: LXXVI. Objection 1. (M. p. 252.) God allowed Solomon's writings on natural things to perish, because he judged the remainder sufficient for his purpose.

units.la: Resp. Haec quae legimus de rebus naturalibus in sacris literis, omnino sufficiunt ad scopum Dei, nimirum ut per ea ad coelestia nos manuducat, quod etiam sufficienter fit per talem earum cognitionem, qualis communiter ab hominibus, communibus mediis cognoscendi haberi potest. At si scientificam institutionem sibi pro scopo propositam habuisset, nego sufficturam ea fuisse, nec dubito, quin ea quae ad hunc scopum apprime faciebant (qualia Salomonis fuisse crediderim) Deus fuisset conservaturus.
units.tr: Answer. What we read about natural things in the sacred writings is entirely sufficient for God's purpose, namely, to lead us through them to heavenly things. This is done sufficiently by such knowledge of them as men can commonly have by ordinary means of knowing. But if God had set before himself the aim of a scientific instruction, I deny that those writings would have sufficed, and I do not doubt that God would have preserved those things which were especially conducive to this aim (such as, I believe, Solomon's were).

units.la: LXXVII. Exc. 2. (M. p. 253.) Quidni eadem Consequentia ratione dicamus leges administratas quondam Republicae Judaicae ex Scriptura addisci non posse nec debere, quoniam librum Recti, cujus ha proculdubio principale fuerunt argumentum, intercidere est passus, Ios. X. Eodem modo quis dicet, res politicas et bellicas in Republ. Judaica quondam gestas non debere addisci ex Scriptura, quod librum bellorum Domini, de quo Num. XXI. 14. interire Deus passus sit. Resp. Si ad meae consequentiae rationem attendas, videbis te per eam de Republica Judaica inferre non posse; Qui enim defectus ex amissione Libri Recti (si tamen non sit intelligendus liber Josuae) et Libri bellorum Domini est exortus, abunde compensatus fuit, per substitutionem aliorum ejus generis et argumenti: at negamus in Scripturis suppletum fuisse, qui ex amissione rerum Philosophicarum scientifice tractatarum a Salomone, obtigit defectus. LXXVIII. Exc. 3. M. p. 253. Similiter colligi debere Physicam prorsus non posse disci ex Aristotele, quia multi ejus libri perierunt. Resp. At ego hic colligo, Deum noluisse Physicam scientiam in sacris literis traderi, quoniam ea, quae Scriptores sacri, de ea conscripserant, intercidere est passus, neque in Canonem, qui semper debuit in Ecclesia conservari, retulit, cujus argumentationis ratio superius est redita. Non vero simpliciter ex eo, quod quidam libri Physici a Scriptoribus ptoribus sacris profecti interierint, colligo, in reliquis nihil Physici reperiri.
units.tr: LXXVII. Objection 2. (M. p. 253.) Why should we not with the same reasoning say that the laws once administered in the Jewish commonwealth cannot and ought not to be learned from Scripture, since the book of the Upright, whose chief subject these doubtless were, has been allowed to perish (Josh. x.)? In the same way someone will say that the political and military affairs once conducted in the Jewish commonwealth ought not to be learned from Scripture, since God has allowed the book of the Wars of the Lord, mentioned at Num. xxi. 14, to perish. Answer. If you attend to the reasoning of my argument, you will see that you cannot infer from it anything about the Jewish commonwealth. For the defect that arose from the loss of the Book of the Upright (unless this is to be understood as the book of Joshua) and of the Book of the Wars of the Lord was fully made good by the substitution of others of the same kind and subject. But we deny that anything was supplied in Scripture for the defect that arose from the loss of the philosophical matters treated scientifically by Solomon. LXXVIII. Objection 3. (M. p. 253.) Similarly it should be inferred that physics cannot be learned at all from Aristotle, because many of his books have perished. Answer. But I do not infer here that God was unwilling for natural science to be delivered in the sacred writings because some physical books by the sacred writers have perished; I infer it because God allowed to perish what the sacred writers had written about it, and did not include it in the canon, which ought always to have been preserved in the Church. The reasoning of this argument has been given above. But I do not infer simply from the fact that certain physical books by the sacred writers have perished that nothing physical is to be found in the rest.

units.la: LXXIX. Exc. 4. M. p. 253. Isti Libri non pertinuerunt ad Canonem Scriptura sacra, Ergo ex illorum interitu nulla ratione potest concludi, Deum voluisse ut à Scripturis rerum Philosophicarum cognitio peteretur.
units.tr: LXXIX. Objection 4. (M. p. 253.) Those books did not belong to the canon of Holy Scripture. Therefore from their loss no conclusion can be drawn that God wished knowledge of philosophical matters to be sought from the Scriptures.

units.la: Resp. Hoc nihil ad rem facit: potuisset enim proculdubio Deus istos libros conservare, & Canonicam auctoritatem iis conferre, quod quia non fecit, nec defectuum hunc compensavit, omnino concludendum est, ejus sententiam non fuisse Physicam scientiam in sacris literis tradere.
units.tr: Answer. This has nothing to do with the matter. For God could doubtless have preserved those books and conferred canonical authority on them. Since he did not do so, and did not make up for this defect, it must be wholly concluded that his purpose was not to deliver natural science in the sacred writings.

units.la: LXXX. Exc. 5. H. p. 13. Absurdum est dicere, Deum libros illos naturales Salomonis interire passum esse, propterea quia non necessarii vel inutiles nobis adsalutem. Cur enim, inquit, nobis usui est scire genealogiam Esau: mensurationem terræ Palestinæ in tribus duodecim? Quid ad salutem est, Reges post Salomonem, eorumque vitam & res gestas scire? &c.
units.tr: LXXX. Objection 5. (H. p. 13.) It is absurd to say that God allowed those natural books of Solomon to perish because they are not necessary or are useless for our salvation. For why, it is said, is it of use to us to know the genealogy of Esau, or the measurement of the land of Palestine among the twelve tribes? What does it matter to salvation to know the kings after Solomon, and their lives and deeds? etc.

units.la: Resp. Ego vero non autumo, Deum ea omnia scripta virorum θεοπνεύστων, concessisse interire, quæ non præcisè ad salutem nobis sunt necessaria; sed tantum statuo, Deum etsi nihil permiserit perire scriptorum, de rebus quæ nobis ad salutem sunt scitu necessariæ, tamen quedam concessisse ut interirent, scripta aliàs utilia, quæ non ad salutem necessaria dogmata complexa fuerunt, quæ eo ipso, quia perierunt, censeo non fuisse canonica.
units.tr: Answer. I do not claim that God permitted all those writings of the divinely inspired men to perish which are not strictly necessary for our salvation. I maintain only this: although God allowed nothing to perish of the writings concerning those things which we must know for salvation, he nevertheless allowed some writings otherwise useful, which contained doctrines not necessary for salvation, to perish; and I judge that these, for the very reason that they have perished, were not canonical.

units.la: CAPUT VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: Sextum Argumentum, quo ostenditur, ea quæ oppositæ sententiæ Patroni ex sacris literis asserunt specimina doctrinæ Philosophicæ, talia non esse.
units.tr: The Sixth Argument, by which it is shown that the things which the advocates of the opposing view claim from the sacred letters as specimens of philosophical doctrine are not such.

units.la: LXXXI. Argumentum sextum. Sed ex ipsa re tandem desumamus Specimina quædam eorum, quæ contrariæ sententiæ Patroni de rerum Physicarum natura in Scriptura se putant reperire. Et Vallesius quidem, ubi Scriptura mentionem aliquam rerum naturalium injicit, occasionem inde sumit de rebus naturalibus differendi, & quidem ex lumine naturali, adeo ut scripturâ vix aliter utatur ac catalogo rerum naturalium, uti patebit ei, qui eum voluerit conferre. Similem fere viam insistit Danæus, quamvis videatur ulterius procedere, & velle probationem desumere ex scriptura de rerum naturalium constitutione & causis. Sed ipse modus procedendi, qua ab illo servatur, satis ostendit, cum rectam viam non institisse, quæ ad Physicæ cognitionem ducat. Nam primò quidem concedit ipse, multarum rerum scripturam ne quidem meminisse: Cometarum, inquit, Lampadum, Doliorum, Chasmatum cœli, Caprarum saltantium, & aliorum ejusmodi meteororum igneorum, quæ nonnunquam in hac expansione (quæ sub cœlo Lunæ est) apparent, nusquam meminit scriptura, quibus & multa alia connecti possent, de variis animalium, plantarum speciebus &c. quæ inter res naturales sunt referenda, & suam habent singularem naturam: Ergò saltem non potest haberi ex scriptura perfecta rerum naturalium cognitio. Et nisi ipse ille Danæus subsidium à ratione & scriptis Philosophicis petiisset, multò pauciora potuisset dicere de rebus naturalibus quam dixit, & multa, quæ ex locis scripturæ obscuris elicere voluit, elicere non tentasset, nisi antea Philosophiæ cognitione imbutus fuisset. Quænam etiam ex scripturis causæ dari possunt Iridis & aliorum meteororum, præter eas de quibus ipsa experientia testatur? Quam causam scriptura assignat albedinis nivis? Ubi demonstratur Tonitrus causa proxima? quidde causâ fluxus & refluxus maris, Salsedinis ejusdem? Quænam causa recensetur stellarum scintillationis? Quid de Lunæ & Solis Eclipsi è scriptura depromi potest, ad causarum intelligentiam faciens, ut taceam sexcenta alia.
units.tr: LXXXI. Sixth argument. But let us at last take from the matter itself some specimens of those things which the advocates of the contrary view think they find in Scripture concerning the nature of physical things. Vallesius, indeed, whenever Scripture introduces some mention of natural things, takes from that an occasion to discourse about natural things, and that from the natural light, so that he hardly uses Scripture otherwise than as a catalogue of natural things, as will be plain to anyone who cares to compare him. Danaeus follows a nearly similar path, although he seems to proceed further and to wish to draw proof from Scripture concerning the constitution and causes of natural things. But the very method of proceeding that he observes shows well enough that he has not taken the right road that leads to knowledge of physics. For first, he himself concedes that Scripture does not even mention many things: "Of comets, torches, barrels, openings of the sky, leaping goats, and other such fiery meteors which sometimes appear in this expanse (which is beneath the sphere of the moon), Scripture nowhere makes mention," to which many other things could be added, concerning the various species of animals, plants, etc., which are to be counted among natural things and have their own singular nature. Therefore at least a complete knowledge of natural things cannot be had from Scripture. And unless Danaeus himself had sought help from reason and philosophical writings, he could have said far fewer things about natural things than he has said, and he would not have attempted to draw out many things which he wished to elicit from obscure passages of Scripture, unless he had first been imbued with the knowledge of philosophy. What causes of the rainbow and of other meteors can be given from the Scriptures, besides those which experience itself attests? What cause does Scripture assign for the whiteness of snow? Where is the proximate cause of thunder demonstrated? What about the cause of the flow and ebb of the sea, and of its saltness? What cause is recounted for the twinkling of the stars? What can be drawn from Scripture about the eclipse of the Moon and the Sun, serving to the understanding of causes? I say nothing of six hundred other things.

units.la: LXXXII. 2. De principio quidem rerum omnium externo, Deo, sive omnium rerum Causa Efficiente Primâ & Universali Scripturam agere non diffitemur, & eâtenus ejus cognitionem prodesse nos met ipsi asserimus, sed non potest Danæus nec quisquam alius, ex scripturâ ostendere, Materiam primam & Formas substantiales, vel Elementa esse rerum omnium Principia, ex quibus componantur & in quæ resolvantur, quæ tamen pro principiis vulgò habentur, alia etiam veriora principia rerum interna à Scripturâ doceri non videmus.
units.tr: LXXXII. 2. We do not deny that Scripture treats of the external principle of all things, God, that is, the first efficient and universal cause of all things, and we ourselves assert that knowledge of him is useful to us to that extent. But neither Danaeus nor anyone else can show from Scripture that prime matter and substantial forms, or the elements, are the principles of all things, out of which they are composed and into which they are resolved, which nevertheless are commonly held to be principles. Nor do we see that Scripture teaches other truer internal principles of things.

units.la: LXXXIII. 2. Multò minus ex scripturâ possunt proferre demonstrationes, quomodo, vel ex vulgaribus illis Peripateticorum Principiis proprietates & effectus rerum naturalium oriantur, vel ex aliis Principiis solidioribus.
units.tr: LXXXIII. 2. Much less can they bring forward from Scripture demonstrations of how the properties and effects of natural things arise, either from those common principles of the Peripatetics or from other, more solid principles.

units.la: LXXXIV. 4. Crassè admodum Danæus philosophatur, ubi se ex scripturis philosophari putat. Sic Trast. I. f. 8. Ex Eph. 5. 13. Lucem definit ab effectu, Lux est quæ omnia manifestat: at ipse hanc definitionem corrigit postea, vel hoc facto suo testatus, eam non fuisse accuratam. Sed nec prior nec posterior definitio multum facit ad Lucis naturam explicandam, de quâ Reusnerus Opt. lib. I. th. 13. conqueritur, eam esse valde abstrusam, idem ferens de colorum natura judicium, ejusdem lib. th. 36. Videtur coloris natura non plus esse comprehensibilis intellectui, quam lux fuit ipsa, causaque tam obscura & difficiles, quam est color ipse promtu adspectuque manifestus. Nec tamen de colorum natura quicquam Scriptura docet. Ita Tract. 2.cap.9. Aërem fere in nihilum redigit, nitens (uti putat) scriptura, aut saltem non pro corpore distincto ab Aqua & Terra habet. Plura similia annotare poterit, cui ejus Physicam perlegere vacabit.
units.tr: LXXXIV. 4. Danaeus philosophizes very crudely when he thinks he is philosophizing from the Scriptures. Thus in Tract. I, p. 8, from Eph. 5:13, he defines light from its effect: "Light is that which makes all things manifest." But he himself corrects this definition afterwards, thereby attesting by this very act that it was not accurate. Yet neither the earlier nor the later definition does much to explain the nature of light, concerning which Reusnerus, Opt. book I, thesis 13, complains that it is very obscure, giving the same judgment on the nature of colours, in the same book, thesis 36: "The nature of colour seems no more comprehensible to the intellect than light itself was, and its cause is as obscure and difficult as colour itself is plain to sight and manifest." Nor does Scripture teach anything about the nature of colours. So in Tract. 2, chap. 9, he reduces air almost to nothing, striving (as he thinks) from Scripture, or at least does not hold it to be a body distinct from water and earth. Anyone who has the leisure to read through his physics may note many more things of this kind.

units.la: LXXXV. 5. Multa, quae ex scriptura probare tentat, talia sunt, ut à quovis, vulgari tantum notitiâ praedito, cognosci possint per experientiam. Ita quando probari vult, nubes elevari ex terra & mari ex Jer. iv. 13. Ecce tanquam nubes ascendit, & 1 Reg. xviii. 44. Fuitque septima vice, ut diceret, ecce nubes parva sicut vola hominis ascendit a mari, nihil praestat, nisi quod à quovis per experientiam cognosci potest: nam quod nubes ita elevantur ex aqua ad oculum patere potest, uti ex posteriori loco apparet.
units.tr: LXXXV. 5. Many things which he tries to prove from Scripture are of such a kind that they can be known by experience by anyone endowed with merely common knowledge. Thus when he wishes to prove that clouds are raised from the earth and from the sea, from Jer. 4:13, "Behold, he shall come up as clouds," and 1 Kings 18:44, "And it came to pass at the seventh time that he said, Behold, there ariseth a little cloud out of the sea, like a man's hand," he achieves nothing except what can be known by anyone through experience: for that clouds are thus raised from water can be plain to the eye, as appears from the latter passage.

units.la: LXXXVI. 6. Multa ex scripturis elicere conatur, quae revera non sequuntur; ex. gr. quando ex locis obscuris & metaphoricis Jobi vult aliquid educere. Sic ex c. xxxvi. 32. vult probare, ex pugna duarum nubium oriri fulmen, qui valde ambiguus est locus, & plane Metaphoricus. Verba ita habent: Manibus obtegit lucem, & interdicit ipsi propter intercedentem. Ex cap. xxxviii. 38. ut perfusio fit fermentanda terra, ut conglutinentur glebae, probare conatur ex pulvere terrae lapides generari, cum nihil aliud indicetur, quam pluvia cadente pulverem terrae in glebas colligi, quemadmodum consideranti patet, & Belgae etiam interpretantur. Similiter ex Jerem. xxxi. 35. Sic ait Jehova, qui disponit Solem ad lucem interdiu, statuta Lunae & stellarum ad lucem noctu, & Jesch. xxx. 26. Et erit lux ipsa Lunae sicut Lux Solis, Lux autem Solis erit septupla, ut lux septem dierum, vult probare stellas habere lucem insitam; quod quamvis de stellis fixis sit verum, quibus tamen fidiculis ex locis istis extorqueri possit, videre quidem nequeo. Eodem in loco, np. Tract. 4. cap. 27. ex Ezech. xxxii. 7. demonstrare conatur, Lunam habere lucem insitam propriam. Verba Ezechielis sic sonant: Et operiam, cum extinguam te, coelos, et stellas eorum: Solem nube operiam, Luna non faciet, ut splendeat lux sua. Forte ex eo id sequi putat, quia dicitur lux sua: at etiam lux in speculo & ab ea reflexa dicitur lux speculi, & à Terra reflexa dicitur Lux terrae: Ergo & Lux Lunae dici potest, propter modificationem, quam accipit à Luna, quia ab ea reflectitur in terram. Psalm.
units.tr: LXXXVI. 6. He tries to elicit many things from the Scriptures which in truth do not follow from them, for example when from obscure and metaphorical passages of Job he wishes to draw something out. Thus from ch. 36:32 he wishes to prove that lightning arises from the clash of two clouds, which is a very ambiguous and plainly metaphorical passage. The words are: "He covereth his hands with the light, and commandeth it to strike the mark." From ch. 38:38, "when the dust runneth into a mass, and the clods cleave fast together," he tries to prove that stones are generated from the dust of the earth, whereas nothing else is indicated than that, when rain falls, the dust of the earth is gathered into clods, as anyone considering it will see, and the Belgians also interpret it so.
