Similarly from Jer. 31:35, "Thus saith the LORD, who giveth the sun for a light by day, and the ordinances of the moon and the stars for a light by night," and Isa. 30:26, "Moreover the light of the moon shall be as the light of the sun, and the light of the sun shall be sevenfold, as the light of seven days," he wishes to prove that the stars have an innate light. Although this is true of the fixed stars, I cannot see by what slender threads it can be extorted from these passages. In the same place, namely Tract. 4, chap. 27, from Ezek. 32:7, he tries to demonstrate that the Moon has its own innate light. The words of Ezekiel sound thus: "And I will cover the heavens, when I shall extinguish thee, and make their stars dark; I will cover the sun with a cloud, and the moon shall not give her light." Perhaps he thinks this follows because it is said "her light"; but light in a mirror, and light reflected from it, is also called the light of the mirror, and light reflected from the earth is called the light of the earth. Therefore the light of the Moon may also be so called, on account of the modification it receives from the Moon, because it is reflected from her onto the earth. Psalm

units.la: CXLVIII. S. Laudate Dominum ignis & grando, nix & exhalatio, ventus tur-bineus, efficiens verbum ejus. Ex his vult educere divisionem vaporum, qua alii sint calidiores & siccriores, alii frigidiores & humidiores. Sed mens Psalmistae non est, ibi species vaporum enumerare, sed tantum quaedam ex meteoris nominare, quae ad laudem Dei homines incitare debeant. Plura recensere defatigor, & facile posset ostendi, vix quicquam à Danaeo esse de natura rei alicujus naturalis ex Scriptura demonstratum. Cui otium est, attente perlegat, & assensum mihi praebebit.
units.tr: CXLVIII. 8. "Praise the LORD, fire and hail, snow and vapours, stormy wind fulfilling his word." From these words he wishes to draw a division of vapours, by which some are hotter and drier, others colder and moister. But the mind of the Psalmist is not to enumerate the kinds of vapours there, but only to name certain meteors which ought to stir men to praise God. I grow weary of listing more, and it could easily be shown that scarcely anything has been demonstrated by Danaeus from Scripture about the nature of any natural thing. Whoever has leisure may read it attentively, and he will give me his assent.

units.la: LXXXVII. Ex hisce omnibus patet, se ipsos valde fallere, qui ne- scio quem honorem scripturae se deferre putant, dum rerum naturalium explicationem exinde deducere conantur.
units.tr: LXXXVII. From all of this it is plain that those greatly deceive themselves who think they pay some honour to Scripture, I know not what kind, when they try to derive from it an explanation of natural things.

units.la: Et hac quidem parte mecum sentit Verulamius, ut argumentum aliquod, ab auctoritate desumtum, ad hominem corollarii loco addam. Is Novo Organo aph. 65. Huic vanitati (qua nempe Theologia Philosophiae admiscetur) nonnulli ex modernis summa levitate ita indulserunt, ut in primo capitulo Genesceos & in libro Job & aliis Scripturis Sacrum Philosophiam naturalem fundare conati sint: inter viva quarentes mortua. Et de Augmentis scientiarum lib. 9. In interpretandi scripturam modo soluto duo interveniunt excessus. Alter ejusmodi in scripturis praesupponit perfectionem, ut & omnis Philosophia ex earum fontibus peti debeat, ac si Philosophia alia quavis res profana esset & Ethnica. Haec intempe-ries in Schola Paracelsi praecipue, nec non apud alios invaluit: Initia autem ejus à Rabbinis & Cabbalistis defluxerunt. Verum istiusmodi homines non id asse-quuntur, quod volunt. Neque enim honorem, ut putant, Scripturis deferunt, sed easdem potius deprimunt & polluunt. Coelum enim materiatum & Terram, qui in verbo Dei quasiverit (de quo dictum est, Coelum & Terra pertransibunt, verbum autem meum non pertransibit:) is sane transitoria inter aeterna temere persequitur. Quemadmodum enim Theologiam in Philosophia quaerere, perinde est, ac si vivos quaeras inter mortuos. Ita è contra Philosophiam in Theologia quarere non aliud est quam mortuos quaerere inter vivos. Huic conjungo Neufvillium, Medicum, dum viveret, & Philosophum Clarissimum, qui ita in Physiologiae suae, sive Physicae generalis praefatione loquitur. Hanc ob causam nonnulli, Scriptura Sacra divinitus nobis revelata auctoritate potissi-mum de rebus naturalibus certi aliquid definiendum esse contendunt: inter quos praecipue est Lambertus Danaeus, qui Physicam Christianam ex sola fere Scriptura collectam & deductam (nempe ex opinione sua, at quam foeliciter, à nobis hactenus ostensum) concinnavit. Idem statuunt Otto Casmannus in Prologomenis Cosmopaeja & Uranographia Christiana praemissis: Conradus Aslacus lib. 1. Physica Mosaica cap. 1. & alii. Et paulo post: Certum ta-men men est, ejusmodi (scilicet de rebus naturalibus) pauca admodum esse, neque eo modo tradita, uti eadem à naturali Philosopho scientia certa atque evidenti comprehendi debent, & constat Scripturam Sacram nobis longe alio fine à Deo esse traditam, videlicet, ut nos de voluntate Divina nostraque salute per Christum obtinendâ, erudiat.
units.tr: In this part I agree with Verulam, and I shall add to the man an argument from his authority, by way of a corollary. In Novum Organum, aphorism 65, he says: "Some of the moderns have indulged this vanity (namely, the mingling of Theology with Philosophy) with such great levity that they have tried to found a sacred natural philosophy on the first chapter of Genesis, on the book of Job and on other Scriptures, seeking the living among the dead." And in the De Augmentis Scientiarum, book 9: "Two excesses arise in the manner of interpreting Scripture that I have just described. The first presupposes in the Scriptures such perfection that all philosophy must be sought from their sources, as though philosophy were any other profane and heathen thing. This intemperance has prevailed chiefly in the school of Paracelsus, and among others as well; but its beginnings flowed from the rabbis and the Cabbalists. Yet such men do not attain what they want. For they do not pay honour to the Scriptures, as they think, but rather debase and defile them. For whoever seeks a material heaven and earth in the Word of God (of which it is said: heaven and earth will pass away, but my word will not pass away) rashly pursues things transitory among things eternal. Just as to seek Theology in Philosophy is as if you sought the living among the dead, so, conversely, to seek Philosophy in Theology is nothing other than to seek the dead among the living." I join to this Neufville, the physician, while he lived, and a most distinguished philosopher, who speaks thus in the preface to his Physiology, or General Physics: "For this reason some contend that, above all, something certain about natural things must be defined on the authority of Holy Scripture divinely revealed to us; among them is especially Lambert Danaeus, who put together a Christian Physics gathered and derived almost solely from Scripture" (namely, according to his opinion, but how happily, we have so far shown otherwise) "Otto Casmann likewise holds this in the Prolegomena prefixed to his Cosmopoeia and Christian Uranography; so does Conrad Aslacus in book 1, chapter 1 of his Mosaic Physics, and others." And a little later: "It is certain, however, that such matters (namely concerning natural things) are very few, and not handed down in such a way as they must be grasped by the natural philosopher with certain and evident knowledge; and it is established that Holy Scripture was given by God to us for a quite different end, namely, to instruct us about the Divine will and about obtaining our salvation through Christ."

units.la: LXXXVIII. Exc. 1. (M. p. 255.)
units.tr: LXXXVIII. Excerpt 1 (M. p. 255.)

units.la: Ex hoc sequte confici posse, Physicam integraliter totam, id est omnibus numeris, membris, particulis consummatam ex Scripturâ non posse constrüi, at quid hoc ad nos, qui afferimus Physicam saltem aliquam essentialiter totam, quae mundum, ejus praecipuas partes, causas, rerum effectus, praecipuas itidem affectiones explicet.
units.tr: From this it follows that Physics cannot be constructed from Scripture in its entirety, that is, complete in all its parts, members and particulars. But what does this matter to us, who maintain that at least some Physics, essentially complete, may be set out, one that explains the world, its chief parts, the causes and effects of things, and their chief affections?

units.la: Resp. 1. Hoc vero contra Danaeum imprimis facit, qui eo sensu Physicam ex Sacris Scripturis voluit petere, quo alii integram Physicam, ut Timplerus, Magyrus in Systemata redduxerunt. An vero hoc contra te esset facturum, nec ne, somniare non potui, qui tuam sententiam nunquam cognoveram. Si ex Scriptura Scientia Physica, vel cognitio rerum naturalium Philosophica, etiamsi non omnium, saltem praecipuarum posset hauriri, adducendi loci Scripturae essent, in quibus rerum naturalium causae proximae atque interior earum constitutio explicetur, quod fieri non potest.
units.tr: Reply 1. This tells especially against Danaeus, who wished to derive Physics from the Holy Scriptures in the same sense in which others, such as Timplerus and Magyrus, have reduced integral Physics to a system. Whether this would tell against you or not, I could not guess, since I had never known your opinion. If physical science, or philosophical knowledge of natural things, even if not of all of them but at least of the chief ones, could be drawn from Scripture, then passages of Scripture would have to be cited in which the proximate causes of natural things and their inner constitution are explained; and this cannot be done.

units.la: LXXXIX. Exc. 2. M. p. 256.
units.tr: LXXXIX. Excerpt 2. M. p. 256.

units.la: At ubinam tradit vester Philosophus causam caloris in igne, proximam & propriam in sole? humectationis in Luna, frigoris in nive? cedo cur Sol lucem habet insitam, reliquae stellae secundum vos nequaquam. Millenas ejusmodi quaestiones Philosophis vestris proponere vel rusticus nullo negotio posset.
units.tr: But where does your philosopher teach the cause of heat in fire, the proximate and proper cause in the sun? The cause of moisture in the moon, of cold in snow? Tell me why the sun has light inherent in it, and the other stars, according to you, by no means do. A rustic could put to your philosophers thousands of such questions without any trouble.

units.la: Resp. Hic homo nec legitimè potest (quod rusticum posse ait) quaestiones proponere Philosophis, & ostendit quam parum sit versatus in Cartesio, contra quem tamen audet insurgere. Ignis & Caloris natura sufficienter explicatur à Philosopho Princ. IV. art. 29. & seqq. item 80. ad 117, nec Calor ab Igne differt, sed est ejusdem essentiae: Calor enim est motus ille particularum primi elementi, qui Ignem constituit. Eadem ratio Solis, quem Cartesius Part. III. aliique flammâ esse demonstrârunt. Itaq; non debet quaeri, quaenam sit Caloris in Igne vel Sole causa, si de externâ id accipias, quemadmodum nec quaeritur, quae sit causa humanitatis in homine &c. Humectatio in Luna nulla est, sed à Luna procedit, estque in rebus humectatis, ac multis modis tùm à Lunâ tum ab aliis causis potest produci. Frigus sive quies particularum in Nive facile explicatur. Vide Meteor. cap. 1. art. 7. Quare Sol & Stellae lucem habeant insitam, Planetae non item (qui hic cum stellis confunduntur) explicat art. 55. seqq. Pp. p. III. Millenas ejusmodi quæstiones explicuit vel saltem sufficientia præbuit fundamenta, quarum ne una quidem ex vulgaribus Scholasticorum Principiis, Materia & Forma, Qualitat. & similibus potuit hactenus explanari.
units.tr: Reply. This man cannot rightly put questions to the philosophers (as he says a rustic can), and he shows how little he is versed in Descartes, against whom he nevertheless dares to rise up. The nature of fire and heat is sufficiently explained by the philosopher in Principles IV, art. 29 ff., also 80 to 117; nor does heat differ from fire but is of the same essence: for heat is that motion of the particles of the first element which constitutes fire. The same reasoning applies to the sun, which Descartes in Part III and others have shown to be a flame. Therefore it should not be asked what the cause of heat in fire or the sun is, if you take it of an external cause, just as one does not ask what the cause of humanity in man is, etc. There is no moisture in the moon; it proceeds from the moon, and it is in moist things, and it can be produced in many ways, both by the moon and by other causes. The cold, or rest of the particles, in snow is easily explained; see Meteorology, chapter 1, art. 7. Why the sun and the stars have light inherent in them, but the planets do not (which are here confused with the stars), he explains in art. 55 ff., Pp. p. III. He has explained thousands of such questions, or at least has provided sufficient foundations for them, not one of which could so far be explained from the common principles of the Scholastics, matter and form, qualities and the like.

units.la: XC. Status autem controversiæ, si recte expendatur (nimirum quæri, An scientifica cognitio rerum naturalium, etsi non omnium saltem multarum, ex quibus corpus Physicum possit confici ex S. Scriptura hauriri possit, quod nego,) concident ea, quæ porro habet M. p. 256. Reliqua quæ reperiuntur p. 257. sunt meri coccyfmi, & falsæ hypotheses, mihi attributæ, quasi ego statuam, Deum de rebus naturalibus loquentem non esse veracem, Scripturam erroribus vulgi scatere, Cælum esse magnitudine immensum, (si hoc intelligas absolute) cum dicam illud definiri non posse &c. quæ ampliori refutatione non habent opus. Cum itaque Institutio Philosophica de rebus naturalibus ad fines Scripturæ non tantum non requiratur, sed etiam expresse à Scripturæ instituto removeatur, cum Deus ab iis scriptoribus sacris, qui Philosophica rerum cognitione pollebant, quales Moses & Daniel, nihil eam concernens voluerit conscribi, & quæ à Salomone scripta sunt, intercidere fuerit passus, iis alibi non suppletis, cumque tandem specimina rerum naturalium ex Scriptura adducta, ad Philosophicam earum cognitionem non spectent (prout demonstratum) quis porro dubitabit, quin Philosophica rerum naturalium cognitio non ex sacris literis, sed ex lumine naturæ debeat hauriri?
units.tr: XC. The state of the controversy, if rightly weighed (namely, the question whether scientific knowledge of natural things, even if not of all of them but at least of many out of which a physical body can be made, can be drawn from Holy Scripture, which I deny), coincides with what he goes on to state on p. 256. The rest that is found on p. 257 are mere jeers and false hypotheses attributed to me, as though I held that God, speaking about natural things, is not truthful, that Scripture abounds in the errors of the common people, that the heaven is immense in magnitude (if you understand this absolutely), since I say that it cannot be defined, etc. These do not need a longer refutation. Since, then, a philosophical account of natural things is not only not required for the ends of Scripture, but is even expressly removed from Scripture's purpose, since God did not wish the sacred writers who possessed philosophical knowledge of things, such as Moses and Daniel, to write anything concerning it, and allowed what Solomon wrote to perish, with nothing supplied elsewhere; and since, finally, the examples of natural things adduced from Scripture do not bear on their philosophical knowledge (as has been shown), who will further doubt that philosophical knowledge of natural things must be drawn not from the sacred letters but from the light of nature?

units.la: CAPUT VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: Objectiones in contrarium adductæ solvuntur & refutantur.
units.tr: The objections brought against us are answered and refuted.

units.la: XCI. Initium facimus à seqq. in quibus mixtæ sunt exceptiones ad nostra argumenta objectionibus, ad eaque conjuncta breviter respondebimus. (L. p. 189.) 1. Præcipuum Theologiæ opus esse, Dei cognoscendi & colendi, hominisque ad æternitatem beata vita perducendi, præcepta tradere non negamus. 2. Sed & licere Spiritui Sancto uti argumentis, à rebus vel natura vel artis petitis, ad hominem persuadendum, convincendum, nisi velimus cum ratione insanire, fateamur. 3. Deinde cæli & terra machina, & utriusque operationes ad Dei notitiam fine suo deducunt: quare qua à se, eadem & ex se instrumenta notitiæ divinæ persuadendæ generare apta sunt. 4. Quid quod ancilla ministerio uti nemo prohibetur: Quare nec Philosophia Theologia. 5. Vel oblectamenti gratia, & lectoris in sacrorum librorum evolutione detinendi, permissum est Spiritui Sancto in res in rerum natura contentas excurrere. 6. Tempore, quo Moses & qui mox eum secuti scripsere, nullos apud Hebraos Philosophiam professos verisimile est. Voluit ergo Deus populum suum, ne crassa rerum caligine premeretur, de quibusdam natura occultis in sacris literis admonere, ceteris experintia & senum denunciationi relictis. 7. Nemo Homero, Poëta & rerum bellicarum scriptori vitio vertit, Geographia & aliarum artium fines invasisse. Et hoc antiquissimo operum, quodque Deum ipsum auctorem habet, non licebit, quod Poëtae fabularum conditori licuit? Et paucis interjectis. Age vero in rerum naturalium judicio ferendo, Deus homines opinioni sua reliquerit, nec calamum scribentium hac in parte direxerit. Nullius ergo judicii fuisse Salomonem statuendum est, cui Deus discertis verbis sapientia omnes homines excedentis testimonium ultro dedit? nec id in populo tantum judicando: sed & in natura obscuritate evolvenda, 1 Reg. IV. Quid Davidem? Quid Propbetas? fungosne fuisse & rerum humanarum aut naturalium omni cognitione exutos arbitramur? Praesertim otio abundantes & ingenii sagacitate propter situm locorum & coeli temperiem, vel Graecis & Italis, ne dum Germanis & Gallis longe praecellentes. Suam igitur vel imperitiam vel judicii iniquitatem produnt, qui ejus affrictione ne quidem sacra maculare erubescunt.
units.tr: XCI. We begin with the following, in which exceptions to our arguments are mixed in with objections. We will reply briefly to these as they are joined together. (L. p. 189.) 1. We do not deny that the chief purpose of Theology is to hand down precepts for knowing and worshipping God and for bringing man to a blessed life for eternity. 2. But we must also grant that the Holy Spirit may use arguments drawn from things, whether from nature or from art, to persuade and convince man, unless we wish to rave against reason. 3. Again, the machinery of heaven and earth, and their workings, lead to the knowledge of God, which is their end. Therefore the instruments that these things can produce for persuading us of the divine knowledge are fit to be drawn from them. 4. What then? No one is forbidden to make use of a handmaid's service. Therefore neither is Philosophy the handmaid of Theology. 5. For the sake of delight, and to hold the reader while he unfolds the sacred books, the Holy Spirit has been allowed to range over things contained in the nature of things. 6. At the time when Moses and those who soon followed him wrote, it is probable that there were no Hebrews who professed Philosophy. God therefore wished to warn his people, lest they be oppressed by the thick darkness of things, about certain hidden matters of nature in the sacred books, leaving the rest to experience and to the teaching of the elders. 7. No one blames Homer, a poet and a writer of warfare, for invading the territory of geography and other arts. And will it not be allowed in this, the most ancient of works, and one that has God himself as its author, what was allowed to the inventor of fables? And after a few words intervene: Come now, in passing judgment on natural things, God has left men to their own opinion and has not guided the pen of the writers in this part. Must we therefore hold that Solomon had no judgment, to whom God of his own accord gave testimony in plain words of a wisdom surpassing all men? And not only in judging the people, but also in unfolding the obscurity of nature, 1 Kings 4. What of David? What of the Prophets? Shall we think they were mere blockheads, stripped of all knowledge of human or natural things? Especially since they abounded in leisure, and in keenness of mind, owing to the situation of their places and the temperature of the sky, they far excelled even the Greeks and Italians, let alone the Germans and Gauls. They therefore betray their own ignorance or the unfairness of their judgment, who are not ashamed to stain even the sacred writings by rubbing this against them.

units.la: XCII. Resp. 1.
units.tr: XCII. Answer to 1.

units.la: Circa primum inter nos convenit. 2. nec negamus secundum: quaeritur tantum, an in talibus argumentis a natura desumtis necesse sit, ut Sp. S. innitatur subtilioribus, & accuratioribus effatis Philosophicis, a veritate rerum naturalium accurata & interiori earum constitutione derivatis, an vero sufficiat ea superstruere vulgari earum cognitioni? nos posterius asserimus & suo loco probavimus. 3. concedimus itidem, per res naturales, per Coeli Terrae machinam nos deduci ad Dei notitiam, sed vicissim dicimus, ad id sufficere cognitionem vulgarem, qualis per sensus a quovis haberi potest, quamvis non negemus, quo penitius natura rerum habetur cognita, eo plura argumenta suppeditari ad potentiae, sapientiae & bonitatis divinae cognitionem. 4. Nec quartum nobis repugnat. Utatur Theologia Philosophia ut ancilla, sed propterea non opus est, ut vel Scriptura Philosophiam doceat, vel de rebus naturalibus accurate loquatur. Sed Theologus, qui ex Scriptura fundamenta fidei suae hausit, ex Philosophia Objectionibus Adversariorum, quas specie rationis obvolvunt satisfaciat, utatur ea ad Illustrandum & similia. quamvis propter usum quem praebet Theologiae non magis Philosophia Theologiae ancilla vocari debet, quam vel Medicina vel Jurisprudentia, vel etiam Theologia, quia Philosophiæ inservit & utilis est, nomine ancillæ insigniri meretur. Quòd si huic modo argumentandi semel aperiatur fenestra, poteris facile hoc nomine quævis tui cerebri figmenta Scripturis tribuere. Exemplo inter alia sit Oleaster, qui quoniam voluit ex Gen. vii. 11. aquas supercœlestes probare, hoc modo contrarium sententium argumenta conatus est diluere: Taxandi sunt, qui potius Sacram Scripturam Philosophiæ regulis subdere, quàm, ut magis decet, Philosophiam tanquam ancillam illi deservire. 5. Non quæritur quid permissum sit Spiritui Sancto, sed quid ipse sapienter facere velit. Suo loco vidimus ex celeberrimis Theologis, quod nolit rudioribus remoram injicere, per ista subtilia Philosophica, quæ non intelligant. Ergò nulla esset causa, quare potiorem haberet rationem doctorum, ut eos oblectet, quam rudiorum, ne eos turbet. 6. De ipso Mose superius vidimus, quod ille fuerit eruditus omni sapientiâ Ægyptiorum. Sed vir antiquitatis & historiarum, ut sibi videtur, peritissimus ex Josepho Antiquit. 1. cap. 3. discere potuisset, Sethi posteros duas columnas erexisse, alteram lapideam, alteram lateritiam, quibus artes à se inventas inscripserant. Item ex cap. 9. Abrahamum docuisse Ægyptios Astronomiam & Arithmeticam, & sic has artes primò à Chaldæis ad Ægyptios, ab his vero tandem ad Græcos traductas. Simile quid Josephum Ægyptiis præstitisse verisimile est, eumque esse, quem Diodorus Siculus Hermem vocat, id est, interpretem, quem tradit disciplinas apud Ægyptios artesque reperisse. Quod si vel solum Polydorum Virgilium inspexisset, ex eo lib. 1. cap. 16 discere potuisset, Philosophos Græcorum Philosophiam à Judæis accepisse, idque ab Eusebio in II. de præparatione Euangelicâ plenissimè demonstrari. Ex his igitur inter se collatis, quia Philosophia inter Sanctos Patriarchas vigucrit, à quibus Israëlitæ sunt orti, ita ut ab iis demum Ægyptii & per eos aliæ gentes acceperint, quia Græci Philosophi à Judæis acceperint, ipseque Moses in ea fuerit insignis, colligere debuisset, longè verisimilius esse, fuisse tempore Mosis eorumque, qui eum secuti sunt, apud Hebræos Philosophiam professos, quàm nullos tales fuisse. Et cum Deus æquè librum Naturæ & Lumen Naturæ hominibus istorum temporum ac nobis concessisset, præterea etiam insignes doctores inter eos excitasset, non opus fuisse, ut arcana Philosophica in sacris traderet, quæ ad alium scopum dirigebantur, sed sufficere ipsis debuisse, quod media prædicta largitus fuisset. 7. Ad septimum annoto, neminem hoc Deo vitio vertere, si voluisset Philosophiam in sacris literis tradere, sed tùm procul dubio fuisse eam demonstratustraturum longe evidentius per causas rerum naturalium interiores quàm ab ullo homine fuit factum. Deinde Salomoni sapientiam non negamus, sed ab eo descriptam sapientiam non exstare amplius, ostendimus. Nec etiam Davidem & Prophetas destitutos rerum naturalium cognitione fuisse asserimus, sed illam sapientiam suam totam in sacras literas retulisse negamus. Ex quibus lectori Judicioso patebit, uti imperitiam suam vel judicii iniquitatem prodant, num illi, qui ipsâ re edocti, Scripturam de rebus naturalibus loquentem formulis uti receptis, veritatem non nudam sed ad homines relatam exprimentibus, contendunt, neque Physicam ex scriptura petendam concedant, num adversarius, qui sine ulla ratione eos arguit macularum sacris literis affricarum.
units.tr: On the first point we agree among ourselves. 2. Nor do we deny the second. The only question is whether, in such arguments drawn from nature, the Holy Spirit must necessarily rest on the more subtle and precise philosophical statements, derived from the accurate truth of natural things and their inner constitution, or whether it is enough to build on their common knowledge. We maintain the latter, and have proved it in its place. 3. We likewise grant that we are led through natural things, through the machinery of heaven and earth, to the knowledge of God. But in turn we say that the common knowledge, such as anyone can have through the senses, is sufficient for this, although we do not deny that the more deeply the nature of things is known, the more arguments are supplied for knowing the power, wisdom and goodness of God. 4. Nor does our position oppose the fourth point. Theology may use Philosophy as a handmaid, but for that reason it is not necessary that either Scripture should teach Philosophy or speak accurately about natural things. Rather, the theologian, who has drawn the foundations of his faith from Scripture, may satisfy himself from Philosophy against the objections of adversaries, which they wrap up in an appearance of reason, and may use it for illustration and the like. Yet, because of the use Philosophy offers to Theology, it should no more be called the handmaid of Theology than Medicine or Jurisprudence, or even Theology itself, which serves Philosophy and is useful to it, deserves to be marked with the name of handmaid. But if once a window is opened to this way of arguing, you could easily attribute to the Scriptures under this name any figments of your own brain. Let Oleaster serve as an example among others: because he wished to prove from Genesis 7:11 that there are waters above the heavens, he tried in this way to dissolve the arguments of the opposing opinion: Those are to be censured who subject Holy Scripture to the rules of Philosophy, rather than, as is more fitting, have Philosophy serve it as a handmaid. 5. The question is not what the Holy Spirit is permitted to do, but what he wisely wishes to do. We have seen in its place, from the most celebrated Theologians, that he is unwilling to place a hindrance before the simpler folk through those subtle philosophical matters which they do not understand. Therefore there would be no reason why he should give greater consideration to the learned, to delight them, than to the simpler folk, so as not to disturb them. 6. We saw above concerning Moses himself that he was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians. But a man who, as he himself thinks, was most expert in antiquity and in histories, could have learned from Josephus, Antiquities book 1, chapter 3, that the descendants of Seth set up two pillars, one of stone and one of brick, on which they had inscribed the arts they had invented. Likewise from chapter 9, that Abraham taught the Egyptians astronomy and arithmetic, and so these arts were first carried from the Chaldeans to the Egyptians, and from them at last to the Greeks. It is probable that Josephus did something similar for the Egyptians, and that he is the one whom Diodorus Siculus calls Hermes, that is, the interpreter, who is said to have discovered the disciplines and arts among the Egyptians. But if he had looked at Polydore Vergil alone, he could have learned from book 1, chapter 16, that the philosophers of the Greeks received their Philosophy from the Jews, and that Eusebius in the second book of the Preparation for the Gospel demonstrates this most fully. From these things, compared with one another, he ought to have concluded that, since Philosophy flourished among the holy Patriarchs, from whom the Israelites sprang, so that the Egyptians and through them other nations received it from them, and since the Greek philosophers received it from the Jews, and Moses himself was distinguished in it, it is much more probable that in the time of Moses and of those who followed him there were Hebrews who professed Philosophy, than that there were none such. And since God had equally granted to men of those times, as to us, the book of Nature and the Light of Nature, and had moreover raised up distinguished teachers among them, there was no need for him to hand down philosophical secrets in the sacred writings, which were directed to another purpose. Rather, it ought to have been enough for them that he had bestowed the aforesaid means. 7. As to the seventh point, I note that no one blames God for this, if he had wished to hand down Philosophy in the sacred writings. But then, without doubt, he would have demonstrated it far more evidently, through the inner causes of natural things, than any man has ever done. Further, we do not deny wisdom to Solomon, but we have shown that the wisdom written by him no longer exists. Nor do we assert that David and the Prophets were without knowledge of natural things, but we deny that they referred all their wisdom to the sacred writings. From these things it will be plain to the judicious reader how those who, having been taught by experience itself, contend that Scripture, when it speaks of natural things, uses the received forms of speech, expressing the truth not bare but as it relates to men, and who therefore do not concede that Physics is to be sought from Scripture, reveal their own ignorance or the unfairness of their judgment, while the adversary, who accuses them without any reason of staining the sacred writings, does the same.

units.la: XCIII.
units.tr: XCIII.

units.la: Sequuntur nunc aliæ Objectiones magis distinctæ & ab invicem separatæ. Prima est Danæi, qui Physicæ Christianæ cap. 3. contra hanc sententiam insurgit, quorum summa hunc redit: Qui est artifex mundi, omniumque in eo creaturarum, ille optimè omnium potest de eo loqui. Quis enim melius de opere suo loqui potest, quam ipse ejus artifex? Quis melius omnium rerum causas, momenta, effecta, existendi modos & tempora quæ fuerint, scit & novit, quam qui ipse eorum omnium est Auctor & perpetuus Administrator? At Deus est artifex mundi &c. Ergò ille potius audiendus, quam Philosophi etiam præstantissimo ingenio præditi, cum illi sæpe pugnantia & veritati contraria doceant & docuerint.
units.tr: Now follow other objections, more distinct and separate from one another. The first is that of Danaeus, who in chapter 3 of his Physica Christiana rises against this opinion. Its substance comes to this: He who is the maker of the world, and of all the creatures in it, can speak of it best of all. For who can speak better of his own work than its maker himself? Who knows and understands better the causes, the motions, the effects, the modes and times of existence of all things, than he who is himself the author and perpetual governor of them all? But God is the maker of the world, etc. Therefore he rather than the philosophers, even those endowed with the most outstanding talent, should be heard, since they often teach, and have taught, things contrary to one another and to the truth.

units.la: XCIV.
units.tr: XCIV.

units.la: Resp. 1. Absit ut omniscientiam Dei in dubium revocemus, è contrario certissimè persuasi, Deum non tantum harum rerum, quas ipse creavit, rationes habere perspectas, sed etiam omnium possibilium, quæ revera sunt infinita; sed non quæritur quid Deus cognoscat, sed tantum quid nobis voluerit in suo verbo revelare? non autem voluisse eum rerum naturalium interiorem naturam ibi explanare, jam ut reor satis superque demonstratum dedimus. 2. non præferimus Philosophos Deo, aut eorum philosophemata sacris oraculis, sed dicimus, cum qui scientiam Physicam acquirere allaborat, eam frustra ex verbo Dei petere, non ad hanc rem inspirato, neque accuratè & scientificè de rerum natura loquente, sed eam quærere debere per lumen Naturæ, quod Deus in hunc finem dedit: neque statuimus, debere hominem quorumvis Philosophorum sequi auctoritatem, cum scientiam intendamus acquirere, non fidem humanam, sed volumus sapientiæ studiosum attendere ad xoinàs ἐννοίας, ad notitias menti insitas, easque cum rebus ipsis conferre, atque ita vel proprio Marte aliquid inde educere, vel alios educentes & demonstrantes audire, quibus tamen assensum non debeat præbere , nisi id quod dixerint clarè demonstraverint.
units.tr: Reply. 1. Far be it from us to call the omniscience of God into doubt. On the contrary, we are most firmly persuaded that God has a perfect understanding not only of the reasons of those things which he himself created, but also of all possible things, which are in fact infinite. But the question is not what God knows, but only what he has been pleased to reveal to us in his Word. We have already given, as I think, sufficient and more than sufficient proof that he did not intend to explain there the inner nature of natural things. 2. We do not set the philosophers above God, nor their philosophical theories above the sacred oracles. We say that one who labours to acquire physical science seeks it in vain from the Word of God, which was not inspired for this purpose, and which does not speak accurately and scientifically about the nature of things; he ought rather to seek it by the light of nature, which God gave for this end. Nor do we hold that a man should follow the authority of any philosophers whatever when he intends to acquire knowledge, not human belief. Rather, we want the student of wisdom to attend to the common notions [κοιναὶ ἔννοιαι], the notions implanted in the mind, and to compare them with the things themselves; and so either to draw something from them by his own effort, or to hear others who draw and demonstrate conclusions, yet without giving assent to them, unless they have clearly demonstrated what they say.

units.la: XCV. Secunda Objectio à Danæo in eodem capite profertur, & in summam collecta huc redit: Heb. xi. 3. legimus : Per fidem intelligimus compactum fuisse mundum verbo Dei, Ergo fide intelligimus mundum atque creaturas, quæ sunt in mundo. Quod si fide : Ergo per Sacram Scripturam, nec enim fides sine illâ esse potest.
units.tr: XCV. The second objection is put forward by Danaeus in the same chapter, and gathered into a summary it comes to this: We read in Heb. 11:3: "By faith we understand that the world was framed by the word of God." Therefore by faith we understand the world and the creatures that are in the world. And if by faith, then by Sacred Scripture, for faith cannot exist without it.

units.la: XCVI. Resp. Plus concluditur, quàm fuit in præmissis. Concedimus libenter, nos fide intelligere, compactum fuisse mundum, id est, ex nihilo solo Dei nutu omnia fuisse creata. At anindeinferre licet? Ergo etiam fide intelligimus omnium rerum interiores naturas, causasque proximas quarumvis proprietatum & effectuum. Rerum itaque existentiam ex creatione cognoscimus, & res omnes ad Deum tanquam auctorem suum referimus, sed essentiam & naturæ interiorem constitutionem aliunde debemus cognoscere.
units.tr: XCVI. Reply. More is concluded than was contained in the premises. We gladly concede that by faith we understand that the world was framed, that is, that all things were created out of nothing by the mere will of God. But what does it follow from this? Therefore by faith we also understand the inner natures of all things, and the proximate causes of any properties and effects whatever? We therefore know the existence of things from creation, and we refer all things to God as their author; but we must learn their essence and inner constitution from elsewhere.

units.la: XCVII. Pergit idem Danæus tertio loco objicere : Moses ille qui Dei jussu & præcepto mundi hujus & originis rerum omnium præclaram illam & verè admirabilem historiam conscripsit, aut vanus erit aut mendax, si Physica cognitio Scripturâ Sacrâ non continetur. Quid enim aliud agit, quàm ut ortum rerum, earumque vires, naturas & effecta, id est Physicen, brevissime quidem, sed tamen verissime & ordine explicet ?
units.tr: XCVII. Danaeus goes on to object in a third place: That Moses, who by God's command and direction wrote that remarkable and truly admirable history of the origin of this world and of all things, would be either vain or lying, if physical knowledge were not contained in Sacred Scripture. For what else does he do than explain, very briefly indeed but yet most truly and in order, the origin of things, their powers, natures and effects, that is, physics?

units.la: XCVIII. Resp. 1. Quodnam Mosis fuerit institutum superius vidimus. 2. concedimus, ex Mose historiam Creationis esse petendam, ab eoque discendum, quæ nam sit omnium rerum Prima Causa & Universalis, & eâtenus Scripturam ad Physicæ cognitionem prodesse largimur, sed cum præter hæc multa alia, causæ nimirum particulares proprietatum omnium & effectuum, cognoscenda sint ei qui Physici nomen vult ferre, quorum explicatio in Scripturis non habetur, uti ostensum, illa certè aliunde, id est, ex lumine naturali sunt petenda. 3. Si Physicam in concreto sumas, pro compendio aliquo Physico, qualia multa habentur, in quo non continentur, nisi quidam rerum naturalium catalogus, cum paucis quibusdam descriptionibus potius quam definitionibus, quibus quædam etiam divisiones sint conjunctæ, possumus concedere, quod Moses Physicen explicet ordine : sed si Physica sumatur in abstracto, pro certâ & indubiâ scientiâ proprietatum & effectuum per causas proximas & immediatas, uti à nobis sumitur, & in hac quæstione sumi debet, negamus eam apud Mosen reperiri.
units.tr: XCVIII. Reply. 1. We have seen above what Moses' purpose was. 2. We concede that the history of Creation is to be sought from Moses, and that from him we are to learn what the first and universal cause of all things is; and so far we grant that Scripture serves for knowledge of physics. But since, besides these, many other things must be known by one who wishes to bear the name of physicist, namely the particular causes of all properties and effects, and their explanation is not found in the Scriptures, as has been shown, these must certainly be sought elsewhere, that is, from the natural light. 3. If you take physics in the concrete, for some physical compendium of the kind that are common, which contains nothing but a catalogue of natural things, with a few descriptions rather than definitions, joined with certain divisions, we may grant that Moses explains physics in order. But if physics is taken in the abstract, as a certain and indubitable science of properties and effects through proximate and immediate causes, as we take it, and as it must be taken in this question, we deny that it is found in Moses.

units.la: XCIX. Quarto loco profert dictum Prov. 8. cap. 22. & seq. ubi omnia per sapientiam Dei & condita esse, & postea per eundem, ut sunt condita dicuntur conservari.
units.tr: XCIX. Fourthly, he cites the passage of Prov. 8:22ff., where it is said that all things were made through the wisdom of God, and afterwards that, as they were made, they are preserved by the same wisdom.

units.la: Resp. Filium Dei, substantialem, sive essentialem Dei sapientiam æque nosse omnium rerum naturas ac Patrem, easque intime habere perspectas, nulli dubitamus. At eam in Scripturam sapientiam hanc retulisse, ineaque res naturales accuratissime explicasse, magnum est postulatum, quod nondum vidimus probatum.
units.tr: Reply. We do not doubt that the Son of God, the substantial or essential wisdom of God, knows the natures of all things just as well as the Father does, and has them most intimately before his eyes. But that this wisdom has been referred to Scripture, and that in it natural things are most accurately explained, is a great assumption which we have not yet seen proved.

units.la: C. Quinto opponit loca Apocrypha Ecclesiastici 42, 17. & lib Sapientia 7, 22. Resp. Sed in loco Eccles. non dicitur, quod Deus sanctos ex scriptura erudiverit de rebus naturalibus, sed tantum quod fecerit eos enarrare mirabilia sua, quod utique nobis non obest. In libro sap. vero docetur tantum, quod sapientiæ insit spiritus intelligens, sanctus &c. At quid hoc confirmet sententiam oppositam non apparet.
units.tr: C. Fifthly, he sets against us passages from the Apocrypha: Ecclesiasticus 42:17 and the book of Wisdom 7:22. Reply. In the passage of Ecclesiasticus it is not said that God taught the saints from Scripture about natural things, but only that he made them declare his wonderful works; which in no way harms us. In the book of Wisdom it is taught only that there is in wisdom an intelligent, holy spirit, etc. But how this confirms the opposite opinion does not appear.

units.la: CI. Tandem Sexto loco objicit authoritates Irenæi, Basilii, Ambrosii, Chrysostomi & Tertulliani. Sed Resp. breviter 1. nos quidem antehac usi fuimus auctoritate, sed non aliter ac argumento ad hominem, quod sciamus, illos cum quibus nobis est negotium auctoritate duci; sed quia ipsi net parum tribuimus auctoritati humanæ, cui videmus refragari lumen naturæ quod sequimur, argumentum tale apud nos non est magni ponderis. 2. Patres in citatis locis à Danæo docent, necessarium esse, ut ex scriptura Creationis cognitionem hauriamus, item ut ex illa cognoscamus causam mundi efficientem supremam ejusque finem ultimum: ostendunt itidem, mundum non ex ullâ præexistente materia esse creatum, sed non docent rerum naturalium cognitionem quoad causas internas, proximas, interioremque constitutionem & similia, adeoque Physicam scientiam ex Scriptura hauriri posse.
units.tr: CI. Finally, in the sixth place, he objects to the authorities of Irenaeus, Basil, Ambrose, Chrysostom and Tertullian. But the reply, briefly: 1. We indeed have used authority before, but only as an argument ad hominem, since we know that those with whom we have to do are led by authority; but because we ourselves attribute little to human authority, which we see is opposed by the natural light that we follow, such an argument carries little weight with us. 2. The Fathers in the passages cited by Danaeus teach that it is necessary to draw the knowledge of Creation from Scripture, and likewise that from it we know the supreme efficient cause of the world and its ultimate end. They also show that the world was created out of no pre-existing matter. But they do not teach the knowledge of natural things as to their internal and proximate causes, their inner constitution and the like; and therefore physical science cannot be drawn from Scripture.

units.la: CII. Aliæ nunc sequuntur Objectiones. Sit ergo Septima. Si Physica non est ex Scriptura petenda: E. nullus usus erit Physicæ in Theologia. Atqui est usus quidam, ut ferè omnes concedunt. E.
units.tr: CII. Other objections now follow. Let the seventh be this: If physics is not to be sought from Scripture, then there will be no use of physics in theology. But there is some use, as almost everyone concedes. Therefore...

units.la: CIII. Resp. 1. Majoris Connexio est nulla. Similiter enim possem inferre: si Physica non est petenda ex Ethica: E. Physicæ nullus est in Ethica usus, cum tamen cognitio subjecti Ethicæ, hominis ab ea informandi aliquatenus prærequiratur, uti sunt passiones quædam naturales. Etsi itaque Theologia Philosophiam non doceat, ejus tamen cognitionem præsupponit in aliquibus, saltem in generalibus: ex. gr. ut cognoscamus differentiam naturæ corporeæ & spiritualis &c. At potest Theologiæ cognitio consistere cum ignorantiâ circa particularia & deceptione sensus circa illa: ex. gr. Terræ motum sive delationem ignorare quis potest & tamen bonus esse Theologus. 2. non quidem est cognitio Physicæ necessaria ad τὸ esse: sed utilis ad τὸ bene esse: ita quis nomen Theologi obtinere nere potest, sed non Disputatoris subtilis ac accuratissimi in Theologicis, si omni Physicæ cognitione sit destitutus, quia hæc sæpe requiritur ad destruenda fundamenta adversariorum Physica abutentium. 3. à Scriptura ad Theologiam non licet argumentari: illa enim quid strictius est, hæc aliquid latius: nam in Theologia etiam reperias argumenta, saltem secundaria, præter scripturam ex ratione depromta: in Theologia invenies refutationes objectionum ex physica desumtarum, quo in casu Physicæ cognitio multum potest prodesse.
units.tr: CIII. Reply. 1. The connection of the major premise is null. For in the same way I could infer: if physics is not to be sought from ethics, then there is no use of physics in ethics; yet a knowledge of the subject of ethics, man, and of certain natural passions, by which he is to be formed in some measure, is presupposed. Thus, although theology does not teach philosophy, it nevertheless presupposes its knowledge in some matters, at least in general ones; for example, that we may know the difference between corporeal and spiritual nature, and so on. But a knowledge of theology can exist alongside ignorance of particulars and of the deception of the senses about them: for example, someone may be ignorant of the motion or movement of the earth and yet be a good theologian. 2. Knowledge of physics is not indeed necessary for existence [τὸ εἶναι], but it is useful for well-being [τὸ εὖ εἶναι]. Thus a man may obtain the name of theologian, but not that of a subtle and most accurate disputant in theological matters, if he is wholly destitute of all physical knowledge, since this is often required for overthrowing the foundations of adversaries who abuse physics. 3. One may not argue from Scripture to theology, for the former is something narrower, the latter something broader. For in theology you will find arguments, at least secondary ones, drawn from reason apart from Scripture; and in theology you will find refutations of objections taken from physics, in which case knowledge of physics can be of great service.

units.la: CIV. Objectionem Octavam ex Vallesio proferimus: Si nulla alia ratione certi aliquid haberi potest de rebus Physicis: E. id ex scriptura petendum: sed verum est prius, cum tot dissentientes Philosophorum reperiantur sententiæ: E.
units.tr: CIV. We set out the eighth objection, taken from Vallesius: If nothing else can be known with certainty about physical things, then it must be sought from Scripture, ergo. But the first claim is true, since so many conflicting opinions of philosophers are found; ergo.

units.la: Resp. Minorem non concedent Philosophi, qui ex Aristotele & Scholasticis, nescio quos thesauros colligi posse putant. Sed nos erimus liberaliores. Concedimus, si vulgari procedendi modo utamur, non innitentes certioribus Principiis, quam materiæ primæ, formis substantialibus, Qualitatibus Realibus, Auctoritati Aristotelis, Thomæ, Scoti & aliorum, vix quicquam certi posse reperiri; quod ipsa experientia docuit eos, qui non præjudiciis mentem habuerunt occupatam: at non itidem negandum, certi aliquid haberi posse, si via rectâ incedens & Principiis firmis innixus ad rerum naturalium cognitionem tendas, si studeas, ut habeas conceptus distinctos, confusos ejicias & reformes; si communibus notionibus recte attendendo iis consectaria superædifices, nihilque judices, nisi de quo clara perceptio præcesserit. Ita certi non aliquid, sed multum inventum esse accuratæ demonstrationes Cartesii loquuntur, & plura inveniri posse, si simili via procedas, non desperandum.
units.tr: Answer: The Philosophers will not grant the minor premise, since they think that a store of knowledge can be gathered from Aristotle and the Schoolmen. We, however, will be more generous. We grant that if we proceed in the common manner, relying on no surer principles than prime matter, substantial forms, real qualities, and the authority of Aristotle, Thomas, Scotus and others, scarcely anything certain can be found. Experience itself has taught this to those whose minds were not occupied by prejudices. Yet it must not likewise be denied that something certain can be had, if you proceed by a straight path, rest on firm principles, and strive toward knowledge of natural things: if you aim to have distinct concepts, and to cast out and reform confused ones; if, by rightly attending to common notions, you build consequences upon them, and judge nothing except what has been preceded by a clear perception. Thus the accurate demonstrations of Descartes declare that not something certain, but much, has been discovered, and that more can be found if you proceed by a similar way; we should not despair of this.

units.la: CV. Obj.Nona(B. p. 16.) Varia de rebus naturalibus aguntur in Psalmis & Iobo.
units.tr: CV. Ninth objection (B. p. 16.): Various things about natural things are discussed in the Psalms and in Job.

units.la: Resp. afferri oporteret aliquam demonstrationem proprie dictam & Philosophicè scientificam explicationem ex scriptura, cum de eâ quæstio exstat, non verò in generalibus hærendum, cum non negem multa naturalia incidenter in scriptura tradi, quatenus faciunt ad Dei sapientiam, bonitatem & potentiam agnoscendam & celebrandam, sed nego, ex illis cognitionem scientificam hauriri posse.
units.tr: Answer: Some proper demonstration and scientific explanation drawn from Scripture ought to be offered, since the question concerns exactly that; we should not linger over generalities. I do not deny that many natural matters are incidentally delivered in Scripture, insofar as they serve to acknowledge and celebrate the wisdom, goodness and power of God. But I deny that scientific knowledge can be drawn from them.

units.la: CVI. Objeƈt.Decima(H. p. 200.) Quicunque nos sua vere docet opera, ille rerum naturalium aliquarum nudam veritatem manifestare vult. Atqui Sp. Sc. &. Resp. Hæc mihi non contrariantur, cum quæstio non existat, An Sp. S. aliquam nudam veritatem rerum naturalium doceat, qualis etiam per communem notitiam haberi potest, sed an accuratam talemque, ex qua cognitio scientifica haberi possit. Videat Lector status Controversiæ constitutionem art. 30.
units.tr: CVI. Tenth objection (H. p. 200.): Whoever truly teaches us his works wishes to reveal the bare truth of certain natural things. But the Holy Spirit etc. Answer: These points do not oppose me, since the question is not whether the Holy Spirit teaches some bare truth of natural things, such as can also be had through common knowledge, but whether it teaches an accurate truth from which scientific knowledge can be had. Let the reader look at the statement of the state of the controversy, art. 30.

units.la: CVII. Obj. Undecima. (H. p. 200.)
units.tr: CVII. Eleventh objection. (H. p. 200.)

units.la: Quicunque de rebus naturalibus aliquando loquitur ex rei veritate, ille nudam quoque rerum naturalium veritatem manifestat: At Sp. S. secundum te aliquando loquitur ex rei veritate: E.
units.tr: Whoever at some time speaks about natural things in accordance with the truth of the matter also reveals the bare truth of natural things. But according to you the Holy Spirit at some time speaks in accordance with the truth of the matter; ergo.

units.la: Resp. Spiritum Sanctum uti aliquando talibus formulis, quæ nudam veritatem exprimunt, omnino dico, sed tum nuda illa veritas talis est, quæ per communem notitiam cognosci potest; sed quæstio est, An scriptura de rebus naturalibus talem veritatem manifestet, ex cujus cognitione scientia gignatur, quod nego.
units.tr: Answer: I altogether affirm that the Holy Spirit sometimes uses such formulas as express bare truth. But that bare truth is of the kind that can be known through common knowledge. The question is whether Scripture reveals in natural matters such a truth from whose knowledge a science may arise; this I deny.

units.la: CVIII. Obj. Duodecima (H. p. 202.)
units.tr: CVIII. Twelfth objection (H. p. 202.)

units.la: Nonne docuit Sp. S. motus Solis & Lunæ distinctionem, coordinationem, vicissitudinem, passiones &c.
units.tr: Did not the Holy Spirit teach the distinction, arrangement, alternation, passions etc. of the motions of the Sun and Moon?

units.la: Resp. Quicquid de iis docuit id omne ad notitiam communem referendum est, non Philosophicam & Scientificam: motum verò solis realem docuisse Sp. S. in scripturis constanter nego.
units.tr: Answer: Whatever it taught about these, all of it must be referred to common knowledge, not to philosophical and scientific knowledge. But that the Holy Spirit constantly taught the real motion of the sun in the Scriptures I deny.

units.la: CIX. Obj. Tertia decima (H. p. 202.)
units.tr: CIX. Thirteenth objection (H. p. 202.)

units.la: Docuit Sp. S. Thubalkainum metalla fundere, Salomonem loqui de bestiis, Hyssopi &c. Danielem instruxit sapientia &c.
units.tr: The Holy Spirit taught Tubal-cain to cast metals, Solomon to speak about beasts, hyssop etc. It furnished Daniel with wisdom etc.

units.la: Resp. Id nihil ad rem; quæstio enim est de Scriptura: An in scriptura nobis voluerit manifestare cognitionem rerum naturalium scientificam: non verò, an Spir. sanctus sit auctor istius luminis, quo Moses, Salomon, Daniel aliique obtinuerunt rerum naturalium cognitionem scientificam, quod libenter concedo.
units.tr: Answer: This has nothing to do with the matter. The question concerns Scripture: whether it has willed to reveal to us scientific knowledge of natural things in Scripture. It is not whether the Holy Spirit is the author of that light by which Moses, Solomon, Daniel and others obtained scientific knowledge of natural things. That I gladly concede.

units.la: CAPUT IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: Cartesii sententia de Mundi extensione & Magnitudine proponitur.
units.tr: The opinion of Descartes on the extension and magnitude of the world is set out.

units.la: CX. Ex his latè fusèque disputatis manifestu[illegible, ~3 letters]or evadet, oleum & operam perdere, qui in scriptura quærentes quod non inest, quodque Deus ei inferere noluit, ex eâ cognitionem rerum naturalium Philosophicam cap. 1, descriptam se consequi posse putant: Atque è concontrario recte facere eos, qui ad lumen naturale confugientes, (quod Deus omnibus hominibus concessit, ut eo si recte utantur, non tantum ab errando sibi caveant, sed etiam veritatem multarum rerum assequantur,) attendunt ad notiones mentii insitas, adque Principia prima & maxime evidentia, ex iisque per manifestas consequentias gradatim institutas, innitentes clare & distincte antea cognitis, rerum naturalium cognitionem accuratam & interiora aperientem acquirunt.
units.tr: CX. From these matters discussed at length and in detail, it will become clear that those who seek in Scripture what is not there, and what God did not wish to put there, waste their oil and labour if they think they can derive from it the philosophical knowledge of natural things described in chapter 1. On the contrary, those act rightly who, taking refuge in the natural light (which God has granted to all men, so that if they use it rightly they not only guard themselves against error but also attain the truth of many things), attend to the notions implanted in the mind and to the first and most evident principles, and from these, by manifest consequences step by step, relying on what has been clearly and distinctly known beforehand, acquire an accurate knowledge of natural things that opens up their inner workings.

units.la: CXI. Id Cartesium fecisse loquuntur scripta ejus Philosophica & in specie Physica, in quibus mille veritates clare retectas & demonstratas reperiri, frustra reclamantibus adversariis, nobiscum cognoscunt omnes, quibus ea oculis mentis ab affectibus & praejudiciis expurgatis inspicere licet. Specimen ejus circa Systema Mundi & Ordinem atque situm Corporum Mundi praecipuorum hic damus, quod in seqq. planius exponere & explanare, atque contra antagonistarum insultus defendere constituimus..
units.tr: That Descartes did this, his philosophical writings, and especially his physical ones, show, in which a thousand truths are found clearly uncovered and demonstrated; though his opponents protest in vain, all who may look upon them with the eyes of the mind, cleansed of emotions and prejudices, recognise this along with us. We here give a specimen of his view of the system of the world and the order and position of the principal bodies of the world, which we intend to set out and explain more plainly in what follows, and to defend against the attacks of his antagonists.

units.la: CXII. Is ergo de Quantitate & Extensione Mundi sic aestimat. Infinitatem soli Deo reservat, propterea quod non tantum in ipso nullos limites agnovit, sed etiam positive nullos esse intellexit. Quoniam vero Mundi tantam reperit in se ideam, ut, quoscunque fines & terminos ci assignet, semper ultra eos spatia extensa concipere oporteat, & sic sub aliqua consideratione nullum finem in ipso reperiat, cum Indefinitum censet habendum & dicendum.
units.tr: He accordingly judges as follows concerning the quantity and extension of the world. He reserves infinity to God alone, because in him he has recognised not only no limits, but has understood that there are positively no limits. But since he finds in himself an idea of the world so great that, whatever bounds and limits one assigns to it, one must always conceive extended spaces beyond them, and so under some consideration finds in it no end, he holds and says that it must be regarded as Indefinite.

units.la: CXIII. Hanc ejus esse sententiam liquet ex seqq. locis inter se ita comparatis, ut obscuriores per clariores, prout convenit legitimo Interpreti, explicentur. Eos prout in ipsius scriptis ordine occurrunt proponemus, atque a detorsione Adversarii liberabimus. Primus locus est Princip. I. art. 26. & 27. Ita nullus unquam fatigabimur disputationibus de infinito: Nam sane cum simus finiti, absurdum esset, nos aliquid de ipso determinare, atque sic illud quasi finire ac comprehendere conari. Non igitur respondere curabimus iis, qui quaerunt, an si daretur linea infinita, ejus media pars esset etiam infinita; vel an numerus infinitus sit par anne impar, & talia; quia de iis nulli videntur debere cogitare, nisi qui mentem suam infinitam esse arbitrantur. Nos autem illa omnia, in quibus sub aliqua consideratione nullum finem poterimus invenire, non quidem affirmabimus esse infinita, sed ut indefinita spectabimus. [illegible, ~10 letters] non possumus imaginari extensionem tam magnam, quin intelligamus adhuc majorem esse posse, dicemus, magnitudinem rerum possibilium esse indefinitam. Et quia non potest dividi aliquod corpus in tot partes, quin singulae adhuc ex his partibus divisibiles intelligantur, putabimus quantitatem esse esse indefinite divisibilem. Et quia non potest fingi tantus stellarum numerus, quin plures adhuc à Deo creari potuisse credamus, illarum etiam numerum indefinitum supponemus; atque ita de reliquis. art. 27. Hacque indefinita dicemus potius quam infinita; tum ut nomen infiniti Deo reservemus, quia in eo solo, omni ex parte, non modo nullos limites agnoscimus, sed etiam positive nullos esse intelligimus; tum etiam quia non eodem modo positive intelligimus, alias res aliquâ ex parte limitibus carere, sed negative tantum eorum limites, si quos habeant, inveniri à nobis non posse confitemur.
units.tr: CXIII. That this is his opinion is plain from the following passages, compared with one another so that the more obscure are explained by the clearer, as befits a lawful interpreter. We will set them out in the order in which they occur in his writings, and free them from the adversary's distortion. The first passage is Principles I, arts. 26 and 27. Therefore we shall never be wearied by disputes about the infinite. Indeed, since we are finite, it would be absurd for us to determine anything about it, and so to try to bound it and comprehend it. Accordingly, we shall not trouble to answer those who ask whether, if an infinite line were given, its half would also be infinite, or whether an infinite number is even or odd, and such things; for these questions seem to occur to no one except those who think their own mind is infinite. But as for all those things in which, under some consideration, we can find no end, we shall not indeed affirm that they are infinite, but shall regard them as indefinite. [illegible, ~10 letters] Since we cannot imagine an extension so great that we do not understand a still greater to be possible, we shall say that the magnitude of possible things is indefinite. And since no body can be divided into so many parts that each of these parts is not still understood to be divisible, we shall judge quantity to be indefinitely divisible. And since no number of stars can be imagined so great that we do not believe God could have created still more, we shall likewise suppose their number to be indefinite; and so on for the rest. Art. 27. We shall call these things indefinite rather than infinite, partly so that we may reserve the name of infinite for God alone, since in him alone do we recognise no limits in every respect, and understand positively that there are none; and partly because we do not understand in the same positive way that other things lack limits in some respect, but only confess that their limits, if they have any, cannot be found by us.

units.la: CXIV. Secundus locus est P. II, 21, 22.
units.tr: CXIV. The second passage is Part II, 21 and 22.

units.la: Cognoscimus praeterea hunc mundum, sive substantiam corporeā universitatem, nullos extensionis sua fines habere. Ubicunque enim fines illos esse fingamus, semper ultra ipsos aliqua spatia indefinite extensa, non modo imaginamur, sed etiam vere imaginabilia hoc est realia esse percipimus; ac proinde etiam substantiam corpoream indefinite extensam in iis contineri. Quia, ut jam fuse ostensum est, idea ejus extensionis, quam in spatio qualicunque concepimus, eadem plane est cum idea substantiae Corporeae §. 22. Hincque etiam colligi facile potest, non aliam esse materiam coeli quam terrae atque omnino si mundi essent infiniti, non posse non illos omnes ex una & eadem materia constare; nec proinde plures, sed unum tantum esse posse: quia perspicue intelligimus illam materiam, cujus natura in eo solo consistit, quod sit substantia extensa, omnia omnino spatia imaginabilia, in quibus alii ísti mundi esse deberent, jam occupare: nec ullius alterius materiae ideam in nobis reperimus.
units.tr: Furthermore, we recognise that this world, or the corporeal universe, has no limits to its extension. For wherever we suppose those limits to be, there always lie beyond them some indefinitely extended spaces, which we not only imagine but also perceive to be truly imaginable, that is, real; and therefore the corporeal substance, indefinitely extended, is contained in them as well. For, as has already been shown at length, the idea of that extension which we conceive in any space whatever is plainly the same as the idea of corporeal substance (§22). And from this it can also easily be gathered that the matter of heaven is not other than the matter of earth; and generally, if the worlds were infinite, they could not but all consist of one and the same matter, and so there could be only one, not several; for we clearly understand that matter, whose nature consists solely in its being extended substance, already occupies all the imaginable spaces in which other such worlds would have to be; nor do we find in ourselves the idea of any other matter.

units.la: CXV. Tertius locus est Princ. III. 1, 2.
units.tr: CXV. The third passage is Princ. III. 1, 2.

units.la: Inventis jam quibusdam Principiis rerum materialium, quae non à praejudiciis sensuum, sed à lumine rationis ita petita sunt, ut de ipsorum veritate dubitare nequeamus, examinandum est, an ex iis solis omnia natura phaenomena possimus explicare; Incipiendumque ab iis, quae maxime Universalia sunt, & à quibus reliqua dependent; nempe à generali totius hujus mundi adspectabilis constructione. De qua ut recte philosophemur, duo sunt imprimis observanda: Unum, ut attendentes ad infinitam Dei potentiam, & bonitatem, ne vereamur nimis ampla, & pulchra, & absoluta ejus opera imaginari; sed è contra caveamus, ne si quos forte limites, nobis non certo cognitos, in ipsis supponamus, nonsatis magnifice de creatoris potentia sentire videamur. §. 2. Alterum, ut etiam caveamus, ne nimis superbe de nobis ipsis sentiamus. Quod fieret non modo, si quos limites, nobis nulla cognitos ratione, nec divina revelatione, mundo vellemus affingere, tanquam si vis nostra cognitionis, ultra id quod à Deo revera factum est, ferri posset; sed etiam maxime, si res omnes propter nos solos ab illo creatas esse fingeremus; vel tantum, si fines fines, quos sibi proposuit in creando Universo, ingenii nostri vi comprehendi posse putaremus.
units.tr: Certain principles of material things having now been found, which are derived not from the prejudices of the senses but from the light of reason, so that we cannot doubt their truth, we must examine whether from these alone we can explain all natural phenomena. We must begin with those things which are most universal and on which the rest depend, namely the general construction of this whole visible world. To philosophize about it rightly, two things must be observed above all. The first: while attending to the infinite power and goodness of God, we should not be afraid to imagine his works as very vast, beautiful and perfect; but on the contrary we should take care that, if we suppose in them any limits not certainly known to us, we do not seem to think too meanly of the power of the Creator. §2. The second: we should also take care not to think too proudly of ourselves. This would happen not only if we wished to attribute to the world some limits known to us by no reasoning and no divine revelation, as if the power of our knowledge could reach beyond what God has really made; but especially if we imagined that all things were created by him solely for our sake, or if we thought that the ends which he set himself in creating the universe could be grasped by the force of our intellect.

units.la: CXVI. Quartus locus est P. III. 29. sin. Ac deinde, juxta usum vulgi, non est cur Fixas consideret ut immotas, potius quam terram, nisi quod putet, ultra ipsas non esse ulla alia corpora, a quibus separentur, & quorum respectu dici possint moveri, terra autem quiescere, illo sensu, quo dicit terram moveri respectu Fixarum. Atqui hoc putare a ratione est alienum; cum enim mens nostra sit talis natura, ut nullos in mundo limites agnoscat, quisquis ad Immensitatem Dei, & sensuum nostrorum infirmitatem attendet, aquius esse judicabit suspicari, ultra illas omnes stellas Fixas quas videmus, forte esse alia corpora, ad qua comparata terra quiescere, ipsa autem omnes simul moveri dici possint, quam suspicari nulla posse talia esse.
units.tr: CXVI. The fourth passage is P. III. 29, near the beginning. And then, according to common usage, there is no reason why one should regard the fixed stars as motionless rather than the earth, unless one thinks that beyond them there are no other bodies from which they are separated, and with respect to which they can be said to move, while the earth rests, in that sense in which he says the earth moves with respect to the fixed stars. But to think this is foreign to reason. For since our mind is of such a nature that it recognizes no limits in the world, whoever attends to the immensity of God and the weakness of our senses will judge it more fitting to suspect that beyond all those fixed stars which we see there may be other bodies, with respect to which the earth may be said to rest while all of them move together, than to suppose that there cannot be any such bodies.

units.la: CXVII. Circa primum locum reprehendit (R. St. p. 83.) quòd Cartesius suam sententiam involvat tanta arte ut qui eum solum legerit, facile Cartesium ab omni errore sit absoluturus, sed serio expensum nihil continere praeter metas tergiversationes, prævaricationes, & propria opinionis eversiones. Primum enim κρησφύγετον, inquit, est in distinctione Infiniti & Indefiniti. Infinitum ei id, in quo omni ex parte nulli limites sint; indefinitum, quod non habet extensionem tam magnam, quin majorem habere possit (id quod vulgo dici solet Infinitum συγκατηγορημα πιχως sive potentiale) & vult videri hoc unum Mundo tribuisse, non autem illud. Alterum est, in distinctione intelle-ctionis positivae a negativa; illam esse, cum in re aliqua intelliguntur nulli li-mites esse, hanc, qua rei alicujus limites, si quos habet, inveniri a nobis non pos-se confitemur, & hanc se, non alteram menti nostra adscripsisse videri vult.
units.tr: CXVII. Concerning the first passage, he (R. St. p. 83.) criticizes Descartes because he wraps up his opinion with such skill that anyone who has read him alone will easily acquit Descartes of every error; but when it is examined carefully it contains nothing but mere evasions, prevarications and overthrows of his own opinion. For, he says, the first last refuge [κρησφύγετον] lies in the distinction between the Infinite and the Indefinite. He takes the Infinite to be that in which there are no limits in any respect; the Indefinite to be that which does not have an extension so great that it cannot have a greater one (what is commonly called the Infinite [συγκατηγορημα πιχως] or potential). And he wants it to seem that he has attributed to the world this one thing and not the other. The second is in the distinction between positive and negative understanding: the former is when no limits are understood to exist in some thing; the latter is when we confess that the limits of some thing, if it has any, cannot be found by us; and he wants it to seem that he has ascribed the latter to our mind and not the former.

units.la: Resp. Discipiamus igitur, num monstrante Adversario illas tergiversationes & propriæ opinionis Cartesii eversiones videre possimus. Cartesius P. I art. 27. Infinitum ita describit: In quo omni ex parte, non modo nullos limites agnoscimus, sed etiam positive nullos esse intelligimus. Indefi-nitum vero P. I. 26. ci est, In quo sub aliqua consideratione nullum finem possu-mus invenire; unde apparet, quam fideliter hic sententia Cartesii fuerit re-lata. Nam definitio Indefiniti adducta, est tantum particularis alicujus Indefiniti, non omnis: at Cartesii est generalis. Ita quidem quoddam Indefinitum est, quod non habet extensionem tam magnam, quin majorem habere possit, sed tale non est omne Indefinitum, cum etiam alia dici possint Indefinita, praeterquam quae extensionis sunt participia. 2. Adeoque nec Indefinitum hic simpliciter Cartesio idem est, quod Potentiale Infinitum, cum hoc illo sit angustius, ita ut omne quidem Potentiale Infinitum sit Indefinitum, sed non omne Indefinitum sit potentiale Infinitum. Hæc prænotanda fuerunt propter ea quæ sequuntur.
units.tr: Reply. Let us therefore examine whether, with the adversary pointing them out, we can see those evasions and the overthrows of Descartes's own opinion. Descartes, P. I, art. 27, describes the Infinite thus: That in which, in every respect, we not only recognize no limits, but also positively understand that there are none. The Indefinite, however, P. I, 26, is that in which, under some consideration, we cannot find any end; from which it is clear how faithfully the opinion of Descartes has been reported here. For the definition of the Indefinite that was cited is only of a particular kind of Indefinite, not of every one; but Descartes's is general. So indeed some Indefinite is that which does not have an extension so great that it cannot have a greater, but not every Indefinite is such, since other things besides extensions can also be called Indefinite. 2. Hence the Indefinite here is not simply the same for Descartes as the Potential Infinite, since this is narrower than that: every Potential Infinite is indeed Indefinite, but not every Indefinite is a Potential Infinite. These things had to be noted beforehand because of what follows.

units.la: CXVIII. Inst. 1. (R. A. p. 61.) Ex iis qua subnectit Cartesius exem-plis patet, eum, quod generalius extulerat, ad particulare hoc Indefinitum extensionis videlicet & Magnitudinis restringere & quomodo fides hic mea in dubium vocabitur, qui generalitatem illam ad rem de qua agitur contraxi, cum de nullo alio Indefinito hic controvertatur, quam de Mundo & ejus extensione? si mihi hac loquendi ratio quidquam commodaret, aut incommodaret Cartesio, rationem sane haberet adversarium expostulandi, nunc tantum nodum in scirpo quærit.
units.tr: CXVIII. Objection 1. (R. A. p. 61.) From the examples that Descartes adds it is clear that he restricts to this particular Indefinite, namely of extension and magnitude, what he had stated more generally; and how is my faith here called into doubt, since I have narrowed that generality to the matter under discussion, when here nothing else is disputed concerning the Indefinite than the world and its extension? If this way of speaking benefited or harmed Descartes in any way, the adversary would certainly have had reason to complain; but now he is looking for a knot in a bulrush.

units.la: Resp. Confitetur ergo, definitionem Indefiniti à Cartesio productam esse generalem, quod accipimus. 2. exempla adducta à Cartesio sunt quidem particularia, quæ tamen non ita restringunt generale ad particulare, ut illud generale ad plura particularia non possit applicari, quemadmodum exempla regulis adjuncta non dicunt, illam regulam in his tantum exemplis locum habere. Ita ergo Indefinitum extensionis & magnitudinis possibilis particulare quidem est Indefinitum, quod sub generali comprehenditur, sed ita ut non excludatur Indefinitum extensionis & magnitudinis realis, quale est Mundi, qui talis ac tantus est, ut in eo nullos limites & fines agnoscamus, sed suppositis quibuscunque finibus semper ulterius adscendamus, de quo Indefinito hic controvertitur. Sic datur Indefinita divisio, cujus non tot possum supponere partes factas, quin intelligam adhuc plures esse. Vid. P. II, 35.3. Multum autem hæc acceptio Indefiniti generalis commodat Cartesio, qui hac ratione liberatur ab accusatione, quod latebras in verbis & tergiversationes quæsiverit.
units.tr: Reply. He therefore confesses that the definition of the Indefinite produced by Descartes is general, which we accept. 2. The examples adduced by Descartes are indeed particular, but they do not so restrict the general to the particular that the general cannot be applied to several particulars, just as examples added to a rule do not say that the rule holds only in those examples. Thus the Indefinite of possible extension and magnitude is indeed a particular Indefinite, which is comprehended under the general one, but in such a way that the Indefinite of real extension and magnitude is not excluded, such as that of the world, which is such and so great that we recognize in it no limits and ends, but, whatever ends are supposed, we always climb further; and it is concerning this Indefinite that the dispute is here. So there is an Indefinite division, of which I cannot suppose so many parts to have been made that I do not understand there to be still more. See P. II, 35.3. This general acceptance of the Indefinite is, however, of great help to Descartes, who by this reasoning is freed from the accusation that he sought hiding places in words and evasions.

units.la: CXIX. Inst. 2. (R. A. p. 62.) Patere, quod Cartesius dicto loco per Indefinitum intellexerit Potentiale Infinitum, 1. quia non alia adducat exempla quam potentialis Infiniti, 2. quia dicat similem esse rationem reliquorum, his verbis; atque ita de reliquis.
units.tr: CXIX. Objection 2. (R. A. p. 62.) It is evident that Descartes in the passage cited understood by the Indefinite the Potential Infinite, 1. because he adduces no other examples than those of the potential infinite, 2. because he says that the reasoning for the rest is similar, in these words: and so on for the rest.

units.la: Resp. Cartef. art. 26. docet, nos de Infinito nihil debere determinare v. g. si linea detur infinita, an etiam ejus media pars sit futura infinita; simul ostendit, quid circa ea sit faciendum, in quibus nullos limites possumus invenire; nempe, non dicendum, ea esse Infinita, quoniam hoc non possumus intelligere, sed Indefinita, atque varia adducit exempla eorum, in quibus sub ulla ratione nullos limites reperire possumus, eaque vult dici Indefinita; ac sic censet dicendum de reliquis, in quibus sub ulla ratione nullos limites possumus reperire. Non autem sequitur; non adducit alia exempla, quam potentialis Infiniti, ergo non alia sub Indefini-to. to generaliter accepto comprehenduntur. Sufficit, quod talis sit generalis cjus natura, ut etiam alia exempla particularia sub eo possimus comprehendere.
units.tr: Reply. Descartes, art. 26, teaches that we ought not to determine anything about the Infinite; for example, if a line is given as infinite, whether its middle part also will be infinite. At the same time he shows what is to be done about those things in which we can find no limits in any way: namely, that they should not be called Infinite, since we cannot understand this, but Indefinite; and he adduces various examples of those things in which we can find no limits in any way, and wishes these to be called Indefinite; and so he holds that the same should be said of the rest, in which we can find no limits in any way. But it does not follow: he adduces no other examples than those of the potential infinite, therefore no other things are comprehended under the Indefinite taken generally. It is enough that its general nature be such that we can comprehend under it other particular examples as well.

units.la: CXX. Circa secundum locum objicitur 1. (R. St. p. 84.) Cartesius loco antea citato, non de eo quod esse possit, egit, sed quod revera sit: mundum, inquam, nullos extensionis sua fines HABERE, in eo spatia REALIA Indefinite extensa ESSE, & substantiam Corpoream Indefinite extensam in iis CONTINERI. At Indefinitum illud, (quod improprie ita vocat) hoc est, Infinitum Potentiale, nunquam actu HABETUR, nunquam EST aut EXISTIT. Exemplo sit divisio continui in infinitas partes, nunquam ad illas pervenitur, sed tantum earum numerum aliquem addi POSSE significatur, & hoc modo mundum non ita magnum esse fatemur, quin major a Deo fieri POSSIT: sed & habere eum, & in illo quoque casu habituruni extensionu sua limites contendimus.
