Nec ex hac potentiali Infinitate, ulla mundi AMPLITUDO sequitur, cum eadem vel minimis corpusculis conveniat, nullum enim tam parvum est, quin minus, nec tam magnum, quin majus fieri possit in Infinitum.
units.tr: CXX. Concerning the second passage, the following objection is made 1. (R. St. p. 84.) Descartes, in the passage cited earlier, was not dealing with what can be, but with what really is: that the world, I mean, HAS no limits of its extension, that in it REAL spaces ARE extended indefinitely, and that corporeal substance extended indefinitely is CONTAINED in them. But that Indefinite (which he improperly calls thus), that is, the Potential Infinite, is never HAD, never IS or EXISTS. Take as an example the division of a continuum into infinite parts: one never arrives at them, but it is only signified that some number of them can be added; and in this way we grant that the world is not so great that a greater cannot be made by God; but we contend that it both has, and in that case too will have, limits to its extension. Nor from this potential infinity does any AMPLITUDE of the world follow, since it applies equally to the smallest corpuscles; for no thing is so small that it cannot be made smaller, nor so large that it cannot be made larger without end.

units.la: Resp. Cartef. P. II. 21. dicit, COGNOSCIMVS praterea, hunc Mundum sive substantia corporea Universitatem, nullos extensionis sua fines habere: quae verba non dextre accepta obnoxia esse potuerunt calumniae: sed si conferantur cum aliis Cartesii verbis, eorum explicatio erit in promtu. P. III. 29. hanc sententiam suam ita profert, Cum mens nostra sit talis natura, ut nullos in Mundo limites agnoscat. Et in Epistola ab ipso ad Morum Anglum scripta ita loquitur. De Mundi extensione, de numero partium, in quas materia est divisibilis & similibus, an sint simpliciter Infinita nec ne, profiteor me nescire, scio tantum me in illis nullum finem agnoscere, atque idcirco respectu mei dico esse Indefinita. Repete verba P. I. 27. ubi dicit, quod in solo Deo omni ex parte non modo nullos limites agnoscimus, sed positive nullos esse intelligimus. Unde patet, verborum P. II. 21. hunc esse sensum: Nos in Mundo nullos fines quos habeat cognoscimus, quod verum est & cum Mente Cartesii convenit. Ergo nulla hic Contradictio. Nam Mundum non vocat Infinitum potentialiter, quemadmodum praecedente articulo intelleximus, sed Indefinitum, ita ut posito quocunque termino ejusdem, semper adhuc major Mundus sit concipiendus. Verum est, ad divisionem continui in infinitas partes nunquam deveniri: at divisionem in indefinitas partes actu fieri demonstravit Cart. Princ. II, 35. Sic omnia, quae hic de Infinito potentiali declamantur, in fumum abeunt.
units.tr: Resp. Cartesius, P. II. 21, says: We acknowledge moreover that this world, or the universe of corporeal substance, has no limits to its extension. These words, if not taken rightly, could be open to calumny; but if they are compared with other words of Descartes, their explanation will be ready to hand. In P. III. 29 he states this opinion in the following way: Since our mind is of such a nature that it recognises no limits in the world. And in a letter he wrote to the Englishman More he speaks thus: Concerning the extension of the world, the number of the parts into which matter is divisible, and similar things, whether they are simply infinite or not, I profess that I do not know. I know only that I recognise no end in them, and therefore I call them indefinite with respect to myself. Compare the words of P. I. 27, where he says that in God alone do we recognise no limits in every respect, but we understand positively that there are none. From this it is clear that the sense of the words in P. II. 21 is this: we recognise in the world no limits which it has, which is true and agrees with the mind of Descartes. Therefore there is no contradiction here. For he does not call the world infinite potentially, as we understood in the preceding article, but indefinite, so that, whatever term of it is posited, a world still greater must always be conceived. It is true that division of the continuum into infinite parts is never reached; but Descartes demonstrated that division into indefinite parts is actually carried out (Princ. II. 35). Thus all the things declaimed here about potential infinity vanish into smoke.

units.la: CXXI. Atque huic formulae antehac verba Cartesii Princip. II. art. 21. aequipollere dixeramus, quod in seqq. contra Antagonistae Instantias tuebimur. Nunc si forte alicui prior hæc æquipollentia videatur coactior (accurate expensis & consideratis iis quæ sequuntur) eam sic explicamus: Cognoscimus, huic mundum nullos extensionis suæ fines, nobis determinabiles, sive quos nos possimus definire, habere. Ex sequentibus hoc fit manifestum, in quibus semper respicitur, quid nostra mens possit definire, percipere. Ubicunque enim fines illos fingamus &c. Id etiam patet ex art. seq. in quo dicitur: Illam materiam omnia omnino spatia imaginabilia jam occupare.
units.tr: CXXI. We had said before that this formula is equivalent to the words of Descartes, Princ. II. art. 21, which in what follows we shall defend against the Antagonist's instances. Now, if to anyone that equivalence seems rather forced (when what follows is weighed and considered carefully), we explain it thus: we recognise that this world has no limits of its extension that are determinable by us, or which we can define. From what follows this becomes manifest, for in those passages it is always regard to what our mind can define and perceive: wherever we may imagine those limits, etc. This is also clear from the following article, in which it is said: that matter now occupies all imaginable spaces.

units.la: CXXII. Inst. 1. (R. A. p. 65.) quid est ad manifestam veritatem oculos claudere, si hoc non est.
units.tr: CXXII. Inst. 1. (R. A. p. 65.) What is it to close one's eyes to manifest truth, if this is not so?

units.la: Hasce duas propositiones æquipollere sensus, nos in Mundo nullos fines possumus cognoscere, & hanc, cognoscimus Mundum nullos extensionis suæ fines habere. Si sic se res habet, idem quoque valebunt hæ duæ. Nos in Ecclesia Dei nullos Electos possumus cognoscere, & hac, Cognoscimus in Ecclesia visibili nullos esse Electos &c.
units.tr: These two propositions are equivalent in sense: we can recognise no limits in the world; and this one: we recognise that the world has no limits to its extension. If the matter stands thus, these two will hold equally: we can recognise no elect in the Church of God; and this: we recognise that there are no elect in the visible Church, etc.

units.la: Resp. Dixi has duas propositiones esse æquipollentes apud Cartesium: Cognoscimus hunc Mundum nullos extensionis suæ fines habere, &, Nos in Mundo nullos fines quos habeat cognoscimus, idque probavi ex locis Cartesii parallelis, in quibus ex professo quàm accuratissime & commodissime suos conceptus de Mundi extensione voluit exprimere. Ex iis enim apparet, Ipsum non Mundum Infinitum statuisse, hoc est, telem, in quo omni ex parte nullos limites agnoscimus, sive positive nullos esse intelligimus, sed Indefinitum, in quo aliquâ ex parte nullos extensionis fines agnoscamus. Cum ergò hæc verba Cartesii possint habere & sensum quem adversarius existimat, & quem ego puto, sintque ita ambigua, ex locis parallelis quem sensum habeant est dispiciendum, quoniam quilibet est optimus interpres suorum verborum. 2. Sic hæ duæ Propositiones, Cognoscimus hunc Mundum nullum certum numerum hominum sive electorum habere, &, Nos in Mundo nullum certum numerum hominum, quem habeat, possumus cognoscere, æquivalere possunt, si id aliunde colligatur, sicut de Cartesii propositionum æquivalen-tiâ factum est.
units.tr: Resp. I said that these two propositions are equivalent in Descartes: "We recognise that this world has no limits to its extension," and "We recognise in the world no limits which it has," and I proved this from parallel passages of Descartes, in which he deliberately wished to express his concepts of the extension of the world as accurately and conveniently as possible. For from them it appears that he did not posit a world that is infinite, that is, one in which we recognise no limits in any respect, or positively understand that there are none, but an indefinite one, in which we recognise, in some respect, no limits of extension. Since therefore these words of Descartes can bear both the sense that the adversary supposes and the one I think is meant, and are so ambiguous, the sense they bear must be examined from parallel passages, since each person is the best interpreter of his own words. 2. Thus these two propositions, "We recognise that this world has no certain number of men or elect," and "We cannot recognise in the world any certain number of men that it has," can be equivalent, if this is gathered from elsewhere, as has been done with the equivalence of Descartes' propositions.

units.la: CXXIII. Inst. 2. (R. A. p. 66.) Quod mundum respecta sui Indefinitum dicat, miror eum nusquam in excusis libris dixisse, quis enim hoc ei non concesserit? sed amplius dixit, nempe, ubicunque fines illius esse FINGAMUS, semper ultra ipsos aliqua spatia indefinite extensa non modo IMAGINAMUR, sed etiam VERE imaginabilia, hoc est, REALIA esse percipimus, ac proinde etiam substantiam indefinite extensam in iis contineri. quis non videt, non modo respecta nostra imperfecta cognitione Indefinitum dici, sed vere in se & realiter &c.
units.tr: CXXIII. Inst. 2. (R. A. p. 66.) That he calls the world indefinite with respect to itself, I wonder that he nowhere said in printed books; for who would not grant him this? But he said more, namely: wherever we suppose its limits to be, we not only imagine, but truly perceive, that beyond those limits some spaces indefinitely extended are always imaginable, that is, that they are real, and consequently that a substance indefinitely extended is contained in them. Who does not see that the world is called indefinite not only with respect to our imperfect knowledge, but truly and really in itself, etc.?

units.la: Resp. Quando Cartesius dicit articulo dicto, semper ultra quoscun-que fines in Mundo suppositos nos percipere spatia realia, non negat mundum respectu sui Indefinitum, imò hoc vel maxime affirmat, dum illis ipsis verbis docet, se nullos in mundo fines posse reperire.
units.tr: Resp. When Descartes says in the article cited that, beyond whatever limits are supposed in the world, we always perceive real spaces, he does not deny that the world is indefinite with respect to itself; indeed he affirms this most strongly, since in those very words he teaches that he can find no limits in the world.

units.la: CXXIV. Inst. 3. (R. A. p. 67.) At si mundus est major omni termino, ut dicis, recte dicitur non nostri tantum respectu, sed in se & in rei veritate, nullos terminos habere.
units.tr: CXXIV. Inst. 3. (R. A. p. 67.) But if the world is greater than every term, as you say, it is rightly said to have no limits not only with respect to us, but in itself and in the truth of the thing.

units.la: Resp. Si mundus sit omni termino major absolute, tum sequeretur id quod infert Antagonista, sed major debet concipi omni termino qui a nobis supponitur vel fingitur, tum quia haec est ejus idea, tum quia non debemus existimare, nos terminos & fines operum Dei posse intelligere.
units.tr: Resp. If the world were greater than every term absolutely, then what the Antagonist infers would follow; but it must be conceived as greater than every term that is supposed or imagined by us, both because this is its idea, and because we ought not to think that we can understand the terms and ends of God's works.

units.la: CXXV. Inst. 4. (R. A. p. 67.) Quod ad eundem More scribit, an Mundi extensio sit simpliciter infinita id se nescire, id quoque mirum, nusquam eum in scriptis suis quae publici juris, profiteri, neque convenit haec ignorantia cum ea quam jactavit cognitione.
units.tr: CXXV. Inst. 4. (R. A. p. 67.) As for his writing to the same More that he does not know whether the extension of the world is simply infinite, this is also strange: nowhere in his writings that are published does he profess it, nor does this ignorance agree with the knowledge he boasted of.

units.la: Resp. Id etiamsi non ἀπλῶς dixerit Cartesius in suis scriptis, tamen dixit verbis aequivalentibus, si conferas P. I. 26. & P III. 1, 2. Nam ex priori constat, nos, Infinitum aliquid praeter Deum esse, non debere determinare; ex posteriori, nos in extensione Mundi nullos fines posse reperire; unde sane colligitur, nos ignorare an sint nec ne. 2. quod autem ea quae nec recta ratio, nec Scriptura determinat, ut in examine argumentorum apparebit, fatear cum Cartesio me ignorare, in eo facio id quod omnes non nimis superbe de se sentientes, nec omnia à se definiri posse fatentes, facere debent.
units.tr: Resp. Even if Descartes did not say simpliciter in his writings, nevertheless he said it in equivalent words, if you compare P. I. 26 and P. III. 1, 2. For from the former it is clear that we ought not to determine anything infinite beside God; from the latter, that we cannot find any limits in the extension of the world; from which it is certainly gathered that we do not know whether they are infinite or not. 2. As for the things which neither right reason nor Scripture determines, as will appear in the examination of the arguments, I confess with Descartes that I do not know them; in this I do what all who do not think too proudly of themselves, and who confess that not everything can be defined by them, ought to do.

units.la: CXXVI. Inst. 5. (R. A. p. 78.) At Cartesius in Epistola ad More inquit, Repugnat conceptui meo, sive quod idem est, puto IMPLICARE CONTRADICTIONEM, UT MUNDUS SIT FINITUS vel DETERMINATUS. Si putet hoc implicare contradictionem, sane putat hoc falsum esse, imo nec verum esse posse. observa porro mirabilem descriptionem implicatae contradictionis, qua videlicet id omne contradictionem involvere putatur, quod repugnat conceptui Cartesiano.
units.tr: CXXVI. Inst. 5. (R. A. p. 78.) But Descartes in his letter to More says: "It is repugnant to my concept, or what is the same, I think it implies a contradiction, that the world should be finite or determinate." If he thinks this implies a contradiction, then surely he thinks this is false, indeed that it cannot even be true. Observe further the remarkable description of an implied contradiction, by which it is thought that everything involves a contradiction which is repugnant to the Cartesian concept.

units.la: Resp. Verba Cartesii in epistola secunda ad More Ep. 69. p. 362. sic habent: Repugnat conceptui meo, sive quod idem est, puto implicare contradictionem, ut mundus sit finitus vel terminatus, quia non possum non concipere spatium ultra quoslibet praesuppositos mundi fines, tale autem spatium apud me est verum corpus: nec moror quod ab aliis imaginarium vocetur, & ideo mundus finitus existimetur, novi enim ex quibus praejudiciis error iste profectus sit. Horum posteriora priora declarant, ita ut ex iis constet, Cartesium statuere implicare contradictionem, mundum esse certu finibus terminatum, eo quod repugnet conceptui suo sive ideæ, quæ talis est, ut suppositis quibuscunque mundi finibus semper tamen reperiamus ulteriorem extensionem, non vero simpliciter esse Finitum, de quo dicit se nihil determinare posse. 2. Hanc autem esse contradictionem, si aliquid repugnet conceptui manifestum. Quæro enim, quo modo alio censeatur implicari contradictio, si non in nostro conceptu, in quo duorum sibi contradicentium invenitur repugnantia? Vel enim illa Contradictionis implicatio est in rebus vel in nostro conceptu. At in rebus uti nulla est falsitas, ita etiam nulla potest esse Contradictio. Restat ergo, ut ea sit in nostro conceptu, quando nempe ei repugnat talia sociare, quæ semetipsa evertunt. Recte itaque Cartesius quod repugnat conceptui suo judicat Contradictorium, quemadmodum tu judicare debes contradictorium id quod tuo conceptui repugnat, alius quod suo, atque ita Cartesius perceptionem sive conceptum suum proprium regulam sui non alterius Judicii constituit, quemadmodum à quolibet judicare legitimè volente fieri debet.
units.tr: Resp. The words of Descartes in the second letter to More (Ep. 69, p. 362) are as follows: "It is repugnant to my concept, or what is the same, I think it implies a contradiction, that the world should be finite or terminated, because I cannot help conceiving space beyond any supposed limits of the world; and such space, for me, is a true body. Nor do I mind that by others it is called imaginary, and that therefore the world is held to be finite; for I know from what prejudices that error has arisen." The latter words explain the former, so that from them it is clear that Descartes holds that it implies a contradiction for the world to be bounded by certain limits, because this is repugnant to his concept or idea, which is such that, whatever limits of the world are supposed, we always find a further extension; but he does not hold that it is simply finite, about which he says he can determine nothing. 2. Now, this is a contradiction, if something is manifestly repugnant to a concept. For I ask, by what other means is a contradiction judged to be implied, if not in our concept, in which the repugnance of two mutually contradictory things is found? For the implication of contradiction is either in things or in our concept. But in things, as there is no falsity, so there can be no contradiction either. It remains, therefore, that it is in our concept, namely when it is repugnant to it to join things that destroy each other. Rightly, then, Descartes judges that which is repugnant to his own concept to be contradictory, just as you ought to judge contradictory that which is repugnant to your concept, and another that which is repugnant to his; and so Descartes makes his own perception or concept the rule of his judgment, not of another's, as must be done by anyone who wishes to judge legitimately.

units.la: CXXVII. Inst. 6. (R. A. p. 67.) Monstrandum esse vel unicum scriptorem, qui Indefiniti vocabulum ita ut Cartesius accipiat, alioqui significationem hanc confictam esse non injuria arbitrabimur.
units.tr: CXXVII. Inst. 6. (R. A. p. 67.) It must be shown that at least one writer uses the term "indefinite" as Descartes does; otherwise we shall not unjustly judge that this meaning has been invented.

units.la: .Resp. Sufficit ostendisse ex ipso Cartesio, hunc quem dixi, esse hujus vocabuli sensum in Cartesii scriptis, hoc enim requirebatur ut liberaretur à tergiversationibus quibus ab adversario gravabatur.
units.tr: Reply: It is enough to have shown from Descartes himself that this is the sense of the term in his writings. That was what was required, so that he might be freed from the evasions with which his opponent burdens him.

units.la: CXXVIII. Videamus quæ contra alteram Cartesii distinctionem 2. objiciuntur (R. St. p. 85.) Perperam etiam huc trahitur distributio Cognitionis in negativam & positivam. Neque enim dixerat, mentem nostram mundi limites, quos habet, invenire non posse, sed eam cognoscere, mundum limites non habere, & ubicunque fines illos fingamus (non putat ergo eos vere dari) semper ultra ipsos spatia realia esse eam percipere.
units.tr: CXXVIII. Let us see what is objected against Descartes's second distinction. (R. St. p. 85.) The distribution of knowledge into negative and positive is also wrongly dragged in here. For he did not say that our mind cannot find the limits the world has, but that it knows the world has no limits, and wherever we imagine such limits (so he does not think they really exist), the mind always perceives real space beyond them.

units.la: Resp. Quàm bene adhibeatur à Cartesio divisio cognitionis in negativam & positivam patebit, si quis tantum ad ea quæ superius à nobis fuerunt allata attendat, ex quibus perspiciet, quæ Cartesii mens fuerit; quando dicit, Cognoscimus hunc mundum nullos extensionis suæ fines habere. Nec mirum est, quod non putet dari limites mundi, quia non statuit mundum esse finitum actu, quod hactenus solidis argumentis non fuit probatum. Neque tamen existimat, ipsum absolutè esse infinitum, quia & hoc ratio manifesta non demonstrat, aliudque ex ipsius verbis inferri non potest, quàm nescivisse, an Mundus aliquos fines haberet nec ne: Sed tædet quæ tam clara sunt, toties inculcare.
units.tr: Reply: How well Descartes uses the division of knowledge into negative and positive will be clear if one attends only to what we have set out above, from which one will perceive what Descartes's mind was, when he says, We know that this world has no bounds to its extension. Nor is it surprising that he does not think the world has limits, since he did not hold that the world is actually finite, which has not so far been proved by solid arguments. Yet neither does he think it is absolutely infinite, since clear reason does not demonstrate this either. Nothing can be inferred from his words except that he did not know whether or not the world had any bounds. But it is tedious to repeat so often what is so clear.

units.la: CXXIX. Inst. (R. A. p. 69.) Itane vero tanto molimine nihil nisi insciitiam suam Cartesius profiteri voluit? & nihil vel hoc ipso paragrapho ego in contrarium demonstravi? &c. quæ tanquam dicteria prætereo.
units.tr: CXXIX. Inst. (R. A. p. 69.) Did Descartes really wish, with such great effort, to profess nothing but his own ignorance? And have I not demonstrated the contrary in this very paragraph? etc., which I pass over as taunts.

units.la: Resp. Duo sunt de quibus agitur, nempe; 1. an mundus sit Indefinitus? 2. an sit Infinitus? posterius se ignorare fatetur Cartesius, & ego cum ipso, non propter ejus auctoritatem, sed quia nullas video firmas ab alterutrâ parte rationes. Prius vero demonstravit firma ratione, & ego ex ipso. Itaque non magno molimine voluit profiteri suam insciitiam, sed firma ratione suam sententiam de Mundi Indefinitate. 2. Verum enim vero exinde patet Philosophica Cartesii modestia, qui non voluit cum aliis magistraliter definire mundi terminos & figuram, nec de re ignotâ audacter judicare, operaque Dei sine ratione evidenti limitare & in arctum constringere, propter quam potius laudandus quàm reprehendendus.
units.tr: Reply: Two matters are at issue: (1) whether the world is indefinite; (2) whether it is infinite. Descartes confesses that he is ignorant of the latter, and I with him, not because of his authority but because I see no firm reasons on either side. The former, however, he demonstrated by firm reasoning, and I with him. So he did not wish to profess his ignorance with great effort, but to set out his opinion on the indefiniteness of the world on solid grounds. Moreover, this makes plain the philosophical modesty of Descartes, who did not wish, like others, to define magisterially the boundaries and shape of the world, nor to judge boldly about an unknown matter, nor to limit and confine the works of God without evident reason. For this he deserves praise rather than blame.

units.la: CXXX. Obj. 3. L. p. 285. Mundum hunc sive substantia corporea universitatem nullos extensionis suæ fines habere, confidenter asseverat. sententia motivum probat à fictione & magnitudine nostra? Firmo scilicet argumento, & ad quævis opinionum monstra inducenda valido. Sive igitur Mundi appellationem nostro, id est, hominum loquentium usu accipiat, sive suo extensionis figmento corporea, neutro modo piaculi violata veritatis crimine purgatur. Nostro loquendi modo Mundus pro cœli & terræ complexu, adjuncta Terræ aqua, cœlo, aëre, usurpatur. hac definito spatio esse corpora omnes qui non delirant unanimi voce docuere. Terram in medio quiescere, cœlum exterius in orbem moveri, etsi non omnium, recepta tamen quam maxime omnium sententia est. Jam si cœlam extremitate sua movetur, extrema ejus poni & fines extensionis necesse est. alioqui ne moveri quidem possit. Tacce, jam nihil rerum humanarum esse ullo modo infinitum actu appellandum: ne propria Deo Infinitas cum rebus creatis confundatur.
units.tr: CXXX. Obj. 3. L. p. 285. He confidently asserts that this world, or the corporeal universe, has no bounds to its extension. With what argument does he prove this, from his fiction and from our magnitude? A firm argument, surely, and one valid for introducing any monstrous opinion! Whether he takes the word "world" in our usage, that is, of men who speak, or in his own corporeal figment of extension, the crime of violated truth is purged in neither way. In our way of speaking, "world" is used for the whole of heaven and earth, with the waters of the earth, the heaven and the air added. That all bodies are in this defined space, all who are not raving have taught with one voice. That the earth rests in the middle and heaven moves outwardly in an orbit, though this is not everyone's view, is nevertheless by far the most received opinion of all. Now if heaven is moved at its outermost extremity, its extremes must be posited and its bounds of extension; otherwise it could not even be moved. So, then, nothing of human things may in any way be called infinite in act, lest the infinity proper to God be confused with created things.

units.la: Resp. Ad hæc sequentia annotamus, 1. Cartesius non asseverat absolute, mundum nullos extensionis suæ fines habere, sed quod mens nostra talis sit naturæ, ut nullos in mundo fines invenire possit, cum id apud se expertus fuerit, & quilibet alius experiri possit, testenturque illi, qui loco spatiorum realium sive corporum spatia imaginaria fingunt. 2. Non desumit probationem Cartesius à fictione nostrâ, sed ab Ideâ mundi, quam quilibet secum circumfert, tali nempe, ut in ea nulli extensionis fines possint reperiri, quæ cum non sit à præjudiciis orta, necesse est, ut à Deo nobis sit indita, & per consequens non aliter ac veritas habet, rem repræsentet. 3. Mundum sumit Cartesius pro Universitate Corporum à Deo creatorum, neque in eo à communi acceptione recedit. Illi enim, qui Mundum τὸ πᾶν Universum appellant, ad hanc significationem attendunt. 4. Quod terra, aqua & aer reliquaque corpora per certum spatium sint determinata, nemo negat; at inde non sequitur, totam Universitatem, quæ in Indefinitum se extendit, esse finitam, uti ex sequentibus patet. Ex quibus etiam constabit, dici non posse, quousque cœlum se ultra stellas fixas extendat, & an aliquis ipsi competat finis, qui quamvis competeret, non sequeretur tamen, Mundum se ultra illum per alia corpora nobis ignota non extendere. 5. an Cœlum moveatur, an Terra, in hoc tractatu determinabitur. Posito autem illud moveri, nihil id ad antagonistæ faceret institutum, qui ultra illud Cœlum stellatum, si de ejus finibus constaret, necessario alia corpora conciperentur. 6. quod hæc Indefinitas Mundi Dei perfectioni nihil detrahat, suo loco etiam ostendetur.
units.tr: Reply: To these points we add the following. (1) Descartes does not assert absolutely that the world has no bounds to its extension, but that our mind is of such a nature that it can find no bounds in the world, since he has experienced this in himself and anyone else can experience it too. Those testify to it who, in place of real spaces or bodies, feign imaginary spaces. (2) Descartes does not derive his proof from our fiction, but from the idea of the world, which everyone carries with him: one in which no bounds of extension can be found. Since this is not born of prejudices, it must be implanted in us by God, and consequently, as truth does, it represents the thing as it is. (3) Descartes takes "world" for the universe of bodies created by God, and in this he does not depart from common usage. For those who call the world the All [τὸ πᾶν], the Universe, attend to this same meaning. (4) That earth, water, air and the other bodies are determined within a certain space, no one denies. But it does not follow from this that the whole universe, which extends into the indefinite, is finite, as will be clear from what follows. From these things it will also be established that it cannot be said how far heaven extends beyond the fixed stars, or whether any end belongs to it. Even if some end did belong to it, it would not follow that the world does not extend beyond it through other bodies unknown to us. (5) Whether heaven moves or earth will be determined in this treatise. But supposing that heaven moves, this would not serve the purpose of the antagonist, who, if its bounds were established, would necessarily conceive other bodies beyond that starry heaven. (6) That this indefiniteness of the world takes nothing from the perfection of God will also be shown in its proper place.

units.la: CXXXI. Inst. (R. A. p. 70.)
units.tr: CXXXI. Inst. (R. A. p. 70.)

units.la: Ex meis verbis præcedente articulo posse meam prævaricationem manibus palpare lectorem, eo quod tum dicam, Cartesium ex Ideâ Mundi probare in ipso nullos extensionis fines posse reperiri, non posisim Cartesio attribuere, quod suam ignorantiam prositeatur.
units.tr: From my words in the preceding article, the reader can feel my prevarication with his hands, because I then said that Descartes proves from the idea of the world that no limits of extension can be found in it, which I cannot attribute to Descartes, since he professes his ignorance.

units.la: Resp. ex responsione prima art. præc. apparet, me distinguere duas quæstiones, nempe, an Mundus sit Indefinitus, & an sit Infinitus: posteriorem concernunt ista mea verba, An extensionis sua fines habeat Mundus nec ne Cartesium non asseverare: priorem verba sequentia, quibus dico, Cartesium ex Idea Mundi probare, se nullos in Mundo fines posse reperire, ac proinde statuere Mundum Indefinitum.
units.tr: Reply: From my first answer to the preceding article it is clear that I distinguish two questions, namely whether the world is indefinite and whether it is infinite. My words, whether the world has limits to its extension or not, Descartes does not assert, concern the latter. The following words, in which I say that Descartes proves from the idea of the world that he can find no limits in it, and therefore holds the world to be indefinite, concern the former.

units.la: CXXXII. Ad locum Quartum observatur (R. St. p. 83.) Cartesium vidisse incommoda, quibus sententia sua ex scriptura posset premi, ideo ne Infinitus hic sums mundus cum innumeris mundis Metrodori, Anaximandri, Anaximenis, Archelai, Aristarchi, Xenophontis, Diogenis, Leucippi, Epicuri & Anaxarchi (cum quibus magnam affinitatem habet) erroribus in fide accenseretur, ea commentum esse, per quae vel perspicacissimos oculos configere se posse speravit. Nam loco dicto pro substantiæ corporeæ universitate supponere stellas fixas quas videmus, pro percipere nobis obtrudere suspicari, pro esse dicere posse esse, imo τὸ vere mutate in fortè, quod profecto hominis sit posticum sibi quærentis, quo elabatur, si quando hanc suam sententiam continuerit examinari. Resp. 1. Cartesius loco quarto, hoc est P. III. 29. non supponit pro substantia corporea universitate stellas fixas, sed eodem modo ac in priori ait, mentem talis esse natura, ut nullos in Mundo limites agnoscat, quemadmodum art. 21. Pars. II. dixerat: sed asserit, forte esse ultra stellas fixas alia corpora, respectu quorum dici possint MOVERI, quod quia non est certum, per forte exprimitur, sed non dicit forte ESSE alia corpora, quod quidem ex indefinita extensione necessario sequitur: esse autem posse corpora ultra stellas fixas, etsi respectu eorum moveri dici non possint, satis puto manifestum: eò pertinet etiam suspicari Cartesii & posse esse. Videat attentus Lector verba art. 29. III. partis, & nihil à me fingi conspiciet. 1. Tantum abest, ut Cartesii sententia affinitatem habeat cum sententiâ eorum, qui infinitos mundos asserebant, ut potius δις δις παντων ab eâ distet; quae enim convenientia eorum, qui infinitos Mundos non tantùm esse posse, sed etiam jàm esse asserunt, cum iis, qui unicum mundum existere ita agnoscunt, ut ne quidem plures esse posse statuant, quae sententia est Cartesii eorumque, qui eum hic sequuntur. 3. quis error in fide, si statuas, mundum esse indefinitae magnitudinis, ejusque finem à nobis comprehendi non posse, esse possit, equidem non video: monstretur ille si fieri potest.
units.tr: CXXXII. On the fourth passage it is observed (R. St. p. 83.) that Descartes saw the difficulties to which his opinion could be exposed from Scripture, and so, lest this infinite world be counted among the errors against the faith along with the innumerable worlds of Metrodorus, Anaximander, Anaximenes, Archelaus, Aristarchus, Xenophanes, Diogenes, Leucippus, Epicurus and Anaxarchus (with whom it has great affinity), he devised contrivances by which he hoped to escape even the keenest eyes. For in the passage cited, he supposes the fixed stars we see to be the whole of corporeal substance; instead of "we perceive," he thrusts on us "we suspect"; instead of "is," he says "can be"; indeed, he changes "truly" into "perhaps." This is surely the trick of a man looking for a back door through which to slip away if his opinion is ever examined. Resp. 1. In the fourth passage, that is III.29, Descartes does not suppose the fixed stars to be the whole of corporeal substance. Rather, in the same way as in the earlier passage, he says that the mind is of such a nature that it recognises no limits in the world, as he had said in art. 21 of Part II. But he asserts that perhaps beyond the fixed stars there are other bodies, with respect to which they can be said to move. Because this is not certain, it is expressed by "perhaps," but he does not say "perhaps there ARE other bodies," which indeed follows necessarily from indefinite extension. That there can be bodies beyond the fixed stars, even if with respect to them they cannot be said to move, I think is clear enough; to this also pertain Descartes' "suspect" and "can be." Let the attentive reader look at the words of art. 29 of Part III, and he will see that I have invented nothing. 2. So far is Descartes' view from having affinity with the view of those who asserted infinite worlds that it is rather diametrically opposed [ἐκ διαμέτρου]. For what agreement is there between those who assert that infinite worlds not only can be but already are, and those who recognise a single world existing in such a way that they do not even allow that several could be? That is Descartes' view, and the view of those who follow him here. 3. What error against the faith there is, if you hold that the world is of indefinite magnitude and that its end cannot be grasped by us, I indeed do not see. Let it be shown, if it can be.

units.la: CXXXIII. Inst. 1. (R. A. p. 59.)
units.tr: CXXXIII. Inst. 1. (R. A. p. 59.)

units.la: Illam meam interpretationem pendere à mutatione interpunctionis Cartesiana, interpungere enim cum post corpora.
units.tr: That my interpretation depends on a change in the Cartesian punctuation, for he punctuates with a stop after "corpora."

units.la: Resp. Et ego idem facio, atque in priori editione feceram; sed dixi verba illa, (ad qua comparata terra quiescere) conjungenda esse cum antecedentibus, forte esse alia corpora, ut sensus sit: Ultra stellas fixas forte esse alia corpora, respectu quorum terra posset dici quiescere, ubi sanè Cartesius non de ipsis corporibus, sed de quiete terrae respectu stellarum fixarum dubitanter loquitur.
units.tr: Reply: I do the same as I did in the earlier edition. But I said that those words, (to which, compared, the earth rests), are to be joined with the preceding words, perhaps there are other bodies, so that the sense is: beyond the fixed stars there are perhaps other bodies, with respect to which the earth could be said to rest. Here, certainly, Descartes is speaking doubtfully not about the bodies themselves but about the rest of the earth with respect to the fixed stars.

units.la: CXXXIV. Inst. 2. (R. A. p. 59.)
units.tr: CXXXIV. Inst. 2. (R. A. p. 59.)

units.la: Rationibus convinci posse, quod Cartesius verbis, de quibus controvertitur, dubitet de existentia aliorum corporum ultra stellas fixas. 1. quia vulgi opinio sit non esse ibi alia corpora, & hinc non putet eas illorum respectu non posse dici moveri, quia videlicet nulla sint. 2. Idem evincere totam Cartesii argumentationem, qua procedat ab immensitate Dei, qua nihil facias ad id ut quiescere dicatur terra, stellae autem moveri respectu hujus vel illius corporis, sed ad ipsam corporum illorum possibilitatem.
units.tr: It can be shown by reasons that Descartes, in the words under dispute, doubts the existence of other bodies beyond the fixed stars. 1. Because it is the common opinion that there are no other bodies there, and so he does not think that with respect to them the stars cannot be said to move, since there are clearly none. 2. The same thing proves that his whole argument, which proceeds from the immensity of God, does nothing toward the claim that the earth is said to rest and the stars to move with respect to this or that body, but rather bears on the very possibility of those bodies.

units.la: Resp. ut evidentissime appareat mens Cartesii, verba ultima art. 29. P. III. paraphrastice exponamus. Ac deinde, juxta usum vulgi, inquit, fiuncndo motum, eo modo, quo supra dictum est, ut à quibusdam corporibus tanquam quam immobilibus spectatis aliorum loca determines, non est cur Philosophus fixas consideret ut immotas potius quam terram, nisi quod putet ille Philosophus, ultra ipsas illas stellas fixas non esse ulla alia corpora à quibus separentur, & quorum respectu stella fixa dici possint moveri, terra autem quiescere, illo sensu quo dicit terram moveri respectu fixarum. Atqui hoc putare est à ratione alienum, quam Philosophus debet sequi. Cum enim mens nostra sit talis naturæ, ut nullos in mundo limites cognoscat, quisquis ad immensitatem Dei sensumque nostrorum infirmitatem attendet, ut ex ea novit, ultra stellas Fixas esse alia corpora, quod ex antecedentibus potuit colligi, ita ex ea probabiliter concludet & suspicabitur, esse illa alia corpora talia, ad quæ comparata terra quiescere, ipsa autem omnes simul moveri dici possint, quam suspicari nulla talia posse esse, quod facere debent ii, qui hoc sensu afferent terram moveri. Ex quibus patet, 1. Cartesium loqui de acceptione motus ex opinione vulgi, non vero hic refutare vulgi opinionem, quâ statuat, non esse ultra stellas fixas alia corpora. Tantum dicit, eos qui considerare velint fixas ut immobiles, & ab iis velint motum Terræ sive variationem ejus loci determinare, debere supponere, ultra stellas fixas nulla esse alia corpora, respectu quorum illæ possint dici moveri, cum tamen contrarium sit probabilius. 2. Ex Immensitate Dei conjunctâ cum naturâ nostræ mentis, quæ nullos in mundo limites agnoscit, certò colligendum esse, dari alia corpora ultra stellas fixas, sed tantum probabiliter, quod eorum respectu terra possit dici quiescere, stellæ verò fixæ moveri. Manet ergo, sententiam Cartesii fuisse, Mundum constituere & asserereIndefinitum, ita ut quoscunque ejus limites supponamus, semper tamen ultra eos aliquam extensionem concipiendam reperiamus.
units.tr: Reply: So that Descartes' mind may appear most evidently, let us paraphrase the final words of art. 29 of Part III. And then, he says, following the common usage in attributing motion, in the way said above, so that you determine the places of others as seen from certain bodies taken as immobile, there is no reason why the philosopher should consider the fixed stars as immobile rather than the earth, unless the philosopher thinks that beyond those fixed stars there are no other bodies from which they are separated, and with respect to which a fixed star can be said to move and the earth to rest, in the sense in which he says the earth moves with respect to the fixed stars. But to think this is foreign to reason, which the philosopher ought to follow. For since our mind is of such a nature that it recognises no limits in the world, whoever attends to the immensity of God and the weakness of our senses will, as he knows from that, that there are other bodies beyond the fixed stars, which could be gathered from what precedes; so from it he will probably conclude and suspect that there are those other bodies, of such a kind that, compared with them, the earth rests while they all together can be said to move; rather than suspect that there could be no such bodies, which those must do who in this sense assert that the earth moves. From these things it is clear: 1. that Descartes is speaking of the sense of motion according to the opinion of the common people, and is not here refuting the common opinion by which one holds that there are no other bodies beyond the fixed stars. He says only that those who wish to consider the fixed stars as immobile, and from them wish to determine the motion or change of place of the earth, must suppose that beyond the fixed stars there are no other bodies with respect to which those stars could be said to move, although the contrary is more probable. 2. From the immensity of God, joined with the nature of our mind, which recognises no limits in the world, it must certainly be concluded that there are other bodies beyond the fixed stars, but only probably that, with respect to them, the earth can be said to rest and the fixed stars to move. It remains, then, that Descartes' view was that the world is indefinite, and he asserts this, so that whatever limits we suppose, we always find some extension to be conceived beyond them.

units.la: CXXXV. Inst. 3. (R. A. p. 57.)
units.tr: CXXXV. Inst. 3. (R. A. p. 57.)

units.la: Ubi Cartesius negaverit plures mundos esse posse, fateor me ignorare &c. Ad rem, de qua agitur, dico, & magnam differentiam esse inter hasce duas opiniones, & magnam tamen affinitatem in eo videlicet, quod illa statuit infinitum numero, hæc vero Infinitum extensione, utrumque autem eadem difficultates patitur.
units.tr: Where Descartes denies that several worlds can exist, I confess I do not know, etc. As to the matter under discussion, I say that there is a great difference between these two opinions, and yet a great affinity between them, namely that the one holds the world infinite in number, while the other holds it infinite in extension; yet both suffer the same difficulties.

units.la: Resp. Ubi Cartesius statuat, non posse esse pluses mundos vel ex Indice potuisses cognoscere. Vide ergo P. II. 22. 2. Objectio vel Censura circa hunc locum qui nunc examinatur, dixerat tantum, magnam esse affinitatem inter has duas sententias, nunc verò cum maxima differentia fuerit ostensa, conceditur & hæc, quæ quomodo cum illâ magnâ affinitate consistere queat non appareat. Nec verò ea magna affinitas inter sententiam Cartesii & eorum qui infinitos mundos asserebant, est ostensa, cum falsum sit Cartesium infinitum extensione statuisse. Difficultates, quibus premitur Cartesii sententia, suo loco videbimus ablatas.
units.tr: Reply. Where Descartes holds that more worlds cannot exist, you could have learned this from the Index. See therefore P. II. 22. 2. The objection or censure on this passage now under examination had said only that there is a great affinity between these two opinions; but now that a great difference has been shown, this too is conceded, though how it can be consistent with that great affinity does not appear. Nor indeed has that great affinity between the opinion of Descartes and that of those who asserted infinite worlds been shown, since it is false that Descartes held the world to be infinite in extension. The difficulties by which Descartes' opinion is burdened we will see removed in their proper place.

units.la: CXXXVI. Inst. 4. (R. A. p. 57.) De Infinito, deque eo, quod mente comprehendere non possumus, hic non agi, sed de Infinito & quidem simpliciter, id enim me hactenus ab omni incommodo liberare conatum fuisse, item de eo quod cognoscimus &c. Hanc sententiam erroneam in fide esse, si illa de Mundi innumerii sit talis. Utramque enim exhaurire omnipotentiam Dei.
units.tr: CXXXVI. Inst. 4. (R. A. p. 57.) Concerning the Infinite, and that which we cannot comprehend with the mind, this is not the point at issue, but the Infinite simply; for I have hitherto tried to free myself from every inconvenience by this, likewise concerning that which we know, etc. This opinion is erroneous in faith, if that about an innumerable world be of such a kind, for each would exhaust the omnipotence of God.

units.la: Resp. Imò verò de Indefinito agi debet, cùm sententia Cartesii à te impugnetur, quæ non est, mundum esse Infinitum, sed Indefinitum. 2. Quamvis nullum incommodum deprehendam in sententiâ, quæ statuit mundum esse Infinitum, hoc est, quamvis nullas videam rationes, quæ contrarium probent, tamen cum & nullæ sint validæ rationes, quæ probent Mundum Infinitum, censeo hic neutram sententiam asserendam, sed de re dubiâ & incertâ assensum cohibendum. 3. Quid de mundo agnoscamus artic. 120. hujus capitis & seqq. ostendimus. 4. An verò hæc sententia de Indefinitate Mundi Omnipotentiam Dei exhauriat in sequentibus videbimus.
units.tr: Reply. Indeed, it must rather be understood of the Indefinite, since the opinion of Descartes is what you attack, which is not that the world is Infinite but Indefinite. 2. Although I find no inconvenience in the opinion that holds the world to be Infinite, that is, although I see no reasons proving the contrary, yet since there are also no valid reasons proving the world infinite, I judge that neither opinion should be asserted here, but that assent should be withheld on a matter that is doubtful and uncertain. 3. What we acknowledge concerning the world we have shown in article 120 of this chapter and those that follow. 4. Whether this opinion of the indefiniteness of the world exhausts the omnipotence of God, we will see in what follows.

units.la: CAPUT X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: Demonstratur sententia Cartesii de Mundi Indefinitate.
units.tr: The opinion of Descartes concerning the indefiniteness of the world is demonstrated.

units.la: CXXXVII. Iltam Mundi Indefinitatem demonstramus ex Idea Mundi, quam de eo omnes omninò homines habent, si modo ad eam attendere velint. Talis enim hic est natura nostræ mentis, ut ubicunque mundi fines supponamus, semper ulterius extensi quid concipiamus, atque ita fines, quos mundo dedimus, eo ipso iterum auferamus, ut quilibet apud se ipsum poterit experiri. Hinc enim enatus est iste spatiorum imaginariorum Conceptus, qui apud plerosque invaluit, ut Localitatem soleant explicare per spatium imaginarium in infinitum protensum in Longum, Latum & Profundum, ex quo tamen potius Mundi Indefinitatem extensionem elicere deberent. Atque hoc argumentum præcipuè isto nititur fundamento, quod, cum omnis clara perceptio sit à Deo, si nihil ultra id quod percepimus judicemus, non possimus falli: cum ergo hic inveniamus apud nos extensionis ideam tantam, ut nullos ejus terminos queamus concipere (in quâ extensione corporis naturam consistere, stere, ut eâ positâ corpus sit ponendum, sublatâ tollendum, à Cartesio abunde est demonstratum) consentaneum est rationi, ut nullos terminos non cognitos Mundo attribuamus, sed cum potius ut Indefinitum nobis repræsentemus.
units.tr: CXXXVII. We demonstrate this indefiniteness of the world from the idea of the world that all men without exception have of it, if only they are willing to attend to it. For it is so much the nature of our mind that wherever we suppose the limits of the world to be, we always conceive something extended further, and so by that very act we remove again the limits we gave the world, as anyone can experience for himself. From this arises that conception of imaginary space which has taken hold among most people, so that they usually explain location by an imaginary space extended to infinity in length, breadth and depth; from which, however, they ought rather to derive the extension of the world's indefiniteness. And this argument rests chiefly on this foundation: since every clear perception comes from God, if we judge nothing beyond what we perceive, we cannot be deceived. Since, then, we find in ourselves an idea of extension so great that we cannot conceive any limits to it (and it has been amply demonstrated by Descartes that the nature of body consists in this extension, so that when it is posited body must be posited, and when it is removed body must be removed), it is consistent with reason that we attribute to the world no limits that are not known to us, but rather represent it to ourselves as indefinite.

units.la: CXXXVIII. Exc. 1. Quod si quis exciperet, hunc conceptum oriri ex præjudicio & errore vulgi, concipientu mundum collocatum tanquam urbem in aliqua planitie; huic Resp. 1. Conceptus vulgi oriri solent ex præjudiciis sensuum & infantiæ (ita vulgus cœlo tribuit extremitates, ibi, ubi se terminat visus; sic putat, se in medio mundi sive Terræ habitare, quia undique circumspiciens se in medio Horizontis reperit,) at hujus sententiæ origo præjudiciis sensuum & Infantiæ adscribi nequit, cum in Infantia de Mundi magnitudine aut finibus non soleamus cogitare, neque etiam sensus huic sententiæ occasionem præbere potuerint. Quinimo 2. vulgus ex sensuum ductu contrarium potius statuit, & fines mundo solet assignare ibi, ubi est cœlum stellatum, quia ultra stellas nulla corpora sensu deprehendere potest.
units.tr: CXXXVIII. Objection 1. But if someone should object that this conception arises from the prejudice and error of the common people, who conceive the world as placed like a city on some plain; to this I reply: 1. The conceptions of the common people usually arise from prejudices of the senses and of infancy (thus the common people assign extremities to the heavens where sight comes to an end; so they think they dwell in the middle of the world or Earth, because looking about on every side they find themselves in the middle of the horizon). But the origin of this opinion cannot be ascribed to prejudices of the senses or of infancy, since in infancy we do not usually think about the magnitude or limits of the world, nor could the senses have provided occasion for this opinion. Indeed, 2. the common people, following the guidance of the senses, rather hold the contrary, and usually assign limits to the world where the starry heaven is, because beyond the stars the senses can detect no bodies.

units.la: CXXXIX. Inst. 1. At etiamsi hic conceptus non sit ortus ex præjudicio Infantiæ, vel sensuum, potest esse Conceptus Nihili, quod in Conceptu nostro solet Ens reale imitari. Quemadmodum solet Nihilum concipi, tanquam vasta solitudo, longe lateque extensa.
units.tr: CXXXIX. Objection 2. But even if this conception has not arisen from prejudice of infancy or of the senses, it may be a conception of nothing, which in our thinking usually imitates a real being, just as nothing is commonly conceived as a vast solitude extended far and wide.

units.la: Resp. Nihili Conceptus fit & fieri debet conveniens, per negationem Entis, ut Ne Hilum concipiamus; at ob summam Nihili Imperfectionem fit, ut mens ei non diu inhærere possit (nullâ enim perfectione mentem afficit, cum ipsum nullâ habeat) sed mox ad Conceptum Entis transiliat, eique Nihili conceptum conformare velit; hunc autem conceptum, quo semper ultra quoscunque fines Mundi positos aliquid concipimus, non esse Nihili, vel exinde manifestum fit, quod, quando volumus ultra Mundi fines à nobis positos Nihil concipere, convenienti & legitimo conceptu, fieri non possit, quin semper extensionem adjungamus Mundo ultra fines quos assignavimus, cum ipsum Nihilum sine extensione facilè concipi possit. 2. Non potest autem dici, hunc Conceptum à nobis esse fictum, similemque conceptui equi alati. Nam quæ sic à Mente sunt ficta, etiam ab eâ possunt dividi, quemadmodum quàm facile possum cogitare equum alatum, tam facile etiam equum non alatum concipere licet, quod hic fieri nequit. Mundum enim sine indefinitâ extensione, id est, cum terminis & finibus concipere non possum, sed semper ultra illos fines aliqua extensio porrò concipienda occurrit.
units.tr: Reply. A conception of nothing is formed, and ought to be formed, suitably by the negation of being, so that we conceive nothing at all, as a mere absence. But because nothing is so very imperfect, the mind cannot long cleave to it (for it affects the mind with no perfection, since it has none), but soon leaps over to the conception of being, and wants to shape its conception of nothing to match. That this conception, by which we always conceive something beyond whatever limits of the world are posited, is not a conception of nothing, is clear from this: when we wish to conceive nothing beyond the limits of the world we have posited, this cannot be done by a suitable and legitimate conception without our always adding extension to the world beyond the limits we assigned, since nothing itself can easily be conceived without extension. 2. Nor can it be said that this conception is fictitious on our part, and similar to the conception of a winged horse. For things thus feigned by the mind can also be separated from it: just as easily as I can think of a winged horse, so easily can I conceive a horse without wings; but this cannot be done here. For I cannot conceive the world without indefinite extension, that is, with terms and limits; rather, some further extension always presents itself to be conceived beyond those limits.

units.la: CXL. Inst. 2. (R. A. p. 15.) Si hic conceptus non est à præjudiciis Infan-tia, tia, neque de Nihilo, neque fictus; Ergo verus est, id est vere Infinitum corpus, aut ut Cartesium loquentem audiamus, infinitam extensionem materiâ repletam, ac consequenter infinitum Mundum credere oportet: quod & patere, inquit, expressu meis verbis art. 2. hujus capitis in fine, hoc est praecedente articulo 139. Mundum enim sine indefinitâ extensione, id est, cum terminis & finibus concipere non possum, sed semper ultra illes fines aliqua extensio porro concipienda occurrit. Ubi ex vi oppositionis evidens fit, indefinitam extensionem mihi esse extensionem sine terminis & finibus, id est infinitam.
units.tr: CXL. Objection 3. (R. A. p. 15.) If this conception is not from the prejudices of infancy, nor of nothing, nor fictitious, then it is true, that is, a truly infinite body; or, to let Descartes speak, an infinite extension filled with matter, and consequently we must believe in an infinite world. This, he says, is evident from my words at the end of article 2 of this chapter, that is, in the preceding article 139: "For I cannot conceive the world without indefinite extension, that is, with terms and limits; rather, some further extension always presents itself to be conceived beyond those limits." Whence, by the force of the opposition, it becomes evident that indefinite extension, to me, is extension without terms and limits, that is, infinite.

units.la: Resp. Conceptus ille verus est Indefiniti corporis, non verè Infiniti, quale mundum non statuo. 2. Cartesius in locis suprà visis non sic loquitur, uti hic loquens introducitur, nec memini me illam formulam in ipsius scriptis observasse. 3. Mea vero verba habere sensum, quem tribuit eis adversarius, non possunt. Nam quamvis non possim mundum concipere cum terminis & finibus, eos tamen propterea non ab eo removeo, sed an habeat nec ne in medio relinquo, dico tantum, naturam humanae mentis esse talem, ut nullos in Mundi conceptu reperire possit. Potest enim aliquid inesse alicui rei, quod tamen ego non invenio; sic multa triangulo inesse possunt, quae tamen in eo nec ego nec alius forte invenit. Indefinita ergo extensio est, non Infinita, in qua nullos possum concipere fines & terminos; Infinita, in quâ etiam positivè cognosco, nullos esse vel esse posse.
units.tr: Reply. That conception is true of an indefinite body, not truly of an infinite one, and I do not assert the world to be infinite. 2. Descartes, in the passages seen above, does not speak as the speaker here is introduced, nor do I remember having observed that formula in his writings. 3. But my words cannot bear the sense the opponent gives them. For although I cannot conceive the world with terms and limits, I do not therefore remove them from it; whether it has them or not I leave undecided, saying only that the nature of the human mind is such that it cannot find any in the conception of the world. For something may belong to a thing which I nevertheless do not find; many properties may belong to a triangle which perhaps neither I nor anyone else finds in it. Therefore the extension is indefinite, not infinite, when I can conceive no limits or terms in it; it is infinite when I positively know that there are none, or that there can be none.

units.la: CXLI. Exc. 2.
units.tr: CXLI. Exc. 2.

units.la: At si Deus annihilaret omnia, totum nempe mundum, omnia mundi corpora, exceptâ unicâ Terrâ; vel etiam, si Deus solam Terram creasset, illa revera esset finita, prout jam est, rotunda quippe, interim tamen nos semper aliquid ultra fuissemus concepturi, quemadmodum nunc facimus, ut ultra quoscunque fines Mundo à nobis assignatos aliquid extensi imaginaremur. Unde non sequitur, quia nostra mens aliquid extensi ultra quoscunque Mundi fines concipit, etiam tale aliquid ultra esse, sed potius hunc mentis nostra conceptum praejudicio alicui esse adscribendum.
units.tr: But if God were to annihilate everything, namely the whole world and all its bodies except the one Earth; or even if God had created only the Earth, which would indeed be finite, as it now is, being round, we would still always conceive something beyond it, just as we now do, imagining some extension beyond whatever limits we assign to the world. Hence it does not follow that, because our mind conceives something extended beyond any limits of the world, such a thing actually exists beyond them; rather, this conception of our mind should be ascribed to some prejudice.

units.la: Resp. Quid posita Terrae solius creatione tantae magnitudinis & figurae, quantae nunc est, aut annihilatione omnium mundi corporum, exceptâ terrâ, concessâ, futurum fuisset in nostrâ mente, nos equidem ignoramus, sive non cognoscimus experimentaliter, quia talem ideam nos nunc non habemus; sufficit ad nostrae sententiae probationem, quod nunc intra nos talem habeamus extensionis ideam, ut ejus nullos fines invenire queamus. Quod si ergo Deo vel omnia corpora in Mundo praeter Terram annihilare liberet, vel solam Terram creare placuisset, tantâ tanta magnitudine & figura praeditam, quanta jam est, etiam proculdubio Terrae finitam Ideam nobis inditurus fuisset, ne fallerentur, saltem nunc id nos concipere non posse certum est. Atque haec sunt Exceptiones, quae a nobis ipsis formatae aliquando remoram injecerunt.
units.tr: Reply. As for what would have happened in our mind if the creation of the Earth alone, of such size and shape as it now has, or the annihilation of all bodies in the world except the Earth, were granted, we indeed do not know this, or do not know it by experience, because we do not now have such an idea. It suffices to prove our opinion that we now have within us such an idea of extension that we cannot find its limits. But if God had been pleased to annihilate all bodies in the world except the Earth, or to create the Earth alone endowed with the size and shape it now has, he would without doubt have implanted in us a finite idea of the Earth, lest we be deceived. That we cannot now conceive this is certain. These are the Exceptions which, formed by ourselves, have at some time put an obstacle in the way.

units.la: CXLII. Inst. 1. (R. A. p. 16.)
units.tr: CXLII. Inst. 1. (R. A. p. 16.)

units.la: Si in hoc casu terra idea finita erit, Ergo vi oppositionis Mundum sive Universum me profiteri Infinitum, & Infinitam ejus ideam statuere.
units.tr: If in this case the idea of the earth will be finite, then by force of your opposition I profess the world or universe to be infinite, and assert its idea to be infinite.

units.la: Resp. Ego vero tuam sequelam non admitto. Dico quidem, me non habere Mundi Ideam finitam (intellige Objective, nam subjective & formaliter omnes Ideae in mente nostra sunt finitae) sed inde non sequitur, illam ergo Ideam esse Infinitam, cum detur tertium, nempe Idea Indefinita. Itaque quoniam ex Idea judicium formo, assero, non Mundum esse Finitum, nec Mundum esse Infinitum, sed cum esse Indefinitum.
units.tr: Reply. I do not admit your inference. I indeed say that I do not have a finite idea of the world (understood objectively; for subjectively and formally all ideas in our mind are finite). But it does not follow from this that the idea is therefore infinite, since a third option is given, namely the idea of the indefinite. Therefore, since I form my judgment from the idea, I assert that the world is neither finite nor infinite, but indefinite.

units.la: CXLIII. Inst. 2. (R. A. p. 17.)
units.tr: CXLIII. Inst. 2. (R. A. p. 17.)

units.la: Cum ais, certum esse, nunc nos id concipere non posse, de mundo videlicet, quod tum conciperemus de Terra, quaero quos intelligas per NOS? omnes ne homines? an Te & Cartesium cum paucis aliis? si omnes, res incredibilis tibi probanda incumbit, nempe omnes hactenus homines Mundum Infinitum putasse.
units.tr: When you say it is certain that we cannot now conceive this, namely of the world, which we would then conceive of the Earth, I ask: whom do you mean by "we"? All men? Or you and Descartes with a few others? If all men, an incredible thing lies on you to prove, namely that all men until now have thought the world infinite.

units.la: Resp. Omnes homines habere Ideam Mundi indefiniti exinde probo, quod semper ultra suppositam quamcunque Mundi extensionem ascendant, quod vel exinde patet, quia spatia imaginaria ultra mundum, cujus fines se posse concipere existimant, concipiunt extensa hoc est vere realia. Quod autem secundum Ideam suam non etiam mundum Indefinitum judicent, ipsorum aberrationi est adscribendum, quae fit, ut ad id, quod in seipsis reperiunt, non satis attendant. 2. Quemadmodum autem non sequitur: si omnes & singuli homines habent notitiam Dei insitam, quod contra Socinianos statuunt Reformati, Ergo etiam omnes & singuli homines Deum existere judicant, cum dari Atheos quosdam etiam speculative tales, qualis Vaninius, negari non possit: ita etiam non procedit, si omnes homines habent Mundi Ideam Indefinitam, Ergo etiam talem mundum judicant.
units.tr: Reply. I prove that all men have an idea of the indefinite world from the fact that they always go beyond any assumed extent of the world. This is evident from the fact that the imaginary spaces beyond the world, whose limits they think they can conceive, they conceive as extended, that is, as truly real. That they do not also judge the world to be indefinite in accordance with their idea must be ascribed to their error, which arises because they do not pay sufficient attention to what they find in themselves. 2. Just as it does not follow that, if all and each men have an innate knowledge of God (as the Reformed maintain against the Socinians), therefore all and each men judge that God exists, since it cannot be denied that some atheists exist even in theory, such as Vanini; so it does not follow, if all men have an indefinite idea of the world, that therefore they judge such a world to exist.

units.la: CXLIV. Inst. 3. (R. A. p. 19.)
units.tr: CXLIV. Inst. 3. (R. A. p. 19.)

units.la: Turpiter tibi contradicis, cum posito illo qui objiciebatur casu, quid futurum fuisset in tua mente, fateris, te IGNORARE, & tamen eodem paragrapho PROCULDUBIO terra finitam Ideam tibi indeudam fuisse affirmas: hac non cohaerent.
units.tr: You shamefully contradict yourself. When that case which was objected is posited, you admit that you DO NOT KNOW what would have happened in your mind; yet in the same paragraph you affirm that without doubt you would have been given a finite idea of the earth. These do not cohere.

units.la: Resp. Fateor, nos hoc ignorare, quatenus ejus Ideam nullam in menmente nunc reperimus, adeoque experimentaliter non cognoscimus; interim tamen, posito fiͤito isto casu, ex Veracitate Dei colligo, nos habituros fuisse Ideam Mundi finitam; quæ optimè inter se cohærent.
units.tr: Reply. I admit that we do not know this, insofar as we now find no idea of it in our mind, and so do not know it by experience. Meanwhile, however, if that case is posited, I gather from the veracity of God that we would have had a finite idea of the world. These cohere very well.

units.la: CXLV. Inst. 4. (B. p. 233.) Me nucleum argumenti non tangere: hæc enim, inquit, est quæstio: posita sola terra rotunda, ejus figura, quam nunc habet, annon spatium vacuum daretur, & concipi posset extensio imaginaria extra eam. Respondes, vos ignorare, quid futurum fuisset in nostra mente: at id non controvertitur, sed an implicaret contradictionem, extra illam Terram dari vacuum.
units.tr: CXLV. Inst. 4. (B. p. 233.) You do not touch the core of the argument. For this, he says, is the question: if only the earth were round, with the shape it now has, would not empty space be given, and an imaginary extension be conceivable outside it? You answer that you do not know what would have happened in our mind; but that is not in dispute. The question is whether it would imply a contradiction that empty space exists outside that Earth.

units.la: Resp. Quæstio est, an posita ista annihilatione cogniturí fuissemus Mundum finitum, ad quam respondeo: Cum non habeamus Ideam nisi Mundi Indefiniti, non vero Ideam Mundi finiti, nos ex ista idea id non posse cognoscere, adeoque id hoc respectu ignorare: sed tamen, posito isto casu, nos ex veracitate & infallibilitate divinâ colligere posse, Deum nobis isto casu inditurū fuisse Mundi ideam finitam, ut ita nihil ulterius conciperemus, adeoque, non ad spatium vacuum & extensionem merè imaginariam delaberemur. At Adversarius, etiam posita Terra rotunda, dicit, se tamen habiturū esse ideam ultra eam spatia imaginaria concipiendi, adeoque Mundi Indefiniti, prout necessario hoc exinde consequitur; quo posito, idea non correspondebit ipsi rei, adeoque si esset à Deo, ut supponi debet, Deus non posset non causa erroris dici.
units.tr: Reply. The question is whether, given this annihilation, we would have come to know the world as finite. To this I answer: since we have no idea except of the indefinite world, and not of a finite world, we cannot know from that idea whether it is finite, and so in this respect we do not know it. Yet, given this case, we can gather from the divine veracity and infallibility that God would have implanted in us an idea of a finite world in this case, so that we would conceive nothing further, and so would not slip into empty space and a merely imaginary extension. But our opponent, even granting the round earth, says that he would still have an idea of imaginary spaces beyond it, and so an idea of the indefinite world, as necessarily follows from this. Given this, the idea would not correspond to the thing itself, and so, if it came from God, as it must be supposed to, God could not avoid being called the cause of error.

units.la: CXLVI. Sed adhuc aliæ nobis proponuntur solvendæ quæstiones, posita sola terra rotunda, & reliquorum corporum annihilatione, nimirum, an Deus tum non posset aliam Terram ejusdem figura creare? si non, cur non in illo nihilo? &c. B. p. 233. quos nodos solvendos esse putat.
units.tr: CXLVI. But other questions are still put before us to be solved, given only the round earth and the annihilation of the remaining bodies, namely: would God then be unable to create another earth of the same shape? If not, why not in that nothing? etc. B. p. 233., which he thinks are knots to be untied.

units.la: Resp. 1. Cùm nunc habeamus Mundi Ideam Indefinitam, non possumus talia percipere, adque tales quæstiones respondere, sed prout antea dictum est, si Deus mundum creasset finitum, etiam ejus finitam Ideam inditurum fuisse, ex ejus veracitate colligimus. 2. Adde, quod prima quæstio sit plane inepta. Nempe supponitur annihilatio omnium corporum exceptâ Terrâ; non ergo potest quæri nisi ineptè, An Deus tum, (hoc est, terra non annihilata, sed aliis omnibus corporibus) non posset aliam terram ejusdem figura creare? Si enim terra supponatur non annihilata, quomodo quæstio institui potest de alia in ejus locum creanda?
units.tr: Reply. 1. Since we now have an idea of the indefinite world, we cannot perceive such things or answer such questions. But, as was said before, if God had created the world finite, we infer from his veracity that he would have implanted in us also a finite idea of it. 2. Add that the first question is plainly absurd. It is supposed that all bodies except the Earth are annihilated; therefore it can only be asked absurdly: Could God then (that is, with the earth not annihilated but all other bodies gone) not create another earth of the same shape? For if the earth is supposed not to be annihilated, how can the question be raised about another to be created in its place?

units.la: CXLVII. Exc. 3. B. p. 234. Indefinita, quam vobis formatis idea, non est à Deo, sed ab erroneo spiritu illo Cartesii, qui omnes conceptus suos illo palliavit velo, quod nisi veri essent, Deus ut illorum inditor, deceptor habendus esset, quasi quasi vero Deus ut justus Judex non aliquando immitteret hominibus spiritum erroneum, ut illis, de quibus Ezech. XIV. 9. & quasi non Cartesium, hominem superbum, qui jactitabat, posse se attenta & saepius iterata meditatione efficere, ut habitum quendam NON ERRANDI acquirat, imò fieri plane NON POSSIT, ut erret, Medit. 4. p. 61. etiam in Philosophicis in perversum sensum tradere potuerit, & revera tradiderit, cum in materiis fidei nec verbo Dei, nec sanae rationi audire dignatus fuerit. Hunc sequimini, non ductum verbi Dei: ac proinde, quam dudum loco stellarum fixarum luminis Prophetici illum Planetam sequendum vobis proposuit is, vos non errare est impossibile.
units.tr: CXLVII. Exc. 3. B. p. 234. The indefinite idea which you have formed is not from God, but from that erroneous spirit of Descartes, who veiled all his conceptions with that cloak, so that, unless they were true, God, as their author, would have to be regarded as a deceiver; as if God, as a just Judge, would never send an erroneous spirit to men, as in Ezekiel 14:9; and as if Descartes, a proud man who boasted that by careful and often repeated meditation he could bring it about that he acquired a certain habit of NOT TO ERR, and indeed that it was completely IMPOSSIBLE for him to err (Med. 4, p. 61), had not been able, even in philosophical matters, to lead others into a perverse sense, and indeed had led them, since in matters of faith he did not deign to listen either to the Word of God or to sound reason. You follow him, not the guidance of the Word of God; and therefore, since he long ago proposed to you that you should follow that planet instead of the fixed stars of prophetic light, it is impossible for you not to err.

units.la: Resp. Pudeat tantae virulentiae Ecclesiae pastorem, quem manifestum esse oportebat; & hujus asseverationis eum, qui Cartesium Scepticisimi accusat. Cartesius statuit: 1. Omnem perceptionem claram esse à Deo, utpote cum sit aliquid boni: 2. Omne judicium debere esse conforme isti claræ perceptioni. 3. Si judicium ei sit conforme, ut np. judicemus tale esse, quod revera ut tale clarè & distinctè percepimus, nos non posse falli, cùm ista clara perceptio sit à Deo, sitque Judicii usus legitimus, ut judicemus de clarè & distinctè perceptis. Quod si igitur posset fieri, ut legitimè adhibentes facultatem judicandi, quam Deus dedit bonam, falleremur, non posset ulla esse certitudo, nec excusari Deus à deceptione. Si enim potest fieri ut fallaris in iis, quæ clarè & distinctè percepisti, quæro per quid certus sis, te etiam nunc non falli, in omnibus iis, quæ hic scripsisti, quomodo certus eris ullam tuam propositionem à te prolatam in tuo libro, esse veram?
units.tr: Reply. The minister of the Church ought to be ashamed of such virulence, which should have been plainly evident to him, and of this assertion of his, when he accuses Descartes of scepticism. Descartes lays down: (1) that every clear perception comes from God, since it is something good; (2) that every judgement ought to conform to that clear perception; (3) that if the judgement conforms to it, so that we judge a thing to be such as we have clearly and distinctly perceived it to be, we cannot be mistaken, since that clear perception comes from God and it is the legitimate use of judgement to judge of what has been clearly and distinctly perceived. But if it could happen that, by legitimately exercising the faculty of judging, which God gave as a good one, we were deceived, there could be no certainty at all, and God could not be cleared of deception. For if you can be wrong about the things you have clearly and distinctly perceived, I ask by what means you can be certain that you are not wrong now, in everything you have written here, and how you will be certain that any proposition you have put forward in your book is true?

units.la: CXLVIII. Quæro porro cum cathedram Ecclesiasticam conscendis, an non clarè & distinctè percipias, id quod es enunciaturus nomine Dei, & tanquam articulum cognitu ad salutem necessarium, esse Dei verbum, & per consequens & tale judices: si non percepisti, nec judicas tale, quâ confidentiâ ergo tale dicis, & ut tanquam tale recipiant auditores, mones? si percepisti & tale judicas, quæro, an in illo tuo judicio possis falli? Si non, ergo certum est, nos non falli in iis quæ clarè & distinctè percepimus, aut nobis desaliam regulam, quâ de re aliquâ certi simus, revera ab hac diversam: si possis falli, eo ipso tibi in reliquis nullam habendam fidem asseres. Egregiè Neufeldt in Judicio de Fidei Catholicæ regula Catholica: Eum characterem, inquit, omnium nostrum animis impressit Veritatis aeternus praes, ut quoties aliquid clare perspicimus, sponte assentiamur, nec ullo modo dubitare queamus, quin sit verum. Vides ergo, Cartesium non jactitâsse, sed verè dixisse, posse se attenta & saepius iterata meditatione efficere, ut habitum quendam non Errandi acquirat. (np. si acquirat habitum judicio suo ita utendi, ut illud non ferat, nisi de clarè & distinctè perceptis, quod sanè possibile esse omnis debet confiteri, qui non omnem certitudinem è rebus humanis vult sublatam.) Item, quoties voluntatem in judiciis ferendis ita contineat, ut ad ea tantum se extendat, quæ illi clarè & distinctè ab intellectu proponuntur (quæ verba, an malitiosè nescio, omittis cum rem declarent) fieri plane non posse ut erret, quia omnis clara & distincta perceptio proculdubio est aliquid, ac proinde à nihilo esse non potest, sed necessario Deum Auctorem habet, Deum, inquam, illum summè perfectum, quem fallacem esse repugnat. Quo non negatur, Deum posse hominibus immittere spiritum erroneum, ita tamen, ut id salva ejus Veracitate & bonitate intelligatur, np. non ut indat facultatem, cujus legitimus usus ad errorem deducat, sed ut permittat, tales abuti facultate judicandi eamque extendere ultra ea quæ perceperunt, item, ut neget ipsis claram & distinctam perceptionem; item ut submînistret occasiones, quibus novit abusuros ad judicium suum extendendum ultra ea quæ perceperunt; &, si quæ alia.
units.tr: CXLVIII. I ask further: when you mount the Church's chair, do you not clearly and distinctly perceive that what you are about to announce in God's name, and as an article necessary to be known for salvation, is God's Word, and so judge it to be such? If you have not perceived this and do not judge it so, with what confidence then do you call it such, and warn your hearers to receive it as such? If you have perceived it and do judge it so, I ask whether you can be mistaken in that judgement of yours. If not, then it is certain that we are not mistaken about what we clearly and distinctly perceive, or else the rule by which we are certain of anything is different from this one. If you can be mistaken, you thereby admit that no trust is to be placed in you in the rest. Neufeldt, in his judgement on the Catholic rule of the Catholic faith, nobly says: The eternal Truth has impressed this mark on the minds of all of us, that whenever we clearly perceive something, we assent to it spontaneously, and cannot in any way doubt that it is true. You see, then, that Descartes did not boast, but spoke truly, in saying that by careful and often repeated meditation he could bring it about that he acquired a certain habit of not erring. (That is, if he acquired the habit of using his judgement in such a way that it gives its verdict only on what is clearly and distinctly perceived. Anyone who does not want all certainty removed from human affairs must admit that this is quite possible.) Likewise, whenever he restrains his will in making judgements so that it extends only to those things which the intellect sets before it clearly and distinctly (whether you omit these words maliciously or not I do not know, since they explain the matter), it is quite impossible for him to err, because every clear and distinct perception is undoubtedly something, and therefore cannot come from nothing, but necessarily has God as its author, that God, I say, who is supremely perfect, and whom it is contrary to reason to think deceitful. This does not deny that God can send a deceiving spirit into men, provided that this is understood in a way consistent with his truthfulness and goodness: not that he gives a faculty whose legitimate use leads to error, but that he permits men to abuse their faculty of judging and to extend it beyond what they have perceived; or that he withholds from them clear and distinct perception; or that he supplies occasions which he knows they will use to extend their judgement beyond what they have perceived; and whatever else there may be.

units.la: CXLIX. Exc. 4. (R. A. p. 26.) Si veritas hæc primo à Cartesio est eruta, ut fateris, falsè ergo dicu, talem esse naturam nostram, ut hanc videlicet veritatem agnoscamus, aut igitur aliam naturam habuit Cartesius quam omnes alii, aut alii etiam hanc veritatem, cum ejusdem natura essem, vidissent.
units.tr: CXLIX. Objection 4 (R. A. p. 26.) If this truth was first brought to light by Descartes, as you admit, then it is false to say that our nature is such that we recognise this truth. Either Descartes had a different nature from all others, or others too, being of the same nature, would have seen this truth.

units.la: Resp. Ego dixi, quod talis sit natura nostræ mentis, ut, si ad eam attendamus, Mundi Ideam in nobis reperiamus talem, ut ultra quoscunque ejus terminos suppositos, semper aliquid extensi nobis imaginemur, atque inde conceptum spatiorum Imaginariorum esse exortum. Sed in eo hucusque erratum, quod homines non advertentes, extensionem naturam Corporis constituere, putarint, se ultra illos suppositos fines tantum imaginarium quid, non reale percipere, quod Cartesius reale ostendit, eo ipso quo naturam corporis in extensione consistere demonstravit. Ex quo apparet, quomodo Cartesius istam veritatem, Mundum esse Indefinitum, alios latentem eruerit; nimirum, præjudiciis renunciando, atque ad ideas menti insitas attendendo, & claras ab obscuris discernendo, quod quia ab aliis non est factum, non mirum, eos hanc veritatem non agnovisse: (falsum enim est, me dixisse, talem esse naturam nostram, ut hanc veritatem agnoscamus.)
