Quemadmodum autem, si quis insignis Mathematicus multas proprietates in Triangulo, Quadrato, Cono &c. reperiat, quas alii non viderunt, non licet inferre: Aut aliam naturam cum habere quàm omnes alios, aut alios etiam, cum ejusdem naturæ essent, eandem veritatem visuros fuisse. Ita & hæc augmentatio inconsequens deprehenditur.
units.tr: Reply. I said that our mind is so constituted that, if we attend to it, we find in ourselves an idea of the world such that, beyond whatever limits are assumed, we always imagine something extended, and from this the concept of imaginary spaces arises. But hitherto men have gone wrong in this: not noticing that extension constitutes the nature of body, they have thought that beyond those assumed limits they perceive only something imaginary, not something real. Descartes showed that it is real, by the very fact that he demonstrated that the nature of body consists in extension. From this it is clear how Descartes brought to light that truth, the world is indefinite, which others had kept hidden: namely, by renouncing prejudices, attending to the ideas innate in the mind, and distinguishing clear from obscure. That others did not do this is no wonder, and it is no wonder that they did not recognise the truth. (For it is false that I said our nature is such that we recognise this truth.) But just as, if some distinguished mathematician discovers many properties of the triangle, the square, the cone and so on which others have not seen, it does not follow that he has a different nature from everyone else, or that others, being of the same nature, would have seen the same truth; so this increase is shown to be an inconsequence.

units.la: CL.* Exc. 5. (R. A. p. 13. 14.) Quaro an extremum illud quod concipis sit finitum an Infinitum? Si finitum fines mundo auferre non potes: si infinitum, nego id te clarè percipere, quod ipse ostendis, cum claram illam perceptionem explicas per impotentiam concipiendi illius spatii terminos, item per non cognitionem illorum terminorum, id est, mentis tua caliginem & ignorantiam pro clara luce nobis venditas.
units.tr: CL. Objection 5 (R. A. p. 13, 14.) I ask whether that extreme limit which you conceive is finite or infinite. If finite, you cannot remove limits from the world. If infinite, I deny that you clearly perceive it, as you yourself show, since you explain that clear perception by the inability to conceive the limits of that space, and by the failure to know those limits; that is, you pass off the darkness and ignorance of your mind as clear light to us.

units.la: Resp. 1. An mundus sit finitus an Infinitus, dico me nolle determinare, sed indefinitum me tantum statuere, propterea quod non ejus ut finiti nec ut infiniti habeam ideam, sed ut indefiniti, h. e. talem ejus extensionis in mente meâ delineationem, ut posita in ea & concepta quacunque quantitate, semper ulterius mihi aliquid restet sumendum, ita ut quaque versus me convertendo & ab hac terra elevando meam cogitationem in indefinitum, non possem tantam supponere extensionem, quin adhuc ulterioris sit in me Idea. 2. Falsum itaque est, me explicare illam perceptionem per impotentiam concipiendi illius spatii terminos, sed per positivam perceptionem quacunque extensione suppositâ extensionis ulterioris, adeoque, adversarium hic & alibi mentem meam vel non percepisse, vel se non percipere simulare.
units.tr: Reply. 1. Whether the world is finite or infinite, I say I do not wish to determine; I hold only that it is indefinite, because I have no idea of it either as finite or as infinite, but only as indefinite. That is, I have such a delineation of its extension in my mind that, whatever quantity is posited and conceived in it, something further always remains to be taken, so that, turning myself in every direction and lifting my thought from this earth into the indefinite, I could not suppose so great an extension that there is not in me an idea of a further one. 2. It is therefore false that I explain that perception by the inability to conceive the limits of that space; I explain it by a positive perception, namely, that whatever extension is supposed, a further extension is always there. So my opponent either has not perceived my mind here and elsewhere, or pretends not to perceive it.

units.la: CLI. Exc. 6. (M. p. 158.) ubi mihi tribuitur tale argumentum: Quicquid mens humana non potest percipere, id non est; sed Mundi fines mens humana non potest percipere: Ergo mundi fines nulli dantur, vel non sunt.
units.tr: CLI. Objection 6 (M. p. 158.) where this argument is attributed to me: Whatever the human mind cannot perceive, that is not; but the limits of the world the human mind cannot perceive. Therefore the limits of the world are nowhere, or do not exist.

units.la: Resp. Illa Conclusio non est mea, & Major falsa, ac plane contra nostram Philosophiam: verum si omnino in formam velis reducere meam argumentationem, hoc modo id fieri oportebat: Eo modo, quo mundi extensionem percipio, eo modo de mundo debeo judicare: At ita eam percipio, ut quacunque ejus quantitate suppositâ, semper ulterius extensi quid concipiam, E. etiam talem debeo judicare. Major nititur hoc fundamento, quòd cùm omnis clara perceptio sit à Deo, non possimus falli in judicio, si secundum illam judicium nostrum formemus. Hæc impugnanda fuissent. Ergo cum umbrà suâ luctatur, quando prolixè argumentum à se propositum, tanquam meum p. 159, 160. refutat.
units.tr: Reply. That conclusion is not mine, and the major premise is false and entirely contrary to our philosophy. But if you really want to reduce my argument to form, it should be done in this way: In whatever way I perceive the extension of the world, in that way I must judge of the world. But I perceive it in such a way that, whatever quantity of it is supposed, I always conceive something further extended; therefore I must judge it to be such. The major premise rests on this foundation: since every clear perception comes from God, we cannot be mistaken in judgement if we form our judgement according to it. This is what should have been attacked. So he wrestles with his own shadow when he refutes at length an argument proposed by himself, as if it were mine, pp. 159, 160.

units.la: 2. Minorem probo ex ipsa idea mundi, quam non ego tantum, sed quilibet habet sibi inditam, dummodo velit attendere. Nonne enim quilibet concipiendo mundum, suppositā quacunque ejus quantitate, semper ulterius terius aliquid extensi concipit? quod quidem etsi spatii imaginarii nomine insigniat, revera tamen, cum in eo extensionem realem concipiat, illi corporeitatem veram attribuit.
units.tr: 2. I prove the minor premise from the very idea of the world, which not only I but everyone has implanted in them, provided they are willing to attend to it. For does not everyone who conceives the world, with any quantity of it supposed, always conceive something further, something else extended? Although they label this with the name of imaginary space, nevertheless, since they conceive real extension in it, they attribute to it true corporeality.

units.la: CLII. Inst. 1. (M. p. 160.) Quamvis quod est extra coelos spatiu imaginarii alias designari solitum, non possumus nisi sub ratione extensi concipere, non tamen ibi concipimus existere Ens aliquod reale praeter Deum. Est enim spatium imaginarium nihil nisi Ens rationis, cujus conceptus objectivus revera sit nihil, aptum tamen recipere corpus in eo locabile.
units.tr: CLII. Inst. 1. (M. p. 160.) Although what lies beyond the heavens, usually designated as imaginary space, we cannot conceive except under the aspect of extension, we do not conceive there to exist any real being besides God. For imaginary space is nothing but a being of reason, whose objective concept is really nothing, yet apt to receive a body to be located in it.

units.la: Resp. Qui necessario adeoque clare concipit in spatiis imaginariis aliquid extensum, ille attributum a corpore inseparabile concipit, adeoque & ipsum corpus, nisi velis statuere cum Pontificiis, Accidens vel attrib. posse esse sine subjecto, Extensionem sine corpore, quod absurdissimum. Si ergo revera concipiamus corpus extra coelos, hoc est, extra terminos mundi a nobis suppositos, etiam judicandum, tale corpus esse, vel statuendum, Deum nos fallere, si ista clara perceptio, quae proculdubio est a Deo, in errorem nos deducat: neque ullum supererit remedium vitandi errores, si possimus falli in iis, quae clare & distincte percipimus. 2. Itaque spatium imaginarium, in quo necessario sit concipienda extensio, non erit Ens rationis, sed Ens reale propter attributi realitatem.
units.tr: Response. He who necessarily and therefore clearly conceives something extended in imaginary spaces conceives an attribute inseparable from body, and therefore the body itself, unless you wish to hold with the Papists that an accident or attribute can exist without a subject, extension without body, which is most absurd. If therefore we really conceive a body beyond the heavens, that is, beyond the limits of the world we have supposed, it must also be judged that such a body exists, or it must be maintained that God deceives us, if this clear perception, which is undoubtedly from God, leads us into error. Nor will any remedy remain for avoiding errors, if we can be deceived in those things which we perceive clearly and distinctly. 2. Therefore imaginary space, in which extension must necessarily be conceived, will not be a being of reason but a real being, on account of the reality of the attribute.

units.la: CLIII. Inst. 2. (M. p. 161.) Si spatia illa revera sint corporea, quatuor absurda educi posse, 1. Mundum fuisse ab aeterno, adeoque ex nihilo creari non potuisse: quoniam illud spatium sive capacitas, in qua mundus jam actu continetur, non potuit non fuisse ante mundi creationem ab aeterno.
units.tr: CLIII. Inst. 2. (M. p. 161.) If those spaces are really corporeal, four absurdities can be drawn: 1. that the world has existed from eternity, and so could not have been created out of nothing, since that space or capacity in which the world is now actually contained could not but have existed from eternity before the creation of the world.

units.la: Resp. Illud vero est quod nego, cum spatium illud, in quo mundus continetur, non nisi ratione ab eo differat, ita ut sine eo nec esse nec concipi possit. Non enim differt illud spatium a mundo, nisi quod mundi extensionem ut singularem consideremus, in spatiis vero unitatem tantum genericam ipsi tribuamus, ita ut hoc mundo annihilato, alius creari possit ejusdem cujus prior extensionis.
units.tr: Response. I deny that, since that space in which the world is contained differs from the world only in aspect, so that neither can exist or be conceived without the other. For that space differs from the world only in that we consider the extension of the world as singular, whereas in the case of spaces we attribute to them only a generic unity, so that, with this world annihilated, another could be created of the same extension as the former.

units.la: At dicis; Illud, quod jam actu capit mundum, ab aeterno potuisse mundum capere nemo, qui quidem Philosophiam a limine salutavit, negare audebit; idem illud spatium sub ratione extensi concipiendum fuisse nemo quoque diffitebitur, siquidem igitur omne id quod sub ratione extensi concipitur sit revera corpus, mundus necessario debuit exstitisse ante mundi creationem, sive ab aeterno.
units.tr: But you say: no one who has even greeted philosophy at its threshold will dare to deny that that which now actually holds the world could have held the world from eternity; nor will anyone deny that the same space had to be conceived under the aspect of extension. If therefore everything conceived under the aspect of extension is really body, the world must necessarily have existed before the creation of the world, or from eternity.

units.la: Resp. Spatium illud quod ratione tantum a mundo distinguitur, ab aeterno non potuit capere mundum, qui ab aeterno non fuit, sed mundo fuit concreatum ut Theologi loquuntur. Itaque negamus illud ante mundum concipiendum, eique extensionem aliquam attribuendam, quia ante mundum illud spatium, cum à mundo non differat, revera nihil fuit, adeoque ante mundum etiam non nisi negativè concipiendum tanquam nihilum.
units.tr: Response. That space which is distinguished from the world only by reason could not have held the world from eternity, since the world was not from eternity but was created together with the world, as the theologians say. Therefore we deny that it is to be conceived before the world, and that any extension should be attributed to it, because before the world that space, since it does not differ from the world, really was nothing; and so before the world too it is to be conceived only negatively, as nothing.

units.la: CLIV. Secundum Absurdum (M. p. 261.) alios mundos ex doctrina Cartesiani à Deo creari non posse duplici ratione evincitur, 1. quia non datur ubi, extra hunc mundum, aptum recipere mundum creandum. 2. quia potentia Dei mundum creans, quae revera eadem est cum ejus Essentia, ita est inclusa huic mundo infinito, ut non possit existere alibi ad creandum ibi novum mundum.
units.tr: CLIV. Second absurdity (M. p. 261.) That other worlds cannot be created by God according to the doctrine of Descartes is proved on a twofold ground: 1. because there is no place outside this world apt to receive a world to be created; 2. because the power of God creating the world, which is really the same as his Essence, is so enclosed in this infinite world that it cannot exist elsewhere to create a new world there.

units.la: Resp. Non est absurdum, si statuamus cum Cartesio & Maresio, mundos à se invicem distinctos & discretos & sic revera plures creari non posse, non quod potentiam Dei imminuamus, vel dicamus, Deum non posse plures soles, terras, stellas &c. creare, sed quod existimemus, contradictionem implicare, ut plures mundi à se invicem discreti creentur, & quod putemus, quibuscunque corporibus, vel creaturis novis creatis, ea omnia unum cundemque mundum cum hoc constituitura esse. Vide Claub. Def. Cartef. p. 487. & seqq. Attamen argumenta duo adversarii, quocunque referantur, sive ad probandum, ex nostra sententia sequi, non posse plures mundos discretos à se invicem adeoque revera plures creari, (quae quidem nostra sententia est, non tamen infertur ex illis argumentis) sive ad ostendendum, non posse plura corpora à Deo producì, nihil efficiunt. Nam etiamsi nullum detur Ubi extra hunc mundum, tamen si Deo libeat corpus extra eum creare, etiam illud Ubi in quo sit, illi erit concreaturus, cum non nisi ratione ab eo differat; Itaque 2. si potentiam suam Deus extra hunc mundum extendere velit & creare nova corpora, non prius essent concipienda quaedam ubi, aut spatia, quam ipsa corpora à Deo creanda, quae ubictatem suam secum afferent; at ea corpora non constituerent novum aliquem mundum, sed cum hoc censenda essent conjuncta.
units.tr: Response. It is not absurd, if we hold with Descartes and Maresius that worlds are distinct and separate from one another, and so that really several cannot be created. This is not because we diminish the power of God, or say that God cannot create several suns, earths, stars and so on, but because we think it involves a contradiction that several worlds separate from one another be created, and because we think that whatever bodies or new creatures are created, all of them will constitute one and the same world with this one. See Clauberg, Defence of Descartes, p. 487 and following. Yet the two arguments of the opponent, however they are referred, accomplish nothing: whether they are meant to prove that it follows from our opinion that several worlds discrete from one another cannot exist and so really several cannot be created (which indeed is our opinion, but is not inferred from those arguments), or to show that several bodies cannot be produced by God. For even if there is no place outside this world, yet if it pleased God to create a body outside it, he would also create that place in which it is, since it differs from the body only in aspect. Therefore, secondly, if God wishes to extend his power beyond this world and create new bodies, certain places or spaces would not first have to be conceived before the bodies themselves that God is to create, which would bring their own placeness with them. But those bodies would not constitute some new world; they would have to be regarded as joined with this one.

units.la: CLV. Tertium Absurdum (M. p. 162.) Mundum admissis hypothesibus Cartesianis non posse annihilari, quia sic non possent annihilari omnia corpora, quin semper superfit illud ubi, in quo illa jam exist unt.
units.tr: CLV. Third absurdity (M. p. 162.) That the world cannot be annihilated on the Cartesian hypotheses, because in that case not all bodies could be annihilated without there always remaining that place in which they already exist.

units.la: Resp. Si annihilentur omnia corpora, cum illud ubi in quo existunt ab iis non differat, etiam illud ipsum annihilatum erit concipiendum, nisi supponas loco istorum corporum annihilatorum alia ejusdem extensionis specificae creari, quo supposito illud ubi manebit, quemadmodum extinc to tinćto uno individuo vel omnibus ejusdem speciei, locoque eorum novis creatis, species tamen remanere dicenda erit.
units.tr: Response. If all bodies are annihilated, then, since that where in which they exist does not differ from them, that very where will also have to be conceived as annihilated, unless you suppose that in place of those annihilated bodies others of the same specific extension are created. On that supposition the place will remain, just as, when one individual or all individuals of the same species are extinguished and new ones created in their place, the species is nevertheless said to remain.

units.la: CLVI. Quartum Absurdum, Mundum de spatio in spatium transferri non posse.
units.tr: CLVI. Fourth absurdity: that the world cannot be transferred from space to space.

units.la: Resp. At illud non est absurdum sed verissimum: corpus enim de spatio in spatium sive potius de loco in locum transportari non posset, nisi supponatur plura esse corpora, quorum unum hunc locum sive situm inter alia occupet, aliud alium, ita ut Corpus dicatur de loco in locum transferri, quia cum prius occupaverit hunc situm respectu horum corporum, postea alium respectu aliorum recipit. At cum non sint plures mundi, non potest etiam unus transferri in locum aliquem, qui non est.
units.tr: Response. But that is not absurd but most true. For a body could not be transported from space to space, or rather from place to place, unless it is supposed that there are several bodies, of which one occupies this place or situation among the others and another occupies another. Thus a body is said to be transferred from place to place, because, having previously occupied this situation with respect to these bodies, it afterwards receives another with respect to others. But since there are not several worlds, one world cannot be transferred into some place which does not exist.

units.la: CLVII. Exc. 7. (M. p. 163.) Se quidem concedere Extensionem a corporis Essentia ita immediate fluere, ut ab eo separari non possit, sed sese habere ad corpus ut accidens proprium ad suum subjectum.
units.tr: CLVII. Exc. 7. (M. p. 163.) He concedes that extension flows so immediately from the essence of body that it cannot be separated from it, but stands to body as a proper accident stands to its subject.

units.la: Resp. Quod corporis Essentia in Extensione consistat, probavit Cartesius Pp. II. art. 11. quæ probatio fuisset refutanda. Vel enim nulla corpori Essentia tribuenda, vel statuendum illud eam constituere, quod solum à corpore, sublatis reliquis, auferri non potest: At tale est sola extensio, reliqua omnia etsi ab hoc vel illo corpore, eo salvo manente auferri nequeunt, tamen possunt à corpore in genere consideratο, adeoque ejus generalem naturam non constituunt. Constat etiam exinde, quia Extensione prius nihil in corpore concipi potest, quodcunque enim asseras, illud ab extensione dependet, ex eâque demonstratur. Sed de hoc plenius in sequentibus.
units.tr: Response. That the essence of body consists in extension Descartes proved in Principles II, art. 11, and that proof should have been refuted. For either no essence is to be attributed to body, or it must be held that the essence is that which alone, with everything else removed, cannot be taken away from body. But such is extension alone; all the other attributes, although they cannot be taken away from this or that body while it remains that body, can nevertheless be considered apart from body in general, and so do not constitute its general nature. This is also clear from the fact that nothing can be conceived in body prior to extension, since whatever you assert of it depends on extension and is demonstrated from it. But of this more fully in what follows.

units.la: CLVIII. Exc. 8. loco afferri potest (R. St. p. 82.) Quid sibi vult, quod Cartesius mentem nostram talis esse natura velut è tripode pronunciat, ut nullos in mundo limites cognoscat? ita enim adversus hoc attentus lector ratio inhabitur: mirum esse de quo mentis statu Cartesius loquatur: Nam in statu Integritatis ea mundum, qualis revera est intellexit, id est, Finitum; In statu corruptionis multi Philosophi & inter eos Aristoteles agnoverunt, infinitum actu non posse dari: in statu renovationis novimus mundi limitem esse calum beatorum; In statu gloriæ idem etiam propriâ Experientiâ sentiemus. Ita quod de mentis naturâ tam confidenter asserit, in merum ludibrium abit.
units.tr: CLVIII. Exc. 8. may be cited at this point (R. St. p. 82.): What does it mean that Descartes pronounces our mind, as if from a tripod, to be of such a nature that it recognises no limits in the world? For against this the attentive reader will be struck by the following reasoning: it is strange what state of mind Descartes is speaking of. In the state of integrity, the mind understood the world as it really is, that is, finite. In the state of corruption, many philosophers, and among them Aristotle, recognised that an actually infinite cannot exist. In the state of renewal, we know that the limit of the world is the heaven of the blessed. In the state of glory, we shall feel the same thing from our own experience. Thus what he so confidently asserts about the nature of the mind turns into sheer mockery.

units.la: Resp. Quid sibi hoc velit, quod mentem nostram talis naturæ esse certa ratione adductus pronunciet, ut nullos in mundo limites agnoscat, nos supra ostendimus 2. Si homo in statu Integritatis mundum intellexit, qualis revera est: Ergone finitum? At quisnam probavit, & unde cognoscitur eum talem esse? aut quare id sine ratione tanquam è tripode de asseritur? Imò si natura mentis humanæ talis sit, ut nullos in mundo limites agnoscere possit, quemadmodum à nobis probatum; cum natura per lapsum non sit mutata, (neque enim per lapsum homo desiit esse homo) E. in statu Integritatis proculdubio etiam talis fuit. 3. Quam firmiter ex Scriptura probatum sit, Cœlum Beatorum esse mundi limitem, ejusque limites nos cognoscere posse, adeoque id nos in statu Regenerationis credere debere, postea videbimus: locum enim Eph. iv. nihil juvare adversarium ostendemus. 4. Quid in statu gloriæ circa mundi fines experientia nobis sit discendum definiri nequit, nec propterea quia sumus futuri in Cœlis, erimus extra mundum vel in ejus finibus, nisi mundi vocabulum nimis stricte accipere velis, pro compage corporum à Terra usque ad stellas collocatorum.
units.tr: Reply. What it means that the mind, moved by sound reasoning, is pronounced to be of such a nature that it recognises no limits in the world, we showed above (2). If man in the state of integrity understood the world as it really is, is it therefore finite? But who has proved this, and how is it known that the world is such? Or why is it asserted, without reason and as if from a tripod? Indeed, if the nature of the human mind is such that it can recognise no limits in the world, as we have proved, then since nature was not changed by the fall (for man did not cease to be man through the fall), it was surely also such in the state of integrity. (3) How firmly it has been proved from Scripture that the heaven of the blessed is the limit of the world, and that we can know its limits, and therefore that we ought to believe this in the state of regeneration, we shall see later; for we shall show that Ephesians 4 does not help the opponent at all. (4) What experience we shall learn about the limits of the world in the state of glory cannot be defined; nor, because we are destined to be in heaven, shall we therefore be outside the world or within its limits, unless you want to take the word "world" too narrowly, as the structure of bodies placed from the earth up to the stars.

units.la: CLIX. Inst. 1. (R. A. p. 44.) Naturam per lapsum non esse mutatam Papisticum & Pelagianum est.
units.tr: CLIX. Inst. 1. (R. A. p. 44.) That nature was not changed through the fall is Papist and Pelagian.

units.la: Resp. Eo sensu, quo ego hoc dico, quatenus nempe homo retinuit Essentiam animæ spiritualem facultate Intelligendi præditam, qua si bene utatur, non erret, non Pelagianum est afferere sed orthodoxum, & principium firmum, quo omnis scepticismus funditus evertitur. At inquis: Hic agitur de mutata hominis cognitione, qua multo obscurior est in statu corruptionis quam in statu Integritatis. Resp. Hic agitur de natura mentis humanæ, an si talis sit, ut nullos in mundo limites agnoscere possit, hoc ei post lapsum sit ablatum. Cognitio hominis post lapsum multò obscurior est facta, non quod Deus ademerit ideas quas indiderat, sed quod ad eas postea homo non attendat, quod præjudiciis involvat, quod confundat, quod sæpe judicium perceptionem earum claram & distinctam antevertat &c. Reliquæ Instantiæ (R. A. p. 54.) de Cœlo Beatorum meræ sunt cavillationes, cum ego nihil de eo præter Scripturam determinem, sed contra Adversarius ad obtinendum institutum, omnes illas quæstiones, de quibus sequenti cap. agetur, debeat determinare.
units.tr: Reply. In the sense in which I say this, namely insofar as man has retained the essence of the soul as spiritual, endowed with the faculty of understanding, which, if he uses it well, will not err, it is not Pelagian to assert it but orthodox, and a firm principle by which all scepticism is utterly overturned. But you object: Here the question is of the changed knowledge of man, which is much more obscure in the state of corruption than in the state of integrity. Reply: here the question is about the nature of the human mind, whether, if it is such that it can recognise no limits in the world, this was taken from it after the fall. Man's knowledge after the fall has become much more obscure, not because God took away the ideas he had implanted, but because man afterwards does not attend to them, because he entangles them in prejudices, because he confuses them, because often judgment anticipates the clear and distinct perception of them, and so on. The remaining instances (R. A. p. 54.) about the heaven of the blessed are mere cavils, since I determine nothing about it except from Scripture; but, on the contrary, the opponent, to achieve his purpose, ought to determine all those questions which will be treated in the following chapter.

units.la: CLX. Inst. 2. (R. A. p. 55.) In statu Gloriæ idem quod hic vel per sanam rationem vel per verbum Dei didicimus, experimento verum esse sentiemus &c. Non futuros autem nos in mundi finibus confidenter dicitur. Probationem quarto. Certè Johannes Apoc. xix. 4. ὅτι εἶπεν, inquit, οἱ ἀκολουθοῦντες τῷ ἀρνίῳ, ὅπου ἂν ὑπάγῃ. An non Christus ad cœli extremum usque se conferre potest? poterunt ergo eum & illuc sequi sui Electi. Resp. 1. Per sanam rationem verbo Dei non refragante didicimus, mundum esse indefinitum. 2. Nos Christum poterimus sequi, quo iverit, quum se posse conferre ad extrema Cœli vel mundi, si habeat, non o negat : at cum extrema mundi mente concipi nequeant, ut antea ostensum, multo minus concipi potest, ea corpore posse permeari.
units.tr: CLX. Inst. 2. (R. A. p. 55.) In the state of glory we shall experientially feel to be true what we have learned here either through sound reason or through the Word of God, etc. But it is confidently said that we shall not be within the limits of the world. Fourth proof. Certainly John, Apoc. xix. 4, says: "those who follow the Lamb, wherever he goes" [οἱ ἀκολουθοῦντες τῷ ἀρνίῳ, ὅπου ἂν ὑπάγῃ]. Can not Christ betake himself even to the farthest edge of heaven? Then his elect too will be able to follow him there. Reply. (1) By sound reason, with the Word of God not opposing, we have learned that the world is indefinite. (2) We shall be able to follow Christ wherever he goes; for he does not deny that he can betake himself to the extremities of heaven or of the world, if he has any. But since the extremities of the world cannot be conceived by the mind, as was shown before, it is much less conceivable that bodies can pass through them.

units.la: CLXI. Manet itaque firmum nostrum argumentum, quod pro mundi Indefinitate adduximus, cum tam facili opera omnes contra illud Exceptiones cum Instantiis fuerint refutatae. Atque ita cognoscitur Mundum esse Indefinitum. Ex quo consequitur tanquam aliquod Corollarium: Nullam certam figuram ei assignari posse: Cum enim figura sit vera determinatio quantitatis, non potest illa tribui, nisi iis corporibus, quae ab aliis separata finitam & terminatam quantitatem obtinent. Quae etiam est sententia Clavii ad Euclid. def. 14. lib. 1. superficies, inquit, infinita vel etiam corpus, cum nullis terminis comprehendatur, Figura vocari nulla ratione potest.
units.tr: CLXI. Our argument, which we brought forward for the indefiniteness of the world, therefore stands firm, since all the exceptions and instances against it have been refuted with such ease. And so it is known that the world is indefinite. From this there follows, as a kind of corollary, that no definite shape can be assigned to it. For since shape is the true determination of quantity, it cannot be attributed except to those bodies which, separated from others, possess a finite and bounded quantity. This is also the opinion of Clavius on Euclid, definition 14, book 1: "An infinite surface, or even an infinite body, since it is not bounded by any limits, can by no means be called a shape."

units.la: CLXII. Exc. 1. (R. A. p. 11.) Hic apparet, authorem hunc mundi nec terminum nec figuram agnoscere, adeoque eum statuere absolute infinitum, ita enim argumentatur: Ea tantum corpora habent figuram, quae ab aliis separata finitam & terminatam quantitatem obtinent: At mundus non est tale corpus.
units.tr: CLXII. Exc. 1. (R. A. p. 11.) Here it appears that this author recognises neither limit nor shape for the world, and so he holds it to be absolutely infinite; for he argues thus: only those bodies have a shape which, separated from others, possess a finite and bounded quantity; but the world is not such a body.

units.la: Resp. Hic apparet adversarium meum pervertere argumentum; tale enim est illud: Iis tantum corporibus certa figura potest attribui, de quibus constat, quod ab aliis separata finitam & terminatam quantitatem obtineant. At an mundus finitam & terminatam quantitatem obtineat non constat: E. Maj. prob. verbis Clavii citatis. Non ergo suppono vel statuo mundum actu Infinitum, nec enim ullibi asserui, quod agnoverim positive, nullos esse in mundo limites, quod requiritur ad Infinitatem, sed tantum, nullas ab ullo hominum in Mundi Idea reperiri posse.
units.tr: Reply. Here it appears that my opponent distorts my argument; for the argument is this: a definite shape can be attributed only to those bodies of which it is established that, separated from others, they possess a finite and bounded quantity. But it is not established whether the world possesses a finite and bounded quantity; therefore (the major premise proved by the words of Clavius cited). Therefore I do not presuppose or assert that the world is actually infinite; for I nowhere asserted that I positively knew there are no limits in the world, which is what infinity requires, but only that no limits can be found in the idea of the world by any human being.

units.la: CLXIII. Exc. 2. (R. A. p. 12.) Verba Clavii nihil mihi commodare, cum non quaeratur, quid sit superficies infinita, sed an talis detur.
units.tr: CLXIII. Exc. 2. (R. A. p. 12.) The words of Clavius do me no good, since the question is not what an infinite surface is, but whether such a thing exists.

units.la: Resp. Imo, multum mihi commodant, dum probant majorem meam propositionem, uti antea dictum. Ridiculum vero quod (M.164. 165.) operose ex meis thesibus tanquam consequens deducat absurdum. Ex Principiis Philosophiae Cartesianae demonstrari nullo modo posse quinam sint termini mundi, cum illud ipsum expresse possuissem in prima Editione, ut hoc labore Antagonista potuerit supersedere. Quod si quid probare voluisset, absurditatem ejus positionis ostendere eum oportuisset.
units.tr: Reply. Indeed they do me a great deal of good, since they prove my major premise, as was said before. But it is ridiculous that he (M. 164, 165.) laboriously deduces an absurdity from my theses as a consequence. That it cannot be demonstrated by the principles of Cartesian philosophy what the limits of the world are in any way, since I had expressly stated that very thing in the first edition, so that the antagonist could have spared himself this labour. But if he had wanted to prove something, he ought to have shown the absurdity of that position.

units.la: CAPUT XI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI.

units.la: Objectio prima contra Indefinitatem Mundi, à spatiis Ima- ginariis desumta proponitur ac refellitur.
units.tr: The first objection against the indefiniteness of the world, drawn from imaginary spaces, is set out and refuted.

units.la: Objectionis primæ loco esse possunt dicta Suarezii de spatiis Imaginariis & præsentia Dei extra mundum in illis, quæ objiciuntur (R. St. p. 78. & seqq.) quæ quia solide refutata sunt à Clariss. Dn. Maresio in Theologo Paradoxo refutato, neque hic pro iis defendendis aliquid novi afferebatur, nos in priori Editione Adversarium ad Maresium remisimus. Sed quoniam nunc objicitur, me hoc onus in alienos humeros rejicere, verba Suarezii recitabo, ac quid in iis reprehendam, succincte dicam. Dicta illa citantur (R. St. p. 78. seqq.) Qui Spatia, inquit, imaginaria in quibus Deus sit extra mundum, EXCOGITARUNT, ita ea explicant, ut talem Deo attribuant modum existendi seu talem dispositionem substantiæ suæ (ut nostro modo loquamur) quæ ex parte sua ita existat, ut sine sui mutatione possit intime & realiter esse in quacunque re, si illam velit creare. Et hunc (ajunt) modum Essendi habet Deus ex vi sua Immensitatis. Quia vero nos non possumus hanc dispositionem in substantia spirituali concipere, nisi per ordinem ad spatium, eo quod Deus ex vi praedicta dispositionis de se aptus est ad existendum in quibuscunque corporalibus spatiis, etiamsi in infinitum usque protendantur, ideo non possumus illam divinæ substantiæ dispositionem & immensitatem concipere, nisi per modum cujusdam extensionis, quam necessario explicamus per ordinem ad corpora, & quando vel reipsa, vel mente realia corpora separamus, necessario apprehendimus veluti quoddam spatium aptum replevi corporibus, cui tota divina substantia sit præsens, & tota in toto, & tota in singulis partibus ejus; per quam præsentiam nihil aliud significamus, quam prædictam divinæ substantiæ dispositionem. Præsentia ergo illa, licet, ut concipitur, NIHIL sit, & mera relatio rationis, illud tamen absolutum, quod per hanc relationem volumus in divina substantia declarare, revera est aliquid in ipso Deo, quod IMMENSITATEM ejus appellamus. Et sic immensitatem Deus habuit, antequam quicquid aliud existeret. Hæc petita sunt ex Suarezio Disp. met. XXX. sect. VII. t. 16. 17. 19. qui addit n. 29. 30. 31. 32. 36. 38. 39. Ex actione Dei immediate infertur actualis præsentia in rebus factis, mediate vero, seu consequenter, potentia, seu aptitudo ex parte Dei ad existendum in omnibus rebus quas in infinitum facere potest, & in hoc consistit immensitas ejus. Nam si Deus Deus concluderetur hoc mundo, non esset immensus, cum mundus infinitus non sit; si, inquam, ita concluderetur, ut in ampliori nec actu esset, nec esse posset, in eo ergo immensitas ejus consistere non potest. Atque ita fit, ut ex actione, quamvis de facto versetur circa res finitas, colligatur tota immensitas, ampliando seu extendendo illam ad actionem possibilem. Et hoc sensu dicitur, Deum sua Immensitate praesentem esse etiam extra hunc mundum, etiam in SS. Literis Job. II. 8. Altior est altissimis coelis quid agas. 9. Longior terra mensura ejus & latior mari cap. XXII. 11. 1 Reg. VIII. 27. Ratio sumitur ex dictis: Quia Deus potest operari extra mundum, sine ulla mutatione sui, ergo ita actu est extra mundum, &c. non ut in aliquo loco, sed in se ipso. (item) sicut aeternitas est in omnibus finitis temporibus, & infinite excedit illa, ita immensitas est in omnibus finitis locis, & infinite superat illa. Et sicut ratione aeternitatis dicere possumus, Deum exstitisse ante reale tempus, in omni Tempore imaginario, ita ratione Immensitatis dicimus, eum esse in omnibus spatiis Imaginariis. Ex quo etiam intelligitur, quid indicent illa adverbia temporalia & localia, cum dicimus, Deum fuisse ab aeterno. Hic, ubi nunc creatus est mundus, vel Ibi ubicunque creari potest, aut tunc fuisse, quando potuit a Deo creari ante totum tempus reale praeteritum. Nam sicut illud tunc non significat aliquam durationem, quae actu extiterit, distinctam a Deo, sed ipsammet durationem Dei, ut aptam ad coexistendum tempori vel instanti, quod antea esse posset: Ita IBI aut HIC non indicat locum Realem actu existentem, sed solam praesentiam Dei per Immensitatem, ut de se aptam ad coexistendum localiter cuicunque corpori realiter ibi existenti. Haec Suarez (inquit R.) recte omnino atque Orthodoxe, quanquam nostro judicio, re probe, ut ab illo explicatur, intellecta, ea quam fingit imaginatione non sit opus, ut alibi monuimus. Quod si tale quid scriptis suis inseruisset Cartesius, non esset, quod illum carperemus: nunc vero ponit spatia nullo fine extensa, non modo per Imaginationem, sed Realiter, & corpoream etiam substantiam eodem modo extensam quae eis continentur: qui nes in universo agnoscunt, eos fingere ait, Infinitae Dei potentia fraudem facere, & ea per superbiam affirmare quae ipsis nec ratione ulla nec revelatione cognita. Vide duo ejus loca primo a nobis citata, & plus eum dicere, quam jam recensuimus, agnoscees.
units.tr: The first objection may be taken from what Suarez says about imaginary spaces and God's presence outside the world within them. These sayings are objected to (R. St. p. 78 and following). Since they were solidly refuted by the most distinguished Mr. Maresius in The Paradoxical Theologian Refuted, and nothing new was offered here in their defence, in the first edition we referred the Antagonist to Maresius. But since it is now objected that I am shifting this burden onto others' shoulders, I will quote Suarez's words and briefly say what I find to blame in them. These sayings are cited (R. St. p. 78 and following): Those who have devised imaginary spaces, in which God is outside the world, explain them in such a way that they attribute to God such a mode of existing, or such a disposition of his substance (to speak in our way), that on its own side it so exists that, without any change in itself, it can be intimately and really present in any thing, if he wishes to create it. And (they say) God has this mode of being from the power of his immensity. But since we cannot conceive this disposition in a spiritual substance except through its relation to space, because God, by virtue of that disposition, is fit to exist in any corporeal spaces, even if they extend to infinity, therefore we cannot conceive that disposition of the divine substance and its immensity except as a kind of extension, which we necessarily explain through its relation to bodies. And when we separate real bodies, either in fact or in the mind, we necessarily apprehend a kind of space fit to be filled with bodies, to which the whole divine substance is present, whole in the whole and whole in each of its parts. By this presence we mean nothing other than that aforesaid disposition of the divine substance. So that presence, although, as it is conceived, it is NOTHING and a mere relation of reason, yet that absolute thing which we wish to declare in the divine substance through this relation really is something in God himself, which we call his IMMENSITY. And thus God had immensity before anything else existed.* These things are taken from Suarez, Disp. Met. XXX, sect. VII, nn. 16, 17, 19, who adds nn. 29, 30, 31, 32, 36, 38, 39. From God's action, actual presence in things made is inferred immediately, but potency or aptitude on God's side to exist in all things which he can make to infinity is inferred mediately, or consequently, and in this his immensity consists. For if God were confined to this world, he would not be immense, since the world is not infinite; if, I say, he were so confined that he neither actually was, nor could be, in a larger one, then his immensity cannot consist in that. And so it comes about that from his action, although in fact it is concerned with finite things, the whole immensity is inferred, by extending it to possible action. And in this sense it is said that God, by his immensity, is present even outside this world, and this is also in Holy Scripture: Job 11:8, "It is higher than the heavens; what can you do?" 9, "Its measure is longer than the earth and broader than the sea." Job 22:11. 1 Kings 8:27. The argument is drawn from what has been said: because God can work outside the world without any change in himself, therefore he is actually outside the world, etc., not as in some place, but in himself. (likewise) As eternity is in all finite times and infinitely exceeds them, so immensity is in all finite places and infinitely surpasses them. And just as by reason of eternity we can say that God existed before real time, in every imaginary time, so by reason of immensity we say that he is in all imaginary spaces. From this it is also understood what those temporal and local adverbs indicate when we say, God was from eternity; here, where the world has now been created, or there, wherever it can be created, or then, when it could be created by God before all past real time. For as that "then" does not signify some duration which actually existed, distinct from God, but God's own duration, as fit to coexist with a time or instant which could previously be, so "there" or "here" does not indicate a real place actually existing, but only the presence of God through immensity, as fit in itself to coexist locally with any body really existing there. Suarez (says R.) says these things entirely rightly and orthodoxly, although in our judgement, the thing is properly understood as he explains it, and the imagination he invents is not needed, as we have elsewhere noted. But if Descartes had inserted something of this kind into his writings, there would be nothing for us to criticise. Now, however, he posits spaces extended without any end, not only in imagination but in reality, and also corporeal substance extended in the same way which is contained in them. He says that those who acknowledge these in the universe commit a fraud against the infinite power of God, and by pride affirm things which are known neither by any reason nor by revelation. See the two passages of his which we cited first, and you will recognise that he says more than we have now recounted.

units.la: CLXV. Resp.
units.tr: CLXV. Reply.

units.la: Ego vero hic primo aliquot argumentis spatia Imaginaria destruam, dein in specie dicam, quid de Suarezii explicatione istorum spatiorum speciali sentiam. Primum quod attinet, quamvis spatia Imaginaria, eo ipso quo talia sementipsa satis refutent, tamen ut eorum inanitas reddatur manifestior, observentur sequentia argumenta. 1 Cum ante mundum nihil fuerit praeter Deum, etiam nihil ante mundum concipiendum: Quid ergo opus imaginari ante mundum conditum spatium extensum? 2. spatium non differt realiter a corpore, E. corpore non existente, non debet concipi existere. 3. spatium imaginarium revera est nihil. Atqui Deus non potest esse in Nihilo. Quomodo enim in coerit? nisi ut in Chimæra, Centauro & aliis figmentis? 4. Ad concipiendum inextensum non opus est concipere extensum; nullam enim ut talia habent convenientiam: Deus autem est inextensus. 5. Imaginariis non possunt neque debent adscribi reales affectiones & realia attributa: Extensio, distantia, & partes diversæ. Cui enim realia attributa conveniunt & cujus conceptum ingrediuntur, illud est reale.
units.tr: I will first destroy imaginary spaces here by several arguments, and then say specifically what I think of Suarez's particular explanation of these spaces. As to the first point, although imaginary spaces refute themselves well enough by the very fact that they are such, the following arguments may be considered, so that their emptiness becomes more manifest. (1) Since before the world there was nothing but God, nothing should be conceived before the world either. Why then imagine an extended space existing before the world was created? (2) Space does not really differ from body; therefore, when no body exists, space ought not to be conceived as existing. (3) Imaginary space is really nothing. But God cannot be in nothing. For how could he be contained there, except as in a chimera, a centaur, or other fictions? (4) To conceive the unextended, there is no need to conceive the extended, for they have no such agreement; yet God is unextended. (5) Imaginary things cannot and should not be ascribed real affections and real attributes, such as extension, distance, and diverse parts. For that to which real attributes belong, and whose concept they enter, is real.

units.la: CLXVI. Dein in Suarezii speciali explicatione sequentia præcipuè, aliis præteritis, reprehendo;
units.tr: CLXVI. Next, in Suarez's particular explanation, I chiefly find fault with the following, setting the others aside.

units.la: 1. Quod dicat, nos non posse illam divina substantia dispositionem & immensitatem nisi per modum cujusdam extensionis concipere. Hic autem quæro ex Adversario, num recte & orthodoxè dictum putet, Deum non posse concipi nisi per modum extensionis, hoc est corporeitatis? Quæro enim an huic conceptui nostro formali correspondeat conceptus aliquis objectivus in ipso Deo, annon? Si prius, Ergo Deus revera est corporeus, si non, ergo falsus & non Orthodoxus est conceptus formalis per quem aliter concipitur ac revera est. 2. Quod dicit, nos necessario apprehendere veluti quoddam spatium aptum repleri corporibus cui tota divina substantia sit præsens. Nam ad omnipræsentiam divinam concipiendam non opus est talibus spatiis quæ sint apta repleri, sed quæ sunt repleta; neque præsentia, cum sit ἐν τ̄ ᾧ εὑρ π, concipienda est sine rebus ad quas referatur. 3. quod existimat, illam præsentiam ad spatia Imaginaria licet, ut concipitur, nihil sit, & mera relatio rationis, tamen esse necessariam ad Immensitatem Dei concipiendam; Nam sic sequitur: Opus esse ad perfectiones Dei concipiendas comparatione cum nihilo sive Imaginatione aliquâ & Nihili tanquam realis, adeoque fictis ad res maxime reales percipiendas, quod non potest non esse absurdum. 4. Quod statuat, Deum Immensitate præsentem etiam esse extra hunc mundum, cum non possit esse præsens nihilo quod non est, quale extra hunc mundum est concipiendum. Dicta vero Jobi xi. & xxi. item Reg. viii. non positive, sed negative Immensitatem Dei describunt, quod nempe totus mundus, quamvis Maximus & Indefinitus juxta superius explicata, non tamen sit tantus, quin Deus possit novis productis creaturis suam præsentiam illis exhibere. 5. Quod dicit, 'Deum extitisse in omni tempore imaginario ante reale tempus, cum è contrario tale imaginarium tempus ad æternam Dei permanentiam concipiendam non sit necessarium.
units.tr: 1. He says that "we cannot conceive that disposition and immensity of the divine substance except by way of a certain extension." Here I ask my opponent whether he thinks it is rightly and orthodoxly said that God cannot be conceived except by way of extension, that is, corporeity. For I ask whether some objective concept in God himself corresponds to this formal concept of ours, or not. If so, then God is really corporeal; if not, then the formal concept by which God is conceived otherwise than he really is, is false and not orthodox. 2. He says that "we necessarily apprehend, as it were, a certain space fit to be filled with bodies, to which the whole divine substance is present." For to conceive divine omnipresence there is no need of such spaces as are fit to be filled, but of those that are filled. Nor can presence, since it is "in that in which it is" [ἐν τῷ ᾧ], be conceived without the things to which it is referred. 3. He thinks that "that presence to imaginary spaces, although as conceived it is nothing and a mere relation of reason, is nevertheless necessary for conceiving the immensity of God." For it follows that to conceive God's perfections we must compare them with nothing, or with some imagination, and treat nothing as if it were real, and so use fictions to perceive the most real things. This cannot but be absurd. 4. He lays down that "God, present by his immensity, is also outside this world." But he cannot be present to nothing, which does not exist, such as must be conceived outside this world. The sayings of Job (xi. and xxi.) and likewise 1 Kings (Reg. viii.) describe God's immensity not positively but negatively: namely, that the whole world, although very great and indefinite as explained above, is not so great that God cannot, by producing new creatures, exhibit his presence to them. 5. He says that "God existed in every imaginary time before real time." On the contrary, such imaginary time is not necessary for conceiving God's eternal permanence.

units.la: CLXVII. Inst. 1. (R. A. p. 28.) Hac tu Wittichi cum dicis omni ratione destituta, vide quid agas, negare enim cogeris, Deum sine mutatione posse interne & realiter esse in quacunque re, si illam velit creare: affirmare adigeris, Deum hoc mundo ita concludi, ut in ampliori nec actu fit nec esse possit, & quod caput est tam multis tamque illustribus Scripturae locis omnem auctoritatem abrogabis.
units.tr: CLXVII. Objection 1 (R. A. p. 28.) In saying this, you say something entirely lacking in all reason; consider what you are doing. For you are forced to deny that God, without change, can be internally and really present in any thing he wishes to create. You are compelled to affirm that God is so enclosed in this world that he neither is nor can be actually present in a wider sphere. And, what is chief, by so many and such illustrious passages of Scripture you abrogate all its authority.

units.la: Resp. Quod ante dixi, spatiorum Imaginariorum introductionem omni ratione esse destitutam, id nunc probatum dedi, atque in superpondium ostendi etiam ea cum recta ratione pugnare. 2. Ex his duobus nec prius negare nec posterius affirmare cogor, etsi spatia imaginaria rejiciam & mundi Indefinitatem adstruam, sin minus, ostendatur quomodo id ex mea sententia consequatur. 3. Auctoritatem Scripturae dictis per meam sententiam non abrogo, nisi hoc apud vos sit Auctoritatem Scripturae derogare, cum sensum quem vos ei tribuitis non recipere.
units.tr: Reply. What I said before, that the introduction of imaginary spaces is entirely lacking in all reason, I have now proved, and I have further shown that they even clash with sound reason. 2. From these two points I am forced neither to deny the former nor to affirm the latter, although I reject imaginary spaces and maintain the indefiniteness of the world. If not, let it be shown how that follows from my opinion. 3. I do not abrogate the authority of Scripture by my opinion, unless among you it is to derogate from Scripture's authority not to accept the sense that you ascribe to it.

units.la: CLXVIII. Porro addit (R. A. p. 29.) Ut autem plenius scias quid de tota hac re sentiam, arbitror Suarezium & te cum Cartesio eodem luto haerere. Ut enim ille ait. Non possumus illam divinae substantiae dispositionem & immensitatem concipere, nisi per modum cujusdam extensionis, ita tu; mundum enim sine indefinita extensione, id est, cum terminis & finibus concipere non possum, sed semper ultra illos fines alia quaedam extensio concipienda porro occurrit, & Cartesius: non possumus imaginari extensionem tam magnam, quin intelligamus adhuc majorem esse posse.
units.tr: CLXVIII. Moreover he adds (R. A. p. 29.) But that you may know more fully what I think of this whole matter, I judge that you and Suarez, with Descartes, stick in the same mud. For as he says: We cannot conceive that disposition and immensity of the divine substance except by way of a certain extension, so you say; for I cannot conceive the world without indefinite extension, that is, with limits and boundaries, but there always occurs to me some further extension to be conceived beyond those boundaries. And Descartes says: we cannot imagine an extension so great that we do not understand a greater can still be.

units.la: Resp. Quis vero non videt differentiam maximam? Suarez loquitur de Deo cui tribuit extensionem quandam: nos de mundo eique attribuimus extensionem indefinitam: convenientia enim quaenam est inter duas propositiones, quorum Subjecta & Praedicata tam sunt diversa?
units.tr: Reply. Who does not see the very great difference? Suarez speaks of God, to whom he attributes a certain extension. We speak of the world, and attribute to it indefinite extension. For what agreement is there between two propositions whose subjects and predicates are so different?

units.la: CLXIX. Tandem R. A p. 29 Sed ille hinc satis feliciter emersit, dum fatetur, praesentiam illam ut concipitur NIHIL esse, sed quod per eam declaratur esse Immensitatem Dei. Vos autem plane absorpsit illa vorago dum spatium ut a vobis concipitur, verum & REALE esse, somniatis, ea tantum ratione quia ita concipitis & imaginamini.
units.tr: CLXIX. Finally, R. A. p. 29. But he has escaped from this fairly happily, in that he confesses that that presence, as it is conceived, is NOTHING, but that what is declared through it is the immensity of God. But you have been wholly swallowed up by that abyss, while you dream that the space, as you conceive it, is true and REAL, for the sole reason that you so conceive and imagine it.

units.la: Resp. E contrario Suarez sese plane immersit, ut antea visum, dum fatetur, praesentiam illam ut concipitur NIHIL esse, & tamen exi-stimat, eam esse necessariam. 2. Nos vero non propterea dicimus spatium illud esse reale, qua ita concipimus & imaginamur, sed quia ejus talem habemus ideam, non aliam, eamque claram & distinctam, quae cum a Deo sit, si cam si eam ad mundum, quem repræsentat, referamus, non possit nos in errorem ducere, nisi velimus Deum statuere fallacem, & omnem certitudinem evertere, uti supra demonstratum.
units.tr: Reply. On the contrary, Suarez has plunged himself entirely into that abyss, as was seen before, while he confesses that that presence, as it is conceived, is NOTHING, and yet thinks it necessary. 2. We, however, do not say that this space is real because we so conceive and imagine it, but because we have such an idea of it, and not another, and a clear and distinct one. Since this idea is from God, if we refer it to the world it represents, it cannot lead us into error unless we wish to hold God deceitful and to overturn all certainty, as demonstrated above.

units.la: CAPUT XII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII.

units.la: Objectio secunda contra Indefinitatem Mundi, à cognitio- ne limitum mundi, quæ omnibus conveniat, expenditur & solvitur.
units.tr: The second objection against the indefiniteness of the world, drawn from our knowledge of the limits of the world, which applies to everyone, is examined and answered.

units.la: CLXX. Obj. Secunda desumta ex eo, quod possimus aliquos Mundi limites cognoscere, ultra quos non sit ulterius ascendendum. Id antecedens probatur 1. ex Eph. iv. 10. (R. St. p. 83.) Manifesto in S. Script. terminus universi statuitur Cœlum Beatorum quod ὑπεράνω πάντων τῶν οὐρανῶν esse dicit Paulus Ephes. iv. 10. ac proinde sub se concludit omnes stellas fixas, quæ proinde in infinitum multiplicari non possunt, nisi cœlum Ubiquitarium nobis commi-niscatur, quod non includat sed pervadat omnia.
units.tr: CLXX. Second objection, taken from the fact that we can know certain limits of the world, beyond which one cannot go further. This premise is proved, first, from Ephesians 4:10 (R. St. p. 83). In Holy Scripture the boundary of the universe is clearly set as the heaven of the blessed, which Paul says is above all the heavens [ὑπεράνω πάντων τῶν οὐρανῶν] in Ephesians 4:10, and therefore he includes under it all the fixed stars, which therefore cannot be multiplied to infinity, unless we invent a ubiquitarian heaven, which does not contain all things but pervades them.

units.la: Resp. 1. Audio Scripturam dicentem: Christum ascendisse ὑπεράνω πάντων τῶν οὐρανῶν; sed ab ea dictum, Cœlum Empyreum esse terminum universi, ipsiusque terminum à nobis posse concipi, non audio. Itaque in citato loco, quemadmodum versu præcedenti illud εἰς τὰ κατώτερα μέρη τῆς γῆς non accipiendum est ita, ac si comparetur Terræ medium, stricte nempe acceptum, cum partibus exterioribus, quasi Christus centrum terræ ingressus fuerit, nisi hic descensum Christi ad inferos cum Pontificiis velis statuminari, sed Terra comparative ad Cœlum est consideranda, uti recte monet Calvinus in hunc locum, Comparatur non una terra pars cum altera, sed tota terra cum cœlo, ac si diceret: ex sede tam excelsa in hoc nostrum profundum barathrum descendisse; similia habet Parkerus de Descensu Christi lib. III. p. 20. Quid vero hinc sequitur? Non enim partes cœli, aut vero terra inter se hic conferuntur, sed supremum cœlum terræ infimæ opponitur: quomodo & Esaias loquitur, apud quem, mentione facta nullâ de inferno animarum, cœlum & terra phrasi eadem sic opponuntur, & c. 4.23. Clangite cœli, clangite inferiores partes terræ: ita etiam illud ὑπεράνω τῶν οὐρανῶν comparate ad terram est concipiendum, ac si diceret: Ex hoc nostro profundo barathro Christum ad sedem tam excelsam ascendisse; quo nihil de terminis mundi & finibus asseritur: si enim absolute hæc verba velles urgere, dicendum esset, etiam supra Cœlum Empyreum Christum ascendisse. Quod si locus bene perpendatur, patebit, nihil aliud ad summum inde concludi posse, quam, Cœlum Beatorum esse supra hoc cœlum visibile stellis repletum, quod nobis non obest. 2. Cum nescianus, quousque illud cœlum se extendat, & annon sit altitudinis Indefinitæ, neque perspectum habeamus, an ultra cœlum illud non alia iterum sint corpora, nobis incognita, neque an undique Cœlum Sidereum ambiat, & adversarius nullum ex his demonstrare possit, imbecillitas istius argumentationis per se patet. 3. Neque tamen hoc cœlum erit Ubiquitisticum, neque dicendum erit omnia pervadere, cum bene colligatur, esse supra omnes hos cœlos visibiles, astris confertos; posset ergo includere omnia corpora, licet à nullo includeretur, & eo usque protenderetur, ut ejus fines assequi non possumus. Manifestum ergo est, hunc locum nequicquam contra Cartesium esse productum.
units.tr: Reply, first. I hear Scripture saying that Christ ascended above all the heavens [ὑπεράνω πάντων τῶν οὐρανῶν]. But that Scripture says the Empyrean heaven is the boundary of the universe, and that we can conceive its boundary, I do not hear. So in the cited passage, just as in the preceding verse the words into the lower parts of the earth [εἰς τὰ κατώτερα μέρη τῆς γῆς] must not be taken as if they were compared with the middle of the earth, strictly understood, with its outer parts, as though Christ had entered the centre of the earth (unless you want to establish with the Papists Christ's descent into hell), but the earth must be considered comparatively with heaven. Calvin rightly advises this on the passage: It is not one part of the earth compared with another, but the whole earth with heaven, as if he said: he descended from so lofty a seat into this our deep abyss. Parker has similar things on the Descent of Christ, book III, p. 20: But what follows from this? For here not parts of heaven, or parts of the earth, are compared with one another, but the highest heaven is set against the lowest earth; just as Isaiah also speaks, in whom, with no mention made of the hell of souls, heaven and earth are set against each other in the same way, etc., and in chapter 4:23, Shout, heavens; shout, lower parts of the earth. So likewise above the heavens [ὑπεράνω τῶν οὐρανῶν] is to be understood comparatively with the earth, as if he said: Christ ascended from this our deep abyss to so lofty a seat. Nothing is asserted here about the limits and boundaries of the world. For if you wanted to press these words absolutely, it would have to be said that Christ ascended even above the Empyrean heaven. But if the passage is weighed carefully, it will be clear that nothing more can be concluded from it at most, than that the heaven of the blessed is above this visible heaven filled with stars, which does not harm us. Second, since we do not know how far that heaven extends, and whether it is not of indefinite height, nor do we have a clear view whether beyond that heaven there are not other bodies again, unknown to us, nor whether the starry heaven surrounds everything on every side, and since the adversary cannot demonstrate any of these things, the weakness of this argument is evident in itself. Third, this heaven will not be ubiquitarian, nor will it have to be said to pervade all things, since it is rightly inferred that it is above all these visible heavens, crowded with stars. It could therefore include all bodies, though it would be included by nothing, and would extend so far that we cannot reach its limits. It is therefore plain that this passage was brought forward in vain against Descartes.

units.la: CLXXI. Inst. 1. (R. A p 30.)
units.tr: CLXXI. Objection 2. (R. A p 30.)

units.la: Inspice ergo primum versiculum Genefeos: porro cœlum tripartito dividitur in aëreum, æthereum & Cœlum Beatorum, quod Paulus τρίτον οὐρανὸν vocat, hoc ὑπερέχων πάντων οὐρανῶν collocat idem Paulus; est ergo terminus universi: nam Universum Cœli & Terra nomine in Scriptura designari, ipse initio Differt. auctor es.
units.tr: Look first at the first verse of Genesis. Further, heaven is divided into three parts: the air, the aether, and the heaven of the blessed, which Paul calls the third heaven [τρίτον οὐρανόν]; this Paul places above all the heavens [ὑπερέχων πάντων οὐρανῶν]. It is therefore the boundary of the universe, for in Scripture the universe is designated by the names heaven and earth, as you yourself, the author, say at the beginning of the Differentia.

units.la: Resp. Argumentum, quod hic adfertur ab adversario, tale ut sit oportet: Cœlum & terra est Universum; At terminus istius cœli & terræ est Cœlum Beatorum, Ergo est terminus Universi. Sed in illo Argumento Minor propof. potest duplici sensu accipi, vel ita ut terminus idem sit quod ultimum corpus, quo sensu etiamsi & Minor & Conclusio concederetur, nihil tamen nobis contrarium esset probatum. Posito enim, quod Cœlum sit ultimum corpus, tamen ad probandum, mundum non esse Indefinitum, esset præterea ostendendum, illud ipsum corpus non esse indefinitæ magnitudinis, ejusque terminum cognoscí posse. Vel Minoris hujus sensus esse potest, ut terminus non tantum ultimum corpus denotet, sed tale utimum corpus, in quo termini queant concipi, quo sensu eam nego, nec probatur per istam divisionem Cœli in Aëreum, Æthereum, & Beatorum, ut per se est clarum.
units.tr: Reply. The argument brought forward here by the adversary must be of this form: heaven and earth is the universe; but the boundary of that heaven and earth is the heaven of the blessed; therefore it is the boundary of the universe. But in that argument the minor premise can be taken in two senses. Either the boundary means the same as the outermost body, and in that sense, even if both the minor premise and the conclusion were granted, nothing contrary to us would have been proved. For granting that heaven is the outermost body, still, to prove that the world is not indefinite, it would further have to be shown that this very body is not of indefinite magnitude and that its boundary can be known. Or the sense of this minor premise can be that the boundary denotes not merely the outermost body but such an outermost body in which boundaries can be conceived. In that sense I deny it, and it is not proved by this division of heaven into the air, the aether, and the heaven of the blessed, as is clear in itself.

units.la: CLXXII. Inst. 2. (R. A. p. 31.)
units.tr: CLXXII. Inst. 2. (R. A. p. 31.)

units.la: Si dicerem, Inferiores partes terræ cum superioribus comparari, nihil praeter textum dicerem, imo ipsam textus literam pro me haberem, nec tamen per illas intelligerem terræ centrum, sed sepulchrum. Tu ergo qui inferiores partes aut etiam medium terræ collatum cum superiori, aut extrema ejus parte putas idem valere quod ejus centrum, Papistarum opinionem vere statuminas, non ego.
units.tr: If I were to say that the lower parts of the earth are to be compared with the upper, I would be saying nothing beyond the text. Indeed, I would have the letter of the text itself on my side, and yet I would not understand by those words the centre of the earth but the sepulchre. You, then, who think that the lower parts, or the middle of the earth compared with the upper, or its outermost part, amount to the same as its centre, are truly propping up the opinion of the Papists, not I.

units.la: Resp. Mens meæ responsionis hæc fuit: quemadmodum non evinci potest, necessario hæc verba, εἰς τὰ κατώτερα μέρη τῆς γῆς, comparative esse intelliintelligenda, vel respectu terrae medii sive centri cum exterioribus comparati, vel, quod nunc addo, respectu inferiorum terrae partium, qualis est sepulchrum, cum superioribus comparatarum; ita etiam illa verba, [illegible, ~2 letters] ... non accipienda esse comparative. Probetur contrarium, si fieri potest. Nos existimamus, Calvini & Belgarum simplicem expositionem de Christi descensu in uterum Beatae Virginis sufficere. 2. Etsi autem hic mihi medium stricte & accuratissime acceptum ac centrum terrae aequivaleat, non tamen dico, quod ubicunque medii & cordis Terrae in Scripturis S. fit mentio, illud vel adeo stricte, vel pro centro Terrae debat sumi.
units.tr: Reply. The sense of my answer was this: just as it cannot be proved that the words εἰς τὰ κατώτερα μέρη τῆς γῆς [eis ta katōtera merē tēs gēs] must necessarily be understood comparatively, either with respect to the middle or centre of the earth compared with its outer parts, or (what I now add) with respect to the lower parts of the earth, such as the sepulchre, compared with the upper, so too the words [illegible] are not to be taken comparatively. Let the contrary be proved, if it can be. We think the simple exposition of Calvin and the Belgians, concerning Christ's descent into the womb of the blessed Virgin, is sufficient. 2. Although here the middle, taken strictly and most exactly, is equivalent to the centre of the earth, I do not say that wherever the middle and heart of the earth is mentioned in Holy Scripture, it must be taken either so strictly or as the centre of the earth.

units.la: CLXXIII. Inst. 3. (R. A. p. 32.) Explicatio Calvini nobis non incommodat, etsi non sit adeo literalis, ut illa altera. Cum enim Terra & Caelum Beatorum fatente adversario, opponantur, sequitur, ut Terra asseritur esse mundi pars infima, ita Caelum, de quo agimus, constitui Mundi partem supremam, ac proinde esse terminum universi in altum, prout Terra in profundum,
units.tr: CLXXIII. Inst. 3. (R. A. p. 32.) The explanation of Calvin does not trouble us, although it is not so literal as the other. For since, as the adversary admits, Earth and the Heaven of the blessed are set in opposition, it follows that just as the Earth is asserted to be the lowest part of the world, so the Heaven of which we speak is set up as the highest part of the world, and therefore is the boundary of the universe upwards, as the Earth is downwards,

units.la: Resp. Quod sequi putat antagonista, illud minime sequitur; nam denominationes hae dextri & sinistri, superioris & inferioris dicuntur a partibus corporis nostri, ut illud superius dicatur, quod est supra capita nostra, inferius quod est sub pedibus nostris. Itaque, etsi Terra concedatur mundi pars infima, eo sensu quia est sub pedibus nostris, quocunque nos vertamus, & Caelum Beatorum pars superior, quatenus est a capitibus nostris magis remotum, quam coeli visibiles, super quibus ab Apostolo hoc loco collocatur, inde tamen non sequitur, quod sit terminus Universi, undique cingens Caelum Sidereum, nec quod ejus ipsius termini possint cognosci, quodque illud ipsum non ut Indefinitum sit concipiendum.
units.tr: Reply. What the opponent thinks follows does not follow at all. For these terms right and left, upper and lower, are named from the parts of our body, so that that is called upper which is above our heads, and lower which is under our feet. Therefore, although the Earth be granted to be the lowest part of the world, in the sense that it is under our feet, whichever way we turn, and the Heaven of the blessed the highest part, inasmuch as it is further removed from our heads than the visible heavens, above which the Apostle places it in this passage, yet it does not follow from this that it is the boundary of the universe, encircling the starry heaven on every side, nor that its limits can be known, nor that it must itself be conceived as unbounded.

units.la: CLXXIV. Inst. 4. (R. A. p. 34.) Non esse absurdum Cajetano, ut dicatur, Christum etiam supra caelum Empyreum ascendisse &c. sed missa illa subtilitate, se negare sequi id quod inferam: Cum enim Christus dicatur ascendisse ad caelum & caelo contineri, e verbis Apostoli hoc unum sequitur, cum ascendisse ad caelum, quod est supra omnes coelos reliquos &c.
units.tr: CLXXIV. Inst. 4. (R. A. p. 34.) It is not absurd, as Cajetan says, that Christ ascended even above the Empyrean heaven, etc. But setting aside that subtlety, he denies that what I infer follows. For since Christ is said to have ascended to heaven and to be contained by heaven, from the words of the Apostle this alone follows: that he ascended to the heaven which is above all the other heavens, etc.

units.la: Resp. Illud quod infero recte infero; sed non infero, Christum ascendisse supra coelum Beatorum, e verbis Apostoli rite intellectis, quod mihi falso hic attribuitur; sed dico, ex verbis illis rigide & absolute acceptis, hoc est, si tantum praecise ad verba, non ad mentem Apostoli attendas, inferri posse, Christum etiam supra Caelum Empyreum ascendisse, quod omnino verum est. Inde itaque concludo, non praecise omnia verba debere bere urgeri, & torqueri, sed ad mentem Apostoli attendendum, ad quam si attendamus, nihil plane pro sua sententia adversarius obtine-bit.
units.tr: Reply. What I infer, I infer rightly. But I do not infer that Christ ascended above the heaven of the blessed from the words of the Apostle rightly understood, which is falsely attributed to me here. I say rather that from those words taken rigidly and absolutely, that is, if you attend only to the bare words and not to the Apostle's meaning, it can be inferred that Christ also ascended above the Empyrean heaven, which is entirely true. From this I conclude that the words should not be pressed and twisted precisely, but that the mind of the Apostle must be attended to. If we attend to that, the adversary will obtain nothing at all for his opinion.

units.la: CLXXV. Inst. 5. loco esse potest (R. A. p. 10.) Quod idem cœlum hariolaris non terminare Universum, nec undiquaque Cœlum Sidereum ambire, sed alicui forte ejus parti incumbere, id ut absurdum sciatet, ita a gravi Theologo alienum esse debet, cujus est loqui & tacere cum Scriptura, ea autem nihil quod supra tertium cœlum sit, usquam memorat, neque uni alicui orbi terrarum partihanc prærogativam dedit, ut inde ad Cœlum Beatorum recta ascendatur, reliquis qui eo contendunt per infinitos gyros circumactu, quod secundum hanc opinionem fieri oporteret..
units.tr: CLXXV. Inst. 5. (R. A. p. 10.) That you conjecture the same heaven does not bound the universe, nor surround the starry heaven on every side, but perhaps rests upon some part of it: as this is known to be absurd, so it ought to be far from a serious theologian, whose task is to speak and be silent with Scripture. Yet Scripture nowhere mentions anything above the third heaven, nor has it given this prerogative to any one part of the world, that one may ascend straight from there to the heaven of the blessed while the rest, who strive towards it, are carried round through infinite circuits, which would have to happen according to this opinion.

units.la: Resp. Nullam ego hic aut alibi extra Scripturam de cœlo Empyreo opinionem profero, neque quicquam hariolor, sed cum Scriptura loquor, & taceo, eo ipso enim, quia Scriptura non determinat, quousque Cœlum Beatorum se extendat &c. Item, an universum undique terminet &c. ea etiam ipsa indeterminata relinquo. Sed si adversarius ex Eph. iv. velit recte inferre, mundum non esse Indefinitum, sed posse ei fines certos assignari, has omnes quæstiones ita determinare debet, ut demonstret, quousque cœlum hoc se extendat, item, nulla esse alia supra hoc cœlum corpora, item, undique cœlum sidereum ambire.
units.tr: Reply. I put forward no opinion here or elsewhere about the Empyrean heaven apart from Scripture, nor do I conjecture anything. I speak with Scripture and am silent, for by that very fact, that Scripture does not determine how far the heaven of the blessed extends, etc. Likewise, whether the universe is bounded on every side, etc.: these things too I leave undetermined. But if the adversary wishes to rightly infer from Eph. 4 that the world is not unbounded, but that fixed limits can be assigned to it, he must settle all these questions by demonstrating how far this heaven extends, that there are no other bodies above this heaven, and that the starry heaven is surrounded on every side.

units.la: CLXXVI. Videamus nunc, quomodo istas quæstiones determinare conetur. R. A. p. 36. Scimus omnes, inquit, cœlum illud non se extendere in infinitum, quia corpus est, scimus supra illud cœlum non esse alia corpora, alioqui ὑπέρουρανον appellationem tueri non posset, quod si ea essent non debuisti Universum cœli & Terra nomine comprehendere, sed addere corpora qua supra ipsum supremum cœlum esse hariolaris.
units.tr: CLXXVI. Let us now see how he tries to settle these questions. R. A. p. 36. We all know, he says, that that heaven does not extend to infinity, because it is a body. We know that there are no other bodies above that heaven, otherwise the expression ὑπέρουρανον could not be defended; and if there were, you ought not to have comprehended the universe under the name of heaven and earth, but to have added the bodies which you conjecture to be above the highest heaven itself.

units.la: Resp. Ex eo quod Cœlum Beatorum sit corpus nego inferri posse, illud non esse indefinitæ extensionis, nec enim corporis naturæ indefinitam extensionem video repugnare. 2. Cœlum Beatorum recte ἐν ὑψί-στῳ dicitur respectu corporum nobis cognitorum & Cœlorum visibilium, sed tamen exinde non sequitur, illud absolute esse supremum, & si sit, habere terminos nobis conceptibiles. Præstat ergo in re incerta, taliqueque quæ quamvis certa sit, non magnum haberet usum, ἀπίχειν, quam aliquid certi determinare velle. 3. Universum Cœli & Terræ nomine cum Scriptura comprehendo; si tamen essent supra Cœlum Beatorum corpora quædam, ea nihilominus ad id, quod cœli nomine intelligitur, essent referenda. Quod est supra cœlos aspectabiles, id nomine cœli tertii venit, quod vel totum potest esse destinatum Beatorum habitationi, vel ex parte tantum, id quod à nobis nequit determinari.
units.tr: Reply. I deny that it can be inferred from the fact that the heaven of the blessed is a body that it is not of indefinite extent, for I see no contradiction between the nature of a body and indefinite extension. 2. The heaven of the blessed is rightly called ἐν ὑψίστῳ [en hypsistō] with respect to the bodies known to us and the visible heavens, but it does not follow from this that it is absolutely the highest, and if it is, that it has limits conceivable by us. It is better, therefore, in an uncertain matter, and one which, however certain it might be, would be of little use, to refrain [ἀπέχειν, apechein] than to wish to determine something certain. 3. I comprehend the universe under the names of heaven and earth with Scripture. Yet if there were certain bodies above the heaven of the blessed, they would nevertheless have to be referred to what is understood by the name heaven. What is above the visible heavens comes under the name of the third heaven, which may be wholly destined for the habitation of the blessed, or only in part, a point which cannot be determined by us.

units.la: CLXXVII. Pergimus cum pergente R. A. p. 36. Coelum supremum si non undique Coelum sidereum ambiret, non tamen careret termino sidereum coelum, sed se ipso terminaretur. Deinde si non ambiret undique Coelum Sidereum, non esset supra omnes coelos, sed supra eorum partem tantum.
units.tr: CLXXVII. We proceed with the author as he proceeds. R. A. p. 36. If the highest heaven did not surround the starry heaven on every side, the starry heaven would not lack a boundary, but would be bounded by itself. Next, if it did not surround the starry heaven on every side, it would not be above all the heavens, but only above a part of them.

units.la: Resp. Si non undique Coelum Sidereum ambiat, sequitur ex indefinitâ extensione mundi, Coeli Siderei terminos cognosci non posse, sed illud se in indefinitum extendere. Deinde Coelum Beatorum esset supra omnes coelos spectabiles, quod dicit Scriptura, etsi non undique coelum sidereum ambiat. Neque enim Scriptura dicit, illud esse undique supra omnes coelos aspectabiles. Quas postea difficultates nectit Antagonista, sive potius nugas prompsit de via, per quam animæ & corpora deberent ascendere ad coelum, si hoc non undiquaque cingeret coelum sidereum, eas tanquam inconsequentes ex nostrâ sententiâ rejicimus, nec opus est, ut de iis simus solliciti. Neque nos γεγωδεις μύθως introducimus, qui dicimus, naturam Coeli Beatorum & extensionis ejus rationem non posse determinari, taliaque, de quibus Scriptura nihil dicit, neque ratio docet, in medio esse relinquenda, sed vos, qui quævis magistraliter vultis determinare.
units.tr: Reply. If it did not surround the starry heaven on every side, it would follow from the indefinite extent of the world that the limits of the starry heaven could not be known, but that it extends indefinitely.
