Next, the heaven of the blessed would be above all the visible heavens, as Scripture says, even if it did not surround the starry heaven on every side, for Scripture does not say that it is on every side above all the visible heavens. As for the further difficulties the opponent ties up, or rather the trifles he brings out about the way by which souls and bodies would have to ascend to heaven if this did not surround the starry heaven on every side, we reject these as inconsequential from our view, and there is no need for us to be anxious about them. Nor do we introduce γραώδεις μύθους [graōdeis mythous, old wives' tales], we who say that the nature of the heaven of the blessed and the reason of its extension cannot be determined, and that matters about which Scripture says nothing and reason teaches nothing must be left open. It is rather you who want to determine everything in a masterly way.

units.la: CLXXVIII. Inst. 6. (R. A. p. 32.) Quomodo coelum potest esse supra omnes coelos visibiles, astris confertos, si astra in infinitum multiplicentur? potestne aliquid superius esse infinito: quomodo potest includere omnia corpora, si non undique Coelum Sidereum ambiat, & ultra ipsum sint alia corpora?
units.tr: CLXXVIII. Inst. 6. (R. A. p. 32.) How can heaven be above all visible heavens, crowded with stars, if the stars are multiplied to infinity? Can anything be higher than the infinite? How can it contain all bodies, if the starry heaven does not surround it on every side and other bodies lie beyond it?

units.la: Resp. Nemo dixit, quod astra actu sint infinita, sed hoc dicimus, eorum numerum determinari non posse, nec certum esse, an ultra stellas fixas, quas oculis usurpamus, aut etiam quas tubo optico assequi possumus, sint aliæ stellæ fixæ, quas nullis ex dictis modis cognoscere possimus, interim cum distribuitur coelum in Aëreum, Sidereum, & Tertium Coelum, per Sidereum intel igitur coelum visibile astris refertum, quæ oculis nostris usurpare possumus, quo respectu Coelum Beatorum supra omnes coelos visibiles esse potest, etsi astrorum numerus iniri non possit. 2. Infinito nihil superius esse potest, adeoque, si Coelum Beatorum undique Coelum Sidereum ambiat, poterimus cognoscere hujus limites, ultra quos non sit altius adscendendum. Quod si vero tantum ab aliqua parte hoc complectatur, etiam tantum ab eâ parte. fines & limites ei erunt adscribendi. 3. Concedimus vero, Coelum Beatorum non posse undique includere omnia corpora, si non undique Coelum Sidereum ambiret; sed hæc duo conjunxinus nullibi. Diximus enim, ad Indefinitatem Mundi destruendam non tantum certum esse oportere, quod cœlum Empyreum undique ambiat cœlum sidereum, sed etiam eo evicto, quod tamen fieri nequit, demonstrari debere, nos cœli Empyrei limites comprehendere vel cognoscere posse.
units.tr: Reply. No one has said that the stars are actually infinite. We say that their number cannot be determined, and it is not certain whether there are other fixed stars beyond those we see with our eyes or can reach with the optical tube, which we cannot know by any of the methods mentioned. Meanwhile, when the heaven is divided into the air, the starry heaven and the third heaven, I understand by the starry heaven the visible heaven filled with stars that we can see with our eyes. In this sense the heaven of the blessed can be above all visible heavens, even though the number of the stars cannot be counted. 2. Nothing can be higher than the infinite. So if the heaven of the blessed surrounds the starry heaven on every side, we shall be able to know its limits, beyond which one cannot ascend higher. But if it embraces the starry heaven only on some side, then limits and boundaries must be assigned to it on that side only. 3. We do concede that the heaven of the blessed could not contain all bodies on every side if the starry heaven did not surround it on every side. But we have joined these two claims nowhere. For we said that, to overthrow the indefiniteness of the world, it is not enough that it be certain that the Empyrean heaven surrounds the starry heaven on every side; it must also be demonstrated, once that is established (which cannot be done), that we can grasp and know the limits of the Empyrean heaven.

units.la: CLXXIX. Tandem (R. A. p. 38.) Cœlum ergo illud vel ubiquitatium necessario erit, quod omnia corpora penetret, vel nullum penitus, cum nullu ei inveniatur locus, stellis fixis, (post terram, aërem, Planetas) omnia omnino loca, quæ imaginari possumus, occupantibus.
units.tr: CLXXIX. Finally (R. A. p. 38.) That heaven, then, will necessarily be either everywhere, if it penetrates all bodies, or wholly nowhere, since no place is found for it, the fixed stars (after earth, air and the planets) occupying absolutely all the places we can imagine.

units.la: Resp. At quis unquam dixit, stellas fixas, post terram, aërem, Planetas omnia omnino loca occupare, cum è contrario dicam, Cœlum Empyreum esse supra omnes hos cœlos visibiles astris refertos, nisi statuas, supra omnes hos cœlos visibiles nullum esse corpus, quod vellent Lutherani.
units.tr: Reply. But who has ever said that the fixed stars, after earth, air and the planets, occupy absolutely all places? On the contrary, I say that the Empyrean heaven is above all these visible heavens filled with stars, unless you maintain that above all these visible heavens there is no body at all, which is what the Lutherans want.

units.la: CLXXX. Prob. Antecced. 2. Potentia pertinet ad materiam, quæ, cum ex se sit Indefinita, origo est infiniti: actus vero ex forma pendet, quæ forma, ut est actus, ita est aliquid sui conditione definitum. Piccol-homineus.
units.tr: CLXXX. Proof of the antecedent 2. Potency pertains to matter, which, since it is indefinite in itself, is the source of the infinite; but actuality depends on form, and form, as it is actual, is by its very condition something defined. Piccolhomineus.

units.la: Resp. Est hic manifestum sophisma, neque probatur, quod probari debebat. Quomodocunque materia & forma differant, sive tantum conceptibus, ut generale & speciale, sive realiter, ut diversa Entia, sive modaliter, de quo hoc loco nolumus disputare, nihil aliud hoc argumento infertur, quam per formam rem in sua specie constitui, & ab aliis Entibus distingui, atque sic finiri & determinari. Sed non procedit argumentum à definitione Metaphysicâ & transcendentali, ad finitionem Physicam, nisi simili modo velis inferre, personas SS. Trinitatis esse finitas, quia natura & persona differunt, ut terminatum & terminans, vocabulis his metaphysice acceptis, uti docent Theologi. 2. Quid si ipsa forma sit infinita, vel indefinita? an non per eam poterit terminari materia, ut tamen non inde exsurgat actu finitum? sic per infinitatem sive perfectionem summam determinatur Ens, ut oriatur conceptus in mente nostra Entis Infiniti, Dei, qui sine omni controversia est actu infinitus.
units.tr: Reply. This is a plain sophism, and it does not prove what it ought to prove. However matter and form differ, whether only in concepts, as the general and the specific, or really, as different beings, or modally (which we do not wish to dispute here), this argument only infers that by its form a thing is constituted in its own kind, is distinguished from other beings, and so is finished and determined. But the argument does not proceed from the metaphysical and transcendental definition to physical finitude, unless you wish to infer in the same way that the persons of the Holy Trinity are finite, because nature and person differ as the terminated and the terminating, these terms being taken metaphysically, as the theologians teach. 2. What if the form itself is infinite or indefinite? Can matter not be terminated by it, without there thereby arising something actually finite? So a being is determined through infinity, or supreme perfection, so that in our mind there arises the concept of an infinite Being, God, who without any controversy is actually infinite.

units.la: CLXXXI. Prob. 3. Antecedentis ex Piccolhomineo. Omne productum & in esse constitutum, ut tale est, etiam præditum dicitur sine & termino sua constitutionis, & propterea contradictionem includeret, si diceremus, esse constitutum in esse, & esse infinitum; ita enim infinitum pertransiretur, nec esset in eo aliquid ultra accipere, devenitum enim esset ad postremum, & infinitum non esset infinitum.
units.tr: CLXXXI. Proof 3. of the antecedent, from Piccolhomineus. Everything produced and set in being, as such, is also said to be bounded by the limit of its constitution, and therefore it would involve a contradiction if we said that it is constituted in being and is infinite; for then the infinite would be traversed, and there would be nothing further to take in it, for one would have arrived at an end, and the infinite would not be infinite.

units.la: Resp. I.
units.tr: Reply. I.

units.la: Resp. 1. Quod productum est, finitum quidem est perfectione, eo ipso, quia est productum, cum certâ & finitâ mensurâ habeat eam sibi communicatam: Sed negamus omne corpus productum, necessario habere finitam extensionem. 2. Omne productum habet terminum suæ constitutionis, quatenus ad illud actio est terminata, sed non ideo Physicè est finitum actu. 3. Nulla ergo est contradictio, si dicamus, productum eo ipso, quia constitutum est in actu, esse hactenus finitum metaphysice, quatenus à non esse ad fieri, & à fieri ad productum esse processit, sed nihil impedit, quin productum corpus possit esse infinitum: neque ita infinitum pertransiretur, dummodo distinctio inter infinitum metaphysice sive transcendentaliter, & infinitum Physice observaretur; quamvis etiam à Deo, qui produxit, comprehenderetur, utpote infinito, nihilominus infinitum maneret, & nobis finitis semper in eo restaret ulterius accipiendum.
units.tr: Reply. (1) What is produced is indeed finite in its perfection, by the very fact that it is produced, since it has received its communicated measure, which is definite and finite. But we deny that every produced body necessarily has a finite extension. (2) Everything produced has a limit of its constitution, insofar as the action is terminated at it, but for that reason it is not physically finite in actuality. (3) There is therefore no contradiction if we say that what is produced, by the very fact that it has been constituted in act, is hitherto finite metaphysically, insofar as it has proceeded from non-being to becoming and from becoming to being produced; but nothing prevents a produced body from being infinite. Nor would the infinite thus be traversed, provided the distinction between the infinite metaphysically or transcendentally and the infinite physically is observed. Even if it were comprehended by God, who produced it, as being infinite it would nonetheless remain infinite, and for us, who are finite, there would always be something further to take in it.

units.la: CLXXXII. Prob. 4. Ejusdem Piccolhom. Conditio corporis actu existentis est, ut sit termino praeditum, quia conditio corporis est terminari superficie.
units.tr: CLXXXII. Proof 4. From the same Piccolhomini: The condition of a body that actually exists is that it be endowed with a boundary, because the condition of a body is to be bounded by a surface.

units.la: Resp. Conditio corporis finiti & terminati omnino est, terminari superficie, sed non corporis quatenus tale est, ad cujus naturam nihil requiritur, præter meram extensionem, reliqua enim omnia ab eo tolli possunt, corpore manente: Tolle enim motum è mundo, nulla erunt corpora terminata & nec finita certâ superficie, sed erunt omnia unum corpus continuum, nec tamen propterea naturam suam amittent. Mirum id quod dico videbitur iis, qui præjudiciis occupati formas nescio quas substantiales fingunt, qui existimant Accidentibus realitatem strictè dictam competere, eaque substantiis, tanquam nova quædam Entia superaddi putant, quinque qualitates sensibiles rebus attribuunt; nec tamen earum rationem formalem intelligunt; sed non mirum erit iis, qui omnia hæc figmenta rejecerunt, qui nihil in corporeis rebus, præter Materiam in Extensione consistentem agnoscunt, in eaque etiam nullam distinctionem concipiunt, præter eam, quæ à Magnitudine, Situ, Motu, & Quiete existit. Vide Cartef. Pp. II. art. 23. Si enim nullus sit motus, nulla erit corporum à se invicem separatio, quoad superficiem externam, quæ sine motu concipi nequit, nulla etiam distinctio texturæ, & variatio partium interiorum. Ubi enim motus non est, ibi pars à proximè cohærente, quoad figuram non distinguitur; cohæret enim, sicque nullum terminum habet; quo posito, Continuitas omnium corporum, omniumque partium, necessario oritur; est enim Continuum, quod alteri immediate ita cohæret, ut penes illud quiescat.
units.tr: Reply: It is indeed the condition of a finite and bounded body to be bounded by a surface, but not of body as such. Nothing is required for its nature except mere extension, for all the other things can be taken away from it while the body remains. Take motion out of the world, and there will be no bodies that are bounded, or limited by a definite surface. Instead, all things will be one continuous body, and yet they will not for that reason lose their nature. What I say will seem strange to those who, occupied with prejudices, invent I know not what substantial forms, who think that accidents have real existence in the strict sense and imagine them added to substances as new kinds of beings, and who attribute the five sensible qualities to things without understanding their formal reason. It will not be strange, however, to those who have rejected all these fictions, who recognise nothing in corporeal things except matter consisting in extension, and who conceive in it no distinction except that which arises from magnitude, situation, motion and rest. See Descartes, Principles, Part II, art. 23. For if there is no motion, there will be no separation of bodies from one another as regards their outer surface, which cannot be conceived without motion. Nor will there be any distinction of texture or variation of the inner parts. For where there is no motion, a part is not distinguished in figure from the part that adheres closely to it. It adheres, and so has no boundary. This being granted, the continuity of all bodies and of all their parts necessarily arises, for a continuum is that which so adheres immediately to another that it rests upon it.

units.la: CLXXXIII.Consequentia vero(R. A. p.47.) ridicula admodū est,de numinis quiescentibus in arcâ, quos ex hac sententia, omnes in unum numinum continuum putat mutatum iri, de quiescentibus in terra lignis & lapidibus, quæ sint futura omnia unum corpus, de quiescentibus noctu animantibus, hominibus, canibus, felibus, quæ sint coalitura in unam massam : &c. An enim, cum quiescunt nummi in arcâ, nullus circa eos est motus aëris, an nulla permeatio materiæ subtilis, quæ omnia transit? 2. an in Animantibus si quiescunt propterea nullus est motus, sanguinis, spirituum? an nihil in iis liquidi? quod eo ipso quo tale est, in perpetuo est motu, an omnes particulæ ita quiescunt, ut nihil circa eas moveatur? Verum hæc omnia inde procedunt, quod non observaverit, à me non dictum, aliquo motu sublato è mundo omnia fore continua,sed indefinite, motu,hoc est,omni sublato è mundo omnia fore Unum corpus continuum.
units.tr: CLXXXIII. The consequence, however (R. A. p.47), is quite ridiculous: concerning coins resting in a chest, which on this view he thinks will all be changed into one continuous coin; concerning sticks and stones resting on the ground, which will all be one body; concerning animals, men, dogs and cats resting at night, which will coalesce into one mass: etc. For when the coins rest in the chest, is there no motion of air around them, or no permeation of subtle matter, which passes through everything? Second, in animals, if they are at rest, is there therefore no motion of blood or of spirits? Is there nothing liquid in them? Yet whatever is liquid is, by that very fact, in perpetual motion. Or do all the particles rest in such a way that nothing moves around them? But all these objections arise from failing to notice that I did not say that with some motion removed from the world, all things will be continuous, but rather, indefinitely, with motion, that is, with all motion removed from the world, all things will be one continuous body.

units.la: Atque hæc dixi præcipua, quæ contra infinitum actu afferri possunt, quod etiamnum dico, quum non videam aliquid urgentius adversarium produxisse, quod non eodem referri queat, aut ex iildem fontibus scaturiat, uti ex dictis apparet, & porro manifestum erit ex iis, quæ occasione datâ, ab adversariis hoc & sequenti capite de infinito actu dicentur.
units.tr: These are the chief points that can be brought against an actual infinite, and I still maintain them, since I do not see that the adversaries have produced anything more pressing that cannot be traced back to the same sources or spring from the same origins, as appears from what has been said. It will become clearer still from what the adversaries will say, when the opportunity arises, about the actual infinite in this chapter and the following one.

units.la: CLXXXIV. Prob. 5. Antecedentis. Corpus infinitum non potest moveri : at totus mundus movetur.
units.tr: CLXXXIV. Proof 5, of the antecedent: An infinite body cannot be moved; but the whole world is moved.

units.la: E. Resp. Movetur mundus tum respectu partium suarum adspectabilium, tùm etiam respectu invisibilium particularum, ex quibus fluida componuntur, sed, an etiam omnes illæ partes mundi superiores, istis partibus adspectabilibus in infinitum usque superpositæ, moverentur, quis dixerit?
units.tr: Therefore, reply: The world is moved both with respect to its visible parts and with respect to the invisible particles of which fluids are composed. But who would say that all those higher parts of the world, placed above these visible parts and extended to infinity, would also be moved?

units.la: CLXXXV. Prob. 6. Anteced. (M. p. 156.) Corpus actu infinitum implicat corpus esse mobile & non posse moveri : Prob. Mobile erit, quia erit corpus naturale; nam ideo habet in se principium motus et quietis, quia natura est principium motus & quietis. Non mobile, quia moveretur aut motu recto, aut circulari; Non recto, quia non esset ubi, quo tenderet, quandoquidem per infinitatem omnia repleret; Non circulari, quia partes corporis infiniti non possent succedere in locum aliarum partium, quod requiritur in motu circulari, eo quod distarent: in infinitum, omnes enim lineæ à centro circulari ductæ, quo longius protenduntur, eo longius inter se distant, quare in infinitum protensæ, in infinitum quoque à se distarent.
units.tr: CLXXXV. Proof 6, of the antecedent (M. p. 156): A body that is actually infinite implies that a body is mobile and yet cannot be moved. Proof: It will be mobile, because it will be a natural body; for it has in itself a principle of motion and rest precisely because nature is a principle of motion and rest. It cannot be mobile, because it would move either with straight motion or with circular motion. Not with straight motion, because there would be no place to which it could tend, since by its infinity it would fill everything. Not with circular motion, because the parts of an infinite body could not succeed into the place of other parts, which circular motion requires, because they would be separated to infinity. For all lines drawn from a circular centre, the further they are extended, the further they are apart from one another; so when extended to infinity, they would also be infinitely distant from one another.

units.la: Resp. Corpus naturale habere principium motus & quietis verum est, si intelligas non de principio activo, sed dispositivo; Activum vero prinprincipium nullum corpus in se habet, quia omne, quod movetur, movetur ab alio, teste Aristot. & ipsa ratione, quæ solis rebus spiritualibus sive cogitantibus hoc privilegium attribuit, ut haberent internum proprium{que} agendi principium: quod si rebus corporeis tribuas, eo ipso cum spiritualibus confundes, quod quidem vitium pessimum est, & tamen in Philosophia Scholastica frequentissimum. Natura ergo est tantum motus & quietis principium dispositivum, quatenus, sicut ab extrinseco agente impellitur & dirigitur, ita pro magnitudine & figura sua motum varie communicat. Itaque corpus naturale eatenus est mobile, quatenus potest moveri ab alio: Corpus autem infinitum potest dici mobile respectu suarum partium in infinitum usque, quia quævis pars potest recedere ab alia, sed an totum sit mobile, sive omnes illæ superiores, quæ ex hypoth. in infinitum extensæ sunt, moveri queant, an non, cum totum ut infinitum non possit comprehendi cogitatione finita, quis dixerit?
units.tr: Reply: It is true that a natural body has a principle of motion and rest, if you understand this not of an active principle but of a dispositive one. No body has in itself an active principle, because everything that is moved is moved by another, as Aristot. teaches, and as reason itself shows, which grants this privilege only to spiritual or thinking beings, that they should have an internal and proper principle of acting. If you attribute this to corporeal things, you confuse them with spiritual ones, which is a very great fault, and yet a most frequent one in Scholastic Philosophy. Nature is therefore only a dispositive principle of motion and rest, inasmuch as, just as it is impelled and directed by an external agent, so according to its magnitude and figure it communicates motion in various ways. Accordingly, a natural body is mobile only so far as it can be moved by another. An infinite body, however, can be called mobile with respect to its parts, extended to infinity, because any part can recede from another. But whether the whole is mobile, or whether all those higher parts, which by hypothesis are extended to infinity, can be moved or not, who would say, since the whole, as infinite, cannot be comprehended by finite thought?

units.la: CLXXXVI. Prob. 7. Anteced. (M. p. 158.)
units.tr: CLXXXVI. Proof 7, the antecedent (M. p. 158.)

units.la: Absurdum est, & contradictorium, esse creaturam, & tamen actu non posse augeri per divinam potentiam: tale autem quid corpus actu infinitum involveret; de creatura constat, non posse autem augeri patet, quia infinito nihil potest accedere.
units.tr: It is absurd and self-contradictory to be a creature and yet be unable actually to be increased by divine power; but such a thing would involve an actually infinite body. That it is a creature is established; that it cannot be increased is plain, since nothing can be added to the infinite.

units.la: Resp. Quomodo mundus posset augeri, nos non possumus intelligere, ergo etiam de eo nihil debemus determinare. In mundo enim cum nullos terminos agnoscere possimus, non etiam intelligere possumus, quomodo augeri queat.
units.tr: Reply: How the world could be increased we cannot understand, so we ought not to determine anything about it either. For since we cannot recognise any limits in the world, neither can we understand how it could be increased.

units.la: CLXXXVII. Prob. 8. Anteced. (M. p. 157.)
units.tr: CLXXXVII. Proof 8, the antecedent (M. p. 157.)

units.la: Si detur corpus actu infinitum, erit sub aliquo certo genere, & tamen sub nulla ejus specie continebitur, esset enim quantum, & tamen sub nulla specie quantitatis, quia nulla species potest esse infinita, eo ipso, quod in esse speciei constituitur per formam, nec essario limitatur per Essentiam.
units.tr: If there is given an actually infinite body, it will fall under some definite genus, and yet it will be contained under no species of it; for it would be a quantity, and yet under no species of quantity, since no species can be infinite, precisely because a species is constituted in being by its form and is necessarily limited by its essence.

units.la: Resp. Hujus argumenti vis similis est cum primo, itaque eadem responsio potest applicari.
units.tr: Reply: The force of this argument is similar to that of the first, so the same answer can be applied.

units.la: CLXXXVIII. Prob. 9. Anteced. Quia tum ex infinitate Christi non formari poterit pro ejus divinitate argumentum.
units.tr: CLXXXVIII. Proof 9, the antecedent. Because from the infinity of Christ no argument can be formed for his divinity.

units.la: Resp. Infinita quando de Deo & Christo usurpatur, significat, infinitatem perfectionis, at de mundo, extensionis, ex qua divinitas nullo modo potest probari.
units.tr: Reply: When "infinite" is used of God and Christ, it signifies infinity of perfection; but of the world it signifies extension, from which divinity can in no way be proved.

units.la: CLXXXIX. Ut tamen appareat, sententiam nostram tantum esse, quod non possint cognosci aliqui mundi limites, ultra quos non ulterius sit adscendendum, non vero nos statuere mundum Infinitum, prout statuimus tuimus, non sufficientia argumenta esse, quæ pro finitate Mundi producuntur, ita etiam ostendemus insufficientiam argumentorum, quæ pro infinitate mundi adduci queunt. Atque primo quidem Objici potest: Cujus Idea talis ac tanta est, ut nullos terminos in eo posse cognoscere, illud est infinitum, Atqui Mundi idea &c.
units.tr: CLXXXIX. Yet so that it may appear that our view is only this, that certain limits of the world cannot be known, beyond which one may not proceed further, and that we do not affirm the world to be infinite, just as we hold that the arguments produced for the finitude of the world are not sufficient, so we shall also show the insufficiency of the arguments which can be brought forward for the infinity of the world. And first, indeed, this may be objected: "That whose idea is such and so great that we cannot know any limits in it, that is infinite; but the idea of the world etc."

units.la: Resp. Negatur Major, quia ut aliquid sit infinitum, requiritur ut idea ejus talis sit, ut concipiamus in eo nullos esse terminos, quod nos negamus de mundo.
units.tr: Reply: The major premise is denied, because for something to be infinite it is required that its idea be such that we conceive no limits in it, which we deny of the world.

units.la: CXC. 2. Obj. Qui est à Deo infinito conditus, ille est infinitus.
units.tr: CXC. Second objection: "That which has been created by an infinite God is itself infinite."

units.la: Resp. Neg. Maj. Prop. Quæ vera esset, si hoc modo esset proposita, Quod est à Deo infinito, illud est tale, ut nos ejus limites non possimus invenire, nisi à revelatione, experientia vel ratione manifestetur, adeoque est Indefinitum.
units.tr: Reply: The major premise is denied. It would be true if it were put in this way: "That which is from an infinite God is such that we cannot find its limits unless they are made manifest by revelation, experience or reason, and so it is indefinite."

units.la: CAPUT XIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIII.

units.la: Objectio tertia ab Infinitate Dei desumpta proposita & refutata.
units.tr: The third objection, drawn from the infinity of God, set out and refuted.

units.la: CXCI. Objectio 3. ex Infinitate Dei hoc modo formari potest: Quæ sententia Deum quendam ex mundo facit, non est admittenda: At sententia de mundi Indefinitate hoc facit. E. Hæc desumi potest ex verbis (R. St. p. 82.) Optarem & eum paulo concinnius argumentari, quam facit, qua enim ἀχολαβία ex immensitate Dei immensitatem creatura deducit? hac ratione Deum quendam alterum ex mundo facere adigitur.
units.tr: CXCI. The third objection, from the infinity of God, can be framed in this way: an opinion that makes some god out of the world must not be admitted; but the opinion about the world's indefiniteness does this. Therefore it. This can be drawn from the words (R. St. p. 82.): I would wish that he argued a little more neatly than he does. For by what consequence [ἀκολουθία] does he deduce the immensity of the creature from the immensity of God? By this reasoning he is compelled to make another god out of the world.

units.la: Resp. Optarem, adversarium aliquanto accuratius ad argumentationem Cartesii attendisse, quam fecit: ubinam enim Cartesius immensitatem creaturæ ex immensitate Dei deducit? ubi vero mundum simpliciter Infinitum dicit? 2. Posito, non concesso, mundum esse simpliciter infinitum sua extensione, quod tamen nullibi dicit Cartesius, nec ego; an inde sequeretur esse Deum? minime vero. Infinitas enim, quæ Deo tribuitur, plane est alterius generis quam infinitas mundi: Illa est perfectionis, quâ significatur, Deum habere omnimodam perfectionem, majoremque, quam ulla creatura cogitatione sua comprehendere possit, cujus nulli sint fines, nulli limites; hæc extensionis, quæ nullo modo in Deum cadit, imo priorem evertit. Quod enim est extensum, etsi esset in infinitum extensum, nihilominus habet partes extra partes, est divisibile &c. quod quam alienum sit à Dei omnimoda perfectione, quilibet videt. Itaque tantum abest, ut per Infinitam extensionem tribuatur mundo infinita perfectio, ut è contrario infinita extensio eo ipso, quia est extensio, multiplicem imperfectionem ponat.
units.tr: Reply: I would wish that the adversary had attended a little more accurately to Descartes's argument than he has done. For where does Descartes deduce the immensity of the creature from the immensity of God? And where does he simply call the world infinite? 2. Granting, though not conceding, that the world is simply infinite in its extension (which Descartes nowhere says, nor do I), would it follow that it is God? By no means. For the infinity ascribed to God is of a wholly different kind from the infinity of the world. The former belongs to perfection, signifying that God possesses every perfection in every way, and greater than any creature can grasp in its thought, a perfection with no ends and no limits. The latter belongs to extension, which in no way applies to God and indeed overturns the former. For what is extended, even if it were extended to infinity, nevertheless has parts outside parts, is divisible, and so on; how alien this is to God's perfection in every respect, anyone can see. So far is it from being the case that infinite perfection is attributed to the world through infinite extension, that on the contrary infinite extension, precisely because it is extension, posits manifold imperfection.

units.la: ·CXCII. Inst. 1. (R. A. p. 39.) Cartesium Pp.III.art.29. ex immensitate Dei immensitatem creaturæ colligere. Causativam enim particulam cùm, evincere, eum vel nullos in mundo limites, id est immensitatem mundi deducere ex immensitate Dei, ut causa, vel hanc ex illa ut effecto.
units.tr: CXCII. Instance 1 (R. A. p. 39.): Descartes, Pp. III art. 29, infers the immensity of the creature from the immensity of God. For the causal particle cum (since) is used to prove that he deduces either no limits in the world, that is, the immensity of the world, from the immensity of God as cause, or this from that as effect.

units.la: Resp. De illo loco supra art. 135. actum, isque legitime explicatus, & quid à Cartesio colligatur, quid non, indicatum. 2. nullos in mundo limites cognoscere, & mundum esse immensum, valde differunt, Cartesius vero ex immensitate Dei nihil aliud colligit, quam ultra stellas fixas alia corpora existere.
units.tr: Reply: That passage was dealt with above at art. 135, and was legitimately explained, and it was shown what Descartes does and does not infer. 2. To know of no limits in the world and to hold that the world is immense are very different things. Descartes, however, infers from the immensity of God nothing more than that other bodies exist beyond the fixed stars.

units.la: CXCIII. Inst. 2. (R. A. p. 40.) Non dixit Cartesius totidem verbis, mundum esse simpliciter infinitum extensione sua, sed dixit quod illis æquivalet, mundum nullos extensionis suæ fines habere.
units.tr: CXCIII. Instance 2 (R. A. p. 40.): Descartes did not say in so many words that the world is simply infinite in its extension, but he said what is equivalent to it: that the world has no limits to its extension.

units.la: Resp. Hæc verba respiciunt Pp. II. art. 21. quem supra art. 120. 121. & seqq. explicuimus, quo lectorem ablegamus.
units.tr: Reply: These words refer to Pp. II art. 21, which we explained above at arts. 120, 121 and following, to which we refer the reader.

units.la: CXCIV. Inst. 3. (R. A. p. 41.) Ex Mundi Infinitate sequeretur, rem extensam esse Deum, quia res extensa ponitur infinita, infinitas autem rei extensa non convenit &c.
units.tr: CXCIV. Instance 3 (R. A. p. 41.): From the infinity of the world it would follow that an extended thing is God, since an extended thing is posited as infinite, but the infinity of an extended thing does not belong, etc.

units.la: Resp. Si hic sit ullum argumentum, deberet hoc modo procedere; Cui convenit Infinitas, ille est Deus, Atqui ex hypoth. mundo convenit. E. At jam responsum erat à me per Infinitatis distinctionem, cum vocabulum Infinitatis dixeram esse ambiguum: Cui ergo competit Infinitas perfectionis, ille est Deus, non cui Infinitas extensionis, qualis esset, si Mundus infinitus statueretur, quod tamen nullibi dico. ·
units.tr: Reply: If there is any argument here, it ought to proceed thus: that to which infinity belongs is God; but by hypothesis infinity belongs to the world. Therefore it is God. But already a reply had been given by me through the distinction of infinity, since I had said that the word "infinity" is ambiguous. To whom infinity of perfection belongs, that one is God; not to whom infinity of extension belongs, such as it would be if an infinite world were posited, which yet I nowhere say.

units.la: CXCV. Inst. 4. (R. A. p. 41.) Infinitas individualis & incommunicabilis proprietas Dei est, mundi infinitas nullius generis i. e. nulla est.
units.tr: CXCV. Instance 4 (R. A. p. 41.): The infinity that is an individual and incommunicable property of God; the infinity of the world is of no kind, i.e. it is nothing.

units.la: Resp Infinitas proprietas Dei est, sed non quocunque sensu vocem illam accipias, verum Infinitas, quæ denotat tot & tantas Dei perfectiones, ut nulli earum limites sint vel esse possint. At Infinitas si mundo tribuatur, non designat infinitatem perfectionis, sed extensionis, quæ auctor, nec ne, non definio; sed si detur, quæritur: an convertat mundum in Deum? quod nego.
units.tr: Reply: Infinity is a property of God, but not in whatever sense you take that word. It is rather the infinity which denotes so many and such great perfections of God that there are, or can be, no limits to any of them. But if infinity is ascribed to the world, it designates not infinity of perfection but of extension. Whether the author is right in this I do not determine; but if it be granted, the question is whether it turns the world into God, which I deny.

units.la: CXCVI. Inst. 5. (R. A. p. 42.) Vos tribuitis rei extensæ talem infinitatem, per quam nullum essentiæ ac perfectionis habet terminum, cum eum nullos extensionis terminos habere fingitis, p. 42. Extensio est perfectio, Infinita ergo Extensio est infinita perfectio.
units.tr: CXCVI. Instance 5 (R. A. p. 42.): You ascribe to an extended thing such an infinity that it has no term of essence or perfection, since you feign that it has no limits of extension (p. 42). Extension is a perfection; infinite extension, therefore, is infinite perfection.

units.la: Resp. Hoc nos non facere saepius est dictum; non enim mundum dicimus infinitum, ut nullos habeat terminos suae extensionis, sed Indefinitum, in quo nulli termini à nobis queant reperiri. 2. Sed nunc quaeritur, an infinitas si tribueretur mundo, esset Essentialis Dei proprietas, quod nos negamus. Dei enim proprietas nō est Infinitas, quovis sensu accepta, sed Infinitas perfectionis, quae mundo non competit. Habebit quidem mundus, si infinitus, nullos Alicujus (nb.) Perfectionis suae, (quae secundum quid tantum talis est, imperfectionemque quandam implicat) limites aliqua ex parte, h. e. Extensionis quatenus talis, sed non perfectionis absolutae, non omnium perfectionum, non omni ex parte, quod ad Infinitatem Dei requiritur.
units.tr: Reply: It has often been said that we do not do this. For we do not call the world infinite so that it has no limits to its extension, but indefinite, in which no limits can be found by us. 2. But now the question is whether, if infinity were ascribed to the world, it would be an essential property of God, which we deny. For the property of God is not infinity in whatever sense taken, but infinity of perfection, which does not belong to the world. The world, indeed, if infinite, would have no limits in some respect of its perfection (which is such only in a certain respect and involves some imperfection), that is, of extension as such; but it would not have absolute perfection, not all perfections, not in every respect, which is what the infinity of God requires. (nb.)

units.la: CXCVII. Iust. 6. (R. A. p. 41, 42.)
units.tr: CXCVII. Iust. 6. (R. A. p. 41, 42.)

units.la: Eo ipso, quo mundus habet partes extra partes & divisibiles est, non potest esse Infinitus, quato enim, an singulae illae partes essent finitae, an infinitae? Si finitae, totum infinitum esse non potest, quia è finitis infinitum non componitur: si infinitae, etiam singulae arbores essent infinitae &c. Concinit M p. 156, 157.
units.tr: By the very fact that the world has parts outside parts and is divisible, it cannot be infinite. For, I ask, are those individual parts finite or infinite? If finite, the whole cannot be infinite, since an infinite is not composed of finites; if infinite, then even the individual trees would be infinite, etc. Agrees with M p. 156, 157.

units.la: Resp. Singulae partes, quae actu ut praecisae conciperentur, essent finitae, ut arbores, homines, tota terra cum omnibus super ea &c. sed si mundus esset infinitus, restarent adhuc semper partes in isto mundo ulterius atque ulterius, in infinitum auferendae & praecidendae, ita ut nulli earum fines sint vel esse possent.
units.tr: Reply: The individual parts, if they were conceived actually as separated, would be finite, such as trees, men, the whole earth with all things upon it, etc. But if the world were infinite, there would still always remain further parts in this world, to be taken away and cut off without end, so that none of them has or could have limits.

units.la: CXCVIII. Inst. 7. (R. A. p. 42.)
units.tr: CXCVIII. Inst. 7. (R. A. p. 42.)

units.la: Quia Extensio multiplicem imperfectionem ponit, E. infinita esse non potest, siquidem infinitas, cum solius Dei sit, omnem imperfectionem excludit.
units.tr: Because extension implies many imperfections, it cannot be infinite; since infinity belongs to God alone, it excludes every imperfection.

units.la: Resp. Non potest esse infinita perfectionibus concedo, nec enim Infinitas quocunque sensu accepta Dei est, sed hoc demum sensu, quatenus dicit tot & tantas perfectiones, ut nulla ex parte earum limites & fines sint vel esse possint.
units.tr: Reply: I grant that it cannot be infinite in its perfections. For infinity is not God's in whatever sense it is taken, but only in this sense: that he has so many and such great perfections that in no respect do limits and ends exist, or could exist, for them.

units.la: CXCIX. Addit R. A. p. 42.
units.tr: CXCIX. He adds, R. A. p. 42.

units.la: Atque hinc quoque insaniens sapientia Clauhergii explodituur, qui ut duo sunt simplicissima, punctum & Deus, ita & duo infinita posse esse cavillatur.
units.tr: And from this also the raving wisdom of Clauberg is exploded, who, just as there are two most simple things, a point and God, mocks that there can also be two infinites.

units.la: Resp. Claub. Def. Cart. p. 512. sic inquit, Ridiculus sit, qui amplius objectionem de duobus infinitis moverit: Plato Materiam vocat infinitam, Deus est infinitus, ergo duo dantur infinita. Nuga. Punctum est res simplicissima, Deus est res simplicissima; ergo duo dantur simplicissima. Nuga & logomachia mera. Quibus ostenditur cavillationem esse in verbo Infinitum, ut in verbo simplicissimum, cum utrumque de Deo usurpatum longe alio sensu accipiatur, quam si aliis quibusvis rebus applicetur. Quod ergo haec non sit λογομαχία ostendendum tibi fuisset, si quid respondere voluisses.
units.tr: Reply: Clauberg, Def. Cart. p. 512, says as follows: Ridiculous is he who has further raised the objection about two infinites: Plato calls matter infinite, God is infinite, therefore two infinites are given. Trifling! A point is a most simple thing, God is a most simple thing; therefore two most simple things are given. Trifling and sheer logomachy. By these words it is shown that the mockery lies in the word infinite, just as in the word most simple, since both, when used of God, are taken in a quite different sense than when applied to any other things. That this is not a logomachy [λογομαχία] should have been shown to you, had you wished to reply to anything.

units.la: CC. Inst. 8. B. p. 128. Sic Dei immensitatem sive infinitatem confundi cum ejus perfectione; Infinitum quidem esse Deum perfectione in omnibus attributis suis, sed neminem Theologorum Reformatorum, illis vocibus simpliciter positis perfectionem intellexisse &c.
units.tr: CC. Inst. 8. B. p. 128. Thus the immensity or infinity of God is confused with his perfection; God is indeed infinite in perfection in all his attributes, but no theologian of the Reformed, taking those words simply, has understood perfection &c.

units.la: Resp. Tu vero dic quaeso, Num definitio supra data art. 195. Infinitatis Divinae sit legitima, nec ne? Si non, cedo vel rationem, vel unum Theologum, qui eam rejiciat; si sit legitima, ex eâ apparet, eam mundo nunquam communicatum iri, etiamsi extensione diceretur Infinitus. Infinitas Dei per omnia attributa, quae sunt ejus perfectiones, sese extendit fatentibus Theologis. E. etiam generaliter est definienda. Vel responde ad hoc argumentum: Mundi Infinitas est extensionis: Dei Infinitas non est Extensionis: E. Dei infinitas non est mundi infinitas. Quod si ulla contradictio inter me & Theologos citatos, ostendendum, quod negent, Infinitatem Dei esse ejus perfectionem & non posse ut perfectionem considerari.
units.tr: Reply: Pray tell me, is the definition of divine infinity given above in art. 195 legitimate or not? If not, I demand either a reason or one theologian who rejects it. If it is legitimate, it appears from it that infinity will never be communicated to the world, even if it were called infinite by extension. The infinity of God extends through all the attributes which are his perfections, as the theologians confess. Therefore it must also be defined in general terms. Or else answer this argument: The infinity of the world belongs to extension; the infinity of God does not belong to extension; therefore the infinity of God is not the infinity of the world. But if there is any contradiction between me and the theologians cited, it must be shown that they deny that the infinity of God is his perfection and that it cannot be considered as a perfection.

units.la: CCI. Inst. 9. Hic porro R. A. p. 76. nescio quem scorpium latere suspicatur, existimans, nos Deo denegare Infinitatem Essentiae, & per Consequ. ejus praesentiam ratione Essentiae, in omnibus locis, inque eum finem adducit verba Cartesii in Epistola ad Morum, ubi sic dicit Cartesius: Hoc ubique non admitto: videris infinitatem in eo ponere, quod ubique existat, (quod intelligendum ratione diffusionis Essentiae in omnibus locis, de qua agebatur) cui opinioni non assentior, sed Deum puto ratione Essentia nullam plane habere relationem ad locum.
units.tr: CCI. Inst. 9. Here, moreover, R. A. p. 76 suspects some scorpion lurking I know not where, supposing that we deny God infinity of essence and, by consequence, his presence in all places by reason of his essence; and to that end he brings forward the words of Descartes in his letter to More, where Descartes says: I do not admit this everywhere: you seem to place infinity in this, that he exists everywhere, (which is to be understood with respect to the diffusion of the essence in all places, which was under discussion) with which opinion I do not agree, but I think that God, with respect to essence, has no relation at all to place.

units.la: Resp. Nullus hic scorpius, nullum periculum. Si Essentia Dei in se consideretur citra operationem ad extra, eam ut talem Cartesius dicit non habere relationem ad locum, quemadmodum ante mundum conditum, antequam operatus erat ad extra, Deus sibi ipsi erat locus & omnia: si vero consideretur cum operatione ad extra, cùm Deus non operetur in distans, & sic respectu suae potentiae sit conjunctus & praesens omnibus rebus, Potentia autem sit idem cum Essentia, etiam Essentia ejus omnibus locis praesens erit dicenda, quod clarum redditur ex epistola Cartesii tertia ad More scripta, quae habetur inter ejus epistolas 72. ubi sic loquitur: Dixi Deum extensum ratione Potentia, quod scilicet illa Potentia se exserat vel exserere possit in re extensa: Certumque est Dei essentiam debere debere esse ubique præsentem, ut ejus potentia ibi possit se exserere, sed nego illam ibi esse per modum rei extensæ, hoc est, eo modo quo paulo ante rem extensam descripsi. Nostra ergo sententia à sententia Vorstii toto cœlo abest. Ille enim Deo tribuebat corpus, existimabat finitū, cœlo includebat respectu essentiæ, quæ omnia ex corporeitate, quam Deo affingebat, procedebant. Nos vero dicimus: Deum esse Spiritum, rem cogitantem, actum purissimum, atq; non minus terræ aliisque quibusvis locis præsente esse respectu essentia, quàm cœlo, cùm cœlum & terram omniaque loca conservet, atq; omnia operetur in omnibus. Hoc tantùm existimamus, Deum ante mundum conditum & nunc non esse in spatiis imaginariis, in quibus nihil operatur, quæque nihil aliud sunt, quàm humani cerebri figmenta, codemque loco habenda, quo chimæra, Cerberus & similia. Unde, cùm nemo id finistrè queat interpretari, si quis neget, Deum esse in chimæra vel in Cerbero, & similibus humani ingenii figmentis, cum nihil sint; Omnipræsentia autem sit ἐκ τ̃ ϖέρς π, ex iis quæ referuntur ad aliquid: neque etiam in pravum sensum detorquendum, si negemus, Deum ibi esse, ubi non operatur, adeoque non esse in spatiis imaginariis. Atque cum hac nostra sententia consentiunt non pauci Theologi. Sic Hyperius Methodi Theol. lib. I. p. 141. Non potest intelligi, Deum ita esse Ubique, quomodo res quapiam in loco est. Cùm namque Deus sit substantia incorporea, ac proinde extremitates nullas admittens, fieri haud potest, ut loco circumscribatur aut contineatur, sed ipse potius circumscribit & continet omnia. Item: Per essentiam est Deus ubique: quia omnes res creatæ cœlum & terra: & quæ in eis sunt, suum esse à Deo accipiunt. Deus namque Principium & Causa Efficiens existit rerum omnium, neque aliunde habent nisi à Deo, ut sint. Igitur hac ratione consideratur Deus ubique per suam essentiam. Et quibusdam interjectis: Deus est ubique per essentiam, h. e. ratione Creationis; per potentiam, i. e. ratione operationis & motionis concessa, quæ in singulis rebus clarè cernitur: denique per præsentiam, i. e. ratione conservationis & gubernationis &c. Quamvis uno verbo simul omnia complectentes, videremur forsitan non inepte dicere: Deum simpliciter esse ubique per potentiam sive operationem. Citat Augustinum ep. 57. ad Dardanum Scriptâ: In eo ipso quod dicitur Deus ubique diffusus carnali resistendum est cogitationi, & mens à corporis sensibus avocanda, ne quasi spatiosa magnitudine opinemur, Deum per omnia diffundi: sicut fumus aut humor, aut aër, aut lux ista diffunditur. (Omnis enim hujusce modi magnitudo minor est in sui parte quàm in toto) sed ita potius, sicuti est magna sapientia etiam in homine, cujus corpus est parvum. Et paulò post: Sic est Deus per cuncta diffusus, ut non sit qualitas mundi, (sed substantia creatrix mundi) sine labore regens, & sine onere continens mundum, non tamen per spatia locorum quasi mole diffusa, ita ut in dimidio mundi corpore sit dimidium &c. sed nullo contentus loco & in se ipso totus. Eadem etiam cum nostra sententia est Tileni in Syntagmate Theologico disp. 12, 28. Vulgata sententia, qua dicimus: Deum esse in rebus omnibus per essentiam, potentiam & praesentiam, intelligenda est, quasi dicatur, Dei essentiam singulis rebus adesse, ut ipsis ὑπαρξιν sive esse suum; potentiam ut vires tribuat: praesentiam ut operationem. Nimirum sicuti causa effectus suo inest, & adest ἐνεργείᾳ. Idem sentit doctissimus Parkerus de Descensu Christi ad inferos libro 2. art. 66. qui post citatos Patres hanc ipsam nostram sententiam à sententia Vorstii distinguens, inquit: Sed nonne ad haeresin illam Augustini Steuchi propendent ista, quam Conradus ille Vorstius irreligiosissimam revocavit ab Orco? Deum nempe substantia sua in coelo duntaxat residere, ubique autem non aliter esse, quam providentia, sapientia, atque potestate sua? Nullo modo. Exprimunt quidem ubiquitatem divinam hi Patres per effectus, utpote nobis notiores, essentiam interim non coarctantes, aut vero etiam à potentia & sapientia separantes: quod nemo hominum, nisi quis forte de grege porci Epicurus attentarit. Concludo verbis Mirandulani: Deus est ubique per essentiam, scilicet per potentiam & praesentiam & hoc nulli creaturae competit. Eadem debet esse sententia eorum omnium, qui substantias spirituales & animas separatas negant esse per essentiam in loco, nisi quatenus illa essentia extra se operatur, sive quatenus est operans (haec enim est mens istorum auctorum) quâ de re videas Parkerum lib. 2. art. 61, 62. qui pro eâ sententiâ varios citat Patres, inter quos Origenes ὡς ἀρχῶν cap. 1. Mens ut moveatur & operetur non indiget loco corporeo NB neque magnitudine sensibili vel corporali habitu, aut colore, aut ullo alio indiget horum, quae corporis vel materiae propria sunt. Gregorius Nyssenus lib. de Anima: Anima non magis locum competit, quam calor. NB Corporum duntaxat propria est ἠ ἐν τόπῳ ϑέσις. Augustinus de 83. quaestionibus: Spiritualia non loci & partibus hujus mundi sursum esse intelligenda nobis sunt, sed merito excellentia sua. Item: Haeresis vestra nihil aliud novit, quam animam & Deum per locorum spatia vel infinita vel indefinita distendere: cum solum corpus talia occupet spatia, vel talibus spatiis occupetur. Claudianus Mamertus, qui librum edidit de statu animae, in quo fusè disputat, animam in loco nullo modo esse, nec moveri localiter posse. Sed & Lavaterus de descensu Christi ad inferos cap. 9. Johannem Picum Mirandulanum pro ea sententia laudat, verbis ejus prolixè recitatis, in quibus eadem sententia confirmatur auctoritate Durandi, Bernhardi de Gannaco, Thomae Anglici, Hervei, Thomae itidem, aliorumque. Adde tandem Mornaeum de Veritate religionis Christianae pag. mihi 301. Hujusmodi verò, inquit, substantiæ (intellectuales) naturâ suâ tota sunt in toto, tota in parte qualibet, non enim addicta sunt ulli loco, sed ibi sunt demum NB ubi operantur, & operantur tota non per partes, quia individuæ sunt; & Zanchium in loco de Angelis pag. mihi 87. Definitivè nihil aliud est, quàm esse in loco sine spatii occupatione, sed operatione duntaxat. NB. Ita angelos simplices spiritus & animas ajunt esse in loco. Ubi enim operantur, ibi ita esse definiuntur, ut simul alibi esse non possint. Si enim hæc sit natura Substantiæ spiritualis, ut non aliter possit dici illa Substantia vel essentia esse in loco, nisi quatenus in loco operatur, cùm Dei substantia maximè sit spiritualis, non potest alio sensu dici Ubique per essentiam, nisi quatenus illa essentia omnia in omnibus operatur. 2. Infinitatem Essentiæ Deo expressè tribuimus, quando dicimus, ei competere tot & tantas perfectiones, ut nulli earum limites esse possint. Essentia autem Dei in eo consistit, quod habeat omnes omnino perfectiones.
units.tr: Reply: There is no scorpion here and no danger. If the essence of God is considered in itself, apart from his outward operation, then, as Descartes says, it has no relation to place, just as before the world was created, before God operated outwardly, God was for himself his own place and all things. But if it is considered together with his outward operation, since God does not operate at a distance, and so is joined and present to all things in respect of his power, and his power is the same as his essence, then his essence must also be called present in all places. This is made clear by Descartes's third letter to More, which is among his letters, number 72, where he speaks thus: I said that God is extended with respect to power, namely that this power exerts itself, or can exert itself, in extended matter. It is certain that the essence of God must be present everywhere, so that his power may exert itself there; but I deny that it is there in the manner of extended matter, that is, in the way I described extended matter a little earlier. Our view, therefore, is as far from the view of Vorstius as heaven is from earth. For he attributed a body to God, thought him finite, and confined him to heaven with respect to his essence, all of which followed from the corporeality he ascribed to God. We, on the other hand, say: God is Spirit, a thinking thing, most pure act, and is present no less to the earth and to any other places with respect to his essence than to heaven, since he preserves heaven and earth and all places, and works all things in all things. We hold only this: that God, before the world was created and now, is not in imaginary spaces, in which he operates nothing, and which are nothing other than figments of the human brain, to be held in the same class as a chimera, Cerberus and the like. Hence, since no one can take it amiss if someone says that God is not in a chimera or in Cerberus, or in similar figments of the human mind, since these are nothing; and since omnipresence is [ἐκ τῶν πρός τι], that is, belongs to things that are related to something else; nor is our statement to be twisted into a bad sense, if we deny that God is there where he does not operate, and therefore is not in imaginary spaces. And not a few theologians agree with this view of ours. So Hyperius, in his Methodus Theologica, book 1, p. 141: It cannot be understood that God is everywhere in the way that some thing is in a place. For since God is an incorporeal substance, and so admits of no extremities, he cannot possibly be circumscribed or contained by a place; rather he himself circumscribes and contains all things. Likewise: God is everywhere by essence, because all created things, heaven and earth and what is in them, receive their being from God. For God exists as the principle and efficient cause of all things, and they have nothing from elsewhere that would allow them to be. Therefore God is considered to be everywhere through his essence in this way. And after some intervening words: God is everywhere by essence, that is, with respect to creation; by power, that is, with respect to the operation and motion granted, which is clearly seen in each single thing; finally by presence, that is, with respect to preservation and government, etc. Although, comprehending all these in one word, we might perhaps not unfittingly say that God is simply everywhere by power or operation. He cites Augustine, letter 57, to Dardanus: In the very statement that God is diffused everywhere, we must resist carnal thought, and the mind must be withdrawn from the senses of the body, lest we suppose, as if by spacious magnitude, that God is spread through all things, as smoke or moisture or air or this light is spread. (For every magnitude of this kind is smaller in its part than in its whole.) But rather he is as great wisdom is even in a man, whose body is small. And a little later: God is so diffused through all things that he is not a quality of the world (but the creating substance of the world), governing the world without labour and containing it without burden, yet not diffused through spaces of places as if by bulk, so that in half the body of the world there is half of him, etc.; but he is contained in no place and is wholly in himself. Tilenus, in his Syntagma Theologicum, disp. 12, 28, also agrees with our view: The common view, by which we say that God is in all things by essence, power and presence, must be understood as if it said that the essence of God is present to individual things so as to give them their existence (ὕπαρξις), his power so as to give them strength, and his presence so as to operate. Just as, of course, a cause is present in its effect and is there [ἐνεργείᾳ], in its working. The very learned Parker, in his book on the Descent of Christ into Hell, book 2, art. 66, thinks the same. After citing the Fathers, distinguishing this very view of ours from that of Vorstius, he says: But do not these statements lean toward that heresy of Augustine Steuchus, which that most impious Conrad Vorstius recalled from the dead? Namely, that God remains in substance only in heaven, but everywhere is only by providence, wisdom and power? By no means. These Fathers indeed express the divine omnipresence through its effects, as more familiar to us, without however confining the essence, or separating it from power and wisdom; which no one of men, unless perhaps someone from the herd of Epicurus's pig, has attempted. I conclude with the words of Mirandula: God is everywhere by essence, that is, by power and presence, and this belongs to no creature. The same must be the view of all those who deny that spiritual substances and separated souls are in a place by essence, except insofar as that essence operates outside itself, or insofar as it is operating (for this is the mind of these authors). On this matter you may see Parker, book 2, art. 61, 62, who cites various Fathers for this view, among them Origen, [περὶ ἀρχῶν], chapter 1: The mind, in order to be moved and to operate, does not need a bodily place, NB nor sensible or bodily magnitude, or colour, or any other of those things that belong to body or matter. Gregory of Nyssa, in his book on the soul: The soul has no more of a place than heat does. NB Being in a place [ἡ ἐν τόπῳ θέσις] belongs only to bodies. Augustine, in the Eighty-three Questions: We must understand spiritual things not to be above in the places and parts of this world, but in virtue of their excellence. Likewise: Your heresy knows nothing else than to stretch the soul and God through the spaces of places, either infinite or indefinite, since only body occupies such spaces, or is occupied by them. Claudianus Mamertus, who published a book on the state of the soul, in which he argues at length that the soul is in no place in any way, nor can it be moved locally. Lavater also, in his work on the descent of Christ into hell, chapter 9, praises Giovanni Pico della Mirandola for this view, quoting his words at length, in which the same view is confirmed by the authority of Durandus, Bernard of Gannacus, Thomas of England, Hervaeus, Thomas likewise, and others. Finally add Mornay, On the Truth of the Christian Religion, p. 301 in my edition: Such substances (intellectual ones), however, are by their nature wholly in the whole and wholly in any part; for they are not bound to any place, but are there only NB where they operate, and they operate wholly, not by parts, because they are indivisible. And Zanchius, in the place on angels, p. 87 in my edition: Definitively, being in a place is nothing other than being in a place without occupying space, but by operation alone. NB Thus they say that angels, simple spirits and souls are in a place. For where they operate, there they are so defined to be, that they cannot at the same time be elsewhere. For if this is the nature of a spiritual substance, that it cannot be said to be in a place, or that its substance or essence is in a place, except insofar as it operates in that place, then, since the substance of God is most of all spiritual, it cannot be said to be everywhere by essence in any other sense than insofar as that essence operates all things in all things. 2. We expressly attribute infinity to the essence of God when we say that so many and such great perfections belong to him that no limits can be set to any of them. Now the essence of God consists in this, that he has all perfections absolutely.

units.la: CCII. Inst. 10. (B. p. 230.) Si absurdum non est dari Creaturam in Infinitum Extensam, ei etiam tribuitur perfectio major, quam ulla creatura cogitatione comprehendere potest.
units.tr: CCII. Inst. 10. (B. p. 230.) If it is not absurd that a creature is extended to infinity, then a perfection greater than any creature can grasp in thought is also attributed to it.

units.la: Resp. Tale hic sit argumentum oportet: Omnis perfectio, quæ major est, quàm ulla creatura cogitatione sua comprehendere potest, est perfectio divina. Atqui posita mundi Infinitate tribueretur ei perfectio talis? Ad quod respondeo: Omnis perfectio, quæ omni ex parte major est, quam ulla creatura sua cogitatione comprehendere potest, est perfectio divina, concedo, sed absolute sumpta Major est falsa, nisi statuas ad Creaturæ intelligentis naturam requiri, ut Dei operum amplitudinem cogitatione sua comprehendere possit, quod nego.
units.tr: Answer: The argument must be framed thus: every perfection that is greater than any creature can grasp in its thought is a divine perfection. But would such a perfection be attributed to the world if its infinity were posited? To this I reply: every perfection that is greater in every respect than any creature can grasp in its thought is a divine perfection, I grant. But the major premise, taken absolutely, is false, unless you hold that it is required of the nature of an intelligent creature that it be able to grasp in its thought the greatness of God's works, which I deny.

units.la: CCIII. Inst. 11. (B. p. 210.) Cum infinitam Extensionem tribuis creaturæ, eam aliqua ratione Deo æqualem statuis in eo, quod nullum possit concipi ubi, in quo creatura non tam sit præsens, quam Creator &c.
units.tr: CCIII. Inst. 11. (B. p. 210.) When you attribute infinite extension to a creature, you make it in some way equal to God, in that no place can be conceived in which the creature is not as present as the Creator, etc.

units.la: Resp. Ubique Deus dicitur, quatenus omnibus rebus tam incorporeis, quam corporeis, adeoque & locis est præsens; primo respectu operationis, quatenus nempe immediatè in omnibus operatur, omnia conservat, & gubernat; deinde ratione potentiæ, quoniam potentia ab operatione separata esse nequit, & tandem cùm potentia idem sit cum Essentia, etiam respectu Essentiæ; At tale quid mundo nequaquam convenire potest. 2. Deus indivisibiliter præsens est omnibus rebus, propter Essentiæ spiritualitatem, quod de mundo dici nequit. Nam, sive mundus finitus, sive infinitus sit, nullum potest dari ubi, in quo non aliqua ejus sit pars: At Deus non per partes est ubique præsens, quas nullas habet. §. Ad locum 1 Reg. xviii. 27. qui pro spatiis extra mundum imaginariis est adductus, superius responsum. 4. Quod vero attinet locutiones Theologorum ad Immensitatem Dei explicandam usitatas, eę hic inter se non conveniunt; Nam Zanchius supra supremum coelum locum sine corpore tribuit mundo, quod Theologi alii non admittunt. Nec mirum, quod Philosophica harum rerum explicatio sit diversa, quoniam alii aliis principiis innituntur. At in re ipsa, quatenus ex verbo Dei haberi potest, summus est consensus. Per haec etiam sufficienter refutata sunt, quae à M. p. 150, 151. contra eandem sententiam afferuntur, quod patebit, cui volupe est haec cum nostris conferre.
units.tr: Answer: God is said to be everywhere insofar as he is present to all things, both incorporeal and corporeal, and so also to places. This is first with respect to operation, insofar as he works immediately in all things, preserves and governs all things. Then it is with respect to power, since power cannot be separated from operation. And finally, since power is the same as essence, it is also with respect to essence. But nothing of this kind can belong to the world in any way. 2. God is present to all things indivisibly, on account of the spirituality of his essence, which cannot be said of the world. For whether the world is finite or infinite, there can be no place in which some part of it is not present, whereas God is not present everywhere by parts, since he has no parts. §. As to the passage 1 Reg. xviii. 27., which was cited for imaginary spaces outside the world, I have answered it above. 4. As for the expressions commonly used by theologians to explain the immensity of God, these do not agree among themselves here. For Zanchius assigns to the world a place beyond the highest heaven, without a body, which other theologians do not admit. Nor is it surprising that the philosophical explanation of these matters is diverse, since different people rest on different principles. But in the matter itself, insofar as it can be drawn from the Word of God, there is the greatest agreement. By these points, too, what is brought against the same opinion at pp. 150, 151 of M. has been sufficiently refuted, as will be clear to anyone who enjoys comparing these things with our arguments.

units.la: CCIV. Inst. 12. Aliud tamen adhuc examinandum (M. p. 152.) ni- mirum:
units.tr: CCIV. Inst. 12. Yet something else still remains to be examined (M. p. 152.), namely:

units.la: Si infinita ponatur mundi magnitudo, omnipotentiam divinam in apertum deduci discrimen, quippe qua unius hujus mundi infiniti creatione ita exhausta statuitur, ut non possit ei vel tantillam quantitatem creando adjungere.
units.tr: If an infinite magnitude of the world is posited, the divine omnipotence is brought into evident danger, since it is held to be so exhausted in the creation of this one infinite world that it cannot add even the smallest quantity to it by creating.

units.la: Resp. Omnipotentia Dei non exhauritur per id, quod eam maximam & infinitam ostendit, sed potius exseritur & manifestatur maxime: si ergo creasset Deus mundum infinitum, non exhausisset suam omnipotentiam, quia viribus ejus nihil decessisset, sed eam exseruisset maxime & infinite. Quemadmodum cum Deus creavit Adamum, Evam &c. etiamsi tum non amplius possit dici, eum posse creare Adamum & Evam, quia creaverat, non tamen dici potest exhausta ejus potentia. Ita etiam, si creavisset Deus mundum infinitum, quamvis tum non amplius possit dici, Deum posse novam creare extensionem, quia jam creavit, non tamen potest dici omnipotentia ejus exhausta. 2. Quod si vero inter nostram sententiam, qua mundus indefinitus statuitur & sententiam Adversariorum, ineatur comparatio, apparebit tantum abesse, ut per eam Dei omnipotentia minuatur, ut potius de ea magnificentissimè sentire simus censendi. Illi enim honestius & magnificentius de Dei potentia sentiunt, qui vacuum nullum agnoscunt atque omnia spatia imaginabilia materia à Deo repleta esse asserunt, & jam in sua plenitudine cuncta regi, conservari atque moveri à potentissimo Creatore statuunt quam ii, qui contrarium tenent.
units.tr: Answer: The omnipotence of God is not exhausted by what shows it to be greatest and infinite; rather it is exercised and manifested most fully. So if God had created an infinite world, he would not have exhausted his omnipotence, because nothing would have been taken from his powers, but he would have exercised it to the greatest degree and infinitely. Just as when God created Adam, Eve, etc., although it can no longer then be said that he is able to create Adam and Eve, because he has created them, it cannot yet be said that his power is exhausted. So too, if God had created an infinite world, although it could no longer be said that God is able to create a new extension, because he has already created one, it still cannot be said that his omnipotence is exhausted. 2. But if a comparison is made between our opinion, which posits an indefinite world, and the view of our opponents, it will appear that far from diminishing God's omnipotence by it, we ought rather to judge that we think of it in the most magnificent way. For those who acknowledge no void, and assert that all imaginable spaces are filled with matter by God, and that all things in their fullness are now ruled, preserved and moved by the most powerful Creator, think more honourably and magnificently of God's power than those who hold the contrary.

units.la: CCV. Corollarii loco examinemus verba L. p. 286. Occurretur nobis ab admiratoribus Cartesii, non eam esse mentem docentis, Coeli & terra spatium esse infinitum; sed mundi nomine comprehendi & spatium Imaginarium extra coelum: Fateor hunc esse verborum ejus sensum; sed hic pauca me respondentem audiant velim. 1. quis illi concesserit vocabula, in medio posita, ad suum & peculiarem sensum detorquere. 2. quis illi spondebit, semper fore qui posteri verborum sensum explicent, & à crassiori & vulgata Mundi appellatione eos avocent? 3. Nego ea, qua extra cœlum immenso spatio imaginamur, mundi esse partem aut additamentum. Rationem primam desumimus à definitione nominis חבל & חלר à finitate, cùm fere semper jungitur in sacru habitatio: Græcus & Latinis ab ornatu, Germanis Welt / quasi von Walten. in eo vero spatio nihil est finitudinis, nihil ornatus, nihil frequentationis 2. à definitione rei: Mundum appellamus compagem rerum.
units.tr: CCV. By way of a corollary, let us examine the words at p. 286 of L.: We shall be met by the admirers of Descartes, who say that this is not the mind of the teacher: that the space of heaven and earth is infinite, but that under the name of the world is comprehended also the imaginary space beyond heaven. I confess this is the sense of his words; but here I would like them to hear me answering briefly. 1. Who would concede to him that words placed in the midst of a discourse are to be twisted to his own peculiar sense? 2. Who will promise him that there will always be those who come after and explain the sense of the words, and turn them away from the cruder and common use of the term world? 3. I deny that those things which we imagine in an immense space beyond heaven are a part or an addition of the world. We take the first reason from the definition of the name חבל [tebel] and חלר [chelel?], from finitude, since it is almost always joined with the sacred habitation; the Greeks and Latins derive it from ornament; the Germans (Welt, as if from "von Walten"). But in that space there is nothing of finitude, nothing of ornament, nothing of frequentation. 2. From the definition of the thing: we call the world the framework of things.

units.la: Resp. Quomodo sententia Cartesii defensa fuerit, ex superioribus liquet, unde duæ illæ responsiones sua sponte concidunt. 2. Quod ea, quæ ultra quosvis mundi fines à nobis positos, sive per cœlum, sive per alia corpora supra illud concipimus, revera sint quid extensum, atque ita corpus; adeoque ad mundum pertineant, sufficienter à nobis demonstratum existimo. Ergo quæ objicit ex locis Topicis à nominis definitione, non præbent argumentum apodicticum, quod nostram sententiam evertat. Nam utraque vox Hebræa, non tam pro universo, quam pro terra sumitur, quam finitam esse nemo unquam negavit; & postea ostendetur, Scripturam uti vocibus usu obtinentibus, quarum derivatio & origo sæpius est opinioni erroneæ adscribenda, aut saltem ab effectu aliquo magis conspicuo & in sensus incurrente est deducta, rarò à natura rerum. Quid autem sit in illo spatio, quod ultra quoscunque mundi fines fictos reperitur, quod nobis reale est, adeoque corpus, aliis imaginarium, quis dixerit: scimus esse quid extensum, & corporeum ex illa idea extensionis indefinitæ, sed quale sit nec Scriptura docet, nec ratio novit. 3. Mundus appellatur compages rerum omnium creatarum, vel compages omnium corporum à Deo creatorum; at inde non sequitur, nos ejus fines assequi posse.
units.tr: Answer: How the opinion of Descartes was defended is clear from what has gone before, whence those two replies fall of their own accord. 2. I consider it sufficiently demonstrated by us that those things which we conceive beyond any limits of the world we have posited, whether through heaven or through other bodies above it, are really something extended, and thus a body; and so they belong to the world. Therefore what he objects from topical arguments drawn from the definition of the name does not provide a demonstrative argument that overturns our opinion. For each Hebrew word is taken not so much for the universe as for the earth, which no one has ever denied is finite; and it will be shown later that Scripture uses words in their established usage, whose derivation and origin is more often to be ascribed to an erroneous opinion, or at least derived from some more conspicuous effect falling under the senses, and rarely from the nature of things. But who would say what is in that space which is found beyond any fictitious limits of the world: what is real to us, and thus a body, to others imaginary? We know it is something extended and corporeal from that idea of indefinite extension, but what sort of thing it is neither Scripture teaches nor reason knows. 3. The world is called the framework of all created things, or the framework of all bodies created by God; but it does not follow from this that we can attain its limits.

units.la: CAPUT XIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIV.

units.la: Refutantur argumenta pro Mundi rotundâ figurâ adducta, & ostenditur, talem figuram nec Cœlo stellato assignari posse.
units.tr: The arguments adduced for the round figure of the world are refuted, and it is shown that no such figure can be assigned even to the starry heaven.

units.la: CCVI. Hucusque refutatio Objectionum, quæ contra mundi Indefinitatem pugnabant, nunc videamus in specie, quid illi, qui mundo certam figuram statuunt assignandam, pro sua sententia adferant. Vulgata est eorum sententia, qui mundo rotundam figuram assignant, atque hi præcipue istis nituntur rationibus, quas videre est, apud Kepl. lib. 2. Astron. Copernic. 1. Quæ figura est capacissima, ea mundo competit: sed figura sphærica est omnium isoperimetrarum capacissima: E. Min. negari non potest, cum certissimis demonstrationibus Geometricis nitatur. Maj. vero quia negari posset, ob hanc rationem, quod Deus potuerit mundum efficere alterius figuræ non isoperimetræ, sed ambitus majoris, quam sphæra, sic probatur. Cum Deus & natura nihil faciant frustra, quandoquidem idem potuerit obtineri, per figuram sphæricam, quod per aliam ambitus majoris, sed ejusdem capacitatis, ex simplicitate Dei operationis colligendum potius, eam figuram sphæricam mundo indidisse.
units.tr: CCVI. So far we have refuted the objections that fought against the indefiniteness of the world. Now let us look more closely at what those who assign a definite figure to the world bring forward for their view. The opinion of those who assign a round figure to the world is the commonly held one, and they rest chiefly on the arguments that may be seen in Kepler, book 2 of his Astronomy of Copernicus, number 1. The figure with the greatest capacity belongs to the world. But the sphere is the most capacious of all isoperimetric figures. Therefore the minor cannot be denied, since it rests on the most certain geometrical demonstrations. The major could be denied on the ground that God could have made the world of some other figure, not isoperimetric but with a greater circumference than a sphere. It is proved thus. Since God and nature do nothing in vain, and since the same result could be obtained through a spherical figure as through another figure of greater circumference but the same capacity, it is rather to be inferred from the simplicity of God's operation that he imposed the spherical figure on the world.

units.la: Resp. Majorem illam futuram esse veram, si nobis de finibus mundi constaret, & si sciremus, unundum aliquam figuram habere, tum enim probabiliter saltem colligi posset, sphæricam figuram potius, quam aliam mundo competere: sed cum mundus non aliter, ac indefinitus possit concipi, hæc Major falsa est. Prob. autem Majoris procedit bene contra eos, qui aliam figuram mundo volunt esse tribuendam: at cum nos dicamus, ignotum esse, an ulla figura mundo competat, quod major supponit, non probat, illa probatio est frustranea.
units.tr: Reply: the major would be true if we were certain of the limits of the world and knew that it has some figure. Then one could at least probably conclude that a spherical figure belongs to the world rather than another. But since the world can be conceived only as indefinite, this major is false. The proof of the major does indeed work well against those who want some other figure to be attributed to the world. But since we say it is unknown whether any figure belongs to the world, which the major presupposes, the proof does not establish anything and is futile.

units.la: CCVII. 2, Obj. Qualis figura mundo Archetypo per Analogiam tribuitur, talis etiam mundo Ectypo est tribuenda; sed mundo Archetypo Deo, tribuitur figura sphærica; quod inde probari potest, quia Ægyptii Deum per circulum soliti fuerint repræsentare, cui consonat illud, Deus circulus est, cujus centrum ubique, circumferentia nusquam. Imo putat Keplerus mysterii Trinitatis in sphæra aliquam similitudinem reperiri, quod ita declarat. 1. Sicut centrum, inquit, est quasi origo sphærici, ita Pater est origo Filii. Quemadmodum superficies est character, & imago centri, & quasi fulgor ab eo, & qui supersuperficiem videt, is eo ipso & centrum videt: ita etiam Filius est charater & imago Patris Hebr. I. & qui videt Filium, videt Patrem, Joh. xiv. 3. Sicut intervallum inter centrum & superficiem resultat ex comparatione Centri cum Superficie, & sic procedit ab utroque: ita Sp. Sanctus procedit à Patre & Filio.
units.tr: CCVII. Second objection. Whatever figure is attributed to the archetypal world by analogy, the same must be attributed to the ectypal world. But a spherical figure is attributed to God, the archetype of the world. This can be proved from the fact that the Egyptians were accustomed to represent God by a circle, to which agrees the saying: God is a circle whose centre is everywhere and whose circumference is nowhere. Indeed Kepler thinks that some likeness to the mystery of the Trinity is found in the sphere, which he explains thus. (1) As the centre is, so to speak, the origin of the sphere, so the Father is the origin of the Son. As the surface is the character and image of the centre, and a kind of radiance from it, and whoever sees the surface sees the centre by that very fact, so the Son too is the character and image of the Father (Heb. 1), and whoever sees the Son sees the Father (John 14:9). (2) As the interval between the centre and the surface results from the comparison of the centre with the surface, and so proceeds from both, so the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.

units.la: CCVIII. Resp. 1. In genere, quicquid sit de illa comparatione Sphaerae cum SS. Trinitate, argumenta talia à proportione & harmoniâ desumpta parum aut nihil demonstrare: harmoniae enim si in rebus inveniantur, sunt considerandae, sed non licet ab harmoniis ad rerum existentiam argumentari, & ut earū pulchritudine delectemur, res quasdam in quibus sint, fingere. Sic non licet inferre; Est Mediator Πανθεωπος, qui homines lapsos cum Deo unit: Ergo est etiam Παγγελος, qui assumsit naturam angelicam, & angelos, qui defecerunt suam originem, cum Deo reconciliat. 2. Deo tribuitur sphaerica figura, non nisi Metaphoricè, sed à Metaphorico sensu ad proprium non procedit argumentum. 3.
