Major est absolute falsa; alias aeque inferrem, omnibus corporibus, imo omnibus creaturis sphaericam competere figuram, cujus tamen contrarium experientia ostendit, si dicerem: Deus est Archetypus omnium tam corporum quam reliquarum Creaturarum: E. cum illi Archetypo tribuatur sphaerica figura, etiam cuilibet Ectypo, cum manifesta absurditate esse tribuenda.
units.tr: CCVIII. Reply. (1) In general, whatever may be said of that comparison of the sphere with the Holy Trinity, arguments of this kind drawn from proportion and harmony prove little or nothing. For if harmonies are found in things, they are to be considered, but one may not argue from harmonies to the existence of things, nor invent certain things in which they might be found in order to delight in their beauty. Thus one may not infer: the Mediator is the Pantheos, who unites fallen men with God; therefore he is also the Pangelos, who took on the angelic nature and reconciles with God the angels who fell from their origin. (2) A spherical figure is attributed to God only metaphorically, and an argument does not proceed from a metaphorical sense to a proper one. (3) The major is absolutely false. Otherwise I could equally infer that a spherical figure belongs to all bodies, indeed to all creatures, and experience shows the contrary. If I said: God is the archetype of all bodies as well as of the other creatures; therefore, since a spherical figure is attributed to that archetype, it must also be attributed to every ectype, I would be asserting something plainly absurd.

units.la: CCIX.
units.tr: CCIX.

units.la: Atque ita vidimus Universo, sive Mundo, nullam posse neque sphaericam, neque aliam figuram adscribi. Huic quaestioni cognata est, quae quaerit de figura Coeli stellati, quod quidem communiter à Philosophis Ethnicis habitum est pro corpore mundi extremo, Christianis communiter Coelum Empyreum supra illud collocantibus. Communis est sententia, Coelo stellato quoad extremum suum ambitum convenire figuram sphaericam. Nos quid in ea sit soliditatis, operae pretium est ut indagemus. Primum igitur, origo hujus sententiae videtur esse desumpta ex perniciosissimo errore, quo statuitur, Coelum esse Deum, quae quidem sententia fuit Aristotelis, teste Plutarcho de Placitis Philosophorum lib. 1. cap. 7. Aristoteles summum quidem Deum formam abjunctam, universi Sphaera innitentem, aethereo corpore, quod ab ipso quintum vocatur. Et patet lib. 2. de Coelo cap. 3. ubi haec reperiuntur verba: Ἐκαστον ἔσιν, ὧν ἔργον ἐστιν, ἕνεκα ἕργου· ἡ δὲ ἐνέργεια. Τὸ δὲ ἐστι ζῷον ἀίδιον. ὥστε ἀνάγκη τῷ ἡείῳ κίνησιν ἀίδιον ἐπαγέχειν. ἐπεὶ ἡ ὁ ἥρανὸς πιστὸ σῶμα ἐς τῷ θεῷ. ἐξ τὰ ἐχὶ τὸ ἐγκύκλιον σῶμα ὁ φύσει κινεῖται κύκλῳ ἀεί. Unumquodque eorum, quorum est opus, id operis causa: Dei vero operatio immortalitau; Hoc autem est perpetua vita. Quare Deo perpetuum inesse motum necesse est. Cum vero coelum sit tale (est enim corpus quoddam divinum) eo corpus habet rotundum, quod natura semper in orbem movetur. Quamvis autem velint quidam Interpretes Aristotelem hic loqui more Platonico, non ex opinione sua, tamen πολυμαθέστατος Vossius satis ostendit hanc fuisse Aristotelis propriam mentem lib. 2. de Idololatria cap. 40. p. 530. & seqq. ita p. 533. concludens: Ut melius sensisse Aristotelem credamus, verba non sinunt, facile autem, ut deterius senserit: quae Achillini Piccolhominei & aliorum sententia fuit. Ex quorum opinione Aristoteli coeli forma informans est anima coelestis; nec aliud est anima haec, quam Intelligentia. Quomodo Coeli movetur componentur ex orbe suo, ut corpore, & anima sive intelligentia ut forma perficiente. Atque ita Deus sit corporeus, quatenus Dei nomine orbis corpus & motem ejus complectimur. Orbis igitur, qui movetur, ignobilior pars divinae fuerit substantia, ut corpus nostrum pars est vilior hominis. At pars nobilior sit motoi, ut anima in nobis. Inde ergo factum est, ut coelo, quod ita habebatur pro Deo, rotunda figura tanquam pulcherrima fuerit attributa. Cum ergo fundamento tam malo haec opinio innitatur, merito nobis suspecta esse debet.
units.tr: And so we have seen that neither a spherical nor any other figure can be ascribed to the universe or world. Related to this question is the one that asks about the figure of the starry heaven. The pagan philosophers commonly held this to be the outermost body of the world, while Christians commonly place the Empyrean heaven beyond it. The common opinion is that the starry heaven, as to its outermost circumference, has a spherical figure. Let us see how much solidity there is in it. First, the origin of this opinion seems to be drawn from the most pernicious error by which heaven is held to be God. This was indeed the opinion of Aristotle, as Plutarch testifies in his Opinions of the Philosophers, book 1, chapter 7: Aristotle held the supreme God to be a separate form, resting on the sphere of the universe, with an ethereal body, which is called the fifth by him. And it is clear from On the Heavens, book 2, chapter 3, where these words are found: [Ἕκαστον ἔστιν ὧν ἔργον ἐστίν, ἕνεκα ἔργου· ... ζῷον ἀΐδιον ...] Each thing whose work it is exists for the sake of its work; the divine is an eternal living being. Hence perpetual motion must belong to God. Since heaven is such a body (for it is a certain divine body), it has a round body, which by nature always moves in a circle. Although some interpreters want Aristotle to speak here in the Platonic manner, not from his own opinion, the most learned Vossius shows well enough that this was Aristotle's own mind, in his On Idolatry, book 2, chapter 40, pages 530 and following, concluding thus on page 533: That Aristotle meant better, the words do not allow; that he meant worse, they readily allow. This was the opinion of Achillini, Piccolomini and others. According to their view, the forming form of the heaven for Aristotle is a heavenly soul, and this soul is nothing other than an intelligence. The heavens that move are composed of their orbit as body, and of the soul or intelligence as perfecting form. Thus God is corporeal, insofar as by the name of God we embrace the body of the orbit and its motion. The orbit that moves is therefore the baser part of the divine substance, as our body is the baser part of man. But the nobler part is the mover, as the soul is in us. Hence it came about that a round figure, as the most beautiful, was attributed to heaven, which was thus regarded as God. Since this opinion rests on so bad a foundation, it ought rightly to be suspect to us.

units.la: CCX. Secundum argumentum nobis inde desumitur, quod, cum ex superioribus pateat, non constare, Utrum undique Coelum Empyreum hoc coelum stellatum circumcingat, incertum sit, an non ab altera parte ita protendatur, ut nos nullum finem quem habeat, cognoscere possimus.
units.tr: CCX. A second argument is drawn from this: since it is clear from what has been said above that it is not established whether the Empyrean heaven surrounds this starry heaven on every side, it is uncertain whether it does not extend on the other side in such a way that we cannot know its limit.

units.la: Sed etiam posito, (quod tamen est dubium) Coelum Empyreum undique hoc Coelum stellatum ambire, cum nemo norit, quaenam illius Coeli Beatorum sit figura concava, & forte nunc inter omnes sit in confesso, coelum esse corpus fluidum, quod terminum accipit ab ambiente, manifestum est, nobis impossibile esse, ut certam determinationem quantitatis, sive figuram coelo stellato assignemus. Itaque cum neque constet, an habeat figuram aliquam coelum stellatum, neque si habeat, quaenam illa sit indagari possit, temerarium est certi aliquid statuere.
units.tr: But even granting (though this is doubtful) that the Empyrean heaven surrounds this starry heaven on all sides, since no one knows what the concave figure of that heaven of the blessed is, and since it is now perhaps agreed among all that heaven is a fluid body which receives its limit from what surrounds it, it is manifest that it is impossible for us to assign to the starry heaven a certain determination of quantity or figure. Therefore, since it is not established whether the starry heaven has any figure at all, and, if it has one, it cannot be discovered what that figure is, it is rash to lay down anything certain.

units.la: CCXI. Sed videamus ea, quae pro Coelorum rotunditate objici solent, ut futilitate istarum rationum cognita tanto magis incertitudo hujus sententiae patefiat. Objici ergo primo solet, Corpori simplici competit simplex figura: Coelum est corpus simplex, sphaerica etiam figura est simplicissima; ut enim circulus inter figuras planas est simplicissima: ita sphaerica figura inter solidas. Nam 1. ut circulum unica linea, ita sphaeram unica superficies claudit. 2. ut in circulo medium ab extremis mis est æqualiter remotum, ita & in sphæra. 3. ut in circulo neque initium est, neque finis; ita neque in sphæra, 4. ut circulus respectu suarum partium non mutat locum, ita sphæra respectu suarum circa centrum convoluta semper eundem occupat locum: (hoc est quaternus & Circulo & sphæra circumvolutis, circa centrum partes illarum figuratum motu suo nulla expellunt corpora, in quorum locum succedant) Aliæ veræ figuræ omnes solidæ vel non terminantur una linea, ut Pyramides, Prismata, sed multis, adeoque non sunt tam simplices, nec reliqua simplicitatis requisita ipsis competunt, ut ex collatione patebit; vel si terminentur unâ lineâ, ut figura Ovalis, Elliptica, medium tamen ab extremis non est æqualiter remotum, nec in motu suarum partium præcise eundem occupant locum, quia motu isto alia corpora expellunt, in quorum locum hæ partes succedunt.
units.tr: CCXI. But let us look at the arguments usually brought against the roundness of the heavens, so that once the weakness of these reasons is recognised, the uncertainty of this opinion may be revealed all the more. It is usually objected, first, that a simple body has a simple figure, that the heaven is a simple body, and that the spherical figure is also the simplest, since among plane figures the circle is the simplest, so among solids the sphere is. For: (1) as a circle is enclosed by a single line, so a sphere is enclosed by a single surface; (2) as in a circle the middle is equally distant from the extremes, so it is in a sphere; (3) as in a circle there is neither beginning nor end, so neither is there in a sphere; (4) as a circle does not change place with respect to its parts, so a sphere, turning about its centre, always occupies the same place with respect to its parts (that is, as long as the circle and sphere revolve, the parts of these figures, by their motion about the centre, expel no bodies into whose place they might succeed). The other true solid figures either are not bounded by one surface, like pyramids and prisms, but by many, and so are not as simple, nor do the remaining requisites of simplicity belong to them, as the comparison will make plain; or if they are bounded by one surface, like the oval or elliptical figure, the middle is nevertheless not equally distant from the extremes, nor do their parts, in their motion, occupy exactly the same place, because by that motion they expel other bodies into whose place these parts succeed.

units.la: CAP. XII. Resp. 1. Falsa est Minor illa, quam experientia multis modis r- efutat; vel enim ex solis Cometis, & maculis in Sole evinci potest, Cœlum non esse corpus simplex & incorruptibile, uti vulgo putatur.
units.tr: CAP. XII. Reply. 1. That minor premise is false, and experience refutes it in many ways; for it can be proved, from the comets and the spots on the Sun alone, that the heaven is not a simple and incorruptible body, as is commonly thought.

units.la: Cometas enim esse in cœlo à Tychone Brahe ita est demonstratum, ut in dubium revocari nequeat; maculæ etiam Solares per tubos opticos sunt deprehensæ, illæque jam densiores, jam rariores, jam crescere, jam decrescere sunt visæ, quod est generationis alicujus & corruptionis argumentum. Clavius Comment. in sphæram de Sacro Bosco p. 211. testatur, Platonem ante Aristotelem, cum multis aliis Philosophis sensisse, cœlum esse corruptibile, & post Christum non paucos, inter quos Ambrosius, Basilius, Gregorius Nyssenus, & cætera fere Ecclesiæ lumina, idem non obscure docuisse. Et vel ipsa imbecillitas rationum, quibus *Aristoteles & ejus sequaces moti, quintam quandam essentiam Cœlo adscripserunt, satis ostendit, quanti debeat haberi hæc sententia ita gratis asserta, & posita, uti ostenditur à Bassone Philosophiæ naturalis lib. 1. de cœlo p. 458. 2. Minor propositæ objectionis etiam vacillat: non enim figura oritur à corporis simplicitate, vel compositione, sed à motu: neque enim ulla futura esset figura, si omnia quiescerent, imo neque corpora forent in mundo, sed omnia in unum essent concreta. Considerari autem debebat potius, cœlum esse corpus fluidum, quod figuram accipiat à continente, quod quale sit, quamque figuram concavam habeat, non satis constat. 3. Retorquetur potius argumentum. Quo corpora sunt simpliciora, eo minus simplex ipsis figura videtur convenire. Nonne enim Aër, Ignis, Aqua, secundum oppositæ sententiæ Patronos sunt corpora simpliciora mixtis? Attamen figuræ, quas habent, plane sunt irregulares, fluxæ, & inconstantes.
units.tr: For that comets are in the heavens has been demonstrated by Tycho Brahe in a way that cannot be called into doubt; the spots on the Sun too have been detected through optical tubes, and they have been seen now denser, now rarer, now growing, now decreasing, which is a sign of some generation and corruption. Clavius, in his commentary on the Sphere of Sacrobosco, p. 211, testifies that Plato, before Aristotle, along with many other philosophers, held that the heaven is corruptible, and that after Christ not a few, among them Ambrose, Basil, Gregory of Nyssa, and almost all the other lights of the Church, taught the same openly. And the very weakness of the reasons by which Aristotle and his followers were moved to ascribe a certain fifth essence to the heaven sufficiently shows how much this opinion, asserted and laid down without cause, ought to be valued, as Basso shows in his Philosophy of Nature, book 1, On the Heaven, p. 458. 2. The minor premise of the objection put forward also wavers: for figure does not arise from the simplicity or compositeness of a body, but from motion; indeed no figure would exist at all if everything were at rest, nor would there be bodies in the world, but everything would be solidified into one mass. It should rather have been considered that the heaven is a fluid body, which receives its figure from what contains it; what kind of body it is, and whether it has a concave figure, is not sufficiently established. 3. The argument is rather turned back upon itself. The more simple bodies are, the less simple a figure seems to belong to them. For according to the patrons of the opposing opinion, are not air, fire and water simpler bodies than mixed ones? Yet the figures they have are plainly irregular, fluid and inconstant.

units.la: CCXIII. 2. Obj. Si cœlum non esset rotundum, sed aut trilaterum, aut quadrilaterum, aut etiam multilaterum, sequeretur & locum aliquem fore vacuum, & corpus aliquod fore sine loco. Vacuus enim locus inter angulos acuminati corporis relinqueretur, & ipsi anguli perpetuo moverentur in Vacuo. Atqui utrumque absurdum est, & naturæ rerum contrarium. Si vero Cœlum esset figura lenticulari, aut conica, vel etiam cylindrica, hæc quidem incommoda non sequerentur, sed alia graviora. Cum enim motus orbium inferiorum sit oblique oppositus motui supremi orbis, sive primi mobilis, fiatque super diversis polis, necesse esset, aut cœlos scindi, aut alios ab aliis penetrari, si non essent figura orbicularI.
units.tr: CCXIII. 2. Objection. If the heavens were not round, but triangular, or quadrangular, or even many-sided, it would follow both that some place would be empty and that some body would be without place. For an empty space would be left between the angles of an angular body, and the angles themselves would move perpetually in a void. But both are absurd and contrary to the nature of things. If indeed the heavens were lens-shaped, or conical, or even cylindrical, these particular inconveniences would not follow, but others more serious. For since the motion of the lower spheres is obliquely opposed to the motion of the highest sphere, or first mover, and takes place about different poles, it would be necessary either that the heavens be split, or that some be penetrated by others, if they were not circular in figure.

units.la: CCXIV. Resp. Objectio hæc procedit ex falsis & incertis hypothesibus, quibus sublatis, hoc argumentum cadere est necesse. Nam 1. præsupponitur; Cœlum Empyreum undique ambire sidereum, quod ratione & revelatione destituitur, adeoque incertum exstit. 2. Superficiem Cœli Empyrei concavam, sive eam quæ respondet Cœlo stellato esse rotundam, quod gratis ponitur. Itaque posito, Cœlum stellatum esse trilaterum aut quadrilaterum &c. dico Cœli Empyrei superficiem talem suturam, ut ei accurate respondeat, vel aliud corpus inter Cœlum Empyreum & Sidereum interpositum iri, quod illam lacunam repleat, & sic remotum iri omnem metum & suspicionem vacui 3. Cœlum constare ex orbibus solidis, qui pellicularum instar in cepis sese invicem ambiant; quod cum fluiditate cœli non convenit, & multis aliis modis est absurdum. 4. Sumitur etiam tanquam in confesso, Orbes illos fictitios, à primo mobili rapi ab Ortu in Occasum, quod itidem falsum esse in sequentibus à nobis demonstrabitur, ubi illam variationem diei & noctis pendere ostendemus, non à Cœli sideréi, sed à Terræ diurna circumvolutione. His itaque hypothesibus, quibus tanquam tibicinibus hæc objectio nitebatur, sublatis, sponte sua corruit.
units.tr: CCXIV. Reply. This objection proceeds from false and uncertain hypotheses, and once these are removed, the argument must fall. For 1. it presupposes that the Empyrean heaven surrounds the starry heaven on every side, which lacks support from reason and revelation, and so remains uncertain. 2. It takes for granted that the concave surface of the Empyrean heaven, that is, the surface corresponding to the starry heaven, is round, which is posited without warrant. Therefore, supposing the starry heaven to be triangular or quadrangular, etc., I say that the surface of the Empyrean heaven will be such that it corresponds exactly to it, or else some other body will be interposed between the Empyrean and the starry heaven, filling that gap, and so all fear and suspicion of a void will be removed. 3. The heavens are said to consist of solid spheres, which enclose one another like layers of skin in onions; this does not agree with the fluidity of the heavens, and is absurd in many other ways. 4. It is also assumed as granted that those fictitious spheres are carried by the first mover from east to west; this too is false, as we shall demonstrate in what follows, where we shall show that the variation of day and night depends not on the motion of the starry heaven but on the daily rotation of the Earth. Therefore, with these hypotheses removed, on which this objection leaned as on props, it collapses of its own accord.

units.la: CCXV. 3. Obj. Si cœlum non esset rotundum, sequeretur, stellarum fixarum alias aliis Terræ propinquiores fore, aut ab ea remotiores; quod absurdum videtur.
units.tr: CCXV. 3. Objection. If the heavens were not round, it would follow that some of the fixed stars would be nearer to the Earth than others, or farther from it; which seems absurd.

units.la: Resp. Non est absurdum, alias stellas nobis propinquiores esse, alias à nobis remotiores; cum enim stellæ fixæ nullam aut vix observabilem habeant parallaxin, de earum distantia nihil certi poterit definiri. Eas autem inæqualiter à terra remotas, ex lucis inæqualitate patet, quæ etiam in minutis stellis valde est vivida, indicatque, quod major & minor stellæ. larum lux ex majori minorive remotione à nobis oriatur, quemadmodum à Cartesio est demonstratum; ut sic sententiam illam, de stellis omnibus in una superficie collocatis, tanquam præjudicium vulgi debeamus abjicere.
units.tr: Reply. It is not absurd that some stars are nearer to us and some farther from us. For since the fixed stars have no parallax, or one scarcely observable, nothing certain can be determined about their distance. That they are unequally distant from the Earth is plain, however, from the unequal brightness of their light, which is very vivid even in the smaller stars, and which indicates that the light of the greater and lesser stars arises from their being nearer or farther from us, as Descartes has demonstrated. Thus we ought to reject, as a prejudice of the common people, that opinion which places all the stars on one surface.

units.la: CAPUT XV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XV.

units.la: De Centro Mundi, nec non circumvolutionum Planetarum.
units.tr: On the Centre of the World, and also on the Revolutions of the Planets.

units.la: CCXVI. Ab Extremis mundi hujus adspectabilis progredimur nunc ad ejus medium, ab ambitu ad centrum, ut disquiramus, quodnam sit Centrum Universi. Atqui hic iterum illud judicium Romanorum usurpare debemus NON LIQUET. Cum enim fines & terminos mundi ignoremus, eumque ut indefinitum concipere necessum habeamus, uti superius est ostensum, non etiam de medio constare poterit, ut appareat ex relatione illa, quæ inter media & extrema existit.
units.tr: CCXVI. We now proceed from the extremities of this visible world to its middle, from the circumference to the centre, to inquire what the centre of the universe is. Here again, however, we must use that Roman verdict: IT IS NOT CLEAR. For since we do not know the limits and boundaries of the world, and must conceive of it as indefinite, as was shown above, its middle cannot be established either, as appears from the relation that exists between the middle and the extremes.

units.la: CCXVII. Quod si vero medium aliquod respectu motus planetarum, circa quod volvantur, assignare velimus, illud necessario Soli erit tribuendum. Atque hic quidem hactenus inter Tychonianos & Copernicanos convenit (profligatâ jam Ptolemaicâ dispositione ob aliquorum phænomenorum repugnantiam) quod circa Solem Saturnus, Jupiter, Mars, Mercurius & Venus; Luna circa Terram moveantur: sed in eo est differentia, quod Tychoniani Solem circa Terram, cum ♄ his Planetis tanquâ suis satellitibus moveri statuant, Copernicani vero inter reliquos planetas constituto loco, etiam Terram circa Solem rotari existiment, quod cum in sequentibus sit demonstrandum, pro certo habendum est, Solem esse illarum circumvolutionum centrum, non Geometricum quidem, sed Physicum, cum ab eo pendeant omnium Planetarum circumvolutiones.
units.tr: CCXVII. If we wish to assign some middle point with respect to the motion of the planets, around which they revolve, it must necessarily be ascribed to the Sun. Here, so far, Tychonians and Copernicans agree (the Ptolemaic arrangement having already been overthrown because of the incompatibility of some phenomena) that Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Mercury and Venus move around the Sun, and the Moon around the Earth. The difference is this: the Tychonians hold that the Sun moves around the Earth, with Saturn and the other planets moving as its satellites, whereas the Copernicans, placing the Sun among the remaining planets, also think the Earth revolves around the Sun. Since this is to be demonstrated in what follows, it must be held as certain that the Sun is the centre of those revolutions, not a geometrical centre but a physical one, since the revolutions of all the planets depend on it.

units.la: CCXVIII. Contra, Terram in medio non tantum circumvolutionum Planetarum, sed totius mundi esse positam, communis est sententia, quæ quibus nitatur rationibus considerare hic libet. Atque 1. ita argumentantur, qui id statuunt: Si stellæ seclusis vaporibus, in quacunque mundi regione, sive ad Ortum sive ad Occasum, quibuscunque temporibus nobis apparent, ejusdem magnitudinis. E. necessum erit, Terram ram collocari in medio mundi: sed verum prius, experientiâ docente, Ergo.
units.tr: CCXVIII. On the contrary, the common opinion holds that the Earth is placed in the middle not only of the revolutions of the planets but of the whole world. It is worth considering here on what reasons this rests. First, those who maintain it argue thus: If the stars, with the vapours excluded, appear to us of the same magnitude in whatever region of the world they are, whether in the East or the West, and at whatever times, then the Earth must necessarily be located in the middle of the world. But the first premise is true, as experience teaches. Therefore...

units.la: CCXIX. Resp. Majoris connexio negatur; fieri enim potest, ut accessus illeTerræ ad firmamentum toto Orbitæ suæ intervallo non habeat tantam proportionem, ut exinde stellarum adspectus quantum ad magnitudinem debeat variari; quemadmodum intervallum diametri Terræ ad stellarum remotionem nullam proportionem habet, ut stella eadem nobis& antipodibus nostris sub eadem appareat magnitudine. Fateor equidem hoc multis, qui non satis attentos oculos habent ad magnalia Dei, adeo videri absurdum, ut propter illud solum sententiæ Copernicanæ, à qua alias non videntur alieni, nuncium mittant. Sed nos suo loco demonstrabimus, hoc nullo modo pro absurdo esse habendum.
units.tr: CCXIX. Reply: The connection of the major premise is denied. For it can happen that the Earth's approach to the firmament, over the whole interval of its orbit, does not have so great a proportion that the appearance of the stars as to magnitude ought to vary from this. Just as the interval of the Earth's diameter has no proportion at all to the distance of the stars, so that the same star appears to us and to our antipodes under the same magnitude. I admit that this seems so absurd to many who do not have sufficiently attentive eyes for the marvels of God that they break off relations with the Copernican opinion on this ground alone, though otherwise they do not seem to be strangers to it. But we shall demonstrate in its place that this is by no means to be held absurd.

units.la: CCXX. Obj. 2. Si Terra non esset in medio mundi, sed propinquior ab una parte firmamento, quam ab altera, tunc is qui existeret in parte Cœlo propinquiori, non videret cœli medietatem, sed minorem partem, quemadmodum alter, qui existeret in parte à Cœlo remotiori, majorem partem conspicaretur: Sed hoc est absurdum, & cum experientia pugnans, quia semper 6. signa Zodiaci nobis oriuntur, totidemque occidunt.
units.tr: CCXX. Objection 2: If the Earth were not in the middle of the world, but nearer the firmament on one side than on the other, then one who stood on the part nearer the heaven would not see half of the heaven but a smaller part, just as the other, who stood on the part farther from the heaven, would behold a greater part. But this is absurd and contrary to experience, because always six signs of the Zodiac rise for us and as many set.

units.la: CCXXI. Resp. 1. Illam propinquitatem Terræ majorem vel minorem ad firmamentum, non esse sensibilem. 2. Circuli omnis imaginarii centrum esse Terram libenter concedimus: oculus enim noster ubicunque sit constitutus, format sibi circulos in cœlo maximos, Horizontem, Æquatorem, Meridianum, Zodiacum, & concipit stellas omnes fixas tanquam in eadem superficie sphæricâ, quia visus eo usque non potest distinguere remota & propinqua. 3. Non est absurdum dicere, eum, qui existeret à Terræ parte cœlo propinquiori, non videre cœli medietatem, sed partem minorem, & contra. Quis enim quæso mensus est id, quod de cœlo simul uno intuitu comprehendit? Quantacunque tamen mundi portio cernitur ea imaginatione sphæræ circa visum descriptæ, censetur esse perfectum hemisphærium. Oculus vero putans, Cœlum esse Terræ extremo circum quaque contiguum, non aliâ semidiametro altitudinem fornicis, quam ipsam latitudinem distantiamve Horizontis metitur.
units.tr: CCXXI. Reply 1: That greater or lesser nearness of the Earth to the firmament is not perceptible. 2: We readily concede that the centre of every imaginary circle is the Earth. For our eye, wherever it is placed, forms for itself great circles in the heavens: the horizon, the equator, the meridian, the zodiac, and it conceives all the fixed stars as lying on one spherical surface, because sight cannot distinguish distant from near objects up to that point. 3: It is not absurd to say that one who stood on the part of the Earth nearer the heaven would not see half the heaven but a smaller part, and conversely. For who, I ask, has measured what he takes in of the heaven at a single glance? Yet however large a portion of the world is seen, by the imagination of a sphere described around the sight it is judged to be a perfect hemisphere. The eye, thinking the heaven to be contiguous on all sides with the extremity of the Earth, measures the height of the vault by no other semidiameter than the very breadth or distance of the horizon.

units.la: CCXXII. Obj. 3. Si Terra non sit in medio mundi, erit vel in plano Æquatoris extra mundi axem, vel in axe mundi, extra planum Æquatoris, vel extra utrumque. Sed omnia hæc sunt absurda: E. erit simul in plano Æquatoris, & in axe mundi, & per consequens in mundi centro.
units.tr: CCXXII. Objection 3: If the Earth is not in the middle of the world, it will be either in the plane of the Equator outside the axis of the world, or in the axis of the world outside the plane of the Equator, or outside both. But all these are absurd. Therefore it will be simultaneously in the plane of the Equator and in the axis of the world, and consequently in the centre of the world.

units.la: P
units.tr: P

units.la: CCXXIII. Resp. 1. Hoc argumento bene infertur, Terram esse in medio Æquatoris, at inde non sequitur eam in medio esse mundi. Æquatoris autem formatio pendet à visus imaginatione, qui, ubicunque sit Terra, Æquatorem concipit. 2. Axis mundi nihil aliud est, quam axis Terræ, circa quem illa motu diurno rotatur; qui dum concipitur continuatus, usque ad fixas, dicitur axis mundi, adeoque Æquator concipitur circulus maximus, medius deductus inter polos Terræ, & extensus usque ad Firmamentum.
units.tr: CCXXIII. Reply 1: It is rightly inferred from this argument that the Earth is in the middle of the Equator, but it does not follow from this that it is in the middle of the world. The formation of the Equator depends on the imagination of sight, which, wherever the Earth may be, conceives an Equator. 2: The axis of the world is nothing other than the axis of the Earth, around which it turns with a daily motion. When this is conceived as continued up to the fixed stars, it is called the axis of the world, and so the Equator is conceived as a great circle, drawn midway between the poles of the Earth and extended up to the firmament.

units.la: CCXXIV. Si Terra non esset in medio mundi sita, non fierent Eclipses Lunæ semper, quando duo luminaria per diametrum opponuntur, ut sint sub signis Zodiaci oppositis: sed Eclipses tunc fieri experientia docet.
units.tr: CCXXIV. If the Earth were not situated in the middle of the world, eclipses of the Moon would not always occur when the two luminaries are opposed along a diameter, so as to lie under opposite signs of the Zodiac. But experience teaches that eclipses do occur then.

units.la: CCXXV. Resp. Eclipsis Lunæ fit, quando inter Solem & Lunam Terra interponitur, ut hæc tria corpora sint in una linea, quo fit ut Terra propter suam magnitudinem, qua Lunam aliquoties excedit, impediat, ne possit hæc à Sole illustrari. Ducta autem linea à Sole ad Lunam, dummodo Terra in illa collocetur, sive in medio istius lineæ, sive propius ad Solem, sive propius ad Lunam, semper fiet Eclipsis, uti attendenti est perspicuum.
units.tr: CCXXV. Reply: An eclipse of the Moon happens when the Earth is interposed between the Sun and the Moon, so that these three bodies lie in one line. Hence the Earth, on account of its size, which exceeds the Moon several times over, prevents the Moon from being illuminated by the Sun. If a line is drawn from the Sun to the Moon, provided the Earth is placed on it, whether in the middle of that line, or nearer the Sun, or nearer the Moon, an eclipse always happens, as is clear to anyone who attends to it.

units.la: CCXXVI. Obj. 5. Quo tendunt omnia gravia illud est centrum mundi: sed ad Terram omnia gravia tendunt. Maj. exinde probatur, quia gravium natura est, ferri & tendere ad mundi centrum.
units.tr: CCXXVI. Objection 5: That to which all heavy bodies tend is the centre of the world. But all heavy bodies tend to the Earth. The major premise is proved thus: it is the nature of heavy things to be carried and to tend to the centre of the world.

units.la: CCXXVII. Resp. Negatur Major illa, aliud enim inferri nequit, quam, istorum gravium, quæ sunt circa Terram, eam esse centrum, id est, locum in quo quiescunt. Nam per se feruntur duntaxat versus Terræ corpus, ut ei uniantur, sed quia id faciunt per brevissimam lineam, quam simul contingit spectare centrum, fit, ut per accidens ad centrum ferri dicantur. Unde autem constabit, gravium eam esse naturam, ut ferantur & tendant ad mundi centrum? an est talis vis insita, quæ faciat gravia cognoscere quodam instinctu naturali suum centrum? at hoc pugnat cum natura corporum, & oritur ille conceptus confusus ex non satis observata distinctione, inter res corporeas, & cogitantes, inde factum, ut attributa rei cogitantis fuerint assignata rebus extensis, & vice versa; ut pluribus ostendi potest exemplis, si ferret institutum. 2. Pugnat talis vis insita, cum principio ab Aristotele sæpe inculcato & demonstrato, quod omne, quod movetur, ab alio movetur. Sed quia videmus corpora gravia tendere deorsum, cum interim visu percipere nequeamus tenuissima corpuscula, à Terra resilientia, quæ illa deorsum premunt, sensus nostros omnium rerum facimus judices, itaque quia nihil videmus, à quo deprimantur, etiam nihil esse putamus, adeoque à se ipsis moveri vulgo statuimus. Et possemus ex Cartefii lib. 1 v. Principiorum gravitatis naturam demonstrare, sed id non requiritur ad nostrum institutum, & sufficit sic ostendisse falsitatem Majoris. 3. Nec Minor etiam probari posset. Unde enim manifestum fiet, an non circa Jovem & Saturnum sint quædam gravia, quæ ad ipsa tendant, quemadmodum gravia, circa Terram ad ipsam feruntur? Quod enim sit alia plane materia, cœlestium & terrestrium, & quinta quædam Essentia, assertum quidem est ab Aristotele ex illo errore, quo statuit, cœlestia esse corpora quædam divina, sed non probatum, imò ab aliis hæc sententia falsitatis convicta.
units.tr: CCXXVII. Reply: The major premise is denied. For nothing else can be inferred than that the Earth is the centre of those heavy bodies which are around it, that is, the place in which they come to rest. Of themselves they are carried only towards the body of the Earth, to be united with it; but because they do this by the shortest line, which happens also to aim at the centre, they are said to be carried to the centre only by accident. But how will it be established that it is the nature of heavy things to be carried and to tend to the centre of the world? Is there some innate force which makes heavy things know their centre by a certain natural instinct? But this conflicts with the nature of bodies, and that confused concept arises from a distinction not sufficiently observed between corporeal and thinking things. Hence it came about that attributes of a thinking thing were assigned to extended things, and vice versa, as could be shown by many examples if the plan of this work allowed. 2: Such an innate force also conflicts with the principle that Aristotle often impressed and demonstrated, whatever is moved is moved by another. But because we see heavy bodies tend downwards, while we cannot perceive with sight the very fine corpuscles rebounding from the Earth which press them downwards, we make our senses the judges of all things. And so, because we see nothing by which they are pressed down, we also think there is nothing, and so commonly hold that they are moved by themselves. We could demonstrate the nature of gravity from Descartes's first book of the Principles, but this is not required for our purpose, and it suffices to have shown thus the falsity of the major premise. 3: Nor could the minor premise even be proved. For how will it become plain whether there are not, around Jupiter and Saturn, certain heavy bodies which tend towards them, just as heavy bodies around the Earth are carried to it? That the heavenly and earthly things are of a wholly different matter, and that there is a certain fifth essence, has indeed been asserted by Aristotle, out of that error by which he held the heavenly bodies to be certain divine bodies; but it has not been proved, and indeed this opinion has been convicted of falsity by others.

units.la: CCXXVIII. Obj. 6. Gravissimum corpus tendit ad infimum locum, nempe ad punctum remotissimum à Cœlo: sed Terra est corpus gravissimum. E.
units.tr: CCXXVIII. Objection 6. The heaviest body tends to the lowest place, namely the point farthest from the heaven. But the earth is the heaviest body. Therefore...

units.la: CCXXIX. Resp. 1. Præsupponitur in hoc argumento, Cœlum sidereum habere rotundam figuram, ut punctum à circumferentia remotissimum pro centro sit habendum: sed ostensum est antea, id valde incertum esse. 2. Negatur Major, nitens eo fundamento, quod vel centro insit aliqua vis corpora ad se attrahendi, vel vis aliqua corporibus competat centrum per se petendi. 3. Minor probatione etiam indiget. Terra enim, proprie loquendo, in se neque gravis neque levis est; gravitas quippe & levitas competit corporibus, quia ad Terram vel accedunt, vel ab ea recedunt: at inde Terra levis vel gravis dici non debet, neque enim centri, puncti imaginarii, talis vis est, ut Terram ad se trahat. Addo tamen ex superabundanti: Si Terra poneretur extra hunc locum naturalem, in quo est, ex. gr. si poneretur in locum Jovis, eam eo delatum iri, ubi nunc est, quod illo in loco commodissime circa Solem deferri possit; uti à Cartefio est demonstratum.
units.tr: CCXXIX. Reply 1. This argument presupposes that the starry heaven has a round figure, so that the point farthest from the circumference is taken as its centre. But it has been shown above that this is very uncertain. 2. The major premise is denied, resting on the ground that either some power inheres in the centre to draw bodies to itself, or some power belongs to bodies to seek the centre for its own sake. 3. The minor premise also needs proof. For the earth, properly speaking, is neither heavy nor light in itself. Heaviness and lightness belong to bodies because they either approach the earth or recede from it. Therefore the earth ought not to be called light or heavy, since the centre, being an imaginary point, has no such power as to draw the earth to itself. I add, however, over and above: if the earth were placed outside this natural place in which it is, for example if it were placed in the place of Jupiter, it would be carried back to where it now is, since in that place it could most conveniently be carried around the sun, as Descartes has demonstrated.

units.la: CCXXX. Obj. 7. Si Terrâ in æquales portiones divisa, ejusdem figuræ & magnitudinis & ponderis, hæ diversis locis sub concavo Lunæ demitterentur, tum omnes partes eodem tempore procul dubio, ad eundem locum tenderent. At hoc non posset fieri, nisi in centro mundi; Ergo Terra est in mundi centro.
units.tr: CCXXX. Objection 7. If the earth were divided into equal portions, of the same shape, size and weight, and these were let down at different places under the concave of the moon, then undoubtedly all the parts would tend to the same place at the same time. But this could not happen unless it were at the centre of the world. Therefore the earth is at the centre of the world.

units.la: CCXXXI. Resp. 1. Major non est vera simpliciter: hoc quidem sequeretur, illas portiones Terræ esse conventuras in unâ aliquâ orbitâ, sed non futura esset eadem cum eâ, in qua nunc Terra defertur, sed tanto magis ad Solem accessuræ essent istæ portiones æquales, quo minores fucfuerint, &, si quaelibet pars talis Mercurio minor esset, caeteris paribus Soli propiores esse futuras, quam ipsum Mercurium. 2. Non etiam necessario eodem tempore nec in eundem istius orbitae locum conventurae essent, sed posset fieri, ut aliae tardius, aliae citius eo pervenirent, prout ab intermediis corporibus varie ista delatio impediri possit. 3. Concessa Majori, Minor falsa nihilominus est; hic enim locus, in quo convenirent, non necessarium esset centrum mundi, sed locus tantum, qui Terrae situi conveniret, in proportione & respectu ad alia corpora.
units.tr: CCXXXI. Reply 1. The major premise is not simply true. It would indeed follow that those portions of earth would meet in some one orbit, but it would not be the same orbit in which the earth is now carried. Rather, those equal portions would come nearer to the sun the smaller they were, and if any such part were smaller than Mercury, other things being equal, it would be nearer the sun than Mercury itself. 2. Nor would they necessarily meet at the same time or in the same place of that orbit. It could happen that some would arrive there more slowly, others more quickly, since that motion could be variously impeded by intervening bodies. 3. Granting the major premise, the minor is nonetheless false. For the place where they would meet would not necessarily be the centre of the world, but only a place that suits the position of the earth, in proportion and in relation to other bodies.

units.la: CCXXXII. Obj. 8. Circuli coeli proportionaliter se habent tam in longum quam in latum. Nam ubivis 15. milliaria Germanica efficiunt unum gradum in Coelo: Ergo erit idem eorum Centrum, scilicet Terrae centrum. CCXXXIII. Resp. Conceditur, Terram esse centrum illorum Cir- culorum imaginariorum, quia describuntur a nobis in Terra constitutis: imo describerentur etiam e Jove, si nos in illo essemus collocati, sive, si Terra nostra eo in loco esset constituta, ubi nunc est Jupiter. 3. sed inde nullis fidiculis potest elici, Terram esse centrum totius Universi. CCXXXIV. Obj. 9. Si Terra non esset in medio mundi, non essent futura Æquinoctia, Sole ingrediente Æquatorem; Atqui negari non potest, quin tunc Æquinoctia fiant. E. CCXXXV. Resp. Major illa est falsa, neque aliud quid infert, quàm, Terram esse in medio Zodiaci & Æquatoris, ad quorum intersectionem, Sol tempore Æquinoctii motu apparenti pervenit, quod nos non nega- mus. Quod autem idem obtineatur, sive Sol motu vero in Zodiaco defe- ratur, sive Terra, norunt omnes, qui levem quandam Astronomiae co- gnitionem sunt adepti. CCXXXVI. Obj. 10. Terrae ignobilissimo corpori totius mundi competit locus etiam ignobilissimus. E. erit in centro Mundi. CCXXXVII. Resp. In hoc argumento multa praesupponuntur, quae tamen dubia, imo salsissima exi stunt: Nam 1. unde constat, quod terra sit corpus ignobilissimum, nisi ex erronea opinione, quod materia coeli sit divinum quid, & Terra non nisi sententia totius mundi. Quid impedit, quin aeque nobilis sit ac Venus, vel Mercurius, vel alius quispiam Pla- neta? 2. Quaenam loco Nobilitas vel Ignobilitas ut tali, competere po- test? Haec enim non nisi respectivum quid important. Quin potius ex hoc argumento a Sole remotissimum censendae esse habere locum, & re- motiorem ipso Saturno, quod tamen etiam cum Tychoniana hypothesi pugnaret. 3. Unde probatur, quod in locatione corporum mundano- rum
units.tr: CCXXXII. Objection 8. The circles of heaven are proportionally related both in length and in breadth. For everywhere 15 German miles make one degree in the heaven. Therefore their centre is the same, namely the centre of the earth. CCXXXIII. Reply. It is granted that the earth is the centre of those imaginary circles, because they are described by us who are situated on the earth. Indeed they would be described from Jupiter too, if we were placed there, or if our earth were situated in the place where Jupiter now is. 3. But from this no thread can be drawn to show that the earth is the centre of the whole universe. CCXXXIV. Objection 9. If the earth were not in the middle of the world, there would be no equinoxes when the sun enters the equator. But it cannot be denied that equinoxes do occur then. Therefore... CCXXXV. Reply. That major premise is false, and it implies nothing other than that the earth is in the middle of the zodiac and of the equator, at whose intersection the sun reaches at the time of the equinox by apparent motion, which we do not deny. That the same result holds whether the sun is carried through the zodiac by true motion or the earth is moved, all know who have acquired a slight knowledge of astronomy. CCXXXVI. Objection 10. The most ignoble body of the whole world, namely the earth, also has the most ignoble place. Therefore it will be at the centre of the world. CCXXXVII. Reply. Many things are presupposed in this argument which are, however, doubtful, indeed most false. For 1. how is it established that the earth is the most ignoble body, except from the erroneous opinion that the matter of heaven is something divine while the earth is not, which is the opinion of the whole world? What prevents the earth from being as noble as Venus, or Mercury, or any other planet? 2. What nobility or ignobility, as such, can belong to a place? For these signify only something relative. Indeed, from this argument the place most remote from the sun would have to be judged to be the centre, and more remote than Saturn itself, which would conflict even with the Tychonic hypothesis. 3. How is it proved that in the placing of worldly bodies

units.la: rum habita fuerit ratio Nobilitatis, vel Ignobilitatis potius, quam Natu-rae? 4. Unde etiam probatur, quod hic praesupponitur, centrum esse locum ignobilissimum? quin potius nobilitas quaedam centro competet, tanquam origini Circumferentiae ex eo ductae.
units.tr: regard was had to nobility, or rather ignobility, rather than to nature? 4. How is it also proved that it is presupposed here that the centre is the most ignoble place? Rather, some nobility belongs to the centre, as to the origin of the circumference drawn from it.

units.la: CCXXXVIII. His objectionibus nunc subjungo Danaei ex scriptura petitas argumentationes. In tractatu 3. Physicae suae Christianae cap. 21. ita suam sententiam ex scriptura sibi videtur firmare. D. Plane igitur Terram meditullium mundi obtinere censes. P. Censeo. Atque cur sic existimem haec ratio est multiplex, quam ex ipsa divina scriptura duco. Prima quod a Coelo (quod totius hujus mundi locum supremum occupare nemo sanus dubitat,) longissime spatii & intervalli ratione distat Terra. Ps. 103. v. 11. Qui verolocum quam longissime a supremo disjungitur, is profecto dubio est infimus. Ergo sit infimo loco necesse est, aut verum non dixerit scriptura, id quod vel omnino cogitasse nefas est. Secunda autem, quod Coelum & Terra inter se opponuntur in scriptura, veluti imum summo, quemadmodum ex Eph. cap. IV. v. 9. apparet. Tertia, quod ubique infima loca tribuuntur Terrae, uti Ps. 95. v. 4. & aliis passim locis, unde Terram infimo omnium loco collocatam esse apparet.
units.tr: CCXXXVIII. To these objections I now add the arguments of Danaeus, drawn from Scripture. In the third tractate of his Christian Physics, chapter 21, he seems to confirm his opinion from Scripture in this way. D. Clearly, then, you hold that the earth occupies the middle of the world. P. I hold so. And the reasons why I think so are manifold, which I draw from divine Scripture itself. First, the earth is separated from heaven (which no sane person doubts occupies the highest place of this whole world) by the greatest distance of space and interval. Ps. 103. v. 11. Whatever place is separated as far as possible from the highest is certainly the lowest. Therefore it must be in the lowest place, or else Scripture would not speak the truth, which it is wicked even to think. Second, heaven and earth are opposed to each other in Scripture, as top to bottom, as appears from Eph. 4. v. 9. Third, the lowest places are everywhere assigned to the earth, as in Ps. 95. v. 4 and in many other passages, whence it appears that the earth is placed in the lowest place of all.

units.la: CCXXXIX. Resp. Tria citata loca haec sunt. Psal. 103. vers. 11. Sed quam alti sunt coeli super terram, praevalet benignitas ejus erga timentes eum. Eph. 4. v. 9. Caeterum illud Ascendit, quid est, nisi quod etiam descenderat prius in infimas partes terrae? Ps. 95. 4. In cujus manu sunt ima vestigia terrae, penes quem sunt vires montium. Sed illa cum judicio consideranda, nobis nihil obesse conspicientur. Coelum sidercum, in quo sunt stellae fixae, locum superiorem inter corpora nobis conspicua occupare concedimus: at, an absolute sit supremum, ut nullum aliud corpus supra se habeat, non constare in superiori capite ostendimus, imo saltem ab aliqua parte supra se habere Coelum Beatorum vidimus. Sed quicquid sit de eo I. Psal. 103. nihil aliud dicitur, quam, Coelos a Terra esse valde remotos, quod nemo negat, imo tantam esse distantiam, ut a nullo hominum hactenus ea potuerit inveniri. Sed inde non sequitur, Terram esse in mundi centro; neque enim hic comparatio inter Terram, Solem, Mercurium instituitur, quasi Coelum stellatum magis a Terra distet, quam ab his corporibus, sed tantum absolute dicitur, magnam esse Coeli supra Terram altitudinem. 2. Eph. 4. uti vidimus superius, ostendit, Christum ex tanta altitudine, ex tam sublimi throno in Terram le demisisse, atque ita mentio fit descensus de loco sublimiori in locum inferiorem, ut simul connotetur status humiliatio. Itaque est comparaparativa locutio, quâ Terra ad Cœlum altius collata valdè humilis est & depressa; sed non absoluta, quasi nullum corpus à Cœlo magis esset remotum quàm Terra, 3. Pf. 95. est planè ἀπροσδιόνυσος; nam ne quidem ibi Cœlum & Terra opponuntur, sed loca Terræ depressiora locis altioribus, nempe montibus.
units.tr: CCXXXIX. Reply. The three passages cited are these. Psalm 103 verse 11: But as high as the heavens are above the earth, so great is his mercy toward them that fear him. Eph. 4 v. 9: Now that he ascended, what is it but that he also first descended into the lower parts of the earth? Ps. 95. 4: In whose hand are the deep places of the earth; the strength of the mountains is his. These, however, are to be considered with judgment, and they will be seen to do us no harm. We grant that the starry heaven, in which the fixed stars are, occupies the higher place among the bodies visible to us. But whether it is absolutely the highest, so as to have no other body above it, we have shown is not established in the chapter above; indeed we have seen that on some side the heaven of the blessed lies above it. Whatever the case, Ps. 103 says nothing else than that the heavens are very remote from the earth, which no one denies; indeed the distance is so great that no man has hitherto been able to find it. But it does not follow from this that the earth is at the centre of the world. For here no comparison is made between the earth, the sun and Mercury, as if the starry heaven were more distant from the earth than these bodies. It is said only absolutely that the height of heaven above the earth is great. 2. Eph. 4, as we saw above, shows that Christ let himself down into the earth from such a height, from so sublime a throne, and so mention is made of a descent from a higher place to a lower, with the humiliation of his state implied at the same time. Therefore it is a comparative expression, by which the earth, compared with the higher heaven, is very humble and low; but it is not absolute, as if no body were more remote from heaven than the earth. 3. Ps. 95 is altogether irrelevant [ἀπροσδιόνυσος]. For not even there are heaven and earth opposed, but the lower parts of the earth are set against higher places, namely mountains.

units.la: CCXL. Coronidis loco respondebimus ad ea quæ R. St. p. 319. opponit: Addimus, inquit, articulum ascensionis Iesu Christi per hanc opinionem evertı. Cum enim Christus non noctu, sed claro die videntibus Apostolis (Act. 1, 9, 10, 11.) ascenderit, sanè caput ad Solem erectum habuit, qui si in imo mundi erat, non ascendisse Christus, sed descendisse dicendus esset. CCXLI. Resp. Nihil est periculi; quis non novit id dici sursum, quod est supra capita nostra, deorsum verò id, quod est sub pedibus nostris? Hæ enim determinationes loci, quales sunt, dextrum & sinistrum, sursum & deorsum, ante & retro, omnes desumtæ sunt à partibus corporis nostri. Igitur quum habuit caput versum ad Solem, eo ipso dici debuit ascendisse, quia motus ille versus cum loco processit, quem caput respiciebat. Quod si Terra vel ibi collocata esset, ubi nunc est Jupiter, nihilominus sursum id esset dicendum, quod esset super capitibus hominum in Terrâ degentium, & vice versâ deorsum, quod sub pedibus. Talem autem communiter esse acceptionem vocabulorum Sursum & Deorsum discere possumus ex Platone in Timæum, cujus verba hic adjungere libet. Sed illud dictu absurdum est, esse duo quædam loca natura à se invicem longo intervallo distincta: & unum quidem deorsum vocari, ad quem locum ea deferuntur omnia, quæcunque molem quandam corporis habent: alterum verò sursum, ad quem vi omnia moveantur. Cum enim Cœlum omne rotundum sit, quæcunque à medio æquè distantia extrema facta sunt, similiter esse oportet extrema. Medium quoque, æqualibus lineis ab extremis utrinque distans, è regione æque omnia respicit. Quoniam igitur ita Mundus dispositus est, si quis dictorum quicquam sursum esse dixerit vel deorsum, non injuria errare videbitur. Medius enim locus in ipso neque sursum neque deorsum dici debet, sed medius. 2. Quamvis autem non diffitear, motum alicujus Corporis versus centrum dici posse ejus descensum, quemadmodum & Cartesius loquitur art. 120. Pp. Part. III, satis tamen clarum, Scripturam potius rationem habuisse locutionis istius communiter receptæ, quâ id, quod capiti nostro imminet, sursum dicitur, & quod à pedibus nostris calcatur, deorsum vocatur, quàm alterius istius à communi loquendi consuetudine remotæ, ac non nisi iis usitatæ, qui Philosophicè rerum naturas rimantur. 3. Non diximus, Solem esse in imo Mundi, sed respectu motuum Planetarum centrum obtinere æstimamus, non quidem Geometricum, sed Physicum: at medium mundi, quod adversarius vocat inum, indeterminabile esse profitemur. 4. Terra ipsa habet vorticem & cœlum suum, quaquà versus sibi circumdatum, cujus ambitus Supra, centrum Infra dicitur. Qui igitur circa vel supra Terram versatur, omnes Cœli vortices & corpora supra se habet. Et sic Christus ascendens, omnes alios vortices, etiam Solem supra se habuit. At ipsa Terra cum vortice suo in vortice Solis in orbem circa Solem, qui ei delationi pro centro est, delata, si appropinquet ad Solem, descendet; at non eâ causâ corpus, quod à Terra versus vortices Cœli alios quoscunque ipsumque Solem feretur, nisi tùm demum cum vorticem Terræ egressum in vortice altero ab extremo ad centrum vergere concipietur.
units.tr: CCXL. By way of a postscript, I reply to what R. St. objects on p. 319: "We add that this opinion overthrows the article of Jesus Christ's ascension. For since Christ ascended not by night but in broad daylight, with the Apostles watching (Acts 1:9-11), he surely had his head turned up towards the Sun; and if the Sun were at the lowest point of the world, it would have to be said that Christ descended, not that he ascended." CCXLI. Reply: There is no danger here. Who does not know that what is above our heads is called "up," and what is beneath our feet "down"? These determinations of place, such as right and left, up and down, before and behind, are all taken from the parts of our bodies. So when Christ had his head turned towards the Sun, he was rightly said to have ascended, because that motion went towards the place his head faced. And if the Earth were placed where Jupiter now is, what is over the heads of men living on the Earth would still be called "up," and what is under their feet "down." We can learn that this is the common usage of the words Up and Down from Plato in the Timaeus, whose words it is worth quoting here: "But it is absurd to say that there are two places, distinct by nature and separated by a long interval, one of which is called down, the place to which all things that have some bulk of body are carried, and the other up, the place to which all things are moved by force. For since the whole heaven is round, whatever extremes are made equally distant from the middle must similarly be extremes. The middle too, being equally distant from the extremes on every side by equal lines, looks equally on all things from its position. Since, then, the world is so arranged, if anyone should say that any of these things is up or down, he will seem to err not without reason. For the middle place in the whole cannot rightly be called up or down, but only middle." 2. Although I do not deny that the motion of any body towards the centre can be called its descent, as Descartes also speaks in art. 120 of Pt. III of the Principles, it is nonetheless clear enough that Scripture took account rather of the commonly received way of speaking, by which what hangs over our head is called up and what is trodden under our feet is called down, than of that other sense, remote from ordinary speech and used only by those who investigate the natures of things philosophically. 3. We did not say that the Sun is at the lowest point of the world; we judge that, with respect to the motions of the planets, it holds the centre, not indeed the geometrical centre but the physical one. But we profess that the middle of the world, which our opponent calls the lowest, cannot be determined. 4. The Earth itself has its own vortex and heaven, spread all around it, whose circumference is called Above and whose centre is called Below. Whoever therefore moves about the Earth or above it has above himself all the vortices and bodies of heaven. And so Christ, ascending, had above himself all the other vortices, even the Sun. But the Earth itself, carried with its vortex in the vortex of the Sun in an orbit about the Sun, which is the centre for that motion, will descend if it approaches the Sun; yet it will not be for that reason that a body which is carried from the Earth towards the vortices of heaven, or towards the Sun itself, is said to descend, unless it is conceived to tend from the outer edge of the Earth's vortex, within another vortex, towards the centre.

units.la: CCXLII. Denique addit ibidem, cum infernus damnatorum à plerisque Theologis non sine magna ratione in imo & à sedibus Beatorum remotissimo loco esse statuatur, scriptura inter hæc magnum chasma ponente Luc. 16, 20, & abyssum, puteum, stagnum, tenebras exteriores passim calamitosum illum locum vocante; sequetur juxta systema Copernicanorum, infernum in ipso Sole esse, quod qua verisimilitudine poßit asseri, prudentioribus expendendum relinquimus.
units.tr: CCXLII. Finally he adds in the same place: since the Hell of the damned is placed by most theologians, and not without good reason, in the lowest place, and the place most remote from the seats of the blessed, while Scripture sets a great gulf between them (Luke 16:20) and everywhere calls that dismal place an abyss, a pit, a lake, and outer darkness, it will follow, according to the system of the Copernicans, that Hell is in the Sun itself. With what plausibility this can be asserted we leave to the more prudent to weigh.

units.la: CCXLIII. Resp. Ubi sit infernus, nos anxiè non disquirimus, sed potius laboramus omnibus modis, ut Christo verâ fide adhærentes ab eo tuti reddamur. Pontificii eum in medio Terræ statuunt, quod quamvis non omninò sit absurdum, tamen est incertum. Sed non sequitur, eum fore in Sole; nam an Sol an Terra vel quodnam aliud corpus à Cœlo Beatorum sit remotissimum quis dixerit? Fatemur ex loco Luc. 16. constare, valdè remota esse à se invicem Cœlum Beatorum & Infernum, sed potest esse aliud corpus ab isto Cœlo adhuc remotius, in quo tamen non necessariò infernus collocandus.
units.tr: CCXLIII. Reply: Where Hell is, we do not anxiously inquire; we rather strive by every means, holding fast to Christ by true faith, to be made safe from it. The Papists place it in the middle of the Earth, which, although not altogether absurd, is uncertain. But it does not follow that it will be in the Sun; for who could say whether the Sun, or the Earth, or some other body, is the most remote from the heaven of the blessed? We grant that from Luke 16 it is clear that the heaven of the blessed and Hell are very far apart from each other; but there may be some other body even more remote from that heaven, and Hell need not necessarily be placed in it.

units.la: CAPUT. XVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVI.

units.la: De situ & Ordine præcipuorum Mundi corporum inter se. Sententia Cartesii & Copernici col- lata cum sententia Ptolemæi & Tychonis Brahe recitatur, porroque origo & vetustas ejus exponitur.
units.tr: On the situation and order of the principal bodies of the world among themselves. The opinion of Descartes and Copernicus is set beside that of Ptolemy and Tycho Brahe, and its origin and antiquity are explained.

units.la: CCXLIV. Sic de Extensione Mundi ex Cartesio actum, atque hac occasione etiam quid de ejus Extremo & Medio censendum, ex recta ratione determinatum. Ut autem Indefinitam istam Mundi extensionem Cartesius ex idea menti insita per legitimum rectæ rationis usum derivavit, ita etiam de Ordine atque Situ corporum Mundi præcipuorum in oculos incurrentium ita disseruit, ut ex Principiis primis & maximè evidentibus per legitimas Consequentias illum ritè deduxerit.
units.tr: CCXLIV. So much for the extension of the world according to Descartes; and on this occasion what is to be judged of its extremity and its middle has also been determined by right reason. But just as he derived this indefinite extension of the world from the idea implanted in the mind, through the lawful use of right reason, so too concerning the order and situation of the principal bodies of the world that fall under our eyes, he reasoned in such a way that he rightly deduced them from first and most evident principles by legitimate consequences.

units.la: CCXLV. Atque primò commodissimè omnium istam Mundi materiam ita dividit, ut totum illud spatium, quod complectitur Solem cum omnibus Planetis, primum Cœlum appellet, innumerabiles verò vortices, qui gyrant circa stellas fixas, ad secundum referat, & denique quicquid ultra istos duos Cœlos reperitur, pro tertio habeat. Vide Pp. III. art. 53. Dein in ipso primo Cœlo, cujus consideratio maximè ad nos spectat, cum Copernico talem ordinem corporum in eo contentorum constituit, ut Solem in medio collocet, quem arctiori ambitu circumit Mercurius, laxiori Venus, tertio loco Terra cum suo satellite Lunâ, quarto Mars, quinto Jupiter cum suis quatuor satellitibus, sexto Saturnus. Motum porrò sive Delationem diurnam Terræ tribuit, dum circa axem suum quotidie convolvi docet. In eo verò à Copernico differt, quòd quamvis Sol ab ipso ponatur in medio istarum circumvolutionum Planetarum, non tamen in medio mundi; deinde quòd stellas fixas non in unâ aliquâ sphærâ collocet, sed hinc inde alias magis, alias minus à Sole removeat.
units.tr: CCXLV. First, and most conveniently of all, he divides this matter of the world so that the whole space that encloses the Sun with all the planets he calls the first heaven; the countless vortices that revolve around the fixed stars he assigns to the second; and finally whatever lies beyond these two heavens he regards as the third. See Part III, art. 53. Then, within the first heaven itself, whose consideration concerns us most, he establishes with Copernicus such an order of the bodies contained in it that he places the Sun in the middle, which Mercury circles in a narrower orbit and Venus in a wider one; in the third place the Earth with its satellite the Moon; fourth Mars; fifth Jupiter with its four satellites; sixth Saturn. Moreover, he attributes to the Earth a motion or daily revolution, since he teaches that it turns every day about its own axis. In this he differs from Copernicus: although he places the Sun in the middle of these circuits of the planets, it is not in the middle of the world; and further, he does not place the fixed stars in one single sphere, but removes some farther from the Sun and others less, here and there.

units.la: CCXLVI. Ab hac dispositione corporum cœlestium recedunt duæ sententiæ celebres, quarum prima est Ptolemæi, qui in medio circumvolutionis Planetarum ponit Terram quiescentem, circa quam proximè volvi statuit Lunam, quam ampliori orbe excipit Mercurius, atque hunc ambit orbita sua Venus, ultra quam quarto loco Orbis solis, quinto Martis, sexto Jovis, septimo Saturni, octavo sphæra Firmamenti collocatur. Atque hos Planetas omnes circa Terram deferri statuit tuit ab Occasu in Ortum alios citius, alios tardius, dum omnes interim à primo mobili ab Ortu in Occasum rapiantur.
units.tr: CCXLVI. Two famous opinions depart from this arrangement of the heavenly bodies. The first is that of Ptolemy, who places the Earth at rest in the middle of the revolution of the planets, and holds that the Moon revolves around it nearest; next, Mercury receives the Moon in a wider orbit, and Venus encircles Mercury with its own orbit. Beyond this, in fourth place, is the orb of the Sun; fifth, that of Mars; sixth, of Jupiter; seventh, of Saturn; and eighth, the sphere of the firmament. He holds that all these planets are carried around the Earth from west to east, some faster, some more slowly, while all of them are meanwhile carried from east to west by the first moving sphere.

units.la: CCXLVII. Secunda dispositio est Tychonis Brahæi nobilis Dani, qui itidem Terram in medio mundi collocat, atque circa eam tria mobilia ferri statuit, proximè Lunam, postea Solem, tertiò Firmamentum. Circa Solem verò moveri dicit quinque errantes, Mercurium proximè, dein Venerem, sed ita ut illi duo suo circuitu Terram non intercipiant, hanc consequitur Mars, ampliori ambitu Jupiter, & adhuc ampliori Saturnus, sed eâ lege, ut suis circumferentiis & Terram cum Lunâ complectantur, & hi omnes, dùm interim propriis motibus circa Solem moveantur, à Sole annuo motu circuitum suum circa Terram absolvente, simul circumvehantur.
units.tr: CCXLVII. The second arrangement is that of the noble Dane Tycho Brahe, who likewise places the Earth in the middle of the world and holds that three moving bodies revolve around it: nearest is the Moon, then the Sun, and thirdly the firmament. He says that five wandering stars revolve around the Sun: Mercury nearest, then Venus, but in such a way that these two do not cut off the Earth in their circuit; Mars follows, then Jupiter in a wider compass, and Saturn in a still wider one. Their circumferences, however, embrace the Earth together with the Moon. All these bodies, while they move by their own motions around the Sun, are at the same time carried around the Earth by the Sun, which completes its circuit around the Earth in a yearly motion.

units.la: CCXLVIII. Prior dispositio Ptolemæi jam communiter rejicitur, quod non satisfiat per eam omnibus Phænomenis, & experientiæ repugnet. Quippe secundum istam dispositionem sæpius Mercurium & Venerem ita constitui oporteret, ut Terram inter se & Solem haberent positum, quod evenire nunquam est observatum. Deinde explicari non possunt phases Veneris experientiâ confirmatæ, quippe quæ deprehensa est augeri & minui lumine suo ut Luna, & plena apparere, tùm quando supra Solem ascendit, nova verò quando inter nos & Solem est interposita, cum secundum Ptolemæum supra Solem nunquam ascendat. Ut nunc alia absurda taceam, quæ hanc dispositionem comitantur.
units.tr: CCXLVIII. The former arrangement of Ptolemy is now commonly rejected, because it does not account for all the phenomena and contradicts experience. For according to that arrangement Mercury and Venus would often have to be placed so that the Earth lay between them and the Sun, which has never been observed to happen. Furthermore, the phases of Venus, confirmed by experience, cannot be explained. For these have been found to wax and wane in light like the Moon, and to appear full when she rises above the Sun, but new when she is interposed between us and the Sun; yet according to Ptolemy she never rises above the Sun. Not to mention the other absurdities that accompany this arrangement.

units.la: CCXLIX. Controvertitur autem præcipuè de Tychoniana & Copernicana hypothesi; Utra nempe cum naturæ Principiis atque adeo veritate conveniat? Atque de duobus imprimis disquiritur: Primò, Utrum Terra circa Solem deferatur intermedia inter Venerem & Martem, an verò Sol circa Terram circumducens quinque Planetas Mercurium, Venerem, Martem, Jovem & Saturnum? Dein, Utrum vicissitudo diei & noctis contingat per Firmamenti Motum diurnum, an vero per Terræ conversionem circa suum axem?
units.tr: CCXLIX. The dispute chiefly concerns the Tychonic and the Copernican hypotheses: which of them agrees with the principles of nature and therefore with the truth? Two questions are chiefly examined. First, whether the Earth is carried around the Sun, lying between Venus and Mars, or whether the Sun, leading around the Earth the five planets Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn, is itself carried around it? Next, whether the alternation of day and night comes about through the daily motion of the firmament, or through the rotation of the Earth around its axis?

units.la: CCL. Quandoquidem ergo prolixius de his quæstionibus agere nobis est constitutum, ab ovo, quod ajunt, rem exordiemur, ac examinabimus primo antiquitatem sententiæ Copernicanæ & originem, deinde statum Controversiæ rectè formabimus per terminorum legitimam explicationem.
units.tr: CCL. Since therefore we have resolved to treat these questions at greater length, we shall begin the matter, as they say, from the egg. We shall first examine the antiquity and origin of the Copernican opinion; then we shall properly frame the state of the controversy by a lawful explanation of the terms.

units.la: CCLI. Ex Veteribus jam diu ante Pythagoram hanc sententiam Numæ Pompilio adscribit Plutarchus in Numâ, quem dicit, templum Vestæ rotundum fecisse ad imaginem Universi, inque medio ejus constituisse æternum ignem, ut solaris ignis symbolum. Numam autem ante Pythagoram vixisse testis est Cicero lib. 2. de Oratore: Et referta quondam Italia Pythagoreorum fuit tum cum erat in hac gente magna illa Gracia: ex quo etiam quidam Numam Pompilium regem nostrum fuisse Pythagoreum ferunt, qui annis permultis ante fuit quam ipse Pythagoras. Idem in lib. 4. Tusculanarum quaestionum ait: Pythagoras fuit in Italia temporibus iisdem, quibus L. Brutus patriam liberavit. Similiter Livius lib. 1. c. 18. Auctorem doctrinae ejus (puta Numae) quia non exstat alius, falso Samium Pythagoram edunt, quem Servio Tullio regnante centum amplius post annos in ultima Italiae ora circa Metapontum Heracleamque & Crotonem juvenum amulantium studia coetus habuisse constat. CCLII. Fuerunt autem teste Laertio, duo Philosophiae Principia, unum quod ab Anaximandro, alterum quod a Pythagora fluxit. Anaximandri praeceptor fuit Thales, Pythagorae vero Pherecydes. Appellatumque est id Philosophiae genus Ionicum, quod Thales ex Ionia fuerit. Hoc autem Italicum, quod illius auctor Pythagoras in Italia ut plurimum philosophatus sit. Haec Principia diversa Philosophi secuti, circa hanc sententiam in contrarias partes iverunt. CCLIII. Ita Aristoteles lib. 2. de coelo cap. 12. docet: Ἐναντίως οἱ περὶ τὸν Ἰταλίαν, καλούμενοι Πυθαγόρειοι, λέγουσιν. ἐπὶ μὲν γὰρ ἓν μέσον πῦρ εἶναι φασι, τὸν δὲ γῆν ἐν τῷ ἄστρων ὧσαν κύκλῳ φερομένην περὶ τὸ μέσον νύκτα καὶ ἡμέραν ποιεῖν, h. e. Contra, qui Italiam incolunt, vocanturque Pythagorei, dicunt. In medio autem ignem esse inquiunt, terram autem astrorum unum existentem circulariter latum circa medium, noctem diemque facere. Idem paulo post: Ἔτι δ' εἴ γε Πυθαγόρειοι καὶ ὅς τὸ μαλίστα ἀπεσχηκεν φυλακὴν τοῦ κυριωτάτου ἐκ πάντος, τὸ μέσον εἶναι πυρὸν, ὁ Διὸς φυλακλὼ ὀνομάζουσι, τὸ πρῶτον ἔχον τὴν χώραν πῦρ, h. e. Amplius autem Pythagorei quidem, propterea quod maxime id convenit servari, quod est principalissimum ipsius universi, medium autem esse tale, quod Jovis carcerem nominat, hanc habere regionem ignem. CCLIV. Pythagoras ipse, quamvis tria volumina scripserit, teste Laertio ex Heraclito Physico, de Institutione, de Civitate, de Natura, tamen quoniam isti libri interierunt, de ejus dogmatibus non nisi ex Pythagoreorum placitis quicquam colligere licet. Hinc factum, ut Archimedes libro de arenae numero dogmatis hujus inventionem adscribat Aristarcho Samio, quem tamen probabilius est, id a conterraneo suo Pythagora accepisse. CCLV. Caeterum qui ex disciplina Pythagorae fuerunt progressi idem dogma cum suo magistro habuere commune. Hinc de Philolao ita Laërtius: Opinatur autem, omnia harmonia ac necessitate fieri, terram juxta primum circulum moveri dicit. De eodem Plutarchus deque aliis Pythagoricis sic l. 3. de Placitis & decretis Philos. scribit: Caeteri (scilicet Philosophi dicunt) terram manere. Philolaus vero Pythagoreus circum ignem verti obliquo in circulo, similiter Soli & Lunae. Heraclides Ponticus, Ecphantus Pythagoricus cient quidem Terram, verum haudquaquam promovent, rota vero instar cardine suo nixam ab occasu ad exortum circa eam volvi. Cicero in Lucullo idem dogma Nicetae sive Hicetae Syracusio & Platoni tribuit; Nicetas, inquit, Syracusius, ut ait Theophrastus, Coelum, Solem, Lunam, Stellas, superva denique omnia stare censet, neque praeter terram rem ullam in mundo moveri: quae cum circum axem se summa celeritate convertat & torqueat eadem effici omnia, quae si stante terra coelum moveretur, atque hoc etiam Platonem in Timaeo dicere quidam arbitrantur, sed paulo obscurius. De quo sic legesin Platone: Terram autem altricem nostram circa polum per universum extensum alligatam, diei noctisque effectricem & custodem esse voluit, nec non primam antiquissimamque Deorum omnium, qui in Coelo sunt geniti.
units.tr: CCLI. Among the ancients, long before Pythagoras, Plutarch in his Life of Numa ascribes this opinion to Numa Pompilius, saying that he made the round temple of Vesta in the image of the Universe, and set up in its middle an eternal fire as a symbol of the solar fire. That Numa lived before Pythagoras is attested by Cicero in the second book of On the Orator: And Italy was once full of Pythagoreans, when that great Greece was in this nation; from which some also say that our king Numa Pompilius was a Pythagorean, who lived many years before Pythagoras himself. The same author says in the fourth book of the Tusculan Disputations: Pythagoras was in Italy in the same times in which Lucius Brutus freed the fatherland. Likewise Livy in book 1, chapter 18: Since there is no other author of his teaching (namely Numa's), they falsely put forward Pythagoras of Samos; it is established that he, while Servius Tullius was reigning, more than a hundred years later, held gatherings of eager young men in the farthest part of Italy, around Metapontum, Heraclea and Croton. CCLII. There were, according to Laertius, two principles of philosophy, one that flowed from Anaximander and the other from Pythagoras. Anaximander's teacher was Thales, while Pythagoras' was Pherecydes. The kind of philosophy derived from Thales is called Ionian, because he came from Ionia; that derived from Pythagoras is called Italian, because its author Pythagoras philosophized mostly in Italy. Philosophers following these different principles went in opposite directions on this opinion. CCLIII. So Aristotle teaches in the second book On the Heavens, chapter 12: "The so-called Pythagoreans of Italy speak in the opposite way. For they say that there is a fire in the middle, and that the earth, being one of the stars, carried round in a circle about the middle, makes night and day." [Ἐναντίως οἱ περὶ τὸν Ἰταλίαν, καλούμενοι Πυθαγόρειοι, λέγουσιν. ἐπὶ μὲν γὰρ ἓν μέσον πῦρ εἶναι φασι, τὸν δὲ γῆν ἐν τῷ ἄστρων ὧσαν κύκλῳ φερομένην περὶ τὸ μέσον νύκτα καὶ ἡμέραν ποιεῖν] Shortly after he says again: "Moreover, the Pythagoreans, since they think it especially fitting to guard what is most principal in the whole, call the middle, which holds the first place, fire, the prison-guard of Jove." [Ἔτι δ' εἴ γε Πυθαγόρειοι καὶ ὅς τὸ μαλίστα ἀπεσχηκεν φυλακὴν τοῦ κυριωτάτου ἐκ πάντος, τὸ μέσον εἶναι πυρὸν, ὁ Διὸς φυλακλὼ ὀνομάζουσι, τὸ πρῶτον ἔχον τὴν χώραν πῦρ] CCLIV. Pythagoras himself, although according to Laertius, who draws on Heraclitus the Physicist, he wrote three volumes, On Instruction, On the State and On Nature, nevertheless, since those books have perished, nothing about his doctrines can be gathered except from the opinions of the Pythagoreans. Hence it happened that Archimedes, in his book on the Sand-Reckoner, ascribes the discovery of this doctrine to Aristarchus of Samos; yet it is more probable that he received it from his fellow countryman Pythagoras. CCLV. Moreover, those who came forth from the school of Pythagoras held the same doctrine in common with their master. Hence Laertius says of Philolaus: He holds that all things come about by harmony and necessity, and says that the Earth moves around the first circle. Plutarch, too, writes of the same man and of the other Pythagoreans in the third book of the Opinions of the Philosophers: The others (namely the philosophers) say that the Earth remains still. But Philolaus the Pythagorean says that it turns around the fire in an oblique circle, similarly to the Sun and the Moon. Heraclides of Pontus and Ecphantus the Pythagorean set the Earth in motion, yet not in a forward progress, but as a wheel fixed on its axle turning around itself from west to east. Cicero in the Lucullus ascribes the same doctrine to Nicetas, or Hicetas, of Syracuse, and to Plato: Nicetas of Syracuse, as Theophrastus says, thinks that the heavens, the Sun, the Moon, the stars, and finally all things above, stand still, and that nothing in the world moves except the Earth; and that, since it turns and spins about its axis with the greatest speed, all the same effects are produced as would be if the Earth stood still and the heavens moved. Some think that Plato also says this in the Timaeus, but a little more obscurely. On this, one reads in Plato as follows: He wanted the Earth, our nurse, wrapped about the pole which extends through the whole, to be the maker and guardian of day and night, and also the first and most ancient of all the gods that have been born in heaven.

units.la: CCLVI.

Dogma hoc ipsum superiori seculo fulcitavit & illustravit Nicolaus Copernicus Prutenus, Astronomus insignis, uti clarum ex eruditissimis libris de revolutionibus coelestium orbium conscriptis, illique dogmati tanquam fundamento superaedificavit explicationem phaenomenorum coelestium, quam longe expeditiorem facilioremque reddidit, sublatis infinitis orbibus & Epicyclis a Ptolemaeo & Astronomis aliis invectis. Hunc feliciter secuti sunt Maesthlinus, Keplerus, Galilaeus de Galliaeis, Guilhelmus Gilbertus Anglus, Philippus Lansbergius & alii multi, ut & Clariss. Dn. Antonius Deusingius in sua Dissertatione de vero systemate mundi, quo ad motum terrae diurnum circa suum axem.
