Novissime vero Renatus des Cartes Philosophorum facile primus hanc sententiam ita explicuit, ut difficultates, quibus sententia Copernici premebatur fultulerit, uti nos in sequentibus ex eo dabimus demonstratum.
units.tr: Nicolaus Copernicus of Prussia, a distinguished astronomer, supported and illustrated this doctrine in the last century, as is clear from his most learned books, On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Orbs. On that doctrine as a foundation he built his explanation of the heavenly phenomena, which he made far simpler and easier, removing the countless orbs and epicycles introduced by Ptolemy and other astronomers. Happily following him were Maestlin, Kepler, Galileo Galilei, William Gilbert of England, Philip Lansbergen and many others, as also the most distinguished Dr. Anthony Deusing in his dissertation on the true system of the world, concerning the daily motion of the earth about its axis. Most recently, René Descartes, first of the philosophers, explained this opinion so that he removed the difficulties by which Copernicus's view was burdened, as we shall demonstrate from him in what follows.

units.la: CCLVII.

In contrariam iverunt sententiam illi, qui Ionicum Philosophiae genus, ab Anaximandro Thaletis discipulo ortum, adoptarunt, quales fuerunt Anaximander, Anaximenes, Anaxagoras, Archelaus, Aristoteles cjusque sequaces, Stoici item, Hipparchus & Ptolemaeus omnesque Ptolemaici, uti & Tycho Brahaeus, qui ex Ptolemaico & Copernicano systemate quandam fecit mixturam, ut in principio hujus capitis videre est.
units.tr: On the opposite side were those who adopted the Ionian kind of philosophy, which arose from Anaximander, the disciple of Thales, such as Anaximander, Anaximenes, Anaxagoras, Archelaus, Aristotle and his followers, the Stoics likewise, Hipparchus and Ptolemy and all the Ptolemaic school, and also Tycho Brahe, who made a certain mixture of the Ptolemaic and Copernican systems, as may be seen at the beginning of this chapter.

units.la: CAPUT XVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVII.

units.la: Termini quæstionum propositarum explicantur, ostenditur quid Terræ nomine veniat, quid itidem per motum intelligamus.
units.tr: The terms of the proposed questions are explained, and it is shown what is meant by the name Earth and what we understand by motion.

units.la: CCLVIII. Terræ nomine intelligi potest 1. globus ille ex Terrâ & aquâ compactus ab aëre & cœlo distinctus. 2. Ille globus unà cum iLis corporibus, quæ se extendunt usque ad concavum Lunæ. His autem modis Terram accipi posse & debere Maimonides More Nebochim Part. II. cap. 30. etiam testatur, cujus verba: Porro & hoc sciendum tibi, quod Erez Terra sit vocabulum homonymum, quod usurpatur tum generaliter, tum specialiter: Generaliter dicitur de omnibus iis, quae sunt sub sphæra Lunæ, hoc est, de quatuor Elementis, specialiter dicitur de uno tantum, & quidem ultimo illorum, quod vocatur Terra. Docet nos hoc scriptura, quando dicit, Et terra erat informis & inanis, & tenebræ erant super facie Abyssi, & spiritus Dei incubabat in superficie aquarum. Ubi ista omnia Terræ vocabulo complectitur. Et paulo post: Et vocavit Deus aridam Erez Terram. Atque hoc quoque est secretum magnum. Quotiescunque enim dictum offendis, Et vocavit Deus tic vel sic, dicitur illud ad distinguendum rem unam ab aliis, cum quibus commune nomen habebat. Ideo hunc versum tibi exposui; In principio creavit Deus superiora & inferiora, & sic proinde per Terram, cujus primo fit mentio (quando videlicet dicitur, Deus creavit cœlum & terram) intelligenda erunt inferiora, hoc est quatuor Elementa, & per terram de qua dicitur: vocavit Deus aridam, Terram, Terra in specie sic dicta.
units.tr: CCLVIII. By the name Earth we may understand (1) that globe compounded of earth and water, distinct from air and heaven; or (2) that same globe together with those bodies which extend as far as the concave sphere of the Moon. That Earth may and should be taken in these senses, Maimonides also attests in More Nebochim, Part II, chapter 30, whose words are: Furthermore, you should also know that Erez, "earth," is an equivocal word, used both generally and specifically. Generally it is said of all those things that lie beneath the sphere of the Moon, that is, of the four Elements; specifically it is said of only one, and indeed the last of them, which is called earth. Scripture teaches us this when it says: "And the earth was without form and void, and darkness was upon the face of the deep, and the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters" (Gen. 1:2). Here it embraces all these things under the word earth. And shortly after: "And God called the dry land Erez, Earth" (Gen. 1:10). This too is a great secret. For whenever you meet with the saying, "And God called this or that," it is said to distinguish one thing from the others with which it had a common name. Therefore I have explained this verse to you: "In the beginning God created the higher and the lower things." Thus, by the earth of which mention is first made (namely where it is said, "God created the heaven and the earth"), the lower things must be understood, that is, the four Elements; and by the earth of which it is said, "God called the dry land Earth," the earth taken specifically in that sense.

units.la: CCLIX. Motus ab Aristotele definitur, quod sit ἐντελέχεια ἡ δυνάμει ὄντος ἢ τοιοῦτον. Sed quid illa ἐντελέχεια sit, cum etiam anima dicatur ἐντελέχεια, similiter actio hoc nomine insigniatur & de aliis rebus hoc vocabulum usurpetur, nondum satis convenit inter Interpretes, ut videatur Aristoteles rem, de qua sibi non satis constabat, obscuro vocabulo voluisse occultatam. Atque si ἐντελέχεια hic designet actum, ut plerique interpretes volunt, omnis actio erit motus. Nam an non omnis actio, quamdiu durat, sive quamdiu res est in fieri, est actus ejus, quod potentia est, quatenus tale est? At omnem actionem esse motum absurdum est, quid enim de creatione dices? quid de satisfactione & aliis actionibus divinis? At dices: Hanc definitionem esse Motus in genere, non motus localocalis. Resp. 1. manere nihilominus, quod sit obscura & latior definito, atque adeo careat proprietatibus bonæ definitionis. 2. si motus ita generaliter accipiatur, nullo modo differet ab actione; quid autem opus est vocabulis uti ambiguis, cum propria sunt in promptu? 3. præsupponitur, aliæ alias motus species, quod falsum esse prolixè ostendi posset, si præsens ferret institutum.
units.tr: CCLIX. Motion is defined by Aristotle as ἐντελέχεια [entelecheia] ἡ δυνάμει ὄντος ἢ τοιοῦτον [the actuality of what is potentially, as such]. But what that entelecheia is has not yet been sufficiently agreed among the interpreters, since the soul too is called an entelecheia, and action is likewise marked by this name, and the word is used of other things as well. So it seems that Aristotle wished to hide, under an obscure term, a matter about which he was not himself sufficiently clear. And if entelecheia here designates actuality, as most interpreters hold, then every action will be motion. For is not every action, as long as it lasts, or as long as the thing is in the process of becoming, "the actuality of that which is potentially, as such"? But it is absurd to say that every action is motion; for what will you say about creation? What about satisfaction and other divine actions? But you will say that this definition is of motion in general, not of local motion. I reply: (1) it nevertheless remains obscure, and broader than what is defined, and so lacks the properties of a good definition; (2) if motion is taken so generally, it will in no way differ from action; but why use ambiguous words when proper ones are at hand? (3) it presupposes that motion has various species, which could be shown to be false at length, if the present plan allowed it.

units.la: CLX. Sed longe clarior est definitio nostri Philosophi, qui Princip. part. II. art. 25. ita Motum definit, quod sit translatio unius partis materiæ, sive unius corporis ex vicinia eorum corporum, quæ illud immediatè continent, & tanquam quiescentia spectantur, in vicinam aliorum. Ex hac enim definitione natura Motus recte agnoscitur, cum omnibus antecedentibus & requisitis ad Motum, præcise rationem formalem Motus ostendat.
units.tr: CLX. But far clearer is the definition of our Philosopher, who in Principles, Part II, article 25, defines motion as the transfer of one part of matter, or of one body, from the vicinity of those bodies which immediately contact it and are regarded as at rest, into the vicinity of others. For from this definition the nature of motion is rightly recognised, since, with all the antecedents and requisites of motion set aside, it shows precisely the formal character of motion.

units.la: CCLXI. Nec aliam naturam Motus reperiemus, dummodo ad rem ipsam attendamus. Simili enim modo August. lib. 2. de Ordine cap. 6. Cognosce nos definire, quid sit moveri: quod si potes facias &c. Quæ cum dicta essent, puer de domo, cui id dederamus negotii, cucurrit ad nos, & horam prandii esse nunciavit. Tum ego: Quid sit, inquam, moveri, non definire no, puer iste sed ipsis oculis cogit ostendere: Eamus igitur, & de isto loco in alium locum transeamus: nam nihil est aliud, ni fallor, moveri &c. Simili ferè modo à Keplero Motus definitur Epit. Astron. Copernicanæ lib. 1. mihi p. 106. Motus est separatio mobilis, quatenus mobile, de loco suo & translatio in locum alium. Sed definitio Philosophi magis perspicua est, quod ex collatione patebit, & sequenti explicatione, in quo vestigia Philosophi sequemur.
units.tr: CCLXI. Nor shall we find any other nature of motion, provided we attend to the thing itself. In a similar way Augustine, in De Ordine, book 2, chapter 6, says: "You know that we define what it is to be moved; if you can, do so, etc. When these things had been said, a boy whom we had sent on an errand from the house came running to us and announced that it was time for lunch. Then I said: 'What it is to be moved, I say, this boy does not define but compels us to show with our very eyes. Let us go, then, and pass from this place to another place; for, unless I am mistaken, to be moved is nothing else, etc.'" Kepler defines motion in much the same way, in the Epitome of Copernican Astronomy, book 1, p. 106 in my edition: "Motion is the separation of the mobile, insofar as it is mobile, from its place and its translation into another place." But the Philosopher's definition is clearer, as will appear from the comparison and from the explanation that follows, in which we shall follow the Philosopher's footsteps.

units.la: CCLXII. Reddit autem Cartesius rationes, ob quas motum vocaverit translationem, non vim vel actionem quæ transfert; quarum prima est, ut ostenderet, illum semper esse in mobili, non in movente, quia hæc duo non satis accurate solent distinguī: secunda ratio est, ut planum faceret, motum duntaxat esse modum rei mobilis, vel mota, non rem aliquam subsistentem, sicut figura est modus rei figuratæ, ac quies rei quiescentis.
units.tr: CCLXII. Descartes gives the reasons why he called motion translation, not the force or action that effects the transfer. The first is that he wished to show that it is always in the moving body, not in the mover, since these two are not usually distinguished with sufficient care. The second reason is to make it plain that motion is merely a mode of the thing that is moved, not some subsisting thing, just as a figure is a mode of the figured thing, and rest is a mode of the thing at rest.

units.la: CCLXIII. Proclives enim admodum esse homines ad confundendum id, quod est in mobili, cum eo quod est in movente, actionem tribuendo mobili, cum tribui debeat moventi, patet 1. ex desin. Arist. supra visa, qui motum definit per actum. 2. ex eo quod vulgo rebus quibuscunque motis insitus motus nescio quis assignatur v. g. cœlis & stellis ad se movendum in orbem, rebus gravibus ad tendendum deorsum, sum, levibus ad tendendum sursum: in quibus est manifesta mobilis cum movente confusio.
units.tr: CCLXIII. That men are very prone to confuse what is in the moved body with what is in the mover, ascribing action to the moved body when it ought to be ascribed to the mover, is evident: (1) from the definition of Aristotle mentioned above, which defines motion through actuality; (2) from the fact that commonly some unknown motion is assigned as inherent in all moved things, for example to the heavens and stars, to move themselves in a circle; to heavy things, to tend downwards; to light things, to tend upwards. In these cases there is a manifest confusion of the moved body with the mover.

units.la: CCLIV. Nec minus vulgare est, motum concipere tanquam rem aliquam subsistentem, unde illæ definitiones: Motus est forma in moto impressa. Scal. exerc. 28. Vel ut alii: Motus est forma fluens, aut: Motus est forma, quæ successivè per partes acquiritur. Et inde respectu communicationis motus facile nobis talia oboriuntur. 1. in genere, non videtur nobis rem unam posse movere alteram, nisi aliquid ei communicet, adeoque, si corpus A motum impellat B, ut B quod antea quiescebat moveatur, vix possumus abstinere, quin putemus corpus A communicare aliquid corpori B, eo quod etiam post separationem à corpore A corpus B pergat ulterius moveri. 2. existimamus saltem in projectis aliquem impulsum concipiendum, qui iis à nostra manu communicatur.
units.tr: CCLIV. Nor is it less common to conceive of motion as some subsisting thing, whence those definitions: Motion is a form impressed on the moved body (Scaliger, Exercitations 28); or, as others have it, Motion is a flowing form, or: Motion is a form which is acquired successively, part by part. And from the point of view of the communication of motion, such notions easily arise in us. (1) In general, it does not seem to us that one thing can move another unless it communicates something to it; so, if body A, striking body B in motion, causes B, which was previously at rest, to move, we can hardly refrain from thinking that body A communicates something to body B, because body B continues to move even after its separation from body A. (2) At least in the case of projectiles, we suppose that some impulse must be conceived, which is communicated to them from our hand.

units.la: CCLXV. Sed si ad Cartesii definitionem & rationem secundam, quam adfert, animum advertamus, nos facile ex his omnibus extricabimus. Quod enim attinet primum; Non opus est, ut aliquid aliud hic inquiramus præter ipsam translationem, sed sufficit, si consideremus illam communicari, non aliquid aliud. Sicuti quando cera confertur figura quadrata, non opus est, ut aliquid aliud inquiramus præter istam determinationem extensionis quadratam. Quemadmodum autem quando in corpus aliquod ex. gr. in ceram alia figura introducitur, eo ipso prior tollitur, ita etiam hic, quando aliud corpus impellitur, eo ipso prius motum suum deperdere debet, vel totaliter vel ex parte, in quantum scilicet communicat; quando enim corpus A movet corpus B, nihil aliud corpori B communicatur, quàm translatio, quæ non est concipienda eadem quæ antea, sed nova. Est enim motus talis natura, ut assidue mutetur sitque continuo alius & alius. Dicitur tamen eadem communicari, respectu habito ad ejus quantitatem, eo quod Deus eandem motus quantitatem conservet in corpore B, quam corpus A habuit, antequam diceretur suum motum communicâsse. Ad secundum quod attinet, dico impulsum non differre à translatione ipsa, nisi hactenus, quod impulsus respectum habeat ad subsequentem translationem. Ut ita impulsus nihil aliud sit, quàm translatio ipsa, quatenus respectum habet ad aliam subsecuturam. In projectis autem nihil aliud fit, quàm ut ponantur in fluido, & versus aliquam partem eorum motus à manu determinetur, simul etiam determinato aëre versus eandem. Unde projecta tamdiu manent in isto statu motus versus istam partem, ad quam sunt determinata, donec à gravitate deprimantur, atque ita alio versus determinentur: quo facto in Terram descendunt, motumque suum cum ejus partibus & aëre quoque circumstante communicant.
units.tr: CCLXV. But if we attend to Descartes's definition and to the second reason he gives, we shall easily free ourselves from all these difficulties. As for the first: we need not look here for anything other than the translation itself, but it suffices to consider that it is communicated, and not something else. Just as when wax receives a square shape, we need not seek anything beyond that determination of square extension. Moreover, just as, when another shape is introduced into a body, for example into wax, the earlier shape is thereby removed, so here too, when another body is struck, it must by that very fact lose its own motion, wholly or in part, insofar as it communicates it. For when body A moves body B, nothing else is communicated to body B except translation, which is not to be conceived as the same as before, but as new. For motion is of such a nature that it is constantly changing and is continually different. Nevertheless it is said to be the same that is communicated, with respect to its quantity, because God preserves in body B the same quantity of motion that body A had before it was said to have communicated its motion. As for the second: I say that the impulse does not differ from the translation itself, except in this, that the impulse has regard to the subsequent translation; so that the impulse is nothing other than the translation itself, insofar as it has regard to another that will follow. In projectiles, however, nothing happens except that they are placed in a fluid, and their motion is determined by the hand towards some part, while at the same time the surrounding air is also determined towards the same part. Hence projectiles remain in that state of motion towards the part to which they have been determined for as long as they are not pressed down by gravity, and so are determined otherwise; when this happens they descend to the Earth, and communicate their motion together with its parts and the surrounding air.

units.la: CCLXVI. Egregie vero Auctor libelli de finito & infinito, Anno 1651. Amstelrodami expressi, ostendit, vim illam in corporibus motis præter respectum ad motum, nihil esse, nisi quid imaginarium. Ita enim p. 16. & 17. inquit: Attendant quaeso (hi nempe qui vim aliquam præter motum rebus motis tribuunt) ad motum ambulantis in navi, qua celerrimè velo & aqua vehitur in contrariam partem ad quam ambulans tendit: liquet non cum majori difficultate ambulantem in contrariam partem ferri, quam si navis plane quiesceret: at si hic vis aliqua præter illam mutationem situs statuenda esset, qua navim impetu perpelleret ad lineam, à qua ambulans recedit: procul dubio majori conatu opus esset, & incassum laboraret homo contendendo in contrariam partem ei ad quam navis vehitur. Considerare autem hic oportet, navim non à vento agitatam, sed flumine placido existente à remis tantum impulsam, ne objicere possis, sentire aliquam resistentiam venti navem impellentis. Postea vero etiam causam reddit hujus hominum præjudicii, quando inquit: Cum autem videamus res motas tantâ vi & impetu objacentia sibi corpora depellere & comminuere, inde male concluditur, vim aliquam ab hac mutatione continua & successiva situs distinctam esse: cum ipse motus sit, qui per suas impressiones & effectus in anima sese distinguens ab aliis rebus vim atque potentiam à nobis vocitetur. Non itaque vim negamus esse in natura: sed vim illam ipsam mutationem situs esse dicimus, qualem hactenus descripsimus. Hæc adscribere volui tanquam præclarè rem istam declarantia.
units.tr: CCCLXVI. The author of the little book On the Finite and the Infinite, printed at Amsterdam in 1651, has rightly shown that the force said to be in moving bodies, apart from their relation to motion, is nothing but something imaginary. At pp. 16 and 17 he says: Let those who attribute some force to moving things, over and above motion, consider the motion of a man walking on a ship that is carried swiftly by sail and water in the direction opposite to that in which he walks. It is clear that he is carried in the opposite direction with no more difficulty than if the ship were standing perfectly still. But if some force besides that change of position had to be posited, by which the ship was driven forward along the line from which the walker moves away, then without doubt more effort would be needed, and the man would labour in vain by striving in the direction opposite to that in which the ship is carried. We must note here that the ship was not driven by the wind but was pushed only by oars on a calm river, so that you cannot object that the ship felt some resistance from the wind driving it. Afterwards he also gives the cause of this prejudice of men, when he says: When we see moving things drive off and crush the bodies lying in their way with such force and impetus, it is wrongly concluded that some force distinct from this continuous and successive change of position exists. Yet it is motion itself, which, distinguishing itself from other things by its impressions and effects on the mind, is called force and power by us. We therefore do not deny that force exists in nature; but we say that this force is the very change of position which we have so far described. I wished to quote these words as clearly explaining the matter.

units.la: CCLXVII. Ex his patet, attentione singulari opus esse, si naturam Motus benè intelligere velimus, neque frivolum fuisse Cartesii institutum, actionem à motu sollicitè distinguentis, uti R. St. p. 170. & L. p. 290. opinantur. Vera quidem est distinctio, ut actio tribuatur motui, quatenus procedit ab agente, & passio quatenus recipitur in patiente, uti Clarifs. Heerebort. in disputatione citata docet; sed hoc totam rem & difficultatem, ad quam Cartesius respexit, non exhaurit, neque etiam ab Heerebortio in eum finem est adductum.
units.tr: CCCLXVII. From these things it is plain that singular attention is needed if we wish to understand the nature of motion well, and that Descartes's undertaking, which carefully distinguishes action from motion, was not frivolous, as R. St. (p. 170) and L. (p. 290) suppose. The distinction is indeed true, that action is attributed to motion as far as it proceeds from the agent, and passion as far as it is received in the patient, as the distinguished Heereboord teaches in the disputation cited; but this does not exhaust the whole matter and difficulty to which Descartes had regard, nor was it introduced by Heereboord for that purpose.

units.la: CCLXVIII. Definitionem Motus art. 25. traditam & probatam Cartesius art. 26. porrò sic declarat. Quippe notandum est, magno nos in hoc præjudicio laborare, quod plus actionis ad motum requiri arbitremur, quam ad quietem. Quid præjudicia sint, & quomodo in nobis formentur, satis docuit Cartesius Pp. I. 71, 72, 73, 74. & vel ipsum non en ostendit, quod sint judicia à nobis facta ante perceptionem sufficientem, adeoque eo ipso, quatenus talia, erronea. Quando vero dicit,nos arbitrari, plus actionis requiri ad quietem, in eoque præjudicio laborare, per actionem intelligit, non actionem tantùm nostram, sed collectivè quamcunque, ut in eo consistat præjudicium, quod, quia plus actionis nostræ sæpius videmus requiri ad motum, quam ad quietem, proclives simus ad statuendum, in genere plus actionis requiri ad motum, non attendentes, plura alia ad motum & quietem concurrere posse, quam nostram actionem, aut nostram ab actione cessationem. Philosophum autem hic loqui de actione, non nostrâ, sed collectivè de omni actione ex sequentibus ipsius verbis est manifestum, præsertim si attendamus ad illa ipsius verba: sumentes sc. actionem pro conatu illo, quo nitimur ad membra nostra, & illorum ope alia corpora permovenda.
units.tr: CCCLXVIII. Descartes, having given and proved the definition of motion in art. 25, then explains it further in art. 26: For it must be noted that we labour under a great prejudice in this, that we think more action is required for motion than for rest. Descartes has sufficiently taught what prejudices are and how they are formed in us (Pp. I. 71, 72, 73, 74), and he himself shows that they are judgments made by us before sufficient perception, and therefore, as such, erroneous. But when he says that we think more action is required for rest, and that we labour under this prejudice, he means by action not merely our own action but action taken collectively, whatever it may be. The prejudice consists in this: since we more often see more of our action required for motion than for rest, we are inclined to conclude that in general more action is required for motion, not noticing that more things than our action, or our ceasing from action, can concur to produce motion and rest. That the philosopher is here speaking not of our action but of all action collectively is plain from the words that follow, especially if we attend to his words: taking action, that is, for that effort by which we strive to move our limbs, and by their help to move other bodies.

units.la: CCLXIX. Ad hoc quia non attendit L.p. 290. vel attendere noluit, verba Cartesii art. 26. tali joco, uti ipse dicit, excipit: Egregium vero inventum, & par illi, aut ex eo deductum, quod libro de Methodo de frugibus terræ sine labore percipiendis promisit. Inventum inquam: nam in hunc diem natura indicio plus actionis ad motum, quàm ad quietem requirebatur. Gratulor ergo jam aurigis, nautis, portitoribus, tabellariis, nuncis, & quicunque iter terrâ marique conficiunt. non plus laboris. Laboris verò? non plus actionis via vel longissima perficienda impendent, quàm si quieti domi desideant. Ab his fabrorum & omnium opificum tabernas perlustrabo, magnam ab iis lato nuntio gratiam initurus. Si quidem & hi, si non pedum saltem brachiorum motu victum quaritabant. Imò si qua & mentis agitatio, quæ sine omni motu & actione interna esse nequit, si qua animi operatio, vel ad virtutem adsequendam laboriosa meditatione instituta, vel ad eruditionis famam non mendacem acquirendam: omnibus bona mentis studiosis jam securis esse impero, ac, omni re jam in vado quiescente in portu navigare, ac ne navigare quidem, sed remos inhibere, vela dejicere jubeo. Nihilo doctiores fient, nec in bonorum virorum officio plus opera navabunt agendo, quàm manibus in tergum rejectis quiescendo. CCLXX. Resp. Quænam quæso est inter hæc Connexio: Præjudicium est, plus actionis in genere ad motum requiri, quàm ad quietem: sive, Non requiritur plus actionis in genere & collectivè sumtæ ad motum, quam ad quietem: Ergo etiam non plus actionis nostræ. Si quis ex illo dicto Poetæ: Non minor est virtus, quam quærere, parta tueri, in Politicis applicato ad Principem, quod non minorem curam debeat adhibere ad conservandum suum regnum, quàm adhibuit ad illud consequensequendum, inferret: Ergo debere Principem, etiam postquam regnum est pacatum, exercitum ducere in hostem, castella expugnare &c. nonne hic Politices Professor ipsum argueret ex Topicis, quod male argumentaretur à genere ad speciem affirmative. Quare ergo & hic ad illum canonem non attendit? Indignabuntur ergo tibi, aurigæ, nautæ, portitores, tabellarii, nuncii, & quicunque iter terrâ marique conficiunt, quod tuo nuncio, læto quidem, sed vano, & ex prave intellectis Cartesii verbis hausto, ipsos deceperis. Quod si ab his fabrorum & omnium opificum tabernas perlustraveris, vide ne malleos, ascias &c. instrumenta sua capiti tuo impingant, quod fidem tuo nuncio habentes operas intermiserint, & ita non levem jacturam rei familiaris fuerint perpessi. Nec majorem gratiam reportabis à bonæ mentis studiosis, qui à te illusi, omnem impositurum impendent operam, ut Satyricum calamum contra te stringentes saltem famam non mendacem styli acuti & perpoliti reportent; ut reciproco joco tecum ludam.
units.tr: CCCLXIX. Because L. (p. 290) either did not notice or did not wish to notice this, he meets Descartes's words of art. 26 with a jest, as he himself calls it: An outstanding discovery, and one equal to, or deduced from, what he promised in his book on Method, that the fruits of the earth can be gathered without labour. A discovery, I say; for up to this day nature indicated that more action was required for motion than for rest. I now congratulate charioteers, sailors, carriers, couriers, messengers, and all who make journeys by land and sea. They spend no more labour, no more action, in completing even the longest journey than if they remained at rest at home. I will go through the shops of smiths and all craftsmen, expecting great thanks from them for my glad news. For even if they sought their living by motion of feet or arms alone... Indeed, if there is any agitation of the mind, which cannot exist without all motion and inner action, any operation of the soul, whether undertaken by laborious meditation to attain virtue or to win the reputation of true learning: I now command all men of good mind to be at ease, and, with everything now at rest in harbour, not even to sail, but to hold back the oars and lower the sails. They will not become more learned, nor will they show more effort in the duty of good men by acting than by lying quiet with their hands folded behind their backs. CCCLXX. Reply: what connection, I ask, is there between these things? The prejudice is that more action in general is required for motion than for rest; or, rather, that not more action in general and collectively taken is required for motion than for rest. Therefore not more of our action either. If someone, from that saying of the poet, Keeping what has been won is no less a virtue than seeking it, applied to politics, were to infer that a prince, after the kingdom is pacified, ought to lead his army against the enemy, storm castles, and so on, would not the professor of politics himself charge him from the Topics with arguing badly from genus to species affirmatively? Why, then, do you not heed that rule here? Charioteers, sailors, carriers, couriers, messengers, and all who make journeys by land and sea will be indignant with you, because you have deceived them with your message, glad but empty, drawn from the wrongly understood words of Descartes. And if you go through the shops of smiths and all craftsmen, take care that they do not strike your head with their hammers, axes and other tools, because, trusting your message, they have stopped their work and so have suffered no slight loss to their household affairs. Nor will you get greater thanks from the men of good mind, whom you have mocked; they will take the greatest pains to wield a satirical pen against you, so that they at least win the reputation of sharp and polished style, not a false one. I will play with you in return with the same jest.

units.la: CCLXXI. Objicit B. p. 103. Secundum eam Cartesii definitionem Motus tantum est superficiei, non corporis totius, saltem non internarum partium: & sic e. g. hinc merces in Indias Orientales transferri poterunt absque ullo eorundem motu, modo compacta sint in navi vehente &c.
units.tr: CCCLXXI. B. (p. 103) objects: According to Descartes's definition, motion belongs only to the surface, not to the whole body, at least not to its inner parts; and so, for example, wares could be carried to the East Indies without any movement of their own, provided they are packed in a ship that is sailing.

units.la: Resp. Nodus in scirpo quaeritur: Clarissimum est pro diverso respectu, eandem rem dici posse moveri & non moveri: Ita nempe merces, quæ in Indiam transferuntur, dum interim in navi sunt compactæ, possunt dici quiescere, & non moveri, si respectus habeatur ad ipsam navem, à quâ non recedunt, nec removentur: verum si considerentur, ut pertinentes ad navim, navisque referatur ad littora, vel ad stellam polarem, quæ tanquam immota spectentur, unà cum navi moveri dici queunt.
units.tr: Reply: they are looking for a knot in a bulrush. It is perfectly clear that the same thing can be said both to move and not to move, depending on the point of view. Thus the wares that are carried to India, while they are packed in the ship, can be said to be at rest and not to move, if we consider them in relation to the ship itself, from which they do not depart or get removed. But if they are considered as belonging to the ship, and the ship is referred to the shores or to the pole star, which are viewed as motionless, they can be said to move together with the ship.

units.la: CCLXXII. Pergit Cartesius & hujus præjudicii causam & fontem aperit, ut eo cognito tanto melius illud vitare possimus. Hocque ideo, inquit, nobis ab ineunte ætate persuasimus, quod corpus nostrum soleat moveri à nostra voluntate, cujus intime conscii sumus, & quiescere ex hoc solo, quod Terra adhæreat per gravitatem, cujus vim non sentimus. Et quidem quia ista gravitas, aliaque plures causæ à nobis non animadversæ, motibus quos in membris nostris ciere volumus resistunt, efficiuntque ut fatigemur, putamus majore actione, sive majore vi opus esse ad motum ciendum, quàm ad illum sistendum, sumentes sc. actionem pro conatu illo, quo utimur ad membra nostra, & illorum ope alia corpora permovenda. His ostendit, præjudicium illud ita formari, inque eo consistere, quod motus membrorum nostrorum sinus conscii, non item quietis, atque ita ad motum requiri actionem perspectum habeamus, ad quietem vero æque necessariam esse non sentiamus. Cujus rei duæ sunt causæ: prior est, quod motus sæpe pendeat à nostrâ voluntate, cujus intime conscii sumus: (velle enim nos scimus, eo ipso dum volumus, quia aliàs, quando volumus, non possemus cum veritate dicere: Ego volo, nisi hoc sciremus: testimonium quippe externum ab interno dissentiret) de quiete vero corporis nostri judicamus ex sensus perceptione, ita concludentes: Ego ad quietem corporis mei nullam vim, nullam actionis gravitatem extra me sentio, percipio: Ergo nulla adest; male sensus nostros constituentes regulam judicandi de iis quæ existunt, vel non existunt. Posterior causa est, quia gravitas membrorum nostrorum resistit eorum motui, quietem vero promovet; hinc fit, ut sentiamus quidem motum membrorum nostrorum propter istam resistentiam, quietem vero propter ejus absentiam non ita sentire queamus.
units.tr: CCLXXII. Descartes goes on to disclose the cause and source of this prejudice, so that once it is known we may avoid it all the better. "We were persuaded of this from early childhood, he says, because our body is usually moved by our will, of which we are intimately aware, and it rests only because it adheres to the Earth through gravity, whose force we do not feel. And indeed, because this gravity, and several other causes not noticed by us, resist the motions we wish to produce in our limbs and make us tired, we think that more action, or more force, is needed to set motion going than to stop it, taking 'action' to mean that effort by which we use our limbs and by their help move other bodies." By this he shows that the prejudice is formed in the following way and consists in this: we have a clear perception that motion of our limbs requires action, of which we are conscious, but we do not perceive that rest is equally necessary. There are two causes of this. The first is that motion often depends on our will, of which we are intimately aware. For we know that we will, in the very act of willing, since otherwise we could not truly say "I will" when we will; the external testimony would disagree with the internal. But concerning the rest of our body, we judge from the perception of the senses, concluding thus: "I perceive no force or weight of action outside myself in the rest of my body; therefore none is present." This wrongly makes our senses the rule for judging what exists and what does not. The second cause is that the weight of our limbs resists their motion but promotes their rest. Hence it comes about that we feel the motion of our limbs because of this resistance, but cannot feel the rest in the same way because of its absence.

units.la: CCLXXIII. Ad hæc notat L. p. 291.
units.tr: CCLXXIII. L. notes on this at p. 291.

units.la: Verum remoto joco, quibus argumentis opinionem suam C. probatum eat, perpendamus. 1. præjudicio nos magno antehac laborasse ait. Itane omnia in quibus vel ratio nobiscum facit, vel populorum consensus, vel integrum sensuum testimonium, si id à pueritia annis noverimus, præjudicii judicio damnandum est? Male de scientiarum jure agitur, si in Novatorum quamvis famosorum gratiam communes animi notiones, vel omnium gentium tàm barbararum quàm eruditarum judicia, præjudicii insimulata deponere cogamur.
units.tr: But, joking aside, let us weigh the arguments by which C. has proved his opinion. 1. He says that he was formerly burdened by a great prejudice. Is it then the case that everything with which either reason agrees, or the consensus of peoples, or the whole testimony of the senses, if we have known it from childhood, must be condemned by the judgment of prejudice? Matters go badly for the right of the sciences if, to gratify certain Innovators, however notorious, we are forced to give up common notions of the mind, or the judgments of all nations, barbarian and learned alike, by accusing them of prejudice.

units.la: CCLXXIV. Resp. Quid sint præjudicia indicatum est superius. Non dicit Cartesius, ea esse præjudicia, in quibus ratio nobiscum facit, vel populorum consensus, vel integrum sensuum testimonium, sed ea effata, de quibus judicavimus, antequam perceperimus, vel rite examinaverimus. Possunt itaque etiam ea esse præjudicia, in quibus ratio nobiscum facit, vel populorum consensus, vel integrum sensuum testimonium, si nempe ea non propter has causas suscepimus, sed tantum credulâ voluntate acceptavimus. Manentque in nobis tanquam præjudicia, donec per legitimum examen resumamus & assentiamur ob rationes manifestas. Fuerunt ergo antea quidem vera, sed nos ea nondum ut talia cognoveramus; fuerunt vera materialiter, at postea vera evadunt formaliter & nobis ipsis. Absit vero, ut communes animi notiones, vel omnium gentium, tàm barbararum quàm eruditarum judicia præjudicii insimulemus. Quin imò hoc adversarii est præjudicium, dum judicat id, quod nec ex Cartesio, nec ex ejus discipulis audivit.
units.tr: CCLXXIV. Reply. What prejudices are has been indicated above. Descartes does not say that those are prejudices in which reason agrees with us, or the consensus of peoples, or the whole testimony of the senses; he means those opinions which we pronounced upon before we perceived them or properly examined them. So there can also be prejudices in which reason agrees with us, or the consensus of peoples, or the whole testimony of the senses, namely if we did not adopt them for these reasons, but merely accepted them with a credulous will. They remain in us as prejudices until we take them up again through legitimate examination and assent to them on manifest grounds. They were therefore indeed true before, but we had not yet known them as true; they were true materially, but afterwards become true formally and for ourselves. Far be it from us to accuse common notions of the mind, or the judgments of all nations, barbarian and learned alike, of prejudice. Indeed, it is the opponent who holds the prejudice, since he judges what he has not heard from Descartes or from his disciples.

units.la: CCLXXV. Porrò non sufficiebat Carteho ostendisse morbum, verum rùm etiam tollere conatur, medicamen nobis monstrando, dùm sic inquit: Quod tamen prejudicium facile exuemus, si consideremus, non modo conatu nobis opus esse ad movenda corpora externa, sed sæpe etiam ad eorum motus sistendos, cum à gravitate aliàve causa non sistuntur. Ut exempli gratia, non majori utimur actione ad navigium in aquâ stagnante quiescens impellendum, quàm ad idem, cùm movetur, subitò retinendum: vel certe non multò majori; hinc enim demenda est aqua ab eâ sublevata gravitas, & ejusdem lentor, à quibus paulatim sisti posset. Præjudicium fuerat: Ad motum plus actionis requiritur, quàm ad quietem, idque ex eo, quia sæpius circa motum actionem experti sumus. non vero circa quietem, malè concludentes: Ubi nullam sentimus actionem, ibi nulla est: Atqui ad quietem procurandam nullam sentimus actionem: Ergo nulla ibi est. Hic Cartesius quidem principaliter & primariò negat Majorem, quia Pp. I. art. 71. ostenderat, malè ita concludi: Ego nihil ibi video, sentio, percipio: Ergo nihil ibi est; adeoque, quamvis gravitatis vim & actionem non sentiamus, non tamen aliquam esse debeat negari. Non enim omnia quæ sunt, sensibus nostris percipere possumus: sic enim nec Deum, nec angelos, nec animas nostras, nec multa minuta corpuscula, quæ sensum nostrum effugiunt, existere esset concedendum. Dein negat quoque Minorem, ostendendo, etiam sæpe fieri, ut sentiamus requiri conatum ad quietem corporibus motis conciliandum, idque declarat exemplo à navigio desumto. Illud quidem sibi relictum ad quietem perducitur, concurrente tùm lentore, tùm etiam gravitate ipsius aquæ, quæ à lateribus navis est sublevata, altiusque quàm reliqua supra eam congregata navem premit, & ejus motui resistit, ut ita ab hac navis sistenda esset, nisi denuò remis propelleretur. Sed si ipsi soli navem ad quietem velimus reducere, quod facimus subitò eam retinendo, (nisi enim hoc fiat, statim habebimus causas alias adjuvantes,) experiemur, non multò minori conatu nobis opus esse, imò majori, quàm si illud quiescens velimus movere. Possumus aliud ad hanc rem adducere exemplum, desumtum à nostris musculis, quibus membra nostra moventur & quiescunt. Docent Anatomici, talem esse musculorum conformationem, ut quàm plurimùm duo ubique sint musculi ibi invicem oppositi, ita ut musculo, qui flectit articulum, opponatur extendens, & ei qui movet partem in anteriora opponatur, qui in posteriora retrahit, atque ita deinceps. Quando itaque duo musculi oppositi simul agunt, & quidem æqualiter, oriri docent motum musculorum tonicum, quo fit, ut pars in eodem situ retineatur & quiescat, ad quam quietem producendam actionem musculorum requiri ajunt.
units.tr: CCLXXV. Moreover, it was not enough for Descartes to have shown the disease; he also tries to remove it, pointing us to a remedy when he says: We shall easily cast off this prejudice if we consider that effort is needed not only to move external bodies, but often also to stop their motions, when they are not stopped by gravity or some other cause. For example, we use no greater action to push a boat resting in still water than to hold it back suddenly when it is moving, or certainly not much greater: for the weight of the water raised by the boat must be removed, and its sluggishness, by which it could gradually be stopped. The prejudice had been: more action is required for motion than for rest, and this because we have more often experienced action in regard to motion and not in regard to rest, concluding badly: where we feel no action, there is none; but we feel no action in bringing about rest; therefore there is none there. Here Descartes principally and primarily denies the major premise, since in Principles part 1, art. 71, he had shown that it is wrongly concluded: I see, feel, perceive nothing there; therefore nothing is there. So, although we do not feel the force and action of gravity, it should not be denied that there is some. For we cannot perceive everything that exists with our senses: thus we would have to concede that neither God, nor angels, nor our souls, nor many tiny corpuscles which escape our senses, exist. Then he also denies the minor premise, showing that it often happens that we feel an effort is required to bring moving bodies to rest, and he makes this clear by an example taken from a boat. That boat, left to itself, is brought to rest by the combined sluggishness and also the weight of the water, which is raised at the sides of the ship and, piled higher than the rest above it, presses on the ship and resists its motion, so that the ship would be stopped by this unless it were pushed again by oars. But if we wish to bring the ship to rest by itself, which we do by suddenly holding it back (for unless this is done, we shall at once have other helping causes), we shall find that we need no smaller effort, indeed a greater one, than if we wanted to move it while it was at rest. We can bring another example to this matter, taken from our muscles, by which our limbs are moved and kept at rest. Anatomists teach that the muscles are so arranged that almost everywhere two muscles lie opposed to each other, so that the muscle which flexes a joint is opposed by the extensor, and the one which moves a part forward is opposed by the one which draws it back, and so on. When therefore two opposing muscles act together, and equally, they teach that a tonic motion of the muscles arises, by which the part is kept in the same position and rests; and they say that action of the muscles is required to produce this rest.

units.la: CCLXXVI. His bene perceptis sponte cadunt Objectiones cont- ra haec Philosophi verba (L. p. 292.) 2.
units.tr: CCLXXVI. Once these points are well understood, the objections raised against these words of the philosopher (L. p. 292.) fall away of their own accord. 2.

units.la: Sape ad corporum externorum motus sistendos conatu aliquo nobis opus esse. (sc. ait Cartesius) Quid tum? ergo semper ad omnia corpora & sistenda, & in quiete retinenda eodem conatu opus est, quo ad ciendum & continuandum motum? pudet me ineptiarum, & tamen a tanto viro pro oraculis haec traduntur & acceptantur. 3. Exemplo utitur navigii in aqua stagnante ad quietem permoti, quod plane contra ipsum militat: nisi & ratio nos fugit, & oculorum sensus saepe decepit. nec eum multum juvit adverbium SVBITO callide insertum. non enim de omni subitanea quiete, sed de quacunque & quidem continuata, ut de motu continuo quaestio est, aut esse debet, si pari hac ratiocinandi modo agimus.
units.tr: Often some effort on our part is needed to stop the motion of external bodies (so Descartes says). What then? Is the same effort always needed to stop all bodies and keep them at rest as is needed to set them in motion and continue their motion? I am ashamed of such silliness, yet these things are handed down and accepted as oracles by so great a man. 3. He uses the example of a ship brought to rest in still water, which plainly works against him, unless reason escapes us too and the sense of sight has often deceived us. Nor does the adverb SUDDENLY, cunningly inserted, help him much. For the question is not about any sudden rest, but about rest of any kind, and indeed continued rest, as the question is, or ought to be, about continuous motion, if we reason in this same way.

units.la: CCLXXVII. Resp. 1. quo tendat Cartesius, quando docet, sape ad corporum externorum motus sistendos conatu aliquo nobis opus esse, ex art. 274. satis patet. Ad Minorem enim illam infringendam unica instantia sufficiebat. Noluit autem neque debuit probare, semper eodem conatu nostro opus esse ad corpora sistenda & in quiete retinenda, imo hoc falsum esse satis novit: neque etiam hic intendit demonstrare, tantum actionis ad quietem requiri, quantum ad motum, quae ejus est thesis; sed contentus fuit antithesin hominum praejudiciis occupatorum infringere: thesin vero suam confirmat Pp. part III. & IV. ubi ex variis exemplis motus & quietis liquet, quod tanta actio ad quietem requiratur, quanta ad procurandum motum. Itaque id, quod de ineptiis Cartesii oggeritur, totum evanescit. 2. quomodo exemplum navigii Cartesio inserviat supra est demonstratum. Voculam SVBITO etiam non callide vel fraudulenter fuisse insertam; sed ad scopum auctoris necessario requisitam, est demonstratum. Ut enim posset nostra actio quietem navigio conciliare, debebat id subito fieri, ne ab aliis causis adjuvaretur; quod tamen vix evitari posse Cartesius ostendit, quando ait, demendam esse aquae a navigio sublevatae gravitatem, & lentorem, a quibus paulatim sisti posset. Hinc tamen non putem adversarium rationem fugere, & oculorum sensum ipsum decepisse, nisi, ut lenissime dicam, non satis accurate attendendo illam a se fugaverit. CCLXXVIII. Pergit Cartesius definitionem suam ulterius deducere & explicare: ita enim art. 27: Cum autem hic non agatur de illa actione, quae intelligitur esse in movente, vel in eo, qui motum sistit, sed de sola translatione ac translationis absentia, sive quiete; manifestum est hanc translationem extra corpus motum esse non posse, atque hoc corpus alio modo se habere cum transfertur; & alio cum non transfertur, sive cum quieseit: adeo ut motus quies nihil aliud in eo sint, quàm diversi modi. Horum verborum iste est sensus. Cùm autem hic non agatur] Propterea enim definiverat motum per translationem, ut ostenderet, actionem non esse de ejus formali ratione, ut à nobis plenius est ostensum. de illa actione quæ intelligitur esse in movente] At objiciat aliquis: Actio non est in agente, sed ab illo, quatenus vel ò terminatur in effecto, passio vocatur. Resp. Actio potest dici ab agente & in agente diverso respectu, uti ex actionibus immanentibus est manifestum.z. In movente esse actionem aliquam facilè intelligitur: nonne enim, si lapidem moves, actio in te exist, vibratio brachii, musculorum extensiones, spirituum influxus & similia? manifestum est] actio enim illa, quæ est in movente extra corpus motum esse potest, & est in jactu lapidis; sed translatio ipsa non potest, cùm sit mobilis, non moventis.atque hoc corpus alio modo] quemadmodum enim figurarum variatio corpus cui insunt variat, ut cera ex gr. aliter se habeat, quando est quadrata, aliter, quando rotunda exístit; aliam enim atque aliam exteriorum partium dispositionem obtinet, aliamque superficiei terminationem: ita etiam motus & quies corporibus aliquam variationem conferunt; quippe motus alium respectum & dispositionem corpori moto ad corpora circumstantia confert, quam quies. adeo ut motus & quies] ad modum enim duo requiruntur, 1. ut insit ei, cujus est modus. 2. ut illud variet, & alio modo se habere faciat; quæ duo motui & quieti competere hactenus ostensum.
units.tr: CCLXXVII. Reply: 1. What Descartes is aiming at, when he teaches that often some effort on our part is needed to stop the motion of external bodies, is quite clear from art. 274. For a single instance was enough to break the minor premise. He did not wish, nor was he obliged, to prove that our effort is always needed to stop bodies and keep them at rest; indeed he knew well enough that this is false. Nor does he here intend to demonstrate that the same amount of action is needed for rest as for motion, which is his thesis. He was content to overturn the antithesis held by men preoccupied with prejudices. He confirms his own thesis in Parts III and IV, where it becomes clear from various examples of motion and rest that as much action is required for rest as for bringing about motion. So what is objected about Descartes' silliness vanishes entirely. 2. How the example of the ship serves Descartes has been shown above. It has also been shown that the little word SUDDENLY was not inserted cunningly or fraudulently, but was necessarily required for the author's purpose. For our action could only bring the ship to rest if it happened suddenly, so that it would not be helped by other causes. Descartes himself shows that this can scarcely be avoided, when he says that the weight and sluggishness of the water lifted by the ship must be removed, since otherwise the ship could be stopped only gradually. Yet I would not think that the opponent escapes reason and has deceived the sense of sight itself, unless (to put it very mildly) by not attending closely enough he has dispelled it from his own mind. CCLXXVIII. Descartes goes on to develop and explain his definition further. In art. 27 he says: But since here we are not concerned with that action which is understood to be in the mover, or in the one who stops the motion, but only with translation and the absence of translation, that is, with rest, it is manifest that this translation cannot exist outside the moved body, and that this body is in one condition when it is translated, and in another when it is not translated, or when it is at rest; so that motion and rest are in it nothing other than different modes. The sense of these words is this. Since here we are not concerned: he had defined motion by translation precisely so as to show that action does not belong to its formal nature, as we have shown more fully. with that action which is understood to be in the mover: but someone may object that action is not in the agent but from it, and insofar as it terminates in the thing affected it is called passion. Reply: action can be said to be from the agent and in the agent, with a different respect, as is clear from immanent actions. It is easily understood that there is some action in the mover: for if you move a stone, is there not action in you, the vibration of the arm, the extension of the muscles, the influx of the animal spirits, and similar things? it is manifest: that action which is in the mover can exist outside the moved body, and it is in the throwing of the stone; but translation itself cannot, since it is a mode of the moved body, not of the mover. and that this body is in another condition: for just as a variation of shapes alters the body in which they inhere, so that wax, for example, is in one state when it is square and in another when it is round, since it takes on a different disposition of its outer parts and a different termination of its surface, so too motion and rest bring some variation to bodies. Motion gives the moved body a different relation and disposition to the surrounding bodies than rest does. so that motion and rest: for a mode requires two things: 1. that it inhere in that of which it is a mode; 2. that it vary the thing and make it be in another condition. Both of these have so far been shown to belong to motion and rest.

units.la: CCLXXIX. Art. 22. declarat Cartesius quare dixerit, translationem fieri ex vicinia corporum immediatè contiguorum in vicinia aliorum, non verò, translationem fieri ex uno loco in alium, quia (inquit) ut supra explicui, art 14. & 15. loci acceptio varia est ac pendet a nostra cogitatione: sed cùm per motum intelligimus eam translationem, quæ fit ex vicinia corporum contiguorum, quoniam una tantùm corpora eodem temporis momento ejusdem mobilis contigua esse possunt, non possumus ipsi mobili plures motus eodem tempore tribuere, sed unum tantùm. Quæ verba sic explico. Quia loci acceptio varia est) aliquando enim designat spatium, quod sibi corpus quodlibet suâ magnitudine determinat, & vocatur locus internus; aliquando verò situm certum inter alia corpora, appellaturque locus externus. Ut ita dicatur corpus in alterius locum succedere, dummodò eundem situm inter corpora circumjacentia obtineat, quem prius, in cujus locum dicitur successisse: sed non dicitur corpus idem spatium occupare cum altero, nisi sit ejusdem magnitudinis. Hinc apparet, definitiones Augustini & Keplerii, quas 260. & 261. articulo adduxinus. ximus, veras quidem esse, sed, quia per vocem ambiguam loci fuerunt formatae, minus esse claras hac definitione Philosophi. Quoniam una tantum corpora, id est, à qualibet superficiei totius parte circumcirca, non nisi unum tantum corpus potest esse contiguum, ab hac parte hoc, ab alia parte aliud. Dicit autem una corpora non unum, quia plura sunt, quae rem illam quae movetur contingunt. Impossibile enim est, ut motus fiat, nisi in circulum, si uno continuo corpore res contineatur. Non possumus isti mobili plures motus] quia eodem tempore non potest, nisi à proxime circumjacentibus corporibus recedere, quae illud immediate contingunt.
units.tr: CCLXXIX. In art. 22 Descartes explains why he said that translation takes place from the vicinity of bodies immediately contiguous to it into the vicinity of others, and not that translation takes place from one place into another. Because (he says), as I explained above in art. 14 and 15, the meaning of place is varied and depends on our thinking. But when by motion we understand that translation which takes place from the vicinity of contiguous bodies, since only one body can be contiguous to the same mobile at the same moment of time, we cannot attribute several motions to the mobile at the same time, but only one. I explain these words thus. Because the meaning of place is varied: sometimes it denotes the space which any body determines for itself by its own magnitude, and this is called internal place; at other times it denotes a fixed situation among other bodies, and this is called external place. So a body is said to succeed into the place of another if it holds the same situation among the surrounding bodies that the earlier one held, into whose place it is said to have succeeded; but a body is not said to occupy the same space as another unless it is of the same magnitude. From this it is clear that the definitions of Augustine and Kepler, which we cited in articles 260 and 261, are indeed true, but since they were framed with the ambiguous word place, they are less clear than this definition of the philosopher. Since only one body: that is, from any part of the whole surface all around, only one body can be contiguous; this body on one side, another on the other side. He says one body rather than one, because there are several bodies that touch the thing that is moved. For motion can only be made in a circle if the thing is enclosed by one continuous body. we cannot attribute several motions to the mobile: because at the same time it cannot recede except from the nearest surrounding bodies, which touch it immediately.

units.la: CCLXXX. Porrò ostendit Cartesius art. 29. quare dixerit, translationem illam fieri ex vicinia, non quorumlibet corporum contiguorum, sed eorum duntaxat, quae tanquam quiescentia spectantur. Ipsa enim, inquit, translatio est reciproca, nec potest intelligi corpus A B transferri ex vicinia corporis C D, quin simul etiam intelligatur corpus C D transferri ex vicinia corporis A B: Ac plane eadem vis & actio requiritur ex una parte atque ex altera. Quapropter, si omnino propriam, & non ad aliud relatam naturam motui tribuere vellemus, cum duo corpora contigua, unum in unam, aliud in aliam partem transferuntur, sicque à se mutuo separantur, tantundem motus in uno quam in altero esse diceremus. Sed hoc à communi loquendi usu nimium abhorreret, cum enim consueti simus stare in terra, eamque ut quiescentem considerare, quamvis aliquas ejus partes aliis minoribus corporibus contiguas, ab eorum vicinia transferri videamus, non tamen ipsam idcirco moveri putamus. Haec verba ita explicanda. Ipsa enim translatio est reciproca] scilicet in rei veritate, secundum illas superficies, secundum quas fit translatio. Supponitur autem in exemplo à Cartesio allato 1. quod fit immediata contiguitas duorum corporum A B & C D, 2. quod illa corpora sint aequalia, 3. habeant superficies congruentes, & 4. libera sint ab omnibus aliis & à nullis corporibus impedita. Illam autem translationem esse reciprocam, etiam colligi potest ex motibus apparentibus Planetarum, quos Astronomi solent vocare veros, quia retrocessisse intelliguntur à vicinia corporum immediate contiguorum. Ac plane eadem vis] non quidem terminatur ista vis & actio ad utrumque corpus, sed ad quodcunque terminetur, cum supponantur esse aequalia, non requiritur major vis, quae terminetur ad corpus A D, quam quae terminetur ad corpus C D, & ad quodcunque corpus ex his duobus actio terminetur, semper erit eadem translatio. Et non ad aliud relatam] nempe, si plane non attendamus ad actionem actionem vel vim moventem, sed meram translationem spectemus, illamque solam pro motu accipiamus & habeamus, uti haberi debet, ut patet ex antecedentibus, manifestum erit, tantum esse translationis in uno corpore, quantum in altero, si duo corpora a se mutuo transferantur, adeoque etiam tantundem motus in utroque. Sed hoc a communi usu loquendi ] hic usus loquendi multum obest indagationi veritatis, & causa est errorum multorum, uti a Philosopho ostenditur Pp.I.art.74. Cum enim vulgus invenerit voces, qui non habuit veram cognitionem rerum, sed praejudiciis infantiae obscuratam, voces ad infantiae praejudicia accommodavit. Hinc est, quod Comenius in Via Lucis optat dari aliquam Linguam Universalem, quae sit rebus accommodata, earumque naturam commodè exprimat, quia enim dum rebus nomina non per rerum naturam imposita sunt, neque sermonis usu rerum deteguntur fundamenta & harmonia mutua fit, ut quoties de rebus controversia incidit, ultro citroque contendentes, nihil nisi verba verbis immisceant, verba sunt Comenii. Saltem quia vix sperandum, ut talis eruditorum consensus sit futurus ad hujusmodi linguae constitutionem, rebus ita stantibus & hominibus variè distractis, nisi specialis gratia Dei accedat, loquendum est cum vulgo, sed sentiendum cum eruditis. Quia itaque, ut ad rem redeamus, non consuevit vulgus tàm accuratè loqui de motu, ut assignet eum unicuique corpori, quod transfertur è vicinia corporis contigui, sive actio moventis ad illud terminetur, sive non, Philosophus illum modum loquendi hic vult sequi, ut ei tantùm corpori motum tribuat, ad quod actio moventis terminatur. Eamque ut quiescentem considerare] quia nos sumus Terrae conjuncti, quamvis deferatur, ut in sequentibus ostendetur, eam solemus respectu nostrae super eâ ambulationis ut quiescentem spectare, quemadmodum is, qui cum navi circumfertur, respectu suae ambulationis in illâ, eam ut quiescentem considerat.
units.tr: CCLXXX. Further, in art. 29 Descartes shows why he said that this translation takes place from the vicinity not of any contiguous bodies whatever, but only of those that are regarded as at rest. For translation itself, he says, is reciprocal, and it cannot be understood that the body AB is transferred from the vicinity of the body CD without it also being understood at the same time that the body CD is transferred from the vicinity of the body AB. Exactly the same force and action is required on the one side as on the other. Therefore, if we wished to assign motion a nature wholly its own, and not one related to something else, then when two contiguous bodies are carried, one into one part and the other into another, and so separate from each other, we would say that there is just as much motion in one as in the other. But this would be too far removed from common usage of speech. For since we are accustomed to stand on the earth and regard it as at rest, although we see some of its parts carried away from the vicinity of smaller bodies contiguous to them, we do not on that account think that the earth itself is moved. These words must be explained thus. For translation itself is reciprocal: that is, in the truth of the matter, according to those surfaces by which the translation takes place. In the example brought forward by Descartes it is supposed: 1. that there is immediate contiguity of two bodies AB and CD; 2. that these bodies are equal; 3. that they have congruent surfaces; and 4. that they are free from all others and not hindered by any bodies. That this translation is reciprocal can also be gathered from the apparent motions of the planets, which astronomers are accustomed to call true, because they are understood to have receded from the vicinity of bodies immediately contiguous to them. Exactly the same force: this force and action is indeed not terminated in each body separately, but wherever it is terminated; since the bodies are supposed to be equal, no greater force is required to be terminated on the body AD than the force terminated on the body CD, and whichever of these two bodies the action is terminated on, the translation will always be the same. and not one related to something else: that is, if we do not attend at all to the action or moving force, but look only at the bare translation, and take that alone as motion, as it ought to be taken, as is clear from what precedes, it will be manifest that there is just as much translation in one body as in the other, if two bodies are carried away from each other, and therefore just as much motion in each. But this would be too far removed from common usage of speech: this usage of speech greatly hinders the search for truth and is the cause of many errors, as the philosopher shows in Part I, art. 74. For the common people, who did not have true knowledge of things but were clouded by the prejudices of infancy, invented words and adapted them to the prejudices of infancy. Hence Comenius, in his Via Lucis, wishes that some universal language might be given, fitted to things and expressing their nature suitably; for while names are imposed on things not according to their nature, and the foundations of things are not uncovered by the use of speech, and no mutual harmony arises, whenever a controversy about things arises, the disputants on either side mix nothing but words with words; these are Comenius' words. At least, since such a consensus of learned men for the construction of a language of this kind is scarcely to be hoped for, with things as they are and men variously divided, unless a special grace of God intervenes, we must speak with the common people but think with the learned. Therefore, to return to the matter, since the common people are not accustomed to speak so accurately about motion as to assign it to each body that is carried away from the vicinity of a contiguous body, whether the action of the mover is terminated on it or not, the philosopher wishes to follow that manner of speaking here, so that he attributes motion only to that body on which the action of the mover is terminated. and to regard it as at rest: because we are joined to the earth, although it is carried along, as will be shown in what follows, we are accustomed, with respect to our walking upon it, to regard it as at rest, just as a man who is carried along with a ship regards it as at rest with respect to his walking in it.

units.la: CCLXXXI. Tandem Philosophus art. 30. rationem reddit, quare hoc in negotio modus loquendi vulgaris sit retinendus.
units.tr: 281. At last the Philosopher, in article 30, gives the reason why the common way of speaking should be kept in this matter.

units.la: Hujusque rei, ait, praecipua ratio est, quod motus intelligatur esse totius corporis quod movetur, nec posset ita intelligi totius Terrae ob translationem quarundam ejus partium, ex vicinia minorum corporum, quibus contigua sunt; quoniam saepe plures ejusmodi translationes sibi mutuo contrarias, in ipsâ licet advertere, esse totius corporis, quod movetur,] id est, secundum omnem superficiem circumcirca e vicinia omnium corporum immediatè contiguorum. Terra verò ex eo solo, quod quaedam ejus partes concipiantur translatae esse è vicinia corporum immediatè contiguorum in viciniam aliorum, quia interim aliae partes propterea non transferuntur, sed vicinitatem suam retinent cum aliis corporibus, non dicetur moveri. Sibi mutuo contrarias:] Sic enim diceretur uno eodemque momento transferri respectu horum corporum in ortum, respectu aliorum in occasum, quod si iterum ad alia atque alia relationem instituas, moveri etiam diceres & ad meridiem & ad septentrionem.
units.tr: "The chief reason for this," he says, "is that motion is understood to belong to the whole body which is moved; and the whole Earth could not be understood to be moved on account of the transfer of certain of its parts out of the neighbourhood of the smaller bodies to which they are contiguous; since very often one may notice in the same body several such transfers which are mutually contrary, yet they belong to the whole body which is moved," that is, according to its whole surface round about, out of the neighbourhood of all the bodies immediately contiguous to it. But the Earth is not said to move merely because certain of its parts are conceived to have been carried from the neighbourhood of bodies immediately contiguous into the neighbourhood of others, while other parts, for that reason, are not transferred but keep their nearness to other bodies. "Mutually contrary": for it would be said that at one and the same moment a part is transferred towards the east with respect to some of these bodies and towards the west with respect to others; and if you were to set up a relation to other and different things again, you would say that it moves both to the south and to the north.

units.la: CCLXXXI. Atque ita, quid Motus proprie loquendo sit, didicimus. Sed solet aliquando Motus vocabulum latius usurpari. Unde nata est distinctio Motus in Communem & Proprium. Proprius est is, de quo egimus, quando nempe corpus aliquod transfertur e vicinia corporum immediate contiguorum. Communis vero est, cum corpus tanquam pars alterius vel alteri conjunctum una cum illo circumfertur, etiamsi illud proprie non moveatur, nec recedat a corporibus immediate contiguis, atque propterea revera quiescat, qui motus Delatio vocatur. Talis motus est Nautae in navi, aut potius hominum in interiori navis sedentium, qui a navi dicuntur deferri. Hactenus ergo terminos quaestionum propositarum consideravimus, prolixius de Motu agentes, partim, quod ejus natura vulgo non ita nota, partim, quia dum sequimur Cartesii Motus explicationem necesse fuit, ut omne quod obscuritatem aliquam continere videretur, & objectionibus vel fuerit impetitum, vel saltem impeti potuerit, elucidaremus.
units.tr: 281. So, having learned what motion properly speaking is, we have also seen that the word motion is sometimes used more broadly. Hence the distinction of motion into common and proper. Proper motion is the kind we have been discussing, namely when some body is carried out of the neighbourhood of bodies immediately contiguous to it. Common motion, however, is when a body, as a part of another or joined to another, is carried along together with it, even though it is not properly moved and does not withdraw from the bodies immediately contiguous to it, and so in truth is at rest; this motion is called carriage (delatio). Such is the motion of the sailor in the ship, or rather of men sitting in the inside of the ship, who are said to be carried along by the ship. Thus far we have considered the terms of the questions proposed, treating of motion at some length, partly because its nature is not commonly so well known, and partly because, while following Descartes' explanation of motion, it was necessary to clarify whatever seemed to contain some obscurity, and either had been or at least could have been assailed by objections.

units.la: CAPUT XVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVIII.

units.la: Demonstratur duobus argumentis, Terram deferri circa Solem annua delatione, & circa axem suum diurna.
units.tr: It is demonstrated by two arguments that the Earth is carried round the Sun by an annual carrying, and round its own axis by a daily one.

units.la: CCLXXXIII. Terminis ita explicatis, nunc ad determinationem quaestionum Cap. xvi, art. 249. propositarum accedimus. Atque pro diversa acceptione subjecti & praedicati, dicimus. 1. Si Terra accipiatur stricte, prout cum aqua unum globum constituit, & distinguitur ab aere & aliis corporibus, ei nullum motum proprie acceptum tribuendum, sicque eam motu proprio moveri negamus. 2. Sed non negamus, motum ei sic acceptae tribui posse communem sive Delationem, quae non nisi improprie motus vocari potest: imo asserimus, eam sic una cum Luna a materia coelesti ambiente deferri circa Solem delatione annua, itidemque singulis diebus circa axem suum convolvi. 3. Quod si vero Terra accipiatur latè pro complexu omnium corporum, usque ad Lunam, neque sic eam proprie moveri asserimus, quia materia, quæ illam defert, tum delatione annuâ, tum diurnâ, nunquam tota simul ab illâ recedit.
units.tr: CCLXXXIII. With the terms thus explained, we now come to determining the questions proposed in Chapter XVI, art. 249. Depending on the different senses of subject and predicate, we say: (1) If the Earth is taken strictly, as it forms one globe together with the water and is distinguished from the air and other bodies, then no motion properly so called is to be attributed to it, and so we deny that it moves by its own motion. (2) But we do not deny that a common motion, or carrying (delatio), which can only improperly be called motion, can be attributed to it so taken. Indeed we assert that it is thus carried, together with the Moon, by the surrounding heavenly matter round the Sun by an annual carrying, and likewise turns round its own axis every day. (3) But if the Earth is taken broadly, for the whole complex of bodies up to the Moon, we do not assert that it moves properly even in this sense, because the matter which carries it, both by the annual and by the daily carrying, never withdraws from it all at once.

units.la: CCLXXXIV. His ita constitutis patet, à Cartesio & nobis, qui hîc eum præeuntem sequimur, multò minus motus terræ tribui, quam vel Tycho, vel Ptolemæus assignaverit, quos inter se quoad motum diurnum convenire superius vidimus. Illi enim aërem vicinum unà cum Cœlo à Terrâ separari statuerunt, vel saltem Cœlum ab aëre subjacente. Cùm autem omnis translatio sit reciproca, ut præcedenti capite est demonstratum, tantum motus Terræ vel ab aëre vicino separatæ, vel unà cum aëre ambiente à proximo Cœlo revulsæ tribuerunt, atque ipsi Cœlo. At Cartesius Terram à materiâ cœlesti ambiente totâ simul nunquam recedere statuit. Ergo multo minùs ei motûs assignat, quàm Tycho aut Ptolemæus. Quod si igitur L. p. 304. naturam veri motus & propriè sic dicti ejusque differentiam à motu communi, hoc est, delatione, mente perspicaci considerasset, nullam in verbis Cartesii contradictionem esse videre potuisset, neque sequentibus verbis Cartesium arguere conatus fuisset. Quomodo, inquit, omnem motum terra detracturus es, & nihilominus eam pro stellâ erranti habebis? Tecum igitur te committo, à te ipso pugnâ plusquam Cadmæâ consumendum. Tirones tamen monitos hic velim, non ex animi sententia motum Terræ ab eo detrahi, nec nudam hic hypothesin fovet, repugnant aperta in contrarium assertiones, repugnat assectarum ejus explicatio.
units.tr: CCLXXXIV. With these things so established, it is clear that Descartes and we, who follow him here as our guide, assign far less motion to the Earth than either Tycho or Ptolemy did, whom we saw above to agree with each other about the daily motion. For they held that the neighbouring air, together with the Heaven, is separated from the Earth, or at least that the Heaven is separated from the air beneath it. But since every translation is reciprocal, as was demonstrated in the preceding chapter, they attributed to the Earth only the motion of being separated from the neighbouring air, or torn away from the nearest Heaven together with the surrounding air, and likewise attributed motion to the Heaven itself. But Descartes holds that the Earth never withdraws all at once from the surrounding heavenly matter. Therefore he assigns it much less motion than Tycho or Ptolemy does. If, then, he had considered with a penetrating mind the nature of true motion, properly so called, and its difference from common motion, that is, carrying, he could have seen no contradiction in Descartes's words, nor would he have tried to refute Descartes with the following words. How, he says, will you strip the Earth of all motion and yet still have it as a wandering star? I therefore leave you to yourself, to be consumed by your own struggle, more than Cadmean. Yet I would like to warn novices here that it is not from his real opinion that Descartes takes motion away from the Earth, nor does he here merely cherish a bare hypothesis; open assertions to the contrary oppose it, and the explanation given by his followers opposes it. L. p. 304.

units.la: Resp. Revera motum Terræ non competere satis, ut puto, patebit Lectoribus ex dictis hoc & præcedenti capite: inde autem nihilominus delationem posse ei tribui etiam conspicuum esse puto, & revera tribuendam in sequentibus demonstrabimus.
units.tr: Reply. That the Earth does not have motion in the full sense, as I think, will be clear to the readers from what has been said in this and the preceding chapter. That carrying can nevertheless be attributed to it, I also think is evident, and indeed we will demonstrate in what follows that it must be attributed.

units.la: CCLXXXV. Ut ergo id aggrediamur, quid nobis incumbat prosequendum, consideremus; nimirum, 1. Terram deferri circa Solem à materiâ cœlesti ambiente delatione annuâ. 2. Eandemque unoquoque <bl>ϰυχηµέρω</bl> converti circa suum axem. Ad hoc præstandum non utar argumentis à Circulorum, Orbium, Epicyclorum per Copernici systema ejectione & faciliori explicatione Astronomicâ motûs corporum cœlestium desumtis. Quamvis enim hæc Circulorum multitudo confundat intellectum, & simplicius semper sit præferendum compositio, tamen non necesse est, ut fiat per talem systematis mutationem, sed præstari potest per plurium Circulorum ad pauciores reductionem, uti hoc
units.tr: CCLXXXV. So that we may take this up, let us consider what remains for us to pursue; namely, (1) that the Earth is carried round the Sun by the surrounding heavenly matter by an annual carrying; (2) and that the same turns about its own axis each day [καθ' ἡμέραν]. To accomplish this I will not use arguments drawn from the removal of circles, orbs and epicycles through the Copernican system, or from the easier astronomical explanation of the motions of the heavenly bodies. For although this multitude of circles confuses the intellect, and the simpler is always to be preferred to the composite, yet it is not necessary that this be done by such a change of system; it can be accomplished by reducing the many circles to fewer, as

units.la: egregiè est præstitum à Clarissimo Deusingio in suo tractatu de vero systemate mundi, quo magnam lucem tum Copernicano, tum etiam Tychoniano systemati intulit. Neque adhibebo argumenta, à proportione & harmoniâ detumpta, quia harmoniæ non sunt in rebus præsupponen-dæ, ut ex illarum hypothesi aliquid concludas, sed tum demum, cùm in rebus fuerint inventæ, agnoscendæ & admirandæ.
units.tr: this has been excellently done by the most distinguished Deusing in his treatise on the true system of the world, by which he has shed great light on both the Copernican and the Tychonian systems. Nor will I employ arguments drawn from proportion and harmony, because harmonies are not to be presupposed in things so that you may conclude something from their hypothesis; they are to be recognised and admired only when they have been found in things.

units.la: CCLXXXVI. Ad ultum censum argumentorum imbecillium etiam refero defumtum argumentum à nimiâ celeritate primi mobilis, quod tamen tantum non pro Achilleo à Copernicanis haberi solet.
units.tr: CCLXXXVI. I also count among the feeble arguments the one drawn from the excessive speed of the primum mobile, which the Copernicans are nevertheless accustomed to treat almost as their Achilles' heel.

units.la: Raptus firmamenti, quem statuunt Ptolemaici & Tychoniani, fieri debet secundum Tychonianam computationem, ut stella fixa motu horario absolvat milliaria circiter 3153333, &, uno scrupulo secundo, sive temporis momento milliaria 26277. Sed tam celerem motum dicunt esse mente imperceptibilem, adeoque impossibilem. Sed mihi videtur istud argumentum esse ejusdem commanatis, cujus est Tychonianorum contra Copernicum à nimiâ altitudine stellarum Fixarum, & nimiâ magnitudine Cœli desumtum, quâ fiat, ut Orbis magnus, in quo Terra defertur, debeat habere ad Cœlum rationem puncti insensibilis, de quo argumento suo loco videbimus.
