units.tr: The rapture of the firmament, which the Ptolemaics and Tychonians posit, must, according to the Tychonian computation, be such that a fixed star completes about 3,153,333 miles in an hour, and 26,277 miles in one second of time, or moment. But they say such swift motion is imperceptible to the mind and therefore impossible. But to me this argument seems to belong to the same class as the Tychonians' argument against Copernicus, drawn from the excessive altitude of the fixed stars and the excessive magnitude of the Heaven, by which it follows that the great orb in which the Earth is carried must bear to the Heaven the ratio of an insensible point. We will see that argument in its proper place.

units.la: Quanquam enim nequeamus distinctè in particulari percipere tantam celeritatem motus, nec imaginatione comprehendere, possumus tamen in genere facilè intelligere, quod motus velocitas possit augeri in infinitum, ita ut adhuc infinities velocior pōt ssit cogitari & dari. Est enim eadem ipsius ratio, quæ magnitudinis, quæ in infinitum augeri potest. Quod si supponamus, Terram cum Firmamento esse unum aliquod continuum corpus, eamque ponamus ita moveri à Deo, ut 24 horis circumvolutionem suam absolveret, rapiet secum eodem tempore convexam Firmamenti, cujuscunque eam amplitudinis supponamus, ut punctum aliquod in eâ, scrupulo secundo possit absolvere milliaria 26277. imò multò plura, prout amplitudinem sphæræ istius supposuerimus majorem. Vel finge rotam extensam usque ad stellas fixas, vel ulterius etiam, eamque moveri suppone, debebunt necessariò eodem tempore, quo partes axi proximæ circuitum suum absolvunt, id etiam præstare remotæ. Pone ergo partes axi proximas horarum 24 spatio circumvolvi. Ergo partes remotissimæ eodem tempore circuitum suum absolvent; adeoque conficient singulis scrupulis secundis milliaria 26277, vel etiam plura, siquidem amplitudinem rotæ majorem supposueris. Quandoquidem ergo illa celeritas Motus in corporibus continuis non est intellectu imperceptibilis, constitue nunc, post impetum impressum, separari vel Firmamentum à Terrâ, vel partem rotæ proximam axi à remotissimâ, eadem utique celeritas poterit permanere.
units.tr: Although we cannot distinctly perceive in particular so great a speed of motion, nor grasp it by imagination, we can nevertheless easily understand in general that the velocity of motion can be increased to infinity, so that something still infinitely faster can be conceived and exist. For its reason is the same as that of magnitude, which can be increased to infinity. If we suppose that the Earth together with the Firmament is one continuous body, and suppose it so moved by God that it completes its revolution in 24 hours, it would carry with it at the same time the convex surface of the Firmament, of whatever size we suppose it to be, so that some point on it could complete 26,277 miles in a second, indeed far more, according as we suppose the size of that sphere to be greater. Or imagine a wheel extended as far as the fixed stars, or even further, and suppose it moved; necessarily, in the same time in which the parts near the axis complete their circuit, the most remote parts must also accomplish theirs. Suppose, then, that the parts near the axis turn round in a space of 24 hours. Therefore the most remote parts will complete their circuit in the same time, and so they will cover 26,277 miles every second, or even more, if you suppose the wheel to be larger. Since, therefore, that speed of motion in continuous bodies is not imperceptible to the understanding, suppose now, after the impetus has been impressed, that either the Firmament is separated from the Earth, or the part of the wheel nearest the axis from the most remote part; the same speed can certainly remain.

units.la: CCLXXXVII. Sed ad obtinendum institutum utar mox §. 291. argumento demonstrativo & evidentissimo, ex nostro Philosopho desumto, illudque tantâ, quantâ potero, brevitate methodo Mathematicâ synthetica per propositiones distinctas proponam. Lectores tamen rogatos volo, ut ipsum Philosophum adeant, & imprimis Princip. partem III. diligenter & attentè pervolvant, ubi accuratè, & Methodo analyticâ demonstrata reperient omnia ea, quæ hic breviter à me proponentur.
units.tr: CCLXXXVII. But to achieve my purpose I will presently use, at §. 291, a demonstrative and most evident argument drawn from our Philosopher, and I will set it out as briefly as I can, in the synthetic mathematical method, through distinct propositions. Yet I wish readers to consult the Philosopher himself, and especially to read through diligently Part III of the Principles, where they will find accurately, and demonstrated by the analytic method, all those things which are briefly proposed here by me.

units.la: CCLXXXVIII. Exc. 1. B. p. 213. 214. me in hisce Propositionibus variis modis peccare in Methodum Mathematicam, 1. quia nullas ponam notiones communes sive axiomata. 2. quia post propositiones subjungam hypotheses, easque probem. 3. quia de eorum veritate dubitem.
units.tr: CCLXXXVIII. Exc. 1. B. p. 213. 214. The objection is that in these propositions I sin in various ways against the mathematical method: 1. because I put down no common notions or axioms; 2. because after the propositions I add hypotheses and prove them; 3. because I doubt their truth.

units.la: Resp. Si voluissem absolutam & plenam instituere probationem materiæ propositæ, potuisset forte ista accusatio aliquam justam habere rationem, sed cùm expresse artic. præcedenti, ut & in fine hujus capitis lectorem ablegem ad Cartesii Principia, dicamque, quod in ea hic tantum digitum intendam, locum ea non invenit. Definitiones ergo omisi brevitatis causâ, quia in ipsis demonstrationibus, si quis terminus obscurus occurrat, explicatus est. Atque notionum communium sive axiomatum eadem est ratio, quæ cùm ex terminis sint manifesta, brevitati studens non lubuit separatim præmittere. 2. Mathematici novum librum inchoantes præmittunt, si necessarium videatur, definitiones, communes notiones & Postulata; & ego ante Propos. XIII. à quâ novus liber potuisset inchoari, præmisi sola Postulata, quæ Hypotheses vocavi, easque non tam probavi quàm declaravi, eo modo quo & Clavius libro 1. Euclidis circa 4. Postulata fecit. 3. Postulata omnia verè poni non est necesse: sufficit enim ostendere, quid eo suppositio consequatur, prout apparet ex Postulato Archimedis, Detur punctum extra terram, & terram movebo. Omnes ergo hic ab adversario adductæ difficultates in fumum abeunt. 4. quod si has hypotheses nomine Postulatorum censere nolis, age sint hypotheses, similes iis, quales in Astronomiâ assumuntur ad salvanda phænomena, propter quarum usum in physicis mihi non magis succensere potes, quàm Astronomis propter usurpatas similes Hypotheses in Astronomiâ.
units.tr: Reply. If I had wanted to set up a complete and full proof of the matter proposed, perhaps that accusation could have some just ground; but since I expressly refer the reader, in the preceding article and again at the end of this chapter, to Descartes's Principles, and say that I intend here only to point to them, the charge does not apply. I therefore omitted definitions for the sake of brevity, because in the demonstrations themselves, if any obscure term occurs, it is explained. The same reasoning holds for common notions or axioms: since they are manifest from their terms, I did not choose, aiming at brevity, to premise them separately. 2. Mathematicians beginning a new book premise, if it seems necessary, definitions, common notions and postulates; and before Prop. XIII, with which a new book could have begun, I premised only the postulates, which I called hypotheses, and these I did not so much prove as declare, in the way Clavius also did around the four postulates of his book 1 of Euclid. 3. It is not necessary that all postulates be truly laid down: it suffices to show what follows from the supposition, as appears from Archimedes' postulate, Let a point be given outside the earth, and I will move the earth. So all the difficulties the adversary has brought forward here go up in smoke. 4. But if you are unwilling to count these hypotheses under the name of postulates, grant that they are hypotheses like those assumed in astronomy to save the phenomena; on account of whose use in physics you can no more be angry with me than with the astronomers for the similar hypotheses they use.

units.la: CCLXXXIX. Exc. 2. B. p. 214. Methodus Mathematica non necesse habet emendicare praejudiciorum depositionem, sed Propositiones Lectores cogunt in assensum, ita ut nullam hactenus passe sint contradictionem: at ex tuis propositionibus ut priores nituntur principio salsissimo, ita & varia sunt, quae cum praecedentibus non habent necessariam connexionem, &, si forsan haec tua probationes non sufficientes comperiantur, vis Lectores rogatos ut ipsum Philosophum adeant.
units.tr: CCLXXXIX. Exc. 2. B. p. 214. The mathematical method does not need to beg for the laying aside of prejudices. Its propositions compel readers to assent, so that they have so far been unable to suffer any contradiction. But in your propositions, just as the earlier ones rest on a most false principle, so there are also various ones which have no necessary connection with what precedes. And if perhaps these proofs of yours are found insufficient, you bid readers to go to the Philosopher himself.

units.la: Resp. Cum mea demonstratio non fit nisi brevis & summaria, non mirum quod Lectores ablegem ad Cartesium, quoniam nolui integram ipsius Physicam describere. 2. agitur hic de rebus Physicis, de quibus varia praejudicia homines hauserunt; ergo hic opus est postulare ut ea deponant, ne impediantur in percipienda veritate, secus se res habet in Geometricis, quas ut quis percipiat nulla praejudicia impediunt. 3. Mathematicae demonstrationes nullam passae sunt contradictionem, nisi a non intelligentibus; exemplo sit Peletarius contra Clavium, vide Clav. Eucl. lib. 3. prop. 16. quo tamen Mathematicae esse non desinunt. Ita etiamsi antagonistae & similes non possint percipere istas demonstrationes, non tamen propterea certae esse desinunt. 4. quod de Principiis falsis & de quarundam Propositionum inutilitate dicit, in seqq. examinabimus.
units.tr: Reply. Since my demonstration is only brief and summary, it is no wonder that I send readers to Descartes, since I did not wish to describe his whole Physics. Second, we are dealing here with physical matters, about which people have drunk in various prejudices. Therefore here it is necessary to demand that they lay these aside, lest they be hindered from perceiving the truth. It is otherwise in geometrical matters, which no prejudices hinder anyone from perceiving. Third, mathematical demonstrations have suffered no contradiction except from those who do not understand them. Let Peletarius against Clavius serve as an example; see Clavius on Euclid, book 3, prop. 16. Yet mathematics does not cease to be mathematics because of this. So even if opponents and such people cannot perceive these demonstrations, they nonetheless do not cease to be certain. Fourth, what he says about false principles and the uselessness of certain propositions we shall examine in what follows.

units.la: CCXC. Sed quoniam idem ille homo etiam p. 211. graviter invehitur in postulatum meum aequissimum, ut praejudicia deponantur, placet uberius de eo cum ipso agere. Inquit: Meum esse vi argumentorum adversarium a praejudiciis liberare, vel ita confutare, ut non habeat, quod ratione reponat; & interjectis sarcasmis, quos facile potuissem in ipsum retorquere, satis acerbe & contra gravitatem Ecclesiasticam quaerit, quaenam sint deponenda praejudicia? Anne, inquit, quod credimus Solem moveri? Anne S. Scripturam ubique veracem esse? Anne Deum esse? additque, se haec praejudicia numquam depositurum, 1. Quodcunque nobis dictat scriptura verum esse, 2. In expositione textus sacri a proprio verborum sensu sine cogente ratione non esse recedendum. Ad quae respondeo 1. apparere hinc candorem Theologicum & charitatem, qua isti homines feruntur in eos, qui ab ipsorum opinionibus quantumcunque recedunt, quorum sententias iniquissime pervertunt, ut pe tulanter iis insultent. Ad se si rediisset adversarius, scire poterat, illa omnia esse praejudicia, quae judicavimus re non satis examinata & perspecta, in quibus judicium contra naturae ordinem perceptionem antecedit, quorum varia hinc & inde sunt indicata, plura a Cartesio Princip. I. art. 71.–75. & a Claubergio in Defensione Cartesianâ sunt collecta. Ea omnia deponenda sunt ei, qui veritatem cognoscere cupit, quod nisi faciat, frustra contra ipsum rationibus egeris. Hoccine vero iniquum putabimus postulatum, ut homo ad aliquam rem examinandam accedens mentem non præoccupatam afferat. Cùm tamen tùm communiter omnes id à veritatis studiosò exigant, tùm in specie nostri Theologi in Pontificiis desiderent. Videsis Ludovicum Crocium de Ecclesiæ Pontificiæ Præjudiciis & præsertim Dissertationem primam. 2. Hoc verò imprimis necessarium est circa res naturales, circa quas ab infantiâ versati, neque satis eas per ætatem examinantes, varia præjudicia hausimus, quæ postea tenacissimè retinentur, nec nisi magno adhibito labore deponi queunt. At non requiritur circa res puras Matheseos, circa quas homines non solent versari, antequam ad usum rationis pervenerint. Verbi gratiâ, persuasus sis ab ineunte ætate, Terram stare & Solem circa eam quotidie convolvi, putesque etiam id testari Scripturam in locis mox examinandis, æquum tamen est, ut si quid veri falsive in tuâ sententiâ sit inquirere velis, de ea, donec evidenter cognoveris veritatem falsitatemve, quidque de ea re Scriptura doceat, judicium suspendas. Æruginem verò suam adversarius prodit, cùm quærit, num velim tanquam Præjudicia deponi, Scripturam ubique veracem esse & Deum existere, cùm me de illâ Scripturæ Veracitate nullatenus dubitare ex meis Dissertationibus satis potuerit cognoscere, in iisque adduxerim rationes, ob quas loca objecta ita interpreter, ut meæ sententiæ nihil quicquam adversentur. De Dei verò existentia nequaquam Cartesium dubitasse, quo sensu id ipsis tribuunt adversarii, clarissimè ostendit Dn. Claubergius de Dubitatione Cap. IV. Refutet id si vir est, sin minus, omittat imposterum calumnias & convitia. 3. Mirum verò est, quòd, cùm hanc sententiam, Cartesium non potuisse errare, contra mentem & protestationes nostras nobis attribuit, nullum ejus ex nostris scriptis afferat fundamentum, atque sic se à calumnia præservet. Ubinam verò Auctoritate Cartesii nituntur vel argumentum ab ea desumimus? ubinam sententiam ejus sine ratione & examine suscipimus? cum è contrario hæc sit nostræ Philosophiæ norma, Nihil esse admittendum pro vero, nisi quod clare & distincte fuerit perceptum. • CCXCI. His ita præmissis ipsæ Propositiones cum vindiciis ab Exceptionibus nunc sequuntur. de colligitur, ista omnia essentialia esse, & ad naturam corporis, in quantum corpus est, pertinere, quod sine iis esse non potest. Inter ea autem, quodnam sit Attributum primum à quo reliqua oriuntur, quodque propterea Essentia corporis sit dicendum, facile reperietur, si consideres, omnia illa, quæ ad extensionem referuntur, eam præsupponere, ac non nisi eâ posità corpori attribui posse. Ac Quantitatem & Magnitudinem quod attinet, si eam spectemus accuratius, atque cum extensione comparemus, reperiemus, hanc esse aliquid magis Absolutum, illa vero magis Respectiva (cum ut Quantum ad Tantum, ita Magnum ad Parvum referatur) adeoque ea Extensionem præsupponere. Neque enim ipsa quantitatis appellatio aliud menti exhibet, quàm certam extensionis determinationem & mensuram. Similiter divisibilitas extensionem in suo conceptu præsupponit, atque ab ea abstrahi nequit. Quod vero partes habeat corpus, quarum una sit posita extra alteram, quæque inter se invicem per extremitates suas conjunctæ continuum faciant, id divisibilitatem, & per consequens extensionem præsupponit. Atque ita Extensio non proprietas stricte sic dicta, sed primum Attributum Corporis est, & proin ejus essentiam constituit. 2. Ineptissimum vero est dicere, formam corporeitatis esse essentiam corporis. Non enim plus dicis, quàm si diceres, essentiam corporis esse essentiam corporis. Atqui de illa ipsa forma corporeitatis quæritur, in quonam illa consistat. Nos in extensione consistere jam dedimus probatum. Cum Cartesio philosophantes rem quærunt, non notiones secundas & nomina, nucleum, non torticem, &, quando eum invenerunt, sunt contenti; ne more Canis Æsopici, dum umbram captant, rem ipsam amittant. Atque hic error est communis in Adversariis, quod Entia multiplicantes citra necessitatem plus quærunt in re quàm revera inest, atque nucleo reperto eum tamen cum cortice commutare velint.
units.tr: CCXC. But since this same man, at p. 211, also attacks vehemently my most fair demand that prejudices be laid aside, it pleases me to deal with him at more length on this point. He says: It is my task to free the opponent from prejudices by the force of arguments, or to refute him in such a way that he has no reason to reply. And, interposing sarcasms, which I could easily have turned back upon him, he asks rather bitterly and contrary to Church gravity: which prejudices are to be laid aside? Is it, he says, that we believe the Sun moves? Is it that Holy Scripture is everywhere true? Is it that God exists? And he adds that he will never lay aside these prejudices: (1) whatever Scripture dictates to us is true; (2) in the exposition of the sacred text one must not depart from the proper sense of the words without a compelling reason. To these things I reply. First, there appears here the theological candour and charity with which these men are carried against those who depart in any degree from their opinions, whose views they most unfairly distort, so that they insult them without restraint. If the opponent had come back to himself, he could have known that all those things are prejudices which we have judged without sufficient examination and clear understanding, in which judgment precedes perception contrary to the order of nature. Various examples of these have been indicated here and there, and more have been collected by Descartes, Principles I, arts. 71–75, and by Clauberg in his Cartesian Defence. All of these must be laid aside by anyone who desires to know the truth. Unless he does so, you will be labouring in vain to argue against him. Yet are we to consider it an unfair demand that a man who approaches some matter for examination should bring a mind not preoccupied? Surely all people in general demand this of a lover of truth, and our theologians in particular require it of the Papists. See Ludovicus Crocius, on the Prejudices of the Papal Church, and especially his first Dissertation. Second, this is above all necessary in natural things, concerning which, having been occupied with them from infancy and not examining them sufficiently with age, we have drunk in various prejudices, which afterwards are retained most tenaciously and cannot be laid aside except with great effort. But it is not required in pure matters of mathematics, with which men are not accustomed to occupy themselves before they reach the use of reason. For example, suppose you have been persuaded from early youth that the Earth stands still and the Sun revolves daily about it, and you think Scripture also bears witness to this in the places soon to be examined. Nevertheless it is only fair that, if you wish to inquire whether there is truth or falsity in your opinion, you suspend judgment about it until you clearly know the truth or falsity, and what Scripture teaches about the matter. The opponent betrays his malice when he asks whether I wish Scripture to be everywhere true and God to exist to be laid aside as prejudices, since from my Dissertations he could have known well enough that I do not in any way doubt the truth of Scripture, and in them I have given the reasons why I interpret the passages objected to in such a way that nothing whatever opposes my view. That Descartes never doubted the existence of God, in the sense in which our adversaries attribute it to him, Mr. Clauberg has most clearly shown in his On Doubt, ch. IV. Let him refute it, if he is a man; if not, let him henceforth omit calumnies and reproaches. Third, it is indeed remarkable that, when he attributes to us this view, that Descartes could not have erred, contrary to our mind and protestations, he brings forward no basis for it from our writings, and so does not protect himself from calumny. Where, then, do we rely on the authority of Descartes, or where do we draw an argument from it? Where do we accept his opinion without reason and examination, when on the contrary this is the norm of our philosophy: that nothing is to be admitted as true except what has been clearly and distinctly perceived? CCXCI. With these things thus premised, the propositions themselves now follow, with their defences against the objections. From this it is gathered that all these things are essential and belong to the nature of body, insofar as it is body, since it cannot exist without them. Among them, moreover, it will easily be found which is the first attribute from which the rest arise, and which is therefore to be called the essence of body, if you consider that all those things which refer to extension presuppose it and can be attributed to body only when it is posited. As for quantity and magnitude, if we look at them more closely and compare them with extension, we shall find that the former is something more absolute, while the latter is more relative (since, as quantum is referred to tantum, so magnum is referred to parvum), and therefore presupposes extension. For the very name of quantity presents nothing else to the mind than a certain determination and measure of extension. Likewise divisibility presupposes extension in its concept and cannot be abstracted from it. And that body has parts, one of which is placed outside another, and which, joined to one another through their extremities, make a continuum, presupposes divisibility and consequently extension. And so extension is not a property strictly so called, but the first attribute of body, and therefore constitutes its essence. Second, it is most absurd to say that the form of corporeity is the essence of body. For you say no more than if you said that the essence of body is the essence of body. Yet it is precisely about that very form of corporeity that the question is, in what it consists. We have already proved that it consists in extension. When philosophers with Descartes seek the thing, they do not seek second notions and names; they seek the kernel, not the husk, and when they have found it they are content, lest, like the dog in Aesop who snatches at the shadow, they lose the thing itself. And this error is common among the adversaries: multiplying entities without necessity, they seek more in the thing than is really in it, and, having found the kernel, they nevertheless want to exchange it for the shell.

units.la: Verùm dices: Nos quærimus subjectum rei, cui omnia ista, Extensio, Quantitas, Magnitudo, divisibilitas &c. insint.
units.tr: But you will say: we seek the subject of the thing, in which all these things, extension, quantity, magnitude, divisibility, etc., inhere.

units.la: Resp. Frustra quæritis, quod jam habetis. Extensio enim est ipsum illud subjectum, cui Quantitas &c. conveniunt. Nihil enim reale post Quantitatem, Magnitudinem, divisibilitatem &c. in corpore præter extensionem remanet. Nolite in infinitum progredi, nolite loco realis subjecti quod habetis, aliquod notionale vel nominale substituere. Ac si omninò velitis subjectum extensionis, dico, illud esse ipsum corpus, quod ab extensione, non nisi nomine, non nisi ut concretum ab abstracto differt; sicut humanitas ab homine, Deitas à Deo.
units.tr: Reply. You seek in vain what you already have. For extension is itself that subject to which quantity etc. belong. For nothing real remains in body after quantity, magnitude, divisibility etc. except extension. Do not go on to infinity; do not, in place of the real subject that you have, substitute some notional or nominal one. And if you absolutely wish to have a subject of extension, I say that it is the body itself, which differs from extension only in name, only as the concrete differs from the abstract, as humanity differs from man, or Deity from God.

units.la: CCXCIV. de colligitur, ista omnia essentialia esse, & ad naturam corporis, in quantum corpus est, pertinere, quod sine iis esse non potest. Inter ea autem, quodnam sit Attributum primum à quo reliqua oriuntur, quodque propterea Essentia corporis sit dicendum, facile reperietur, si consideres, omnia illa, quae ad extensionem referuntur, eam praesupponere, ac non nisi eâ posità corpori attribui posse. Ac Quantitatem & Magnitudinem quod attinet, si eam spectemus accuratius, atque cum extensione comparemus, reperiemus, hanc esse aliquid magis Absolutum, illa vero magis Respectiva (cum ut Quantum ad Tantum, ita Magnum ad Parvum referatur) adeoque ea Extensionem praesupponere. Neque enim ipsa quantitatis appellatio aliud menti exhibet, quàm certam extensionis determinationem & mensuram. Similiter divisibilitas extensionem in suo conceptu praesupponit, atque ab ea abstrahi nequit. Quod vero partes habeat corpus, quarum una sit posita extra alteram, quaeque inter se invicem per extremitates suas conjunctae continuum faciant, id divisibilitatem, & per consequens extensionem praesupponit. Atque ita Extensio non proprietas strictè sic dicta, sed primum Attributum Corporis est, & proin ejus essentiam constituit. 2. Ineptissimum vero est dicere, formam corporeitatis esse essentiam corporis. Non enim plus dicis, quàm si diceres, essentiam corporis esse essentiam corporis. Atqui de illa ipsa forma corporeitatis quaeritur, in quonam illa consistat. Nos in extensione consistere jam dedimus probatum. Cum Cartesio philosophantes rem quaerunt, non notiones secundas & nomina, nucleum, non torticem, &, quando eum invenerunt, sunt contenti; ne more Canis Æsopici, dum umbram captant, rem ipsam amittant. Atque hic error est communis in Adversariis, quod Entia multiplicantes citra necessitatem plus quaerunt in re quàm revera inest, atque nucleo reperto eum tamen cum cortice commutare velint.
units.tr: CCXCIV. From this it is gathered that all these are essential, and belong to the nature of body insofar as it is body, since without them it cannot exist. Among them, it will easily be found which attribute is the first, from which the rest arise, and which is therefore to be called the essence of body, if you consider that all those things which are referred to extension presuppose it and can be attributed to body only when it is posited. As for quantity and magnitude, if we look at them more closely and compare them with extension, we will find that the former is something more absolute, while the latter is more relative (for as "quantum" is referred to "tantum," so "magnum" is referred to "parvum"), and therefore they presuppose extension. For the very word "quantity" presents to the mind nothing other than a certain determination and measure of extension. Similarly, divisibility presupposes extension in its concept and cannot be abstracted from it. Moreover, that body has parts, one of which lies outside another, and which, joined together through their extremities, make a continuum, this presupposes divisibility and consequently extension. And so extension is not a property, strictly so called, but is the first attribute of body, and therefore constitutes its essence. 2. It is most absurd to say that the form of corporeity is the essence of body. For you say no more than if you said that the essence of body is the essence of body. Yet it is precisely about that form of corporeity that the question arises, in what it consists. We have already proved that it consists in extension. Those who philosophize with Descartes seek the thing itself, the kernel and not the husk, and are content when they have found it; lest, like the dog in Aesop who snatches at the shadow, they lose the thing itself. And this error is common among our opponents: multiplying entities without necessity, they seek more in the thing than is really in it, and even when they have found the kernel, they still wish to exchange it for the shell.

units.la: Verùm dices: Nos quaerimus subjectum rei, cui omnia ista, Extensio, Quantitas, Magnitudo, divisibilitas &c. insint.
units.tr: But you will say: We are seeking the subject of the thing, in which all these things, extension, quantity, magnitude, divisibility, etc., inhere.

units.la: Resp. Frustra quaeritis, quod jam habetis. Extensio enim est ipsum illud subjectum, cui Quantitas &c. conveniunt. Nihil enim reale post Quantitatem, Magnitudinem, divisibilitatem &c. in corpore praeter extensionem remanet. Nolite in infinitum progredi, nolite loco realis subjecti quod habetis, aliquod notionale vel nominale substituere. Ac si omninò velitis subjectum extensionis, dico, illud esse ipsum corpus, quod ab extensione, non nisi nomine, non nisi ut concretum ab abstracto differt; sicut humanitas ab homine, Deitas à Deo.
units.tr: I answer: You seek in vain what you already have. For extension is itself that subject to which quantity etc. belong. For nothing real remains in body after quantity, magnitude, divisibility, etc., except extension. Do not proceed to infinity; do not substitute for the real subject which you have some notional or nominal thing. And if you wish absolutely to have a subject of extension, I say that it is the body itself, which differs from extension only in name, only as the concrete differs from the abstract, as humanity differs from man, and Deity from God.

units.la: CCXCIV. Exc. 3. (B. p. 218.) Cartesium confundere extensionem prout inest corpori, cum ea quae fit per abstractionem intellectus. Cum enim nominat quid extensum, tum comprehendit duo, videlicet, & subjectum cui extensio adhaeret, & adjunctum videl. extensionem subjecto inhaerentem: At in spatio, quod vacuum appellatur, per abstractionem concipitur extensio non dato subjecto extenso, qualis est abstractio Mathematica & Astronomica &c.
units.tr: CCXCIV. Exc. 3. (B. p. 218.) Descartes confuses extension as it is present in body with that which is produced by the abstraction of the intellect. For when he names something extended, he then comprehends two things, namely both the subject to which extension adheres and the adjunct, namely extension inhering in the subject. But in space, which is called empty, extension is conceived by abstraction, without a given extended subject, as is the case in mathematical and astronomical abstraction, etc.

units.la: Resp. Quin extensio ita possit a corpore distingui, quemadmodum humanitas ab homine nemo negat: neque negamus, quod extensio possit in genere considerari, prout non est ad hoc vel illud corpus restricta, adeoque, quod possit abstrahi ab hoc vel illo corpore in particulari, sicut & humanitas potest abstrahi ab hoc vel illo homine. Verum, quemadmodum humanitas in genere non differt ab homine in genere spectato, nisi ut abstractum & concretum, ita nec extensio a corpore generatim accepto. Atque haec est abstractio Mathematica in genere sic dicta, quae contemplatur magnitudines & figuras, parum curans, utrum tales sint actu in rerum natura, an vero tantum tales esse possint. Unde dicitur, Mathematicam quidem abstrahere a materia sensibili, hoc est, hac vel illa, non vero a materia intelligibili. 2. Astronomia vero non in abstracto contemplatur distantiam, magnitudinem &c. sed distantiam & magnitudinem stellarum; & quamvis in distantia immensurandā non habeat rationem vel aëris, vel aliorum corporum certorum, tamen non posset distantiam considerare corporum, si inter duo, quorum distantiam spectat, nulla alia corpora intercederent, hoc est, si non distarent inter se invicem. Nulla ergo hic confusio adscribi potest Cartesio, cum non neget, extensionem posse abstrahi a re extensa modo dicto, sed negat ab ea realiter differre, & per consequens posse inde separari. 3. Si in spatio, quod vacuum appellatur, consideretur per abstractionem extensio, tum consideraretur ea in genere quidem, sed non tamen oppositè ad corpus. At si dicatur, eam revera existere, etiam subjectum ejus corpus revera existere oportet confiteri. Apparet ergo sufficienter probatam esse a Cartesio propositionem primam, neque quid solidi objectum.
units.tr: I answer: Indeed extension can be distinguished from body in the way that nobody denies humanity can be distinguished from man; nor do we deny that extension can be considered in general, insofar as it is not restricted to this or that body, and so that it can be abstracted from this or that body in particular, just as humanity can be abstracted from this or that man. But just as humanity in general does not differ from man considered in general, except as the abstract differs from the concrete, so neither does extension differ from body taken generally. And this is what is called mathematical abstraction in general, which contemplates magnitudes and figures, caring little whether such things actually exist in the nature of things or only could exist. Hence it is said that mathematics indeed abstracts from sensible matter, that is, from this or that matter, but not from intelligible matter. 2. Astronomy, however, does not contemplate distance and magnitude in the abstract, but the distance and magnitude of the stars; and although in measuring an immeasurable distance it has no regard to air or to other certain bodies, yet it could not consider the distance of bodies if no other bodies lay between the two whose distance it considers, that is, if they were not at a distance from one another. No confusion can therefore be imputed to Descartes here, since he does not deny that extension can be abstracted from the extended thing in the way described, but he denies that it really differs from it and consequently can be separated from it. 3. If extension is considered by abstraction in space, which is called empty, then it would be considered in general, but not however as opposed to body. But if it is said that it really exists, then one must also confess that its subject, body, really exists. It therefore appears that the first proposition has been sufficiently proved by Descartes, nor is there any solid objection.

units.la: PROPOSITIO II.
units.tr: PROPOSITION II.

units.la: CCXCV. Vacuum dari non potest, art. 16. Quia contradictionem implicat. Quodcunque enim fingas, aut voces vacuum, cum ei semper extensionem videas esse tribuendam, reipsa tale non concipis, nec concipere potes, adeoque nec tale esse judicare debes, quia judicium perceptioni conforme esse debet. Quia autem extentionem ei attribuis, eo ipso totam corporis naturam ei assignas (per propos. 1.) & sic quod vacuum vocas, re ipsa corpus esse ostendis.
units.tr: CCXCV. A vacuum cannot exist, art. 16. Because it implies a contradiction. For whatever you imagine, or call a vacuum, since you must always attribute extension to it, you do not actually conceive such a thing, nor can you conceive it, and so you ought not to judge it to be such, since judgment must conform to perception. But because you attribute extension to it, you thereby assign to it the whole nature of body (by prop. 1), and so what you call a vacuum you show in fact to be body.

units.la: SCHOLIUM,
units.tr: SCHOLIUM,

units.la: CCXCVI. Exc. 1. (B. p. 219.) Mathematicorum stylus est ipsis propositionibus, non earum demonstrationibus propositiones sequentes superaedificare, quod hic à me sit factum.
units.tr: CCXCVI. Objection 1 (B. p. 219.) It is the style of mathematicians to build the following propositions on the propositions themselves, not on their demonstrations; and this is what I have done here.

units.la: Resp. Nisi brevitati studuissem, & non digitum intendissem ad Cartesium, istamque materiam tanquam non actam tractassem, tum debuissem propositionem hanc praemittere: corporis naturam in extensione consistere, & sic hinc & inde plures formare Propositiones, sed quia brevitati studui, illam Propositionem in demonstratione primae consideravi, & sic ad illam demonstrationem hic potui provocare.
units.tr: Reply: Had I not aimed at brevity, and had I not pointed my finger at Descartes, treating this matter as if it had never been handled, I ought to have prefaced this proposition: that the nature of body consists in extension, and so to draw several propositions from it on either side; but because I aimed at brevity, I considered that proposition in the demonstration of the first, and so could here refer to that demonstration.

units.la: CCXCVII. Exc. 2. (B. p. 220, 221.) Spatium vocamus, quod corpus comprehendere potest, & locum nominamus, cum corpus continet. Locus enim est spatium corpore plenum. Spatium vero est revera nihil, sed ita spatiose consideratum, ut in eo corpus locari possit. Spatium autem consideratur vel ut indeterminatum vel ut terminatum. Indeterminatum est, quod nullos, ne quidem in conceptu nostro terminos habet. Terminatum, quod saltem in conceptu nostro terminis est comprehensum. Et sic consideratur in Mathematica per abstractionem mentis nulla materia habita ratione.
units.tr: CCXCVII. Objection 2 (B. p. 220, 221.) We call space that which a body can comprehend, and we name place when a body contains it. For place is space filled with body. But space is really nothing, though it is considered spatially so that a body can be located in it. Space is considered either as indeterminate or as determinate. Indeterminate is that which has no boundaries, not even in our conception. Determinate is that which is comprehended by boundaries at least in our conception. And so it is considered in mathematics, by an abstraction of the mind, with no regard to matter.

units.la: Resp. Si τὸ Nihilum recte consideres, non opus est, ut in eo aliud quam negationem omnis realitatis spectes, utque neges habere extensionem, cogitationem & quae alia cum iis sunt connexa, quo sensu, si ad potentiam Dei referatur, nihil aliud potest dici, quàm Deum posse res omnes sive extensas sive cogitantes ex nihilo condere, & creare, sed tunc male tribuis isti nihilo, quod possit corpus comprehendere, cum id non conveniat, nisi ei quod est extensum. Nam necessario distaret ea pars istius nihili, quae posset hanc corporis partem comprehendere, ab ea quae posset oppositam, nisi velis dicere, ab eadem ejus parte omnes corporis partes simul posse comprehendi, quod est contradictorium. Quod autem ut extensum debet concipi, debet concipi, ut corpus, ac proinde ut tale judicari, ut judicium cum perceptione concordet. Videre ergo potes, te non recte Spatium Loco contradistinguere, sed praeferendam Cartesii distinctionem, quae clara est & ab omni confusione libera. Vide Princ. II. art. 14.
units.tr: Reply: If you rightly consider the nothing [τὸ Nihilum], there is no need to regard in it anything other than the negation of all reality, and to deny that it has extension, thought, and whatever else is connected with these. In this sense, if it is referred to the power of God, nothing else can be said than that God can produce and create all things, whether extended or thinking, out of nothing. But then you wrongly attribute to that nothing that it can comprehend a body, since this belongs only to what is extended. For that part of this nothing which could comprehend this part of body would necessarily be distinct from the part which could comprehend the opposite part, unless you wish to say that all parts of body could be comprehended at once by the same part of it, which is contradictory. But what must be conceived as extended must be conceived as body, and so judged to be such, so that judgment agrees with perception. You see, then, that you do not rightly distinguish space from place; rather Descartes's distinction is to be preferred, for it is clear and free from all confusion. See Princ. II, art. 14.

units.la: 2. Quod si ante mundum conditum debuerunt concipi attributa corporum, quale est extensio, tum etiam ipsa corpora, & si debuerunt concipi, etiam debent judicari exstitisse,& per consequens, mundum fuisse ab æterno. 3. Mathematici considerant spatium quidem, & corpus in genere & abstracte, ut non referatur ad hoc vel illud corpus physicum in specie, sed non tamen sine ulla materiæ ratione, quia, ut dictum, Mathematici non abstrahunt à materiâ intelligibili, etsi à materiâ sensibili, hoc est, hâc vel illâ.
units.tr: 2. If the attributes of bodies, such as extension, must be conceived before the world was made, then the bodies themselves must also be conceived; and if they must be conceived, they must also be judged to have existed, and consequently the world would have existed from eternity. 3. Mathematicians consider space, and body, in general and abstractly, not as referred to this or that physical body in particular; yet not without some regard to matter, since, as said, mathematicians do not abstract from intelligible matter, though they do abstract from sensible matter, that is, this or that matter.

units.la: CCXCVIII. Inst. 1. (B. p. 221.) Deus in vase manentibus terminis omne corpus nullo alio succedente tollere potest.
units.tr: CCCXCVIII. Inst. 1 (B. p. 221.) God can remove every body from a vessel, the boundaries remaining, with nothing else taking its place.

units.la: Resp. At hæc est manifesta contradictio: Manere in vase terminos à se invicem distantes, & tamen nihil esse intermedium. Distantia enim quidem est duorum corporum, sed tamen fundamentum ejus non est in ipsis corporibus distantibus, sed in tertio aliquo intermedio corpore. Si enim in ipsis corporibus, ergo habebunt distantiam, quocunque modo fuerint posita, etiamsi se immediate contingant, quod non potest non esse absurdum. Nihilum vero efficere distantiam non potest, cum ejus nullæ sint affectiones, nullæ operationes.
units.tr: Reply: But this is a plain contradiction: for boundaries distant from one another to remain in a vessel, and yet for nothing to lie between them. For distance indeed belongs to two bodies, but its ground is not in the distant bodies themselves, but in some third, intermediate body. For if it were in the bodies themselves, they would have distance however they were placed, even if they touched immediately, which cannot but be absurd. But nothing cannot produce distance, since it has no affections and no operations.

units.la: CCXCIX. Inst. 2. (B. p. 221.) At hallucinamini in voce Nihil, cùm eâ tantum negetur corpus aliquod intermedium, non verò spatium tale, quod intellectu abstrahente ab omni materiâ concipitur &c.
units.tr: CCXCIX. Inst. 2 (B. p. 221.) But you are mistaken about the word Nothing, since by it only some intermediate body is denied, not such a space as is conceived by the intellect abstracting from all matter, etc.

units.la: Resp. Spatium absque omni materia concipi non potest, cum non possit concipi sine extensione, quæ est materiæ sive corporis essentia, uti demonstratum. Tò nihil à nihilo non differt, sed reale à nihilo differt. Spatium ergo illud si differat à nihilo, reale erit dicendum, & per consequens vel aliquid extensum erit, vel aliquid spirituale. At spirituale distantiam efficere non potest. Extensum vero si sit, eo ipso corpus erit dicendum.
units.tr: Reply: Space cannot be conceived without all matter, since it cannot be conceived without extension, which is the essence of matter or body, as has been shown. The nothing does not differ from nothing, but the real differs from nothing. If that space therefore differs from nothing, it must be called real, and consequently it will be either something extended or something spiritual. But a spiritual thing cannot produce distance. If it is extended, then by that very fact it must be called body.

units.la: CCC. Inst. 3. (B. p. 222.) At Deus potuit Angelos creare ante substantia corporea universitatem, ergo potuerunt fuisse aliquo Ubi, in quo versarentur, quod debet considerari tantum ut spatium vacuum, sunt enim essentia finita, quas de loco in locum migrare testatur pagina sacra.
units.tr: CCC. Inst. 3 (B. p. 222.) But God could have created the angels before the universe of corporeal substance; therefore they could have been in some where, in which they dwelt, which must be considered merely as empty space, for they are finite essences, which the sacred page testifies to pass from place to place.

units.la: Resp. Angeli ad suam essentiam præcise consideratam non opus habent aliquo ubi, cum ea in cogitatione consistat, quæ ubi quidem considerat, sed formaliter ad ipsum nullam habet relationem. Dicuntur autem in ubi esse, quando operantur extra se in corpora, in quibus Ubi consideratur, & quoniam eorum essentia non potest separari ab eorum operatione, etiam tum eorum essentia ad ubi habet relationem. Itaque dico, Angelos ante universitatem corporum creatos nullum respectum ad ubi habituros fuisse, cum nullum tale fuisse supponatur. Nihili enim nullæ sunt qualitates, nullæ affectiones. Finitudo vero Angelorum non infert, ut necessario ad extra in corpora operentur, sed tantum, si ad extra operentur, & sic relatione ad ubi recipiant, quod eorum operatio non ad omne ubi, ut Dei, sed ad certum aliquod & determinatum se extendat.
units.tr: Reply: Angels, considered precisely in their essence, have no need of any where, since their essence consists in thought, which indeed considers where, but formally has no relation to it. They are said to be in a where when they act outside themselves upon bodies, in which Where is considered; and since their essence cannot be separated from their operation, their essence too then has a relation to a where. So I say that angels created before the universe of bodies would have had no respect to a where, since no such thing is supposed. For nothing has no qualities, no affections. But the finitude of angels does not imply that they must necessarily act outwardly upon bodies, only that, if they do act outwardly, they receive a relation to a where, since their operation extends not to every where, as God's does, but to a certain and determinate one.

units.la: CCCI. Exc. 3. (B.p.223.) Ex hac sententia inferri mundi æternitatem, quia ante mundum conditum possum fingere spatium replebile, sicut ante mundi principium possum concipere tempus possibile.
units.tr: CCCI. Objection 3 (B. p. 223.) From this opinion it follows that the world is eternal, because before the world was made I can imagine a space capable of being filled, just as before the beginning of the world I can conceive a possible time.

units.la: Resp. Illud vero ex vestra sententia sequi superius art. 297. ostendi. Nos enim negamus, ante mundum conditum, præter Deum aliud debere concipi quàm nihil, non Ens, negationem omnis realitatis, omnisque extensionis &c. adeoque non spatium replebile. 2. Ut vero tempus ante mundum quidem potes concipere possibile, non quod esset, sed quod fieri posset, ita etiam tantum spatium possibile ut corpus possibile concipere licet, quod non negamus, sed dicimus, illud sine extensione concipi non posse, adeoque à corpore non differre realiter.
units.tr: Reply: That this follows from your opinion I have shown above, at art. 297. For we deny that before the world was made anything other than God should be conceived except nothing, not Being: the negation of all reality, of all extension, and so not a space capable of being filled. 2. Just as you can indeed conceive time before the world as possible, not as existing but as able to come to be, so too one may conceive a possible space as a possible body. This we do not deny; but we say that it cannot be conceived without extension, and so does not really differ from body.

units.la: CCCII. Exc. 3. (B.p.224.) Nostram doctrinam contra spatia imaginaria magnam sibi ingenerare suspicionem, quod clam negetur mundi creatio ex nihilo, & foveatur opinio de æternitate mundi. Idque eo magis, quod illud axioma, ex nihilo nihil fit, ut veritas quædam æterna à Cartesio consideretur Princ. I. art. 49.
units.tr: CCCII. Objection 3 (B. p. 224.) Our doctrine against imaginary spaces creates a great suspicion that the creation of the world out of nothing is secretly denied, and that the opinion of the eternity of the world is fostered; and this all the more because Descartes treats that axiom, out of nothing nothing comes, as an eternal truth Princ. I, art. 49.

units.la: Resp. Si suspicionibus & consequentiis agere licet, multo magis adscribenda adversariis opinio de mundi æternitate, quàm nobis, quoniam ex ipsorum principiis sequi ostendimus, à nostra vero sententia removimus. Tantum abest, ut existimem mundum esse ab æterno, ut & contra scholasticos negem, æternitatem mundi possibilem esse. 2. Axioma illud, ex nihilo nihil fit, intelligendum secundum subjectam materiam in Physica, in qua agitur de viribus naturæ, de qua semper verum est, eam ex nihilo nihil posse producere. Ad reliqua, quæ de infinitate mundi hic disputat, superius jam responsum.
units.tr: Reply: If it is allowed to argue from suspicions and consequences, the opinion that the world is eternal must be ascribed far more to our adversaries than to us, since we show that it follows from their principles, while we have removed it from ours. So far am I from thinking the world is from eternity, that I also deny, against the Schoolmen, that the eternity of the world is possible. 2. That axiom, out of nothing nothing comes, is to be understood with respect to the subject matter in Physics, in which the powers of nature are treated; of these it is always true that they cannot produce anything out of nothing. As to the rest, which he disputes here about the infinity of the world, I have already replied above.

units.la: PROPOSITIO III.
units.tr: PROPOSITION III.

units.la: CCCIII. Rarefactio non fit, nisi quando corpora quædam poros alterius corporis ingrediuntur, eaque diducunt: Condensatio contra, quando corpora ex poris alicujus corporis recedunt, ut intervalla ista imminuantur vel plane tollantur. art. 6. Non potest enim cognosci, quomodo nova extensio accedat sine novæ substantiæ corporeæ additamento; ubicunque enim extensionem ponis, ibi corpus te ponere necesse est, & vice versâ (ex propos. 1.)
units.tr: 303. Rarefaction happens only when certain bodies enter the pores of another body and spread them apart; condensation, on the other hand, happens when bodies withdraw from the pores of some body, so that those intervals are diminished or entirely removed. Art. 6. For it cannot be understood how a new extension can arise without the addition of new corporeal substance; for wherever you posit extension, you must necessarily posit body there, and conversely (from Prop. 1).

units.la: SCHOLIUM.
units.tr: SCHOLIUM.

units.la: CCCIV. Exc. (B. p. 135.) Hanc propositionem inutiliter hic inseri, cùm in sequentibus non habeat usum, praeterquam in propositione ultimâ, & in controversiâ alienâ, videl. cur Luna non magis accesserit ad terram.
units.tr: 304. Exc. (B. p. 135.) This proposition is inserted here to no purpose, since in what follows it has no use, except in the final proposition and in a controversy foreign to the matter, namely why the Moon has not come closer to the earth.

units.la: Resp. Si vel in unâ propositione habeat usum est necessaria: nec illa controversia aliena. Nam ostenditur ibi, quòd Luna materiam coelestem inter se & terram interjectam in modum vorticis contorquet, & sic istâ materiâ interveniente terram circa suum axem circumvolvat; ad id ostendendum requirebatur, ne Luna propius ad terram accederet, quod ostenditur factum esse ex globulorum resistentiâ, quae nititur propos. hàc tertiâ, uti in demonstratione propositionis ultimae videre est.
units.tr: Reply: Even if it had a use in a single proposition, it would be necessary; nor is that controversy foreign. For it is shown there that the Moon twists the celestial matter lying between itself and the earth into the form of a vortex, and so, with this matter intervening, turns the earth about its axis. To show this, it was required that the Moon not approach the earth more closely; and this is shown to have happened from the resistance of the globules, which rests on this third proposition, as can be seen in the demonstration of the final proposition.

units.la: PROPOSITIO IV.
units.tr: PROPOSITION IV.

units.la: CCCV. Omne corpus, quantumvis parvum, in infinitum potest dividi. art. 20. Quia nulla pars corporis potest esse tam parva, quin habeat extensionem: secus enim corporea esse desineret, & vel in nihilum abiret, vel in rei spiritualis sive immaterialis naturam mutaretur, quod est impossibile. Omne autem extensum, cum hoc ipso habeat longitudinem, latitudinem & profunditatem, iterum minui potest.
units.tr: CCCV. Every body, however small, can be divided to infinity. art. 20. Because no part of a body can be so small that it lacks extension. Otherwise it would cease to be corporeal and would either pass into nothing or be changed into the nature of a spiritual or immaterial thing, which is impossible. Now everything extended, since it has length, breadth and depth, can again be diminished.

units.la: SCHOLIUM.
units.tr: SCHOLIUM.

units.la: CCCVI. Hanc propositionem dicit (B. p. 236.) se concedere posse, cum hac cautelâ, nullam dari realem divisionem in infinitum.
units.tr: CCCVI. He says (B. p. 236.) that he can concede this proposition, with this caution, that there is no real division to infinity.

units.la: Resp. Hoc libenter admitto, imò consequens hujus nostrae propositionis existimo. At quòd hinc putat, se probare posse infinitatem mundi implicare contradictionem, id non videmus consequi.
units.tr: Reply. I gladly admit this; indeed I regard it as a consequence of our proposition. But that he thinks he can thence prove that the infinity of the world implies a contradiction, we do not see follows.

units.la: Inquit: Omne corpus habet partem extra partem, ergò varias & diversas partes; partium autem illarum, qualescunque vel quantacunque considerentur, numerus est par vel impar, & sic unitate potest augeri, ac proinde, quemadmodum numerus in infinitum auctus dari non potest, sic nec extensio corporis, quod ex partibus est compositum, in infinitum aucta: ac proinde terminos & fines habet extensionis suae. Resp. Simile hoc est argumentum ei, ad quod supra responsum est cap. xiii. Nam numerus partium mundi, quae actu à reliquis separatae intelliguntur, semper est finitus, adeoque par vel impar; quod si vero mundus esset infinitus, dico, nunquam tantum numerum partium auferri posse, quin semper in infinitum restet aliquid sumendum, adeoque numerus partium mundi, quae in eo continentur, infinitus erit dicendus. Sed haec ex hypothesi infinitatis mundi respondeo, de quâ nihil certi posse determinari statuo.
units.tr: He says: Every body has part outside part, therefore various and diverse parts; and the number of those parts, however small or large they are considered, is either even or odd, and so can be increased by one; and therefore, just as a number increased to infinity cannot be given, so neither can the extension of a body, which is composed of parts, be increased to infinity: and therefore it has limits and ends of its extension. Reply. This argument is similar to the one to which an answer was given above, in chapter xiii. For the number of parts of the world, which are actually understood as separated from the rest, is always finite, and so either even or odd. But if the world were infinite, I say that a number of parts could never be removed without something always remaining to be taken, in infinity; and so the number of parts of the world contained in it will have to be called infinite. But I answer these things on the hypothesis of the world's infinity, about which I hold that nothing certain can be determined.

units.la: PROPOSITIO V.
units.tr: PROPOSITIO V.

units.la: CCCVII. Quocunque corpore moto semper integer ambitus corporum simul movetur art. 33. Cùm enim vacuum non detur (per prop. 2.) non potest ullum corpus moveri, nisi aliud corpus ante se protrudat, nec hoc, nisi iterum aliud, & sic consequenter. Non datur autem locus, quò recedat corpus ultimum, nisi quem derelinquere conatur primum, quo facto, penultimum in locum ultimi succedit, & sic porrò. Itaque quocunque moto corpore semper integer ambitus sive circulus corporum simul movetur.
units.tr: CCCVII. Whenever a body is moved, a whole ring of bodies is moved at the same time art. 33. For since there is no void (by prop. 2), no body can be moved unless it pushes another body ahead of itself, and that body cannot move unless another moves, and so on in sequence. Yet there is no place for the last body to withdraw into, except the one which the first body is trying to leave. When this happens, the second-last body moves into the place of the last, and so on. Thus, whenever a body is moved, a whole ring or circle of bodies is moved at the same time.

units.la: SCHOLIUM.
units.tr: SCHOLIUM.

units.la: CCCVIII. Exc. I. (B. p. 239.) Se quomodo ea propositio in omni motu corporum omnium locum habeat vel non capere, vel ut falsum concipere. Ponamus enim sagittam vel glandem ex sclopeto celerrimè per liquidum aërem emissam, quomodo corpora illa vel aëris protensi particula moveantur in circulum ostendendum esset. Ponamus etiam navem, & quidem satis magnam in circumferentiâ lacûs aggere concluso celerrimè motam, protrudit quidem partes proximas à lateribus recedentes, sed non aquas totius circumferentia.
units.tr: CCCVIII. Exc. I. (B. p. 239.) I do not see how this proposition holds in every motion of all bodies, or else I conceive it to be false. For let us suppose an arrow or a bullet discharged very swiftly from a musket through the liquid air; it would need to be shown how those bodies, or the particles of the stretched air, are moved in a circle. Let us suppose also a ship, and a fairly large one, driven very swiftly within the circumference of a lake enclosed by an embankment. It indeed pushes the nearby parts, which recede from its sides, but not the waters of the whole circumference.

units.la: Resp. Sive capiat antagonista sive non, nihil ad veritatem refert. Interim ea difficultas quam objicit, nulla est. Nam sagitta non posset procedere, nisi tanta pars aëris recedat, quanta est sagitta, nec illa pars aëris recedere potest, nisi sibi cedat alia, & sic porrò, atque ita aëris partes proximae sagittae iterum se conferant in locum sagittae, ubi spatium inveniunt, cùm aliud reperiant nusquam. Sic navis celerrimè mota non necessariò protrudit aquas totius circumferentiae lacûs, si ille sit satis magnus, sed intra illam circumferentiam alium ambitum efficere potest, ita nempe, ut semper novus ac novus ambitus, prout ulterius navis promovetur, efficiatur.
units.tr: Reply. Whether my opponent grasps it or not makes no difference to the truth. Meanwhile, the difficulty he raises is no difficulty at all. For the arrow could not advance unless as much air withdrew as the arrow fills; nor can that part of the air withdraw unless another part yields to it, and so on. Thus the parts of air nearest the arrow move back again into the place the arrow has left, where they find space, since they find none anywhere else. Likewise, a ship moved very swiftly does not necessarily push the waters of the whole circumference of the lake, if the lake is large enough. Rather, within that circumference it can produce another ring, namely one which is always new, as the ship is carried further forward.

units.la: CCCIX. Exc. 2, Ad fugam vacui sufficit corpora sibi mutuo cedere & succedere, quamvis id non fiat in circulo.
units.tr: CCCIX. Exc. 2. For the flight of a void, it is enough that bodies yield to one another and succeed one another, even though this does not happen in a circle.

units.la: Resp. Nec nos, nec Cartesius de circulo proprie dicto vel perfecto loquitur, sed per ambitum intelligit circulum quantumlibet irregularem, modo primum corpus succedat in locum secundi, secundum in locum tertii, tertium in locum quarti, & sic porro, ut ultimum locum primi vicissim occupet: quo sensu dicitur circulatio sanguinis, item circulatores, qui post varia loca peragrata tandem ad primum redeunt. Circulus ergo dicitur, quia semper solet fieri aliqua curvatura, etiamsi quaedam in illo circulo secundum lineam rectam moveantur. Ergo eo ipso si ad fugam vacui corpora sibi mutuo cedant ac succedant in omni motu, erit in omni motu circulus sive corporum ambitus, quod erat probandum.
units.tr: Reply. Neither I nor Descartes speaks of a circle in the strict or perfect sense, but by "ring" he means a circuit of whatever irregular shape, provided that the first body succeeds into the place of the second, the second into the place of the third, the third into the place of the fourth, and so on, until the last body in turn occupies the place of the first. In this sense we speak of the circulation of the blood, and likewise of hawkers (circulatores) who, after wandering through various places, at last return to the first. It is called a circle because some curvature always tends to occur, even if some bodies in that circle are moved along a straight line. Therefore, if in every motion bodies yield to one another and succeed one another for the flight of a void, then in every motion there will be a circle, that is, a ring of bodies, which was to be proved.

units.la: PROPOSITIO VI.
units.tr: PROPOSITIO VI.

units.la: CCCX. In hoc motu circulari omnes locorum inaequalitates inaequali motuum celeritate debent compensari art. 33. Quandoquidem enim vacuum dari non potest (per prop. 2.) ideo necessario minora corpora citius transeunt, ubi majora simul non possunt, vel etiam unum aut duo majora corpora reliqua motu praevenire debent. Et quia se invicem premunt, alterutri major vis ad motum celerem communicatur, ei nempe, quod ad motum aptissime est dispositum.
units.tr: CCCX. In this circular motion, all the inequalities of places must be compensated by unequal speeds of motion. Art. 33. For since a vacuum cannot be given (by Prop. 2), the smaller bodies necessarily pass more quickly wherever the larger ones cannot move together with them, or else one or two larger bodies must outstrip the rest by their motion. And because they press upon one another, a greater force is communicated to whichever body is most fitted for rapid motion.

units.la: SCHOLIUM
units.tr: SCHOLIUM

units.la: CCCXI. Exc. (B. p. 240.) Haec propositio si intelligatur de corporibus fluidis, in lateribus circumferentia conclusis, ut in aquis, qua in circumferentia lacus concluduntur, tota facile conceditur.
units.tr: CCCXI. Excerpt (B. p. 240). If this proposition is understood of fluid bodies enclosed by sides on their circumference, as waters enclosed on the circumference of a lake, it is easily granted in full.

units.la: Resp. Haec propositio est intelligenda de omnibus corporibus fluidis, quandocunque nempe contingit, ut a latere ea comprimantur ab aliis corporibus cedere nescīis, tum enim propter rationem allatam corpora per angustius spatium celerius moveri debent, ut ita per celerem motum latitudo spatii compensetur.
units.tr: Reply: This proposition is to be understood of all fluid bodies, whenever it happens that they are pressed from the side by other bodies that do not know how to give way. For then, for the reason given, the bodies must move more swiftly through the narrower space, so that the width of the space is compensated by the swifter motion.

units.la: PROPOSITIO VII.
units.tr: PROPOSITIO VII.

units.la: CCCXII. Deum primaria est motus causa, eandemque semper motus quantitatem, quam semel creavit, conservat. art. 36. Prius facile concedet, qui attendet ad Dei perfectionem, à quâ oritur, ut omnia ab ipso independente dependeant. Nec posterius etiam facile quis negabit, qui ad Dei constantiam animum suum adjecerit, quam eum in operando semper exprimere cogitandum, donec mutatio aliqua ex effectibus evidenter cognoscatur.
units.tr: CCCXII. God is the primary cause of motion, and he always preserves the same quantity of motion that he once created. Art. 36. The former will readily be conceded by anyone who attends to the perfection of God, from which it follows that all things depend on him who depends on nothing else. Nor will anyone easily deny the latter who has fixed his mind on the constancy of God, which we must always think of him as expressing in his working, until some change is clearly recognised in the effects.

units.la: SCHOLIUM.
units.tr: SCHOLIUM.

units.la: CCCXIII. Exc. 1. (B. p. 241.) Hanc non esse Methodum Mathematicam, quia hac propositio non demonstretur ex antecedente aliqua propo-sitione.
units.tr: CCCXIII. Excerpt 1 (B. p. 241). That this is not the mathematical method, because this proposition is not demonstrated from some preceding proposition.

units.la: Resp. At sufficit, si ex communi notione demonstretur, quod à me est factum, quamvis brevitatis causâ illa communis notio propositioni non fuerit praemissa. Communis est notio: Ab Ente perfectissimo omnia dependere. Si enim id negetur, simul negabitur illud Ens perfectissimum existere. Inde ergo etiam motum dependere evincitur.
units.tr: Reply: But it is enough if it is demonstrated from a common notion, which I have done, although for the sake of brevity that common notion was not set before the proposition. The common notion is this: All things depend on the most perfect Being. For if this is denied, it will at the same time be denied that the most perfect Being exists. From this it is therefore also proved that motion depends on him.

units.la: CCCXIV. Exc. 2. (B. p. 243.) quâ impugnatur art. Cart. 36. Princ. II. ad quem provocavimus. Concedimus Deum omnis motus, qui in rerum natura reperitur, esse causam primam. At duo sunt in Philosophia Cartesiana principia, quibus assentiri non possumus. Primum est, ad rerum omnium constitutionem nihil requiri praeter materiam, figuram & motum, ita ut creatio, quam Theologi vocare solent secundam, non in alia re consistat, quàm quòd motum specialem dederit variis partibus materiae &c.
units.tr: CCCXIV. Excerpt 2 (B. p. 243), in which is attacked Art. 36 of Descartes, Principles II, to which we appealed. We concede that God is the first cause of all the motion that is found in the nature of things. But there are two principles in the Cartesian philosophy to which we cannot assent. The first is that nothing beyond matter, figure and motion is required for the constitution of all things, so that creation, which theologians are accustomed to call secondary, consists in nothing else than that he gave a special motion to various parts of matter, etc.

units.la: Resp. Illud quod de creatione secundâ adducit, est plane impertinens: neque enim in nostra propositione, prout nec à Cartesio, aliud quid intenditur, quàm motum dependere à Deo tanquam à causâ, & eandem ejus quantitatem in mundo semper remanere, quorum si alterum concedat, habemus quod intendimus. Quod autem omnes materiae proprietates, quae clarè & distinctè possunt concipi, reducantur ad id, quod sit mobilis & partibilis, id ex Cartesii Principiis patet, quoniam per haec omnia in corporibus demonstrata sunt & demonstrari possunt. Quod si antagonista & alii plura requiri putent, formas nempe nescio quas substantiales, qualitates reales, ea ab ipsis probari oportebat. Ad Dei vero opera extollenda non opus est, ut aliquid iis affingamus, quod non reperitur, sed ea satis evadunt magnifica, si 1. consideremus, esse amplissima, & nobis imperscrutabilia. 2. Si non præsumamus nos ea perfecte exhaurire, ita ut non aliam putemus in iis posse adhuc latere proprietatem, quam non cognoscimus. 3. Si ejus immediatam operationem in iis agnoscamus. 4. Si omnibus momentis ab ipso dependere & conservari statuamus, &c. qualia in Cartesiana Philosophia reperiuntur. Creatio vero secunda satis distinguitur à Mechanici actione. 1. quod sit productio rei ex materia nullam habente naturalem ad id, quod inde fit, dispositionem. 2. quod Deus sit auctor legum naturæ, & secundum eas omnia ipse dirigat. 3. quod ea quæ produxit, comparatè ad opera Mechanica, infinitè sint artificiosa, ut ea non possit ullus Mechanicus imitari. 4. quod creaverit motum, porroque creet sive conservet, cum Mechanicus non nisi motum possit determinare, nullum vero novum producere. 5. quod ad omnia opera Dei simul sese extendat & respectu omnium quæ sunt in iis, cum Mechanici uno tempore non nisi unum opus illudque imperfectum possint efficere. Probetur vero, ad creationem secundam opus esse, ut Deus novas formas substantiales, quæ realiter distinguantur à materia, producat. Est ergo creatio secunda omnipotens Dei actio, ad omnia opera Dei sese extendens, quâ motûs certam quantitatem in mundo produxit, & secundùm leges naturæ à se positas cum direxit, atque sic ex materia inhabili & informi sex diebus opera ea, quæ in Genesi describuntur, per immediatam suam operationem & in materiam influxum persecit.
units.tr: Reply: What he adduces about secondary creation is quite irrelevant. For in our proposition, as also in Descartes, nothing else is intended than that motion depends on God as on a cause, and that the same quantity of it always remains in the world. If he concedes one of these, we have what we intend. As for the claim that all the properties of matter which can be clearly and distinctly conceived are reducible to what is movable and divisible, this is plain from the principles of Descartes, since all of these have been, and can be, demonstrated in bodies by means of them. But if the opponent and others think that more is required, namely certain substantial forms, I know not what, and real qualities, it was incumbent on them to prove these. To extol the works of God, however, we need not attach to them anything that is not found there; they are magnificent enough if (1) we consider that they are most vast and inscrutable to us; (2) we do not presume that we have exhausted them perfectly, so as to think that some other property which we do not know may still lie hidden in them; (3) we acknowledge his immediate operation in them; (4) we hold that they depend on him and are preserved by him at every moment, etc., as is found in the Cartesian philosophy. Secondary creation, however, is sufficiently distinguished from the action of a mechanic: (1) in that it is the production of a thing out of matter that has no natural disposition towards what is made from it; (2) in that God is the author of the laws of nature and directs all things according to them; (3) in that the things he has produced are, compared with mechanical works, infinitely skilful, so that no mechanic could imitate them; (4) in that he has created motion, and will go on creating or preserving it, whereas a mechanic can only determine motion and cannot produce anything new; (5) in that he extends himself to all the works of God at once, and to all that is in them, whereas mechanics can make only one work at a time, and that imperfect. It must, moreover, be proved that for secondary creation it is necessary that God produce new substantial forms that are really distinct from matter. Secondary creation is therefore the omnipotent action of God, extending to all the works of God, by which he produced a certain quantity of motion in the world, and, when he had directed it according to the laws of nature set by himself, thus brought to completion, out of unfit and formless matter, in six days, the works described in Genesis, by his immediate operation and influence upon matter.

units.la: CCCXV. At dices: Creatio est substantiarum. At motus non est substantia. Ergo non potest creari. Item, Secunda creatio est creatio. Ergo per eam producta sunt substantia, & per consequens forma substantiales.
units.tr: CCCXV. But you will say: Creation is of substances. But motion is not a substance. Therefore it cannot be created. Likewise, secondary creation is creation. Therefore substances, and consequently substantial forms, have been produced by it.

units.la: Resp. Ad primum. Creatio proprie dicta est substantiarum, sed improprie dicta, qualis est creatio motus, potest etiam esse modorum, quam si malis concreationem vocare, me non habebis repugnantem. Ad secundum. Et secundum nos creationis secundæ terminus est substantia, non aliqua ex nihilo producta materia, (quod nec dicent adversarii, cum illa materia sit primæ creationis effectum:) sed illa ipsa materia variata hoc modo & dispósita, ut aliquod singulare corpus inde oriretur, quod vel Sol, vel stella, vel planta &c. posset vocari, idque propter vim omnipotentem & immediatam, quæ sese hic exseruit, ut aliquid produceret, quod à nulla creatura produci potuisset. Reliqua, quae hic adversarius debacchatur in Cartesium de arrogantiâ & superbiâ, ne par pari referre cogamur, intacta relinquimus.
units.tr: Reply: To the first: creation properly so called is of substances, but creation improperly so called, such as the creation of motion, can also be of modes. If you prefer to call it concreation, you will not find me opposed. To the second: according to us, the term of secondary creation is a substance, not some matter produced out of nothing (which the opponents will not say either, since that matter is the effect of the primary creation), but that very matter varied and disposed in such a way that some single body arose from it, which could be called a sun, a star, a plant, etc., and this on account of the omnipotent and immediate power which here put itself forth to produce something that could not have been produced by any creature. As for the rest, in which this opponent rages against Descartes about arrogance and pride, we leave it untouched, lest we be forced to return like for like.

units.la: CCCXVI. Pergit (B. p. 244.) Secundum Cartesii principium est, quod ex Deo merum faciat tornionem, & in rebus creatis nullum agendi principium internum relinquatur, & sic secundum ipsius theoriam non agunt creaturae, sed Deus in creaturis, & ad earum praesentiam; sic urit in igne &c.
units.tr: CCCXVI. He goes on (B. p. 244): The second principle of Descartes is that he makes God a mere machinist, and leaves no internal principle of action in created things; and so, according to his theory, creatures do not act, but God acts in creatures, and in their presence; thus he burns in fire, etc.

units.la: Resp. 1. Quomodo actio Mechanici cujusvis actione Dei distinguatur actio jam ostendimus. 2. Neque sequitur, Deum urere in igne, &c. quamvis Deus sit causa istius actionis propter suum Concursum, quem omnes Philosophi agnoscunt, quia actio denominatur ab eo corpore, à cujus dispositione determinatur, sic ustio ab igne, latratus à cane &c.
units.tr: Reply: (1) How the action of any mechanic is distinguished from the action of God we have already shown. (2) Nor does it follow that God burns in fire, etc., although God is the cause of that action on account of his concurrence, which all philosophers acknowledge; for an action is named from the body by whose disposition it is determined. Thus burning is named from fire, barking from the dog, etc.

units.la: 3. Internum agendi principium rebus corporeis inditum, diversum à magnitudine, figurâ, motu & quiete, esset probandum: nos hoc privilegium solis creaturis rationalibus dicimus reservatum.
units.tr: (3) An internal principle of action implanted in corporeal things, distinct from magnitude, figure, motion and rest, would have to be proved. We say that this privilege is reserved for rational creatures alone.

units.la: CCCXVII. Exc. contra secundam Propositionis partem. (B p. 245.) In motu luminarium coelestium Deus eundem motum continuo conservat, sed in aliis rebus non agnoscimus motum illum, quo materia ad rerum constitutionem modificetur, ut & negamus, Deum eandem motus quantitatem in universo conservare.
units.tr: CCCXVII. Excerpt against the second part of the Proposition (B. p. 245). In the motion of the heavenly luminaries God continually preserves the same motion, but in other things we do not acknowledge that motion by which matter is modified for the constitution of things, and we deny that God conserves the same quantity of motion in the universe.

units.la: Resp. In istâ Propositione ostenditur generaliter, quod Deus eandem motus quantitatem tam in coelestibus quam subcoelestibus conservet, non quidem, ut iste motus certis quibusdam corporibus sit alligatus, sed quod, licet ab his procedat ad illa, non tamen augeatur, nec minuatur ejus quantitas; argumentum nostrum sumentes ab immutabilitate Dei, quod an adversarius enervet, videamus.
units.tr: Reply. In this proposition it is shown in general that God preserves the same quantity of motion both in the heavenly and in the sublunary realm. This is not meant in the sense that the motion is bound to certain bodies, but that, although it passes from these to those, its quantity is neither increased nor diminished. We take our argument from the immutability of God; let us see whether the adversary weakens it.

units.la: CCCXVIII. Inquit (p. 245.) Immutabilitas Dei non violatur mutatione operum suorum. Non est in se mutabilis factus, cum mundum ex nihilo creavit.
units.tr: 318. He says (p. 245): The immutability of God is not violated by a change in his works. He is not made mutable in himself, since he created the world out of nothing.

units.la: Resp. Per se manifesta est hujus Propositionis secunda pars, ut nempe statuamus, Nullam in universo variationem esse quantitatis motus, quamdiu nec ratio nec revelatio aliquam mutationem docet. Similiter ac tamdiu statuitur sensus alicujus orationis proprius, quamdiu nulla necessitas ab eo recedere cogit. Potuisset itaque etiam ista Propositio sine probatione tanquam notio communis admitti. Cartesius tamen fundamentum istius veritatis in immutabilitate Dei consistere ex superabundanti demonstrat, hoc modo: Qui est constans & immutabilis, illius operibus nulla debet tribui mutatio, nisi quam evidens experientia vel divina revelatio certam reddit. At motus quantitatem variari, ita ut Deus partem nunc interire sinat, nunc novam vicissim creet, nec divina revelatio, nec evidens experientia certum reddit. E. id non est statuendum. Major probatur exinde, quòd quanta maxima potest conformitas operantis & operationis est agnoscenda: item, quia ubi variatio, ibi quædam imperfectio: at qui est immutabilis etiam perfectus est, qui autem perfectus est, is talia opera condit, ut sint durabilia. Variatio autem, quam evidens docet experientia, non pugnat cum Dei immutabilitate & constantiâ, quia non pugnat cum legibus naturæ, sed ex ipsis oritur, iisque est conformis. Variatio, quam revelatio testatur, eo ipso creditur non obesse divinæ immutabilitati, etsi id percipere non queamus. Et sanè simili modo Theologi ex immutabilitate Dei, immutabilitatem fidei, justificationis & sanctificationis solent colligere, quod argumentum, si nostrum non procedat, similiter claudicare erit dicendum.
units.tr: Reply. The second part of this proposition is evident in itself, namely that we hold: There is no variation in the quantity of motion in the universe, so long as neither reason nor revelation teaches any change. In the same way, the proper sense of any sentence is held to be fixed so long as no necessity compels us to depart from it. So this proposition too could have been admitted without proof, as a common notion. Nevertheless Descartes, out of abundance, demonstrates the foundation of this truth as resting on the immutability of God, in this way: To whatever is constant and immutable, no change ought to be ascribed in its works, except what clear experience or divine revelation makes certain.
