But that the quantity of motion varies, so that God now allows a part to perish and again now creates a new part, is made certain neither by divine revelation nor by clear experience. Therefore it is not to be affirmed. The major premise is proved as follows: because the greatest possible conformity between the agent and the operation must be recognised; likewise, because where there is variation there is some imperfection; but what is immutable is also perfect, and what is perfect constructs such works as are durable. The variation, however, which clear experience teaches does not conflict with God's immutability and constancy, because it does not conflict with the laws of nature but arises from them and conforms to them. A variation which revelation attests is for that very reason believed not to hinder the divine immutability, even though we cannot perceive how. And indeed, in a similar way, theologians are accustomed to infer from the immutability of God the immutability of faith, of justification and of sanctification; if our argument does not hold, that argument too must be said to limp in the same way.

units.la: PROPOSITIO VIII.
units.tr: PROPOSITION VIII.

units.la: CCCXIX. Unaquaque res, quantum in ipsâ est, semper manet in eodem statu, sicque quod semel movetur, semper moveri pergit art. 37. Hæc Propositio videtur naturâ nota esse, neque demonstratione indigere, sed tantùm hâc cautione, nisi ab alio ex illo statu deturbetur, vel in motu impediatur. Quare enim moveri cessaret, si nulla sit causa, quæ motum impedias?
units.tr: 319. Every thing, so far as it is in itself, always remains in the same state, and so what has once been set in motion always continues to move; art. 37. This proposition seems to be known by nature and to need no demonstration, only this caution: unless it is thrown out of that state by another, or hindered in its motion. For why would it cease to move, if there is no cause which might impede the motion?

units.la: SCHOLIUM.
units.tr: SCHOLIUM.

units.la: CCCXX. Hanc exagitat (B. p. 246.) & cum Methodo Mathematica non convenire inquit. Cui responsionis loco inservire potest, quod ab initio ad præcedentem Propositionem annotavimus.
units.tr: 320. He (B. p. 246.) attacks this, saying it does not agree with the mathematical method. In place of a reply, what we noted at the beginning, on the preceding proposition, can serve.

units.la: Pergit, videtur ea Propositio fere in omnibus sublunaribus falsa esse.
units.tr: He goes on: this proposition seems to be false in almost all things below the moon.

units.la: Resp. Naturâ nota esse videtur omnibus iis, quæ præjudicia sensuum & infantiæ depositerunt, falsa verò esse videtur hominibus, qui, postquam ab ineunte ætate judicarunt eos motus, qui à causis, quæ nostros sensus latent, sistebantur, sua sponte desinere, nitentes hac fallaci regulâ: Quas causas sensibus non percipio, ea non sunt, quique postea illud de omnibus existimant, quod videntur in multis esse experti.
units.tr: Reply: It seems known by nature to all those who have laid aside the prejudices of the senses and of infancy; but it seems false to those men who, having judged from early age that those motions which were halted by causes hidden from our senses cease of their own accord, and resting on this deceptive rule, Those causes which I do not perceive by the senses do not exist, afterwards judge this of all things, because they seem to have experienced it in many.

units.la: CCCXXI. Ad meam rationem, quare moveri cessaret &c. respondet, hoc fieri, quod vis à motore corpori moto impressa sensim evanescit, cum & hic locum habeat illud vulgare, nullum violentum est diuturnum.
units.tr: 321. To my reason, why it would cease to move, etc., he replies that this happens because the force impressed on the moved body by the mover gradually fades away, since here too that common saying holds, that nothing violent is lasting.

units.la: Resp. Meæ rationis vis hæc est, Quod non habet causam, ob quam moveri cesset, illud pergit moveri; at quælibet res mota in se nullam habet causam, ut in motu impediatur, nec supponitur alia impediens. E. quæ erat refutanda. 2. Objectio ejus nullius est momenti; nam vis illa à primo motore impressa, ut sensim dicatur evanescere, absurdum est. Nec enim illa vis aliud est quam ipse motus, qui, prout paulo post est futurus, vis vel potentia potest appellari. 3. Et quid moveret Deum eam creare motûs quantitatem, cui aliquid demendum sibi sciret in posterum? Si enim postea evanesceret motus, quem Deus corpori impressit, demeret Deus de quantitate motûs, atque sic cessaret ab opere, quod sapientissime constituerat is, qui est immutabilis. 4. Violenti vox dupliciter potest accipi, vel pro eo quod pugnat cum aliquâ alicujus rei naturâ, vel pro eo quod pendet à causâ externâ. Nullum violentum est diuturnum, priori sensu verum est, posteriori falsum: at posteriori modo, non priori motus potest dici violentus.
units.tr: Reply: The force of my reasoning is this: what has no cause for ceasing to move continues to move; but any moved thing has in itself no cause by which it is hindered in its motion, nor is any hindering agent supposed. Therefore what was to be refuted. 2. His objection is of no weight; for that force impressed by the first mover, supposing it gradually fades, is absurd. For that force is nothing other than the motion itself, which, as it will be a little later, can be called force or power. 3. And what would move God to create a quantity of motion which He knew would have to be diminished in the future? For if the motion which God impressed on the body were afterwards to fade, God would be diminishing the quantity of motion, and so would cease from the work which He who is immutable had most wisely established. 4. The word violent can be taken in two ways: either for what conflicts with the nature of some thing, or for what depends on an external cause. "Nothing violent is lasting" is true in the former sense, false in the latter; but in the latter sense, not in the former, can motion be called violent.

units.la: CCCXXII. Pergit adversarius, (p. 247.) & exempla affert trochi, & eorum, quæ in longum projiciuntur, quibus putat se confirmare posse suam con- tra hanc propositionem oppositionem, ad quæ quoniam sufficiens responsio haberi potest ex iis, quæ à Cartefio art. 37. & 38. dicuntur, lectorem eò remitto, quamvis etiam initio hujus scholii ista Objectio à nobis sit præoccupata. CCCXXIII. Quærit tandem, quare non usu fuerim ratione Cartefii, putatque eam a me non habitam fuisse pro firma & sufficienti.
units.tr: 322. The adversary goes on (p. 247.) and brings forward examples of a top and of things thrown far, by which he thinks he can confirm his objection against this proposition. Since a sufficient reply can be drawn from what Descartes says in art. 37 and 38, I refer the reader there, although at the beginning of this scholium we have already anticipated this objection. 323. Finally he asks why I did not use Descartes' reasoning, and thinks I did not hold it to be firm and sufficient.

units.la: Resp. Hæc Propositio sufficienter per se erat clara, quia communi axiomate nitebatur, Nihil fieri sine causa, itaque alteram rationem non adhibui. 2. Sed ut videat, me non rejicere, eam nunc subjungo, hoc modo. Cui Deus conservat perfectionem semel datam, illud nunquam sponte & per se eam abjicit, sed si abjiciat, hoc alii imputandum est. At Deus & rei motæ, & rei quiescenti conservat hanc perfectionem, nempe motum illi, huic quietem. E. Min. prob. Qui est constans & immutabilis, illum, quod semel dedit, conservare, statuendum est, nisi evidens ratio de mutatione certum quem reddat, quæ est, quando aliud corpus externam rem de suo statu deturbat. Illudque eodem modo clarum potest reddi, quo probatio præcedentis Propositionis.
units.tr: Reply: This proposition was of itself sufficiently clear, because it rested on the common axiom, Nothing happens without a cause; therefore I did not employ the other reason. 2. But so that he may see that I do not reject it, I now add it, in this way. He to whom God preserves a perfection once given never casts it off of his own accord and by himself; but if he does cast it off, this must be imputed to another. But God preserves this perfection both for the moved thing and for the thing at rest, namely motion to the one, rest to the other. Therefore the minor premise is proved. Whoever is constant and immutable must be held to preserve what he has once given, unless a clear reason makes a change certain, which is when another body drives an external thing out of its state. And this can be made clear in the same way as the proof of the preceding proposition.

units.la: CCCXXIV. Hic porrò arripit adversarius terminum immobilitatis à Cartefio usurpatum, quem insolentem & hactenus Theologia inauditum inquit; sed sciat, cum potuisse in genere usurpari, prout ab adversariis motus usurpatur pro omni mutatione: ut sic similiter Immobilitas idem esset, quod Immutabilitas. Atque ea vox usurpatur à Parćo Theologo in commentario Epistolæ ad Romanos cap. 1. ad versum 19. prope finem, qui inquit: Ostendit ea (puta cognitio Dei naturalis) hominibus utcunque, quod sit Deus, quod sit æterna & immobilis substantia &c. I nunc & dic, hunc terminum Theologis inauditum. Argumentum vero Cartesii quale sit hic est declaratum, ut frustra illud arrodat, transformet, & debile reddat adversarius, quantum potest.
units.tr: 324. Here moreover the adversary seizes on the term immobility, used by Descartes, which he calls unusual and hitherto unheard of in theology; but let him know that it could be used in general, just as motion is used by our opponents for every change, so that immobility would likewise be the same as immutability. And this word is used by the theologian Pareus in his commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, chapter 1, near the end on verse 19, who says: It shows them (namely the natural knowledge of God) in some measure to men, that God is an eternal and immovable substance, etc. Go now and say that this term is unheard of among theologians. The argument of Descartes, however, is here set out in such a way that the adversary, as far as he can, gnaws at it in vain, transforms it, and makes it weak.

units.la: PROPOSITIO IX.
units.tr: PROPOSITIO IX.

units.la: CCCXXV. Omnis motus ex se ipso est rectus, & ideo, quæ circulariter moventur, tendunt semper, ut recedant a centro sui circuli, quem describunt, idque obtinent, nisi ab aliis corporibus impediantur, art. 39. Cum enim Deus motus sit primaria causa (per prop 7.) ex Simplicitate Dei colligere licet, talem inditurum fuisse, qui maximè sit simplex, qualis solus est rectus. Ipsa experientia etiam hanc Propositionem confirmat. Ita enim lapis in funda circumrotatus in quavis parte circuli, etiam superiori, (ne dicas id à gravitate pendere) tendit semper, ut à manu secundùm lineam rectam recedat.
units.tr: CCCXXV. Every motion is of itself straight, and therefore bodies that move in a circle always tend to recede from the centre of the circle they describe, and they keep this tendency unless other bodies impede them, art. 39. For since God is the primary cause of motion (by prop. 7), we may infer from the simplicity of God that he would impart a motion that is most simple, and such is only the straight one. Experience itself also confirms this proposition. For a stone whirled in a sling, at any point of the circle, even the highest (do not say that this depends on gravity), always tends to leave the hand along a straight line.

units.la: SCHOLIUM.
units.tr: SCHOLIUM.

units.la: CCCXXVI. Exc. (B. p. 250.) negando, quod ea propositio in omnibus subjectis locum habeat, quia, inquit, corpora cælestia nullam ex se ipsis habeant inclinationem ad recessum a centro.
units.tr: CCCXXVI. Excerpt (B. p. 250.): denying that this proposition holds for all subjects, because, he says, the heavenly bodies have no inclination of their own to recede from the centre.

units.la: Resp. Cùm de omni motu loquatur Propositio ejusque demonstratio, ex vi universalitatis etiam motui cœlestium corporum talis competit proprietas. Cur autem Planetæ non ulterius recedant demonstratum à Cartesio, in specie verò de Luna à me quoque Prop. 28. Idem Cartesius rationem reddit, quare stellæ fixæ centra sua non deserant, quæ ratio non obstat, quò minùs sua natura habeant inclinationem ad motum rectum. Propositionem istam primo demonstravi ex Simplicitate Dei, dein auctarii loco etiam per ipsam experientiam, valdeque errat B. p. 25. quòd primum argumentum in duo dispertit, ut vim ejus enervet. Est verò meum argumentum, si omnino ad syllogismum reduci velit tale. Qui est simplex, ejus operibus nulla tribui debet irregularitas & difformitas, nisi quam evidens experientia, & divina revelatio certam reddit: Atqui motus est opus Dei Simplicis: E. ut à Deo inditur, non potest esse nisi maximè regularis & simplex, qualis est rectus. Ut autem varietur, id habet non quatenus à Deo inditur, sed quatenus communicatur cum aliis corporibus, poribus, Maj. probatur simili ratione, quâ argumentum circa priorem Propof. probatum. Atque hæc Major non est inepta, ut clamat B. p. 251. modo legitimè proponatur, non ut hi ab adversario.
units.tr: Reply: Since the proposition and its demonstration speak of every motion, by the force of its universality such a property belongs also to the motion of the heavenly bodies. Why the planets do not recede further has been demonstrated by Descartes, and in particular concerning the Moon, by me also in prop. 28. The same Descartes gives the reason why the fixed stars do not abandon their centres, and this reason does not prevent them from having, by their nature, an inclination to straight motion. I first demonstrated this proposition from the simplicity of God, and then, by way of an addition, from experience itself. And he greatly errs (B. p. 25) in dividing my first argument into two parts, in order to weaken its force. My argument, if it must be reduced to a syllogism at all, runs thus: What is simple should not be credited with any irregularity or unevenness in its works, except what clear experience and divine revelation make certain. But motion is a work of the simple God. Therefore, insofar as it is imparted by God, it cannot be anything but most regular and simple, such as straight motion is. That it is varied, however, it has not from being imparted by God, but from being communicated with other bodies and pores. The major premise is proved by a reasoning similar to that by which the argument about the earlier proposition was proved. And this major premise is not absurd, as he cries out (B. p. 251), provided it is properly stated, and not in the way the adversary states it.

units.la: CCCXXVII. Pergit B. p. 252. Equidem similiter ex aliis attrib. licet argumentari. Deus est æternus, immensus, omnipotens, ergo tales etiam sunt ejus creatura.
units.tr: CCCXXVII. He goes on, B. p. 252: Indeed, one may argue in the same way from the other attributes. God is eternal, immense, omnipotent; therefore his creatures are also such.

units.la: Resp. Nullum dubium, quin ex attributis Dei quibuscunque simili modo liceat inferre, Deum in operibus suis similitudinem suorum attributorum, quantum fieri potest, expressisse, & quantum creaturæ istius sunt capaces, quamdiu vel evidens experientia, vel divina revelatio contrarium non suadeat. Quanta enim potest maxima conformitas operantis & operationis est agnoscenda.
units.tr: Reply: There is no doubt that from any of God's attributes one may in the same way infer that God has expressed the likeness of his attributes in his works, as far as this is possible, and as far as creatures are capable of it, so long as clear experience or divine revelation does not suggest otherwise. For the greatest possible conformity between the agent and the action must be acknowledged.

units.la: Reliqua quæ contra Cart. art. 39. à nobis citatum objicit p. 253. inde oriuntur, quòd argumentum non perceperit, quare ad ea non opus est aliâ responsione, quàm, quæ suprà est facta, argumenti nempe legitimæ propositione.
units.tr: The remaining objections he raises against Descartes, art. 39, which we cited, on p. 253, arise from the fact that he has not grasped the argument. Therefore no other answer is needed for them than the one already given above, namely the proper statement of the argument.

units.la: CCCXXVIII. Tandem Cartesii verba art. 39. arrodit. Neque enim illum (scil. motum Deus) conservat, nisi præcise qualis est eo ipso temporis momento, quo conservat, nulla habita ratione ejus, qui forte fuit paulo ante. Quorum hic est sensus. Probat ex simplicitate Dei simplicitatem operationis Dei in indendo & conservando motu tali, quo materia tendat moveri secundùm lineas rectas, & nequis dicat, fieri nihilominus, ut multiplici modo corpora cogantur deflectere ob occursum aliorum, respondet, Dei conservationem, ex quâ oritur simplicitas motûs, præcise respicere motum in se & suâ naturâ consideratum, adeoque ex illâ habiturum, ut ex se tendat secundum lineas rectas, etsi forte ante propter occursum aliorum corporum hoc non potuerit obtinere. Hæc interpretatio si attendatur, apparebit aëra exdere B. p. 254. suâ objectione contra verba ista, quod manifestum evadet. si lector benevolus conferre dignetur. Vim corporibus inditam, qua se ipsa moveant negamus, solarum creaturarum rationalium hoc statuentes esse privilegium, ut internum habeant propriumque agendi principium.
units.tr: CCCXXVIII. Finally, he nibbles at the words of Descartes, art. 39: For God does not conserve it (scil. the motion) except precisely as it is at that very moment of time in which he conserves it, with no account taken of what it perhaps was a little before. Their sense is this. From the simplicity of God he proves the simplicity of God's action in imparting and conserving a motion by which matter tends to move along straight lines. And if someone should say that it nonetheless happens that bodies are compelled to deflect in many ways because of the collision of others, he replies that God's conservation, from which the simplicity of motion arises, looks precisely at motion considered in itself and in its own nature. Hence it will have, from that nature, the tendency to move of itself along straight lines, even if perhaps before, on account of the collision of other bodies, it could not attain this. If this interpretation is attended to, it will appear that in his objection against these words, on p. 254, he clearly errs, as will become manifest if the kindly reader deigns to compare. We deny that a force impressed on bodies, by which they move themselves, exists; we hold that an internal and proper principle of acting is the privilege of rational creatures alone.

units.la: PROPOSITIO X.
units.tr: PROPOSITION X.

units.la: CCCXXIX. Corpus alteri fortiori occurrendo, quod propellere non potest, nihil amittit de suo motu, sed tantum determinationem aliam accepit: occurrendo vero minus forti, tantum amittit, quantum in illud transfert art. 40. Nulla enim ratio est, cur amitteret, quia alteri non communicat, sed manet in illo suo statu motus (per prop. 8.) Tantum etiam amittere, quantum transfert, exinde cognoscitur, quia non potest retinere illud, quod alteri communicavit.
units.tr: CCCXXIX. A body that meets a stronger body, which it cannot push back, loses nothing of its motion but only receives a different direction; but when it meets a weaker body, it loses exactly as much as it transfers to that body. Art. 40. For there is no reason why it should lose anything, since it does not communicate it to the other body, but remains in its own state of motion (by prop. 8). That it loses exactly as much as it transfers is known from this: it cannot retain what it has communicated to another.

units.la: SCHOLIUM.
units.tr: SCHOLIUM.

units.la: CCCXXX. Exc. B. Haec propositio repugnat experientiae: detur enim globus explosus e tormento inhaerens vallo vel parieti, quae propellere nequit, revera motum suum amittit, ut & sagitta, &c. similiter ut rota quae vehementer mota ligno vel alio instrumento puncto temporis sistitur.
units.tr: CCCXXX. Exc. B. This proposition contradicts experience. For suppose a cannonball, fired from a gun, lodges in a rampart or wall, which it cannot push; it truly loses its motion, as does an arrow, etc., just as a wheel moving violently is brought to rest in an instant by a piece of wood or another instrument.

units.la: Resp. Hic vero iterum laborat isto praejudicio adversarius, quo circa prop. 8. eum laborasse ostendimus, nimirum, quia sensibus non percipit, quibus corporibus motus globi tormentarii, sagittae & rotae communicetur; itaque communicari negat. Sciat ergo, globum tormento explosum & sagittam primo quidem, dum moventur per aërem, tantundem motus, quantum ipsa amiserunt, aëri communicasse, & infixa vallo vel parieti non quidem propulisse tota, sed tantum partes v. g. muri & valli propulisse eas, quae locum fecerant globo & sagittae, illas vero partes aëri circumstanti, quod acceperant motus, reddidisse; ut hoc experimento prob. nostra non refutetur, quae firma demonstratione est fulta, hactenus frustra ab adversario impetita. Similiter rota mota sistitur à ligno, sed ita, ut partem sui motus ligno, partem manui & partem aëri circumstanti communicet.
units.tr: Reply. Here again the adversary labours under the same prejudice under which we showed him labouring in prop. 8, namely that, because he does not perceive with his senses to which bodies the motion of the cannonball, the arrow and the wheel is communicated, he denies that it is communicated at all. Let him know, then, that a cannonball fired from a gun, and an arrow, while they move through the air, first communicate to the air as much motion as they themselves lose; and when they lodge in a rampart or wall, they do not push the whole of it, but only push those parts of the wall and rampart which made room for the ball or arrow, and those parts in turn pass on to the surrounding air the motion they had received. So this experiment does not refute our proof, which rests on a firm demonstration and has hitherto been assailed by the adversary in vain. Similarly, a wheel that is moving is brought to rest by the wood, but in such a way that it communicates part of its motion to the wood, part to the hand, and part to the surrounding air.

units.la: PROPOSITIO XI.
units.tr: PROPOSITION XI.

units.la: CCCXXXI. Omne fluidum corpus est divisum in multas particulas exiguas, motibus à se mutuo diversis agitatas, art. 54. Hoc enim vocamus corpus fluidum, quod facile cedit alteri corpori moto. At cum motus motui non sit contrarius, quies vero sit, facile percipitur, id corpus, quod jam in motu est, facilius cedere alteri corpori, quam illud, quod quiescit. Ergo quanto minus quiescit, tanto facilius cedit, quod fieri manifestum est, si constet particulis exiguis, motibus à se mutuo diversis agitatis.
units.tr: CCCXXXI. Every fluid body is divided into many tiny particles, agitated by motions that differ from one another, art. 54. For we call a body fluid when it readily yields to another body that is moving. But since motion is not contrary to motion, whereas rest is, it is easily perceived that a body already in motion yields more readily to another body than one that is at rest. Therefore the less a body is at rest, the more readily it yields. This is clearly seen if it consists of tiny particles agitated by motions that differ from one another.

units.la: SCHOLIUM.
units.tr: SCHOLIUM.

units.la: CCCXXXII. Exc. (B. p. 256.) Haec mea & Cartesii definitio fluidorum dorum si sit vera, se non videre quomodo cineres & farina & arena non etiam inter fluida poßint referri.
units.tr: CCCXXXII. Objection (B. p. 256.) If my definition of fluids, and that of Descartes, is true, I do not see why ashes, flour and sand cannot also be counted among fluids.

units.la: Resp. Omnia mundi corpora in universum in has duas species possunt distpesci, ut eorum alia sint dura, alia fluida; atque ea à posterioi sic definiuntur à Cartesio. Fluida, quod eorum partes facile recedant ex suis locis, atque ideo manibus nostris versus illa motis non resistant. Dura, quod eorum partes ita sibi mutuò cohærent, ut non sine vi, quæ sufficiat ad istam illorum cohærentiam superandam, sejungi possint. A priori verò, quod Fluida sint corpora divisa in multas exiguas particulas motibus à se mutuo diversis agitatas. Dura verò, quorum omnes particulæ juxta se mutuo quiescunt. Hæc sunt duo extrema & immediatè opposita: at inter ea multa sunt intermedia corpora, nec perfectè dura, alia magis ad fluida accedentia, aliaque etiam intermediam naturam obtinentia: unde apparet, quid de farina, arena, cinere & similibus sit statuendum, nimirum, nulla ex his esse perfectè fluida vel dura, sed respectu interjacentis materiæ mobilis & subtilis, quæ particulas farinæ & cineris circumdat, dici fluida, si tanta ejus sit copia, ut illas particulas secum movere possit, sin minus, singulas quidem particulas farinæ, singulas arenulas dici dura, sed respectu circumstantis materiæ totam massam farinæ &c. mixtum quid ex duro & fluido posse appellari. 2. Confundit antagonista communi errore in Philosophia fluidum cum humido, quæ tamen valdè sunt diversa, cum etiam sicca possint esse fluida, ut ignis, materia Solis & stellarum.
units.tr: Answer. All bodies in the world can be divided in general into these two kinds, so that some are hard and others fluid. Descartes defines them as follows. Fluid is that whose parts readily withdraw from their places, and so do not resist our hands when they are moved toward them. Hard is that whose parts cohere with one another so firmly that they cannot be separated without a force sufficient to overcome that cohesion. Or, from the other side, fluids are bodies divided into many tiny particles agitated by motions that differ from one another, whereas hard bodies are those whose particles all rest beside one another. These are two extremes and directly opposed. But between them lie many intermediate bodies, not perfectly hard, some approaching fluids more closely and others having an intermediate nature. From this it is clear what must be said of flour, sand, ashes and similar things: none of them is perfectly fluid or hard, but in relation to the intervening mobile and subtle matter that surrounds the particles of flour and ash, they may be called fluid if there is so great an amount of it that it can move those particles along with it; otherwise the single particles of flour and the single grains of sand are called hard, though in relation to the surrounding matter the whole mass of flour, etc., may be called a mixture of the hard and the fluid. 2. The opponent, through a common error in philosophy, confuses fluid with liquid, which are nonetheless very different, since dry things can also be fluid, as fire and the matter of the Sun and stars.

units.la: CCCXXXIII. Excipit præterea B. p. 257. contra Propof. demonstrationem. Motus species revera sibi contrariari, quales sint antrorsum & retrorsum, dextrorsum & sinistrorsum, sursum & deorsum &c.
units.tr: CCCXXXIII. Moreover, he objects (B. p. 257.) against the demonstration of the proposition: Kinds of motion really are contrary to one another, such as forward and backward, rightward and leftward, upward and downward, etc.

units.la: Resp. Quomodo motus motui non sit contrarius, intelligere licet ex Cartesio art. 43. & 44. Is art. 43. ostendit, quod vis cujusque corporis ad agendum in aliud, vel ad alterius actioni resistendum, in hoc uno consistat, quod unaquæque res tendat, quantum in se est, ad permanendum in eodem statu, in quo est. Unde colligere licet, motum per se, ut talem, non esse alteri contrarium. Contraria ergò corpora esse sibi invicem, quando unum alterum de illo statu, in quo est, expellere conatur. Quod non fit per duorum corporum motum, quatenus is in se spectatur; sed contrarietas est inter motum & quietem, item inter motum celerem & tardum, non respectu motûs, sed respectu quietis, de quâ motus tardus participat. Dein, contrarietas est inter determinationem motûs versus unam partem, & occursum corporis ad illam partem quiescentis, vel aliter ter moti, tardius nempe, vel dissentiente determinatione. Si enim talia duo corpora sibi invicem occurrant, conatur unum alterum impedire in eo statu in quo est, quò facit obj. adducta, quæ mihi propterea non contrariatur, sed ex male intellecta mea mente procedit.
units.tr: Answer. How motion is not contrary to motion may be understood from Descartes, art. 43 and 44. Article 43 shows that the power of each body to act upon another, or to resist the action of another, consists in this alone: that each thing tends, as far as it is in itself, to remain in the state in which it is. From this it may be gathered that motion, as such, considered in itself, is not contrary to another motion. Bodies are therefore contrary to one another when one tries to drive the other out of the state in which it is. This does not happen through the motion of two bodies, so far as that is considered in itself; rather, contrariety lies between motion and rest, and likewise between swift and slow motion, not with respect to motion but with respect to rest, in which the slower motion partakes. Next, contrariety lies between the direction of a motion toward one part and the encounter of a body that is at rest toward that part, or moving otherwise, namely more slowly, or in a differing direction. For if two such bodies meet one another, each tries to impede the other in the state in which it is. This is what the objection adduced does; but that contrariety is not mine, and it arises from my mind being misunderstood.

units.la: Exemplum de duobus globis ejusdem magnitudinis & gravitatis eadem vi actis, ita ut unus ab oriente in occidentem, alter ab occidente in orientem moveatur, quos, si sibi mutuo occurrant & in puncto oppositionis contingant, putat B. p. 257. quieturos, alienum est, & cum omni ratione pugnat; nam tali posito casu, ista corpora reflecterentur, & pergerent moveri retro, versus illos terminos, unde venerant. Alienum est, quia non ego, quin sit contrarietas inter duo corpora versus invicem mota, respectu nempe ejusmodi determinationis. Et, si præterea supponas, ea duo corpora esse perfecte dura, item à reliquis omnibus sic divisa, ut eorum motus à nullis aliis circumjacentibus impedirentur, nec juvarentur, post occursum & reflexionem pergerent ita moveri versus illas partes, à quibus venerant, nullâ parte suæ celeritatis amissâ. Vide hæc clarissimè demonstrata à Cartef. Pp. II. art. 45, 46.
units.tr: The example of two globes of the same size and weight, driven with the same force, so that one moves from east to west and the other from west to east, which, if they meet one another and touch at the point of opposition, B. p. 257. thinks will come to rest, is foreign to the matter and contradicts all reason. For in such a case those bodies would be reflected and would go on moving back toward the places from which they came. It is foreign, because I do not deny that there is contrariety between two bodies moving toward each other, namely with respect to that kind of direction. And if you suppose besides that these two bodies are perfectly hard, and separated from all the rest so that their motion is hindered or helped by no other surrounding bodies, then after the meeting and the reflection they would continue to move toward those parts from which they came, without losing any part of their speed. See this most clearly demonstrated by Descartes, Principles II, art. 45, 46.

units.la: CCCXXXIV. Porrò hic nescio quod (B. p. 258.) argumentum mihi affingit: In Syllogismum, inquit, si redigatur meum argumentum, talem fore ejus formam. Quod corpus facilius cedit corpori quiescenti, illud jam est in motu, corpus fluidum facilius cedit corpori quiescenti. Ergo. cùm tale quid ex demonstratione meâ elici non posset: si tamen forte sit προὸεγμα, ut pro quiescenti voluerit scribere moto, dico sequens argumentum ex istâ meâ demonstratione debere formari. Quod facilè cedit corpori moto, illud non quiescit, sed est in motu, & quò facilius cedit, eo minus de quiete participat, cujus ratio est, quia, si quiesceret, non cederet facile, propterea quod quies motui sit contraria, non verò ipse motus in se consideratus. Sed, inquit, dicimus, ad facilem cessionem corporum sufficere, si particulæ à se mutuo vel sint distinctæ, vel facillimè possint separari, ut videre est in ligno, quod totum durum est; at si ferrae in particulas minutas dissecetur, facile movetur, & eo facilius, quo particulæ sunt minores, fragmentis tamen nullum motum indidit ferra, sed ea tantum secavit, & à se mutuo divulsit.
units.tr: CCCXXXIV. Next, he attributes to me here some argument I do not know (B. p. 258.): If my argument, he says, is reduced to a syllogism, its form would be this: A body that yields more readily to a body at rest is already in motion; a fluid body yields more readily to a body at rest. Therefore. Since no such thing can be drawn from my demonstration, yet if perhaps this is the assumption [πρόσλημμα], as he wished to write moving instead of at rest, I say that the following argument should be formed from my demonstration: What readily yields to a moving body is not at rest but is in motion, and the more readily it yields, the less it partakes of rest. The reason is that if it were at rest, it would not yield readily, because rest is contrary to motion, not motion considered in itself. But, he says, we say that for the easy yielding of bodies it is enough that their particles are either distinct from one another or can very easily be separated, as can be seen in wood, which is wholly hard; yet if iron is cut into tiny particles, it moves easily, and the more easily the smaller the particles are. The iron, however, imparts no motion to the fragments, but only cuts them and tears them apart from one another.

units.la: Resp. Verùm, si mea demonstratio recte percipiatur, hæc mihi nihil contrariantur. Antea visum est, inter corpora perfecte dura & fluida esse varia intermedia corpora, quæ partim de natura duri, partim de natura fluidi, participant. Sed quò facilius cedunt corpori moto, eo magis fluida sunt judicanda, quò minùs eò minùs, ita quo magis resistunt, eo magis dura, quo minus, eo minus. Lignum non est corpus perfecte durum, rum, sed multos habet poros materiâ fluidâ repletos, quod etiam, quo ejus pori sunt minores, eo majorem duritiem obtinet, ac eo difficilius serræ cedit, prout in ligno Brasiliensi videre est: scobis vero particulæ facilè moventur, quia sunt à se invicem divisæ, & materiâ fluidâ circundatæ, quæ dum movetur, eas secum aufert, uti Cartesius observat de corporibus duris, quæ in fluido sunt posita. Ut autem moveantur deorsum versus, à vi gravitatis habent, sive actione materiæ cœlestis, quæ motum istarum particularum versus terram determinat, prout per eam actionem naturam gravitatis Cart. explicuit. Unde apparet, Maj. meam propositionem ut à me adducta, veram esse, nempe, & corpus, quod est in motu, facilius cedere, quàm quiescens, & , quo facilius cedit, eo minus quiescere. 2. Lignum quiescens non tam facilè cedit corpori moto, quàm quod est in motu, quod longè facilius impelli potest; serra vero non agit in totum lignum simul, sed nunc in has, nunc alias ejus partes, quas separat; interim difficilius agit in eas ante separationem, quando quiescunt, quàm post, quando motum tum à serrâ, tum à gravitate acceperunt. 3. Itaque quod facillimè cedit,& nihil planè resistit corpori moto, illud æquè veloci motu movetur, quàm corpus motum; quod aliquantum resistit, illud tardius movetur; quod magis, adhuc tardius; quod facillimè potest separari, illud minus durum est, ejusque partes minus quiescunt; quod habet particulas à se mutuo distinctas est fluidum, cui corpus durum dum innatat facilius ejus motui obsequitur.
units.tr: Answer. Indeed, if my demonstration is rightly understood, these points do not oppose me in any way. It was shown earlier that between perfectly hard and fluid bodies there are various intermediate bodies, which partake partly of the nature of the hard and partly of the nature of the fluid. But the more readily they yield to a moving body, the more they are to be judged fluid; and the less they yield, the less fluid they are, so that the more they resist, the harder they are, and the less they resist, the less hard. Wood is not a perfectly hard body, but has many pores filled with fluid matter; and the smaller its pores are, the greater its hardness, and the more difficultly it yields to the saw, as may be seen in Brazilwood. But the particles of sawdust are moved easily, because they are divided from one another and surrounded by fluid matter, which, as it moves, carries them away with it, as Descartes observes of hard bodies placed in a fluid. That they move downward, however, they owe to the force of gravity, or to the action of heavenly matter, which determines the motion of these particles toward the earth, as Descartes explained the nature of gravity through that action. From this it is evident that my major premise, as I have stated it, is true: that a body in motion yields more readily than one at rest, and the more readily it yields, the less it is at rest. 2. Wood at rest does not yield so readily to a moving body as what is in motion, which can be pushed far more easily; the saw, moreover, does not act on the whole piece of wood at once, but now on these parts, now on those, which it separates; meanwhile it acts with more difficulty on those parts before they are separated, when they are at rest, than afterward, when they have received motion from both the saw and gravity. 3. Therefore, what yields most readily and resists a moving body in no way at all, is moved with a speed equal to that of the moving body; what resists somewhat is moved more slowly; what resists more, more slowly still; what can be separated most easily is less hard, and its parts are less at rest; what has particles distinct from one another is fluid, and a hard body floating in it yields more easily to its motion.

units.la: PROPOSITIO XII.
units.tr: PROPOSITION XII.

units.la: CCCXXXV. Corpus durum in fluido collocatum defertur à fluido versus eam partem, ad quam ipsum corpus fluidum tendit. art. 61. Vel enim imponetur quiescens, & sic (per propof. 10.) facilè motum accipiet à fluido, quod totum simul versus aliquam partem tendit, quo ipso fluidum illud totum simul fortius erit duro quocunque: vel imponetur cum impetu tendente aliorsum, quàm fluidum, & sic iterum, cum totum fluidum fit fortius, determinationem accipiet versus eam partem, ad quam fluidum fertur, (per candem prop. 10.) vel denique imponetur, ut motus duri determinetur versus eam partem, ad quam fluidum fertur, & sic tanto facilius ab eo poterit deferri.
units.tr: CCCXXXV. A hard body placed in a fluid is carried along by the fluid towards the part to which the fluid itself tends. Art. 61. For either it will be placed at rest, and so (by prop. 10) it will readily receive motion from the fluid, which as a whole tends at once towards some part; and by that very fact the whole fluid will be stronger than any hard body whatever. Or it will be placed with an impetus tending in a different direction from the fluid, and so again, when the whole fluid becomes stronger, it will receive its determination towards the part to which the fluid is carried (by the same prop. 10). Or finally it will be placed so that its motion is determined towards the part to which the fluid is carried, and so it can be carried along by it all the more easily.

units.la: SCHOLIUM.
units.tr: SCHOLIUM.

units.la: CCCXXXVI. B. p. 259. Se posse hanc propositionem totam concedere, si excipiantur ea, quae feruntur in contrarium, sive motu proprio, ut aves in aëre, pisces in aquis &c. sive motu violento, ut naves actae velis & remis.
units.tr: CCCXXXVI. B. p. 259. He says he can grant this whole proposition, if excepted are those things which are carried in the opposite direction, either by their own motion, such as birds in the air, fish in the waters, etc., or by violent motion, such as ships driven by sails and oars.

units.la: Resp. Illa exceptione non erat opus; praesupponitur enim corpus durum in fluido collocatum, & eo modo collocatum relictum, quod per se est manifestum, & sic in secundo casu etiam post impetum acceptum sibi relinquitur: at aves post acceptum iuspetum semper alium atque alium accipiunt, neque eo modo, quo post unum impetum in aëre ponuntur, relinquuntur, sed alium atque alium accipiunt à spiritibus, à quibus alae moventur. Similiter navis remis & velis impulsa non eo modo, quo collocata est, relinquitur, sed semper novum à remis & velis impetum recipit.
units.tr: Reply: That exception was not needed. For a hard body placed in a fluid, and left in the state in which it was placed, is presupposed, and this is evident in itself; and so in the second case also, after receiving its impetus, it is left to itself. But birds, after receiving an impetus, always receive another and another, and they are not left in the state in which they are placed after a single impetus in the air; they receive one impetus after another from the spirits by which their wings are moved. Similarly a ship driven by oars and sails is not left in the state in which it was placed, but always receives a fresh impetus from the oars and sails.

units.la: CCCXXXVII. His propositionibus ex lib. II. Cart. Principiorum tanquam fundamentis generalibus praemissis, nunc ut ad nostrum institutum propius accedamus, utque naturam coelorum & terrae, atque inde huius duplicem delationem cognoscamus, opus est, non, uti nunc sunt in statu suae perfectionis absoluto, uno quasi obtutu ea inspicere, sed prout paulatim fieri potuissent ac debuissent, ex legibus naturae à Deo positis, (si Deus paulatim oriri ea ac fieri voluisset, donec tandem talia evaderent, qualia esse experimur, dum consummata & absoluta sunt,) ea contemplari. Res enim sunt eaedem in fieri, quae in facto esse, eandemque habent naturam, qualem, si successive essent factae, per leges naturae fuissent consecuturae. Nam per ττ fieri acceperunt omnia, quae nunc habent in facto esse, naturam nempe, quae cum principiis & legibus naturae convenit: At talis est ea quae successive iis fuisset tribuenda, quippe quae à Cartesio ostenditur cum legibus naturae convenire. Quod si ergo in fieri res spectemus, easdem illas contemplabimur & perfectius, quoniam quod primo obtutu in iis cernere non possumus variis ordine actibus lustrabimus, & perfectius cognoscemus. Atque ita propter imperfectionem nostri intellectus solet ac debet fieri in quibuscunque rebus. Ita ad hominis naturam perfectius cognoscendam, opus est eum considerare, prout paulatim in utero formatus & perfectus est. Sic planta spectanda prout paulatim e semine orta, & adulta, ultimumque complementum consecuta sit, &, ne dicas, iflam Methodum contemplandi quidem locum habere in iis, quae successive fiunt, quamvis ratio antehac allata generalis sit, do etiam exem-pla. pla eorum, quæ indivisibilia in se sunt, nec tamen à tali consideratione excluduntur. Sic etiamsi Deus homines quosdam in momento regenerat, debemus tamen regenerationem spectare, prout & Theologi faciunt, per varias partes, secundum ordinem naturæ, ut primo intellectus, deinde voluntas illuminentur atque regenerentur. & variis actibus cognitionis & fidei intervenientibus tandem regeneratio plenè perficiatur. Sic resurrectio mortuorum, quamvis momento sit futura, ab Ezechiele 37. cap. ut successiva describitur, & ut talis à nobis potest considerari.
units.tr: CCCXXXVII. Having laid down these propositions from the second book of Descartes' Principles as general foundations, we now need, in order to come closer to our purpose, and to know the nature of the heavens and the earth and hence their twofold motion, not to look at them in a single glance as they now are in the completed state of their perfection, but to contemplate them as they could and ought to have come into being gradually, according to the laws of nature established by God (as if God had wished them to arise and be made gradually, until at last they became such as we experience them to be now that they are finished and complete). For things in the process of becoming are the same as things in existence, and have the same nature which they would have attained, had they been made successively, through the laws of nature. For all the things that now exist were received through becoming, namely a nature which agrees with the principles and laws of nature; and such is the nature which would have been given to them successively, since Descartes shows that it agrees with the laws of nature. If then we regard things in their becoming, we shall contemplate those same things more perfectly, since what we cannot discern in them at a first glance we shall survey through various acts in order, and so know them more perfectly. And so, on account of the imperfection of our intellect, this is and ought to be done in all things whatever. Thus, to know human nature more perfectly, we must consider it as it is gradually formed and perfected in the womb. So a plant is to be viewed as it gradually arises from the seed, grows to maturity, and attains its final completion. And lest you say that this method of contemplation has a place indeed in those things which come to be successively, although the reason stated above is general, I also give examples of things which are indivisible in themselves, and yet are not excluded from such consideration. Thus, even if God regenerates some men in a moment, we must nevertheless consider regeneration, as the theologians also do, through its various parts, according to the order of nature: first the intellect is enlightened, then the will is illuminated and regenerated, and through various intervening acts of knowledge and faith, regeneration is at last fully completed. Likewise the resurrection of the dead, although it is to happen in a moment, is described by Ezekiel in chapter 37 as successive, and as such it can be considered by us.

units.la: CCCXXXVIII. Atque ut paucis absolvam, hanc methodum nostram confirmat quàm maximè consideratio decretorum divinorum inter Theologos frequentata. Norunt ii, ea non, ut inter homines contingit, successivè esse facta, ut unum post alterum prævia deliberatione, ordine quem sapientia dictat, fuerit factum, sed unico & simplicissimo actu, quo Deus omnia intelligit & vult; non tamen verentur ea spectare, ac si sic successivè essent formata, ordinemque in iis constituunt talem, qui legibus sapientiæ est conveniens, si successivè unum post alterum esset lancitum. Quidni ergo licebit opus creationis, de quo saltem constat, quod non momento, sed sex diebus fuerit absolutum, & de quo quæri potest, num non cujuslibet diei opus, etiam successivè fuerit peractum, ita ut totum spatium ⟨Greek⟩ ei consummando fuerit adhibitum, successivè & per partes modo dicto contemplari. Si id licet de operibus Dei internis, quæque cum Deo ipso convertuntur, atque ipsè sunt Deus, quidni licebit circa opera Dei externa, quæ ab ipso Deo realiter differunt? Ac, quemadmodum in decretis divinis necessitatem ea distinguendi nobis imponit imbecillitas nostri intellectus, quod illa unico actu intelligere nequeamus; ita ea ipsa est causa, propter quam opera Dei in creatione, etsi indivisim sint facta, distincte & per partes spectemus. Sicut porro in decretis divinis rationem ordinis inde petit Theologus, quod unus ille actus divinus simplex æquivaleat actibus creatis, quorum unus alterum consequitur consecutione naturali, vel, quod unicus actus divinus multiplicem volendi varietatem eminenter continet. Ita in operibus creationis rationem ordinis inde petit Philosophus, quod una actio divina, momentanea quamvis & indivisa, æquivaleat actibus naturæ, secundum leges à Deo positas, Dei concursu interveniente agentis, quorum unus alterum consequitur consecutione naturali. Ut etiam ratio considerandi varios actus in decretis divinis exinde sumitur, quia in operioperibus illis, de quibus facta sunt decreta, est quædam varietas & successio; ita, quia in operibus naturæ, quæ Deus nunc per naturam operatur, quædam est successio & v. g. stella fixa mutatur in Planetam & Cometam, prout Cartesius demonstravit, etiam ab initio tale quid prius debet concipi. Sicut tandem ordo in decretis divinis secundum leges & regulas sapientiæ divinæ constituitur: ita ordo in operibus creationis secundum leges divinas, quas in natura tulit, est constituendus. Verum cui hæc plenius cognoscere libet, &, quomodo hæc nostra sententia ab adversariorum objectionibus sufficienter sit vindicata, percipere, adeat Exercit. Clausbergii 94---100.
units.tr: CCCXXXVIII. To be brief: our method is strongly confirmed by the consideration of God's decrees, which is frequent among the theologians. They know that these were not made successively, as happens among men, so that one thing was done after another, after prior deliberation, in an order dictated by wisdom; but by a single and most simple act, by which God understands and wills all things. Yet they do not hesitate to regard them as if they had been formed successively, and they set up in them an order which agrees with the laws of wisdom, as if it had been decreed one after another. Why then should it not be permitted to contemplate successively and part by part, in the manner described, the work of creation, of which it is at least certain that it was completed not in a moment but in six days, and about which it can be asked whether the work of each day was not also carried out successively, so that the whole span of time [χρόνον] was devoted to bringing it to completion? If this is allowed concerning God's internal works, which are one with God himself and are God, why should it not be allowed concerning God's external works, which really differ from God himself? And just as the weakness of our intellect obliges us, in the case of the divine decrees, to distinguish them because we cannot understand them by one act, so that very weakness is the cause for which we consider the works of God in creation distinctly and part by part, even though they were made without division. Furthermore, just as the theologian derives the ground of order in the divine decrees from the fact that that one simple divine act is equivalent to created acts, of which one follows another by natural succession, or from the fact that a single divine act eminently contains the manifold variety of willing; so the philosopher derives the ground of order in the works of creation from the fact that one divine action, though momentary and undivided, is equivalent to acts of nature according to the laws established by God, acting with God's concurrence, of which one follows another by natural succession. Likewise, just as the reason for considering the various acts in the divine decrees is taken from the fact that in those works concerning which the decrees were made there is a certain variety and succession, so, because in the works of nature, which God now works through nature, there is a certain succession (for example, a fixed star is changed into a planet and a comet, as Descartes demonstrated), such a thing must also be conceived from the beginning. Finally, just as the order in the divine decrees is established according to the laws and rules of divine wisdom, so the order in the works of creation is to be established according to the divine laws which he set down in nature. But whoever wishes to know these things more fully, and to perceive how this our opinion has been sufficiently defended against the objections of its opponents, let him consult the Exercitationes of Clauberg, 94–100.

units.la: CCCXXXIX. Excipit B.p. 260. Ortum rerum naturalium qua in sua Esse à mera creatione dependent à priori considerare, prout sensim oriri possint ac debeant (addere debuisset, quod ego addidi, si Deus ipsa paulatim oriri voluisset) non tantum impossibile & impervestigabile judicamus, sed & id tentare ut temeraria præsumptionis indicium habeamus.
units.tr: CCCXXXIX. He takes exception, B. p. 260: we judge it not only impossible and unsearchable to consider a priori the origin of natural things, which depend in their being on mere creation, as to how they can and ought to arise gradually (he ought to have added what I have added: if God had wished them to arise gradually), but also that to attempt this is a sign of rash presumption.

units.la: Resp. Possibile esse demonstravimus, & facto paulo post ipso ostendemus; debere autem fieri exinde manifestum est, quia alio modo non possunt opera Dei distincte cognosci, nisi earum successivam compositionem saltem possibilem, à primis rudimentis ad ultimam usque perfectionem inspiciamus; præsumptioni vero temerariæ istum agendi modum non esse obnoxium patebit, si quis illum modū procedendi conferat cum modo considerandi Dei decreta, quæ à Theologis spectantur, non prout facta sunt unico actu, sed certo quodam ordine, qui convenienter sapientiæ divinæ est instituendus. Si enim illi temerariæ præsumptionis non possunt accusari, multo minus ii, qui opera Dei, etsi momento essent facta, certo quodam ordine convenienti naturæ ipsarum rerum considerant.
units.tr: Reply: We have demonstrated that it is possible, and we shall show it in fact shortly afterwards. That it ought to be done is clear from this: the works of God cannot otherwise be known distinctly unless we examine their successive composition, at least as a possibility, from the first rudiments to the final perfection. That this way of proceeding is not liable to the charge of rash presumption will be plain if anyone compares this mode of proceeding with the mode of considering God's decrees, which the theologians regard not as made by a single act, but in a certain order which is to be arranged in agreement with divine wisdom. For if those men cannot be accused of rash presumption, much less can those who consider the works of God, even though they were made in a moment, in a certain order suited to the nature of the things themselves.

units.la: CCCXL. Exc. porro B. p. 261. Gloria divina non parum detrahi per hanc sententiam, cum inde sequatur creationem secundam tantum consistere in mechanica motione &c.
units.tr: CCCXL. Exc. porro B. p. 261. The glory of God is not a little diminished by this opinion, since it follows from it that the second creation consists only in mechanical motion, etc.

units.la: Resp. Ad hanc objectionem sufficiens responsio est in schol. Prop. 7. ubi ostendimus, quantum hæc actio divina à Mechanica actione differat, unde etiam patebit, quod Angelis communicari non possit. Sed secundum istos homines gloriæ divinæ detrahitur, si non quælibet commenta, nempe formas substantiales, qualitates reales, vires movendi corporibus inditas, velimus agnoscere, easque ad Deum tanquam auctorem, referre. Gloria divina multò magis elucet, si statuamus, Deum per motum & divisionem, observationemque legum naturæ, quas posuit, tam admirandos effectus potuisse efficere, quam si existimemus, non potuisse eum hæc, quæ videmus effectu, producere sine formis substantialibus, qualitatibus & nescio quibus viribus, per quas semetipsa moveant, quamvis hæc non nisi ab hominibus sint effecta. Quod porrò clamat adversarius: Hæc quæ à me statuuntur esse indigna Theologo Reformato, si de ipsâ meâ sententiâ intelligat, lectori judiciioso cuicunque judicanda relinquo, si verò de consequente, quod ex eâ se educere putat, interpretetur, cum illud minimè consequatur, non est, quod me istius sententiæ pudeat.
units.tr: Reply. A sufficient answer to this objection is in the scholium to Prop. 7, where we showed how far this divine action differs from mechanical action, and from that it will also be clear that it cannot be communicated to angels. But according to these men, the glory of God is diminished unless we acknowledge those fancies, namely substantial forms, real qualities, and powers of moving implanted in bodies, and refer them to God as their author. The glory of God shines out much more if we hold that God, by motion, division and the observance of the laws of nature which he established, could bring about effects as admirable as those we see, than if we think he could not produce these effects without substantial forms, qualities and I know not what powers by which things move themselves, although these are the contrivances of men alone. As for the adversary's outcry that these things which are laid down by me are unworthy of a Reformed theologian: if he means my own opinion, I leave it to any judicious reader to judge; if he interprets it of the consequence he thinks he draws from it, since that does not follow at all, there is no reason I should be ashamed of this opinion.

units.la: CCCXLI. Exc. B. p. 267. Non esse hic quæstionem, an Deus opera uniuscujusque diei unico momento absolverit, an verò eo spatio, quod dies vocatur, produxerit, sed 1. An creatio secunda tantum consistat in materia corporea divisione & motione. 2. An fluidorum natura consistat in motione circa propria centra.
units.tr: CCCXLI. Exc. B. p. 267. The question here is not whether God finished the works of each day in a single moment, or produced them in the space that is called a day, but 1. whether secondary creation consists only in the division and motion of corporeal matter. 2. whether the nature of fluids consists in motion around their own centres.

units.la: Resp. Et ego ipse hanc quæstionem, An Deus opera uniuscujusque diei momento absolverit, in medio relinquo, cum ad negotium nostrum patum faciat ejus determinatio. Verum quæstio in hoc articulo est: An non sicut in decretis divinis divisio & ordo legibus sapientiæ divinæ conveniens, spectatur, licet sint indivisa; ita similiter, licet opera creationis unico momento facta sint, possimus ordinem & divisionem convenientem sapientiæ divinæ & naturæ legibusin iis spectare? quod plane dissimulat adversarius, neque quicquam respondet NB. ad comparationem operum Dei creationis cum decretis divinis à me ita institutam, ut efficacissimum argumentum pro negotio præsenti inde desumeretur. De reliquis autem duabus quæstionibus suo loco est actum, & quid de creatione secundâ statuamus ad Prop. VII. ostensum, & ad Hypoth. tertiam demonstrabitur, quod ad fluida requiratur motio circa propria centra.
units.tr: Reply. I myself leave undecided the question whether God finished the works of each day in a moment, since its determination has little bearing on our business. The question in this article, however, is this: just as in God's decrees division and order, fitting the laws of divine wisdom, are considered although the decrees are undivided, may we not similarly consider in the works of creation, although they were made in a single moment, an order and division fitting divine wisdom and the laws of nature? The adversary plainly evades this, and he makes no reply NB. to the comparison of God's works of creation with his decrees, as I set it up, from which a very powerful argument for the present matter would be drawn. As for the other two questions, they have been dealt with in their place: what we hold about secondary creation was shown at Prop. VII, and it will be demonstrated at the third Hypothesis that motion around their own centres is required for fluids.

units.la: CCCXLII. His ita constitutis, quatuor Hypotheses, sive, si malis, Postulata ad considerationem operum Dei successivam instituendam, præmittemus, quæ quidem facile à quovis possunt admitti, tradita à Cartesio Pp. III. art. 46.
units.tr: CCCXLII. Having thus laid these foundations, we will set down four Hypotheses, or if you prefer, Postulates, for undertaking the successive consideration of God's works. These can readily be admitted by anyone, as taught by Descartes, Pp. III. art. 46.

units.la: Hypothesis sive Postulatum I.
units.tr: Hypothesis or Postulate I.

units.la: Deus materiam illam, ex quâ mundus adspectabilis est factus, unam & eandem omnium corporum existentem (per prop. I.) divisit in varias particulas, ut ita corpus fluidum constituerent (per prop.XI.) Declaratio. Necessario enim requirebatur divisio, ut separatim à se invicem hæ particulæ moveri moveri possent, atque ita, quæ per motum oriuntur, proprietates esse possent. Ante divisionem autem & motum est eadem, & omnes proprietates materiæ ad hoc unum reducuntur, quod sit divisibilis & mobilis. An vero æquales, an inæquales supponanrur istæ particulæ, parum refert, quia qualiscunque figuræ sint, & quantæcunque parvitatis (dummodo ea tanta sit, ut corpus fluidum componant) semper idem secundùm leges naturæ sequetur, ut & Philosophus monet art. 47. sed probabilius tamen est, eas supponere æquales, quia magis æqualitas & ordo Deo convenire videtur.
units.tr: God divided that matter, out of which the visible world was made, and which is one and the same for all bodies (by Prop. I), into various particles, so that they would constitute a fluid body (by Prop. XI). Declaration. For division was necessarily required, so that these particles could be moved separately from one another could be moved, and so that what arises through motion could be properties. Before the division and motion, however, the matter is the same, and all the properties of matter are reduced to this one thing, that it is divisible and movable. Whether these particles are supposed to be equal or unequal matters little, since whatever their shape and however small they are (provided they are small enough to make up a fluid body), the same thing will always follow according to the laws of nature, as the Philosopher also notes in art. 47. Still, it is more probable that they are supposed to be equal, because equality and order seem more fitting to God.

units.la: SCHOLIVM
units.tr: SCHOLIUM

units.la: CCCXLIII. Excipit B. p. 262. Hanc Hypothesin supponere salsissima principia. 1. Materiam omnem in prima productione ex nihilo fuisse eandem, quod repugnat authoritati sacræ.
units.tr: CCCXLIII. B., p. 262, objects: This hypothesis presupposes most absurd principles. 1. That all matter was the same in the first production out of nothing, which contradicts sacred authority.

units.la: · Resp. Ostendi prop. primâ, quod una & eadem sit omnium corporum materia, eandemque Prop. ab Exc. adversarii vindicavi. Quod intelligendum, uti per se patet, de materiâ, quatenus in genere consideratur, & in hoc consistit, quod res sit extensa in longum, latum & profundum; sed non suppono, quod non in primâ creatione quædam jam facta fuerit distinctio istius materiæ. Non enim dico, quid fecerit Deus, & quomodo formaverit corpora (illud enim non determino: An Deus momento uniuscujusque diei fecerit opera? An vero intervallo istius temporis, quod dies vocatur? atque historiam creationis à Mose descriptam immotam relinquo) sed dico tantum, quod ordine debeant corpora à Deo facta considerari, eo modo, quo Theologi dicunt: Deum primum considerasse finem, dein media; quod intelligitur non respecta ipsius Dei, sed in modo nostro considerandi.
units.tr: Reply. I showed in the first proposition that the matter of all bodies is one and the same, and I defended that proposition against the opponent's objection. This must be understood, as is plain in itself, of matter as it is considered in general, and which consists in this, that a thing is extended in length, breadth and depth. But I do not suppose that some distinction of that matter had not already been made in the first creation. For I do not say what God made, or how he formed bodies (I do not determine that: whether God made the works in the moment of each day, or rather in the interval of that time which is called a day; and I leave the account of the creation described by Moses untouched). I say only that the bodies made by God ought to be considered in the order in which the theologians say that God first considered the end and then the means. This is understood not with respect to God himself, but in our manner of considering.

units.la: CCCXLIV. 2. Secundum falsum principium, quod mihi tribuit, est, Creationem secundam tantum consistere in operatione mechanica.
units.tr: CCCXLIV. 2. The second false principle which he attributes to me is: that the second creation consists only in mechanical operation.

units.la: Resp. De eo in schol. prop. 7. sufficienter est actum.
units.tr: Reply. This has been sufficiently dealt with in the scholium to Proposition 7.

units.la: CCCXLV. 3. Tertium falsum principium: Rerum creationem nobis esse perceptibilem, cujus contrarium testatur mortalium sapientissimus Eccl. 3. 11. Ipsum unumquodque facere pulchrum suo tempore etiam quamdiu saeculum est, exponere animo illorum (excepto eo, quod non assequitur homo) opus quod fecit ipse Deus à principio ad finem usque.
units.tr: CCCXLV. 3. The third false principle: that the creation of things is perceptible to us, which the wisest of mortals testifies to the contrary, Eccl. 3. 11: "He has made everything beautiful in its time, and also has set the world in their heart (except that man cannot grasp) the work which God himself has done from the beginning to the end."

units.la: Resp. Et nos concedimus, perfectè opera Dei à nobis cognosci non posse, vide schol, prop. 7. quod tantum testatur Ecclesiastes, sed non negat, ea debere considerari (imo vel hoc ipsum citato in loco confirmat) nec negat, in iis considerandis debere ordinem adhiberi naturæ & sapientiæ divinæ convenientem, prout scriptura non prohibet, ut decreta divina consideremus, & iis spectandis certum ordinem adhibeamus.
units.tr: Reply. We too concede that the works of God cannot be known by us perfectly; see the scholium to Proposition 7. Ecclesiastes testifies only to this, and does not deny that these works ought to be considered (indeed, the very passage cited confirms this). Nor does he deny that in considering them an order should be observed which agrees with the nature and wisdom of God, just as Scripture does not forbid us to consider the divine decrees and to observe a certain order in contemplating them.

units.la: CCCXLVI. Tandem dicit B. disquisitionem esse ridiculam, an particulas supponenda sint æquales, an inæquales, per quas facta est ista divisio, & argumentum pro æqualitate earum esse vanissimum, quod tantum propter authoritatem Cartesii recipiamus.
units.tr: CCCXLVI. Finally, B. says: that the inquiry whether the particles through which that division was made are to be supposed equal or unequal is ridiculous, and that the argument for their equality is most vain, which we accept only because of the authority of Descartes.

units.la: Resp. Parum refert, quid antagonistæ videatur ridiculum, quid serium; facile enim fieri potest, ut ex ridiculis faciat seria, & contra. 2. Argumentatio ab attributis Dei ad ejus operationes, ut quantum fieri potest maximam inter Deum operantem & ejus operationes conformitatem agnoscamus, valida suo loco satis ostensa. Falsissimum est autem & contrarium tot nostris protestationibus, quod nos propter authoritatem Cart. vel minimum arripiamus, cum illud ipsum sit, de quo accusamus alios Philosophos, scientes, quod in Philosophiâ non authoritas humana, sed ratio debeat obtinere.
units.tr: Reply. It matters little what seems ridiculous or serious to the opponent; for it can easily happen that he makes serious things ridiculous, and the reverse. Second, the argument from the attributes of God to his operations, so that we may recognise as far as possible the greatest conformity between God working and his operations, has been shown to be sound in its proper place. It is most false, and contrary to all our protestations, that we accept anything, even the smallest point, merely because of the authority of Descartes, since this is exactly the thing for which we accuse other philosophers, knowing that in philosophy it is not human authority but reason that ought to prevail.

units.la: Hypothesis II.
units.tr: Hypothesis II.

units.la: CCCXLVII. Deus istam materiam ita divisam movit, tantundemque motûs indidit, quantum jam in mundo reperitur. Declaratio. Hoc requirebatur si distincta & varia corpora ex illâ materiâ successivè producere vellet. Posterius patet ex prop. 7.
units.tr: CCCXLVII. God moved this matter, so divided, and imparted to it exactly as much motion as is now found in the world. Declaration. This was required if he wished to produce distinct and varied bodies successively out of that matter. The latter is evident from proposition 7.

units.la: SCHOLIUM.
units.tr: SCHOLIUM.

units.la: CCCXLVIII. Hanc hypothesin ut vanissimam se rejicere, ut propositionem septimam, inquit B. p. 264.
units.tr: CCCXLVIII. Him rejecting this hypothesis as most vain, as the seventh proposition, says B., p. 264.

units.la: Resp. At nos, ut solidissimam ostendimus illam prop. septimam; ita hanc hypothesin convenienter legibus naturæ dicimus constitutam.
units.tr: Reply. But we, just as we have shown that proposition seven is most solid, so we declare this hypothesis to have been established in accordance with the laws of nature.

units.la: Hypothesis III.
units.tr: Hypothesis III.

units.la: CCCXLIX. Deus istas particulas singulas movit circa propria centra separatim. Declaratio. Hoc enim requirebatur ad naturam fluidi (per prop. II.) prop. 11.) quod debere constituere præsupponuntur; item, ut à seinvicem istæ particulæ sejungerentur.
units.tr: CCCXLIX. God moved these individual particles separately, each about its own centre. Declaration. For this was required by the nature of a fluid (by Prop. II and Prop. 11), which must be presupposed to constitute it; and likewise so that these particles should be separated from one another.

units.la: . SCHOLIUM,
units.tr: SCHOLIUM

units.la: CCCL. Ad id, quod toties repetit B. nempe, per hanc meam sententiam Deum transformari in merum tornionem, semel est responsum.
units.tr: CCCL. To what B. repeats so often, namely, that by my view God is transformed into a mere turner, a reply has been given once already.

units.la: 2. Quod ad naturam fluidi, qualetunc poterat spectari, requiratur,ut Deus singulas particulas circa propria moveret centra, patet ex prop. 11. in quâ ostensum, fluidi particulas agitari motibus à se mutuo diversis: Motus enim à se mutuo diversi, hoc est,ut quælibet particula habeat motum proprium, & ab altera distinctum, esse nequeunt, si non quælibet circa proprium centrum convertatur; nam hoc non posito, plures habebunt eundem motum.
units.tr: 2. That, with respect to the nature of a fluid as it could then be regarded, God should be required to move the individual particles each about its own centre is clear from Prop. 11, where it was shown that the particles of a fluid are agitated by motions differing from one another. For motions differing from one another, that is, such that each particle has its own motion distinct from another's, cannot exist unless each one is turned about its own centre; for if this is not granted, several particles will have the same motion.

units.la: CCCLI. At B. putat, hic me in varias absurditates incidere. Quarum prima, quod hæc non convenuant cum prop. 9. in qua dixeram, omnem motum natura sua esse rectum.
units.tr: CCCLI. But B. thinks that here I fall into various absurdities. The first of these is that these things do not agree with Prop. 9, in which I had said that every motion is by its nature straight.

units.la: Resp. Quomodo hæc coaveniant, Cartesius art. 39. in prop.9. citato declarat his verbis: Esi multa cogantur sæpè deflectere propter occursum aliarum NB. atque in quolibet motu fiat quodammodo circulus ex omni materia simul mota. Idque etiam ex ipsa illâ prop. patet, in quá dico, quod illa, quæ circulariter moventur, recedant sua natura à centro sui circuli & actu egressum istum obtineant, nisi ab aliis impediantur. Conferat etiam lector Schol. ad prop. 9.
units.tr: Reply. How these agree, Descartes declares in art. 39, on the passage cited in Prop. 9, in these words: Although many things are often forced to deflect because of the meeting of others, NB. and in every motion a kind of circle is made out of all the matter moved together. This is also clear from that same proposition itself, in which I say that those things which are moved circularly recede by their nature from the centre of their circle and actually obtain that outward course, unless they are impeded by others. Let the reader also consult the Scholium on Prop. 9.

units.la: CCCLII. Secunda absurditas ab adversario objecta est: quod, cum omnia quæ circa centra moventur, in circulum moveantur, videatur necessario dandum vacuum inter illos vortices, prout enim circulus circulum tangit in puncto, ita & vortex vorticem &c.
units.tr: CCCLII. The second absurdity is objected by the opponent: that, since all things that are moved about centres are moved in a circle, it seems that a void must necessarily be admitted between those vortices; for just as one circle touches another at a point, so also one vortex touches another vortex, and so on.

units.la: Resp. Negamus, quod vortex vorticem tangat tantum in puncto,ita enim compositi sunt inter se vortices, ut inæqualitas alterius per alterum suppleatur, atque totâ superficie alter alterum contingat, & quoniam tota materia cujusque vorticis, est fluida, facile unius vorticis materia cedit alteri vortici motu, ut non necessarium sit vacuum admittere. Verum de vorticibus ipsis hic non quæritur, sed de particulis eorum, quæ non sphæricæ supponuntur, sed angulosæ, quia postea ex ipsorum angulis abrasis, materia primi elementi dicitur orta. Illæ ergo dum circa centra motæ fuerunt anguli illarum paulatim fuerunt abrasi, quæ rasura spatia inter ipsas relicta replevit. Nulla ergo hic potest esse vel suspicio vacui, si rem attente inspiciamus.
units.tr: Reply. We deny that a vortex touches another vortex only at a point. For the vortices are so composed among themselves that the unevenness of one is made good by the other, and each touches the other over its whole surface; and since the whole matter of each vortex is fluid, the matter of one vortex readily yields to another vortex by motion, so that it is not necessary to admit a void. But the question here is not about the vortices themselves, but about their particles, which are supposed not to be spherical but angular, because afterwards the matter of the first element is said to arise from the rubbing away of their angles. Therefore, while these particles were moved about their centres, their angles were gradually worn away, and the matter rubbed off filled the spaces left between them. There can therefore be no suspicion of a void here, if we examine the matter carefully.

units.la: Hypothesis IV.
units.tr: Hypothesis IV.

units.la: CCCLIII. Deus plures particulas tales simul movit circa alia quaedam puncta aque a se mutuo remota, & eodem modo dispositas, ac jam sunt centra fixarum, nec non etiam circa alia aliquanto plura, que aequent numerum Planetarum. Declaratio. Ut enim possent misceri, & varia corpora inde fieri, non debebant in eodem loco consistendo circa propria tantum centra convolvi. Et cogitare hic licet, Deum voluisse ita obscura quasi lineamenta effingere corporum maxime conspicuorum per motum talem circa commune centrum.
units.tr: CCCLIII. God set many such particles moving at once around certain other points, equally remote from one another and arranged in the same way as the centres of the fixed stars are now, and also around some more points, equal in number to the Planets. Declaration. For these particles to be mixed together and so form various bodies, they could not stay in one place and merely revolve around their own centres. Here one may also reflect that God willed to sketch, as it were, the obscure outlines of the most conspicuous bodies by such a motion around a common centre.

units.la: SCHOLIUM.
units.tr: SCHOLIUM.

units.la: CCCLIV. Exc. B. p. 266. Me in hac una hypothesi quinque supponere, que ne una quidem ratione probem.
units.tr: CCCLIV. Exc. B. p. 266. In this one hypothesis I assume five things, none of which I can prove even by one reason.

units.la: Resp. Nihil hic suppono, nisi quod ordini isti spectandi opera Dei successive est conveniens secundum leges naturae, quod quidem de his 4. quae hic ponuntur ostendo.(Non enim 5, verum 4 pono.) Primum est, plures particulas simul esse motas circa alia quaedam puncta, quod requirebatur ad mixtionem. 2. Ea puncta aque a se mutuo remota & dispositas esse, ac nunc sunt centra fixarum; quod colligitur ex ipsa dispositione fixarum, quarum ortum cum suis vorticibus postea Cartesius demonstrat. 3. Nec non circa alia aliquanto plura, quia praeter fixas etiam considerandi Planetae. 4. Ea puncta aquare numerum Planetarum, quia tot debent centra praeter stellarum fixarum considerari, quot sunt planetae.
units.tr: Reply. I assume nothing here except what agrees with the order in which God's works are successively to be considered, according to the laws of nature. I show this for the four points set out here. (For I do not assume five, but four.) The first is that several particles are moved at once around certain other points, which was required for mixing. Second, that those points are equally remote from one another and arranged as the centres of the fixed stars now are; this is gathered from the very arrangement of the fixed stars, whose origin, together with their vortices, Descartes later demonstrates. Third, that there are also some more points, because besides the fixed stars the planets too must be considered. Fourth, that these points are equal in number to the planets, because as many centres must be considered besides those of the fixed stars as there are planets.

units.la: CCCLV. Non sunt autem hae hypotheses omnino falsae & veritati e diametro adversae. Licet enim talis praecise divisio & ordo a Deo non fuerit observatus, tamen actio divina una, qua ista opera facta fuerunt, illis actionibus diversis, quae hic spectantur, aequivalet, cum per eam res naturam legibus naturae convenientem acceperint. Eodem modo, quo hypotheses circa decreta divina explicanda adhibitae, (quales sunt, quod Deus prius finem, postea media decreverit, cum tamen in Deo nihil sit prius vel posterius,) non sunt omnino falsae; illud enim decretum in Deo unicum aequipollet actibus creatis, inter quos prior spectat finem, posterior media. Repete plures rationes istius convenientiae ex art. 338. Ut tamen hae hypotheses faciunt ad intellectum decretorum divinorum, ita illae ad intelligentiam operis creationis. Y CCCLVI. Exc.
units.tr: CCCLV. These hypotheses, however, are not wholly false nor diametrically opposed to the truth. For although God did not observe precisely such a division and order, yet the one divine action by which these works were made is equivalent to those diverse actions considered here, since through it things received a nature agreeing with the laws of nature. In the same way, the hypotheses employed to explain the divine decrees (such as that God decreed the end first and the means afterwards, although in God there is nothing prior or posterior) are not wholly false. For that one decree in God is equivalent to created acts, among which the former regards the end and the latter the means. Repeat several reasons for this agreement from art. 338. However, just as these hypotheses serve to understand the divine decrees, so those serve to understand the work of creation. CCCLVI. Exc.

units.la: CCCLVI. Exc. B. Has hypotheses postea assumi ut media probationis, media autem probationis ex parte falsa nobis non posse formare certas conclusiones.
