units.tr: CCCLVI. Exc. B. These hypotheses are afterwards assumed as means of proof, and since we cannot form certain conclusions from means of proof that are partly false.

units.la: * Resp. Non assumuntur aliter in sequentibus, quàm divisio & ordo decretorum divinorum à Theologis ad hæc vel illa probanda. Non enim argumenta ex falsâ hypothesi quâtenus tali petuntur, sed ex legibus naturæ, quas, his hypothesibus præmissis, distinctè possumus inspicere, quemadmodum à Theologis argumenta desumuntur ex regulis sapientiæ divinæ, quas præmissâ divisione & ordine decretorum divinorum, distinctè possumus considerare.
units.tr: Reply. In what follows they are assumed in no other way than the division and order of the divine decrees are assumed by Theologians to prove this or that. For arguments are not drawn from a false hypothesis as such, but from the laws of nature, which, with these hypotheses premised, we can distinctly examine, just as Theologians draw arguments from the rules of divine wisdom, which, with the division and order of the divine decrees premised, we can distinctly consider.

units.la: PROPOSITIO XIII.
units.tr: PROPOSITION XIII.

units.la: CCCLVII. Illæ particulæ æquales hypothesēos prima non potuerunt esse sphæricæ. Quia sic vacuum relinqueretur (contra Prop. 2.) sed cujuscunque figuræ primò fuerint, debuerunt tandem fieri sphæricæ, art. 48. Quia fuerunt motæ (ex hypoth. 2.) & quidem variè, tùm circa propria centra, tùm circa alia (per hypoth. 3. & 4.) Quare eminentiæ omnes necessariò tandem fuerunt abrasæ.
units.tr: 357. The equal particles of the first hypothesis could not have been spherical, for thus a vacuum would be left (contrary to Proposition 2). But whatever shape they were at first, they must in the end have become spherical (art. 48), because they were moved (by hypothesis 2), and indeed variously, both about their own centres and about others (by hypotheses 3 and 4). Hence all protuberances were necessarily worn away in the end.

units.la: SCHOLIUM.
units.tr: SCHOLIUM.

units.la: CCCLVIII. Exc. B. p 268. Futilem esse probationem, quia nititur hypothesibus vanissimis non probatis.
units.tr: 358. Exc. B. p. 268. That the proof is futile, because it rests on most empty hypotheses that have not been proved.

units.la: Resp. Nititur legibus naturæ, quas positis divisione, motu & ordine, in operibus divinis contemplandis, consideramus: sicut enim posito ordine aliquo in decretis divinis, ac suppositâ eorum divisione, sequitur primò, Deum decrevisse de fine, dein de mediis ex legibus sapientiæ, ita & posito ordine in operibus divinis ac suppositâ divisione & motu materiæ, sequitur, ex legibus naturæ eas particulas debuisse evadere sphæricas.
units.tr: Reply. It rests on the laws of nature, which we consider when, the division, motion and order being posited, we contemplate the works of God. For just as, given some order in the divine decrees and their division supposed, it follows first that God decreed concerning the end, and then concerning the means, according to the laws of wisdom, so too, given an order in the divine works and the division and motion of matter supposed, it follows, according to the laws of nature, that those particles must have turned out spherical.

units.la: PROPOSITIO XIV.
units.tr: PROPOSITION XIV.

units.la: CCCLIX. Circa ista particulas sphæricas debuit alia esse materia subtilius, art. 49. Orta est enim ex abrasione angulorum & eminentiarum (per prop. 13.) Quia autem mansit eadem extensio totius istius materiæ collectivè consideratæ post divisionem & abrasionem, ideò spatia inter globulos relicta debuit implere, quod facilè potuit præstare propter tenuitatem, nuitatem. niuitatem, quia non nisi tenue potuit esse id, quod unâ vice ab istis æqualibus partibus fuit abrasum, propter quam tenuitatem etiam facile dividi potuit in infinitum (per Prop. 4.) ut in quælibet spatiola se potuerit insinuare.
units.tr: CCCLIX. Around these spherical particles there ought to have been another, more subtle matter, art. 49. For it arose from the abrasion of the corners and projections (by Prop. 13). Because the same extension of the whole of this matter, considered collectively, remained after the division and abrasion, it ought to have filled the spaces left between the globules. It could easily do this because of its thinness, since whatever was abraded at one time from these equal parts could not be anything but thin. Because of this thinness it could also easily be divided into infinitely many parts (by Prop. 4), so that it could insinuate itself into any small spaces whatever.

units.la: SCHOLIVM.
units.tr: SCHOLIUM.

units.la: CCCLX. Obj. B. p. 269. Hæc corpuscula spatia inter sphæras intermedia replere nequeunt, nisi talis sint concavitatis & tales habeant proeminentias & angulos acutissimos, ut undiquaque sphærulas circumcingant.
units.tr: CCCLX. Objection, B. p. 269. These little bodies cannot fill the spaces lying between the spheres unless they have such concavity, and such projections and very sharp angles, that they surround the little spheres on every side.

units.la: Resp. Ad illam obj. responsum est in ipsa demonstratione. Ista abrasio eminentiarum & angulorum, ut sphærulæ fuerint formatæ, non potuit fieri unâ vice, sed sæpius debuit repeti: Quod autem unâ vice fuit abrasum, valde fuit tenue, & sic facile potuit dividi, ut in quælibet spatia se potnerit insinuare; quod si una particula ad aliquod spatium implendum non apta esset, potuerunt plures id præstare, idque tanto magis, quod variarum sint figurarum; potuit etiam quælibet varie flecti propter tenuitatem, & dividi ulterius, ut quodlibet spatium minimum ab aliis corpusculis sive particulis relictum impleret. Evanescunt ergo omnia, quæ de superficiebus istarum particularum vel convexis vel concavis proferuntur p. 269, 270. cum superficies debuerint esse omnis generis, & magnitudines etiam indefinitæ istarum particularum. Spatium enim quodvis repleri potest per corpuscula indefinitæ magnitudinis, & cujuscunque figuræ. Si enim unum corpusculum sit nimis parvum, conjunguntur plura; si nimis magnum, aliud aptum inter tot indefinitæ magnitudinis adest. Si figura sit inconveniens vel superficies, aliud alterius figuræ id præstabit; facile etiam dividi potest id, quod propter figuræ inconvenientiam spatium suppositum non potest intrOIre.
units.tr: Reply. This objection has been answered in the demonstration itself. The abrasion of the projections and corners, by which the little spheres were formed, could not take place all at once but must have been repeated many times. What was abraded at one time was very thin, and so it could easily be divided so as to insinuate itself into any spaces whatever. If one particle were not suited to filling some space, several could do it, and all the more so because they are of various shapes. Any particle could also be bent in various ways because of its thinness, and divided further, so that it would fill any smallest space left by other corpuscles or particles. Therefore everything that is said on pp. 269 and 270 about the surfaces of these particles, whether convex or concave, vanishes away, since their surfaces must be of every kind, and their magnitudes too must be indefinite. For any space whatever can be filled by corpuscles of indefinite magnitude and of any shape whatever. If one corpuscle is too small, several are joined together; if it is too large, another suited to such an indefinite variety of magnitudes is at hand. If the shape or the surface is unsuitable, another of a different shape will do the job; and whatever cannot enter the supposed space because of its unsuitable shape can easily be divided.

units.la: CCCLXI. At contra meam rationem inquit, me Propof. IV. tantum probasse, posse corpora dividi in infinitum, sed non actu divisa, qualia secundum hanc doctrinam darentur.
units.tr: CCCLXI. But against my argument he says that I, in Prop. IV, have proved only that bodies can be divided into infinity, but not that they are actually divided, as they would be according to this doctrine.

units.la: Resp. Negatur, quòd secundùm hanc doctrinam darentur corpora actu in infinitum divisa, sed tantùm, nullum corpus tam parvum, quin adhuc possit dividi ulterius, &, si necesse sit, etiam ulterius dividatur, ita tamen, ut nunquam ad ultimam divisionem perveniatur, vel etiam perveniri possit; quod cùm statuamus, eo ipso negamus, dari corpora actu in infinitum divisa.
units.tr: Reply. It is denied that, according to this doctrine, bodies actually divided into infinity would exist. Rather, no body is so small that it cannot still be divided further, and, if necessary, it is divided further, yet in such a way that the ultimate division is never reached, or even can be reached. Since we maintain this, we thereby deny that bodies actually divided into infinity exist.

units.la: PROPOSITIO XV.
units.tr: PROPOSITION XV.

units.la: CCCLXII. Confluxit etiam ista materia ad centra ea, circa quae ex hypoth. quartaconseries particularum fuit mota, indeque sidera sunt orta, art. §4. Aucta enim est valde ex continua illa abrasione, ut major longè fuerit copia, quàm requirebatur ad spatia interjecta replenda. Cùm autem (per Propos. 9.) globuli moti circulariter à centro conarentur recedere, propulerunt illi proximos, & hi alios. Sed vacuum dari non potest (per Prop. 2.) & in corporibus motis semper fit circulus (per Propos. 5.) Necessariò ergò globulis à centro recedentibus alia quædam materia debet succedere. Globuli autem nulli ad centra potuerunt accedere, quia hactenus omnes fuerunt æquales, adeoque æqualem habuerunt conatum à centro recedendi. Ergò necessario materia subtilis, quæ facile recipit motus aliorum corporum, utpote tenuis & facile sese insinuare valens, ad centra fuit depulsa, sicque sidera sunt orta proportionalia ad materiam, quæ circa illa in orbem movetur.
units.tr: CCCLXII. This matter also flowed together to those centres around which, by hypothesis four, a series of particles was moved, and from it the stars arose, art. §4. For the matter was greatly increased by that continual abrasion, so that its quantity was far greater than was needed to fill the intervening spaces. Now since (by Prop. 9) the globules moved circularly tried to recede from the centre, they pushed the nearest ones, and these pushed others. But a vacuum cannot exist (by Prop. 2), and in bodies in motion a circle is always formed (by Prop. 5). Therefore, as the globules recede from the centre, some other matter must necessarily take their place. But no globules could approach the centres, since until now they had all been equal and so had an equal endeavour to recede from the centre. Therefore the subtle matter, which easily receives the motions of other bodies, being thin and able to insinuate itself readily, was necessarily driven to the centres; and so stars arose in proportion to the matter that moves in an orb around them.

units.la: SCHOLIUM
units.tr: SCHOLIUM

units.la: CCCLXIII. Rogat hic B.p. 272. Annon illa corpuscula angulata, quæ per abrasionem mutata sint in sphæras, tantum amiserint à sua magnitudine, quantum ab ipsis fuit abrasum? si amiserint, quidnam repleverint spatium abrasarum particularum? si dicatur, illa materia subtilis, undenam auctio illius materia, si replere debuit illa spatia, quibus abrasa & in sphærulas mutata corpuscula sunt imminuta? vel, unde fiat, quod materia subtilis ex abrasione orta jam majora & spatia occupet post abrasionem, quàm cùm corpusculis aliis adhuc erat annexa? hasque putat difficultates inextricabiles.
units.tr: CCCLXIII. Here B.p. 272 asks: Have not those angular corpuscles, which by abrasion were changed into spheres, lost from their magnitude exactly as much as was rubbed off them? If they have lost that much, what filled the space of the rubbed-off particles? If you say that subtle matter did, whence came the increase of that matter, if it had to fill those spaces by which the corpuscles, abraded and changed into little spheres, were diminished? Or how does it come about that the subtle matter arising from the abrasion now occupies larger spaces after the abrasion than when it was still joined to the other corpuscles? And he thinks these are inextricable difficulties.

units.la: Resp. Qui non intelligit, nec percipit demonstrationes Mathematicas, ei difficultates inextricabiles oriri nullum est dubium, quæ tamen alii in mentem venire non possunt. Nullû dubium, quin tantum amiserint corpuscula angulata de sua magnitudine, quantum fuit abrasum, &, cùm dixerimus, varias esse particulas, quarum anguli debuerint abradi, item omnes fuisse & circa centra propria & circa alia puncta quædam agitatas, facile patet, simul varias particulas debuisse abradi, quarum hæ hoc spatium, aliæ aliud repleverint sibi conveniens, præsertim, cùm, si hæ non essent aptæ, facile per ea, quæ ad propositionem præcedentem diximus, potuerint aptitudinem acquirere. Præterea, quarum eminentiæ fuerunt abrasæ, illæ eo, quod fuit relictum, immediate particulas contiguas attigerunt, atque in illud spatium, quod per istum accessum fuit relictum, facile quævis particulæ aliunde abrasæ, si, quod hic abrasum non esset conveniens, potuerunt sese insinuare. Post abrasionem autem materiæ non fuerunt spatia majora facta, quàm ante abrasionem illa materia replevit, sed eadem manserunt in tota illa materiâ, quam motam dicimus; verum propter accessum particularum, post ablatos angulos, & remotionem ab aliis, alia spatia majora, alia minora fuerunt facta, quæ eo ipso materiâ abrasâ fuerunt repleta, secundùm ea, quæ ad Propos. præced. fuerunt dicta.
units.tr: Answer: Whoever does not understand or grasp mathematical demonstrations will undoubtedly find inextricable difficulties, which yet cannot occur to others. There is no doubt that the angular corpuscles lost from their magnitude exactly as much as was rubbed off. And since we have said that the particles were of various kinds, whose angles had to be worn away, and that all of them were agitated both about their own centres and about certain other points, it is easy to see that various particles had to be abraded at the same time, and that these filled this space and those filled another, each suitable to it. This is especially so because, if they were not suitable, they could easily acquire suitability through what we said about the preceding proposition. Moreover, where the projections were abraded, the particles that had been left touched the neighbouring particles directly, and into the space left by this approach any other particles abraded elsewhere could easily insinuate themselves, if they were suitable for a place that was not worn away here. After the abrasion, however, the spaces were not made larger than the matter had filled before the abrasion; they remained the same throughout all that matter which we call moved. But because of the approach of the particles after the angles were removed, and their removal from others, some spaces became larger and some smaller, and these, by that very fact, were filled by the abraded matter, according to what was said in the preceding propositions.

units.la: CCCLXIV. Pergit B. p. 273. Nullam dari rationem, unde fulgor ille, qui conspicitur in Sole, oriatur, & quomodo particularum imminutio tantam lucem gignere possit.
units.tr: CCCLXIV. B.p. 273 goes on: There is no reason given whence that brightness which is seen in the Sun arises, or how a diminution of particles can produce so great a light.

units.la: Resp. Fulgor in Sole non potest considerari, nisi postquam ipse formatus consideratur; at ut ille fulgor à me hic demonstraretur, ad institutum meum planè non erat necesse: id tamen factum abunde à Cartesio Pp. III. 77, 78, 80, 81.
units.tr: Answer: The brightness in the Sun cannot be considered except after the Sun itself has been considered as formed. But it was not at all necessary for my purpose to demonstrate that brightness here. Nevertheless, Descartes has done this amply: Pt. III, 77, 78, 80, 81.

units.la: CCCLXV. Tandem p. 273. Si Sol sit centrum, necessariò ab omnibus peripheriis vorticum planetarum æqualiter distare debet; at hoc falsum esse testatur tota Astronomia. Habent enim omnes planetæ, qui in vorticibus suis secundum Cartesium circa Solem feruntur, sua Aphelia & Perihelia &c.
units.tr: CCCLXV. Finally, B.p. 273: If the Sun is the centre, it must necessarily be equally distant from all the peripheries of the planetary vortices; but the whole of astronomy testifies that this is false. For all the planets, which according to Descartes are carried round the Sun in their vortices, have their aphelia and perihelia, etc.

units.la: Resp. De eâ, quam existimat, difficultate, quoniam pleniùs agetur ad Propos. 21. igitur ejus explicationem eò usque differemus; ubi tantum observaverimus, non à Cartesio dici Planetas moveri in vorticibus suis, cùm illorum omnium vortices absorptos à vortice Solis ostendat, sed intra globulos secundi elementi quemlibet in suo circuitu, quem obtinent in vortice Solis, exceptâ tamen Terrâ & Jove ac fortè Saturno.
units.tr: Answer: This difficulty he thinks of will be treated more fully at Proposition 21, so we will defer its explanation until then. Here we need only observe that Descartes does not say the planets move in their own vortices, since he shows that all their vortices are absorbed into the vortex of the Sun. Rather, each planet moves, in its circuit within the vortex of the Sun, through the globules of the second element, except the Earth, Jupiter and perhaps Saturn.

units.la: PROPOSITIO XVI.
units.tr: PROPOSITION XVI.

units.la: CCCLXVI. Illa porrò materia subtilis, quàm primùm ad centra pervenit, mota est motu ejus vorticis in circulum. art. 72. Hic enim motus facilè à vicinis globulis poterat imprimi, unde posteà subsequens materia similem impressionem suscepit, donec omnis superflua materia in centrum descenderit, quæ tota simul gyrare debuit.
units.tr: CCCLXVI. That subtle matter, as soon as it reaches the centres, is moved in a circle by the motion of its vortex. Art. 72. For this motion could easily be impressed by the neighbouring globules; whence the matter that follows afterwards receives a similar impression, until all the superfluous matter has descended into the centre, where the whole of it must at once whirl round.

units.la: SCHOLIUM.
units.tr: SCHOLIUM.

units.la: CCCLXVII. B. p. 274. inquit, Se hanc Propof. facile concessurum, si demonstratum, dari tales vortices, globulos & materiam subtilem, quae omnia cum ex legibus naturae demonstraverimus efficacissimè, nos hanc concessionem adversarii accipimus.
units.tr: CCCLXVII. He says at p. 274 that he will readily concede this proposition, if it is demonstrated that such vortices, globules and subtle matter exist; and since we have demonstrated all these things most effectively from the laws of nature, we take this concession from the adversary.

units.la: PROPOSITIO XVII.
units.tr: PROPOSITION XVII.

units.la: CCCLXVIII. Vortices jam debent ita inter se esse compositi, ut unusquisque in eam partem feratur, secundum quam reliquorum omnium circumstantium motus minus illi adversantur art. 65. Nam (ex Propos. 10.) colligi potest, motum quodcunque corpus alterius occursu ita facile flecti posse, ut in suo motu quàm minimum impediatur, quod futurum esse mutuo huc & illuc impulsu, concipi facilè potest.
units.tr: 368. Vortices must now be so mutually arranged that each one is carried in that direction in which the motions of all the others surrounding it offer it the least resistance art. 65. For (from Prop. 10) it can be inferred that any moving body, upon meeting another body, can be turned aside so easily that it is hindered as little as possible in its motion; and it can easily be conceived that this will happen through mutual pushing hither and thither.

units.la: SCHOLIUM.
units.tr: SCHOLIUM.

units.la: CCCLXIX. Ad hanc Propositionem B. p. 275. eandem cantilenam repetit, & dicterium se dignum annectit, itaque pergo ad Propositionem XVIII.
units.tr: 369. On this Proposition he repeats the same old refrain, and attaches a saying worthy of himself; so I pass on to Proposition XVIII.

units.la: PROPOSITIO XVIII.
units.tr: PROPOSITION XVIII.

units.la: CCCLXX. Minus autem se impediunt vortices, si poli cujusque non tam vicini sint polis aliorum vorticum contiguorum, quam partibus ab ipsorum polis valde remotis, hoc est, ecliptica, art. 67. Si enim duorum poli se mutuò tangerent, vel ambo in eandem partes ferrentur, & sic in unum vorticem coalescerent, at nos distinctos jam supposuimus; vel in contrarias, & sic sibi mutuò quàm maximè repugnarent.
units.tr: 370. Vortices, however, hinder one another less if the poles of each are not so near the poles of the neighbouring contiguous vortices as they are to parts far removed from their own poles, that is, to the ecliptic, art. 67. For if the poles of two vortices touched each other, and both were carried in the same direction, they would coalesce into one vortex, whereas we have already supposed them distinct; or if they were carried in opposite directions, they would be mutually and most strongly opposed to each other.

units.la: PROPOSITIO XIX.
units.tr: PROPOSITION XIX.

units.la: CCCLXXI. Vortices isti sunt latiores & ampliores versus eclipticam quàm versus polos. Globuli enim vehementius versus eclipticam pelluntur, quod ex circumgyratione est manifestum. Ecliptica autem oppositi sunt poli, (per Prop. 18.) qui minus resistunt, quòd globuli versus polos los non ita vehementer pellantur: Polis vero eclipticæ, quæ magis.
units.tr: 371. The vortices are wider and larger toward the ecliptic than toward the poles. For the globules are driven more forcefully toward the ecliptic, which is plain from the circular motion. Now the poles are opposed to the ecliptic (by Prop. 18), and they resist less, because the globules are not driven as vehemently toward the poles; but the poles of the ecliptic are the ones that resist more.

units.la: SCHOLIUM.
units.tr: SCHOLIUM.

units.la: CCCLXXII. Ad has duas propositiones nihil annotat Adversarius, quàm, vortices à Cartesio non esse probatos; quod an factum sit, non ipsius, sed lectoris attenti & cordati judicio permittimus.
units.tr: 372. The Adversary makes no remark on these two propositions except that the vortices have not been proved by Descartes. Whether this is so, we leave not to him but to the judgment of the attentive and sensible reader.

units.la: PROPOSITIO XX.
units.tr: PROPOSITION XX.

units.la: CCCLXXIII. Materia subtilis ex polis cujusque vorticis versus centrum, & ex centro versus alias partes fluit, art. 69. Omnis enim materia recedere conatur à centro, (per prop. 9.) & vehementius pellitur versus eclipticam, quàm versus polos (per Prop. 19.) Cum ergò ad Ecliptican occurrat polis (per Prop. 18.) qui minus resistunt, certum est, illam ibi ingressuram, egressuramque ex partibus versus eclipticam.
units.tr: CCCLXXIII. Subtle matter flows from the poles of each vortex towards the centre, and from the centre towards other parts (art. 69). For all matter tends to recede from the centre (by Prop. 9), and is driven more violently towards the ecliptic than towards the poles (by Prop. 19). Since, therefore, the matter meets the ecliptic at the poles (by Prop. 18), which offer less resistance, it is certain that it will enter there and leave again from the parts towards the ecliptic.

units.la: SCHOLIUM.
units.tr: SCHOLIUM.

units.la: CCCLXXIV. Objicit hic B. p. 277. Si detur talis fluxus & refluxus materia ex polo ad centrum, & ex centro rursus ad alias partes, non videmus, quomodo fieri possit, quin Planeta descendant versus Solem, ut centrum, & inde rursus ad alias partes circumferentiarum recedant, nec Luna aquabiliter à centro suo distabit, modò verget versus illud, modò in alias partes circumferentia feretur, & sic omnia tandem in unum chaos convertentur.
units.tr: CCCLXXIV. Here B. objects, p. 277: If there is such a flow and reflux of matter from the pole to the centre, and from the centre again to other parts, we do not see how it can be avoided that the planets descend towards the Sun, as the centre, and thence recede again to other parts of the circumferences; nor will the Moon keep an even distance from its centre, but now it will incline towards it, now it will be carried off into other parts of the circumference, and so all things will at last be turned into one chaos.

units.la: Resp. Scilicet, quia antagonista videre non potest aliud, idcirco hoc, quod imaginatur, fiet! At Cartesius demonstrativam dedit rationem, Princip. III. art. 120. & seqq. quare aliquis Planeta, quem ordine naturæ prius consideravit ut stellam fixam, neque ulterius versus centrum descendat, neque magis ab eo recedat. Materia verò subtilis, quæ ex aliis vorticibus per partes polo vicinas versus centrum cujusque vorticis fluit, & refluit, non habet tantam vim, ut Planetam aliquem versus Solem, ut centrum vorticis, vel versus circumferentiam vorticis propellere possit, quamvis hinc & inde aliquantum eum possit propellere, prout & Cartesius demonstravit Pp. III. 142.
units.tr: Reply. Of course, because my opponent cannot see anything else, this will happen, just as he imagines! But Descartes gave a demonstrative reason (Principles III, art. 120 and following) why a certain planet, which in the order of nature he first considered as a fixed star, neither descends further towards the centre nor recedes further from it. Subtle matter, however, which flows and reflows from other vortices through the parts near the pole towards the centre of each vortex, does not have such great force that it could drive any planet towards the Sun, as the centre of the vortex, or towards the circumference of the vortex. Although it can push it to some extent from this side and that, as Descartes also demonstrated (Pp. III. 142).

units.la: PROPOSITIO XXI.
units.tr: PROPOSITION XXI.

units.la: CCCLXXV. Proximi sideri globuli celerius feruntur, quam paulo remotiores ad certam distantiam, art. 84, Quia, cum materia subtilis in centro vorticis semper circumvolvatur, (per Prop. 16.) & semper aliquid sui per angustos meatus, qui sunt inter globulos secundi Elementi, versus Eclipticam emittat, & versus polos recipiat, (per Prop. 20.) non dubium est, quin habeat vim secum rapiendi globulos istos usque ad certam distantiam. Idcircoque quo propiores sunt, tanto magis in istos vim suam exserere potest, quo remotiores, tanto minus.
units.tr: CCCLXXV. The nearer globules of a star move more swiftly than those somewhat more distant, up to a certain distance, art. 84. Because the subtle matter always revolves in the centre of the vortex (by Prop. 16), and always sends some part of itself through the narrow passages between the globules of the second element towards the Ecliptic and takes it back at the poles (by Prop. 20), there is no doubt that it has the power to carry those globules along with it up to a certain distance. Therefore the nearer they are, the more strongly it can exert its force on them, and the more distant they are, the less.

units.la: SCHOLIUM
units.tr: SCHOLIUM

units.la: CCCLXXVI. In hac Propositione examinanda B. prolixior est, ac citatis Pp. III. art. 30. & 148. tres quaestiones ventilandas proponit.
units.tr: CCCLXXVI. In examining this Proposition, B. is rather long-winded, and, citing Pp. III. arts. 30 and 148, he puts forward three questions to be discussed.

units.la: 1. An Sol sit centrum Planetarum. 2. An circa proprium centrum celerrime gyrando secum rapiat materiam coelestem, in qua versantur Planeta. 3. An ejus partes Soli viciniores velocius moveantur remotioribus.
units.tr: 1. Whether the Sun is the centre of the planets. 2. Whether, by turning rapidly about its own centre, it carries along with it the celestial matter in which the planets move. 3. Whether its parts nearer the Sun move more swiftly than the more distant ones.

units.la: CCCLXXVII. De priori sic inquit p. 278. Solem esse centrum Planetarum vult Cartesius, & proinde typum suum Planetarum ita construxit, ut Sol accurate in centro omnium Planetarum sit locatus, ut in schemate videre est &c.
units.tr: CCCLXXVII. On the first point he says, at p. 278: Descartes wishes the Sun to be the centre of the planets, and therefore constructed his figure of the planets so that the Sun is placed exactly in the centre of all the planets, as can be seen in the diagram, etc.

units.la: Resp. Ridiculum est, quod ex schemate velit colligere, Cartesium statuisse, Solem esse centrum Planetarum Geometricum & exactum, cum nec Cartesius curiosus fuerit circa figuras, nec solent multi Mathematici accuratissimi. Vide Clavii figuras in Euclide, quae saepe non conveniunt cum propositionibus, sed supponuntur tantum convenire; & aliunde satis sit manifestum, cum non alio modo statuere Solem esse centrum circuitus Planetarum, quam circuitus ipsorum circulus appellatur. At ipsorum circuitus circulus appellatur non perfecte, sed valde imperfecte, eo modo, quo circulus designat ambitum aliquem, in quo alicubi incipiendo tandem ad eundem locum fit regressus, a quo initium fuerat desumtum. Ipso illo par. 30. ab adversario citato inquit: Ut in fluminum locis, si varie festucae aquae incumbant, videbimus eas, quamvis semper motus circulares affectent, vix tamen unquam circulos omnino perfectos describere, quod & de Planetis vult intelligi, ac per ea omnia eorum phaenomena explicari. Quod si enim haec proportionaliter conferas, ad vortic em illum magnum, in quo Sol centrum, & omnes Planetæ circa eum transferuntur, nulla potest esse difficultas. Porro Pp. III. 34. inquit: Ne putemus omnia centra Planetarum in eodem plano semper consistere NF. nec circulos, quos describunt, esse omninò perfectos NB. sed ut in omnibus aliis rebus naturalibus contingere videmus, ista tantum praterpropter talia esse, ac etiam labentibus seculis continuò mutari. Item art. 36. expressè agnoscit Aphelia & Peribelia Planetarum. Sic & art. 82. dum dicit, globulos HQ in sphaeroide HNQR impendere triginta annos vel etiam plures, satis manifestum reddit, Saturnum, qui triginta annis circuitum absolvit, & per istos globulos deferitur, in tali sphaeroide moveri, & sic Solem non esse centrum ejus Geometricum. Conf. etiam art. 84, 134, 136. in quo expressissimè dicit, sphæram Saturni intra illum terminum contineri, intra quem globuli coelestes non sunt æquales, cùm extra eum æquales statuantur, qui terminus art. 82. dicitur sphæroides. Statuit ergò, Solem esse centrum circuitûs Planetarum, eo modo, quo quivis alii Astronomi Copernicani, & quo etiam Tycho, qui tamen non ignorant Aphelia & Parhelia Saturni, ejusque excentricitatem.
units.tr: Reply. It is ridiculous that he wants to infer from the diagram that Descartes held the Sun to be the exact geometrical centre of the planets, since Descartes was not fussy about figures, and very accurate mathematicians often are not either. See Clavius's figures in Euclid, which often do not agree with the propositions but are merely assumed to agree. In any case it is clear enough that to say the Sun is the centre of the planets' orbits is no different from calling their orbit a circle. Yet their orbit is called a circle not perfectly but very imperfectly, in the sense that a circle designates some circuit in which, starting from some point, one eventually returns to the same place from which one began. In the very passage, art. 30, cited by our opponent, he says: As in places of rivers, if straws lie in the water in various ways, we see them, although they always tend to circular motions, hardly ever describing perfectly complete circles; and this is to be understood also of the planets, and by these means all their phenomena are explained. If you compare these things in proportion, there can be no difficulty about that great vortex in which the Sun is the centre and all the planets are carried around it. Further, at Pp. III. 34 he says: Let us not suppose that all the centres of the planets always stand in the same plane NF, nor that the circles they describe are altogether perfect NB, but, as we see happens in all other natural things, these are only approximately such, and are continually changing even as the centuries pass. Likewise at art. 36 he expressly acknowledges the aphelia and perihelia of the planets. So too at art. 82, where he says that the globules HQ in the spheroid HNQR take thirty years or even more, he makes it sufficiently plain that Saturn, which completes its circuit in thirty years and is carried by those globules, moves in such a spheroid, and so the Sun is not its geometrical centre. Compare also arts. 84, 134, 136, where he most explicitly says that Saturn's sphere is contained within the limit inside which the celestial globules are not equal, since they are assumed to be equal outside it, which limit is called the spheroid in art. 82. He therefore holds that the Sun is the centre of the planets' circuit in the same way as any other Copernican astronomers, and as Tycho too, who nevertheless are not ignorant of the aphelia and perihelia of Saturn and its eccentricity.

units.la: CCCLXXVIII. At dices: Non tribui Cartesio, quod statuat Solem esse centrum Planetarum Geometricum, sed quaestionem esse, an centrum circuitûs Planetarum possit vocari.
units.tr: CCCLXXVIII. But you will say: I did not attribute to Descartes the view that the Sun is the geometrical centre of the planets, but the question is whether it can be called the centre of the planets' circuit.

units.la: Resp. Verba B. citata hoc inferunt, quod Cartesius eo modo Solem statuat centrum, quo modo in typo planetarum Sol conspicitur; ad quæ subsumo: At in typo planetarum à Cartesio adjuncto accuratè ponitur in medio, estque centrum Geometricum, Ergo & Cartesius secundum te statuit Solem esse centrum Geometricum: Ego vero & contrarium ostendi & Majorem Propositionem falsitatis convici. Si hic non sit sensus verborum citatorum, assignetur iis alius si fieri potest. 2. Nisi centrum sumatur accuratissimè, nulla erit quæstio ex mente adversarii inter ipsum & Cartesium; concedit enim paulo post, Solem posse vocari centrum Planetarum late sumtum. Qui plura de isto lapsu adversarii cognoscere velit, adeat libellum, cujus titulus: Demonstratio Mathematica Ignorantia & ineptiarum &c. p. 27. seqq. Item Den Hollenden Astronomus p.9, 10. ut & Den Verstrickte Astronomus p. 16, 17.
units.tr: Reply. The words of B. cited here imply that Descartes holds the Sun to be the centre in the way the Sun appears in the planetary diagram. To which I assume: but in the planetary diagram added by Descartes the Sun is accurately placed in the middle, and is the geometrical centre. Therefore, by your account, Descartes also holds that the Sun is the geometrical centre. I, however, have shown the opposite and convict the major premise of falsehood. If this is not the sense of the words cited, let another sense be assigned to them, if that is possible. 2. Unless the centre is taken with the greatest precision, there will be no question, on our opponent's view, between him and Descartes; for he concedes a little later that the Sun can be called the centre of the planets in a loose sense. Anyone who wishes to learn more about this slip of our opponent may consult the little book entitled Mathematical Demonstration of Ignorance and Trifles, etc., p. 27 ff. Also The Hollow Astronomer, pp. 9, 10, and The Entangled Astronomer, pp. 16, 17.

units.la: CCCLXXIX. Progredimur ad secundam quæstionem, quam propositit adversarius; An Sol circa proprium centrum celerrimè gyrando secum rapiat materiam cœlestem, in quâ versantur Planetæ? cujus affirmativam cum Cartesio statuo.
units.tr: CCCLXXIX. We proceed to the second question, which our opponent put forward: Whether the Sun, by turning rapidly about its own centre, carries along with it the celestial matter in which the planets move? I affirm this with Descartes.

units.la: Hic primo inquit B. p. 281. Nondum certum est, Solem circa proprium cencentrum itagyrare. Id enim ex motu maculatum solarium colligere imbecille nimis est, cum aliunde motus ille causari possit.
units.tr: Here, first, B. says at p. 281: It is not yet certain that the Sun turns about its own centre. For to infer this from the motion of the solar spots is too weak, since that motion can be caused otherwise.

units.la: Resp. Quod Sol circa proprium centrum gyret demonstratum est Prop. 16. Nam quod per materiam subtilem intelligatur cujuvis sideris, adeoque & Solis materia, liquere potuit ex collatione hujus Propositi cum Cartes. art. 84. unde desumta est. At B. nihil reposuit, quàm, vortices & materiam subtilem non esse demonstrata, quod an factum sit nec ne Prop. 15. judicet Lector attentus. 2. Remoris formis substantialibus & vi insitâ, quâ corpora à seipsis moveantur, & solis his nostris principiis suppositis, non alia potest esse causa motus maculatum solarium circa Solem, quàm gyratio Solis circa proprium centrum, quod à Cartesio abunde demonstratum.
units.tr: Reply. That the Sun turns about its own centre was demonstrated in Prop. 16. For that the subtle matter of any star, and so also of the Sun, is meant can be clear from comparing this Proposition with Descartes art. 84, from which it is taken. But B. has replied nothing except that vortices and subtle matter have not been demonstrated; let the attentive reader judge whether this was done in Prop. 15. 2. Setting aside substantial forms and the inherent power by which bodies move themselves, and with only these principles of ours assumed, there can be no other cause of the solar spots' motion around the Sun than the rotation of the Sun about its own centre, which Descartes has amply demonstrated.

units.la: CCCLXXX. 2. inquit B. p. 281. Eo motu Solis concesso non poterit tamen dici celerrimus. Nam macula illa superficiei Solis contigua, ut vult Cartesius Pp. III. 22. Solem circumeunt spatio viginti sex dierum. Unde sequetur, Solem ferè quadruplo tardius circumgyrationem suam absolvere, quàm ex ipsius hypothesi terra.
units.tr: CCCLXXX. 2. says B. at p. 281: Even if that motion of the Sun is granted, it cannot yet be called most rapid. For that spot lying next to the surface of the Sun, as Descartes holds at Pp. III. 22, goes round the Sun in a space of twenty-six days. From which it will follow that the Sun completes its rotation almost four times more slowly than, on its own hypothesis, the earth.

units.la: Resp. Quod ille motus sit celerrimus, patet ex natura materiae, ex quâ Sol constat, quae est fluidissima & celerrimae agitationis, utpote ejusdem naturae, cujus ignis, nisi quod ignis hic noster partes terrestres & aereas multas habeat intermixtas, & propterea hujus motus tardior sit. Difficultatem vero objectam jam solverat ipse Cartesius, Pp. III. 148. quae verba adscribere lubet. Nec interim, inquit, mirabimur, quod macula, quae in ejus superficie apparent, multo tardius feruntur, quàm ullu Planeta: (quippe in brevissimo suo circuitu viginti sex dies impendunt, Mercurius autem in suo plusquam sexagies majori vix tres menses, & Saturnus in suo forte bis millies majori annos tantum triginta, qui nisi celeriùs ipsis moveretur, plus centum deberet impendere.) Hoc enim putabimus accidere ex eo, quod particula tertii elementi, orta à continuâ maculârum dissolutione, congregatae sint circa Solem, atque ibi magnam quandam molem aëris sive atheris componant, forte usque ad sphaeram Mercurii, vel etiam ulterius extensam, cujus atheris particulae càm sint valdè irregulares & ramosa, sibi invicem sic adhaerent, ut non disjunctim concitentur, quemadmodum globuli materiae coelestis, sed omnes simul à Sole rapiantur, & cum ipsis tum macula solares, tum etiam pars coeli Mercurio vicina; unde fit, ut non multo plures circuitus, quàm Mercurius, eodem tempore absolvant, nec proinde tam cito moveantur. Apparet ergo adversarium parum legisse Cartesium, quod tamen ejus refutatorem decebat, qui hic & alibi ea objicit, ad quae jam diu à Cartesio responsum. Non ergo Sol tam tardè movetur ac maculæ solares, nec propterea tardius quàm terra, sed longè celerius. Et novum hinc paralogismum antagonistæ videre licet.
units.tr: Reply. That this motion is most rapid is evident from the nature of the matter of which the Sun consists, which is most fluid and of the most rapid agitation, being of the same nature as fire, except that our fire has many earthly and airy parts mixed in, and therefore its motion is slower. But Descartes himself had already solved the difficulty raised, at Pp. III. 148, and I am pleased to quote his words. Nor meanwhile, he says, shall we be surprised that the spots which appear on its surface move much more slowly than any planet (for they take twenty-six days in their very short circuit, while Mercury in its more than sixty times larger one takes scarcely three months, and Saturn, in its perhaps two thousand times larger one, only thirty years, which, unless it moved more swiftly, would have to take more than a hundred). For we shall think this happens from the fact that particles of the third element, arising from the continual dissolution of the spots, have gathered about the Sun and there form a great mass of air or aether, perhaps extended as far as the sphere of Mercury or even beyond; and since the particles of this aether are very irregular and branching, they cling to one another so that they are not set in motion separately, as the globules of celestial matter are, but all are carried along together by the Sun, and with them both the solar spots and also the part of the heavens near Mercury; whence it comes about that they do not complete many more circuits than Mercury in the same time, and therefore do not move so quickly. It appears, then, that our opponent has read Descartes little, which nevertheless befitted his refuter, who here and elsewhere raises objections to which Descartes replied long ago. Therefore the Sun does not move as slowly as the solar spots, nor for that reason more slowly than the earth, but far more quickly. And from this one may see a new paralogism of the antagonist.

units.la: CCCLXXXI. 3. Absurdum esse putat B. p. 262. quod hinc consequitur, nimirum, tardius moveri materiam cœlestem circa verticem terræ quàm circa Solem.
units.tr: CCCLXXXI. 3. He thinks it absurd, B. p. 262, that the following consequence follows: namely, that celestial matter moves more slowly around the pole of the earth than around the Sun.

units.la: Resp. Hæc absurditas consequitur ipsi ex priori; nimirum, prius existimavit Solem longè tardius moveri circa axem suum, quàm terra circa Solem moveatur, & hinc comparatione institutâ tribuerat diurno motui superficiei solaris milliaria 1572. nunc autem reperit ex hypoth. Copernici & Lansbergii materiæ cœlestis circa terram motui diurno competere milliaria 16785. Verum, quin uno absurdo dato alia consequantur, non negamus, sed & uno absurdo sublato alia auferri necesse est. Quoniam itaque ostendimus, nequaquam ex nostra sententia consequi, Solem tardius circa axem suum gyrare, quàm Terra circa Solem defertur, adeoque longe plus diurno motui superficiei solaris competere, quàm milliaria 1572. etiam cadit id, quod inde educit, materiam solarem tardius moveri quàm materiam cœlestem, quæ circa terram existit, totaque ista computatio frustrà est instituta.
units.tr: Reply: This absurdity follows from his earlier one. Namely, he previously judged that the Sun rotates on its own axis far more slowly than the earth moves around the Sun, and by making that comparison he had assigned to the solar surface's daily motion 1572 miles. Now, however, he finds from the hypothesis of Copernicus and Lansbergius that the daily motion of celestial matter around the earth amounts to 16785 miles. Now, we do not deny that from one absurdity other absurdities may follow, but when one absurdity is removed the others must also be taken away. Since therefore we have shown that by our view it does not at all follow that the Sun turns on its axis more slowly than the Earth is carried around the Sun, and that the daily motion of the solar surface is therefore far greater than 1572 miles, the conclusion he draws, that solar matter moves more slowly than the celestial matter that exists around the earth, also falls, and this whole calculation has been made in vain.

units.la: CCCLXXXII. 4. Inquit B. p. 283. Galilæus Galilei magnus ille macularum solarium inventor & observator, qui ex maculis illis magis præsupponit, quàm certo affirmavit corpus solare in gyrum verti, probat Dial. 3. polum macularum illarum diversum esse à polo ecliptica, unde porro sequetur, etiam polos motus corporis solaris esse diversos à polis ecliptica, circa quos Planetæ omnes moventur. Jam velim ostendi, quomodo circumgyratio Solis circa propriios polos secum possit abripere & movere vortices circa alios polos.
units.tr: CCCLXXXII. 4. He says, B. p. 283: Galileo Galilei, that great discoverer and observer of the solar spots, who from those spots presupposed rather than with certainty affirmed that the solar body turns in a circle, proves in the third Dialogue that the pole of those spots is different from the pole of the ecliptic; whence it further follows that the poles of the motion of the solar body are also different from the poles of the ecliptic, around which all the planets move. Now I should like it shown how the rotation of the Sun around its own poles can carry with it and move the vortices around other poles.

units.la: Resp. Agnoscimus, quod poli macularum, qui iidem sunt cum polis corporis solaris, ut & Cartesius statuit Princ. III. 95. quando dicit, maculas Solis in orbem circa Solis polos moveri, differant à polis ecliptica. Et sic Cartesius art. 35. ex Scheinero ponit Solis maculas in planis septem gradibus aut amplius ad eclipticam inclinatis circa Solem volvi, adeo ut earum motus hac in re non differat à motibus Planetarum, quorum nullus movetur circa polos ecliptica, exceptâ solâ terrâ secundum nos, secundum Ptolemæum & Tychonem unico Sole. Poli autem macularum cum iidem sint cum polis Solis, quærendum tantum, quare fiat, ut poli Solis non sint iidem cum polis ecliptica, & cum polis motuum Planetarum, & tamen Sol circa se Terram & reliquos Planetas faciat gyrare. Ad quod Resp. Solem, quantum in se est, ita rapere hos globos, ut via ipsorum rum motus parallela sit corporis solaris ecliptica, sed quod inde deflectant, Terra septem gradibus, alii Planetæ magis minusve, oritur ex aliis causis, nempe, quod materia primi elementi per polos hujus cœli, in quo Sol, ingrediens & sic in sphæroides illud, intra quod versantur Planetæ, irruens & transiens corpus Planetæ, eum vel possit attollere super planum Solis vel infra illud deprimere, per quam exaltationem & depressionem motus in latitudinem indicatur.
units.tr: Reply: We acknowledge that the poles of the spots, which are the same as the poles of the solar body, as Descartes also holds in Principles III, 95, where he says that the Sun's spots move in a circle around the Sun's poles, differ from the poles of the ecliptic. And so Descartes, art. 35, following Scheiner, holds that the Sun's spots revolve around the Sun on planes inclined seven degrees or more to the ecliptic, so that in this respect their motion does not differ from the motions of the planets, none of which moves around the poles of the ecliptic, except the earth alone according to us, and according to Ptolemy and Tycho the single Sun. Since, then, the poles of the spots are the same as the poles of the Sun, the only question is why it happens that the poles of the Sun are not the same as the poles of the ecliptic and the poles of the planets' motions, and yet the Sun makes the Earth and the other planets revolve around itself. To this we reply that the Sun, as far as it is in itself, carries these globes so that the path of their motion is parallel to the ecliptic of the solar body; but that they deviate from it, the Earth by seven degrees and the other planets more or less, arises from other causes: namely, that the matter of the first element, entering through the poles of this heaven in which the Sun lies, and so rushing into and passing through that spheroid within which the planets move, is able either to lift the body of the planet above the plane of the Sun or to press it down below it, and by this elevation and depression the motion in latitude is produced.

units.la: CCCLXXXIII. 5. Inquit B. p. 283. Cum Sol non sit centrum Planetarum, nisi admodum late sumtum, & Saturni centrum nulla ratione dici queat, ostendi etiam debet, quomodo Sol secum possit rapere orbes eccentricos circa varia, & tam à Sole quam à se invicem distita centra?
units.tr: CCCLXXXIII. 5. He says, B. p. 283: Since the Sun is not the centre of the planets, except in a very loose sense, and the centre of Saturn cannot in any way be said to be the Sun, it must also be shown how the Sun can carry with it eccentric orbits around various centres, distant both from the Sun and from one another?

units.la: Resp. Neg, quod non possit Sol dici centrum Saturni, quum ambiat Solem circuitus Saturni. 2. quod petit ostendi adversarius, jam ostendit Cartesius, quando rationes reddidit apheliorum & periheliorum Planetarum, nempe Pp. III. 141. Motus quidem Planetarum circa Solem pendent ab ipso Sole & materia cœlesti, infra cujus ambitum Planeta aliquis est detrusus, sed quia spatium, in quo simul cum tota materia cœli rotatur, non est perfecte sphæricum, fit, ut, ubi illud latius est, lentius fluat materia cœli, adeoque Planeta magis à Sole removeatur, ubi angustius, celerius fluatista materia, & sic Planeta magis ad Solem accedat.
units.tr: Reply: First, I deny that the Sun cannot be called the centre of Saturn, since Saturn's circuit surrounds the Sun. Second, what the adversary asks to have shown, Descartes has already shown, when he gave the reasons for the aphelia and perihelia of the planets, namely in Principles III, 141: The motions of the planets around the Sun depend indeed on the Sun itself and on the celestial matter, beneath whose circuit some planet is thrust; but because the space in which the whole matter of the heaven rotates together with it is not perfectly spherical, it happens that where it is wider the celestial matter flows more slowly, and so the planet is carried farther from the Sun, and where it is narrower the matter flows more quickly, and so the planet approaches the Sun more closely.

units.la: Duabus his difficultatibus, quartæ nempe & quintæ, hic ab antagonista objectis jam satisfecerat Cartesius art. 141. — 146. Quod si quis hæc quæ à nobis ad eas sunt dicta, non satis possit percipere, operam impendat in evolvendo lib. III. Princip. nec enim, quæ ex interioribus penetralibus hujus Philosophiæ petuntur, aliter, quam multis aliis, quibus innituntur, admissis & intellectis, intelligi queunt.
units.tr: Descartes had already answered these two difficulties, the fourth and the fifth, which the adversary raised here, in art. 141–146. If anyone cannot sufficiently grasp what we have said in reply to them, let him take the trouble to work through Book III of the Principles; for what is drawn from the inner recesses of this philosophy cannot be understood otherwise than by admitting and understanding the many other things on which it rests.

units.la: CCCLXXXIV. Quærit 3. B. p. 283. An materia cœlestis partes Soli viciniores velocius moveantur quam remotiores? Cujus negativam prolixe se putat demonstrasse, verum, quoniam Auctor Demonstrationis Mathematicæ ignorantia & ineptiarum du Bois ad incitas hic redegit adversarium, nos lectorem eo remittimus.
units.tr: CCCLXXXIV. He asks, third, B. p. 283: Do the parts of celestial matter nearer the Sun move more swiftly than those more remote? He thinks he has demonstrated the negative of this at length; but since the author of the Mathematical Demonstration of the Ignorance and Trifles of du Bois has here reduced the adversary to nothing, we refer the reader to him.

units.la: PROPOSITIO XXII.
units.tr: PROPOSITION XXII.

units.la: CCCLXXXV. Globuli sideri proximi sunt minores remotioribus, art. 85. Esse enim inter eos quoad magnitudinem differentiam, patet exinde, quia etsi ab initio omnes fuerint æquales, fieri tamen non potuit, quin lapsa temtemporis ob inæqualitatem spatiorum quæ percurrunt, & motûs inæqualitatem inde ortam (per Propof. 6.) aliqui aliis minores evaderent. Jam autem celerius moventur priores remotioribus (per Propof. 21.) si ergo centro proximi essent majores vel æquales superioribus, eo ipso plus vel tantum haberent virium à centro recedendi, & sic evaderent superiores.
units.tr: 385. The globules nearest the star are smaller than the more remote ones, art. 85. That there is a difference in size between them is plain from this: even if at the beginning all were equal, it could not but happen, as time passed, that some became smaller than others, because of the unequal spaces they traverse and the unequal motion arising from this (by Prop. 6). Now the earlier ones move more swiftly than the remote ones (by Prop. 21). So if those nearer the centre were larger than or equal to the upper ones, they would by that very fact have more or as much force for receding from the centre, and so they would become the upper ones.

units.la: SCHOLIVM.
units.tr: SCHOLIUM.

units.la: CCCLXXXVI. Exc. B. p. 291. Si motus velocior arguat globulos & minores esse, & propinquiores centro, necessario sequetur, globulos orbis terra, (posito, eam in vortice suo ferri circa Solem) minores esse globulis orbis Veneris, & terram Soli multo propinquiorem, cum Veneris orbu tardius, terra velocius moveatur, ut ad Propof. 21. latè probatum est.
units.tr: 386. Excerpt from B., p. 291. If greater speed indicates that the globules are both smaller and nearer the centre, it will necessarily follow that the globules of the earth's orb (supposing that the earth is carried in its vortex about the Sun) are smaller than the globules of Venus's orb, and that the earth is much nearer the Sun, since the orb of Venus moves more slowly and the earth more swiftly, as has been widely proved at Prop. 21.

units.la: Resp. Ego in hujus Propositionis demonstratione probo 1. esse globulos aliis minores. 2. eos qui minores sunt, sideri esse proximos. Primum necessario ex eo consequitur, (non obstante, quod primum dicantur fuisse æquales,) quod debuerunt inæqualia spatia percurrere propter vorticis inæqualitatem, qui non est accurate rotundus, & hinc alii aliis celerius moveri per Propof. 6. Hoc enim facto, illi, qui habuerunt majorem celeritatem, quam acquisiverunt transeundo per spatia angusta, debuerunt fortius inter se collidi, & sic plus de suâ materiâ perdiderunt. Secundum vero clarissime probato priori consequitur. Cum enim centro proximi celerius moveantur quàm remotiores. Ergo posito, quod propiores fuissent centro, tamen ob majorem vim à centro recedendi, quam habuissent præ minoribus, debuissent minores antevertere, easque in locum à se relictum detrudere versus centrum. Adversarius vero hic, quid impugnet nescit. Ex eo enim, quod aliqui globuli sint proximi sideri, ostendi, etiam celerius moveri remotioribus Propof. præcedente. Hic vero, dum vortex esset in fieri, demonstravi, globulos ejus alios aliis minores factos, quod majorem quidem celeritatem acquisiverint transeundo per spatia angustiora, adeoque fortius debuerint collidi, & sic plus materiæ abradi. Quæ vero ad Propof. 21. oppositum, eorum inanitas clarissime est demonstrata. Accurate attendens ad articulos Cartesii, unde desumpta hæc sunt, videbit eorum soliditatem.
units.tr: Answer. In the demonstration of this proposition I prove, first, that some globules are smaller than others; second, that those which are smaller are nearer the star. The first follows necessarily from this (although they are said to have been equal at first): because, on account of the unevenness of the vortex, which is not exactly round, they had to traverse unequal spaces, and hence some move more swiftly than others by Prop. 6. For this happening, those which had greater speed, acquired by passing through narrow spaces, must have collided more violently with one another, and so they lost more of their matter. The second follows very clearly from the first. For since those nearer the centre move more swiftly than the more remote ones, then, supposing they were nearer the centre, yet because of their greater force for receding from the centre than the smaller ones had, they must have outstripped the smaller ones and thrust them down, towards the centre, into the place they had left. But the adversary here does not know what he is attacking. For from the fact that some globules are near the star, it was shown by the preceding Prop. that they also move more swiftly than the remoter ones. Here, however, while the vortex was in process of formation, I demonstrated that its globules became smaller than one another, because they acquired greater speed by passing through narrower spaces, and so must have collided more violently, and thus more of their matter was worn away. As for the opposite argument against Prop. 21, its emptiness has been most clearly demonstrated. Attending carefully to the articles of Descartes, from which these things are drawn, he will see their soundness.

units.la: PROPOSITIO XXIII.
units.tr: PROPOSITION XXIII.

units.la: CCCLXXXVII. Terra fuit aliquando sidus Pp. IV. 1. 2. Cum enim ex hypothesi quartâ, in ipsa centrum etiam fuerit, circa quod quædam materia movebatur, cætera omnia ex demonstratis eodem modo contingere debuerunt, ut materia subtilis in istud centrum confluxerit, & sic sidus constituerit.
units.tr: CCCLXXXVII. The earth was once a star. Pp. IV. 1. 2. For since, on the fourth hypothesis, there was also a centre in it, around which a certain matter was moving, everything else ought to have happened in the same way, as shown above: subtle matter flowed together into that centre and so constituted a star.

units.la: SCHOLIVM.
units.tr: SCHOLIUM.

units.la: CCCLXXXVIII. Hæc Propositio & sequentes intelligendæ sunt secundum ea, quæ ad hypotheses superius annotavi. Ergo terra fuit aliquando sidus, intellige, in modo nostro considerandi ex hypothesi, quod debeat considerari, prout successive secundum leges naturæ debuisset & potuisset fieri, sive, Terra prius consideranda est tanquam sidus, quoniam integram & totam simul non possumus spectare, sed quomodo paulatim talis fieri potuerit, etsi historia Creationis testaretur, quod Deus momento talem fecerit. Dico ergo, si ejus natura debeat cognosci, oportere hoc modo considerari, quomodo secundum leges naturæ, si Deus voluisset successive efficere, debuerit formari, assumendo omnes formas ordine, donec tandem ad hanc, quam habet, pervenerit; sicut enim nunc stella fixa mutatur in Planetam vel Cometam, ita in terræ natura accurate percipienda, quæ hactenus cum Planetis convenit, tale ejus initium considerandum.
units.tr: CCCLXXXVIII. This proposition and those that follow must be understood in line with what I have noted above concerning the hypotheses. So the earth was once a star is to be understood as in our way of considering it on the hypothesis, that is, it is to be considered as it ought to have, and could have, come about successively according to the laws of nature. In other words, the Earth must first be considered as a star, since we cannot view the whole of it at once, but only how it could gradually have become such, even though the history of Creation tells us that God made it such in a moment. I say, therefore, that if its nature is to be known, it must be considered in this way: how, according to the laws of nature, it ought to have been formed if God had willed to produce it successively, taking up all the forms in order until it finally reached the one it now has. For just as a fixed star now changes into a planet or a comet, so in accurately grasping the nature of the earth, which so far agrees with the planets, its beginning must be considered in this way.

units.la: CCCLXXXIX. Contra hanc propositionem vehementer insurgit B. p. 292. (utrùm ex imperitiâ, an malitia non facile dixerim) ac clamat, hanc propositionem Mosi in os contradicere, doctrinam continere ἀνιγεάφον & futilißimam, quæ in Theologia Professore sit intolerabilis.
units.tr: CCCLXXXIX. B. p. 292. vehemently rises up against this proposition (I can hardly say whether from ignorance or malice) and cries out that this proposition directly contradicts Moses, contains an unwritten [ἄγραφον] and most trifling doctrine, and is intolerable in a professor of theology.

units.la: Resp. Si Theologis dicentibus: Deus prius fecit decretum de fine, quàm de mediis, vel, Deus decrevit prius, hominem creare, dein decrevit lapsum permittere, oggeras, eos in os contradicere simplicitati divinæ, nonne responderetur, hoc intelligendum esse de modo nostro considerandi? quidni ergo eandem responsionem ex art. 338. potuisses circa hanc quæstionem depromere? Methodum enim hanc considerandi opera Dei supponere creationis historiam veram, neque ei quid velle derogatum, apparet ex Pp. III. 45. sed hæc non impedit, quo minus possimus considerare Terram, prout fieri potuisset à Deo, si Deo successive cessive agere placuisset, ad cognoscendam ejus naturam & reddendas causas variorum Phænomenon; quoniam ex hac consideratione cognoscitur, eam nihilominus habere talem naturam, ac si successive fuisset creata.
units.tr: Reply: If, when theologians say that God first made the decree concerning the end and then concerning the means, or that God decreed first to create man and then decreed to permit the fall, you were to object that they contradict the divine simplicity, would it not be answered that this must be understood in our way of considering things? Why, then, could you not bring forward the same answer from article 338 on this question? For that this method of considering God's works presupposes the true history of creation, and that nothing is meant to detract from it, appears from Pp. III. 45. But this does not prevent us from considering the earth as it could have been made by God, had God been pleased to act successively, in order to know its nature and to give the causes of its various phenomena; for from this consideration it is known that it nonetheless has such a nature as if it had been created successively.

units.la: CCCXC. Ex his ita declaratis apparet: Propositionem istam Terra fuit aliquando sidus, non esse absurdam, quamvis si sola inspiciatur (non consideratis iis, quæ art. 6. hujus capitis etiam in priori editione dixeram, facientibus quàm maxime ad istius & seqq. Propositionum intellectum) absurditatem manifestam involvere videatur. In quem finem, utque sententias Cartesii & eorum, quos in Methodo philosophandi ipsum sequi non pudet, odiosas publico redderet, hanc Propositionem, ut & alias ex meis Dissertationibus citavit Suetonius Tranquillus in suo libello Belgico: Naerder openinge van eenige stucken in de Cartesiaensche Philosophie &c. qui modus agendi si obtineat, sique verba quædam separata ab aliis, ex quibus eorum sensus evadit conspicuus, liceat seorsim proponere ad sententiam alicujus publico proponendam, nec ipsa Scriptura ab accusatione de maxime absurdis libera esse potest.
units.tr: CCCXC. From what has now been explained it is clear that this proposition, the earth was once a star, is not absurd, although if it is looked at alone (without considering what I said in article 6 of this chapter, even in the earlier edition, which contributes greatly to understanding this and the following propositions), it may seem to involve a manifest absurdity. To this end, and so as to make the opinions of Descartes and of those who are not ashamed to follow him in the Method of Philosophizing odious to the public, Suetonius Tranquillus, in his Dutch booklet Closer explanation of some points in Cartesian philosophy, etc., cited this proposition, as well as others, from my Dissertations. If this way of acting were to prevail, and if it were allowed to put forward certain words separately from others, by which their meaning becomes evident, in order to expose someone's opinion to public odium, then not even Scripture itself could be free from the charge of being most absurd.

units.la: PROPOSITIO XXIV.
units.tr: PROPOSITION XXIV.

units.la: CCCXCI. Terra obducta est tandem maculis, & vortex ejus absumptus fuit à vortice potentiore vicini Solis Pp. IV. 2. Cum enim fuerit sidus, (per Prop. 23.) nunc autem tam crassa existat, debuit necessario tam densis maculis obvolvi. Facile sane potuit contingere, ut materiæ illius subtilis partes irregulares & minus subtiles sibi mutuo adhærerent, & non tam facile circumagi possent. Itaque sic tanto commodius aliæ atque aliæ minutiæ adhærere potuerunt, donec tandem tam crassa facta fuerit obductio, ut materia subtilis, quæ intra istam maculam circumvolvebatur, (per Prop. 16. & 8.) nullam vim ad circumrapiendum globulos sui vorticis potuerit exserere, quo facto iste vortex facile ab adjacente potentiori fuit absorptus.
units.tr: CCCXCI. The earth was at last covered with spots, and its vortex was absorbed by the more powerful vortex of the neighbouring Sun Pp. IV. 2. For since it was a star (by Prop. 23), but is now so dense, it must necessarily have been enveloped in such thick spots. It could quite easily happen that the irregular and less subtle parts of that subtle matter adhered to one another and could not so easily be made to revolve. Thus, all the more conveniently, one and another tiny particle could adhere, until at last the covering became so thick that the subtle matter revolving within that spot (by Props. 16 and 8) could exert no force to snatch away the globules of its own vortex. Once this happened, that vortex was easily absorbed by the more powerful neighbouring one.

units.la: SCHOLIUM
units.tr: SCHOLIUM

units.la: CCCXCII. Quæ hic iterum objiciuntur à B.p.293. similia sunt præcedentibus, cum non evincant, non posse terram considerari, prout successivè à Deo potuit creari. Cur enim nobis non sit concessum considerare res naturales secundum eos status, in quibus quidem diversis vicibus non exstiterunt, quando primum creatæ sunt & productæ, sed tamen si successivè fuissent factæ, debuerunt exstitisse.
units.tr: CCCXCII. What B. p. 293 objects here again is similar to the preceding, since it does not prove that the earth cannot be considered as having been created successively by God. For why should we not be allowed to consider natural things according to those states in which they did not exist at the same time when they were first created and produced, but which, had they been made successively, they ought to have existed in?

units.la: PROPOSITIO XXV.
units.tr: PROPOSITION XXV.

units.la: CCCXCIII. Terra fuit detrusa versus Solem. Pp. IV. art. 2. Cum enim vortex ejus fuerit absorptus à vortice Solis (per Prop. 24.) etiam ipsum sidus maculâ obductum à vortice absorbente necessariò debuit rapi: Materia autem circa Solem circumvoluta conabatur magis magisque semper recedere à centro (per Prop. 9.) Itaque omne illud, quod sibi obstabat, ut hic Terram, depellere debuit versus centrum, ut in ejus locum ascenderet, quamdiu nempe in isto sidere maculis obducto, sive Terrâ, nullus alius motus consideratur.
units.tr: CCCXCIII. The earth was thrust down towards the Sun. Pp. IV. art. 2. For since its vortex was absorbed by the vortex of the Sun (by Prop. 24), the star itself, also covered with spots, must necessarily have been carried off by the absorbing vortex. But the matter circulating around the Sun kept striving to recede ever more from the centre (by Prop. 9). Therefore everything that stood in its way, such as the Earth here, had to be pushed down towards the centre, so as to rise into its place, for as long, namely, as no other motion is considered in that star covered with spots, or Earth.

units.la: SCHOLIUM.
units.tr: SCHOLIUM.

units.la: CCCXCIV. Ad hanc Propositionem cum nihil reponat B. 294. nisi quod modum quo res creatæ fuerint opponat modo considerandi successivo, quæ non repugnare ostendi, pergimus ad Prop. 26.
units.tr: CCCXCIV. Since he replies to this Proposition with nothing except that he opposes to the successive mode of considering things the mode in which created things were made, and I have shown that these do not conflict, we proceed to Prop. 26.

units.la: PROPOSITIO XXVI.
units.tr: PROPOSITION XXVI.

units.la: CCCXCV. Terra fuit detrusa in locum, in quo nunc est, Pp. III. 40. In eum enim locum debuit descendere, ubi sunt globuli cœlestes, quibus in soliditate, sive in aptitudine ad perseverandum in suo motu sunt lineas rectas est æqualis. Si enim propius versus Solem accederet, versaretur ibi inter globulos cœlestes paulo minores, (per Prop. 27.) quos superaret vi ad recedendum à centro, circa quod gyrat, & sic superior evaderet: versaretur etiam inter globulos paulo celerius motos (per Prop. 21.) à quibus vim majorem ad recedendum à centro acciperet, atque ita inde rursus egredi deberet. Si verò magis recederet à Sole, ei occurrerent globuli cœlestes aliquanto minus celeriter moti (per Prop. 21.) qui proinde ejus agitationem sive vim recedendi à centro minuerent, & paulo majores (per Prop.22.) qui proinde vim haberent ipsam depellendi.
units.tr: CCCXCV. The earth was thrust into the place in which it now is, Pp. III. 40. For it had to descend into that place where the heavenly globules are equal in solidity, or in aptitude for persisting in their motion along straight lines. For if it came closer to the Sun, it would be there among heavenly globules slightly smaller (by Prop. 27), which it would surpass with its force of receding from the centre around which it gyrates, and so would become the higher. It would also be among globules moving slightly faster (by Prop. 21), from which it would receive greater force of receding from the centre, and so would have to be driven out again from there. But if it withdrew further from the Sun, it would meet heavenly globules moving somewhat more slowly (by Prop. 21), which would therefore diminish its agitation, or its force of receding from the centre, and slightly larger ones (by Prop. 22), which would therefore have the force of thrusting it down.

units.la: SCHOLIUM.
units.tr: SCHOLIUM.

units.la: CCCXCVI. Hanc propositionem antecedentibus niti, ex iisque demonstratis fluere agnoscit B. p. 295. in quo acquiescimus.
units.tr: CCCXCVI. He acknowledges that this proposition rests on the preceding ones and follows from what has been demonstrated, and in this we acquiesce.

units.la: PROPOSITIO XXVII.
units.tr: PROPOSITION XXVII.

units.la: CCCXCVII. Terra in eo loco, in quo est, defertur à materia ambiente annua delatione. Fuit enim absorptus à vortice Solis vortex Terræ (per Prop. 25.) & detrusa Terra in eum locum, in quo nunc est, (per Prop. 26.) ubi materia cœlestis eam ambit, quæ fluida est, (ex antecedentibus) & in circulum movetur (ex hypoth. 4.) Ergò (per Prop. 12.) corpus durum, quod inibi est positum, secum defert. Quo autem tempore Terra ita delata redeat ad locum eundem, ex phænomenis discendum. Fit illud, quando Sol sub eodem signo iterum conspicitur, sub quo antea fuit conspectus, ut si ex. gr. fuerit conspectus sub Ariete, quando iterum sub eodem signo conspicitur, censenda est circuitum suum absolvisse, quod annuo spatio fieri, experientia docet.
units.tr: 397. The earth is carried along, in the place where it is, by the surrounding matter with an annual motion. For the vortex of the Earth was absorbed by the vortex of the Sun (by Prop. 25), and the Earth, thrust out into the place where it now is (by Prop. 26), is surrounded there by celestial matter, which is fluid (from what precedes) and is moved in a circle (by hypothesis 4). Therefore (by Prop. 12) the hard body that is placed within it carries the Earth along with it. At what time the Earth, so carried, returns to the same place is to be learned from the phenomena. This happens when the Sun is seen again under the same sign under which it was seen before: for example, if it was seen under Aries, and is seen again under the same sign, the Earth is to be judged to have completed its circuit. Experience teaches that this happens in the course of a year.

units.la: SCHOLIUM.
units.tr: SCHOLIUM.

units.la: CCCXCVIII. Excipit B. p. 296. Hac Propositio, qua prima directè concludit pro motu terræ, est fundata tota in quarta hypoth. ex illa siquidem ortum habent vortices minores & majores, absorbentes & absorpti; item materia fluida, quæ in circulum circa Solem movetur, ita ut minimè necessarius fuerit tantus apparatus tot Propositionum & Hypothesium, cum hypothesis quarta sola sufficere potuisset.
units.tr: 398. Page 296 of B. objects: "This proposition, by which the first conclusion in favour of the motion of the earth is drawn directly, rests entirely on the fourth hypothesis. For from that hypothesis arise the lesser and greater vortices, the absorbing and the absorbed, and likewise the fluid matter that moves in a circle about the Sun. So the great apparatus of so many propositions and hypotheses was by no means necessary, since the fourth hypothesis alone could have sufficed."

units.la: Resp. Si lector ipse hanc demonstrationem inspiciat, videbit eam niti Prop. 25, 26. & 12. quæ iterum proxime antecedentibus nituntur, & sic deinceps, donec veniatur ad ipsas regulas naturæ, unde omnia, quæ hîc reperiuntur, fluunt. Hypothesis vero quarta tantum eo facit, ut possimus opera Dei successivè & per varias partes, & ut in fieri sunt, ordine considerare, quod necessarium esse ostendi. Quis vero in demonstrationibus Euclidis versatus aliquem ita ferat argumentantem? Hæc vel illa Prop. Euclidis v. g. 10. lib. 12, Omnis conus tertia pars est Cylindri eandem cum ipso basin habentis & altitudinem æqualem, nititur variis communibus axiomatibus, quia in ea resolvitur, E. omnes intermediæ Propositiones lõnga serie deducte ex istis axiomatibus, ut tandem proxime posset hæc ipsa Propositio demonstrari, non sunt necessariæ, & inutilis tantum apparatus; vel aliud quodcunque exemplum sumatur, ubi propositio aliqua nititur longa Propos. concatenatarum serie, quæ tandem in communes notiones, & quasdam hypotheses similes nostris resolvuntur.
units.tr: Reply: If the reader himself examines this demonstration, he will see that it rests on Propositions 25, 26 and 12, which in turn rest on the propositions immediately preceding them, and so on, until one comes to the very laws of nature from which all the things found here flow. The fourth hypothesis merely serves to let us consider the works of God successively and part by part, in the order in which they come into being; and I have shown that this is necessary. But who that is versed in the demonstrations of Euclid would put up with such an argument? This or that proposition of Euclid, for example the 10th of Book 12, "Every cone is a third part of a cylinder having the same base and an equal height," rests on various common axioms, because it is resolved into them. All the intermediate propositions, deduced through a long series from those axioms, so that at last this very proposition could be demonstrated, are not necessary, and are only a useless apparatus. Or let any other example be taken where some proposition rests on a long series of linked propositions, which at last are resolved into common notions and certain hypotheses similar to ours.

units.la: CCCXCIX. Pergit B. p. 297. Demonstrationem non posse esse solidam, quia supponatur, dari vortices, Solem esse centrum, dari verticem terræ, deferentem corpus terræ, quæ omnia neget.
units.tr: 399. Page 297 of B. goes on: "The demonstration cannot be sound, because it presupposes that there are vortices, that the Sun is the centre, that there is a vortex of the earth carrying the body of the earth, all of which he denies."

units.la: Resp. Quid supponatur, quid probetur, ex antecedentibus constat; suppositiones tantum faciunt ad successivam considerationem rerum naturalium, quâ posita evincitur ex naturæ legibus & principiis naturâ notis, talem esse rerum naturam, quæ per vortices & similia, quæ superius posuimus, non per alia possit explicari. Quod si in fieri talis est terra ut necessario legibus naturæ sic ferentibus debuerit rotari circa Solem: Ergo etiam in facto esse debet talis agnosci. Quid vero neget adversarius parum curamus, dummodo contra ejus negationem firma fuerit nostra argumentatio.
units.tr: Reply: What is presupposed and what is proved is clear from what precedes. Suppositions serve only for the successive consideration of natural things, by which, once they are granted, it is shown from the laws of nature and principles known by nature that the nature of things is such that it can be explained through vortices and similar things, which we set out above, and not through other things. And if the earth in its coming into being was such that, by the laws of nature so directing, it must necessarily have revolved about the Sun, then it ought also to be recognised as such in fact. As for what the adversary denies, we care little, provided our argument stands firm against his denial.

units.la: PROPOSITIO XXVIII.
units.tr: PROPOSITION XXVIII.

units.la: CCCC. Terra simul circumvolvitur à materia cœlesti ambiente circumvolutione diurna. Nam cum vicissitudo diei & noctis, positis his omnibus, quæ antea sunt demonstrata, non possit fieri motu Solis circa terram diurno, nec alia causa afferri queat, necessario id fieri debet per Terræ conversionem. 2. Cum Terra fuerit sidus (per Propos. 23.) ergo potuit retinere illum motum, quem antea habuit, materiaque subtilis in ejus centro, cum procul dubio adhuc moveatur (per Prop. 8.) Terram impellere potest. 3. Quia Luna movetur circa Terram (uti satis constat ex phænomenis) debuit hoc ex antea demonstratis inde contingere, quod cum non minorem habeat vim agitationis quam Terra, in eadem sphæra debuerit versari, (per Prop. 26.) &, cum molem minor, æqualem habens vim agitationis, celerius debeat fieri. Ergo fuit delata versus terram in eadem sphæra. Est autem Luna quantitate satis magna, ita ut secundum Clavium ad terram proportionem habeat, qualem 1. ad 39 1/2. Vacuum etiam dari nequit, (er Prop. 2.) nec minui potest extensio, non minutâ substantiâ corporeâ (per Prop. 3.) Quare ita versus Terram delata mole sua compressit globulos versus Terram, qui cum tam cito non potuerint cedere, ut circulus fieret, (per Prop. 5.) propter nimiam miam Lunæ agitationem, restiterunt, ut Luna ad Terram non potuerit magis accedere, quàm accessit. Quare Luna (per Prop. 10.) etiam determinationem motûs accepit, ita ut circa Terram gyret, dum interim unà cum illa circa Solem defertur à materiâ cœlesti ambiente. Quia ergò vis & quantitas magna est Lunæ, ex antecedentibus, facile potuit materiam cœlestem inter se & Terram interjectam in modum vorticis contorquere, quæ simul Terram circa axem suum convolvit (per Prop. 12.)
units.tr: 400. The earth is at the same time turned around by the heavenly matter surrounding it, in a diurnal circular motion. For since the alternation of day and night, with all the things demonstrated above laid down, cannot be brought about by the diurnal motion of the Sun around the earth, and no other cause can be brought forward, it must necessarily happen through the rotation of the Earth. 2. Since the Earth was a star (by Prop. 23), it could retain the motion it had before. The subtle matter at its centre, which without doubt is still moving (by Prop. 8), is able to impel the Earth. 3. Because the Moon moves around the Earth (as is sufficiently clear from the phenomena), this must come about from what was demonstrated before.
