Since it has no less force of agitation than the Earth, it must have been situated in the same sphere (by Prop. 26), and, being smaller in mass but having equal force of agitation, it must be made to move more swiftly. Therefore it was carried towards the earth in the same sphere. The Moon is indeed quite large, so that according to Clavius it has to the earth a proportion of about 1 to 39 1/2. A vacuum also cannot be granted (by Prop. 2), nor can extension be diminished without a diminution of corporeal substance (by Prop. 3). Therefore, carried thus towards the Earth, by its mass it compressed the globules towards the Earth. Since these could not yield quickly enough for a circle to form (by Prop. 5), on account of the excessive agitation of the Moon, they resisted, so that the Moon could not approach the Earth any more than it did. Hence the Moon (by Prop. 10) also received a determination of motion, so that it revolves around the Earth while meanwhile it is carried along with it around the Sun by the surrounding heavenly matter. Therefore, since the force and quantity of the Moon are great, from what has gone before it could easily twist the heavenly matter lying between itself and the Earth in the manner of a vortex, which at the same time rolls the Earth around its axis (by Prop. 12).

units.la: Nec mirum esse debet, quod Terra fere tricies circa axem suum convolvatur, dum Luna tantum semel circumferentiam circuli sui circa Terram percurrit. Cum enim hæc circumferentia sit circiter sexagesies major terræ ambitu, sic Luna duplo celerius adhuc fertur, quàm Terra, & cum ambæ agantur ab eadem materia cœlesti, quam credibile est, non minus celeriter moveri prope Terram quàm prope Lunam, non alia causa videtur esse majoris in Luna celeritatis, quàm quod Terra sit minor.
units.tr: Nor ought it to be surprising that the Earth turns about its axis some thirty times while the Moon runs only once around its circle about the Earth. For since this circumference is about sixty times greater than the circuit of the earth, the Moon is carried twice as fast as the Earth. And since both are driven by the same heavenly matter, which it is credible moves no less swiftly near the Earth than near the Moon, no other cause seems to account for the greater speed of the Moon than that the Earth is smaller.

units.la: SCHOLIUM.
units.tr: SCHOLIUM.

units.la: CCCCI. Hæc Propositio triplicem, ut apparet, habet demonstrationem.
units.tr: 401. As appears, this Proposition has a threefold demonstration.

units.la: Ad primum B. p. 298. inquit, nondum esse probatum in antecedentibus, Solem motu suo circa terram vicissitudinem noctu non efficere.
units.tr: To the first, Baxter (p. 298) says that it has not yet been proved in the preceding that the Sun, by its motion around the earth, does not effect the alternation of night.

units.la: Resp. Quid probatum, quid non probatum, non judicio adversarii, sed lectoris à partibus alieni, & qui tantum operæ impendere voluerit, ut non tantum meas demonstrationes obiter aspicere, sed imprimis Cartesii principia, ad quæ digitum intendi, opera diligenti & attentione animi dignatus fuerit perlustrare, permitto.
units.tr: Reply. What has been proved and what has not, I leave to the judgment not of the adversary but of a reader free from partisanship, one who is willing to spend enough effort not merely to glance over my demonstrations in passing, but above all to go through with diligent care and close attention the principles of Descartes, to which I have pointed.

units.la: CCCCII. Ad secundam Probationem excipit. 1. Comperta fuit Propositio 23. vanissimum commentum historiæ sacræ contrarium, in vorticoso cerebro confictum.
units.tr: 402. To the second proof he objects: 1. Proposition 23 has been shown to be the most vain fiction of sacred history, contrived in a vortical brain.

units.la: Resp. Imò compertum fuit, te ei non nisi ignorantiam, ut lenissime dicam, opposuisse.
units.tr: Reply. Rather it has been shown that you have opposed nothing to it but ignorance, to put it most mildly.

units.la: CCCCIII. 2. Addit, darj talem materiam subtilem in centro terra nondum liquere.
units.tr: 403. 2. He adds that it is not yet clear that there is such subtle matter in the centre of the earth.

units.la: Resp. Ex eo id liquet, quod talis natura ejus, prout in fieri consideratur, debeat spectari, ut habuerit formam sideris, quod macula est obducta; at non potuit illa macula omnem materiam subtilem, quam obtexit, planè expellere.
units.tr: Reply. This is clear from the fact that its nature, as it is considered in its becoming, must be regarded as having had the form of a star, which is covered by a spot. But that spot could not wholly expel all the subtle matter which it covers.

units.la: CCCCIV. 3. Cupit probatum, eam materiam adhuc moveri.
units.tr: 404. 3. He desires it to be proved that this matter is still moving.

units.la: Resp. Si ibi sit materia subtilis, uti probatum dedimus, quæ in circulum necessariò movetur ex Prop. 16. Ergò, cum nulla res possit dari, quæ ejus motum impediat ex Prop. 8. facillimè ab oppositionibus adversarii defensa, debet manere in eodem statu; cum nihil quicquam possit excogitari, quod eam ab hoc statu deturbet.
units.tr: Reply. If there is subtle matter there, as we have shown, it is necessarily moved in a circle (by Prop. 16). Therefore, since no thing can be granted which would impede its motion (by Prop. 8), it is most easily defended against the adversary's objections, and it must remain in the same state, since nothing whatever can be conceived that would drive it from this state.

units.la: CCCCV. Ad tertiam Probationem objicit B. p. 300. me hic quidem videri prima facie probare Propositionem, sed interim nihil minus agere; me enim ingredi dissertatiunculam de motu Lunæ circa terram, quā tutò possit praeteriri, cum nitatur principiis & hypothesibus gratis assumptis & falsis, &c.
units.tr: 405. To the third proof he objects, at p. 300, that I indeed seem at first sight to prove the Proposition here, but meanwhile accomplish nothing less; for I enter upon a little dissertation on the motion of the Moon about the earth, which may safely be passed over, since it rests on principles and hypotheses gratuitously assumed and false, etc.

units.la: Resp. An revera probem, nec ne, lectori cordato expendendum relinquo, saltem adversarii fuisset defectum ostendere. Ut enim de motu Lunæ circa Terram dicam, satis ad rem factum apparet, cum exinde Terræ circa axem suum convolutionem deduxerim. Quæ verò de hypothesibus & principiis gratis assumptis saepius inculcat, ad ea negando respondeo, ac ad antecedentia lectorem remitto.
units.tr: Reply. Whether I really prove it or not I leave to the discerning reader to weigh; at least it was the adversary's business to show a defect. For as to what I say about the motion of the Moon about the Earth, it appears sufficiently to the point, since from it I have deduced the rotation of the Earth about its axis. As for what he repeatedly insists upon, namely hypotheses and principles gratuitously assumed, I answer by denying them, and refer the reader to what has gone before.

units.la: CCCCVI. Ita thesis nostra evidentissima, iis qui diligenter attendunt ad omnia, demonstratione est probata; Nunc etiam Antithesis Tychonis est evertenda, quo simul habebimus argumentum aliud ad nostræ sententiæ, quam hic propugnamus, confirmationem. Tychonis autem dispositionem absurdam esse inde est conspicuum. Cum enim Sol circa axem suum circumvolvatur, uti experientia comprobavit per Solis maculas, quæ spatio 26 dierum circiter circumvolvi cernuntur, & à Sole circumtrapiantur 5 Planetæ per hypoth. Tychonis, non potest ulla ratio concipi, quare etiam Terra intermedia inter proximos & remotiores Planetas, uti ex Systematis inspectione patet, non simul à Sole rapiatur, nisi fingas maximam aliquam vim, quæ, tractis à Sole remotioribus Planetis, corporibus longe majoribus, terram retineat immotam. Ad extraordinariam autem Dei potentiam hic confugere, cum quaerantur causæ naturales, est prorsus <bl>ἀπεγοδιόνωον</bl>.
units.tr: 406. Thus our thesis, most evident to those who attend diligently to everything, has been proved by demonstration. Now the antithesis of Tycho must also be overthrown, which will at the same time give us another argument confirming the opinion we here defend. That Tycho's arrangement is absurd is evident from this. For since the Sun turns about its own axis, as experience has confirmed through the spots on the Sun, which are seen to turn in about 26 days, and according to Tycho's hypothesis five planets are carried around by the Sun, no reason can be conceived why the Earth too, lying between the nearer and the more remote planets, as is plain from inspection of the system, is not likewise carried along by the Sun. Unless you feign some very great force which, with the more remote planets drawing bodies far larger, holds the earth motionless. But to flee here to the extraordinary power of God, when natural causes are being sought, is utterly absurd [ἀπεγοδιόνωον].

units.la: CCCCVII. Excipit B. D. p. 34. Si aliqua darentur argumenta verè demonstrativa, pro motu terræ diurno & annuo, ea à phænomenis & apparentiis deduci deberent.
units.tr: 407. He objects, at p. 34: If there were any arguments truly demonstrative for the diurnal and annual motion of the earth, they would have to be deduced from phenomena and appearances.

units.la: Resp. 1. Argumentum nostrum per propositiones 28 deductum, ut & quod præcedenti articulo adjectum, esse revera demonstrationem, patebit lectori benevolo, qui citra præjudicium rem voluerit perpendere, adhibitâ simul in consilium parte II. & III. Principiorum Philosophi, ubi omnia latius sunt deducta; nec existimo quicquam contra illa excipi posse, ad quod non facilis mihi parata sit responsio. 2. Argumentum, quod per causas naturales nexu evidentissimo inter se cohærentes effectum demonstrat, esse demonstrativum nemo negare potest, qui quid sit demonstratio ἐκ διότι cognitum habet; tale autem hoc nostrum esse inspectio docebit. Quam præferendam esse demonstrationi ἐκ ὅτι, quæ ab effectu ad causam procedit, accuratiores Logici ostendunt. Quamvis itaque forte apparentiæ æque per Tychonianam hypothesin salvari queant, ac per Copernicanam, adeoque demonstratio ἐκ τοῦ ὅτι haberi non queat, illius tamen defectum facile demonstratio à priori supplebit.
units.tr: Reply. 1. That our argument, deduced through Propositions 28, and also what was added in the preceding article, is in truth a demonstration, will be clear to the well-disposed reader who, without prejudice, is willing to weigh the matter, taking into counsel at the same time Parts II and III of the Principles of the Philosopher, where everything is set out more fully. Nor do I think anything can be objected against those things to which I do not have an easy and ready answer. 2. No one who knows what demonstration from the reason [ἐκ διότι] is can deny that an argument which demonstrates an effect through natural causes cohering among themselves by a most evident connection is demonstrative; and inspection will show that this argument of ours is such. That this is to be preferred to demonstration from the fact [ἐκ τοῦ ὅτι], which proceeds from effect to cause, the more accurate logicians show. Although, therefore, perhaps the appearances can be saved equally well by the Tychonic hypothesis as by the Copernican, and so demonstration from the fact cannot be had, nevertheless demonstration from the prior cause will easily supply its defect.

units.la: CCCCVIII. Excipit B. p. 301. Primo, Theologum magis decuisse argumento Theologico refellere sententiam Tychonis quàm Philosophico : ac si Theologum decet μεταβαίνειν εἰς ἄλλο γένος & Philosophica Theologicè tractare, aut non liceat Theologo Philosophicam considerationem rerum naturalium instituere. Nugæ!
units.tr: 408. He objects, at p. 301. First, that it would have better befitted a theologian to refute Tycho's opinion with a theological argument rather than a philosophical one. As if it befits a theologian to pass over into another genus [μεταβαίνειν εἰς ἄλλο γένος] and to treat philosophical matters theologically, or as if it were not permitted to the theologian to undertake a philosophical consideration of natural things. Trifles!

units.la: CCCCIX. Secundo proponit B. p. 202. Systematis Tychonis schema, ac inquit, tantùm abesse ut hæc dispositio absurditatis alicujus insimulari posit, ut potius ipse Cartesius fateatur eam à Copernicana non multum differre, citatis verbis Cartesii, Pp. III, §. 17.
units.tr: 409. Secondly, he sets out, at p. 202, the diagram of Tycho's system, and says that this arrangement is so far from being chargeable with any absurdity, that Descartes himself admits it differs little from the Copernican, citing the words of Descartes, Pp. III, §17.

units.la: Resp. Ita Cartesius fatetur non multum differre Tychonianam hypothesin à Copernicana, ut Pp. III art. 39. absurditatis accusat, quod nempe, dum Tycho conatur motum Terræ detrahere, eum revera ipsi tribuat, quòd necessariò ex ejus hypothesi sequatur, Terram vi aliqua separari à partibus istius materiæ sibi contiguis, atq; in eâ circulum describere. Verba Cartesii hæc sunt: Ex eadem Tychonis hypothesi Sol motu annuo circa terram gyrans, non modo Mercurium & Venerem, sed etiam Martem, Jovem & Saturnum, qui ab eo remotiores sunt quam terra, secum ducit: quod intelligi non potest, præsertim in cœlo fluido, quale illud supponunt, quin tota cœli materia interjacens simul feratur, & interim terra vi aliqua separetur, à partibus istius materiæ sibi contiguis, atque in eâ circulum describat. Quapropter hæc rursus separatio, quæ est totius terræ, ac peculiarem in ea actionem requirit, ejus motus erit dicendus. Unde rectè deduco, illam vim, quæ retineat terram, ut non simul cum toto systemate Planetarum ex hypothesi Tychonis circumrapiatur, sine ratione & absurde statui, cum non possit ab extraordinaria Dei potentia pendere, utpote ordinaria, neque causa aliqua naturalis, à qua ista vis oriatur, possit excogitari.
units.tr: Reply: Cartesius indeed admits that the Tychonic hypothesis does not differ much from the Copernican. He accuses it of absurdity in Principia III art. 39, namely that while Tycho tries to take away the motion of the Earth, he in fact attributes it to her, because it necessarily follows from his hypothesis that the Earth is separated by some force from the parts of that matter contiguous to it, and describes a circle in it. The words of Cartesius are these: From the same hypothesis of Tycho, the Sun, revolving annually about the earth, carries with it not only Mercury and Venus but also Mars, Jupiter and Saturn, which are more remote from it than the earth is. This cannot be understood, especially in a fluid heaven such as they suppose, without the whole interposed matter of the heavens being carried along at the same time, and the earth meanwhile being separated by some force from the parts of that matter contiguous to it, and describing a circle in it. Wherefore this separation again, which belongs to the whole earth and requires a peculiar action in it, is to be called its motion. Hence I rightly infer that that force which keeps the earth from being swept round together with the whole system of planets on Tycho's hypothesis is posited without reason and absurdly, since it cannot depend on an extraordinary power of God, being an ordinary one, and no natural cause from which that force might arise can be devised.

units.la: CCCCX. Tertio contra ipsum illud nostrum argumentum, hypothesi Tychonis oppositum, excipit p. 303. At jam probavimus 1. circumvolutionem illam Solis circa suum axem non ita certam esse. 2. Si daretur, eumfieri circa polos à polis ecliptica diversos, ac proinde vortices Planetarum secum raperapere non posse. 3. In Orbe Veneris raptum illum Planetarum propinquiorum velociorem & remotiorem tardiorum salsissimum reperiri.
units.tr: CCCCX. Thirdly, against that very argument of ours, opposed to the hypothesis of Tycho, he objects on p. 303: But we have now proved (1) that that rotation of the Sun about its own axis is not so certain; (2) that if it were given, it would take place about poles different from the poles of the ecliptic, and therefore the vortices could not carry the planets along with them; (3) that in the orb of Venus that carrying of the nearer planets, being swifter, and of the more remote, being slower, is found to be most absurd.

units.la: Resp. Nos ad Prop. 21. omnes illas probationes inconsequentiae & falsitatis convicimus, quo lectorem remittimus.
units.tr: Reply: In reply to Prop. 21 we have refuted all those proofs as inconsequent and false, to which we refer the reader.

units.la: CCCCXI. Pergit. Quamvis caelum circa terram moveatur, non est tamen mirum terram in medio quiescere, cum Deus illi & locum & quietem ibidem ordinaverit, unde non dimovebitur, ita ut non recurratur ad extraordinariam Dei potentiam, sed ad ordinem, qui ut a summo & sapientissimo Creatore constitutus est in prima creatione, ita etiamnum conservatur & conservabitur usque ad finem mundi.
units.tr: CCCCXI. He goes on: Although the heaven moves about the earth, it is nevertheless not strange that the earth rests in the middle, since God has ordained for it both its place and its rest there, whence it will not be moved; so that one does not have recourse to an extraordinary power of God, but to the order which, as it was established by the highest and most wise Creator in the first creation, so it is still preserved and will be preserved until the end of the world.

units.la: Resp. At nos quam parum haec ad rem faciant ostendemus. Quaeritur qui fiat, quod circumraptis a Sole ex hypoth. Tychonis reliquis Planetis Terra intermedia (quod apparet ex systemate) inter Solem circumrapientem Mercurium, Venerem ab una parte, Martem, Jovem, & Saturnum ab extrema parte, non simul circumrapiatur; hoc est, quaenam sit causa, quae retineat Terram per aliquam vim, & a qua vis illa dependeat, num sit naturalis, pendens ab ordine & constitutione divina, in prima creatione lata, adeoque ordinaria Dei providentia, num vero sit immediata & extraordinaria Dei manus. Ordinaria Dei potentia esse nequit. Ordo enim naturae est, ut, si corpora propinqua & remota, rapiantur ab aliquo, etiam intermedium, inter propinquum & remotum, simul circumferri necesse sit, nisi aliquid impediat. Ducantur lineae ex Sole per Terram & Planetas, per has lineas debet concipi vis Solis quasi dissundi secundum Tychonem, ut rapiat Planetas superiores, & inferiores; quod si ergo rapiat Planetas superiores, nonne clarum, quod etiam terram debeat circumrapere intermediam. Vel posito, quod intermedium non circumraplatur, ut ponit Tychoniana hypothesis, necesse est ostendi, quid illud sit, quod impediat; Nos id dicimus vel futurum immediatam & extraordinariam Dei manum, vel causam naturalem. At causa naturalis ab adversario non adfertur, nec ulla afferri potest, neque ad extraordinariam Dei potentiam sibi recurrendum censet. Ergo nulla talis datur, & per consequens hypoth. Tychoniana est absurda, nihilque ad eam ab absurdo liberandam ab adversario est responsum.
units.tr: Reply: But we shall show how little these things bear on the matter. The question is how it comes about that, while the remaining planets are swept round by the Sun on the Tychonic hypothesis, the Earth, lying between them (as appears from the system), namely between the Sun sweeping round Mercury and Venus on one side and Mars, Jupiter and Saturn on the far side, is not swept round at the same time; that is, what is the cause that keeps the Earth by some force, and on what that force depends: whether it is natural, depending on the order and constitution of God laid down in the first creation, and so on ordinary providence of God, or whether it is the immediate and extraordinary hand of God. It cannot be the ordinary power of God. For it is the order of nature that, if bodies near and far are carried along by something, then whatever lies between the near and the far must of necessity be carried along with them, unless something hinders. Let lines be drawn from the Sun through the Earth and the planets; through these lines, according to Tycho, the force of the Sun must be conceived as it were spreading out, so that it carries along the superior and the inferior planets. If therefore it carries the superior planets, is it not clear that it ought also to sweep round the intervening Earth? Or, granting that the intervening body is not swept round, as the Tychonic hypothesis posits, it must be shown what that is which hinders. We say that this will be either the immediate and extraordinary hand of God, or a natural cause. But a natural cause is not brought forward by the opponent, nor can any be brought forward; nor does he think that recourse must be had to an extraordinary power of God. Therefore no such cause is given, and consequently the Tychonic hypothesis is absurd, and the opponent has offered no answer by which it might be freed from absurdity.

units.la: CAPUT XIX.
units.tr: CAPUT XIX.

units.la: Objectiones contra delationem terræ à sensu & ratione desumptæ refutantur.
units.tr: Objections against the motion of the earth, drawn from sense and reason, are refuted.

units.la: CCCCXII. Nostram sententiam firmissimis niti rationibus superiori capite probavimus, sed ut nullum superfit dubium, operæ pretium est, ostendere, quam infirmæ sint rationes, quæ pro Terræ quiete & Solis circa eam delatione proferuntur.
units.tr: CCCCXII. In the preceding chapter we have shown that our opinion rests on the firmest reasons. But so that no doubt remains, it is worth showing how weak are the reasons that are brought forward for the rest of the earth and the motion of the Sun around it.

units.la: 1. Objectio à sensu desumta maximè movet homines vulgares, quorum præcipua notitia in sensu & ex sensu consistit, talisque potest formari. Solem moveri & circumire circa Terram quotidie sensu oculorum percipimus: At Terram moveri nullus nobis sensus testatur: Ergo illud potius, quàm hoc nobis est credendum.
units.tr: 1. The objection drawn from sense moves ordinary people most, whose chief knowledge consists in and comes from the senses, and it can be framed thus: We perceive by the sense of sight that the Sun moves and goes around the Earth every day. But no sense tells us that the Earth moves. Therefore we ought to believe the former rather than the latter.

units.la: CCCCXIII. Resp. Non est, quod sensui admodum fidamus, cum propter illam magnam sensibilis remotionem nos facile fallere possit, præsertim ubi ratio contrarium plane docet, uti superius vidimus. Sensus verò neque Solem neque Terram moveri nobis manifestum reddere potest. Apparentia enim sensus semper hic erit eadem, sive ipse visus, sive res ipsa moveatur, adeoque, quando nobis apparet Sol ex Cancro in Leonem, ex Leone in Virginem progredi, id duobus modis contingere potest; vel ut Sol ipse respectu horum signorum mutet locum suum, & sub illis circumferatur, vel etiam ut Terra cum vortice suo usque ad Lunam (ea significatione quam supra annotavimus) locum suum ita mutet, delata à materiâ ambiente, ut spectator in Terrâ constitutus Solem nunc sub his, nunc sub aliis signis conspicere possit. Similis ratio est, si motum diurnum, sive Solis sive Terræ spectes. 2. Sed ut illa fallacia visûs tanto melius deprehendatur, consideremus eos, qui navi, vel etiam curru vehuntur, quibus videntur littora, montes & arbores recedere, (hinc Virgilius: provehimur portu, terræque urbesque recedunt,) cum tamen illi ipsi, qui in navi sunt, simul cum navi à terrâ montibusque recedant, eaque respectu ipsorum revera sint ut quiescentia spectanda, & cogitemus, eodem modo contingere posse, ut nobis unà cum terrâ circumvectis, videantur Sol & astra recedere. Ponamus autem porrò hominem aliquem in navi esse natum atque educatum, neque unquam extra eam fuisse, aliunde etiam edoctum non esse, terram & littora respectu sui ut quiescentia esse spectanspectanda, sitque illa navis in vasto mari constituta, inque eo perpetuò agitetur, sed tamen ita ut littora conspici possint, is firmissime persuasum sibi habebit, & vel Jovem lapidem jurabit, non navem, in qua est, à littoribus, sed littora à navi recedere. Cum ergò nos ab incunabulis nostris in terra vixerimus, neque unquam extra eam fuerimus collocati, non mirum est, si Solem & astra aspicientes, ea respectu nostri moveri putemus, nosque in terrâ quiescente consistere existimemus. Idque tanto magis, quod is, qui in navi ita consideratur natus & educatus, saltem si extra navim in terrâ deponatur, hunc errorem etiam adminiculo sensûs possit corrigere: nos verò hoc adminiculo sumus destituti, nunquam in hac vitâ extra Terram collocandi. Inde ergò oriri existimemus, quod tam firma idea de motu Solis & astrorum per ista sensuum praejudicia nobis sit impressa, ut etiam, postquam rationem contrariam edocentem audiverimus, vix tamen illam priorem ideam ejicere possimus. Quemadmodum etiam contingit circa magnitudinem Solis, cujus in nobis per sensuum praejudicia idea est impressa, non major, quàm bipedalis. Quamvis enim postea rationibus Astronomicis evidentissimis edocti simus, Solem multo majorem esse ipsa Terrâ, quoties tamen visu nostro Solem iterum usurpamus, prior idea semper recurrit. Non ergò sensum in tam ardua quaestione, sed rationem consulamus, qua si rectè utamur (possumus autem si velimus) percipiemus, delationem duplicem non Soli, sed Terrae convenire.
units.tr: CCCCXIII. Reply. We need not place great trust in the senses, since because of that great distance of the sensible object they can easily deceive us, especially where reason plainly teaches the contrary, as we have seen above. Yet the senses cannot make it manifest to us that either the Sun or the Earth moves. For the appearance to the senses will always be the same, whether the sight itself or the thing itself is moving. So when the Sun appears to us to advance from Cancer into Leo and from Leo into Virgo, this can happen in two ways: either the Sun itself changes its place with respect to these signs and is carried around beneath them, or else the Earth, together with its vortex, as far as the Moon (in the sense we noted above), changes its place, carried along by the surrounding matter, so that a spectator placed on the Earth can see the Sun now under these signs, now under others. The same reasoning holds if you consider the daily motion, whether of the Sun or of the Earth. 2. But so that this deception of sight may be detected all the better, let us consider those who are carried in a ship or even in a chariot, for whom shores, mountains and trees seem to recede (hence Virgil: "we are carried from the harbour, and lands and cities recede"), although those very people who are in the ship recede together with the ship from the land and mountains, and these things are, with respect to them, truly to be regarded as at rest. Let us think that in the same way it may happen, while we are carried around together with the Earth, that the Sun and stars seem to recede. Let us suppose further that some man was born and brought up in a ship, never having been outside it, and not otherwise taught, and that the land and shores are to be regarded as at rest with respect to him; and let that ship be placed in the vast sea and be constantly tossed about in it, yet in such a way that the shores can be seen. He will hold most firmly to the persuasion, and will swear by Jupiter the stone, that it is not the ship in which he is that recedes from the shores, but the shores that recede from the ship. Since, then, we have lived on the earth from our cradles and have never been placed outside it, it is no wonder if, looking at the Sun and stars, we think they move with respect to us, and suppose that we stand on a resting earth. And this is all the more so because the man who is thus imagined to be born and brought up in a ship, at least if he is set down on land outside the ship, can correct this error with the aid of sense; but we are deprived of this aid, since we are never to be placed outside the Earth in this life. From this, then, we may suppose it arises that the idea of the motion of the Sun and stars has been so firmly impressed upon us by these prejudices of the senses that, even after we have heard reason teaching the contrary, we can hardly cast out that earlier idea. Just as also happens with the size of the Sun, the idea of which has been impressed upon us by the prejudices of the senses as no larger than two feet. For although we are afterwards taught by the most evident astronomical reasons that the Sun is much larger than the Earth itself, nevertheless whenever we again use our sight on the Sun, the earlier idea always returns. Let us therefore consult not the senses in so difficult a question, but reason; if we use it rightly (and we can, if we wish), we shall perceive that the double motion belongs not to the Sun but to the Earth.

units.la: CCCCXIV. 2. Obj.
units.tr: CCCCXIV. 2. Objection.

units.la: At saltem sentiremus motum ipsius Terrae, dum cum ipsa circumvehimur, etiam clausis oculis, quemadmodum navi vectus motum navis sentire potest. Nihil autem tale quispiam hominum expertus est: Ergo Terra non movetur.
units.tr: But at least we would feel the motion of the Earth itself while we are carried along with it, even with our eyes closed, just as a man carried in a ship can feel the motion of the ship. But no one among men has experienced anything of the kind. Therefore the Earth does not move.

units.la: CCCCXV. Resp. Ex antecedentibus cognoscere licuit totum vorticem usque ad Lunam una cum terra circumferri, cujus magna est quantitas, ut ejus diameter censeatur esse 2000000 milliarium Germanicorum; non mirum ergo esse debet, si Terra in isto vortice delata non impingat, cum revera in eo quiescat, uti superius est ostensum. 2. Navis motus non sentitur, si planè aequabiliter deferatur, nec à ventis vel fluctibus concutiatur; cum ergo & Terrae aequabilis sit delatio, quandoquidem nihil est, in quod impingere possit, fieri nequit, ut nos cum ipsa delati motum ejus sentiamus.
units.tr: CCCCXV. Reply. From what has gone before it has been possible to recognise that the whole vortex as far as the Moon is carried around together with the Earth, whose quantity is so great that its diameter is reckoned to be 2,000,000 German miles. It ought not to be surprising, therefore, if the Earth, carried in this vortex, does not strike against anything, since in truth it rests in it, as was shown above. 2. The motion of a ship is not felt if it is carried along quite evenly and is not shaken by winds or waves. Since, then, the carrying of the Earth is also even, there being nothing against which it could strike, it cannot come about that we feel its motion while we are carried along with it.

units.la: CCCCXVI Obj. 3. Si Terra delatione diurna ferretur versus Ortum, montes qui sunt ad Occasum, dum una cum terrâ deferuntur versus Ortum viderentur adscendere; at experientia nihil de eo docet. Ergo. CCCCXVII. Resp. 1. Visus hoc æstimare non potest: montes enim non recedunt ab aëre sibi contiguo, sed unà cum illo, imò cum toto cœlo usque ad Lunam circumferuntur. 2. Visus illud, in quo existit immotus, moveri non putat; ita si adspiciat navim, etiamsi ab illa deferatur, moveri non putabit: quia ergò montes sunt in illa planitie, cui nos insistimus, dum à Terrâ deferimur, illorum delatio videri non potest.
units.tr: CCCCXVI. Objection 3. If the Earth were carried by a daily motion towards the East, the mountains which lie to the West would, while they are carried together with the Earth towards the East, seem to rise; but experience teaches nothing of the kind. Therefore... CCCCXVII. Reply. 1. Sight cannot judge this: for the mountains do not recede from the air contiguous to them, but are carried along together with it, indeed together with the whole heaven as far as the Moon. 2. Sight does not think that moving which it is in and which is motionless; so if it looks at a ship, it will not think the ship is moving even though it is carried along by it. Therefore, since the mountains are on that plain on which we stand while we are carried along with the Earth, their motion cannot be seen.

units.la: CCCCXVIII. Obj. 4. Si Terra ferretur versus Ortum ab Occasu, apparerent aves, nubes, aliaque in aëre suspensa rapidissime semper ferri in Occasum tanquam relicta à nimio terræ raptu. At hoc experientia non testatur.
units.tr: CCCCXVIII. Objection 4. If the Earth were carried towards the East from the West, birds, clouds and other things suspended in the air would always appear to be borne most swiftly towards the West, as if left behind by the excessive rapid seizure of the Earth. But experience does not bear witness to this.

units.la: CCCCXIX. Resp. Neg. Connexio majoris; hæc enim omnia una cum terra feruntur, ab Occasu versus Ortum, neque à corporibus proximis & immediatè sibi contiguis recedunt, uti satis apparet ex eo, quod ostenderimus, non Terram separatim, sed à vortice suo delatam, qui longe sese ab utraque parte extendit, deferri. Quemadmodum autem pisces in scapha piscatoris aquæ plena & navi alligata, etsi huc & illuc discurrunt, semper tamen cum navi transferuntur, ita etiam cogitandum de volucribus & nubibus in aëre motis, quod semper in & cum isto vortice transferuntur.
units.tr: CCCCXIX. Reply. I deny the connection of the major premise. For all these things are carried together with the Earth from the West towards the East, and they do not recede from the bodies nearest and immediately contiguous to them, as is sufficiently clear from what we have shown, namely that the Earth is not carried separately but together with its vortex, which extends itself a long way on either side. Just as fish in a fisherman's boat full of water and tied to the ship, although they swim hither and thither, are always carried along with the ship, so we must think also of birds and clouds moved in the air: they are always carried in and with this vortex.

units.la: CCCC XX. Obj. 5. Si Terra hoc velocissimo raptu ab Occasu in Ortum deferretur, ventus ex opposito sentiri deberet perpetuus, quod experientia non docet.
units.tr: CCCCXX. Objection 5. If the Earth were carried from the West into the East by this most swift seizure, a constant wind from the opposite direction ought to be felt, which experience does not show.

units.la: CCCCXXI. Resp. Procedit hæc objectio, ut & aliæ quam multæ, ex falsa sententia nostræ interpretatione; hoc enim sequi deberet, si Terra aëri circumjacenti subriperetur, at cum ille una cum omnibus corporibus à terra usque ad concavum Lunæ circumrapiatur, nihil quicquam tale poterit consequi.
units.tr: CCCCXXI. Reply. This objection, like many others, proceeds from a false interpretation of our opinion. For this would follow if the Earth were slipping away from the air lying around it; but since that air, together with all bodies from the Earth up to the concave sphere of the Moon, is carried around, nothing of the kind can follow.

units.la: CCCC XXII. Qbj. 6. Sequitur altera remora, ex ratione desumpta contra delationem terræ annuam speciatim objecta, quæ vel sola multis viris doctis obest, ne hanc sententiam veram amplecti queant. Est autem illa, quod tum orbis magnus, in quo terra circa Solem defertur, cujus diameter secundum Copernicum continet milliaria Germanica 2000000 sit habiturus ad firmamentum rationem insensibilis puncti, adeoque mundi magnitudo in nimium sit excretura, & quasi infinita futura.
units.tr: CCCCXXII. Objection 6. There follows another hindrance, drawn from reason and specially raised against the yearly motion of the Earth, which alone hinders many learned men from being able to embrace this true opinion. It is this: that the great orb in which the Earth is carried about the Sun, whose diameter according to Copernicus contains 2,000,000 German miles, will have, in relation to the firmament, the proportion of an insensible point; and so the magnitude of the world will be excessively enlarged and will become, as it were, infinite.

units.la: CCCCXXIII. Resp. 1. Hoc argumentum movet eos, qui magnalia Dei nimis parva consueverunt concipere, eaque metiri volunt ad decempedam suæ imaginationis, quæ valdè est restricta, nec ulterius se extenextendit, quàm ad concipienda illa corpora, quæ visus circumeundo lustrare potest. At sanè nos parum afficit hæc objectio, imò potius nostram sententiam confirmat, cum nos mundi fines nullos possumus cognoscere, mundumque ut indefinitum concipiamus, uti ex superioribus potuit liquere. 2. Hominibus ex sensu solo opera Dei judicantibus etiam absurdum videbitur, si dicas, Terram, cujus diameter continere dicitur milliaria 17 18 vel etiam plura secundum alios, rationem habere insensibilis puncti ad firmamentum collatam, sed Astronomi certa demonstratione aliter edocti, hoc pro absurdo non habent: quod si ergo firmamenti ambitum, vel potius circumferentiam, in qua una aliqua stella fixa collocatur, longè ampliorem concipias, quàm vulgo concipi solet, (quidni enim posses, cum nullis certis demonstrationibus hactenus potuerit certa mensura ei assignari) etiam licebit illud punctum insensibile longe majus concipere. Imo amplius dico, non absurdum fore, si statuatur, totum illud planetarum systema, usque ad Saturnum, adeoque sphæram Saturni, quæ longè major concipi debet orbe illo magno, ad Firmamentum habere insensibilis puncti rationem. Cum enim nemo illam proportionem, quæ inter hæc intercedit, indagaverit, neque ullus indagare possit, si ad magnitudinem immensitatemque Dei attendamus & secundum eam ipsius opera concipiamus, præstat, illa potius maxima, quam parva, concipere. Quemadmodum autem argumentum Copernicanum, à nimis veloci raptu firmamenti desumptum, ostendi infirmum esse, neque rem benè attendenti persuadere posse, ita idem judico de hac objectione, eamque ad magnalia Dei attendens, tanquam leviculam rejicio.
units.tr: CCCCXXIII. Reply 1. This argument moves those who are accustomed to conceive God's great works too small and want to measure them by the yardstick of their own imagination, which is very narrow and extends no further than to conceiving those bodies that the eye can take in by looking around. But this objection troubles us very little; indeed it rather confirms our view, since we cannot know any limits of the world and must conceive the world as indefinite, as can be gathered from what has gone before. 2. To people who judge God's works by sense alone, it will also seem absurd if you say that the earth, whose diameter is said to be 17 or 18 miles, or even more according to others, has the proportion of an insensible point compared with the firmament. But astronomers, taught otherwise by certain demonstration, do not regard this as absurd. If therefore you conceive the circuit, or rather the circumference, of the firmament, on which a certain fixed star is placed, to be far larger than is commonly conceived (for why should you not, since no certain measure has yet been assigned to it by any sure demonstration?), then you may also conceive that insensible point to be far larger. I say more: it will not be absurd if it is held that the whole planetary system, up to Saturn, and so the sphere of Saturn, which must be conceived far larger than that great orbit, has the proportion of an insensible point to the firmament. For since no one has investigated the proportion that lies between these, and no one can investigate it, if we consider the greatness and immensity of God and conceive his works according to it, it is better to conceive those things as very great rather than small. Just as I have shown that the Copernican argument, drawn from the excessively swift carrying of the firmament, is weak and cannot persuade anyone who considers the matter carefully, so I judge the same of this objection, and, looking at God's great works, I reject it as quite trivial.

units.la: CCCCXXIV. Inst. At si orbita, in qua terra defertur, habet rationem insensibilem respectu firmamenti: Ergo Sol, qui in ejus centro collocatur, erit quavis stellâ fixâ minor.
units.tr: CCCCXXIV. Instance. But if the orbit in which the earth is carried has an insensible proportion to the firmament, then the Sun, which is placed at its centre, will be smaller than any fixed star.

units.la: CCCCXXV. Resp. 1. Nulla est Majoris connexio; fieri enim potest, ut stellæ fixæ habeant minorem circa se vorticem, quàm Sol, atque ita sint minores; colligi enim potuit ex cap. præcedenti, proportionem aliquam inter vorticem & centrum ipsius intercedere, sed nihil certi de eo concludi potest. 2. Neque id, quod tanquam absurdum in Minore assumitur, tale potest ostendi; quis enim dixerit, an non stellæ quædam, quæ ob nimiam forte à nobis distantiam nobis videntur valdè parvæ, sint majores Sole? Sed hic nihil certi determinari potest.
units.tr: CCCCXXV. Reply 1. There is no connection between the major and the minor; for it may be that the fixed stars have a smaller vortex around them than the Sun does, and so are smaller. For it could be gathered from the preceding chapter that some proportion holds between a vortex and its centre, but nothing certain can be concluded about it. 2. Nor can what is assumed in the minor premise, as something absurd, be shown to be such. For who would say whether some stars, which seem to us very small perhaps because of their great distance from us, are not larger than the Sun? But nothing certain can be determined here.

units.la: CCCCXXVI. Succedunt nunc aliæ objectiones minoris momenti. Sit ergo objectio 7. Si Terra delatione annua circa Solem fertur, Sol non erit dicendus Apogæus, & Perigæus, si vero circumducitur diurnâ circumvolutione Sol non dicetur oriri & occidere, quæ omnia sunt absurda.
units.tr: CCCCXXVI. Other objections of lesser weight now follow. Let the seventh objection be this: If the earth is carried annually around the Sun, the Sun will not be called apogee and perigee; and if the Sun is carried about by a daily revolution, the Sun will not be said to rise and set. All these things are absurd.

units.la: CCCCXXVII. Resp. 1. Astronomi receptas & vulgares voces non rejiciunt, etiamsi accuratiores dari possint, quia reddere debent causas apparentiarum, quæ vocibus à vulgo receptis efferuntur. Absque hoc foret, non absurdum forte futurum, si Terra Aphelios & Perihelios diceretur. 2. Sol nihilominus Oriri & Occidere dici potest, quia, sive Terra circa axem suum convolvatur, ita ut nunc hoc, nunc alterum hæmisphærium Soli obvertat, sive Sol Terram circumeat, tamen semper ei parti Terræ Sol dicetur ortus, super cujus Horizontem fuerit elevatus, hoc enim Ortus denotat, alteri vero hemisphærio occidisse dicetur, sub cujus Horizonte latuerit.
units.tr: CCCCXXVII. Reply 1. Astronomers do not reject the received and common terms, even if more accurate ones can be given, because they must give the causes of the appearances, which are expressed by the terms commonly received. Without this, it would perhaps not be absurd if the earth were called aphelion and perihelion. 2. Nevertheless the Sun can be said to rise and set, because, whether the earth turns about its own axis, so that now this and now the other hemisphere faces the Sun, or whether the Sun goes around the earth, the Sun is still said to have risen for that part of the earth over whose horizon it has been raised, for this is what "rising" denotes; and it is said to have set for the other hemisphere, beneath whose horizon it has lain hidden.

units.la: CCCCXXVIII. Obj. 8. Si Terra circa Solem deferretur, non futuri essent tales Planetarum adspectus, quales nunc sunt, Eclipses Solis & Lunæ, phases ejusdem non ita essent apparituræ, uti nunc apparent, quod utique absurdum esset futurum.
units.tr: CCCCXXVIII. Objection 8. If the earth were carried around the Sun, the aspects of the planets would not be such as they now are; the eclipses of the Sun and Moon, and the phases of the same, would not appear as they now appear, which would certainly be absurd.

units.la: CCCCXXIX. Resp. Negari connexionem Majoris. Nam harum omnium apparentiarum causas æque, imo forte melius explicare queunt Copernicani, quàm Tychoniani, vel Ptolemaici. Planetis enim, Mercurio, Veneri, Marti, Jovi, Saturno, & Lunæ, motus non demitur à Copernico. Ergo quando percurrunt Zodiacum, sub quo etiam Sol è Terra conspicitur, varias nihilominus habere poterunt configurationes, & cum Sole, & inter se invicem, Eclipsis vero Lunæ semper continget, quando Terra erit in eádem linea recta inter Solem & Lunam interposita: Solis, quando Luna inter Terram & Solem interjicitur, quæ omnia non minus fieri posse in systemate Copernicano & Tychoniano, luce meridiana clarius est. Similiter phases Lunæ ob circuitum, quem ea circa Terram conficit, sese eodem modo semper habebunt.
units.tr: CCCCXXIX. Reply. The connection of the major is denied. For the Copernicans can explain the causes of all these appearances equally well, or perhaps even better, than the Tychonians or Ptolemaists. For the motion of the planets, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn and the Moon, is not taken away by Copernicus. Therefore, when they run through the zodiac, under which the Sun too is seen from the earth, they can nevertheless have various configurations, both with the Sun and with one another. An eclipse of the Moon will always occur when the earth is interposed on the same straight line between the Sun and the Moon; an eclipse of the Sun, when the Moon is interposed between the earth and the Sun. That all these things can happen no less in the Copernican system than in the Tychonian is clearer than midday light. Likewise the phases of the Moon, because of the circuit it makes around the earth, will always present themselves in the same way.

units.la: CCCCXXX. Obj. 9. Si Terra deferretur circa Solem, ea inter Planetas erit referenda, quod oppido quàm absurdum multis videtur.
units.tr: CCCCXXX. Objection 9. If the earth were carried around the Sun, it would have to be counted among the planets, which many think is extremely absurd.

units.la: CCCCXXXI. Resp. Absurdum fortasse erit illis, qui nominibus potius, quàm rebus inhærent, & ex illis potius scientiam suam consarciunt, quàm ex ipsis rebus. Cum enim putent, Planetas, Venerem, Lunam, &c. nos propter propinquitatem plus vel æque aut saltem non multo minùs lumine suo afficere, quàm multas stellas fixas, vix aliam differentiam inter ipsos & stellas fixas, imo & Solem ipsum quoad lucem agnoagnoscunt. At qui ultra voces ascendere amant, & potius penetralia rerum scrutari volunt, quam vocabulorum apicibus inhærere, illi norunt, magnam inter Planetas ab una parte, & Solem atque fixas ab altera esse differentiam, quod illi sint corpora opaca, lucem nullam insitam habentia, sed tantum eam, quam à Sole acceperunt reflectentia, & cùm cælestium eadem sit materia, quæ terrestrium, & simili modo reliqui Planetæ sint formati, quo Terra, uti ex demonstratione nostrâ cap. præcedenti propositâ colligi potest, nihil absurdi erit, si Terram in eodem ordine collocemus.
units.tr: CCCCXXXI. Reply. It will perhaps be absurd to those who cling to names rather than things, and who patch together their knowledge from words rather than from the things themselves. For since they think that the planets, Venus, the Moon, and so on, affect us by their light, because of their nearness, more or at least equally, or at any rate not much less, than many fixed stars, they hardly acknowledge any difference between them and the fixed stars, or even the Sun itself, as far as light is concerned. But those who love to rise above words, and want to search the inner recesses of things rather than cling to the letters of vocabulary, know that there is a great difference between the planets on the one hand and the Sun and fixed stars on the other: the planets are opaque bodies, having no light of their own, but only reflecting that which they have received from the Sun. And since the matter of the heavenly bodies is the same as that of earthly bodies, and the other planets were formed in the same way as the earth, as can be gathered from our demonstration proposed in the preceding chapter, there will be nothing absurd if we place the earth in the same order.

units.la: CCCCXXXII. Obj. 10. At L. p. 300. & 301. multis hanc sen- tentiam sibi premere videtur argumentis, quæ breviter perstringemus:
units.tr: CCCCXXXII. Obj. 10. But L. (pp. 300 and 301) seems to press this opinion with many arguments, which we will briefly set out:

units.la: Cùm stellæ omnes sint vel errantes vel inerrantes, Planetam esse non persuadebit, nisi stellam esse constiterit. Stellarum autem numero Terram comprehendi, tam peregrinum rationi est, quam quod maxime. Stella sibi & Orbi lucent, idque noctu maxime. Terra nisi luce cælestium corporum detegatur, tenebris demersa latet; nec unquam navigando Terram è longinquo videre potui, nec sideribus cæli abscondis, unquam ea nobis lucebat, quin & ne impingeremus in eam incauti, si propinquam esse suspicaremur, timebamus. Stella cum cælo devehuntur, & in eo esse ab omnibus creduntur. Terra quàm maximè Coelo opposita est, & locutione hominum & Sacra Scriptura testimonio. Vel principem apicem earum lege: In principio creavit Deus Coelum & Terram. Et hoc respectu sæpè divini oraculo verbi ἀξυος Terra, Coelum ὐψῷ appellatur, & ut inter res remotissimas comparatio inde sumitur Psal. 103. Stella & omnia cœlestia fluida corpora sunt & subtilia: Terra crassa, arida, & tactui resistens, inde & ab ariditate הארץ quasi proprio nomine insignitur Gen. 1. 2. Terra hominum & belluarum habitationi data est: Planetæ nullis incolis frequentantur: & explosa jamdiu veterum quorundam opinio est, ad Luciani veram historiam ableganda, Lunam arboribus, aquis stagnantibus, & profluentibus, montibus & hominum cultu esse habitabilem. 3. Coelum esse negat, ad quod adspiramus, qui Terram inter Planetas numerat, aut jam sumus in Coelo, si Terra est inter Planetas: aut ne Planeta quidem & Stella & Sol ipse in Coelo fertur, atqui ita Coelum in nuda verbi appellatione, fundamentum vana rationis, non in rei veritate subsistit. 4. Scriptura Sacra hac opinio, quàm maximè adversatur Scommata, quæ hac occasione in Cartesium jactat, lubens prætereo, nec enim par pari referre est animus.
units.tr: Since all the stars are either wandering or fixed, one will not be persuaded that the Earth is a planet unless it has first been established that it is a star. Yet that the Earth should be counted among the stars is as foreign to reason as anything could be. A star shines for itself and for the world, and most of all at night. The Earth, unless it is revealed by the light of the heavenly bodies, lies hidden, sunk in darkness; nor have I ever been able to see the Earth from afar while sailing, nor has it ever shone on us from the stars of heaven. Indeed, if we suspected that it was near, we would be afraid lest we run into it unawares. Stars are carried along with the heavens and are believed by everyone to be in heaven. The Earth is most opposed to heaven, both in the common speech of men and by the testimony of Holy Scripture. Read its first verse: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth. And in this respect the divine oracle often calls the Earth low [ἀξυος] and heaven on high [ὑψοῦ], and a comparison is drawn from the most distant things, as in Psalm 103. Stars and all heavenly bodies are fluid and subtle bodies; the Earth is thick, dry, and resistant to touch, and for this reason it is marked, almost by a proper name, from its dryness as הארץ [ha-arets], Gen. 1.2. The Earth is given for the habitation of men and beasts; the planets are frequented by no inhabitants. The opinion of certain ancients, that the Moon is habitable with trees, stagnant and flowing waters, mountains, and the cultivation of men, has long been exploded and is to be relegated to Lucian's True History. 3. He denies that it is heaven to which we aspire, who counts the Earth among the planets; otherwise we are already in heaven, if the Earth is among the planets; or else not even the planets, the stars, and the Sun itself are carried in heaven. But heaven, in this bare verbal sense, rests on the foundation of vain reasoning, not on the truth of the matter. 4. I gladly pass over the sneers which he hurls at Descartes on this occasion, since this opinion is strongly opposed to Holy Scripture; for it is not my intention to return like for like.

units.la: CCCCXXXIII. Resp. Qui bene consideraverit demonstrationem meam cap. antecedenti propositam, eamque cum Cartesii lib. II. & III. Principiorum contulerit, has objectiones ne responsione quidem dignas judijudicabit; ne tamen triumphum ante victoriam adversarius, uti consuevit, canat, pauca haec regerere lubet. Ad primum argumentum velim notari, hoc argumentum oppido quam imbecillum esse, proinde ex Logica ἀκρoαματικῇ ostendi posse. Livisio enim stellarum in errantes & inerrantes vulgata cum sit generis in species, debet necessario ex ipsis speciebus sive particularibus suum fundamentum habere. Cum Genus colligatur ex speciebus, species ex individuis, uti omnes fere, qui doctrinam universalium tradunt, docent: Ergo prius constare debet, Planetas esse stellas, quàm ex hac divisione aliquid queat inferri, ad quod natura Planetarum debet esse cognita atque perspecta. Quo facto facile sciam, an Terra sit inter Planetas referenda, prout cum iis vel convenire, vel non convenire comperero. Manifesta est ergo in hoc argumento petitio principii. Dein luditur in voce Stellae: si per stellam intelligatur id, quod lumen aliquod praebet de se aliis corporibus, sive proprium sive reflexum, Planetas esse stellas non negabo: sed si vox stellae non nisi iis corporibus convenit, quae lucem habent propriam insitam, quam de se emittunt, manifestum erit, hos inter stellas non esse referendos. Quibus observatis, sequentia sua sponte concidunt. Quemadmodum enim Planetae reliqui, Luna imprimis, Venus, &c. lumen ad Terram reflectunt à Sole receptum: ita vicissim Terram lumen ad Lunam & Aerem reflectere, nimis quam est notum; tenue enim illud lumen, quod aliquando in Luna nova conspicitur, non aliunde quàm à Terra provenire judicandum, & communiter Physici infimam Aëris regionem determinant ibi, ubi radii solares à Terra reflexi ita deficiunt & languent, ut calorem Aëris sensibiliter augere amplius non possint. Ut in tirone Physicae vel Astronomiae non sit ferenda illa argumentatio: Terra noctu non lucet; Ergo nullum lumen reflectit. Cum enim nullum habeat lumen insitum, non potest lumen reflectere, nisi praesente Sole, à quo recipit, quemadmodum & Luna tempore novilunii, lumen à Sole ad nos non reflectit, quia à parte nobis obversa, tum non est illuminata. Cui genuina est illa p. 303. qua ex eo, quod à Terra ne vicina quidem maria, delitescentibus coelo sideribus, ad dispellendas noctis tenebras, scintillam ullam lucis accipiunt, inferre vult: Lunam in novilunio non recipere lumen à Terra reflexum, ignorans quod Novilunium fiat, in Lunae cum Sole conjunctione, eaque non noctu, sed interdu concipi debeat à Terra lumen reflexum recipere. Sed profecto, qui talia capere non potest, à Cartesii impugnatione, cujus profundam doctrinam omnes cordati mirantur, abstinere debuisset. Terram porro à materia coelesti devehi, ex mea demonstratione liquere potest, sed propterea non est ipsum Cœlum, eique nihilominùs opponi potest, quemadmodum & Sol & Planetæ possunt. Cœli vero vocem varie in Scriptura sumi, nimis quam notum est, ut non absurdum sit, si quodam sensu Terra in Cœlo esse dicatur, quatenus Aëre fluido, qui nomine cœli etiam venit, circumcingitur. Quomodo Cœlum dicatur ♂♃⊙, Terræ vero imum tribuatur, liquere potest ex superioribus. Tertia etiam differentia, quam inter stellas & Terram constituit, nobis nihil quicquam obest. Agnoscimus, stellas fixas esse corpora fluida & subtilia, sed Planetas opacos esse ex luminis reflexione pater. Nec igitur Terram in numerum stellarum fixarum referimus, sed ut pro Planetâ habeatur, absurdum esse non putamus.
units.tr: CCCCXXXIII. Reply. Anyone who has carefully considered my demonstration set out in the preceding chapter, and compared it with Descartes' Principles, Books II and III, will judge these objections unworthy even of an answer. Nevertheless, lest my adversary sing his triumph before the victory, as he is wont to do, I wish to offer a few points in return. As to the first argument, I would have it noted that this argument is exceedingly feeble, and can be shown to be so from acroamatic logic [ἀκροαματικῇ]. For the division of the stars into wandering and fixed, though commonly accepted, is a division of a genus into species, and so must necessarily have its foundation in the species themselves or in the particulars. Since a genus is gathered from its species, and species from individuals, as almost all who teach the doctrine of universals teach, it must first be established that the planets are stars, before anything can be inferred from this division; and for that, the nature of the planets must be known and thoroughly understood. Once this is done, I shall easily know whether the Earth is to be counted among the planets, insofar as I find that it agrees or does not agree with them. There is therefore a plain petitio principii in this argument. Next, there is a play on the word "star". If by a star is meant that which gives some light of its own to other bodies, whether its own or reflected, I will not deny that the planets are stars. But if the word "star" applies only to those bodies which have an innate light of their own, which they send out from themselves, it will be clear that they are not to be counted among the stars. With these points observed, what follows falls of its own accord. For just as the other planets, the Moon above all, Venus, and so on, reflect to the Earth the light received from the Sun, so conversely it is well known that the Earth reflects light to the Moon and to the air; for that faint light which is sometimes seen in the new Moon must be judged to come from nothing other than the Earth. And physicists commonly determine that the lowest region of the air is where the solar rays reflected from the Earth fail and grow so weak that they can no longer sensibly increase the heat of the air. So that argument, "the Earth does not shine at night; therefore it reflects no light," is not to be tolerated in a beginner in physics or astronomy. For since it has no innate light, it cannot reflect light except when the Sun is present, from which it receives it, just as the Moon at new moon does not reflect light from the Sun to us, because the part turned toward us is then not illuminated. To this belongs the authentic passage at p. 303, in which he wishes to infer, from the fact that "not even the nearby seas receive from the Earth any spark of light to dispel the darkness of night, the stars being hidden by the sky," that the Moon at new moon does not receive light reflected from the Earth, ignoring that new moon occurs at the conjunction of the Moon with the Sun, and that it must be understood to receive reflected light from the Earth not at night but by day. But indeed, whoever cannot grasp such things ought to have refrained from attacking Descartes, whose profound doctrine all men of judgment admire. Further, it can be clear from my demonstration that the Earth is carried along with the heavenly matter; but on that account it is not heaven itself, and yet it can nevertheless be opposed to heaven, just as the Sun and the planets can be. The word "heaven," however, is used in various senses in Scripture, as is only too well known; so it is not absurd, if in a certain sense the Earth is said to be in heaven, insofar as it is surrounded by the fluid air, which also comes under the name of heaven. How heaven is said to be [♂♃⊙], and the lowest place is assigned to the Earth, can be clear from what has gone before. The third difference which he draws between the stars and the Earth also does nothing to hinder us. We acknowledge that the fixed stars are fluid and subtle bodies, but that the planets are opaque is evident from the reflection of light. Nor therefore do we count the Earth among the fixed stars; but we do not think it absurd that it should be regarded as a planet.

units.la: CCCCXXXIV. Ad secundum argumentum respondeo 1. sufficere, si Terra in luminis reflexione adeoque opacitate, ut & motu circa Solem, uti demonstratum, cum Planetis conveniat, ut ad unum Planetarum redigi possit. 2. An vero Luna arboribus &c. sit referta, non constat, sed tantùm, quod partes quasdam habeat altiores quasdam depressiores, impossibile tamen esse, aut, omnino absurdum non judicamus, malo verò ab eo determinando abstinere, quia hactenus nullæ sufficientes rationes visæ quæ vel hoc vel contrarium evincerent. Ad tertium dico: Si Cœlum pro Aëre sumatur, nos omnino jam esse in cœlo, sed non propterea in cœlo Beatorum, ad quod aspiramus, & in quo Terram esse negamus. Ad quartum, hanc sententiam nostram Scripturæ Sacræ non adversari, paulo post sumus ostensuri. CCCCXXXV. Obj. 11. Contra Terræ delationem talis profertur. Si Terræ competeret motus circularis, sive is sit motus conversionis diurnæ circa proprium axem, sive etiam annuæ circa Solem, hujusmodi motus deberet ei esse naturalis, & ab interno aliquo ejus principio provenire. Neque enim explicari posse videtur, à quonam principio externo iste motus efficiatur, nisi ad causam primam Deum videlicet, vel in-telligentiam aliquam hunc effectum referamus. Non potest Terræ esse naturalis hic motus, quia corpori simplici unus tantùm motus convenire potest, qui, cum rectus sit Terræ conveniens, non potest alius quispiam ei attribui. Urgetur istud argumentum hoc modo à Gerhardo de Neufville, Philosopho dum viveret acuto, qui si solidiora principia habuisset, magni quid suisset præstiturus, in disputatione prima (quam an plures fuerint subsecutæ me latet) qua Terræ delationem evertere conatur. CCCCXXXVI. Resp. Varia in hoc argumento sunt notanda.
units.tr: CCCCXXXIV. To the second argument I reply: (1) it is enough, if the Earth agrees with the planets in reflecting light, and therefore in opacity, as also in motion about the Sun, as has been demonstrated, that it may be reduced to one of the planets. (2) Whether the Moon is filled with trees and so on is not established; it is only known that it has some parts higher and some lower. Yet we do not judge it impossible, or altogether absurd, but I prefer to refrain from determining the matter, because hitherto no sufficient reasons have been seen that would prove either this or the contrary. To the third I say: if heaven is taken to mean air, then we are already altogether in heaven; but not on that account in the heaven of the blessed, to which we aspire, and in which we deny that the Earth is. To the fourth, we shall show shortly that this opinion of ours is not opposed to Holy Scripture. CCCCXXXV. Obj. 11. Against the motion of the Earth the following is brought forward. If the Earth were fitted for circular motion, whether that is the motion of daily rotation about its own axis or also of annual revolution about the Sun, such a motion would have to be natural to it and come from some internal principle of its own. For it does not seem possible to explain from what external principle this motion is produced, unless we refer it to God as first cause or to some intelligence. This motion cannot be natural to the Earth, because only one motion can belong to a simple body, and that motion, since it is straight and suits the Earth, cannot be attributed to it as any other. This argument is pressed in this way by Gerhard de Neufville, a philosopher of keen mind while he lived, who would have achieved something great if he had had firmer principles, in the first disputation (I do not know whether more followed) in which he tries to overturn the motion of the Earth. CCCCXXXVI. Reply. Several points are to be noted in this argument.

units.la: I. Motus circularis, qui Terræ tribuitur, vel potius Delatio posset dici Naturalis, si consideretur ei convenire secundum ordinem & leges naturæ, uti à nobis demonstratum, & sic omnis Motus naturalis dici potest: Potest etiam dici Non-naturalis, tum hoc sensu, quatenus pendet à principio externo, nempe materiâ coelesti ambiente, & sic iterum omnis motus non-naturalis dici potest, cum nihil quicquam à se ipso moveatur: tum illo sensu, quo Motus is non requiritur ad Terræ essentiam, cum, etiamsi quiesceret, sinam naturam non dicenda esset mutâsse, quâ ratione Motus quibusdam corporibus est naturalis, verbi gratiâ, igni qui sine motu esse non potest. Alium autem motum naturalem, qui conveniat corpori, ex sua natura, eique sit insitus, non admittimus: Formas etiam aliquas substantiales realiter distinctas à materia in aliis corporibus præterquam humanis dari negamus, quod ut prolixius demonstremus, non est hujus loci. 2. Corpori cuilibet simplici, si separatim ab aliis corporibus consideretur, competere, ut à centro sui motûs secundum lineam rectam recedere conetur Prop.9. cap. precedentis demonstravimus, sed propter alia corpora circumstantia fieri potest, ut in circulum feratur, idque eatenus etiam ipsi est naturale, quatenus secundum leges naturæ ei contingit. 3. Terram esse corpus simplex facilius asseritur, quàm probatur, oriturque hæc opinio, ex illa fictitia compositione omnium corporum, ex quatuor elementis vulgò ita dictis; Igne, Aëre, Aquâ, Terrâ. Terra verò ex pluribus partibus heterogeneis constiit, quam vel plumbum, vel lapis. 4. Terræ rectum motum per se competere alio sensu, quam quatenus circulariter delata à centro sui circuli semper recedere conatur, non admittimus. Inst. At dicas: Motus, qui partibus Terræ competit, etiam toti Terræ convenire est censendus: At motus rectus deorsum ad centrum Terræ partibus competit: Ergo etiam Terræ naturaliter convenit motus rectus. Inde enim Terræ partes hunc motum rectum obtinent, quia cum Toto naturam communem habent. Resp. Motus ille, quo tanquam graves Terræ partes tendunt deorsum, non competit ipsis ex principio aliquo insito, sed quod globuli Coelestes in Terram impingentes undiquaque dum ab ea resiliunt, corpora quæ in Aëre inveniunt, ut sibi spatium à Terra recedendi faciant, versus illam deprimunt, uti id à Cartesio Princip. IV. art. 20. & seqq. uberius demonstratur. Hic ergo idem motus non potest ipsi Terræ competere, sed alius quispiam, quo, si extra suum locum posita esset sive versus Solem propius, sive ab eo remotius, semper ad hunc locum, in quo nunc est, esset depellenda, ex Prop, 26, cap. precedentis.
units.tr: I. The circular motion attributed to the Earth, or rather the Earth's motion of carrying, could be called natural, if it is considered to belong to the Earth according to the order and laws of nature, as we have demonstrated; and in this sense every natural motion can be so called. It can also be called non-natural: first, in the sense that it depends on an external principle, namely the surrounding celestial matter, and in this sense every non-natural motion can be so called, since nothing moves itself; second, in the sense that this motion is not required for the Earth's essence, since even if it were at rest its nature would not be said to have been changed. On this reasoning some motion is natural to certain bodies, for example to fire, which cannot exist without motion. We do not, however, admit any other natural motion that belongs to a body from its own nature and is innate in it. We also deny that any substantial forms really distinct from matter exist in bodies other than human ones; to demonstrate this at greater length is not the place here. 2. Any simple body, if considered separately from other bodies, tends to recede from the centre of its motion along a straight line; we demonstrated this in Proposition 9 of the preceding chapter. But because of other surrounding bodies it can happen that it is carried in a circle, and to that extent this motion is natural to it, in so far as it happens to it according to the laws of nature. 3. That the Earth is a simple body is asserted more easily than proved, and this opinion arises from that fictitious composition of all bodies out of the four so-called elements: fire, air, water and earth. The Earth, however, is made up of many heterogeneous parts, such as lead or stone. 4. We do not admit that the Earth has, of itself, a straight motion in any sense other than that, being carried circularly, it always tends to recede from the centre of its circle. Objection: But you may say: a motion that belongs to the parts of the Earth must also be judged to belong to the whole Earth; yet the straight motion downward toward the centre of the Earth belongs to its parts; therefore a straight motion also belongs naturally to the Earth. For the parts of the Earth obtain this straight motion because they share a common nature with the whole. Reply: That motion by which the Earth's parts, as heavy bodies, tend downward does not belong to them from some innate principle, but because the celestial globules, striking the Earth and rebounding from it on every side, press downward upon the bodies they find in the air, so as to make room for themselves to recede from the Earth. This is shown more fully by Descartes, Principles IV, art. 20 and following. Hence this same motion cannot belong to the Earth itself; rather some other motion does, by which the Earth, if it were placed outside its own position, whether nearer to the Sun or farther from it, would always be driven back to this place in which it now is, as shown in Proposition 26 of the preceding chapter.

units.la: CCCCXXXVII. Obj. 12. Si Terra moveretur motu adeo rapido, ut spatio 24 horarum circa axem suum convolveretur, verendum, ne illa per hunc motum dissiparetur, aedificia corruerent, turres conquassa- rentur, crescentia hoc motu impedirentur, & destruerentur. B. D. p. 46. argumentum latius deducit.
units.tr: CCCCXXXVII. Objection 12. If the Earth were moved by a motion so rapid that it revolved about its axis in the space of 24 hours, we should fear that buildings would collapse, towers would be shaken, and growing things would be hindered and destroyed by this motion, and that the Earth itself would be dissipated. B. D. p. 46 develops the argument at greater length.

units.la: Nihil est, quod facilius sub intellectum nostrum cadit, quam, quod illud debeat esse quietum, in quo homo, aliaque animalia vivent, movebuntur, & actiones suas peragent, prout multo commodius in Terra firma ambulamus & nostra peragimus, quam in navi celerrime mota : contra vero; quomodo Terra tam rapide motu duplici acta commodum posset exhibere hominibus aliisque habitaculum, hactenus, quae mea est stupiditas, quidquid dicant Galilaeus, Lansbergius, aliique Copernicani, percipere non potui: & hac occasione rationem meam paucis aperiam: Motum tribuunt Terra duplicem, Diurnum & Annuum, Diurno semel circumvolvitur terra spatio 24 horarum; ambitus autem Terrae, est milliarium 5400, quorum quindecim uni gradui correspondent, quae fere aequalia sunt viginti milliaribus horariis, quorum unum cum virgu 1600 fere convenit, ita ut ambitus Terrae comprehendat milliaria horaria, 7200, quae si in horas 24 dividantur, palam erit habitatores sub Aequatore spatio horario ab Ortu in Occasum moveri milliaria 300. & scrupulo primo milliaria 5, scrupulo autem secundo, id est, puncto temporis, virgas 133. Sed & hic motus exiguus respectu ejus, quem spatio annuo in Zodiaco absolvere debebit, semidiameter enim orbis magni Terra comprehendit ex sententia Lansbergii, Uranom. p. 122, 1498, cum dimidio semidiametros Terrae, id est, milliaria 1717155, & per consequens totus diameter 3434310, unde porro liquet, ex proportione diametri ad circumferentiam, ambitum magni Orbis esse milliarium horariorum 10789193, qui si dividantur in dies 365, hor. 5-49. habebitur motus diurnus in Zodiaco milliar. horar. 29539, eritque motus uniu hora, milliarium 1230, & scrupuli primi milliar. 20. secundi autem virgarum 533, qui motus rapidissimus cum quiete hominum & animalium in terra degentium, ambulantium, quiescentium &c. meo judicio est irreconciliabilis.
units.tr: Nothing falls more easily under our understanding than that the place where man and other animals live, move, and carry out their actions ought to be at rest, since we walk and do our business far more conveniently on solid ground than on a ship moving very swiftly. On the other hand, how the Earth, carried by so rapid a double motion, could offer men and other creatures a convenient dwelling, I have not been able to grasp up to now, whatever Galileo, Lansberg and the other Copernicans may say. This occasion lets me set out my reasoning briefly. They attribute to the Earth a double motion, diurnal and annual. By the diurnal motion the Earth turns once round in the space of 24 hours. The circumference of the Earth is 5400 miles, of which fifteen correspond to one degree; these are nearly equal to twenty hourly miles, of which one is about 1600 yards. So the circumference of the Earth comprises 7200 hourly miles. If these are divided into 24 hours, it will be plain that the inhabitants under the Equator are carried from east to west through 300 hourly miles in an hour, 5 miles in a first minute, and 133 yards in a second minute, that is, in a moment of time. But this motion is also small compared with the motion which the Earth must complete in the Zodiac in the space of a year. For according to Lansberg's view (Uranometria p. 122), the semidiameter of the great orbit comprehends the Earth 1498 and a half times over, that is 1717155 miles, and consequently the whole diameter is 3434310. From this it further follows, by the proportion of diameter to circumference, that the circuit of the great orbit is 10789193 hourly miles. If these are divided into 365 days and 5 hours 49 minutes, the daily motion in the Zodiac will be 29539 hourly miles. The motion in one hour will be 1230 miles, in a first minute 20 miles, and in a second minute 533 yards. In my judgment such a most rapid motion cannot be reconciled with the rest of men and animals dwelling on the earth, walking, resting, and so on.

units.la: CCCCXXXVIII. Resp. Nihil est in nostra sententia hic periculi. Si enim statueremus, omnia spatia circa Terram, quae ab ipsius materia non occupantur, nihil continere, nisi corpus, quod motus aliorum corporum nulla ratione impediret, nec juvaret, tum quidem futurum esset, ut propter circumvolutionem Terrae circa suum axem, illae omnes ejus partes, quae sibi mutuo non essent firmiter alligatae hinc inde versus Coelum dissilirent: Eodem modo, quo videre licet, dum turbo gyrat, arena supra ipsum conjiciatur, eam statim ab illo recedere, atque ein omnes partes dispergi, uti Cartesius docet Princip. IV. art. 21. At cum nostra sit sententia, Terram in vortice tanto, qui se extendat usque ad Lunam, deferri, tum annuâ delatione circa Solem, tum diurnâ circa proprium axem, globulosque cælestes omnia corpora gravia versus Terram deprimere, uti art. 20. Cartesius Princip. IV. ostendit, quomodo motus hic quieti animalium, ædificiorum, crescentium in Terra &c. obesse possit, non video. Terra enim planè quieta cum omnibus corporibus usque ad concavum Lunæ circumfertur, uti sæpius sententiam nostram hanc esse testati sumus.
units.tr: CCCCXXXVIII. Reply. In our view there is no danger here. For if we held that all the spaces around the Earth which are not occupied by its matter contain nothing but a body which hinders or helps the motion of other bodies in no way, then indeed it would follow that, because of the Earth's rotation about its axis, all those parts of it which were not firmly bound to one another would be flung outwards towards heaven. In the same way we see that when a whirlwind spins, sand thrown above it is at once carried away from it and scattered in all directions, as Descartes teaches in Principles IV, art. 21. But since our view is that the Earth is carried in a vortex which extends as far as the Moon, both by its annual motion about the Sun and by its daily motion about its own axis, and that the heavenly globules press all heavy bodies down towards the Earth, as Descartes shows in Principles IV, art. 20, I do not see how this motion could hinder the rest of animals, buildings, growing things on the Earth, and so on. For the Earth, quite at rest, is carried along with all bodies up to the concave surface of the Moon, as we have often testified that this is our view.

units.la: CCCCXXXIX. Obj. 13. Si Terra deferretur duplici delatione, tunc nullum corpus aut sursum emissum, aut superne demissum ad per- pendiculum caderet, si dum volaret in aëre, locus Terræ subduceretur: quemadmodum emissa sagitta dum navis transfertur, ad perpendiculum non recidit.
units.tr: CCCCXXXIX. Objection 13. If the Earth were carried by a double motion, then no body thrown upwards or dropped from above would fall perpendicularly, if the place of the Earth were withdrawn while the body was in the air, just as an arrow shot off does not fall back perpendicularly while the ship is carried along.

units.la: CCCCXL. Resp. Supponitur ac si nostra sententia esset, Terram ab aëre separatam proprie moveri. Cum vero dicamus, Terram in suo vortice deferri, cogitandum est, etiam omnia quæ in illo vortice continentur, simul deferri. Quare delato Terræ loco, è quo sagitta emittitur, etiam ipsa sagitta emissa in aëre motu communi istius vorticis circumfertur, unde fit, ut perpendiculariter decidat. Quod si vero sagitta quædam transmitti posset ultra Lunam, illa quia non communi istius vorticis delatione deferretur, si recideret in Terram, ad perpendiculum utique delapsura non esset. 2. Experimentum adductum aliter se habet. Observatum enim sagittam è puppi emissam in eam recidere, quod exinde contingere potest, quod navis suum motum toti circun stanti aëri imprimat, qui sagittam simul defert, ut ita delapsa in eundem recidat locum. 3. Quamvis experimentum in Objectione propositum ita se haberet, attamen nobis non efficeret, cum navis revera moveatur, sed Terra in vortice suo delata revera quiescat. 4. Motus lapidis projecti ad Terram, vel etiam sagittæ emissæ motus versus Terram non est exacte rectus & per lineam rectam, sed potius super lineam parabolicam, quia interim, dum ad Terram lapis vel sagitta deprimitur, defertur à vortice Terræ. Apparet tamen omnibus rectus, quia non animadvertunt eam delationem, per quam unà cum Terra circumferuntur, quemadmodum etiam accidit navi vectis.
units.tr: CCCCXL. Reply. It is assumed as if our view were that the Earth is moved properly, separated from the air. But since we say that the Earth is carried along in its vortex, we must consider that all the things contained in that vortex are carried along together. Hence, when the place of the Earth from which the arrow is shot is carried along, the arrow itself, once shot into the air, is also carried round by the common motion of that vortex, and so it falls perpendicularly. But if some arrow could be shot beyond the Moon, it would not, since it is not carried along by the common motion of that vortex, fall perpendicularly if it came back down to the Earth. (2) The experiment cited is otherwise. For it is observed that an arrow shot from the stern falls back into the same place; this can happen because the ship impresses its motion on all the surrounding air, which carries the arrow along with it, so that, having fallen, it returns to the same spot. (3) Even if the experiment in the Objection were as stated, it would not help us, since the ship is really moving while the Earth, carried in its vortex, is really at rest.
