(4) The motion of a stone thrown towards the Earth, or of an arrow shot towards it, is not exactly straight and along a straight line, but rather along a parabolic line, because while the stone or arrow is descending to the Earth, it is carried along by the vortex of the Earth. Yet it appears straight to everyone, because they do not notice that carrying, by which they are borne round together with the Earth, just as happens to a passenger in a ship.

units.la: CCCCXLI. Obj. 14. Si Terra circumvolveretur ab Occasu in Ortum, tunc globus bombardicus versus Occasum emissus longius tenderet: subduceretur enim interim ipsa machina; is vero, qui versus Ortum exploderetur, brevius ferretur, quia machina eum consequeretur: quæ omnia cum Experientia pugnant.
units.tr: CCCCXLI. Objection 14. If the Earth revolved from west to east, then a bombard ball fired towards the west would travel farther, for the gun itself would be withdrawn in the meantime; but the ball fired towards the east would travel a shorter distance, because the gun would follow it. All these things are contrary to experience.

units.la: CCCCXLII. Resp. Nulla est in Majore connexio Antecedentis cum Consequente. Nam globo versus Occasum emisso, quantum ei subducitur machina, tantum etiam ille globus versus machinam à motu communi vorticis repellitur: & contra globo in Ortum exploso, quantum machina subsequitur, tantum etiam additur delationis globo à vortice Terræ. 2. Quod si Minor negaretur, ea experientia probari non posset (quamvis si Terra proprie inveretur, hoc est, ab aere vicino separaretur, rem ita se habituram, ut Minor ponit, per rationem colligi posset) esset enim hæc differentia celeritatis insensibilis, cum 2 temporis minutis eum milliare absolvere compertum sit.
units.tr: CCCCXLII. Reply. There is no connection in the major premise between the antecedent and the consequent. For as much as the gun is withdrawn from a ball fired towards the west, so much also is that ball driven back away from the gun by the common motion of the vortex; and conversely, for a ball fired towards the east, as much as the gun follows, so much is added to the ball's motion by the vortex of the Earth. (2) But if the minor premise were denied, it could not be proved by that experience. (Although, if the Earth were truly moved, that is, separated from the neighbouring air, the matter would turn out as the minor premise states, which can be inferred by reasoning.) For this difference of speed would be imperceptible, since it has been found that a ball covers a mile in 2 minutes of time.

units.la: CCCCXLIII. Hæ sunt Objectiones, quas nobis contra hanc sententiam prolatas videre contigit, nunc Corollarii loco addam refutationem eorum, quæ L. p. 307. porrò contra hanc sententiam deprom it. Observandum, inquit, 1. Terram in Cælo suo esse, ex sententia Cartesii, ut Planeta suo quique coelo volvuntur. 2. Navis exemplam magis evertere motum Terræ, quam stabilire. Si quidem navis malacia deprehensa, nec ventis ullis aut remis propulsa, etsi in latus interdum concutiatur, nihil tamen aut parum admodum progreditur. 3. Si Terra suo coelo circumfertur, Planeta suo, & Sol, qui Cartesio inter stellas fixas, finstra à Josua Sol stare jussu, & Luna quiescere, si Terra nihilominus coeli sui motu rapta est, nec diei stationem & quietem morata. Sed Scriptura ad opinionem vulgi, non ad rei veritatem Cartesio judice loquitur; ideoque hoc & similia facta non urgemus. 4. Si Terra suo in Coelo quiescit, alieno tantum motu delata, Sole in medio mundi quiescente, circa quem omnes Planetarum orbes in gyrum torqueantur: altera pars Terræ nunquam à Sole aversa, perpetuo die fruitur, altera eidem semper aversa, nocte sempiterna premetur, quod ratio & experientia secus esse docet. 5. Mercurium tribus mensibus cursum suum absolvere, contra Astronomorum circa phaenomena observationem est: quod tamen fieri non miremur si interiori prope Solem gyro vertatur.
units.tr: CCCCXLIII. These are the objections which we have chanced to see raised against this view. Now, by way of a corollary, I shall add a refutation of the points which L. p. 307 further brings forward against this view. "It must be noted," he says, (1) that according to Descartes' view the Earth is in its own heaven, as each planet revolves in its own heaven. (2) The example of a ship rather overturns the motion of the Earth than establishes it: for indeed a ship caught in a calm, pushed neither by winds nor oars, though sometimes shaken from side to side, nevertheless advances not at all or very little. (3) If the Earth is carried round in its own heaven, as the planets are, and the Sun, which for Descartes is among the fixed stars, was made to stand still at Joshua's command, and the Moon to rest, then if the Earth was nevertheless snatched away by the motion of its own heaven, it would neither delay the stopping and rest of the day. But Scripture speaks, in Descartes' judgment, according to the opinion of the common people, not according to the truth of the matter; and therefore we do not press this and similar facts. (4) If the Earth rests in its own heaven, carried only by another's motion, with the Sun resting in the middle of the world, around which all the orbits of the planets are turned in a circle, then one part of the Earth, never turned away from the Sun, enjoys perpetual day, while the other part, always turned away from it, would be oppressed by everlasting night; which reason and experience teach is not so. (5) That Mercury completes its course in three months is contrary to the observation of the astronomers regarding the phenomena; yet we should not wonder at this if it revolves in a circle very near the Sun.

units.la: CCCCXLIV. Resp. In primo, quod observari vult, nihil esse absurdi, jam ante art. 431. est evictum. Ad secundum considerandum, Cartesium exemplo navis nullis remis nec ventis impulsæ, nec anchoris alligatæ, quæ in medio maris possit quiescere, etsi forte aquæ ingens moles occulto cursu delabens ipsam secum ferat, uti, ad ostendendum, delationem cum quiete corporis delati non pugnare. Supponit autem, illam navem deferri vel à mari æstu marino defluente, vel à mari tenden-te. te versus Ortum (quod ex eo deprehenditur, quod magnæ navigationes sint multò tardiores & difficiliores versus partes Orientales quàm Occidentales,) vel collocatam etiam esse in quibusdam maris angustiis, in quibus aqua semper fluit versus Occasum. Ad tertium respondebimus suo loco. Notamus tantum, nullibi dicere Cartesium Solem circumferri suo coelo, quin contra, Solem esse causam circumvolutionis sui cœli circa se, dum circa axem suum circumvolvitur, discere potuisset ex art. 84.
units.tr: CCCCXLIV. Reply. As to the first point, which he wishes to be observed, that there is nothing absurd in it has already been established before art. 431. As to the second, let us consider that Descartes, by the example of a ship driven by neither oars nor winds, nor tied with anchors, which can rest in the middle of the sea, even if perhaps a huge mass of water, gliding by a hidden course, carries it along with it, uses this to show that being carried along does not conflict with the rest of the body that is carried. But he supposes that the ship is carried either by the tidal flow of the sea, or by the sea tending towards the East (which is perceived from this, that great voyages are much slower and more difficult towards the Eastern parts than towards the Western), or even that it is placed in certain narrows of the sea, in which the water always flows towards the West. We shall answer the third point in its place. We note only that Descartes nowhere says that the Sun is carried around within its heaven; on the contrary, he could have learned from art. 84 that the Sun is the cause of the revolution of its heaven around itself, while it turns about its own axis.

units.la: Pp. III. In quarto & quinto ostendit, quàm parum sit aptus ad congressum cum Cartesio, cùm tam leviter res Astronomicas & Physicas, etiam vulgò notas, habeat perspectas. Nonne enim omnes, qui Copernicanam sententiam habent perspectam, nôrunt, ipsum statuere, dum Terra circumvolvitur circa suum axem, fieri, ut nunc hæc pars, nunc altera die aut nocte fruatur? quæ eadem sententia est Cartesii & nostra, quam hic defendimus. Similiter, nonne in confesso est apud Astronomos nunc fere omnes, Mercurium tribus mensibus circa Solem cursum suum absolvere? Ipse Tycho, & omnes qui ipsum sequuntur, hoc statuunt, idque cum phænomenis benè convenire agnoscunt. Unicum cito Gassendum (nec enim plures in re adeò notâ lubet aperire) qui Iustit. Astronom. cap. 12. in quo Tychonianum systema mundi describit, ita loquitur: Adhæc (statuit sc. Tycho) quinque stellas errantes motus speciales circa Solem tanquam circa centrum obire, Mercurium scilicet trimestrem, Venerem octimestrem, Martem biennem &c. Sed fortasse non assurrexit adversarius ultra levem quandam cognitionem Systematis Ptolemaici, quod quidem nunc ab omnibus fere Astronomis rejicitur, propter multitarias absurditates; in quo Mercurius & Venus eodem fere tempore cum Sole cursum suum statuuntur circa Terram absolvere; qui tamen tàm audacter proclamare possit, id esse contra Astronomorum circa phænomena observationes, satis nequeo mirari! Cartesius autem quando dicit art. 31. Pp. III. Mercurium circuitum suum tribus mensibus absolvere, expressè circa Solem mentionem facit.
units.tr: Pp. III. In the fourth and fifth points he shows how little he is fit to engage with Descartes, since he has so lightly grasped the astronomical and physical matters, even those commonly known. For do not all who have grasped the Copernican opinion know that it holds that, while the Earth turns about its own axis, it comes about that now this part and now the other enjoys day or night? This is the same opinion as Descartes's and ours, which we defend here. Likewise, is it not agreed among astronomers, now almost all of them, that Mercury completes its course about the Sun in three months? Tycho himself, and all who follow him, hold this and acknowledge that it agrees well with the phenomena. I shall cite only Gassendi (for I do not wish to set out more in a matter so well known), who in his Institutio Astronomica, chapter 12, in which he describes the Tychonian system of the world, speaks thus: "Moreover (Tycho holds, that is) the five wandering stars perform their special motions about the Sun as about a centre, namely Mercury in three months, Venus in eight months, Mars in two years, etc." But perhaps the opponent has not risen beyond a slight acquaintance with the Ptolemaic system, which indeed is now rejected by almost all astronomers on account of its many absurdities; in it Mercury and Venus are held to complete their course about the Earth at almost the same time as the Sun. I can scarcely wonder enough how he could so boldly proclaim that this is contrary to the astronomers' observations of the phenomena! But Descartes, when he says in art. 31, Pp. III, that Mercury completes its circuit in three months, expressly mentions the Sun.

units.la: CCCCXLV. Atque hæ sunt Objectiones contra hanc Terræ delationem militantes, quas mihi videre licuit, ex quibus refutatis, apparebit, opinor, quàm infirmis contraria sententia tibicinibus nitatur, nostraque magis confirmabitur. Quod si verò hæ responsiones ad objectiones alicui videantur fluere ex aliis Principiis, quàm vulgò receptis, nec tamen à me omnia demonstrata inveniat, sciat, hoc operis institutum pati non potuisse, & mihi satis fuisse, quòd Objectiones adversariorum enervaverim, eas invalidas esse plane demonstrando. Ac si non gravetur Cartesii in hanc rem edita, Meditationes & Principia, cum attentione accuratâ pervolvere, non dubito, quin ea omnia quæ in Objectionibus resolvendis à me sunt assumta, sit ibi demonstrata reperturus.
units.tr: CCCCXLV. These are the objections against this motion of the Earth that I have been able to see, and once they have been refuted, it will appear, I think, how weakly the contrary opinion rests on its supports, and our view will be the more confirmed. But if these replies to the objections seem to someone to flow from principles other than those commonly received, and he does not find everything demonstrated by me, let him know that the plan of this work could not allow it, and that it was enough for me to have weakened the objections of the adversaries, by plainly demonstrating that they are invalid. And if he does not mind turning over with careful attention Descartes's writings published on this matter, the Meditations and the Principles, I do not doubt that he will find there demonstrated all the things that I have assumed in resolving the objections.

units.la: CAPUT XX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XX.

units.la: Cartesius Auctoritatem Scripturæ omnibus suis ratiociniis anteponit, & ego cum ipso. Ejus Auctoritati ut nec in- fallibilitati, repugnat sententia de stylo Scripturæ vul- gari circa res naturales. Status Controversiæ istius quæstionis constituitur.
units.tr: Descartes places the authority of Scripture above all his reasonings, and I agree with him. The view that Scripture commonly speaks of natural things in an ordinary style does not conflict with its authority or infallibility. The state of this controversy is set out.

units.la: CCCCXLVI. Specimen vidimus Cartesianæ Methodi Philosophandi, quâ non quærens in libro Scripturæ doctrinam, quæ non inest, Philosophicam, sed in semetipso & vasto mundi volumine, attendendo ad notiones menti insitas, & per sensus sæpe excitatas, distinctâque à confusis secernens, à primis causis & Principiis, maximè evidentibus, per manifestas consequentias varias speciales veritates deduxit. At libro Scripturæ omnino divinam attribuit Auctoritatem & infallibilem veritatem, cui sese debeat omnis intellectus subjicere, quandocunque de isto testimonio est persuasus, sive, quando novit, hoc vel illud Spiritum S. in suo verbo testari.
units.tr: CCCCXLVI. We have seen a sample of the Cartesian method of philosophizing. It does not seek in the book of Scripture a philosophical doctrine that is not there. Instead it attends to itself and to the vast volume of the world, looking to notions implanted in the mind and often roused by the senses. Separating distinct notions from confused ones, it deduces various particular truths from first causes and principles, which are most evident, through clear consequences. But to the book of Scripture it ascribes divine authority and infallible truth, to which every intellect ought to submit whenever it is persuaded of this testimony, that is, whenever it knows that the Holy Spirit bears witness to this or that in his Word.

units.la: CCCCXLVII. Huc faciunt loca seqq. Pp. I. art. 25. Itaque forte nobis Deus de se ipso, vel aliis aliquid revelet, quod naturales ingenii nostri vires excedat, qualia jam sunt mysteria Incarnationis & Trinitatis, non recusabimus illa credere, quamvis non clare intelligamus; nec ullo modo mirabimur, multa esse tùm in immensâ ejus naturâ, tum etiam in rebus creatis quæ captum nostrum excedant, Et Art. 76. Præter cetera autem, memoriæ nostræ pro summâ regulâ est infigendum, ea quæ nobis à Deo revelata sunt, ut omnium certissima esse credenda. Et quamvis forte lumen rationis, quàm maximè clarum & evidens, aliud quid nobis suggerere videretur, soli tamen auctoritati divinæ potius, quàm proprio nostro judicio, fidem esse adhibendam: sed in iis, de quibus fides divina nihil nos docet, minimè decere hominem Philosophum, aliquid pro vero assumere, quod verum esse nunquam perspexit; & magis fidere sensibus, hoc est, inconsideratis infantiæ suæ judiciis, quam maturâ rationi.
units.tr: CCCCXLVII. The following passages bear on this. Principles, Part I, art. 25: So God may perhaps reveal to us something about himself or about other things that exceeds the natural powers of our intellect, as the mysteries of the Incarnation and the Trinity already do. We shall not refuse to believe these, although we do not clearly understand them, and we shall in no way be surprised that there are many things, both in his immense nature and in created things, that exceed our capacity. And art. 76: Besides other things, this must be fixed in our memory as the highest rule: that what has been revealed to us by God is to be believed as the most certain of all. And although perhaps the light of reason, very clear and evident, seemed to suggest something else to us, faith must nevertheless be placed in the divine authority alone, rather than in our own judgment. But in those matters about which divine faith teaches us nothing, it is by no means fitting for a man who is a philosopher to take as true something he has never perceived to be true, and to trust his senses, that is, the unconsidered judgments of his infancy, more than mature reason.

units.la: CCCCXLVIII. Huic sententiæ totus consentio, atque apud me tanta est Scripturarum S. Auctoritas & Infallibilitas, ut omnem meam rationem & sensus potius velim ejurare, quam vel dubitare de eo, quod cognoverint à Scripturâ doceri, sive à Deo loquente in eâ affirmari vel negari, paratusque sim renunciare omni sententiæ, quam S. Scripturæ verè repugnare fuerit ostensum. Atqui hæc Authoritas & Infallibilitas Scripturæ S. communiter obtinet apud omnes Christianos, nisi quòd Sociniani existiment: Scriptores sacros in levioribus quibusdam errare potuisse, quibus ab omnibus aliis contradicitur, hoc præcipuè argumento nitentibus, quod Sp. S. illa, quæ iis Scriptoribus inspiravit, ac per eos voluit testari, sine maculâ erroris voluit testata relinquere. Sed quænam sint illa, quæ Scriptura testatur, quæ docet atque credenda proponit, de eo disquiritur adhuc hodiè inter varias sectas & religiones, illudque ejus testimonium (quod sunt verba Scripturæ ritè intellecta) per media interpretandi ritè adhibita est cognoscendum.
units.tr: CCCCXLVIII. I agree entirely with this view. My own estimation of the authority and infallibility of the holy Scriptures is so high that I would rather renounce all my reasoning and my senses than doubt what I have learned is taught by Scripture, or what the God who speaks in it affirms or denies. I am ready to abandon any opinion that has been shown to be truly contrary to Holy Scripture. Now, this authority and infallibility of the holy Scripture is commonly held by all Christians, except that the Socinians think that the sacred writers could have erred in some rather minor matters. All others contradict them, relying chiefly on this argument: that the Holy Spirit, who inspired those writers and wished to bear witness through them, meant to leave what they bore witness to without the stain of error. But what it is that Scripture bears witness to, what it teaches and proposes to be believed, is still disputed today among various sects and religions. That testimony of Scripture, which is the words of Scripture rightly understood, must be learned by the proper means of interpretation.

units.la: CCCCXLIX.
units.tr: CCCCXLIX.

units.la: Quantumvis autem Cartesius Respons. ad secundas Obj. p. 75. occasione data per object. contra Dei Infallibilitatem inquiat: Omnibus est nota distinctio inter modos loquendi de Deo ad sensus vulgi accommodatos, & veritatem quidem aliquam, sed ut ad homines relatam continentes, quibus Sacra litera uti solent; atque alios nudam magis veritatem, nec ad homines relatam exprimentes, quibus omnes inter Philosophandum uti debent; atque nos eosdem modos loquendi à Scriptura de rebus naturalibus dicamus usurpari, id tamen cum Scripturæ Authoritate vel Infallibilitate pugnare nullatenus existimamus, prout in sequentibus ostendemus. Ordine itaque progredientes, primo demonstrabimus, hunc Scripturæ stylum esse, quem posteà, Authoritati & Infallibilitati Scripturæ nihil quicquam detrahere evincemus.
units.tr: However, although Descartes, in his Replies to the Second Objections, p. 75, when the occasion arose through an objection against God's infallibility, says: Everyone knows the distinction between ways of speaking about God that are adapted to the senses of the common people, which contain some truth but related to men, and which Sacred Letters customarily use, and other ways that express bare truth more, not related to men, which everyone ought to use when philosophizing; we nevertheless do not think that this is in any way contrary to the authority or infallibility of Scripture, if we say that these same ways of speaking are used by Scripture about natural things, as we shall show in what follows. Proceeding therefore in order, we shall first demonstrate that this is the style of Scripture, and then we shall prove that it takes nothing whatever away from the authority and infallibility of Scripture.

units.la: CCCCL.
units.tr: CCCCL.

units.la: Ut autem prius rectè peragatur, ante omnia, quid hic in quæstionem veniat, bene considerandum, ad quod intelligendum, velim Lectorem repetere caput primum hujus tractatûs, & imprimis art. 21, 22, & 23. In isto capite ostendimus, quid sit notitia communis & vulgaris, &, quomodo sermo, à vulgo inventus, sit ei appropriatus. Prout enim notitia illa communis veritatem assequitur, ita & sermo ei accommodatus eam exprimit: si ea nudam veritatem fuerit assecuta, etiam sermo nudam exprimit; sin veritatem quidem aliquam generalem, sed confusè perceptam, atque homines & eorum sensus relatam atque præjudiciis involutam notitia communis deprehenderit, etiam sermo vulgaris talem veritatem exprimit.
units.tr: So that this may be done properly, first of all it must be carefully considered what is at issue here. To understand this, I would have the reader go back to the first chapter of this treatise, and especially to articles 21, 22 and 23. In that chapter we showed what common and popular knowledge is, and how speech found among the common people is adapted to it. For just as common knowledge attains the truth, so the speech adapted to it expresses it. If that knowledge has attained bare truth, the speech also expresses bare truth; but if it has grasped some general truth, yet perceived it confusedly, and if it has taken that truth as relating to men and their senses and wrapped up in prejudices, then popular speech also expresses such a truth.

units.la: CCCCLI.
units.tr: CCCCLI.

units.la: Statuimus ergo, Scripturam de rebus naturalibus loquentem sermone vulgari uti, sive nudam veritatem exprimat, sive ad homines eorumque sensu relatam atque prajudiciis & erroribus involutam. Ac prius quidem extra dubium est, sed de posteriori inter nos & adversarios controverti videtur. Nec alius, quàm sequens potest esse status Controversiæ, si sint, qui omnino adhuc nobiscum contendere velint: An Scriptura de rebus naturalibus loquens adhibeat formulas communi usu tritas, veritatem quidem aliquam, sed ad homines eorumque sensus relatam & prajudiciis atque erroribus involutam referentes, κείνην suam circa prajudicia non interponendo; An vero, ubi vulgares locutiones innituntur multis firmissimè radicatis & necdum depositis prajudiciis, eas mutet in accuratas & Philosophicas? Ego prius affirmo, posterius nego.
units.tr: I therefore lay down this: Scripture, when it speaks of natural things, uses ordinary language, whether it expresses the bare truth or refers it to men and their senses and wraps it in prejudices and errors. The first part is beyond doubt, but between us and our opponents the second part seems to be disputed. The issue can only stand as follows, if there are people who still wish to contend with us at all: Does Scripture, when it speaks of natural things, use formulas worn smooth by common usage, which refer to some truth, but one related to men and their senses and wrapped in prejudices and errors, without itself interposing any correction of those prejudices? Or, where ordinary expressions rest on many deeply rooted prejudices not yet laid aside, does it change them into precise and philosophical ones? I affirm the former and deny the latter.

units.la: CCCCLII. Quid hic per nudam veritatem intelligatur, ex oppositione est manifestum, nimirum talis, quæ ad homines eorumque sensus non sit relata, quæque prajudiciis & erroribus non sit involuta. Veritas vero, ad homines eorumque sensus relata, est, quando res denominantur à varietatibus istis & qualitatibus, quas in nostris sensibus efficiunt: v. g. quando rebus tribuimus lucem, colorem, sonum, odorem, calorem, gravitatem &c. propterea quod sensus nostros his diversis modis afficiunt. Quod si quis sic loquens etiam putaverit, revera lucem, colorem, sonum, &c. his ipsis rebus, quæ inde denominantur, inesse, etiam Prajudiciis involuta est veritas, sermoque iis prajudiciis innititur, quo tamen generalis aliqua veritas ita significatur, ut modus significandi eam à prajudiciis habeat ortum. Ita dum res colorata, calida, gravis &c. dicitur, veritas quidem significatur, quod sit aliqua in re illa varietas, propter quam sensus coloris, caloris, gravitatis &c. in me excitatur. Ita sermo prajudiciis est involutus, quando Sol oriri & occidere dicitur &c. CCCCLIII. Semper tamen Scriptura his phrasibus utens aliquam veritatem exprimit, sed generalem, quæ sub illis involucris latet, quæque ab iis est separanda. Quid enim & quantum per tales formulas doceatur & significetur ex circumstantiis sermonis & personâ iis utente est judicandum. Si utens isto sermone sit homo, qui ultra vulgarem cognitionem non ascenderit, Philosophicâ cognitione non imbutus, vel in universum, vel de re de quâ loquitur, atque ex circumstantiis sermonis patet, quod prajudiciorum & errorum, quibus ejus sermo innitetur, significatio ad ejus institutum faciat, quin ea per suum sermonem significet & doceat non est dubitandum. Si sit homo sapiens, Philosophicâ cognitione rerum imbutus, vel in universum, vel circa rem de quâ loquitur, multò magis, si sit Spiritus Sanctus omnis sapientiæ auctor, qui nullis erroribus vel prajudiciis obnoxius esse potest, sique ex circumstantiis stantiis sermonis fiat manifestum, eorum significationem non requiri ad ipsius scopum, nullum dubium esse potest, quin non præjudicia, sed veritatem tantum generalem, sub illis involucris latentem, verba illa docent & significent.
units.tr: CCCCLII. What is meant here by bare truth is clear from the contrast: namely, a truth that is not related to men and their senses and is not wrapped in prejudices and errors. Truth, however, is related to men and their senses when things are named from those variations and qualities which they produce in our senses; for example, when we ascribe to things light, colour, sound, smell, heat, weight and so on, because they affect our senses in these various ways. If someone speaking in this way also thinks that light, colour, sound and the rest truly inhere in the very things named from them, then the truth is wrapped in prejudices, and the speech rests on those prejudices, although a general truth is still signified in such a way that the manner of signifying it has its origin in prejudice. Thus when a thing is called coloured, warm, heavy and so on, the truth signified is that there is some variation in the thing, on account of which the sensations of colour, heat, weight and so on are excited in me. So speech is wrapped in prejudice when the sun is said to rise and set, and so on. CCCCLIII. Nevertheless, Scripture, using such phrases, always expresses some truth, but a general one, which lies hidden under those wrappings and must be separated from them. What and how much is taught and signified by such formulas must be judged from the circumstances of the discourse and from the person using it. If the one using such language is a man who has not risen above ordinary knowledge, not imbued with philosophical knowledge either in general or about the matter he is speaking of, and it is clear from the circumstances of the discourse that the signification of the prejudices and errors on which his speech rests bears on his purpose, there can be no doubt that he does not teach or signify those prejudices by his speech. If he is a wise man, imbued with philosophical knowledge of things, either in general or about the matter he speaks of, far more so if it is the Holy Spirit, the author of all wisdom, who cannot be liable to any errors or prejudices; and if it becomes plain from the circumstances of the discourse that their signification is not required for his purpose, there can be no doubt that those words teach and signify not the prejudices but only the general truth lying hidden under those wrappings.

units.la: CCCCLIV. Atque in hac ipsa sententiâ, quam articulo 451 constitui, mecum consentiunt adversarii, contra quos in sequentibus sum disputaturus, ut ita à limine statim appareat, eos, dum sese mihi opponunt, cum umbrâ suâ vel secum ipsis luctari. Sic B. p. 261, inquit: Non omnis qui secundum apparentiam loquitur, negat rei veritatem, sed sæpè tantum determinat rei veritatem, prout sese nobis exhibet. Hoc autem est quod ego volo; patet enim ex dictis hîc & in Dissertationibus, quod nec ego statuam, Spiritum Sanctum secundum apparentiam loquentem, veritatem rei negare. P. 105. ad locum Jud. com. 13. concedit per ἀστέρας πλανήτας Planetas proprie dictos intelligi, eosque ab Astronomis, ita, inquit, appellatos, quia ab ipsis observantur varii illorum motus apparentes, quibus hominibus errantibus similes videntur. Ergò denominationem acceperunt ab apparentia, quæ cum rei veritate non convenit; reverà enim non errant, adeoque utitur Spiritus Sanctus formulis usu tritis, etsi opinionibus erroneis nitantur, ut nunc in alia loca adversarii non inquiram. Similiter M. p. 115 dicit, sufficere dummodò statuamus cordu vocabulum ea vere significare, quæ Spiritus Sanctus eo nobis significare intendit, sive ea vera significatio errorem aliquem auctorum istius phraseologiæ supponat sive non; quo non commodius meam potuisset exprimere sententiam. Sic p.215. Concedimus libenter, posse Scripturam proponi linguâ aliquâ vulgari, in quâ multa sunt locutiones vulgares & à communi loquendi usu desumpta, erroneis opinionibus innitentes NB. id est, talibus ubi rei vera erronea opinio vulgi hoc vel illud imponit nomen; quæ interim rem intentam usu vere significet, NB. Sic p.216. Concedimus 1. non omnes hujusmodi locutiones errori alicui vulgari innitentes, dummodò ex usu rem significandam vere significent, esse evitandas. 2. Nec etiam tum orationem in contrarium esse flectendam. 3. Multo minùs errorem in rebus naturalibus esse notandum & refutandum, (omne ergò conceditur quod ego intendo.) Hoc tantum dicimus, multa in se falsa in Scripturam debuisse admisti, potiùs istorum falsorum mentionem plane supprimendam fuisse, cùm ad nihil sit utilis (quæ prout oppositè intelligenda ad antecedentia, ut designetur, Scripturam non docere, testari, significare falsum, libentissimè admitto.) Judicet nunc æquus Lector, num ego, num adversarius cum umbrâ suâ luctetur. Nec video aliam sententiam esse H. p. 198, quando inquit: Balbutivit Spiritus Sanctus in modo NB proponendi rem, non autem in re ipsâ.
units.tr: CCCCLIV. Indeed, my opponents agree with me in this very view which I laid down in article 451, and against whom I am going to dispute in what follows, so that from the outset it appears plainly that, while they set themselves against me, they are wrestling with their own shadow or with themselves. So B., p. 261, says: Not everyone who speaks according to appearance denies the truth of the thing, but often he only determines the truth of the thing as it presents itself to us. This is exactly what I want; for it is clear from what has been said here and in the Dissertations that I too do not hold that the Holy Spirit, speaking according to appearance, denies the truth of the thing. P. 105, on the passage Jude 13, he grants that by wandering stars [ἀστέρας πλανήτας] are properly meant the planets, and that they are so called by astronomers, he says, because their various apparent motions are observed by them, and these seem like wandering men. Therefore they took the name from appearance, which does not agree with the truth of the thing; for in reality they do not wander, and so the Holy Spirit uses formulas worn by common usage, even though they rest on erroneous opinions; I will not now look into other places in my opponents. Similarly M., p. 115, says: It is enough if we hold that the word cordu... truly signifies what the Holy Spirit intends it to signify to us, whether that true signification presupposes some error in the authors of this phraseology or not; by which he could not have expressed my view more conveniently. So p. 215: We gladly grant that Scripture can be set forth in some ordinary language, in which there are many colloquial expressions taken from common usage, resting on erroneous opinions NB. that is, such where the erroneous opinion of the common people imposes this or that name on a thing; which nevertheless truly signifies the intended thing by usage NB. So p. 216: We grant, first, that not all such expressions which rest on some popular error are to be avoided, provided that by usage they truly signify the thing to be signified. Second, nor is the discourse to be bent to the contrary. Third, much less is error in natural things to be noted and refuted (so everything I intend is granted here). We say only this, that many things false in themselves ought to have been admitted into Scripture; rather, the mention of those falsehoods ought to have been wholly suppressed, since it is useless for anything (which, understood in the opposite sense to what precedes, so as to make clear that Scripture does not teach, attest or signify what is false, I most gladly admit). Let the fair reader now judge whether I or my opponent is wrestling with his own shadow. Nor do I see any other meaning in H., p. 198, when he says: The Holy Spirit stammered in the mode of proposing the matter, not in the matter itself.

units.la: Quod autem mihi videtur tribuere, Spiritum Sanctum balbutire in re ipsa cum vulgo, ut falsum significet & testetur cum ipso, id à Sacrâ Scriptură & mente meâ alienum esse protestor. Sed manifestius consensus nostER patefit ex ipsius verbis, p. 248. Spiritus Sanctus mutuatus hic est verbum seu nomen opinionis à populo, non verò opinionem, quæ est ipsissima sententia mea, quam hîc defendo. Item p. 239. Spiritus Sanctus nautarum more loquendi phrases, sicuti prolatæ sunt, describi jussit. Item: Esse locutionem à communi visûs errore desumptam Act. xxvii. 27. De illo adversariorum consensu qui plura cognoscere voluerit, legat caput hujus nostri Tractatus xxiii. Et sane nemo eorum, cum quibus hactenus fui congressus, negare fuit ausus, in linguâ vulgari, quâ Sp. Sanctus utitur, dum voluntatem suam de salute nobis revelat, reperiri phrases erroneis vulgi opinionibus innitentes, iisque Spiritum Sanctum solere uti, non per eas ullos errores exprimendo, sed semper aliquam veritatem docendo. Et hoc solum est, quod & nos negare non audemus. Quemadmodum vero illi negant, Spiritum Sanctum in Scripturâ loquentem adoptare vulgi prajudicia & errores, eosque in Scriptura docere, ita & ego hoc ipsum constanter nego.
units.tr: But what seems to me to attribute to the Holy Spirit a stammering in the thing itself, as though with the common people he signified and attested something false along with them, I protest is alien both to Holy Scripture and to my own mind. But the consensus between us is more clearly revealed in their own words, p. 248: The Holy Spirit here borrowed from the people the word or name of an opinion, not the opinion itself, which is precisely my own view, which I defend here. Likewise p. 239: The Holy Spirit ordered the phrases of sailors' speech to be described just as they were uttered. Likewise: It is an expression taken from a common error of sight, Acts xxvii. 27. Whoever wishes to know more of the agreement of my opponents, let him read the twenty-third chapter of this our treatise. And indeed none of those with whom I have contended so far has dared to deny that in the ordinary language which the Holy Spirit uses, when he reveals his will about our salvation, there are found phrases resting on the erroneous opinions of the common people, and that the Holy Spirit is accustomed to use them, not by them expressing any errors, but always by teaching some truth. And this alone is what we too do not dare to deny. But just as they deny that the Holy Spirit, speaking in Scripture, adopts the prejudices and errors of the people and teaches them in Scripture, so I too constantly deny this very thing.

units.la: CCCCLV. Hanc meam sententiam satis etiam mihi videbar expressisse in editione Dissertationum.
units.tr: CCCCLV. I seemed to myself to have expressed this view of mine sufficiently in the edition of the Dissertations.

units.la: Quamvis enim usus fuerim formulâ à Copernicanis usurpatâ, dicendo: Spiritum Sanctum sæpe loqui ex opinione vulgi & secundum apparentiam, non secundum rei accuratam veritatem. Item, Scripturam sæpissime de rebus naturalibus loqui ut apparent, non ut sunt secundum ἀκρίβειαν Philosophicam. Item: Scripturam de rebus naturalibus loquentem non accuratam semper veritatem, sed potius sensum & opinionem vulgi sapius sequi, tamen satis ex explicatione passim data potuit patere, me non statuere, Spiritum Sanctum destertâ veritate opinionem erroneam vulgi assumere, ei assentiri, eam docere, testari vel significare in S. litteris, quod communiter adversarii mihi videntur tribuere. Loqui enim duplici sensu aliquis potest dici secundum vulgi erroneam opinionem, vel verba tantum usurpando iisque veritatem generalem exprimendo, quo sensu id Spiritui Sancto tribui, vel opinionem ejus assumendo, ei assentiendo, & sic sermonem secundum eam formando, quo sensu id de Spiritu Sancto constanter nego. Vidit hunc duplicem sensum istius phraseos jam olim Melchior Canus Loc. Theol. lib. ii. cap. 5. p. 586. Falsa vulgi opiniones, inquit, in duplici sunt differentiâ. Quaedam, quæ non nisi verbis falsis signisicari atque exprimi possunt. Ut Christum esse Johannem Baptistam, vel Hieremiam, vel unum ex prioribus Prophetis. Atque hujusmodi opiniones semper auctores sacri ita referunt, ut non ex se, sed ex vulgi nomine retulisse videantur. Alia sunt vulgi opiniones falsæ quidem, sed verbis iis expressæ ac significatæ, quæ in sensu aliquo vulgari veræ sint. Ut Ioseph esse patrem Christi ad vulgi sensum falsum omnino erat, sed vere tamen pater, & sine falsitate dicebatur. Tam quoniam nutritius erat, tam quoniam Vir matris erat. Et licet vulgi sermone, vere tamen privignus filius vocatur, mater noverca, vitricus pater. In quibus rebus, fateor, vera historia lex est vulgi opinionem exprimere. Nam si de priore rerum genere sermo sit, in historia profana absurdus est, in sacra etiam impius. Sapientes quippe cum vulgo loquuntur fere, sed non sentiunt cum vulgo. Nec mendacii tamen rei sunt, quoniam, quæ loquuntur, ea secundum aliquem verbi significatum vera esse intelligunt.
units.tr: For although I used the formula employed by the Copernicans, saying: the Holy Spirit often speaks according to the opinion of the common people and according to appearance, not according to the exact truth of the thing. Likewise: Scripture, when speaking of natural things, very often speaks as they appear, not as they are according to philosophical accuracy [ἀκρίβεια]. Likewise: Scripture, when speaking of natural things, does not always follow the exact truth but more often follows the sense and opinion of the common people. Nevertheless, it could be sufficiently clear from the explanation given throughout that I do not hold that the Holy Spirit, departing from the true fact, adopts the erroneous opinion of the common people, assents to it, teaches it, or affirms or signifies it in the holy writings, which my opponents generally seem to attribute to me. For a person may be said to speak according to the erroneous opinion of the common people in two senses: either by merely using the words and expressing a general truth by them, in which sense I grant this of the Holy Spirit; or by adopting their opinion, assenting to it, and so forming his speech according to it, in which sense I constantly deny this of the Holy Spirit. Melchior Canus already saw this twofold sense of the expression long ago, Loc. Theol. bk. 2, ch. 5, p. 586: False opinions of the common people, he says, are of two kinds. Some can be signified and expressed only by false words, as that Christ is John the Baptist, or Jeremiah, or one of the earlier prophets. And sacred authors report opinions of this kind in such a way that they seem to report them not on their own authority but in the name of the common people. Other opinions of the common people are indeed false, but are expressed and signified by words which are true in some popular sense. Thus that Joseph was the father of Christ was entirely false in the sense of the common people, yet he was truly a father and was called so without falsehood: both because he was the foster-father and because he was the husband of the mother. And, in the common manner of speaking, a stepson is truly called a son, a stepmother a mother, a stepfather a father. In these matters, I admit, it is the rule of true history to express the opinion of the common people. For if the discourse concerns the first kind of thing, it is absurd in profane history and impious even in sacred history. Wise men, indeed, generally speak with the common people, but do not think with them. Nor are they guilty of lying, since they understand that what they say is true in some sense of the word.

units.la: CCCCLVI. Art. 8. cap. 1. diff. 3. sic explicavi meam mentem, ut appareret, me nihil aliud statuere, quàm quod etiam art. 45, hujus capitis posui. Sic enim dico: Uti quidem Spiritum Sanctum illis formulis, quibus vulgus suam opinionem exprimit, qui præter veritatem generalem præjudicium etiam, quod eam involvit, solet significare: at non ideo etiam Spiritum Sanctum hanc opinionem suam facere, sed id, quod more recepto & formulis è trivio desumptis profert, recte intelligere, hoc est, significare tantum veritatem generalem, non verò consignificare istud præjudicium, quo in ista formula veritas est involuta. Idque declaravi exemplo Astronomorum, qui, quamvis formulis receptis ab apparentiis & præjudiciis sensuum derivatis, sive quæ præjudiciis innituntur, utantur, non tamen ista præjudicia sua faciunt, hoc est, non significant ea, sed tantum veritatem generalem iis involutam. Interim non velle dixi Spiritum Sanctum in Scripturâ nudam NB. veritatem (nudam dixi, non simpliciter veritatem; non enim nego, quin aliquam semper istis formulis veritatem doceat, sed eam dico ratione formularum esse involutam præjudiciis & erroribus) circa res naturales, quas optimè cognitas habet, manifestare (intellige, nisi etiam cognitio vulgaris ad nudam hujus vel illius rei veritatem pertingat) sed eam in medio relinquere, permittendo interea literatis hominibus, ut locutiones tales conferant cum Philosophiâ, & inde, num accurata sint, num vulgares discant, hoc est, ut, postquam per generalis veritatis significationem scopo Sp. S. satis factum esse viderint, videant, num in iis formulis forte præjudicium aliquod sit implicatum, quod non à Spiritu Sancto, sed à vulgo, tum tali formulâ utitur, significetur, atque sic sint vulgares; num accuratæ, ut nudam veritatem exprimant.
units.tr: CCCCLVI. In article 8, chapter 1, dissertation 3, I explained my view in such a way that it would appear that I hold nothing other than what I also laid down in article 45 of this chapter. For I say this: Indeed the Holy Spirit uses those formulas by which the common people express their opinion, which, besides the general truth, usually also signifies the prejudice that the truth involves. Yet the Holy Spirit does not on that account make this opinion his own, but rightly understands what he utters in the accepted manner and in formulas taken from common speech, that is, he signifies only the general truth and does not co-signify that prejudice by which the truth is wrapped up in that formula. I illustrated this with the example of the astronomers, who, although they use formulas, accepted and derived from appearances and from the prejudices of the senses, or which rest on prejudices, do not thereby make those prejudices their own; that is, they do not signify them, but only the general truth involved in them. Meanwhile I said that the Holy Spirit does not wish to make plain in Scripture the bare NB. truth (I said bare, not simply truth; for I do not deny that by these formulas he always teaches some truth, but I say that by the nature of the formulas it is wrapped up in prejudices and errors) concerning natural things, which he has perfectly known (understand: unless ordinary knowledge also reaches the bare truth of this or that thing) but leaves it undecided, allowing learned men meanwhile to compare such expressions with philosophy, and from this to learn whether they are accurate or whether they are vulgar; that is, once they have seen that the purpose of the Holy Spirit has been sufficiently served by the signification of the general truth, they should see whether some prejudice is perhaps implicated in those formulas which is signified not by the Holy Spirit but by the common people, who use such a formula, and so whether they are vulgar; and whether they are accurate, so as to express the bare truth.

units.la: CCCCLVII. Similiter Diff. prima p. 89. ipsis illis verbis, quibus hic usus fui art. 45, statum controversiæ expresseram, dicendo: Disquirendum itaque restat, num ad puritatem Scriptura requiratur, ut non proponatur lingua aliqua vulgari, in qua sunt multa locutiones vulgares erroneis opinionibus innitentes, a sensuum praejudiciis plerumque haustis: aut, si proponatur lingua vulgari, an saltem omnes tales locutiones evitari debeant, imo, ubi occasio fert, in contrarium sermo vertendus, errorque vulgaris notandus & refutandus? Nos dicimus, hoc modo nihil quicquam puritati Scripturae decedere. Lx his enim & similibus sententia nica explicanda, & ad haec referenda ea, quae, ab aliis separata, durius quid sonare videntur. Quoniam tamen quidam ex solo titulo librum priorem judicantes phrasi Copernicana fuerunt offensi, nos in eorum gratiam ab ea hic abstinebimus, & propterea statum controversiae art. 451. aliis verbis propositimus.
units.tr: CCCCLVII. Similarly, in the first dissertation, p. 89, I stated the state of the controversy in the very words by which I used it in article 45, saying: It remains, therefore, to inquire whether purity of Scripture requires that it not be set forth in any vernacular language, in which there are many vulgar expressions resting on erroneous opinions, drawn for the most part from prejudices of the senses; or, if it is set forth in a vernacular language, whether at least all such expressions ought to be avoided, or rather, where occasion arises, the discourse ought to be turned the other way, and the popular error noted and refuted? We say that in this way nothing whatever detracts from the purity of Scripture. For this single opinion must be explained by these and similar statements, and those things which, when separated from them, seem to sound somewhat harsh must be referred to these. Nevertheless, since some who judged the first book from its title alone were offended by the Copernican phrase, for their sake I shall abstain from it here, and therefore I have set forth the state of the controversy in article 451 in other words.

units.la: CCCCLVIII. Sed ut adhuc manifestius evadat, me per phrasin Copernicanam nihil aliud, quam quod art. 451 dixi, voluisse expressum, occasione examinis objectionum seqq. nostram illam phrasin ulterius declarabimus. Objicit B. p. 25. Multa dici secundum apparentiam non consideratâ opinione vulgi, atque hoc esse πεδον meum pseudos, quod secundum apparentiam & secundum opinionem erroneam mihi aequivaleat.
units.tr: CCCCLVIII. But so that it may become even clearer that by the Copernican phrase I meant nothing other than what I said in article 451, we shall explain that phrase further on the occasion of examining the following objections. B., p. 25, objects: Many things are said according to appearance without regard to the opinion of the common people, and this is my πεδον [ground], my pseudos [falsehood], which to me amounts to the same as according to appearance and according to an erroneous opinion.

units.la: Resp. Phrasin hanc secundum apparentiam loqui in sua latitudine consideratam mihi eandem esse cum eâ, loqui secundum opinionem erroneam nego, sed tunc demum mihi aequivalent, quando prior vel aperte vel implicitè opponitur τῷ loqui secundum rei veritatem accuratam.
units.tr: Reply: I hold that this phrase to speak according to appearance, considered in its full range, is the same as to speak according to an erroneous opinion; I deny it. It amounts to the same only when the former is opposed, either openly or by implication, to speaking according to the accurate truth of the thing [τῷ].

units.la: CCCCLIX. Pergit B. p. 26. Unde etiam liquet alter Wittichii error, quod hanc phrasin, secundum apparentiam, ponat ut unisonam illi, non secundum rei veritatem: nam non omnis qui secundum apparentiam loquitur, negat rei veritatem: sed saepe tantum determinat rei veritatem prout sese nobis exhibet.
units.tr: CCCCLIX. B. goes on, p. 26. From this there also appears another error of Wittich, that he puts this phrase, according to appearance, as if it were equivalent to not according to the truth of the thing: for not everyone who speaks according to appearance denies the truth of the thing, but often only determines the truth of the thing as it presents itself to us.

units.la: Resp. Non oppono istam phrasin secundum apparentiam veritati simpliciter, ac si sub illa apparentia non aliqua lateat veritas sed veritati accuratae, exactae, nudae. Secundum apparentiam ergo loqui oppositè ad veritatem accuratam nihil aliud est, quam uti sermone, non veritatem nudam, sed praejudiciis visus involutam exprimente, secundum ea quae superius fuerunt dicta.
units.tr: Reply: I do not set this phrase according to appearance simply against truth, as if under that appearance there were no truth hidden, but against accurate, exact, bare truth. To speak according to appearance, therefore, as opposed to accurate truth, is nothing other than to use a form of speech which expresses not bare truth but truth wrapped up in the prejudices of sight, according to what was said above.

units.la: CCCCLX. Tuitus praeterea fueram in priore editione hanc meam sententiam exemplo Astronomorum, quod etiam hic facio cap. 1. art. 2 dicendo, quod Astronomi etiam post detectos errores phrases consuetas utuntur &c. contra quod B. p. 36. sic excipit: Sic cum Astronomus assignat locum apparentem Planetae, non negat, eum esse verum ejus locum, sed docet in quo loco sit resp nostri & à nobis videatur, unde & illum verum locum secundum Astronomorum stylum vocabit: sic cum Lunam dicimus plenam vel dimidiam, ita loquimur, quia talis nobis apparet, ergo secundum apparentiam, & tamen etiam secundum rei veritatem, vid. respectu nostri, quia Luna, revera nobis est plena, vel dimidia, id est, ab illo latere, quo nobis videtur vel plenaria vel dimidia parte illuminata. Et p. 31. inquit, non esse quod Astronomorum exemplo me tueat, se enim negare eos uti phrasibus ab erronea vulgi opinione desumptis, vel nominare apparentias quae rei veritati repugnent. Locum apparentem Planeta etiam vocare locum verum, tempus apparens, tempus verum.
units.tr: CCCCLX. Moreover, in the earlier edition I defended this view of mine by the example of the astronomers, which I also do here in chapter 1, article 2, saying that the astronomers, even after errors have been detected, still use the customary phrases, etc. Against this, B., p. 36, objects as follows: Thus when an astronomer assigns the apparent place of a planet, he does not deny that this is its true place, but shows in what place it is with respect to us and as seen by us; whence he will also call that the true place according to the style of the astronomers. So when we say that the moon is full or half, we speak so because it appears so to us, therefore according to appearance, and yet also according to the truth of the thing, namely with respect to us, because the moon really is full or half to us, that is, from that side from which it is seen by us as fully or half illuminated. And on p. 31 he says: There is no reason for him to defend himself by the example of the astronomers, for he, indeed, denies that they use phrases taken from the erroneous opinion of the common people, or name appearances which contradict the truth of the thing. The apparent place of a planet they also call the true place, the apparent time the true time.

units.la: Resp.- Non est utique veritas illa nuda, quando locus Planetae verus dicitur is, qui est tantum apparens, sed relata ad sensus nostros & fallacia visus obvoluta. Secundum enim nudam & accuratam rei veritatem, cum planetae in suis circulis singulis diebus aequalia spatia permeent, non possunt ea spatia mensurari singulis diebus per lineas motus apparentis, sed per lineas motus medii. Lineae ergo motus apparentis, designantes locum planetae apparentem, non designant locum ejus exacte & accurate verum, hoc enim si fieret, dicendum, planetas singulis diebus inaequalia spatia, modo majora, modo minora percurrere, sed verum dicitur ille locus apparens, quod respectu nostri oculi revera talem planeta habeat situm. Nos autem non negamus, quin tales locutiones veritatem aliquam exprimant, sed dicimus, eam non esse nudam & accuratam, verum fallacia visus involutam. Sic Luna dimidia dicitur apparenter, opposite ad accuratam rei veritatem, quia secundum accuratam rei veritatem semper hemisphaerii ejus pars illuminatur, ut semper sit plena, nunquam dimidia vel corniculata. At quin sub illo involucro lateat quaedam generalis veritas quam solam Astronomi, hac locutione utentes, significant, non negamus. Quid vero dicet adversarius de Eclipsi Solis, quae non ei, sed oculo nostro competit, de ingressu stellarum fixarum in Solis radios atque ex iis emersione & similibus, per quas locutiones sane nullus motus realis stellis fixis tribuitur. Nullius fere ponderis sunt quae M. p. 197, 198. contra hoc Astronomorum exemplum excipit, sed facile ex dictis refutabuntur, si lectori placeat conferre. Quicquid tamen sit de vero & commodo sensu istius phraseos, Scripturam loqui secundum erronea vulgi praejudicia; vel, secundum vulgi erroneam opinionem, cum ea nunc passim ab adversariis hoc sensu accipiatur, ac si significaret, Spiritum Sanctum in Scripturis & errare cum vulgo, & errorem docere (quamvis nemo antiquorum & recentio-rum Theologorum, cum quibus in Dissertationibus Anno 53 editis fueram locutus, hoc sensu ea phrasi fuerit usus; nec ego unquam eam, ne per somnium quidem, hoc sensu acceperim) constanter ab ea ab Anno §9 abstinui, firmiterque constitui eā imposterum non amplius uti. Nunquam enim censui de verbis litigandum, ubicunque de re ipsa est consensus; adeoque refugiam illam, non quia, quod dicitur, non bene dicitur, sed quia quod bene dicitur, non bene intelligitur. Non est ergo quaestio: An Spiritus Sanctus in Scripturis erret cum vulgo & errorem doceat, adeoque si quis per hanc phrasin, Scripturam loqui secundum vulgi erroneam opinionem, intelligat, Spiritum Sanctum in Scripturis loquentem & errare cum vulgo & errorem docere, idque affirmet, ei tanquam blasphemo anathema dico, atque hanc sententiam toto corde abominor.
units.tr: Reply: That is not the bare truth at all when the planet's place is called true although it is only apparent. Rather, that place is referred to our senses and wrapped in the deceptions of sight. For according to the bare and exact truth of the matter, since the planets traverse equal spaces in their circles each day, those spaces cannot be measured day by day by the lines of apparent motion, but only by the lines of mean motion. The lines of apparent motion, then, which mark the apparent place of the planet, do not mark its place exactly and accurately true. For if they did, we would have to say that the planets cover unequal spaces each day, now larger, now smaller. Rather, that apparent place is called true because, with respect to our eye, the planet really has that position. We do not deny that such expressions convey some truth, but we say that it is not bare and exact; it is wrapped in the deception of sight. So the Moon is said to be half in appearance, in contrast to the exact truth of the matter, since according to the exact truth a part of its hemisphere is always illuminated, so that it is always full and never half or crescent. But that some general truth lies hidden under this covering, which alone the Astronomers signify when they use this expression, we do not deny. What the adversary will say about the Eclipse of the Sun, which belongs not to him but to our eye, about the entry of the fixed stars into the rays of the Sun and their emergence from them, and similar things, by which expressions no real motion is certainly ascribed to the fixed stars? The objections which M. raises against this example of the Astronomers, pp. 197, 198, are of almost no weight, and they will easily be refuted from what has been said, if the reader cares to compare them. Whatever the true and proper sense of this phrase, Scripture speaks according to the erroneous prejudices of the common people, or according to the erroneous opinion of the common people, since our opponents now everywhere take it in such a sense as if it meant that the Holy Spirit in the Scriptures both errs along with the common people and teaches error (although none of the ancient or recent Theologians, with whom I spoke in the Dissertations published in the year 1653, used that phrase in this sense, and I myself never understood it in this sense, not even in a dream), I have constantly abstained from it since the year 1659, and I have firmly resolved not to use it any more in future. For I have never thought that words should be disputed over where there is agreement about the thing itself. Hence I take refuge in that expression, not because what is said is not well said, but because what is well said is not well understood. So the question is not: Whether the Holy Spirit in the Scriptures errs along with the common people and teaches error. Accordingly, if anyone understands by this phrase, Scripture speaks according to the erroneous opinion of the common people, that the Holy Spirit speaks in the Scriptures, errs along with the common people and teaches error, and affirms this, I pronounce him accursed as a blasphemer, and I utterly abominate this opinion.

units.la: CAPUT XXI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXI.

units.la: Scripturam uti debere formulis usu tritis, etsi praejudiciis ex innitantur atque veritatem iis involutam referant, probatur Argumento ex Esai. VIII. 1. desumto.
units.tr: That Scripture ought to use commonly worn phrases, even though they rest on prejudices and carry truth wrapped up in them, is proved by an argument drawn from Isaiah 8:1.

units.la: CCCCLXI. Probemus tamen argumentis hanc sententiam, quod Scriptura ut utatur formulis usu tritis, etsi praejudiciis innitantur, atque veritatem iis involutam referant. Primum ad obtinendum nostrum institutum argumentum desumimus ex Esaiae 8. cap. v. 1. ubi mandatur Esaiae, ut scriberet stylo humano, hoc est, tali Scriptura, quam quilibet posset legere, vel secundum modum qui erat in usu, vel juxta stylum communem & consuetudinem, interpretibus Belgis. Ergo non debebat aliter loqui, quam verbis, quae a quovis intelligi possent. Ergo porro dum incideret in mentionem rerum naturalium, debuit adhibere formulas communi usu tritas, non accuratas: Atqui tales formulae usu tritae saepe innituntur praejudiciis, & veritatem non nudam, sed relatam ad homines & praejudicis involutam referunt. Ergo etiam talibus debuit Propheta uti. Similis ratio est aliorum Scriptorum ἡ οπνδ;ων; ubi enim communis est causa; id quod dictum est uni, omnibus dici intelligendum est. Haec sententia est Calvini, qui in commentario in Genesews cap. I. 16, ita notat: Quia Moses non minus indoctis & rudibus, quam doctis ordinatus erat magister, non aliter potuit partes suas implere, quam si se demitteret ad crassam istam rationem. Si de rebus vulgo ignotis loquutus fuerat, causari poterant idiota altiora haec esse captu suo. Denique cum Sp. S. hic promiscuam omnibus scholam aperiat, non mirum est, si ea maxime deligat, quae possunt ab omnibus intelligi. Haec autem dicit, quando declarat, quomodo Moses Lunam referat inter ter Luminaria magna, quæ secundùm Astronomos à stellis fixis magnitudine longè superatur, ostenditque respectum habeti ad apparentiam sensuum nostrorum. Atque, ut istud argumentum nostrum rectius intelligatur, cogitandum est nobis, linguam & stylum humanum proculdubio esse cum, qui exprimit conceptus & ideas humanas de rebus quibuscunque obviis, prout ab hominibus illæ formari solent. Inter illas ideas, sive conceptus sunt variæ de rebus sensibilibus, de Sole, Lunâ, stellis, terrâ, mari, plantis, arboribus &c. de lumine, de colore, de calore, de frigore &c. de magnitudine, figura, quiete, motu &c: Has ideas formamus ab ineunte ætate per sensus, illæque ad Notitiam Communem pertinent, quâ de re CAP. I. prolixius fuit actum. Hæ ideæ intervenientibus sensuum organis in mente nostrâ formatæ merâ apparentiâ nituntur, atque tales sunt, ut rem exprimant, non, prout in se est, &, prout à nudo intellectu sive purâ mente potest cognosci, sed, prout sensus nostri ab illis rebus assiciuntur. Ita de Solis magnitudine omnes habemus ideam bipedalem: tales sunt ideæ de comâ & caudâ cometarum, de remo fracto in aquâ, de nummo ad superficiem aquæ conspecto, & quæ sunt similes aliæ. Quæ omnes ideæ ejusmodi impressionem per sensus fecerunt in mente, ut, quamvis ex certis ratiociniis simus persuasi, Solem ipsam Terram multis vicibus excedere, remum integrum esse, nullâ fractura corruptum, & sic de reliquis, nihilominus dum Solem adspicimus & remum &c. non possumus non eandem ideam sensualem repetere. Quando igitur de rebus istiusmodi incidit sermo, non potest ille aliter formari, quàm ut cum istiusmodi ideis plané conveniat, adeoque non potest is esse nisi vulgaris, non accuratam nudam & Philosophicam veritatem exprimens, sed eam, quæ apparentiis & præjudiciis sensuum sit involuta. Scriptura igitur eo ipso, quo voluit stylo humano uti, Spiritus Sanctus quia novâ linguâ noluit scribere, sed receptâ aliquâ & notâ inter homines voluit uti, eodem sermone de rebus quibuscunque obviis, quæ sub sensus nostros cadunt, debuit loqui, quo homines uti consueverunt; idque tanto magis, quia etiam hic sermo veritatem aliquam exprimit, quæ Notitia Communi ab omnibus hominibus cognoscitur, quem Sp. S. istis in locis voluit designare.
units.tr: CCCCLXI. Let us nonetheless prove this opinion by arguments: that Scripture uses commonly worn phrases, even though they rest on prejudices and convey truth wrapped up in them. First, to establish our purpose, we take an argument from Isaiah 8:1, where Isaiah is commanded to write in human style, that is, in such Scripture as anyone could read, either according to the manner that was in use or in the common and customary style, as the Dutch translators render it. Therefore he ought not to speak otherwise than in words that anyone could understand. Further, therefore, when he came to mention natural things, he ought to employ phrases worn by common use, not exact ones. But such commonly worn phrases often rest on prejudices, and they convey truth not bare, but related to men and wrapped up in prejudice. Therefore the Prophet ought to have used such phrases too. The reasoning is similar for the other writers; for where the cause is common, what is said to one must be understood as said to all. This is the view of Calvin, who in his commentary on Genesis 1:16 remarks as follows: Since Moses was appointed teacher no less for the unlearned and rude than for the learned, he could not fulfil his task except by lowering himself to that crude manner of reckoning. Had he spoken of things unknown to the common people, the uneducated could have objected that these things were beyond their grasp. Finally, since the Holy Spirit here opens a school common to all, it is no wonder if he chose above all those things which can be understood by all. He says this when he explains how Moses reckons the Moon among the two great lights, although according to the astronomers it is far surpassed in magnitude by the fixed stars, and he shows that regard is had to the appearance presented to our senses. And so that this argument of ours may be understood more correctly, we must consider that human language and style is without doubt that which expresses human concepts and ideas about any common things whatever, as men are accustomed to form them. Among those ideas or concepts there are various ones about sensible things: about the Sun, the Moon, the stars, earth, sea, plants, trees, and so on; about light, colour, heat, cold, and so on; about size, shape, rest, motion, and so on. We form these ideas from early childhood through the senses, and they belong to the common notion, a matter treated at more length in Chapter I. These ideas, formed in our mind through the organs of sense, rest on mere appearance, and they are such that they express the thing not as it is in itself, nor as it can be known by bare intellect or pure mind, but as our senses are affected by those things. Thus we all have the idea that the Sun is two feet across; such are the ideas of the tail and hair of comets, of an oar broken in water, of a coin seen at the surface of water, and other similar ones. All these ideas have made such an impression on the mind through the senses that, although by sure reasoning we are persuaded that the Sun is many times larger than the Earth, and that the oar is whole and undamaged, and so on for the rest, nevertheless whenever we look at the Sun, or at the oar, and so on, we cannot help repeating the same sensory idea. When talk therefore turns to things of this kind, it cannot be formed otherwise than in full agreement with such ideas, and so it cannot be anything but common, not expressing exact, bare and philosophical truth, but truth that is wrapped up in the appearances and prejudices of the senses. Scripture therefore, by the very fact that it chose to use human style, since the Holy Spirit did not wish to write in some new language but wished to use an established one known among men, was bound to speak about any common things whatever that fall under our senses in the same way men are accustomed to speak; and all the more so because this speech too expresses some truth which is known to all men by the common notion, which the Holy Spirit wished to designate in those passages.

units.la: CCCCLXII. Exc. I. (B. p. 42.) Scribere potest Auctor aliquis, Scriptura legibili secundùm modum, qui est in usu, juxta stylum communem & consuetudinem, verbis quæ à quovis intelligi possunt, & simul exactam rei veritatem docere, & male præsupponitur, hanc talibus modu loquendi non posse tradi, cum non melius quam tali stylo doceatur.
units.tr: CCCCLXII. Objection I (B. p. 42.) An author can write Scripture in a legible manner according to the mode in use, in the common and customary style, in words which anyone can understand, and at the same time teach the exact truth of the matter; and it is wrongly presupposed that this cannot be conveyed by such a mode of speaking, since it is taught no less well than by such a style.

units.la: Resp. Concedimus, quod si aliquando formula vulgaris de rebus naturalibus exprimat veritatem accuratam, (quod fieri praecedenti cap. diximus in iis, in quibus Notitia Communis accuratam rei veritatem est assecuta) etiam Sp. S. eâ utatur, sed non potest auctor aliquis scribere juxta communem stylum & consuetudinem, quin utatur phrasibus, quae cum ideis sensuum conveniunt, & hic quaeritur: an si formula vulgaris proserat veritatem ad sensus hominum relatam & praejudiciis involutam, adeoque, si ista formula praejudicio sit involuta, an non Sp. S. eandem debuerit retinere, si verbis, quae à quovis intelligi possint, debuerit uti? quod ego affirmo, tanquam ad perspicuitatem Scripturae imprimis necessarium, illudque art. praeced. probavi.
units.tr: Reply. We concede that if at some time a common formula expresses exact truth about natural things (which we said in the preceding chapter happens in those matters in which the common notion has attained the exact truth of the thing), the Holy Spirit also uses it. But no author can write in the common style and custom without using phrases that agree with the ideas of the senses. And the question here is this: if a common formula conveys truth that is related to the senses of men and wrapped up in prejudice, and so if that formula is wrapped up in prejudice, ought not the Holy Spirit to have kept that same formula, if he ought to use words that anyone could understand? This I affirm, as something especially necessary for the perspicuity of Scripture, and I proved it in the preceding article.

units.la: CCCCLXIII. Exc. 2. B. p. 42. Futile nimium esse quod addam,
units.tr: CCCCLXIII. Exc. 2. B. p. 42. It would be far too trivial to add what follows,

units.la: Prophetas non potuisse intelligi si de rerum natura semper, uti est, subtiliter & accurate fuissent locuti. Quasi vero si Spiritus Sanctus dixisset, Terram moveri & Solem quiescere, id a vulgo non potuisset intelligi.
units.tr: The prophets could not have been understood if they had always spoken subtly and accurately about the nature of things, as it is. As if, indeed, had the Holy Spirit said that the earth moves and the sun stands still, this could not have been understood by the common people.

units.la: Resp. Solidissimum est quod dixi. Quis enim non videt, quod si Prophetae formulis à communi usu remotis fuissent usi, intelligi non potuerint nisi ab iis, à quibus formulae istae usurpatae? Quis dicet formulas abstrusas & ab usu remotas posse à quovis intelligi? Quòd si vero Sp. Sanctus ad significandam prolongationem diei tempore Josuae factam dixisset: Terram à suâ gyratione cessasse, nonne eo ipso res per se clara, phrasi istâ abstrusâ & ab usu remotâ multum fuisset involuta?
units.tr: Reply: What I said is entirely sound. For who does not see that if the prophets had used expressions remote from common usage, they could have been understood only by those who used those expressions? Who would say that abstruse expressions remote from usage can be understood by anyone? But if the Holy Spirit, to signify that the day was lengthened in the time of Joshua, had said the earth ceased from its rotation, would not the thing itself, clear in its own right, have been greatly obscured by this abstruse and unusual phrase?

units.la: CCCCLXIV. Exc. 3. B. p. 43. Stylo humano scribere est literis distinctis, claru & magnis scribere, quae ab omnibus praetereuntibus legi possint, ita ut respiciatur non sensus perspicuitas, sed literarum claritas & legibilitas. Sic Junius, Calvinus, Genevenses.
units.tr: CCCCLXIV. Exc. 3. B. p. 43. To write in human style is to write in distinct letters, clearly and in large characters, which can be read by all passers-by, so that what is regarded is not the clarity of the sense but the clarity and legibility of the letters. So Junius, Calvin, and the Genevans.

units.la: Resp. Utrumque hic respicitur, imò unum ex altero sequitur. Et Calvinus utrumque conjungit, quod dissimulat adversarius. Primum, inquit Calvinus, quo melius populum expergefaciat, Deus jubet hanc prophetiam publicari ac proscribi, ut ab omnibus intelligatur. Posteà denique verba ab antagonistâ citata de claritate & magnitudine literarum subjungit. Inspiciatur ipse Calvinus. Ad quid verò claritas literarum nisi ad sensus perspicuitatem? Et quare debebat ista Scriptura ab unoquoque legi, si non potuisset intelligi? Sententia ergo Junii & Genevensium nobis non contrariatur. Videmus autem, quàm tali exceptione Reformatorum sententia de Scripturae perspicuitate contra Pontificios enervetur.
units.tr: Reply: Both are regarded here; indeed, the one follows from the other. And Calvin joins the two, which your opponent conceals. "First," says Calvin, "so that he may better awaken the people, God commands this prophecy to be published and posted up, so that it may be understood by all." Afterwards he adds the words cited by our opponent about the clarity and size of the letters. Let Calvin himself be consulted. But to what end is the clarity of the letters, if not for the clarity of the sense? And why ought this Scripture to be read by everyone, if it could not be understood? The opinion of Junius and the Genevans, therefore, does not conflict with ours. We see, moreover, how by such an objection the Reformers' view of the perspicuity of Scripture is weakened against the Papists.

units.la: CCCCLXV. Exc.4. M. p. 27. Illa verba quatuor לנחר טלל חו בו de-
units.tr: CCCCLXV. Exc. 4. M. p. 27. Those four words [לנחר טלל חו בו] de-

units.la: debebant tantum clare & distincte scribi, ut à quovis legi possent, etiam à properante in transcursu.
units.tr: ought only to be written clearly and distinctly, so that they can be read by anyone, even by a person hurrying past in passing.

units.la: Resp. Negamus versum primum tantum de illis verbis intelligendum, & contrarium patuit ex Calvino & dictis.
units.tr: Reply: We deny that the first verse is to be understood only of those words, and the contrary has been shown from Calvin and what has been said.

units.la: • CCCCLXVI. Exc. 5. M. p. 27. Stylo hominis loqui ad summum nihil aliud est, quam veritatem exprimere phrasibus vulgò tritis.
units.tr: • CCCCLXVI. Exc. 5. M. p. 27. To speak in human style is, at most, nothing other than to express the truth in commonly worn phrases.

units.la: Resp. Atqui hoc ipsum est quod volumus & urgemus. Cùm formulæ tritæ sæpè respondeant apparentiis, atque præjudiciis innitantur, si formulas tritas debuit adhibere Propheta, sæpe, non quidem falsitas debuit doceri, vel tradi, sed veritas ad homines eorumque sensus relata, & præjudiciis involuta.
units.tr: Reply: Indeed this very thing is what we maintain and press. Since worn phrases often correspond to appearances and rest upon prejudices, if the prophet ought to have used worn phrases, then often it was not falsehood that had to be taught or handed down, but truth related to men and their senses, and wrapped in prejudices.

units.la: CCCCLXVII. Exc. 6. B. p. 45. Ad sententiam Calvini pro me citatam art. 46. Agit Calvinus contra illos argutos homines, qui Mosen imperitia arguebant, quod Lunam faceret secundum luminare. Itaque dicit Calvinus, Mosen populariter scribere, quæ sine doctrina & literis omnes idiotæ communi sensu percipiunt.
units.tr: CCCCLXVII. Exc. 6. B. p. 45. Regarding the opinion of Calvin cited by me in article 46: Calvin is arguing against those clever men who accused Moses of ignorance because he called the moon the "lesser luminary." So Calvin says that Moses writes popularly, in the way that all the unlearned, without teaching or letters, perceive by common sense.

units.la: Resp. Hæc exceptio nihil quicquam nobis obest: Verba enim Calvini ad nostræ sententiæ confirmationem faciunt, præsertim si jungantur cum iis, quæ postea sequuntur: Moses duo fecit magna luminaria. Atqui Astrologi firmis rationibus probant, Saturni sidus, quod omnium minimum propter longinquitatem apparet, lunari esse majus. Et paulò post: Verum id est reconditum: oculis enim aliud apparet. NB. Item: Neque nos in cœlum evocat, sed proponit tantum quæ ante oculos patent. Itaque ad crassam rationem se demittere, nihil aliud est Calvino, quàm ad apparentiam sensuum respicere oppositè al Astronomorum rationes, qui veram Lunæ magnitudinem indagant. Dein reconditum illud circa Lunæ magnitudinem est, quòd Saturno sit minor, idque verum demonstrant Astronomi ex mente Calvini: at ei opponitur aliud, quod oculis apparet, quod proinde non est verum, sed phænomenon & sensuum præjudicium. Eadem ergo est sententia mea & Calvini, nimirum, Scripturam de rebus naturalibus loqui secundùm apparentiam, sive, uti formulis veritatem ad sensus hominum relatam & præjudiciis involutam referentibus. Et mirum, quod Adversarius clarissima verba Calvini audeat adeò detorquere.
units.tr: Reply: This objection does us no harm at all. Indeed, Calvin's words serve to confirm our view, especially if they are joined with what follows: Moses made two great lights. But the astrologers prove by firm arguments that the planet Saturn, which appears the smallest of all because of its distance, is larger than the moon. And a little later: But this is hidden: for something else appears to the eyes. NB. Likewise: Nor does he call us up into heaven, but sets before us only what lies open before our eyes. Thus, for Calvin, "to descend to a crude reckoning" means nothing other than to attend to the appearance of the senses, in contrast to the reasonings of the astronomers, who investigate the true size of the moon. Then that "hidden" matter concerning the size of the moon is that it is smaller than Saturn, and this truth the astronomers demonstrate; but opposed to it is something else, which appears to the eyes, which is therefore not true but a phenomenon and a prejudice of the senses. The opinion of Calvin and mine is therefore the same: namely, that Scripture speaks of natural things according to appearance, or, in other words, uses phrases that relate truth to the senses of men and wrap it in prejudices. It is remarkable that the adversary dares to twist Calvin's very clear words so far.

units.la: CAPUT XXII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXII.

units.la: Secundum Argumentum pro sententia dicta à modo agen- di Scripturæ Dialectico desumtum.
units.tr: The second argument for the above opinion, drawn from the dialectical manner of Scripture's speaking.

units.la: CCCCLXVIII. Secundum Argumentum. Dialectici est non recedere à communi loquendi consuetudine: in eo enim differt ab Analytico, qui naturas ipsas rerum rimatur: id egregiè explicat Neldelius, qui ex Aristotele Logicam accuratius eruit; quàm ulli Peripatetici, dum inter 55 differentias Analyticarum & Dialecticarum rationum hanc facit nonam decimam in Prato suo Logico p. 36. In Dialecticis rationibus explicandis, inquit, non recedit à communi & vulgo recepta loquendi consuetudine NB. etiamsi verba non semper ipsis rebus conveniant. Ideoque κατηγορεῖν τὰς ὀνομασίας τὰ πράγματα καθ' ἃπερ οἱ πολλοί, inquit, Philos. lib. 2. Topicorum c. 2. id est, appellare, nos oportet res nominibus, sicut Vulgus appellat, & ut vulgo dicitur, loquendum cum multis, sentiendum cum doctis & sapientibus, & inter ἁμαρτίας sive vitia Dialecticorum problematum recensetur sub finem cap. 1. ejusdem libri τὸ ἀξιοῦν τῶν ποιημάτων λέξιν, id est, si quis discedat à communi loquendi consuetudine. At Analyticus qui naturas ipsas rerum rimatur, non solet loqui cum vulgo, nisi fortasse verba rebus congruant, &c. Atque hinc Aristot. opponit inter se non tantùm Analytice & Logice, sed etiam καὶ' ἀλήθειαν & ἐξ δόξαν πραγματικῶς, quod hæc sint eadem teste Neldelio p. 318. Atqui Scriptores sacri circa res naturales debuerunt agere dialecticos, cum hæ non proprium eorum objectum spectent, atque exemplo Christi appareat, eum similitudinibus à rebus terrestribus fuisse usum, possitque id aliis modis ostendi. Non ergo debuerunt recedere à communi loquendi consuetudine: At ea inter alia in eo consistit, ut phrases phænomenis sive apparentiis convenientes adhibeantur, & susque deque habeas, sive illæ phrases præjudiciis debeant originem, sive res uti sunt accuratè, & nude exprimant.
