units.tr: CCCCLXVIII. Second argument. It is the mark of the dialectician not to depart from common ways of speaking, for in this he differs from the analyst, who searches out the very natures of things. Neldelius explains this well; he draws out the Logic of Aristotle more accurately than any other Peripatetic, when among the 55 differences between analytical and dialectical reasoning he makes this the nineteenth, in his Pratum Logicum, p. 36: In explaining dialectical arguments, he says, one does not depart from the common and popularly received manner of speaking, NB, even if the words do not always fit the things themselves. Hence the Philosopher, in the second book of the Topics, chapter 2, says that one should "name things by names as the many do" [κατηγορεῖν τὰς ὀνομασίας τὰ πράγματα καθ' ἃπερ οἱ πολλοί], that is, we must call things by names as the common people call them, and speak as the crowd does, but think as the learned and wise do. Among the faults of dialectical problems, near the end of chapter 1 of the same book, he lists "to insist on a word not in common use" [τὸ ἀξιοῦν τῶν ποιημάτων λέξιν], that is, when someone departs from the common manner of speaking. But the analyst, who searches out the natures of things, is not accustomed to speak with the crowd, unless perhaps the words agree with the things, etc. From this, too, Aristotle sets against one another not only analytical and logical but also truth [καὶ' ἀλήθειαν] and opinion [ἐξ δόξαν] in the manner of things, which, according to Neldelius, p. 318, are the same. But the sacred writers ought to speak dialectically about natural things, since these do not concern their proper object, and the example of Christ shows that he used comparisons drawn from earthly things, and this can be shown in other ways too. Therefore they ought not to depart from the common manner of speaking. Now that manner consists, among other things, in using phrases that fit appearances or phenomena, whether or not those phrases owe their origin to prejudices, and whether or not one states the things accurately and plainly as they are.

units.la: CCCCLXIX. Exc. 1, B. p. 67. Hoc argumentum desumtum est ab auctoritate humanâ.
units.tr: CCCCLXIX. Exc. 1, B. p. 67. This argument is drawn from human authority.

units.la: Resp. Neg. Est desumtum ex naturâ modi agendi Dialectici, qui à Logicâ docetur, cum enim finis Dialectici non sit scientia, nec naturas rerum explicet, ejusque rationes quibus utitur, sint communes, probabiles, non propriæ & necessariæ, cumque agat cum iis quorum intellectus Atus non est capax accuratiorum locutionum, debet omnino adhibere minus accuratas & vulgares.
units.tr: Reply: I deny it. It is drawn from the nature of the dialectical manner of proceeding, which is taught by Logic. For since the aim of dialectic is not science, and it does not explain the natures of things, and the reasons it uses are common and probable, not proper and necessary, and since it deals with those whose understanding is not capable of more exact speech, it must by all means use less exact and popular language.

units.la: CCCCLXX. Exc. 2. M. p. 69. Conceditur, licere in dialectici disquisitionibus aliquando ad veritatem exprimendam adhibere locutiones minus accuratas, minus distinctas, παχυλῶς & minus adaquatè veritatem exprimentes, quod nobis nihil quicquam adversatur.
units.tr: CCCCLXX. Exc. 2, M. p. 69. It is granted that in dialectical disquisitions it is sometimes lawful to use, in expressing the truth, expressions that are less exact, less distinct, [παχυλῶς] rough, and that express the truth less adequately; this in no way opposes us.

units.la: Resp. Sed evici, etiam dialectico licere usurpare verba, quae non semper ipsis rebus conveniant; item, loquendum cum vulgo & sentiendum cum doctis, quo nihil clarius dici potest pro usu formularum usu tritarum, veritatem non nudam, sed praejudiciis involutam &c. referentium.
units.tr: Reply: But I have shown that even the dialectician may use words that do not always agree with the things themselves; likewise, one must speak with the crowd and think with the learned. Nothing can be said more clearly in favour of the use of customary formulas, which refer to the truth not bare but wrapped in prejudices, etc.

units.la: CCCCLXXI. Exc. 3. M. p. 70. Si non sit recedendum à communi consuetudine, ergo non licet motum Terrae exprimere verbis communi & vulgo receptâ loquendi consuetudine motum Solis exprimentibus.
units.tr: CCCCLXXI. Exc. 3, M. p. 70. If one must not depart from common usage, then it is not lawful to express the motion of the Earth in words that, in common and received speech, express the motion of the Sun.

units.la: Resp. Ubinam verò hoc à nobis est dictum, per phrases Scripturae exprimi vel significari motum Terrae? nos è contrario suo loco ostendemus, locis illis, quae contra Terrae gyrationem producuntur, aliquod Phaenomenon sive apparentiam coelestem, quae hoc modo se oculis ingerit, denotari, ita ut non disquirant in modum vel in causam, cui illud phaenomenon debeat ortum.
units.tr: Reply: Where, pray, have we said that the motion of the Earth is expressed or signified by the phrases of Scripture? On the contrary, in its proper place we will show that those passages which are brought against the Earth's rotation denote a certain celestial phenomenon or appearance, which presents itself to the eyes in this way, so that they do not inquire into the mode or the cause to which that phenomenon owes its origin.

units.la: CCCCLXXII. Exc. 4. M. p. 70. Non sequitur, quod licet Philosophis in dialecticis, id licet Spiritui Sancto in Scripturâ.
units.tr: CCCCLXXII. Exc. 4, M. p. 70. It does not follow that what is permitted to philosophers in dialectic is permitted to the Holy Spirit in Scripture.

units.la: Resp. Cum Scriptores sacri dialecticos agant circa res naturales, utpote non spectantes ad suum scopum sive institutum, debuerunt modum agendi dialecticum sive topicum usurpare.
units.tr: Reply: Since the sacred writers handle natural things dialectically, as not bearing on their scope or purpose, they ought to use the dialectical or topical manner of proceeding.

units.la: CCCCLXXIII. Exc. 5. (B. p. 33.) Si totus Philosophi contextus inspiciatur, comperietur eum contra te loqui. Hoc ergo vult Philosophus, simplices rerum denominationes assumi debere secundum stylum vulgarem, at in terminis complexis non loquendum cum vulgo: videat lector, si tanti sit B. p. 33 & 34.
units.tr: CCCCLXXIII. Exc. 5, (B. p. 33.) If the whole context of the Philosopher is examined, it will be found that he speaks against you. So the Philosopher means this: simple denominations of things must be taken according to the common style, but in complex terms one must not speak with the crowd. Let the reader see whether it is worth the trouble: B. pp. 33 and 34.

units.la: Resp. Ut, quis sit sensus verborum Aristotelis, appareat, plenius verba cap. 1 & 2. lib. 2. Top. Arist. ad quae in hoc argumento respexi citabimus. Cap. 1. inquit, Διορίσασθαι ἢ δεῖ καὶ τὰς ἁμαρτίας τὰς ἐν τοῖς ἀγελλήμασιν, ὅτι εἰσὶ διτλαί ἢ τῷ ψευδέσθαι, ἢ τῷ φαίνεσθαι τὸν κεκμηλῶν λέξιν, οἱ πὸ ψευδόμενοι, καὶ τὸ μὴ ὑπάρχον ὑπάρχειν πνὶ λέγοντες, ἁμαρτάνουσι. καὶ οἱ τῆς ἀλοτοίοις ὀνόμασιν, τὰ πεπραγμένα ἀγοσαγαγόντες, οἷον τὸν θνατάνον, ἄνθρωπον, φαίνεσθαι τὸν κεκμηλῶν ὀνομασίαν. In quaestiones autem duo peccata incidunt, quae exponenda sunt: peccatum autem aut mentiendo, aut discedendo à verbis, quæ imposita sunt rebus. Nam & ab iis peccatur, qui quod non cadit in aliquem, cadere confirmant: & ab iis qui res minus usitatis & tritis nominibus appellant, ut qui hominem platanum appellant, nominum impositorum fines transeunt. Et cap. 2. Ἐπὶ διορίζεσθαι, ποῖα δεῖ καλεῖν ὡς οἱ πολλοὶ, καὶ ποῖα ἀ χρήσιμον ἦ καὶ πρὸς τὸ κατασκευάζειν καὶ πρὸς τὸ ἀνασκευάζειν. οἷον ὅτι, ταῖς μὲν ὀνομασίαις τὰ πράγματα προσαγορεύοντος, καθάπερ οἱ πολλοὶ. ποῖα ἢ τῶν πραγμάτων ἐστι ποιῶτα, ἢ ὑ ποιῶντα, ἐκεῖ προσεκτέον τοῖς πολλοῖς. οἷον ὑγιεινὸν μὲν ῥῆτέον, τὸ ποιητικὸν ὑγιείας, ἢ ὑ, ἐκεῖ ὡς οἱ πολλοὶ λεκτέον, ἀλλ' ὡς ὁ ἰατρός. Jam vero exponendum est, quæ appellanda sunt, ut plerique solent, quæque non sint appellanda: qui locus & ad confirmandum & ad refutandum valet: ut res nominibus iis quæ trita sunt vulgo & usitata appellandas esse: at vero in constituendo quæ res tales, vel non tales sint, non audiendam esse multitudinem: veluti salubria ea quæ valetudinis efficientia sint, vocanda sunt illa quidem vulgi opinione: sed utrum id de quo id agit, efficiens sit nec ne valetudinis, de eo non jam vulgi, sed medicorum judicium exspectare debemus. Ex illis enim manifestum fit 1. quod non tantum loquatur de simplicibus rerum denominationibus, sed etiam de terminis complexis: si enim salubria vocanda sunt ea, quæ ex opinione vulgi efficiunt valetudinem, ergò de hâc vel illâ herba, quam vulgus opinatur causam efficientem valetudinis dicendum, esse salubrem, quia vulgus ita loquitur. 2. Eo ipso quod in simplicibus hoc licitum, etiam in complexis licere æstimandum, sive enim attributum adscribatur rei citra propositionem & interventum copulæ Est, sive per talem interventum, res eodem plane redit. Sed de eo uberius suo loco. CCCCLXXIV. Exc. 6. (B. p. 35.) Aristoteles quidem dicit vocem salubris usurpandam esse vulgari significatione, sed cum de re aliquâ quaeritur, non amplius loquendum ut vulgus, sed ut medicus. Jam quæro cum quonam loquendum in quæstione de Motu Terræ aut Solis, an cum Deo, an vero cum Cartesio, &c. Resp. Id maximè promefacit, inde enim sequitur, Scripturam tamdiu, quàm quæstio non fuit in populo Dei de motu Solis vel Terræ, debuisse loqui cum vulgo: At in locis pro Solis motu allatis non agebatur de determinatione istius quæstionis, sed de alia re, quam etiam vulgari formula Spiritus Sanctus voluit significare, ut patebit in examine locorum controversorum. 2. Sic etiam nobis, ubi decisio istius controversiæ ad rem præsentem non facit, loquendum cum vulgo & Scriptura, sed ubi de illa re quæritur, non amplius loquendum ut vulgus, sed ut Philosophus loquitur.
units.tr: Reply: So that the sense of Aristotle's words may appear, let the words of chapters 1 and 2 of the second book of Aristotle's Topics, to which I have referred in this argument, be cited more fully. In chapter 1 he says: one must also define the faults that occur in the replies, which are twofold, either by lying or by appearing to use a word in a sense other than that in which it is imposed; for those who lie, and those who say that what does not belong to something belongs to it, err; and those who call things by words not in use, as when they call a plane tree a man, pass beyond the limits of the imposed names [ὀνομασίαι]. In questions, moreover, two faults occur, which must be explained: the fault either by lying, or by departing from the words that have been imposed on things. For men err both when they assert that something which does not fall under a thing falls under it, and when they call things by names not usual and common. And in chapter 2: It remains to determine which things ought to be called as the many call them, and which things are useful both for establishing and for refuting. For example, things should be named by the names used in common, as the many do. But as to whether a thing is a quality or a cause of qualities, here we must attend to the many no longer. For example, one should say that a thing is healthful, if it produces health, as the many do; but whether it is a cause of health, here we must speak not as the many do but as the physician does. Now from these passages it is clear, first, that he speaks not only of simple denominations of things but also of complex terms. For if those things are to be called healthful which, by the opinion of the crowd, produce health, then one must say of this or that herb, which the crowd supposes to be an efficient cause of health, that it is healthful, because the crowd speaks so. Second, since this is allowed in simple terms, it must be judged to be allowed in complex ones as well; for whether an attribute is ascribed to a thing without a proposition and without the intervention of the copula is, or through such an intervention, the matter comes to exactly the same thing. But of this more fully in its place. CCCCLXXIV. Exc. 6, (B. p. 35.) Aristotle indeed says that the word healthful is to be used in its common meaning, but when a thing is inquired into, one must no longer speak as the crowd does but as the physician does. Now I ask: with whom must one speak in the question about the motion of the Earth or the Sun? With God, or with Descartes, etc.? Reply: This is most of all to our purpose. For it follows that Scripture, as long as the question about the motion of the Sun or Earth was not among the people of God, ought to have spoken with the crowd. But in the passages cited for the motion of the Sun, there was no question of settling that controversy, but of another matter, which the Holy Spirit also wished to signify in the common formula, as will be clear in the examination of the disputed passages. Second, in the same way, for us too, where the decision of that controversy does not bear on the present matter, we must speak with the crowd and with Scripture; but where that very matter is inquired into, we must no longer speak as the crowd does, but as the philosopher speaks.

units.la: CAPUT XXIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIII.

units.la: Argumentum tertium ab Inductione eorum Scripturæ lo- corum, quæ continent formulas vulgares referentes phænomena atque veritatem ad sensus relatam & præjudiciis involutam.
units.tr: The third argument, from the induction of those passages of Scripture which contain common expressions that refer phenomena and truth to the senses and are wrapped in prejudices.

units.la: CCCCLXXV. Sequitur Inductio quorundam locorum è multis, in quibus sunt locutiones vulgares sensuum præjudiciis innitentes, quæ veritatem ad hominum sensus relatam & præjudiciis involutam referunt, qualia sunt primò, ea quæ de extremitate cœlorum loquuntur, ex. gr. Deut.xxx.4. Etiamsi quis ex tuis depulsus esset ad extremitatem coeli, inde colligam te: cui similis est locus Esa.xiii.5. Veniunt è terra longinqua ab extremitate coelorum, Jer. xlix. 36. Adducam enim contra Elamitas quatuor ventos à quatuor extremitatibus coelorum, & multi alii, in quibus extremitates cœlo attribuuntur, per locutionem manifeste desumptam à præjudiciis sensuum. Ita enim videtur ei, qui solis sensibus innititur, ac si Cœlum esset Hemisphærium, quod in extremis Terræ finibus deficiat, ita ut Terræ innitatur, & progredientibus eò usque videatur occursurum, impediens progressum ulteriorem. Hoc præjudicio sensuum occupatus Homerus Æthyopas collocat ad extremitates Ortûs & Occasûs, existimans Solem ob hanc Cœli & Terræ contiguitatem, adeò propinquum eis fieri, ut eorum cutem adurat. Ita enim Odyss. A. Αἰθίοπας τοι διχθα δεδαίαται ἐσχατοι ἀνδρῶν, οἱ μὲν δυσομένης ὑπερίονος, οἱ δ᾽ ἀνίστοντος, id est, Æthiopas, qui bifariam divisi sunt, ultimi hominum. Alii quidem Occidentalis Solis, alii vero Orientalis. Huic sententiæ quoad locum Deut. xxx. adstipulatur Junius, in ejus analytica explicatione: id est, in ultimis terris, qui cœlo ad aspectum nostrum videntur terminari (sic enim Hebrei LOQVVNTVR POPVLARITER.) Certum enim est, Cœlo rotundo nullam competere extremitatem proprie loquendo. Sed quoniam loca longinqua & remota solent per extremitates Cœli vulgo designari, Spiritus Sanctus eâdem formulâ voluit uti, quamvis veritas designata, nempe loca remota, sit præjudicio sensuum antea dicto involuta.
units.tr: CCCCLXXV. There follows an induction from some of the many passages in which there are common expressions resting on prejudices of the senses, which refer truth to human senses and wrap it in prejudices. Such are, first, those which speak of the extremities of the heavens, for example Deut. 30.4: If anyone of yours were driven out to the extremity of heaven, from there I will gather you. Similar is Isa. 13.5, They come from a distant land, from the extremity of the heavens, and Jer. 49.36, For I will bring against the Elamites the four winds from the four extremities of the heavens, and many others, in which extremities are attributed to heaven through an expression plainly taken from the prejudices of the senses. For so it seems to one who relies only on the senses, as if heaven were a hemisphere, which ends at the far limits of the earth, so that it rests upon the earth, and to those who advance as far as that it seems to meet them, blocking further progress. Occupied by this prejudice of the senses, Homer places the Ethiopians at the extremities of rising and setting, thinking that the sun, because of this contiguity of heaven and earth, becomes so near to them that it scorches their skin. For so in the Odyssey, book 1: Αἰθίοπας τοι διχθα δεδαίαται ἐσχατοι ἀνδρῶν, οἱ μὲν δυσομένης ὑπερίονος, οἱ δ᾽ ἀνίστοντος [Ethiopians, who are divided in two, the last of men: some where the sun sets, others where it rises], that is, The Ethiopians, who are divided in two, the last of men. Some toward the setting sun, others toward the rising sun. Junius agrees with this view as regards Deut. 30, in his analytical explanation: that is, in the furthest lands, which seem to be bounded by heaven to our sight (for so the Hebrews SPEAK POPULARLY). For it is certain that a round heaven properly speaking has no extremity. But since distant and remote places are commonly designated by the extremities of heaven, the Holy Spirit wished to use the same expression, although the truth signified, namely remote places, is wrapped in the prejudice of the senses mentioned above.

units.la: CCCCLXXVI. Exc. 1. (B. p. 84.) Junium mihi contrariari, qui per cælum intelligat orbem terrarum, qui circumclusus est cælo μετωνυμικῶς, ut videre sit in notis ad Deut. IV. 32.
units.tr: CCCCLXXVI. Objection 1 (B, p. 84): Junius contradicts me, since he understands by heaven the orb of the earth, which is surrounded by heaven metonymically, as can be seen in the notes on Deut. 4.32.

units.la: Resp. Hæc non contrariantur. Nam ad extremitates has formandas debuerunt concurrere & cœlum & terra, non realiter, sed apparenter, ubi videntur se invicem contingere. Sufficit ergo, si hinc colligam, esse formulam loquendi apparentiis convenientem & præjudicio innitentem.
units.tr: Answer: These do not contradict one another. For heaven and earth had to meet to form these extremities, not really but apparently, where they seem to touch each other. It is enough, therefore, that I conclude from this that it is a form of speech conforming to appearances and resting on prejudice.

units.la: CCCCLXXVII. Exc. 2. M. p. 93.
units.tr: CCCCLXXVII. Objection 2 (M, p. 93).

units.la: Est in illis locis manifesta hyperbole, qualis etiam Psalm. cxxx. x. si scanderem cœlos. Significatur igitur per extremitates cœli spatium longissime distitum locutione synecdochica, ubi res in specie magna ponitur pro magna in genere.
units.tr: In those places there is a plain hyperbole, such as also in Psalm 139.8 (130.10 in some editions): if I climbed up to the heavens. The extremities of heaven therefore signify, by synecdoche, a space at the greatest distance, where a thing great in its kind is put for what is great in general.

units.la: Resp. Non designantur extremitates cœli sursum versus, sed extremitates, quas videtur ejus contiguitas cum Terra efficere, quia, ut antea vidimus, sunt eadem cum extremitatibus Terræ. Hæ extremitates quia videntur longè dissitæ à nobis, in meditullio Horizontis constitutis, sumuntur pro quâvis distantiâ longè remotâ.
units.tr: Answer: The extremities of heaven are not designated as those toward the heights, but the extremities which its contact with the earth seems to form, because, as we saw before, they are the same as the extremities of the earth. Since these extremities seem to be far distant from us, placed in the middle of the horizon, they are taken for any distance far removed.

units.la: CCCCLXXVIII. Exc. 3. M. p. 94.
units.tr: CCCCLXXVIII. Objection 3 (M, p. 94).

units.la: Per Synecdochen partis per cœlum potest intelligi pars cœli, quousque scilicet illud hujus aut illius visui est expositum, ita ut extremitates suas cœlum sic sumtum revera habeat à visu humano.
units.tr: By synecdoche of a part, heaven can be understood as a part of heaven, namely as far as it lies open to the sight of this or that person, so that heaven, taken in this way, really has its extremities from human sight.

units.la: Resp. Id mihi non contrariatur, imò est ipsissima mea sententia, quam defendo, quamvis male dicatur Cœlum habere extremitates revera à visu humano, ille enim nihil cœlo confert. Cœli igitur extremitates, quas à visu accipit, non sunt tales revera, sed tantummodo apparentes, adeoque phrasis, quæ mentionem facit extremitatum cœli innititur præjudicio sensus, atque propterea veritatem refert ad hominum sensus relatam atque præjudiciis involutam.
units.tr: Answer: This does not contradict me; indeed it is my very own opinion, which I defend, although it is wrongly said that heaven really has its extremities from human sight, for sight adds nothing to heaven. The extremities of heaven which it receives from sight are therefore not such in reality, but only apparent, and so the phrase which mentions the extremities of heaven rests on a prejudice of the senses, and for that reason refers truth to human senses and wraps it in prejudices.

units.la: CCCCLXXIX. Exc. 4. H. p. 130.
units.tr: CCCCLXXIX. Objection 4 (H, p. 130).

units.la: Homerum non fuisse eo præjudicio excæcatum, neque id probari posse ex illis verbis citatis.
units.tr: That Homer was not blinded by that prejudice, nor can this be proved from the words cited.

units.la: Resp. Ea quæ de Homero dixi illustrationis gratiâ adduco. Si quis ejus auctoritatem tanti faciat, ut putet alienum esse hoc de tanto Poëta opinari, per me fruatur suo judicio, neque propterea quicquam nostræ probationi decedet. Quòd si quis verba attentius inspiciat, apparebit saltem, hic respexisse infantiæ præjudicium, ut parum referat, num & ipse illud adhuc foverit. 2. Minus alienum hoc de Homero credere, quàm de Lactantio, qui lib. 3. Instit cap. 24. Antipodas negavit, statuitque, terram deorsum infinitis extendi radicibus. Vide Parkerum de Descensu Christi, qui multos Patrum citat, quibus hæc fuerit sententia lib. 2. p. 123. & seqq. Nec ea sententia isto sæculo magis indigna Homero, quàm Theodecte, qui referente Strabone lib. xv. p. m. 695. sic canit:
units.tr: Answer: I bring forward what I said about Homer by way of illustration. If anyone holds his authority so high that he thinks it improper to hold this opinion about so great a poet, let him enjoy his own judgment; nothing will be lost to our proof on that account. But if anyone examines the words more closely, it will at least appear that he had in mind the prejudice of infancy, so it matters little whether he himself still cherished it. 2. It is less improper to believe this of Homer than of Lactantius, who in Institutes book 3, chapter 24, denied the Antipodes and held that the earth extends downward with infinite roots. See Parker, On the Descent of Christ, who cites many of the Fathers who held this opinion, book 2, p. 123 and following. Nor is that opinion more unworthy of Homer in this age than of Theodectes, who, as Strabo reports in book 15, p. 695, sings thus:

units.la: Ἡς ἀρχιπέμωι ἡλιῷ διφρηλατῶν Σκοτεινὴν ἀνθῷ ἐξίχεωσι λιγυρὸν Εἰς σῶμα. ἀὼμαὶ ἀνδρῶν καὶ συνίσρεψεν νόμας Μοέφαις ἀναγκήτηση σωμήξας πυρός. Quorum propinqua Sol adurens orbita Fuliginoso corpora colore imbuit Æstu-que tostas sicco crispavit comas. Materiemque adolescendi consumtam abstulit. Eadem mens Propertio lib. 3. eleg. 13. de Indis. Quos Aurora suis rubra colorat equis. Affinis isti opinioni & consentanea illa, quâ Solem Oceano mergi, indeque emergere perhibent, de quâ suo loco ad Psal. xix. agemus.
units.tr: Whose near orbit, where the sun drives his chariot, scorching, poured out a clear-sounding fire upon the body of the men [ἡς ἀρχιπέμωι ἡλιῷ διφρηλατῶν Σκοτεινὴν ἀνθῷ ἐξίχεωσι λιγυρὸν Εἰς σῶμα]. The flames and the glowing winds... the sun, burning with its nearby circuit, dyed their bodies with a sooty color, and, scorching their hair dry, it crisped it, and it took away the fuel of growing things, consumed. The same mind is in Propertius, book 3, elegy 13, about the Indians: Whom the rosy Dawn colours with her horses. Akin to that opinion, and consistent with it, is the view that the sun sinks into the Ocean and rises out of it again, which we will discuss in its place on Psalm 19.

units.la: CCCCLXXX. Secunda Classis est eorum locorum, quæ de fundamentis & columnis Cœlorum loquuntur: Job. xxvi. 11. Ʋsquedum Columnæ cœli concutiantur & stupescant ab increpatione ejus. Et 2 Sam xxii. 8. Et concutitur ac movetur Terra, fundamenta Cœlorum commoventur, concutiuntur autem, cum ira accenditur ei, cum quo si conferas locum parallelum (Psal. xviii. 8. Et concutitur ac movetur Terra, fundamentaque montium commoventur, concutiuntur autem cum ira accenditur ei:) apparet, quæ priori loco vocantur Fundamenta Cœlorum, posteriori vocari fundamenta montium, quibus simul ipsi montes connotantur, ut ita montes dicantur fundamenta Cœlorum. Utraque autem locutio satis est vulgaris, inmitens illi sensuum præjudicio, quod cœlum montibus incumbat, unde & Poëtæ Atlantem portare cœlum dixerunt, nominatim Homerus Odyss. A. Montes autem in priori loco dicuntur columna, quatenus attenditur ad interstitium, quod inter illos datur, fundamenta vero simpliciter, quatenus cœlum iis incumbere videtur. Cum hac nostra interpretatione consentientes producit Mercerus in Jobi locum citatum. Metaphoricè hæc dicuntur, non quod alioqui cœlum columnas habeat, quibus nitatur, sed quod in vehementiori orbis concussione videatur nobis perinde, ac si nutent ejus columnæ. Alii terram & montes & solidiores Terræ partes putant columnas Cœli dici, quod velut illi innituntur, & Terra velut orbis totius fundamentum ac firmamentum sit. Ipse autem in genere nobis assentitur, dicendo, quod sit locutio secundum id quod videtur. Eodem modo exponit hæc loca inter se collata Ravanellus, qui ad vocem Fundamentum sic annotat p. 656. Fundamentum cœlorum i. e. montes altissimi, quibus videtur cœlum quasi incumbere, & inniti, sicut Poëta de Atlante fabulati sunt 2 Sam. xxii. 8. Psal. xviii. 8. Hactenus ille. Veritas autem his locis significata est: Cœlum cum Terra & montibus per iram Dei corruere, innitens isti præjudicio, quod cœlum videatur incumbere montibus & Terræ.
units.tr: CCCCLXXX. The second class is of those passages which speak of the foundations and pillars of the heavens: Job 26.11, The pillars of heaven tremble and are astonished at his rebuke. And 2 Sam. 22.8, The earth shakes and quakes, the foundations of the heavens move and are shaken, because he is angry. If you compare with this the parallel passage (Ps. 18.8, The earth shakes and quakes, and the foundations of the mountains move and are shaken, because he is angry), it appears that what in the former place are called the foundations of the heavens are in the latter called the foundations of the mountains, by which the mountains themselves are also implied, so that mountains are called the foundations of the heavens. Both expressions are quite common, resting on that prejudice of the senses that heaven rests on the mountains, whence also the poets said that Atlas carries the heavens, namely Homer in the Odyssey, book 1. The mountains in the former place are called pillars insofar as attention is paid to the interval that lies between them, but foundations simply insofar as heaven seems to rest upon them. Mercerus, agreeing with our interpretation, adduces this on the cited passage of Job: These things are said metaphorically, not because heaven otherwise has pillars on which it rests, but because in a more violent shaking of the globe its pillars seem to us to totter in the same way. Others think that the earth and the mountains and the more solid parts of the earth are called pillars of heaven, because heaven rests upon them as it were, and the earth is, as it were, the foundation and support of the whole globe. He himself agrees with us in general, saying that it is an expression according to what appears. Ravanellus, comparing these passages, explains them in the same way, and on the word Foundation he notes thus, p. 656: The foundations of the heavens, that is, the highest mountains, on which heaven seems as it were to lean and rest, as the poets fabled of Atlas (2 Sam. 22.8; Ps. 18.8). Thus far he. The truth signified in these passages, however, is this: heaven together with the earth and the mountains falls through the wrath of God, resting on the prejudice that heaven seems to lean on the mountains and the earth.

units.la: CCCCXXXI. Ad collationem istam duorum locorum, in quâ tamen vis interpretationis meæ consistit, nihil habet B. Sed excipit p.86. Mercerum mecum non consentire, quia dicat tantum Cœlum montibus VELVT inniti, & Terram VELVT totius orbis fundamentum & firma-mentum esse.
units.tr: CCCCXXXI. I have no answer to this comparison of the two passages, on which the force of my interpretation rests. But he objects on p. 86: that Mercer does not agree with me, because he says only that the heavens rest on the mountains, as it were, and that the earth is, as it were, the foundation and firmament of the whole world.

units.la: Resp. Mercerum non quoad hunc locum mecum consentientem citavi, sed alios ab ipso sine nomine commemoratos, qui eo ipso, quo dicunt: Cœlum montibus VELUT inniti &c. mecum consentiunt; quomodo enim cœlum VELVT innititur Montibus &c. nisi exinde, quia ita appareret, quia hoc est phænomenon, nisi quia Cœlum montes & Orbem Terræ videtur contingere. Ut enim quod respectu alterius superiori in loco est constitutum, illudque inferius contingit, dicitur ei inniti, ita & hic, quia respectu Terræ & Montium Cœlum superiori est loco constitutum, idque Terram & montes videtur desuper contingere, dicitur Terræ & montibus inniti.
units.tr: Answer: I did not cite Mercer as agreeing with me on this passage, but others whom he mentions without naming them, who by the very words they use, "the heavens rest on the mountains, as it were," agree with me. For how do the heavens rest on the mountains, as it were, unless because it so appears, because this is the phenomenon, namely that the heavens seem to touch the mountains and the orb of the earth? For just as that which is placed in a higher position relative to something else, and touches what is lower, is said to rest on it, so here too, since the heavens are placed higher relative to the earth and the mountains, and seem to touch the earth and the mountains from above, they are said to rest on the earth and the mountains.

units.la: CCCCLXXXII. Exc. 2. B. p. 86. Ratio similitudinis est, ut fundamenta sese habent ratione locationis sub adificio: ita montes, imo tota terra sub coelo.
units.tr: CCCCLXXXII. Exc. 2. B. p. 86. The reason for the comparison is that foundations stand in relation to a building by their position beneath it; so the mountains, indeed the whole earth, stand beneath the heavens.

units.la: Resp. Nego hoc modo exhauriri vim similitudinis. Fundamentum enim non potest dici id, quod respectu alterius inferius est, nisi id contingat, ei conjungatur, aut saltem videatur contingere. Nec fundamentum ædificii dicetur quod respectu ejus est inferius, nisi contactus accedat eique alterum innitatur. Sic inepte dices terram fundamentum Solis & stellarum, dum in medio cœli sunt constituta, nec videntur Terram contingere.
units.tr: Answer: I deny that the force of the comparison is exhausted in this way. For a thing cannot be called a foundation merely because it is lower than another, unless it touches that other, is joined to it, or at least seems to touch it. Nor is the foundation of a building called so merely because it is lower than the building, unless contact is present and the building rests on it. Thus you would absurdly call the earth the foundation of the sun and the stars, since these are placed in the middle of the heavens and do not seem to touch the earth.

units.la: CCCCLXXXIII. Exc. 3. B. p. 86. Quidnam est quod videtur? an-ne quod coelum montibus incumbit? id non dicit Mercerus, sed quod in vehementi orbis concussione quasi NUTENT ejus columna, ita ut to videri referat ad nutare, non ad columnas.
units.tr: CCCCLXXXIII. Exc. 3. B. p. 86. What is it that seems? Is it not that the heavens rest on the mountains? Mercer does not say that, but that in a violent shaking of the world its pillars, as it were, totter, so that "to seem" refers to "totter," not to "pillars."

units.la: Resp. At quomodo possunt videri nutare Columnæ cœli? nisi vel revera montes & terra sint Columnæ cœli, quod non dicet adversarius, vel videantur tales, & sic in concussione orbis quasi nutare; itaque to videri & ad columnas & ad to nutare est referendum.
units.tr: Answer: But how can the pillars of the heavens seem to totter, unless either the mountains and the earth really are the pillars of the heavens, which my opponent will not say, or they appear to be such, and so in a shaking of the world seem, as it were, to totter? Therefore "to seem" must refer both to the pillars and to "totter."

units.la: CCCCLXXXIV. Exc, 4. p. 86: Sed dixerit Mercerus, montes videri columnas cœli, & ita vocentur propter apparentiam respectu visu, non tamen inde inferri poterit illam denominationem fieri propter errorem vulgi &c.
units.tr: CCCCLXXXIV. Exc. 4. p. 86. But Mercer may say that the mountains seem to be the pillars of the heavens, and so are called such because of their appearance to sight; yet it cannot be inferred from this that this designation arises from the error of the common people, etc.

units.la: Resp. Ex eo, quòd montes videntur columnæ cœli, infertur, hoc ipsum esse phænomenon, quod cum oriatur exinde, quod propter distantiam corpora inter montes & cœlum intercedentia non possunt animadverti, inde sequitur, in reiveritate cœlum non incumbere montibus, adeoque eoque, quando montes dicuntur fundamenta vel columnæ cœlorum, locutionem esse vulgarem apparentiæ & præjudiciis sensuum innitentem, quod est quod hic urgeo & intendo.
units.tr: Answer: From the fact that the mountains seem to be the pillars of the heavens it follows that this itself is the phenomenon. Since it arises from the fact that, because of the distance, the bodies lying between the mountains and the heavens cannot be observed, it follows that in reality the heavens do not rest on the mountains. Consequently, when the mountains are called the foundations or pillars of the heavens, the expression is a common one, resting on the appearance and on the prejudices of the senses. This is what I press and insist upon here.

units.la: CCCCLXXXV. Exc. 5. B. p. 87. Si montes vocentur columna cœli propter errorem à præjudicio sensuum, propter quam rationem aut quæ præjudicia sensuum tribuitur ipsis stupor &c? Si ergo hic mera Metaphora, dicatur & idem de montibus.
units.tr: CCCCLXXXV. Exc. 5. B. p. 87. If the mountains are called the pillars of the heavens because of an error arising from the prejudice of the senses, for what reason, or what prejudices of the senses, are attributed to them, stupor, etc.? If therefore this is a mere metaphor, the same should be said of the mountains.

units.la: Resp. Quod Metaphora locum non possit habere nisi hoc præjudicium præsupponatur, patet ex responsione ad exceptionem secundam.
units.tr: Answer: That a metaphor can have no place unless this prejudice is presupposed is clear from my reply to the second objection.

units.la: 2. Non sequitur, si in phrasi conjuncta non sit respectus ad id quod videtur, ergo nec in altera, aut quâ arte Logicâ hoc elicies? quasi vero idem modus loquendi, idem tropus in phrasibus conjunctis locum debeat habere.
units.tr: 2. It does not follow that, if there is no reference to what seems in the conjoined phrase, there is none in the other. By what logical art will you draw this conclusion? As if the same mode of speaking and the same trope must necessarily occur in conjoined phrases.

units.la: CCCCLXXXVI. Exc. 6. M. p. 95. Supponi in meo argumento, per fundamenta Cœlorum & fundamenta montium significari unam eandemque rem.
units.tr: CCCCLXXXVI. Exc. 6. M. p. 95. It is presupposed in my argument that by the foundations of the heavens and the foundations of the mountains one and the same thing is signified.

units.la: Resp. Ex collatione locorum apparet, quod cum fundamentis montium simul ipsi montes connotentur, quod & Ravanellus vidit.
units.tr: Answer: From the comparison of the passages it appears that, together with the foundations of the mountains, the mountains themselves are connoted, as Ravanellus also saw.

units.la: CCCCLXXXVII. Exc. 7. M. p. 95. Me supponere, per fundamenta montium denotari ipsos montes.
units.tr: CCCCLXXXVII. Exc. 7. M. p. 95. That I presuppose that by the foundations of the mountains the mountains themselves are denoted.

units.la: Resp. Non suppono denotari, sed dico connotari, & ex collatione demonstrari, & terram quæ est fundamentum montium contremiscere, & ipsos montes, qui fundamenta cœlorum appellantur, concuti & commoveri.
units.tr: Answer: I do not presuppose that they are denoted, but I say that they are connoted, and it is shown from the comparison that the earth, which is the foundation of the mountains, trembles, and the mountains themselves, which are called the foundations of the heavens, are shaken and moved.

units.la: CCCCLXXXVIII. Exc. 8. M. p. 95. Si ex loco Jobi potest colligi, Montes dici columnas cœli, quia iis videtur cœlum inniti, Ergo etiam Montes videbuntur vel apparebunt animalia, qui obstupescant & rationalia, qui à Deo increpentur.
units.tr: CCCCLXXXVIII. Exc. 8. M. p. 95. If from the passage in Job it can be gathered that mountains are called pillars of the heavens because the heavens seem to rest on them, then the mountains will also seem or appear to be animals that are stupefied, and rational beings that are rebuked by God.

units.la: Resp. In loco Jobi, ut ex collatione reliquorum patet, duo sunt, Metaphora in voce fundamenta, quæ in textu habetur, & ratio istius Metaphoræ, quam probavi inde desumi, quod visui appareat, cœlos super montibus inniti. Similiter in voce stupor Metaphoram agnosco, sed rationem metaphoræ dico non esse eandem, sed dici stupere, quod in externo statu post motum similes sint animalibus stupentibus, non verò quòd videantur vel appareant animalia.
units.tr: Answer: In the passage in Job, as is clear from comparison with the others, there are two things: the metaphor in the word "foundations," which is in the text, and the ground of that metaphor, which I have shown is drawn from the fact that to sight it appears that the heavens rest on the mountains. Similarly, I recognise a metaphor in the word "stupor," but I say that the ground of this metaphor is not the same, but that they are said to be "stupefied" because in their outward state after the shaking they are like stupefied animals, not because the mountains seem or appear to be animals.

units.la: CCCCXXXIX. Exc. 9. M. p. 95. Probandum erat per columnas cœli non intelligi angelos robustissimos.
units.tr: CCCCXXXIX. Exc. 9. M. p. 95. It had to be proved that by the pillars of the heavens the most powerful angels are not meant.

units.la: Resp. At sententia illa quorundam Peripateticorum, qui putarunt affixos fixos Angelos orbibus & sphæris cœlestibus volvendis jam diu explosa, est, tum, quod istius Angelorum officii nullam faciat Scriptura mentionem, tum quod Deus naturæ nexum tam firmum constituerit, & leges ordinis, quas est observatura quamdiu erit, modò Deus manu sua sustentet & conservet, ut Angelorum operâ hic non sit opus.
units.tr: Answer: But that opinion of certain Peripatetics, who thought that angels fixed to the orbs and celestial spheres turn them, has long been exploded. This is so, first because Scripture makes no mention of such an office of the angels; second, because God has established the bond of nature so firmly, and the laws of order which it will observe as long as it lasts, provided God sustains and preserves it with his hand, that there is no need here of the angels' work.

units.la: CCCCXC. Exc. 10. M. p. 96. Quid si ipsi cœli intelligantur per fundamenta cœlorum, ut per fundamenta montium ipsi montes.
units.tr: CCCCXC. Exc. 10. M. p. 96. What if the heavens themselves are understood by the foundations of the heavens, as the mountains themselves are by the foundations of the mountains?

units.la: Resp. Dico connotari Montes, non designari per fundamenta montium. Quando enim fundamenta Montium tremunt, ipsi montes contremiscere sunt dicendi. De reliquis vide Responsum §. CCCCLXXXVI.
units.tr: Answer: I say that the mountains are connoted, not designated, by the foundations of the mountains. For when the foundations of the mountains tremble, the mountains themselves are to be said to tremble. On the rest see my reply at §. CCCCLXXXVI.

units.la: CCCCXCI. Exc. 10. M. p. 96. Quid si cœlorum vires, robur & potentia intelligatur, item firmitas & constantia per ista fundamenta.
units.tr: CCCCXCI. Exc. 10. M. p. 96. What if by these foundations the powers, strength and might of the heavens are understood, likewise their firmness and constancy?

units.la: Resp. Non opus est, ut probato, quid debeat intelligi per fundamenta cœlorum & columnas, omnes alienas interpretationes refutem, sed ab antagonistâ aliqua contraria fuisset eligenda, quam contra me defenderet, neque ita crebrò desiliendum ab uno ad aliud.
units.tr: Answer: It is not necessary, once it is proved what must be understood by the foundations and columns of the heavens, that I refute all the foreign interpretations. Rather, my opponent should have chosen some contrary view and defended it against me, instead of leaping so often from one thing to another.

units.la: CCCCXCII. Quæ porro ab H. p. 232. — 235. sunt objecta, procedunt exinde, quod mentem meam non rectè fuerit assecutus, ad quæ hæc tantùm annoto. 1. Columnas hîc dici cœli, ergo attendi ad rationem sustentandi debere. 2. Neque opus esse, ut Judæi adulti crediderint inniti cœlum montibus, sufficere quod sit phænomenon hoc, super quo præjudicium infantiæ est formatum, quod occasionem dedit isti locutioni, quæ mansit etiam post ejus depositionem in adulta ætate. 3. Non sequitur, omnia quæ metaphoricè tribuuntur montibus, fundari debere in sensuum apparentiis, sed ubi phænomenon aliquod est, & locutio ei innixa, ibi illius rationem ex eo esse desumendam, ut ita locus Psal. civ. & nihil ad rem faciat. 4. Quin Poëtæ & alias habuerint rationes, quare Atlantem dixerint humeris suis cœlum portare à me non negatur. Quod vero ad illud phænomenon respexerint mihi quàm verissimum videtur, & fuisse opinionem à quibusdam receptam patet ex eo, quod Aristot. lib. 2. de Cœlo eam debuerit refutare, & ex ipso H. qui p. 234. dicit Incolas Cæli columnam Atlantem montem dixisse. Videatur Aristoteles lib. 2. de Cœlo cap. 1. Διόπερ ἔ τε χ' ... ἀνάγκλω ἐμψυχον. Idcirco neque putandum est, ipsum in sese habere, ut veterum fabula dicit, qui quidem salutem ipsius Atlante quodam inquiunt indigere. Et ii namque qui hanc sententiam attulerunt, idem, quod posteri videntur existimasse. Nam quasi pondus haberent supera corpora omnia terreaque essent, necessitatem animam participem ipsi fabulose supposuere.
units.tr: CCCCXCII. The objections that H. raises on pp. 232–235 arise from his not having grasped my meaning properly, to which I only note the following. 1. Here the heavens are called columns; therefore attention must be paid to the manner of sustaining. 2. It is not necessary that adult Jews believed the heavens rest on the mountains; it is enough that this is a phenomenon, on which a prejudice of infancy was formed, which gave occasion to that way of speaking, and which remained even after that prejudice was laid aside in adult life. 3. It does not follow that all things attributed to mountains metaphorically must be grounded in appearances to the senses; but where there is some phenomenon and a locution resting on it, its explanation must be drawn from that, as in Ps. civ., and this has nothing to do with the matter. 4. That the poets had other reasons for saying that Atlas carries the heavens on his shoulders, I do not deny. That they looked to that phenomenon seems to me most true, and that it was an opinion received by some is clear from the fact that Aristotle in book 2 of On the Heavens had to refute it, and from H. himself, who on p. 234 says that the inhabitants called the mountain Atlas the pillar of heaven. See Aristotle, On the Heavens, book 2, ch. 1: [Διόπερ ... ἔμψυχον.] Therefore it should not be thought, as the fable of the ancients says, that it has in itself, as they say, a need of some Atlas for its preservation. For those who advanced this view seem to have held the same opinion as later writers: as if the upper bodies had weight and all things were earthly, they fabulously supposed a necessity of a soul participating in them.

units.la: CCCCXCIII. Tertiam Classem locorum constituimus in iis, quae Extremitatum Terrae faciunt mentionem, qualia sunt inter alia Psal. 11.8. Pete a me, & donabo gentes in possessionem tuam, & fines terrae ius possessionis tuae. Psal. xxii. 8. Recordabuntur & convertentur ad Jehovam omnes fines terrae. Psal. xlviii. 11. Laudem tuam esse usque ad extremitates terrae. Jer. x. 13. Qui effert vapores ab extremitate Terrae. Sic Dan. iv. 11. de arbore, quam vidit Nebucadnezar in somnio: Crevit arbor & invaluit, & altitudo ejus accedebat ad coelum, & conspectus ejus ad finem totius terrae; quibus duobus posterioribus locis plane respicitur ad horizontem, ubi Terra & coelum apparent inter se invicem se contingere, adeoque Terra terminari per coelum, propter quod ulterius non liceat progredi. Sic enim conspiciuntur vapores ad horizontem exturgere & se elevare versus coelum, atque ita vita est arbor suos ramos extendere usque a l horizontem.
units.tr: In the third class of passages we place those that mention the extremities of the earth. Among others are Psalm 11.8, "Ask of me, and I will give the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession"; Psalm 22.8, "All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to Jehovah"; Psalm 48.11, "Your praise reaches to the ends of the earth"; and Jeremiah 10.13, "He who brings up vapours from the end of the earth." So too Daniel 4.11, on the tree that Nebuchadnezzar saw in a dream: "The tree grew and became strong, and its height reached to heaven, and its sight to the end of the whole earth." In the last two of these passages, the reference is plainly to the horizon, where earth and heaven appear to meet one another, so that the earth is bounded by the heavens and one cannot go further. For the vapours are seen to rise at the horizon and lift themselves towards heaven, and in this way the tree is said to extend its branches as far as the horizon.

units.la: In omnibus his locis fit mentio Terrae finium & extremitatum, non habito respectu ad Terrae interiora, quomodo potest vocari Terrae extremitas illud totum, quod pedibus calcamus, sive ipsa Terrae superficies (quod quidem per se clarum est, nec enim alias extremitates Terrae possent opponi habitationibus Judaeorum, cum secundum istum sensum omnes homines aequaliter in extremitatibus Terrae habitare sint dicendi:) sed respectu ipsius superficiei, cum tamen nullibi Terra habeat fines in rei veritate, sed rotunda existat, quod concedunt & norunt hodie omnes Geographi. Talium locutionum pleni sunt profani auctores, ad quod exemplis probandum non pigebit describere ea, quae habet Bochartus in Phaleg lib. 3. cap. 7. p. M. 191. Merito Iberi dicti, qui ex Phaenicum sententia terrarum fines ultimos occupárunt; Hispani nempe, quorum urbem Calpen Tyrii putaverunt esse τέρμονας τῆς οἰκουμένης, ut in Strabone habetur. Tale est, quod Gaditanum templum Poseidonius scribit esse καὶ γῆς καὶ ἁλὸς ἄκρα τὸ πέρας maris & terrae terminum. Et quod in Homero Proteus Menelaum ita compellat: Ἀλλά σ' ἐς Ἠλύσιον πεδίον καὶ πείρατα γαίης, Ἀθάνατοι πέμψουσιν, Tefe I ad Elysios campos atque ultima terrae mittere Diis libitum, id est in Hispaniam, ut interpretatur Strabo. Quos secutus Claudianus de Stilichone dicit; in extremos aciem mittebat Iberos. Pro quo alibi primos vocat, sed eodem sensu lib. 1. in Rufinum: à primis Ganges horrebat Iberis. Et in Apollonio Philostratus lib. 2. cap. 14. In ipso (Lypeo) Hercules insculptus erat terminus terrae penes Gades collocans. Et lib. 5. initio: De columnis, quas veluti terminos posuisse Herculem ferunt. Itaque in Pindaro nihil frequentius, quàm ultra Herculis columnas non posse navigari. Vide illum imprimis Olympiâ 3. in fine, ubi de his sermonem ita claudit: Τὸ πόρσω δ' ἐςι σοφοῖς ἄδαπυ καὶ ὀφοις, ὑ μλιὼ διώξω, κενὸς ἔλω. Quod ultra eas est sapientibus & insipientibus æque inaccessum. Itaque non prosequar, nam vanus essem. In quem locum dicit Scholiastes Herculem voluisse ulterius progredi. At inquit: χαὶ ὁ ὄρων ἡ ζόφον ἐςιν σήλας, ἀὶ ὧν ἐμήνυσι τὸ πέλ ⊙ ἡ ἁλάσσης, ὡς μηδὲν ἔναι περαντέων ἀλωτὸν, cùm chaos & tenebras reperisset, columnas constituit, per quas significavit hunc esse finem maris, ita ut ulterius nihil sit navigabile. Quibus consona hac anonymi Geographi sub Constantio: Inde Oceanum esse dicitur, & huius partem quam nemo hominum narrare potest. Deinde barbarus scriptor quasi cunctabundus addit: Sed quid ibi esse potest? Est enim desertum, & sicut ajunt, est ibi finis mundi. Plura vide apud Erasmum in adagio Ἡ σ ἡ ἡ κλέια σήλα. Inde nuga illa olim credita apud Posidonium & Artemidorum, Solem cum prope Gades occumbit videri ἐκάτον ἀλασίοα, id est centuplo majorem, quàm alibi appareat, & in ipso Solis occasu stridorem edi, ὡσανεὶ σίζοντ ⊙ ξ πελάγης ἡ σ εἰσὶν αὐτὸ δ ὁ ἐμπίπτειν εἰς τ βύθον, tanquam stridete pelago, cùm extinguitur Sol, quia in abyssum demergitur: Et statim ab occasu noctem ingruere, demerso scilicet & extincto Sole. Et quo tempore excrescens Oceani aqua regionem inundat, animas morientes non deserere. Quales nugas referunt non Graeci solum, sed & Romani Scriptores. In his Florus cujus verba sunt lib. 2. c. 17. Decimus Brutus aliquando latius, Celticos Lusitanosque, & omnes Gallaeciæ populos, formidatumque militibus flumen OBLIVIONIS, peragratoque victor Oceano, non prius signa convertit, quàm cadentem in mare Solem, obrutumque aquis ignem, non sine quodam sacrilegii metu & errore deprehendit. Sed nec Aristoteli visum est incredibile, quod nonnulli opinantur σωά̈πλειν τ ᾳ̈ὲ τὰς Ἡρακλέας σήλας τόπον τῷ ᾳ̈ὲ τὴν Ἰνδικῷ locum qui est circa columnas Herculeas ei conjungi qui est circa Indicam. Atque eadem de causa terra sua terminos apud Abdiam ארמת Sarphath & ספרד Judai volunt esse Galliam & Hispaniam, quia Ps. lxxii.8. Psaltes Christi imperium extendit usque ad fines terræ, quos Aben Ezra in illum locum scribit esse בסוף מערב in extremo occidente. Denique ab Hispanis ipsis Nerium vel Celticum promontorium in Artabris vocatur Finis Terræ. Hactenus Bochartus. Nititur ergo hæc locutio præjudicio ex fallacia visûs desumpto, secundùm quæ ab infantiâ putamus extremitatem Terræ ibi esse, ubi Cœlum & Sol occidens & oriens Terram quasi contingere videtur, & Terram deorsum infinitis radicibus extendi. Et sanè hoc præjudicio infantiæ adhuc innexos mansisse etiam eos, qui inter literatos nomen suum sunt professi, apparet ex iis, quæ ex Bocharto adduximus. Addit his multos ex Patribus Parkerus de Defcensu Christi ad inferos Lib. II. §. 74. Persuasum habebant fere omnes ad unum, Terram ultra horizontem non exstare habitabilem, totam aquis innatare, quas vocabant Abyssos mundi, ibi esse & Abrahæ sinum (infulam silicet aut saltem regionem maritimam, sinum enim Abrahæ portum interpretantur) & subterraneum ignis thesaurum. Motum coeli negarunt Origenes, Diodorus Tharsensis, Eusebius Emissenus, omnis fere Theologorum schola, ut apud Senensem videre est. Sic Justinus Martyr. Coelum esse sphæricum, vel spharico motu moveri impossibile est. Sic HIERONYMUS. Si quis coelum putat fornicis more curvatum, Esaiæ quem non intelligit verbis deceptus, stultiloquium est.
units.tr: In all these places the mention is of the boundaries and extremities of the earth, without regard to the interior of the earth. That whole surface which we tread underfoot, or the very surface of the earth, cannot be called its extremity in this sense (which is clear enough in itself, for otherwise the extremities of the earth could not be set over against the dwelling places of the Jews, since on that understanding all men would have to be said to dwell equally at the extremities of the earth). Rather the extremity is spoken of with respect to the surface itself, although in truth the earth nowhere has boundaries but is round, as all geographers concede and know today. Profane authors are full of such expressions, and to prove this by examples it will not be tedious to set out what Bochart has in Phaleg, book 3, chapter 7, p. 191: "Rightly were they called Iberians, who, according to the Phoenicians, occupied the furthest limits of the lands, namely the Spaniards, whose city Calpe the Tyrians thought to be the termonas tēs oikoumenēs, as is found in Strabo." Similar is what Posidonius writes of the temple at Gades, that it is "kai gēs kai halos akra to peras," the extremity and boundary of land and sea. And in Homer, Proteus addresses Menelaus thus: "Alla s' es Ēlysion pedion kai peirata gaiēs, Athanatoi pempsousin," "But to the Elysian plain and the ends of the earth the immortals will send you." That is, into Spain, as Strabo explains. Claudian, following them, says of Stilicho: "He was sending his battle line against the farthest Iberians." Elsewhere he calls them the first, but in the same sense, in book 1 against Rufinus: "From the first Iberians the Ganges shuddered." And Philostratus in Apollonius, book 2, chapter 14: "On the shield itself Hercules was carved, placing a boundary of the earth near Gades." And at the start of book 5: "Concerning the pillars which Hercules is said to have set up as boundaries." So in Pindar nothing is more frequent than that one cannot sail beyond the pillars of Hercules. See especially Olympian 3, near the end, where he closes his discourse on these matters thus: "To porso d' esti sophoisi abaton kai ophroisi (?) ... " What lies beyond is inaccessible alike to the wise and to the foolish; therefore I will not pursue it, for I would be vain. On this passage the scholiast says that Hercules wished to go further. But he goes on: "kai hōs chaos kai zophon heurōn stēlas esthsen, di' hōn emēnusen to pelagos tēs thalassēs, hōs mēden einai peranteōn alōton," when he had found chaos and darkness, he set up pillars, through which he showed that this is the limit of the sea, so that nothing beyond is navigable. In agreement with this is the anonymous geographer under Constantius: "From there the Ocean is said to begin, and a part of it which no man can describe." Then the barbarous writer adds, as if hesitating: "But what can be there? For it is a desert, and, as they say, there is the end of the world." See more in Erasmus, in the adage Herculea stēlē [Ἡρακλέους στήλη]. Hence that old trifle believed by Posidonius and Artemidorus, that the sun, when it sets near Gades, appears "hekaton(taplasiona)," a hundredfold larger than elsewhere, and that at the very setting of the sun a hissing is heard, "hōsanei sizontos tou pelagous, hote sbennutai ho hēlios," as if the sea were hissing when the sun is extinguished, because it sinks into the abyss; and immediately from sunset night comes on, the sun having sunk and been extinguished. And at the time when the rising water of the Ocean floods the region, they say, it does not forsake the dying souls. Such trifles are reported not only by Greek but also by Roman writers. Among these is Florus, whose words are in book 2, chapter 17: "Decimus Brutus once travelled further, through the Celtic and Lusitanian peoples and all the peoples of Gallaecia, and the river of Oblivion, which the soldiers dreaded; and having traversed the Ocean as victor, he did not turn back his standards until he saw the sun falling into the sea and its fire submerged in the waters, not without a certain dread and error of sacrilege." But Aristotle also did not think it incredible what some believe, "symplein tēn te Hērakleos stēlas topon tē te Indikē," that the place about the Pillars of Hercules is joined to that about India. And for this same reason the Jews take the land of Sarphath and Sepharad in Obadiah to be France and Spain, because in Psalm 72.8 the psalmist extends Christ's rule to the ends of the earth; and Aben Ezra, on that passage, writes that these are "besof ma'arav," [בסוף מערב] "at the end of the west." Finally, the Nerium or Celtic promontory in Artabria is called by the Spaniards themselves Finis Terrae, "the end of the earth." So far Bochart. This way of speaking therefore rests on a prejudice drawn from a deceptive sight, by which from infancy we suppose the extremity of the earth to be where the heavens and the setting and rising sun seem to touch the earth, and the earth to extend downwards with endless roots. And that these prejudices of infancy still held fast even those who have professed themselves learned men is plain from what we have quoted from Bochart. Parker, in his De Descensu Christi ad Inferos, book 2, §74, adds many of the Fathers: "Almost all of them were persuaded, to a man, that the earth beyond the horizon is not habitable, that the whole of it floats on waters, which they called the Abysses of the world; that there too is Abraham's bosom (an island, or at least a maritime region, for they interpret the bosom of Abraham as a harbour), and the subterranean treasure of fire." Origen, Diodorus of Tarsus, Eusebius of Emesa, and almost the whole school of theologians denied the motion of the heavens, as may be seen in Senensis. So Justin Martyr: "It is impossible that the heaven be spherical or move with a spherical motion." So JEROME: "If anyone thinks the heaven is curved like a vault, deceived by the words of Isaiah which he does not understand, he speaks foolishly."

units.la: PROCOPIUS autem Gazaeus: si quis coelum dicat esse figura sphærica, eum contradicere Mosi, Prophetis, Paulo, & ipsi Christo contendit Cæsarius Nazianzeni frater, coelum appellat hemisphærium non sphæram. Sol non ascendit (inquit) sed egreditur Psalm. 19. & redit ad orientem occulte, Borealem plagam permeans: nox autem fit, elevante se Cappadocum solo. Hinc de infimo hemisphærio ita exclamat O miraculum; quomodo solubili innatat terra? quomodo per liquidum non penetrat grave? quomodo montes in molli non submerguntur? Resonat huic Chrysostomus. Contra aquarum naturam est ferre corpus tam grave, & interim contra naturam terra sedem in alio fundamento habere. Deus autem contra quam homines in omnibus operatur: Illi aquam in fundamentu fugiunt, hic appeiit: illi tectum, hic fundamentum posterius adificavit. Sic Basilius, Theodoretus, Theophylactus, Elias Cretensis Nazianzeni Scholiastes, sic denique omnes prope divinarum rerum periti patres, figuram & motum cœli rejecerunt tanquam figmentum Græcorum & a ratiocinando profectum. Subjungit Parkerus §. 76. Augustinum de quo sic loquitur: Cum ante dubitasset, tandem inferos sub terris esse concludit: sub terris cum dicit, idem dicit cum Tertulliano, sub corpore terræ. Post quæ hæc ironice addit Parkerus: Jam enim factum scilicet prudentior damnarat Antipodas, quos juvenis ante probarat. Sic solent homines proficere. Ridet postea Hieronymi argumenta risu quoque digna, quibus commotus Hieronymus, Vir cætera doctissimus, Infernum sub terra esse, extra omnem dubitationis aleam ponit, hunc in modum §. 82. in Hieronymum insurgens: Quibus vero ille rationibus pugnarit, & extra omnem ambiguitatem (ut ille quidem opinabatur) suum sensum hunc posuerit, posteru denique suii persuaserit, pudet equidem me referre. Ex hoc quod dicitur, usque ad fundamenta lacti, distinius quod Infernus sub terra sit. Ridicule. Infernus sub terra est, quia cor terræ appellatur. Puerile, Nec minus absurde ista. Noverimus loca ergastulorum secundum fidem Scripturarum inter immenſes abyssi aquas constituta. Probat vero ex Psalm. LXIII. & Job. XXXVI. Gemunt gigantes sub aquis, hoc est, Diaboli in Inferioribus terra, ubi inferi esse perhibentur. Aqua enim ejus natura suni, ut sine terra esse non possint. Sic Lactantius lib. 3. Instit. cap. 24. ridet Philosophos, qui statuebant, Terram esse rotundam, & dari Antipodes. Nihil tamen contra eos affert, quo refutentur, nisi talia praejudicia sensuum, contra quae quia Philosophorum sententia militabat, ridicula ipsi fuit visa, non aliter ac nunc vulgo ridentur, qui firmis rationibus inducti Terram circa Solem deferri existimant. Ita idem ille Lib. 3. de falsa sapientia cap. 24. adeo ineptis argumentis impugnat Antipodes, ut nunc vix sit hominum qualemcunque cognitionem historiarum habens, qui non risu potius quam refutatione digna arbitretur; quod ut constet audiamus ipsum loquentem Lactantium: Quid illi, qui esse contrarios vestigiis nostris antipodas putant; num aliquid loquuntur? aut est quisquam tam ineptus, qui credat esse homines, quorum vestigia sint superiora, quam capita? aut ibi qua apud nos jacent, inversa pendere? fruges & arbores deorsum versus crescere? pluvias & nives, & grandinem sursum versus cadere in terram? Et miratur aliquis hortos pensiles inter septem mira narrari; cum Philosophi & agros, & maria, & urbes, & montes pensiles faciant? Tam altas autem egerunt praejudicia ista radices, ut Johannes Aventinus lib. 3. Annalium Bojorum referat, Episcopum quendam Germanum, nomine Virgilium, Mathematicis artibus institutum, a Zacharia Papa Romam accersitum & haereseos damnatum esse, propterea quod antipodes statuerit; neque potuit illa opinio ex hominum mentibus eradicari, donec Christophorus Columbus illam Orbis partem, in qua sunt Antipodes detexisset. Unde vis praejudiciorum patet quam clarissime, quae uti sentiendi ita & loquendi libertati fibulam imposuerunt. Inde Terra sortita est nomen Orbis, quia videtur quasi planities sive diffus, a Coelo undique in rotundum conclusus. Sub illis tamen loquendi formulis de Terra finibus haec veritas latet, ut per eas designentur remotissimae gentes & loca: at praejudicium, quo illa est obvoluta, est fallacia illa visus, qua, ubi est Sol oriens & occidens, Coelum Terram contingere videtur.
units.tr: PROCOPIUS of Gaza states: if anyone says that heaven is spherical in shape, he contradicts Moses, the Prophets, Paul, and Christ himself. Caesarius, the brother of Gregory Nazianzen, calls heaven a hemisphere, not a sphere. The sun (he says) does not rise but comes forth, Psalm 19, and returns secretly to the east, passing through the northern region; and night falls when the soil of the Cappadocians rises up. From this, he exclaims about the lowest hemisphere: O miracle! How does the earth float on a liquid that dissolves? How does heavy matter not sink through the fluid? How are the mountains not submerged in the soft substance? Chrysostom echoes this. It is contrary to the nature of water to bear so heavy a body, and at the same time it is contrary to nature for the earth to have its seat on another foundation. But God works in ways contrary to men in all things: they flee the water for a foundation, he appears on it; they build the roof, he built the foundation afterwards. Thus Basil, Theodoret, Theophylact, Elias of Crete, the scholiast of Nazianzen, and finally almost all the Fathers skilled in divine things, rejected the figure and motion of heaven as a fiction of the Greeks, derived from reasoning. Parker adds, at §. 76, concerning Augustine, of whom he speaks thus: When he had first doubted, at last he concludes that hell is under the earth. When he says "under the earth," he says the same as Tertullian, "under the body of the earth." After these things Parker adds ironically: "For, having grown wiser, he had condemned the Antipodes, whom as a young man he had approved. Thus men tend to make progress." Afterwards he mocks the arguments of Jerome, which deserve laughter as well: moved by them, Jerome, otherwise a most learned man, lays it down beyond every shadow of doubt that hell is under the earth. Parker, rising against Jerome at §. 82 in this manner: As for the reasons by which he fought, and by which he set down his view beyond all ambiguity (as he himself believed), and finally persuaded himself of it, I am ashamed to report them. From this, that it is said, "down to the foundations of the milk," it is clear that hell is under the earth. Ridiculous. Hell is under the earth because it is called the heart of the earth. Childish. Nor are these things less absurd. Let us know that the places of the prisons, according to the faith of the Scriptures, are set amid the immense waters of the abyss. He proves this from Psalm 63 and Job 36: the giants groan under the waters, that is, the devils in the lower parts of the earth, where hell is said to be. For their nature is water, so that they cannot exist without earth. Thus Lactantius, Book 3 of the Institutes, chapter 24, mocks the philosophers who held that the earth is round and that there are Antipodes. Yet he brings nothing against them to refute them except such prejudices of the senses. Since the opinion of the philosophers went against these, it seemed ridiculous to him, just as those are now commonly laughed at who, led by solid reasons, think that the earth is carried around the sun. So the same Lactantius, Book 3 of On False Wisdom, chapter 24, attacks the Antipodes with arguments so inept that there is now scarcely anyone with even a modest knowledge of history who does not think them worthy of laughter rather than refutation. To make this clear, let us hear Lactantius himself speaking: What of those who think there are Antipodes whose feet are opposite to ours? Do they say anything at all? Or is there anyone so foolish as to believe there are men whose feet are higher than their heads? Or that things which lie here hang upside down there? That fruits and trees grow downward, and rain and snow and hail fall upward to the earth? And does anyone wonder that gardens hanging in the air are told of among the seven wonders, when the philosophers make fields, seas, cities, and mountains hang in the air? Yet these prejudices have struck such deep roots that Johannes Aventinus, Book 3 of the Annals of the Boii, reports that a certain German bishop, named Virgilius, trained in the mathematical arts, was summoned to Rome by Pope Zachary and condemned as a heretic because he had taught that there are Antipodes. Nor could that opinion be eradicated from men's minds until Christopher Columbus discovered that part of the globe in which the Antipodes are. From this the force of prejudices is most clearly evident, which have placed a clasp upon the freedom of thinking and of speaking alike. Hence the earth has received the name orb, because it seems to be a flat plain or expanse, enclosed on all sides by heaven as a circle. Under these forms of speech, however, concerning the limits of the earth, this truth lies hidden, so that by them the most distant peoples and places are designated. But the prejudice in which that truth is wrapped is that deceptive appearance of the sight, by which, where the sun rises and sets, heaven seems to touch the earth.

units.la: Per extremitates & fines terrae intelligi debent extremitates habitationum, quibus homines degunt, quales revera dari in orbe rotundo terrarum certo certius est, probatur, quia agitur in dicto loco de regno Christi extendendo in omnes nationes, ita ut respiciatur non figura terra, sed genus humanum. Hoc vero p. 88. per extremitates Terrae intelligit illas. illas, quae mari quaquaversum terminantur, lambuntur, distinguuntur, claudantur.
units.tr: The extremities and borders of the earth must be understood as the extremities of the habitations in which men dwell, which really exist in the round world of lands beyond all doubt. This is proved because the passage speaks of the kingdom of Christ being extended to all nations, so that what is regarded is not the shape of the earth but the human race. But on p. 88 he understands by the extremities of the earth those parts which are bounded, washed, separated and enclosed on every side by the sea.

units.la: Resp. Quaenam sint illae extremitates habitationum in terra rotunda, debuisset à B. explicari, quòd si per eas idem intelligat, quod H. dico, habitationum terrae extremitates, ut nec ipsius Terrae, non posse dici, nisi respicias ad aliquid, quod eas extremitates faciat, vel efficere videatur. At cum ultra mare iterum sit terra stabilis, ut ex Geographia constat, non possunt dici extremitates vel Terrae vel habitationum, nisi ex illo Terrae & Coeli confinio. 2. agitur de regno Christi extendendo in remotissimas regiones, quae censendo à terra Judaica sunt ex, quae ab illo centro sunt maximè remotae, ut ex globo Geographico apparet, quae per extremitates Coeli & Terrae designantur, ita ut veritas ista formulâ denotata praejudicio dicto sensuum sit involuta. 3. si ex partes intelliguntur, quae mari undiquaque terminantur, cum Terra sancta ab Oriente terminetur Syria & Arabia, à Meridie deserto Pharan & Ægypto, ab Occidente mari magno sive Mediterraneo, à Septentrione Libanum montem fines habeat, erit dicendum, ab una parte intelligi regiones & nationes Mediterraneo mari adjacentes, quales sunt Tyriorum, Philistinorum, ab altera verò parte usquedum undique tum à Syria & Arabia ad mare rubrum, tum ab Ægypto ad mare Æthiopicum, tum à Libano monte longo demum tractu ulterius pergendo usque ad Oceanum pervenias, & sic excludendae erunt ex partes, quae ultra Oceanum jacent, & mare Mediterraneum, quod absurdum apparet. Nostra ergo interpretatio istorum locorum longè concinnior censenda.
units.tr: Reply. The author should have explained what the extremities of habitations on a round earth are. If he means by them the same thing I do, the extremities of the habitations of the earth, then, since they are not the extremities of the earth itself, they cannot be called such unless one looks to something that makes them extremities or seems to make them so. But since there is again solid land beyond the sea, as geography makes clear, they cannot be called the extremities either of the earth or of the habitations, except by reference to that boundary between earth and heaven. 2. The passage speaks of the kingdom of Christ being extended into the most remote regions, which, reckoned from the land of Judea, are those most distant from that centre, as the geographical globe shows; these are what is designated by the extremities of heaven and earth, so that this truth, signified by the phrase, is wrapped up in the prejudice of the senses just mentioned. 3. If the parts meant are those bounded on every side by the sea, then, since the Holy Land is bounded on the east by Syria and Arabia, on the south by the desert of Paran and Egypt, on the west by the Great Sea or Mediterranean, and on the north by Mount Lebanon, it must be said that on one side the regions and nations adjoining the Mediterranean are meant, such as those of the Tyrians and Philistines; on the other side, however, if you proceed onward, both from Syria and Arabia to the Red Sea, and from Egypt to the Ethiopian sea, and from Mount Lebanon through a long stretch until you finally reach the Ocean, then the parts lying beyond the Ocean would have to be excluded, and the Mediterranean too, which is absurd. Our interpretation of these passages is therefore to be judged far more consistent.

units.la: CCCCXCV. Exc. 2. H. p. 236. Verba Psalmi ad aeternum Dei Fi- lium facta esse, non ad vulgum.
units.tr: CCCCXCV. Exc. 2. H. p. 236. The words of the Psalm were spoken to the eternal Son of God, not to the common people.

units.la: Resp. Sed ita ut nobis sint revelata, adeoque ad captum nostrum proposita. 2. illa quae in Psalmis reliquis habentur, non ad Filium sunt facta.
units.tr: Reply. Yes, but in the way they have been revealed to us, and so set before our understanding. 2. The other things found in the Psalms were not spoken to the Son.

units.la: CCCCXCVI. Exc. 3. B. p. 88. A vulgo credi terram deorsum infinitis radicibus extendi & quidem errore a praejudicio sensuum orto numquam innotuit.
units.tr: CCCCXCVI. Exc. 3. B. p. 88. That the common people believe the earth extends downward by infinite roots, and that this error, arising from a prejudice of the senses, has never been recognised.

units.la: Resp. Praejudicium esse infantiae quilibet, si, quas in infantia ea de re habuerit cogitationes memoriâ recolat, experietur, idque exemplo Patrum & Lactantii aliorumque plurimorum, qui ante Christophorum Columbum vixerunt, exemplis §. cccexc iii. aperte fuit confirmatum.
units.tr: Reply. Anyone who recalls the thoughts he had about this matter in infancy will find that it is a prejudice of childhood. This has been clearly confirmed by the example of the Fathers and of Lactantius and very many others who lived before Christopher Columbus, as shown by the examples at §. cccexc iii.

units.la: CCCCXCVII. Quartum Inductionis exemplum suppeditat locus Job. xxvi. 7. Qui extendit Aquilonem super inane, suspendens Terram super pi-
units.tr: CCCCXCVII. The fourth example of the induction is supplied by the passage Job xxvi. 7. He stretcheth out the north over the empty place, and hangeth the earth upon nothing.

units.la: nihilum. Per Aquilonem commodè hic intelligitur cœli pars illa quæ habet Polum Arcticum, constituta à Circulo Æquinoctiali, qui cœlum dividit in duas partes. Atque huic interpretationi Mercerus consentit, dicendo: Possumus generaliter accipere Aquilonis nomine totum hemisphærium nostrum, quod Aquilonare est & superius. Item Buxtorfius in Lexico יָרַע dicit per illam intelligi plagam Mundi septentrionalem quasi Abditam dictam nempe à sole, qui ad eam non accedat, adductis quibusdam exemplis. Inane autem explicandum est de Aere, quem vulgus nihil esse putat, unde sæpe audias, hominibus idiotis Aërem & Nihilum pro eodem sumi, adeoque spatium illud inter Cœlum & Terram inane judicari. A parte nostra sunt Piscator in notis ad Jobum, & Mercerus commentario in eundem: quorum ille ad hæc verba (super inane) notat: id est, super aërem, cujus spatium imperitis natura rerum videtur inane. Hic vero. Super inane, sive vacuum dicit juxta vulgi opinionem, juxta quam SÆ-PE SCRIPTVRA LOQVITVR, qui putat vacuum esse totum illud spatium, quod est à Terra hinc ad Cœlum usque, cùm sit aëre plenum & occupatum. Veritas ergo hic significata est, Deum extendere Cœlum super aërem, qui ei nullum fulcrum præbere potest, & terram suspendere super eodem, qui ejus pondus sustinere nequit. Præjudicium vero, cui veritas illa est involuta, est, quod aërem homines ab infantia, quamdiu nullum in eo ventum, nec frigus aut calorem experiuntur, pro nihilo prorsus ducant, illudque spatium, quod à Terra ad Cœlum extenditur, inane judicent.
units.tr: nothing. By "north" is fittingly understood here that part of the heavens which has the Arctic Pole, marked off by the equinoctial circle, which divides the heavens into two parts. Mercerus agrees with this interpretation, saying: We may generally take the name of the north to mean our whole hemisphere, which lies to the north and above. Likewise Buxtorf in his Lexicon says that by the word [יָרַע] is understood the northern quarter of the world, as it were hidden, namely so called because the sun does not approach it, citing certain examples. The empty place must, however, be explained of the air, which the common people think is nothing; hence you may often hear that with uneducated people air and nothing are taken to be the same, and so that space between heaven and earth is judged to be empty. On our side are Piscator in his notes on Job and Mercerus in his commentary on the same book. Piscator, on these words (over the empty place), notes: that is, over the air, whose space seems empty to the unlearned in the nature of things. Mercerus says: He calls it empty or void according to the popular opinion, in accordance with which SCRIPTURE OFTEN SPEAKS, which supposes that the whole space that lies from the earth up to heaven is empty, when it is full and occupied with air. The truth signified here, then, is that God stretches out heaven over the air, which can offer it no support, and hangs the earth upon the same air, which cannot bear its weight. The prejudice, however, by which this truth is wrapped up, is that men, from infancy, as long as they experience no wind in it, nor cold or heat, regard the air as absolutely nothing, and judge that space which extends from earth to heaven to be empty.

units.la: CCCCXCVIII. Exc. 1. B. p. 89. Vocem הָרָא interpretes Belgæ vertunt het woeste, Hieronymus Vatlum, Genevenses le Vuide, Junius & Tre- mellius inane, omnes tamen simul intelligere videntur totum illud spatium quod est à Coelo usque ad terram.
units.tr: CCCCXCVIII. Exc. 1. B. p. 89. The Belgic translators render the word [הָרָא] het woeste, Jerome renders it Vatlum, the Genevans le Vuide, and Junius and Tremellius inane. Yet all of them seem to understand by it that whole space which extends from heaven to earth.

units.la: Resp. Hæ interpretationes non pugnant cum interpretatione Piscatoris & Mercerí, quas pro me adduxi. Neque enim ille, neque ego nego, quod per inane & nihil debeat intelligi totum illud spatium, quod est à Cœlo usque ad Terram, cujus pars Terræ proxima solet Aër appellari, unde Genevenses dicunt, Il soustient la terre comme par de contrepois en l'air. Sustentat terram in aëre ut per contralibrationem. Sed quæstio est, annon aër vel illud spatium, quod est à Cœlo usque ad Terram Inane & nihil appelletur ex præjudicio Infantiæ suprà explicato? quod ego affirmo.
units.tr: Reply. These interpretations do not conflict with the interpretation of Piscator and Mercerus, which I have adduced in my favour. Neither he nor I deny that by "void" and "nothing" that whole space must be understood which extends from heaven to earth, and whose part nearest the earth is usually called air. Hence the Genevans say, Il soustient la terre comme par de contrepois en l'air [He holds up the earth as if by a counterweight in the air], and Sustentat terram in aëre ut per contralibrationem [He sustains the earth in the air as by a counterbalance]. But the question is whether air, or that space which extends from heaven to earth, should be called "void" and "nothing" on account of the prejudice of infancy explained above. This I affirm.

units.la: CCCCXCIX. Exc. 2. B. p. 90. Alia potest dari ratio meo judicio multo solidior, videlicet vocem illam usurpari, ut denotetur, nullum esse soli-
units.tr: CCCCXCIX. Exc. 2. B. p. 90. In my judgment another reason, much more solid, can be given: namely that this word is used to denote that there is no solid

units.la: solidum fundamentum Coelorum circumquaque extensorum &c.
units.tr: solid foundation of the heavens stretched out on every side, etc.

units.la: Resp. Non statim id, quod non est solidum, dici potest inane, vel nihilum in rei veritate, nisi habeatur respectus ad præjudicia, adeoque nihil quicquam hæc exceptio meæ sententiæ contrariatur. Itaque probationes adversarii sunt frustraneæ.
