Non quæritur enim inter nos, an hic Jobus velit potentiam Dei probare, quod libenter concedimus; nec quæritur, an hoc sit argumentum potentiæ divinæ, quòd cœlum expanderit super inane & Terram super nihilum, sed quid per illud inane intelligatur & nihilum, &, si Aër intelligatur sive spatium à Cœlo usque ad Terram, quare illud Nihilum & inane vocetur? annon propter præjudicium? quod ego existimo cum Mercero & Piscatore, neque hactenus contrarium ostensum.
units.tr: Reply. What is not solid cannot at once be called void, or nothing, in the truth of the matter, unless regard is had to prejudices. So this exception does not in any way contradict my opinion, and the adversary's proofs are therefore pointless. For the question between us is not whether Job here wishes to prove the power of God, which we gladly concede; nor is it asked whether this is an argument of divine power, that he stretched out heaven over the void and earth over nothing. The question is what is meant by that void and nothing. If air, or the space from heaven to earth, is meant, why is it called nothing and void? Is it not because of prejudice? This I hold with Mercerus and Piscator, and nothing to the contrary has yet been shown.

units.la: D. Exc. 3. H. p. 238. Extensio illa proprie Aquiloni vento Boreali tribui potius debet.
units.tr: D. Exc. 3. H. p. 238. That extension ought rather properly to be attributed to the north wind, Boreas.

units.la: Resp. Contrarium patet ex voce extendit, quæ de Cœlo non de vento solet usurpari. 2. ex phrasi adjectâ. Eo enim modo Deus extendere dicitur Aquilonem super inane, quomodo Terram suspendit super nihilum. At Terram suspendit super Aërem. Ergò similiter Cœlum Aquilonare sive partem Boreæ'em super Aërem extendit.
units.tr: Reply. The contrary is evident, first from the word extends, which is usually applied to heaven, not to wind. Second, from the added phrase. For God is said to stretch out the north wind over the void in the same way as he suspends the earth over nothing. But he suspends the earth over the air. Therefore similarly he stretches out the northern quarter of heaven, that is the north wind, over the air.

units.la: DI. Ad reliqua quæ hic H. p. 237, & 238. item M. p 98. habent, noto, 1. si concedatur, Spiritus Sancti effectum esse, quod vulgus de inani sensit, confirmatur quod intendo, nimirum ad præjudicia infantiæ respexisse, quæ vulgus, hoc est, ii quibus aëris corporeitas non est demonstrata, retinent. 2. Per Aërem præjudiciis infantiæ capti non intelligunt nihilum positivum, privativum ego dixero, hoc est, ut explicat H. quod non est id quod inesse debet, quemadmodum urna dicitur vacua, quæ non continet lac vel aquam vel simile aliquid, sed ex illo modo judicandi. Ubi nihil sentio, ibi nihil est, merum nihil sive negativum intelligitur. 3. Si concedas, errori vulgari superstructam esse locutionem, uti non videtur valde negare M. tum concedis id, quod ego hic intendo.
units.tr: DI. As for the rest that H. has at pp. 237 and 238, and likewise M. at p. 98, I note the following. 1. If it is conceded that the common people's notion of the void was the effect of the Holy Spirit, then what I intend is confirmed: namely that it had regard to the prejudices of infancy, which the common people retain, that is, those to whom the corporeality of air has not been demonstrated. 2. By air, those held captive by the prejudices of infancy do not understand a positive nothing (I would call it privative), that is, as H. explains it, that which is not what ought to be in it. A jar is called empty which contains no milk or water or anything similar. Rather, by that manner of judging, Where I perceive nothing, there is nothing, a mere nothing, or negative nothing, is understood. 3. If you concede that the expression is built upon a common error, as M. does not seem strongly to deny, then you concede what I intend here.

units.la: DII. Quintum inductionis exemplum desumimus ex Gen. I. 16. Fecit Deus duo illa luminaria magna, luminare majus ad præsecturam diei & luminare minus ad præsecturam noctis atque stellas. Sol & Luna vocantur luminaria magna oppositè ad reliquas stellas: quod apparet ex eo, i. quoniam Moses dicit: Deus fecit duo luminaria magna, atque NB. stellas, si enim non diceretur oppositè ad stellas, non duo luminaria facta esse dicendum fuisset, sed plura. 2. Dicit Moses: duo illa luminaria magna. Ergò in hac phrasi his duobus, præ aliis, insignis magnitudo adscribitur, cùm accuratè loquendo potiùs stellæ oppositè ad Lunam sint illa lumi-naria magna. At certum est, apud Astronomos plurimas stellas tam fixas quàm Planetas superare Lunam suâ magnitudine. Videsis Clavium in Sphæram de sacro Bosco p. 205, 206. Ergò hîc iterum est exemplum Scripturæ uturpantis formulam Phænomeno convenientem & veritatem præjudicio involutam referentem. Atque veritas hîc significata à Spiritu Sanƈto est, quod Deus fecerit duo illa corpora, quæ nobis præ aliis majorem usum præbent, magisque nos illuminant interdiu & noƈtu. Præjudicium, quo involuta est veritas formulâ receptâ, est ma-gnitudo Luminis & Corporis præ stellis tanquam causa illius majoris usus & illuminationis. Consentiunt Belgæ interpretes: De welcke groot genoemt worden, ten aensien van haer uyterlijcke gedaente, soo die in onse ogen staen, en haer uytnemende werckingen, id est, quæ magna appellantur respectu ipsorum externa speciei, ut illa in oculos nostros incidit, & excellentium operationum. Verba Calvini digna sunt consideratu, multumque prosunt ad totam nostram Controversiam. Is in vers. 14. cap. 1. Genef. Tenendum est illud, inquit, Mosen NON ACUTE PHILOSOPHARI de occultis mysteriis: sed referre quæ passim etiam RUDIBUS NOTA sunt, & posita in vulgari usu. Item ad vers. 15. Iterum repetere opera pretium est, quod prius dixi: non hic philosophicè disseri, quantus Sol in Cœlo, & quàm magna vel parva Luna: sed quanta lux ex ipsis ad nos perveniat. SENSUS enim nostros hîc compellat, ne donorum Dei, quibus fruimur, cognitio præterfluat. Et ad vers. 16. Hoc interest, quod Moses populariter scit, si, quæ sine doctrinâ & literis omnes Idiotæ, communi sensu percipiunt: illi autem (Astronomi puta:) magno labore investigant, quicquid humani ingenii acumen assequi potest. Paræus conformiter satis huic nostræ sententiæ in hunc locum loquitur: Lunâ minores sunt stellæ alia, non quidem REVERA, SED APPARENTER. Nam & corpus lunare majus apparet, quia est astris infimum, & oculis nostris vicinius, proximum Terræ &c. Sic Perkinsius tom. 1. pag 1136. in Baςανολογία: Scriptura sæpenumero de rebus loquitur, non quemadmodum in se sunt, sed quemadmodum nobis videntur. Hoc sensu affirmatur, Deum fecifle duo luminaria magna Solem & Lunam: cùm tamen Luna sit multo stellis minor: quia verò Terra tam propinqua est, nobis major cæteris videtur, idcircò luminare magnum appellatur. Similiter Piscator in quæstione, in Pentat. Quo sensu Sol & Luna dicuntur luminaria magna? Resp. Sic vocantur respectu nostri sensùs & judicii oculorum. Et Alstedius in notis ad Genesin. Luna est luminare magnum non SECUNDUM REM, sed secundùm SPECIEM duntaxat & VIRTUTEM. Consentientium nobiscum in hujus loci interpre-tatione tatione agmen claudat Polanus, qui in suo Synt. Theol. lib. 5. cap. 23. Sic, inquit, Sol & Luna dicuntur luminaria magna, quamvis stellæ fixæ sint longè majores quantitate Lunæ &c. partim quoad δόξαν sive opinionem communem vulgi, quod de rebus loquitur non ut sunt, sed ut videntur esse, & AD CUJUS CAPTUM SP. S. IN HIS TALIBUS SESE ACCOMMODARE DIGNATUR.
units.tr: DII. We take the fifth example of induction from Gen. 1:16. God made those two great lights, the greater light to rule the day and the lesser light to rule the night, and the stars. Sun and Moon are called the great lights in contrast to the other stars. This is clear from the fact that Moses says: God made two great lights, and NB, the stars. For if it were not said in contrast to the stars, he would have had to say that not two lights but more were made. 2. Moses says: those two great lights. So in this phrase these two are singled out for exceptional greatness above the others, although, speaking strictly, the stars are rather the great lights in contrast to the Moon. But it is certain that, according to the astronomers, very many stars, both fixed and planets, surpass the Moon in size. See Clavius on Sacrobosco's Sphere, pp. 205, 206. So here again we have an example of Scripture using a form of words that fits the appearance and expresses a truth wrapped in a prejudice. The truth signified here by the Holy Spirit is that God made those two bodies which give us more use than the others and illuminate us more by day and by night. The prejudice in which the truth is wrapped in the accepted form of words is the greatness of the Light and the Body compared with the stars, taken as the cause of that greater use and illumination. The Belgic translators agree: Who are called great with respect to their outward appearance, as they stand before our eyes, and their excellent workings; that is, which are called great with respect to their external appearance, as it strikes our eyes, and their excellent operations. The words of Calvin deserve consideration and greatly help our whole controversy. He says on verse 14 of Genesis chapter 1: It must be held that Moses does NOT PHILOSOPHISE SUBTLY about hidden mysteries, but relates what is commonly known even to the UNLEARNED and is in everyday use. Likewise on verse 15: It is worth repeating what I said before: the question here is not philosophically how large the Sun is in the heavens, or how great or small the Moon is, but how much light reaches us from them. For it addresses our SENSES, lest the knowledge of God's gifts, which we enjoy, slip past us. And on verse 16: This is the difference, that Moses speaks popularly, as all unlearned people perceive by common sense what is without teaching and letters; but those others (the astronomers, namely) investigate with great labour whatever the sharpness of human wit can reach. Paraeus speaks quite in agreement with our view on this passage: The stars are smaller than the Moon, not indeed in REALITY, but in APPEARANCE. For the lunar body also appears larger, because it is the lowest of the heavenly bodies and closer to our eyes, nearest to the Earth, etc. So Perkins, vol. 1, p. 1136, in his Basanologia [βασανολογία]: Scripture often speaks of things not as they are in themselves, but as they seem to us. In this sense it is affirmed that God made two great lights, the Sun and the Moon, although the Moon is much smaller than the stars: but because the Earth is so near, it seems larger to us than the others, and so it is called the great light. Similarly Piscator in his question on the Pentateuch: In what sense are the Sun and Moon called great lights? Answer: they are so called with respect to our sense and the judgement of our eyes. And Alsted in his notes on Genesis: The Moon is a great light not ACCORDING TO THE THING, but according to APPEARANCE only and POWER. Closing the line of those who agree with us in interpreting this passage is Polanus, who in his Syntagma Theologiae, book 5, chapter 23, says: Thus, he says, the Sun and Moon are called great lights, although the fixed stars are far greater in quantity than the Moon, etc., partly as regards the common opinion of the crowd, since Scripture speaks of things not as they are but as they seem to be, and TO WHOSE CAPACITY THE HOLY SPIRIT CONDESCENDS TO ACCOMMODATE HIMSELF IN SUCH MATTERS.

units.la: DIII. Exc. 1. R. Analectorum Theologicorum disp. 47. th. 5. ad hunc locum. Imò ex rei veritate (scil. dicitur Luna luminare majus:) cùm magnitudo non modò de substantiâ, sed etiam de potentiâ & operationibus dicatur Gen. XXIV. 35. Eccles. II. 10. Luc. I. 15. 1 Cor. XIII. 13. ita hîc intelligendum. Additur enim, luminare majus ad præfecturam diei & luminare minus ad præfecturam noctis. Verè ergò notatum Basilio aliisque, magna hæc luminaria nos posse accipere, non tam aliorum comparatione, quàm suo munere.
units.tr: DIII. Exc. 1. R. Analectorum Theologicorum disp. 47, th. 5, on this passage: Indeed, in the truth of the matter (namely, the moon is called the greater light), since greatness is said not only of substance but also of power and operations, as in Gen. XXIV. 35, Eccles. II. 10, Luke I. 15, 1 Cor. XIII. 13, so it is to be understood here. For it is added: the greater light for the rule of the day, and the lesser light for the rule of the night. Rightly therefore Basil and others have noted that these great lights we can take not so much by comparison with others as by their office.

units.la: Resp. Concedimus, quòd à Spiritu Sancto significetur, ea luminaria majorem usum nobis præbere, atque nos magis illuminare quàm stellas, interim tamen ipsa illa veritas est hoc præjudicio involuta, quòd majora sint respectu corporis & respectu lucis, uti vidimus ex interpretibus citatis, atque id præjudicium vulgo censetur causa istius majoris operationis & illuminationis.
units.tr: Reply. We grant that the Holy Spirit signifies that these lights afford us greater use and illuminate us more than the stars do. Yet that truth is itself wrapped up in this prejudice: that they are greater in respect of body and in respect of light, as we have seen from the interpreters cited. And this prejudice is commonly held to be the cause of that greater operation and illumination.

units.la: DIV. L. p. 177. Novæ suæ sapientiæ similia exceptionis loco adfert. Distinguo, inquit, magnitudinem, quæ non tantùm quantitatis est, sed aliarum quoque rerum, inprimis virtutis & operationis. Nisi forte viri magni nomen nisi in gigante non admittas. Luna inter majora lumina, sed ut Lumen, & respectu in terris operationum. En tibi parmam hanc ereptam. Nam ad cetera, quæ proferre queas, facilior etiam solutio. His conjungo B. D. p. 18. responsionem, quam putat. Dico verò ibi respici non ad magnitudinem corporum, sed ad rationem illuminandi, quia majus Lumen præbent in Terrâ, quatenus sunt מארת luminaria: quod vel ex ipso Mose clarissimè liquet. Nam agitur de eâ magnitudine, quâ Sol major apparet Lunâ, at discus Solis non major apparet, quam discus Lunæ, sed multo majus præbet nobis lumen, ac eâ ratione est majus luminare quàm Luna; quæ etiam ob majus lumen multo majus luminare est, quàm vel Venus, vel Jupiter, vel maxima ex stellis prima magnitudinis.
units.tr: DIV. L. p. 177. He brings forward, as if by way of exception, something like his own new wisdom. I distinguish, he says, between greatness, which pertains not only to quantity but also to other things, especially to power and operation. Unless perhaps you will not admit the name "great man" except of a giant. The moon is among the greater lights, but as a light, and with respect to its operations on earth. There, you have this shield wrested from you. For the rest of what you may bring forward, the solution is even easier. To this I add the reply of B. D. p. 18, which he thinks is decisive. I say, however, that there the reference is not to the magnitude of bodies, but to the manner of giving light, because they give a greater light on earth, inasmuch as they are מארת [me'orot], lights: which is clear enough from Moses himself. For the question concerns that greatness by which the sun appears larger than the moon; yet the disc of the sun does not appear larger than the disc of the moon, but it gives us much more light, and on that account it is a greater light than the moon. The moon too, because of its greater light, is a much greater light than either Venus or Jupiter, or the greatest of the stars of the first magnitude.

units.la: Resp. Præter responsionem datam art. precedente, vel ex eo apparet, quod sit locutio accommodata ad sensuum apparentiam, quia Luna vocatur luminare, & in eodem ordine cum Sole collocatur, cùm tamen non nisi æquivocè luminare dici possit: quippe tanta, imo major est differentia ferentia inter Solem & Lunam, quanta est inter flammam candelæ & lapidem aliquem ejus lumen reflectentem. Trium enim generum sunt corpora in mundo: quædam emittunt lumen, ut Sol, Stellæ, Ignis; quædam transmittunt, ut Aër, Cœlum, Vitrum; quædam remittunt, ut omnia Corpora opaca, Terra, Luna & reliqui Planetæ. Certum equidem est, Lunam nullam habere lucem insitam, uti apparet satis ex eo, quod tempore Novilunii etiam tenuissima serenissimâ non conspicua sit, nisi quod aliquando lumen in eâ tenue conspiciatur, quod existimandum est, esse à Terrâ ad Lunam reflexum: stellis autem fixis lucem insitam competere, constat. Illa ergo procul dubio in se longè major est, tum quia est propria, tum quia eorum corpora longè sunt majora Lunæ corpore: sed ob maximam à nobis remotionem & distantiam fit, ut illa lux nobis non ita appareat, neque oculos nostros tam fortiter feriat. Itaque si absolutè loqui voluisset Scriptura, nullo habito respectu ad sensus nostros, & eorum apparentiam, Luna vix luminare dici potuisset, sed id nominis accuratè loquendo tantùm stellis fixis & Solis fuisset tribuendum: &, si etiam ea, quæ lumen reflectunt, saltem æquivocè inter luminaria sint recensenda, potiori jure Terra luminare accuratè loquendo appellanda, cùm Lumen longè & majus & fortius reflectat quàm Luna ob magnitudinem majorem. 2. Quando Moses dicit, Fecit Deus duo illa Luminaria magna, oppositè ad stellas, illa phrasis refertur ad majorem apparentiam, tum respectu magnitudinis, tum respectu luminis, & significatur major usus & illuminatio, quam nobis ista luminaria præbent. Quando autem postea dicit sequentibus verbis, luminare majus ad præfecturam diei & luminare minus ad præfecturam noctis, comparationem instituit inter ipsa hæc duo luminaria, quæ oppositè ad stellas absolutè magna dixerat, majorem & minorem illuminationem significasse concedimus, ita tamen, ut & illæ phrases phænomenon respiciant, quod hic cum rei veritate concordat.
units.tr: Reply. Apart from the answer given in the preceding article, this appears from the fact that the language is accommodated to the appearance to the senses, since the moon is called a light and is placed in the same order as the sun, although it can be called a light only equivocally. Indeed the difference between the sun and the moon is as great, or greater, as that between the flame of a candle and some stone reflecting its light. There are three kinds of bodies in the world: some emit light, as the sun, the stars and fire; some transmit it, as air, heaven and glass; some reflect it, as all opaque bodies, the earth, the moon and the other planets. It is certain indeed that the moon has no inherent light, as is clear enough from the fact that at new moon it is not visible even in the clearest sky, except that sometimes a faint light is seen on it, which must be thought to be reflected from the earth to the moon. But that the fixed stars have their own inherent light is established. Those therefore are without doubt far greater in themselves, both because they have their own light and because their bodies are far greater than the body of the moon. But because of their very great remoteness and distance from us, that light does not appear to us in the same way, nor strike our eyes so strongly. Thus if Scripture had wished to speak absolutely, with no regard to our senses and their appearance, the moon could scarcely have been called a light; the name would have been given strictly speaking only to the fixed stars and the sun. And even if those things which reflect light must be counted among the lights at least equivocally, the earth should with better right be called a light, strictly speaking, since it reflects a light both farther and stronger than the moon, by reason of its greater size. 2. When Moses says, God made those two great lights, set against the stars, that phrase refers to the greater appearance, both in respect of size and in respect of light, and it signifies the greater use and illumination which those lights afford us. But when he afterwards says in the following words, the greater light for the rule of the day, and the lesser light for the rule of the night, he institutes a comparison between those two lights themselves, which he had called absolutely great in contrast to the stars. We grant that he signifies a greater and a lesser illumination; yet in such a way that those phrases also regard the phenomenon, which here agrees with the truth of the matter.

units.la: DV. Exc. 3. B. p. 92. Me in responsionibus non distinguere, contra quem agam.
units.tr: DV. Exc. 3. B. p. 92. I do not distinguish in my replies, against whom I am arguing.

units.la: Resp. Ubi communiter excipiunt adversarii, ibi me communia regerere non est mirum.
units.tr: Reply. Where my adversaries commonly make an exception, it is no wonder that I answer with common points.

units.la: DVI. Exc. 4. B. p. 93. Calvini interpretationem consentire cum interpretatione meorum adversariorum, sic enim illum ad vers. 15. Gen. 1. commentari. Minus luminare dicit comparativè, quia exigua est lucis portio, quam nobis emittit, prout est immensus Solis fulgor.
units.tr: DVI. Exc. 4. B. p. 93. Calvin's interpretation agrees with the interpretation of my adversaries; for he comments thus on verse 15 of Genesis 1: "He calls it the lesser light comparatively, because the portion of light it gives us is small, compared with the immense brilliance of the sun."

units.la: Resp. Calvinus ad vers. 16. totus noster est, uti superius vidimus; sed nec verbis hic citatis nobis contradicit. Agit enim de Luna oppositè ad Solem, quare ea in hac oppositione vocetur luminare minus, quid verò hoc ad sententiam adversariorum? Non enim quæritur, quomodo Luna respectu Solis minus luminare dici possit, sed quomodo Luna dicatur magnum luminare oppositè ad stellas, ita ut hic aliquanto accuratius ad id quod est in quæstione attendi oportuisset.
units.tr: Reply. Calvin's comment on verse 16 is wholly on our side, as we have seen above; but neither does he contradict us in the words cited here. For he is speaking of the moon in contrast to the sun, and therefore it is called the lesser light in this contrast. But what has this to do with the opinion of my adversaries? For the question is not how the moon can be called a lesser light with respect to the sun, but how the moon is called a great light in contrast to the stars. So here he ought to have paid somewhat closer attention to what is in question.

units.la: DVII. Exc. 5. B. p. 93. Negatam fuisse consequentiam mea majoris. Si Sol & Luna vocantur luminaria magna oppositè ad stellas, ergo hic iterum est exemplum Scripturæ usurpatis formulam phænomeno convenientem, & veritatem præjudicio involutam referentem: addità ratione, quod appellentur magna luminaria non propter apparentiam, sed propter operationem potentiam & magnitudinem.
units.tr: DVII. Exc. 5. B. p. 93. The consequence of my major premise was denied. If the sun and the moon are called great lights in contrast to the stars, then here again is an example of Scripture using a form of words suited to appearance, and expressing a truth wrapped up in prejudice: with the added reason that they are called great lights not on account of their appearance, but on account of their operation, power and magnitude.

units.la: Resp. Si per phrasin istam Gen. 1, 16. potentia operationum & magnitudo sit intelligenda, & simul ea involuta sit præjudicio de magnitudine apparente corporis atque luminis Lunæ, orto ex apparentia, ut ostendi, omnino firmata est meæ majoris connexio.
units.tr: Reply. If by that phrase in Genesis 1:16 power of operation and magnitude is to be understood, and at the same time it is wrapped up in the prejudice concerning the apparent size of the body and light of the moon, arising from its appearance, as I have shown, then the connection of my major premise is wholly established.

units.la: Inst. B. p. 94. Hâc meâ negatâ consequentiâ nec à me probatâ obtineri contrarium, nempe Scripturam loqui ex rei veritate.
units.tr: Inst. B. p. 94. Since my denied consequence has not been proved by me, the contrary is to be maintained, namely that Scripture speaks according to the truth of the matter.

units.la: Resp. Cùm ostenderim art. 501, 502. Lunam, quia ita apparet, vocari à vulgo luminare magnum, cùm & majorem vim illuminandi habeant stellæ quàm Luna, & majus lumen de se fundant, licet id propter remotionem non possit à nobis percipi, manet; Scripturam loqui convenienter phænomenis sive apparentiis, & phrasin istam præjudicio esse involutam, quamvis, prout à Spiritu Sancto usurpatur, tantum veritatem exprimat.
units.tr: Reply. Since I have shown in articles 501 and 502 that the moon is called by common people a great light because it so appears, although the stars have a greater power of illuminating than the moon and pour forth a greater light from themselves (even if this cannot be perceived by us because of their remoteness), it stands that Scripture speaks in accordance with phenomena or appearances, and that this phrase is wrapped up in prejudice, although, as it is used by the Holy Spirit, it expresses only the truth.

units.la: DVIII. Exc. 6. B. p. 95. Illa luminaria magna vocantur propter Luminis nobis exhibiti magnitudinem.
units.tr: DVIII. Exc. 6. B. p. 95. Those great lights are called great on account of the greatness of the light shown to us.

units.la: Resp. At illa magnitudo tantum est apparens eo ipso, quod nobis sit lumen magnum exhibitum. Majus enim de se fundere lumen stellas est certissimum, quamvis non majus appareat. Itaque si Luna vocatur luminare magnum, propter magnitudinem & corporis & illuminationis apparentem: Ergo exinde recte concluditur, Scripturam convenienter phænomenis loqui, non judicando de istorum phænomenon causis, num ea sensus fallaciæ, num ipsis rebus adscribi debeant.
units.tr: Reply. But that greatness is only apparent, precisely because a great light is shown to us. For that the stars pour forth a greater light from themselves is most certain, although it does not appear greater. Therefore if the moon is called a great light on account of the apparent greatness both of its body and of its illumination, then it is rightly concluded from this that Scripture speaks in accordance with phenomena, without judging whether these phenomena should be ascribed to the deceptions of the senses or to the things themselves.

units.la: DIX. Exc. 7. B. p. 96. Me mihimet contrariari videri in eo, quod dicam, Lunam vocari luminare magnum propter magnitudinem illuminationis & luminis, & tamen dicam, tantum æquivoce luminare vocari.
units.tr: DIX. Exc. 7. B. p. 96. I seem to contradict myself in saying that the moon is called a great light on account of the greatness of its illumination and light, and yet saying that it is called a light only equivocally.

units.la: Resp. Dixi, Lunam luminare magnum appellari, quod magna appareat, & respectu magnitudinis corporis & respectu illuminationis; quoniam vero simul ostendi, nullum habere lumen insitum, etiamsi ad nos magnum lumen inde perveniat, dixi, nonnisi æquivoce luminare magnum dici posse, inter quæ nulla planè contradictio existit. Corpora enim quæ ex se lumen emittunt, proprie illuminant, exque sua natura lumen fundunt; sed quæ aliunde receptum tantum remittunt, ex se vero nullum præbent, luminaria non nisi æquivoce & per accidens dicentur. Nisi enim essent alia illa luminaria proprie sic dicta, nihil hæc quicquam luminis essent præbitura.
units.tr: Reply. I said that the moon is called a great light because it appears great, both in respect of the size of its body and in respect of its illumination. But since I showed at the same time that it has no inherent light, even though a great light comes to us from it, I said that it can be called a great light only equivocally; and between these there is clearly no contradiction. For bodies which emit light from themselves properly illuminate, and pour forth light from their own nature; but those which only reflect what they have received from elsewhere, and give none of their own, will be called lights only equivocally and by accident. For unless those other things were properly so called lights, these would have no light to give at all.

units.la: DX. Exc. 8. B. p. 96. Speculum radios solares in locum tenebricosum reflectens potest dici illi loco luminare,
units.tr: DX. Exc. 8. B. p. 96. A mirror reflecting the rays of the sun into a dark place can be called a luminary for that place,

units.la: Resp. Concedo, eo modo quo Luna, sed tantum æquivoce, non univoce & proprie.
units.tr: Answer. I grant it, in the same way as the Moon, but only equivocally, not univocally and properly.

units.la: DXI. Exc. 9. B. p. 97. Ex articulis fidei & sacris literis me istam phraseologiam potuisse discere, videlicet eandem denominationem sæpe attribui & causæ efficienti & subjecto recipienti. Sic enim Spiritum vocari sanctum & Ecclesiam sanctam, Christum vocari Lucem & Ecclesiam, nec tamen dici posse, Ecclesiam vocari sanctam & Lucem habito respectu ad sensus nostros, non ex rei veritate.
units.tr: DXI. Exc. 9. B. p. 97. I could have learned this way of speaking from the articles of faith and the Holy Scriptures, namely that the same name is often applied both to the efficient cause and to the recipient subject. Thus the Spirit is called holy and the Church is called holy, and Christ is called Light and the Church is called light; yet it cannot be said that the Church is called holy and light with regard to our senses, not in the truth of the matter.

units.la: Resp. Negando quod simili ratione Sol & Luna dici possint luminaria, qua Christus dicitur sanctus & Ecclesia sancta; sanctitas enim Ecclesiæ, quamvis à Christo dependeat, inhæret & Ecclesiæ modificationem aliquam internam confert, quod de lumine Lunæ dici nequit, quod ei plane est externum, neque internam variationem confert.
units.tr: Answer. I deny that Sun and Moon can be called luminaries by the same reasoning by which Christ is called holy and the Church holy. For the holiness of the Church, although it depends on Christ, inheres in the Church and confers some internal modification on it. This cannot be said of the light of the Moon, which is wholly external to it and does not confer any internal change.

units.la: DXII. Exc. 10. B. p. 97. Ex rei veritate & accurate, non ex mera apparentia loquitur is, qui subjectum recipiens denominat ab adjuncto inhærente, quod facit Scriptura, dum Lunam dicit luminare.
units.tr: DXII. Exc. 10. B. p. 97. He who names a subject receiving something from an inhering adjunct speaks in terms of the truth of the matter and accurately, not from mere appearance; and this is what Scripture does when it calls the Moon a luminary.

units.la: Resp. At lux quæ in Luna esse dicitur, non aliter ei inhærere censeri potest, quàm radius reflexus corpori, à quo reflectitur. Unde plane extrinseca Lunæ est censenda, ac propterea proprie loquendo inhærere dici nequit. Evanescit ergo & ista exceptio, si hanc responsionem cum præcedente conferas.
units.tr: Answer. But the light said to be in the Moon cannot be regarded as inhering in it any differently from a ray reflected from the body from which it is reflected. Hence it must be regarded as wholly external to the Moon, and therefore, speaking properly, it cannot be said to inhere. So this objection also vanishes, if you compare this answer with the previous one.

units.la: DXIII. Exc. 11. B. p. 97. Me tantum pro authoritate dicere, stellæ fixæ lucem insitam competere constat.
units.tr: DXIII. Exc. 11. B. p. 97. It is agreed that I say, on the authority of others, that the fixed stars have innate light.

units.la: Resp. Quia hoc habui pro tali, quod extra quæstionem inter Principes Philosophos est positum, probatio ejus hic mihi videbatur superfvacanea. Nunc tamen in gratiam adversarii unum argumentum, quod instar omnium sit, afferam; quale est, quod stellæ fixæ valde vivi-dos dos radios vibrent, & tamen longissime à nobis & Sole distent; unde evinci posse puto, eis lucem insitam competere.
units.tr: Answer. Because I took this to be something settled beyond dispute among the leading philosophers, a proof of it seemed to me superfluous here. Now, however, to oblige my opponent, I will offer one argument which may serve for all: the fixed stars send out very bright rays, and yet they are at a very great distance from us and from the Sun. From this I think it can be shown that they have innate light.

units.la: DXIV. Exc. 12. B. p. 98. Valde dilutum esse, quod dicam Terram potiori jure pro luminari habendam. 1. Quia Moses refert quenam luminaria Deus dederit Terræ, ineptum ergo futurum fuisse de Terra ut alio luminari agere.
units.tr: DXIV. Exc. 12. B. p. 98. It is very weak to say that the Earth should rather be regarded as a luminary. 1. Because Moses reports which luminaries God gave to the Earth; it would therefore be absurd for the Earth to act as another luminary.

units.la: Resp. At ego non dixi, debuisse id facere Moßen, atque contra usum loqui, sed tantum consideratione habita reflexionis radiorum & magnitudinis corporum potiori jure pro luminari habendam, quam Lunam; atque homines si accurate loqui voluissent, potius Terram hoc titulo debuisse insignire, atque eam in absentia Solis magis homines fuisse illuminaturam, si extra ejus globum & in loco, ubi nunc est Luna, ponere-tur.
units.tr: Answer. But I did not say that Moses ought to have done this and spoken contrary to usage. I said only that, considering the reflection of rays and the size of the bodies, the Earth should rather be regarded as a luminary than the Moon. And if men had wished to speak accurately, they ought rather to have given the Earth this title, and in the absence of the Sun the Earth would light men more, if it were placed outside its globe and in the place where the Moon now is.

units.la: Inst. B. p. 98. At reflexionis luminis magnitudo maxime dependet non à corporis reflectentis magnitudine, sed ejusdem ad reflectendum apta dispositione.
units.tr: Objection. But the magnitude of the reflection of light depends chiefly not on the size of the reflecting body but on its suitable disposition for reflecting.

units.la: Resp. Si par sit dispositio utriusque corporis, Terræ & Lunæ, uti existimo & ostendi, dico magnitudinem majorum corporum reflectentium efficere, ut illa luminaria etiam majus lumen reflectant.
units.tr: Answer. If the disposition of both bodies, Earth and Moon, is equal, as I believe and have shown, I say that the greater size of the larger reflecting bodies makes those luminaries reflect a greater light as well.

units.la: DXV. Exc. 13. (H. p. 52. qui prolixior hic paulo, quàm ad rem) Deum fecisse Solem & Lunam magna luminaria novis, ut calceum sutor pedi minori.
units.tr: DXV. Exc. 13. (H. p. 52., which is here somewhat longer than the matter requires) God made the Sun and the Moon great luminaries, as a shoemaker makes a shoe too small for the foot.

units.la: Resp. Quæritur, an non illa phrasis, qua Sol & Luna dicuntur luminaria magna, oppositè ad stellas (quæ ex demonstrationibus Astronomicis longe majores sunt, quàm Luna) ortum habeat ex præjudicio? quod ego affirmo. Neque id per istam exceptionem elidi-tur; quòd enim Moses per istam phrasin significet veritatem ad nos relatam non nego.
units.tr: Answer. The question is whether that phrase, by which the Sun and Moon are called great luminaries, as opposed to the stars (which by astronomical demonstrations are far larger than the Moon), does not arise from prejudice. I affirm that it does. Nor is this refuted by that objection; for I do not deny that Moses, by this phrase, signifies a truth related to us.

units.la: 2. Calceus Petræ applicatus est magnus vel parvus, major vel minor: at si æque stellæ nobis applicarentur ac Luna, hoc est, si in eadem sint distantia, accurate loquendo, nobis etiam majores dici deberent. Ergò etiam secundùm istam exceptionem locutio dicta phænomeno est accommodata, & præjudicio involuta.
units.tr: 2. A shoe applied to a rock is large or small, greater or lesser. But if the stars were applied to us in the same way as the Moon, that is, if they were at the same distance, then, speaking accurately, they too ought to be called larger. Therefore, according to this objection also, the expression is adapted to the appearance and wrapped in prejudice.

units.la: DXVI. Exc. 14. H. p. 55. Quia eorum quantitas non restringitur, non determinatur: ideo quorum respectu Luna major vel minor sit, hinc decidere non possumus, si vel omnes subtilissimi ingenii exhauriamus vires.
units.tr: DXVI. Exc. 14. H. p. 55. Because their quantity is not restricted, it is not determined; so we cannot decide from this passage in relation to which things the Moon is larger or smaller, even if we exhaust all the powers of the most subtle wit.

units.la: Resp. Non posse nos aliud ex isto loco decidere, quàm id quod Spiritus Sanctus per verba citata voluit significatum, quod art. 503. indicavimus, vimus, libenter concedo, sed quæritur: an non formula illa, qua voluit Sp. S. hanc veritatem significare, sit præjudicio involuta, & ad sensus hominum relata? Id ex Scriptura decidi non potest, sed ex usu vulgari & origine hujus formulæ, quæ est opinio, quod Luna sit luminare majus quàm stellæ, à quâ hanc formulam dicimus ortam.
units.tr: Answer. I readily grant that we cannot decide anything from that passage except what the Holy Spirit wished to signify by the words cited, which I indicated in art. 503. But the question is whether that form of words, by which the Holy Spirit wished to express this truth, is not involved in prejudice and related to the senses of men. This cannot be decided from Scripture, but from common usage and the origin of this form, which is the opinion that the Moon is a larger luminary than the stars, and from which we say this form arose.

units.la: DXVII. Exc. 15. (H. p. 56.) Nondum probatum esse Solem & Lunam vocari luminaria magna oppositæ ad stellas.
units.tr: DXVII. Exc. 15. (H. p. 56.) It has not yet been proved that the Sun and Moon are called great luminaries as opposed to the stars.

units.la: Resp. Id attendenti textum per se futurum erat manifestum. Sed videat lector art. 501. hujus capitis, ubi id clare probatum invenier.
units.tr: Answer. For one who attends to the text, this would have been clear in itself. But let the reader see art. 501 of this chapter, where he will find it clearly proved.

units.la: Inst. (H. p. 56.) Restrictionem ad reliquas stellas in textu citato non esse, sed comparari Lunam cum Sole atque ejus respectu vocari luminare minus.
units.tr: Objection. (H. p. 56.) In the cited text there is no restriction to the remaining stars; rather the Moon is compared with the Sun, and in relation to it is called the lesser luminary.

units.la: Resp. Hoc verò non nego, nec id prolixe opus erat probari; sed quemadmodum in illis verbis, luminare majus & luminare minus, est oppositio inter Solem & Lunam, ita in illis: Deus fecit duo luminaria magna atque stellas, est oppositio inter Solem & Lunam conjunctim ab una parte & stellas ab altera.
units.tr: Answer. This I do not deny, nor was it necessary to prove it at length. But just as in the words greater luminary and lesser luminary there is an opposition between Sun and Moon, so in those words, God made two great luminaries and the stars, there is an opposition between Sun and Moon taken together on one side and the stars on the other.

units.la: DXVIII. Exc. 16. (H. p. 58.) Sancta materia & textûs expositionem esse simplicissimam secundum veritatis rotunditatem debere, non ad hypothesin Geometricam reflectendam, meam vero & Belgarum interpretum non esse simplicissimam, nec secundum veritatis normam.
units.tr: DXVIII. Exc. 16. (H. p. 58.) A holy subject and the exposition of the text ought to be most simple, according to the roundness of truth, and not bent back to a geometrical hypothesis; but my interpretation and that of the Dutch interpreters is not most simple, nor according to the standard of truth.

units.la: Resp. Expositionem nostram esse simplicissimam & rotundam ex art. 501. apparet, cui non repugnat, si dicamus, formulam loquendi, quæ quidem ut à Spiritu Sancto abhibetur veritatem significat, præjudicio alicui ortum debere, quod hic tantum intendimus. Quæ porro disputat (H. p. 58. & seqq.) contra Calvinum, ea quantum ad me faciunt, jam sunt refutata: præsupponit torqueri Scripturam, & pollui ejus veritatem à nobis &c. quæ probata oportebat. Philosophari dicit Moses; at unde hoc constat? cum naturas rerum & affectiones non doceat, nec demonstret, sed phrasibus utatur communibus & vulgaribus ad phænomena accommodatis, & in descriptione rerum naturalium, postquam omnia ad Deum auctorem retulisset, supra communem notitiam se non extollat. Videatur hujus tractatûs primum caput, ad quod velim attendi ab adversario; sic enim plurima dubia, quæ movet, p. 60, 61, 62. ipsi eximentur.
units.tr: Answer. That our exposition is most simple and round appears from art. 501, which is not contradicted if we say that the form of speech, which indeed as used by the Holy Spirit signifies truth, ought to have arisen from some prejudice; and this is all we are here intending. As for what he argues (H. p. 58 and following) against Calvin, this, so far as it concerns me, has already been refuted. He presupposes that Scripture is twisted, and its truth is polluted by us, etc., which ought to have been proved. He says Moses philosophizes; but how is this established? Moses does not teach or demonstrate the natures and affections of things, but uses common and popular phrases adapted to appearances, and in describing natural things, after he has referred everything to God as author, he does not raise himself above common knowledge. Let the adversary attend to the first chapter of this treatise, for by it most of the doubts he raises on pp. 60, 61, 62 will be removed.

units.la: DXIX. Exc. 17. (H. p. 61.) Si, quæ hic loci de luminaribus dicuntur, occulta intelligit mysteria, involvit contradictionem Calvinus.
units.tr: DXIX. Exc. 17. (H. p. 61.) If what is said here about the luminaries is understood to be hidden mysteries, Calvin involves himself in a contradiction.

units.la: Resp. Per occulta mysteria intelligit Calvinus veram Solis, Lunæ, & stellarum magnitudinem, quæ occulta sunt plebejis hominibus, de quibus loquitur Calvinus. Ubi ergò contradictio? Videtur in eo conflituí stitui ab adversario, quod rerum naturalium qualitates & proportio occulta mysteria esse nequeant; verum si attendat, quibus occulta esse dicat, plebejis nempe non indagantibus, omne contradictionis phantasma evanescet.
units.tr: Reply: By hidden mysteries Calvin means the true magnitude of the Sun, Moon and stars, which is hidden from common people, of whom Calvin speaks. Where, then, is the contradiction? The opponent seems to rest his case on the claim that the qualities and proportions of natural things cannot be hidden mysteries. But if he considers to whom Calvin says they are hidden, namely to common people who do not investigate them, every appearance of contradiction will vanish.

units.la: DXX. Exc. 18. (H.p. 62.) Calvinus forte non negat Mosen philosophari, sed negat acutè philosophari.
units.tr: DXX. Exc. 18. (H. p. 62.) Perhaps Calvin does not deny that Moses philosophises, but he denies that he philosophises acutely.

units.la: Resp. Contrarium constat exinde, quod το philosophari opponit referre quae rudibus etiam nota sunt: at hoc nec est philosophari, nec acute philosophari.
units.tr: Reply: The contrary is clear from the fact that Calvin sets against "to philosophise" [τὸ φιλοσοφεῖν] the phrase "to relate things that are known even to the unlearned." But this is neither philosophising nor philosophising acutely.

units.la: DXXI. Exc. 19. (H. p.63.) Refert Calvinus ibidem mysteria non ad luminaria, sed ad signa.
units.tr: DXXI. Exc. 19. (H. p. 63.) Calvin there refers the mysteries not to the luminaries but to the signs.

units.la: Resp. Quod referat ad luminaria manifestum est ex nota ejus ad v. 16. Dixi, Mosen hic non subtiliter differere de natura arcanis, ut Philosophum, quod in his verbis videre est &c. Moses duo facit luminaria: Atqui Astrologi firmis rationibus probant, Saturni sidus, quod omnium minimum propter longinquitatem apparet, lunari esse majus.
units.tr: Reply: That he refers them to the luminaries is plain from his note on v. 16: "I have said that Moses does not here discuss the secret nature of things subtly, as a philosopher would, as can be seen in these words, etc. Moses makes two luminaries." Yet astrologers prove by firm arguments that the planet Saturn, which appears smallest of all because of its distance, is larger than the Moon.

units.la: DXXII. Exc. 20. (H. p. 73.) Aliud est, quaerere quam ob causam Moses ista luminaria magna appellaverit. Aliud, ob quam jam & hodie magna appellentur. Moses non fecit id, quia talia apparebant; adeoque non ad apparentiam, sed ad Jehova collocutoris sui eloquia attendit. Huic affine est, quod p. 76,77. cujus summa huc redit: Mosen contemplatum esse in Sancto Spiritu istam universitatem, atque ita literis consignasse, absque cogitatione terra vel hominum.
units.tr: DXXII. Exc. 20. (H. p. 73.) It is one thing to ask why Moses called those luminaries great, and another to ask why they are now and already called great. Moses did not do it because they appeared so; therefore he attended not to appearance but to the utterances of Jehovah, his speaker. Related to this is what he says on pp. 76–77, the sum of which comes to this: Moses contemplated this universe in the Holy Spirit, and so committed it to writing without thought of earth or of men.

units.la: Resp. Concedimus, Mosen scripsisse ea quae Deus inspirabat, & ea ipsa verba: at quia Deus ea scribi voluit hominibus, ut ab iis sensus eorum perciperetur, censendum est, voluisse proponere phrasibus receptis, quas circa res naturales phaenomenis respondere, & sæpe præjudiciis involutas esse certum est, atque id ipsum est, quod ego probandum suscepi. An verò hoc pugnet cum Spiritu Sancto & verbo ejus, ut sæpius repetit antagonista, nos in Obj. refutatione examinabimus. 2. Dubium non est, quin Sp. Sanctus phrasi recepta utens, veritatem per eam significet, quamvis per eandem phrasin homo præjudiciis præoccupatus, errorem confisignificet; adeoque hactenus, aliam ob causam Sp. S. adhibere phrasin receptam, nempe ad solam veritatem docendam, aliam ob causam homines præjudiciis occupatos, nempe ad consignificandum errorem, nequaquam negamus.
units.tr: Reply: We grant that Moses wrote what God inspired, and those very words. But because God wished these things to be written for men so that their sense might be perceived by them, it must be judged that he wished to set them forth in received phrases, which correspond to the appearances of natural things and which are certainly often wrapped up in prejudices. This is exactly what I undertook to prove. Whether this conflicts with the Holy Spirit and his word, as the antagonist often repeats, we shall examine in our refutation of the objections. 2. There is no doubt that the Holy Spirit, using a received phrase, signifies the truth through it, even though a man preoccupied with prejudices may signify error through the same phrase. Thus we by no means deny that the Holy Spirit uses a received phrase for one reason, namely to teach the truth alone, while men occupied with prejudices use it for another reason, namely to signify error as well.

units.la: DXXIII. Haec sunt, quæ in verboso H. discursu contra me facere videbantur. Et jam satis prolixe de loco per se claro est actum, Atque hacte-
units.tr: DXXIII. These are the points which seemed to tell against me in the wordy discourse of H. And now the matter, which is clear in itself, has been treated at sufficient length. And so far

units.la: hactenus observata applicari possunt iis, quæ M. à p. 98. ad 112. objici, cùm homogenea sunt objectionibus & exceptionibus B. & H. paucis his specialiter adhuc notatis. Ac primo quoniam negat, Lunæ omne lumen esse adventitium, item stellas habere lucem insitam, nos id prolixius ostendimus. Atque ut de Luna primum agamus, præmittendum, eam semper eandem nobis obvertere plagam, quo posito dicimus, si lux aliqua Lunæ esset, ea apertissime se ostenderet in Eclipsibus Lunaribus, quod tamen experientiæ contrariatur. Corpus enim lucidum tanto clarius apparet, quanto ambiens est obscurius, quod observare licet in stellis fixis, quæ interdiu non minus lucent, quam nocte, sed ob circumfusum Solis lumen cerni nequeunt. 2. Interdum subito Luna tota penitus amittitur, ut ne vestigium quidem ejus appareat, cum tamen proxime locum ejus cerni possint fixæ quartæ vel quintæ magnitudinis: quare tunc locum non habet suspicio caliginosi nimium Aëris. Sic factum est anno 1620 Junii. Hoc est argumentum Kepleri. Quod vero lumen in Luna conspicuum sit ex reflexione Terræ, apparet inde, quia videmus illud lumen secundarium biduo vel triduo ante aut post conjunctionem omnium maximum esse, post autem, prout Luna magis, magisque recedit à Sole, etiam lucem hanc secundariam in Luna decrescere, ut tandem post primam quadraturam nulla plane appareat, idque nullam aliam ob causam, nisi quod Luna tunc tanto intervallo à Sole digreditur, ut radii à Terra reflexi eam assequi nequeant. Ex quibus patet, non posse debilitatem istius lucis insitæ causam esse, quare lumen Lunæ non conspiciatur eo tempore; quantacunque enim illa sit, cum stellæ quartæ & quintæ magnitudinis appareant, quæ infinito longius distant, etiam Lunam adeo propinquam videri oporteret; dispositio vero & habitudo ad nos inepta non potest prætendi cum M. quoniam experientia teste, Luna eandem semper plagam nobis obvertit. Nec dici potest, contiguam radiationem aliorum astrorum illud turbare; cum non turbet illud lumen, quod à Terra reflexum in eâ conspicitur. Ac tandem corpus, quod interjici diceres (ponitur enim serenus Aër, nulla nubes) nullum dari potest, nisi forte dicas per miraculum novum corpus creatum, quod frigidum est satis.
units.tr: what has been observed so far can be applied to those things which M. objects from pp. 98 to 112, since they are homogeneous with the objections and exceptions of B. and H., with these few points still specially noted. First, since he denies that all the light of the Moon is borrowed, and likewise that the stars have innate light, we shall show this more fully. And to deal first with the Moon: it must be premised that it always turns the same side toward us. Given this, we say that if the Moon had any light of its own, it would show itself most plainly in lunar eclipses, which however is contrary to experience. For a luminous body appears all the brighter the darker its surroundings are, as may be observed in the fixed stars, which by day shine no less than by night but cannot be seen because of the surrounding light of the Sun. 2. Sometimes the Moon is suddenly lost altogether, so that not even a trace of it appears, although fixed stars of the fourth or fifth magnitude can be seen very close to its place. So the suspicion of an overly misty air has no place here. This happened in June 1620. This is Kepler's argument. That the light visible in the Moon comes from reflection from the Earth is shown by the fact that we see this secondary light is greatest two or three days before or after conjunction, and afterwards, as the Moon recedes more and more from the Sun, this secondary light in the Moon decreases, until finally after the first quadrature it appears not at all, and this for no other reason than that the Moon then lies at such a distance from the Sun that the rays reflected from the Earth cannot reach it. From these things it is plain that the weakness of that innate light cannot be the cause why the light of the Moon is not seen at that time. For however great it might be, since stars of the fourth and fifth magnitude are visible, which are infinitely farther away, the Moon, being so near, ought to be seen too. Nor can M. plead an unsuitable disposition and relation to us, since, as experience witnesses, the Moon always turns the same side toward us. Nor can it be said that the adjacent radiation of other stars disturbs it, since that light which is seen in it reflected from the Earth is not disturbed. And finally, any body which you might say intervenes (for the air is assumed to be clear, with no cloud) cannot exist, unless perhaps you say that by a new miracle a body has been created, which is cold enough.

units.la: Objeƈt. Tempore defectus aliquando rubicunda apparet. Ergo habet insitam lucem.
units.tr: Objection. At times during an eclipse the Moon appears reddish. Therefore it has innate light.

units.la: Resp. Ille rubor nullo modo proprio ipsius lumini adscribi potest, sed potius ætheri Lunæ circumfuso, & radiis Solaribus ab eo refractis, umbramque Terræ adstringentibus, qui facile Lunæ per umbram apogæam transeunti aliquem colorem subrufum inducere possunt. Idque necessa-rio rio huic causæ adscribendum, quoniam si hoc ex luce ei insita penderet, semper Luna Aëre sereno rubicunda apparere deberet. Stellis lucem insitam competere, art. 512. probavi.
units.tr: Reply: That redness cannot in any way be ascribed to its own light, but rather to the ether surrounding the Moon and to the solar rays refracted by it, which contract the Earth's shadow, and which can easily impart some reddish colour to the Moon as it passes through the shadow at its apogee. And this must necessarily be ascribed to this cause, since if it depended on light innate in it, the Moon ought always to appear reddish in clear air. I have proved in article 512 that innate light belongs to the stars.

units.la: DXXIV. Sed 2. notamus contra M. objectiones: Absurdam esse ejus interpretationem qua putat: Moses duo vocare luminaria, sed tamen forte unum intelligere, cujus absurditas, modo proponatur lectori per se est manifesta. 3 Satis manifeste probavimus, quando Sol & Luna dicuntur luminaria magna, id dici oppositæ ad stellas, quibus in ista vulgari locutione in hoc tertio magnitudinis opponuntur. 4. Quod majus corpus cæteris paribus, id est, si eadem sit ejus raritas vel densitas in superficie externa, majus lumen reflectat, quam minus, ex te satis apertum est. 5. Quid sit Æquivocum, non opus erat, ut M. tam operose me doceret. Cùm lumen illud, quod à Lunâ reflexum ad nos pervenit, non sit Lunæ, sed Solis, non magis univoce Lunam luminare dici posse, quam speculum, manifestum est, adeoque & nocte ipsâ à Sole nos illuminari, si accurate loquive velimus, esset dicendum. 6. Exinde etiam manifestum est, majorem esse convenientiam Solis & candelæ, quam Lunæ & Solis, cum lux candelæ ei sit propria, Lunæ verò nulla. 7. Cum Solis lumen sit maxime forte & vividum, nimisque Sol distet à stellis fixis, Lunæ verò & planetarum reliquorum, ut etiam ipsius terræ sit tenue & debile, non nisi absurdissime philosophando dices, Solis lucem esse collectam ex luce stellarum fixarum & Planetarum. 8. Quod verò M. videat in responsione meâ ad Objeẚt. B. quod ipse B. non potuit videre, nimirum, me concessis pramisso negare conclusionem, in eo se satis oculatum ostendit. Argumentum B. tale proponit: Eo modo Luna dicitur luminaribus major, quo Sol dicitur Lunâ major. Atqui Sol non dicitur ideo Lunâ major, quod major appareat extensio, & moles Solis, ergo nec Luna: Verum ex mea responsione liquet, me istam Majorem propositionem; Quo modo Sol dicitur major Lunâ, eo modo Luna dicitur major stellis, negare: si enim illa vera, subsumere liceret; atque Sol Lunâ est major ratione magnitudinis, extensionis & illuminationis simul. Ergò etiam Luna, quod tamen aperte est falsum. 9. Contradictio vero nulla est inter ea verba, ubi major & diffusior lux apparet in corpore lucido, ibi etiam ipsum corpus lucidum majus apparere necessarium est, & : Sol etsi Luna major sit illuminatione, non tamen disco & magnitudine apparet major. Non enim dico, quod in Sole major & diffusior lux appareat quam in Luna, quod si dicerem, non possem concedere ejus discum Lunæ disco æqualem, sed tantum quod intensior & vividior; Major autem illuminatio respectu nostri oriFtur tur tum exinde, si alicujus corporis, cujus discus æqualis est alteri, lux sit intensior, & vividior, & sic major à Sole, quam à Luna oritur ; tum etiam, si magnitudo alterius corporis appareat multoties major, etsi Lumen non sit adeo vividum, & sic Luna majus est luminare quam stellæ. 10. Similis ratio est alterius contradictionis, quam mihi affingit ; quamvis enim Lunæ competat illuminatio, non tamen lux insita, quia per lucem reflexam, quæ propterea ejus lux dici potest, illuminare est dicenda. Et mirum est, quod tanti Astronomi, qui negant competere Lunæ lucem insitam, & tamen statuunt illuminare, debuerint exspectare hunc hominem, qui ipsis ostenderet contradictionem, quam in sua sententia mecum comminiscerint.
units.tr: DXXIV. But second, we note against M.'s objections: his interpretation, by which he thinks that Moses calls them two luminaries, but perhaps means one, is absurd, and its absurdity is plain of itself once it is set before the reader. 3. We have sufficiently clearly proved that when the Sun and Moon are called the great luminaries, this is said in contrast to the stars, which in this common mode of speaking are opposed to them in the third degree of magnitude. 4. That a larger body, other things being equal (that is, if its rarity or density at the outer surface is the same), reflects more light than a smaller one, is clear enough from your own statement. 5. There was no need for M. to teach me so laboriously what an equivocal term is. Since the light that reaches us reflected from the Moon is not the Moon's but the Sun's, the Moon cannot be called a luminary univocally any more than a mirror can; so, if we wished to speak accurately, it would have to be said that we are lit even at night by the Sun. 6. From this it is also plain that the Sun and a candle have a closer likeness than the Moon and the Sun, since the light of a candle belongs to it, but the Moon has none. 7. Since the light of the Sun is very strong and vivid, and the Sun is very far from the fixed stars, while the light of the Moon and of the other planets, as well as of the Earth itself, is faint and weak, you will say nothing except in the most absurd kind of philosophising if you say that the light of the Sun is gathered from the light of the fixed stars and the planets. 8. But that M. sees, in my reply to B.'s objection, what B. himself could not see, namely that I deny the conclusion while granting the premises, shows him to be rather sharp-sighted in that. B. puts his argument thus: In the same way the Moon is said to be greater than the luminaries as the Sun is said to be greater than the Moon. But the Sun is not called greater than the Moon because its extension and bulk appear larger; therefore neither is the Moon. But from my reply it is clear that I deny that major premise: "In the way the Sun is said to be greater than the Moon, in that way the Moon is said to be greater than the stars." For if that were true, one might assume the minor; and the Sun is greater than the Moon in respect of magnitude, extension and illumination together. Therefore the Moon too, which is nevertheless clearly false. 9. There is no contradiction between these words: where a greater and more diffuse light appears in a luminous body, there the luminous body itself must necessarily appear larger, and: although the Sun is greater than the Moon in illumination, it does not appear greater in disc and magnitude. For I do not say that a greater and more diffuse light appears in the Sun than in the Moon; if I said that, I could not grant that its disc is equal to the Moon's disc, but only that its light is more intense and vivid. A greater illumination with respect to us arises partly from this: if the light of one body, whose disc is equal to another's, is more intense and vivid, and so the Sun produces greater light than the Moon does; and partly also if the apparent magnitude of one body is many times greater, even though its light is not so vivid. So the Moon is a greater luminary than the stars. 10. A similar argument answers another contradiction which he attributes to me. For although illumination belongs to the Moon, innate light does not, because what is illuminated by reflected light, which may therefore be called its light, must be said to be illuminated. And it is remarkable that such great astronomers, who deny that innate light belongs to the Moon and yet hold that it illuminates, should have needed this man to show them the contradiction which they had themselves devised in their view along with me.

units.la: DXXV. Sextum inductionis exemplum suppeditat locus Act. xxvii. 27. Nautæ circa medium noctis suspicati sunt, προσάγειν, appropinquare sibi aliquam regionem.
units.tr: DXXV. The sixth example of induction is supplied by Acts 27:27: "The sailors suspected about midnight that they were drawing near [προσάγειν, prosagein] some region."

units.la: Locutio hæc desumpta est à vulgari visus fallacia, quâ fit, ut, dum navi vehimur, littora accedere vel recedere videantur, terraque urbesque recedunt. Similiter dicere solemus iter facientes, daer komt een berg, cum tamen mons non adveniat, sed nos ad illum accedamus. Sic appropinquantes urbi, ut videre illam possint, dicere consueverunt, daer komt defe of defe stadt. Ipsa quidem appropinquatio est mutua, quæ fit per imminutionem distantiæ, quæ exsistit inter duo corpora, ob alia corpora interjecta, sed tamen τὸ appropinquare, cum connotet actionem, proprie & accurate loquendo non potest tribui, nisi ei, in quo est ista actio, non vero alteri. Atque ita proprie loquendo navis appropinquat regioni, non regio navi, cum motus denique iis proprie & ἀχεῖσθαι tribuatur, quæ simul recedunt ab omnibus corporibus immediate contiguis, non vero iis, quæ tantum ab uno vel altero recedunt, patet iterum accurate loquendo navi competere motum, adeoque appropinquationem, non regioni, cum illa ab omnibus corporibus immediate contiguis simul recedat, non ita regio. Interea tamen vicissim Sp. S. per hanc locutionem vulgarem & minus accuratam significat, Nautas suspicatos fuisse, se propiores fieri alicui regioni, quod verum est, quamvis ea veritas & à nautis & à Spiritu Sancto efferretur phrasi, quæ fallaciæ visûs & infantiæ præjudicio, quo motus & appropinquatio rebus extra nos positis ac visui propioribus factis, adscribi solet, innitatur.
units.tr: This expression is taken from the common illusion of sight, by which, while we are carried in a ship, the shores seem to approach or recede, and the land and cities seem to move away. We similarly say when travelling, daer komt een berg ("there comes a mountain"), although the mountain does not come to us, but we approach it. So too, when people draw near a city so that they can see it, they are accustomed to say, daer komt defe of defe stadt ("there comes this or that city"). The approach itself is mutual, brought about by the lessening of the distance between two bodies, caused by other bodies lying between them. But since to approach (appropinquare) implies an action, it can properly and strictly speaking be ascribed only to that which performs the action, and not to the other. So, strictly speaking, the ship approaches the region, not the region the ship. For motion is properly and strictly ascribed to those things which recede at the same time from all the bodies immediately contiguous to them, and not to those which recede only from one or another. It is clear again that, strictly speaking, motion, and therefore approach, belongs to the ship, not to the region, since the region does not recede simultaneously from all the bodies immediately contiguous to it. Meanwhile, conversely, the Holy Spirit by this common and less exact expression signifies that the sailors suspected they were coming nearer to some region. This is true, although that truth is expressed both by the sailors and by the Holy Spirit in a phrase that rests on the deception of sight and on the prejudice of infancy, by which motion and approach are commonly ascribed to things outside us which become nearer to the sight.

units.la: DXXVI. Exc. I. B. p. 102. Dicere Sp. S. non quod regio appropin- quaret, sed quod talis fuerit nautarum suspicio.
units.tr: DXXVI. Exception I, B, p. 102: the Holy Spirit does not say that the region drew near, but that such was the sailors' suspicion.

units.la: Resp. Suspicio nautarum erat, quod aliqua regio sibi propinquior fieret, atque ea postea experientia comprobata, quam suam suspicionem & ipsi & Sp. S. verbis communiter receptis fallacia visus & praejudicio infantiæ obvolutis, significarunt. Nihil ergo hâc exceptione mihi contradicitur. Uti nec Exc. 2. B. p. 102. Visus non fallit, sed judicium mentis.
units.tr: Answer: The sailors' suspicion was that some region was becoming nearer to them, and this was afterwards confirmed by experience. They and the Holy Spirit both expressed this suspicion in commonly accepted words, wrapped in the deception of sight and the prejudice of infancy. Therefore nothing is contradicted in me by this exception. Nor is it so with Exception 2, B, p. 102: Sight does not deceive, but the judgement of the mind does.

units.la: Resp. Non ita absurdus est Cartesius & nos cum eo, ut visui oppositè ad judicium mentis errorem tribuamus, sed quando dicimus visum errare, sumimus concretè, complectendo omnes tres visûs gradus. Vid. Claub. Exercitatione XVIII. de Cognitione Dei & nostri.
units.tr: Answer: Descartes is not so absurd, nor are we with him, as to attribute error to the judgement of the mind as opposed to sight. But when we say that sight errs, we take the word in the concrete sense, embracing all three degrees of sight. See Clauberg, Exercise XVIII, on the knowledge of God and of ourselves.

units.la: DXXVII. Exc. 3. B. p. 102. Quando objecta remota appropinquare dicuntur, non respicitur, in quo subjecto fiat motus, sed quodnam sit illud subjectum, cui appropinquatio tribuitur.
units.tr: DXXVII. Exception 3, B, p. 102: When distant objects are said to approach, one does not consider in which subject the motion takes place, but what that subject is to which the approach is ascribed.

units.la: Resp. Id mihi planè non incommodat: sufficit enim ad meum scopum, quòd corpus illud, cujus ego, dum iter facio, quasi partem constituo, cujusmodi est navis, sit id cui competit motus, cùm tamen in locutione præsenti ille motus non mihi nec isti corpori tribuatur, sed potius illi corpori, quod quiescit, quale est urbs vel littora, propter sensus apparentiam & præjudicium, quod super eâ est fundatum.
units.tr: Answer: This does not trouble me at all. For it is enough for my purpose that the body of which I, while travelling, am as it were a part, such as the ship, is the one to which the motion belongs. Yet in the present expression that motion is ascribed neither to me nor to that body, but rather to the body which is at rest, such as the city or the shores, on account of the appearance to the senses and the prejudice founded upon it.

units.la: DXXVIII. Quæ H. hic habet p. 239. pro me potius faciunt. Concedit, esse locutionem à communi visus errore desumptam; atqui ego similiter doceo, phrasin adhiberi phænomeno convenientem: item Spiritus Sanctus, inquit, nautarum more loquendi phrases sicuti prolatæ sunt describi jussit. Quod est illud ipsum, quod ego intendo, Spiritum Sanctum à receptis formulis non recedere, etsi illæ præjudiciis infantiæ innitantur.
units.tr: DXXVIII. What H. says here at p. 239 rather favours me. He concedes that the expression is taken from the common error of sight. Yet I likewise teach that a phrase is used which agrees with the phenomenon. Likewise: The Holy Spirit, he says, bade the phrases to be described just as they were uttered, in the manner of the sailors' way of speaking. This is exactly what I intend: that the Holy Spirit does not depart from received forms of speech, even though these rest on prejudices of infancy.

units.la: DXXIX. Exc. 4. M. p. 212. Forte esse in verbis tropum, quem Hypallagen vocant, ut apud Virgilium: dare classibus Austros.
units.tr: DXXIX. Exception 4, M, p. 212: Perhaps there is in the words a trope which they call hypallage, as in Virgil: "to give the winds to the fleets".

units.la: Resp. Ad illud forte, ego si per forte non respondeam, satisfecero isti exceptioni; quod verò locutio sit à visus fallacia desumpta, phænomeno conveniens, supra ostendi.
units.tr: Answer: If I answer to this "perhaps" with "perhaps not", I have satisfied this exception. That the expression is taken from the deception of sight and agrees with the phenomenon I have shown above.

units.la: DXXX. Septimum inductionis exemplum desumimus ex Epistolâ Judæ com. 3. ubi de Pseudo-prophetis dicit, quòd sint ἀστέρες πλανῆται stellæ erraticæ. Erit enim hic iterum exemplum formulæ loquendi ab erronea opinione desumptæ, si per planetas intelligamus corpora ista opaca in æthere constituta, Solis lumen ad nos reflectentia, qualia sunt Luna, Mars, Venus &c. Non enim revera errant, cum leges sui motûs exactissimè servent, uti ex Astronomia constat. Sed Planetæ dicuntur, quia secundum sensuum apparentiam errare videntur. Et sanè nihil impedit, quo minus ita sumamus, quum voluerit Apostolus exprimere istorum hominum inconstantiam & instabilem doctrinam, quemadmodum Belgæ interpretes hic nobis consentiunt, apud quos hæc nota reperitur, dat is, Planeten, welcker loop hoewel se seecker is, so schijnense ons nochtans te dwaelen, om dat haer en loop niet eenparigh en is, met de andere sterren. Dacr by vergelijckt by haere ongestadigheyt, quæ verba sic Latine reddimus: hoc est, Planetæ, quorum cursus quamvis sit certus, videntur tamen errare, quia ipsorum cursus non conformis est reliquarum stellarum cursui. Huic comparat ipsorum inconstantiam. Veritas ergo hâc phrasi expressa erit, irregularis astrorum[?] corporum situs respectu oculorum variatio, obvoluta hoc præjudicio, quod sine norma hinc inde discurrunt. Attamen quia alii interpretes per Planetas intelligunt ignem fatuum, alii stellas cadentes, non multum de hoc loco disputabimus, sufficient reliqui loci adducti.
units.tr: DXXX. We take the seventh example of induction from the Epistle of Jude, verse 3, where he speaks of false prophets as ἀστέρες πλανῆται [asteres planetai], "wandering stars". Here again there will be an example of a form of speech taken from a mistaken opinion, if by planets we understand those opaque bodies situated in the ether which reflect the light of the sun to us, such as the Moon, Mars, Venus and so on. For they do not really wander, since they keep exactly to the laws of their motion, as is clear from astronomy. But they are called planets because they seem to wander according to the appearance to the senses. Indeed nothing prevents us from taking it so, since the Apostle wished to express the inconstancy and unstable teaching of those men. So the Belgian translators agree with us here, and among them this note is found: that is, the planets, whose course, although it is certain, yet seems to wander to us, because their course is not uniform with the other stars. He compares to this their inconstancy. The truth expressed by this phrase will therefore be the irregular variation of the position of the heavenly bodies with respect to the eyes, wrapped in the prejudice that they run hither and thither without rule. However, since other interpreters understand by the planets will-o'-the-wisps and others falling stars, we shall not dispute much about this passage; the other passages adduced will suffice.

units.la: DXXX. B. p. 105. Hic intelligit Planetas proprie dictos, atque dicit: iis ab Astronomis nomen impositum Planetarum, quia ab ipsis observantur varii illorum motus apparentes, quibus hominibus errantibus similes videntur.
units.tr: DXXX, B, p. 105. Here he understands the planets properly so called, and says: they were given the name of planets by the astronomers, because their various apparent motions are observed by them, and these seem to be like erring men.

units.la: Resp. At hoc est illud ipsum, quod hic intendimus; Scripturam usurpare phrases & voces, quæ phænomenis conveniunt, quaque propter apparentiam rebus sunt impositæ, à quocunque illa impositio ortum habeat, sive Astronomus sit, sive alius quicunque.
units.tr: Answer: But this is exactly what we are arguing: that Scripture uses phrases and words which agree with the phenomena, and which have been imposed on things because of their appearance, whatever the source of that imposition may be, whether it is an astronomer or any other person.

units.la: DXXXI. H. p. 240. Non ideo Planetæ sidera errantia vocantur, quia motus ordinem non servant & revera errant.
units.tr: DXXXI, H, p. 240: The planets are not called wandering stars because they do not keep the order of motion and really wander.

units.la: Resp. Nec ego hoc dico, sed quia apparent errare; nec affirmo, quòd vulgus communiter putet, verum errorem illis competere, quia non attendit; sed quod illis qui attendunt ad eorum motus, quicunque sint, videantur similes hominibus errantibus. Ad reliqua patet responsio ex dictis.
units.tr: Answer: Nor do I say this, but because they appear to wander. Nor do I affirm that the common people generally think that a true error belongs to them, because they do not attend to it. Rather, to those who attend to their motions, whoever they may be, they seem like erring men. The rest of the answer is clear from what has been said.

units.la: DXXXII. Exc. 3, H. p. 242. Locutionem esse metaphoricam.
units.tr: DXXXII, Exception 3, H, p. 242: The expression is metaphorical.

units.la: Resp. Est metaphora si compares cum hominibus errantibus Planetas, attamen illa ipsa comparatio originem habet ex visus apparentia.
units.tr: Answer: It is a metaphor if you compare the planets with erring men. Yet that very comparison has its origin in the appearance to sight.

units.la: DXXXIII. Exc. 4. M. p. 113. Quid si cum Cicerone statuamus Planetas stellas erraticas appellari per antiphrasin, quod minimum errent.
units.tr: DXXXIII, Exception 4, M, p. 113: What if we hold with Cicero that the planets are called wandering stars by antiphrasis, because they wander least?

units.la: Resp. At hoc debebas probasse, nec enim dicere sufficit: quod autem hæc Etymologiæ ratio locum habere non possit, apparet, quia etsi Planetæ observent in suo motu leges & ordinem naturæ, quod ex diligenti eorum observatione apparet, tamen videntur oculis errare, & propter istam apparentiam hoc nomen sortitos esse omnino statuendum.
units.tr: Answer: You ought to have proved this, for it is not enough to say it. That this etymological reason cannot hold is clear, because although the planets observe in their motion the laws and order of nature, as careful observation of them shows, yet they seem to the eyes to wander, and it must be wholly maintained that they received this name on account of that appearance.

units.la: DXXXV. Exc. 5. M. p. 115. Barbarum fuisset Spiritus Sanctus si vo-ce antiqua abolita novam substituisset.
units.tr: DXXXV, Exception 5, M, p. 115: The Holy Spirit would have been barbarous if, having abolished an ancient word, he had substituted a new one.

units.la: Resp. Hoc est, quod ego volo, debuisse nimirum Spiritum Sanctum retinere vocabula recepta, ut intelligeretur.
units.tr: Answer: This is just what I want: namely, that the Holy Spirit ought to have retained the received words, so that they might be understood.

units.la: DXXXVI. Adjiciamus prioribus Inductionis Exemplum Octavum ex Eccl. xii. 2. Dum non obtenebratur Sol & lux, & Luna & stella, & redeunt nubes post pluviam; ubi figurata locutione ostenditur, quænam incommoda maneant senectutem, quòd nempe oculi ipsorum ita obtenebrentur, ut Solem & lucem, Lunam & stellas amplius videre non possint, ubi Soli & Lunæ & stellis tribuitur id, quod potius in eorum oculis existit. Atque ita locum istum explicant Belgæ Interpretes, qui ad marginem hujus versus sic annotant: Niet in der daet, maer den ouden half blinden dunckt het soo te sijn: quasi dicerent: obtenebrantur Sol, Luna & stella non reipsa, sed senibus caecutientibus hæc ita videntur.
units.tr: DXXXVI. Let us add to the earlier examples of induction an eighth, from Eccl. 12:2: While the sun and the light are not darkened, and the moon and the stars, and the clouds return after the rain. Here a figurative expression shows what troubles remain for old age, namely that their eyes are so darkened that they can no longer see the sun and light, the moon and the stars. What really exists in their eyes is attributed to the sun, moon and stars. The Belgian interpreters explain the passage this way and note in the margin of the verse: Not in fact, but it seems so to the old, who are half blind, as if to say: the sun, moon and stars are not darkened in themselves, but to old men whose sight is failing they appear so.

units.la: DXXXVII. Sed excipiet aliquis in genere contra hæc inductionis exempla: multis Scripturæ locis probatum quidem esse, Scripturam usurpare terminos simplices, qui respectu habito ad phænomena & præjudicia inde exorta, ab auctoribus fuerunt impositi; sed probandum fuisse, adhiberi à sacris literis Propositiones sive terminos complexos phænomenis quidem convenientes, sed non intellectui legitime judicanti ex veris causis & natura rerum. Sic B. p. 128. Veritas, inquit, & falsitas logica proprie non est simplicium terminorum, sed axiomatum, nec in simplici conceptu, vel nominatione rerum vel fictarum vel verarum, ex. gr. Chimera, Solis &c. aliqua est veritas vel falsitas, sed ea tum demum locum habere incipit, cum de iis aliquid affirmatur vel negatur, ut esse, vel non esse; moveri, vel non moveri &c.
units.tr: DXXXVII. But someone will object in general to these examples of induction: it has indeed been proved from many passages of Scripture that Scripture uses simple terms which the authors imposed with regard to appearances and the prejudices arising from them. But it should have been proved that Scripture employs complex propositions or terms that agree with appearances but not with the intellect judging rightly from true causes and the nature of things. Thus B. p. 128: Logical truth and falsity, he says, properly belong not to simple terms but to axioms. In a simple concept or naming of things, whether fictitious or true, e.g. chimera, sun, etc., there is no truth or falsity. It begins to have a place only when something is affirmed or denied of them, such as to be or not to be, to move or not to move, etc.

units.la: Resp. Falsitatem in conceptibus Solis, quatenos eos homines ad nihil aliud extra se referunt, non consistere libenter concedo; sic quando conceptum angeli, mentis, trianguli, chimerae, &c. formo, atque nihil extra me refero, fateor nullam falsitatem in iis locum habere; sed de eo non est quæstio, verum de conceptibus quatenus ad aliquid extra nos referuntur, sive per terminos simplices id faciamus, sive per terminos compositos, de quibus dico, veritatem vel falsitatem in iis reperiri, prout vel conveniunt cum eo, ad quod referuntur, per terminos sive simplices, sive complexos, vel non conveniunt. Si conveniunt, veritas iis adscribenda, si non, falsitas, quod illa relatio horum conceptum non fiat nisi intercedente judicio. si cogites de substantia subtili fluida transitum luci permittente, habente extremitates, ubi terram contingere apparet, item de substantia lucida, ex se radios emittente, mota circulariter, & de substantia magna lumen reflectente, nihil veri vel falsi logice cogitabis; sed si conceptum priorem referas ad Coelum judicio praecedaneo, veri aliquid vel falsi dices, & sic de aliis.
