units.tr: Reply: I readily grant that falsity does not consist in concepts of the sun insofar as men refer them to nothing outside themselves. So when I form the concept of an angel, a mind, a triangle, or a chimera, and refer nothing outside myself, I admit that no falsity can lie in them. But that is not the question. The question concerns concepts insofar as they are referred to something outside us, whether we do this through simple terms or through compound terms. I say truth or falsity is found in them according as they agree or do not agree with that to which they are referred, whether through simple or complex terms. If they agree, truth is to be ascribed to them; if not, falsity, because this relation of concepts is made only through an intervening judgment. If you think of a subtle fluid substance permitting light to pass, having extremities where it seems to touch the earth, or of a luminous substance emitting rays from itself and moving in a circle, or of a great substance reflecting light, you will think nothing logically true or false. But if you refer the former concept to heaven by a prior judgment, you will say something true or false, and so with the others.

units.la: DXXXVIII. Exc. I. B. p. 115. Signum esse causa desperata, quod cum ipse mihi moveam hanc objectionem, vel non conatus fuerim, vel non potuerim unicum exemplum proferre talis connexionis terminorum, quae facta sit ad opinionem erroneam vulgo, sive (ut haec exceptio accommodetur ad phrasin, qua status controversiae exprimitur) quae innitatur praejudicio infantiae eoque sit involuta.
units.tr: DXXXVIII. Exc. 1. B. p. 115. It is a sign of a desperate cause that, since I myself raise this objection, either I have not tried, or I have not been able, to produce a single example of such a connection of terms made according to a commonly held erroneous opinion, or (so that this exception fits the phrase by which the state of the controversy is expressed) which rests on the prejudice of infancy and is thereby involved.

units.la: Ref. Lectori hoc relinquebam, cui facile id poterat patere ex locorum inspectione. Sic cognoscere poterat Job. xxvi. 7. dici Aquilonem sive hemisphaerium superius, in quo est Polus arcticus, esse extensum super juane, quod est praejudicium infantiae. Sic Gen. I. 26. est connexio terminorum, Lunae cum luminaribus magnis, adeo ut ibi dicatur: Luna oppositae ad stellas est luminare magnum; atque ita de aliis. Et connexio terminorum etiam ibi est, ubi non adest copula Est, ut cuivis patet; licet enim facile illam supplere, atque sic Propositiones Logicas formare; & quidem in interpretatione Scripturarum, nihil frequentius, quam ut propositiones formentur variae, ex una expressae posita. Sumamus unum exemplum, Eph. iv. 16. Ex quo totum corpus congruenter coagmentatum & compactum per omnes suppeditatas commissuras, ex vi intus agente, pro mensura uniuscujusque membri incrementum capit corpori conveniens ad sui ipsius exstructionem per charitatem. Hic enim una tantum est Propositio logica. Corpus Christi, congruenter coagmentatum &c. capit incrementum, reliqua sunt determinationes subjecti & praedicati, ex quibus Logice conjunctis variae propositiones Logico formantur, quales sunt. 1. Christi corpus est totum sive integrum corpus. 2. Corpus Christi est ex Christo coagmentatum. 3. Coagmentatio facta est per commissuras suppeditatas. 4. Vis intus agens coagmentavit Christi corpus &c. sed taedet in re tam clara explicanda tempus terere.
units.tr: Ref. I left this to the reader, for whom it could easily become clear by looking at the passages. Thus he could recognise that Job 26:7 says the north, or the upper hemisphere in which the north pole lies, is stretched out over empty space, which is a prejudice of infancy. So Gen. 1:26 contains a connection of terms, of the moon with the greater lights, so that there it is said: the moon, opposite the stars, is the greater light; and so with others. There is also a connection of terms where the copula is is absent, as is plain to anyone. For although it is easy to supply it and so form logical propositions, indeed in the interpretation of Scripture nothing is more frequent than that various propositions are formed from one stated proposition. Let us take one example, Eph. 4:16: From whom the whole body, fitly joined and knit together through every supporting joint, according to the working of each individual part, makes increase of the body to the building up of itself in love. Here there is only one logical proposition: the body of Christ, fitly joined together, etc., receives increase. The rest are determinations of subject and predicate, from which, logically combined, various logical propositions are formed, such as: 1. The body of Christ is the whole or entire body. 2. The body of Christ is joined together by Christ. 3. The joining is made through the supporting joints. 4. An inwardly working force joined the body of Christ, etc. But it is tedious to waste time explaining so clear a matter.

units.la: DXXXIX. Exc. 2. B. p. 115. Posito terminos simplices fundaros esse in aliqua opinione erronea vulgi, non tamen inde sequitur, eum qui in sententia tali aliquo termino utitur, si subjectum & praedicatum tantum connectat, non loqui ex rei veritate &c.
units.tr: DXXXIX. Exc. 2. B. p. 115. Even granting that simple terms are founded in some erroneous popular opinion, it does not follow that one who uses such a term in a statement, if he only connects subject and predicate, is not speaking according to the truth of the matter, etc.

units.la: Resp. Ex eo quod termini simplices fundati sunt in aliqua opinione erronea vulgi, sequitur eum, qui in sententia tali aliquo termino utitur, non loqui ex rei veritate accurata, hoc est, uti verbis, quae non veritatem nudam & accuratam, sed quae phaenomenis convenientem ad sensus relatam & praejudiciis involutam significant; non vero inde sequitur, eum falsum testari, aut docere, quod semper à scriptoribus sacris remo-vi.
units.tr: Reply: From the fact that simple terms are founded in some erroneous popular opinion, it does follow that one who uses such a term in a statement is not speaking according to exact truth. That is, he uses words which signify not bare and exact truth but what agrees with appearances, is referred to the senses, and is involved in prejudices. But it does not follow from this that he asserts or teaches what is false, which I have always kept away from the sacred writers.

units.la: DXL. Exc. 3. B. p. 116. Termini simplices ex usu vulgi adhibiti saepe sumuntur tantum ab apparentiis & similitudinibus, non semper ortum habent ex falsis complexis &c.
units.tr: DXL. Exc. 3. B. p. 116. Simple terms used in common speech are often taken only from appearances and resemblances; they do not always arise from false complex statements, etc.

units.la: Resp. Demonstravimus, tales locutiones ortum habere ex praejudiciis infantiae atque eo ipso ex falsis complexis, quamvis à plurimis non omnia postea retineantur. Vide ea, quae in genere de iis dixi, cap. I. Similia his habet M.p.116. ad quae proinde haec responsiones satis poterunt applicari.
units.tr: Reply: We have shown that such expressions arose from prejudices of infancy and so, by that very fact, from false complex statements, although many of them are afterwards not all retained. See what I said about these in general in chapter I. M. p. 116 has similar points, to which these replies can therefore well be applied.

units.la: DXLI. Exc. 4. M. p. 116. Falsa complexa multo efficaciora, quam incomplexa falsa, in una tantum re consistentia.
units.tr: DXLI. Exc. 4. M. p. 116. False complex statements are far more effective than false simple ones, which consist in a single thing only.

units.la: Resp. Incomplexa non possunt esse falsa; Veritati incomplexae, nulla opponitur falsitas. Ergo etiamsi termini incomplexi saepe videantur, tamen eo ipso, quia revera non competunt iis, quibus attribuuntur, sunt complexa falsa, licet non formaliter, tamen materialiter, & subintelligitur copula: ut in hoc: Luna luminare magnum scilicet est.
units.tr: Reply: Simple terms cannot be false; no falsity is opposed to simple truth. Therefore, even if simple terms often seem to be so, nevertheless by that very fact, because in reality they do not belong to the things to which they are attributed, they are complex falsehoods. They are not formally so, but materially, and the copula is understood, as in this: the moon is the greater light, namely is.

units.la: CAPUT XXIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIV.

units.la: Quartum Argumentum, quo sententiae nostrae veritas ostenditur & demonstratur.
units.tr: The Fourth Argument, by which the truth of our view is shown and demonstrated.

units.la: DXLII. Quartum Argumentum desumimus à circumcisione, cujus observatio ad tempus ab Apostolis in Ecclesia fuit permissa, hoc modo inferentes: Si Apostoli debuerunt sese accommodare Judaeis in retinenda ad tempus, & observanda circumcisione in Ecclesia, quae tamen per Christum facta erat non tantum inutilis, sed etiam perniciosa, uti apparet ex Epist. ad Gal. v. 2. Ecce ego Paulus dico vobis si circumcidamini, Christum vobis nihil profuturum, quatenus illa sua natura, quemadmodum aliae ceremoniae legales ad Christum venturum respiciebat; si inquam, Apostoli retinuerunt in Ecclesia ad tempus circumcisionem, donec Judaica synagoga honeste sepeliretur: Ergo multo magis scriptores ἀποστόλοι debuerunt buerunt retinere formulas receptas de rebus naturalibus, quamvis præjudiciis inniterentur, & veritatem præjudiciis involutam referrent, atque sic sese accommodare notitiæ vulgari & communi, donec similiter mundus præsens, in quo cognoscimus tantum ex parte, per speculum & per ænigma, sepeliatur. Quemadmodum igitur Circumcisionis & aliarum ceremoniarum observationem ad tempus concedebant Apostoli inspirante Spiritu Sancto, ne infirmi offenderentur, si adeo repugnantia opinioni sui præconceptæ & diu fotæ atque adultæ inter Judæos, de legis Ceremonialis absoluta necessitate, audivissent: ita & Spiritus Sanctus condescendere voluit hominibus simplicioribus, retinendo formulas receptas de rebus naturalibus; quamvis præjudiciis inniterentur, nec eas mutando in accuratas, quibus veritas nuda & à notitia vulgari abscondita significata fuisset, ne eos turbaret, si per formulas accuratas opiniones & præjudicia evertisset, quæ per sensus hauserunt, quæque pro tam firma habent veritate, ac si de ea à natura edocti fuissent. Neque est quod dicas: Non concessisse Apostolos circumcisionem, nisi iis, qui ut rem mediam habebant: Illi enim, qui pro re media eam habebant, & plane indifferente, non poterant per ejus neglectum scandalizari. Ergo potius in eorum gratiam fuit facta hæc concessio, qui inter Judæos eam pro necessaria habebant. Simili modo licet aliquando in praxi sese accommodare præconceptæ hominum opinioni, quando res sine certa perturbatione mutari non potest, ut obtinet, ex. gr. in imaginum toleratione in Templis, Papisticarum quarundam ceremoniarum retentione, & aliis multis, ubi notatu digna verba Clarissimi Maresii in Judicio de controversiis Theologicis in Hungaria &c. motis. Censeo multa tolerari debere à piis, quæ non probent, plurimaque pacis studio multitudini & consuetudini esse condonanda.
units.tr: DXLII. We draw the fourth argument from circumcision, the observance of which the Apostles allowed in the Church for a time, and we reason as follows: If the Apostles ought to have accommodated themselves to the Jews by retaining circumcision and observing it in the Church for a time, even though through Christ it had become not only useless but harmful, as appears from Gal. 5.2, Behold, I Paul say to you that if you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing, in so far as circumcision by its own nature, like the other legal ceremonies, pointed forward to the coming of Christ; if, I say, the Apostles retained circumcision in the Church for a time, until the Jewish synagogue was honourably buried, then much more the apostolic writers [ἀπόστολοι] ought to have retained the formulas received concerning natural things, although they rest on prejudices and express a truth wrapped in prejudices, and so accommodate themselves to common and popular knowledge, until the present world, in which we know only in part, through a glass and in a riddle, is in like manner buried. Just as the Apostles, moved by the Holy Spirit, allowed the observance of circumcision and the other ceremonies for a time, lest the weak be offended if they heard things so opposed to the opinion they had long held and nurtured among the Jews concerning the absolute necessity of the ceremonial law, so the Holy Spirit also chose to condescend to simpler men by retaining the received formulas concerning natural things, although they rest on prejudices. He did not change them into exact ones, by which the bare truth, hidden from common knowledge, would have been signified, lest he disturb them, if by exact formulas he had overturned the opinions and prejudices which they have absorbed through the senses, and which they hold to be as firmly true as if nature had taught them. Nor can you say that the Apostles only conceded circumcision to those who regarded it as an indifferent matter. For those who regarded it as an indifferent thing, and quite unimportant, could not be scandalized by its neglect. Therefore this concession was made rather for the sake of those who held it to be necessary among the Jews. In a similar way it is sometimes lawful in practice to accommodate oneself to men's preconceived opinion, when a matter cannot be changed without definite disturbance. This happens, for example, in the toleration of images in churches, in the retention of certain Papist ceremonies, and in many other cases, where the words of the most distinguished Maresius in his Judgment on the Theological Controversies stirred up in Hungary &c. are worth noting: I think that many things which the godly do not approve must be tolerated, and that for the sake of peace most things must be pardoned to the multitude and to custom.

units.la: DXLIII. Exc. 1. B. p. 48. Si hac argumentandi ratio concedatur, nihil certi ex sacris literis poterit erui, & in materiis fidei nulla erit certitudo, & in aliis articulis, modo non evertatur fundamentum salutis, simili ratione concludet Spiritus quidam erroneus.
units.tr: DXLIII. Excerpt 1, B. p. 48. If this method of argument is granted, nothing certain can be drawn from the sacred letters, there will be no certainty in matters of faith, and by a similar reasoning some erring spirit may conclude concerning other articles, provided the foundation of salvation is not overturned.

units.la: Resp. Non quæritur quid aliquis erronee posset concludere, sed quid juste & legitime. Sunt autem certæ regulæ, quarum adminiculo, quid his vel illis locutionibus Scriptura doceat, significet & testetur, possumus cognoscere.
units.tr: Answer: The question is not what someone might wrongly conclude, but what may be concluded rightly and lawfully. There are, however, certain rules by the aid of which we can know what Scripture teaches, signifies and attests by these or those expressions.

units.la: DXLIV. Exc. 2. B. p. 49. Nullam esse in majori terminorum connexionem, quia respectu circumcisionis prægnans erat ratio, utpote quam, quoniam erat instituta in fœdus perpetuum, nondum poterant capere fideles ex Judais esse esse annihilatam. Tenacissimi enim jam pridem fuere religionis avita. Periculum ergo erat ne totum Christum abjicerent &c. quid simile vero in rebus naturalibus & speciatim in materia de motu Solis vel Terrae? an unquam fuit ulla doctrina divina, propter quam credere debuerint populus Dei, Solem moveri, quae postea esset mutata.
units.tr: DXLIV. Excerpt 2, B. p. 49. There is no parallel in the major premise, because with respect to circumcision the reason was weighty: since it had been instituted as a perpetual covenant, the faithful from among the Jews could not yet grasp that it was annulled. For they were very tenacious of their ancestral religion. There was therefore danger that they would reject Christ altogether, &c. What is similar to this in natural things, and especially in the matter of the motion of the Sun or the Earth? Was there ever any divine doctrine for which the people of God ought to have believed that the Sun moves, and which was afterwards changed?

units.la: Resp. At quis non videt his ipsis confirmari egregie meum argumentum? Si enim propterea debuit tolerari circumcisio, quia inter Judaeos erat recepta, nec ii intelligebant annihilatam, ne totum Christum rejicerent: Ergo multo magis debuerunt retineri formulae de rebus naturalibus praejudiciis innitentes, quia receptae, nec intelligebant homines, eas non esse accuratas. 2. Simile non est idem, nec opus est, ut in omnibus sit convenientia, sufficit ad meum scopum illa, quod sicut Judaei circumcisionem putabant esse perpetuae observationis & necessariam, sed erronee, ita homines praejudicia infantiae & sensuum putant vera, atque propterea sermonem super iis suum fundarunt. Si ergo debuerunt Apostoli illi opinioni sese accommodare, neque illam evertere per contrarium praeceptum: Ergo nec scriptores sacri debuerunt opiniones praejudicatas evertere per formularum usum iis non innitentium.
units.tr: Answer: But who does not see that my argument is splendidly confirmed by these very points? For if circumcision had to be tolerated because it was received among the Jews, and they did not understand that it had been annulled, lest they reject all of Christ, then much more ought the formulas concerning natural things, which rest on prejudices but are received, to have been retained, since men did not understand that they were not exact. Second, the case is not the same, and there is no need for agreement in every respect. It is enough for my purpose that, just as the Jews thought circumcision was of perpetual observance and necessary, though wrongly, so men think the prejudices of infancy and of the senses are true, and for that reason have founded their speech upon them. If therefore those Apostles ought to have accommodated themselves to that opinion, and not overturned it by a contrary precept, then neither ought the sacred writers to have overturned preconceived opinions by using formulas that do not rest on them.

units.la: DXLV. Exc. 3. B. p. 50. Tolerabatur praxis circumcisionis, non docebatur; at in motu Solis non toleraretur error in populo, sed doceretur illa doctrina propria & diversis verbis.
units.tr: DXLV. Excerpt 3, B. p. 50. The practice of circumcision was tolerated, not taught; but in the motion of the Sun an error among the people would not be tolerated; rather that doctrine would be taught, in its own proper words.

units.la: Resp. Hoc vero est, quod nego, & cujus negationis rationes in examine istorum locorum affero,
units.tr: Answer: This is what I deny, and I set out my reasons for the denial in my examination of those passages.

units.la: DXLVI. Exc. 4. B. p. 50. Maximum imminebat periculum defectus multorum a Christo, nisi concessa fuisset circumcisio; putatne Wittichius vulgus a Deo defecturum, vel auctoritatem sacrarum literarum rejecturum fuisse, si Spiritus Sanctus secundum rei veritatem docuisset, non Solem, sed Terram moveri? Unde ergo haec Cartesianorum audacia, quod hanc doctrinam in vulgus spargere ausint, &c.
units.tr: DXLVI. Excerpt 4, B. p. 50. The greatest danger threatened that many would fall away from Christ, unless circumcision had been allowed. Does Wittich think that the common people would have fallen away from God, or rejected the authority of the sacred letters, if the Holy Spirit had taught according to the truth of the matter that the Earth, not the Sun, moves? Whence then this audacity of the Cartesians, who dare to spread this doctrine among the common people, &c.?

units.la: Resp. Maxima futura fuisset confusio, si termini recepti, atque phrases vulgares communi notitiae ortum debentes a Spiritu Sancto de rebus naturalibus loquente fuissent immutatae, quam precul dubio Spiritus Sanctus hoc modo prudenter voluit evitare. 2 Quod autem nos de hac materia scribimus, id facimus impulsi clamoribus adversariorum, hanc sententiam populo reddentium invisam; ut audita & altera parte vel suspendant judicium, si rationum momenta ab utraque parte non possint expendere, vel si rationum vim pro hac sententia militantium percipere possint, ei assensum praebeant. Quod si ex professo Scripturae hanc materiam teriam tractare placuisset, non dubitamus, quin Spiritui Sancto in promptu futurae fuissent tales rationes, quibus veritatem hujus sententiae clarissime potuisset explicare; quia vero noluit Spiritus Sanctus ea, quae ad scopum Scripturae non necessaria erant, pertractare, sapientissime ab eo factum, quod phrases receptas retinuerit.
units.tr: Answer: There would have been the greatest confusion if the received terms and common phrases, which arise from common knowledge, had been changed by the Holy Spirit when he spoke of natural things. Without doubt the Holy Spirit wisely chose to avoid this. As for my writing on this subject, I do it impelled by the outcry of my opponents, who make this opinion hateful to the people. I want them, having heard both sides, either to suspend judgment if they cannot weigh the force of the reasons on each side, or, if they can perceive the force of the reasons that support this opinion, to give it their assent. But if Scripture had purposely chosen to treat this matter, I do not doubt that the Holy Spirit would have had at hand such reasons as could have set out the truth of this opinion most clearly. But since the Holy Spirit did not wish to treat those things which were not necessary for the purpose of Scripture, it was most wisely done by him that he retained the received phrases.

units.la: DXLVII. Exc. 5. H. p. 228. Condescenderunt Apostoli circumcisionem etiam inutilem concedendo, sed 1. Judaei condescenderunt ad factum, ut facerent, non ad captum ut intelligerent. 2. Descenderunt ad factum hominum, inter quos docti etiam erant. 3. fecerunt hoc invíti &c. sed quid hoc ad rem tam controversam.
units.tr: DXLVII. Excerpt 5, H. p. 228. The Apostles condescended by allowing circumcision even though it was useless; but (1) the Jews condescended to the deed, so that they might do it, not to the understanding, so that they might grasp it. (2) They came down to the deeds of men, among whom there were also learned men. (3) They did this unwillingly, &c. But what has this to do with so controverted a matter?

units.la: Resp. Agnosco hanc diversitatem, sed ea nihil ad rem praesentem facit. Ad argumentum melum sufficit convenientia, quam antea adduxi. Et, si opinio recepta de circumcisionis necessitate fuit toleranda, & ex ea orta praxis quamvis inutilis fuit retinenda: Ergo multo magis toleranda opinio recepta de rebus naturalibus, quamvis erronea, atque phrasis ei innitens retinenda, nec per phrasin accuratam refutanda. Quis non videt unum ex altero aperte consequi? Si majus fecerunt Apostoli, quare & minus non fecissent? Majus erat retentio circumcisionis, quae pugnabat cum Christi adventu; Minus usurpatio formularum vulgarium, ex qua nullum periculum, cum per eas ut à Spiritu Sancto adhibitas, non errores consignificentur, sed tantum veritas generalis, uti suo loco declaramus.
units.tr: Answer: I acknowledge this difference, but it has nothing to do with the present point. For my argument the parallel I adduced earlier is enough. If the received opinion about the necessity of circumcision had to be tolerated, and the practice that arose from it had to be retained, though it was useless, then much more ought the received opinion about natural things to be tolerated, though it is erroneous, and the phrase resting on it to be retained, and not refuted by an exact phrase. Who does not see that the one clearly follows from the other? If the Apostles did the greater thing, why would they not also have done the lesser? The greater was the retention of circumcision, which clashed with the coming of Christ. The lesser is the use of common formulas, from which there is no danger, since through them, as used by the Holy Spirit, errors are not signified along with them, but only the general truth, as we shall declare in its proper place.

units.la: DXLVIII. Exc. 6. H. p. 229. Probat errorem & pravam opinionem de rebus naturalibus esse peccatum.
units.tr: 548. Exc. 6. H. p. 229. He proves that error and a perverse opinion about natural things is sin.

units.la: Resp. Id parum facit ad rem praesentem, unde ei non multum refragabor, cum in priori editione non simpliciter negaverim, tales errores esse peccata, sed tantum negem, pugnare cum doctrina salutis, quemadmodum alii errores de rebus salutaribus cum eâ pugnant.
units.tr: Answer: This has little bearing on the present matter, so I will not greatly contradict it, since in the earlier edition I did not simply deny that such errors are sins, but only denied that they clash with the doctrine of salvation, as other errors about saving matters clash with it.

units.la: DXLIX. Exc. 7. M. p. 46. Deum in hujusmodi erroribus, qui non constituunt peccatum, nec salutem tangunt, se accommodare captui vulgari, quantum scilicet hoc salva veracitate sua fieri potest, ex quo non sequitur, ipsum debere in gratiam erroris falsa loqui.
units.tr: 549. Exc. 7. M. p. 46. That God, in errors of this kind, which constitute no sin and do not touch salvation, accommodates himself to the capacity of the common people, as far as this can be done while his truthfulness is preserved; from which it does not follow that he must speak falsely for the sake of someone's error.

units.la: Resp. Hoc concesso obtinui causam, cum veracitati Dei non repugnet, uti formulis receptis, etiamsi opinionibus erroneis innitantur, nec propterea dici possit falsa loqui, cum his formulis generalem aliquam veritatem semper significet.
units.tr: Answer: Granting this, I have won the case, since it does not conflict with the truthfulness of God that received formulas, even if they rest on erroneous opinions, should be used, nor can it therefore be said that he speaks falsely, since these formulas always signify some general truth.

units.la: DL. Exc. 8. M p. 46. Negando Majorem Propositionem mei argumenti, quia magna sit differentia inter actum positivum, & inter actum tantum permissivum.
units.tr: 550. Exc. 8. M. p. 46. By denying the major proposition of my argument, because there is a great difference between a positive act and a merely permissive act.

units.la: missivum : concedere autem, dicere solum actum permissivum, loqui vero falsum actum notare permissivum : item permissionem circumcisionis non intulisse approbationem & consensum.
units.tr: missivum: but to concede that it is only a permissive act, and yet to say that speaking of it marks a permissive act as false; likewise, that the permission of circumcision did not imply approval and consent.

units.la: Resp. Vis mei argumenti tali modo non eliditur, nec quicquam mihi haec verba obsunt. Uti formulis receptis, quae praejudiciis innituntur, minus periculosum, quam permittere aliquod, quod infert abnegationem adventus Christi, quale eo tempore erat circumcisio. 2. Usus illarum formularum nullatenus infert earum approbationem & consensum, sed tantum <bl>xεἰστως</bl> intermissionem.
units.tr: Answer: The force of my argument is not overturned in this way, nor do these words harm me. Using received formulas, which rest on prejudices, is less dangerous than permitting something that brings with it the denial of the coming of Christ, as circumcision was at that time. (2) The use of those formulas in no way implies their approval and consent, but only a temporary tolerance.

units.la: DLI. Exc. 9. M. p. 47. Hoc tantum ex praemissis sequi : Deum debere vulgo in erroneâ suâ sententiâ tantum concedere, ut falsa sua opinione fruatur, circa ea, quae non tangunt salutem.
units.tr: 551. Exc. 9. M. p. 47. That only this follows from the premises: that God ought to concede to the common people, in their erroneous opinion, only so much that they may enjoy their false view about matters which do not touch salvation.

units.la: Resp. Si hoc sequitur ex praemissis, tum sequitur omne id, quod intendo. Hoc enim fecit Deus usurpando formulas receptas veritatem ad sensus relatam & praejudiciis involutam referentes.
units.tr: Answer: If this follows from the premises, then everything I intend follows. For God has done this by using received formulas, which refer to the truth as it relates to the senses and is wrapped in prejudices.

units.la: DLII. Exc. 10. M. p. 47. Deus alibi diserte declaravit, sese non approbare circumcisionem, idem demonstretur de hac Propositione.
units.tr: 552. Exc. 10. M. p. 47. God has plainly declared elsewhere that he does not approve of circumcision; the same should be shown of this proposition.

units.la: Resp. De illa exceptione plenius agetur cap. 29. quod videat lector.
units.tr: Answer: That exception will be treated more fully in chapter 29, which the reader may consult.

units.la: DLIII. Exc. 11. M. p. 48. Circumcisio permissione divina fit licita, at vero sententia falsa elocutione divina non potest fieri vera.
units.tr: 553. Exc. 11. M. p. 48. Circumcision becomes lawful by divine permission, but a false statement cannot become true through divine utterance.

units.la: Resp. Antecedens negatur, quia illa permissio non inferebat approbationem, sed tantum tolerationem, quali modo se habebat permissio divortii in V. T. 2. Phrasis vulgaris & recepta praejudiciis innitens non fit quidem conformis veritati accuratae & nullae per elocutionem divinam, sed quia per eam non approbatur, nihil inde fallitatis infertur menti divinae vel humanae.
units.tr: Answer: The antecedent is denied, because that permission did not imply approval but only toleration, in the way the permission of divorce stood in the Old Testament. (2) A common and received phrase, resting on prejudices, is indeed not made conformable to accurate truth, nor through divine utterance; but because it is not approved by it, no falsity is thereby imputed to the divine or the human mind.

units.la: CAPUT XXV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXV.

units.la: Sententiam de Usu formularum receptarum veritatem ali- quam praejudiciis involutam referentium non pugna- re cum Auctoritate & Veritate Scripturae pro- batur argumento ex locutionibus Scripturae de Corde usurpatis.
units.tr: The view that the use of received forms of speech, which refer to some truth involved in prejudices, does not conflict with the authority and truth of Scripture, is shown by an argument drawn from the ways Scripture speaks of the heart.

units.la: DLIV. Hactenus argumenta, quibus probatum fuit, debuisse scriptores ptores sacros, de phænomenis loquentes, adhibere phrases iis convenientes referentes veritatem quidem aliquam, sed ad sensus relatam & præjudicis involutam, idque fecisse manifeste ostendimus: nunc ut aditum paremus, ad solvendas objectiones Adversariorum, qui putant ea sententiâ labefactari Veritatem & Auctoritatem Scripturæ, adjiciemus argumenta, quibus juste id factum esse & convenienter Veritati & Auctoritati Scripturæ demonstremus. Atque huc spectant sequentia.
units.tr: DLIV. So far we have shown by argument that the sacred writers, when speaking of phenomena, ought to use expressions suited to them, which refer to some truth but relate it to the senses and involve it in prejudices, and that they have clearly done so. Now, to prepare the way for answering the objections of our opponents, who think this view undermines the truth and authority of Scripture, we will add arguments to show that this has been done justly and in agreement with the truth and authority of Scripture. To this end the following points bear.

units.la: DLV. Error est vulgi statuentis, Animæ præcipuam in corde esse sedem: qui postea adoptatus est ab Aristotele & ejus sequacibus, & rationibus quibusdam speciem veritatis habentibus est stabilitus, sed à Galeno & tota fere Medicorum schola, paucis exceptis, rejectus, teste Lemnio Medico de occultis naturæ miraculis Lib. 1. cap. 12. Ubi sic scribit. Quâ autem in parte collocetur anima quamve sedem occupet, multi Veterum in quæstionem vocant. Philosophi cordis medullium ei assignant. Quod designare videtur sapiens, cum inquit, Omni cura custodi cor tuum, quoniam ex ipsa vita procedit. At Medici qui exactius naturæ opera sunt perscrutati in cerebro illam constituunt, ex quo omnes sensus & facultates animæ, omnesque actiones procedunt. Sic Sennertus Epit. Naturalis scientiæ lib. 6. cap. 1. Eadem quæstio est, quænam sit sedes animæ, & quod membrum principale. Sed quodnam illud sit membrum Princeps Platonicis, quibus Galenus & Medici multi se adjungunt, cum Peripateticis lu est. Plato & Galenus tres præcipuas partes, Epar, Cor & Cerebrum, Cerebroque principatum, quod in eo sensus motusque principium anima rationalis resideat, deferunt. Hanc esse sententiam communem Medicorum testatur & Bartholinus Controversiarum Anatomicarum quæst. 4 de partibus, earumque facultatibus & functionibus, ubi inter alia sic inquit: Dicet forte quispiam pro Medicorum communi opinione primatum cerebro deferente &c. Atque hæc Medicorum sententia evidentissime nititur ratione: Nam 1. in cerebro fit concursus omnium nervorum, per quos & corpus dirigitur, & ea quæ exterius fiunt in corpore vel extra illud animæ repræsentantur. Ibi ergo sedem habet præcipuam, ubi omnia quæ ad corpus spectant potest percipere, & unde totum corpus potest dirigere. Cerebro affecto varias passiones animæ contingere videmus, ut amentiam, furorem, phrenesin &c. quæ oriuntur ex vario spirituum motu in cerebro, propter ejus læsionem, quo fit ut glandula pinealis varie movetur, & menti diversum quid significet; at corde male habente, non ideo talia animam opprimunt pathemata.
units.tr: DLV. The people's error, which holds that the principal seat of the soul is in the heart, was later adopted by Aristotle and his followers, and was established by certain arguments that have a semblance of truth. But it was rejected by Galen and almost the whole school of physicians, with few exceptions, as Lemnius the physician testifies in his book On the Hidden Miracles of Nature, Book 1, chapter 12, where he writes thus: Many of the ancients call into question in what part the soul is located, or what seat it occupies. The philosophers assign it the marrow of the heart. The wise man seems to point to this when he says, "Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it proceed the issues of life." But physicians, who have examined the works of nature more exactly, place it in the brain, from which all the senses and faculties of the soul and all its actions proceed. So too Sennert, Epitome of Natural Science, Book 6, chapter 1: The same question arises, what is the seat of the soul, and which is its principal member. But which member is the chief one, the Platonists, to whom Galen and many physicians join themselves, dispute with the Peripatetics. Plato and Galen assign the principal parts to three: the liver, the heart and the brain; and they give the principate to the brain, in which the rational soul, the source of sense and motion, resides. Bartholin, Anatomical Controversies, question 4 on the parts and their faculties and functions, also testifies that this is the common view of physicians, where among other things he says: Someone will perhaps say that, according to the common opinion of physicians, the primacy belongs to the brain, etc. And this opinion of the physicians rests most evidently on reason. For first, in the brain all the nerves meet, through which the body is directed, and what happens outside it or on the body is represented to the soul. There, then, it has its principal seat, where it can perceive all that concerns the body and from where it can direct the whole body. We see that when the brain is affected various passions of the soul arise, such as madness, rage, frenzy and so on, which come from the varied motion of the spirits in the brain on account of its injury, so that the pineal gland is moved in different ways and signifies something different to the mind. But when the heart is unwell, such disorders do not on that account oppress the soul.

units.la: DLVI. Ab hoc errore vulgi otiæ sunt locutiones in omnibus fere linguis obviæ, quæ huic errori innituntur. Sic in Latinâ linguâ homo prudens & sapien< vocatur cordatus: sic Recordari significat in mentem nobis aliquid redire : excordes & vecordes appellantur ii, qui carent intellectu & sapientia : Cic. 1. Tusc. Et Nasica ille prudens, bis Consul, corculum appellatus. In lingua Gallica Apprendre par cœur significat memoriæ mandare; prendre a cœur considerare diligenter; de bon cœur, ex animo; il a eu le cœur aux lettres, animum intendit ad studia. In lingua Germanica, ein ding zu hertzen nehmen, behertzigen, id est, animo perpendere. Aus guttem hertzen ex sincero animo. Ita dicimus: Wes das hertz vollist, dessen gehet der mundt über, hoc est, ex plenitudine cordis os loquitur. Atque has phrases imitatur Scriptura, cor ponendo vel pro ipsa anima, Psal. xxiv. 4. Innocens manibus & puro corde. Psal. xxxiv. 4. Cor meum & caro mea clamant ad Deum fortem, vel pro voluntate, Matth. vi. 21. ubi fuerit thesaurus vester, ibi erit & cor vestrum: vel pro cogitationibus, unde Deus dicitur corda scrutari & esse καρδιογνώστης, vel pro sapientia & ejus sede, Prov. II. 10. Cum venerit sapientia in cor tuum, Prov. xv. 14. Cor prudentis quaerit scientiam, Prov. vii. 7. Vidi inter fatuos, animadverti inter filios puerum defectu cordis. In quibus locutionibus est Metonymia subjecti recipientis pro adjuncto, quod hæ locutiones hanc opinionem supponant, non tantum animæ præcipuam sedem esse in corde, sed etiam intellectum & voluntatem animi potentias in corde radicari. Ex quibus observatis tale argumentum formamus: Cujus auctoritati & veritati non repugnat, ut utatur formulis receptis de corde, quæ ortum habent ex opinione erronea, illius Auctoritati multo minus repugnat, ut utatur phrasibus receptis circa phænomena, etiamsi præjudiciis infantiæ innitantur. Sed: Ergo.
units.tr: DLVI. From this error of the people come expressions found in almost all languages, which rest upon it. Thus in Latin a prudent and wise man is called cordatus; recordari means for something to come back into our mind; those who lack understanding and wisdom are called excordes and vecordes. Cicero, Tusculan Disputations 1: And that prudent Nasica, twice consul, was called "little heart." In French, apprendre par cœur means to commit to memory; prendre à cœur means to consider diligently; de bon cœur, from the heart; il a eu le cœur aux lettres, he has set his mind on his studies. In German, ein ding zu hertzen nehmen, behertzigen, that is, to weigh a thing in the mind; aus guttem hertzen, from a sincere heart. So we say: Wes das hertz vollist, dessen gehet der mundt über, that is, out of the fullness of the heart the mouth speaks. Scripture imitates these expressions, using the heart either for the soul itself: Ps. 24:4, The innocent in hands and pure in heart; Ps. 34:4 (LXX numbering), My heart and my flesh cry out to the living God; or for the will: Matt. 6:21, where your treasure is, there will your heart be also; or for the thoughts, whence God is said to search the hearts and to be καρδιογνώστης [heart-knower]; or for wisdom and its seat: Prov. 2:10, When wisdom enters into your heart; Prov. 15:14, The heart of the prudent seeks knowledge; Prov. 7:7, I saw among the simple, I noticed among the young men, a lad lacking heart. In these expressions there is a metonymy of the subject receiving for the adjunct, since these expressions presuppose this opinion: not only that the principal seat of the soul is in the heart, but also that the understanding and the will, the powers of the mind, are rooted in the heart. From these observations we form the following argument: whoever does not conflict with the authority and truth of Scripture in using the received forms about the heart, which arose from an erroneous opinion, is much less in conflict with it when it uses received phrases about phenomena, even if these rest on prejudices of infancy. But the first holds; therefore the second holds.

units.la: DLVII. Exc. 1. B. p. 107.
units.tr: DLVII. Exc. 1. B. p. 107.

units.la: Postquam aliquantum more solito in Cartesianos debacchatus esset, sic non bene credidistis Deum καρδιογνώστην, simpliciter videlicet intelligendo, Deum scrutari secretissimas cogitationes animæ residentis in corde &c.
units.tr: After he had raged against the Cartesians in his usual way, he said: "Thus you did not rightly believe that God is καρδιογνώστης [kardiognōstēs, knower of hearts], understood simply as meaning that God searches the most secret thoughts of the soul residing in the heart, etc."

units.la: Resp. Ut intelligamus, Deum esse καρδιογνώστην, sufficit si sciamus, Deum scrutari secretissimas cogitationes, sive putemus animam reverä sedem habere in corde, sive ei cerebrum pro sede assignemus; per cor enim nihil aliud talibus locis, quam animam cum secretissimis cogitationibus Scriptura voluit designare.
units.tr: Reply: To understand that God is καρδιογνώστης [kardiognōstēs], it is enough to know that God searches the most secret thoughts, whether we think the soul really has its seat in the heart or assign the brain as its seat. For in such passages Scripture meant by "heart" nothing other than the soul together with its most secret thoughts.

units.la: DLVIII. Exc. 2. B. p. 107. An ergo mille loca, quibus Cor per Me- ton. subjecti sumitur pro anima, credenda erunt supponere errorem vulgarem?
units.tr: DLVIII. Exc. 2. B. p. 107. Must we then believe that a thousand passages, in which the heart is taken by metonymy of the subject for the soul, suppose a common error?

units.la: Resp. Quia illæ phrases sunt receptæ, eas, ne barbari sint scriptores sacri, noluerunt mutare, nec refutare errorem receptum, cum id nulla necessinecessitas requirat. Eorum vero mens erat, significare actiones Dei, circa animam nostram, ejus voluntatem & intellectum, similiter ipsius animæ actiones; id ut phrasi recepta exprimerent, nihil videmus impedi-re.
units.tr: Reply: Because those phrases are in common use, the sacred writers did not want to change them, lest they seem barbarous, nor did they refute the received error, since no necessity required it. Their meaning was to signify God's actions towards our soul, His will and understanding, and likewise the soul's own actions; and we see no obstacle to their expressing this in the current idiom.

units.la: DLIX. Exc. 3. B. p. 107. Theologi aliter statuunt, nominatim Bucanus Instit. Theol. 4. 27. & professj, Leydenses disp. 13. th. 21. synops.
units.tr: DLIX. Exc. 3. B. p. 107. The theologians hold a different view, namely Bucanus, Institutes of Theology 4.27, and the professors of Leiden, Disputation 13, thesis 21, Synopsis.

units.la: Resp. His Theologis oppono Polanum Syntag. Theol. lib. 5. cap. 30. Cerebrum, inquit, anima rationalis, seu mentis sedes est. Victorinum Strigelium in notis ad libellum Philippi Melanchthonis de anima, p. 31. Sedem animæ proprie assignandam cordi non satis evincitur, hoc argumento, quod Sacra Scriptura multis in locis etiam vim cognoscentem videatur cordi tribuere. Hoc enim facit Spiritus Sanctus tum ratione usurpati sermonis, NB. tum etiam ratione συμπαθείας, qua actiones mentis, voluntatis & cordis sunt copulatæ. Theologos Salmuriensses in thesibus de Fide Parte priore th. 16. Cor in Scriptura & apud alios bonos auctores mentem denotat, quia olim ἡ γνώμη ἔ ἀνθρώπῳ ἐν τῇ λαιῇ κοιλίῃ τὸ καρδίας εἶναι, ut loquitur Hippocrates, atque inde τὸ ἀΐδιος ψυχῆς ἄρχειν putabatur; neque ergo magis reprehendendus ero, quod recedo à sententia Leydensium, quam adversarius, qui à sententia Theologorum à me citatorum dissentit. Auctoritates tales sunt humanæ, neque quicquam veritati præjudicare possunt.
units.tr: Reply: Against these theologians I set Polanus, Syntagma of Theology, book 5, chapter 30: "The brain," he says, "is the seat of the rational soul, or of the mind." I set Victorinus Strigelius, in his notes on Philip Melanchthon's little book on the soul, p. 31: "That the seat of the soul should properly be assigned to the heart is not sufficiently proved by the argument that Holy Scripture in many places seems to attribute cognitive power to the heart. The Holy Spirit does this both by the manner of speaking, NB, and also by reason of the sympathy by which the actions of mind, will and heart are joined." I set the theologians of Saumur in the theses on Faith, first part, thesis 16: "In Scripture and among other good authors, 'heart' denotes the mind, because of old, as Hippocrates says, [ἡ γνώμη ἐν ἀνθρώπῳ ἐν τῇ ἀριστερῇ κοιλίῃ τῆς καρδίης εἶναι, the understanding of man is in the left ventricle of the heart], and from this it was thought that [τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν τῆς ψυχῆς ἄρχειν, the ruling part of the soul governs]." Therefore I shall not be blamed any more for departing from the opinion of the Leiden professors than my opponent is for dissenting from the theologians I have cited. Such authorities are human, and they can prejudice nothing against the truth.

units.la: DLX. Exc. 4. B. p. 111. Etiam corde male affecto, humoribus biliosis & melancholicis, animam iracundam vel melancholicam percipimus: Ergo eadem consequentia animæ sedem esse in corde probo.
units.tr: DLX. Exc. 4. B. p. 111. Even when the heart is ill affected by bilious and melancholic humours, we perceive the soul as angry or melancholic. Therefore by the same reasoning I prove that the seat of the soul is in the heart.

units.la: Resp. Meum argumentum inde procedit, quod alibi anima non possit affici à spiritibus animalibus quàm in cerebro, cum non alibi sint ad hunc effectum sufficientes; itaque etiam humores biliosi & melancholici non possunt animam iracundam reddere, nisi interveniente motu spirituum in cerebro. Sed nihil attinet prolixius cum adversario & similibus disputare, cum hæc in libello Pass. à Cart. optimè sint explicata.
units.tr: Reply: My argument proceeds from this: the soul cannot be affected by animal spirits anywhere except in the brain, since they are not sufficient for this effect elsewhere. So bilious and melancholic humours cannot make the soul angry unless a motion of the spirits in the brain intervenes. But it is pointless to dispute at greater length with my opponent and others like him, since these matters have been very well explained in the book by Descartes, Les passions de l'âme.

units.la: DLXI. Exc. 5. (B. p. 111.) Licet talia pathemata ut amentia, furor, ex corde male affecto potius oriantur, tamen alias affectiones inde ortum habere jam ostensum est.
units.tr: DLXI. Exc. 5. (B. p. 111.) Although such affections as madness and frenzy arise rather from a heart ill affected, it has already been shown that other affections also arise from it.

units.la: Resp. Quomodo ex illis præcisè affectibus argumentum petamus videat antagonista supra. 2. Non aliter excitant humores biliosi & melancholici affectus iracundiæ & melancholiæ in animâ, quàm quatenus ex illis humoribus tales convenientes iis spiritus animales generantur, qui animam in cerebro principalem sedem tenentem iracundiâ & melancholiâ afficiunt.
units.tr: Reply: Let my opponent, see above, 2, consider how we might draw an argument from those very affections. Bilious and melancholic humours excite the affections of anger and melancholy in the soul only insofar as from those humours there are generated animal spirits suited to them, which affect the soul, holding its principal seat in the brain, with anger and melancholy.

units.la: DLXII. Exc. 6. B. p. III. Annon ipsa cordis oppressio, quae fit per melancholici humoris copiam, ipsum cerebrum inficere & furorem gignere possit, consulatur Medicorum schola.
units.tr: DLXII. Exc. 6. B. p. III. Let the school of physicians be consulted: can the very oppression of the heart, which is caused by an abundance of melancholic humour, infect the brain itself and beget frenzy?

units.la: Resp. Si illud nescit Adversarius, quid ergo responsionis loco id affert? dico autem id fieri posse, sed non immediatè, verùm infecto cerebro, ut ipse dicit, & per spiritus animales, qui ex melancholico humore melancholiæ excitandæ convenientes generantur.
units.tr: Reply: If my opponent does not know this, what does he bring forward by way of answer? I say, however, that it can happen, but not immediately: rather, the brain is first infected, as he himself says, and this happens through animal spirits, which are generated from the melancholic humour and are suited to stir up melancholy.

units.la: DLXIII. Exc. 7. B. p. III. Quod cerebro male affecto amentiam, furorem &c. consequi videmus, mirum non est: unde per hoc argumentum nihil aliud poterit probari, quàm animam in cerebro fungi facultatibus intellectualibus, vel ad summum animam esse essentialiter in cerebro, non autem quod non sit etiam essentialiter in corde.
units.tr: DLXIII. Exc. 7. B. p. III. That we see madness, frenzy, etc. follow a brain ill affected is no surprise. Hence by this argument nothing else can be proved than that the soul performs its intellectual faculties in the brain, or at most that the soul is essentially in the brain, but not that it is not also essentially in the heart.

units.la: Resp. Sic causam tradit. Hoc enim argumento probare intendi, non quòd essentialiter anima tantùm sit in cerebro, & non in corde, sed quòd in cerebro anima præcipuam NB sedem habeat, & potentiâ intelligendi & volendi in cerebro fungatur anima, cujus contrarium supponunt phrases vulgares etiam ab ipsâ Scripturâ adhibitæ.
units.tr: Reply: He misrepresents the point. For the intention of this argument is not to prove that the soul is essentially only in the brain and not in the heart, but that the soul has its principal NB seat in the brain, and that the soul exercises the power of understanding and willing in the brain. The common phrases, which Scripture itself uses, suppose the contrary.

units.la: DLXIV. Præter hæc observata contra ea quæ H. habet à p. 251 ad 255 sequentia possunt notari. 1. Me non dicere, quod omnes Tropi erroneis vulgi opinionibus innitantur, sed dico, hunc Tropum in citatis locis, in quo supponitur, cor esse præcipuam animæ sedem, in variis linguis adhibitum, etiam usurpari in Scripturâ, non obstante, quòd inventores ejus Tropi respexerint opinionem erroneam, quam non opus est Sp. S. refutare. Vana ergò sunt omnia quæ p. 252. tractat. 2. Vox Cordatus & theoreticè sapientem & practicè prudentem notat, uti ex usu apud Auctores patet. Sed quicquid sit de eo, cor non est magis virtutum sedes quàm animæ. Virtutes enim inhærent animæ & voluntati, ideoque cordatus non fuit dictus ab iis, qui hoc nomen invenerunt, nisi habito respectu ad istam opinionem. 3. Sufficit, quòd origo istius impositionis talis sit, etiamsi non omnis is, qui eâ utitur voce, ad istam originem in usu attendat. Atqui hæc contra p. 253. dicta sunto. 4. Cadunt vero facilè, quæ de voce Recordari & aliis observat p. 254. Nam eæ voces ab inventoribus similiter usurpatæ sunt, habito respectu ad istam vulgarem opinionem, quod mihi sufficit ad obtinendam meam sententiam.
units.tr: DLXIV. Besides these remarks, the following points may be noted against what he says on pages 251 to 255. 1. I do not say that all tropes rest on erroneous popular opinions; I say that this trope in the passages cited, in which it is supposed that the heart is the principal seat of the soul, is used in various languages and is also employed in Scripture, even though its inventors had in view an erroneous opinion, which the Holy Spirit has no need to refute. So everything he treats on page 252 is empty. 2. The word cordatus denotes one who is wise in theory and prudent in practice, as is clear from its use among authors. But whatever the case, the heart is no more the seat of the virtues than of the soul. For the virtues inhere in the soul and the will, and so those who coined the term did not call a man cordatus except with regard to that opinion. 3. It is enough that the origin of this way of speaking is such, even if not everyone who uses the word attends to that origin in ordinary use. Yet what he says on page 253 is to be said against this. 4. What he observes on page 254 about the words recordari and others easily falls. For those words were likewise used by their inventors with regard to this common opinion, which is enough for me to maintain my view.

units.la: DLXV. M. p. 115. mecum convenit, dum dicit, sufficere dummodo statuamus Cordis vocabulum ea vere significare, quæ Spiritus Sanctus eo nobis significare intendit, sive ea vera significatio errorem aliquem auctorum istius phraseologiæ supponat, sive non. Hoc enim est quod toto libro docco, recce-ptis ptis phrasibus uti sacras literas, quæ impositæ sæpe sunt ab auctoribus ad errorem aliquem respicientibus. Quæ vero hic mihi opponit, nullius sunt momenti; quod enim vocabulum בלב citatis locis non tantùm genere medium, sed in specie hoc medium, nempe partem hanc corporis humani, quæ Cor appellari solet, significet, nimis quàm manifestum est; quod autem per Cor anima intelligatur tropicè, ipse etiam dico.
units.tr: DLXV. M. p. 115. He agrees with me when he says: it is enough, provided we hold that the word "heart" truly signifies what the Holy Spirit intends to signify by it, whether or not that true signification supposes some error in the authors of this phraseology. This is indeed what I teach throughout the whole book: that Holy Scripture uses received phrases, which were often coined by authors looking to some error. But what he objects to me here has no weight. That the word בלב [belev, "in the heart"] in the passages cited signifies not merely a neutral genus but specifically this organ, namely the part of the human body which is usually called the heart, is more than manifest; and that by "heart" the soul is understood tropically, I myself also say.

units.la: CAPUT XXVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVI.

units.la: Idem probatur secundò Argumento desumto ex locutio- nibus in Scripturâ usurpatis de moralibus & practicis apparentiæ & opinioni super eâ fundare innitentibus.
units.tr: The same is proved secondly by an argument drawn from the expressions used in Scripture about moral and practical matters, which rest on appearance and on opinion founded upon it.

units.la: DLXVI. Sententiam superioribus capitibus probatam non repugnare Auctoritati & Veritati Scripturæ, etiam hoc modo videmur evincere posse. Si cum Auctoritate & Veritate Scripturæ non pugnant locutiones de rebus moralibus & practicis in Scripturâ sæpe frequentatæ, quibus veritas aliqua relata ad externam apparentiam & opinione erronea involuta significatur? Ergo pari ratione non repugnat ejusdem Auctoritati & Veritati, si circa phænomena & res naturales utatur phrasibus receptis, Veritatem ad hominum sensus relatam & præjudiciis involutam referentibus. Sed verum est prius, uti ex seqq. manifestum. Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: DLXVI. We seem able to show in this way too that the opinion proved in the preceding chapters does not conflict with the authority and truth of Scripture. If expressions about moral and practical matters, which Scripture often uses, do not conflict with its authority and truth, when they signify some truth referred to outward appearance and wrapped in a mistaken opinion, then by the same reasoning it does not conflict with that same authority and truth if it uses the accepted phrases about phenomena and natural things, phrases that refer to truth as it is related to human senses and wrapped in prejudices. But the first is true, as will be clear from what follows. Therefore so is the second.

units.la: DLXVII. Exc. M. p. 71. Isto modo omnem certitudinem ex hu textibus tolli. Si enim subinde de rebus moralibus & practicis secundum errores aliorum Spiritus S. locutus deprehenditur, quidni in aliis idem fieri potuisse rationabiliter suspicabimur?
units.tr: DLXVII. Cited from M., p. 71: In this way all certainty is removed from these texts. For if the Holy Spirit is found to have spoken in moral and practical matters according to the errors of others, why should we not reasonably suspect that the same could have happened elsewhere?

units.la: Resp. Non sufficit suspicio, sed opus est illud ostendere, quemadmodum in locis citatis à me est factum. In illis enim phrases tales reperiri, vel ex rei naturâ ipsâ ex. gr. Josh. xi. quem nono loco adduximus, colligitur. Idem ergo est hoc argumentum cum argumento Maldonati in Harmon. ad cap. xxvi. Matth. quo utitur contra nostros, qui in verbis: Panis est corpus Christi, tropum esse dicunt, quando inquit: Cur non & ibi figuras quærunt, ubi Marcion, ubi Arius, ubi Manes, ubi Origenes? quod quàm nullius sit momenti nemo non videt.
units.tr: Reply. Suspicion is not enough; one must show it, as I have done in the passages cited. For that such phrases are found in them is gathered from the nature of the matter itself, for example Joshua 11, which I cited in the ninth place. So this argument is the same as the argument of Maldonatus in his Harmony on Matthew, chapter 26, which he uses against our people, who say that in the words This is the body of Christ there is a trope. He says: Why do they not seek figures there too, where Marcion, where Arius, where Manes, where Origen? That this is of no weight, no one fails to see.

units.la: DLXVIII. Probamus nostram Minorem inductione variorum locorum, quibus Veritas aliqua relata ad externam apparentiam & erronea opinione involuta significatur, quo evicto eo ipso constabit, illas cum Auctoritate & Veritate Scripturae optime consistere. Primam Classem constituunt loca, in quibus justi dicuntur ii, qui tales sunt in externa apparentia, & opinione super ea fundata vel sua vel aliorum, qualia sunt, 1. Ef. xl ix. 24. collato cum v. 25. An Auferretur a robusto captura? an etiam captiva turba justi eriperetur? Quin sic ait Jehova, & turba captiva robusti auferetur, & captura violenti eripietur. Hic is, qui priori versu vocabatur justus, sequenti vocatur violentus, tyrannus. Itaque ista justitia non est nisi in opinione istius tyranni, qui omnia sua violenta facta titulo justitiae novit obtegere, & eorum, qui ejus partes sequuntur. Nam ut suspicemur mendum irrepsisse, ita ut pro יְרִיק in priori versu sit legendum יְרִיק ut quidam interpretes volunt, nulla necessitas cogit. Marloratus ad hunc locum consideretur, cujus haec sunt verba ex Calvino. Interea haec similitudo diligenter notanda est, quod Ecclesia opprimatur tyrannide Principum, & faucibus luporum expositia sit, & nihilominus JVSTA eorum prada esse EXISTIMETVR! Sed utcunque JVSTOS se Dominos jactitent, & inani titulo glorientur, Dominus eos praedones iniquissimos esse declarat, cum se vindicem fore atque ita pradam suam erepturum esse significat. Similes huic sunt loci Prov. xviii. 17. ubi secundum Hebraeum textum haec habentur verba, Justus, qui primus est in lite sua, advenit proximus ejus & perrestigat eum, in quo loco interpretes per Justum intelligunt eum, qui sibi videtur Justus. Vide Cartwrightum, Belgas & Junium. Matth. ix. verf. 13. Non enim veni vocatum justos, sed peccatores ad resipiscentiam. Christus per justos intelligit Pharisaeos, qui turgebant propria justitia & sibi justi videbantur, cum tamen nihil minus quam tales essent, in qua explicatione consentiunt interpretes, nominatim Belgae, Pareus, Musculus. Simili modo locum Ezech. III. 20. Jun. 5. Sin averteretur justus a justitia sua & faciet iniquitatem interpretantur Belgae; (qui quamvis forte aliter accipi possit, eorum tamen verba adscribam) Een rechtveerdige] te weeten in den schijn voor de menschen, niet in der waerheyt voor Godt, aldoo is het woort rechtveerdigh genomen, Prov. xviii. 17. Ezech. xviii. 24, 26. &c. cap. xxxiii. 13. Matth. ix. 13. Luc. xviii. 9, 14. item geloove voor den schijn-geloove. Luc. viii. 13. Act. viii. 13. ende liefde voor schijn-liefde.
units.tr: DLXVIII. We prove our minor premise by induction from various passages in which some truth referred to outward appearance and wrapped in a mistaken opinion is signified. When this is established, it will at once be clear that these passages agree very well with the authority and truth of Scripture. The first class consists of passages in which the just are those who are such in outward appearance, and in an opinion founded on it, either their own or others'. Such are: (1) Isaiah 49:24, compared with verse 25: Shall the prey be taken from the mighty? or the lawful captive be delivered? But thus says the LORD: Even the captives of the mighty shall be taken away, and the prey of the terrible shall be delivered. Here he who was called just in the former verse is called violent, a tyrant in the next. So that justice exists only in the opinion of that tyrant, who knows how to cover all his violent deeds with the title of justice, and of those who follow his party. For there is no necessity to suspect that an error has crept in, so that for yārîq in the first verse one should read yārûq, as some interpreters want. Let Marloratus be consulted on this passage; his words, taken from Calvin, are these: Meanwhile this likeness must be carefully noted: that the Church is oppressed by the tyranny of princes, and is exposed to the jaws of wolves, and yet is THOUGHT to be their JUST prey! But however much they boast of being JUST lords and glory in an empty title, the Lord declares them to be most unjust plunderers, when he signifies that he will avenge and so take away his prey. Similar to this are passages in Proverbs 18:17, where according to the Hebrew text these words occur: The just man who is first in his cause comes, and his neighbour comes and searches him out. In this place the interpreters understand by the just one who seems just to himself. See Cartwright, the Belgians and Junius. Matthew 9:13: For I came not to call the just, but sinners to repentance. Christ by the just means the Pharisees, who were puffed up with their own righteousness and seemed just to themselves, though they were nothing less than such. In this explanation the interpreters agree, especially the Belgians, Pareus and Musculus. In a similar way the Belgians interpret Ezekiel 3:20, and Junius on 5: But if the just turns away from his righteousness and commits iniquity. (Although this might perhaps be taken otherwise, I will cite their words.) A righteous one: that is, in appearance before men, not in truth before God; in that place the word "righteous" is taken so. Proverbs 18:17; Ezekiel 18:24, 26, etc.; chapter 33:13; Matthew 9:13; Luke 18:9, 14. Likewise faith for apparent faith: Luke 8:13; Acts 8:13. And love for apparent love.

units.la: 1 Job. III. 12. quae ita Latine reddo, Justus] scilicet in apparentia coram hominibus, non in rei veritate coram Deo: ita accipitur vox justus Prov.xviii. 17. Ezech. xviii. 24, 26. &c. cap. xxxiii. 13. Matth. ix. 13 Luc. xvi ii. 9, 14. item fides pro fide apparenti Luc. viii. 13. Act. viii. 13. & charitas pro charitate apparente 1 Joh. iii. 12.
units.tr: 1 John 3:12, which I render into Latin thus: The just: that is, in appearance before men, not in the truth of the matter before God; the word "just" is taken in this way. Proverbs 18:17; Ezekiel 18:24, 26, etc.; chapter 33:13; Matthew 9:13; Luke 18:9, 14. Likewise faith for apparent faith, Luke 8:13; Acts 8:13; and charity for apparent charity, 1 John 3:12.

units.la: DLXIX. Exc. 1. B. p. 71. ad locum Esaiae, Prado dicitur justus, quia jus belli prae se fert, sed omnibus per se notum est ipsum esse injustum,
units.tr: DLXIX. Cited from B., p. 71, on the passage of Isaiah: he is called just by the plunderer because he bears the right of war before him, but it is evident to all in itself that he is unjust.

units.la: Resp. Omnibus notum est quos violenter aggreditur, sed non ipsi nec iis qui ejus partes sequuntur, quibus justus videtur eo ipso, quia jus belli prae se fert. 2. Si hoc per se notum sit, tanto evidentius probat meam Minorem, hocque est exemplum locutionis, qua veritas relata ad externam apparentiam & erronea opinione involuta significatur, a Scriptura usurpatae.
units.tr: Reply. It is known to all whom he attacks violently, but not to him or to those who follow his party, to whom he seems just for the very reason that he bears the right of war before him. Second, if this is evident in itself, it proves my minor premise all the more clearly, and this is an example of the expression, used in Scripture, by which truth referred to outward appearance and wrapped in a mistaken opinion is signified.

units.la: DLXX. Exc. 2. H. p. 244. Non acceptandum esse argumentum ad probationem, quod interpretum adhuc styło laceretur.
units.tr: DLXX. Cited from H., p. 244: An argument should not be accepted as proof because the style of the interpreters is still being torn apart.

units.la: Resp. At sine causa interpretes quidam hunc locum aliter legunt, cum Scripturas V. & N. T. incorruptas contra quosdam Pontificios sufficienter a Protestantibus sit evictum. (Unde apparet M. pag. 72. primam notam ex mera contradicendi libidine profectam, cum non suspicari mendum non excludat negationem mendi:) Omnino ergo hoc argumentum ad probationem nostrae sententiae recte adhibetur.
units.tr: Reply. Some interpreters read this passage otherwise without good cause, since the Protestants have sufficiently shown against certain Papists that the Old and New Testament Scriptures are uncorrupted. (From this it appears that M.'s first objection, on page 72, proceeds from mere love of contradiction, since not to suspect an error does not exclude the denial of error.) Altogether, then, this argument is rightly used to prove our view.

units.la: DLXXI. Contra reliqua quae M. hic habet p. 73, 74. quae inspiciat cui volupe est, observo sequentia. 1. Non esse necessarium, ut Spiritus Sanctus istum tyrannum justum appellaverit in gratiam Tyranni, vel in gratiam vulgi, sed eum appellare justum & violentum simul, ut ostendat ejus justitiam non veram esse sed apparentem, viderique potius suis & sibi justum, quam revera esse, ad consolandam Ecclesiam, ut ex explicatione Calvini apparet. 2. Si Tyrannus appelletur justus eo modo, quo reprobi populus Christi &c. omnino spectanda est apparentia externa & judicium, super ea fundatum, tum ipsorum tyrannorum, tum aliorum, quod tamen cum veritate non convenit. 3. Verum est, Spiritum Sanctum indicare quomodo illud זדיק intelligi velit, atque eo ipso patet, quod debeat sumi secundum opinionem. Hoc enim nostrum confirmat argumentum. 4. Quod si vero το צדיק referre velis ad שבי idem nihilominus erit sensus, illam nempe captivam turbam iustam dici, hoc est, juste captam propter opinionem istius tyranni & sectatorum.
units.tr: DLXXI. Against the remaining points that M. makes here, on pages 73 and 74, let whoever enjoys such things examine them. I observe the following. (1) It is not necessary that the Holy Spirit called this tyrant just out of regard for the tyrant, or for the sake of the common people; rather he calls him just and violent at the same time, to show that his justice is not true but apparent, and that he seems just to his own people and to himself rather than really being so. This serves to console the Church, as appears from Calvin's explanation. (2) If the tyrant is called just in the way that the rejected people of Christ, etc., are called so, then the outward appearance and the judgment founded on it must be considered altogether, both that of the tyrants themselves and that of others; and this does not agree with the truth. (3) It is true that the Holy Spirit indicates how the word zadiq is to be understood, and from this it is plain that it must be taken according to opinion. For this confirms our argument. (4) But if you wish to refer tsaddiq to shevi, the sense will nonetheless be the same: that captive crowd is called just, that is, justly captured on account of the opinion of that tyrant and his followers.

units.la: DLXXII. B. p. 71. Circa Matth. IX. 13. consentit, dicendo, illos dici justos suo judicio & propria imaginatione, quos revera injustos fuisse ex Evangelio clare liquet.
units.tr: DLXXII. Cited from B., p. 71. On Matthew 9:13 he agrees, saying that they are called just by their own judgment and private imagination, though it is clear from the Gospel that they were in fact unjust.

units.la: Resp. Et hoc est quod ego intendo, vocari justos aliquos secundum apparentiam externam, secundum suum judicium sive opinionem, quae hîc hic est erronea, quoniam eos injustos fuisse revera ex Euangelio clarè liquet. Sic ergo Minor mea confirmatur.
units.tr: Reply. This is exactly what I mean: some people are called just according to outward appearance, according to their own judgement or opinion, which here is mistaken, since it is clear from the Gospel that they were in fact unjust. So my minor premise is confirmed.

units.la: DLXXIII. H. vero p. 244. — 247. nihil præter verba objicit, quibus non impugnatur mea probatio, sed potius stabilitur, itaque non est quod operosus sim in iis refutandis. Sufficit enim 1. quod probatum sit, justos appellari eos, qui revera tales non erant, sed tantùm in opinione sua & aliorum. Hoc enim tantùm requiritur ad probationem meæ Minoris suprà positæ. Quod autem per justos intelligat Christus Pharisæos, qui sibi justi videbantur, dicatque, se non venisse vocatum eos sic turgidos propriâ justitia, apparet ex textu: ii enim intelliguntur per justos, qui opponuntur publicanis, ii, qui murmurabant. Atqui hi erant Pharisæi propria justitia turgidi. At dicis: Christus tamen etiam Pharisæos vocavit; quod apparet ex effectu, quia crediderunt in eum, ergo eos hic concrete non exclusit.
units.tr: In DLXXIII, at pp. 244–247, he objects with nothing but words, which do not refute my proof but rather support it. There is therefore no need for me to labour over refuting them. For it is enough, first, that it has been shown that those are called just who were not really such, but only in their own opinion and that of others. This alone is required to prove my minor premise stated above. That Christ, by "the just", means the Pharisees, who seemed just to themselves, and that he says he has not come to call people so puffed up with their own righteousness, appears from the text itself: for those who are meant by "the just" are those set against the tax collectors, namely those who were grumbling. But these were the Pharisees, puffed up with their own righteousness. You reply: Yet Christ also called the Pharisees; this is evident from the result, since they believed in him; therefore he did not here exclude them concretely.

units.la: Resp. Designantur hîc Pharisæi in communi, qui se legaliter justos putabant, cui non repugnat, quod quosdam ex iis vocaverit. 2. Non semper ad captum sese accommodant Scriptores sacri per tales locutiones, sive, non semper propterea usurpant Scriptores sacri ejusmodi phrases, quia aliæ superent vulgi captum, (istius enim loquendi modi variæ possunt esse causæ, ut & suprà §. 57. observatum) sed sufficit aliquando adhiberi, quod usu sint receptæ, & applicatæ his vel illis subjectis. 3. Qualem veritatem habere possimus ex illis verbis in explicatione hujus loci ostensum, sic & in locis qui de rebus naturalibus loquuntur, veritatem habere possum, sed non eam, quam quis præjudicio occupatus conformiter suo præjudicio ex istis phrasibus inferre solet. Sed & concedo, eam veritatem ex Christi verbis haberi posse, quod Pharisæi non sint verè justi, sed in sua opinione; quod tamen ex nudis illis verbis non patet, sed ex textus circumstantiis & historia Pharisæorum descripta in Euangelio. 4. Nec ego is sum, qui putem vulgus semper errare, uti videtur mihi tribuere p. 246. & contrarium ejus patuit ex cap. 1.
units.tr: Answer: Here the Pharisees are meant in general, those who thought themselves justified by the Law. That does not conflict with his calling some of them. 2. Sacred writers do not always adapt themselves to the understanding of their hearers through such expressions. That is, they do not always use such phrases because others would exceed the grasp of the common people. (There can be various reasons for this manner of speaking, as was also noted above in §. 57.) It is sometimes enough that the phrase is in common use and is applied to these or those subjects. 3. Just as the truth we may get from those words has been shown in the explanation of this passage, so we may also have truth in passages that speak of natural things, but not the truth that a man preoccupied with prejudice usually infers from such phrases in line with his prejudice. Yet I also grant that the truth can be had from Christ's words that the Pharisees were not truly just, but only in their own opinion. This does not appear from those bare words, however, but from the circumstances of the text and from the account of the Pharisees given in the Gospel. 4. Nor am I one who thinks that the common people always err, as you seem to attribute to me on p. 246. The contrary of this has been shown in chap. 1.

units.la: DLXXIV. Ad Prov. xviii. Exc. 1. M. p. 75. posse vocabulum justus sumi ironicè.
units.tr: DLXXIV. On Prov. 18. Objection 1, M. p. 75: that the word "just" may be taken ironically.

units.la: Resp. 1. Ironiæ adhibentur vel ad reprehendendum cum, quem ironicè appellas, vel ad ei illudendum, quod hîc locum habere non potest, neque illud indicant verba sequentia, sed potius, quod non sit verè justus. 2. Quòd si ironicè hîc sumatur, non conficies inde, δοξαστικῶς sumi non posse, cùm hæc sæpe sint inter se invicem conjuncta.
units.tr: Answer: 1. Irony is used either to rebuke the person whom you call ironically, or to mock him. This cannot take place here, nor do the following words indicate it; rather they indicate that he is not truly just. 2. But even if it is taken ironically here, you will not conclude from this that it cannot be taken in a complimentary sense [δοξαστικῶς], since these are often joined with one another.

units.la: DLXXV. Exc. 2, M.p. 75. Comparando hæc verba cum Matth.v. ut hic sensus, Justus primò semetipsum pervertiget, antequam proximum suum ad censuram revocet, item justum dici qui pronunciatur justu in judicio: quae omnia sensum hujus loci pervertunt potiùs quàm exponunt. Et quia sufficit ipsi varias afferre interpretationes, quae tamen & semetipsas & saepe textum pervertunt, me eas negare sufficiet.
units.tr: DLXXV. Objection 2, M., p. 75. By comparing these words with Matt. 5, so that the sense is: "The just man first perverts himself before he calls his neighbour to account; likewise one is called just who is pronounced just in judgement": all these things pervert the sense of this passage rather than explain it. And since it is enough for him to bring forward various interpretations, which nevertheless both pervert themselves and often the text, it will be enough for me to deny them.

units.la: DLXXVI. Quod circa Matth. ix. M. p. 76. observat, jam refutatum est, nisi quod dicat, hîc agi de re fidei & quidem articulo fundamentali. Ad quod facilis est responsio. Nam etiamsi ipsa vocatio ad salutem per Christum sit articulus fundamentalis, tamen, justos esse aliquos secundum apparentiam, atque tales dici cum nullo articulo fundamentali pugnat, ut per se est manifestum.
units.tr: DLXXVI. What he observes about Matt. 9, M., p. 76, has already been refuted, except that he says the matter here concerns the faith, and indeed a fundamental article. The reply to this is easy. For even if the calling itself to salvation through Christ is a fundamental article, nevertheless that some are just according to appearance, and are called such, is in conflict with no fundamental article, as is evident in itself.

units.la: DLXXVII. Secundum Inductionis exemplum praebet locus Prov. xxx. 19. Tria ista occulta à me, imò quatuor haec non novi, viam aquilae in coelo, viam serpentis in rupe, viam navis in alto mari, & viam viri in virgine. Ita est via mulieris adulterae: comedit, deinde abstergit os suum, tum dicit, non sum operata iniquitatem. Hic in Hebraeo habetur vox עלמה, quam interpretes statuunt semper significare virginem intactam, quae nondum virum cognovit, idque ad tuendam Virginitatem B. Mariae Matris Domini nostri, de qua praedixerat Esaias cap. vii. Cùm autem Judaei objiciunt hunc locum Prov. xxx. 19. in quo volunt vocem עלמה sumi pro virgine corrupta, quia versu sequenti dicitur: Ita est via mulieris scortantis, respondent, hîc sumi pro tali, quae sit virgo secundum δοξαν, quod sese pro virgine venditet. Ita Cartwright ad hunc locum: Non attendunt Judaei, Prophetam hoc in loco συγχωρητικῶς per concessionem loqui, prout ver-sus sequens aperte declarat; quia sulicet tamen si vitiata sit, pro virgine tamen sese venditet. Ad eundem modum incantatores, quamvis insigni stultitiâ sint, quia tamen sapientes habere voluerunt & habiti sunt, sapientes in Scriptura nec semel appellantur. Similiter Scultetus in Ef. vii. Quamvis locum Prov. xxx. de corruptâ juvenculâ loquatur, virginem tamen eam dici non quidem ἀληθῶς sed vel ἐρωτικῶς vel δοξαστικῶς (ubi nota, quod ἐρωτικῶς de aliquo dicitur etiam simul δοξαστικῶς esse intelligendum) non est absurdum. Ita & Ursinus in cap. Ef. vii. vocat virginem, id est, quae videtur aut videri vult virgo, etiamsi non sit virgo, id est, non virginem veram, sed simulatam.
units.tr: DLXXVII. The second example of induction is provided by Prov. 30:19: There are three things hidden from me, nay four which I do not know: the way of an eagle in the heavens, the way of a serpent on a rock, the way of a ship on the deep sea, and the way of a man with a maiden. Such is the way of an adulterous woman: she eats, then wipes her mouth, and says, I have done no iniquity. Here the Hebrew has the word almah [עלמה], which the translators hold always signifies an intact virgin who has not yet known a man; and this is to defend the virginity of the Blessed Mary, Mother of our Lord, of whom Isaiah had foretold in chapter 7. When the Jews object to this passage, Prov. 30:19, in which they want the word almah [עלמה] to be taken for a corrupted virgin, because in the following verse it is said, Such is the way of a harlot, they reply that here it is taken for one who is a virgin according to opinion [δοξαν, doxan], in that she offers herself as a virgin. So Cartwright on this passage: The Jews do not notice that the Prophet here speaks συγχωρητικῶς [synchōrētikōs, by concession], as the following verse clearly declares; because, although she may have been defiled, yet she offers herself as a virgin. In the same way, enchanters, although they are of remarkable folly, because they wished to be and were held to be wise, are nowhere in Scripture called wise, not even once. Similarly Scultetus on Isa. 7: Although the passage of Prov. 30 speaks of a corrupted young girl, it is not absurd to call her a virgin, not indeed ἀληθῶς [alēthōs, truly], but either ἐρωτικῶς [erōtikōs, in love-language] or δοξαστικῶς [doxastikōs, according to opinion] (where note that what is said ἐρωτικῶς of someone is also to be understood δοξαστικῶς). So also Ursinus on Isa. 7 calls her a virgin, that is, one who seems or wishes to seem a virgin, even though she is not a virgin, that is, not a true virgin but a feigned one.

units.la: DLXXVIII. Exc. i. B. p. 72. Vitiata se nominat Virginem, sed admittendo viros se mentiri probat.
units.tr: DLXXVIII. Objection 1, B., p. 72. She calls herself a virgin though she is defiled, but by admitting that men are involved she proves that she is lying.
