units.la: Resp. At etiam Spiritus Sanctus Virginem appellat, ergo si probet talis Virgo se mentiri, apparet adhiberi à Spiritu S. locutionem, quae super apparentia & opinione est fundata, quod sufficit ad meum scopum.
units.tr: Reply. But the Holy Spirit also calls her a virgin. Therefore, if such a virgin is shown to be lying, it is evident that the Holy Spirit has used an expression founded upon appearance and opinion, which is enough for my purpose.

units.la: DLXXIX. Exc. 2. M. p. 74. Vocabulo עלמה non designari Virgi-nem corruptam. Sic enim Judaos fortius posse urgere suum argumentum contra Ef. vi 1. Vocabulo autem דרך significari machinationes mirabiles, quibus adulteri & scortatores solent inhiare Virginum pudicitia. Verbis vero sequenti-bus, sic via mulieris adultera, comparari conatus adulterarum, quibus scelera perpetrata à se amoliri nituntur, cum iis, quibus scortatores virginum pudicitia insidiantur.
units.tr: DLXXIX. Objection 2, M., p. 74. That by the word almah [עלמה] a corrupted virgin is not designated. For in this way the Jews could press their argument more strongly against Isa. 7:1. The word derech [דרך] signifies the wonderful devices by which adulterers and fornicators are accustomed to aim at the chastity of virgins. By the following words, "so is the way of an adulterous woman", are compared the attempts of adulteresses, by which they strive to remove the crimes committed by them, with those by which fornicators lay snares for the chastity of virgins.

units.la: Resp. Quòd vox עלמה hic tribuatur Virgini corruptæ propter externam apparentiam, quâ virgo videtur & opinionem super eâ fundatam, apparet ex textu. Non enim fit comparatio inter quatuor propositá v. 19. & quintum v. 20. Sed comparantur hæc tria, via aquilæ in cælo, via serpentis in rupe, via navis in alto mari, cum quarto, quod est via viri in virgine. Illud autem quartum v. 20. ulterius illustratur & contrariore similitudine declaratur, cùm scortum quod antea vocaverat עלמה propter apparentiam externam, ei assimilat, qui aliquid sibi denegatum expetens illud comedit & ne comedisse deprehendatur, os & dentes detergit. Quartum enim imprimis hic fuit, cujus insignem difficultatem vult exaggerare. Unde & numerus Cardinalis quatuor videtur poni pro ordinali quartum, quemadmodum & Lutherus interpretatur. Et cùm cohæreat v. 20. cum præcedente, non potest commodiùs exponi, quàm si dicatur, illo versu rationem reddi, quare viri via in virgine, quæ pro tali se venditet sit occulta, nimirum, quia talis sit similis comedenti & abstergenti os suum. In quâ expohendi ratione consentientem habeo Junium in Parallelo quarto, qui postquam dixisset ea, quæ citabimus art. 675, edit: Eodem modo accipiendum est Puellæ nomen in eo Proverbiorum loco: quod nemo Judæus aut ullus infensissimus Evangelicæ veritatis adversarius negaverit, si attendas ad sapientis verba. Nam postquam dixit Tria illa occulta sunt à me &c. Si rogesquâ virgine? obsecro, audiamus Salomonem ipsum hoc genus virginum explicantem sequente versu &c. Hu certè verbis demonstrat Salomo evidentissimè, eam à se nominatim perstringi, quæ se impudenter affirmat virginem, ac proinde humanâ opinione habetur virgo. 2. Quod verò Judæis sic detur occasio fortius urgendi argumentum suum, non potuerunt videre interpretes citati, qui hoc modo iverunt Judæis obviam, statuentibus vocem עלמה significare juvenculam, adeoque hoc vaticinium posse uxori Prophetæ Esaiæ applicari. Hæc enim responsione data omninò eorum exceptio concidit. Sed non posse Ef. vii. vocem עלמה significare virginem corruptam, vel ex eo contra Judæos ostendi potest, quòd Esaias istam conceptionem & partum tanquam miraculum propo-nat, nat, id quod de conceptione & partu scorti dici nequit.
units.tr: Reply. That the word almah [עלמה] is here ascribed to a corrupted virgin on account of the outward appearance by which she seems a virgin, and the opinion founded upon that, is clear from the text. For no comparison is made between the four things proposed in v. 19 and the fifth in v. 20. Rather, these three are compared: the way of an eagle in the heavens, the way of a serpent on a rock, the way of a ship on the deep sea, with a fourth, which is the way of a man with a maiden. That fourth point, however, in v. 20 is further illustrated and explained by a more contrary likeness, since the harlot, whom he had earlier called almah [עלמה] on account of her outward appearance, is compared to one who, desiring something denied to him, eats it, and to avoid being caught having eaten, wipes his mouth and teeth. For the fourth point was above all the one whose remarkable difficulty he wishes to heighten. Whence the cardinal number four seems to be put for the ordinal fourth, as Luther also interprets it. And since v. 20 coheres with the preceding, it cannot be explained more conveniently than by saying that in that verse a reason is given why the way of a man with a virgin, which she who offers herself as such conceals, is hidden: namely, because she is like one who eats and wipes his mouth. In this manner of explaining I have Junius as an agreeing witness, in his Parallel, fourth, who, after saying those things which we shall cite at art. 675, writes: In the same way the word "maiden" must be understood in that passage of the Proverbs, which no Jew or any most hostile adversary of evangelical truth will deny, if you attend to the words of the sage. For after he said, "These three things are hidden from me", etc. If you ask, with what virgin? I beg you, let us hear Solomon himself explaining this kind of virgin in the following verse, etc. Surely by these words Solomon most clearly shows that he is naming and censuring her who shamelessly affirms that she is a virgin, and therefore by human opinion is regarded as a virgin. Second, that the Jews are thus given an occasion of pressing their argument more strongly, the interpreters cited did not see, who went to meet the Jews in this way, holding that the word almah [עלמה] signifies a young girl, and so this prophecy could be applied to the wife of the Prophet Isaiah. For by giving this reply, their whole objection collapses. But that in Isa. 7 the word almah [עלמה] cannot signify a corrupted virgin can be shown against the Jews from this, that Isaiah sets forth that conception and birth as a miracle, which cannot be said of the conception and birth of a harlot.

units.la: DLXXX. Tertium Inductionis exemplum ponimus locum Jer. xxviii.1. Allocutus est me Chanania filius Hazzurii Propheta, qui erat e Gib-bone & v. 5. Tum alloquens Iirmeja Propheta Chananiam Prophetam illum. Chanania hic aeque vocatur Propheta, hoc est, futura praedicens ac Jeremias, cum tamen ille nihil minus esset, sed Pseudopropheta & seductor populi. Prophetae ergo vocabulum de Chananiâ usurpatum externa apparentia & opinione Judaeorum, qui ab ipso decipiebantur, nituntur. Et ita Piscator in notis in Jeremiam annotat. Qui se profitebatur Prophe-tam. Dictum ☩ ☩.
units.tr: DLXXX. We put forward a third example of this method, the passage Jer. xxviii.1: Hananiah the son of Azzur the prophet spoke to me, who was of Gibeon, and v. 5: Then Jeremiah the prophet spoke to Hananiah the prophet. Here Hananiah is called a prophet just as Jeremiah is, that is, one who foretells the future, although he was anything but this, being a false prophet and a seducer of the people. The title of prophet, then, which is applied to Hananiah, rests on the outward appearance and the opinion of the Jews, who were deceived by him. And Piscator thus notes in his notes on Jeremiah: He who professed himself a prophet. Said ☩ ☩.

units.la: DLXXXI. Exc. 1. B. p. 72. Chanania Prophetam se jactitabat, sed Pseudo-propheta se prodidit.
units.tr: DLXXXI. Exc. 1. B. p. 72. Hananiah boasted that he was a prophet, but the false prophet betrayed himself.

units.la: Resp. At erat talis secundum apparentiam, & hinc sese jactitabat, atque pro tali à Judaeis habebatur (plurimis, licet forte non omnibus) prout apparet ex v. 15. tu fecisti, ut fiduciam poneret populus in falso. Id autem non poterat fieri, nisi eum pro Prophetâ habuisset, quamvis postea fraus ejus fuerit a Jeremiâ detecta, ut apparet, si istud caput integrum libeat alicui inspicere. Haec etiam observare volo H. nihil enim his consideratis video, quod in ipsius verbis p.247, 248. mihi obstat: probandum enim fuisset Hananiam non propterea vocatum fuisse Prophetam, quia talis habitus à populo, licet non esset. At contrarium ex textu constat & à me probatum.
units.tr: Reply: He was indeed a prophet in appearance, and on this basis he boasted of it and was regarded as such by the Jews (by most of them, though perhaps not all), as is clear from v. 15: You have made the people put their trust in a lie. This could not have happened unless they had regarded him as a prophet, although his fraud was later exposed by Jeremiah, as will be clear if anyone cares to read the whole chapter. I also want the reader to note this, since in these considerations I see nothing that stands in the way of what H. says in his words on pages 247 and 248. For it would have had to be proved that Hananiah was not called a prophet because he was regarded as one by the people, even though he was not. But the opposite is established from the text, and I have proved it.

units.la: DLXXXII. Exc. 2. Tandem addit H. p. 248. Spiritus Sanctus mutuatus hi est verbum seu nomen opinionis à populo, non vero opinionem. Et ideo nomen istud eloquitur, sed opinionem erroneam dicere Deum non potest. At quam optime haec conveniunt mea sententiae! Quando enim dixi antehac, Scripturam vel Spiritum Sanctum loqui secundum opinionem aliquando, nihil aliud volo, quam quod nomen, verbum vel phrasin opinionis à populo sit mutuatus, illudque nomen vel phrasin fuerit elocutus. Nullibi vero dixi, quod doceat Spiritus Sanctus ipsam opinionem erroneam, neque verba mea eo trahi volo. Quae vero hic objicit M. p. 78. ea ex haectenus dictis sufficienter reperiet refutata. DLXXXIII. Quartum Exemplum Inductionis desumimus ex Marc. vi. 14. Audivit autem hac Rex Herodes, ubi Antipas vocatur Rex, cum tamen non Rex fuerit, sed tantum Tetrarcha, quemadmodum vocatur Matth. xiv. Et refert Josephus lib. 17. antiquit. quod post mortem Herodis Magni Caesar Augustus Archelao mediam partem regni, quod pater tenuerat, concesserit, alteram vero partem distribuerit inter reliquos duos Herodis Magni Filios, Antipam & Philippum. Nullus autem istorum Herodis filiorum Rex fuit factus, ne Archelaus quidem, cui dimidia pars regni obtigerat, & promissum fuerat regnum, quod etiam fuisset consecutus, nisi in iram Cæsaris incurrisset, quemadmodum ex Josepho satis potest colligi. Quare Antipas non aliter potuit Rex dici, nisi quod se ut Regem gesserit, adeoque in opinione sua & populi pro Rege fuerit habitus, quo non obstante vulgo receptam Regis appellationem ei Sp. S. non dubitat assignare. Cum hac acceptione vocis Regis à me allatâ consentit Dieter. in Dom. 21. post Trinit. qui in textus Joh. iv. 46. explicatione inquit, Etsi Herodes Rex non esset, sed Tetrarcha, Rex tamen à vulgo dicebatur Marc. vi. 14.
units.tr: DLXXXII. Exc. 2. Finally H. adds on p. 248: The Holy Spirit borrows the word or name of opinion from the people, but not the opinion itself. And so he uses that name, but God cannot call an erroneous opinion true. But how well these words agree with my view! For when I said before that Scripture or the Holy Spirit sometimes speaks according to opinion, I meant nothing other than that he borrows the name, word or phrase of opinion from the people and uses that name or phrase. I nowhere said that the Holy Spirit teaches the erroneous opinion itself, nor do I want my words to be taken that way. As for what M. objects on p. 78, the reader will find it sufficiently refuted by what has been said so far. DLXXXIII. We take a fourth example of this method from Mark vi. 14: Now King Herod heard of this, where Antipas is called king, although he was not a king but only a tetrarch, as he is called in Matt. xiv. And Josephus, in book 17 of the Antiquities, reports that after the death of Herod the Great, Caesar Augustus granted Archelaus the middle part of the kingdom that his father had held, and divided the other part between the two remaining sons of Herod the Great, Antipas and Philip. None of these sons of Herod was made king, not even Archelaus, to whom half the kingdom had fallen and who had been promised the kingdom, which he would indeed have obtained had he not incurred the anger of Caesar, as can sufficiently be gathered from Josephus. Hence Antipas could be called king only because he conducted himself as a king, and so in his own opinion and that of the people he was regarded as king; and despite this, the Holy Spirit does not hesitate to assign to him the title of king, which was commonly accepted. Dieter agrees with this sense of the word king which I have given, for in his explanation of John iv. 46, in his twenty-first Sunday after Trinity sermon, he says: Although Herod was not a king but a tetrarch, he was nevertheless called king by the common people, Mark vi. 14.

units.la: DLXXXIV. Exc. i. B. p: 71. Antipas vocatur Rex, quia titulo illo delectabatur, cum Magni Regis esset filius.
units.tr: DLXXXIV. Exc. i. B. p. 71. Antipas is called king because he delighted in that title, although he was the son of the Great King.

units.la: Resp. Hæc non pugnant, imo unum ex altero sequitur, quia enim titulo illo delectabatur, se gessit ut Regem, ut opinionem talem de se populus conciperet, adeoque se Regem appellaret, quam appellationem Spiritus Sanctus dum retinere voluit, eo ipso nobis præbuit exemplum Scripturæ usurpantis phrasin externæ apparentiæ & opinioni super ea fundatæ convenientem.
units.tr: Answer: These statements do not conflict; indeed, the one follows from the other. Because he delighted in that title, he behaved as a king, so that the people would form such an opinion of him, and therefore he called himself king. By retaining this designation, the Holy Spirit gave us an example of Scripture using language that fits outward appearance and the opinion founded upon it.

units.la: DLXXXV. Exc. 2. H. p. 249. Vulgus appellavit Regem sed non eum esse credebat, Joh. xix. 12. Omnis qui se Regem facit contradicit Cæsari. Et v. 15. Non habemus inquiunt Regem nisi Cæsarem.
units.tr: DLXXXV. Exc. 2. H. p. 249. The crowd called him king, but they did not believe that he was one, John 19:12. Everyone who makes himself king contradicts Caesar. And at v. 15: They say, We have no king but Caesar.

units.la: Resp. Sensus Judæorum apud Johannem est, partes Imperatoris Romani sibi vindicare, qui sine ejus auctoritate vult regnare, ut Grotius hic annotat, idque clamabant impulsi à sacerdotibus, non tam, quod adeo libenter Cæsari subjecti essent, sed quod desiderium Christum trucidandi hunc ipsis clamorem exprimeret. Christum ergo accusabant tanquam talem, qui sine auctoritate Cæsaris regnum sibi assereret, (cum tamen ejus regnum non esset terrenum & de hoc mundo, sed spirituale & alterius generis.) Quod si autem propius exceptionem hanc consideremus, tali modo procedat oportet. Qui nullum volebant Regem recipere præter Cæsarem, illi non credebant Herodem Regem. Atqui illi ipsi Judæi Galilæi nullum volebant Regem recipere. Ergo. Ad hanc respondeo, 1. distinguendo. Noluerunt Regem recipere præter Cæsarem non ex animo, sed simulatè, ut hic Pilato persuaderent Christi homicidium. Quàm enim aliàs proni fuerint ad excutiendum jugum Cæsaris, ex historia Josephi patet. 2. Si tamen seria hic quorundam voluntas fuerit, dico hoc sensisse, se nolle recipere Regem, qui sine Cæsaris auctoauctoritate regnaret. At dum Herodem Antipam Regem esse putavit populus, non sine Cæsaris auctoritate regnare autumasse censendum est.
units.tr: Answer: The meaning of the Jews in John is that they claim the rights of the Roman Emperor, who wishes to reign without his authority, as Grotius notes here. They shouted this, urged on by the priests, not so much because they were willingly subject to Caesar, but because their desire to put Christ to death forced this cry from them. They therefore accused Christ of being one who claimed a kingdom for himself without Caesar's authority, although his kingdom was not earthly and of this world, but spiritual and of another kind. But if we consider this objection more closely, it must proceed in this way: those who wanted to receive no king except Caesar did not believe Herod to be king. But those same Galilean Jews wanted to receive no king. Therefore... I answer this: first, by distinguishing. They did not want to receive a king except Caesar not sincerely, but in pretence, so that they might persuade Pilate to kill Christ. For how eager they were at other times to shake off Caesar's yoke is clear from the history of Josephus. 2. If, however, the will of some of them here was serious, I say they meant only that they would not receive a king who reigned without Caesar's authority. But while the people thought Herod Antipas was king, it must be judged that they did not suppose he reigned without Caesar's authority.

units.la: DLXXXVI. Quem movent exceptiones M. p. 79, 80, 81. eum attendere velim ad sequentia, quæ ex Josephi historia depromsi. Is lib. 17. Antiq. cap. 10. dicit, quòd Archelaum ab Herode per Testamentum fuerit Rex constitutum, à Regis nomine tamen sibi abstinendum censuerit, quòd ab auctoritate & assensu Cæsaris penderet, penes quem sit Testamenti à patre conscripti confirmatio, cap. 11. in fine inquit, Cæsarem Archelaum dignum regno pronunciasse, atque testamenti paterni confirmationem promisisse, sed viso hac promissione confirmatum in spe juvenem, nihil tum amplius super eo statuisse, sed deliberasse secum, unine regnum ratum faceret, an commune sineret Herodis generi? Cap. 12. referTur accusatio Judæorum contra Herodem Magnum jam mortuum & Archelaum. Cap. 13. testatur, Cæsarem Archelaum non declarasse Regem, sed dimidia parte ditionis, quæ Herodis fuerat, et concessa Ethnarcham eum constituisse, regnum quoque pollicitum fuisse. quamprimum ille se tali honore dignum redderet, alteram dimidiam partem partitum esse inter alios duos Herodis Filios, Philippum & Antipam eum, qui cum Archelao de toto regno contenderat. Tandem Cap. 15. docet, Archelaum jam Ethnarcham in Judæam reversum decimo principatus sui anno a primatibus Judæorum fuisse delatum ad Cæsarem, à quo postquam auditus esset, Viennam Galliæ in exilium fuisse missum. Ex quibus patebit, nec Archelaum nec Herodem Antipam vere Regem fuisse. Nec ego nego, Principem tributarium posse Regem vocari, sed dico ex Josepho, neminem potuisse Regem vere appellari, nisi qui à Cæsare fuerit constitutus, uti ex historia Josephi est manifestum. Unde & absurdum esse patebit, quod dicit Adversarius, Antipam, Philippum & Archelaum eodem modo fuisse Reges, quo Herodes Magnus eorum parens, cum expresse id ipsis à Cæsare fuerit denegatum. De Agrippa alia ratio, qui Rex fuit constitutus à Cajo Cæsare, impositio in ejus caput diadema, teste eodem Josepho lib. 17. antiquit. cap. 8. fine. Consentiunt meum omnes fere docti horum temporum. Instar omnium sit Isaacus Casaubonus Exercit. I. contra Baronium Sect. 2. in fine pag. mihi 16. b. Auxit vero calamitas, & unus quasi gradus ad perniciem ultimam est factus, anno post natum Dominum circiter decimo, cum Archelao Viennam relegato, Judæa in formulam provinciæ est redacta: quod quam vim habeat, peritis rerum Romanarum satis est compertum. Ab eo tempore nullus unquam postea Judæa neque Rex fuit, neque Ethnarcha: planeque tum accidit, quod modo Justinus dicebat, & Judæi sic proprie dicti, Ἰουδαῖοι βασιλέως ἐπαιονται. ἰπαύοντο εἶναι proprio sibi Regi desierunt esse subjecti. Nam quod Eusebius, & eum secutus Baronius, Agrippam juniorem Regem ultimum Judaeorum appellant; quasi ille Hierosolymorum Rex fuerit: meraeft virorum eruditissimorum hallucinatio. Fuerunt quidem & senior Agrippa & junior reges Judaeorum; sed non Hierosolymorum, neque τ κυρίως λεγομένων, hoc est, proprie dictorum Judaeorum; de quâ distinctione alio loco erit dicendum. Herodes Antipas & Philippus, neque Reges unquam fuerunt, sed Ethmarchae, id quoque non Hierosolymorum, sed adjacentium regionum. Vera Judaea, amoto Archelao, in formulam provinciae, sicuti dicebamus, redacta, Syriae accessit; cepitque tum in eum mitti, qui vocabatur 'Procurator Caesaris in Judaea', vel etiam procurator Judaeae, de quo multa inferius.
units.tr: DLXXXVI. Whoever is moved by the objections of M., pp. 79, 80, 81, I would like him to attend to what follows, which I have drawn from the history of Josephus. In Antiquities book 17, chapter 10, he says that Archelaus was appointed king by Herod's will, but that he judged he should abstain from the title of king, because it depended on the authority and assent of Caesar, in whose power lay the confirmation of the will drawn up by his father. In chapter 11, near the end, he says that Caesar pronounced Archelaus worthy of the kingdom and promised to confirm his father's will; but when the young man saw this promise and was confirmed in hope, Caesar then decided nothing more about him, but deliberated with himself whether to ratify the kingdom or to let it remain common to Herod's family. Chapter 12 relates the accusation of the Jews against Herod the Great, now dead, and against Archelaus. Chapter 13 testifies that Caesar did not declare Archelaus king, but, having granted him half of the territory that had belonged to Herod, appointed him ethnarch, and also promised him the kingdom, as soon as he should show himself worthy of such honour; the other half was divided between two other sons of Herod, Philip and Antipas, the latter of whom had contended with Archelaus for the whole kingdom. Finally, chapter 15 teaches that Archelaus, having returned to Judaea as ethnarch, was in the tenth year of his rule denounced to Caesar by the leading men of the Jews, and after being heard by him, was sent into exile at Vienne in Gaul. From these things it will be clear that neither Archelaus nor Herod Antipas was truly king. I do not deny that a tributary prince may be called king, but I say from Josephus that no one could truly be called king unless he had been appointed by Caesar, as is manifest from the history of Josephus. Hence it will also be clear that what my opponent says is absurd, namely that Antipas, Philip and Archelaus were kings in the same way as Herod the Great, their father, since this was expressly denied them by Caesar. Agrippa is another case, for he was appointed king by Caius Caesar, and a diadem was placed on his head, as the same Josephus witnesses in Antiquities book 17, chapter 8, near the end. Almost all the learned men of our time agree with me. Let Isaac Casaubon, Exercitation I against Baronius, section 2, near the end, page 16b in my copy, stand for all: "Calamity increased, and it became, as it were, one step to final ruin, when, about the tenth year after the birth of the Lord, Archelaus having been banished to Vienne, Judaea was reduced to the form of a province; and it is well enough known to those versed in Roman affairs what force this has. From that time no one afterwards was ever king or ethnarch of Judaea; and then came to pass what Justin had just said, and the Jews, as they are properly so called, 'ceased to be subject to a king of their own' (Ἰουδαῖοι βασιλέως ἐπαίοντο) [ἐπαύοντο εἶναι]. For what Eusebius, and Baronius following him, call the younger Agrippa the last king of the Jews, as though he had been king of Jerusalem, is pure delusion of most learned men. There were indeed both the elder and the younger Agrippa, kings of the Jews; but not of Jerusalem, nor of the Jews in the proper sense (τῶν κυρίως λεγομένων) [of those properly so called]; concerning this distinction something will have to be said in another place. Herod Antipas and Philip were never kings, but ethnarchs, and not of Jerusalem but of the neighbouring regions. True Judaea, with Archelaus removed, was reduced to the form of a province, as we were saying, and was added to Syria; and then began to be sent there a man who was called 'Procurator of Caesar in Judaea', or even procurator of Judaea, concerning whom much more below."

units.la: DLXXXVII. Quintum Exemplum Inductionis suppeditat 2 Cor. IV. 4. In quibus Deus hujus seculi excaecavit mentes, nempe in infidelibus.
units.tr: DLXXXVII. The fifth example of induction is supplied by 2 Cor. 4:4: In whom the God of this age has blinded the minds, namely of unbelievers.

units.la: Hic Diabolus vocatur Deus hujus seculi, quod non nisi δοξαστικῶς & putativè intelligendum est, quemadmodum etiam fieri debet, quando idola gentium passim in Scripturâ dii vocantur, ut inter alia Exod. 23. 24. Ne incurvando te honorem habeto Dii eorum, scil. Cananaeorum & reliquarum gentium, quas Deus coram Israelitis expulit. Unde & Theologi, nominatim Leyd. in Synopsi Theol. Disp. VI. art. 13. quando de nomine Dei agunt, annotant, illud vel proprie vel improprie sumi; improprie itidem vel κοινωνητῶς, quando Angelis vel hominibus propter excellentem dignitatem &c. tribuitur, vel δοξαστικῶς ex opinione & errore falsis Diis.
units.tr: Here the devil is called "the god of this age," which must be understood only by opinion [δοξαστικῶς] and as a matter of supposition, just as must be done wherever the idols of the Gentiles are called gods throughout Scripture, as in Exod. 23:24, among other places: You shall not bow down to their gods, namely of the Canaanites and the other nations whom God drove out before the Israelites. Hence the theologians, notably Leyden in the Synopsis of Theology, Disp. VI, art. 13, when they treat of the name of God, observe that it is used either properly or improperly. Improperly, again, it is used either in common [κοινωνητῶς], when it is given to angels or men on account of their excellent dignity, etc., or by opinion [δοξαστικῶς], from the belief and error of false gods.

units.la: DLXXXVIII. Quae hic M. p. 81, 82. excipere conatur, ea magis meam sententiam confirmant.
units.tr: DLXXXVIII. What M. tries to object to on pages 81 and 82 confirms my view even more.

units.la: Nam quòd Diabolus dicatur Deus hujus seculi, quia ab Impiis pro Deo habetur, eique major cultus exhibetur quàm vero Deo, atque sic practice Deus aestimatur, hoc & ego dico, & unà cum Theologis contendo. Hoc enim ad meum scopum sufficit, ut probem Scripturam aliquando uti phrasibus, quae apparentiae & opinioni super eâ fundatae conveniunt. 2. Quod porro dicit, Diabolum vere Deum esse quamvis metaphorice, quod in malis faciendis primatum revera obtineat, haud secus ac Deus Opt. Max. in bonis facere consuevit: sive quod justo Dei judicio talem in filios inobedientiae obtineat potestatem, qualem Deus habet in universum mundum, id referens horresco; malim tamen judicare ex studio contradicendi, cui totum sese dedisse videtur, hominí excidisse. Nam, si Diabolus verè Deus dicendus, quod in malis faciendis principatum revera obtineat, ut Deus in bonis, nonne sic duo Principia duosque Deos introduces cum Manichaeis, unum bonum alterum malum? Dein, si propter similem aliquam potestatem, sed tamen valde limitatam & restrictam, aliquis est vere Deus, quidni recte fecit Alexander Magnus, qui se pro Deo adorari volebat, magnam habuerit potestatem? Videat Lector, quo tandem studium contradicendi hos homines deducat.
units.tr: For that the devil is called the god of this age, because he is regarded as God by the impious, and greater worship is paid to him than to the true God, so that in practice he is esteemed God, I too say this, and I contend along with the theologians. For this is enough for my purpose, namely to prove that Scripture sometimes uses phrases that suit appearance and the opinion founded upon it. 2. Furthermore, when he says that the devil is truly God, though metaphorically, because he actually holds the primacy in doing evil, just as God Most Good and Great is accustomed to act in good things; or because by God's just judgment he holds over the sons of disobedience such power as God has over the whole world, I shudder to repeat it. I would rather judge that he has fallen into this out of a zeal for contradiction, to which he seems to have given himself entirely. For if the devil must truly be called God, because he actually holds the principate in doing evil, as God does in good, do we not thus introduce two principles and two gods with the Manichaeans, one good and the other evil? Next, if on account of some similar power, though very limited and restricted, someone is truly God, why did Alexander the Great not rightly do so, who wished to be worshipped as God, since he had great power? Let the reader see where this zeal for contradiction finally leads these men.

units.la: DLXXXIX. Sextum Exemplum locutionum talium desumimus ex Epist. ad Gal. I. 6. Miror vos ita cito, deserto eo, qui vocavit vos in gratiam Christi, transferri in aliud Euangelium. Doctrinam Pseudo-Apostolorum vocat Paulus aliud Euangelium, innitente ista appellatione opinioni istorum hominum, cum esset oppositum Euangelio Christi, adeoque nomine Euangelii indignum. Atque ita interpretes exponunt. Perkins. ad haec verba ita annotat. Ad aliud Euangelium] ad aliam doctrinam salutis, quae juxta opinionem & verba falsorum Doctorum, est aliud Euangelii genus, absolutius & excellentius, quam id quod Paulus tradidit. Musculus: Fieri potuit ut vel ipsi suam doctrinam aliud Euangelium vocarint, vel auditores illorum dixerint. Hoc aliud Euangelium est ab eo, quod vobis Paulus praedicavit, atque ita Apostolus μιμητικῶς seductricem illam doctrinam aliud Euangelium appellavit. Nam alias, quod non est Euangelium, non potest vere aliud esse Euangelium, quemadmodum alius homo esse nequit, qui non est homo, & alius Christus, qui non est Christus, & alius Deus, qui non est vere Deus.
units.tr: DLXXXIX. We take the sixth example of such expressions from Galatians 1:6: I marvel that you are so quickly turning away from him who called you into the grace of Christ to another gospel. Paul calls the teaching of the false apostles "another gospel", a name resting on the opinion of those men, since it was opposed to the gospel of Christ and so unworthy of the name of gospel. And so the interpreters explain it. Perkins annotates on these words thus: To another gospel: to another doctrine of salvation, which, according to the opinion and words of the false teachers, is another kind of gospel, more perfect and excellent than that which Paul delivered. Musculus: It could be that either they themselves called their doctrine another gospel, or their hearers said so. This "another gospel" differs from that which Paul preached to you, and so the Apostle mimetically [μιμητικῶς] called that seductive doctrine another gospel. For otherwise, what is not the gospel cannot truly be another gospel, just as another man cannot be a man who is not a man, and another Christ who is not Christ, and another God who is not truly God.

units.la: DXC. Cum autem ibi vox Euangelii non sumatur generaliter pro quovis laeto nuncio, sed pro laeto nuncio de salute, apparet, non potuisse dici doctrinam Pseudo-Apostolorum verum Euangelium, quemadmodum M. p. 82. quem videat lector, exstimat. Illud enim est Euangelium verum, quod vera salutis media annunciat, non aliud; nisi veram doctrinam practicam appellare velis, quae ad finem bonum per contraria media deducit, vel etiam salutis, quae ad infernum tendit. Quid tandem non audebit eructare zelus perversus, modo contradixisse dici possit?
units.tr: DXC. But since the word gospel here is not taken generally for any joyful news, but for joyful news of salvation, it is clear that the doctrine of the false apostles could not be called the true gospel, as M. supposes on page 82, which the reader may see. For that is the true gospel which announces the true means of salvation, and not another, unless you wish to call it true practical doctrine, which leads to a good end by contrary means, or even of salvation, which tends to hell. What will perverse zeal not dare to belch out at last, provided it can be said to have contradicted?

units.la: DXCI. Septimum Exemplum locutionum innitentium opinioni hominum suppeditat Jos. II. caput, in quo dicitur de exploratoribus ab Israelitis missis, quod illos persecuti fuerint quidam ex Hierichuntinis, v. 7. Viri illi persecuti fuerunt illos via ad Jordanem per vada singula, v. 16. ad ipsum montem ite ne occurrant vobis, qui persequuntur, v. 22. Abeuntes venerunt in montem illum ac manserunt ibi tribus diebus, donec redissent, qui persequebantur, quaesiverant enim eos, qui persequebantur tota via illa, sed non invenerunt. In Hebraeo habetur ורדפו אחריהם, quod si verbotenus reddas, erit, persecuti sunt post ipsos. At fuerunt illi viri abscondati primum in stipulis lini, quae erant super tecto aedium Rachabae, dein tribus diebus in monte latuerunt ex Rachabæ consilio. Non poterant ergò in rei veritate persequi post eos; sed denuo hic habemus exemplum Scripturæ usurpantis locutionem innitentem opinioni hominum.
units.tr: DXCI. The seventh example of expressions resting on the opinion of men is supplied by Joshua chapter 2, where it is said of the spies sent by the Israelites that certain of the people of Jericho pursued them, v. 7: Those men pursued them by the way to the Jordan, by the fords. v. 16: Go to the mountain, lest those who pursue meet you. v. 22: Going away they came to that mountain and stayed there three days, until those who were pursuing returned; for those who pursued had sought them all along that way, but did not find them. In the Hebrew it reads ורדפו אחריהם [veradfu acharehem], which, if rendered word for word, is "they pursued after them." But those men were first hidden among the stalks of flax that lay on the roof of Rahab's house, and then for three days lay hidden in the mountain on Rahab's advice. They therefore could not, in the reality of the matter, "pursue after them"; here again we have an example of Scripture using an expression that rests on the opinion of men.

units.la: DXCII. Hic verò quam ineptum audias effugium B. p. 79. Hierichuntini cum consilium sequerentur mentientis Rachabæ, persecuti sunt illos, sed quos? Verone exploratores? non, sed fictos, de quibus mentita erat Rachab, illos jam exivisse: intendebant enim veros exploratores persequi & assequi, sed revera tantum enim fictos persequebantur. Illud cum refert Spiritus Sanctus annon loquitur ex rei veritate?
units.tr: DXCII. Here indeed hear what a foolish escape B. offers on page 79: The people of Jericho, when they followed the counsel of lying Rahab, pursued them, but whom? The true spies? No, but the feigned ones, about whom Rahab had lied, saying that they had already gone out. For they intended to pursue and overtake the true spies, but in fact they were pursuing only the feigned ones. When the Holy Spirit relates this, does he not speak from the reality of the matter?

units.la: Resp. Verba sunt, quibus contradicendi studium proditur, nec tamen contra licitur. Versu 7. dicitur, viri illi persecuti fuerunt אחריהם post eos NB. Quinam illi? pronomen illud refertur ad antecedens aliquod substantivum, de quo sermo erat factus: at ad quod aliud referetur, quam ad exploratores, quos egressos mentita erat Rachab, quosque persequi intendebant Hierichuntini? An vero de fictis mentionem fecerat Rachab dicendo: Ficti exploratores exierunt? an fictos volebat intelligi, idque significabat verbis? nequaquam; omnino ergò dicuntur persecuti veros exploratores; adeoque Spiritus Sancti locutio opinioni istorum Hierichuntinorum innititur, non rei veritati.
units.tr: Reply. These are words that betray a zeal for contradiction, and yet they are not permitted against it. In verse 7 it says that those men pursued אחריהם [acharehem], "after them." NB. Who were they? That pronoun refers to some antecedent noun about which the discourse had been made. To what other thing will it refer, then, than to the spies, whom Rahab said had gone out and whom the people of Jericho intended to pursue? Or did Rahab mention the feigned ones when she said, "The spies went out"? Did she wish the feigned ones to be understood, and signify this by her words? By no means. So they are altogether said to have pursued the true spies, and therefore the Holy Spirit's expression rests on the opinion of those people of Jericho, not on the reality.

units.la: DXCIII. Quod verò M. p. 86. dicit, non posse dici Scripturam hac formula usam, ne turbaret lectorem, id fateor; nec unquam dixi, ubique ad illud attendi: sed usa est hac formulâ, quia ea est recepta ad significandum, aliquem eam viam ingressum, qua alium, quem assequi vult, putat incessisse, sive illud verè, sive falso putaverit, innitens opinioni erroneæ, quod hic videmus factum. Ad reliqua, quæ ibidem opponit, agnosco, vocabulum Persequi in sacris literis significare idem, quod alicujus vitæ &c. insidiari; at tum sumitur impropriè pro machinationibus animi, sed hic simul includitur motus corporis, corpore enim dicuntur persecuti post ipsos, hoc est, eâ viâ secuti, qua putabant fugisse. Nec tantum intentio persecutorum narratur, sed ipse actus, qui talis est, ut in rei veritate sub isto formali non potuerit prædicari de Hierichuntinis.
units.tr: DXCIII. As for what M. says on page 86, that Scripture cannot be said to have used this formula so as not to disturb the reader, I admit it. Nor have I ever said that this was attended to everywhere. But it used this formula because it is the accepted way of signifying that someone has entered upon the road by which he thinks the man he wishes to overtake has gone, whether he thought so truly or falsely, resting on an erroneous opinion, which is what we see happening here. As to the rest of what he objects there, I acknowledge that the word "to pursue" in the sacred letters means the same as "to lie in wait for someone's life" and so on; but then it is taken improperly, for machinations of the mind. Here, however, bodily motion is included at the same time, for they are said to have pursued after them with their bodies, that is, by the way they thought the men had fled. Nor is only the intention of the pursuers narrated, but the act itself, which is such that, in the reality of the matter, it could not have been predicated of the people of Jericho under that formal description.

units.la: DXCIV. Octavum Inductionis nostræ exemplum desumimus ex I Sam. xxviii. 12. Cum autem videret mulier Samuelem, v. 14. agnoscens Saul Samuelem esse, v. 15. dixit autem Samuel Sauli, quare commovisti me evocando me. v. 16. cui dicit Samuel, quare ergo consulis me? v. 20. adeo rimebat valde à verbis Samuelis. Eum, qui hic evocatus fuit à Pythonissa ad Saulis instantiam, fuisse Diabolum, constat inter omnes Orthodoxos, vel maxime eo argumento, quod nullo modo Diabolo, cujus opera utuntur magi & necromantīci, tanta potestas à Deo concedatur, ut mortui sancti ejus imperio sint subjecti, quo de eorum animis disponere possit, pro suo lubitu: interim non semel dicitur Samuel, unde & Ecclesiasticus Apocryphus occasionem videtur sumpsisse, hæc vero Samuelis applicandi. Vocatur ergo Samuel, quia speciem Samuelis referebat, ex opinione Saulis & Pythonissæ, non ex rei veritate. Consentit nobiscum Perkinsius tom. I. p. 1136. Βασκανολογία dicens: Scriptura se frequenter ad captum intelligentiamque nostram demittit, de rebus non prout se habent, sed more humano loquens. Eodem illa respectu etiam Samuelem imaginarium nomine veri Samuelis appellat, propterea, quod talis Sauli videretur.
units.tr: DXCIV. The eighth example of our induction we take from 1 Samuel 28. v. 12: When the woman saw Samuel; v. 14: Saul, perceiving that it was Samuel; v. 15: Samuel said to Saul, "Why have you disturbed me by calling me up?" v. 16: Samuel says to him, "Why then do you consult me?" v. 20: So greatly did he fear the words of Samuel. That the one who was here called up by the Pythoness at Saul's urging was the devil is agreed among all the orthodox, chiefly for this argument: God in no way grants to the devil, whose work magicians and necromancers employ, such power that his holy dead are subject to his command, so that he could dispose of their souls at his pleasure. Yet more than once he is called Samuel, whence the Apocryphal Ecclesiasticus seems to have taken occasion to apply these things to Samuel. So he is called Samuel because he presented the appearance of Samuel, according to the opinion of Saul and the Pythoness, not according to the reality. Perkins agrees with us, vol. I, p. 1136, in the chapter on Baskanologia [Βασκανολογία], saying: Scripture frequently lowers itself to our capacity and understanding, speaking of things not as they are, but in human fashion. In that same respect it also calls the imagined Samuel by the name of the true Samuel, because he seemed such to Saul.

units.la: DXCV. Exc. B. p. 72. Dæmon credebatur & vocabatur Samuel, quia faciem & habitum ejus referebat.
units.tr: DXCV. Exc. B. p. 72. The demon was believed and called Samuel, because he resembled Samuel's face and bearing.

units.la: Resp. Consensus ergo est inter nos manifestus, adeoque est exemplum Scripturæ usurpantis formulam, quæ apparentiæ externæ & opinioni super ea fundatæ innititur.
units.tr: Reply: There is therefore a clear agreement between us, and so this is an example of Scripture using a form of expression that rests on external appearance and on the opinion founded upon it.

units.la: DXCVI. M. tamen p. 87. inquit, hic esse metaphoram, quâ Scriptura similitudines appellare solet nomine rerum ipsarum, sicut imagines lignea appellantur Cherubim &c. Atque ea metaphora Diabolum appellari Samuelem propter speciem & similitudinem Samuelis quam referebat.
units.tr: DXCVI. M. nevertheless, p. 87, says that here there is a metaphor, by which Scripture is accustomed to call likenesses by the names of the things themselves, just as wooden images are called Cherubim, etc.; and by that metaphor the devil is called Samuel on account of the appearance and likeness of Samuel which he bore.

units.la: Resp. Quando imagini tribuitur rei ipsius nomen, v. g. quando de eo, qui vidit imaginem Cæsaris dicitur, vidit Cæsarem, sensus proprius istius locutionis est hic, quod viderit signum Cæsarem repræsentans: at quando dicitur, quod Saul agnoverit Samuelem, seque ei incurvaverit, & consilium ejus expetiverit, hic sensus, nisi admodum absurde, esse nequit, quod agnoverit signum repræsentans Samuelem &c. quod ei signo se incurvaverit; sed potius exinde constat, quod Saul cum vero Samuele negotium sibi esse putaverit, adeoque istam appellationem à Spiritu Sancto ex ejus ore acceptam & usurpatam eo ipso innixam fuisse erroneæ ejus opinioni, quod hoc loco conamur probare.
units.tr: Reply: When the name of a thing is given to its image, for example when of one who has seen the image of Caesar it is said, "he saw Caesar," the proper sense of that expression is that he saw a sign representing Caesar. But when it is said that Saul recognised Samuel, bowed himself down to him, and sought his counsel, the sense cannot be (unless in a thoroughly absurd way) that he recognised a sign representing Samuel, etc., and bowed himself down to that sign. Rather it follows from this that Saul believed he was dealing with the real Samuel, and so that this appellation, received and used by the Holy Spirit from Saul's own mouth, rested on his mistaken opinion, which is what we are trying to prove in this place.

units.la: DXCVII. Simile exemplum præbet locus Deut. xviii, 10, 11. Ne invenitor in te utens incantatione, aut inquirens Pythonem, aut Ariolus aut mortuos consulens. Hic Necromantici dicuntur mortuos consulere, cum hoc fiat tantum in ipsorum opinione & aliorum, non in rei veritate: putant se mortuos hos vel illos consulere, & colloquium cum iis instituere, cum tamen sit Diabolus, qui sub specie mortuorum iis apparet, eosque sal-lit.
units.tr: DXCVII. The passage Deut. 18:10, 11 provides a similar example: "Let there not be found among you anyone who uses enchantment, or who inquires of a Python, or a soothsayer, or who consults the dead." Here necromancers are said to consult the dead, although this happens only in their own opinion and that of others, not in the truth of the matter: they think they are consulting this or that dead person and holding conversation with them, whereas it is the devil who, under the appearance of the dead, appears to them and deceives them.

units.la: DXCVIII.
units.tr: DXCVIII.

units.la: DXCVIII. Exc. M. p. 88. Necromantici vere consulunt mortuos, quamvis responsum accipiant à Diabolo, sub mortuorum cadaveribus latente.
units.tr: DXCVIII. Exc. M. p. 88. Necromancers truly consult the dead, although they receive an answer from the Devil, who lies hidden under the corpses of the dead.

units.la: Resp. Neg. quod verè consulant mortuos. Consulere enim mortuos non tantum est, petere consilium, sed etiam accipere à mortuis, cum sit Diabolus à quo consilium capiunt. Consulunt ita ut colloquium instituant, quod sane non instituunt cum mortuis, sed cum Diabolo, qui sub specie eorum apparet; ergo vicissim est exemplum locutionis secundum apparentiam & opinionem ei innitentem.
units.tr: Answer: I deny that they truly consult the dead. For to consult the dead is not merely to seek counsel but also to receive it from the dead, whereas the one from whom they take counsel is the Devil. They hold a consultation, but not with the dead, which they certainly do not hold; they hold it with the Devil, who appears under the form of the dead. Therefore, conversely, this is an example of speech according to appearance and the opinion resting upon it.

units.la: DXCIX. Decimum Inductionis Exemplum petimus ex Joh. v.31.
units.tr: DXCIX. For the tenth example of induction we take Joh. v. 31.

units.la: Si ego testor de me ipso, testimonium meum non est firmum, nempe secundum vestram opinionem, cum vos possitis de eo dubitare; alias enim in rei veritate testimonium Christi semper est firmum, cum sit ipsa veritas, ipseque docet Joh. vi. 11, 14. Etiamsi ego testor de me ipso, firmum est meum testimonium. Designat autem Christus testimonium suum apud Judaeos nullum effectum habiturum, locutione innitente opinioni erroneae, quod Christi testimonium nullam habeat firmitatem.
units.tr: If I bear witness of myself, my witness is not true: that is, according to your opinion, since you may doubt it. For otherwise, in the truth of the matter, the testimony of Christ is always true, since he is truth itself, and he himself teaches this at John vi. 11, 14: Even if I bear witness of myself, my witness is true. Christ, however, means that his testimony will have no effect among the Jews, speaking in a way that accords with their erroneous opinion, that the testimony of Christ has no firmness.

units.la: DC. Exc. 1. B. p. 80. Hic Christum in collatione cum adversariis ipsis aliquid concedere, ut argumentis ad eos confutandos fortioribus constringantur, atque de eo facile inter nos convenire posse, sed hoc parum pertinere ad scopum meum. Consentit M. p. 89. Esse in hoc loco concessionem manifestam, quae aequipolleat his verbis, dato, non concesso.
units.tr: DC. Exc. 1. B. p. 80. Here Christ concedes something to his adversaries in the course of disputing with them, so that they may be pressed by arguments that are stronger for refuting them; and that it can easily be agreed between us, but this has little bearing on my purpose. M. agrees, p. 89: There is in this place a manifest concession, which is equivalent to these words: granted, not conceded.

units.la: Resp. Si concedit hic aliquid Christus adversariis, non concedit, quasi in rei veritate sit concedendum, sed relinquit ipsorum opinionem sine refutatione, atque phrasi utitur, quae eorum opinioni erroneae innititur. Atque sic probatur Minor mei argumenti articulo 566. propositi, quae Minor probata quomodo faciat ad meum scopum ex initio hujus capitis apparet, quod lector benevolus consulat.
units.tr: Answer: If Christ here concedes something to his adversaries, he does not concede it as though it must be conceded in the truth of the matter; rather, he leaves their opinion without refutation and uses a form of speech that rests upon their erroneous opinion. And thus my minor premise is proved, the one set out in article 566 of my argument; how this proved minor premise bears on my purpose appears from the beginning of this chapter, which the kind reader may consult.

units.la: DCI. Exc. 2. M. p. 88. qui hic in omnes formas se vertit, Testimonium Christi respectu Judaeorum quorundam, quibus non constabat veracitas Christi, vere non fuisse idoneum f. ἀληθὲς, quod alias in se consideratum satis est firmum & infallibile.
units.tr: DCI. Exc. 2. M. p. 88, who here turns himself into every shape: The testimony of Christ, with respect to certain Jews who were not convinced of Christ's truthfulness, was truly not fit, or true, which otherwise, considered in itself, is firm and infallible enough.

units.la: Resp. Si respectu Judaeorum non fuit firmum, cum in se esset, itaque in eorum opinione tantum non erat firmum, non erat idoneum. Adeoque non vere, cum in se idoneum esset, atque sic nihilominus obtineo institutum.
units.tr: Answer: If it was not firm with respect to the Jews, although it was in itself, then it was not firm only in their opinion, and so it was not fit. Hence it was not fit in truth, since in itself it was fit; and thus I nevertheless obtain my aim.

units.la: DCII. Tandem addit M. p. 90. Quatenus autem Spiritus Sanctus salva veracitate sua falsas aliorum opiniones possit referre, & ad tempus absque maxime eo argumento, quod nullo modo Diabolo, cujus opera utuntur magi & necromanti-ci, tanta potestas à Deo concedatur, ut mortui sancti ejus imperio sint subjecti, quo de communi animis disponere possit, pro suo lubitu: interim non semel dicitur Samuel, unde & Ecclesiasticus Apocryphus occasionem videtur sumpsisse, hæc vero Samuelis applicandi. Vocatur ergo Samuel, quia speciem Samuelis referebat, ex opinione Saulis & Pythonissæ, non ex rei veritate. Consentit nobiscum Perkinsius tom. I. p. 1136. Βασιανολογία dicens: Scriptura se sese frequenter ad captum intelligentiamque nostram demittit, de rebus non prout se habent, sed more humano loquens. Eodem illa respectu etiam Samuelem imaginarium nomine veri Samuelis appellat, propterea, quod talis Sauli videretur.
units.tr: DCII. Finally, M. adds, p. 90: But insofar as the Holy Spirit, while his truthfulness is preserved, could relate the false opinions of others, and for a time, without especially by that argument, that God in no way grants to the Devil, whose work magicians and necromancers use, such power that his holy dead are subject to his command, by which he could dispose the common minds at his pleasure. Meanwhile Samuel is named more than once, from which the Apocryphal Ecclesiasticus seems to have taken occasion, but these things are to be applied to Samuel. Therefore he is called Samuel because he bore the likeness of Samuel, according to the opinion of Saul and the woman of Endor, not according to the truth of the matter. Perkins, vol. I, p. 1136, agrees with us, calling it basanologia [Βασιανολογία], saying: Scripture often lets itself down to our capacity and understanding, speaking of things not as they are in themselves, but in human fashion. In that same respect it also calls the imagined Samuel by the name of the true Samuel, because it seemed to be such to Saul.

units.la: DXCV. Exc. B. p. 72. Daemon credebatur & vocabatur Samuel, quia faciem & habitum ejus referebat.
units.tr: DXCV. Exc. B. p. 72. The demon was believed to be, and was called, Samuel, because he bore his face and appearance.

units.la: Resp. Consensus ergo est inter nos manifestus, adeoque est exemplum Scripturæ usurpantis formulam, quæ apparentiæ externæ & opinioni super ea fundatæ innititur.
units.tr: Answer: Therefore there is plain agreement between us, and so this is an example of Scripture using a formula that rests upon external appearance and the opinion founded upon it.

units.la: DXCVI. M. tamen p. 87. inquit, hic esse metaphoram, quâ Scriptura similitudines appellare solet nomine rerum ipsarum, sicut imagines lignea appellantur Cherubim &c. Atque ea metaphora Diabolum appellari Samuelem propter speciem & similitudinem Samuelis quam referebat.
units.tr: DXCVI. M. nevertheless, p. 87, says that here there is a metaphor, by which Scripture is accustomed to call likenesses by the names of the things themselves, just as images of wood are called cherubim, etc. And by that metaphor the Devil is called Samuel because of the appearance and likeness of Samuel which he bore.

units.la: Resp. Quando imagini tribuitur rei ipsius nomen, v. g. quando de eo, qui vidit imaginem Cæsaris dicitur, vidit Cæsarem, sensus proprius istius locutionis est hic, quod viderit signum Cæsarem repræsentans: at quando dicitur, quod Saul agnoverit Samuelem, seque ei incurvaverit, & consilium ejus expetiverit, hic sensus, nisi admodum absurdè, esse nequit, quod agnoverit signum repræsentans Samuelem &c. quod ei signo se incurvaverit; sed potius exinde constat, quod Saul cum vero Samuele negotium sibi esse putaverit, adeoque istam appellationem à Spiritu Sancto ex ejus ore acceptam & usurpatam eo ipso innixam fuisse erroneæ ejus opinioni, quod hoc loco conamur probare.
units.tr: Answer: When the name of the thing itself is given to an image, for example when of one who has seen an image of Caesar it is said that he saw Caesar, the proper sense of that expression is that he saw a sign representing Caesar. But when it is said that Saul recognised Samuel, bowed himself to him, and sought his counsel, this sense cannot be otherwise than absurd: that he recognised a sign representing Samuel, etc., and bowed himself to that sign. Rather, it is clear from this that Saul thought he had to do with the true Samuel; and so this appellation, received and used by the Holy Spirit from his mouth, rested precisely upon his erroneous opinion, which we are attempting to prove in this place.

units.la: DXCVII. Simile exemplum præbet locus Deut. XVIII. 10, 11. Ne inveniator in te utens incantatione, aut inquirens Pythonem, aut Ariolus aut mortuos consulens. Hic Necromantici dicuntur mortuos consulere, cum hoc fiat tantum in ipsorum opinione & aliorum, non in rei veritate: putant se mortuos hos vel illos consulere, & colloquium cum iis instituere, cum tamen sit Diabolus, qui sub specie mortuorum iis apparet, eosque sal-lit.
units.tr: DXCVII. A similar example is given by the passage Deut. xviii. 10, 11: Let there not be found in you anyone who uses enchantment, or who inquires of a Python, or a soothsayer, or who consults the dead. Here necromancers are said to consult the dead, although this happens only in their own opinion and that of others, not in the truth of the matter: they think they are consulting these or those dead, and holding converse with them, whereas it is the Devil who appears to them under the form of the dead and deceives them.

units.la: DXCVIII.
units.tr: DXCVIII.

units.la: DXCVIII. Exc. M. p. 88. Necromantici vere consulunt mortuos, quamvis responsum accipiant à Diabolo, sub mortuorum cadaveribus latente.
units.tr: DXCVIII. Exc. M. p. 88. Necromancers truly consult the dead, although they receive an answer from the Devil, who lies hidden beneath the corpses of the dead.

units.la: Resp. Neg. quod verè consulant mortuos. Consulere enim mortuos non tantum est, petere consilium, sed etiam accipere à mortuis, cum sit Diabolus à quo consilium capiunt. Consulunt ita ut colloquium instituant, quod sane non instituunt cum mortuis, sed cum Diabolo, qui sub specie eorum apparet; ergo vicissim est exemplum locutionis secundum apparentiam & opinionem ei innitentem.
units.tr: Reply: I deny that they truly consult the dead. To consult the dead is not merely to seek counsel but also to receive it from the dead, whereas the one from whom they take counsel is the Devil. They consult in the sense that they hold a conversation, but they do not hold it with the dead; they hold it with the Devil, who appears to them under the guise of the dead. Therefore, conversely, this is an example of a manner of speaking that follows appearance and the opinion resting upon it.

units.la: DXCIX. Decimum Inductionis Exemplum petimus ex Joh. v.31. Si ego testor de me ipso, testimonium meum non est firmum, nempe secundum vestram opinionem, cum vos possitis de eo dubitare; alias enim in rei veritate testimonium Christi semper est firmum, cum sit ipsa veritas, ipseque docet Joh. vi. 11, 14. Etiamsi ego testor de me ipso, firmum est meum testimonium. Designat autem Christus, testimonium suum apud Judaeos nullum effectum habiturum, locutione innitente opinioni erroneae, quod Christi testimonium nullam habeat firmitatem.
units.tr: DXCIX. We take the tenth example of the induction from John 5:31. If I bear witness of myself, my witness is not true, namely according to your opinion, since you can doubt it; for otherwise, in the truth of the matter, the testimony of Christ is always true, since he is the truth itself, as he teaches in John 6:11, 14: Even if I bear witness of myself, my witness is true. Christ indicates, however, that his testimony will have no effect among the Jews, using a form of speech that rests on their erroneous opinion, namely that the testimony of Christ has no firmness.

units.la: DC. Exc. 1. B. p. 80. Hic Christum in collatione cum adversariis ipsis aliquid concedere, ut argumentis ad eos confutandos fortioribus constringantur, atque de eo facile inter nos convenire posse, sed hoc parum pertinere ad scopum meum. Consentit M. p. 89. Esse in hoc loco concessionem manifestam, quae aequipolleat his verbis, dato, non concesso.
units.tr: DC. Exc. 1. B. p. 80. Here Christ concedes something to his adversaries in argument, so that they may be pressed by stronger arguments for their refutation; and it can easily be agreed between us that this has little bearing on my purpose. M. p. 89 agrees: There is in this place a manifest concession, which is equivalent to the words "granted, not conceded".

units.la: Resp. Si concedit hic aliquid Christus adversariis, non concedit, quasi in rei veritate sit concedendum, sed relinquit ipsorum opinionem sine refutatione, atque phrasi utitur, quae eorum opinioni erroneae innititur. Atque sic probatur Minor mei argumenti articulo 566. propositi, quae Minor probata quomodo faciat ad meum scopum ex initio hujus capitis apparet, quod lector benevolus consulat.
units.tr: Reply: If Christ concedes something here to his adversaries, he does not concede it as though it ought to be conceded in the truth of the matter; he leaves their opinion unrefuted and uses an expression that rests on their erroneous opinion. And so the minor premise of my argument, set out in article 566, is proved. How this proved minor bears on my purpose is apparent from the beginning of this chapter, which the kind reader may consult.

units.la: DCI. Exc. 2. M. p. 88. qui hic in omnes formas se vertit, Testimonium Christi respectu Judaeorum quorundam, quibus non constabat veracitas Christi, vere non fuisse idoneum s. αληθὲς, quod alias in se consideratum satis est firmum & infallibile.
units.tr: DCI. Exc. 2. M. p. 88, who here turns himself into every shape: The testimony of Christ, with respect to certain Jews, to whom the truthfulness of Christ was not established, was not truly fit, or true [αληθὲς], although in itself considered it is otherwise firm and infallible enough.

units.la: Resp. Si respectu Judaeorum non fuit firmum, cum in se esset, itaque in eorum opinione tantum non erat firmum, non erat idoneum. Adeoque non verè, cum in se idoneum esset, atque sic nihilominus obtineo institutum.
units.tr: Reply: If it was not firm with respect to the Jews, although in itself it was, then it was not firm only in their opinion, and so it was not fit. Hence it was not truly fit, since in itself it was fit; and thus I nonetheless obtain what I set out to show.

units.la: DCII. Tandem addit M. p. 90. Quatenus autem Spiritus Sanctus salva veritate sua falsas aliorum opiniones potest referre, & ad tempus absque absque speciali refutatione permittere saepius dictum est.
units.tr: DCII. Finally M. p. 90 adds: Insofar as the Holy Spirit, while his truth remains intact, can report the false opinions of others, and for a time permit them without any special refutation, this has been said quite often.

units.la: Resp. Si hoc posset fieri, ergo consensus est inter nos; nec erat, quod objiceret, Spiritum Sanctum in rebus fidei secundum me se componere ad falsam aliorum opinionem. Quod enim hoc eam non refutando fieri possit, salva Spiritus Sancti veracitate conceditur.
units.tr: Reply: If this can be done, then there is agreement between us; nor was there any reason for him to object that the Holy Spirit, according to me, accommodates himself in matters of faith to the false opinion of others. For it is granted that this can be done without refutation, with the veracity of the Holy Spirit preserved.

units.la: DCIII. Undecimum Exemplum desumimus ex Phil. III. 7. Sed quae mihi erant lucra, ea duxi propter Christum damna esse. Quae mihi lucra erant, non revera, sed in mea opinione, quam habebam, cum nondum essem conversus, de observatione Decalogi, & aliarum constitutionum, tum Dei tum etiam hominum, per quas volui justificari, ea nunc detrimentosa, luce divina illustratus judicio recto judico.
units.tr: DCIII. We take the eleventh example from Philippians 3:7: But what things were gain to me, those I counted loss for Christ. These were gains to me, not in reality but in my opinion, which I held when I was not yet converted, concerning the observance of the Decalogue and of other constitutions, both of God and of men, by which I wished to be justified. These things, now enlightened by the divine light, I judge with a right judgment to be harmful.

units.la: DCIV. Exc. M. p. 90. Appellat hoc loco Apostolus bona opera damna, non absolute, sed respectu Christi, propter Christum. Observatio legis est lucrum in se, damnum quatenus spectatur ut meritum.
units.tr: DCIV. Exc. M. p. 90. The Apostle here calls good works losses, not absolutely, but with respect to Christ, on account of Christ. The observance of the law is gain in itself; it is loss insofar as it is regarded as merit.

units.la: Resp. Haec mihi non contrariantur: illa enim ante conversionem vel revera lucra erant Paulo, vel tantum in opinione ipsius; quod si dicatur, uti dici debet, est exemplum locutionis, quo adhibetur formula, quae opinioni innititur.
units.tr: Reply: These statements do not conflict with mine. For before his conversion those things were either truly gains to Paul, or only in his opinion; and if it is said, as it must be said, that this is an example of a manner of speaking, the expression is used that rests on opinion.

units.la: DCV. Duodecimum Exemplum adducimus ex Tit. I. 12. Epimenides vocatur Cretensium Propheta: at is non fuit sane secundum rei veritatem, sed tantum secundum eorum opinionem, cum in tanto apud illos fuerit honore, ut ei etiam post mortem sacrificaverint, quem admodum refert Diogenes Laertius. Notetur Calvini explicatio ad hunc locum: Cum Poetae interdum Graecis Prophetae dicantur, quemadmodum apud Latinos Vates: simpliciter pro Doctore accipio. Hinc autem appellatio (ut videtur) orta est, quod semper HABITI SUNT genus Θεου και ενθουσιαστικον. Unde & Adimantus apud Platonem 2, de Rep. postquam vocavit Poetas Deorum filios, addit eorum quoque factos fuisse Prophetas. Quare mihi videtur Paulus ad COMMUNEM USUM sermonem accommodare.
units.tr: DCV. We adduce the twelfth example from Titus 1:12: Epimenides is called a prophet of the Cretans; but he was surely not so in the truth of the matter, only according to their opinion, since he held such honour among them that they even sacrificed to him after his death, as Diogenes Laertius reports. Note Calvin's explanation of this passage: "Since the poets are sometimes called prophets by the Greeks, just as vates among the Latins, I take it simply to mean teacher. Hence the name (as it seems) arose, because they were always regarded as belonging to a kind of divine and inspired [γένος θεοῦ καὶ ἐνθουσιαστικόν] race. Whence also Adimantus in Plato, Republic 2, after calling the poets sons of the gods, adds that they also became prophets. Therefore it seems to me that Paul accommodates his speech to COMMON USAGE."

units.la: DCVI. Nihil hic excipitur a M. p. 91. quod ad rem faciat. Nam Epimenides vel revera fuit, & verus Cretensium Propheta, vel in eorum opinione. Non revera, uti per se patet, nec enim revelationem divinam habuit: Ergo in opinione. 2. Doctores dicuntur Prophetae, quia teste Calvino, semper habiti sunt genus Θεου και ενθουσιαστικον. At Epimenides non revera fuit divinus & ενθουσιαστικος, quia nullam revelationem habuit divinam. Ergo tantum in opinione talis. In his vis argumenti continetur, ad quod debuisset responderi, non in genere dicendum, quod ad rem nihil facit.
units.tr: DCVI. M. p. 91 here excepts nothing that bears on the matter. For Epimenides either truly was, and was a true prophet of the Cretans, or he was so in their opinion. Not in truth, as is plain in itself, for he had no divine revelation; therefore in opinion. Second: teachers are called prophets because, as Calvin testifies, they were always regarded as belonging to a kind of divine and inspired race. But Epimenides was not truly divine and inspired, because he had no divine revelation. Therefore he was such only in opinion. The force of the argument lies in these points, to which a reply should have been made; it is not enough to say in general what has nothing to do with the matter.

units.la: DVII. Tertium decimum tandem Exemplum suppeditatur 2 Pet. II. 1. Fuerunt autem etiam Pseudo-prophetæ in populo &c. etiam Dominum, qui illos mercatus est, abnegantes. Si veritatem hic spectemus, dici sanè non potest, Christum eos mercatum fuisse, à peccato & servitute Diaboli liberasse, cùm contrarium appareat ex eorum operibus, quibus ostendunt, se adhuc manere sub dominio peccati & Diaboli. Sed quia sunt in externa communione Ecclesiæ, & Christum profitentur, videntur pertinere ad pusillum illum gregem, quem Christus ex faucibus Satanæ eripuit. Ita phrasis illa innititur opinioni tum ipsorum, tum aliorum, qua pro redemptis habebantur. Et hæc est communis interpretatio Orthodoxorum, quando Christi mortis efficaciam ad solos electos pertinere ostendunt.
units.tr: DVII. Lastly, the thirteenth example is supplied by 2 Peter 2:1: But there were also false prophets among the people, &c., even denying the Lord who bought them. If we look at the truth, it cannot be said that Christ bought them, that is, freed them from sin and the servitude of the Devil, since the contrary appears from their works, by which they show that they still remain under the dominion of sin and the Devil. But because they are in the external communion of the Church and profess Christ, they seem to belong to that little flock which Christ snatched from the jaws of Satan. Thus that phrase rests on the opinion both of themselves and of others, by whom they were regarded as redeemed. And this is the common interpretation of the Orthodox, when they show that the efficacy of Christ's death pertains only to the elect.

units.la: DCVIII. Sic Belgæ ad hunc locum notant: Defe worden hier gefeght van den Heere gekocht te sijn, ten aensien datse haer voor soodanige uytgeven, ende van andere nae de liefde daer voor gehouden sijn, soo lange als sy in de gemeynschap der Kercke waeren, siet diergelijcke iwijse vae spreecken. Joh. xv. 2. Apoc. xxii. 19. Want Christus heeft door sijn bloet waerlijck en in der daet alleen sijne gemeynte gekocht. Actor. xx. 28. Eph. v. 25. Dat is, alleen de waere geloovige, die altijt by Christum blyven, ende hem niet en verlochenen, siet 1 Joh. II. 19. Apoc. xiv. 3, 4. Hoc est, isti hic dicuntur empti à Domino, eo respectu, quod sese pro talibus venditarent, & ab aliis ex charitate tales haberentur, quamdiu erant in communione Ecclesia. Vide similem loquendi formulam Joh. xv. 2. Apoc. xxii. 19. Nam Christus suo sanguinè revera & actu tantum suam Ecclesiam redemit. Actor. xx. 28. Eph. v. 25. hoc est, tantum vere fideles, qui semper apud Christum manent, & ipsum non abnegant. Vide 1 Joh. II. 19. Apoc. xiv. 3, 4. Similis est Interpretatio Paræi. Erant redempti, id est, respectu sufficientia λύτρε, seu quoad magnitudinem pretii, 2. ipsorum professione & gloriatione. Christus enim pro omnibus solvit pretium, & multi impii gloriantur de Christi redemptione, sed fide eum sibi non applicant. Aliud verò est gloriari, aliud certo statuere, Deum sibi esse propitium propter Christi meritum.
units.tr: DCVIII. So the Belgians note on this passage: Here it is said of the false teachers that they were bought by the Lord, with respect to the fact that they presented themselves as such, and were held to be such by others out of charity, as long as they were in the communion of the Church. See similar forms of speech: John 15:2; Revelation 22:19. For Christ by his blood truly and in deed alone bought his congregation, Acts 20:28; Ephesians 5:25, that is, only the truly faithful, who always remain with Christ and do not deny him. See 1 John 2:19; Revelation 14:3, 4. That is, these are said here to have been bought by the Lord, with respect to the fact that they gave themselves out as such and were held to be such by others out of charity, as long as they were in the communion of the Church. Compare a similar manner of speaking in John 15:2 and Revelation 22:19. For Christ truly and actually redeemed his Church only by his blood, Acts 20:28; Ephesians 5:25, that is, only the truly faithful, who always abide with Christ and do not deny him. See 1 John 2:19; Revelation 14:3, 4. Parens' interpretation is similar: they were redeemed, that is, with respect to the sufficiency of the ransom [λύτρου], or as to the greatness of the price; and secondly, with respect to their own profession and boasting. For Christ paid the price for all, and many impious persons boast of Christ's redemption, but do not apply him to themselves by faith. Indeed, to boast is one thing, and to determine with certainty that God is propitious to oneself for the sake of Christ's merit is another.

units.la: 3. HOMINVM OPINIONE. Consentit Alstedius in Pleiade Apostolica, ubi inter alia ad hunc locum notat: Ratione applicationis mortis Christi oportet distinguere fidem justificantem, temporariam, & historicam, itemque gloriationem, opinionem, & judicium charitatis. Quantum ad fidem salvificam, Christus omnes & solas suas oves mercatus est, Joh. x. quantum ad reliqua, Christus etiam mercatus est hypocritas.
units.tr: 3. Of the opinion of men. Alstedius agrees in his Pleias Apostolica, where, among other things, he notes on this passage: With regard to the application of Christ's death, one must distinguish justifying faith from temporary and historical faith, and likewise boasting, opinion, and the judgment of charity. As to saving faith, Christ has bought all and only his sheep, John 10. As to the rest, Christ has also bought hypocrites.

units.la: DCIX. Sed dices, an non sufficiet? si dicas, Christum ita dici cos mercatum fuisse, ut pretium, quod in se erat sufficiens, ad illos redimen-dos dos persolverit, ut non opus sit altera expositione de redemptione, quoad ipsorum opinionem.
units.tr: DCIX. But you will say: is this not enough? If you say that Christ is said to have bought them in such a way that he paid a price which in itself was sufficient to redeem them, then there is no need for another explanation of the redemption, as far as their own opinion is concerned.

units.la: Resp. Non sufficit: hic enim est sermo de illis hominibus, qui erant in externa communione Ecclesiæ, ac propterea judicabantur etiam esse in internâ communione cum Christo, uti fieri debet ex judicio charitatis. Itaque singulari ratione Christus eos hic dicitur mercatus, hoc est, vocasse ad externam communionem Ecclesiæ, quod significatur per phrasin innitentem opinioni erroneæ, qua pro revera redemptis habebantur.
units.tr: Answer: It is not enough. For this is a discussion about those men who were in the external communion of the Church, and who for that reason were also judged to be in internal communion with Christ, as must be done by the judgment of charity. Therefore Christ is said here to have bought them in a particular sense, that is, to have called them into the external communion of the Church. This is signified by a phrase resting on an erroneous opinion, by which they were held to be truly redeemed.

units.la: Inst. At saltem satis erit, si dicas, eos redemptos dici, quoad professionem suam.
units.tr: Objection: At least it will be enough if you say that they are called redeemed with respect to their profession.

units.la: Resp. Illa professio oritur ex opinione ipsorum falsa. 2. Ex illa prosessione oritur etiam opinio aliorum de ipsis erronea. Itaque nihilominus vox illa in opinione erronea fundatur, quod erat probandum.
units.tr: Answer: That profession arises from their false opinion. Second, from that profession there also arises the erroneous opinion of others about them. Therefore that word is nonetheless founded on an erroneous opinion, which was what had to be proved.

units.la: DCX. Exc. B. p. 83. Pro ista instantia salvanda. 1. Quid tum? modo Professio sit causa, cur à Domino empti dicantur, 2. me probare debuisse hominum opinionem erroneam & non Professionem Pseudo-prophetarum causam esse illius Phraseologiæ, alias hoc loco pro mea sententia nihil profuturum.
units.tr: DCX. Exc. B. p. 83. To save this objection: What then? Provided the profession is the cause why they are said to be bought by the Lord. 2. I ought to have proved that the erroneous opinion of men, and not the profession of the pseudo-prophets, is the cause of that phraseology; otherwise nothing would help my view in this place.

units.la: Resp. Si professio ipsorum sit causa, cur à Domino empti dicantur, eo ipso eorum opinio erronea erit causa istius phraseologiæ. Sic enim dicentur tales redempti, quia se tales venditabant; atqui tales se dicebant ex opinione erronea, neque hæc ab ipsorum professione potest separari. Ergo tales dicuntur etiam quoad opinionem suam. 2. Si Professio non sit causa istius appellationis citra opinionem erroneam, obtinui institutum; neque enim probandum mihi, quod sola opinio erronea sit causa istius phraseologiæ.
units.tr: Answer: If their profession is the cause why they are said to be bought by the Lord, then by that very fact their erroneous opinion will be the cause of this phraseology. For such men would be called redeemed because they claimed to be such; but they claimed this out of an erroneous opinion, and this cannot be separated from their profession. Therefore they are also called such with respect to their opinion. 2. If the profession is not the cause of this appellation apart from the erroneous opinion, then I have gained my point. For I need not prove that the erroneous opinion alone is the cause of this phraseology.

units.la: DCXI. Porrò adversarii dissimulatis auctoritatibus Belgarum, Parei, Alstedii, quas pro mea sententia adduxi, opponunt alias. B. quidem p. 81, 82. Molinæi, Amesii, in Coronide & Antisynod. Heidani & Collationis Hagiensium, M. p. 92. Gomari & Amesii in Explanatione Epistolæ Petri, qui per ἐ δεσπότην non intelligant Christum, sed Patrem & emptionem explicent de aggregatione externa.
units.tr: DCXI. Furthermore, the adversaries, passing over the authorities of the Belgians, Paraeus and Alstedius, which I adduced for my view, bring forward others: B. indeed at pp. 81, 82; Molinaeus and Amesius in the Coronis and Antisynodus; Heidanus and the Collatio Hagiensis, M. p. 92; Gomarus and Amesius in the explanation of Peter's Epistle, who do not understand Christ by the word despotēn [δεσπότην], but the Father, and explain the buying as external aggregation.

units.la: Resp. 1. Non agitur hic de committendis inter se auctoribus orthodoxis & nostris, sed de veritate interpretationis, an nempe illa interpretatio dicti Petrini, à me adducta sit legitima? 2. An per δεσπότην hic sit intelligendus Pater, nolim disputare: nam si Patrem intelligas, cum agat omnia per Filium, & imprimis opus redemptionis per eundem exsequatur, quatur, recte etiam Christus dicendus est istos homines fuisse mercatus. 3. Pars etiam citatorum auctorum meam sententiam stabiliunt. Heidanus p. 396. expresse hanc meam interpretationem admittit his verbis: Die hoewel sy in der waerheyt geen part nochte deel en hebben aen den woorde, ende met geheylight en waeren door het bloet Christi, nochtans uyterlycke professie deeden van de Christelycke Religie, ende door de uyterlycke besprenginge des doops, en mondelycke belijdenisse (ichenen NB gereynight te sijn, ende nae den ichijn goede Christenen. Hoc est, quibus etiamsi in veritate nulla pars aut sors erat in verbo, nec sanctificati fuerant per sanguinem Christi, tamen externe profitebantur Christianam religionem, & per externam aspersionem Baptismi & oralem confessionem videbantur NB mundati & secundum apparentiam boni Christiani. Amesius vero in 2 Pet. tres responsiones affert, quarum prior cum nostra explicatione convenit.
units.tr: Answer: 1. Here we are not concerned with setting orthodox authors and ours against one another, but with the truth of the interpretation: namely, whether the interpretation of the Petrine passage which I adduced is legitimate. 2. Whether the Father is to be understood here by despotēn [δεσπότην] I am not willing to dispute. For if you understand the Father, since he does all things through the Son and especially carries out the work of redemption through him, it is rightly said that Christ bought these men. 3. Part of the authors cited also confirm my view. Heidanus, at p. 396, expressly admits this my interpretation in these words: Although in truth they had no part or lot in the word, nor were they sanctified by the blood of Christ, yet they outwardly professed the Christian religion, and through the outward sprinkling of baptism and oral confession they seemed NB cleansed and, by appearance, good Christians. Amesius, indeed, in his commentary on 2 Peter, offers three answers, of which the first agrees with our explanation.

units.la: DCXII. Sed observatu digna hic est responsio Amesii in Antisynodalibus, quam Arminianis, Reformatorum responsionem, similem meae ad argumenta pro Solis motu objecta, onerantibus iisdem absurdis, quibus meam Antagonistae premunt sententiam, reponit. Verba illa, quae huc faciunt, referre non pigebit cap. 6. de morte Christi, art. 5. Sic autem Remonstrantes objiciebant: Ajunt alii Apostolum non agere de iis, pro quibus Christus revera mortuus est, sed qui pro talibus debent haberi, ex judicio charitatu, sed 1. sic nihil erit certi, in tota Scriptura (Nota quoties hoc mihi objiciatur) Christus similiter ipse dici potest homo fuisse, non revera, sed opinione & phantasia quadam. 2. Sic infringitur argumentum Apostoli, quia nihil est periculi in talium offensione, nisi ut hypocrisis ipsorum in lucem protrahatur, quod est optandum.
