Respondet Amesius inter alia: Hinc etiam cuilibet intelligenti facile apparebit, qualis sit illa comparatio declamatoria, quam hic suo more instituunt Remonstrantes inter istam interpretationem, quae quosdam non proprie redemptos, redemptis tamen conjunctos propter illam conjunctionem redemptos vocari dicit, & eorum insaniam, qui dicerent humanam Christi naturam fuisse imaginariam tantum, cum ibi sit manifesta ratio usu loquendi approbata, NB passim in Scripturis, ubi omnes qui sunt in Ecclesia vocantur sancti, hic autem nihil praeter insaniam meam. Quod autem addunt de hypocrisi nihil habet sani. Neque enim sunt omnes illi, qui ad tempus aliquo modo credunt, sed absque radice propria loquendo hypocrita, & peccatum quod in tales admittitur, dum tales nobis apparent, non minus est, quam si revera tales essent & culpa nostra perderentur.
units.tr: DCXII. But the response of Amesius in the Antisynodalia is worth noting here. It answers the Arminians, and is the Reformed reply, similar to my answer to the arguments against the motion of the Sun. It burdens my opponents with the same absurdities with which they press my view. It will not be tedious to report those words which bear on this, from chapter 6 on the death of Christ, art. 5. The Remonstrants objected as follows: Others say that the Apostle is not speaking of those for whom Christ truly died, but of those who must be held to be such by the judgment of charity. But then, first, nothing will be certain in all of Scripture (note how often this is thrown at me). Christ himself could likewise be said to have been a man not in reality but by a certain opinion and fancy. Second: Thus the Apostle's argument is undermined, since there is no danger in the offence of such people, unless their hypocrisy be brought to light, which is to be desired. Amesius replies, among other things: From this, too, it will easily appear to anyone who understands what sort of declamatory comparison the Remonstrants, as is their habit, set up here between that interpretation, which says that some are not properly redeemed but are called redeemed because they are joined to the redeemed on account of that connection, and the madness of those who would say that Christ's human nature was merely imaginary. There is a clear reason, approved by usage NB everywhere in the Scriptures, where all who are in the Church are called saints. Here, however, they find nothing but my madness. What they add about hypocrisy has nothing sound in it. For not all those who believe for a time in some way, but who lack a proper root, are hypocrites strictly speaking. And the sin which is committed against such people, while they appear to us as such, is no less than if they really were such and were lost through our fault.

units.la: DCXIII. Ex his apparet, non posse Minorem meam Propositionem art. 565. propositam negari, quam his Scripturae locis volui confirmatam. tam. Atque ut magis fiat manifestum, quomodo eadem confirmetur consensu Adversarii, per ejus exceptiones generales, videamus. Ita ergo B. p. 70. In illis locis Scriptura vel aliquam dictionem improprie sumptam a me arripi ad probandam totam locutionem non secundum rei veritatem dictam, sed ad erroneam vulgi opinionem (quod de suo addit, dixeram enim hominum quorumcunque quatenus ex externis judicant,) esse accommodatam, vel aliquid praedicatum subjecto me velle attribui tantum secundum opinionem hominum, non rei veritatem ut Hebr. vii. (ubi nota, quod non dicam, Melchisedecum secundum opinionem dici talem, prout ex sequentibus patebit) Ios. II. 7. &c. & prioris quidem generis loca quod attinet, inquit, non negamus in terminis simplicibus aliquando titulos vel attributa subjectis tribui, quae tamen ipsis secundum rei veritatem non competunt, ut in loco citato videre est. Habemus ergo confitentem reum, saltem ex parte, atque Minorem meam Propositionem approbantem, scriptores sacros usurpare locutiones correspondentes opinioni quamvis erroneae, xeíẅ suam non interponentes, nec mutare in accuratas, sed negat, id fieri in terminis complexis, ita ut praedicatum tribuatur subjecto, cui non inest, vel negetur de subjecto cui inest.
units.tr: DCXIII. From these things it appears that my minor proposition, set out at art. 565, cannot be denied, and I wished to confirm it by these passages of Scripture. And so that it may become clearer how the same is confirmed by the consent of the adversary, let us look at his general exceptions. Thus B. at p. 70: In those passages Scripture either takes some expression used improperly, which I seize upon to prove that the whole locution is not said according to the truth of the matter but is adapted to the erroneous opinion of the common people (which he adds on his own, for I had said of men whoever they are, insofar as they judge by externals), or else I wish some predicate to be attributed to the subject only according to the opinion of men and not the truth of the matter, as in Heb. 7 (where note that I do not say Melchizedek is called such according to opinion, as will be clear from what follows), Josh. 2:7, etc. As far as passages of the former kind are concerned, he says, we do not deny that sometimes, in simple terms, titles or attributes are assigned to subjects which nonetheless do not belong to them in the truth of the matter, as can be seen in the passage cited. We have, therefore, the accused confessing, at least in part, and approving my minor proposition, that the sacred writers use expressions corresponding to an opinion, however erroneous, without interposing any correction or changing them into accurate ones. But he denies that this happens in complex terms, so that a predicate is attributed to a subject in which it does not inhere, or is denied of a subject in which it does inhere.

units.la: Resp. Contrarium est ostensum, in hoc capite, & plenius adversario est responsum in fine capitis XXIII.
units.tr: Answer: The contrary has been shown in this chapter, and the adversary has been answered more fully at the end of chapter XXIII.

units.la: DCXIV. Sed & sequentia Adversarii instituto meo inserviunt, B. p. 71. Datur in talium complurium terminorum usu aliqua ratio manifesta, propter quam titulus illi subjecto attribuitur, & ex qua cognoscitur ipsi revera non competere: quae si absit, non licet dicere, titulum subjecto tributum ei revera non inesse. Item p. 72. in hisce ergo (loquitur de 1 Sam. XXVIII.) & similibus locis clare videmus & aliquas subesse rationes, propter quas attributa subjectis proprie non competentia illis tribuantur, & etiam certa dari judicia, unde nobis pateat illos titulos subjectis proprie non convenire, quae si non dantur, non licet in alicujus phraseos expositione dicere, attributa subjecto non secundum rei veritatem, sed apparentiam tribui.
units.tr: DCXIV. But the following points of my opponent also serve my purpose, p. 71. There is some clear reason for the use of such terms in many passages, on account of which a title is ascribed to a subject, and from which it is known that the title does not truly belong to it. If that reason were absent, one could not say that a title ascribed to a subject is not really present in it. Likewise p. 72, where he speaks of 1 Sam. 28: in these and similar places we clearly see both that there are some reasons on account of which attributes that do not properly belong to subjects are ascribed to them, and also that there are certain judgments from which it is plain to us that those titles do not properly fit the subjects. If these judgments were not available, one could not say, in explaining any phrase, that attributes are ascribed to a subject according to appearance and not according to the truth of the matter.

units.la: Resp. Et hic iterum inter nos convenit; neque enim dico, vel terminos simplices adhiberi ex usu vulgi, vel complexos, nisi subsit aliqua ratio, propter quam talis locutio sit agnoscenda; si itaque ad Spiritus Sancti institutum non requiratur, ut formulis receptis aliud doceat, quam generalem aliquam veritatem, & ex ratione constet, illas locutiones, prout vulgo usurpantur, ortum habere ex opinione erronea, omnino sententia, quam defendo, erit comprobata. Ne ergo imposterum Auctoritas & Veritas Scripturae objiciatur; cum de illa non sit quaestio, sed disquiratur: utrum in locis proSolis motu adductis formulis receptis aliquid aliud praeter ter veritatem generalem, quam suis in locis indico, doceatur. Item, utrum sit aliqua ratio certa, quæ in locis, pro quiete Terræ & Solis motu adductis, ostendit, locutionem reperiri, quæ ex præjudicio & opinione erronea habet ortum. Ego verò suis in locis talem dedi, quam non video ita impugnatam, quin facile contra Objectionem adversarii potuerit defendi.
units.tr: Answer. Here again we agree. For I do not say that either simple or compound terms are used in the common manner unless some reason underlies them, on account of which such a way of speaking must be recognised. So if, in the purpose of the Holy Spirit, it is not required that He teach something other than some general truth by means of the received formulas, and if it is clear from reasoning that those expressions, as they are commonly used, arose from an erroneous opinion, then my position, which I defend, will be wholly confirmed. Therefore let the authority and truth of Scripture not be objected against from now on, since that is not in question; rather the question is whether, in the passages I have just cited about the motion of the Sun, the received formulas teach anything other than the general truth, which I point out in their proper places. Likewise, whether there is some certain reason which, in the passages cited about the rest of the Earth and the motion of the Sun, shows that a way of speaking is found that arises from prejudice and erroneous opinion. For my part, in their proper places I have given such a reason, which I do not see has been so attacked that it could not easily be defended against the opponent's objection.

units.la: CAPUT XXVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVII.

units.la: Tertium Argumentum, quo probatur, sententiam dictam cum Auctoritate & Veritate Scripturæ nequaquam pugnare, ex eo desumtum, quod Scriptura ali- quid neget, non quia revera est negandum, sed quia à nobis non est cognitum.
units.tr: The third argument, by which it is proved that the said opinion does not at all conflict with the authority and truth of Scripture, drawn from the fact that Scripture denies something, not because it really must be denied, but because it has not been known by us.

units.la: DCXV. Tertium argumentum. Si Scriptura sine læsione Auctoritatis & Veritatis suæ possit aliquid negare, non quod revera sit negandum, sed quia à nobis non est cognitum: Ergò multo minus repugnabit ejus Auctoritati & Veritati, ut utatur phrasibus receptis, quæ ex infantiæ præjudiciis habent ortum, suam κεἶνν non apponendo; Sed verum prius. Min. probatur Heb. 7, 3. De Melchisedeco dicitur, quod fuerit sine patre, sine matre, sine genere, nec initium dierum, neque vita finem habens, sed assimulatus filio Dei, manet sacerdos in perpetuum. Utique hæc quæ negantur de Melchisedeco, non possunt secundum veritatem negari; (nisi velimus sequi sententiam Cunæi de Republ. Hebræorum, qui per Melchisedecum intelligit ipsum filium Dei, cujus sententiæ inter alia repugnat imprimis, quod filius Dei non potuerit esse typus sui ipsius) cum enim fuerit homo, uti probabilior fert sententia, & quidem Rex Salem, proculdubio etiam habuit suos parentes, genealogiam &c. sed tantum secundum cognitionem nostram, quod ejus parentes &c. sint incognita. Quemadmodum ergo Scriptura in superioribus exemplis sese accommodavit ad nostram opinionem, ut locuta fuerit, quemadmodum opinantur de rebus; ita sese hic accommodat ad nostram cognitionem, ut non quod verum est, dicat, sed quia nos non cognoscimus, neget. Consentiunt hic interpretes: sic enim Paræus, dicitur sine patre, sine matre, non quod revera talis fuerit, sed quod talem Spiritus Sanctus historiâ repræsentat. Eodem modo Scultetus in Epistolam ad Hebræos, quibus similia habet Gualtherus: Talem proponit Scriptura, non quod REVERA talis fuerit aut superfit adhuc, sed ut assimulatus filio Dei, id est, typi causa eundem proponit.
units.tr: DCXV. The third argument. If Scripture, without any injury to its authority and truth, can deny something, not because it really must be denied, but because it has not been known by us, then much less will it conflict with its authority and truth if it uses received expressions which have arisen from the prejudices of infancy, without adding its own [κεἶνν]. But the first is true. The minor premise is proved from Heb. 7:3: of Melchisedec it is said that he was "without father, without mother, without descent, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but made like unto the Son of God, abideth a priest continually." Now those things which are denied of Melchisedec cannot be denied according to the truth (unless we wish to follow the opinion of Cunaeus in De Republica Hebraeorum, who understands by Melchisedec the Son of God himself; this opinion is opposed above all by the fact that the Son of God could not be a type of himself). For since he was a man, as the more probable opinion holds, and indeed the king of Salem, he undoubtedly also had his parents, a genealogy, and so on, but only according to our knowledge is it that his parents and so on are unknown. Just as, therefore, Scripture in the earlier examples accommodated itself to our opinion, so that it spoke as people think about things, so here it accommodates itself to our knowledge, so that it does not state what is true but denies it because we do not know it. The interpreters agree here. Thus Paraeus: "He is said to be without father, without mother, not because he really was such, but because the Holy Spirit represents him in history as such." In the same way Scultetus on the Epistle to the Hebrews, and Gualther has similar things: "Scripture sets forth such a person, not because he REALLY was such or still survives, but so that, made like the Son of God, that is, he is set forth as a type."

units.la: DCXVI. Excipit hic B. p. 73. & 74. multis verbis inaniter profusis quorum summa: Scopo meo convenienter ostendi debuisse, hanc fuisse erroneam opinionem vulgi, quod ℳ Melchisedecus fuerit sine patre.
units.tr: DCXVI. Here B., pp. 73 and 74, objects, with many words poured out in vain, the sum of which is: "It ought to have been shown, in keeping with my purpose, that it was the erroneous opinion of the common people that Melchisedec was without father."

units.la: Resp. Hoc necessarium non fuisse ex meo argumento patet, quod hic nunc magis in forma propositi, quamvis & id antehac ab attento lectore potuerit cognosci. Quo argumento meo observato etiam cadunt, quae M. p. 84. similia objicit, ac si hoc modo scopo meo non fuerit satisfactum.
units.tr: Reply: From my argument it is clear that this was not necessary, which is now stated more formally, although an attentive reader could have recognized it even before. With this argument of mine observed, those things also fall which M., p. 84, objects in a similar way, as if my purpose had not been satisfied in this manner.

units.la: DCXVII. Inst. B. p. 74. Haec duo multum differunt: Nam rem incognitam esse, notat negativum quod, cum negetur rei cognitio; at opinio notat affirmativum quod, quae si a veritate deflectat, fit erronea; probandum autem fuisse Spiritum Sanctum sese accommodare ad opinionem erroneam.
units.tr: DCXVII. Inst., B., p. 74: "These two differ greatly. For that a thing is unknown denotes a negative that, since knowledge of the thing is denied; but opinion denotes an affirmative that, which, if it departs from the truth, becomes erroneous. But it ought to have been proved that the Holy Spirit accommodated himself to an erroneous opinion."

units.la: Resp. Quid probandum fuerit & probatum sit ex argumento agnoscet. Homines autem isti semper praesupponunt, idem mihi esse loqui secundum opinionem erroneam & loqui opinionem erroneam, vel affirmare & testari opinionem erroneam, quod nunquam in mentem mihi venit, & ab ea sententia sum alienus; unde & factum est, ut prudens abea phrasi in posterum velim abstinere, quamvis nihil aliud denotaverit, quam ea ipsa, qua nunc utor, nempe, Spiritum Sanctum uti Phrasibus receptis, quae ex praejudiciis infantiae & sensuum habent ortum, veritatem aliquam, sed ad sensus nostros relatam atque praejudiciis involutam exprimentibus. Itaque haec instantia nihil quicquam mihi obest.
units.tr: Reply: What ought to have been proved, and what has been proved, will be recognized from the argument. These men, however, always presuppose that to speak according to an erroneous opinion is the same as to speak an erroneous opinion, or to affirm and attest an erroneous opinion. This never came into my mind, and I am a stranger to that view. Hence it has come about that, being prudent, I would in future wish to abstain from that phrase, although it has signified nothing other than that very phrase which I now use, namely, that the Holy Spirit, using received expressions which have arisen from the prejudices of infancy and of the senses, sets forth some truth, but one referred to our senses and wrapped up in prejudices. Therefore this objection does me no harm at all.

units.la: DCXVIII. Exc. 2. B. p. 75. Sed & negamus hac de Melchisedeco dici respectu cognitionis nostrae, cum ignorantia nostra non possit inferre rationem typicam, ac proinde afferimus, Apostolum sic de Melchisedeco loqui, propter modum revelationis divinae.
units.tr: DCXVIII. Exception 2, B., p. 75: "But we also deny that these things are said of Melchisedec with respect to our knowledge, since our ignorance cannot supply a typical reason; and therefore we affirm that the Apostle speaks thus of Melchisedec on account of the mode of divine revelation."

units.la: Resp. Haec non pugnant, sed unum ex altero consequitur. Si enim Apostolus neget de Melchisedeco patrem, matrem, &c. propter negatam revelationem divinam: Ergo etiam negat propter negatam cognitionem nostram, quae sine revelatione de his esse non poterat; unde apparet, nihil repugnare, quin ignorantia nostra ob negatam revelationem inferat rationem typicam. Non autem opus erat, ut tot auctores citaret Adversarius, quum nullus citatorum mihi repugnet, neque ullus neget, hac negari de ℳ Melchisedeco propter negatam cognitionem nostram; quae est sententia mea, cui non repugnat illa, quae dicit, ea negari de Melchisedeco propter negatam revelationem divinam, cum hujus negatio alteram inferat. Unde liquet, non quàm ego inepte argumenter, sed quàm inepte ex eo, quod citati auctores dicunt, Melchisedecum dici sine patre &c. propter Spiritus Sancti propositionem & revelationem, (hoc est, quod Spiritus Sanctus nihil de iis revelet) inferat Adversarius, eos negare, quod ratio habeatur nostra ignorantia, cum hæc negatam revelationem divinam, de re, quæ aliunde non potest cognosci, consequatur.
units.tr: Reply: These things do not conflict, but one follows from the other. For if the Apostle denies of Melchisedec a father, a mother, and so on, on account of the denied divine revelation, then he also denies them on account of our denied knowledge, which without revelation could not be had of these things. From this it appears that nothing prevents our ignorance, owing to the denied revelation, from supplying a typical reason. Nor was it necessary for the adversary to cite so many authors, since none of those cited opposes me, and none denies that these things are denied of Melchisedec on account of our denied knowledge, which is my opinion; nor does that which says these things are denied of Melchisedec on account of the denied divine revelation oppose it, since the denial of the one infers the other. Hence it is clear that it is not I who argue foolishly, but rather the adversary who argues foolishly, when from what the cited authors say, namely that Melchisedec is said to be without father, and so on, on account of the proposition and revelation of the Holy Spirit (that is, that the Holy Spirit reveals nothing about these matters), he infers that they deny that account is taken of our ignorance, since this denied divine revelation follows concerning a matter which cannot otherwise be known.

units.la: DCXIX. Exc. 3. H. p. 249. Hoc dubium esse principium ex quo argumentor, quia enim ille ἀπάτωρ & ἀμήτωρ fuerit, adhuc controvertitur.
units.tr: DCXIX. Exception 3, H., p. 249: "This is a doubtful principle from which I argue, for whether he was ἀπάτωρ and ἀμήτωρ is still disputed."

units.la: Resp. Melchisedecum fuisse ex historiâ constat eum, qui dicitur ἀπάτωρ & ἀμήτωρ, cum autem eum Scriptura describat, ut Regem Salem, & ut hominem, non est, quod de eo dubitemus. Quis autem fuerit ille homo, non necesse est à nobis cognosci, imo ex illa ignorantia, sive negata cognitione hic argumentor. Quæ præterea habet, nihil lectorem attentum remorari possunt, si modo hæc nostra, quæ prioribus articulis sunt dicta cum ipsius p. 250. conferre velit.
units.tr: Reply: From history it is established that Melchisedec was the one who is called [ἀπάτωρ and ἀμήτωρ], fatherless and motherless. Since, however, Scripture describes him as king of Salem and as a man, there is no reason for us to doubt about him. Who that man was, however, need not be known by us; indeed, I argue here precisely from that ignorance, or denied knowledge. What else he has can detain an attentive reader not at all, if only he is willing to compare these things of ours, which were said in the earlier articles, with his own p. 250.

units.la: DCXX. Exc. 4. M. p. 85. Vere dici Melchisedecum ἀπάτωρ &c. quia vere non recensentur à Mose, non secus ac aliquis appellatur anonymus, qui nomen suum libello non subjecit.
units.tr: DCXX. Exception 4, M., p. 85: "It is truly said that Melchisedec was ἀπάτωρ, and so on, because he is truly not recorded by Moses, just as someone is called anonymous who did not attach his name to his little book."

units.la: Resp. Qui dicitur sine patre, is negatur habere patrem, matrem, initium finemque dierum. At de Melchisedeco hoc revera non potest negari. Nam revera habuit Patrem. Ergo quia non fuit revelatus pater, & à nobis non cognitus. Sic anonymus non dicitur revera talis, si enim revera sit talis, tum nullum habebit nomen, quod est falsum; sed quia non addidit scripto suo, & propterea nos illud ignoramus. Atqui ex eo ipso fui argumentatus.
units.tr: Reply: He who is said to be without father is denied to have a father, a mother, a beginning and end of days. But this truly cannot be denied of Melchisedec, for he truly had a father. Therefore it is because his father was not revealed, and not known by us. Thus an anonymous author is not said to be truly such; for if he were truly such, then he would have no name, which is false; but he is so called because he did not add his name to his writing, and therefore we do not know it. Yet it was from this very point that I argued.

units.la: CAPUT XXVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVIII.

units.la: Quartum Argumentum pro sententia dicta desumptum ex argumentationibus ad hominem in Scriptura usurpatis.
units.tr: The fourth argument for the said opinion, drawn from the arguments ad hominem used in Scripture.

units.la: DCXXI. Sequitur Argumentum quartum. Si Scripturæ Veritati & Auctoritati non repugnat, ut assumat propositiones falsas, falsaque principia, ea non refutans, quæ iis, contra quos disputat, videntur vera, ex iisque veritatem aliquam educat: Ergo multo minus ut utatur formulis receptis, etsi erroneis opinionibus innitantur &c, Si enim non repugnat assuassumere aliquod falsum, illudque proponere in argumento, ut veram propositionem, & ex illo argumentari, non indicato, te illud habere pro falso, non video, quare illud posterius magis repugnare debeat, aut, si aliter sit, ratio diversitatis detur oportet; sed non repugnat, quia videmus id fieri in Scriptura, ex qua unum aut alterum exemplum nobis sufficiet.
units.tr: DCXXI. There follows the fourth argument. If it is not inconsistent with the truth and authority of Scripture for it to assume false propositions and false principles, without refuting them, which seem true to those against whom it disputes, and to draw some truth from them, then much less is it inconsistent for it to use accepted formulas, even if they rest on erroneous opinions, and so on. For if it is not inconsistent to assume something false, to put it forward in an argument as a true proposition, and to argue from it without indicating that you hold it to be false, I do not see why the latter should be more inconsistent. If it is otherwise, a reason for the difference ought to be given. But it is not inconsistent, because we see this done in Scripture, from which one or another example will be enough for us.

units.la: Matth.xix.16,17. Et ecce quidam accedens dixit ei: Doctor bone, quid boni faciam, ut habeam vitam aeternam? Ipse vero dicit ei: cur me dicis bonum? nullus est bonus, nisi unus nempe Deus. Si vis autem ad vitam ingredi, serva mandata. Horum Christi verborum sensus omnibus bene consideratis est iste; Parcius utere hoc titulo boni, qui soli Deo vere & proprie convenit, & quanquam aliquo modo etiam Creaturis tribui possit, non tamen iis tribui debet sine restrictione, si non expressa, saltem tacita: quod cum a te non fieri cognoscam, neque tamen me habeas pro Deo, monendus primo fuisti, de hac compellatione Quandoquidem autem existimas, te faciendo vitam aeternam posse consequi, fac & observa mandata, a Deo praescripta. Quod si Logice haec verba Christi resolvas, deprehendes duplex in iis latere argumentum ad hominem. Primum. Omnis vere, proprie & sine restrictione dicendus bonus, est Deus: Atqui ego non sum Deus (secundum te) Ergo non sum ita bonus sine restrictione, neque talem me appellare debes. Secundum. Cui per justitiam propriam acquirenda est vita aeterna, is debet servare mandata: Atqui tibi per justitiam propriam acquirenda est vita aeterna (quae erat opinio communis inter Judaeos ex Pharisaeorum doctrina derivata) ergo debes servare mandata. In utroque hoc argumento Minor est falsa absolute loquendo, sed vera erat ex mente istius juvenis; eam igitur Christus assumit tanquam veram, & exinde in primo coarguit istum juvenem lapsus in compellatione. In altero satis facit quaestioni ab illo propositae. Quamvis autem dici possit, ita indirecte Christum ostendere voluisse falsitatem istarum propositionum, fieri tamen potuerat, ut hoc iste juvenis non satis assequeretur, ita ut, si secundum istorum hominum sententiam lingua Christi fuisset dirigenda, ex professo & directe debuerit hanc Minorem refutasse.
units.tr: Matth. xix. 16, 17. And behold, one came up and said to him: Good Teacher, what good thing shall I do, that I may have eternal life? But he said to him: Why do you call me good? There is none good but one, namely God. But if you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments. The sense of these words of Christ, when all is carefully considered, is this: Use the title of "good" more sparingly, since it belongs truly and properly only to God, and although in some way it can also be attributed to creatures, it ought not to be attributed to them without restriction, if not expressly then at least tacitly. Since I know you do not do this, and yet you do not regard me as God, you were first to be admonished about this form of address. Since, however, you think you can obtain eternal life by doing, then do and keep the commandments prescribed by God. But if you resolve these words of Christ logically, you will find that there lie hidden in them a double argument ad hominem. First: Whoever is to be called good truly, properly and without restriction is God. But I am not God (according to you). Therefore I am not good in that unrestricted sense, and you ought not to call me so. Second: Whoever is to acquire eternal life by his own righteousness ought to keep the commandments. But eternal life is to be acquired by your own righteousness (which was the common opinion among the Jews, derived from the teaching of the Pharisees). Therefore you ought to keep the commandments. In each of these arguments the minor premise is false in an absolute sense, but it was true in the mind of this young man. Christ therefore takes it as true, and from it, in the first case, he convicts this young man of a slip in his form of address; in the second he satisfies the question put to him. Although it may be said that Christ thus wished to show indirectly the falsity of these propositions, nevertheless it could have happened that this young man would not have grasped this sufficiently. So, if the tongue of Christ had had to be directed according to the opinion of these men, he ought to have refuted this minor premise expressly and directly.

units.la: DCXXII. Alterum Exemplum est, 1 Cor. xv. 29. Alioqui quid facient, qui baptizantur super mortuis? si omnino mortui non suscitantur, cur baptizantur super mortuis? Variae sunt hujus loci interpretationes, quas recensere, & quid in unaquaque difficultatis vel probabilitatis lateat, enucleare, non est hujus loci. Videat, qui voluerit Musculum, Calvinum, Martyrem, Paraeum in hunc locum. Celebriores autem interpretationes sunt duae: quarum prior est, respexisse Apostolum ad morem pravum tunc temporis usitatum, quo factum, ut differrent multi Baptismum ad mortem usque, & tum demum voluerint baptizari, cum illam præsentirent, ut ita abluti à peccatis cœlum ingrederentur, qui inde dicti sunt Clinici: altera; rationem habuisse Apostolum alterius cujusdam consuetudinis in primâ Ecclesiâ receptæ, qua factum, ut si quis morte præventus sine baptismo decesserat, alter in ejus locum fuerit substitutus, qui loco defuncti baptismum suscepit.
units.tr: DCXXII. The second example is 1 Cor. xv. 29. Otherwise, what will they do who are baptized for the dead? If the dead do not rise at all, why are they baptized for the dead? There are various interpretations of this passage. To review them, and to explain what lies hidden in each of their difficulties or probabilities, is not the business of this place. Whoever wishes may consult Musculus, Calvin, Martyr and Paraeus on this passage. The two more famous interpretations are these. The first is that the Apostle had regard to a wicked custom then in use, by which many put off baptism until death, and then at last wished to be baptized when they sensed death was near, so that, washed from their sins, they might enter heaven; these were accordingly called Clinics. The second is that the Apostle took account of another custom received in the primitive Church, by which, if anyone had died before baptism, prevented by death, another was substituted in his place, who received baptism on behalf of the deceased.

units.la: DCXXIII. Utram autem ex his sententiam eligas, erit Argumentum hoc Apostoli ad hominem è principio falso desumptum, quod si redigas in formam talem erit: Baptizari pro mortuis eumque baptismum approbare est tacitè confiteri mortuorum resurrectionem: At sunt inter vos qui baptizantur pro mortuis, vosque eum baptismum approbatis. Ergò eo ipso confitemini mortuorum resurrectionem. Factum itaque illicitum tam secundum priorem quàm posteriorem sententiam assumitur, ac si legitimum esset, ex eoque aliquid scopo Apostoli inserviens infertur. Nec de hoc exemplo idem dici potest, quod de priori: neque enim directè neque indirectè Apostolus hanc opinionem voluit refutare, sed eam omninò pro verâ assumsit.
units.tr: DCXXIII. Whichever of these opinions you choose, this argument of the Apostle will be an argument ad hominem drawn from a false principle. If you reduce it to form, it will be this: To be baptized for the dead, and to approve that baptism, is tacitly to confess the resurrection of the dead. But there are among you those who are baptized for the dead, and you approve that baptism. Therefore by that very fact you confess the resurrection of the dead. Thus an unlawful act is assumed as if it were lawful, on both the former and the latter opinion, and from it something serving the Apostle's purpose is inferred. Nor can the same be said of this example as of the former. For the Apostle neither directly nor indirectly wished to refute this opinion, but assumed it entirely as true.

units.la: DCXXIV. Excipit B. pag. 63. existimans argumentum ad hominem, qualia sunt recensita, & deductionem ad absurdum unum idemque genus esse argumentandi; in quo miserè hallucinatur. Observet ergò sequentes differentias inter syllogismum deducentem ad incommodum, & argumentum ad hominem. 1. In deductione ad incommodum conclusio deducta non directè adversatur thesi adversarii, unde vocatur hic syllogismus indirectus; in argumento ad hominem directè adversatur; ut ex argumentis citatis patet. 2. In deductione ad incommodum conclusio est absurda & falsa, sed in argumento ad hominem est vera. 3. In Ded. ad absurdum altera præmissarum est adversarii Propositio, quæ per indirectum refutatur; non ita in argumento ad hominem ex. gr. deductio ad absurdum est apud Paulum 1 Cor. xv. 14. Si resurrectio mortuorum non est: Christus quoque non est suscitatus: Atqui resurrectio mortuorum non est, ergò Christus non est suscitatus. Hæc conclusio est absurda. Ergò vel major vel minor. Non major. Ergo minor, quæ est eorum, contra quos Paulus disputat. Sed argumentum ad hominem est. Qui est absque limitatione Bonus, ille est Deus; Atqui ego secundum te non sum Deus, ergo non debes me, quem tanquam creaturam consideras, Bonum appellare. Quæ Conclusio est vera. Sic, Baptizari pro mortuis, talemque baptismum approbare, est tacitè confiteri mortuorum resurrectionem. At sunt inter vos tales vosque cum baptismum approbatis. Ergo. Vides ergo in argumento ad hominem propositionem adversarii assumtam non rejici nec refutari, simili modo quo formula aliqua vulgaris non rejicitur nec refutatur. 4. Deductio ad absurdum habet locum etiam in ordine ad propriam mentem dirigendam, quae sibi potest aliquando absurda & incommoda proponere, ut vitet eam sententiam, ex qua talia sequantur. Argumentum vero ad hominem semper est ad alium. 5. Deductio ad absurdum opponitur Demonstrationi ostensivae ab omnibus Logicis; argumento ad hominem opponunt omnes Logici argumentum ad rem. 6. In deductione ad incommodum absurdum & falsum sumo, qua tale est & videtur & mihi & alteri quicum ago; in argumento ad hominem sumo absurdum saepe, (& in eo est convenientia) sed non qua tale mihi & alteri quicum ago, sed quatenus verum & minime absurdum videtur adversario (& haec est differentia) At tamen non semper sumo absurdum revera tale, sed saepe id quod adversario videtur, mihi nondum exploratum, adeo ut ego de eo judicium suspendam, & tantum id assumam in ordine ad adversarium, quem ex sua perceptione ad judicium verum conor deducere. Consentit Danhaverus, qui argumentum ad hominem ita definit pag. 52. Ideae boni Interpretis, quod sit ex principio ab altero quoquam disputatur concessO, esto id principium saepe falsum sit, stat tamen pro principio, quia alter hoc nunquam est negaturus. 7. Deductio ad absurdum ordinarie ad demonstrandum; argumentum ad hominem ad disputandum adhibetur.
units.tr: DCXXIV. B., p. 63, objects, thinking that an argument ad hominem, such as those listed, and reduction to absurdity are one and the same kind of arguing; in this he is sadly mistaken. Let him therefore observe the following differences between a syllogism leading to absurdity and an argument ad hominem. 1. In reduction to absurdity the conclusion drawn is not directly opposed to the thesis of the adversary, whence this syllogism is called indirect; in an argument ad hominem it is directly opposed, as is clear from the arguments cited. 2. In reduction to absurdity the conclusion is absurd and false, but in an argument ad hominem it is true. 3. In reduction to absurdity one of the premises is the proposition of the adversary, which is refuted indirectly; this is not so in an argument ad hominem. For example, the reduction to absurdity in Paul is at 1 Cor. xv. 14: If the resurrection of the dead is not, then Christ also has not been raised; but the resurrection of the dead is not; therefore Christ has not been raised. This conclusion is absurd. Therefore either the major or the minor premise is false. Not the major. Therefore the minor, which is the position of those against whom Paul disputes. But the argument ad hominem is: Whoever is good without limitation is God; but I, according to you, am not God; therefore you ought not to call me good, whom you regard as a creature. This conclusion is true. Likewise: To be baptized for the dead, and to approve such a baptism, is tacitly to confess the resurrection of the dead. But there are among you such people, and you approve that baptism. Therefore... You see, then, that in an argument ad hominem the adversary's proposition is assumed, not rejected nor refuted, in the same way that some common formula is neither rejected nor refuted. 4. Reduction to absurdity also has a place in directing one's own mind, which can sometimes set before itself absurd and inconvenient things, so as to avoid the opinion from which such things follow; but an argument ad hominem is always addressed to another. 5. Reduction to absurdity is opposed to ostensive demonstration by all logicians; all logicians oppose the argument ad hominem to the argument ad rem. 6. In reduction to absurdity I take the absurd and false as such, as it is, and as it seems both to me and to the other person with whom I deal. In an argument ad hominem I often take the absurd (and in this there is agreement), but not as such to me and to the other person with whom I deal; rather, insofar as it seems true and by no means absurd to the adversary (and this is the difference). Yet I do not always take what is really absurd, but often what seems so to the adversary, not yet examined by me, so that I suspend my judgment on it and assume it only with respect to the adversary, whom I try to lead from his own perception to a true judgment. Danhauer agrees, who at p. 52 defines the argument ad hominem thus: It is from a principle conceded by another with whom one disputes; although that principle is often false, it stands as a principle, because the other will never deny it. 7. Reduction to absurdity is ordinarily used for demonstrating; the argument ad hominem is used for disputing.

units.la: DCXXV. Exc. 2. b, p 66. Si Christus secundum opinionem hujus juvenis locutus fuisset, tum vel dixisset: Ita sum bonus, vel saltem denominationis silentio annuisset, dixisset etiam, saltem annuisset vitam aeternam operibus acquirendam &c.
units.tr: DCXXV. Exc. 2. b, p. 66. If Christ had spoken according to the opinion of this young man, then he would either have said, "Thus am I good," or at least by his silence have assented to the title, and he would also have said, or at least assented, that eternal life is to be acquired by works, etc.

units.la: Resp. Atqui ostendi Minores propositiones, Ego Christus non sum Deus: Tibi per justitiam propriam acquirenda est vita aeterna: Vos approbatu baptismum pro mortuis, assumi, non refutari eo in loco, sed in medio relinqui, & ex iis elici quid, quod cum adversariorum sententia pugnat, quod hic sufficit.
units.tr: Reply: But I showed that the minor propositions, "I, Christ, am not God"; "eternal life is to be acquired by you through your own righteousness"; "you approve baptism for the dead", are assumed in that place, not refuted, but left open, and from them is drawn something that conflicts with the opponents' opinion, which is enough for this point.

units.la: DCXXVI. Exc. 3. B. p. 66. At cum de motu solo loquitur Scriptura, non argumentatur ab absurdo ad homines erroris alicujus convincendos.
units.tr: DCXXVI. Exc. 3. B. p. 66. But when Scripture speaks of motion alone, it does not argue from absurdity to convict men of some error.

units.la: Resp. Nec ego hoc dixi, neque infero, sed infero quod ejus auctoritati non repugnet uti formulis receptis, quae opinioni erroneae innituntur, ut patet ex adducto argumento.
units.tr: Reply: I did not say this, nor do I infer it. I infer only that its authority does not prevent the use of accepted formulas that rest on an erroneous opinion, as is clear from the argument I adduced.

units.la: DCXXVII. Quae M. p. 281. objicit, ut nihil quicquam mihi obesse possunt, cum neget quidem majorem propositionem, sed nulla allata ratione
units.tr: DCXXVII. What M. objects on p. 281 can do me no harm at all, since he indeed denies the major proposition, but without offering any reason

units.la: tione diversitatis inter hæc duo, ob quam ab uno ad alterum argumentari non liceat.
units.tr: for a difference between these two, on account of which one may not argue from the one to the other.

units.la: DCXXVIII. Tandem ad ea quæ prolixè M. p. 65, 66, 67 contra hoc meum argumentum opponit, hæc generalia annoto. 1. Me non divisse argumenta ad hominem niti SOLA falsâ hypothesi adversarii. Niituntur enim duabus propositionibus, quarum una est falsa hypothesis adversarii, altera vera Propositio, uti ex descriptione argumenti ad hominem liquet.
units.tr: DCXXVIII. Finally, as to what he objects at length against this argument of mine, at pp. 65, 66, 67, I note the following general points. 1. I did not divide arguments ad hominem as resting ONLY on a false hypothesis of the adversary. For they rest on two propositions, of which one is the false hypothesis of the adversary and the other a true proposition, as is clear from the description of the ad hominem argument.

units.la: DCXXIX. 2. Non nego, quòd argumentum ad hominem hoc modo proponi queat. Qui statuit hoc, ille etiam necessariò statuere debet istud. Atqui tu statuis hoc. Ergò. Nam exempli gratiâ hoc argumentum; Qui statuit Christum non esse Deum, ille eum non debet vocare Bonum. Atqui tu statuis. Ergò. æquivalebit huic, Solus Deus est Bonus vocandus sine restrictione: Atqui Christus non est Deus (scil. secundùm te) Ergò. Verùm 4. in posteriori constitutione argumenti magis manifesta est vis Majoris Propositionis. 5. Minor Propositio utrobique assumitur, atque in medio relinquitur, neque ibi refutatur, quod est quod hic intendo. Idem enim dico fieri in assumtione formularum loquendi vulgarium phænomenis quidem respondentium, sed non semper veritatem accuratam significantium.
units.tr: DCXXIX. 2. I do not deny that an argument ad hominem can be put in this way. Whoever holds this must necessarily hold that. But you hold this. Therefore. For example, this argument: Whoever holds that Christ is not God ought not to call him good. But you hold it. Therefore. This will be equivalent to: God alone is to be called good without restriction; but Christ is not God (namely, according to you); therefore. Indeed, 4. in the latter form of the argument the force of the major proposition is more manifest. 5. The minor proposition is in both cases assumed and left in the middle, and is not refuted there, which is what I am aiming at here. For I say the same happens in the assumption of common forms of speech which correspond to the appearances of things, but do not always express accurate truth.

units.la: DCXXX. 3. Non semper qui argumentatur ad hominem id expressè profitetur, sed id sæpe est aliunde colligendum, & Christi argumentum fuisse argumentum ad hominem nobis quidem constat, qui novimus Christum esse verum Deum, sed non Judæis, non aliis qui hoc ignorant vel etiam negant. Similiter qui utitur formulis apparentiarum sive φαινομένων non correspondentibus accuratæ veritati, non semper id expressè profitetur, neque hoc omnibus constat, sed tantùm iis, qui de accuratâ veritate sunt instructi. 4. Immutatur Conclusio ab Adversario in argumentis propositis, quæ non est: Ergo ego sum Deus, sed, ergo tu me non debes Bonum vocare sine restrictione. 5. Eundem hic errorem errat, cum B. confundendo deductionem ad absurdum cum argumento ad hominem, de quorum distinctione vide supra.
units.tr: DCXXX. 3. Whoever argues ad hominem does not always profess this openly, but it is often to be gathered from elsewhere; and that Christ's argument was an argument ad hominem is clear to us, who know that Christ is the true God, but not to the Jews, nor to others who are ignorant of this or even deny it. Similarly, whoever uses forms of appearance, or phenomena, that do not correspond to accurate truth does not always profess this openly, nor is it evident to all, but only to those who are instructed in accurate truth. 4. The adversary changes the conclusion of the arguments put forward, which is not: "Therefore I am God," but: "Therefore you ought not to call me good without restriction." 5. Here he commits the same error, when B. confuses the reductio ad absurdum with the argument ad hominem; concerning their distinction see above.

units.la: DCXXXI. 6. Quod attinet locum 1 Cor. xv. 29. certum est, argumentum Apostoli, quicquid sit de sensu loci, esse tale, quale suprà propositum est, atque sic melius proponi & clarius quàm per an bages ab Adversario usurpatas. Qui statuit &c. Hæc qui conferre volet cum iis, quæ habet M. p. 65, 66, 67. videbit inania esse quæ hic oggerit, & vim mei argumenti hactenus manere inconcussam.
units.tr: DCXXXI. 6. As for the passage 1 Cor. xv. 29, it is certain that the Apostle's argument, whatever the sense of the passage may be, is of the kind set out above, and so is better and more clearly put than in the roundabout forms used by the adversary: "Whoever holds, etc." Whoever wishes to compare these points with what M. has at pp. 65, 66, 67 will see that what he brings forward here is empty, and that the force of my argument so far remains unshaken.

units.la: CAPUT XXIX.
units.tr: CAPUT XXIX.

units.la: Quintum Argumentum ex phrasibus de Deo adhibitis desumtum proponitur & defenditur.
units.tr: The fifth argument, drawn from the expressions used of God, is set out and defended.

units.la: DCXXXII. Quintum Argumentum hoc modo formamus: Si scriptura loquens de Deo multas adhibet phrases, quae innituntur praejudiciis infantiae & sensuum, atque veritatem relatam ad homines & praejudiciis involutam referentes citra laesionem Auctoritatis & Veritatis suae, Ergo multo minus ejus Auctoritati & Veritati repugnabit, si idem faciat circa res naturales. Sed verum est prius. Ergo & posterius. Ad Minorem illam probandam inservient nobis locutiones, quas Theologi vocare solent Anthropopathicas, in quibus explicandis praeeuntem sequemur Majmonidem More Nebochim dicentem; In his scripturam loqui secundum linguam filiorum hominum. Author ille insigni laude dignus, & reliquis Rabbinis longe praeferendus est, unde Casaub. in Exercit. ad Annales Baronii tali eum ornat elogio. Moses Maimonides (qui & Moses Ægyptius dicitur) solidae atque ingentis doctrinae vir, de quo videor mihi posse id vere dicere, quod Plinius olim de Diodoro Siculo, primum illum inter suos desiisse nugari. Cunaeus vero de Republ. Hebraica lib. I. c. 2. his verbis tantum non ad Coelum tollit. Est in admiratione hominum scriptor maximus, Rabbi Moses Ben Maimonis, qui Thalmudicam doctrinam sepositis nugamentis feliciter complexus est divino illo opere quod מִשְׁנֵה תּוֹרָה appellat. Nunquam ita magnifice quidquam de illo authore dicemus, quin id virtus superet ejus. Fato enim quodam & forte nascendi primus solusque in illa gente recte intellexit, quid illud sit non ineptire. In genere is docet parte I. cap. 33, Legem loqui lingua filiorum hominum, quia haec ratio commoda & facilis est, ut ab ea incipiant pueri, mulieres & communis plebs, in quorum viribus non est, res secundum veritatem apprehendere.
units.tr: DCXXXII. We frame the fifth argument thus: If Scripture, speaking of God, uses many phrases that rest on the prejudices of infancy and of the senses, and that refer a truth related to men and wrapped in such prejudices, without harm to its authority and truth, then it will much less conflict with its authority and truth if it does the same concerning natural things. But the first is true. Therefore the second is also true. To prove the minor, we shall use the expressions that theologians commonly call anthropopathic, and in explaining them we shall follow Maimonides, who in his More Nebochim says that in these places Scripture speaks according to the language of the sons of men. That author deserves distinguished praise and is to be preferred far above the other rabbis, whence Casaubon, in his Exercitationes on Baronius's Annales, honours him with this tribute: Moses Maimonides (who is also called Moses the Egyptian) was a man of solid and great learning, of whom I think I can truly say what Pliny once said of Diodorus Siculus, that he was the first among his own people to stop trifling. Cunaeus, in his work on the Hebrew Commonwealth, book I, ch. 2, almost raises him to heaven in these words: Rabbi Moses ben Maimon, the greatest writer, is an object of men's admiration; he happily gathered the Talmudic teaching, its trifles set aside, in that divine work which he calls Mishneh Torah [מִשְׁנֵה תּוֹרָה]. We shall never speak so magnificently of that author that his merit does not surpass it. For by a certain fate and the chance of his birth, he alone, first and only, in that nation understood rightly what it is not to trifle. In general he teaches, part I, ch. 33, that the Law speaks in the language of the sons of men, because this manner of speech is convenient and easy, so that boys, women and the common people, whose powers do not reach to grasping things according to truth, may begin with it.

units.la: DCXXXIII. In specie vero parte I. cap. 26. quia [a] vulgus hominum non apprehendunt ab initio cogitationis Entitatem vel Essentiam, nisi in rebus corporeis, (& quicquid non est corpus vel res in corpore existens, imo quicquid non est crassum corpus, ut fortiter sensum moveat, quia faciunt sensus suos judicem cognoscendi, an res existant an non, non creditur ab iis esse vel existere) describitur Deus per attributa & nomina corporea, ut doceatur, ipsum esse Ens.
units.tr: DCXXXIII. More particularly, in part I, ch. 26, because the common sort of men at the start of their thinking do not grasp being or essence except in bodily things (and whatever is not a body, or a thing existing in a body, or indeed whatever is not a gross body so as to move the senses strongly, is not believed by them to be or to exist, since they make their senses the judge of whether things exist or not), God is described through bodily attributes and names, so that it may be taught that he is a Being.

units.la: DCXXXIV. Et cùm [b] omnia corporea attributa imperfectionem quandam in se & suâ naturâ involvant, saltem divisibilitatem & mutationem, est tamen quædam differentia inter ea; nam quædam imperfectionem ex consensu & opinione omnium atque etiam vulgi denotant; alia vero imperfectionem inferre cernuntur acutiùs demùm cernentibus, scriptura quidem ea Deo non tribuit, quæ consentientibus omnibus imperfectionem important: at reliqua de Deo prædicare non veretur. Unde [c] motus & quies Deo tribuitur, quando dicitur, Adscendere, Descendere, stare, sedere, Habitare, Ambulare, quoniam non capit vulgus, quomodo aliquid vivere possit sine motione, cùm tamen motus non sit de essentiâ vitæ generaliter acceptæ, sed accidens ab eâ separabile. Itaque motus ad vitam Dei designandam à scripturâ sæpiùs adhibetur. Sic sensus [d] Deo attribuuntur, Visus, Auditus, Odoratus, quia non tantùm vulgus, sed etiam multi viri docti ex præjudicio infantiæ nondum depositò supponunt: Nihil esse in Intellectu quod non prius fuerit in sensu, quod quidem absolutè est falsum, ut fusiùs posset demonstrari, si id ratio instituti nostri ferret. Itaque ad notandam Dei cognitionem Intellectualem Sensus ipsi adscribuntur. Eadem de causâ loquela Deo attribuitur ad significandam Influentiam ipsius in res creatas, unde sæpe locutus dicitur Prophetis, quando tantùm menti ipsorum singulari quodam modo ea, quæ dicere debuerunt indidit: quia vulgus non intelligit, quomodo aliquid ex unius hominis animo in alterum transferri possit, nisi per sermonem.
units.tr: DCXXXIV. And since all bodily attributes involve in themselves and by their nature some imperfection, at least divisibility and change, there is nevertheless a certain difference among them. For some indicate imperfection by the agreement and opinion of all, even of the common people; others are seen to imply imperfection only to those who see more keenly in the end. Scripture indeed does not attribute to God those things which all agree imply imperfection, but it does not hesitate to predicate the rest of God. Hence motion and rest are ascribed to God when it is said: to ascend, to descend, to stand, to sit, to dwell, to walk, because the common people do not grasp how anything can live without motion, although motion is not of the essence of life taken in general, but an accident separable from it. Accordingly, Scripture often uses motion to designate the life of God. So too sight, hearing, smell are attributed to God, because not only the common people but many learned men too, from the prejudice of infancy not yet laid aside, suppose that there is nothing in the intellect which was not first in the senses, which is indeed absolutely false, as could be shown at greater length if the purpose of our undertaking allowed it. Therefore the senses themselves are ascribed to God to mark his intellectual knowledge. For the same reason speech is attributed to God to signify his influence on created things; hence he is said often to have spoken to the prophets, when he put into their minds in some singular manner what they were to say, because the common people do not understand how anything can be transferred from the mind of one man to another except by speech.

units.la: DCXXXV. At quia ex communi hominum sententiâ aliqua imperfectio est in ægrotando, dormiendo, eo quod manifestè imbecillitatem & defatigationem præsupponant, item in edendo & bibendo, quia à siti & fame ea oriri necesse est, ea Deo nullibi in scripturâ tribui legimus. Ita etiam reliqui duo sensus [e] Gustus & Tactus Deo non tribuuntur, quia hos duos tantùm per contactum fieri vulgus supponit, tres alios sine contactu, quamvis verè doceat Aristoteles 3 de Animâ cap. 13. Nullum sensum absque tactu haberi posse, corpus enim animalis omnis habere vim sentiendi tangendo. Deum vero non conjungi cum corporibus per contactum corporalem verè quidem existimant, sed ex pravo principio, quia videre Deum nequeunt: malè enim colligunt: Ego non video hoc vel illud, ergo non est. Similiter [f] Humeri Deo non attribuuntur, quia communiter adhibentur portandis oneribus, quibus summoperè homines defatigantur: multo minùs organa illa, quæ cibis & alimentis capiendis inserviunt. Nam illa etiam in principio cogitationis manifesta sunt imperfectionis signa & indicia. Ex quibus apparet, tantoperè in his Anthropopathiis rationem haberi opinionis vulgi, ut id, in quo perfectionem constituunt, licet erroneè, Deo tribuatur; contrà verò, ubi imperfectionem deprehendunt, ab illo removeatur.
units.tr: DCXXXV. But since, by the common opinion of men, there is some imperfection in being sick, sleeping, since these plainly presuppose weakness and fatigue, likewise in eating and drinking, since these necessarily arise from thirst and hunger, we read that Scripture nowhere attributes these to God. Thus too the other two senses, taste and touch, are not attributed to God, because the common people suppose that these two come about only by contact, while the other three come without contact; yet Aristotle truly teaches, De Anima III, ch. 13, that no sense can be had without touch, for the body of every animal has the power of sensing by touching. That God is not joined to bodies by bodily contact, men indeed rightly believe, but from a wrong principle, because they cannot see God; for they reason badly: I do not see this or that, therefore it is not. Likewise shoulders are not attributed to God, because they are commonly used for carrying burdens, by which men are greatly wearied; much less those organs which serve for taking food and nourishment. For even these, at the start of thinking, are plain signs and indications of imperfection. From these things it appears that in these anthropopathic expressions so much regard is had to the opinion of the common people that what they place perfection in, even though erroneously, is attributed to God; on the contrary, where they perceive imperfection, it is removed from him.

units.la: DCXXXVI. Adhæc {g} notandum, quòd scriptura Deum proponat tanquam hominem mutabilem & flexibilem, eo quod hoc in precibus tacitè quasi solet supponi, cùm tamen respectu suæ providentiæ, secundùm quam omnia, quæ fieri debent ab æterno, dispositit, sit planè immutabilis. Cùm itaque scriptura tales locutiones innitentes præjudiciis Infantiæ de Deo non dubitet usurpare; unde majus periculum videbatur imminere, hoc nempe, ut homines Deo corpus tribuant, quemadmodum & ex malâ interpretatione horum locorum ab Audianis & Anthropomorphitis factum, multò potiùs Deum hoc facturum fuisse circa res naturales, circa quas si erremus, error ille periculo caret, est exi-stimandum. DCXXXVII. {a} Ad hoc argumentum B. post multa cavilla & convitia p. 54. præmissa (de quibus quia in præfatione conquesti sumus, neque volumus par pari referre, eaque ad rem non facere confiteatur, ea sicco pede præterimus, & ad rem ipsam cum eo accedimus) Exc. 1. p. 55. Deum esse Ens nihil aliud infert quàm Deum esse, sive dari Deum qui existat. Itaque cum Deo attribuuntur oculi, aures &c. nihil aliud notabitur, quam dari Deum qui est, quo nihil ineptius dici potest. Et ad denotandum Dei Entitatem sufficit dicere Deum esse: at cùm dicitur Deum habere aures &c. aliquid superadditur in conceptu nostro Entitati, sive Essentia divina &c. vide totam p. 56. Resp. 1. Imò verò ineptum est statuere, quod Ens de Deo usurpatum nihil aliud significet quàm existere, cùm Ens tanquam concretum non tantùm existentiam denotet, sed essentiam & attributa realia secundùm Metaphysicam. Itaque qui dicit Deum Ens, non tantùm dicit Deum existere, sed & habere Essentiam & attributa realia, quæ ex illâ Essentiâ consequuntur. 2. Dixi in genere usurpari attributa corporea de Deo ad ostendendum ipsum esse Ens reale non evanidum, cui non repugnat, quod ea speciatim considerata etiam aliquid aliud designent, præter ipsum existere, cum libenter concedam, per Oculos Dei omniscientiam ejus & providentiam, per Dextram Dei ejus omnipotentiam & efficaciam in operando designari. Ineptus ergo est adversarius, quod distinguere nesciat ea, quae distincte fuerunt explicata. 3. Nulla autem hic pugna inter me & Theologos ab adversario citatos. Distinguendae enim hic sunt quaestiones diversae, quarum aliae spectant τὸ ὅτι, aliae τὸ διότι. Τὸ ὅτι spectant, si quaeras. 1. Quid attributa corporea de Deo praedicata in ipso denotent in genere considerata? 2. Quid designent attributa corporea haec vel illa in specie Deo assignata, ut aures, dextera &c? Ad priorem respondeo, designari per ea, quod Deus sit Ens reale & verum, habeatque realem Essentiam, Existentiam aliaque attributa vera. Ad secundam dico cum Theologis citatis adhiberi ea ad proprietatem efficientiamque Dei designanda. Sed cum responsum est ad istas duas Ϛ ὅτι quaestiones, restant adhuc quaestiones de τῶ διότι, nimirum. 1. Quare scriptura Deo assignet attributa corporea?
units.tr: DCXXXVI. Furthermore, it is to be noted that Scripture presents God as a changeable and flexible man, because this is commonly tacitly presupposed in prayers, although with respect to his providence, according to which he has disposed from eternity all things that are to be done, he is altogether immutable. Since, therefore, Scripture does not hesitate to use such expressions resting on the prejudices of infancy concerning God, where a greater danger seemed to threaten, namely that men would attribute a body to God (as happened from the bad interpretation of these places by the Audians and Anthropomorphites), it is to be judged that God would much more do this concerning natural things, about which, if we err, that error is free from danger. DCXXXVII. To this argument B., after many cavils and insults set forth at p. 54 (of which, since we have complained in the preface, and do not wish to repay like with like, and which he himself admits have nothing to do with the matter, we pass over dryshod and come to the thing itself), says at Exc. 1, p. 55: That God is a Being implies nothing other than that God is, or that there is a God who exists. So when eyes, ears, etc. are attributed to God, nothing else will be noted than that there is a God who is, than which nothing can be said more absurdly. And to denote the Being of God it is enough to say God is; but when it is said that God has ears etc., something is added in our concept to the Entity, or divine Essence, etc. See the whole of p. 56. Reply 1. On the contrary, it is absurd to state that Being, used of God, signifies nothing other than to exist, since Being, as a concrete term, denotes not only existence but essence and real attributes according to Metaphysics. Therefore whoever says God is a Being says not only that God exists, but also that he has an Essence and real attributes that follow from that Essence. 2. I said that bodily attributes are used of God in general to show that he is a real and non-empty Being, to which it is not opposed that these, considered specifically, also designate something else besides existing; for I readily concede that by the eyes of God his omniscience and providence are designated, and by the right hand of God his omnipotence and efficacy in working. Therefore the adversary is foolish in not knowing how to distinguish things that were distinctly explained. 3. Yet there is no quarrel here between me and the theologians cited by the adversary. For different questions must be distinguished here, of which some concern the that [τὸ ὅτι], others the why [τὸ διότι]. The questions about the that are, if you ask: 1. What do the bodily attributes predicated of God denote in him, considered in general? 2. What do these or those bodily attributes assigned to God in particular designate, such as ears, the right hand, etc.? To the former I reply that they designate that God is a real and true Being, and has a real Essence, Existence and other true attributes. To the second I say, with the theologians cited, that they are used to designate the property and efficacy of God. But when an answer has been given to these two questions of the that, there remain questions of the why [τὸ διότι], namely: 1. Why does Scripture assign bodily attributes to God?

units.la: 2. Quare haec vel illa attributa corporea? ad priorem respondeo, id fieri, quia ii, qui sensuum ductum tantum sequuntur, non apprehendunt ab initio cogitationis Entitatem vel Essentiam, nisi in rebus corporeis &c. Ad posteriorem in sequentibus responsio habetur. Atque ita satisfactum est primae, secundae, tertiae & quintae adversarii, quam vocat, responsioni.
units.tr: 2. Why these or those corporeal attributes? To the first part I answer that this happens because those who follow only the guidance of the senses do not, at the outset of their thinking, grasp Entity or Essence except in corporeal things, etc. The answer to the second part is given in what follows. And so the first, second, third and fifth parts of what my opponent calls his response have been dealt with.

units.la: DCXXXVIII. Exc. 2. B. p. 56, quae est quarta ejus responsio.
units.tr: DCXXXVIII. Exc. 2. B. p. 56, which is his fourth response.

units.la: Si per corporea attributa notetur Dei Entitas, ergo cum alibi corporeitas & affectiones corporales quae fortiter sensus movere solent, de Deo negantur, etiam negaretur Dei Entitas, ut cum Deus dicitur Spiritus, Invisibilis, saltem abduceretur vulgus a ratione concipiendi Entitatem Dei.
units.tr: If the Entity of God is signified by corporeal attributes, then, since elsewhere corporeity and bodily affections, which usually strongly move the senses, are denied of God, the Entity of God would also be denied, as when God is called Spirit and Invisible; at least the common people would be drawn away from the way of conceiving the Entity of God.

units.la: Resp. Superius dixi, Attributa corporea in genere considerata de Deo praedicari, ut per ea designetur, quod Deus sit verum Ens reale, & veram habeat realemque Essentiam, Existentiam aliaque Attributa. Itaque argumentum hic obiectum simile est huic: Si attributa corporea, nempe, quod Deus habeat dextram, aures, oculos &c. adhibentur a scriptura ad proprietatem efficientiamque Dei denotandam, uti Theologi citati ab adversario loquuntur, Ergo quando illa de Deo negantur, ut saepe fit, negaretur Dei proprietas & efficientia. Itaque nego istam connexionem, atque dico; corporea attributa adhiberi aliquando, ut per ea designetur crassiori modo realis Dei essentia, aliquando vero spiritualia Deo attribui, ut sine tropo proprie & accurate realis illa Dei essentia significetur.
units.tr: Reply. I said above that corporeal attributes, considered in general, are predicated of God so that by them it is signified that God is a true real Being, and has a true and real Essence, Existence and other attributes. So the argument raised here is similar to this one: If corporeal attributes, namely that God has a right hand, ears, eyes, etc., are used by Scripture to denote the property and efficacy of God, as the Theologians cited by my opponent say, then when those attributes are denied of God, as often happens, the property and efficacy of God would be denied. I therefore deny this connection, and say that corporeal attributes are sometimes used to signify, in a cruder manner, the real essence of God, while at other times spiritual attributes are ascribed to God so that that real essence of God is signified properly and accurately, without a trope.

units.la: DCXXXIX. Exc. 3. B. p. 56. Quis credet tam inepto modo Entitatem suam designare voluisse, cum dentur phraseologiae multo commodiores.
units.tr: DCXXXIX. Exc. 3. B. p. 56. Who would believe that he wished to designate his Entity in such an inept way, when more convenient phrases are available?

units.la: diores ad denotandum, quod sit Ens Entium, aeternum, per se subsistens, & causa omnium rerum, ut vox יהוה.
units.tr: more convenient expressions for denoting that he is the Being of beings, eternal, self-subsisting, and the cause of all things, such as the word [יהוה] (Yahweh).

units.la: Resp. Similiter dicam: Quis credet Deum tam inepto modo suas proprietates designare voluisse, quali Theologi ab ipso citati existimant, cum dentur phraseologiae multo commodiores, nempe vox שרי אל &c. itaque quod superius est responsum, huic etiam applicari velim, Deum & crasso modo & accurate voluisse haec significare, ut quocunque modo intelligerentur.
units.tr: Answer. Similarly I say: who would believe that God wished to designate his properties in so inept a way, as the theologians cited by the adversary think, when more suitable phrases are available, namely the phrase [שרי אל] and so on? So what was answered above I would like applied to this too: God wished these things to be signified both in a crude way and accurately, so that they could be understood in either way.

units.la: [b] DCXL. Exc. 4. B. p. 57. Quasi vero Vulgus, quod tam stupidum faciam, ut Entitatem rei concipere non possit, nisi sub rebus corporeis, nec de illa doceri, nisi sub harum nominibus &c. tam subtiliter distinguere queat inter sensuum vel majorem vel minorem imperfectionem, ob quam attributa quaedam de Deo praedicari vel non praedicari possint.
units.tr: [b] DCXL. Exc. 4. B. p. 57. As if indeed I made the common people so stupid that they could not conceive the entity of a thing except under corporeal things, nor be taught about it except under their names, etc., and could distinguish so subtly between a greater or lesser imperfection of the senses, on account of which certain attributes can or cannot be predicated of God.

units.la: Resp. 1. Non dixi vulgus esse tam stupidum, ut Entitatem rei concipere non possit nisi sub rebus corporeis, (quamvis etiam non negaverim, multos esse tam stupidos, ut nullam substantiam intelligant nisi imaginabilem & corpoream vel etiam sensibilem) sed dixi cum Maimonide, ab initio cogitationis non apprehendere ea, hoc est, quamdiu nititur praejudiciis infantiae. 2. Non opus est, ut vulgus distinguat inter majorem sensuum perfectionem vel imperfectionem in actu signato, sufficit, quod distinguat in actu exercito, & in edendo, bibendo &c. ex sensuum judiciis aliqua imperfectio agnoscatur, uti patet ex art. DCXXXIV. a me dictis.
units.tr: Answer 1. I did not say that the common people are so stupid that they cannot conceive the entity of a thing except under corporeal things (although I would not deny that many are so stupid that they understand no substance except an imaginable, corporeal or even sensible one). But I said, with Maimonides, that at the start of thought they do not apprehend these things, that is, as long as they rely on the prejudices of infancy. 2. It is not necessary that the common people distinguish between a greater or lesser perfection of the senses in the abstract; it is enough that they distinguish in the exercised act, in eating, drinking, etc. From the judgments of the senses some imperfection is recognised, as is clear from what I said in article DCXXXIV.

units.la: [c] DCXLI. Exc. 4. B. p. 58. Si per motum denotetur Dei vita, quid per quietem designabitur nisi carentia vita? &c. quae videat Lector, si operae pretium sit.
units.tr: [c] DCXLI. Exc. 4. B. p. 58. If by motion the life of God is denoted, what will be denoted by rest except lack of life? etc. Let the reader look at this, if it is worth the effort.

units.la: Resp. 1. Neg. propos. Maj. Nam motus quidem immediate in Deo significat actionem ad extra, sed mediate vitam, quae ex actione tali colligitur; quies vero cessationem ab hac actione tantum in Deo designat, non vero mortem, quia recte quidem concludes, ubi est haec actio, ibi est vita; sed non similiter, ubi non est haec actio, ibi est cessatio a vita. 2. Non nego, quod vita Dei etiam propriis vocibus designetur, quando dicitur Deus vivens &c. sed dico aliquando accuratius eam significari, aliquando crassius & popularius, uti & supra de Dei Entitate sive realitate vidimus.
units.tr: Answer 1. I deny the major premise. For motion in God signifies immediately an action directed outward, but mediately life, which is inferred from such action; rest, however, designates in God only the cessation from this action, not death. For you rightly conclude that where this action is, there is life; but not similarly that where this action is not, there is cessation from life. 2. I do not deny that God's life is also designated by proper words when God is called living, etc., but I say that it is sometimes signified more accurately, sometimes more crudely and popularly, as we also saw above concerning the entity or reality of God.

units.la: [d] DCXLII. Exc. 5. B. p. 29. Praejudicium illud, de quo somniem esse vanissimum meum commentum &c. videat, cui placet, totam paginam. Resp. Hoc axioma, Nihil est in intellectu, quod non prius fuerit in sensu, esse praejudicium infantiae, patet, quoniam procedit ex eo axiomate, ubi nihil video, sentio, nihil est, quod praejudicium infantiae esse suo loco ostendimus. 2. Hoc axioma absolute falsum esse, patet exinde, quia intellectus habet Dei cognitionem insitam, aliarumque rerum ideas innatas, quae ad intelligendum plane sunt necessariae: nisi enim talis esset natura mentis, ut quarumlibet rerum ideas ex semetipsa posset formare, nihil quicquam intelligere posset. Sensus autem nihil aliud conserunt quam ut, vestigium in cerebro imprimendo, animae dent occasionem hanc vel illam cogitationem sive conceptum formalem sive ideam tunc ex semetipsa depromendi. Nego autem, quod natura caecus non possit concipere, quod sit lux, color, &c. Sensualiter cognoscere non posse concedo, sed intellectualiter ejus essentiam apprehendere omnino potest. Unde videre est, quam vana sint omnia, quae adducit hic adversarius.
units.tr: [d] DCXLII. Exc. 5. B. p. 29. That prejudice, of which my own invention is a most empty dream, etc. Let whoever likes look at the whole page. Answer. That axiom, There is nothing in the intellect that was not first in the sense, is a prejudice of infancy. This is clear, since it proceeds from that axiom: where I see nothing and sense nothing, nothing is; which we have shown in its place to be a prejudice of infancy. 2. That this axiom is absolutely false is clear from this: the intellect has an innate knowledge of God and innate ideas of other things, which are plainly necessary for understanding. For unless the nature of the mind were such that it could form the ideas of whatever things from itself, it could understand nothing at all. The senses, however, contribute nothing other than, by imprinting a trace in the brain, giving the soul occasion to draw forth from itself this or that thought, whether formal concept or idea. I deny, however, that a man who is blind by nature cannot conceive that light or colour exists, etc. I concede that he cannot know it by sense, but he can altogether apprehend its essence intellectually. Hence one can see how vain are all the things this adversary adduces.

units.la: [e] DCXLHI. Exc. 6. B. p. 60. Quis unquam audivit, quod vulgus judicet illum sensum esse imperfectum, qui fit per contactum, vel quod nescias auditum fieri per contactum soni ad aures, odoratum per contactum vaporum odoriferorum &c.
units.tr: [e] DCXLIII. Exc. 6. B. p. 60. Who has ever heard that the common people judge that sense to be imperfect which comes about by contact, or that you do not know that hearing happens by the contact of sound with the ears, smell by the contact of odoriferous vapours, etc.

units.la: Resp. Quis vero unquam audivit, non esse imperfectionem, contactu objecti opus habere ad ejus perceptionem? & quis negaverit, vulgum supponere, contactu eo opus tantum esse in Gustu & Tactu, non in reliquis sensibus, cum & Philosophi Scholastici id doceant, cumque noverit vulgus, audiri posse sonum e loco remotiori editum, non existimat, cum pervenire ad aures per contactum, atque rem odoriferam posse odore percipi, etsi in aliqua distantia a naribus sit remota; de vaporum odoriferorum exhalatione vulgus revera non cogitat. Non ergo vanae sunt subtilitates, quas putat antagonista, etiamsi oculorum ejus aciem forte valde obtusam effugiant.
units.tr: Answer. But who has ever heard that it is not an imperfection to need contact with the object for its perception? And who would deny that the common people suppose such contact is needed only in taste and touch, not in the other senses, since the Scholastic philosophers also teach this? Since the common people know that a sound produced from a more distant place can be heard, they do not think that it reaches the ears by contact, nor that a fragrant thing can be perceived by smell when it is at some distance from the nostrils. The common people do not really think about the exhalation of odoriferous vapours. So the subtleties which the antagonist thinks are vain are not vain, even if they escape his perhaps very dull eyesight.

units.la: [f] DCXLIV. Exc. 7. B. p. 61. Humeros Christo adscribi Ef. IX. 5. Et erit principatus super humerum ipsius. Et Deus comparatus Bajulo dicitur omnia ferre verbo potentiae suae.
units.tr: [f] DCXLIV. Exc. 7. B. p. 61. Shoulders are ascribed to Christ, Is. 9:5: "And the government shall be upon his shoulder." And God, compared to a porter, is said to bear all things by the word of his power.

units.la: Resp. Humeri Deo non adscribuntur Ef. ix. 5. quia Christus ibi non praecise consideratur qua Deus, sed qua Θεάνθρωπος, itaque Humeri ei assignantur respectu habito ad ejus humanitatem. Quod autem Deus Heb. I. 3. dicitur omnia portare, id nihil ad rem. Est enim quaestio: An Humeri Deo adscribantur? non vero an dicatur portare, cum hoc non ita omnium consensu imperfectionem designet.
units.tr: Answer. Shoulders are not ascribed to God at Is. 9:5, because Christ there is not considered precisely as God, but as the God-man, so shoulders are assigned to him with regard to his humanity. As for God being said at Heb. 1:3 to bear all things, that has nothing to do with it. For the question is whether shoulders are ascribed to God, not whether he is said to bear, since this does not, by universal agreement, designate imperfection.

units.la: DCXLV.
units.tr: DCXLV.

units.la: [g] DCXLV. Exc. 8. B. p. 61. Deum in precibus mutabilem & flexibilem consideari ob mutabilitatem actionum divinarum.
units.tr: [g] DCXLV. Exc. 8. B. p. 61. That God is considered in prayers as mutable and flexible because of the mutability of the divine actions.

units.la: Resp. Quando Scriptura Deum ut mutabilem & flexibilem proponit, hoc quidem respectu mutabilitatis actionum divinarum esse explicandum censeo, sed inde non consequitur, quod istam locutionem de Deo non adhibeat sese accommodando nostro Judicio erroneo.
units.tr: Answer. When Scripture presents God as mutable and flexible, I think this must indeed be explained with respect to the mutability of the divine actions; but it does not follow from this that it does not use this way of speaking about God, accommodating itself to our erroneous judgment.

units.la: DCXLVI. De consequentia argumenti quoniam non vult litigare, B. p. 62. & nos firmam Minorem probaverimus, nostrum argumentum inconcussum manet.
units.tr: DCXLVI. On the consequence of the argument: since he does not wish to dispute it (B. p. 62), and we have proved the minor premise firm, our argument remains unshaken.

units.la: DCXLVII. Exc. 9. H. p. 161, 162. Se ab explicatione Maimonidae non plane abhorrere inquit, sed negat, quod Deus velit condescendere ad apprehensionem eam vulgi, qua ex se & per se vulgus Deum cum membris humanis concipit. Ex. XL, 18, quia vulgus Deum per alicujus hominis individuum temere & interdum parum decore concipit.
units.tr: DCXLVII. Exc. 9. H. p. 161, 162. He says he does not altogether shrink from Maimonides' explanation, but he denies that God wishes to condescend to the vulgar's apprehension, by which the common people conceive God from themselves and through themselves with human members. Ex. XL, 18, because the common people rashly, and sometimes indecorously, conceive God through the individual of some man.

units.la: Resp. Quod Deus velit condescendere ad apprehensionem vulgi, qua Deum cum membris humanis concipit, apparet ex phrasibus illis a Deo adhibitis ab initio hujus capitis adductis, quibus quid velit docere, est indicatum. Sed condescendit Deus quoad modum loquendi vulgo erranti, non quoad ipsam illam opinionem erroneam, quam phrasibus istis non docet, quo facit locus Ex. XL. 18.
units.tr: Reply. That God wishes to condescend to the vulgar's apprehension, by which he conceives God with human members, appears from those phrases used by God, cited at the beginning of this chapter, by which what he wishes to teach is indicated. But God condescends in the manner of speaking to the erring vulgar, not to that erroneous opinion itself, which he does not teach by those phrases; to this the place Ex. XL. 18 applies.

units.la: DCXLVIII. Exc. 10. H. p. 163. Deo corporea membra hac vel illa adscribi, quia in generis humani forma per singularem suam dispensationem hominibus apparuit. Et quia visu ita est a Patribus, filii etiam Deum ad eundem modum concipiunt &c.
