units.tr: DCXLVIII. Exc. 10. H. p. 163. Corporeal members are ascribed to God, this or that, because in the form of the human race he appeared to men through his singular dispensation. And because it is so seen by the Fathers, the sons also conceive God in the same way, etc.

units.la: Resp. In apparitionibus Dei figurae illae senis, columbae, fuerunt symbola praesentiae Dei, non Dei imagines; unde nego Deum concessisse hunc modum se ita concipiendi, ut non reputetur nobis in peccatum, neque enim adhibitae fuerunt istae apparitiones anthropopathicae, ut nos imaginem Dei conciperemus per eas, sed tantum, ut designarent singularem Dei praesentiam aliquodque Dei attributum. Quod enim nolit corporeus concipi, apparet ex illis locis Scripturae, ubi se invisibilem & spiritum appellat, & possumus ideam sive conceptum Dei formare, ita ut conceptum Dei non ingrediatur ullus corporeae rei conceptus, si cogitemus de Ente perfectissimo, omnipotente, misericorde, justo &c. Atque hic plus mihi concedit adversarius quam petebam. Ego tantum volo phrases vulgares de Deo adhiberi, quamvis ex opinione erronea habeant ortum, ille etiam vult, Deum a nobis debere secundum opinionem erroneam concipi, quod est falsum, neque a me intentum.
units.tr: Reply. In God's appearances, those figures of an old man and of a dove were symbols of God's presence, not images of God. Hence I deny that God granted this mode of conceiving himself in such a way that it is not reckoned to us as sin. For those anthropopathic appearances were not employed so that we would conceive an image of God through them, but only to designate God's singular presence and some attribute of God. That he does not wish to be conceived as corporeal appears from those passages of Scripture where he calls himself invisible and spirit. And we can form an idea or concept of God in such a way that no concept of a corporeal thing enters into the concept of God, if we think of the most perfect, omnipotent, merciful, just Being, etc. Here my opponent concedes more to me than I was asking. I only want common phrases about God to be used, although they arise from an erroneous opinion; he also wants God to be conceived by us according to the erroneous opinion, which is false and not what I intend.

units.la: DCXLIX. Exc. 11. M. p. 56, 57. videtur excipere, quæ planè non tangunt scopum. Summa huc redit. Spiritum sanctum tali phrasi anthropopathicâ significare intendere rem ipsam secundum absolutam perfectionem consideratam, v. gr. per visum scientiam Dei: phrasin verò consignificare aliquam imperfectionem. Id enim mihi non repugnat, sed est ipsa mea sententia, cum nullibi doceam, quod Scriptura per illas phrases impersectionem aliquam in Deo significet, id enim mihi affingitur ab adversariis; sed quæstio est, quare tali modo ista perfectio exprimatur, annon propterea, quod voluerit non rejicere phrasin præjudiciis infantiæ & sensuum innitentem, eo quòd illa esset recepta, cum aliàs etiam absque tali phrasi istam perfectionem potuerit exprimere.
units.tr: DCXLIX. Exc. 11. M. p. 56, 57. seems to except things which do not touch the point at all. The sum comes to this: that the Holy Spirit, by such an anthropopathic phrase, intends to signify the thing itself considered according to absolute perfection, e.g., the knowledge of God through sight; but the phrase co-signifies some imperfection. This does not oppose me; it is my very view, since I nowhere teach that Scripture by those phrases signifies any imperfection in God. That is attributed to me by my opponents. The question is rather why this perfection is expressed in such a way: is it not perhaps because Scripture wished not to reject a phrase resting on prejudices of infancy and the senses, since that phrase was received, although it could otherwise have expressed that perfection even without such a phrase?

units.la: DCL. Exc. 12. M. p. 58. post multa. Absolutè loquendo dantur formulæ perfectionem divinam distinctius exprimentes quàm Anthropopathicæ: relinquunt tamen omnes divinam perfectionem in infinitum post se. Verùm hic ea formulæ dicenda sunt perfectiores, quæ fini magis inserviunt, nempe ædificationi Ecclesiæ, quales sunt Anthropopathicæ, quæ plurium, nempe vulgi, ædificationem promovent.
units.tr: DCL. Exc. 12. M. p. 58. after many things. Absolutely speaking, there are formulas expressing the divine perfection more distinctly than the anthropopathic ones; yet all of them leave the divine perfection infinitely beyond them. But here those formulas are to be called more perfect which serve the end more, namely the edification of the Church; such are the anthropopathic ones, which promote the edification of the many, namely the common people.

units.la: Resp. Totus hic discursus nihil quicquam mihi adversatur. Sufficit mihi, illas formulas anthropopathicas inniti præjudiciis infantiæ & sensuum, quod quamdiu non refutatur nihil efficitur.
units.tr: Reply. This whole discourse opposes nothing to me. It is enough for me that those anthropopathic formulas rest on prejudices of infancy and the senses; as long as this is not refuted, nothing is achieved.

units.la: DCLI. Exc. 13. M. p. 59. Ista locutiones nec falsæ, nec rem falsam sed inadæquatis verbis rem veram exprimunt, adeóque nec falsæ sed imperfectæ potiùs locutiones sunt appellandæ.
units.tr: DCLI. Exc. 13. M. p. 59. These expressions are neither false, nor do they express a false thing; rather, they express a true thing by inadequate words, and so they should be called not false but imperfect expressions.

units.la: Resp. Nec ego uilibi dico, vel illas locutiones falsè, vel rem falsam exprimere, sed esse præjudiciis sensuum & infantiæ innixas, quibus tamen Scriptura utens eo ipso hæc nolit docere, nec tamen etiam refutare.
units.tr: Reply. Nor do I say anywhere that these expressions either are false or express a false thing, but that they rest on prejudices of the senses and of infancy. Yet Scripture, using them, by that very fact does not wish to teach these things, nor, however, to refute them.

units.la: DCLII. Sequuntur ea, quæ S. p. 407. huic argumento oggerit. 1. inquit, Quanta non intercedit distantia inter Deum creatorem & res naturales ab eo creatas. Quoniam Deus ut Infinitus excedit sphaeram intellectus nostri, Spiritus sanctum nobiscum quasi balbutire cogitur, eumque, cujus faciem intueri non possumus, quasi a tergo nobis propenit, juxta ea ipsa quae Mosi acciderunt. Exod. XXXIII. Sed alia planè ratio est rerum naturalium, quamvis enim eas plenissimè & sufficientissimè cognoscendo non qucamus perspicere (ut subsequenti capite distinctius fusiusque offendemus) interim tamen eas ipsas, quod ad cognitionem proportionatas esse, ostendunt illi ipsi, cum quibus hic nobis negotium est: Spiritum sanctum enim in scriptura loquentem eum in finem nituntur circumscribere, ut submoto illius testimonio, tanquam sibi adversante facilius summ thesin tutari, aliisque persuadere queant. 2. Haec, ut Deo tribuuntur metaphoricè, & pro metaphora ratione explicari debent, sic non est existimandum (quemadmodum Audiani & Anthropomorphita somniabant) aliquid horum Deo convenire proprie & formaliter, sed duntaxat secundum effectum. Et uti tropus non implicat mendacium, ita hæc ipsa convenienter explicata nihil falsi continent: siquidem hæ locutiones frequentantur, ut operationes Dei verè describantur, nobisque convenienter proponantur, quod pro caliginosibus mentis oculis supremum illud numen tale, quale illud in se est, intueri non queamus. 3. Quæ verò consequentia ab his locutionibus ad eas, quæ in scripturâ de rebus naturalibus frequentantur? Dato, in hisce locutionibus similem notandum esse scopum, hoc solum sequetur, allegoricè duntaxat & obscuriùs naturam rerum naturalium in scripturâ proponi, neutiquam verò res naturales cognoscendas proponi secundum erroneum judicium: nisi quis pariter dicere voluerit, Deo membra & affectus & similia tribui secundum erroneum vulgi judicium. Pariter quippe dixerunt ex vulgi judicio Deum in scripturâ ut avem proponi, quod tribuantur eidem ala atque pennæ Psal. XVII. 8. Psal. XCI. 4. Aug. Ep. 3. ad Paulinum. Quæ de membris assiduè scriptura commemorat, ne quisquam secundum carnis hujus formam & figuram non esse crederet similes Deo: propterea eadem & alas Deum habere dixit, quas utique nos non habemus. Hic Clarissimo viro visum fuit infringere vim hujus argumenti.
units.tr: DCLII. There follows what S. p. 407 brings against this argument. (1) How great a distance there is between God the creator and natural things created by him! Since God, as infinite, exceeds the sphere of our intellect, the Holy Spirit is forced to stammer with us, as it were, and to present him whose face we cannot behold, as it were from behind, in accordance with what happened to Moses, Exod. XXXIII. But the case of natural things is quite different. For although we cannot perceive them by knowing them most fully and sufficiently (as we shall show more distinctly and at greater length in the following chapter), nevertheless those very people with whom we have business here show that they are proportionate to our knowledge. For they strive to circumscribe the Holy Spirit speaking in Scripture to this end, so that, with his testimony removed as opposing them, they can more easily defend their highest thesis and persuade others. (2) Just as these things are attributed to God metaphorically, and must be explained according to the metaphor, so it is not to be thought (as the Audians and Anthropomorphites dreamed) that any of these belong to God properly and formally, but only according to effect. And as a trope does not involve a lie, so these very things, suitably explained, contain nothing false. For these expressions are frequent so that God's operations may be truly described and suitably set forth to us, since we cannot behold that supreme deity as it is in itself with our mental eyes so clouded. (3) But what is the consequence from these expressions to those which are frequent in Scripture about natural things? Granted that a similar aim must be noted in these expressions, this only follows: that the nature of natural things is set forth in Scripture allegorically and more obscurely, and by no means that natural things are set forth to be known according to an erroneous judgment. Unless someone wishes to say likewise that members, affections and the like are attributed to God according to the erroneous judgment of the common people. Likewise indeed they said that God is presented in Scripture as a bird according to the judgment of the common people, because wings and feathers are attributed to him Psal. XVII. 8. Psal. XCI. 4. Augustine, Ep. 3 ad Paulinum. What Scripture constantly relates about members, lest anyone believe that we are not like God in the form and figure of this flesh, it also says that God has wings, which of course we do not have. Here it seemed good to that most distinguished man to weaken the force of this argument.

units.la: DCLIII. Ad quæ nos sequentia reponimus, quibus existimamus argumentum nostrum satis roborari.
units.tr: DCLIII. To these points we reply as follows, and we think our argument is thereby sufficiently strengthened.

units.la: 1. Fatemur, distantiam magnam esse inter Deum & res naturales, quippe infinitum: Concedimus etiam, hanc unam esse causam, ob quam Deus nobiscum balbutire velit, quia Deus ut Infinitus excedit sphæram intellectus nostri: sed quia etiam ad Scripturæ scopum spectabat, Dei naturam nobis explicare in tantum, quantum hoc salutis necessitas, requirebat, non itidem rerum naturalium, potior etiam erat ratio, cur Scriptura de Deo loqueretur secundum rei veritatem, quousque sese extenderet infirmus noster intellectus. Itaque nisi alia accederet ratio, quam nos dedimus, quod scriptura debeat promiscuè legi ab omnibus, quorum major pars variis prajudiciis est occupata, potuisset Scriptura omisisse locutiones tales anthropopathicas, quas initi ostendimus vulgi prejudiciis, & Dei describere naturam, quod sit spiritualis, æterna, perfectissima, immensa &c. quemadmodum aliis in locis facit, ex quibus Theologi hæc attributa deducunt & probant: hæc enim ut apprehendat & cognoscat, in quantum opus est, infirmus noster intellectus nihil repugnat.
units.tr: 1. We admit that there is a great distance between God and natural things, since he is infinite. We also concede that this is one reason why God wishes to stammer with us, because God as Infinite exceeds the sphere of our understanding. But since Scripture's aim was also to explain the nature of God to us as far as the necessity of salvation requires, and not in the same way the nature of natural things, there was an even stronger reason why Scripture should speak of God according to the truth of the matter, as far as our weak understanding can reach. Thus, unless another reason were added to the one we gave, that Scripture ought to be read indiscriminately by all, most of whom are occupied with various prejudices, Scripture could have omitted such anthropopathic expressions, which we have shown to be based on the prejudices of the common people, and could have described the nature of God, that he is spiritual, eternal, most perfect, immense, and so on, as it does in other places, from which theologians deduce and prove these attributes. For our weak understanding has no difficulty in apprehending and knowing these things, as far as is necessary.

units.la: DCLIV. 2. Illi, cum quibus negotium sibi dicit esse vir Clarissimus, nihil aliud moliuntur, quàm ut ostendentes, dogma de Terræ delatio ne non esse contrarium Scripturæ, absurditates amoveant, quibus solet gravari, & sic lectori aditum faciant ad perpendendas rationes, quibus firmissimis nititur.
units.tr: DCLIV. 2. Those with whom the most distinguished man says he has to deal do nothing else than, by showing that the doctrine of the earth's motion is not contrary to Scripture, remove the absurdities with which it is usually burdened, and so open the way for the reader to weigh the arguments on which it rests most firmly.

units.la: DCLV. 3. Verum est, hæc Scripturæ dicta Θεοπέπνως esse intelligenda, & Metaphoricè explicanda per similitudinem effectuum; quin tamen superstruantur fundamento erronearum vulgi opinionum exinde non evincitur, cum susè à nobis ostensa sint talium locutionum fundamenta. Non ergò debent dici mendacia, at & concedendum erroribus inniti; nec tamen ideo Spiritus sanctus errores confirmat, nec suos facit, sed tantum non refutat & ad illos sese accommodat, cum non sint damnosi. Quamvis autem peccarint Audiani & Anthropomorphitæ, Deum ut corporeum concipiendo, & minus recte fiat, si Deus ita concipiatur, quotusquisque tamen est, qui non nescio quid extensi in conceptu Dei implicet? De vulgo hoc est certum, quamvis in actu signato neget, & sciat non debere fieri, in actu tamen exercito fieri sæpissimè experientia docet. De multis etiam eruditis idem dixero, paucis, qui diuturno exercitio mentem suam assuefecerunt ad accuratos conceptus formandos, & benè distinguendum naturam substantiæ corporeæ à natu-rà substantiæ intelligentis, exceptis; quam tamen imbecillitatem Deum hominibus condonaturum confidimus. Et hæc ad secundam responsionem sufficiunt.
units.tr: DCLV. 3. It is true that these sayings of Scripture must be understood as divinely inspired [θεοπνεύστως] and explained metaphorically, through the likeness of effects. Yet it does not follow from this that they are built on the foundation of erroneous popular opinions, since we have shown at length the foundations of such expressions. Therefore they should not be called lies, and yet it must be conceded that they rest on errors. Nor for that reason does the Holy Spirit confirm errors or make them his own; he merely does not refute them and accommodates himself to them, since they are not harmful. Although the Audians and the Anthropomorphites erred in conceiving God as corporeal, and it is less correct if God is so conceived, how few are there who do not somehow implicate something extended in their concept of God? This is certain of the common people: although in explicit thought they deny it and know it should not be done, in practice experience shows that it very often happens. I would say the same of many learned people, except the few who by long exercise have accustomed their minds to form precise concepts and to distinguish well the nature of corporeal substance from the nature of intelligent substance; yet we trust that God will pardon men this weakness. These things suffice for the second reply.

units.la: DCLVI. 4. Quænam sit consequentia in nostra ratiocinatione attentus lector deprehendere potuit ex initio hujus capitis. Nec sequitur Deum ut avem concipi à vulgo, eo quod ipsi tribuantur alæ; sed vulgus celeritatem actionum concipere solet per celeritatem motus, hanc autem alarum ministerio optimè fieri solere existimat, ut multæ vulgares locutiones testantur, ex. gr. quando dicimus in linguâ Germanicâ, Er läufft so geschwindt als wann er sloge: item überhin fliegen. sic Galli à la volée, Latini avolare, advolare, & apud Poëtas multa reperies exempla, in quibus per alas & volatum designatur celeritas. Sic Ovid. in Metam. de Atalantâ Virgine: passu volat alite virgo. Inde factum est, ut Mercurio nuncio Deorum alas attribuerint. Confirmatur nostra sententia à Celeberrimo Vossio lib. 1. de Orig. Idolol. p. m. 2. Ad Angeli-cam hanc potentiam, quæ intellectus ac voluntatis est instrumentum, incredi-bilis etiam velocitas refertur. Atque ob hanc attributa iis ala. Ita Cherubim in Exodo cum aliis facta. Jesaias ait, Seraphim ad se volasse. Daniel etiam & Ezechiel advolantes conspexere. Hoc Chrysostomus homil. ὥσπερ ἀκαταλήπ-τως fieri fieri ait per συγκατάβασιν q. d. condescensionem, quia describuntur, non quales sunt natura; sed prout facilius à simplicibus CONCIPIVNTVR & intelliguntur. Et paulo post. Nempe, quomodo & ventis ad eorum velocitatem denotandam, penna tribuuntur. Unde & Deus dicitur Psalm. XVII. & CIII. volare & ambulare super pennas ventorum, ac Poëtis similiter alati fingun-tur: ut liquet ex Ovidio, Silio, Juvenale. Etiam Boreæ filii Calais & Zethus, πτερωτοὶ Apollodoro. Imò non aliâ de causâ quam in celeritatis Symbolum, quâ ventos referrent, Ælius Verus Cæsar cursoribus suis, tùm Noti, Borea, aliorum-que ventorum nomina imponebat; tum alas etiam apponebat, ut author Spartianus. Quamobrem non dubito, quin, quòd Angeli referuntur alati, id maximè pertineat ad velocitatem indicandam. Concinit Perkinsius tom. 2. p. 53 Tractatu III de Officiis & dignitatibus Ministerii, ubi ad vocem advolavit ex Ef. 6, 6 sic annotat: Phrasis ad nostrum concipiendi modum accommodata est, ut significet, quàm promte & celeriter Angelus exierit ad consolationem Prophetæ ministrandam. Sicut enim nihil sensibus nostris celerius moveri videtur, quàm creatura volans: & sicut nos dicimus, illum ad opus suum advolare, qui illud citò & diligenter exsequitur: sic hîc Spiritus sanctus agilitatem & alacritatem Angeli proponit ad consolationem huic sancto Prophetæ afferendam. Itaque & Deo alæ tribuuntur, & volatus ad velocitatem actionum ipsius denotandam, quam vulgus concipere solet per volatum, latetque etiam in citatis his Scripturæ locis locutio, quæ fundamentum habet in vulgi præjudicio.
units.tr: DCLVI. 4. An attentive reader could have grasped the logic of our reasoning from the beginning of this chapter. It does not follow that God is conceived by the common people as a bird because wings are attributed to him. Rather, the common people are accustomed to conceive the speed of actions through the speed of motion, and they think this is best achieved by means of wings, as many common expressions attest: for example, when we say in German, He runs as fast as if he flew; likewise überhin fliegen. So the French say à la volée, the Latins avolare and advolare, and among the poets you will find many examples in which speed is denoted by wings and flight. So Ovid in the Metamorphoses of the virgin Atalanta: the virgin flies on winged feet. Hence it came about that they gave wings to Mercury, the messenger of the gods. Our opinion is confirmed by the most celebrated Vossius, book 1 On the Origin of Idolatry, p. 2: To this angelic power, which is the instrument of intellect and will, an incredible speed is also ascribed, and for this reason wings are attributed to them. Thus the Cherubim in Exodus are made with wings, along with others. Isaiah says that the Seraphim flew to him. Daniel and Ezekiel also saw them flying toward them. Chrysostom, in his homily, says this is done, as it were, [ὥσπερ] by condescension [συγκατάβασιν], because they are described not as they are in nature, but as they are more easily conceived and understood by simple people. And a little later: Just as wings are attributed to the winds to denote their speed, so God is said in Psalms 17 and 103 to fly and walk upon the wings of the winds, and in the same way the poets feign winged beings, as is clear from Ovid, Silius and Juvenal. Also the sons of Boreas, Calais and Zethus, are winged [πτερωτοί] in Apollodorus. Indeed, the Caesar Aelius Verus gave his couriers the names of the winds, Notus, Boreas and the others, and also put wings on them, as the author Spartianus reports, and for no other reason than as a symbol of the speed by which they carried the winds. Therefore I do not doubt that the fact that angels are described as winged pertains chiefly to indicating their speed. Perkins agrees, in volume 2, p. 53, Treatise III, On the Offices and Dignities of the Ministry, where on the word advolavit from Ef. 6, 6 he annotates thus: The phrase is adapted to our way of conceiving, to signify how promptly and swiftly the angel went out to minister consolation to the prophet. For just as nothing seems to move more quickly to our senses than a flying creature, and just as we say that someone who carries out his work quickly and diligently flies to it, so here the Holy Spirit sets forth the agility and eagerness of the angel to bring consolation to this holy prophet. Thus wings are attributed also to God, and flight is used to denote the speed of his actions, which the common people are accustomed to conceive through flight. And in these cited passages of Scripture lies a manner of speaking which has its foundation in the prejudice of the common people.

units.la: DCLVII. Inst. ad Resp. 1. præced. art. M. pag. 61.
units.tr: DCLVII. Objection to the first reply in the preceding article, M. p. 61.

units.la: Ex eo quod perfectioribus loquendi formulis essentiam & attributa sua sublinde Deus describit, satis constat, ut sapissime cum vulgo balbutiat, non tamen cum eo errare, adeo ut ejus omniscientia, veritas, fides, in discrimen venire non possint &c. Atque hæc est generalis acceptio à multis adhibita, ut & ab H. pag. 255. cujus summa eò redit, Scripturam si alicubi loquendi modos usurpet veritatem præjudiciis involutam referentes alibi semet explicare.
units.tr: From the fact that God sometimes describes his essence and attributes in more refined forms of speech, it is quite clear that, as very often, he stammers with the common people, yet he does not err with them, so that his omniscience, truth and faithfulness cannot be brought into doubt, etc. This is the general view adopted by many, and also by H. p. 255, whose gist comes to this: if Scripture at any point uses modes of speech that express truths wrapped in prejudices, it explains itself elsewhere.

units.la: Resp. 1. Falsum esse quod dicitur, Scripturam utentem locutionibus vulgaribus, semper se explicare, vel hoc in loco vel in aliis. Nam ubi quæso docet accurate loquendo, Lunam non esse luminare majus, sed minus stellis? ubi explicat non competere fines Cœlo & Terræ? Aërem non esse inane? ut vocatur Job. xxvi, 7. Ubinam docet, cor non esse sedem intellectus, & voluntatis, quod præjudicium multis locutionibus de corde supponitur? 2. Qua quæso occasione sese explicaret? anne adhibendo alibi locutiones accuratas? at supra ostendimus, nolle immutare sermonem hominum vulgarem, qui etiam ab ipsis Philosophis & Astronomis, quamvis causam errorum cognoscentibus, non est immutatus: an differendo ex professo & philosophicè, ut faciunt philosophi, retinendo quidem formulas vulgares, sed causas errorum detegendo, & veras in medium proferendo? at sic munus Philosophi arriperet, quod nec facere vult, nec commode, propter scopum alienum à philosophia, facere posset, rem alienam à suo munere existimans. 3. Sed si absolute illicitum esset loqui cum vulgo, sive uti sermone vulgari etiam praejudiciis innitente, illud per subsequentem explicationem licitum fieri non posset, quemadmodum Mendacium, quod ex hac sententia fluere putat adversarius, per subsequentem explicationem licitum non redditur. 4. Locutionum de Moralibus, in quibus concedunt adversarii, scripturam loqui secundum id quod homo praesumit, ut & locutionum de Attributis divinis alia plane est ratio: de his agere ex professo, (eo sensu, quo de naturalibus in scriptura tractari nego) scripturae est propositum, suntque fori scripturae, de naturalibus non item: illorum cognitio saepe aliunde quam ex scriptura haberi non potest, naturalium potest: errores circa illa saepe sunt noxii in Theologia, circa haec innoxii.
units.tr: Reply 1. It is false that Scripture, when it uses common expressions, always explains itself, either in this place or in others. For where, I ask, does it teach with precision that the Moon is not a greater light but a lesser one than the stars? Where does it explain that the boundaries do not belong to Heaven and Earth? That the air is not empty, as it is called in Job 26:7? Where does it teach that the heart is not the seat of the understanding and the will, a prejudice presupposed in many expressions about the heart? 2. On what occasion, I ask, would it explain itself? By using precise expressions elsewhere? But above we have shown that it is unwilling to change the common speech of men, which was not changed even by the philosophers and astronomers themselves, although they knew the cause of the errors. Or by treating the matter expressly and philosophically, as philosophers do, retaining the common formulas but uncovering the causes of the errors and bringing the true ones into the open? But in that case it would be taking over the office of the philosopher, which it neither wishes to do nor could fittingly do, since its aim is foreign to philosophy, and it would regard the matter as lying outside its own office. 3. But even if it were absolutely unlawful to speak with the common people, or to use common speech resting on prejudices, that could not be made lawful by a later explanation, just as a lie, which our opponent thinks follows from this view, is not made lawful by a later explanation. 4. The case of expressions about moral matters, where our opponents concede that Scripture speaks according to what man supposes, is clearly different, and so is the case of expressions about the divine attributes. To treat these matters expressly (in the sense in which I deny that natural things are treated in Scripture) is Scripture's purpose, and they belong to Scripture's domain; natural things do not. Knowledge of the former often cannot be had from any source other than Scripture, while knowledge of natural things can be. Errors about the former are often harmful in theology; about the latter they are harmless.

units.la: DCLVIII. Hanc exceptionem magis urgere videtur B. p. 30. dum sic inquit.
units.tr: DCLVIII. This objection seems to be pressed more strongly by B., p. 30, where he says as follows.

units.la: Qui phrasi, quae opinio erronea exprimitur, & quae conceptus hominum per se ad opinionem erroneam ducit, continuo utitur, nec unquam, quomodo eam intelligat, vel intelligi velit, exponit, revera illam locutionem approbat, licet illam recte intelligat, ut si quis inter Turcas degens Mahometem semper vocaret Prophetam Dei, nec unquam indicaret, quo sensu id diceret, ille phrasin & doctrinam per eam expressam revera suam faceret. Qui phrasi vulgari utitur, eam sensu vulgari usurpare praesumitur, nisi mentem suam aperiat, quod ni faciat, hypocritam agit, illudit, decipit & omnibus sese in eadem cum vulgo esse sententia fidem ingenerat.
units.tr: He who continually uses a phrase by which an erroneous opinion is expressed, and which of itself leads men's concepts to that erroneous opinion, and never explains how he understands it or wishes it to be understood, in truth approves that expression, even though he understands it rightly. For example, if someone living among the Turks were always to call Mahomet the Prophet of God, and never indicate in what sense he said it, he would in truth make the phrase and the doctrine expressed through it his own. Whoever uses a common phrase is presumed to employ it in its common sense, unless he makes his meaning plain; and if he does not, he acts the hypocrite, deceives and cheats, and by letting everyone think he is of the same opinion as the common people, he creates belief in that agreement.

units.la: Resp. Munus istarum phrasium, sive formularum (quibus Scripturam uti defendo) duplex est, & distinctum: vel enim significant tantum aliquam generalem veritatem, vel etiam consignificant aliquid speciale, sive illud verum sive erroneum fuerit, quod ex reipsa est judicandum. Ita quando dicit, Jon. III, 4. quod inceperit progredi Jonas in urbe itinere unius diei, significatur haec generalis veritas, quod intra urbem circumiens variis in locis urbis fuerit concionatus, non quòd longitudo urbis tanta fuerit, ut ad eam transeundam itinere unius diei fuerit opus, quod propterea ex verbis Jonae non potest elici. Sic hujus phrasis, Sol ambulat ab extremitate ad extremitatem, duplex est munus, sed distinctum & diversum atque separatum; in genere significat noctis & diei vicissitudinem, sed dein consignificat causam huius vicissitudinis motum Solis realem; verum non ubique & apud omnes ista phrasi utentes utrumque hoc munus obtinet. A doctis & rem intelligentibus si adhibeatur, significat tantum generalem aliquam veritatem. Ita dum a sapientibus & rationem motus corporum caelestium intelligentibus, dicitur, Solem oriri ab una extremitate calorum & occidere in altera, nihil aliud ab iis significatur, quam vicissitudo diei ac noctis, die initium faciente ab aurora, nocte vero initium faciente a vespera. Atque ad eundem modum Scriptura his phrasibus usa, nihil quoque aliud, quam vicissitudinem diei ac noctis per eas significat. Indocti & rerum ignari ea utentes, etiam consignificant errorem phrasi dictae, nempe causam falsam huius effectus, motum Solis realem. Quod si velis cognoscere, quid quis significet per tales phrases, semper quidem certum est, & manifestum, quod quivis generalem illam veritatem significet, sed an praeterea errorem consignificet ex persona utentis & circumstantiis sermonis est cognoscendum. Quod si ergo ex circumstantiis sermonis non appareat, phrasi dicta consignificari Solis motum realem, & constet aliunde, hanc sententiam esse praejudicium, censendum est, illud a Spiritu sancto non consignificari, sed istam phrasin praejudicio inniti. Alia plane est ratio istius phraseos, si quis Mahometem vocaret Prophetam Dei; quoniam 1. illa phrasis tantum hoc nec aliud praeterea inter Turcas significat, nempe Mahometem a Deo missum esse, & inspirationem seu revelationem habere divinam; non ergo posset quis sine hypocrisi ista phrasi uti, si non illud praecise significaret, vel non satis indicet, aut explicet, quod ironice tantum, & ex sensu Turcarum istam phrasin usurparet. Itaque 2. si quis Mahumetem vocat Prophetam, neque tamen semel explicet, alterutrum ex his erit dicendum, vel ex animi sententia significare, eum esse missum a Deo &c. vel agere hypocritam, cum tertium non detur. At si quis dicat, Solem ambulare ab extremitate ad extremitatem non necessario erit dicendum, eum, vel ex animi sententia Soli motum realem tribuere, vel hypocritam agere, quoniam tertium datur, nempe significare tantum generalem aliquam veritatem, quae est vicissitudinem dierum vel noctium a variatione situs Solis ortum habere, non vero etiam consignificare errorem.
units.tr: Reply: These phrases, or formulas (which I maintain Scripture uses), have a twofold and distinct function. They either signify only some general truth, or they also co-signify something specific, whether that specific thing is true or false, which must be judged from the matter itself. So when Jonah 3:4 says that Jonah began to go through the city a journey of one day, the general truth signified is that he preached while going around the city and in various places within it. It does not mean that the city was so large that crossing it would take a day's journey, which therefore cannot be inferred from Jonah's words. Likewise this phrase, the sun walks from one end to the other, has a twofold function, but one that is distinct, different and separate. In general it signifies the alternation of night and day, but it also co-signifies the real motion of the sun as the cause of this alternation. However, this function is not always, and not for everyone who uses the phrase, present in both respects. When it is used by learned people who understand the matter, it signifies only some general truth. So when wise people who understand the motion of the heavenly bodies say that the sun rises at one end of the heavens and sets at the other, they signify nothing more than the alternation of day and night, the day beginning at dawn and the night beginning at evening. In the same way, Scripture, when it uses these phrases, signifies through them nothing more than the alternation of day and night. Ignorant people, and those unfamiliar with the facts, who use them also co-signify an error in the phrase itself, namely the false cause of this effect, the real motion of the sun. If you want to know what someone signifies by such phrases, it is always certain and plain that he signifies that general truth. But whether he also co-signifies an error must be known from the character of the speaker and the circumstances of the discourse. If, then, the circumstances of the discourse do not show that the real motion of the sun is co-signified by the phrase, and it is established from elsewhere that this view is a prejudice, it must be judged that the Holy Spirit does not co-signify it, but that the phrase rests on a prejudice. The case of the phrase is entirely different if someone called Mahomet the Prophet of God. For (1) that phrase, among the Turks, signifies only this and nothing else, namely that Mahomet was sent by God and has divine inspiration or revelation. One therefore could not use that phrase without hypocrisy if he did not mean exactly that, or did not sufficiently indicate or explain that he used it only ironically and in the sense of the Turks. Thus (2) if someone calls Mahomet a prophet and yet does not explain himself even once, one of two things must be said: either he signifies from his real conviction that Mahomet was sent by God, or he is acting the hypocrite, since there is no third option. But if someone says that the sun walks from one end to the other, it need not be said that he either attributes real motion to the sun from his conviction or is acting the hypocrite, since a third option exists: he signifies only some general truth, namely that the alternation of days or nights arises from the changing position of the sun, and does not also co-signify an error.

units.la: DCLIX. Inst. 1. ad resp. quartam (nam ad reliqua jam saepe respon- sum est, & porro respondebitur.) M. p. 64.
units.tr: DCLIX. Inst. 1. To the fourth reply (for the rest has already often been answered, and will be answered further.) M. p. 64.

units.la: Ex nostra sententia sequi maxime, Deum ut avem concipi a vulgo, quod pateat hunc syllogismum consideranti deranti. derunt. Quodcunque repræsentatur locutionibus anthropopathicis id secundum vos est vel debet esse præjudicium vulgi: At repræsentatur Psf. XVII, 8. Psf. XCI, 4. Deus alatus. Ergo Deum alatum sive avem esse, est præjudicium vulgi. 2. In locis citatis, alas non significare actionis celeritatem, vel levissime textus inspicienti apparere potuisset.
units.tr: It follows, above all, from our opinion that God is conceived by the common people as a bird, as anyone considering this syllogism will see. Whatever is represented in anthropopathic expressions is, according to you, or ought to be, a prejudice of the common people. But God is represented as winged (Ps. 17:8; Ps. 91:4). Therefore, that God is winged, or is a bird, is a prejudice of the common people. 2. In the passages cited, wings do not signify the speed of an action; this could have been seen by anyone who looked even lightly at the text.

units.la: Resp. Diximus supra: locutiones anthropopathicas inniti alicui præjudicio infantiæ & sensuum, atque ostendimus, etiam hanc locutionem, qua Deo alæ tribuuntur, diciturque volare supra alas ventorum, celeritatem ejus actionum designare, idque sufficienter probavimus; sed syllogismi ab adversario adducti Major non est nostra. 2. Neque diximus, semper per alas designari celeritatem actionum, verum tum demum, cum alæ tribuuntur cum respectu ad volandum: At Psal. 17, & 91. alæ tribuuntur Deo ad designandam metaphorice protectionem & defensionem ab ipso exhibitam.
units.tr: Reply: We said above that anthropopathic expressions rest on some prejudice of infancy and of the senses, and we showed that this expression also, by which wings are attributed to God and it is said that he flies upon the wings of the winds, designates the speed of his actions; and we have proved this sufficiently. But the major premise of the syllogism brought forward by the adversary is not ours. 2. Nor have we said that wings always designate the speed of actions, but only then, when wings are attributed with reference to flying. But in Psalms 17 and 91 wings are attributed to God to designate metaphorically the protection and defence exhibited by him.

units.la: DCLX. Inst. 2. H. p. 171. Psf. 139, 17. dicitur, si sumpsero pennas diluculi &c. illic tenebit me dextra tua, quaero an ibi homo ut avis a vulgo concipiatur.
units.tr: DCLX. Inst. 2. H. p. 171. Ps. 139:9, 10. It is said: "If I take the wings of the morning... there shall your hand lead me." I ask whether there man is conceived by the common people as a bird.

units.la: Resp. Dicit David, etiamsi haberet pennas & volaret, hoc est, etiamsi celerrime se moveret, se tamen non posse manum Dei effugere; quid vero absurdi, si dicamus: illam locutionem etiam, prout de Davide usurpatur, habere ortum ex præjudicio, quo celeritas motus solet concipi per ministerium alarum?
units.tr: Reply: David says that even if he had wings and flew, that is, even if he moved most swiftly, he still could not escape the hand of God. What absurdity is there, then, if we say that this expression, even as it is used of David, arises from a prejudice by which speed of motion is commonly conceived through the agency of wings?

units.la: CAPUT XXX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXX.

units.la: Sextum Argumentum ab usu versionis LXX Interpretum in N. T. proponitur ac defenditur.
units.tr: The sixth argument, from the use of the Septuagint version in the New Testament, is set forth and defended.

units.la: DCLXI. Sextum Argumentum nobis inde suppeditatur, quod Apostoli in V. T. usi fuerint versione Græca V. T. quæ vulgo dicitur LXX Interpretum, non adeo pura, sed multis in locis erronea; non tantum iis in locis, ubi correspondet fonti Hebræo, sed etiam ubi ab eo discessit, atque ita in errore est, quod illa tum temporis inter Judæos fuerit recepta. Docet hoc Rivetus, Isagoges ad scripturam sacram p. 137. quæ verba, quia multum faciunt ad controversiæ nostræ elucidationem, adscribere non pigebit. Negari non debet, inquit, versionem illam tunc apud Græcos communem Apostolos & Evangelistas Græce scribentes sape usurpasse. usurpasse, aliquando etiam citasse, Ubi Discrepantia quaedam à Textu Hebraeo manifestissima est, quia Apostoli & Apostolici viri, in ponendis testimoniis de V. T. non semper verba consideraverunt, sed sensum, nec eadem sermonum calcarunt vestigia, dummodo à sententiis non recederent, ut loquitur Hieron. Comment. in Amos. Hanc ergo interpretationem secuti sunt, in iis solum rebus, quae nihil per se de veritate fidei derogabant, praesertim cum discessionem à recepta inter Hellenistas editione periculosam & sine fructu Ecclesiae futuram animadverterent. Exemplo potest esse Luc. 3, 36. in Christi Genealogia, nomen Kainan secundo adductum, quod in Hebraea editione non est, sed in editione, qua Hellenista utebantur. Existimant enim viri docti, visum fuisse Sp. S. cum historia Euangelii Graece traderetur, ad gentes manatura (quae narrationem hanc Lucae cum Editione Graeca fuerant comparatura) illud errori jam recepto condonare, quamvis PRAETER VERITATEM; quia res sine fructu, & cum gravissimo offensionis periculo, fuisset conjuncta, si Lucas veritatem historiae secutus praecise hoc argumentum vulgo ad charitatem publicam & unitatem Ecclesiae labefactandam suppeditasset. Extitissent enim Multi, qui hac una occasione minime necessaria cum ofsensi fuissent ipsi, tum graves Tragaedias adversus Ecclesiam & Euangelium Lucae excitassent. Quae res omnibus Christianis exemplo est, ut charitati donare discant, quicquid sine detrimento fidei condonari vident oportere, donec res ex veritate emendari possit. Neque enim putandum est, Lucam adversari historiae veritati, sed tantum publico Errori, qui tum altius radicatus erat, aliquid indulgere ad tempus, & per provisionem (ut dicitur) donec commodior esset Ecclesia de ea re instituenda sine damno graviori locum. Et quamvis de illa voce Kainan aliam foveat sententiam, nostram tamen sententiam disertissimis verbis asserit.
units.tr: DCLXI. The sixth argument is supplied to us by the fact that the Apostles, in quoting the Old Testament, used the Greek version of the Old Testament commonly called that of the Seventy Interpreters. This version is not altogether pure but is erroneous in many places: not only where it agrees with the Hebrew source, but also where it departs from it, and so is in error, because it was then received among the Jews. Rivet teaches this in his Isagoge ad scripturam sacram, p. 137. Since his words contribute much to clarifying our controversy, I will not hesitate to quote them. It must not be denied, he says, that the Apostles and Evangelists, writing in Greek, often used that version, which was then common among the Greeks, and sometimes even cited it, where some discrepancy from the Hebrew text is very plain, because the Apostles and apostolic men, in setting down testimonies from the Old Testament, did not always weigh the words but the sense, and did not follow the very footsteps of the language, provided they did not depart from the meanings, as Jerome says in his commentary on Amos. They therefore followed this translation only in those matters which in themselves took nothing away from the truth of the faith, especially since they noticed that a departure from the edition received among the Hellenists would be dangerous and of no benefit to the Church. An example can be Luke 3:36, in Christ's genealogy, where the name Kainan is given a second time, which is not in the Hebrew edition but is in the edition the Hellenists used. For learned men think that the Holy Spirit, when the history of the Gospel was to be delivered in Greek for the nations (who were going to compare this narrative of Luke with the Greek edition), saw fit to overlook that error, already accepted, though it was CONTRARY TO THE TRUTH; because the matter would have been bound up with no benefit and with the gravest danger of offence, had Luke, following the truth of the history, supplied this point, which was commonly held, for overturning public charity and the unity of the Church. For many would have arisen who, offended on this one unnecessary occasion, would themselves have stirred up serious tragedies against the Church and the Gospel of Luke. This matter is an example to all Christians, that they learn to overlook for the sake of charity whatever they see can be overlooked without loss to the faith, until the matter can be corrected in accordance with the truth. For we should not think that Luke was opposed to the truth of history, but only that for a time he indulged the public error, which was then more deeply rooted, and did so by providence (as it is called), until the Church could be better placed to set the matter right without greater harm. And although he holds a different view about the word Kainan, he nonetheless asserts our view in the plainest words.

units.la: DCLXII. Vossius etiam consentit, qui in Disputationibus selectis p. 60. ad locum Luc. 3, 36.
units.tr: DCLXII. Vossius also agrees, who in his Disputationes selectae, p. 60, on Luke 3:36, says:

units.la: Dicendum Kainan citari ex versione Hellenistica, Et paulo post: Cur errorem 70 Interpretum suum fecit Lucas? siquidem error fit, saltem suum non fecit, cum citat integrum illum contextum: citando enim nec improbat, nec approbat Versionis παροιμίας, nec ἀκεισθαι ejus ex professo ad examen revocavit, ne homines versioni illi & secundum eam genealogiam assuetos turbaret. Suffecit illi ad probationem Genealogiae Christi loca Biblica citasse ex versione vulgata maxime omnium nota & recepta, imprimis à Alexandrina illa Judaica Alexandrina, quā qua cum usum fuisse, teste est Scaliger in notis ad N. T. Porrò versionem illam a scriptoribus N. T. suo loco relictam, at ex ea omnia fere loca de verbo ad verbum citata (Quamvis saepe tam docte aut accurate Veritatem Hebraicam non exprimeret) nimis notum est. Institutio & scopo illorum hoc sufficiebat: Hactenus ille.
units.tr: Kainan must be said to be cited from the Hellenistic version. And a little later: Why did Luke make the Seventy's error his own? If it is an error, at least he did not make it his own, since he cites the whole context: in citing it he neither disapproves nor approves of the version's proverbs [?], nor did he call its accuracy into question on purpose, lest he disturb people accustomed to that version and to the genealogy according to it. It was enough for him, to prove Christ's genealogy, to cite Biblical passages from the version most widely known and received of all, above all from that Alexandrian Jewish version, which, as Scaliger testifies in his notes on the New Testament, was in use. Moreover, that the writers of the New Testament left that version in its place, and cited almost all the passages from it word for word (although it often did not express the Hebrew truth so learnedly or accurately), is too well known. For their purpose and aim this was sufficient. So far he.

units.la: DCLXIII. Concordat Junius tum in genere, tum respectu vocis Kainan, quae verba digna sunt ut transcribantur.
units.tr: DCLXIII. Junius agrees, both in general and with respect to the word Kainan, and his words are worth transcribing.

units.la: Post rejectas duas solutiones: Restat, inquit, solutio tertia, fuisse Kainanis vocem à Luca additam, sed ex Interpretum Graecorum fide, quam solutionem his verbis expositi Beda. Nomen & generatio Kainan juxta Hebraicam veritatem neque in Genesi, neque in verbis aliorum invenitur, sed Arphaxad Selaa vel Sale filium nullo interposito genuisse perhibetur. Scito ergo Lucam hanc generationem de septuaginta interpretum Editione sumpsisse, ubi scriptum est, quod Arphaxad centum triginta quinque annorum genuerit Kainan &c. Tanquam si diceret, Lucam id officii cum Graecorum interpretationi, tum recepta in vulgus opinioni tribuisse, prout multa in Scripturis δοξαστικῶς sunt enunciata, & accommodata opinioni vulgi: NB. Neque intempestivo certamine de causa alicujus nominis voluisse committere, ut Ecclesiae pax, aut piarum mentium quies in discrimen vocaretur; nutaret eorum fides, vel periclitaretur Scriptura auctoritas. Hujus itaque responsi NB. religionem probo & solutionis primae veritatem. Sed quia summa Patrum, Interpretum Arabu & Syri omniumque fere exemplarium consensione comparet Cainanis nomen, nos solutioni postremae NB facile acquiescimus, &c. Sed & pag. seq. occurrit Objectionibus contra hanc sententiam, quae homogeneae sunt iis, quibus contra me adversarii utuntur: Hic vero, inquit, non sumus nescii, obstrepere nonnullos veritatis hostes, & de auctoritate ipsius Luca, atque Euangelii ab eo scripti, hoc argumento fidem detrahere. Falsum est, inquiunt, illud, & falso adhibetur Kainanis nomen. Respondemus, etsi re falsum fuisse dabimus, tamen fuisse opinabile, imo in opinione fuisse Vulgi, ad quam opinionem in vulgo receptissimam respexit Lucas, NB. ut ex verbis ipsius modo ostendimus. Opinioni autem falsae jamdiu auctores fuerant septuaginta illi, Lucas vero bona fide exemplum illorum opinionemque vulgi, & certo consilio secutus est. In illis ergo, ac non in Luca desideratur fides. At Lucas, inquient, falsum esse scivit. Scivit quidem illud, sed hoc ejusmodi esse scivit, quod rei tantum unius historicae, non autem fidei Catholicae veritatem offenderet. Nam Kainane interposito veritatis quidem historicae aliquid additur, sed nihil fidei adimitur; cujus certitudo unius aut alterius historiae, sermonis aut vocis errore NB. minime convellitur, nisi contra fidei Christiana fundamentum, aut articulos ejus (ut vocant) fundamentales veniat. Hoc itaque non est μνημονικὸν ἁμαρτημα, sed συγγνώμης ἀνα-μάρτητου, id est modesta confessio peccato vacans, quo genere sermonum Scriptura non raro utitur. Quid ergo? Nonne Lucas hoc modo errorem confirmaverit? NB minime omnium. Nam & publicus error a privato differt, & inveteratus a recente novoque. Lucas autem errorem neque publicum ex privato facit, neque nascentem aluit, sed publicum errorem jamdiu inveteratum pertulit, quia auctore Spiritu Dei, ex duobus malis vidit eligendum minus, quod vulgo dici solet. Malum quidem fuit illud, quod septuaginta ausi sunt a veritate historia discedere, quocunque tandem studio, & consilio fecerint, ac proinde eorum factum falsum invaluit in sacra historia. Sed cum ille error historicus per se fidei non afferat damnum, gravius malum eventurum esse vidit, si illud inveteratum atque apud omnes receptum tentaret intempestive eximere, &c.
units.tr: After rejecting two solutions, he says: There remains a third solution: that the word Kainan was added by Luke, but in faithfulness to the Greek translators, as Bede expounds the matter in these words. The name and generation of Kainan are found neither in Genesis nor in the words of others according to the Hebrew truth, but Arphaxad is said to have begotten Shelah, or Salah, with no one interposed. Know, then, that Luke took this genealogy from the edition of the Septuagint, where it is written that Arphaxad, at the age of 135, begot Kainan, and so on. As if he were saying that Luke gave this service both to the Greek interpretation and to the opinion received among the common people, as many things in the Scriptures are stated according to opinion and adapted to the opinion of the people. NB. Nor did he wish to bring into peril, by an ill-timed dispute over the cause of a name, the peace of the Church or the quiet of pious minds; their faith would waver, or the authority of Scripture would be endangered. Therefore I approve the reverence of this answer, NB, and the truth of the first solution. But since the consensus of the Fathers, the Arabic and Syriac interpreters, and nearly all the copies, favours the name Kainan, we easily assent to the last solution, NB, etc. But on the following page there also occurs an objection against this view, which is of the same kind as those which my opponents use against me: Here, he says, we are not unaware that some enemies of the truth clamour, and detract from the authority of Luke himself and of the Gospel written by him, by this argument. That is false, they say, and the name Kainan is wrongly introduced. We reply: even if we grant that it is false in fact, it was still something held as opinion, indeed the opinion of the common people, to which the most widely received opinion Luke looked, NB, as we have just shown from his own words. Those seventy men had long been the authors of that opinion, but Luke followed their example and the common opinion in good faith and with a deliberate purpose. The fault therefore lies with them, and not with Luke. But Luke, they will say, knew it to be false. He indeed knew it, but he knew it to be of such a kind that it touched only the truth of one historical matter, and not the Catholic truth of the faith. For by inserting Kainan something is added to historical truth, but nothing is taken away from the faith; its certainty is in no way shaken by an error of one or another history, word, or term NB. unless it attacks the foundation of the Christian faith, or its so-called fundamental articles. This, then, is not a memory-slip [μνημονικὸν ἁμαρτημα] but a pardonable fault, free of sin [συγγνώμης ἀναμαρτήτου], that is, a modest confession free of sin, a kind of speech Scripture not infrequently uses. What then? Has Luke not in this way confirmed the error? NB by no means. For a public error differs from a private one, and an ancient one from a recent, newly arisen one. Luke does not make a public error out of a private one, nor does he nourish one just beginning, but he endured a public error long since rooted, because, under the guidance of the Spirit of God, he saw that of two evils the lesser must be chosen, as is commonly said. The evil indeed was that the Seventy dared to depart from the truth of history, whatever zeal or purpose they had, and so their false act prevailed in the sacred history. But since that historical error does not in itself bring any harm to the faith, he saw that a greater evil would follow if he ill-timedly tried to remove what was ancient and received by all, etc.

units.la: DCLXIV. Adjungo testimonium Calvini, qui simpliciter docet; Scriptores N. T. usos esse versione LXX etiam in iis, in quibus a fonte Hebraeo recessit.
units.tr: DCLXIV. I add the testimony of Calvin, who plainly teaches that the writers of the New Testament used the Septuagint version even where it departs from the Hebrew source.

units.la: Sic enim ille ad Heb. xi. 21. annotat: Non dubium est, quin Moses de lectuli capite loquitur, cum dicit על ראש המטה Graeci autem, quasi scriptum esset Matthcb transtulerunt, caput virga, quod vulgo receptum erat, Apostolus non dubitat suo instituto accommodare. Judaeis quidem scribebat, sed qui in varias regiones dispersi, patriam linguam Graeca commutaverant. Scimus autem Apostolos hac in parte non fuisse adeo scrupulosos, quia se rudibus attemperarent, quibus adhuc lacte erat opus, & in ea re nihil est periculi, modo semper revocentur lectores ad sinceram nativamque Scriptura lectionem. Item Heb x. 5. Apostolus Graecos secutus dixit, Corpus aptasti. Neque in verbis recitandis adeo religiosi fuerunt. Drusius in eadem plane est sententia in Parallelis p. 6. ubi sic inquit: Apostoli & Evangelistae quandoque editionem Graecam LXX. referunt, etiam quando satis oscitanter Ebraea converterunt. Causa hujus, ut credibile est, quod editio illa in omnium manibus tum versaretur, vulgoque lecta in Synagogis, usuque recepta esset. Spanhemius Dub. Euangelicorum Parte III. p. 48. & 49. haec habet de LXX. Interpretibus: Evangelistae secutos versionem LXX. in plerisque, quae & maxima auctoritatu erat apud Hellenistas, & multis pro manibus, quando id fieri poterat salva dictorum Propheticorum substantia, tum ut libertatem suam ostenderent, tum ne in re levi & adiaphora malis cavillorum, infirmis scandali ullam occasionem praberent. Coccejus in Habac. I. 5. Apparet, tempore Apostolorum in frequenti usu fuisse versionem illam, quae dicitur LXX. Interpretum, sive Paulus sic Grace locutus fuerit in Synagogâ Græcanicâ Antiochiæ Pisidiæ, sive Lucas ita retulerit. Et quanquam verba Græca exacte Hebræis non conveniant, causa tamen non fuit, quare versionis usitatæ verbis abstineret: quia quam culpam in genere indicat Græca vox καταφρονητὴ, eam in specie Hebraum designat.
units.tr: For on Heb. 11:21 he remarks: There is no doubt that Moses is speaking of the head of the bed when he says upon the head of the bed [על ראש המטה]. The Greeks, however, as if the text had been written matteh, translated "the head of the staff," which was commonly accepted, and the Apostle does not hesitate to adapt it to his purpose. He was writing indeed to Jews, but to Jews who had been scattered into various regions and had exchanged their native tongue for Greek. We know, moreover, that the Apostles were not so scrupulous in this matter, since they accommodated themselves to rude hearers who still needed milk, and in such a matter there is no danger, provided that readers are always brought back to the pure and native reading of Scripture. Likewise on Heb. 10:5: The Apostle, following the Greeks, said, "a body you have prepared." Nor were they so scrupulous in quoting words. Drusius is quite of the same opinion in his Parallels, p. 6, where he says: The Apostles and Evangelists sometimes cite the Greek edition of the Seventy, even when they have rendered the Hebrew rather carelessly. The reason for this, it is credible, is that this edition was then in everyone's hands, was read commonly in the synagogues, and was in general use. Spanheim, in Dubia Evangelica, Part III, pp. 48 and 49, says this about the Seventy translators: The Evangelists, in most places, followed the version of the Seventy, which was of the greatest authority among the Hellenists and was at hand for many, whenever this could be done without harm to the substance of the prophetic words; partly to show their own freedom, and partly so that, in a slight matter of indifference, they might give the weak no occasion of scandal from the malice of the scoffers. Coccejus, on Habakkuk 1:5: It appears that in the time of the Apostles that version which is called the version of the Seventy Interpreters was in frequent use, whether Paul spoke thus in Greek in the Greek synagogue at Antioch of Pisidia, or Luke so reported it. And although the Greek words do not agree exactly with the Hebrew, there was no reason for him to refrain from the words of the customary version, because the fault which the Greek word καταφρονητής indicates in general, the Hebrew designates in particular.

units.la: DCLXV. Consentiunt Lutherani quoque Theologi. Flacius Illyricus Clavi Scripturæ II. Parte p. 204. Observandum est, ἐᾶ apostolos in LXX. versione citandâ non immerito aliquid dedisse in beneficium Christianorum & communi consuetudini, quod non aliter aliquoties dicta Scriptura citaverint, quàm sicut jam dudum apud vulgus ex illa versione innotuerant. Sic enim illi pusillu Christi lac præbentes ad eorum captum se accommodantes loqui non sunt dedignati. Sequatur Helvicus: Neque soliciteþ inquit, laborandum est, quomodo Scriptores N. T. cum Hebræo conveniant, quia ex Græca versione tum temporu usitatissima allegabant: Neque quomodo Græca cum Hebræo conveniant; certum enim est, sæpe illos ab Hebræa veritate discessisse, cujus rei plerumque causa est tam defectus punctorum, quibus illi destituti aliter legerunt, quam authentica exemplaria requirebant: tunc deceptio in literis, quando unam pro alia legerent. Ex eodem ordine est Frantzius in tract. de Interp. script. part. I. p. 38 Omnino apparet ex collatione locorum N. T. versionem LXX. temporibus Apostolorum fuisse in manibus Judæorum & Gentium & tritiorem familiarioremque, quam fontes Hebræos. Et quia Apostoli citare tunc temporis non ex fontibus Hebræis, sed ex versione Græca LXX. sententias & alia voluerunt suis de causis, idcirco quandoque retinent versionem LXX, ut eam reperant non correctam. Noluerunt ex leviorībus suspicionem quamcunque apud infirmos movere. Item Glassius Phil. sacræ p. 173. Ex Græca LXX. Interpretum versione sæpe allegationes in N. T. fieri, has autem à textu Hebræo discedere certum est. Ex his observatis tale nobis exsurgit Argumentum: Si Apostoli citra læsionem auctoritatis & veritatis Scripturæ V. T. potuerunt uti versione LXX. vulgo receptâ, etiam in iis, in quibus cum textu Hebræo non conveniebat: Ergo scriptores sacri citra læsionem īstius veritatis & auctoritatis etiam potuerunt usurpare formulas receptas de rebus naturalibus phænomenis convenientes, etiamsi opinionibus erroneis & præjudiciis inniterentur; atqui verum est prius ex dictis & consensu Theologorum: Ergò & posterius.
units.tr: DCLXV. The Lutheran theologians also agree. Flacius Illyricus, Clavis Scripturae, Part II, p. 204: It must be observed that the Apostles, in citing the version of the Seventy, not undeservedly granted something for the benefit of Christians and for common usage, since they quoted the Scripture on several occasions in no other way than as it had long been known among the people from that version. For thus, feeding the little ones of Christ with milk, they did not disdain to speak in a manner adapted to their capacity. Let Helvicus follow: Nor, he says, must we labour anxiously over how the writers of the New Testament agree with the Hebrew, since they cited the Greek version, which was then most in use; nor over how the Greek agrees with the Hebrew. For it is certain that they often departed from the Hebrew truth, the chief cause of which is the lack of vowel points, by which they, lacking them, read otherwise than the authentic copies required; then the error lay in letters, when they read one for another. In the same vein is Frantzius, in his treatise on the interpretation of Scripture, Part I, p. 38: It clearly appears from a comparison of New Testament passages that in the times of the Apostles the version of the Seventy was in the hands of Jews and Gentiles, and was more common and more familiar than the Hebrew sources. And since the Apostles at that time wished, for their own reasons, to cite sentences and other matters from the Greek version of the Seventy rather than from the Hebrew sources, therefore they sometimes keep the version of the Seventy, as they found it uncorrected. They did not wish to stir up any suspicion among the weak over trifling matters. Likewise Glassius, Philologia Sacra, p. 173: Allegations in the New Testament are often made from the Greek version of the Seventy Interpreters, and it is certain that these depart from the Hebrew text. From these observations there arises for us the following argument: If the Apostles, without any injury to the authority and truth of the Old Testament, could use the commonly received version of the Seventy even where it did not agree with the Hebrew text, then the sacred writers, without any injury to this truth and authority, could also employ received expressions about natural phenomena that agree with them, even if those expressions rest on erroneous opinions and prejudices. But the first is true, by the statements and consensus of the theologians; therefore the second is true also.

units.la: . DCLXVI. Excipit B. p. 52. Negando Majorem Propositionem.
units.tr: DCLXVI. B. objects at p. 52, denying the major premise.

units.la: Resp. Est Argumentum à majori ad minus. Qui citra læsionem Auctoritatis & Veritatis V. T. potuerunt tantum concedere errori recepto in versione LXX. Interpr. ut eam citarent ad probationem scopi sui, illi multo magis potuerunt uti ad suum scopum formulis receptis &c. Illud enim
units.tr: Reply: This is an argument from the greater to the less. Those who, without injury to the authority and truth of the Old Testament, could grant so much to an error received in the version of the Seventy Interpreters, so that they might cite it to prove their purpose, could much more readily use received expressions for their purpose, and so on. For that

units.la: cnim enim majus est, & magis videtur adversari Auctoritati Scripturæ, hoc minus & minus videtur repugnare.
units.tr: for that is the greater matter, and seems more opposed to the authority of Scripture; this is the lesser, and seems less to conflict with it.

units.la: DCLXVII. Exc. 2. B. p. 51. Aliqua ratione valeret forsitan hæc consequentia ad excusandum illum modum loquendi, sed ad eum probandum efficax esse non poterit.
units.tr: DCLXVII. Exception 2, B. p. 51. This consequence might perhaps hold for excusing that manner of speaking in some way, but it cannot be effective in proving it.

units.la: Resp. Adduxi in eum finem, ut ostenderem non repugnare istam sententiam meam Auctoritati & Veritati Scripturæ, quod hic sufficit.
units.tr: Reply: I adduced it for this purpose, to show that my view does not conflict with the authority and truth of Scripture, which is enough here.

units.la: DCLXVIII. Exc. 3. B. pag. 52. Hi citarunt versionem Græcam, ut verbα quidem discrepent ab Hebræo, sed non sensu verborum. Iste enim dissensus quamvis in translatoribus errorem verbalem notet, in citatoribus, (dummodo exprimant mentem Sp. S.) nequaquam, qui non tam ad verba, quam ad verborum sensum solent attendere.
units.tr: DCLXVIII. Exception 3, B. p. 52. They cited the Greek version so that the words indeed differ from the Hebrew, but not the sense of the words. For this disagreement, although it marks a verbal error in the translators, does not do so in the citers (provided they express the mind of the Holy Spirit), who are accustomed to attend not so much to the words as to the sense of the words.

units.la: Resp. 1. At hoc sufficit; si enim errorem Græcorum quoad verba assumpserunt, eoque sunt usi citra refutationem; Ergo similiter licuit illis uti verbis receptis, quibus phænomena exprimuntur, licet ea verba præjudiciis infantiæ & sensuum ortum suum debent. Neque enim ullibi dixi, errorem ipsum, sive præjudicium suum fecisse Sp. S. aut usurpasse sensum ejus præjudicii, sed verba adhibuisse, quibus tamen errorem noluit docere. Atque ita etiamsi in inventoribus phrasium phænomenis convenientium error sit aliquis, tamen non in Sp. S.; qui errorem eum non attendit, nec ibidem significat, sed in medio relinquit. 2. Velim verò Dn. du Bois ea quæ hic dixit conciliare cum iis, quæ scripsit in libro Belgico Oude tijdt Tijdtsthresoor appellato, pag. 80. De H. Martelaer Stephanus seght, Hand. VI.I. 1. dat Jacob in Egypten gekomen is met alle sijn geslachte bestaende in 75. zielen; daer nochtans Moses nergens van booger getal gewag maakt als van 70. Waer in die heilige man wederom spreeckt nae het gemeen gevoelen van de Joden (gelijck oock voor in een ander exempel op het 2706de Jaer van de Peri. Jul. gesien is) het welcke by haer schijnt ingekropen te zijn uyt de Grieck se oversettinge van de LXX Overzetters, die by haer seer in 't gebruyck was (gelyck die mede dickmaels in het N. T. gevolgt word) in welcke, in dit stuck, een misslag ingekropen is.
units.tr: Reply 1: This is enough. For if they took up the Greeks' error as to words, and used it without refutation, then it was likewise lawful for them to use the received words by which the phenomena are expressed, even though those words owe their origin to the prejudices of infancy and the senses. For nowhere have I said that the error itself, or their own prejudice, was made by the Holy Spirit, or that the Holy Spirit adopted the sense of that prejudice; but that they employed words, by which, however, he did not wish to teach the error. And so, even if there is some error in the inventors of expressions agreeing with phenomena, it is not in the Holy Spirit, who does not attend to that error, nor signify it there, but leaves it undecided. 2. I would indeed like Mr. du Bois to reconcile what he has said here with what he wrote in the Dutch book called Oude tijdt Tijdtsthresoor (Treasury of Old Times), p. 80: Stephen the martyr says, Acts 7:14, that Jacob came into Egypt with all his kindred, numbering seventy-five souls; yet Moses nowhere makes mention of a larger number than seventy. In this the holy man again speaks according to the common opinion of the Jews (as was seen before in another example, in the year 2706 of the Julian period), which seems to have crept in among them from the Greek translation of the Seventy Translators, which was very much in use among them (as it is also often followed in the New Testament), in which, in this point, a mistake has crept in.

units.la: DCLXIX. Exc. 4. B. p. 52. At vult Auctor noster, Deum in rebus naturalibus uti sermone, qui quoad præcipuum sensum verborum à rei veritate dissentiat.
units.tr: DCLXIX. Exception 4, B. p. 52. But our author adds that God, in natural matters, uses a manner of speech which, as to the principal sense of the words, departs from the truth of the thing.

units.la: Resp. Cùm formulæ de quibus est quæstio, & significent generalem aliquam veritatem, & ex usu vulgi errorem, quo ea est involuta, præcipuus sensus dici potius debet illa veritas generalis, quia ea & à vulgo à Spiritu Sancto utente tali phrasi significatur; error verò quia respectu vulgi ab ipso simul significatur ejus respectu minus præcipuus sensus poteft vocari; at respectu Spiritus Sancti, cùm ab illo error non significetur, nec præcipuus nec minus præcipuus ejus sensus est appellandus. Accusatio ergò adversarii à veritate aberrat.
units.tr: Answer. Since the formulas in question both signify some general truth and, through the common usage of the people, involve an error, the principal sense ought rather to be called that general truth, because the Holy Spirit, using such a phrase, signifies it both to the common people and to himself. The error, however, since it is signified by the phrase to the common people, can be called a less principal sense with respect to them. But with respect to the Holy Spirit, since the error is not signified by him, his sense should be called neither principal nor less principal. Therefore the adversary's accusation strays from the truth.

units.la: DCLXX. Exc. 5. M. p. 48. Spiritus Sanctus in N. T. interdum adducit loca V. T. convenienter translationi, quæ vocatur LXX. Interpretum, sed semper verè absque ullo errore.
units.tr: 670. Exc. 5. M. p. 48. The Holy Spirit in the New Testament sometimes cites passages of the Old Testament in agreement with the translation called that of the Seventy Interpreters, but always truly and without any error.

units.la: Resp. Sic etiam quando utitur phrasibus receptis, id enim toto libro inculco. Videantur porro ea, quæ habet p. 49. plane facientia pro mea sententia.
units.tr: Answer. So also when he uses the received phrases, for I insist on this throughout the whole book. Moreover, let what he says on p. 49 be considered, since it clearly supports my opinion.

units.la: DCLXXI. Exc. 6. M. p. 50. Dato, non concesso, Sp. S. citare LXX etiam quoad sensum ab originali textu recedentes, negamus tamen constanter, sententiam citatam eousque posse esse falsam, quousque facit ad scopum citantis. Citans enim citatum in tantum suum facit, in quantum ad scopum applicat, quoad catera, si falsum quid citationi insit, correctionem tantum suspendit.
units.tr: 671. Exc. 6. M. p. 50. Granting, though not conceding, that the Holy Spirit cites the LXX even where their sense departs from the original text, we nevertheless constantly deny that the cited sentence can be false so far as it serves the purpose of the one citing. For the one citing makes the cited words his own insofar as he applies them to his purpose. As to the rest, if something false is contained in the citation, he only suspends the correction.

units.la: Resp. At hæc denuo egregie meæ causæ serviunt; neque enim formulis ulterius utitur Sp. S. quàm quantum ad scopum suum faciunt, ut egregie ostensum à Dn. Velthusio, & sæpius à me dictum; quoad cætera, si falsum quid his formulis insit, hoc est, si inventæ & usurpatæ fuerint ad errorem significandum, Sp. S. correctionem tantum suspendit.
units.tr: Answer. But these points again serve my cause admirably. For the Holy Spirit does not use such formulas any further than they serve his purpose, as Mr. Velthusius has excellently shown and as I have often said. As to the rest, if something false is contained in these formulas, that is, if they were devised and used to signify an error, the Holy Spirit only suspends the correction.

units.la: DCLXXII. De voce Cainan novi varias esse conciliationes, neque hic meus est scopus, quæ vera sit ostendere, cum quicquid de eo sit, nihilominus generalis sententia vera maneat, hoc est, Minor mea propositio, quia non adduxi Rivetum, nisi quatenus generaliter meæ Minori testimonium præbet. Dn. Voetium non aliter etiam cito, nisi quatenus ejus verba ad Minoris meæ probationem faciunt, quid de conciliatione istorum locorum sentiat, parum hic attinet; quod enim citent Apostoli versionem Græcam, etsi Hebr. veritatem non tam rectè & accuratè exprimat, adeoque error sit in verbis, nimis quam aperte dicit.
units.tr: 672. There are various reconciliations of the word Cainan, and it is not my aim here to show which is true, since whatever be the case, my general thesis, that is, my minor proposition, remains true. I did not cite Rivet except insofar as he gives general testimony to my minor. What Mr. Voetius thinks about the reconciliation of these passages matters little here, since I cite him only insofar as his words bear on the proof of my minor. For that the Apostles cite the Greek version, even though it does not express the Hebrew truth so fully and accurately, and so there is an error in the words, he says quite openly, indeed all too openly.

units.la: DCLXXIII. Exc. M. p. 51. Non dicit Rivetus, Sp. S. usurpasse errores LXX. Interpretum, sed usurpasse aliquando Græcam versionem, etiam ubi discrepantia quaedam est à textu Hebræo manifesta.
units.tr: 673. Exc. M. p. 51. Rivet does not say that the Holy Spirit used the errors of the LXX Interpreters, but that he sometimes used the Greek version, even where some discrepancy from the Hebrew text is manifest.

units.la: Resp. Quod dicit Rivetus mihi sufficit ad Minoris meæ confirmationem, uti ex argumento meo art. 665. apparet. Sed & operæ pretium est annotare ea, quæ idem Rivetus Exercit. in Genef. 69 p. 331. tradit: Nollem atro calculo, inquit, notare eorum sententiam, qui errorem in 70. editione agnoscentes non tamen putant erasse B. Lucam, cum ex eorum codice genealogiam describit, in quâ sciebat errorem fuisse commissum, ne in re quæ fidem non tangebat displiceret novitate apud Hellenistas &c. Et paulò post: Neque tamen propterea existimandum esset, Scripturam vel Spiritum Sanctum errâsse; neque enim accusatur alibi erroris, cum Scriptura aliquando loquitur ex hominum opinione, quibus se accommodat, ubi ferri potest sine dispendio veritatis necessaria. Parum enim valent objectiones eorum, qui dicunt: Sacer scriptor non errat volens, quia illius scriba est, qui neminem decipit; neque dignum est Spir. Sanctum scribere mendacia &c. Quia neque in eo error est scriptoris, neque mendacium, sed tantum erroris alieni non periculosi tolerantia ob causas graves &c.
units.tr: Answer. What Rivet says is enough for me to confirm my minor, as appears from my argument at art. 665. But it is also worth noting what the same Rivet sets out in Exercit. in Genef. 69, p. 331: "I would not wish to mark with a black pencil the opinion of those who, acknowledging an error in the 70 edition, nevertheless do not think that St. Luke erred when he describes the genealogy from their codex, in which he knew the error had been committed, lest in a matter which did not touch the faith he should give offence by novelty among the Hellenists, etc." And a little after: "Nor should it therefore be thought that Scripture or the Holy Spirit erred. For he is nowhere accused of error, since Scripture sometimes speaks according to the opinion of men, to which it accommodates itself, where this can be borne without loss of the necessary truth. For the objections of those who say, 'The sacred writer does not err when he is willing, because he is the scribe of one who deceives no one; nor is it worthy of the Holy Spirit to write lies,' etc., carry little weight. For in this there is neither the error of the writer nor a lie, but only the tolerance of another's error, which is not dangerous, for weighty reasons, etc."

units.la: CAPUT XXXI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXI.

units.la: Consensus Theologorum cum nostra sententia ostenditur.
units.tr: The agreement of the theologians with our opinion is shown.

units.la: DCLXXIV. Nihil nunc adderemus probationibus nostris evidentissimis, nisi itidem nos accommodare vellemus ad ingenium eorum, qui auctoritatibus humanis duci solent, ac vel propterea hanc sententiam rejiciunt, quia putant eam consensui Theologorum adversari. In istorum ergo gratiam adducam auctoritates magni nominis Theologorum; ut ita videant, tum veritatem à parte nostra stare, tum etiam consensum Theologorum nobis militare. Plurimi autem jam superius ad partes sunt vocati, quos nunc congregamus. Laudati jam sunt: Chrysostomus, Calvinus, Maimonides, Rivetus, Paræus, Mercerus, Piscator, Polanus, Alstedius, Belgæ Interpretes, Marloratus, Cartwright, Junius, Musculus, Scultetus, Ursinus, Theologi Leydenses in synopsi purioris Theol. Perkinsius, qui omnes uno ore hanc, quam hactenus defendi sententiam, pronunciant. Chrysostomus: Describi angelos alatos, non quales sunt natura, sed prout facilius à simplicibus concipiantur. Calvinus: Moses non acute philosophatur, Moses populariter scripsit (intellige de Luna, quam vocat luminare magnum) illi autem (Astronomi) magno labore investigant, quicquid humani ingenii acumen assequi potest. Maimonides: Scriptura loquitur secundum linguam filiorum hominum. Rivetus: Apostoli erroris publico voluerunt aliquid indulgere ad tempus. Paræus: Luna minores sunt stellæ aliæ, non revera, sed apparenter, (respicit autem ad Genes. 1.) Mercerus: Juxta opinionem vulgi Scriptura sæpe loquitur: Piscator: Reperiuntur in Scriptura dicta ita πρὸς δόξαν: dicuntur luminaria magna respectu nostri sensus & judicii oculorum, (ad Genef. 1.) Polanus: dicuntur talia quoad δόξαν seu communem opinionem vulgi, quod de rebus loquitur, non ut sunt, sed ut videntur esse, & ad cujus captum Sp. S. in his talibus se accommodare dignatur. Alstedius:Dici quaedam in sacris literis non secundum rem, sed secundum speciem & virtutem. Belgae Interpretes: 'Dici quaedam talia secundum apparentiam coram hominibus, non secundum rei veritatem coram Deo. Marloratus: Captiva turba justi dicitur, quia justa eorum praeda existimatur. Cartwrightus: Scriptura nominat hos vel illos tales, quia pro talibus se venditant. Junius: Hebraei loquuntur populariter coeli extremitates nominando. Musculus: Appellatur Evangelium quod vere tale non est. Scultetus: Scriptura vocat aliquid tale δοξαστικῶς non ἀληθῶς. Ursinus: Vocatur aliquid tale, quia videtur, aut videri vult tale. Leydensis: Nomen Dei tribuitur falsis Diis δοξαστικῶς ex opinione & errore. Perkinsius: Scriptura saepenumero de rebus loquitur, non quemadmodum in se sunt, sed prout nobis videntur.
units.tr: DCLXXIV. We would add nothing now to our most evident proofs, unless we also wished to accommodate ourselves to the temper of those who are usually led by human authorities and reject this opinion for the very reason that they think it conflicts with the consensus of the theologians. For their sake, then, I will adduce the authorities of theologians of great name, so that they may see both that the truth stands on our side and that the consensus of the theologians fights on our behalf. Many of these have already been called to our side earlier, and we now gather them together.
