Already cited are: Chrysostom, Calvin, Maimonides, Rivet, Paraeus, Mercerus, Piscator, Polanus, Alsted, the Belgic interpreters, Marlorat, Cartwright, Junius, Musculus, Scultetus, Ursinus, the Leiden theologians in the Synopsis of Purer Theology, and Perkins, who all with one voice pronounce this opinion that I have so far defended. Chrysostom: Angels are described as winged, not as they are by nature, but as simple people can more easily conceive them. Calvin: Moses does not philosophize keenly; Moses wrote in popular fashion (understand this of the moon, which he calls the greater light), whereas the astronomers investigate with great labor whatever the acuteness of human intellect can reach. Maimonides: Scripture speaks according to the language of the sons of men. Rivet: The apostles were willing to indulge a public error for a time. Paraeus: Other stars are smaller than the moon, not in reality but in appearance (he refers to Gen. 1). Mercerus: Scripture often speaks according to the common opinion of the people. Piscator: Such expressions are found in Scripture according to appearance [πρὸς δόξαν]: the great lights are so called with respect to our sense and the judgment of our eyes (on Gen. 1). Polanus: Such things are said with respect to opinion [δόξα], or the common view of the people, about which he speaks, not as they are but as they seem to be, and to whose grasp the Holy Spirit deigns to accommodate himself in such matters. Alsted: Some things in the sacred letters are said not according to the thing itself but according to appearance and power. The Belgic interpreters: Certain such things are said according to appearance before men, not according to the truth of the thing before God. Marlorat: The captive crowd of the just is so called because their booty is judged to be just. Cartwright: Scripture names these or those as such because they pass themselves off as such. Junius: The Hebrews speak popularly when they name the extremities of heaven. Musculus: The Gospel is so called, though it is not truly such. Scultetus: Scripture calls something such doxastically [δοξαστικῶς], not truly [ἀληθῶς]. Ursinus: Something is called such because it seems to be such, or wishes to seem such. The Leiden theologians: The name of God is attributed to false gods doxastically [δοξαστικῶς], from opinion and error. Perkins: Scripture very often speaks of things not as they are in themselves, but as they appear to us.

units.la: DCLXXV. Adduco nunc aliud testimonium Parei, quod superioribus adjungo. Is Genef. 1. ad v. 1. quando disquirit, quare Moses mentionem nullam fecerit explicitam creationis Angelorum, respondet, simplicior est ratio Chrysostomi, hom. 2. in Genef. quam & Basilius attingit, hom. 1. in Hexam. Moses historiam suam ruditati Judaeorum accommodasse, erant enim homines terreni, tantum SENSIBILIA sapientes. Item Junii in Parallelo quarto: Res omnes in Scriptura ex vulgi usu duobus modis appellari solent; alia quidem ἀληθῶς ἢ πρὸς τὸ τῆς οὐσίας ἀληθεσιν, id est, prout res ipsa sunt ex veritate, sive propria sive translata sint earum nomina: alia vero εὐδοξῶς vel δοξαστικῶς id est ex opinione, sive quod ita habeantur quamvis non ita sint, sive συγχωρητικῶς quod ita haberi velint: quemadmodum idola gentium magi & gastrologi appellationem Deorum vel sapientum obtinent, cum nihil sint minus, quam quod dicuntur esse. Sed & Rivetus Exercit. in Genesin p. 595. Hic locum, inquit, habent regula in scripturarum interpretatione observanda, quarum prima est: Aliquando Scriptura se accommodat hominum opinioni. Altera, huic gemina: Aliquando res ab hominum existimatione falsa nomen assumunt. Sic sapientes in Scriptura dicuntur, quos vulgus tales judicat, licet alioqui sint insipientes ut Matth. xi. 25. Qui abscondisti haec a sapientibus &c. His Theologis adscocio Rainholdum virum eruditum, qui in Censura librorum Apocryphorum praelect. 90. p. 1103. ita inquit: Animadvertendum est, ut in Sacris Scripturis attribuuntur rerum nomina, rerum imaginibus, ita etiam in actibus verba accipi solere, non ex Veritate, sed ex opinione; ubi etiam consentientem citat Aben Efræ in Exod. xx. & paulò post: Apparet ex circumstantiis S. Scripturæ, rectè ab eo, (sc. Aben Efræ) esse observatum, non rei veritatem, sed opinionem à Scriptura esse spectatam, cum dicitur Saul intellexisse, quod esset Samuel, quia opinabatur eum esse. Cum his jungo Glassium Theologum Lutheranum, qui Rhet. sacra, p. 62. statuit esse metonymiam adjuncti, quando opinio hominum pro ipsa re ponitur, quam sic porro declarat, Res denominatio sit quandoque ab externo adjuncto opinionis hominum; alii ita: in sacris literis res sæpe nominatur & describitur uti est φαινομένως καὶ κατὰ δόξαν, non κατὰ τὸ εἶναι, καὶ ἀληθέως, seu qualis hominibus videtur esse, non qualis est, in sua natura. Exempla quædam ex ipso hausimus, & uberius declaravimus. Claudat agmen Finckius, Professor dum viveret Giessensis, qui in centuria canonum Theologicorum hunc facit quartum: In Scriptura Sacra sæpe res describitur, ut est φαινομένως & κατὰ δόξαν non κατὰ τὸ εἶναι.
units.tr: DCLXXV. I now add another testimony of Paraeus, which I join to the above. On Gen. 1 at verse 1, when he inquires why Moses made no explicit mention of the creation of the angels, he answers: The reasoning of Chrysostom in homily 2 on Genesis is simpler, and Basil also touches on it in homily 1 on the Hexaemeron. Moses accommodated his history to the crudeness of the Jews, for they were earthly men, wise only in sensible things. Likewise Junius in the fourth Parallel: All things in Scripture are commonly named in two ways according to popular usage. Some are named truly [ἀληθῶς], that is, according to the truth of the thing itself, whether their names are proper or figurative. Others are named according to opinion [εὐδοξῶς] or doxastically [δοξαστικῶς], that is, from opinion, either because they are held to be so although they are not so, or condescendingly [συγχωρητικῶς], because they wish to be held so: as the idols of the nations, magicians and gastromancers obtain the title of gods or wise men, although they are the least of what they are called. But also Rivet, in his Exercitationes in Genesin, p. 595: Here, he says, there is a rule to be observed in interpreting the Scriptures, the first of which is: Sometimes Scripture accommodates itself to the opinion of men. The second, twin to this: Sometimes things take names from human estimation that is false. Thus in Scripture those are called wise whom the crowd judges to be such, although otherwise they are foolish, as in Matt. 11:25: "Thou hast hidden these things from the wise," etc. To these theologians I add Reinhold, a learned man, who in his Censura librorum Apocryphorum, lecture 90, p. 1103, says: It must be observed that just as in the Holy Scriptures the names of things are attributed to the images of things, so also actions and words are usually to be taken not from truth but from opinion; where he also cites Aben Ezra in Exodus 20 as agreeing, and shortly after: It is evident from the circumstances of Holy Scripture that he (namely Aben Ezra) rightly observed that Scripture regards not the truth of the thing but the opinion, when it is said that Saul understood it to be Samuel, because he supposed him to be him. With these I join the Lutheran theologian Glassius, who in his Rhetorica sacra, p. 62, holds that it is a metonymy of the adjunct when the opinion of men is put for the thing itself, which he further explains thus: The naming of a thing is sometimes from an external adjunct, the opinion of men. Others say: in the sacred letters things are often named and described as they are, phenomenally and according to opinion [φαινομένως καὶ κατὰ δόξαν], not according to being and truth [κατὰ τὸ εἶναι, καὶ ἀληθέως], that is, as they seem to men, not as they are in their own nature. Some examples I have drawn from these men themselves and have explained more fully. Finally, Finck, who while he lived was professor at Giessen, closes the line; he makes this the fourth in his Centuria of theological canons: In Holy Scripture things are often described as they are phenomenally and according to opinion, not according to being.

units.la: DCLXXVI. Adjocio his Jeremiam Dycke, pium Theologum Practicum, qui in suo Nosce te ipsum cap. 5. ad objectionem ex Luc. viii. 13. desumtam sic respondet;
units.tr: DCLXXVI. To these I add Jeremiah Dyke, a pious practical theologian, who in his Nosce te ipsum, chapter 5, answers an objection drawn from Luke 8:13 as follows:

units.la: Quod si ita est, (nempe quod temporarii non sint vere fideles.) quare ergo Luc. viii. dicitur, quod tales homines credant, si id non faciunt? Responsio, sic sæpe loquitur Scriptura de rebus, secundum id quod communiter de iis judicatur. Sic Luna dicitur unum ex duobus maximis luminaribus, cum tamen omnium Planetarum sit minima. Sic Satanas vocatur Samuel, quum sub forma Samuelis Sauli apparebat, ab eoque pro Samuele habebatur. Ita etiam temporaria fides vocatur fides, quia in multis vera fidei est similis & tam à temporariis, quam ab aliis pro vera fide habetur. Accedit Ravanellus supra ad Gen. I. 26. citatus. Item Chamierus tom. 3. lib. 9. cap. 9. art. 13. Quia positum est loqui Scripturas de reprobis illis, qui admixti sunt electis in externa fidei professione, observare debemus, illos ἐμφανίμως dici Christianos, nimirum, quia externa aut omnia aut ferme omnia eadem habent cum electis, nec nos possumus judicare, nisi ex iis quæ apparent. Quare κατὰ τὸ φαίνεσθαι, ἀλλ' ὁ κατὰ τὸ εἶναι sic solent appellari. Et lib. 13. cap. 21. art. 18. ad Gal. 5. respondet. Ergo justificari inquit Benedictus Justinianus non pro re ipsa, sed pro opinione justitiæ accipitur. Nempe quia quæ videntur esse, NB. appellantur quasi essent. Parkerus de Descensu Christi ad inferos Lib. II. p. 122. Καταχθόνιος nominunquam in sacris popularitèr accipiuntur, pro iis quæ in aquis sunt, quia vulgi sententia est, aquas subesse Terræ, eo quòd è littore atque è ripa in aquam descendatur. Spanhemius Dub. Evangelicorum Part. II. p. 525. Atqui Scriptura id αὐτολεξεὶ edisserit illi (nempe Herodi) fuisse illusum. Resp. Solemne Scriptura loqui de rebus interdum quales sunt, interdum, quales apparent, interdum secundum rei naturam, interdum secundum opinionem vel nostram vel aliorum. Exempla obvia, sic Sol & Luna luminaria magna dicuntur pra omnibus aliis, Dii Damascenorum dicuntur percussisse Achabum. Sic Christus non venit vocatum justos, aufert ab habente, solvit Sabbathum, qui invenit animam, perdit eam, qui invenit, perdit. Sic Apostolus se ἀφρονα appellat, commemorat τὸ μωρὸν ἢ Θεοῦ sapientiam mundi. Sic stella decidunt de Cœlo. Innumera talia ubique obvia. Idem p. 313. ad Objectionem eorum, qui putabant, Stellam, quæ apparuit magis, fuisse stellam fixam, vel erraticam, desumtam ex nomine, quòd constanter stella vocatur, sic respondet: Nomenclationem Scriptura sæpe rebus tribui κατ' ἀλήθειαν secundum earum veritatem, sæpe κατὰ φαῖνον, secundum earum apparentiam, sæpe κατὰ δόξαν secundum hominum de iis opinionem. Vocatur itaque hoc φαινόμενον ἀστρον. 1. Ob figuram, quia corpus rotundum erat & sphæricum. 2. Ob lucem, quia lucidum. 3. Ob situm, quia in loco superiori. 4. Ob motum, quia movebatur, instar astri cujusdam. 5. Ob opinionem magorum, quia illis videbatur sidus. Et revera magis accedebat ad sideris, quàm ad corporis alius naturam. Sic Angeli sæpe vocantur Viri: Sic φαιστὰ μὲν, quæ in manibus Christi, stellæ Apoc. I. 16. Sic illud, quod videbatur cecidisse è cœlo, stella magna Apoc. XIII. 10, 12. Sic Luna luminare magnum pra aliis sideribus Gen. I. 16. Multi justi, sapientes suâ, vel aliorum opinione. Euangelium & ejus prædicatio μωρία & κηρύγματα 1 Cor. I. 21. Tota Scriptura idgenus exemplis referta. Capellus Ispicileg. ad Matth. v. 18. Hyperbolica omnino est locutio, qua Christus absolutissima legis complementum significavit, phrasi accommodata ad Judæorum de legis mysteriis opinionem & sententiam NB. at non qua comprobet tamen usquequaque illam sententiam &c. Item Critic. sacra p. 674. Scriptura non raro de rebus loquitur, non prout sunt, in se revera, sed ex hominum de illis opinione & sententia.
units.tr: But if this is so (namely, that temporary believers are not truly faithful), why then does Luke 8 say that such men believe, if they do not? Answer: Scripture often speaks of things according to what is commonly judged of them. Thus the moon is called one of the two greatest lights, although it is the smallest of all the planets. Thus Satan is called Samuel, when he appeared to Saul in Samuel's form and was taken for Samuel. So also temporary faith is called faith, because in many respects it resembles true faith, and it is taken for true faith both by temporary believers and by others. Ravanellus, cited above on Genesis 1:26, agrees. Likewise Chamier, vol. 3, book 9, chapter 9, art. 13: Since it has been laid down that the Scriptures speak of those reprobates who are mixed with the elect in the outward profession of faith, we must observe that they are called Christians phenomenally [ἐμφανῶς], namely, because they have outwardly all or nearly all the same things as the elect, and we cannot judge except from what appears. Hence they are usually called Christians according to appearance [κατὰ τὸ φαίνεσθαι], but not according to being [κατὰ τὸ εἶναι]. And in book 13, chapter 21, art. 18, on Galatians 5, he answers: Therefore, says Benedict Justinian, justification is taken not for the thing itself but for the opinion of righteousness. Namely, because things which seem to be are, NB, called as if they were. Parker, on the Descent of Christ into Hell, book 2, p. 122: "Subterranean" [καταχθόνιος] is sometimes taken in sacred writings in a popular sense, for those things which are in the waters, because the common opinion is that the waters lie beneath the earth, since one descends into the water from the shore and bank. Spanheim, Dubia Evangelica, part 2, p. 525: But Scripture sets forth verbatim [αὐτολεξεί] that Herod was mocked. Answer: It is the custom of Scripture to speak of things sometimes as they are, sometimes as they appear, sometimes according to the nature of the thing, sometimes according to the opinion either of ourselves or of others. Obvious examples: the sun and moon are called the great lights above all others; the gods of Damascus are said to have struck Ahab; so Christ did not come to call the righteous, he takes away from him who has, he breaks the Sabbath, he who finds his life loses it, and he who loses finds it; so the Apostle calls himself a fool [ἄφρων], and mentions the foolishness [τὸ μωρὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ] of God and the wisdom of the world; so stars fall from heaven. Countless such things are everywhere. The same author, p. 313, answers the objection of those who thought that the star which appeared to the Magi was a fixed star or a planet, drawn from the name, because it is constantly called a star, as follows: Scripture often ascribes names to things according to truth, that is, according to their reality; often according to appearance, that is, according to how they appear; often according to opinion, that is, according to the opinion of men about them. So this appearing thing is called a star: (1) because of its shape, since the body was round and spherical; (2) because of its light, since it was luminous; (3) because of its position, since it was in a higher place; (4) because of its motion, since it moved like a certain star; (5) because of the opinion of the Magi, since to them it seemed to be a star. And indeed it came closer to the nature of a star than to that of any other body. So angels are often called men; so the stars in Christ's hand are called stars in Revelation 1:16; so that which seemed to have fallen from heaven is called a great star in Revelation 13:10, 12; so the moon is called the great light above the other stars in Genesis 1:16. Many righteous men are called wise by their own or others' opinion. The Gospel and its preaching are called foolishness [μωρία] and preaching [κηρύγματα], 1 Corinthians 1:21. The whole of Scripture is full of examples of this kind. Capellus, Ispicilegium, on Matthew 5:18: The expression is entirely hyperbolical, by which Christ signified the most complete fulfilment of the law, in a phrase adapted to the opinion and judgement of the Jews concerning the mysteries of the law, NB, but not so as to approve that opinion in every respect, etc. Likewise in the Critici Sacri, p. 674: Scripture not infrequently speaks of things not as they are in themselves in reality, but according to men's opinion and judgement about them.

units.la: DCLXXVII. Dignæ quoque consideratu Responsiones Piscatoris, quibus Vorstii Objectiones, homogeneas objectionibus meorum adversariorum, solvit. Sic autem Parte tertia responsionis ad amicam duplicationem Vorstii, p. 55. Cavillaris & calumniaris, dum ex verbis meis, quæ de sanctificatione Apostolorum scripsi, infers, me arguere Apostolum mendacii, ac proinde blasphemare; scripsi ego ex Apostoli verbis illis concludi non posse Apostatas illos verè fuisse per sanguinem fœderis sanctificatos.
units.tr: DCLXXVII. Also worthy of consideration are the answers of Piscator, by which he solves Vorstius's objections, which are similar to the objections of my opponents. In the third part of his reply to Vorstius's friendly duplication, p. 55, he writes thus: You cavil and calumniate when, from my words which I wrote about the sanctification of the Apostles, you infer that I accuse the Apostle of lying and therefore of blasphemy. I wrote that it cannot be concluded from the Apostle's words that those apostates were truly sanctified through the blood of the covenant.

units.la: Hinc tu infers, me eadem opera dicere potuisse, Apostolum non vera, sed falsa hic scripsisse. Item me nihil aliud hic facere, quam quod Apostolo re ipsa in os contradicam: dum quod ille magno cum zelo de Apostatis pronunciat, id ego non verè ita se habere audacter accipiam. Resp. 1. Non sequitur, Apostolus dicit, Apostatas illos fuisse sanctificatos per sanguinem foederis: ergo intelligit ac significare vult, eos fuisse vere sanctificatos: & per consequens, qui hoc negat, is Apostolo in os contradicit, eumque mendacii arguit &c. Et p. 56. 2. Sed pergis cavillari & argutari, sic porrò disputans; si non vere sanctificati fuerunt Apostatae illi: ergo falso. Nam alterum ex duobus immediate oppositis hic locum habere oportet. Si falso: igitur falsum dicit Apostolus, qui illos ita fuisse sanctificatos scripsit. Resp. Fallis ex homonymia phraseos. Nam cum dicitur, Apostatas illos non fuisse vere sanctificatos, hac phrasi non innuitur distributio: quasi scilicet sanctificatio fiat aut vere aut falso: sed hoc tantum intelligitur, non esse verum, quod illi fuerint sanctificati proprie loquendo. Neque Apostolus hoc dicit: sed simpliciter & indefinite dicit, eos fuisse sanctificatos: non autem adjecit vocem vere vel falso.
units.tr: From this you infer that I could, by the same token, say that the Apostle wrote not true things here but false. Likewise that I do nothing else here than contradict the Apostle to his face, since I boldly take as untrue what he pronounces with great zeal about the apostates. Answer 1: It does not follow that, because the Apostle says those apostates were sanctified through the blood of the covenant, he therefore means and wishes to signify that they were truly sanctified; and consequently whoever denies this contradicts the Apostle to his face and accuses him of lying, etc. And p. 56: 2. But you go on cavilling and quibbling, arguing thus: if those apostates were not truly sanctified, then falsely. For one of two immediately opposed things must hold here. If falsely, then the Apostle, who wrote that they were so sanctified, says what is false. Answer: You are deceived by the ambiguity of the phrase. For when it is said that those apostates were not truly sanctified, this phrase does not imply a distinction, as if sanctification were done either truly or falsely; it is only understood that it is not true that they were sanctified in the proper sense of the word. Nor does the Apostle say this; he simply and indefinitely says that they were sanctified, and he did not add the word truly or falsely.

units.la: DCLXXVIII. Notatu etiam digna sunt, quae habet Flacius in Clave Scripturae, qui parte secunda ex Augustino primo de Trinit. cap. 12: hanc ponit regulam: Nullo locutionis genere utitur Sacra Scriptura, quod in consuetudine hominum non inveniatur, quia utique hominibus loquitur, quam confirmat testimonio Hilarii, super Psalmum cxxv 1. Sermo enim divinus secundum intelligentiam nostram consuetudinem naturamque se temperat communibus rerum vocabulis ad significationem doctrinae suae & institutionis aptatis: nobis enim non sibi loquitur: atque ideo nostris utitur in loquendo. Item ex Hieronymo in Jerem. cap xxviii. & Matth. xiv. haec verba citat: Multa in Scripturis sancte dicuntur juxta opinionem temporis, quo gesta referuntur, & non juxta id quod veritas continebat. Ita Flacius ad verba Hieronymi in epist. ad Gal. cap. 3. Paulus sermone trivii utitur nonnunquam in Epistolis, sic annotat p. 203. Quod dicitur: O insensati Galatae, quis vos fascinavit? digne Paulo (qui etsi imperitus est sermone, non tamen sententia) debemus exponere: non quod scierit esse fascinum, quod vulgo putatur nocere, si usus sermone sit trivii; ut in caeteris, item in hoc quoque loco, verbum quotidiana sermocinationis assumserit &c. Dicitur Fascinus proprie infantibus nocere & aetati parvulae, & his qui firmo vestigio figant gradum. Unde & quidam ex gentilibus: Nescio quis teneros oculus mihi fascinat agnos. Hoc utrum verum sit, nec ne, Deus viderit: quia potest fieri, ut & daemones huic parato serviant, & quoscunque in Dei opere vel capisse vel profecisse cognoverint, eos a bonis operibus avertant. Nunc illud in causa est, quod ex opinione vulgi sumtum putamus exemplum: ut, quomodo tenera aetas noceri dicitur fascino, sic etiam Galatae in Christi fide nuper nati & nutriti lacte, & non solido, veluti quodam fascinante fitlasi, & stomacho fidei accusante, Sp. S. cibum evomuerint. Quod si aliquis contradicat, exponat, quomodo modo de communi opinione sit sumtum; vallis Titanorum in regum libris, Sirena & Onocentauri in Esaiâ, Arcturus & Orion & Plejades in Job; & cetera hiis similia: quae utique vocabula Gentilium fabularum & causas & origines habent. Idem p. 283. Vocabula singula phrases & dicta aut sententiae integra accipiuntur aliàs secundum communem quandam opinionem, apparentiam aut existentiam Job, V. 31. Si ego de me ipso testor testimonium meum non est verum. i. e. Sic omnium hominum more ac opinione receptum est, ut, cum omnes sint mendaces & sui nimium amantes, nulli de se ipso gloriosè aut in suum commodum testanti credatur. Huc possis referre, quod Christus dicit Joh. xv. 22. Si non venissem, & locutus essem eis peccatum non haberent, i.e. possent aliquam speciem insontium suâ excusatione sibi accersere. Alias secundum hominum opinionem eamque usitatam quidem sed plerumque falsam. Sic Christus dicitur filius Josephi, & ille ipsius Pater Joh. vi. 42. Christus est scandalum & stultitia 1 Cor. I. 23. & quod stultum est Dei ibid. vers. 25. scil. ut ab hominibus habetur ac vocatur. Joh. VII. 28. Vos nostis quis sim & unde sim, sc. ut vos falsò opinamini & jactatis &c. Alias secundum solam quandam externam speciem. Sic accedit regio Act. xxvii. 27. ut illud, Provehimur portu, terraeque urbesque, recedunt. Sic columnae terrae, lingent pulverem pedum tuorum Es. xlix. 23. i. e. incurvabunt se, ut videantur lingere &c. Sic exponunt quòd montes concurrerint navigantibus Miniis in Argo: quia navigantibus inter angustias promontoriorum anteriora ad quae accedunt videntur à se invicem digredi, & posteriora loca denuo videntur congredi. Sic Pilatus vocat Jesum in inscriptione Regem Judaeorum Matth. xxvii. 37. &c. Idem p. 285. Cratylus apud Platonem disputat: res tales esse, quales hominibus videantur. Sic quoque p. 409. Sermo Hebraeus saepe admodum secundum cognitionem, judicium aut opinionem praesentium hominum de rebus magis loquitur, quàm secundum ipsius rei existentiam; sive rei veritas conveniat cum illa hominum cognitione sive non. Loquor autem non de articulis aut dogmatibus religionis, sed de communibus phrasibus. Et post adducta exempla inquit: Talia sunt multa apud Poëtas cum profanos, tum sacros. Sic Debora canit Jud. V. 20. Stellas pugnâsse cum Siserâ sc. quia talis quaedam species visa est, dum Deus grandinem immisit super ejus exercitum. Sic Æneid. 1. Mirantur Julum i. e. Cupidinem, quem putabant esse Julum, &, Magnis exterrita monstris, i. e. qua putabat Andromacha esse monstra & spectra. p. 410. Sic etiam p. 413, 414. Non tantum profanus sermo & sacer, non tam rei ipsius veritatem, quam auditorum de rebus cogitationes, seu res, ut sunt in auditorum animu concepta, respicit. Ut cum Baptista negat, se esse Heliam aut Prophetam, sc. talem, qualem Sacerdotes animo conceperant. Sic dicit Christus, se in proverbiis locutum esse Apostolis Joh.xvi. 15. non indicans doctrina obscuritatem, sed Apostolorum ruditatem, quibus ejus dogmata saepe mera aenigmata erant. Et p. 415. Falsa aut simulata aliquando verorum nomina obtinent, ut Augustinus annotat c. 11. de Mirabilibus Scriptura. Addimus his omnibus seqq. adhuc Theologos, quorum omnium hanc sententiam durissimis verbis expressit Twisus lib. I. Vindic. Gratiae &c. pag. mihi 194. b. Plurima in sacris literis enunciantur ad sensum vulgarem accommodata, etiam ad judicium humanum, quamvis erroneum, NB ut de duobus luminaribus magnis. Sic Mollerus in Ps. lxix.29. Saepe enim Scriptura sermonem magis accommodat ad sensum & opinionem hominum quam ut revera id ita esse affirmet. Chamierus tomo 3. p.174. fine: Nam quod Bellarminus excipit, morem esse Scriptura, ut loquatur de multis quasi de omnibus, frequentissimum esse non negaverim, quandoquidem ita vulgo solent homines, quorum vocibus conexta est Scriptura. Coccejus in Psalm. cxxxix. vers. 10. In his autem Scripturam se accommodare sermonibus humanis, ad indicandum, quod vulgo tali sermone exprimebatur, planum est. Significabatur res difficillima &c. Grotius in Jerem. xviii. 7. Non proprie Deus aut poenitentiam agit suorum decretorum, aut ea mutat, sed ita agit quasi mutet, cum mutatio sit in re non in ipso. Sic dicimus navigantibus terras recedere. Claudat agmen Arriaga Philosophus p. 382. Respondeo, in eo Christum locutum more humano & vulgari, quia vulgariter censetur cibus abire in excrementa &c. Nec tamen propterea Christus quicquam decidit, an aliquando exiguum alimentum natura valde conforme convertatur in substantiam aliti; unde non est putanda de Fide hac opinio de nutritione. Plures attento lectori auctores ubivis occurrent. Et vix credo, esse Interpretem Scripturae extra partes positum, qui non pedibus in illam sententiam plane eat.
units.tr: DCLXXVIII. Also worth noting is what Flacius says in his Clavis Scripturae, in the second part, drawing on Augustine, On the Trinity, book 1, chapter 12. He lays down this rule: Holy Scripture uses no kind of expression that is not found in common human usage, since it speaks to men. He confirms this by the testimony of Hilary on Psalm 125 (124), verse 1: The divine word adapts itself, according to our understanding and nature, to the common words of things, fitted to signify its teaching and instruction. For it speaks to us, not to itself; and therefore it uses our manner of speaking. Likewise, from Jerome on Jeremiah 28 and Matthew 14, he cites these words: Many things in the Scriptures are rightly said according to the opinion of the time in which the deeds are related, and not according to what the truth contained. So Flacius, on Jerome's words in the Epistle to the Galatians, chapter 3. Paul sometimes uses the language of the street in his Epistles. He notes this on page 203: When he says, "O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you?" we ought to explain it in a way worthy of Paul, who, though unskilled in speech, was not unskilled in thought. He did not mean that he knew there was a spell, which people commonly think harms, if he used the language of the street; as elsewhere, so also in this place, he took up a common phrase of everyday speech, etc. Fascinus properly harms infants and tender age, and those who plant their step with a firm foot. Hence some of the Gentiles also said: "I know not who bewitches my tender lambs with his eye." Whether this is true or not, God will see; for it may happen that demons serve this practice, and turn away from good works whoever they know to have taken up or advanced in God's work. Now the point at issue is that we think the example was taken from the opinion of the common people: just as tender age is said to be harmed by a spell, so the Galatians, newly born and nourished in Christian faith on milk and not on solid food, as if bewitched by some charm, and with their stomach of faith rejecting it, vomited up the food of the Holy Spirit. But if anyone objects, let him explain how such expressions have been taken from common opinion: the valley of the Titans in the books of Kings, the Sirens and Onocentaurs in Isaiah, Arcturus and Orion and the Pleiades in Job, and other things like these; words which surely have the causes and origins of Gentile fables. The same author, page 283: Single words, phrases, and whole sayings or sentences are sometimes taken according to a common opinion, appearance, or existence. Job 5:31: If I bear witness of myself, my witness is not true. That is: It is so received by the custom and opinion of all men that, since all are liars and overly fond of themselves, no one is believed when he testifies about himself with glory or for his own advantage. To this you may refer what Christ says in John 15:22: If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin, that is, they could have procured for themselves some appearance of innocence by their excuse. At other times it is according to the opinion of men, usual indeed but for the most part false. So Christ is called the son of Joseph, and that man his father, John 6:42. Christ is a stumbling block and foolishness, 1 Corinthians 1:23, and "that which is foolish of God" (ibid. verse 25), namely as it is regarded and called by men. John 7:28: You know who I am and where I am from, namely as you falsely suppose and boast, etc. At other times only according to a certain outward appearance. So the land draws near, Acts 27:27; and as in "We are carried past the harbour, and lands and cities recede." So "they shall lick the dust of your feet," Isaiah 49:23, that is, they will bend down so that they seem to lick, etc. So they explain that the mountains seemed to come together for the sailors of the Argo, as Minyas says: because for those sailing between the narrows of headlands, the forward points they approach seem to draw apart from one another, and the places behind them seem again to come together. So Pilate calls Jesus in the inscription "King of the Jews," Matthew 27:37, etc. The same author, page 285: Cratylus, in Plato, argues that things are such as they appear to men. Likewise on page 409: The Hebrew language very often speaks of things more according to the knowledge, judgment, or opinion of the men present than according to the actual existence of the thing, whether the truth of the thing agrees with that human knowledge or not. I speak, however, not of the articles or dogmas of religion, but of common phrases. And after citing examples he says: Many such things occur among the poets, both profane and sacred. So Deborah sings in Judges 5:20: The stars fought against Sisera, that is, because a certain kind of appearance was seen while God sent hail upon his army. So in the Aeneid, book 1: they admire Iulus, that is Cupid, whom they thought to be Iulus; and terrified by great portents, that is, by what Andromache thought were portents and apparitions. Page 410. So also on pages 413 and 414: Not only profane and sacred speech, not so much the truth of the thing itself, but the thoughts of the hearers about things, or things as they are conceived in the minds of the hearers, are regarded. As when the Baptist denies that he is Elijah or the Prophet, that is, such as the priests had conceived him in their minds. So Christ says that he has spoken to the apostles in proverbs, John 16:25, not indicating obscurity of doctrine but the dullness of the apostles, to whom his teachings were often mere riddles. And page 415: False or feigned names sometimes obtain the names of true things, as Augustine notes in chapter 11 of On the Wonders of Scripture. To all these we add the following theologians, whose whole opinion Twisse expressed in the harshest words in book 1 of the Vindiciae gratiae, page 194 of my edition, column b: Very many things in the sacred letters are stated accommodated to the common sense, even to human judgment, though erroneous, NB as about the two great lights. So Mollerus on Psalm 69:29: For Scripture often adapts its speech more to the sense and opinion of men than to affirm that the thing is really so. Chamier, volume 3, page 174, near the end: For as to Bellarmine's exception, that it is the custom of Scripture to speak of many things as if of all, I would not deny that it is very frequent, since men, to whose voices Scripture is joined, commonly speak in this way. Cocceius on Psalm 139, verse 10: That in these matters Scripture accommodates itself to human speech, in order to indicate what was commonly expressed in such speech, is plain. The most difficult thing was being signified, etc. Grotius on Jeremiah 18:7: God does not properly repent of his decrees, nor change them; but he acts as if he changed them, since the change is in the thing and not in him. So we say that the lands recede to sailors. Let Arriaga the philosopher, page 382, close the line: I answer that Christ spoke there in the human and common manner, because food is commonly thought to pass into excrement, etc. Nor on that account does Christ assert anything, whether nature, very suitably, converts a small amount of nourishment into the substance that nourishes; so that this opinion about nutrition is not to be thought a matter of faith. Many more authors will be found everywhere by the attentive reader. And I hardly believe that there is an interpreter of Scripture, standing outside the parties, who does not go entirely along with that opinion.

units.la: DCLXXIX. Exc. B. p.122. Essent adducendi Theologi, qui loca Scriptura, quae de motu Solis & quiete Terrae loquuntur, sic interpretentur, ut tu fuisti interpretatus, si illa sententia debeat a novitate liberari.
units.tr: DCLXXIX. Exc. B. p.122. There would have to be theologians cited who interpret the passages of Scripture that speak of the motion of the Sun and the rest of the Earth just as you have interpreted them, if that opinion is to be freed from novelty.

units.la: Resp. Ad meum scopum sufficit, generalem istam sententiam, quam hic defendo, a novitate vindicasse. Si enim non sit blasphemum, Scripturam loqui secundum opinionem non accuratam semper veritatem, hoc est, ut interpretor, si utitur formulis receptis veritatem praejudiciis involutam referentibus: si certum sit in genere, tales locutiones in Scriptura saepe reperiri, uti testantur tot Theologi, quaestio tantum erit: An etiam in locis pro Solis motu adductis sint agnoscenda? propter quod solum, si generalis sententia consensu tot Theologorum est confirmata, tot fluctus non fuissent movendi ab adversariis.
units.tr: Reply. For my purpose it is enough to have defended from the charge of novelty this general opinion which I maintain here. For if it is not blasphemous to say that Scripture, speaking according to an inaccurate opinion, does not always state the truth (that is, as I interpret it, when it uses received formulas that refer to the truth wrapped in prejudices), and if it is certain in general that such expressions are often found in Scripture, as so many theologians testify, then the only question will be: "Are they also to be recognised in the passages cited for the motion of the Sun?" For this reason alone, if the general opinion has been confirmed by the consensus of so many theologians, there would have been no need for the adversaries to stir up so many waves.

units.la: DCLXXX. Exc. 2. B. p. 123. Cum quaestio nostra principalis quoad loca spectantia motum Solis, sit de terminis complexis, si te in hisce phrasibus consentientes habere magnos illos viros probare velis, produc talia loca, in quibus non de voce aliqua, sed de tota sententia Scripturam ita loqui dicant.
units.tr: DCLXXX. Exc. 2. B. p. 123. Since our principal question, as regards the passages concerning the motion of the Sun, concerns complex terms, if you wish to prove that those great men agree with you in these phrases, produce such passages in which they say that Scripture speaks thus not about some single word but about the whole sentence.

units.la: Resp. Supra ostensum, parem hic esse rationem terminorum complexorum, atque incomplexorum; sed & multi loci sunt adducti continentes terminos complexos originem habentes ex praejudicio vel falsa opinione, ac Theologi citati promiscue loquuntur de terminis complexis & incomplexis, ut lectori patebit, si inspicere libeat & hoc capite & superioribus capitibus citatos: ut mirum valde sit, hunc hominem tota p. 124. & 125. me provocare ad producendum consensum Theologorum, qui superabundanter est adductus. Sed haec est consuetudo istorum Bellatorum, ut victi & prostrati magnis clamoribus contrarium velint spectatoribus ridicule persuadere.
units.tr: Reply. It has been shown above that the reasoning for complex terms is the same as for incomplex ones. Moreover, many passages have been adduced containing complex terms that arise from prejudice or false opinion, and the theologians cited speak indiscriminately of complex and incomplex terms, as the reader will see if he cares to inspect the authors cited both in this chapter and in the preceding ones. So it is very strange that this man, across pp. 124 and 125, challenges me to produce the consensus of theologians, which has already been adduced more than abundantly. But this is the habit of these warriors: when defeated and prostrate, they try with loud shouting to persuade the onlookers of the opposite, and ridiculously so.

units.la: DCLXXXI, Exc. 3. B. p. 126. Ad testimonium Parei dicendo: Parœum stupiditatem Judæorum, tantum sensibilia sapientium causam facere, cur Moses siluerit de creatione Angelorum, me vero praejudicii sensuum causam facere, cur Sacra Scriptura in iis quae refert, non locuta fuerit ex rei veritate, sed secundum erroneam opinionem vulgi.
units.tr: DCLXXXI, Exc. 3. B. p. 126. Speaking of the testimony of Pareus: that Pareus makes the stupidity of the Jews the only cause why Moses kept silent about the creation of angels, the sensible things being the concern of the wise; but I make the prejudice of the senses the cause why Holy Scripture, in what it relates, has not spoken according to the truth of the matter, but according to the erroneous opinion of the common people.

units.la: Resp. Pareus dicit, Mosen historiam suam ruditati Judæorum accommodasse, quod essent homines terreni, sensibilia tantum sapientes: unde omnino consequitur, Sp. S. phrases usurpasse referentes veritatem ad sensus relatam & sensuum praejudiciis involutam.
units.tr: Reply. Pareus says that Moses adapted his history to the rudeness of the Jews, since they were earthly men, wise only in sensible things. From this it wholly follows that the Holy Spirit used expressions that refer the truth to the senses and are wrapped in the prejudices of the senses.

units.la: DCLXXXII. Exc. 4. B. p. 126. ad testimonium Rainholdi. Eum non dicere attributa subjectis attribui, non ex veritate, sed ex erronea opinione, sed tantum de terminis simplicibus dicta intelligere ut rerum imagimibus, rerum nomina, sic etiam actibus verba ex vulgi opinione aliquando tribui &c.
units.tr: DCLXXXII. Exc. 4. B. p. 126. Against the testimony of Rainholdus: that he does not say that attributes are ascribed to subjects not according to truth but according to erroneous opinion, but understands it only of simple terms, saying that just as the names of things are given to images of things, so also verbs of acts are sometimes ascribed according to the opinion of the common people, etc.

units.la: Resp. Quid dicatur his verbis ipsum excipientem ignorare pro certo habeo. Plenius Rainholdi locum adscribam: Nam animadvertendum est, ut in sacris literis attribuuntur rerum nomina rerum imaginibus, ita etiam in actibus verba accipi solere, non ex veritate, sed ex opinione. Quod recte observavit in hunc locum Aben Ezra, ubi ait, Scripturam cum mentionem facit Dei alieni, loqui secundum cognitionem servientium illi; hujusmodi autem locutionis producit tria exempla, ex illo ipso loco Exodi, primum ubi dicuntur Dii gentium, qui putabantur esse Dii, alterum ex Josh. II. &c. Tertium est hoc loco, 1 Sam. XXVIII. de Samuele a Pythonissa excitato &c. Quod ex circumstantiis S. Scriptura apparet recte ab eo observatum, non rei veritatem, NB sed opinionem a Scriptura esse spectatam cum dicitur, Saul intellexit, quod esset Samuel, quia opinabatur eum esse, nā observentur ipsa verba contextus &c. Ex iis apparet manifeste, quod statuat, Scriptura loqui ex opinione, nō ex rei veritate, quod sive in terminis simplicibus fiat, sive in complexis, perinde est, ut superius demonstratum. 2. per actus intelligit hic scientiam, cognitionem, cursum &c. adeoque actum sciendi, cognoscendi alicui tribui, circa hoc vel illud, ex opinione, non ex rei veritate statuit, & sic actionem hanc, sequi post exploratores vult convenire Hierichuntinis, non ex rei veritate, sed opinione. Similiter actum cognoscendi, quod Diabolus Samuel esset, non ex rei veritate tributum Sauli, sed ex ejus opinione. Et tamen adhuc quis somniabit, istam phrasin eo sensu, quo ego antehac adhibueram, à Rainholdo non usurpari.
units.tr: Reply. I am certain that the objector himself does not know what is meant by these words. I shall quote Rainholdus' passage more fully: "For it must be noted that just as in the sacred letters the names of things are attributed to images of things, so also verbs of acts are usually understood not according to truth but according to opinion. Aben Ezra rightly observed this on the passage, where he says that Scripture, when it mentions a foreign god, speaks according to the knowledge of those who serve him. He produces three examples of this kind of speech from that very passage of Exodus: first, where they are called gods of the nations, who were thought to be gods; second, from Josh. 2, etc.; third, in this place, 1 Sam. 28, about Samuel raised by the Pythoness, etc. That Aben Ezra rightly observed this is clear from the circumstances in Holy Scripture; NB, it is not the truth of the thing but opinion that Scripture regards when it says, 'Saul understood that it was Samuel,' because he supposed that it was; for let the very words of the context be observed, etc." From these words it plainly appears that he holds that Scripture speaks from opinion, not from the truth of the thing; whether this happens in simple or complex terms makes no difference, as shown above. Second, by acts he here understands knowledge, cognition, course, etc., and so he holds that the act of knowing or perceiving is ascribed to someone regarding this or that according to opinion, not according to the truth of the thing; and thus he wishes this action, the following of the spies, to be attributed to the people of Jericho according to opinion, not according to the truth of the thing. Similarly, the act of knowing that the devil was Samuel is ascribed to Saul not according to the truth of the thing but according to his opinion. And yet who will still dream that this phrase is not used by Rainholdus in the sense in which I had used it before?

units.la: DCLXXXIII. Ut hoc concludam caput observandum, reliquorum citatorum Theologorum testimonia intacta relinqni, quæ ipsa tacita est confessio eos mecum consentire.
units.tr: DCLXXXIII. To conclude this chapter, it should be observed that the testimonies of the remaining theologians cited have been left untouched, and this silence is itself a tacit confession that they agree with me.

units.la: CAPUT XXXII.
units.tr: CAPUT XXXII.

units.la: Objectiones contra hanc sententiam examinantur, quarum prima urget, quod ex eâ sequatur, Scripturam falsum docere.
units.tr: Objections against this opinion are examined. The first urges that it follows from it that Scripture teaches what is false.

units.la: DCLXXXIV. Prima Objectio: Qui adhibet formulas vulgares, veritatem quidem aliquam referentes, sed ad homines relatam, & prejudiciis involutam, sub quibus latet, ille falsum docet: Atqui Spiritus Sanctus; Ergo.
units.tr: DCLXXXIV. First Objection: Whoever uses common formulas, which express some truth but as it is related to human beings and wrapped in prejudices, under which it lies hidden, teaches falsehood. But the Holy Spirit does so. Therefore...

units.la: Resp. Neg. Maj. propositio absolute sumpta, nisi velis eodem modo inferre, omnes formulas vulgares usu receptas, quæ præjudiciis sunt involutæ, esse tollendas, novamque linguam inveniendam, in qua verba rem nude exprimunt, sine præjudiciorum involucro, quod est sermonis usum è mundo tollere. Tali enim formula utitur Scriptura, quia est recepta, non omne illud, ad quod illa ab aliis adhibetur, per eam significando; sed tantum id quod communiter significatur, & quod verum est; idque non ex nuda illa formula est intelligendum. Sed ex circumstantiis sermonis & personâ ejus, qui loquitur. Si ergo ad scopum Sp. S. non sit necessarium, ut doceat in locis contra nos objectis, Solem circa Terram realiter moveri, ergo per talem formulam tantum Sp. S. indicat hanc veritatem, tem, nempe quod variationem situs Terra accipiat respectu Solis, vel Sol respectu Terræ. Si plus tali formula doceat, id ex circumstantiis textus demonstretur. Nec infrequens est, ut eådem formulâ vel signis aliis arbitrariis utentes alii aliis plus vel minus significent. Ita Baptismo, quo à Judæis proselytus initiabatur, significabatur tantùm receptio in gentem & religionem Judaicam, sed à Christo præter istam receptionem ad Christianismum regeneratio per Spiritum Sanctum. Sic per Coronæ impositionem ab aliis lætitia tantum, ab aliis etiam victoria vel aliud quid præterea significatur. Utimur nominibus dierum Solis, Lunæ, &c. non omne id quod primi inventores Ethnici cogitârunt significantes, sed tantùm distinctionis dierum causâ. Vox Canonicorum apud Ultrajectinos olim designabat homines Ecclesiasticos cultui spirituali Idololatrico destinatos, quibus adjuncta erat potestas politica, ut primum Reipubl. Ultrajectinæ membrum constituerent, nunc per eam merè Politici designantur. Talia plura afferri possent exempla.
units.tr: Answer: I deny the major premise as it stands, unless you want to infer from it that all commonly received popular formulas that are wrapped in prejudices must be abolished, and a new language invented in which words express the thing bare, without the wrapping of prejudice. That would mean removing the use of speech from the world. Scripture uses such a formula because it is the accepted one, and it does not, by using it, signify everything that others mean by it, but only what is commonly meant and is true. Nor is this to be understood from the bare formula, but from the circumstances of the discourse and the person who speaks. If, then, it is not necessary for the purpose of the Holy Spirit to teach, in the passages objected to us, that the sun really moves about the earth, then by such a formula the Holy Spirit only indicates this truth, namely that the earth undergoes a change of position with respect to the sun, or the sun with respect to the earth. If it teaches more by such a formula, this must be shown from the circumstances of the text. Nor is it uncommon for people who use the same formula or other arbitrary signs to signify more or less by them. Thus by the baptism by which proselytes were initiated among the Jews, only reception into the Jewish nation and religion was signified; but in Christ, besides that reception, regeneration by the Holy Spirit into Christianity is signified. So by the placing of a crown, joy alone is signified by some, and by others victory or something else besides. We use the names of the days, Sun, Moon, and so on, not signifying everything the first pagan inventors had in mind, but only for the sake of distinguishing the days. The term "Canons" among the people of Utrecht once designated ecclesiastical men destined for spiritual idolatrous worship, to whom political power was attached so that they constituted the first member of the Utrecht commonwealth; now by that term only politicians are designated. Many more such examples could be cited.

units.la: 2. Hoc tantùm ex illo antecedente inferre licet; ergo Scriptura non emendat locutiones vulgares, eas mutando in accuratas, & sic fundamenta istarum locutionum vulgarium non refutat; vel: Ergo de eo loquitur Scriptura, quod est falsum, illudque in medio relinquit, quorum neutrum est absurdum, adque neutrum Scriptura tenetur; imò si prius faceret, crucem figeret animis plebejis, quibus talia incredibilia viderentur. Ita plebejis istis animis non facilè persuadebis, quod Luna sit minor quam stella fixa, quod Terra non sit corpus maximum, imò cœli respectu puncti insensibilis habeat rationem, cùm sensus ipsos videantur aliud docere, nec possit præjudicium eximi istud, nisi per accurtissimas demonstrationes, quarum isti non sunt capaces, nec satis præparati ad illas percipiendas. Quæ ergo supra vidimus de versione LXX. Interpretum, ex Riveto & Voetio ea etiam hic applicari possunt.
units.tr: 2. From that antecedent one may infer only this: therefore Scripture does not correct common expressions by changing them into exact ones, and so it does not refute the foundations of those common expressions; or else: therefore Scripture speaks of what is false and leaves it undecided. Neither of these is absurd, and Scripture is bound to neither; indeed, if it did the former, it would place a cross before the minds of common people, to whom such things would seem incredible. So you will not easily persuade those plebeian minds that the moon is smaller than a fixed star, that the earth is not the greatest body, indeed that it bears the relation of an insensible point to the heavens, since the senses themselves seem to teach otherwise, and this prejudice cannot be removed except by the most exact demonstrations, which these people are not capable of, nor sufficiently prepared to grasp. What we saw above concerning the translation of the Septuagint, from Rivetus and Voetius, can be applied here as well.

units.la: Et sanè rectè faciunt Concionatores & prudenter, si Scripturæ exemplum sequentes in concionibus suis vulgo sese accommodent. Ita enim v. g. de Terra debent loqui tanquam de maximo aliquo corpore, cum tamen illa respectu Cœli puncti habeat rationem, quod coram vulgo dicere ἀ ὡς ἐγοσδιόνναυ foret. Ita possunt sæpe Concionatores suas adhortationes superstruere opinioni vulgi ex. gr. dicendo: Deo obedit mare, cum dicit, consiste; Deo obedit Terra, cum dicit: Aperi os tuum & degluti impios; Deo obediunt montes, cum eos transponit: Quare ergo vos homines rationales estis tam immorigeri? &c. cum proprie & accuratè loquendo obedientia non possit attribui, nisi Creaturis rationalibus, & revera communis sit error, quo omnibus rebus communis quidam sensus & appetitus attribuitur. Simili modo in aliis fieri potest.
units.tr: And indeed preachers do rightly and wisely if, following the example of Scripture, they accommodate themselves in their sermons to the common people. For example, they ought to speak of the earth as of some very great body, although with respect to the heavens it bears the relation of a point; to say this before the common people would be [ἀ ὡς ἐγοσδιόνναυ] (unseemly). In this way preachers can often build their exhortations on the opinion of the people, for example by saying: The sea obeys God when he says, Be still; the earth obeys God when he says: Open your mouth and swallow the wicked; the mountains obey God when he moves them: Why then are you rational men so unruly? etc. whereas, speaking properly and exactly, obedience can be attributed only to rational creatures, and in fact there is a common error by which some common sense and appetite is attributed to all things. In the same way it can be done in other cases.

units.la: DCLXXXV. Instant. 1. B. p. 129. Probatur major negata. Qui de subjecto praedicat, quod ei non competit, vel negat quod ei competit, falsum docet: at qui adhibet formulas vulgares &c. Ergo: sive, quod eodem redit, qui dicit rei inesse quod non inest, peccat: At Sp. Sanctus dicit rei inesse &c. Ergo.
units.tr: DCLXXXV. Further objection. 1. B. p. 129. The major premise, denied, is proved thus: whoever predicates of a subject what does not belong to it, or denies of it what does belong to it, teaches falsehood. But whoever uses common formulas etc. Therefore; or, which comes to the same thing: whoever says that something is in a thing when it is not, sins. But the Holy Spirit says that something is in a thing etc. Therefore.

units.la: Resp. Negando minorem propositionem utriusque syllogismi, cum sit ipsa inter nos quaestio, an dicat, id est, testetur Spiritus S. inesse Soli ex, gr. Motum realem, an praedicet aliquid per formulas vulgares de subjecto quod ei non competit? cum, quid praedicet, quid non, qui utitur formulis receptis ex ipsa persona utente iis & circumstantiis textus sit intelligendum. Illud ergo praedicat Scriptura de subjecto, illud dicit Spiritus Sanctus subjecto inesse, non quod verba primo aspectu praese ferunt, sed quod sensus verborum per media interpretandi legitime demonstratus infert. Itaque negamus, Spiritum Sanctum testari vel docere per illa loca Scripturae, in quibus sunt formulae praejudiciis involutae, ipsa praejudicia, sed ea in medio relinquere dicimus.
units.tr: Answer: I deny the minor premise of each syllogism, since the very question between us is whether the Holy Spirit says, that is, testifies, that real motion is in the sun, for example, or whether by common formulas he predicates of a subject something that does not belong to it. For what is predicated and what is not is to be understood from the very person using the received formulas and from the circumstances of the text. Scripture therefore predicates of the subject that which the Holy Spirit says is in the subject, not what the words seem at first sight to carry, but what the sense of the words, legitimately demonstrated by the proper means of interpretation, implies. Therefore we deny that the Holy Spirit testifies or teaches the prejudices themselves through those passages of Scripture in which there are formulas wrapped in prejudices; we say he leaves those prejudices undecided.

units.la: DCLXXXVI. Inst. 2. M. p. 190. Hoc modo procedere istam objectionem. Quicunque loquens non loquitur ex veritate, ille loquitur ex falsitate &c. sed forte negaveris, Deum loquendo falsum docere falsum, quod nihil aliud est quam nugari; cum dicere vel eloqui rem aliquam nihil aliud significet, quam auditorem de re aliqua docere &c. sic omnia poterunt elidi, si dicas, Scripturam errorem tantum non refutare, sed simpliciter referre hoc falsum &c.
units.tr: DCLXXXVI. Further objection, 2. M. p. 190. The objection proceeds in this way: whoever speaks not from truth speaks from falsehood, etc. But perhaps you will deny that God, in speaking, teaches falsehood falsely, which is nothing other than trifling, since to say or to utter a thing means nothing other than to teach the hearer about some thing, etc. In this way everything could be overturned, if you say that Scripture does not refute error but simply reports this falsehood, etc.

units.la: Resp. Major non recte proponitur, non enim dixi simpliciter, Scripturam non loqui ex rei veritate, sed ex rei veritate accurata, cui non opponitur falsitas, sed veritas non accurata seu praejudiciis involuta. Quid autem Scriptura dicat vel doceat locis pro Solis motu objectis suis locis ostendemus. Non omne id dicit, quod homines praejudiciis obstiti imaginantur se in ea reperire, sed id demum dicit, quod verba recte intellecta inferunt. Verbum Dei demum est sensus verborum legitimus. Illa vero instantia, posse nempe hoc modo omnia elidi, si dicatur, Scripturam errorem tantum non refutare, tum demum valeret, si diceremus, nullis verbis Scripturam docere, cum e contrario dicamus, illis formulis referri & doceri veritatem aliquam, sed non nudam, verum ad homines relatam, quam quoque doceat ex accurata inspectione quorumvis locorum poterit facile cognosci. Supra vidimus Theologos dicentes, dum Sp. S. in N. T. citat versionem LXX, etiam in illis locis ubi erronea est, eum errorem non refutare, qui tamen tuam consequentiam, sic omnia posse elidi, non admittent.
units.tr: Answer: The major premise is not rightly stated. I did not say simply that Scripture does not speak from the truth of the thing, but from the exact truth of the thing, to which falsehood is not opposed, but truth that is not exact, or wrapped in prejudices. What Scripture says or teaches in the passages objected concerning the motion of the sun we will show in their proper places. It does not say everything that men, held by prejudices, imagine they find in it, but only what the words, rightly understood, imply. The Word of God is in fact the legitimate sense of the words. As for that instance, namely that in this way everything could be overturned, if it is said that Scripture does not refute error but only reports it, it would hold only if we said that Scripture teaches nothing by its words; whereas, on the contrary, we say that some truth is conveyed and taught by those formulas, but not bare truth, rather truth as related to human beings, which anyone who carefully examines the passages can easily recognise as also taught. Above we saw theologians who, when the Holy Spirit in the New Testament cites the Septuagint version even in those places where it is erroneous, say that he does not refute that error; yet they would not accept your consequence, that thus everything could be overturned.

units.la: DCLXXXVII. Inst. 3. M. p. 192. Uno eodemque modo dicit Scriptura, Sol currit, & sanguis Christi purgat à peccatis, quaeritur ergo, quare posterior ista phrasis vim habeat majorem asserendi quàm prior.
units.tr: DCLXXXVII. Further objection, 3. M. p. 192. Scripture says in one and the same way, The sun runs, and, The blood of Christ cleanses from sins; the question therefore is why the latter phrase has greater force in asserting than the former.

units.la: Resp. Quando Scriptura dicit, sanguinem Christi nos purgare à peccatis 1 Joh. I. 7. ex scopo & circumstantiis textus apparet doceri, communionem nostram cum Christo fieri per sanguinis ipsius ablutionem à peccatis, sive per remissionem peccatorum. At quando dicit Psal. xix. 6. Sol laetatur tanquam robustus decursurus viam, circumstantiae textus tantùm requirunt, ut his verbis doceatur, Soli variationem quandam situs obtingere respectu terrae, ut cùm tempore nocturno latuerit, manè iterum appareat & conspiciatur, adeoque variaverit situm suum, & porrò celerrimè sit variaturus, non verò ut realis motus ei tribuatur, ut etiam realis laetitia ei non competit, prout id apparebit manifestius in istius loci examine.
units.tr: Answer: When Scripture says that the blood of Christ cleanses us from sins (1 John 1:7), it appears from the aim and circumstances of the text that it teaches that our communion with Christ takes place through the washing away of sins by his blood, that is, through the remission of sins. But when it says (Psalm 19:6) The sun rejoices as a strong man to run his course, the circumstances of the text only require that by these words it be taught that some change of position in relation to the earth befalls the sun, so that, having been hidden in the night time, it appears and is seen again in the morning, and so has changed its position and will continue to change it very swiftly; not that real motion is attributed to it, just as real joy does not belong to it, as will appear more clearly in the examination of that passage.

units.la: DCLXXXVIII. Inst. 4. B. p. 130. Sic poterunt excusari etiam salsissimae locutiones, ex. gr. dicam, Papa est caput Ecclesiae, Christi vicarius &c. si accuser falsitatis, excipiam tantùm, non loquor ex rei veritate, quia est locutio in Papatu vulgaris, quam non muto in accuratam, videl. quod sese venditat esse talem &c. sic si quis in foro ita agat verbis esset excipiendus M. item p. 191. inquit: Sic Jesuitarum technas posse excusari.
units.tr: DCLXXXVIII. Inst. 4. B. p. 130. Thus even the most absurd expressions could be excused, for example: "I will say, the Pope is the head of the Church, Christ's vicar, etc." If I am accused of falsehood, I shall only answer: "I do not speak according to the truth of the matter, because it is a common expression among the Papacy, which I do not change into a precise one, namely, that he presents himself as being such, etc." So if anyone in court acted in this way, he should be excused by these words. M. likewise says on p. 191: "Thus the wiles of the Jesuits can be excused."

units.la: Resp. Si utar his locutionibus incidenter inter Pontificios neq; ex circumstantiis sermonis appareat, me per illas testari vel docere velle, nisi aliquid generale, sed eam controversiam jam nolle tractare, nemo poterit me falsae doctrinae accusare: ex. gr. si ita quis dicat, Greg. Magnus caput Ecclesiae, & vicarius Christi dixit, Eum qui se vocaverit universalem Episcopum esse vel Anti-Christum vel ejus praecursorem. Ergò quoniam hoc fecit Bonifacius & faciunt omnes Romani Episcopi, merito pro AntiChristo sunt habendi; nemo poterit inferre me docere per illa verba, Papam esse caput Ecclesiae, vel esse verum vicarium Christi: verù si quis absolutè ita loqueretur, & ex circumstantiis pateret, eum hoc velle significare & testari, vel ad effugiendum martyrium, vel ad ostendendum consensum suum cum Papatu, ei haec excusatio eo ipso ademta esset, ut non posset dicere, se id docere non voluisse, adeoque hac formula non locutum ex rei veritate, sed tantum rem falsam in medio reliquisse. Unde verò illud, quod saepius solet dici? Hac verba in ore Orthodoxi possunt legitimum sensum habere adeoque vera esse: at in ore Arminiani Socinianismo laten-tis vel Socin-iani falsa sunt. Sic Heydanus ad primam quaestionem Catech. Arminii, Sic saepe Calvinus lib. 4. Instit. cap. 7. Romanum Pontificem vocat Episcopum, quem tamen postea, quando ad ipsam illam quæstionem deventum est §. 24. Episcopum negat expresse. Ergone inferes: falsum locutus est vel falsum docuit Calvinus. Et quid crebrius in usu est quàm tales loquendi formulæ? 2. Ineptissimè exemplum reorum in judicium vel mendaciis vel æquivocationibus Jesuitarum utentium huc adducitur, cum coram judicio teneantur illam ipsam veritatem, de quâ quæritur, testari vel profiteri. At Spiritus Sanctus semper testatur veritatem aliquam, sed non omnibus necessariò verbis, non omnem quam quis se putat colligere ex formulis receptis, cum ab eo sine animo attentiendi & præjudicia per eas confirmandi proferantur.
units.tr: Reply. If I use these expressions incidentally among the Papists, and it does not appear from the circumstances of the discourse that I wish to testify or teach anything through them, except something general, but I am unwilling to treat that controversy now, no one will be able to accuse me of false doctrine. For example, if someone says: "Gregory the Great, the head of the Church and vicar of Christ, said that whoever called himself universal bishop was either Antichrist or his forerunner. Therefore, since Boniface did this and all the Roman bishops do the same, they are rightly to be held as Antichrist," no one will be able to infer that I teach, by those words, that the Pope is the head of the Church or the true vicar of Christ. But if someone spoke in such a way absolutely, and it were clear from the circumstances that he meant to signify and testify this, whether to escape martyrdom or to show his agreement with the Papacy, then this excuse would be taken away from him by that very fact, so that he could not say that he did not wish to teach this, and so he would not have spoken according to the truth of the matter with this formula, but would merely have left a false thing in the middle. Whence then is that which is so often said: "These words can have a legitimate sense in the mouth of an Orthodox man, and so be true; but in the mouth of an Arminian hiding Socinianism, or of a Socinian, they are false"? So Heydanus, on the first question of Arminius's Catechism; so Calvin often, in Institutes book 4, chapter 7, calls the Roman Pontiff a bishop, whom he afterwards, when the question itself is reached (§ 24), expressly denies to be a bishop. Will you therefore infer: Calvin spoke falsely or taught falsely? And what is more frequent in use than such forms of speech? 2. The example of defendants in court who use lies or equivocations, like the Jesuits, is very foolishly brought in here, since before a court they are bound to testify or profess that very truth which is in question. But the Holy Spirit always testifies some truth, though not in all necessarily the same words, and not every truth which someone thinks he gathers from received formulas, since these are brought forward without any intention of attending to them and of confirming prejudices by them.

units.la: DCLXXXIX. Instit. 5. B. p. 132. Quasi verò tam perniciosa fuisset doctrina, si Spiritus veritatis populum docuisset, non Solem sed Terram moveri, cùm non minùs incredibilia referat, ut aquæ quondam steisse instar murorum &c. 2. Nulla etiam figura crux est, qui semetipsum totum Dei subjecerit, & Deus potuisset aque per demonstrationem præjudicia tollere, ut nos caperemus.
units.tr: DCLXXXIX. Instit. 5. B. p. 132. As if indeed the doctrine would have been so pernicious, if the Spirit of truth had taught the people that not the Sun but the Earth moves, since it relates no less incredible things, such as that the waters once stood like walls, etc. 2. Nor is any figure a cross to one who has wholly subjected himself to God; and God could have removed prejudices by demonstration, so that we might grasp it.

units.la: Resp. Crux esset satis perniciosa si Scriptura formulas adhiberet veritatem nudam & ad hominum captum non accommodatam referentes; sic enim difficultatem intelligendi pareret præter necessitatem. Alia ratio est miraculorum; in quibus aliquid præter naturam extraordinariè factum esse testatur, quod necessarium est relatu, & quia docetur à Scriptura propterea est credendum, sed si Scriptura adhiberet formulas correspondentes accuratæ rerum notitiæ eam ab hominibus omnibus requireret, quod sanè magnam difficultatem inferret. 2. Hoc etiam posset oggeri sententiæ eorum qui existimant, ideò usurpâsse Apostolos versionem Græcam, ne crucem figerent in rebus non necessariis. 3. Omne quod Deus testatur credimus, & sic ei nos libenter subjicimus, sed negamus, eum per has formulas testari aliud, quàm veritatem generalem, præjudiciis, quoad ipsas formulas loquendi, involutam. 4. Quæritur, non quid Deus facere potuerit, sed quid fecerit: an nempè, cum noluerit uti demonstrationibus, debuerit & voluerit doctrinam de motu Solis reali credendam proponere, quod nos negamus.
units.tr: Reply. The cross would indeed be quite pernicious if Scripture used formulas that report the bare truth and are not adapted to the understanding of men; for in that way it would create difficulty in understanding beyond what is necessary. The case of miracles is different: in them Scripture testifies that something beyond nature was done extraordinarily, which must needs be related, and because Scripture teaches it, it is therefore to be believed. But if Scripture used formulas corresponding to an exact knowledge of things, it would require that knowledge of all men, which would certainly bring great difficulty. 2. This could also be objected to the opinion of those who think the Apostles used the Greek version for this reason, lest they should set up a cross in matters that were not necessary. 3. Whatever God testifies, we believe, and so we willingly submit ourselves to him; but we deny that he testifies through these formulas anything other than a general truth, involved in prejudices as regards the very forms of speech. 4. The question is not what God could have done, but what he did: namely, whether, since he was unwilling to use demonstrations, he ought and wished to propose the doctrine of the real motion of the Sun to be believed, which we deny.

units.la: DCXC. Inst. 6. B. p. 132. cui consentit M. p. 209. si formula ista impedirent intellectum vulgi, poterant ergo in totum prateriri & sileri, quid necesse erat eo uti argumento ad probandam Dei gloriam in Cœlis conspicuam Psalm xix.
units.tr: DCXC. Inst. 6. B. p. 132. With which M. agrees, p. 209: "If these formulas would hinder the understanding of the common people, they could therefore have been passed over and kept silent altogether; what need was there to use this argument for proving the glory of God visible in the heavens?" Psalm 19.

units.la: Resp. Realis motus Solis, de quo nihil docetur Psalm. xix. non est argumentum ad probandam Dei gloriam, sed illa vicissitudo dierum noctium, Solisque influentia, quæ efficitur per variationem situs sui cum Terrâ, quæ debebat formulâ receptâ exprimi, quâ quidem ista veritas denotabatur, sed obtecta involucris præjudiciorum, propter hoc ipsum, quia ista formula erat recepta.
units.tr: Reply. The real motion of the Sun, of which nothing is taught in Psalm 19, is not the argument for proving God's glory; rather it is that alternation of days and nights, and the influence of the Sun, which is brought about by the variation of its position relative to the Earth. This ought to have been expressed by the received formula, by which indeed this truth was denoted, but was hidden under the veils of prejudices, for this very reason, that this formula was received.

units.la: DCXCI. Inst. 7. B. p. 133. Si fuit hæc Spiritus Sancti prudentia, ut utatur istâ formulâ, unde jam ista Cartesianorum audacia, quod doctrinam hanc in vulgus spargere ausint?
units.tr: DCXCI. Inst. 7. B. p. 133. If it was the prudence of the Holy Spirit to use this formula, whence then this audacity of the Cartesians, that they dare to spread this doctrine among the common people?

units.la: Resp. Nihil hic ego vel alii qui Cartesii sententiam hic defenderunt, agunt, ad quod non vestrâ importunitate fuerunt adacti. Ego non coram vulgo defendi sententiam meam, sed coram orbe erudito, tum adhibitis demonstrationibus, tum respondendo ad vestras objectiones. At cum vos eam doctrinam vulgo invisam redderetis vestris ad populum declamationibus motus est Dn. Velthuysen, ut & coram vulgo, quod vos concitare conabamini, causæ hujus defensionem susciperet. Itaque si quid hic peccatum, ab adversariorum importunitate est commissum.
units.tr: Reply. Neither I nor the others who have here defended the opinion of Descartes do anything for which we were not driven by your importunity. I did not defend my opinion before the common people, but before the learned world, both by employing demonstrations and by answering your objections. But when you made that doctrine odious to the common people by your declamations before the people, Mr. Velthuysen was moved to take up the defence of this cause, even before the common people, which you were trying to stir up. Therefore, if any wrong has been committed here, it was committed through the importunity of the adversaries.

units.la: DCXCII. Inst. 8. M. p. 210. Spiritus Sanctus rerum naturalium accuratam veritatem usque adeo perspicuè potuisset tradere, ut vel ipsi plebeji eam perspexissent: sin minus, eorum intellectum eò potuisset elevare, ut non minus accuratam rerum naturalium veritatem comprehendissent, quàm quidem veritatem rerum cœlestium captu multò difficiliorum actu comprehendant.
units.tr: DCXCII. Inst. 8. M. p. 210. The Holy Spirit could have delivered the accurate truth of natural things so plainly that even the common people would have perceived it; but if not, he could have raised their understanding so far that they would have comprehended the accurate truth of natural things no less than they actually comprehend the truth of heavenly things, which is far more difficult to grasp.

units.la: Resp. Si voluisset uti demonstrationibus & agere Philosophum, atque docere sapientiam mundi potuisse concedo, sed nego voluisse, vel id necesse fuisse, quod patebit ex sequentibus. 2. Veritatem rerum cœlestium intelligunt salutariter fideles per illuminationem Spiritus Sancti, at ad intelligendum veritatem naturalem ea non requiritur. 3. Quæritur, quidnam convenientius fuerit Spiritui Sancto, omitterene locutiones de rebus naturalibus, quod non potuisse fieri manifestum, an uti accuratis, ac ad eas intelligendas illuminare intellectum hominum, quod existimat adversarius, an verò uti formulis vulgaribus? nos postremum existimamus, cum illæ sufficere possint Spiritus Sancti scopo, neque accuratarum formularum usus ad salutem sit necessarius.
units.tr: Reply. If he had wished to use demonstrations and act as a philosopher, and to teach the wisdom of the world, I concede he could have; but I deny that he wished it, or that it was necessary, as will become clear from what follows. 2. The faithful understand the truth of heavenly things savingly through the illumination of the Holy Spirit, but for understanding natural truth this is not required. 3. The question is, what would have been more fitting for the Holy Spirit: to omit statements about natural things, which could not have been done without it being obvious, or to use exact expressions and illuminate the understanding of men so that they might grasp them, as the adversary thinks; or rather to use common formulas? We hold the latter, since these can suffice for the purpose of the Holy Spirit, and the use of exact formulas is not necessary for salvation.

units.la: DCXCIII. Inst. 9. B. p. 134. Boni Pastoris non est talibus uti phrasibus quæ per se & suâ naturâ tales conceptus ingenerant, qui rei veritati repugnant, prout auctor noster vult Spiritum Sanctum docere motum Solis, cum ejus quies sit intelligenda. 2. Non est necesse falsitatibus Ecclesiam pascere.
units.tr: DCXCIII. Inst. 9. B. p. 134. It is not the part of a good Shepherd to use such phrases which by themselves and by their nature generate such conceptions as contradict the truth of the matter, as our author wants the Holy Spirit to teach the motion of the Sun, when its rest is to be understood. 2. It is not necessary to feed the Church with falsehoods.

units.la: Resp. Pastor debet uti formulis receptis, etiamsi sciat, eas apud imperitiores, non quidem præjudicium ingenerare, quod potius jam factum esse præsupponunt, vide cap. I. sed non refutare, non rejicere; quo modo tamen falsitatibus Ecclesiam absurdissimè pascere diceretur, nisi putes falsitatibus pascere alios eos omnes, qui formulis in præjudiciis fundatis utuntur. 2. Nego, quòd ego velim, per loca Scripturæ pro motu Solis adducta quietem debere intelligi, cum neutrum iis determinare Scriptura velit, & sæpius dixerim, Spiritum Sanctum per suas formulas non docere motum Solis, sed istum in medio relinquere; unde colligere est, quòd quietem quoque non doceat.
units.tr: Reply. A minister ought to use received formulas, even if he knows that among the less learned they generate, not indeed a prejudice (which they presuppose has rather already been done, see chapter I), but yet do not refute or reject it; in what way, however, it would be said most absurdly that he feeds the Church with falsehoods, unless you think that all those feed others with falsehoods who use formulas founded in prejudices. 2. I deny that, as I would wish, the passages of Scripture adduced for the motion of the Sun must be understood of rest, since Scripture wishes to determine neither of these, and I have often said that the Holy Spirit by his formulas does not teach the motion of the Sun, but leaves that in the middle; whence it may be gathered that he does not teach rest either.

units.la: DCXCIV. Inst. 10. B. p. 136. Negamus tales locutiones, (quibus dicitur, Deo obedit Terra &c.) fundatas in communi errore vulgi, sed metaphoricas dicimus.
units.tr: DCXCIV. Inst. 10. B. p. 136. We deny that such expressions (by which it is said, "the earth obeys God," etc.) are grounded in the common error of the crowd, but we call them metaphorical.

units.la: Resp. Id verò probatum exinde, quod communis sit error, quo omnibus rebus communis quidam sensus & appetitus tribuitur: Illas phrases primo intuitu quivis adspiciens diceret, per eas obedientiam mari attribui, cum tamen iis nihil aliud docetur, quàm quod, sicut ad nutum Dei sequitur in creatura irrationali effectus, ita debeat etiam sequi in rationali.
units.tr: Reply: This is proved from the fact that the error is common, by which a certain common sense and appetite is attributed to all things. Anyone who looks at those phrases at first glance would say that obedience is ascribed to the sea by them, although nothing else is taught by them than that, just as an effect follows in irrational creatures at God's nod, so it ought also to follow in rational ones.

units.la: DCXCV. Atque hæc fuit prima ratio Negatæ Majoris in objectione propositâ, nimirum, quod ex illo antecedente tantum sequatur, Scripturam non refutare fundamenta erronea vulgarium locutionum. Altera ratio est, quemadmodum in visionibus ecstaticis aliud videtur & narratur, aliud intelligitur, ex. gr. videtur senex sedens in throno excelso &c. & intelligitur Deus Judex Terræ, non tamen propterea dicendum, in talibus visionibus fallitatem hærere: ita etiam Spiritus Sanctus ubi formulis receptis cum vulgo loquitur, aliud verbis efferre videtur ei, qui præjudiciis est occupatus, nempe prout res apparet, aliud intelligit, prout res revera se habet. Et sic is, cui rei veritas est cognita, etiam Spiritum Sanctum loquendi formulis vulgaribus utentem intelliget, nimirum, quòd iis veritatem tantum generalem & ad homines relatam, non nudam & specialem docet: nec tamen alii, qui cum vulgo sentit & errat, is error oberit saluti. Sicut ergo is, qui se repræsentat forma viri &c. non docet se esse virum, ita non sequitur, qui utitur formulis receptis, ex quibus alicui videtur præjudicium significari, ille docet id ipsum. Itaque omnino illa appositè adhibetur comparatio, quicquid adversarii opponant. Simile quidem non est idem, sed tamen est simile, & sufficit ad infringendam vim Majoris Propositionis in objectione. H. hic pag. 24. aliquanto plus dicit, quàm ego, Fallitas nulla est in visione rei, sed in modo visionis, qui fuit œconomia divina, quod secundum meam explicationem ut dicatur non est opus.
units.tr: DCXCV. This was the first reason for denying the major premise in the objection put forward, namely, that from that antecedent only this follows: that Scripture does not refute the erroneous foundations of common expressions.
