The second reason is this: just as in ecstatic visions one thing is seen and narrated, and another is understood (for example, an old man is seen sitting on a high throne, etc., and God the Judge of the earth is understood), yet it should not therefore be said that falsehood lies in such visions, so also when the Holy Spirit speaks with the crowd in received formulas, He seems to express to the man who is occupied with prejudices one thing in words, namely, as the matter appears, and understands another, namely, as the matter really is. And so he to whom the truth of the matter is known will also understand the Holy Spirit, using common forms of speech, to teach by them only a general truth related to men, not a bare and special truth; yet this error will not harm the salvation of another who thinks and errs with the crowd. Just as he who presents himself in the form of a man, etc., does not teach that he is a man, so it does not follow that he who uses received formulas, from which to someone it seems that a prejudice is signified, teaches that very thing. Therefore that comparison is aptly adduced, whatever the opponents may object. It is indeed not the same thing, but it is similar, and it is enough to weaken the force of the major premise in the objection. H. here, p. 24, says somewhat more than I do: There is no falsity in the vision of the thing, but in the mode of the vision, which was the divine economy; but according to my explanation there is no need for this to be said.

units.la: DCXCVI. Inst. 1. B. p. 138. In visionibus ad rem significatam est argumentum comparatorum, & quidem similium: at in motu Solis ad ejus quietem est argumentum contradicentium.
units.tr: DCXCVI. Inst. 1. B. p. 138. In visions the argument concerns the thing signified by comparisons, and indeed similar ones; but in the motion of the sun the argument concerns its rest, and the arguments are contradictory.

units.la: Resp. Quaenam sit convenientia inter visiones ecstaticas & inter locutiones receptas jam indicavi, eaque mihi hîc sufficit, nec ad meum scopum ulterior requiritur: nullibi vero docui, in locis quae pro motu Solis adducuntur, significari Terrae quietem, adeoque nec eam à nobis intelligi oportet, cùm saepius dixerim, illis locutionibus non exprimi vel signisicari vel doceri, nisi veritatem relatam ad homines, non nudam, qualis est, Terram moveri, sive potius, cum suo vortice gyrare circa suum axem.
units.tr: Reply: I have already indicated what agreement there is between ecstatic visions and received expressions, and that is enough for me here; nor is a further account required for my purpose. But nowhere have I taught that in the passages adduced for the motion of the sun the rest of the earth is signified, and therefore it ought not to be understood by us in that way, since I have often said that those expressions do not express, signify or teach anything except a truth related to men, not a bare one, such as that the earth moves, or rather, that it turns with its vortex about its own axis.

units.la: DCXCVII. Inst. 2. M. p. 197. Contradictio est manifestissima, si dicas, aliud videri, aliud intelligi.
units.tr: DCXCVII. Inst. 2. M. p. 197. It is a most manifest contradiction if you say that one thing is seen and another understood.

units.la: Resp. Si est contradictio, ergo falsum erit in visionibus illis videri virum senem sedentem in throno, & intelligi Deum ab aeterno in aeternum omnia regentem, quod cum omnium Interpretum expositione pugnabit.
units.tr: Reply: If it is a contradiction, then it will be false that in those visions an old man is seen sitting on a throne, and God is understood as ruling all things from eternity to eternity; and this will clash with the exposition of all the interpreters.

units.la: DCXCVIII. Inst. 3. B. p. 139. Typi & figurae sunt umbrae, quae suam habent obscuritatem &c. at in locis referentibus motum Solis verba tam sunt clara & rem ipsam ita nude proponunt, ut nulla veritas ullis terminis clarius proponi queat.
units.tr: DCXCVIII. Inst. 3. B. p. 139. Types and figures are shadows, which have their own obscurity, etc.; but in the passages referring to the motion of the sun the words are so clear and set forth the thing itself so bare that no truth could be set forth more clearly in any terms.

units.la: Resp. Claritatem verborum non negamus, & satis clarè significari mutationem aliquam & variationem situs Solis respectu Terrae dicimus, sed negamus, quod in illis claris verbis motus Soli realis clarè attribuatur, cùm plane non tribui certi sinus; & in eo quaestio inter nos & adversarios consistat.
units.tr: Reply: We do not deny the clarity of the words, and we say that some change and variation of the position of the sun with respect to the earth is signified quite clearly; but we deny that in those clear words a real motion is clearly attributed to the sun, since it is plainly not attributed at all, and in this the question between us and our opponents consists.

units.la: DCXCIX. Inst. 4. At etiamsi Spiritus Sanctus non doceat errorem hiis phrasibus, tamen fiet, ut alius, qui veritatem aliunde non habet cognitam in errore confirmetur.
units.tr: DCXCIX. Inst. 4. But even if the Holy Spirit does not teach error by these phrases, nevertheless it will come about that another person, who has not known the truth from elsewhere, is confirmed in error.

units.la: Resp. Hoc sibi imputet, non Spiritui Sancto, cùm ex circumstantiis scripturarum colligere debuisset, quid Sp. S. iis voluerit testari: quemadmodum, si quis imperitus ex sermone Astronomi, loquentis de phaenomenis vulgari modo, existimat, eum etiam modo vulgari judicâsse, & suum testimonium expressisse, fallaciam non Astronomo & sapienti, sed sibi ipsi debet imputare; ita si quis ex his Scripturae verbis errorem colligat, non Scripturae, sed suae inconsiderantiae adscribat oportet. Attendere enim debuisset, istas phrases, quas Scriptura usurpat, è trivio desumtas, esse de rebus à sensu longè remotis, quae ob hanc remotionem ideas rebus valdè similes repræsentare non possunt, atque ita sernicnem rebus non sic esse convenientem, ac is, qui de rebus magis propinquis, quæ non uno, sed multis sensibus simul usurpari possunt, instituitur. 2. Ille error non oberit saluti, cùm doctrina ista sit philosophica, de quâ salvâ fide dissentire licet, nisi omnes errores velis facere fundamentales; itaque non mirum, quod Spiritus Sanctus non refutaverit in Scripturâ, vel occasionem eum refutandi præbuerit.
units.tr: Reply: Let him impute this to himself, not to the Holy Spirit, since he ought to have gathered from the circumstances of the Scriptures what the Holy Spirit meant to testify by them. Just as, if some unskilled person from the speech of an astronomer, speaking of phenomena in the common manner, supposes that he also judged in the common manner and expressed his own testimony, he must impute the fallacy not to the astronomer and the wise man but to himself, so if someone draws an error from these words of Scripture, he must ascribe it not to Scripture but to his own thoughtlessness. For he ought to have observed that those phrases which Scripture uses, taken from the street, concern things far removed from the senses, and because of this remoteness cannot represent ideas very similar to the things; and thus they are not so suited to the things as is the case with those that concern nearer things, which can be used by many senses at once rather than one. 2. That error will not harm salvation, since this doctrine is philosophical, and one may dissent from it with faith intact, unless you wish to make all errors fundamental; therefore it is not surprising that the Holy Spirit did not refute it in Scripture, or did not give occasion for refuting it.

units.la: DCC. At inquit B p. 139. Egregiè vero. Ergo non erit, quod impesterum carpamus eos, 1. quorum verba tantum secundum apparentiam sunt vera. 2. quaque per se & genuino sensu rei veritati repugnant. 3. falsum docent, & 4. quorum sensus ex doctrinâ contrariâ hauriri debet, 5. quibusque vulgus in errores inducitur, modo is error non obsit saluti &c.
units.tr: DCC. But he says, p. 139: Excellently! Therefore there will be no reason for us to criticise in future those 1. whose words are true only according to appearance; 2. and which, in their own and genuine sense, contradict the truth of the thing; 3. and teach falsehood; and 4. whose sense must be drawn from a contrary doctrine; 5. and by which the crowd is led into errors, provided that the error does not harm salvation, etc.

units.la: Resp. Ad primum. Imo vero non sunt carpendi, qui formulis receptis utuntur, etsi præjudiciis innitantur sive obvolutæ sint, quamvis alii qui præjudiciis sunt occupati sibi falso videantur præjudiciorum suorum reperire in iis confirmationem. Ad secundum & tertium, Calumniæ sunt, quod doceam, per se & genuino sensu Scripturæ verba repugnare veritati, vel falsum docere, neque possum, quin eum qui talia mihi affingit pro pessimo calumniatore habeam & proclamem. Ad quartum. Verborum locorum Scripturæ, quæ utuntur formulis receptis &c. sensus debet hauriri ex textûs circumstantiis, non ex doctrinâ contrariâ, qualem nullam esse dico, cùm negemus, verba Scripturæ pro motu Solis adducta contrariari doctrinæ de Terræ delatione. Ad quintum. Neminem per se à Scripturâ in errores induci dico, sed per suam ignorantiam, putando se convenientia in Scripturâ cum suo errore reperire, cùm tamen verba Scripturæ ultra scopum ejus extendere non deberet.
units.tr: Reply: To the first. On the contrary, those who use received formulas are not to be criticised, even if they rest on prejudices or are wrapped up in them, although others who are occupied with prejudices wrongly seem to themselves to find in them a confirmation of their prejudices. To the second and third, it is calumny to say that I teach that the words of Scripture, in their own and genuine sense, contradict the truth or teach falsehood; nor can I help regarding and proclaiming as a most wicked calumniator the man who fastens such things on me. To the fourth. The sense of the words of those passages of Scripture which use received formulas, etc., must be drawn from the circumstances of the text, not from a contrary doctrine, of which I say there is none, since we deny that the words of Scripture adduced for the motion of the sun conflict with the doctrine of the earth's motion. To the fifth. I do not say that anyone is led by Scripture itself into errors, but by his own ignorance, supposing that he finds in Scripture agreement with his error, whereas Scripture ought not to be stretched beyond its purpose.

units.la: DCCI. Tertia ratio negatæ Majoris est, quòd tantùm ex antecedente inferri possit, Scripturæ locutiones esse exotericas, quòd de rebus naturalibus acroamaticè agere ejus non sit institutum. Illa autem distinctio est communis inter locutiones vulgares sive exotericas & acroamaticas, inter probationes didascalicas & dialecticas, per quam sæpè multa falsa ab auctoribus prolata excusantur, si dicatur, librum in quo hæc vel illa continentur esse exotericum, non acroamaticum, ut videre est apud Peripateticos, qui quando urgentur iis, quæ Aristoteles habet in Problematibus, sæpe confugiunt ad hanc distinctionem, dicendo, librum hunc esse exotericum, non acroamaticum. Ita Vossius de origine Idololatriæ lib. 3. p. 848. scio Philosophum (de Aristotele loquitur) in exotericis, atque ubi obiter & perfunctorie aliquid dicendum vulgares sequi opiniones folisolitum : quomodo & hoc loco Aristotelem excusant Alexander Aphrodiensis & Augustinus Niphus. Cùm itaque Scriptura de rebus sensibilibus & naturalibus nolit acroamaticè, sed tantùm exotericè agere, non mirum, si & hic sectetur exotericas locutiones, non accuratè veritatem exprimentes, sed præjudiciorum involucris vestitam.
units.tr: DCCI. The third reason for denying the major premise is that only this can be inferred from the antecedent: that the expressions of Scripture are exoteric, because it is not its purpose to treat natural things acroamatically. That distinction, however, is common between popular or exoteric expressions and acroamatic ones, between didactic and dialectical proofs, and by it many falsehoods put forward by authors are often excused, if it is said that the book in which this or that is contained is exoteric, not acroamatic; as may be seen among the Peripatetics, who, when they are pressed with what Aristotle has in the Problems, often take refuge in this distinction, saying that this book is exoteric, not acroamatic. So Vossius, On the Origin of Idolatry, book 3, p. 848: I know that the Philosopher (he is speaking of Aristotle) was accustomed, in his exoteric works, and where something had to be said in passing and cursorily, to follow common opinions; and in this place too Alexander of Aphrodisias and Agostino Nifo excuse Aristotle. Since, therefore, Scripture does not wish to treat sensible and natural things acroamatically, but only exoterically, it is not surprising if here too it follows exoteric expressions, which do not express the truth precisely, but are clothed in the wrappings of prejudices.

units.la: DCCII. Inst. 1. B. p. 141. Notam quidem esse distinctionem librorum Aristotelis in libros Exotericos & Acroamaticos, sed non locutionum.
units.tr: DCCII. Inst. 1. B. p. 141. It is indeed known that Aristotle's books are divided into Exoteric and Acroamatic, but not the expressions (locutions).

units.la: Resp. Locutiones Acroamaticæ mihi sunt eæ, quæ accuratè rem exprimunt, quibus nuda veritas & accurata docetur: Locutiones verò exotericæ sunt communes & vulgares, respondentes notitiæ communi, atque propterea veritatem ad homines relatam & præjudiciis involutam exprimentes. Exoterica locutio est eadem quæ popularis, Dialectica; Acroamatica, quæ Analytica. At popularis locutionis meminit Scaliger Exerc. 313. 'Popularuer, inquit, locutus est in quinto Politicorum philosophus. Dialecticam locutionem distinguit ab Analyticâ Neldelius in Prato Logico p. 418: At, inquit, in 8. Topicorum cap. 3. Aristoteles ἐπιστήμων seu scientiam non analytice, ut in Ethicis, sed Dialecticè tantùm accipit. Idem pag. 361, 362. Analytico tribuit suam αἰτείαν γλῶτταν, contradistinctam à communi & receptâ loquendi consuetudine, quam Dialectico assignat; illam non convenire, inquit, cum sermone imperitæ multitudinis, eamque adhibitam ab Aristotele in libris Analyticis, quod pateat eos cum Topicis conferenti.
units.tr: Reply. By acroamatic expressions I mean those which express a thing accurately, by which bare truth and exact doctrine are taught; but exoteric expressions are common and popular, corresponding to common notions, and therefore expressing truth as it relates to men and wrapped up in prejudices. An exoteric expression is the same as a popular one, a dialectical one; an acroamatic one is the same as an analytic one. Scaliger mentions the popular expression in Exercitation 313: "The philosopher spoke popularly," he says, "in the fifth book of the Politics." Neldelius, in the Prato Logico, p. 418, distinguishes the dialectical expression from the analytic: "But," he says, "in the eighth book of the Topics, chapter 3, Aristotle takes epistēmē, or science, not analytically, as in the Ethics, but only dialectically." The same author, pp. 361 and 362, assigns to the analytic its own proper language (aitian glōttan), set apart from the common and received manner of speaking, which he assigns to the dialectical; he says that the former does not agree with the speech of the unskilled multitude, and that Aristotle used it in the Analytics, as is clear to anyone who compares them with the Topics.

units.la: DCCIII. Inst. 2. B. p. 142. Sic dicendum erit, utilem esse eam distinctionem ad excusanda multa falsa in Scripturâ : aliàs non potest applicari.
units.tr: DCCIII. Inst. 2. B. p. 142. "It must be said that this distinction is useful for excusing many false statements in Scripture; otherwise it cannot be applied."

units.la: Resp. Quasi verò aliqua distinctio non possit diversis modis applicari. A me quomodo ad Scripturæ loca applicetur ex superioribus est manifestum, nimirum ad ostendendum, in locutionibus exotericis in Scripturâ usurpatis non omnia verba Scripturæ ad vivum resecanda, quasi singulis veritas aliqua doceretur, sed tantùm ea, quæ ex circumstantiis ad scopum directè facere colliguntur.
units.tr: Reply. As if some distinction could not be applied in different ways! How I apply it to the passages of Scripture is clear from what has been said above: namely, to show that in the exoteric expressions used in Scripture, not every word of Scripture is to be pressed to the quick, as though some truth were taught by each single word, but only those things which are gathered from the circumstances as bearing directly on the purpose.

units.la: CAPUT XXXIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXIII.

units.la: Objectio secunda, quòd per istam sententiam omnis cer- titudo significationis Scripturæ evertatur, eaque in nasum cereum commutetur, proponitur & refutatur.
units.tr: The second objection, that by this opinion all certainty of Scripture's meaning is overthrown and Scripture is turned into a wax nose, is set out and refuted.

units.la: DCCIV. Secundo loco contra sententiam nostram sic objicitur: Si Scriptura circa res naturales utitur formulis receptis, non accuratam veritatem, sed ad homines relatam & præjudiciis involutam referentibus: Ergo nihil certi ex Scriptura poterit concludi; adeoque statuendum erit cum Pontificiis, Scripturam esse cereum nasum qui pro lubitu possit flecti. Hanc objectionem urget B. D. p. 14. Eo modo agendi semel concesso, nihil tandem certi ex Scriptura colligi & concludi poterit: imo ne quidem in materiis fidei. Nam si in Physicis & Astronomicis pro lubitu verba in se ipsa facilia & propria ut tropos vel phrases loquendi nostro modulo accommodata exponere nobis liceat, cur non & in Theologicis & materiis fidei?
units.tr: DCCIV. Second, our view is objected to as follows: if Scripture, in speaking of natural things, uses received formulas that express not the exact truth but things related to men and involved in prejudices, then nothing certain can be concluded from Scripture. Therefore, with the Papists, we must hold that Scripture is a wax nose that can be bent at will. B. D. presses this objection at p. 14: Once this manner of acting is granted, nothing certain can at last be gathered and concluded from Scripture, indeed not even in matters of faith. For if we are allowed, at our pleasure, to expound in physics and astronomy words that are in themselves plain and proper as tropes or phrases of speech adapted to our manner, why not also in theology and matters of faith?

units.la: Resp. Neg. Conn. Majoris. Nam 1. ex circumstantiis textus semper patet, quid Scriptura his vel illis formulis doceat & significet, quidque propterea ex iis sit colligendum: itaque nunquam pro lubitu exponendæ, sed ex circumstantiis textus & scopo Spiritus Sancti declarandæ. 2. posito, non tamen concesso nec concedendo, quod circa res naturales nihil certi ex locis Scripturæ de iis, formulis vulgaribus loquentibus, posset colligi, alia tamen ratio est materiarum fidei, hoc est, eorum, quæ sola revelatione sunt cognoscibilia, cum de talibus Scriptura loquens formulis accuratam eorum veritatem referentibus soleat uti, neque circa præjudicia sensuum sint formata, utpote sub eos non cadentia, imo nec sub lumen naturæ, quod ejus sphæram activitatis longe excedant.
units.tr: Answer: I deny the connection of the major premise. For (1) from the circumstances of the text it is always clear what Scripture teaches and means by these or those formulas, and what is therefore to be gathered from them. They are therefore never to be expounded at will, but are to be declared from the circumstances of the text and the purpose of the Holy Spirit. (2) Granting, though not conceding nor ever to be conceded, that nothing certain about natural things could be gathered from passages of Scripture that speak in common formulas, the case is different with matters of faith, that is, with those things which can be known only by revelation. When Scripture speaks of such things, it customarily uses formulas that express their exact truth, and these are not shaped by the prejudices of the senses, since such matters do not fall under the senses, nor even under the light of nature, which they far exceed in their range.

units.la: 3. Res fidei & Theologicas debet Scriptura accurate docere, cum pertineant ad ejus scopum, non ita res naturales, circa quas satis est assumere ea, quæ per vulgarem notitiam de iis sunt cognita, easque formulis receptis exprimere. Itaque debet ita loqui de rebus fidei, ut non tantum formulas adhibeat, designantes veritatem aliquam generalem, prout circa res naturales contingere ostendimus, sed etiam tales, quibus specialem veritatem doceat opponendam erroribus Ethnicorum & ἀπαιδεύτων [?] Scripturæ.
units.tr: (3) Scripture ought to teach matters of faith and theology accurately, since they belong to its purpose; natural things are not so, for in them it is enough to assume what is known about them by common knowledge and to express these in received formulas. So Scripture ought to speak of matters of faith not only by using formulas that designate some general truth, as we have shown happens with natural things, but also by using such formulas as teach a specific truth to be set against the errors of the Gentiles and of the ignorant [ἀπαιδεύτων].

units.la: DCCV. Inst. 1. B. p. 144. Probari Majorem Propositionem ex eo posse, quod alibi dicam, Loqui Deum cum Vulgo, sed non cum eo sentire. Nam, inquit, si Deus loquitur cum vulgo, sed non sentit cum eo, hoc est (li utitur formulis à vulgo inventis & communiter receptis, quibus exprimitur veritas relata ad homines & praejudiciis involuta, sed non praejudiciis ipsis assentitur, neque docet) Ergo cum quaeritur de sensu verborum Spiritus Sancti nulla potest dari determinatio, cum quibus sentiat Spiritus Sanctus, an cum sapientibus, & cum quibus, num cum Ptolemaicis, Tychonianis, an Copernicanis & Cartesianis. Ergo Scriptura est nasus cereus.
units.tr: DCCV. Inst. 1. B. p. 144. The major premise can be proved from what I say elsewhere: God speaks with the common people, but does not share their opinion. For, he says, if God speaks with the common people but does not think with them, that is (he uses formulas devised by the common people and commonly received, by which a truth related to men and involved in prejudices is expressed, but does not assent to the prejudices themselves nor teach them), then when the meaning of the words of the Holy Spirit is asked, no determination can be given as to what opinion the Holy Spirit shares: whether with the wise, and with which of them, whether with the Ptolemaics, the Tychonians, or the Copernicans and Cartesians. Therefore Scripture is a wax nose.

units.la: Resp. Cum quaeritur de sensu verborum Spiritus Sancti, ex textus circumstantiis & mediis interpretandi sufficienter poterit intelligi, quid sentiat Spiritus Sanctus, nempe id, quod hoc vel illo textu docere intendit, quid vero de ipsa illa formula, per quam veritatem aliquam exprimit, Deus sentiat, num sit accurata, num vero ex praejudiciis ortum habeat, non est Spiritus Sancti determinare in Scriptura, sed ex ipsa natura & inventione vocum est discendum. Si enim ex recta ratione constet, aliquem sermonem originem debere praejudiciis, atque homines, qui praejudiciis illis sunt imbuti, utentes isto sermone solere praeter veritatem generalem etiam praejudicia significare: certum est, Spiritum Sanctum, quippe qui est auctor rectae rationis, tantum veritatem generalem significare, non etiam ipsa praejudicia. 2. Scriptura est verbum Dei quoad verum & legitimum sensum, non quoad verba quocunque modo intellecta. Cum ergo ille sensus unicus certo & infallibiliter possit colligi ex Scriptura, non obstante nostra sententia, non ex ea sententia ullo modo nasus cereus est dicenda.
units.tr: Answer: When the meaning of the words of the Holy Spirit is asked, what the Holy Spirit thinks can be sufficiently understood from the circumstances of the text and the means of interpretation, namely what he intends to teach by this or that text. But what God thinks of that very formula by which he expresses some truth, whether it is accurate or whether it arises from prejudices, it is not for the Holy Spirit to determine in Scripture; this must be learned from the nature and origin of the words themselves. For if it is clear from right reason that some way of speaking owes its origin to prejudices, and that men imbued with those prejudices, using such speech, commonly signify, besides the general truth, the prejudices also, it is certain that the Holy Spirit, who is the author of right reason, signifies only the general truth and not the prejudices themselves. (2) Scripture is the Word of God as to its true and lawful sense, not as to words understood in any way at all. Since that one sense can be gathered from Scripture with certainty and infallibly, notwithstanding our view, it cannot in any way be called a wax nose because of that view.

units.la: DCCVI. Inst. 2. B. p. 145. Si verba Sacra opinioni meae consentiant, dicam, loquitur Spiritus Sanctus ex rei veritate, sin repugnent, non loquitur ex rei veritate, Ergo denuo nasus cereus.
units.tr: DCCVI. Inst. 2. B. p. 145. If the sacred words agree with my opinion, I will say that the Holy Spirit speaks according to the truth of the matter; if they conflict with it, he does not speak according to the truth of the matter. Therefore again a wax nose.

units.la: Resp. Si haec argumentatio valeret, ergo similiter inferte possent Lutherani & Pontificii, ex nostra sententia, qua statuimus in verbis his, Panis est corpus Christi, esse tropum, sequi, Scripturam esse cereum nasum. Sic enim quis dicet: si verba sacra opinioni meae consentiant, dicam, loqui Sp. S. proprie, si repugnent, loqui tropice. At ut non sufficit hoc dicere, sed ostendendum ex textu per interpretandi regulas, ea verba tropice accipi debere, ita etiam hic non sufficit dicere, spiritum Sanctum non per omnia ea verba, quae in formula usitata & praejudiciis innitente reperiuntur, docere aliquam veritatem, sed videndum, an textus natura & scopus Spiritus Sancti requirat, ut omnibus praecise verbis aliqua veritas doceatur, an non: quod si pateat, non requirere id scopum & naturam textus, & praeterea constet, formulam esse vulgarem, satis manifestum erit, Spiritum Sanctum non per omnia praecise verba docere voluisse
units.tr: Answer: If this argument were valid, then by the same reasoning the Lutherans and the Papists could infer, from our view, which holds that in these words, This is the body of Christ, there is a trope, that Scripture is a wax nose. For someone could say: if the sacred words agree with my opinion, I will say that the Holy Spirit speaks properly; if they conflict, that he speaks tropically. But just as it is not enough to say this, but it must be shown from the text by the rules of interpretation that those words must be taken tropically, so here too it is not enough to say that the Holy Spirit does not teach some truth through every word found in a usual formula resting on prejudice. Rather, it must be considered whether the nature and purpose of the text require that some truth be taught by every single word, or not. If it is clear that the purpose and nature of the text do not require this, and besides it is established that the formula is a common one, it will be sufficiently plain that the Holy Spirit did not intend to teach through every precise word.

units.la: DCCVII. Inst. 3. B. p. 146. Stante vestra sententia veritas ex textu sacro hauriri non debebit, sed verborum sensus ex cognita veritate formandus erit, qui modus quidem exponendus textibus obscurioribus est convenientissimus, cum alibi rei veritatem clare explicat idem spiritus, sed in naturalibus controversiis est pessimus, cum nemo non intelligat rei veritatem; & sic nemo non dicet se recte intelligere, & pro sua opinione verbis hunc vel illum sensum attribuet. Item, quilibet poterit dicere, Scripturam loqui exoterice, non acroamatice.
units.tr: DCCVII. Inst. 3. B. p. 146. On your view, the truth will not be drawn from the sacred text, but the meaning of the words will have to be shaped from the truth already known. This manner is indeed most suitable for expounding obscure texts, since the same Spirit elsewhere explains the truth of the matter clearly; but in disputes about natural things it is the worst, since everyone understands the truth of the matter, and so everyone will say that he understands it rightly, and will assign this or that meaning to the words for the sake of his own opinion. Likewise, anyone will be able to say that Scripture speaks exoterically, not acroamatically.

units.la: Resp. Verborum sensus formandus est ex circumstantiis textus, quousque nempe iis aliquid Spiritus Sanctus voluerit testari. 2. An vero reliqua verba, quae non ad scopum directe faciunt, ortum habeant ex praejudiciis, ex natura & origine sermonis est deducendum. 3. Non quaeritur, quo quis queat effugio uti, quidque excipere possit ad scripturae loca contra se objecta, sed quid vere quid solide respondeat, nec sufficit si dicat, se intelligere veritatem, sed opus est ut eam demonstret, quod a nobis circa Terrae motum factum exitimamus. Nos autem non dicimus, verborum scripturae sensum ex cognita veritate naturali formandum, sed tantum, postquam verborum Scripturae sensus ex ipsius Scripturae inspectione est cognitus, ex ratione debere cognosci, num formula adhibita praejudiciis innitatur. Sic ergo clarissime liquet, ex nostra sententia non sequi, Scripturam esse cereum nasum, nisi dicas, quavis responsiones & modos interpretandi Scripturam quibusvis locis applicari posse, quod oppido quam absurdum.
units.tr: Answer: The meaning of the words must be shaped from the circumstances of the text, namely as far as the Holy Spirit has wished to bear witness to something by them. (2) Whether the remaining words, which do not bear directly on the purpose, have their origin in prejudices, must be deduced from the nature and origin of the speech. (3) The question is not by what escape a man may save himself, or what he may except to the passages of Scripture objected against him, but what he truly and solidly answers. Nor is it enough to say that he understands the truth; he must demonstrate it, as we think has been done concerning the motion of the earth. We, however, do not say that the sense of the words of Scripture must be shaped from a known natural truth, but only that, once the sense of the words of Scripture has been known from inspecting Scripture itself, it must be known by reason whether the formula used rests on prejudices. Thus it is quite clear that our view does not make Scripture a wax nose, unless you say that any answers and modes of interpreting Scripture may be applied to any passages, which is utterly absurd.

units.la: DCCVIII. Inst. 4. M. p. 199. Relinquitur saltem, majorem partem Scripturae nobis esse inutilem, quoniam nihil certi ex ea concludere possumus, quod in naturalibus plerunque loquatur contra veritatem ex captu vulgi.
units.tr: DCCVIII. Inst. 4. M. p. 199. It follows at least that the greater part of Scripture is useless to us, since we can conclude nothing certain from it, because in natural matters it for the most part speaks against the truth, according to the grasp of the common people.

units.la: Resp. Meam sententiam non esse, Scripturam loqui contra veritatem, ex toto tractatu puto liquere: quomodo autem, & quid certi ex locutionibus Scripturae de rebus naturalibus colligi possit, hoc ipso capite ostendi jam aliquoties. Hominibus vero istis, nisi calumniis saevissimis contra propriam conscientiam prolatis, onerent proximum, nihil esse pro sidii, & hinc & ex aliis infinitis locis constat.
units.tr: Answer: I think it is clear from the whole treatise that my view is not that Scripture speaks against the truth; and how, and what certainty can be gathered from the expressions of Scripture about natural things, has already been shown several times in this very chapter. As for those men, unless they bring slanders most savage and contrary to their own conscience to burden their neighbour, there is nothing in them that is sound, as this and countless other passages make plain.

units.la: DCCIX. Inst. 5. B. p. 15. Quamvis Scriptura Sacra tantum incidenter ageret de rebus naturalibus & Astronomicis, tamen de illis vere loqui credis anima pia, quae totam Scripturam ut veram recipit.
units.tr: DCCIX. Instance 5. B. p. 15. Although Holy Scripture treats of natural and astronomical matters only incidentally, a pious soul that accepts all of Scripture as true nevertheless believes that it speaks truly about them.

units.la: Resp. Et ego id credo, & concedo, vere loqui Scripturam de rebus naturalibus. Quomodo enim phrasis mea prius adhibita sit intelligenda, ex cap. xx. patet; nempe, quicquid docet, quicquid testatur, vere testatur Scriptura, atque hoc sensu vere loquitur de rebus naturalibus, hocque sensu non alio pia anima Scripturam ut veram recipit: sed ad hanc veritatem non requiritur, ut eam exprimat verbis iis, quae nullis praejudiciis innituntur, cum possit uti formulis receptis, ut tamen omnibus verbis xeisiv suam non interponat.
units.tr: Answer. I too believe this and concede that Scripture speaks truly about natural things. How my earlier phrase is to be understood is clear from chapter 20: whatever Scripture teaches or affirms, it affirms truly, and in this sense it speaks truly about natural things, and in this sense alone does a pious soul accept Scripture as true. But this truth does not require that Scripture express it in words that rest on no preconceptions. It may use the received forms of speech, provided it does not insert its own opinion into every word [λέξεσιν].

units.la: DCCX. Inst. 6. B. p. 16. Negamus, sacras literas mere incidenter Physica & Astronomica referre, quia licet ad speciales scopum non faciant, tamen faciunt ad generalem, videlicet gloriam Dei, quam etiam in Physicis & Astronomicis ostendit, cum ex illis argumenta elicit, quibus gloria divina manifestatur. Sic M. p. 201. omnia quae in Scriptura exstant faciunt ad proprium ejus institutum, quia omnis Scriptura est utilis ad doctrinam, praeterquam quod a diametro repugnet enti summe rationali, quale Spiritus Sanctus in Scriptura loquens, aliquid proferre quod ad institutum suum non faciat.
units.tr: DCCX. Instance 6. B. p. 16. We deny that the sacred writings refer to physical and astronomical matters merely incidentally. Although they do not bear on their particular aim, they do bear on the general one, namely the glory of God, which they also display in physical and astronomical matters, when they draw from them arguments by which the divine glory is made manifest. So M. p. 201: all that is found in Scripture bears on its proper purpose, since all Scripture is profitable for teaching; besides, it is utterly contrary to the nature of the supremely rational being, such as the Holy Spirit speaking in Scripture is, to set forth anything that does not bear on his purpose.

units.la: Resp. Ad hanc Instantiam responsio sufficiens habetur capite tertio, quod vide.
units.tr: Answer. A sufficient reply to this instance is given in chapter 3, which see.

units.la: DCCXI. Inst. 7. B. p 17. Hominum praesumtio non potest esse justa ratio infringendi hanc objectionem. Nam etiam multi sunt opinati, in materiis fidei Scripturam loqui secundum apparentiam, ut Marcionitae.
units.tr: DCCXI. Instance 7. B. p. 17. The presumption of men cannot be a just ground for overturning this objection. For many have thought that in matters of faith Scripture speaks according to appearance, as the Marcionites did.

units.la: Resp. Non praesumo, quod de materiis naturalibus utatur formulis receptis, sed id ex ipsis formulis manifeste cognosco, & ex sacro textu perspicio, non necessarium esse ad scopum ejus, ut quaelibet verba praecise urgeantur, quod Marcionitae non possunt dicere, & facile contra ipsos ostendi potest ex Scriptura veritas Christi humanae naturae, & in specie corporis ejus. Vide ea quae dicentur uberius cap. 37. art. 752, 753.
units.tr: Answer. I do not presume that it uses received forms of speech in natural matters; I recognise this plainly from the forms themselves and perceive from the sacred text that it is not necessary for its purpose that every word be pressed precisely. The Marcionites cannot say this, and from Scripture it can easily be shown against them that Christ's human nature, and in particular his body, is true. See what will be said more fully in chapter 37, articles 752 and 753.

units.la: DCCXII. Inst. 8. M. p. 202. Ergo in solis iis, quae absque revelatione cognosci non possunt, Scripturae infallibilitas agnosci debet: in reliquis non necessarium est accuratam scitari veritatem, adeoque ex iis nihil certi potest concludi.
units.tr: DCCXII. Instance 8. M. p. 202. Therefore the infallibility of Scripture must be acknowledged only in those things that cannot be known without revelation; in the rest it is not necessary to seek exact truth, and so nothing certain can be concluded from them.

units.la: Resp. Negatur haec sequi, cum antea ostenderim, illas formulas, quae quidem veritatem exprimunt, sed non nudam, non accuratam, verum praejudiciis involutam, non repugnare Scripturae infallibilitati, quia id, quod per illas vult Scriptura testari, verum est & infallibile.
units.tr: Answer. This does not follow. I have already shown that those forms which do express the truth, though not bare or exact but wrapped in preconceptions, do not conflict with the infallibility of Scripture, because what Scripture wishes to attest by them is true and infallible.

units.la: DCCXIII. Inst. 9. M. p. 202. Etiam circa articulos fidei possunt foveri praejudicia. Sic de creatione omnium ex nihilo, & de sacrosanctâ Trinitate foverunt Ethnici praejudicia.
units.tr: DCCXIII. Instance 9. M. p. 202. Even concerning the articles of faith, preconceptions can be nourished. Thus the Gentiles nourished preconceptions about the creation of all things out of nothing and about the most holy Trinity.

units.la: Resp. 1. Non tamen praejudicia infantiae & sensuum, quibus sermo communis innititur, de quibus hic agitur, & eo modo quo cap. 1. sunt descripta. Quòd enim circa revelationem possint foveri errores non nego. 2. omnia ex nihilo creata etiam ex lumine naturae potest cognosci & demonstrari estque res non ex sola revelatione cognoscibilis, quâ de re articulo 704. fui locutus.
units.tr: Answer. 1. These are not, however, the preconceptions of infancy and of the senses on which common speech rests, which are what is at issue here, and which are described as in chapter 1. That errors can be fostered concerning revelation I do not deny. 2. That all things were created out of nothing can also be known and demonstrated from the light of nature; it is a matter not knowable from revelation alone, concerning which I spoke in article 704.

units.la: DCCXIV. Inst. 10. Jam docuimus Sacra Scriptura scopum esse, docere, quomodo gloria divina in creaturis sit manifesta, quae arguuntur errores male cogitantium de rebus naturalibus.
units.tr: DCCXIV. Instance 10. We have already taught that the aim of Holy Scripture is to teach how the divine glory is manifest in creatures, and by this errors of those who think badly about natural things are refuted.

units.la: Resp. Et nos jam ad id cap. 1. respondimus, nec enim requiritur ad gloriam Dei manifestandam ex creaturis, ut tota natura rerum explicetur, sed aliquis creaturarum effectus sufficit, qui ad sensum cognoscitur. Sic Ps. xix gloriam Dei deducit Psalmista, ex hoc Solis effectu, quod Terram illuminet & calefaciat per variationem situs, quod quidem sine motu Solis reali sufficienter fieri potuit.
units.tr: Answer. We have already replied to this in chapter 1. For to make the glory of God manifest from creatures it is not required that the whole nature of things be explained; a single effect of creatures suffices, one that is known by the senses. Thus in Psalm 19 the Psalmist infers God's glory from this effect of the sun, that it illuminates and warms the earth through its changing position, which indeed could be done sufficiently without any real motion of the sun.

units.la: DCCXV. Inst. 11. B p. 141. Sic tamen non parum derogat auctoritati Scripturae & doctrinae Ecclesiarum reformatarum. Multi sunt nobis adversarii, quorum alii divinitatem & auctoritatem Scripturae sacrae in totum negant, alii pro lubitu Scripturae affingere volunt, ut Pontifici: Qui sacrarum literarum auctoritatem negant, satis habent, si illas multis in locis falsitatis arguere possint, quod ex tuâ sententiâ habebunt.
units.tr: DCCXV. Instance 11. B. p. 141. Yet in this way the authority of Scripture and the teaching of the reformed Churches are not a little diminished. We have many adversaries: some altogether deny the divinity and authority of Holy Scripture, others want to attribute to it whatever they please, as the Papist does. Those who deny the authority of the sacred letters are content if they can charge them with falsehood in many places, which they will have from your opinion.

units.la: Resp. Negatur, quod ex mea sententia sequatur, Scripturam falsum docere, & satis me ab illa sequela puto liberasse, coram omnibus rerum aequis aestimatoribus, qui citra affectum judicare volunt; alios non moror, cum vix aliquid dici possit tam clarum, quod verborum captatores non in alium sensum trahere possint. Atque ita nihil habebunt Ethnici, quod contra auctoritatem Scripturae usurpare possint.
units.tr: Answer. It is denied that what follows from my opinion is that Scripture teaches falsehood. I think I have freed myself well enough from that charge before all fair judges of things who wish to judge without partisanship; I will not dwell on others, since there is hardly anything so clear that word-catchers cannot twist it into another sense. And so the Gentiles will have nothing that they can use against the authority of Scripture.

units.la: DCCXVI. Inst. 12. B. p. 148. Si dicas Scripturam quidem in naturalibus uti formulis, quae praejudiciis innituntur, non in materiis fidei, audies, qui in minori est mendax, nec in majori fide dignus. 2. Deus est totus veritas.
units.tr: DCCXVI. Instance 12. B. p. 148. If you say that Scripture indeed uses in natural matters forms that rest on preconceptions, but not in matters of faith, you will hear: he who is a liar in the lesser matter is not to be trusted in the greater. 2. God is wholly truth.

units.la: Resp. At ego nego & pernego, sequi ex mea sententia. Deum esse mendacem: vide istam sequelam plane refutatam in sequentibus; qui vero id tanquam meam sententiam conatur mihi attribuere, cum non possum non columniae atrocissimae reum habere.
units.tr: Answer. But I deny and utterly deny that this follows from my opinion: that God is a liar. See this inference thoroughly refuted in what follows. But whoever tries to attribute this to me as my opinion lays himself open to the most atrocious slander.

units.la: DCCXVII. Inst. 13. B. p. 149. Si distinctione locutionum in Acroamaticas maticas & Exotericas in medium procedu, risum movebis adversario,illam non recipienti.
units.tr: DCCXVII. Instance 13. B. p. 149. If you bring forward the distinction of expressions into acroamatic and exoteric, you will make your opponent laugh, since he does not accept it.

units.la: Resp. Imò risum movebit adversarius eam rejiciens, cum sit manifestissima, uti suprà demonstratum.
units.tr: Answer. Rather, the opponent who rejects it will make himself laughable, since it is most manifest, as shown above.

units.la: DCCXVIII. Inst. 14. B. p. 149. Si ad probandum dogma aliquod Anti-Pontificium urgere velis verba Scriptura sacra, audies sensum verborum illorum à cognitione rei ipsius dependere, veritatem autem cognosci judicio Pontificis Romani, plane ut hic sensum verborum sacra Scriptura in naturalibus vis dependere à veritate Philosophicâ, quam Cartesius docet.
units.tr: DCCXVIII. Instance 14. B. p. 149. If you wish to press the words of Holy Scripture to prove some anti-Papal doctrine, you will hear that the sense of those words depends on knowledge of the thing itself, and that the truth is known by the judgment of the Roman Pontiff. Just so, you here want the sense of the words of Holy Scripture in natural matters to depend on philosophical truth, which Descartes teaches.

units.la: Resp. Ineptissimè Pontificii sic essent excepturi, cum statuam cum nostris, sensum Scripturæ verborum debere per medium interpretandi cognosci, qualia sunt scopi consideratio, antecedentium & consequentium collatio &c. nec ullibi dixerim, sensum verborum Scripturæ dependere à veritate Philosophicâ.
units.tr: Answer. The Papists would object most absurdly in this way, since I hold with our people that the sense of the words of Scripture must be known through the usual means of interpretation, such as consideration of the aim, comparison of what precedes and follows, and so on. Nor have I ever said anywhere that the sense of the words of Scripture depends on philosophical truth.

units.la: DCCXIX. Inst. 15. B. p. 149. Alios adversarios auctoritatem Scripturæ quidem admittentes, sed in materiâ fidei errantes, posità hac sententiâ, quomodo sis constrictarus videre nequeo.
units.tr: DCCXIX. Instance 15. B. p. 149. I cannot see how, once this opinion is laid down, you can constrain other adversaries who admit the authority of Scripture but err in matters of faith.

units.la: Resp. Hoc simili ratione fiet, quâ superiores constrinxi, ostendendo, eos prave ex mea doctrinâ conclusisse, quod ex eâ nullatenus educi potest; nimirum, Scripturam falsum docere in rebus naturalibus, vel mentiri &c. adeoque malè ea tanquam certa supponere, cum à me planè rejiciantur. Sic ergo nihil periculi erit contra adversarios, quando indubitata auctoritas Scripturæ in omnibus retinetur, quod ego facio, cum inter nos de sensu locorum Scripturæ ex ipso textu colligendo sit quæstio, non de auctoritate & veritate Scripturæ. Atque hoc est πεῶτον ψεῦδος ad-versariorum, si non πεῶτη ἀληθεια, agi de auctoritate & veritate Scripturæ, stentorea voce clamantium.
units.tr: Answer. This will be done in the same way as I constrained them above, by showing that they drew wrong conclusions from my doctrine, which cannot be deduced from it in any way: namely, that Scripture teaches falsehood in natural matters, or lies, and so on, and that they therefore wrongly assume these things as certain, since they are utterly rejected by me. So there will be no danger against the adversaries when the indubitable authority of Scripture is kept intact in all things, as I do, since between us the question is about gathering the sense of passages of Scripture from the text itself, not about the authority and truth of Scripture. And this is the first falsehood [πρῶτον ψεῦδος] of the adversaries, if not the first truth [πρώτη ἀλήθεια], that they cry out in stentorian voices that the authority and truth of Scripture is at issue.

units.la: DCCXX. Inst. 16. M p. 200. Et secundum te, Scriptura loquitur secundum erroneam opinionem vulgi de rebus moralibus & practicis cap. 7. art. 1. de articulis fidei ratione aliquomodo cognoscibilibus cap. 10. art. 1. de veritate Christi cap. 7. Joh. V. 31. de redemtione per ejus sanguinem cap. 7. art. 14. Itaque verborum protestatio diserte contradicit factis.
units.tr: DCCXX. Instance 16. M. p. 200. And according to you, Scripture speaks according to the erroneous opinion of the common people about moral and practical matters (chapter 7, article 1); about the articles of faith that are in some measure knowable by reason (chapter 10, article 1); about the truth of Christ (chapter 7, John 5:31); about redemption through his blood (chapter 7, article 14). Therefore the protestation of the words flatly contradicts the facts.

units.la: Resp. 1. Ipse adversarius dicit, quatenus Sp. S salvâ veracitate suâ falsas opiniones aliorum posset referre, & ad tempus absque speciali refutatione premittere, sæpius nisi fallor, dictum est. Ergo apparet, posse id fieri salva veracitate, quod est illud ipsum quod ego intendo; ergo non hic negavi simpliciter, Scripturam etiam circa res morales &c uti phrasibus innitentibus apparentiæ & opinioni erroneæ super eâ fundatæ, quod suis locis explicuiplicui, sed nego istius Maj. Connexionem: Si Scriptura circa res naturales adhibet formulas praejudiciis sensuum & infantiae innitentes, Ergo idem facit circa res fidei. Hae enim consequentiae quidem sunt legitimae: Si de rebus moralibus & practicis loquentes Scripturae saepe usurpant locutiones correspondentes vel simpliciter opinioni, vel externae apparentiae aut opinioni, quae super externa apparentia fundata est, ergo Scripturae non repugnat, ut utatur formulis receptis circa res naturales etiam in praejudiciis fundatis. Item: si Scriptura loquens de Deo multas adhibet phrases, quae praejudiciis infantiae & sensuum innituntur, atque veritatem relatam ad homines & praejudiciis involutam referentes, Ergo multo minus ejus auctoritati & veritati repugnabit, si idem faciat circa res naturales; quia per se patet, si harum formularum usus laederet auctoritatem Scripturae, maxime laederet in rebus fidei, ubi maxime ea necessaria, adeoque minus essent ibi usurpandae: sed non vice versa possum colligere: si Scriptura de iis, quae non pertinent ad institutum formulis vulgaribus utitur, Ergo similiter de iis quae ad institutum pertinent. Hoc ex priori illo sequi nego: quia non licet dicere, si minus non laedit, Ergo nec majus; sed si majus non laedit, quod maxime videbatur laesurum, sequitur etiam minus non laedere. Et de iis, quae ad institutum pertinent debet ita loqui, ut quamvis alicubi utatur formulis vulgaribus, tamen, (ut loquuntur adversarii,) alibi se explicet, de rebus vero naturalibus tali explicatione accurata non est opus.
units.tr: Reply 1. The adversary himself says: "that the Holy Spirit, while keeping his truthfulness intact, could report false opinions of others and set them down for a time without special refutation, has been said often, unless I am mistaken." So it is clear that this can be done while truthfulness is preserved, which is exactly what I maintain. I have not simply denied that Scripture, also in moral matters and the like, uses phrases that rest on appearance and on the erroneous opinion founded upon that appearance; I explained this in its own places. What I deny is the connection of this major premise: if Scripture, when dealing with natural things, employs expressions that rest on the prejudices of the senses and of infancy, then it does the same in matters of faith. The following inferences are indeed valid: if Scripture, speaking of moral and practical matters, often uses expressions that correspond either simply to opinion or to outward appearance, or to an opinion founded on outward appearance, then it is not inconsistent for Scripture to use the accepted forms of speech about natural things, even those founded on prejudices. Likewise: if Scripture, speaking of God, uses many phrases that rest on the prejudices of infancy and of the senses, and refers truth related to men and wrapped in prejudices, then it will be even less inconsistent with its authority and truth if it does the same concerning natural things; for it is evident in itself that if the use of these expressions damaged the authority of Scripture, it would damage it most in matters of faith, where they are most necessary, and so they should be used there least. But the converse does not follow: if Scripture uses common forms concerning things that do not belong to its purpose, then similarly concerning things that do belong to it. I deny that this follows from the former, for it is not permitted to say: if the lesser does no harm, then neither does the greater. But if the greater does no harm, which seemed most likely to do harm, it follows that the lesser does no harm either. And concerning things that belong to its purpose, Scripture ought to speak in such a way that, although it uses common forms somewhere, it nevertheless (as the adversaries put it) explains itself elsewhere; but concerning natural things such exact explanation is not needed.

units.la: DCCXXI. Inst. 17. M. p. 203. Si Spiritus Sanctus errores Ethnicorum circa Scripturae veritatem tenetur eximere, non tenetur ponere obicem, quod faceret res multas falsas asserendo.
units.tr: DCCXXI. Inst. 17. M. p. 203. If the Holy Spirit is bound to free the errors of the Gentiles concerning the truth of Scripture, he is not bound to place an obstacle in the way, which he would do by asserting many things that are false.

units.la: Resp. Omnino hunc obicem esse futurum concedo, sed nego, hanc meam esse sententiam, cum integro capite hanc sequelam ex mea sententia non fuere satis manifeste ostenderim.
units.tr: Reply. I concede that this obstacle would indeed arise, but I deny that this is my opinion, since I have not sufficiently shown clearly enough, in the whole chapter, that this consequence follows from my view.

units.la: DCCXXII. Inst. 18. M. p. 203. Anne propterea, quod Scriptura non tenetur eximere errores, qui de rebus naturalibus cogitantur, quando loquitur secundum erroneam opinionem hominum, non erit nasus cereus? quomodo ista cohaerent?
units.tr: DCCXXII. Inst. 18. M. p. 203. Will it not therefore be a wax nose, because Scripture is not bound to free from the errors that are thought concerning natural things, when it speaks according to the erroneous opinion of men? How do these things hang together?

units.la: Resp. Argumenta fuerunt duo artic. 704. propter affinitatem conjuncta, ad quorum posterius, (quod tale erat: si in Physicis verba facilia, ut tropos vel phrases loquendi nostro modulo accommodatas exponerenobis liceat, Ergo etiam hoc licebit in rebus Theologicis & materiis fidei) recte ostenderam, negari consequentiam ob rationem disparem hanc: quia Scriptura tenetur eximere errores circa res Theologicas & fidei, adeoque ita loqui, ut, quamvis aliquando formu'as vulgares adhibeat, tamen ex aliis locis cognoscatur accurata veritas, secus se res habet in naturalibus.
units.tr: Reply. There were two arguments, article 704, joined together because of their affinity. Concerning the second of these, which ran: if we are allowed to explain in physics words that are easy, such as tropes or phrases of speech adapted to our manner, then this will also be allowed in theological matters and matters of faith, I had rightly shown that the inference is denied for this disparate reason: Scripture is bound to free from errors concerning theological matters and matters of faith, and so to speak in such a way that, although it sometimes uses common forms, the accurate truth is nevertheless known from other passages. It is otherwise with natural things.

units.la: DCCXXIII. Inst. 19. M. p. 206. Si Scriptura alicubi de Deo & attributis ejus utitur formulis accuratis, nihil morans captum vulgi, tum alicubi animo plebejis crucem figeret, aut in iis locis, in quibus de Deo & ejus attributis minus accurate loquitur, id praeter necessitatem agere censendum erit; quoniam si necessitas compelleret, in uno loco aeque ac in alio faciendum fuisset.
units.tr: DCCXXIII. Inst. 19. M. p. 206. If Scripture somewhere uses exact forms concerning God and his attributes, without regard to the grasp of the common people, then somewhere else, in the passages where it speaks less accurately about God and his attributes, it must be judged to do so beyond necessity; for if necessity compelled it, it would have had to do the same in the one place as in the other.

units.la: Resp. Dixi equidem, Sp S. de rebus naturalibus loquentem voluisse uti formulis vulgaribus, ne crucem vulgo figeret, recedendo à receptâ loquendi consuetudine, ubi accuratam veritatem significari non erat necesse: at alia est ratio Dei & attributorum ejus; ibi etsi Scriptura etiam locutionibus vulgaribus utatur, quando accuratam veritatem significari non est necesse, tamen quoniam aliquando est necesse accuratam veritatem significari, opus etiam est, ut Scriptura formulis accuratis utatur.
units.tr: Reply. I did indeed say that the Holy Spirit, when speaking of natural things, wished to use common forms, so as not to set a cross before the common people, departing from the accepted manner of speaking, where it was not necessary to signify the accurate truth. But the case of God and his attributes is different. There, although Scripture also uses common expressions when it is not necessary to signify the accurate truth, nevertheless, since it is sometimes necessary to signify the accurate truth, it is also needful that Scripture use exact forms.

units.la: DCCXXIV. Inst. 20. M. p. 206. At etiam res morales & practicae articulos fidei concernunt, de quibus tamen dicis, usurpari formulas innitentes opinioni super externa apparentia fundata: si enim nullos fidei articulos concernunt, tum omnis tractatio de vivendi ratione, de virtutibus & vitiis ex fidei doctrina limitibus plane exterminabitur.
units.tr: DCCXXIV. Inst. 20. M. p. 206. But moral and practical matters also concern the articles of faith, though you say that expressions resting on opinion founded on outward appearance are used about them. For if they concern no articles of faith, then all discussion of the rule of life, of virtues and vices, will be utterly banished from the limits of the doctrine of faith.

units.la: Resp. Per fidei articulos intelligo strictè sic dictos, hoc est, sola revelatione cognoscendos, uti satis explicatum, cùm alias non nesciam, omne quod docetur in Scripturis esse fide acceptandum, adeoque etiam qua virtutes & vitia concernit, quoniam omni illi propter divinae auctoritatis testimonium assentimur, quod tamen quatenus ex lumine rationis cognoscitur & per eam demonstratur, scientiae sive certae cognitionis nomen sortitur.
units.tr: Reply. By articles of faith I understand those strictly so called, that is, those knowable by revelation alone, as has been sufficiently explained; for I am not unaware that everything taught in the Scriptures is to be accepted by faith, and so also that which concerns virtues and vices, since we assent to all of it on account of the testimony of divine authority. Yet insofar as it is known from the light of reason and demonstrated by it, it receives the name of science, or certain knowledge.

units.la: DCCXXV. Inst. 21. B. p. 147. Eundem modum exponendi sacras literas, etiam in materiis fidei, ut in attributis Dei, Melchisedeco, verbu Christi Job. V. 31. 1 Pet. II. introducere conatur, nec te mere intra terminos naturalium comitnes.
units.tr: DCCXXV. Inst. 21. B. p. 147. He tries to introduce the same mode of expounding the sacred letters also in matters of faith, as in the attributes of God, Melchizedek, the words of Christ in John 5:31, 1 Peter 2, and he does not merely keep you within the bounds of natural things.

units.la: Resp. Quomodo illis argumentis utar salvâ Scripturae auctoritate. & verit. videat lector suis in locis. Hic tantum dixi, de rebus Theologicis ita debere loqui Scripturam, ut etiamsi non omnibus formulis accuratam & specialem veritatem designet, id tamen faciat aliquibus, cum ejus sit scopus eas docere.
units.tr: Reply. How I would use those arguments while preserving the authority and truth of Scripture, let the reader see in their own places. Here I have only said that Scripture ought to speak of theological matters in such a way that, even if it does not designate the accurate and specific truth by all its forms, it nevertheless does so by some, since its purpose is to teach them.

units.la: CAPUT XXXIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXIV.

units.la: Objectio tertia desumta ex Joh. xvi. 13. cum instantiùs proponitur & refutatur.
units.tr: The third objection, drawn from John 16:13, is set out more forcefully and refuted.

units.la: DCCXXVI. Sequitur Objectio tertia contra nostram sententiam, quam desumimus ex S. p. 402. Cùm Apostolis Christi, & in eorum persona omnibus amanuensibus Sp. S. hæc promissio facta fuerit Joh. xvi. 13. Spiritus ille veritatis dux via vobis erit in omnem veritatem: quis est qui existimet citra blasphemiam in Sp. S. dici posse, quod suos amanuenses, quotiescunque aut ex professo, aut incidenter de rebus naturalibus verba factuři erant, non eruditi de ipsa veritate, sed solummodo monuerit, quid ab errante vulgo statueretur? Similia habet p. 406. Accommodat se quidem Scriptura nostro captui & infirmitati, sic tamen, ut non desinat esse veritatis Spiritus, quo elogio sane condecorari non posset, si sic sese demitteret ad nostram infirmitatem, ut cum mentientibus mentiretur, cum errantibus erraret.
units.tr: DCCXXVI. The third objection against our view follows, which we take from page 402: Since this promise was made to the apostles of Christ, and in their person to all the amanuenses of the Holy Spirit, John 16:13, "That Spirit of truth will guide you into all truth": who would think it possible, without blasphemy, to say of the Holy Spirit that when his amanuenses were going to speak, whether professedly or incidentally, about natural things, he did not teach them the truth itself, but only warned them what the erring crowd held? He says something similar on page 406: Scripture indeed adapts itself to our capacity and weakness, yet in such a way that it does not cease to be the Spirit of truth. That praise could hardly belong to him if he so lowered himself to our weakness that he lied with liars and erred with those who err.

units.la: DCCXXVII. Resp. Verba Christi Joh. xvi. 13. sunt intelligenda secundum subjectam materiam, & vox omnis secundum illam restringenda. Dixerat Christus versu præcedenti, se habere multa dicenda suis discipulis: at an illa erant veritates Physicæ? non utique; sed veritates cœlestes de Euangelio Christi, quod debebant annunciare per totum mundum. Illa ergo Sp. S. erat suppleturus, & reipsa supplevit, habemusque in scriptis Apostolicis consignata, in quibus rerum naturalium scientificam explicationem non reperimus. Et ita Belgæ Interpretes: in alle waerheyt] namelijck die u noodigh sal zijn te weten tot uytvoeringe van u ampt, Matth. xxv. 19. alsoo dat ghy de selve niet alleen sult weten, maer oock in het leeren der selve niet en sult konnen duralen, id est, in omnem veritatem quae vobis scitu erit necessaria ad muneris vestri functionem, Matth. xxv iii. 19. ita ut illam non solum sciatis, sed etiam in ea docen-da errori non sitis obnoxii suturi.
units.tr: DCCXXVII. Reply: The words of Christ in John 16:13 must be understood according to the subject matter, and the word all must be restricted accordingly. In the preceding verse Christ had said that he had many things to say to his disciples. But were those things truths of physics? Certainly not; they were heavenly truths about the gospel of Christ, which they were to proclaim throughout the whole world. The Spirit was therefore to supply these, and indeed did supply them, and we have them recorded in the apostolic writings, in which we find no scientific explanation of natural things. The Dutch translators also render it so: in alle waerheyt, namely what will be necessary for you to know for the discharge of your office (Matt. 25:19), so that you will not only know it but also will not be liable to err in teaching it; that is, "into all truth which shall be necessary for you to know for the performance of your ministry (Matt. 25:19), so that you not only know it but also will not be liable to err in teaching it."

units.la: 2. Non ergo est ulla inter hæc connexio: Sp. S. vos ducet in omnem veritatem cœlestem: Ergo ubi incidenter agit de rebus naturalibus, formulis utetur talibus, quæ earum nudam veritatem proponant, nullis involucris opinionum à fallaciis sensuum obtectam. Sed potius, quia hic erat Sp. S. scopus, veritatem cœlestem docere non tantum eruditos, sed etiam plebejos homines, de rebus naturalibus vulgarem & communem notitiam tantum habentes, noluit se occupare in rerum naturalium lium explicatione philosophica, sed ad scopum suum collimans, dum incideret in res naturales, satis habuit uti formulis ex vulgari notitia ortis, etiamsi ea aliquando erronea essent. 3. Quare nulla blasphemia in Sp. S. committitur, cum non negetur, id Sp. S. potuisse, sed tantum asseratur, id illum pro singulari sapientia noluisse, uti superius ex Calvino & Paraeo vidimus. 4. Nihil veracitati Sp. S. detrahitur per nostram assertionem; non enim, ut supra notavimus, etsi cum vulgo loquatur, etiam cum eo sentit, nec errat cum errantibus, sed usurpando formulas dictas, veritatem generalem per eas docet, de praejudiciis vero quibus innituntur necem suam non instituit.
units.tr: 2. There is therefore no connection between these two claims: "The Holy Spirit will lead you into all heavenly truth," and "Therefore when he incidentally deals with natural things he will use such formulas as set out their bare truth, covered by no wrappings of opinion arising from the deceptions of the senses." Rather, since the Spirit's purpose here was to teach heavenly truth not only to the learned but also to common people, who had only a vulgar and ordinary knowledge of natural things, he did not wish to occupy himself with a philosophical explanation of natural things. Aiming at his purpose, when he came to natural things he was content to use formulas arising from ordinary knowledge, even if these were sometimes erroneous. 3. Hence no blasphemy is committed against the Holy Spirit, since it is not denied that he could have done so, but only asserted that for his singular wisdom he did not wish to, as we saw above from Calvin and Paraeus. 4. Nothing is taken from the Spirit's truthfulness by our assertion. For, as we have noted above, although he speaks with the common people, he does not therefore think with them, nor does he err with those who err; by using the formulas in question, he teaches a general truth through them, but he does not work to destroy the prejudices on which they rest.

units.la: DCCXXVIII. At inquit: Si tua obtineat sententia, sequetur Sp.S. cum mentientibus mentiri & cum errantibus errare.
units.tr: DCCXXVIII. But he says: If your view prevails, it will follow that the Holy Spirit lies with liars and errs with those who err.

units.la: Resp. Negatur ista sequela, cujus infirmitas sufficienter potest cognosci ex cap. 30. in quo ostendimus, Scripturam per formulas tales vulgares errorem non testari; sed tamen ut evidentius id hic appareat, consideremus tantum, quid sit mendacium, ex quo apparebit, ejus definitionem non posse Sp. S. sermonibus ex nostra sententia applicari. Mendacium ab Augustino libro contra Mendac. ad Crescentium ita describitur: Mendacium est falsa significatio cum voluntate fallendi, & a Wollebio lib. 2. cap. 13. Mendacium est, quo falsum animo fallendi verbis factisque significatur. At per illas locutiones a Sp. S. adhibitas nec falsum significatur, nec animus fallendi adest: Ergo. Quid per eas significetur, & jam dictum & porro dicetur, nempe verum, sed generale & latens sub involucro praejudicii, quod non consignificatur, sed a vero est devolvendum.
units.tr: Reply: That consequence is denied. Its weakness can sufficiently be recognised from chapter 30, in which we showed that Scripture does not attest error through such common formulas. Yet, to make this clearer here, let us consider only what a lie is, and it will appear that its definition cannot be applied to the Holy Spirit's words on our view. Augustine, in his book against lying to Crescentius, describes a lie thus: A lie is a false signification with the will to deceive. And Wollebius, book 2, chapter 13: A lie is that by which what is false is signified, in words or deeds, with the intention of deceiving. But by those expressions used by the Holy Spirit neither something false is signified, nor is there an intention to deceive. Therefore, etc. What is signified by them has already been said and will be said further: namely the truth, but a general truth, hidden beneath the covering of a prejudice, which is not co-signified, but must be unrolled from the truth.

units.la: DCCXXIX. Inst. 1. M. p. 207. Mea responsiones ad hoc argumentum, ad unum omnes ne vim ejus quidem attingere.
units.tr: DCCXXIX. Inst. 1, M., p. 207: My replies to this argument do not touch its force at all, not even on one point.

units.la: Resp. Id judicandum relinquimus lectori.
units.tr: Reply: We leave that judgement to the reader.

units.la: DCCXXX. Inst. 2. M. p. 208. Promittitur Spiritus Sanctus qui eos ducturus sit in omnem veritatem & consequenter in nullam falsitatem, quod sit locutione falsi.
units.tr: DCCXXX. Inst. 2, M., p. 208: The Holy Spirit is promised, who is going to lead them into all truth, and consequently into no falsehood, which is a manner of speaking of what is false.

units.la: Resp. Promittitur Sp. S. qui est ducturus in omnem veritatem, hoc sensu, ut nulla non veritatem coelestem & salutare sit docturus. 2. Ex mea sententia non sequi, Sp. S. in falsitatem homines deducere cap. 32. cliendi.
units.tr: Reply: The Holy Spirit is promised as one who is going to lead into all truth, in the sense that he will teach every heavenly and saving truth. 2. From my view it does not follow that the Spirit leads men into falsehood; see chapter 32.

units.la: DCCXXXI. Inst. 3. M. p. 209. At dum probare allaboras, Sp: S. non debere plebejis crucem figere, sive obstaculum cognitioni objicere, ipse Spiritui Sancto crucem manifeste figis, dum illum huc adigis, ut non possit ullibi ex stricta rei veritate loqui, ubi quidem illa opinioni vulgi repugnat, nisi velit audire, plebejorum cognitioni obstaculum objecisse.
units.tr: DCCXXXI. Inst. 3, M., p. 209: But while you labour to prove that the Holy Spirit ought not to set a cross before common people, or put an obstacle in the way of their knowledge, you clearly set a cross before the Holy Spirit himself, while you drive him to this point, that he could nowhere speak from the strict truth of the matter where it contradicts the opinion of the crowd, unless he were willing to be heard as having put an obstacle in the way of the knowledge of common people.

units.la: Resp. Negatur, me hîc velle quicquam præscribere Spiritui S. Id agit ipse pro sapientia sua, ut sese accommodet ad captum, &, ubi non opus est, nullam difficultatem injiciat, usurpando formulas inusitatas, ad veritatem scopo suo convenientem significandam, & proinde non intelligibiles.
units.tr: Reply: It is denied that I wish here to prescribe anything to the Holy Spirit. He himself acts according to his wisdom, so as to accommodate himself to our capacity, and where there is no need he throws in no difficulty, by using unusual formulas to signify a truth suited to his purpose, which therefore are not intelligible.

units.la: DCCXXXII. Inst. 4. M. p. 210. Blasphemia saltem proximum est, statuere: Sp. S. in omnem veritatem ducturum cœlesti veritati propugnanda falsa naturalia admiscepe debuisse. 2. Spiritum veritatis ex vestra hypothesi non potuisse in naturalibus semper accuratam veritatem loqui.
units.tr: DCCXXXII. Inst. 4, M., p. 210: It is at least close to blasphemy to hold that the Holy Spirit, who was to lead into all truth, ought to have mixed false natural claims in with the defence of heavenly truth. 2. According to your hypothesis, the Spirit of truth could not always speak with accurate truth in natural matters.

units.la: Resp. At calumnia est, hoc mihi affingere, quum satis ostenderim, non sequi, quod illis formulis voluerit fallitatem docere, vel testari: videatur cap. 32. in quo prolixè hæc objectio refutata. 2. Negamus, ex nostra hypothesi sequi, non potuisse veritatem accuratam loqui, sed tantum, noluisse uti formulis accuratis, idque sapienter & convenienter suo instituto.
units.tr: Reply: This is a slander to attribute to me, since I have sufficiently shown that it does not follow that he wished to teach or attest falsehood by those formulas; see chapter 32, where this objection is refuted at length. 2. We deny that on our hypothesis it follows that he could not speak accurate truth; it follows only that he did not wish to use accurate formulas, and he did this wisely and in keeping with his purpose.

units.la: DCCXXXIII. Inst. 5. M. p. 211. Mendacium nihil aliud est, quàm Enunciatio falsa scienter facta, hujus enunciationis effectum est decipere, hoc autem sive proferens intendat, sive non, definitionem mendacii non mutat.
units.tr: DCCXXXIII. Inst. 5, M., p. 211: A lie is nothing other than a false statement made knowingly; the effect of such a statement is to deceive, and whether the speaker intends this or not does not change the definition of a lie.

units.la: Resp. Intentionem fallendi ad mendacium requiri ex Augustino & Wollebrio supra vidimus. Quod si hæc M. sit sufficiens definitio mendacii, etiam ironiæ mendacia erunt dicenda, cum sint enunciationes falsæ scienter factæ: Effectus verò decipiendi nihil quicquam ad rationem formalem mendacii facit, cum ille merè sit eventualis, nec semper, nec necessariò mendacium consequatur. Sic sunt mendacia in Deum, qui tamen decipi nequit, sic mentitur qui coram sapiente, vel aliter de re informato rem falsam contra animi sententiam animo decipiendi, sive fide suâ interpositâ narrat, etsi talis actu non decipiatur.
units.tr: Reply: We have seen above, from Augustine and Wollebius, that an intention to deceive is required for a lie. If this definition of M. were sufficient, then ironical statements would also have to be called lies, since they are false statements made knowingly. But the effect of deceiving contributes nothing to the formal nature of a lie, since it is merely eventual, and a lie does not always and necessarily result in deception. Thus there are lies told against God, who yet cannot be deceived; and one lies who, before a wise man, or about a matter known otherwise, tells a false thing against his own conviction with intent to deceive, even on his oath, though such a person is not actually deceived.

units.la: DCCXXXIV. Inst. 6. M. p. 9. Si Spiritus S. iis formulis loquendi aliud proferat, aliud intelligat, & sentiat, tum incurrit in formale vitium mendacii.
units.tr: DCCXXXIV. Inst. 6, M., p. 9: If the Holy Spirit, in such forms of speech, says one thing and intends and thinks another, then he incurs the formal fault of lying.

units.la: Resp. Qui ita loquitur, ut per suam loquelam aliquid significet, cujus contrarium sentit, intentione decipiendi, cum mentiri dicimus, sed negamus, id facere eum qui utitur formulis receptis. Sp. S. ergo per iStas formulas profert, hoc est, significat veritatem generalem, quam etiam in mente concepit, non verò præjudicium, quod in medio reliquit.
units.tr: Reply: One who speaks so as, by his utterance, to signify something whose contrary he thinks, with intent to deceive, is someone we say lies; but we deny that he does so who uses received formulas. The Holy Spirit therefore uses these formulas to express, that is, to signify, the general truth which he has also conceived in his mind, and not the prejudice which he has left in the middle.

units.la: CAPUT XXXV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXV.

units.la: Objectiones quarta & quinta, quarum illa desumitur à po- tentia & voluntate Dei, hæc à comparatione Dei cum artificibus manuariis, proponuntur & refelluntur.
units.tr: The fourth and fifth objections are set out and refuted: the fourth is drawn from the power and will of God, the fifth from the comparison of God with manual craftsmen.

units.la: DCCXXXV. Sequitur Objectio Quarta S. p. 402. Si statuendum sit, Spiritum Sanctum de rebus naturalibus loqui ex mente vulgi, aut non potuerit suos erudire de veritate rerum naturalium, aut si potuerit noluit. At neutrum dici potest. Prius si statuatur, definit Sp. S. verus esse Deus, eo ipso, quod non sit omniscius & omnipotens: Posterius autem adversatur titulo consolatorio, quem passim in Scriptura fert: nam ut pra invidia (absit blasphemia) videri posset nobis subduxisse, quod ab naturalia, veritatis patefactionem; sic eo ipso definit esse consolator, quod menti ad veritatem anhelanti, videatur destinato voluisse crucem figere.
units.tr: DCCXXXV. The fourth objection follows (p. 402): If it must be held that the Holy Spirit speaks of natural things in the manner of the common people, then either he could not instruct his own people about the truth of natural things, or, if he could, he was unwilling. But neither can be said. If the first is maintained, the Holy Spirit ceases to be the true God, by the very fact that he is not omniscient and omnipotent. The second, however, conflicts with the consoling title which he bears throughout Scripture: for it could seem (God forbid the blasphemy) that out of envy he had withheld from us the revelation of the truth about natural things; and so by that very fact he would be shown not to be a consoler, since to a mind longing for truth he would seem to have deliberately fixed a cross.

units.la: DCCXXXVI. Resp. Hoc dilemma nos non stringit, aperta enim est adhuc via, quâ sine omni violentiâ facile possimus evadere. Concedimus libenter, potuisse Spiritum Sanctum quam accuratissimè enucleare naturam rerum naturalium. Quis enim verè Christianus hoc audeat negare? cum enim ab illo res omnes habeant existentiam & essentiam, eas utique cognovit, etiam antequam essent, in suis æternis ideis, secundum quas eas in tempore produxit: Et qui fieri posset, ut Sp. S. qui auctor est omnis luminis & dator omnis scientiæ, ipse quædam ignoraret? 2. Dicimus itque, Sp. S noluisse per Scripturas nos erudire de rebus naturalibus, quoad ipsarum naturam interiorem, & attributa; cum & ad illarum rerum intelligentiam hominibus lumen naturæ concesserit, ad quod cui vacet attendere, is possit exinde sufficientem cognitionem naturæ rerum haurire, dummodo eo recte utatur; & noluerit in Scripturis per formulas accuratas de rebus naturalibus adhibitas mentes rudiorum turbare, ne dicere possent, altiora hæc esse captu suo, uti superius ex Calvino & Paræo didicimus. 3. Non ergo vel titulus consolatoris Sp.S. propterea subtrahendus, vel invidiæ nota ipsi inurenda. Quid enim quæso consolationis ad homines redit, sive putent, Terram moveri, sive Cælum; (nisi forte dicas, ut jocôutar, si putent Terram quiescere, metuum illis hunc eximi, ne forte unà cum Terra in Cœlum ruant,) sive sciant, stellas majoris esse quantitatis, & lucem quoque in se habere, quàm Lunam, nam, sive contrarium existiment. Est equidem Spiritus S. consolator, sed hoc suo officio fungitur, dum mentes miseras sensu iræ divinæ dejectas erigit, ipsis dicendo: Confide fili mi, remissa sunt tibi peccata tua; dum molestias, quæ ipsis in hac terrâ sunt exhauriendæ, lenit, spe & expectatione vitæ æternæ, ex cujus consideratione erumpunt cū Paulo in has voces: Reor, minimè pares esse præsentis temporis passiones gloriæ in nobis revelandæ; dum luctantes cum metu, ne iterum excidant sua salute, certos reddit, nihil esse quod possit eos separare à dilectione Dei quæ est in Christo Iesu. His & similibus modis Sp. S. officio consolatoris fungitur. Inst. At menti ad veritatem anhelanti crucem destinato videtur figere voluisse. Resp.
