Verum equidem est, quod omnes homines naturaliter scire desiderent, sed hoc desiderium in his vel illis variè restringitur, dum vident, se non ad scientiam nisi multo sudore & vigiliis pervenire posse, quas sustinere vel nolunt, vel etiam non possunt, propter corporis vel mentis imbecillitatem, curam rei familiaris, aliasque causas, ut non multum sint solliciti, qui fiat, quod magnes trahat ferrum, quæ causa æstus marini, unde salsedo maris oriatur &c. imò vix unquam de iis cogitationem suscipiant, aliis negotiis impediti: etsi autem in quibusdam remaneat desiderium cognoscendi viam salutis, illis sufficienter satisfit in Scriptura sacra; cui verò præterea volupe est opera Dei accuratè cognoscere, ei lumen naturale est concessum; quo si recte utatur, ut judicium semper sequatur perceptionem, saltem ab errore potest esse immunis, & ad multarum rerum naturalium cognitionem accuratam pervenire.
units.tr: DCCXXXVI. Reply: This dilemma does not press us, for there is still an open way by which we can easily escape without any violence. We gladly concede that the Holy Spirit could have explained the nature of natural things most accurately. For who that is truly a Christian would dare to deny this? Since all things have their existence and essence from him, he certainly knew them even before they existed, in his eternal ideas, according to which he brought them into being in time. And how could it happen that the Holy Spirit, who is the author of all light and the giver of all knowledge, should himself be ignorant of certain things? 2. We say, then, that the Holy Spirit was unwilling to instruct us through Scripture about natural things as regards their inner nature and attributes; since he has granted men the light of nature for understanding those things, and whoever gives heed to it may thence draw a sufficient knowledge of the nature of things, provided he uses it rightly. And he was unwilling, in Scripture, by means of exact terms about natural things, to disturb the minds of the simple, lest they should say that these matters were beyond their grasp, as we learned above from Calvin and Pareus. 3. Therefore the title of consoler is not to be withdrawn from the Holy Spirit on this account, nor is the mark of envy to be branded upon him. For what consolation, I ask, does it bring to men whether they think the earth moves or the heavens (unless perhaps, to joke, you say that if they think the earth is at rest they are freed from the fear that they may fall into heaven together with the earth), or whether they know that the stars are of greater size and have light in themselves, more than the moon, or whether they believe the contrary? The Holy Spirit is indeed a consoler, but he performs this office when he raises up wretched minds cast down by a sense of divine wrath, saying to them: Be of good cheer, my son, your sins are forgiven you; when he soothes the troubles which they must endure in this earth, by the hope and expectation of eternal life, from the consideration of which they break out with Paul into these words: I reckon that the sufferings of the present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to be revealed in us; when he makes certain those who struggle with fear lest they again fall from their salvation, that there is nothing which can separate them from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus. In these and similar ways the Holy Spirit fulfils the office of consoler. Objection: But he seems to have wished to fix a cross for a mind longing for the truth. Reply: It is indeed true that all men naturally desire to know, but this desire is variously restrained in this or that person, since they see that they cannot attain knowledge except with much sweat and watching, which some are unwilling to endure, and others are unable to endure, on account of weakness of body or mind, care of household affairs, and other causes; so that they are not much concerned how it happens that a magnet attracts iron, what causes the tide of the sea, whence the saltness of the sea arises, and so on. Indeed they hardly ever take such thoughts to heart, being hindered by other business. And although in some there remains a desire to know the way of salvation, this is sufficiently satisfied in Holy Scripture; but whoever moreover takes pleasure in knowing accurately the works of God, to him the natural light has been granted, which, if he uses it rightly, so that judgment always follows perception, can at least be free from error and attain to an accurate knowledge of many natural things.

units.la: DCCXXXVII. Objectio quinta S. p. 403. Sententia hac, inquit, à diametro pugnat cum intentione cujuscunque doctoris, abjectissimi quoque, atque ex tribu mechanicorum; quis enim ex omnibus illis, qui non quemcunque ex suis discipulis, saltem nitatur manu ducere ad eam veritatem, quam in arte sua censetur exploratam habere? secus qui faciunt, invidi, si non malefici haberi debent. Sed, si audiantur illi, quos obiter hic notamus, Spiritus Sanctus hac in parte inferior censendus fuerit vilissimo aliquo artifice?
units.tr: DCCXXXVII. The fifth objection (p. 403): This opinion, he says, flatly contradicts the intention of every teacher, even the most abject, and of men of the mechanical class. For who among all those who do not, at least, strive to lead by the hand some one of their pupils to that truth which he is held to have tested in his art? Those who do otherwise ought to be considered envious, if not malicious. But if we listen to those whom we here note in passing, will the Holy Spirit be judged inferior in this respect to some most worthless craftsman?

units.la: DCCXXXVIII. Resp. 1. Si hoc argumentum aliquam vim habere debeat: Ergo pariter inferet, debere omnes veritates Physicas, Mathematicas &c. in Scriptura doceri, quod quàm absurdum sit nemo non videt. Si enim Spiritus Sanctus debet docere omnem veritatem, quam censetur exploratam habere, cum omnes habeat exploratissimas; nulla erit, quæ in Scriptura non sit quærenda. Sed si hoc sic intelligendum de veritate, quæ facit ad scopum Artificis & quæ propria est istius artis, quam profitetur: Ergo cum ad scopum Spiritus Sancti sufficiat veritas Euangelica de reconciliatione gratuitâ hominis peccatoris coram Deo, & quæ ei sunt connexæ, sufficit, illas veritates à Spiritu doceri, quod ab eo fieri quàm plenissimè, statuimus: quid verò faciant ad istum scopum veritates Physicæ ex. gr. Terram moveri, Lunam esse minorem stellu &c. & cur non sine iis scopum suum obtinere possit, equidem non video. Quemadmodum enim sufficit artifici Mechanico, si usum instrumentorum, in artis exercitio necessariorum discipulo suo monstret: ex. gr. fabro ferrario, si usum mallei, incudis & aliorum instrumentorum, dexteramque eorum applicationem ostendat, etiamsi non doceat, quæ sit natura ferri, quænam ejus generatio &c. quamvis etiam sciat fortè, discipulum erroneas de materiâ, formâ & constitutione instrumentorum fovere opiniones: ita etiam sufficit Spiritui Sancto si ostendat, quomodo res naturales nos ducant ad cognitionem Dei, sapientiæ ejus, bonitatis & potentiæ, ad quod sufficit cognitio, quæ de iis per sensus haberi potest, quamvis errores quosdam habeat adjunctos. Inst. At dicas: saltem nihil falsi debet tradere. Resp. Concedo, non debere docere aliquam falsitatem, quod cum non facere cap. 32. ostendi; at nego, propterea non posse assumere locutiones vulgares ab opinione falsâ defumtas, iisque incidenter uti: non enim tenetur falsitatem ubique refutare, sed potest eam in medio relinquere, & interim cum vulgo loqui, ne ille turbetur, & rem quam principaliter Scriptura tractat, intelligere queat. 2. Non ergo inferior erit censendus Spiritus Sanctus hac in parte quovis vilissimo artifice, cum veritates cœlestes, quæ propriæ sunt istius artis, voce artis generaliter accepta, quam in Scripturâ Sacrâ tradit, sufficientissimè, dexterrimè & sapientissimè explicet, ita ut in illâ explicatione nihil possit desiderari; de rebus naturalibus etiam tantum delibet, quantum opus ad salutarem rerum divinarum cognitionem.
units.tr: DCCXXXVIII. Reply: 1. If this argument ought to have any force, then it will likewise follow that all physical and mathematical truths and so on must be taught in Scripture, and how absurd that is nobody fails to see. For if the Holy Spirit must teach every truth which is held to be tested, since all of them are most thoroughly tested, then there will be none which should not be sought in Scripture. But if this is to be understood of the truth which serves the artisan's purpose and is proper to the art which he professes, then, since for the purpose of the Holy Spirit the Gospel truth of the free reconciliation of sinful man before God, and what is connected with it, is sufficient, it suffices that those truths are taught by the Spirit, which we affirm has been done as fully as possible. But what physical truths, for example that the earth moves, that the moon is smaller than the stars and so on, contribute to that purpose, and why it cannot be attained without them, I indeed do not see. For just as it suffices for a mechanical craftsman if he shows his pupil the use of the instruments necessary in the exercise of the craft, for example a blacksmith if he shows the use of the hammer, the anvil and the other instruments and their correct application, even if he does not teach what the nature of iron is, or how it is generated, and so on, although perhaps he knows that the pupil fosters erroneous opinions about the matter, form and make-up of the instruments: so too it suffices for the Holy Spirit if he shows how natural things lead us to the knowledge of God, his wisdom, goodness and power, for which knowledge that can be had of them through the senses suffices, even though some errors are attached to it. Objection: But you may say: at least he ought to deliver nothing false. Reply: I concede that he ought not to teach any falsehood, which I showed in chapter 32 that he does not do. But I deny that for this reason he cannot adopt common expressions drawn from a false opinion and use them incidentally. For he is not bound to refute falsehood everywhere; he can leave it in the middle, and meanwhile speak with the common people, so that they are not disturbed and can understand the matter which Scripture principally treats. 2. Therefore the Holy Spirit is not to be considered inferior in this respect to any most worthless craftsman, since he explains the heavenly truths, which are proper to this art, in the language of art taken in a general sense, which he hands down in Holy Scripture, most sufficiently, most skilfully and most wisely, so that nothing can be desired in that explanation. Of natural things too he touches only as much as is needed for the saving knowledge of divine things.

units.la: CAPUT XXXVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXVI.

units.la: Objectio sexta à puritate Scripturæ divinæ desumta proponitur & refutatur.
units.tr: The sixth objection, drawn from the purity of divine Scripture, is set out and refuted.

units.la: DCCXXXIX. Sextæ Objectionis loco sunt ea, quæ habet S.p.403. Quod scriptum censeri debet purissimum, atque ab omnibus sordibus, nævisque defecatum, in eo non debet notari quid falsi, aut quod serviat corroborando errori; Sed talis est Scriptura. Consequentia est certissima. Quia enim scriptum illud purum & defecatum esse censeat, in quo, sive studio ipsius auctoris, sive per imprudentiam ejusdem, sive quacunque alia ratione errores aliqui commissi notentur? Minor vero ex pluribus Scripturæ textibus probari potest: ex quibus hi præcipui Psal. xii. 7. Dicta Jehova dicta pura; argentum purgatum in catino lectissimo Terræ. Psal. xix. v. 9. Præceptum Jehova purum illuminans oculos. Prov. xxx. 5. Totus sermo Dei purgatissimus est. 1 Pet. ii. 2. Lac sermonis sincerum. Apoc. xix. 9. Verba Dei vera sunt. Necessum ergo periculosa sententia Patroni, quod major propositio invicti sit roboris, in dubium vocent assumtionem, ac pariter ipsius Scripturæ infallibilem Auctoritatem.
units.tr: DCCXXXIX. The sixth objection is what the author gives on p. 403: What must be judged most pure, and cleansed from all filth and blemish, ought not to have anything false noted in it, or anything that serves to strengthen error. But such is Scripture. The consequence is quite certain. For why would a writing be judged pure and clean if, whether by the study of its author, or through his carelessness, or for any other reason, some errors are noted in it? The minor premise can be proved from several texts of Scripture, of which these are the chief: Ps. 12:7, "The words of the LORD are pure words, silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times." Ps. 19:9, "The commandment of the LORD is pure, enlightening the eyes." Prov. 30:5, "Every word of God is most pure." 1 Pet. 2:2, "the sincere milk of the word." Rev. 19:9, "These are the true words of God." Therefore the proponent of this dangerous opinion must of necessity call into doubt either the major premise, that it is of invincible strength, or likewise the assumption, and the infallible authority of Scripture itself.

units.la: DCCXL. Resp. 1. Purum variis modis accipi potest: Est enim 1. mundum sive, quod à sordibus corporis est liberum; 2. Purum est, in quo nihil est heterogenei admixtum, quod non sit ejusdem naturæ specificæ cum eo, cui puritas tribuitur. Sic aurum & argentum vocantur pura, non tantum si nullas habeant scorias, sed etiam si non sint colliquata cum aliis metallis. 3. purum accipi potest pro vero, cui nulla est admixta falsitas. 4. pro sancto, cui nullum vitium, nulla macula adhæret. 5. pro simplici, nudo: ut purus homo, qui non est Deus. Prior ex his significationibus Scripturæ applicari non potest: secunda significatione Scriptura est pura, non ex parte, sed in totum, quatenus sola Dei verba revelata proponit, nihilque traditionum vel commentorum humanorum habet admixti: tertia significatio etiam locum habet, quia nihil quod in ea traditur & docetur, credendumque proponitur, est falsum, sed pura puta veritas: de quarta significatione res est certa; sanctissima est Scriptura, à Deo quippe sanctissimo & fonte omnis sanctitatis profecta: quinta item significatio applicari Scripturæ potest, quatenus est verbum solius Dei, non hominum. Disquirendum itaque restat, num ad puritatem Scripturæ requiratur, ut non proponatur lingua aliqua vulgari, in qua sunt multa locutiones vulgares à comà communi loquendi usu desumta, erroneis opinionibus innitentes, à sensuum prajudiciis plerumque hausta? aut, si proponatur linguâ vulgari, an saltem omnes tales locutiones evitari debeant, imò, ubi occasio fert, in contrarium sermo vertendus, errorque vulgaris notandus & refutandus? Nos dicimus, hoc modo nihil quicquam puritati Scripturæ decedere: si enim sic quicquam decederet puritati Scripturæ, non fuisset illa exaranda lingua aliqua vulgari recepta, qualis Hebræa & Græca & quævis aliæ; multas enim esse locutiones vulgares in Hebræa & Græca lingua, nimis quam clarum est, & superius ex Junio ad Deut. III. didicimus, qui inquit, Scripturam Veteris T. loqui, quemadmodum Hebrai loquuntur populariter. Invenienda ergo fuisset nova lingua, in qua voces accuratissimè rebus responderent, omnesque vulgares locutiones fuissent exterminatæ. Sed à quo intellecta fuisset? saltem vulgus fidelium, cujus tamen usui est tradita, vix quicquam in ea profecisset. Si verò debuisset semper, ubi occasio ferret, loco locutionum vulgarium usurpare accuratas, & errores vulgares refutare, major perturbatio fuisset orta, quam si scriptores N.T. à versione vulgata 70. in omnibus debuissent recedere, per quam causam à Riveto & Voetio Apostolicum hoc factum defensum fuisse superius cap. 30. art. 660. vidimus, quemadmodum hoc jam aliquoties monuimus. Distinguamus ergo hic res enunciatas & modum enunciandi. Res enunciatæ in Scriptura à Deo nobis credendæ & faciendæ propositæ, sunt purum Dei verbum. Modum enunciandi etiam quod attinet ipsarum linguarum originalium respectu, eatenus Scriptura etiam est verbum Dei, quatenus omnia & singula verba censemus à Spiritu S. esse inspirata: sed si in illo modo enunciandi consideres, reperiri formulas loquendi vulgares & receptas, etiam innitentes opinionibus erroneis, dicimus, eo sensu non esse purum Dei verbum, si spectes tantum Dei naturam, quomodo ab ipso proficisci potuerit & debuerit conformiter divinæ naturæ, si forte Angelis tantum loqui voluisset, cum se accommodare voluerit ad hominum naturam, quibuscum ipsi esset negotium. Sed absolutè loquendo hoc nihil de puritate decerpit; si enim concionatorum verba dicantur purum Dei verbum, quatenus consentiunt cum Sacrâ Scripturâ, etiamsi modus proponendi plane sit humanus, multo magis purum Dei verbum dici potest id, quod tum quoad res enunciatas, tum quoad modum enunciandi à Deo est profectum, quamvis locutionibus utatur vulgaribus, quæ commodè evitari non possunt. Major itaque Objectionis propositæ, quæ invicti habetur roboris, hoc modo limitata non procedit: si Scriptura habet quasdam locutiones vulgares ab errore defumtas, quem non refutat, eoque refutato veritati convenienter loquitur: Ergo non est pura. Ostendimus enim, hoc puritati Scripturæ nihil detrahere.
units.tr: DCCXL. Reply, 1. "Pure" can be taken in various ways. For it can mean (1) clean, that is, free from bodily filth; (2) pure, where nothing foreign is mixed in that is not of the same specific nature as that to which purity is ascribed. In this sense gold and silver are called pure, not only if they have no dross, but also if they are not alloyed with other metals; (3) pure can be taken to mean true, with no falsehood mixed in; (4) holy, to which no vice or stain adheres; (5) simple and unadorned, as a pure man, who is not God. Of these meanings the first cannot be applied to Scripture. In the second sense Scripture is pure, not in part but wholly, since it sets forth only the revealed words of God and has nothing of human traditions or inventions mixed in. The third meaning also applies, since nothing that is delivered and taught, and proposed for belief in it is false, but it is pure truth. Concerning the fourth meaning there is no doubt: Scripture is most holy, having proceeded from God, who is most holy and the fountain of all holiness. The fifth meaning too can be applied to Scripture, insofar as it is the word of God alone and not of men. It remains, then, to inquire whether purity of Scripture requires that it not be set forth in some vernacular language, in which there are many colloquial expressions taken from the common use of speech, resting on erroneous opinions, and for the most part drawn from the prejudices of the senses? Or, if it is set forth in a vernacular language, whether at least all such expressions ought to be avoided, or rather, where the occasion arises, the speech ought to be turned to the contrary, and the common error noted and refuted? We say that in this way nothing whatever is taken away from the purity of Scripture. For if anything were taken away from the purity of Scripture in this way, then Scripture should not have been written in any received vernacular language, such as Hebrew, Greek, or any others. For that there are many colloquial expressions in the Hebrew and Greek languages is all too clear, and we learned above from Junius on Deut. 3 that he says Scripture of the Old Testament speaks just as the Hebrews speak in popular fashion. A new language would therefore have had to be invented, in which words corresponded most exactly to things, and all colloquial expressions had been banished. But by whom would it have been understood? At least the common body of the faithful, for whose use it was given, would have gained scarcely anything from it. And if the writers had been obliged always, where the occasion arose, to use exact expressions in place of colloquial ones, and to refute common errors, a greater confusion would have arisen than if the writers of the New Testament had been obliged to depart in every case from the Vulgate translation of the Seventy. For this reason Rivetus and Voetius defended this apostolic practice, as we saw above in chapter 30, article 660, as we have already pointed out several times. Let us therefore here distinguish the things stated and the manner of stating them. The things stated in Scripture, which God sets before us to believe and to do, are the pure word of God. As for the manner of stating them, even with respect to the original languages themselves, Scripture is also the word of God insofar as we judge all and each of the words to be inspired by the Holy Spirit. But if you consider in that manner of stating, you will find common and accepted forms of speech, even resting on erroneous opinions; we say that in that sense it is not the pure word of God, if you look only at the nature of God, as to how it could and ought to have proceeded from him in conformity with the divine nature, had he perhaps wished to speak only to angels, whereas he willed to accommodate himself to human nature, with which he had to deal. But speaking absolutely, this takes nothing away from its purity. For if the words of preachers are called the pure word of God, insofar as they agree with Holy Scripture, even though the manner of setting them forth is plainly human, much more may that be called the pure word of God which has proceeded from God both as to the things stated and as to the manner of stating them, although it uses colloquial expressions, which cannot conveniently be avoided. Therefore the major premise of the objection put forward, which is held to be of invincible strength, when limited in this way does not hold: "If Scripture has certain colloquial expressions taken from an error, which it does not refute, and speaks in agreement with the truth when that error has been refuted, then it is not pure." For we have shown that this takes nothing away from the purity of Scripture.

units.la: DCCXLI. 2. Quod si speciatim loca allata consideremus, videbimus ea parum ad rem facere. Psal. xii. verf. 6. præcedente, Dominum ipsum induxerat dicentem: se jam surrecturum & populo suo vastato & afflicto salutem allaturum, id v. 7. confirmat, ostendendo, verbo Dei omni dubitatione rejectâ, quam firmissimè & securissimè esse credendum & innitendum. Sermo est ergo de veritate promissionum divinarum: unde non sequitur, verbum Dei in locutionibus de rebus naturalibus & aliis nullam formulam vulgarem errori vulgi innitentem adhibere debere. Psal. xix. v. 9. ostenditur, ex verbo Dei regulam vitæ posse hauriri, ut non opus sit commentis & figmentis humanis; cui non adversatur, si verbum Dei circa alia loquatur populariter sensu sæpius dictq Proverb. xxx. 5. quia præcedenti versu ostensum fuerat, sapientiam & viam ad salutem cognitu esse difficilem, hoc versu remedium huic difficultati docetur esse paratum per verbum Dei, quod sit purum & immaculatum & ab omnibus commentis liberum; atque inde nihil magis contra nos infertur, quam ex præcedenti loco. Similiter 1 Pet. II. 2. nihil aliud indicatur, quam, si velimus augeri & crescere incremento Spirituali, nos non alio nutrimento debere uti, quam verbo Dei ab omnibus humanis commentis sejuncto. Apoc. xx. 9. dicitur, quod verba illa præcedentia, quibus vocatis ad cœnam spiritualem salus promittitur, sint vera & firma, ut tuto quis iis inniti possit, & ad cœnam illam spiritualem sine metu accedere. Cui veritati nihil decedit, etiamsi verbum Dei per occasionem in declaratione istius vocationis & salutis, quæ continetur in toto Canone V. & N. Testamenti, aliquando incidat in locutiones vulgares, atque adeò minus accuratas, quemadmodum satis ostensum in responsionibus nostris ad objectionem primam.
units.tr: DCCXLI. 2. If we consider the places cited one by one, we shall see that they bear little on the matter. In Ps. 12, verse 6, the preceding verse, the Lord himself is introduced as saying that he will now rise up and bring salvation to his people, who have been laid waste and afflicted; verse 7 confirms this, showing, with every doubt cast aside, that the word of God is to be believed and relied upon most firmly and most securely. The discussion is therefore about the truth of the divine promises, whence it does not follow that the word of God, in its statements about natural things and other matters, must employ no vernacular form of speech that rests on the error of the common people. Ps. 19:9 shows that a rule of life can be drawn from the word of God, so that there is no need for human inventions and fictions; this is not opposed to the word of God speaking in popular fashion about other matters, as it often does. Prov. 30:5 is cited because the preceding verse had shown that wisdom and the way to salvation are hard to know; in this verse the remedy for this difficulty is taught to be ready through the word of God, which is pure and spotless and free from all inventions. Nothing more is inferred against us from this place than from the preceding one. Likewise 1 Pet. 2:2 indicates nothing other than that, if we wish to be increased and to grow by spiritual nourishment, we ought to use no other food than the word of God, separated from all human inventions. Rev. 19:9 says that those preceding words, by which salvation is promised to those called to the spiritual supper, are true and firm, so that one may safely rely upon them and approach that spiritual supper without fear. Nothing is taken from this truth, even if the word of God, on the occasion of declaring that calling and salvation, which is contained in the whole canon of the Old and New Testaments, sometimes falls into colloquial and therefore less exact expressions, as has been sufficiently shown in our replies to the first objection.

units.la: DCCXLII. Inst. 1. M. p. 113. Si concedas in secunda, tertia, quarta, & quinta significatione Scripturam esse purissimam & purgatissimam, tuam ipsius sententiam jugulas: quod sic patet 1. quod ita purum, ut nihil commenti humani sibi admixti habeat, illud non potest dici ullas falsitates ad captum vulgi compositas continere. Quid enim ista falsitates sint aliud quam commenta ingenii vulgaris. Item. Saltem non posset dici purissimum.
units.tr: DCCXLII. Inst. 1. M. p. 113. If you grant that in the second, third, fourth and fifth senses Scripture is most pure and purified, you cut the throat of your own opinion. This is clear, first, because what is so pure that it contains no human invention mixed into it cannot be said to contain any falsehoods composed to suit the grasp of the common people. For what are such falsehoods but the inventions of the common mind? Likewise: at least it could not be called most pure.

units.la: DCCXLIII. Resp. Hæc recte se habent bene intellecta, sed nobis non repugnant. Commenta humana admiscentur divinis verbis, quando ea docentur tanquam divinum verbum, quando afferuntur, quando quis ea conatur persuadere, quod non facit Scriptura, sed utitur tantum formulis, quæ originem habent ex commento humano, eas quia receptæ sunt, non immutando; unde nihil commenti humani admiscetur, nisi velis dicere verba hominum recepta non debuisse usurpari in sacris literis, quod absurdum.
units.tr: DCCXLIII. Resp. These points are correct when rightly understood, but they do not conflict with us. Human inventions are mixed in with divine words when they are taught as the divine word, when they are brought forward, or when someone tries to persuade others of them. Scripture does not do this. It merely uses formulas that have their origin in a human invention, and it does not change them because they are already in common use. So nothing of human invention is mixed in, unless you wish to say that words received from men ought not to be used in Holy Letters, which is absurd.

units.la: DCCXLIV. Inst. 2. M. p. 213. Si secundum tertiam puri significationem omnia quæ in Scripturis docentur & ad credendum proponuntur, sint pura, puta veritas, tum omnia quæ in ea traduntur sunt talia &c. omnia itidem quæ in ea traduntur etiam docentur 2 Tim. III. 16. Rom. xvi. 4.
units.tr: DCCXLIV. Inst. 2. M. p. 213. If, according to the third sense of purity, all the things that are taught in the Scriptures and proposed for belief are pure, namely true, then all the things that are handed down in it are such, etc. Likewise, all the things that are handed down in it are also taught 2 Tim. III. 16. Rom. xvi. 4.

units.la: Resp. Omnia quæ traduntur in Sacrâ Scripturâ sunt vera & pura sine omni falsitate: atqui ea demum possunt dici tradi in sacris literis, quæ Sp. S. vult in iis significare; sensus Scripturæ legitimus est id, quod tradit Scriptura, in quo nihil falsitatis reperiri dicimus.
units.tr: Resp. Everything that is handed down in Holy Scripture is true and pure, without any falsehood. But things can be said to be handed down in Holy Letters only when the Holy Spirit wishes them to be signified in them. The legitimate sense of Scripture is what Scripture hands down, and in this we say nothing of falsehood is to be found.

units.la: DCCXLV. Inst. 3. M. p. 213. Si juxta quartam significationem Scriptura sit sanctissima, est etiam verissima.
units.tr: DCCXLV. Inst. 3. M. p. 213. If, according to the fourth sense, Scripture is most holy, it is also most true.

units.la: Resp. Hoc nihil contra me, cum Scripturæ veritatem nullatenus in dubium vocem, & hunc totum laborem suscepserim ad conciliandam ejus veritatem cum sententia Cartesii.
units.tr: Resp. This is nothing against me, since I in no way call the truth of Scripture into doubt, and I undertook this whole labour precisely to reconcile its truth with the opinion of Descartes.

units.la: DCCXLVI. Inst. 4. M. p. 215. Statum controversiæ esse: An ad Scripturæ puritatem requiratur, ut nullas locutiones contineat in se quidem falsas, sed opinione tantum vulgi veras. Item p. 219. Quæstionem esse an Scriptura possit loqui quod in se erroneum est, quod nego.
units.tr: DCCXLVI. Inst. 4. M. p. 215. The state of the controversy is this: whether, for the purity of Scripture, it is required that it contain no expressions which are indeed false in themselves but true only by the opinion of the common people. Likewise p. 219: the question is whether Scripture can speak what is erroneous in itself, which I deny.

units.la: Resp. Hunc statum controversiæ non esse, ostensum 20. capite, adeoque toto Cœlo aberrat adversarius.
units.tr: Resp. That this is not the state of the controversy has been shown in chapter 20, and so the adversary wanders far from the truth.

units.la: DCCXLVII. Inst. 5. M. p. 216. In Hebraâ & Græcâ linguâ omnia tam accurate possunt exprimi, quam nova Philosophia Cartesiana omnia potuit accurate exprimere lingua Latina multo his imperfectiori.
units.tr: DCCXLVII. Inst. 5. M. p. 216. Everything can be expressed as accurately in the Hebrew and Greek language as the new Cartesian philosophy has been able to express everything accurately in the Latin language, which is much less perfect than these.

units.la: Resp. Vanissimum effugium, quis enim hoc neget? aut quis non concedat, si Spiritus S. voluisset philosophiam conscribere, quin potuerit Græcâ & Hebraâ linguâ, imo quâvis aliâ, omnia non tantum tam accurate, sed longè acuratiùs exprimere quàm Cartesius, sed quia non voluit ultra cognitionem vulgarem procedere, non etiam opus habuit aliis phrasibus quàm ei convenientibus. 2. Non tamen possunt ullâ in linguâ res accuratius exprimi, quàm ejus phrases à vulgo inventæ permittunt; unde & Cartesius non semper potuit reperire verba satis philosophica, sive accuratè rerum veritatem exprimentia, sed coactus fuit interdum loqui cum vulgo.
units.tr: Resp. This is a most empty escape. For who would deny this? Or who would not concede that, if the Holy Spirit had wished to write a philosophy, he could have done so in the Greek and Hebrew language, or indeed in any other language, expressing all things not only as accurately but far more accurately than Descartes? But since he did not wish to go beyond ordinary knowledge, he had no need of any phrases other than those suited to it. 2. Nevertheless, no matter is expressed more accurately in any language than its phrases, as found by the common people, allow. Hence Descartes too could not always find words sufficiently philosophical, that is, words expressing the truth of things accurately, but was sometimes forced to speak with the common people.

units.la: DCCXLVIII. Inst. 6. M. p. 217. Res enunciata proprie non est verbum bum Dei, sed ipsa rei enunciatio, modus enunciandi & verba ac phrases enuntiata sub verbi divini appellatione veniunt.
units.tr: DCCXLVIII. Inst. 6. M. p. 217. The thing enunciated is not properly the word of God, but the very statement of the thing; the mode of enunciating and the words and phrases enunciated come under the name of the divine word.

units.la: Resp. Imò vero propriissimè. Nonne enim id est verbum Dei quod à Deo pronuntiatur: at tale procul dubio est res enunciata. Nonne id est verbum Dei quod Deus nobis significat? Quòd si hic verbo- rum debeat esse sensus, non solùm rem enunciatam, sed etiam modum enunciandi, quatenus omnia & singula verba à Spiritu S. sint inspirata, esse à Deo, nihil mihi contradicitur, cùm hæc expresse docuerim art. 740.
units.tr: Resp. On the contrary, most properly. For is not that the word of God which is pronounced by God? Yet without doubt the thing enunciated is such. Is not that the word of God which God signifies to us? But if the sense of "word" here should also include not only the thing enunciated but also the mode of enunciating, insofar as all and each of the words are inspired by the Holy Spirit and are from God, nothing is contradicted to me, since I have taught exactly this in art. 740.

units.la: DCCXLIX. Inst. 7. M. 219. Πάρεργα sunt ista explicationes locorum in objectione adductorum, nisi minorem vel iu negare.
units.tr: DCCXLIX. Inst. 7. M. 219. These explanations of the passages adduced in the objection are side-issues [πάρεργα], unless the minor premise or the inference is denied.

units.la: Resp. Si πάρεργα sunt atque nihil faciunt ad rem, quid opus fuit ut contra ea instantiæ formarentur? Sed si consideretur, quomodo ostendi- derim, ex illis dictis non sequi, Scripturam non posse uti formulis vulgaribus in præjudiciis fundatis, apparebit non πάρεργα fuisse quæ de iis à nobis fuerunt adducta.
units.tr: Resp. If they are side-issues [πάρεργα] and contribute nothing to the matter, why was there any need to form instances against them? But if one considers how I showed that it does not follow from those sayings that Scripture cannot use common formulas founded on prejudices, it will appear that what we adduced about them was not side-issues.

units.la: DCCL. Inst. 8. M. p. 220. ad Psal. xix. Negry quidem est in isthoc textu de commentis humanis.
units.tr: DCCL. Inst. 8. M. p. 220. on Psalm xix. It can indeed be denied that there is anything about human inventions in this text.

units.la: Resp, Negry quidem ergo vidit Calvinus, qui in Commentariis ad hæc verba sic inquit: In fine versus, regulam divinæ legis puram esse & oculos illuminare, tradens subindicat, perperam aliunde peti boni & mali discrimen, quia vita puritatem inquinet suis facibus, quicquid ex se comminiscuntur homines. Deinde cum toto suo acumine cæcos esse & semper in tenebris errare, donec ad cœlestis doctrinæ lucem convertant oculos. 2. Sed nonne hoc infertur ex illis verbis? Non enim posse verbum Dei esse certum & purum, ut simplices possit reddere vere sapientes, si commentis humanis esset inquinatum.
units.tr: Resp. So Calvin indeed saw that it could be denied, who in his Commentaries on these words says: "At the end of the verse, by stating that the rule of the divine law is pure and enlightens the eyes, he hints that the distinction between good and evil is wrongly sought elsewhere, because life is polluted by its own torches, whatever men devise for themselves. Then, though with all their acuteness they are blind and always wander in darkness, until they turn their eyes to the light of heavenly teaching." 2. But is this not inferred from those words? For the word of God cannot be certain and pure, so as to make the simple truly wise, if it were polluted by human inventions.

units.la: DCCLI. Inst. 9. M. p. 220. Dato haberi quid de commentis humanis, fortius tamen sententiam refellet. Si enim verbum regulam vitæ ita contineat, ut non opus habeamus commentis atque figmentis humanis; Ergo non opus habemus falsitatibus ad captum vulgi compositis.
units.tr: DCCLI. Inst. 9. M. p. 220. Granted that something of human inventions is found, it would nevertheless refute the opinion more strongly. For if the word contains the rule of life in such a way that we have no need of human inventions and fictions, then we have no need of falsehoods composed to suit the grasp of the common people.

units.la: Resp. Ad illud jam satis fuit responsum. Neque enim attingitur status controversiæ. Tandem, dum M. p. 220. & p. 221. vindicare vult reliqua loca in objectione adducta, pugnat cum suâ umbrâ, sumens sibi oppugnandam sententiam hanc, ac si mea esset, Scripturam habere in se falsitates, sive falsa loqui, tradere, testari, vel significare, quod ego non secus ac ipse rejicio.
units.tr: Resp. An answer to this has already been given enough. For the state of the controversy is not touched upon. Finally, while on pages 220 and 221 he wishes to vindicate the other passages adduced in the objection, he fights with his own shadow, taking up as his opponent a view that he imagines to be mine: that Scripture has falsehoods in it, or speaks, hands down, testifies or signifies falsely, which I reject no less than he does.

units.la: CAPUT XXXVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXVII.

units.la: Septima Objectio inde desumta, quod posita nostra sen- tentia sufficiens habeant hæretici fundamentum negandi, Christum esse hominem.
units.tr: The seventh objection, drawn from the fact that, on our opinion, heretics have sufficient grounds for denying that Christ is man.

units.la: DCCLII. Septimam Objectionem habet S. p. 404. Si quid tribui mereatur sententia, quam recentiores quidam mordicus tuentur in thesi quasi, sed pro hypothesi Pythagoreo-Copernicana, vicerint Valentiniani, Marcionita, Basilidiani, Anabaptista, Weigeliani, & quotquot negant Christum Dei filium, veram humanam naturam assumsisse, si quidem, ut libro proximo videlicet, Marcion jam olim dicere solet, carnem & ea quæ sunt hominis Christo in Scriptura tribui duntaxat secundum externam speciem. Homogeneæ sunt his quæ habet B. D. p. 14. quando sic inquit: Marcion ejusque Asseclæ negabant, Christum fuisse verum hominem & eum hominem vocatum volebant, quia videbatur homo, non quod revera talis esset. Nemo nostrum non abhorret ab illo modo interpretandi S. literas. At quomodo possibile est tutari Orthodoxam S. Scripturæ interpretationem, contra illos, aliosque similis farinæ hæreticos, nisi fundamentum jam positum, de non recedendo à proprio verborum sensu, absque necessaria ratione firmiter retineamus? Et quis tandem absurditatum finis, quave porta hæresibus quibuscunque non aperietur?
units.tr: DCCLII. The seventh objection is found at p. 404: If any weight is to be given to the opinion which some more recent writers defend stubbornly in theory, but as a Pythagorean-Copernican hypothesis, then the Valentinians, Marcionites, Basilidians, Anabaptists, Weigelians, and all who deny that Christ, the Son of God, took a true human nature have won, if indeed, as in the next book, Marcion has long been accustomed to say, that flesh and the things that belong to man are attributed to Christ in Scripture only according to outward appearance. Similar to these is what B. D. says at p. 14, when he writes: Marcion and his followers denied that Christ was a true man, and wanted him to be called a man only because he appeared to be one, not because he really was such. None of us does not shrink from that manner of interpreting the Sacred Letters. But how is it possible to uphold the orthodox interpretation of Holy Scripture against those heretics and others of the same stripe, unless we firmly hold to the principle, already laid down, of not departing from the proper sense of the words without a necessary reason? And where at last will the end of absurdities be, or through what door will the heresies of every kind not be opened?

units.la: DCCLIII. Resp. Non ita facilem concedimus his hæreticis victoriam, neque enim in Majori ulla connexio antecedentis cum consequente, ob magnam diversitatem dogmatum fidei & naturæ: nam 1. de Christo ejusque naturâ humanâ agit Scriptura non incidenter, sed ex instituto, eltque illa doctrina propria Scripturæ, cum directè faciat ad salutem illam; ergò accuratè in Scripturâ explicari, negari non debet: at de rebus naturalibus agit incidenter, non ut earum naturam explicet, cum hoc ad salutem non requiratur, sed ut per earum cognitionem, quamvis πκχυλω sive crassam, nos ad Dei, sive divinarum rerum cognitionem deducat. Adeoque 2. non tantum semel Scriptura carnis & ossium Christi mentionem facit, sed ejus conceptionem, nativitatem, educationem, conversationem diuturnam cum hominibus, ejus partes, animam & corpus, proprietates humanas &c. tam accurate describit, ut hæc omnia attente consideranti, mente à Sp. S. illuminatâ, non possit talis hæretica cogitatio in mentem venire; at non similiter ex textuum circumstantiis stantiis, in quibus formulas vulgares dicimus usurpari, patet, ea dogmata, quae adversarii ibi putant tradi, reperiri; quod si tam clare posset ostendi, ut veritas humanae naturae Christi ex sacris literis potest, nos his assensum praebere non retragabimur. 3. In exemplis, quae de rebus naturalibus adduximus, non tantum circumstantiae textus non requirunt, ut formulis, quae praejudiciis innituntur, ipsa illa praejudicia doceantur, sed & sanior Philosophia vel ipsa Scriptura ostendit, praejudiciis involutam esse veritatem, quae his formulis docetur; at simile quid haeretici circa locA humanam Christo naturam tribuentia dicere non possunt. Imo Philosophia sana supponens ea, quae Scriptura de Christo tradit, ut, cum dicitur, quod nobis esse similis quoad omnia debuerit, excepto peccato, elicit & concludit: Christo ergo veram naturam humanam, corpus finitum, locale & circumscriptum competere.
units.tr: DCCLIII. Reply: We do not concede such an easy victory to these heretics. For in the major premise there is no real connection between antecedent and consequent, because of the great difference between the doctrines of faith and of nature. First, Scripture treats of Christ and his human nature not incidentally but deliberately, and that doctrine belongs properly to Scripture, since it bears directly on that salvation. Therefore it must not be denied that it is explained accurately in Scripture. But it treats of natural things incidentally, not in order to explain their nature, since that is not required for salvation, but so that through the knowledge of them, however crude [παχυλῶς], it may lead us to the knowledge of God or of divine things. Hence, second, Scripture does not mention the flesh and bones of Christ only once; it describes his conception, birth, upbringing, and long life among men, his parts, soul and body, human properties, and so on, so accurately that anyone who considers all these things carefully, with a mind enlightened by the Holy Spirit, cannot have such a heretical thought come into his mind. But it is not similarly clear, from the circumstances of the texts in which we say common formulas are used, that those doctrines which our opponents think are taught there are to be found. And if it could be shown as clearly as the truth of Christ's human nature can be shown from the Sacred Letters, we would not hesitate to give assent to them. Third, in the examples we have adduced from natural things, the circumstances of the text not only do not require that those prejudices on which the formulas rest be taught, but sounder philosophy, or Scripture itself, shows that the truth taught by these formulas is wrapped in prejudices. But the heretics cannot say anything similar about the passages which ascribe a human nature to Christ. Indeed, sound philosophy, supposing those things which Scripture teaches about Christ, as when it is said that he ought to have been made like us in all things, except sin, draws the conclusion that a true human nature, a finite, local and circumscribed body, belongs to Christ.

units.la: DCCLIV. Inst. B. p. 21. multa affert ad hoc argumentum Marcionis defendendum, ac inquit: Quid si Marcion illam distinctionem non admittat. 2. Quid si neget in iis, in quibus sacra litera tantum incidenter agunt, magis licere absque ratione recedere a proprietate verborum. 3. Quid si neget, illas tantum incidenter Physica & Astronomica referre sine peculiari scopo. 4. Quid si probet sacras literas etiam in materiis fidei tropicis loquendi modis uti, quod facile efficiet, si absque cogente necessitate in Physicis liceat tropos effingere.
units.tr: DCCLIV. The Institutes, p. 21, brings forward many things in defence of this argument of Marcion, and says: What if Marcion does not admit that distinction? 2. What if he denies that in those matters where the Sacred Letters treat only incidentally, it is more lawful to depart from the proper sense of the words without reason? 3. What if he denies that they relate physical and astronomical matters only incidentally, without a special purpose? 4. What if he proves that the Sacred Letters use figurative modes of speech even in matters of faith, which he will easily do if it is allowed to invent tropes in physical matters without any compelling necessity?

units.la: Resp. Ad primum & tertium. Quid si vero ego firmiter probavero (ut factum cap. 3. & seq.) Scripturam rerum naturalium essentiam & interiorem constitutionem non explicare, nec propterea cognitionem earum accuratam ex sacris literis hauriendam, nonne eo ipso haec distinctio satis censenda firmata? Ad secundum & quartum dico; quid si vero attulerim rationes, ex quibus appareat, non singulis verbis & phrasibus Scripturae praecise insistendum, sed scopum & circumstantias textus inspicienda, ut de mente Sp. S. certus esse queas? habebitne quicquam B. pro Marcione ad me solide refutandum?
units.tr: Reply to the first and third: What if I have firmly proved (as is done in chapter 3 and following) that Scripture does not explain the essence and inner constitution of natural things, and that therefore an accurate knowledge of them is not to be drawn from the Sacred Letters? Would not this distinction, by that very fact, be considered sufficiently established? To the second and fourth I say: What if I have brought forward reasons from which it appears that one must not keep strictly to single words and phrases of Scripture, but must look to the purpose and circumstances of the text, so that you may be sure of the mind of the Holy Spirit? Will he have anything with which to refute me solidly on behalf of Marcion?

units.la: DCCLV. Inst. 2. B. p. 22. Argumentum meum quod pro veritate carnis Christi adduxi, in se esse optimum, hoc fundamento posito, de non recedendo a proprio verborum sensu absque necessaria ratione.
units.tr: DCCLV. The Institutes, 2nd book, p. 22: My argument, which I adduced for the truth of Christ's flesh, is in itself excellent, given this foundation, that one must not depart from the proper sense of the words without a necessary reason.

units.la: Resp. At hoc ego fundamentum suppono: itaque optimum hoc est meum argumentum.
units.tr: Reply: But I take this as a foundation; therefore my argument is excellent.

units.la: DCCLVI. Inst. 3. B. p. 27. At fere Cartesiani infinita loca Scripturae, quae beatiis vitam, sensum, cognitionem tribuunt, improprie volunt intelligi, & vitam & sensum & cognitionem in ipsis negantes. Et tu ipse vis cor sumi pro anima anima per metonymiam subjecti propter errorem vulgi, credentis animam essentialiter residere in corde, cum illa phraseologia plus centies in sacris literis repetiatur.
units.tr: DCCLVI. The Institutes, 3rd book, p. 27: But the Cartesians almost wish that the infinite passages of Scripture which attribute life, sense and knowledge to beasts be understood improperly, denying life, sense and knowledge in them. And you yourself want the heart to be taken for the soul by metonymy of the subject, on account of the error of the common people who believe that the soul resides essentially in the heart, although that phraseology is repeated more than a hundred times in the Sacred Letters.

units.la: Resp. Cartesiani vitam & sensum non negant in bestiis, sed recte ea explicant. Videat lector D. Velthusii Nader Bewijs &c. pag. 105. & seqq. Cognitionem vero non asserunt in iis, quia vident omnes earum actiones sufficienter per materialia principia posse explicari. At ego exinde non simpliciter argumentor, quod Scriptura non semel carnis & ossium mentionem faciat, sed quod ejus conceptionem, nativitatem, educationem &c. accuratissime describat, quodque ex scopo & circumstantiis textuum appareat, veram naturam humanam Christo attribui. An vero simpliciter & proprie cogitationem bestiis Scriptura tribuit & an similiter longe lateque cordis compositionem, functiones & proprietates describit & ea occasione sedem animae statuit? Nihil ergo hoc meae sententiae obest, quod cum insignibus Theologis & Medicis, Cor non esse sedem anima praecipuam, defendam.
units.tr: Reply: The Cartesians do not deny life and sense in beasts, but explain them rightly. Let the reader see Velthuysen's Nader Bewijs etc., p. 105 and following. They do not assert knowledge in them, because they see that all their actions can be sufficiently explained by material principles. But I do not argue simply from the fact that Scripture mentions the flesh and bones of Christ more than once; I argue that it describes his conception, birth, upbringing and so on most accurately, and that from the purpose and circumstances of the texts it appears that a true human nature is attributed to Christ. But does Scripture simply and properly attribute thought to beasts? Does it describe the composition, functions and properties of the heart in the same wide and long way, and on that occasion establish the seat of the soul? Therefore this does nothing against my opinion, which I defend together with notable theologians and physicians: the heart is not the principal seat of the soul.

units.la: DCCLVII. Inst. 4. B. p. 23. At etiam attente consideranti loca Scriptura, quibus motum Solis diurnum docent, non potest talis cogitatio in mentem venire, vid. quod non Sol, sed Terra moveatur.
units.tr: DCCLVII. The Institutes, 4th book, p. 23: But also to one who considers carefully the passages of Scripture by which it teaches the daily motion of the Sun, such a thought cannot come into mind, namely, that the Sun does not move but the Earth does.

units.la: Resp. Imo vero attente consideranti circumstantias textuum, non potest aliud in mentem venire, quam formulis receptis vicissitudinem dierum & noctium exprimi; de praejudicio isto, cui istae formulae innituntur Scripturam ξείζιν suam non instituere.
units.tr: Reply: On the contrary, to one who considers carefully the circumstances of the texts, nothing else can come into mind than that the alternation of days and nights is expressed in the accepted formulas. Scripture does not establish its own mode of speech on that prejudice on which these formulas rest.

units.la: CAPUT XXXVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXVIII.

units.la: Octava, nona, decima, undecima & duodecima Objecti- ones refutantur.
units.tr: The eighth, ninth, tenth, eleventh and twelfth Objections are refuted.

units.la: DCCLVIII. Objectionis octavae loco esse possunt ea, quae habet S. p. 406. Verum quidem est, per Scripturam nos a rebus inanibus ad coelestia & perennia invitari, interim tamen propterea non debuit loqui de rebus naturalibus cum errante vulgo: sic enim ostenderet sese delectari rebus inanibus, quid enim errore vulgi inanius censeri potest?
units.tr: DCCLVIII. The eighth objection may be taken from what the author writes on p. 406: It is true that Scripture invites us away from empty things to heavenly and enduring ones; yet for that reason it ought not to have spoken about natural things with the errant common people. For in this way it would show that it delights in empty things, since what can be judged emptier than the error of the common people?

units.la: Resp. 1. Scriptura Sacra descendendo ad captum vulgi, ita ut usurpet formulas a vulgo inventas & praejudicio innitentes, non propterea ostendit, se delectari rebus inanibus, sed tantum, se eo usque etiam velle demittere, ut, quemadmodum pater cum suis infantibus loquitur & balbutit, etsi sciat illas formulas loquendi infantium non exacte quadrare ad veritatem, ita pariter nobiscum balbutire velit: sapientia divina letificat deliciis suis filios hominum. Prov. viii. 31. Is qui se accommodat alterius infirmitati, non propterea ista infirmitate delectatur; sed cum quidem vellet mutatam, si fieri posset: Sed Deus, quia alia media concessit, per quae error circa res naturales tolli possit, lumen nempe naturae, quo si quis recte utatur certum est, non futurum erroribus obnoxium, eo ipso velle censendus est, ut errores circa res naturales, quatenus sunt quaedam imperfectiones, tollerentur, attamen quia talis error, talis imperfectio saluti non obest, non vult cum per Scripturam tollere, quod aliàs proculdubio esset facturus, sed tamen propterea non gaudet, non delectatur eo, sed fert, tolerat. Et quemadmodum Deus terendo divortium, & certas formulas ei praescribendo, videbatur condescendisse Judaeorum duritiei, ita hic loquendo cum vulgo, ejus ruditati se accommodasse dicendus est; at inde vel divortio vel ruditate & erroribus cum delectatum fuisse non censendum. Sic Deus etiam tollere posset peccatum, an vero quia non tollit, censendus est eo delectari? Init. At dices; sic etiam confirmaret errorem. Resp. Ad hoc responsum peti potest ex primae objectionis refutatione; nam etsi loquatur Scriptura eum vulgo, eam tamen cum eo sentire, dici non debet.
units.tr: Answer 1. Holy Scripture, in descending to the understanding of the common people, so that it uses expressions devised by the common people and resting on prejudice, does not for that reason show that it delights in empty things. It shows only that it is willing to stoop so far that, as a father speaks and stammers with his infants, although he knows that the infants' way of speaking does not exactly fit the truth, so likewise it is willing to stammer with us: divine wisdom rejoices in its delights with the sons of men (Prov. 8:31). One who adapts himself to another's weakness does not thereby delight in that weakness; he would rather wish it changed, if that could be done. But God, since he has granted other means by which error about natural things can be removed, namely the light of nature, which, if a person uses it rightly, is certain not to be subject to errors, must be taken to wish that errors about natural things be removed insofar as they are certain imperfections. Yet because such an error or imperfection does not stand in the way of salvation, he does not wish to remove it through Scripture, which he would doubtless otherwise have done; nevertheless he does not for that reason rejoice in it or delight in it, but bears with it and tolerates it. And just as God, by tolerating divorce and prescribing certain forms for it, seemed to accommodate himself to the hardness of the Jews, so here, by speaking with the common people, he is to be said to have accommodated himself to their rudeness; yet it should not be judged that he took pleasure in divorce, or in rudeness and errors. So too God could remove sin; but is he therefore to be judged to delight in it because he does not remove it? Init. But you will say: so also it would confirm error. Answer: To this objection the answer can be drawn from the refutation of the first objection; for although Scripture speaks with the common people, it ought not on that account to be said to agree with them.

units.la: DCCLIX. Nona objectio est, quâ utitur Vallesius in suâ Philosophiâ sacrâ, quae tali modo proponi posse videtur: Si Scriptura de rebus naturalibus loqueretur ex vulgi opinione: Ergo videretur velle nobis celare rerum naturalium cognitionem. At nulla est causa ob quam debeat celare. Ergo.
units.tr: DCCLIX. The ninth objection, which Vallesius uses in his Sacred Philosophy, may be put in this form: If Scripture spoke about natural things according to the opinion of the common people, it would seem to want to hide from us the knowledge of natural things. But there is no cause for which it should hide them. Therefore...

units.la: Resp. Hoc tantum colligi ex nostra sententia potest; quia Scriptura de rebus naturalibus loquitur, non accuratas formulas adhibens, sed e trivio desumptas & praejudiciis innitentes, nolle Deum, ut ex Scriptura petamus explicationem, non vero, velle Deum eas nobis absolute esse incognitas; nam ad eas inquirendas lumen naturae concessit, uti jam saepe est ingeminatum. Causae etiam, ob quas eas in Scriptura nolit explicare, jam sunt datae, quod accurata earum explicatio non conveniret auditoribus promiscuis Scripturae, quorum imbecillitas eas non caperet, quique facile turbarentur, si in Scriptura reperirent, quae tam manifeste pugnarent cum sensuum praejudiciis, quae ipsi habent pro veritatibus per lumen naturae cognitis.
units.tr: Answer. From our opinion only this can be inferred: since Scripture speaks about natural things without using exact expressions, but ones taken from the common run of speech and resting on prejudices, God does not wish us to seek an explanation from Scripture; but it does not follow that he wishes these things to be absolutely unknown to us. For he has granted the light of nature for investigating them, as has often been repeated already. The reasons also why he is unwilling to explain them in Scripture have already been given: an exact explanation of them would not suit the mixed audience of Scripture, whose weakness would not grasp them, and who would easily be disturbed if they found in Scripture things that so plainly conflicted with the prejudices of the senses, which they hold to be truths known through the light of nature.

units.la: DCCLX. Hisce subjungamus Objectionem decimam ex R. St. p. 47. desumtam: Si Scriptura loquatur aliquando ex opinione erronea vulgi, Ergo Ergo nemo certus erit, an non ea quae de Cæli & Terra creatione &c. docentur, sint ejusdem natura.
units.tr: DCCLX. Let us add the tenth objection, taken from R. St. p. 47: If Scripture at some point speaks according to an erroneous opinion of the common people, then no one will be certain whether those things which are taught about the creation of heaven and earth, etc., are of the same nature.

units.la: Resp. Regula, per quam quis scire possit, quid Scriptura doceat, est data, nimirum, ad scopum & circumstantias textus esse attendendum, ex quibus patere possit, quid phrasibus adhibitis docere velit, quâ regulâ applicatâ ad descriptionem Creationis Cœli & Terræ, cuilibet facile patebit, ea, quæ de iis repériuntur consignata in sacris literis, talia esse, ut ex iis sufficienter possit cognosci, Deo vero Creationem Cœli & Terræ verè & realiter competere, item, ordinem eum observatum, qui in Hexaëmero describitur.
units.tr: Answer. A rule has been given by which anyone can know what Scripture teaches, namely that one must attend to the purpose and circumstances of the passage, from which it may be clear what the author wishes to teach by the phrases he uses. When this rule is applied to the description of the creation of heaven and earth, it will easily be evident to anyone that the things found there recorded in the sacred letters are such that from them one can sufficiently know that the creation of heaven and earth truly and really belongs to God, and likewise the order observed that is described in the Hexaemeron.

units.la: DCCLXI. Objectio undecima peti potest ex verbis L. pag. 84. Hanc sententiam vel ad Dei contemtum vel ad puriorís religionis negationem stadium aperire.
units.tr: DCCLXI. The eleventh objection may be taken from the words of L. p. 84: This opinion opens the way either to contempt of God or to the denial of the purer religion.

units.la: Resp. Nullum est periculum, nam res fidei semper excepimus, in iisque Scripturam hominibus veritatem nudam, quantum ea ad salutem cognitu est necessaria, proponere dicimus, ut quod in uno loco obscurius est dictum, vel ubi Scriptura se ad intellectum infirmiorum accommodavit, in altero plenius nihilominus explicetur. Scimus puriorem religionem non aliunde petendam, quam ex revelatione; illam autem posse haberi sine accuratâ rerum naturalium cognitione, æque novimus.
units.tr: Answer. There is no danger, for we always except the matters of faith, and in these we say that Scripture sets forth to men the bare truth, as far as it is necessary to know for salvation; so that what is said more obscurely in one place, or where Scripture has accommodated itself to the understanding of the weaker, is nevertheless explained more fully in another. We know that the purer religion is not to be sought from anywhere other than revelation; and we equally know that it can be had without an exact knowledge of natural things.

units.la: DCCLXII. Objectionis duodecimæ loco esse possunt verba L. p. 177. Sententiam nostram insignem esse non magis novitate, quam impiâ arrogantiâ.
units.tr: 762. The twelfth objection may be the words of the author at p. 177: "Our opinion is remarkable not so much for its novelty as for its impious arrogance."

units.la: Ref. 1. Quod ad novitatem attinet, sciendum est, à novitate non debere alicui sententiæ præjudicium creari, nisi eâdem operâ omnia, quæ homines sentiunt de rebus quibuscunque, velimus rejicere: omnia enim hæc aliquo tempore fuerunt nova, tum nempe quando primum inventa sunt. Et per talem ratiocinationem, omnia quæ habet Aristoteles contra veterum Philosophorum placita ab ejus sequacibus essent rejicienda. Id quod nunc est novum, aliquando fiet antiquum, & quod est antiquum, aliquando novum fuerit necesse est. 2. Si spectes lumen naturale menti inditum, illud satis est antiquum, sed cum per illud aliqua veritas eruitur, ea quidem quatenus tunc demum detegitur, nova dici potest, sed tamen quoniam est veritas, antiqua sat est, utpote quæ ab æterno in mente Dei fuerit. 3. Quemadmodum novas terras detexisse gloriosum est, & Vespucio, Columbo & aliis insignis gloria inde accessit; ita novas veritates detegere, proculdubio si rem ipsam spectes, gloriâ & laude est dignum, quamvis ab invidis antiquariis, qui verentur, ne ipsi tandem cum suis veteramentis exhibilandi sint, dente Theonino rodatur. Sic novas veritates in Mathesi detexisse quovis tempore fuit gloriosum: sic ex Scriptura novas observationes depromsisse multis in laudem cessit, qui etiam librorum titulos his Epithetis condecorare non erubuerunt, uti patet ex. gr. ex libello d'Espagne, qui inscribitur Nouvelles observations sur le symbole de la Foy & similibus. 4. An verò ea sententia pro nova sit habenda, quae calculo tot Theologorum nititur, uti suo loco est demonstratum, judicent lectores: quanquam non differam his hominibus videri novam, ut & multa alia, quae ab ipsis non sunt cognita, sed nos hoc illorum judicium parum curamus. 5. Quomodo vero impia arrogantia haec sententia sit insignis, ostendat, si possit, adversarius. Nihil in eo impietatis, ut patet ex objectionum superiorum refutatione: Nihil arrogantiae si asseras, id quod ipsa res docet, firmisque rationibus comprobes, nisi forte nimis magna sit arrogantia ab istis Patronis veritatis scilicet in omnia alia abire.
units.tr: Reply 1. As to novelty, it must be understood that no prejudice should be formed against any opinion merely from its being new, unless we are willing at the same time to reject everything men think about any subject whatever. For all such things were at some time new, namely when they were first discovered. By such reasoning, everything Aristotle holds against the opinions of the ancient philosophers would have to be rejected by his followers. What is now new will at some time become old, and what is old must at some time have been new. 2. If you look at the natural light implanted in the mind, that is old enough; but when some truth is brought to light through it, that truth, insofar as it is then first uncovered, may indeed be called new; yet since it is a truth, it is old enough, inasmuch as it has been in the mind of God from eternity. 3. Just as it is glorious to have discovered new lands, and Vespucci, Columbus and others gained distinguished fame thereby, so to uncover new truths is undoubtedly, if you look at the thing itself, worthy of glory and praise, even though it is gnawed at by the Theonine tooth of envious antiquarians, who fear that they themselves may in the end be hissed off the stage together with their old wares. Thus to have uncovered new truths in mathematics has at all times been glorious; and to have drawn new observations from Scripture has brought praise to many, who were not ashamed to adorn the titles of their books with such epithets, as is evident, for example, from the little book by d'Espagne entitled Nouvelles observations sur le symbole de la Foy and similar works. 4. Whether this opinion is to be regarded as new, when it rests on the agreement of so many theologians, as has been shown in its proper place, let the readers judge; although I will not deny that it may seem new to these men, as many other things do that are not known to them; but we care little for their judgment. 5. How this opinion is remarkable for impious arrogance, let the adversary show, if he can. There is nothing impious in it, as is clear from the refutation of the objections above. There is nothing arrogant in it if you assert what the matter itself teaches and confirm it with firm reasons, unless perhaps it is too great an arrogance to depart from these patrons of truth in every other respect.

units.la: CAPUT XXXIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXIX.

units.la: Objectio tertia decima à comparatione rerum naturalium cum mysteriis prophetiis & Chronologicis desumta proponitur & refellitur.
units.tr: The thirteenth objection, drawn from the comparison of natural things with mysteries, prophecies and chronology, is set out and refuted.

units.la: DCCLXIII. Si Scriptura tradit alias res multo difficiliores, de iisque loquens adhibet formulas nudam & accuratam veritatem referentes, nihil morans imbecillitatem & captum hominum: Ergo similiter non fuit opus, ut de rebus naturalibus loquens, habitâ ratione captûs & imbecillitatis humanæ, utatur formulis è trivio desumtis innitentibus præjudiciis: Sed verum est prius, quod exinde apparet, quia mysteria omnem rationis captum excedentia tradit; item manifestum est ex prophetiis, in quibus multa, quæ à vulgo non intelliguntur, multa, quæ ne quidem à doctissimis Interpretibus explicari potuerunt ante eventum; liquet etiam ex Chronologicis & aliis non paucis in Scriptura intellectu difficilibus.
units.tr: DCCLXIII. If Scripture teaches other matters that are much more difficult, and when speaking of them uses expressions that state the bare and exact truth, without regard to human weakness and capacity, then likewise, when speaking of natural things, there was no need to take account of human capacity and weakness and to use expressions drawn from common speech that rest on prejudices. But the first is true. This appears from the fact that Scripture sets out mysteries that exceed all the grasp of reason; it is plain also from the prophecies, in which many things are not understood by the common people, and many things could not be explained even by the most learned interpreters before the event; it is clear too from the chronological passages and not a few others that are hard to understand in Scripture.

units.la: DCCLXIV. Resp. 1. Magna hic est diversitas, quæ facit, ut Majoris Propositionis nulla sit connexio. Nam primo, si spectemus mysteria, quæ nec ratio humana, postquam revelata sunt, intelligere potest, de iis antehac nulla præjudicia sensuum sunt formata, cum quibus pugnent, adeoque sermonem iis non accommodavit, imo nihil quicquam de iis cogitavit; itaque quando proponuntur à Scriptura, ab hominibus idiotis τὸ ὅτι illorum mysteriorum creditur propter auctoritatem & veracitatem divinam, de τῷ διότι vix NB ab iis cogitatur. Sic circa mysteria Trinitatis & Incarnationis &c. vulgares homines vix cogitarunt de Personalitate, an ea multiplicatâ individua etiam debeant multiplicari, an vero fieri possit, ut uni essentiæ individuæ plures personalitates conveniant. Similiter non cogitarunt, an individua essentia possit carere personalitate & ἑνυπόστατος fieri? Hæc & similia ne quidem in mentem ipsis veniunt, sed sufficit iis credere, quod sint tres personæ, quarum quælibet sit Deus, nec tamen sint tres dii, quoniam hæ personæ sunt unum essentia. Quod autem Philosophos Ethnicos attinet, illi in Lumine rationis nihil inveniunt, quod his veré contradicat, quemadmodum à nostris contra Socinianos ostendi solet. At de rebus naturalibus vulgus contrarias sententias veritati sæpe concepit, illasque tam firmiter habet radicatas, ut putet, à natura se de iis esse edoctum, adeoque quicquid eis repugnat, pro commento soleat habere; quod si ergo Scriptura formulâ accuratâ uti debuisset & per eam significare veritatem Philosophicam sine demonstratione, facile etiam ab aliis credendis populum rudem avertisset. Circa Chronologica, prophetias & similia, quia hæc non sunt cognitu ad salutem necessaria, non ita versatur vulgus, & quando hic in Scriptura difficilia quædam invenit, ea prætermittit, tanquam captum suum superantia, nihil de iis judicando. Quibus adde, quod cùm Chronologica & prophetiæ ante revelationem non fuerint ab infantia cognita, non potuerint circa ea præjudicia infantiæ & sensuum formari, quibus propterea sermo fuerit accommodatus.
units.tr: DCCLXIV. Reply 1. There is a great difference here, which means that the major premise has no connection with the conclusion. For first, if we consider the mysteries which human reason cannot grasp even after they have been revealed, no prejudices of the senses have been formed about them with which they could conflict, and so Scripture did not adapt its language to them; indeed people never thought anything at all about them. Therefore, when they are set before people by Scripture, uneducated men believe that (τὸ ὅτι) those mysteries are so on account of the divine authority and truthfulness, and hardly ever think about why (τῷ διότι). So with the mysteries of the Trinity, the Incarnation and so on, ordinary people have scarcely considered whether personality, when multiplied, must also multiply the individual, or whether it can happen that several personalities belong to one individual essence. Likewise they have not considered whether an individual essence can lack personality and become hypostatically (ἑνυπόστατος) subsistent. Such questions do not even come into their minds; it is enough for them to believe that there are three persons, each of whom is God, and yet that there are not three gods, because these persons are one in essence. As for the heathen philosophers, they find nothing in the light of reason that truly contradicts these doctrines, as our writers are accustomed to show against the Socinians. But concerning natural things the common people have often formed opinions contrary to the truth, and hold them so firmly rooted that they think they have been taught them by nature itself; so whatever conflicts with these they are accustomed to regard as an invention. If therefore Scripture had had to use exact language and by it signify philosophical truth without demonstration, it would easily have turned the unlearned people away from the other things to be believed. Concerning chronology, prophecies and similar matters, since these are not necessary to know for salvation, the common people are not much concerned with them, and when they find some difficult points in Scripture they pass them by as beyond their grasp, judging nothing about them. To these add that, since chronology and prophecies were not known from infancy before revelation, prejudices of infancy and of the senses could not have been formed about them, and therefore language did not need to be adapted to them.

units.la: DCCLXV. 2. Altera ratio diversitatis est, quod mysteriorum cognitio sit fidei, quæ propterea debebant in Scriptura tradi, & quamvis essent difficilia, tamen fide admitti ea oportebat; at res naturales pertinent ad scientiam, & citra salutis periculum possunt ignorari. Omittuntur ergo, ne, si earum veritas accurata, quæ sensuum cognitioni & apparentiæ sæpius adversatur, ac proinde incredibilis videtur, vulgo decerceretur, homines, qui de rebus naturalibus vix aliam quàm sensualem habent notitiam, turbarentur, & ita etiam ab aliis, quæ in Scriptura traduntur revelata, averterentur. Itaque nostra mens hæc est, sapientissimè Sp. S. egisse, quod omittendo ea quæ sunt levioris momenti, vel contentus notitia vulgari noluerit ab omnibus revelatis homines avertere. Cùm autem dicimus, mus, Sp. S. propter res fidei non declarasse res naturales, nemo hoc applicare debet ad ipsas res fidei, cum Scripturæ sit has tam accurate tradere, quàm ad salutem adipiscendam requirebatur.
units.tr: DCCLXV. 2. The other reason for the difference is that knowledge of the mysteries belongs to faith, and therefore they had to be delivered in Scripture, and although they were difficult, they had to be accepted by faith; but natural things belong to science, and can be unknown without danger to salvation. They are therefore left out, lest, if their exact truth, which often runs counter to the knowledge and appearance of the senses and so seems incredible, were disclosed to the common people, men who have hardly any knowledge of natural things beyond the sensory would be disturbed, and so would be turned away also from the other things revealed in Scripture. Our view, then, is that the Holy Spirit acted most wisely: by omitting things of lesser importance, or by being content with common knowledge, he did not wish to turn people away from all the revealed truths. When we say that the Holy Spirit did not declare natural things because of the matters of faith, no one should apply this to the matters of faith themselves, since it is the task of Scripture to deliver these as accurately as was required for obtaining salvation.

units.la: DCCLXVI. Inst. 1, M. p. 30. Deus infallibili suâ veracitate facilè potuisset retundere & reprimere hujusmodi præjudicia de rebus naturalibus, quemadmodum in rebus fidei actu videmus fieri, adeò ut non necesse fuerit propter ista præjudicia veritatem deserere. Item p. 32. Debebant homines ut circa res fidei, ita circa res naturales captivare intellectum.
units.tr: DCCLXVI. Inst. 1, M. p. 30. God, by his infallible truthfulness, could easily have overthrown and restrained such prejudices about natural things, just as we actually see done in matters of faith, so that there was no need to abandon the truth on account of these prejudices. Likewise p. 32. Men ought to have their intellect brought into captivity concerning natural things just as they are concerning matters of faith.

units.la: Resp. Non deseruit Sp. S. veritatem, quando usus est formulis receptis, sed, ut præjudicia non docuit, verùm tantùm veritatem aliquam generalem sub iis latentem, ita etiam ea per usum formularum accuratatarum noluit rejicere. Cùm autem falso hoc fundamento adversarius nitatur, ac si ex mea sententia Deus veracitatem deseruisset, falsum locutus fuisset, errores admisisset, apparet ea, quæ p. 31. ad istam Dei veracitatem probandam affert, nihil quicquam contra me facere. 2. Intellectûs captivatione opus non est, quando nihil docetur, quod eum excedit. At per istas formulas vulgares tantum docetur generalis veritas, quæ à quovis notitiâ communi utente potest intelligi.
units.tr: Reply. The Holy Spirit did not abandon the truth when he used the accepted expressions; but just as he did not teach the prejudices, and only some general truth lying hidden under them, so he did not wish to reject them by using exact expressions. Since, however, the opponent rests on the false foundation that, according to my view, God would have abandoned his truthfulness, would have spoken falsely, and would have admitted errors, it appears that what he brings forward on p. 31 to prove this truthfulness of God does nothing at all against me. 2. There is no need for captivity of the intellect when nothing is taught that exceeds it. But through those common expressions only a general truth is taught, which can be understood by anyone who uses ordinary knowledge.

units.la: DCCLXVII. Inst. 2. M. p. 32. Si vulgus per Philosophos de veritate edoctus deprehendisset, Scripturam neglectâ veritate errores vulgi sectari, nonne totam Scripturam ut scriptum erroribus scatens rejecisset?
units.tr: DCCLXVII. Inst. 2. M. p. 32. If the common people, taught about the truth by the philosophers, had perceived that Scripture, neglecting the truth, pursued the errors of the common people, would they not have rejected the whole of Scripture as a writing full of errors?

units.la: Resp. Si vulgus errores in Scripturâ tradi doceri & testimonio approbari vidisset, omninò id sequeretur, sed hanc meam esse sententiam nego. Non autem erat, quòd propter formularum receptarum usum Scripturam rejicerent, quia si ad textûs circumstantias attenderent, poterant cognoscere, iis veritatem quidem generalem doceri, & Scripturam obtinere munus significandi istam veritatem generalem, sed non etiam errorem, quem à præjudiciis nondum liberati per eas formulas significarent.
units.tr: Reply. If the common people had seen that errors were taught and approved by testimony in Scripture, this would certainly follow; but I deny that this is my view. Nor was there any reason for them to reject Scripture because of the use of accepted expressions, since if they had attended to the circumstances of the text they could recognise that a general truth was indeed taught there, and that Scripture had the function of signifying that general truth, but not also the error which those who were not yet freed from prejudices would have signified by those expressions.

units.la: DCCLXVIII. Inst. 3. M. p. 32. Homines etiam circa res pura puta fide cognitas præjudiciis capiuntur, quia ex 1 Cor. 11. animali homini ea quæ spiritus sunt stultitia. Nonne Judæi præjudicia formarunt de justificatione ex operibus, de exacta observatione legis, de comestione carnis & libitione sanguinis Christi &c. Consentit H. p. 216.
units.tr: DCCLXVIII. Inst. 3. M. p. 32. Men are also captivated by prejudices even concerning things known purely by faith, because according to 1 Cor. 11 the things of the Spirit are foolishness to the natural man. Did not the Jews form prejudices about justification by works, about the exact observance of the law, about eating the flesh and drinking the blood of Christ, and so on? H. p. 216 agrees.

units.la: Resp. Concedimus, quòd circa res quasdam fide cognitas præjudicia quædam formentur, sed negamus, ea esse præjudicia sensuum & infantiæ, adeoque similiter communem sermonem iis esse involutum, ut propterea utens eo Scriptura ad veritatem aliquam generalem significandam, non potuerint formularum praejudiciis innitentium usum evita-re.
units.tr: Reply.
