We grant that some prejudices are formed concerning certain things known by faith, but we deny that these are prejudices of the senses and of infancy, and so that common speech is similarly involved in them; therefore Scripture, when using such speech to signify some general truth, could not avoid using expressions that rest on prejudices.

units.la: DCCLXIX. Inst. 4. H. p. 218. Vulgus circa mysteria etiam de τῶ Διόν cogitare manifestum esse exemplo B. Virginis, quia mysterium Incarnationis secundum τὸ ὃν crediderat quidem, veruntamen τὸ διόν non intellexerat.
units.tr: DCCLXIX. Inst. 4. H. p. 218. That the common people, even concerning the mysteries, think about the that rather than the why is plain from the example of the Blessed Virgin, because she had believed the mystery of the Incarnation according to the that (τὸ ὃν), but had not understood the why (τὸ διόν).

units.la: Resp. Haec mihi non obsunt. Nam ego locutus sum de Idiotis in communi, & dixi, quòd vix de τῶ Διόν cogitent, non quòd nunquam id contingat. Sunt quidam ex Idiotis curiosi, sed plurimi aliis rebus intenti non inquirunt ulterius.
units.tr: Reply. These points do not harm me. For I spoke of the uneducated in general, and said that they hardly ever think about the why (τῷ διόν), not that this never happens. Some of the uneducated are curious, but most, occupied with other things, do not inquire further.

units.la: DCCLXX. Quae porrò objicit M. p. 34. & init. 35. ea observatis sequentibus cadunt. Nam 1. nituntur ista objecta hâc ejus opinione, quâ putat me statuere, Scripturam de rebus naturalibus loquentem falsum docere vel testari, quam sententiam toto hoc tractatu à me sum amolitus. 2. falso etiam supponit, potuisse Sp. S. abstinere ab omnium istarum rerum mentione, circa quas vulgus praejudiciis fuisset occupatus, cujus contrarium suo loco est ostensum. Similiter ad ea quae hic objicit H. p. 220. ex dictis sufficiens potest haberi responsio, prout lectori conferre volenti patebit. Omnia enim exinde procedunt, quod mentem meam non recte fuerit assecutus.
units.tr: DCCLXX. As for what M. objects on p. 34 and the beginning of p. 35, these fall away when the following points are observed. For first, these objections rest on his opinion that I hold that Scripture, when speaking of natural things, teaches or testifies falsehood; I have removed that view throughout this treatise. Second, he also wrongly supposes that the Holy Spirit could have abstained from mentioning all those things about which the common people were occupied with prejudices; the contrary has been shown in its proper place. Similarly, a sufficient reply to what he objects here from H. p. 220 can be had from what has been said, as will be plain to a reader who cares to compare. For all these arise from the fact that he has not rightly grasped my meaning.

units.la: DCCLXXI. Ad ea vero quae habet H. p. 221. noto sequentia, 1. nos non dicere, quòd Sp. S. contrarium loquatur veritati, quod hîc supponitur. 2. qualis metus turbandi indoctiores esset futurus, jam antehâc est dictum, nimirum, turbarentur idiotae, si locutionibus abstrusis & à communi usu remotis veritatem nudam sub cognitionem vulgarem non cadentem referentibus Sp. S. fuisset usus; quod non fit, quando in Scripturis mentio fit aquarum, quae in superâ parte sunt expansi, quales sunt nubes, item, quando dicuntur flumina ex mari fluere, & eodem rursus refluere & similibus.
units.tr: DCCLXXI. As for what H. says on p. 221, I note the following. First, we do not say that the Holy Spirit speaks contrary to the truth, which is what is assumed here. Second, what kind of fear of troubling the less learned would arise has already been said earlier: the uneducated would be disturbed if the Holy Spirit had used abstruse expressions, remote from common usage, that set forth bare truth not falling within ordinary understanding. That does not happen when mention is made in the Scriptures of the waters that are above the firmament, such as the clouds; likewise when rivers are said to flow from the sea and flow back again into it, and things of that sort.

units.la: DCCLXXII. Inst. 5. M. p. 35. Si vulgus circa prophetias non versatur, quare ergo Deus jussit Ef. VIII. 1. Prophetam exarare prophetiam stylo hominis? id est, stylo falso ad placitum vulgi compositio?
units.tr: DCCLXXII. Inst. 5. M. p. 35. If the common people are not concerned with prophecies, why then did God order the prophet (Isa. 8:1) to write the prophecy with a human stylus? That is, with a false stylus, composed to suit the taste of the common people?

units.la: Resp. 1. Nego stylum humanum, hoc est, formulis e trivio desumtis constantem & stylum falsum ad placitum vulgi compositum mihi eundem esse. 2. non dixi, quòd vulgus plane non versetur circa prophetias, sed dixi, quod non ita versetur circa eas ac circa res fidei, & ea, quorum cognitio simplex & quoad τὸ ὃν ad salutem est necessaria. Non enim ita inquirit nec inquirere tenetur in praedictiones, in quibus multa ante eventum tum sunt obscura, quam in ea quæ scire tenetur ad salutem. Circa prophetiam autem Esaiæ vulgus illius temporis debuit versari, ut ad pœnitentiam excitaretur, quæ ideo stylo humano, modo, quo suo loco est dictum, debuit exarari,
units.tr: Reply: First, I deny that a human stylus, that is, a style made up of formulas taken from the street-corner, and a false style composed to suit the common people, are the same thing for me. Second, I did not say that the common people are wholly unconcerned with prophecies; I said that they are not concerned with them in the same way as with the matters of faith, and with those things whose simple knowledge is necessary for salvation, as to what is essential [τὸ ὃν]. For they do not inquire into predictions in the same way, nor are they bound to inquire into them, since in predictions many things are obscure before the event, much more than in what one is bound to know for salvation. But the common people of Isaiah's time ought to have been concerned with his prophecy, so that they might be roused to repentance; and for this reason it had to be written in a human style, in the manner which, as I have said in its place,

units.la: CAPUT XL.
units.tr: CHAPTER XL.

units.la: Objectio quarta decima à fide Spiritui Sancto debitâ.
units.tr: Objection fourteen, from the faith owed to the Holy Spirit.

units.la: DCCLXXIII. Consideremus nunc verba S. p. 405. Frustra sunt, quicunque existimant, Spiritum Sanctum de rebus naturalibus loqui ex mente errantis vulgi potiùs quàm ex rei veritate: quod si hoc modo loqueretur, minùs fidem promereretur. Hoc enim si verum foret, pariter sequeretur, homines de rebus naturalibus philosophantes magis sufficere ad ingenerandam fidem in aliis quàm ipsum Spiritum Sanctum, quæ nobis suppeditare queunt objectionem quartam decimam, cujus hæc vis esse potest. Si homines de rebus naturalibus accuratè philosophantes & formulis accuratis eas exprimentes fidem merentur. Ergo, quamvis Sp. S. non uteretur formulis loquendi vulgaribus ex præjudiciis ortum habentibus, fidem in omnibus mereretur: Sed verum est priùs; Ergo.
units.tr: DCCLXXIII. Let us now consider the words of S. p. 405. They are wrong who think that the Holy Spirit speaks of natural things in the manner of the mistaken common people rather than according to the truth of the matter. If he spoke in this way, he would deserve less faith. For if this were true, it would follow equally that men who philosophise accurately about natural things are more sufficient for producing faith in others than the Holy Spirit himself. These words can supply us with the fourteenth objection, which may have this force: If men who philosophise accurately about natural things and express them in exact formulas deserve faith, then the Holy Spirit, even if he did not use the common forms of speech that arise from prejudices, would deserve faith in all things. But the first is true; therefore the second is too.

units.la: DCCLXXIV. Resp. Ad eam objectionem quoniam M. conquestus est me antehàc obscuriùs respondisse, operam dabo, ut clariùs meam responsionem exprimam. Dico ergo 1. nos non statuere, Spiritum Sanctum non esse fidem meriturum, si uteretur formulis accuratam veritatem exprimentibus. Fidem enim meretur Sp. S. in omnibus quæ testatur, quæ docet. Fides enim est assensus exhibitus testimonio divino, ubi autem testimonium divinum non est, ibi nec fides locum habere potest. At quando utitur formulis receptis, non testatur nisi generalem veritatem, cui propterea assensus est præbendus, non vero speciale præjudicium, quod homines præjudiciis obnoxii hisque formulis utentes exprimerent.
units.tr: DCCLXXIV. Reply. Since M. has complained that I answered this objection too obscurely before, I shall take care to state my answer more clearly. I say, therefore, first, that we do not hold that the Holy Spirit would not deserve faith if he used formulas that express the exact truth. The Holy Spirit deserves faith in everything that he attests and teaches. For faith is assent given to divine testimony, and where there is no divine testimony, faith cannot have a place. But when he uses received formulas, he attests only a general truth, to which assent is therefore to be given, and not a particular prejudice, which men subject to prejudices who use these formulas would express.

units.la: 2. Quod si vero voluisset Sp. S. loqui de rebus naturalibus formulis accuratis, perque eas specialem veritatem exprimere, & testari, fidem quidem meruisset, sed tamen hominibus, quibus præjudicia nondum ablata, difficile fuisset fidem exhibere, propterea quia tales de rebus naturalibus plerumque contrarias sententias conceperunt, easque pertinaciter fovent tanquam tales, de quibus à naturâ se esse edoctos putant: Ergo go sine demonstratione & praejudiciorum ablatione audientes contraria iis doceri, ea assequi non potuissent, & sic quamvis fidem adhibere debuissent,id tamen non facile fecisssent; quam difficultatem Sp.S. voluit evitare, utendo formulis receptis, etiamsi opinionibus erroneis niterentur. Distinguo itaque inter fidem debitam, & inter ipsam fidem actu adhibitam. Neque vero illud est mirum, si potius demonstrationibus accuratis aliquis a praejudiciis liberatus & praerequisitis ad demonstrationem cognitu necessariis recte praeimbutus assentiatur NB. quam praejudiciis occupatus, & existimans ea, quae a Sp.S. dicerentur, lumini naturali contrariari, subscribat testimonio Sp. S. Aeque quidem, imo majori jure fides Apostolis debita fuisset, si in citationibus V.T. nunquam secuti fuissent versionem LXX, quam viris doctis ostendentibus, ei versioni non ubique cum fontibus convenire. At antea vidimus ex Riveto, Voetio, Junio, Spanhemio, aliisque Theologis, placuisse Sp.S. Apostolos dirigenti sese hic accommodare hominibus, ne illi turbarentur. Similis ratio est formularum receptarum, quas propter usum diuturnum ab Apostolis dico retentas, quod observet H. contra ea quae habet p. 222. Nec fides deberetur hominibus demonstrantibus, sed assensus propter demonstrationem perceptam, qui assensus non nomine Fidei, sed nomine Scientiae esset insigniendus.
units.tr: Second, if the Holy Spirit had wished to speak of natural things in exact formulas, and through them to express and attest a particular truth, he would indeed have deserved faith, but it would have been difficult for men, whose prejudices were not yet removed, to give faith, because such men have for the most part formed contrary opinions about natural things and cling to them stubbornly, as things of which they think they have been taught by nature. Therefore, hearing things contrary to these taught without demonstration and without the removal of their prejudices, they could not grasp them, and so, although they ought to have given faith, they would not easily have done so. The Holy Spirit wished to avoid this difficulty by using received formulas, even though they rested on erroneous opinions. I therefore distinguish between the faith that is owed and the faith actually given. Nor is it surprising if someone freed from prejudices by accurate demonstrations, and rightly imbued with the prerequisites needed for understanding the demonstration, assents rather than one who is occupied with prejudices and thinks that what is said by the Holy Spirit runs counter to the natural light, and yet subscribes to the testimony of the Holy Spirit. NB. Indeed, faith would have been owed to the Apostles with equal, or even greater, right if they had never followed the Septuagint version in their citations from the Old Testament, which learned men have shown does not everywhere agree with the sources. But we saw earlier, from Rivetus, Voetius, Junius, Spanheim, and other theologians, that it pleased the Holy Spirit, directing the Apostles, to accommodate himself here to men, so that they would not be disturbed. The reason is similar for received formulas, which I say the Apostles retained because of long usage, as H. may observe, contrary to what he says on p. 222. Nor would faith be owed to men who demonstrate, but assent on account of the demonstration perceived; such assent should be designated not by the name of Faith but by the name of Knowledge.

units.la: DCCLXXV. Ex quibus observatis, omnia quae M. in contrarium affert p. 38. & 39. refelluntur. Nam 1. non dico, Sp. S. docentem non mereri fidem; vel ei fidem non debere adhiberi. 2. Sed nego, quod per illas formulas praecise testetur id, quod putant praejudiciis occupati.
units.tr: DCCLXXV. From these observations, everything that M. brings against this on pp. 38 and 39 is refuted. For, first, I do not say that the Holy Spirit, when teaching, does not deserve faith, or that faith should not be given to him. Second, I deny that through those formulas he attests precisely what men occupied with prejudices think.

units.la: 3. Nego, quod si voluisset per formulas accuratas testari veritatem contrariam praejudiciis sensuum sine demonstrationibus, facile fidem fuisset reperturus: saltem non sine magno offendiculo, & nisi singulari & occulta ratione mentes lectorum instruxisset & gubernasset, fidem invenisset, testando ea de rebus naturalibus, quae praejudiciis sensuum plane adversarentur. 4. Nullam blasphemiam ego admitto, sed pervertit verba adversarius, quando mihi tribuit, quod statuam, a praejudiciis liberatum magis debere NB. demonstrationibus a se formatis assentiri, quam praejudiciis captum testimonio Sp. S. quod non somniavi. 5. Suppositiones, quas mihi attribuit pag. 39. duas, non admitto, nec ex meis verbis possunt elici.
units.tr: Third, I deny that if he had wished to attest through exact formulas a truth contrary to the prejudices of the senses, without demonstrations, he would easily have found faith; at least not without great offence, and unless he had instructed and guided the minds of readers by a singular and hidden method, he would have found faith only by attesting, concerning natural things, things that plainly oppose the prejudices of the senses. Fourth, I admit no blasphemy, but the opponent perverts my words when he attributes to me the view that a man freed from prejudices ought rather to assent NB. to demonstrations formed by himself than to the testimony of the Holy Spirit when held captive by prejudice; I never dreamed of that. Fifth, the two suppositions that he attributes to me on p. 39 I do not admit, nor can they be drawn from my words.

units.la: DCCLXXVI.· Inst. p. 9. Insulsum esse, quod dicam, a vulgo homines supponi ea, quae dicunt, clarissimis & verissimis demonstrationibus evincere &c.
units.tr: DCCLXXVI. Inst. p. 9. It is foolish of me to say that people commonly suppose what they say to be proved by the clearest and truest demonstrations, etc.

units.la: Resp. Ego vero non a vulgo dixi supponi, homines ea quae dicunt demonstrationibus evincere, sed à me ipso in hac responsione, si clarissimis demonstrationibus homines evicerint sua dogmata, iis assensum deberi; si enim non faciant, nullo modo iis assensus adhibendus. Quo observato facilè cadunt ea quæ B. objicit p. 9. & 10. si etiam notetur, nos loqui de verissimis demonstrationibus, quibus assentiens tales debet percepisse, quod circa eorum argumenta, quæ adhibent Solis motûs defensores, fieri non potest, cùm non sint demonstrationes, sed paralogismi facilè solubiles, ut suis locis vidimus. Reliqua mera verba sunt & clamores rem non tangentes.
units.tr: Reply. I indeed did not say that people commonly suppose that what they say is proved by demonstrations; I said it myself in this reply: if men have proved their doctrines by the clearest demonstrations, assent is owed to them; for if they do not, assent is in no way to be given to them. With this observed, the points that B. objects to on pp. 9 and 10 easily fall away, if it is also noted that we speak of the truest demonstrations, which the one assenting ought to have properly perceived. This cannot happen with the arguments used by the defenders of the motion of the Sun, since they are not demonstrations but paralogisms easily solved, as we have seen in their places. The rest are mere words and clamours not touching the matter.

units.la: CAPUT XLI.
units.tr: CAPUT XLI.

units.la: Objectio quinta decima à Comparatione rerum natura- lium cum Miraculis.
units.tr: The fifteenth objection, from the comparison of natural things with miracles.

units.la: DCCLXXVII. Objectionem quintam decimam desumimus ex verbis S. p. 403. Nec audiendi sunt, qui sibi pro asserendo duro & periculoso commento, humanæ rationis pariterque sensuum infirmitatem imaginantur. Nam, si omnes Scripturæ filii (Atheos & Libertinos tanquam profanes à sacris his arcere fas est) qui invitantur ad considerationem rerum supernaturalium sive miraculorum, ea intellectu suo apprehendere possunt, cur non magis apprehendant naturalia? Imò cùm Scriptura proponat ea, quæ acciderunt circa naturalia, tanquam extraordinaria & miraculosa, cur non credendum, eam de rebus naturalibus ex præscripto veritatis loqui; ad hoc ut miraculosa & supernaturalia, imò contra-naturalia ex naturalibus intelligi possint? quod argumentum si in formam reducatur, tale poterit esse. Si homines præjudiciis occupati possunt miracula apprehendere: Ergo etiam interiora rerum naturalium. Itaque ut illa debent doceri in sacris literis; ita etiam rerum naturalium interiora in iis sunt explicanda, & per consequens Scriptura debuit formulis non innitentibus præjudiciis, sed accuratè & sine præjudiciorum involucris veritatem exprimentibus uti: Sed verum est prius, Ergo.
units.tr: DCCLXXVII. We take the fifteenth objection from the words of S. at p. 403: Nor are they to be heard who, to defend a harsh and dangerous opinion, imagine the weakness of human reason and likewise of the senses. For if all the sons of Scripture (it is right to keep Atheists and Libertines away from these sacred things as profane) who are invited to consider supernatural things or miracles can grasp them with their understanding, why should they not grasp natural things even more? Indeed, since Scripture presents those things which happened in connection with natural things as extraordinary and miraculous, why should it not be believed that it speaks of natural things according to the prescription of truth, so that miraculous, supernatural, and even contra-natural things may be understood from natural ones? If this argument is reduced to form, it may go like this: If men preoccupied with prejudices can grasp miracles, then they can also grasp the inner workings of natural things. Therefore, just as the former must be taught in the sacred letters, so too the inner workings of natural things must be explained in them, and consequently Scripture ought to use formulas that do not rest on prejudices but express the truth accurately and without the wrappings of prejudice. But the first premise is true; therefore the conclusion follows.

units.la: DCCLXXVIII. Resp. Argumentum non procedit à tractatione miraculorum ad tractationem & explicationem rerum naturalium, ob diversam rationem miraculorum & rerum naturalium. Nam 1. Miraculorum narratio necessaria est ad confirmandam fidem & auctoritatem verbi divini, non ita rerum naturalium accurata explicatio per formulas accuratas. 2. Miracula quando præsentia sunt, sensus circa ea fidem possunt juvare, atque ita facilius creduntur & cognoscuntur rita ex. gr. quando divisum fuit mare rubrum, illam divisionem factam esse sensus cognoverunt; quando verò facta sunt, & tanquam facta creduntur, etsi tunc sensibus usurpari non queant, sensibus iterum ordinarium naturæ cursum percipientibus, nihil tamen impedit, quin credi possit, cursum naturæ aliquando fuisse mutatum, eamque mutationem sensibus perceptam fuisse, quinimo miracula, quando fiunt, sensibus ut plurimum apparere debent; fiunt ergo quidem contra naturæ ordinem consuetum, non vero contra sensuum apparentias: at cùm accurata veritas circa res naturales ut plurimum repugnet sensuum apparentiæ, quæ à vulgo pro ipsâ veritate recipitur, manifesta satis est ratio diversitatis inter miraculorum & rerum naturalium tractationem à Scriptura institutam, hæcque repugnantia impedit, ut vulgus credere potuerit, si accuratis verbis simplex naturalium rerum veritas fuisset ostensa. 3. non tenebatur Scriptura de rebus naturalibus ex præscripto veritatis loqui, hoc est, uti formulis nudam veritatem referentibus, ad hoc ut miraculosa & supernaturalia, imò contra-naturalia ex naturalibus intelligi possint; nam ad id sufficiebat cognitio rerum naturalium, qualis per sensus haberi potest, adeoque vulgaris & omnibus communis, & si quid contra vel præter cursum naturæ à sensibus notatum fieret, id pro miraculo habendum: ex. gr. ad cognoscendum miraculum per Elisæum factum, ut ferrum enataret 2 Reg. vi. sufficiebat vulgaris cognitio, quod ferri natura sit, ut sub aquâ mergatur: at unde talis sit ferri natura, & quæ ratio gravitatis, ad miraculi cognitionem nosse non fuit necessarium.
units.tr: DCCLXXVIII. Reply: The argument does not proceed from the treatment of miracles to the treatment and explanation of natural things, because miracles and natural things differ in their nature. For, first, the narrative of miracles is necessary to confirm the faith and authority of the divine Word, whereas an exact explanation of natural things through precise formulas is not. Second, when miracles are present, the senses can help faith concerning them, and so they are more easily believed and recognised. For example, when the Red Sea was divided, the senses perceived that division; and when miracles have been done and are believed as done, although the senses can no longer be applied to them, the senses, perceiving the ordinary course of nature again, nevertheless do not prevent it from being believed that the course of nature was at some time changed and that the change was perceived by the senses. Indeed, miracles, when they occur, ought for the most part to appear to the senses; they happen, then, indeed against the customary order of nature, but not against the appearances to the senses. But since accurate truth about natural things for the most part conflicts with the appearance to the senses, which the common people accept as the truth itself, the reason for the difference between the treatment of miracles and of natural things in Scripture is clear enough, and this conflict would have prevented the common people from believing if the simple truth of natural things had been shown in exact words. Third, Scripture was not bound to speak of natural things according to the prescription of truth, that is, to use formulas expressing the bare truth, so that miraculous, supernatural, and even contra-natural things may be understood from natural ones; for knowledge of natural things, of the kind that can be had through the senses, and therefore common and shared by all, was sufficient for this. And if anything occurred against or beyond the course of nature, as noted by the senses, that was to be held as a miracle. For example, to recognise the miracle performed by Elisha, that the iron floated (2 Kings 6), common knowledge was sufficient, namely that the nature of iron is to sink under water. But to know from what cause such a nature of iron arises, and what the reason of its gravity is, was not necessary for knowing the miracle.

units.la: DCCLXXIX. Instantiæ, quas M. p. 40, 41. contra responsionem primam affert, facilè enervantur, si observetur, primò Objectionem propositam procedere tam à tractatione miraculorum ad explicationem rerum naturalium, quàm à miraculorum intellectione ad intellectionem rerum naturalium, quod patet, si quis attendat ad artic. 777. 2. Me hic non agere opponentem argumentando, sed respondentem defendendo, adeoque sufficere, si dederim rationem, propter quam Major propositæ Objectionis sit inconsequens. 3. Non necessariam esse ad confirmandam fidem rerum naturalium accuratam explicationem, sed sufficere superficialem, atque talem, qualis per communem notitiam potest haberi, prout initio hujus tractatus est inculcatum. 4. Non opponi explicationem falsam accuratæ, sed minùs accuratam, falsam verò opponi veræ, prout sæpiùs dictum.
units.tr: DCCLXXIX. The instances which M. brings at pp. 40 and 41 against the first reply are easily weakened, if it is observed: first, that the proposed objection proceeds from the treatment of miracles to the explanation of natural things, as much as from the understanding of miracles to the understanding of natural things, which is clear if one attends to art. 777. Second, I am not here acting as the objector arguing, but as the respondent defending, and so it is enough if I have given the reason on account of which the major premise of the proposed objection is inconsequent. Third, an accurate explanation is not necessary to confirm the faith concerning natural things, but a superficial one suffices, such as can be had through common knowledge, as was urged at the beginning of this treatise. Fourth, a false explanation is not opposed to an accurate one, but a less accurate one is; a false one is opposed to a true one, as has often been said.

units.la: DCCLXXX. Inst. 1. contra secundam responsionem M. p. 42. quid fiet de illis miraculis quae sensus non incurrunt?
units.tr: DCCLXXX. Instance 1 against the second reply, from M. at p. 42: What will be done about those miracles which do not fall under the senses?

units.la: Resp. Circa illa prior responsio, quae generalis est, sufficit.
units.tr: Reply: As to those, the former reply, which is general, is sufficient.

units.la: DCCLXXXI. Inst. 2. M. p. 42. Miracula judicio intellectus praesertim vulgaris & ab ipso miraculo remoti e diametro saepe repugnant, adeoque intellectui captu multo sunt difficiliora, eo quod ordinem totius universi semel constitutum transcendant, & superent, quod capere sine dubio intellectu difficillimum est. Similiter B. p. 8. Praesertim cum multo incredibiliora narret, quae non simplici judicio sensuum, sed omnium avorum experientia contraria &c.
units.tr: DCCLXXXI. Instance 2, M. at p. 42: Miracles, especially in the judgment of the intellect of the common people and remote from the miracle itself, often flatly contradict it, and so are much more difficult for the understanding to grasp, because they transcend and surpass the order of the whole universe once established, which without doubt is the most difficult thing for the intellect to grasp. Likewise B. at p. 8: Especially since he relates things much more incredible, which are contrary not to the simple judgment of the senses but to the experience of all ages, etc.

units.la: Resp. Imo vero facilius credi potest, cursum naturae aliquando esse mutatum, quamvis credatur, semper aliter se eum habere, quam sensus eum iis videntur repraesentare, qui ultra vulgarem notitiam non adscenderunt.
units.tr: Reply: Indeed, it can more easily be believed that the course of nature was at some time changed, even though it is believed that it always behaves otherwise than the senses represent it to those who have not risen above common knowledge.

units.la: DCCLXXXII. Contra tertiam responsionem instat M. p. 43. & 44. Ad quae observet lector, cui ea ibi inspicere licet 1. ut cognoscam mutationem esse factam, sufficere, si habeam cognitionem per sensus rerum ipsarum naturalium: sed ut cognoscam ipsum miraculum, utrum falsum, alia requiri non nego; neque dixi unquam, ad eam differentiam percipiendam sufficere judicium ex sensuum apparentia defuntum, cum Diabolus etiam suis praestigiis sensus deludere possit. 2. ex naturalibus ita perspectis, ut fit a communi notitia, quatenus vera est, sufficienter possumus cognoscere supernaturalia, quia comparationes inter haec instituta non in notitia Philosophica, sed notitia communi fundantur. Quod autem hoc modo, quo proponit adversarius, miracula fidem vere confirment, libenter concedo, nempe si, prout dicit, judicio intellectus vere persuasus fueris, illud a potentia divina esse profectum.
units.tr: DCCLXXXII. Against the third reply M. insists at pp. 43 and 44. To these the reader, who may look at them there, should note: first, that I do not deny that to know that a change has been made, it is enough to have knowledge through the senses of the natural things themselves; but that other things are required in order to know the miracle itself, whether it is false, I do not deny; nor have I ever said that judgment drawn from the appearance to the senses is sufficient for perceiving that difference, since the Devil too can deceive the senses by his illusions. Second, from natural things so perceived as they are from common knowledge, insofar as it is true, we can sufficiently know supernatural things, because the comparisons instituted between these are founded not on philosophical knowledge but on common knowledge. But that miracles, in the way the adversary proposes, truly confirm faith, I gladly concede, namely if, as he says, you are truly persuaded by the judgment of the intellect that it proceeded from divine power.

units.la: CAPUT XLII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XLII.

units.la: Objectio sexta decima desumta a comparatione rerum naturalium cum rebus gravibus, & captum nostrum excedentibus.
units.tr: The sixteenth objection, drawn from the comparison of natural things with weighty matters that exceed our understanding.

units.la: DCCLXXXIII. Objectio sexta decima desumi potest ex verbis B. D. p. 13. Probandum esset, non dicendum tantum, S. Scripturam tam ruditer & tam crasse loqui, ut rei ipsius veritas ex verbis eruinon possit. Sit ita, ut in maltmateriis quibusdam ad modulum nostrum se nobis accommodans, nobiscum balbutias, id sit in materiis gravibus, & conceptum nostrum excedentibus, non autem in Physicis, non in Astronomicis. Licet enim Sacra Scriptura subtiles Astronomiae quaestiones non tractet, in iis tamen quae de Astronomia profert, ita loquitur, ut nisi praeconcepta opinione sententiae contrariae laboremus, impossibile sit alias ex iis formare cogitationes. Ex quibus verbis tali modo obiectio potest formari: Si ad summum Scriptura est dicenda balbutire in rebus gravibus & conceptum nostrum excedentibus: Ergo non debet dici sese demittere ad nostrum captum per formularum non accuratarum usum in Physicis & Astronomicis: Sed verum est prius: Ergo.
units.tr: DCCLXXXIII. The sixteenth objection can be drawn from the words of B. D., p. 13: "It would have to be proved, not merely said, that Holy Scripture speaks so rudely and so crudely that the truth of the matter cannot be drawn out of the words. Granted, that in certain matters it accommodates itself to our measure and stammers with us, that is, in weighty matters that exceed our conception, but not in physical matters, not in astronomical ones. For although Holy Scripture does not treat the subtle questions of astronomy, yet in what it says about astronomy it speaks in such a way that, unless we labour under a preconceived opinion to the contrary, it is impossible to form other thoughts from those words." From these words the objection can be framed thus: If at most Scripture must be said to stammer in weighty matters that exceed our conception, then it should not be said to lower itself to our capacity by using inaccurate formulas in physics and astronomy. But the first is true; therefore the second.

units.la: DCCLXXXIV. Resp. 1. Dedimus rationem, ob quam fiat, quòd Scriptura de rebus naturalibus sæpè tam crassè loquatur, ut rei ipsius veritas ex verbis erui non possit specialis, hoc est, ut quando ex. gr. per formulam hanc, Sol currit, ostendit variationem situs corporis solaris velocem, non possit ex illâ hæc veritas erui, istam variationem situ pendere a Terra gyratione, nec tamen etiam contrarium, quia his præcisè verbis nihil aliud quàm illa variatio situs doceatur: atque τὸ διότι protulimus, quod requisivit hæc methodus Elenchtica: τὸ ὅτι etiam testimoniis quibusdam Scripturæ supra manifestum est redditum. 2. si concedatur, Scripturam Sacram in rebus gravibus ad modulum nostrum se accommodare & nobiscum balbutire, atque inde nullum periculum imminet Sp. S. arguendi (absit blasphemia) mendacii & falsitatis, multò magis hoc credendum est de rebus Physicis & Astronomicis, cùm hæ non ita sint cognitu necessariæ, ut materiæ graviores. Et quamvis res Physicæ & Astronomicæ captum hominis absolutè non excedant, attamen excedunt captum hominis idiotæ, præjudiciis multis mentem habentis occupatam, & non per prævias doctrinas ad ea capienda sufficienter instituti, quod cum Scriptura noluerit facere, non mirum est, si dicatur, eam etiam ipsam veritatem circa res Physicas & Astronomicas noluisse explicare. 3. an in iis, quæ de Astronomia profert ita loquatur, ut nisi præconcepta opinione sententiæ contrariæ laboremus, impossibile sit alias ex iis formare cogitationes, videbimus in sequentibus. 4. Invertimus potiùs hoc argumentum & dicimus: Quæ non ita sunt necessaria cognitu ad salutem, in iis minùs opus est, ut accuratè loquatur Scriptura Sacra; quæ verò magis sunt necessaria de iis magis accuratè debet loqui: quoniam quo magis accurate de iis Scriptura loquitur, eò magis accuratè cognoscuntur. Unde tamen non sequitur, quod existimat H. p. 226. Oracula Dei sine veritate concipienda, prout sæpiùs demonstratum.
units.tr: DCCLXXXIV. Response 1. We have given the reason why Scripture so often speaks about natural things so crudely that the truth of the matter cannot be drawn out of the words, specifically: when, for example, through the formula "the sun runs" it shows the rapid change in the position of the solar body, this truth cannot be drawn from it, that this change of position depends on the rotation of the earth; yet neither can the contrary be drawn, because these very words teach nothing but that change of position. We have also put forward the "why" (to dioti), which this elenctic method required, and the "that" (to hoti) has been made clear by certain testimonies of Scripture above. 2. Even if it is granted that Holy Scripture in weighty matters accommodates itself to our measure and stammers with us, and that from this there is no danger that the Holy Spirit be charged (far be the blasphemy) with lying and falsehood, much more must this be believed of physical and astronomical matters, since these are not so necessary to know as the weightier matters. And although physical and astronomical things do not absolutely exceed human capacity, they do exceed the capacity of an untrained man, whose mind is occupied with many prejudices and who has not been sufficiently prepared by prior teaching to grasp them. Since Scripture did not wish to do this, it is no wonder if it is said that it also did not wish to explain the truth itself concerning physical and astronomical matters. 3. Whether, in what it says about astronomy, it speaks in such a way that, unless we labour under a preconceived opinion to the contrary, it is impossible to form other thoughts from those words, we shall see in what follows. 4. We rather invert this argument and say: where things are not so necessary to know for salvation, there is less need for Holy Scripture to speak accurately; but where things are more necessary, it must speak more accurately about them, since the more accurately Scripture speaks about them, the more accurately they are known. Yet it does not follow from this, as H. p. 226 holds, that "the oracles of God are to be conceived without truth", as has been shown often enough.

units.la: DCCCLXXXV. Inst. 1. H. p. 227. Si naturales res homini minùs necessaria sunt, quare condescendit Deus? Cur proponit quæ necessaria non sunt?
units.tr: DCCLXXXV. Objection 1. H. p. 227: "If natural things are less necessary for man, why does God condescend? Why does he set forth things that are not necessary?"

units.la: Resp. Cognitio earum accurata non est necessaria ad scopum Sp. S. sed cognitio communis & vulgaris, igitur prior quia minus est necessaria, non etiam utitur Sp. S. formulis accuratis eam exprimentibus, sed formulas, quibus homines notitiam communem sectantes utuntur, usurpat.
units.tr: Response. Accurate knowledge of these things is not necessary for the purpose of the Holy Spirit, but common and ordinary knowledge is. Therefore the Spirit, because the former is less necessary, does not also use accurate formulas expressing it, but uses the formulas which men pursuing common knowledge employ.

units.la: DCCLXXXVI. Inst. 2. H. p. 227. Res Physicæ & Astronomicæ captum hominis Idiota excedunt tantùm per accidens.
units.tr: DCCLXXXVI. Objection 2. H. p. 227: "Physical and astronomical things exceed the capacity of the unlearned only per accidens."

units.la: Resp. Quamvis per accidens excedant, nempe propter mentem præjudiciis occupatam, tamen quia illa præjudicia Sp. S. noluit tollere, omninò hic debuit formulas receptas retinere, neque usurpare formulas, quæ vulgi captum excedunt; præsertim cùm per res naturales voluerit eos deducere ad spiritualia: Ergo formulas maximè captui accommodatas debuit usurpare, ne obscurum per æquè obscurum illustraret.
units.tr: Response. Although they exceed it per accidens, namely on account of a mind occupied with prejudices, nevertheless, since the Holy Spirit did not wish to remove those prejudices, it had altogether to retain the received formulas here, and not to use formulas that exceed the grasp of the common people. This is especially so since it wished to lead them through natural things to spiritual ones. Therefore it had to use formulas most suited to their capacity, lest it illuminate the obscure by means of the equally obscure.

units.la: DCCLXXXVII. Reliqua, quæ H. p. 227. & 228. habet inania sunt, affinia iis quæ B. p. 113. & jam refutata, cùm res naturales in Scripturis non ita tradantur, ut ex iis philosophice quis possit instrui; & quid per idiotam hîc intelligatur satis est manifestum, nempe omnino privative ignarus, qui præjudiciis est occupatus &c. cujus sane captum excedit rerum naturalium accurata doctrina, non præmissâ demonstratione & præjudiciorum exemptione, qualis ex mente adversariorum in Scriptura deberet reperiri.
units.tr: DCCLXXXVII. The remaining points which H. p. 227 and 228 contain are empty, akin to those which B. p. 113 has already refuted, since natural things are not so presented in the Scriptures that one could be philosophically instructed from them. And what is meant here by "the unlearned" is clear enough: entirely privatively ignorant, occupied with prejudices, and so on. The accurate teaching of natural things certainly exceeds such a person's capacity, not being preceded by demonstration and freedom from prejudice, which, on the opponents' view, ought to be found in Scripture.

units.la: DCCLXXXVIII. Inst. 3. B. p. 4. Hanc esse argumenti sui vim, quòd citra cogentem necessitatem à proprietate verborum ad tropicam & figuratam expositionem verborum deflectendum non sit, quod negare non fuerim ausus, nec tamen potuerim dare rationem.
units.tr: DCCLXXXVIII. Objection 3. B. p. 4: "This is the force of his argument: that without compelling necessity one need not turn from the proper meaning of words to a tropical and figurative exposition of them. I did not dare to deny this, but nor could I give a reason for it."

units.la: Resp. Hanc tamen vim argumenti hujus non præ se ferunt verba citata art. 783. hujus capitis, ut lectori patebit. 2. nos non recedimus à proprietate verborum in locis Scripturæ exponendis, in quibus dicimus reperiri formulas præjudiciis innitentes, sed quid per eas Sp. S. voluerit significare ex scopo & circumstantiis textus colligimus, & quod circumstantiæ textus non requirunt, illud etiam non dicimus significari, itaque non tam est quæstio deacceptione verborum propriâne an impropriâ, sed quid & quousque Spiritus Sanctus his vel illis verbis voluerit testari.
units.tr: Response. 1. However, the words cited in art. 783 of this chapter do not display this force of the argument, as the reader will see. 2. We do not depart from the proper meaning of words in expounding passages of Scripture. In those places we say that there are formulas resting on prejudices; but what the Holy Spirit meant to signify by them we gather from the scope and circumstances of the text, and what the circumstances of the text do not require, we do not say is signified. So the question is not so much whether the words are taken in their proper or improper sense, but what, and how far, the Holy Spirit wished to attest by these or those words.

units.la: DCCLXXXIX. Inst. 4. B. p. 7. Hæc, nempe, quod homines præjudiciis sint obruti & veritatem exprimant formulis, quæ in præjudiciis habent ortum, quibus etiam Spiritus Sanctus voluerit uti, ne turbareutur homines, gratis dicuntur.
units.tr: DCCLXXXIX. Objection 4. B. p. 7: "That men are overwhelmed by prejudices and express the truth in formulas that have their origin in those prejudices, which the Holy Spirit also wished to use lest men be disturbed, is said without warrant."

units.la: Resp. Probatum hoc est ab initio, & ipsa experientia docet, talia esse præjudicia, talemque sermonem, quem non immutandum fuisse à Spiritu Sancto in hoc libro ostendimus.
units.tr: Response. This has been proved from the beginning, and experience itself teaches that such prejudices exist, and that such speech, which we have shown should not have been changed by the Holy Spirit in this book.

units.la: DCCXC. Inst. 5. B. p. 7. Vulgus fidelis magis supponit, Spiritum Sanctum intimam habere cognitionem naturâ quàm homines (quod concedo) ac per consequens magis certiusque loqui secundum veritatem (hoc est uti formulis veritatem nudam exprimentibus) quàm homines (nempe Philosophos, de quibus est sermo.)
units.tr: DCCXC. Objection 5. B. p. 7: "The faithful common people assume more than men do that the Holy Spirit has an intimate knowledge of nature (which I grant), and consequently speaks more certainly and more truly according to the truth (that is, uses formulas that express the bare truth) than men (namely the philosophers, of whom we are speaking)."

units.la: Resp. Illud vero est inconsequens, cum mutatio non sit exspectanda ab eo, qui tantum propter aliud & non philosophice rem declarat.
units.tr: Response. That is indeed inconsistent, since change is not to be expected from one who explains a thing only for another purpose and not philosophically.

units.la: DCCXCI. Inst. 6. B. pag. 11. & seq. Cum Deus nobiscum balbutit utitur phrasibus tropicis à rebus humanis desumtis, in quibus nullum est periculum, quod Sp. S. mendacii vel falsitatis sit arguendus, cum non notent contrarium vel contradictorium rei per tropum designatae, sed rem ipsam sub tropico loquendi modo; verùm in phraseologiâ quam Cartesiani nobis fingunt notatur contrarium rei significata.
units.tr: DCCXCI. Objection 6. B. p. 11 f.: "When God stammers with us, he uses tropical phrases drawn from human affairs, in which there is no danger that the Holy Spirit be charged with lying or falsehood, since they do not mark the contrary or contradictory of the thing designated by the trope, but the thing itself under a figurative mode of speech. In the phraseology which the Cartesians invent for us, however, the contrary of the thing signified is indicated."

units.la: Resp. Est par utriusque ratio: falsum enim est, quod dicamus per istas formulas contrarium significari, sed dicimus, generalem veritatem significari, non vero consignificari errorem, qui quidem à præjudiciis obsesso significaretur.
units.tr: Response. The reasoning of both is the same. For it is false that we say the contrary is signified by those formulas; we say that a general truth is signified, not that error is co-signified, which would indeed be signified in a man beset by prejudices.

units.la: DCCXCII. Inst. 7. B. p. 12. Cum Sacra Scriptura nobiscum balbutit, id fit vel propter verborum defectum, vel propter nostram incapacitatem ad rei ipsius conceptum, quorum neutrum in materiâ de motu Solis vel Terrae locum habet.
units.tr: DCCXCII. Objection 7. B. p. 12: "When Holy Scripture stammers with us, this happens either because of a lack of words or because of our incapacity to grasp the thing itself. Neither of these has a place in the matter of the motion of the Sun or Earth."

units.la: Resp. Id fit propter incapacitatem hominum, præjudiciis occupatorum, quales omnes sunt ab infantiâ & plurimi in virili ætate manent, quam incapacitatem quoniam noluit tollere Sp. S. iis sese accommodare habuit necesse.
units.tr: Reply: It happens because of the incapacity of men, who are occupied by prejudices, as all are from infancy and most remain so into manhood. Since the Holy Spirit was unwilling to remove this incapacity, He was necessarily obliged to accommodate Himself to it.

units.la: DCCXCIII. Inst. 8. B. p. 13. Mentem habere præjudiciis occupatam non dicit, mentem non esse capacem ad rem apprehendendam si clarè doceretur.
units.tr: DCCXCIII. Institutio, 8th objection, p. 13. He does not say that the mind is occupied with prejudices; he says that the mind is not capable of grasping the matter if it were taught clearly.

units.la: Resp. Nec ego habeo ista duo pro iisdem, sed dico, mentem præjudiciis occupatam & cui debito modo ista non exempta sunt, non esse capacem ad rem apprehendendam, quæ sine demonstratione simpliciter proponeretur.
units.tr: Reply: I do not hold these two to be the same. I say that a mind occupied with prejudices, and not freed from them in the proper way, is not capable of grasping a matter that is simply put forward without demonstration.

units.la: DCCXCIV. Tandem non consistere videntur ea quæ habet B. in fine p. 14. Quamvis forsan posses probare, verba sacra secundum apparentiam ob necessarias rationes debere intelligi, hoc tamen maneret certum, ipsum textum sacrum per se, non alios in nobis posse formare conceptus, quàm Terrâ quiescente Solem circa eam motu diurno moveri.
units.tr: DCCXCIV. Finally, the things which the author has at the end of p. 14 do not seem to hold together. Although perhaps you could prove that the sacred words must be understood according to appearance, for necessary reasons, this would nevertheless remain certain: the sacred text itself, by itself, cannot form in us any other concepts than that, with the earth at rest, the sun moves around it in a daily motion.

units.la: Resp. Si enim posterius sit verum: Ergo nullæ possunt esse rationes, ob quas aliter deberet sacer textus intelligi, nisi phrasi, per se non posse formare in nobis alios conceptus, intelligas, homines præjudiciis occupatos incidentes in textus, in quibus formulæ iis innitentes reperiuntur, existimare primo intuitu, ea præjudicia à Spiritu Sancto designari, à quâ tamen cogitatione postquam quis circumstantias textus rite examinavit, est recedendum.
units.tr: Reply: For if the latter is true, then there can be no reasons why the sacred text should be understood otherwise, unless by the phrase cannot by itself form other concepts in us you mean this: men occupied with prejudices, coming upon passages in which formulas resting on those prejudices are found, at first glance think that those prejudices are signified by the Holy Spirit; yet from this thought one must withdraw once someone has duly examined the circumstances of the text.

units.la: CAPUT XLIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XLIII.

units.la: Objectiones à septima decima usque ad vigesimam septi- mam proponuntur & refutantur.
units.tr: Objections from the seventeenth to the twenty-seventh are put forward and refuted.

units.la: DCCXCV. Succedunt nunc aliæ Objectiones, quas de novo ex Adversariorum scriptis collegi, quarum tamen quasdam si potius inter Exceptiones velis numerare, non multum refragabor. Septima decima desumitur ex M. pag. 8. dicente: Hâc ratione omnium auctorum falsitates excusavero, dicendo, auctorem quidem uti hac vel illâ formulâ falsum significante, interim ipsum verum sentire.
units.tr: DCCXCV. Now follow other objections, which I have newly gathered from my opponents' writings, though if you would rather count some of them among the exceptions, I shall not greatly object. The seventeenth is taken from M. p. 8, where he says: By this reasoning I shall excuse all the falsehoods of authors, by saying that the author indeed uses this or that formula signifying something false, while he himself nevertheless means the truth.

units.la: Resp. Nullo modo, si id ita explices ut ego, nempe, Auctorem uti formula quâdam veritatem generalem significante, etiamsi alius quis ea utens per eam præter istam veritatem, etiam quandam falsitatem consignificaret. Id enim faciens auctor, cum tali sermone non falsum, sed verum significet, nullius etiam falsitatis poterit accusari.
units.tr: Answer: Not at all, if you explain it as I do, namely: The author uses a formula signifying some general truth, even though another person using it signifies, through it, besides that truth, also some falsehood. For in doing this, the author, since by such speech he signifies not what is false but what is true, cannot be accused of any falsehood.

units.la: DCCXCVI. Objectionis octavæ decimæ loco sint sequentia (M. p. 9.) Quando Paulus formulam Menandri 1 Cor. xv. 33. Epimenidis Tit. I. 2. Arati Act. xvii. 28. suam facit, quis dicat eum sensum illarum & sententiam auctorum illorum non suam facere.
units.tr: DCCXCVI. In place of the eighteenth objection let the following serve (M. p. 9): When Paul makes his own the formula of Menander (1 Cor. 15:33), of Epimenides (Titus 1:2), and of Aratus (Acts 17:28), who would say that he does not make his own the sense and meaning of those authors?

units.la: Resp. Si in illâ formulâ munus significandi sit tantum unum, tum omnino is, qui eâ utitur, illum etiam unum sensum suum facit, si se non alibi explicet, ut superius vidimus; sed si munus illa formula obineat duplex, tum tantum generalem sensum suum facit, non etiam necessario specialem, quem cum eo auctor conjunxit, v. g. ponamus Aratum per illa verba, ἔ χρ ἡμ ἡμῶ ἐσμέν, significasse primo quidem & generaliter, nos à Deo Originem nostram habere. 2. speciliter, ita ab eo origine nem habere, ut etiam partem divinæ essentiæ simus consecuti, tum proculdubio Sp. S. tantum prius significavit, non posterius consignificavit.
units.tr: Answer: If the formula has only one function of signifying, then whoever uses it does indeed make that one sense his own, unless he explains himself otherwise, as we saw above. But if the formula has a twofold function, then he makes his own only the general sense, not necessarily also the special sense which the author joined with it. For example, let us suppose that Aratus, by the words "for we are also his offspring" [τοῦ γὰρ καὶ γένος ἐσμέν], signified first and generally that we have our origin from God, and secondly, in particular, that we have our origin from him in such a way that we are also parts of the divine essence. Then undoubtedly the Holy Spirit signified only the former, and did not co-signify the latter.

units.la: DCCXCVII. Sequitur Objectio nona decima M. p. 9. Quicunque formulis loquendi sciens volens alio sensu utitur, quam is cui loquitur, u non barbarus modo, sed & fallax est, quod utrumque blasphemum est de Spiritu Sancto cogitare.
units.tr: DCCXCVII. Next follows the nineteenth objection, M. p. 9: Whoever knowingly and willingly uses forms of speech in a sense other than that in which the one he addresses understands them is not only a barbarian but also deceitful; and to think of the Holy Spirit as either is blasphemous.

units.la: Resp. Qui in sensu principali & generali utitur formulis loquendi, quo utitur is, cui loquitur, ille nec barbarus, nec fallax est, etiamsi speciem illum sensum non consignificet, quem omnis is, cui loquitur, dum illis formulis uteretur, significaret. At Sp. S. utitur formulis isto sensu generali & principali.
units.tr: Answer: Whoever uses forms of speech in the principal and general sense in which the one he addresses understands them is neither a barbarian nor deceitful, even if he does not co-signify that special sense which every hearer, while using those forms, would signify. But the Holy Spirit uses the forms in this general and principal sense.

units.la: DCCXCVIII. Objectio vigesima M. p. 13. Qua sententia infert, Deum aliquando esse falsum testem, ea prorsus est falsa & absurda; sed id facit vestra sententia, Ergo. Min. quia Deus loquens secundum falsam opinionem vulgi, (hoc est, utens formulis receptis, etsi opinionibus erroneis innitantur) profert testimonium à re dissentiens. Probatur vicissim Minor: quia testatur moveri Solem, & Terram quiescere, cum revera Sol non moveatur.
units.tr: DCCXCVIII. Objection twenty, M. p. 13: Whatever opinion implies that God is sometimes a false witness is wholly false and absurd; but your opinion does this. Therefore. The minor premise: because God, speaking according to the false opinion of the common people (that is, using received forms, even though they rest on erroneous opinions), gives a testimony that differs from the thing. The minor is proved in turn: because he testifies that the Sun moves and the Earth rests, when in truth the Sun does not move.

units.la: Resp. Neg. Min. cum probationibus. Quod enim testatur Sp. S. formulis dictis, quod significat, quod docet optimè cum veritate convenit: salsissimum autem est, ullibi testari vel docere Sp. S. Solem moveri & Terram quiescere. Atque hæc mera est petitio Principii, & assumtio ejus, quod est in quæstione.
units.tr: Answer: I deny the minor premise, with its proofs. For what the Holy Spirit testifies by those said forms, what he signifies, what he teaches, agrees most perfectly with the truth. But it is utterly absurd to say that the Holy Spirit anywhere testifies or teaches that the Sun moves and the Earth rests. This is mere begging of the question, and an assumption of what is in dispute.

units.la: DCCXCIX. Inst. M. p. 15. Cui fides est adhibenda, illud est testimonium: At omnibus quæ Deus loquitur est fides adhibenda, Ergo.
units.tr: DCCXCIX. Inst. M. p. 15: That to which faith is to be given is a testimony; but faith is to be given to everything God says. Therefore.

units.la: Resp. Concedi totum argumentum: id enim Deus loquitur formaliter & proprie, quod per verba significat, eique fidem esse adhibendam una cum omnibus vere Christianis contendo, & propugnabo, quamdiu Spiritus hos regit artus; sed Deum loqui formaliter, Solem motu reali moveri & similia, quæ homines Scripturis tanquam nolis sonantibus affingunt, nego.
units.tr: Answer: I grant the whole argument. For God speaks formally and properly that which he signifies by his words, and faith is to be given to it; this I maintain and will defend, together with all truly Christian people, as long as the Spirit rules these limbs. But that God speaks formally that the Sun moves with real motion, and similar things which men attribute to the Scriptures as if the Scriptures sounded so, I deny.

units.la: DCCC. Objectio vigesima prima M. p. 16. Deus loquens secundum falsam opinionem vulgi (hoc est, utens formulis vulgi, ex præjudiciis originem habentibus) sciens volens abludit à veritate, Ergo constituitur mendax.
units.tr: DCCC. Objection twenty-one, M. p. 16: God, speaking according to the false opinion of the common people (that is, using the forms of the common people, which have their origin in prejudices), knowingly and willingly departs from the truth; therefore he is made a liar.

units.la: Y.y 3
units.tr: Y.y 3

units.la: Resp. Min. Neg. & quia ejus fundamentum (quod per illas formulas testentur falsitatem ex nostra sententia) est refutatum, atque de eo etiam superius actum, non est quod hic plura dicamus.
units.tr: Answer: The minor premise is denied. And since its foundation (that by those forms they testify falsehood according to our opinion) has been refuted, and was also dealt with above, there is no need to say more here.

units.la: DCCCI. Objectio vigesima secunda M. p. 16. Per eam sententiam evertitur omnis fides divina; quod evincere inde conatur, quia ea sententia veritatem tollit à testimonio.
units.tr: DCCCI. Objection twenty-two, M. p. 16: By that opinion all divine faith is overthrown; which he tries to prove from this, because that opinion removes truth from testimony.

units.la: Resp. Illud superius refutatum.
units.tr: Answer: That has been refuted above.

units.la: DCCCII. Inst. 1. M. p. 17. At haec sententia tollit hoc axioma, quicquid Deus dicit verum est: Ergo tollit omnem fidem divinam.
units.tr: DCCCII. Inst. 1, M. p. 17: But this opinion removes this axiom, whatever God says is true; therefore it removes all divine faith.

units.la: Resp. Negatur Antecedens, ejusque falsitas ex dictis patet.
units.tr: Answer: The antecedent is denied, and its falsity is plain from what has been said.

units.la: DCCCIII. Inst. 2. M, p. 18. At qui statuit Deum loqui aliquando falsum, secundum opinionem vulgi, ille negat omne quod Deus dicit verum esse.
units.tr: DCCCIII. Inst. 2, M. p. 18: But whoever holds that God sometimes speaks falsely, according to the opinion of the common people, denies that everything God says is true.

units.la: Resp. Nullibi dixi, Deum loqui falsum, sed tantum dico, uti formulis receptis; quo nullatenus nego, omne quod Deus dicit verum esse; sed quaestio est, quid sit illud quod Deus dicit? utique id quod significat, quod testatur, quod docet; quod non esse falsum ex nostra sententia supra evictum.
units.tr: Answer: I nowhere said that God speaks falsely; I only say that he uses received forms. In that I by no means deny that everything God says is true. The question is, what is that which God says? Surely that which he signifies, which he testifies, which he teaches; and that this is not false has been proved above from our opinion.

units.la: DCCCIV. Objectio vigesima tertia M. p. 19. Per istam sententiam, errare, fit bonum morale, quod hic ostendere conatur: Ad quodcunque tenemur lege divina, id est bonum morale. Atqui (ex hypothesi adversarii statuentis, Deum in naturalibus loqui quod in se falsum est &c.) tenemur lege divina ad errandum: Ergo.
units.tr: DCCCIV. Objection twenty-three, M. p. 19: By this opinion error becomes a moral good, which he tries to show thus: Whatever we are bound to by divine law is a moral good. But (on the hypothesis of the adversary, who holds that God in natural matters speaks what is in itself false, etc.) we are bound by divine law to err. Therefore.

units.la: Resp. Neg. hanc meam esse hypothesin, Deum in naturalibus loqui quod in se falsum est, cum dixerim, quod his formulis verum loquatur.
units.tr: Answer: I deny that this is my hypothesis, that God in natural matters speaks what is in itself false, since I have said that by these forms he speaks what is true.

units.la: DCCCV. Objectio vigesima quarta M. p. 20. Haec sententia convenit cum Pontificiis statuentibus, fidem divinam non resolvi ultimo in Scripturam Sacram, sed in Ecclesiam. Et cum Socinianis docentibus, quicquid repugnat rationi non esse credendum, in eo, quod cum illis constituit normam quandam extra Scripturam, ad quam Scriptura sensus examinari debet, quaque de eo judicare possit.
units.tr: DCCCV. Objection twenty-four, M. p. 20: This opinion agrees with the Papists, who hold that divine faith is not ultimately resolved into Holy Scripture but into the Church. And it agrees with the Socinians, who teach that whatever is repugnant to reason is not to be believed; in that he sets up with them a certain norm outside Scripture, by which the sense of Scripture must be examined, and by which one can judge about it.

units.la: Resp. Negando, me aliquam normam extra Scripturam agnoscere, ad quam ejus veritas examinari debet; neque enim aliud quid ex mea sententia colligi potest, quam id, quod adversarius statuit p. 22. Rationem ut medium recto Scripturae sensui eliciendo adhiberi posse. Probandum ergo contrarium ab Adversario ex meis verbis fuisset.
units.tr: Answer: I deny that I acknowledge any norm outside Scripture to which its truth must be examined. Nothing else can be gathered from my opinion than what the adversary himself states on p. 22: that reason can be used as a means of eliciting the right sense of Scripture. He should therefore have proved the contrary from my own words.

units.la: DCCCVI. Pergit: In hoc vero dissentiunt, quod Wittichius statuat veram aliquam falsitatem in Scriptura existere: illi vero id prorsus inficientur. 2. quod hic tantum locutiones de rebus moralibus & naturalibus rationis judicio velit subesse, in rebus vero puris putis fidei Scriptura suprematum libenter agno-scere profitetur.
units.tr: DCCCVI. He goes on: They differ in this, that Wittich holds that some real falsehood exists in Scripture, whereas they flatly deny it. 2. That here he wishes only the expressions about moral and natural matters to be subject to the judgment of reason, but in pure matters of faith he freely professes that Scripture has supremacy.

units.la: Resp. Falsissimum prius, me judicare veram aliquam falsitatem in Scripturis existere, idque saepius a me negatum, neque talia verba ulla in meis Dissertationibus reperiuntur. 2. neque dico, locutiones de rebus naturalibus & moralibus debere subesse rationis judicio, ut ad eam tanquam normam examinentur, sed tantum: rationem esse medium, per quod cognosci possit, quales sint locutiones illae, num accuratae, num vulgares, quae praejudiciis quidem innitantur, veritatem tamen aliquam significent.
units.tr: Answer: The first point is most false: I do not judge that any real falsehood exists in the Scriptures, and I have often denied it; nor are any such words to be found in my Dissertations. 2. Nor do I say that expressions about natural and moral matters must be subject to the judgment of reason, so as to be examined by it as a norm. I say only that reason is the means by which it can be known what sort of expressions those are, whether accurate or popular, which indeed rest on prejudices yet signify some truth.

units.la: DCCCXVII. Quandoquidem ergo haec mea non est sententia, frustra p. 23, 24, & 25. argumenta contra me proferuntur, quibus probetur, rationem non esse normam, ad quam Scriptura debeat examinari, cum de eo nulla inter me & adversarios fuerit aut unquam futura sit quaestio.
units.tr: DCCCXVII. Since, then, this is not my opinion, the arguments brought against me on pp. 23, 24 and 25 are in vain, by which it is proved that reason is not the norm to which Scripture ought to be examined; for there has been, and never will be, any dispute between me and my adversaries about this.

units.la: DCCCXVIII. Objectio vigesima quinta potest formari ex verbis H. p. 215, ubi dicit: Deum ideo nobis condescendere, ut judicemus, non autem quia praejudicavimus (reliqua contra me non faciunt, nam ad nostrum captum Sp. S. descendere in spiritualibus atque mysteriis non negamus.)
units.tr: DCCCXVIII. The twenty-fifth objection can be framed from the words of H., p. 215, where he says: God condescends to us so that we may judge, not because we have prejudged (the rest does not count against me, for I do not deny that the Holy Spirit descends to our level in spiritual matters and mysteries).

units.la: Resp. Utrumque verum est, adeoque haec duo conjungenda, non sejungenda sunt, quia praejudicavimus & hinc istis praejudiciis sermonem accommodavimus, Sp. S. voluit se nobis accommodare, dum utitur isto sermone, prout superius est demonstratum.
units.tr: Reply: Both things are true, and so these two must be joined, not separated: because we have prejudged, and therefore have adapted our speech to those prejudices, the Holy Spirit chose to accommodate himself to us when he uses that speech, as has been demonstrated above.

units.la: DCCCIX. Objectionem vigesimam sextam suppeditare possunt verba H. p. 227, 228. Ex sancti Spiritus mente scripta verba sunt: quae altissimi mens ex divinarum Scripturarum sensu petenda omnino est & evincenda.
units.tr: DCCCIX. The twenty-sixth objection can be supplied by the words of H., p. 227, 228: "The words were written from the mind of the Holy Spirit; the mind of the Most High is certainly to be sought and established from the sense of the divine Scriptures."

units.la: Resp. Haec omnia libenter concedo, neque enim alio sensu dixi, Sp. S. loqui secundum opinionem vulgi, quam phrases vulgi usurpando, & per eas veritatem generalem significando.
units.tr: Reply: I gladly concede all of this, for I did not say in any other sense that the Holy Spirit speaks according to the opinion of the common people, than by using the common phrases and by them signifying a general truth.

units.la: DCCCX. Tandem objectionem vigesimam septimam desumimus ex H. p. 279. Aut Deus se nobis accommodavit integris aut corruptis. Non prius, Ergo posterius. At si corruptis, detur ratio quare aut quomodo istud fieri debuit, vel potuit, cum nondum conditi ad Dei imaginem, ne dicam corrupti in eadem effemus. Resp. Deus in Scriptura, quam curavit consignari, se accommodavit nobis corruptis, in eo quod formulas loquendi, quas præjudiciis accommodaveramus, retinuerit, ob id quod receptæ erant, itaut per eas non omnëid quod nos, quatenus tales, sed tantum id quod verum, significaret, ut ex superioribus patet. Quando Verbum suum literis exarari curavit, utique jam existebant homines corrupti, quos per Scripturam voluit de via salutis & liberatione ex illa corruptione instruere, quibus usque ad nos continuo succesȿerunt simili corruptione laborantes.
units.tr: DCCCX. Finally, we take the twenty-seventh objection from H., p. 279: "Either God accommodated himself to us in our integrity or in our corruption. Not the former; therefore the latter. But if in corruption, let a reason be given why or how this had to be done, or could be done, since we were not yet created in the image of God, let alone corrupted in it." Reply: In the Scripture, which he took care to have written down, God accommodated himself to us in our corruption, in that he retained the forms of speech which we had adapted to our prejudices, because they were already in use, so that through them he signified not everything that we, as such, mean, but only what is true, as is clear from what was said above. When he had his Word committed to writing, men were already existing in corruption, whom he willed to instruct through Scripture about the way of salvation and deliverance from that corruption; and after them, down to us, there have continually followed others labouring under the same corruption.

units.la: CAPUT XLIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XLIV.

units.la: Sententiam de Gyratione Telluris non adversari auctori- tati & veritati sacrarum literarum ostenditur. In specie vero cum ista sententia conciliatur Josuæ capitis x. versus 12. & 13.
units.tr: It is shown that the opinion concerning the rotation of the Earth does not conflict with the authority and truth of the Holy Scriptures. In particular, this opinion is reconciled with Joshua chapter 10, verses 12 and 13.

units.la: DCCCXI. Hactenus evicta est sententiæ nostræ generalis (ex quâ dicimus, Scripturam de rebus naturalibus uti sermone recepto, etiamsi ex præjudiciis sensuum & infantiæ habeat ortum) veritas, atque ostensum, eam cum sacrarum literarum Auctoritate & Veritate nullatenus pugnare. Nunc in specie ostendendum, sententiæ Cartesii de gyratione Terræ circa axem suum, nullum esse dissidium cum sacris literis. Fatemur, Scripturam loquentem de vicissitudine dierum & noctium, uti illis ipsis phrasibus & formulis loquendi, quibus Vulgus eam vicissitudinem exprimere solet, quamvis Vulgus sub illis loquendi formulis præterea errorem, quem de causâ istius vicissitudinis adoptavit, significet. Vulgus nimirum à Terræ partibus, tanquam immobilibus spectatis, Solis & stellarum loca determinat, atque Solem Stellasque eâtenus moveri judicat, quatenus à locis ita determinatis recedunt, atque ita situm suum ratione Terræ mutant, & per istam situs mutationem vicissitudinem dierum atque noctium introducunt; in eo vero errat, quod existimat, Terram revera in medio mundi ita quiescere, ut à Cælo & aëre circumjacente non deferatur: Solem vero è contrario, ut & stellas fixas, singulis diebus circa Solem una cum cœlo circumferri, atque hanc Solis, stellarumque fixarum unà cum cœlo circumlationem vel rotationem circa Terram esse istius vicissitudinis causam. Illum errorem vulgus connotat, dum Solem oriri & occidere, progredi ab unâ extremitate cœlorum an alteram &c. dicit, sed primariò denotat variationem situs Solis & stellarum respectu nostri oculi, cui sententiæ exprimendæ hæ formulæ sunt inventæ. Sapientes, dum de his rebus loquendū, non possunt aliis loqui formulis, quàm iis, quæ à vulgo sunt inventæ & in communi sunt usu, nec tamen magis iis turbantur, quàm Mathematici per schemata figurarum non satis accurata, quibus non minus commodè uti possunt ad demonstrationes etiam accuratissimas conficiendas, quàm schematibus longè accuratioribus, quoniam non tantoperè ad ea, quæ per sensus repræsentantur, quàm ad rei ipsius naturam & essentiam attendunt. An ergo putabimus Sapientissimum Deum, non æquè posse uti ad suum obtinendum scopum illis formulis loquendi à vulgo inventis, etsi non satis accuratæ fuerint, & à vulgo quoque adhibeantur ad aliquos errores denotandos? an non Deus per has formulas potest veritatem denotare eam, quæ ab errore est separata, quamvis vulgus, & si qui docti hâc in parte communem cum vulgo foveant errorem, dum iis utuntur, errorem cum veritate conjunctum per has phrases & loquendi formulas designent; quamvis etiam hi ipsi, dum legunt Scripturam, veritatem & errorem unà significari putent, adeoque illum ipsum errorem pro liquidâ veritate amplectantur. Quod si igitur potest Deus per dictas formulas loquendi veritatem hanc designare, quod singulis 24 horarum spatiis fiat vicissitudo diei & noctis ob variatum situm Solis & stellarum respectu oculi nostri; &, si circumstantiæ illorum locorum Scripturæ, in quibus istæ formulæ occurrunt, etiam asserere cogant, per illas formulas hanc veritatem designari, quis dubitabit, quin Deus etiam istam veritatem per illas loquendi formulas revera voluerit exprimere? Si verò similiter circumstantiæ illorum locorum nos eò adigant, ut præter hanc veritatem utrinque concessam simul etiam designari putemus, hanc variationem situs oriri ex diurnâ rotatione Solis & stellarum fixarum unà cum Cœlo circa Terram, & hoc ipsum erit asserendum, & pro veritate certissimâ erit habendum; sin è contrario circumstantiæ illorum locorum hâc de re nihil determinent, etiam à nobis non erit asserendum, tale quid in dictis locis denotari; quid verò de ipsâ illâ re fuerit ex rationis lumine erit determinandum. Nihil ergo nunc amplius nobis agendum restat, quàm ut indagemus, an loci illi ab adversariis adducti ad probandum, quod Sol cum Cœlo & stellis fixis singulis 24 horarum spatiû circa Terram quiescentem circumvolvatur, id ipsum revera designent? quod ex circumstantiis istorum locorum, ex scopo imprimis, antecedentibus & consequentibus &c. est inquirendum. Ad rem ergo ipsam nos accingentes singula loca ordine examinexaminemus. Primus locus est Iof.x.12,13. Tunc allocutus est Iehoschuah Iehovam, quo die exposuit Iehova hunc Emorrhaum filiis Israëli, & dixit ante oculos Israëlis: Sol in Gibhone subsiste & Luna in valle Ajalonis. Substitit ergo Sol & Luna stetit, donec vindicata esset Gens Israëlitica ab hostibus suis. Nonne hoc scriptum est in libro rectì? Stabat autem Sol in medio Cœlo, neque festinabat ad occasum, quasi diem integrum. Hunc locum B. D. p. 13. ita urget: Quenam erit probabilitatis species, quod Iosua plenus Spiritu Sancto, tam ruditer, sensu rei veritati contrario, loqui voluerit. Ad quem locum cum nostra sententia conciliandum observamus. 1. Non absurdum esse, si dicamus, Iosuam non omnia scivisse, quæ pertinebant ad res naturales, quamvis Spiritu Sancto fuerit plenus, non enim ad hoc ipsi Spiritus Sanctus erat datus. Quidni enim nobis idem liceret statuere de Iosua, quod Celeberrimus Vossius lib. 3. de Idololatria c. 99. statuit de Apostolis, his verbis: Nec enim, inquit, necesse est, credamus, Clementem scisse omnia, quæ facerent ad arcana natura. Ne id quidem credere est opus de Apostolis: licet Christus promiserat, missurum se Spiritum Sanctum, qui in omnem eos duceret veritatem. Quippe hoc restringendum ad veritatem earum rerum, quæ ad salutis pertineant negotium; imo ne harum quidem omnium, quia Apostoli ipsi ex parte viderunt ac probarunt: sed omnium, quas scire est opus alteram ad vitam consequendam. Nihil ergo inconvenientiæ futurum, si dicamus, Iosuam ibi opinionem vulgi secutum, & opinatum fuisse, quod Sol vero motu sive rotatione circa Terram diem efficeret, & hinc petiisse, ut ejus motus aliquamdiu sisteretur.
units.tr: 811. Thus far has been established the truth of our general thesis (from which we say that Scripture, concerning natural things, uses the accepted manner of speech, even though that speech has its origin in the prejudices of the senses and of infancy), and it has been shown that this thesis by no means clashes with the authority and truth of the Sacred Writings. Now it must be shown in particular that there is no disagreement between the sacred writings and the opinion of Descartes concerning the rotation of the Earth about its axis. We admit that Scripture, speaking of the alternation of days and nights, uses those very phrases and forms of speech by which the common people are wont to express that alternation, although under those forms of speech the common people also signify the error which they have adopted concerning the cause of that alternation. For the common people, regarding the parts of the Earth as immobile, determine the places of the Sun and stars, and judge that the Sun and stars move only insofar as they recede from the places so determined, and thus change their position relative to the Earth, and by this change of position introduce the alternation of days and nights. Their error lies in this, that they think the Earth in truth rests in the middle of the world in such a way that it is not carried along by the heavens and the surrounding air; and that, on the contrary, the Sun, as well as the fixed stars, is carried every day around the Earth together with the heavens, and that this circulation or rotation of the Sun and fixed stars together with the heavens about the Earth is the cause of that alternation. The common people imply that error when they say that the Sun rises and sets, proceeds from one extremity of the heavens to the other, and so on; but they chiefly denote the variation of the position of the Sun and stars with respect to our eye, for which purpose these phrases were invented. Wise men, when they must speak of these things, cannot use other phrases than those which have been devised by the common people and are in general use; nor are they any more troubled by them than mathematicians are by figures drawn not very accurately, which they can use no less conveniently to construct even the most exact demonstrations than far more accurate diagrams, since they attend not so much to what is represented by the senses as to the nature and essence of the thing itself. Shall we then think that the most wise God cannot equally use, to attain His purpose, those forms of speech invented by the common people, even if they are not sufficiently accurate, and which the common people also employ to denote some errors? Can not God, through these phrases, denote the truth that is separated from error, even though the common people, and some learned men who in this matter share the common error, when they use them, designate by these phrases and forms of speech error joined with truth; even though these very men, when they read Scripture, may think that truth and error are signified together, and so embrace that very error as clear truth? If then God can, by the said forms of speech, designate this truth, that the alternation of day and night takes place in each span of 24 hours because of the varying position of the Sun and stars with respect to our eye; and if the circumstances of those passages of Scripture in which these forms occur also compel us to assert that this truth is designated by those forms, who will doubt that God really intended to express this truth by those forms of speech? But if, similarly, the circumstances of those passages drive us to think that, besides this truth conceded on both sides, there is also designated this: that this variation of position arises from the daily rotation of the Sun and fixed stars together with the Heavens about the Earth, then this very thing must be asserted and held as most certain truth; but if, on the contrary, the circumstances of those passages determine nothing in this matter, then neither shall we assert that any such thing is denoted in the said passages; but what is to be determined about the thing itself must be determined by the light of reason. Nothing more remains for us to do now, then, than to inquire whether those passages which the adversaries have adduced to prove that the Sun, together with the Heavens and the fixed stars, revolves around the resting Earth in each span of 24 hours, do in fact designate this very thing? This must be inquired from the circumstances of these passages, above all from their scope, the things going before and following, and so on. Setting ourselves therefore to the matter itself, let us examine the individual passages in order. The first passage is Josh. 10:12,13. Then spoke Joshua to Jehovah, on the day when Jehovah delivered up the Amorite before the children of Israel, and he said before the eyes of Israel: Sun, stand thou still in Gibeon, and thou, Moon, in the valley of Aijalon. So the Sun stood still and the Moon stayed, until the nation of Israel had avenged itself on its enemies. Is not this written in the book of the upright? And the Sun stood in the midst of heaven, and did not hasten to set, as for a whole day. The author of the B. D., p. 13, presses this passage thus: What probability is there that Joshua, full of the Holy Spirit, should have wished to speak so crudely, in a sense contrary to the truth of the matter? In reconciling this passage with our opinion, we observe: 1. It is not absurd to say that Joshua did not know everything that pertained to natural things, although he was full of the Holy Spirit; for the Holy Spirit was not given to him for this purpose. For why should we not be allowed to hold the same about Joshua that the most celebrated Vossius, in book 3 of On Idolatry, chapter 99, holds about the Apostles, in these words: For it is not necessary, he says, that we believe Clement knew everything that pertains to the secrets of nature. Nor is it even necessary to believe this of the Apostles, although Christ had promised that He would send the Holy Spirit, who would lead them into all truth.
