Indeed this must be restricted to the truth of those things which pertain to the business of salvation; nay, not even of all these, since the Apostles themselves saw and approved them only in part; but to those of all which it is necessary to know in order to attain the life to come. Nothing inconvenient, therefore, will follow if we say that Joshua there followed the opinion of the common people, and supposed that the Sun, by its true motion or rotation about the Earth, makes the day, and hence asked that its motion be stopped for a while.

units.la: DCCCXII.
units.tr: DCCCXII.

units.la: 2. Sive autem sciverit Iosua, sive non, cujus motui tribuenda diei & noctis vicissitudo, Solis ne an Terræ, adhuc facilis est solutio. Consideremus tantùm, quid hoc in loco Iosua à Deo efflagitaverit. Is proculdubio ex instinctu Sp. S, qui fidem miraculorum in corde ipsius accenderat, exoptavit, ut dies continuaretur, quo vindictam sumere posset, de inimicis Dei & populi Israëlitici. Itaque suum votum expressit hac formulâ, ut Solem stare juberet: si enim scivit, Terram gyrare, non opus erat, ut propterea alia formula loquendi uteretur, quàm vulgo erat recepta; si verò nescivit, non multum intererat, neque tempestivum erat, ut tunc, quid sit de causis vicissitudinis dierum ac noctium accuratè examinaret, & reperto, causam istam Terræ gyrationi esse adscribendam, formulâ accuratâ uteretur. Sed sciebat, Deum intellecturum suam intentionem, quibuscunque verbis eam exprimeret, modò tales illæ essent, quæ ad continuationem diei significandam essent aptæ. Itaque cum porrò de exauditione ejus dicitur, Scriptura ipsius formulæ loquendi respondet, ut, quemadmodum ipse diei prolongationem petiit per hanc formulam : Sol sta, ita Scriptura ostendat, simili formulâ, illud quod petierat factum esse, ut nempe dies fuerit prolongatus.
units.tr: 2. Whether Joshua knew or did not know to which motion the alternation of day and night is to be ascribed, the Sun's or the Earth's, a solution is still easy. Let us consider only what Joshua asked of God in this place. He, without doubt, by the impulse of the Holy Spirit, who had kindled in his heart faith in the miracles, desired that the day be prolonged, so that he might take vengeance on the enemies of God and of the people of Israel. Accordingly he expressed his prayer in this form of words, bidding the Sun to stand still. For if he knew that the Earth turns, there was no need for him to use a different form of speech from the one commonly received; and if he did not know it, it made little difference, nor was it the right time for him to examine accurately what is the cause of the alternation of days and nights, and, having discovered that this cause is to be ascribed to the Earth's rotation, to use a precise form of words. But he knew that God would understand his intention, whatever words he used to express it, provided only that they were such as were suited to signifying the prolongation of the day. Therefore, when it is afterwards said that his prayer was heard, Scripture answers to the very form of his speech: just as he asked for the lengthening of the day by this form, "Sun, stand still," so Scripture shows, in a similar form, that what he had asked was done, namely that the day was prolonged.

units.la: DCCCXIII. 3. Voluit ut Sol sibi staret ad scopum suum obtinendum, id est, supra suum Horizontem maneret, quod fieri potuit, sive motus Solis apparens sisteretur, per Terræ, sive verus per Solis quietem, quæ responsio est ex Keplero desumta, cui similis est Foscarini, qui ita dicit: Iosua imperium, Sol ne movearis, & miraculum immoti Solis, ab eo perpetratum ita potest accipi, ut non proprie corpus solare, sed Solis splendor super Terrâ subsiterit, ex eo, quod non ipse Sol (per se jam prius immotus) sed ipsa Terra ejus splendorem recipiens motum suum stiterit: qua sicut ordinarium suum motum Orientem versus indesinenter persequendo, Solis splendorem in Occidentem accivisset, ita immota manens, immotus & stetit Solis splendor in eam impressus. 4. Subjungamus tandem Belgarum Interpretationem, qui ad verba in Gibbone, ita annotant : Dat is, staet stille te dier plaetse, daer ghy nu zijt, want Josua was te deser tijdt te Gibeon vers. 10. Item ad verba, in Convalle Ajalonis. De sinn der woorden Josua is, Sonne en gaet ons niet onder, ter wijle wy in Gibeon strijden, ende Maene en brengt ons den nacht niet. aen, hoc est, consiste in hoc loco, in quo nunc es, nam Josua erat tunc temporis in Gibeone. Item, Sensus verborum Josuæ est, Sol ne occidas nobis, quamdiu pugnamus in Gibeone, & Luna, ne nobis adducas noctem. Ex quâ interpretatione hæc duo pro nostra sententia colligimus, 1. in eo cognosci debere vulgarem locutionem, quod Soli tribuitur existentia in Gibeone, quæ tamen conveniebat Josuæ; inde non mirum esse debet, si etiam in illo ipso STARE talem annotemus. 2. Josuam petere, hancque ipsius esse intentionem, ne Sol sibi occidat. Soli autem ortus & occasus convenit & tribuitur tam ab iis, qui Copernici systema corporum cœlestium admittunt, quàm à Ptolemaicis vel Tychonianis.
units.tr: DCCCXIII. 3. He willed that the Sun should stand still for him in order to attain his purpose, that is, that it should remain above his horizon. This could happen either if the apparent motion of the Sun were stopped, through the motion of the Earth, or if its true motion were stopped, through the rest of the Sun. This answer is taken from Kepler, and similar to it is that of Foscarini, who speaks thus: Joshua's command, "Sun, do not move," and the miracle of the unmoving Sun wrought by him, can be understood in such a way that it was not properly the solar body but the light of the Sun that stood still above the Earth. For it was not the Sun itself (already previously unmoving in itself) but the Earth, receiving its light, that stopped its motion. Just as the Earth, by continually pursuing its ordinary motion eastward, would have caused the light of the Sun to move westward, so, remaining unmoved, the light of the Sun impressed upon it stood still as well. 4. Let us finally add the interpretation of the Belgians, who annotate the words in Gibeon thus: That is, stand still in the place where you now are, for Joshua was at that time at Gibeon, verse 10. Likewise, on the words in the valley of Aijalon: The meaning of Joshua's words is: Sun, do not set for us while we fight at Gibeon, and Moon, do not bring us the night. That is, remain in this place in which you now are, for Joshua was then at Gibeon. Likewise: The sense of Joshua's words is: Sun, do not set on us while we fight at Gibeon, and Moon, do not bring us night. From this interpretation we draw two things in support of our view: 1. It should be recognised that the common manner of speaking is in this, that existence at Gibeon is attributed to the Sun, which nevertheless fitted Joshua; hence it should not be surprising if we note such a usage also in this very word STAND. 2. Joshua asked, and this was his intention, that the Sun should not set for him. Rising and setting, however, belong to the Sun and are attributed to it both by those who admit Copernicus's system of the heavenly bodies and by the Ptolemaic or Tychonic followers.

units.la: DCCCXIV. Exc. 1. B p. 152. ad Observationem primam, præter scommata in Cartesium conjecta, quas sordes lubens prætereo; Quamvis Josua non omnia naturalia noverit, nullo modo tamen est credibile, ipsum ignorasse illa naturalia de quibus loquebatur: & cum precabatur ut afflatus Spiritu Sancto, ipsum nescivisse, an vere, an secundum apparentiam loqueretur. Simile quid habet M. cap. 7. art. 4. & 6. quæ si ita videatur poterunt conferri.
units.tr: DCCCXIV. Excerpt 1, B, p. 152, on the first Observation. Setting aside the jeers aimed at Descartes, which I gladly pass over as filth: Although Joshua did not know all natural things, it is in no way credible that he was ignorant of those natural things of which he was speaking; and when he prayed, moved by the Holy Spirit, that he did not know whether he was speaking truly or according to appearance. Something similar is found in M., chapter 7, articles 4 and 6, which may be compared if it seems fit.

units.la: Resp. Quodnam verò hic habebis argumentum, quò probes, Josuam scivisse, an Terra, an Sol reali corporis sui motu vicissitudinem dierum & noctium causetur? Hoc proculdubio vis dicere; qui loquitur de rebus naturalibus ex afflatu Sp. S. habuit etiam illarum naturam inti-mè perspectam. At Josua; Ergo. At ambiguitas in Majori erit manifesta, hanc enim duplici sensu poteris intelligere: vel hoc; qui in tantum in quantum loquitur de rebus naturalibus habet afflatum Sp. S. & ad hoc ipsum sibi datum, ut accuratè earum naturam per istum afflatum disceret, ille habet illarum naturam intimè perspectam, quo sensu Maj. concedo. Min. nego. Vel hoc; Qui cum loquitur de rebus naturalibus afflatus est Sp. S. ad hoc, ut preces ardentes coram Deo effundat & fide de exauditione sit certus, ille habet illarum naturam intimè perspectam. Sic Min. conceditur, Maj. negatur: non enim afflatus Sp. S. ulterius extendendus, quam ad id, ad quod datus fuit. Quasi vero non possint preces fundi afflatu Sp. S. in quibus etiam mentio fit rerum naturalium, ut tamen illarum natura non sit intimè perspecta. Velim hic Dn. du Bois in memoriam sibi revocare, quae antehac scripsit in libro, quem vocat Ondetijdts Tydt-threfoor p. 55. eaque applicare suæ objectioni hic factæ. Verba sic habent: Stephanus was wel gedreven door den H. Geest, soo dat hy in de grond van de leere niet gemist heeft: maer dat en strydt daer niet tegen, dat hy in eenige omstandigheden van bysondere historien noch niet alle beschreidene kennisse gehadt, of op die selvige soo nauw gelet heeft, hoc est, Stephanus erat quidem actus à Spiritu Sancto, ita ut in fundamento doctrinæ non erraverit: sed hoc non repugnat ei, quod in aliquibus circumstantiis singularium historiarum nondum habuit satis distinctam cognitionem, aut ad illas tàm precisè attendit.
units.tr: Reply. What argument, then, will you have here by which to prove that Joshua knew whether the alternation of day and night is caused by the Earth or by the Sun through the real motion of its body? You will say, no doubt: whoever speaks of natural things by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit has also a thorough insight into their nature. But Joshua did so; therefore... But the ambiguity in the major premise is plain, for you can understand it in two senses. Either this: whoever, in so far as he speaks of natural things, has the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, and has been given it for this very purpose, that he might learn their nature accurately through that inspiration, has a thorough insight into their nature; in this sense I grant the major and deny the minor. Or this: whoever, when he speaks of natural things, is inspired by the Holy Spirit so that he may pour out fervent prayers before God and be certain of being heard, has a thorough insight into their nature. Thus the minor is granted and the major denied: for the inspiration of the Holy Spirit is not to be extended further than to that for which it was given. As if prayers could not be poured out by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit in which mention is made of natural things, without their nature being thoroughly understood! I would have Mr. du Bois call to mind here what he wrote earlier in the book he calls Ondetijdts Tydt-threfoor, p. 55, and apply it to his objection made here. The words run thus: Stephen was indeed moved by the Holy Spirit, so that he did not miss the foundation of the doctrine; but this does not contradict the fact that in some circumstances of particular histories he had not yet full knowledge of all that is written, or did not attend to them so precisely; that is, Stephen was indeed moved by the Holy Spirit, so that he did not err in the foundation of doctrine, but this does not conflict with his not yet having a sufficiently distinct knowledge of some circumstances of particular histories, or not attending to them so precisely.

units.la: DCCCXV. M. p. 23.
units.tr: DCCCXV. M. p. 23.

units.la: fere simili hic argumento utitur, sed præterea contra hanc primam meam observationem sic argumentatur: Josua fuit usus præceptore Mose per multos annos; Ergo novit veram causam vicissitudinis dierum & noctium.
units.tr: He uses almost the same argument here, but in addition argues against this first observation of mine as follows: Joshua was for many years a pupil of his teacher Moses; therefore he knew the true cause of the alternation of day and night.

units.la: Resp. Nonne multò magis liceret colligere, Apostolos omnia scivisse, qui longè sapientiori præceptore fuerant usi ipso Christo, quos tamen Vossius negat, omnia scivisse & omnes res naturales habuisse cognitas. Quousque Josuæ cognitio in rebus naturalibus sese extenderit, & an circa hanc quæstionem fuerit informatus, difficile est divinare. Quod vero addit, isthoc comma non videri multum recedere à sententia Socini dicentis, scriptores sacros memoriâ labi & in levioribus errare potuisse; ad id respondeo, videri mihi tantum recedere quantum inde receditur, si quis dicat, Apostolorum dicta quædam etiam in libros sacros relata, qualia de regno terreno Messiæ, de præeminentia &c. errorea fuisse, quo sane non diceretur, eos in iis, quæ tanquam ψευδῶς scripserunt, errare potuisse. DCCCXVI. Exc. H. p. 40. ubi praecedentia sua verba in summam colligit: Qui repletus est sapientia Domini Spiritu, ille non est de vulgo, ille sapienter, ille vere cum Spiritu sapientia & non falso cum vulgo sentit & loquitur. Spiritui quippe ejus quem dederat ei Dominus, non ideo sapientia tribuitur, quia cum vulgo falso loqui & sentire, sed quia supra vulgum sapere debet. At Josua &c. Ergo sapientia, quae est supra vulgum, pugnat cum opinione vulgi; ideo quippe vulgi faecibus eximimur, ut meliora sapiamus, meliora loquamur.
units.tr: Reply. Would it not be much more reasonable to infer that the Apostles knew everything? They had used as their teacher Christ himself, who was far wiser, and yet Vossius denies that they knew everything or had all natural things known to them. How far Joshua's knowledge of natural things extended, and whether he was informed about this question, is hard to guess. As for what he adds, that this passage does not seem to depart much from the opinion of Socinus, who says that the sacred writers could forget things and err in minor matters; to that I reply that it seems to me to depart only as far as one departs if one says that certain sayings of the Apostles, also related in the sacred books, such as those about the earthly kingdom of the Messiah, about pre-eminence, etc., were erroneous. Surely it would not be said by that that they could err in those things which they wrote as [ψευδῶς] false. DCCCXVI. Exc. H. p. 40. where he gathers his preceding words into a summary: He who is filled with the Spirit of wisdom from the Lord is not of the common crowd; he is wise, he truly is wise with the Spirit, and he does not think and speak falsely with the crowd. For wisdom is not attributed to the Spirit that the Lord gave him because he speaks and thinks falsely with the crowd, but because he ought to be wise above the crowd. But Joshua, etc. Therefore wisdom which is above the crowd conflicts with the opinion of the crowd; for we are indeed freed from the dregs of the crowd so that we may think better things and speak better things.

units.la: Resp. 1. Applicetur eadem responsio, quae art. 814. fuit data. Neque enim, an ad vulgus talis sit referendus, opus est multum litigare: multi enim vulgi faecibus exemti sunt, qui tamen quatenus praejudicia quaedam retinent, eatenus supra vulgus se non extulerunt: sufficit, si ostendamus, hoc argumento non probari, Josuam scivisse cujusnam motui debeat attribui causa vicissitudinis diei & noctis: dico itaque, Majorem esse limitandam; Qui repletus est Spiritu sapientiae Domini in omnibus & quoad omnia, tam naturalia quam supernaturalia & politica, is non cum vulgo falso sentit & loquitur. Sic demum vera est Major. At nego Minorem sic subsumtam, quae non magis ex Num. xxvii. 18. probatur, quam ex Joh. xvi. 13. probari potest, Apostolos per Spiritum Sanctum cognovisse omnes veritates physicas; vide responsionem meam ad hunc locum capite 34.
units.tr: Reply 1. Let the same answer be applied that was given at art. 814. For it is not necessary to dispute at length whether he is to be counted among the crowd. Many who are freed from the dregs of the crowd nevertheless, insofar as they retain certain prejudices, have not raised themselves above the crowd. It is enough if we show that this argument does not prove that Joshua knew to what motion the cause of the alternation of day and night should be attributed. I say, therefore, that the major premise must be limited: he who is filled with the Spirit of the wisdom of the Lord in all things and with respect to all things, both natural and supernatural and political, does not think and speak falsely with the crowd. Only so is the major premise true. But I deny the minor premise as thus assumed, which is no more proved from Num. 27:18 than it can be proved from John 16:13 that the Apostles through the Holy Spirit knew all physical truths. See my reply to this passage in chapter 34.

units.la: DCCCXVII. Pergit B. p. 153. & inquit: Comparationem inter Apostolos & Josuam nihil esse ad rhombum: nam de illis quae ignoraverunt nihil esse locutos: at de quiete Solis & Lunae miraculosa locutum esse Josuam & historiam facti referre historicum sacrum.
units.tr: DCCCXVII. He continues, p. 153 of B., and says: The comparison between the Apostles and Joshua is nothing to the point, for they said nothing about the things they did not know; but Joshua spoke of the miraculous rest of the Sun and Moon, and the sacred historian reports the history of the event.

units.la: Resp. Comparatio a me hactenus tantum fuit instituta: Si non absurdum est statuere, Apostolos afflatos Sp. S. non omnia tamen scivisse; Ergo etiam non est absurdum illud Josuae attribuere. Ex eo vero quod locutus fuerit de quiete Solis & Lunae, hoc est, quod formulas usurpaverit, quibus vulgus praeter veritatem generalem etiam quietem Solis & Lunae significat, non inferri, cum veras causas vicissitudinis dierum habuisse perspectas, antea est ostensum.
units.tr: Reply. So far I have made only this comparison: if it is not absurd to hold that the Apostles, inspired by the Holy Spirit, nevertheless did not know everything, then it is not absurd to attribute the same to Joshua. But it has been shown above that from the fact that he spoke of the rest of the Sun and Moon, that is, that he used expressions by which the common people, beyond the general truth, also signify the rest of the Sun and Moon, it does not follow that he had clearly perceived the true causes of the alternation of days.

units.la: DCCCXVIII. Addit B. p. 153. Quando in Apostolis alicujus rei ignorantia percipitur, ejus certa esse indicia, quae in Josua debuissent etiam dari alias intolerabilem esse audaciam, si rei, de qua agebatur, insitiam vel lapsum ipsis tribuamus.
units.tr: DCCCXVIII. B. adds, p. 153: When an ignorance of some matter is perceived in the Apostles, there are certain sure signs of it, which ought also to have been given in Joshua; otherwise it would be an intolerable audacity if we attributed to them ignorance or error in the matter under discussion.

units.la: Resp. Cadet haec Objectio, si quis consideret, quodnam sit officium respondentis; ei enim sufficit argumenti adversarii infirmitatem ostendisse disse per petitionem ulterioris probationis, nec requiritur ut ipse contrarium probet. Dico igitur, ex precibus Josuae non posse inferri sententiam oppositam; cum potuerit fieri, ut Josua veram causam vicissitudinis diei ignoraverit, cujus contrarium ostendendum ei, qui huic argumento firmitatem velit conciliare.
units.tr: Reply. This objection falls if one considers what the duty of the respondent is. For it is enough for him to have shown the weakness of the opponent's argument by asking for further proof; he is not required to prove the contrary himself. I say, therefore, that from Joshua's prayer the opposite opinion cannot be inferred, since it may have happened that Joshua did not know the true cause of the alternation of day. The contrary of this must be shown by anyone who wishes to lend firmness to this argument.

units.la: DCCCXIX. Ad secundam observationem Exc. 1. B. p. 155.
units.tr: DCCCXIX. On the second observation of Exc. 1, B., p. 155.

units.la: Non tantum referri scopum generalem Josuae, respectu prolongationis diei, sed etiam modum sive remedium, quo prolongari petebat, videl. stationem Solis & Lunae: absurdum autem fuisset petere prolongationem diei per tale medium quod impetrari non poterat. Simile habet M. p. 126. In petitione Josua &c. quae videat cui vacat.
units.tr: Not only is the general aim of Joshua with respect to the prolongation of the day referred to, but also the means or remedy by which he sought that it be prolonged, namely the standing still of the Sun and Moon. But it would have been absurd to ask for a prolongation of the day by means of something that could not be obtained. M. has a similar statement at p. 126: In the petition of Joshua, etc. let whoever has time look it up.

units.la: Resp. Unde vero probabitis, & Josuam petiisse ut hoc medio, nempe per stationem Solis & Lunae dies prolongaretur, & a Deo hoc medio illud factum fuisse? Dicetis ex illis verbis: Sol cтa, & Sol stetit. Verum sic petetis principium & pro certo assumetis, quod est in quaestione. Dico itaque, cum formulae receptae de vicissitudine dierum & noctium loquentium sint: Solem moveri, Solem progredi &c. (quibus tamen sapientes utentes nihil aliud denotant, quam illam vicissitudinem & variationem situs corporis solaris, quamvis praejudiciis occupati & ex prima institutione etiam causam istius vicissitudinis falsam connotent:) non potuisse miraculum circa vicissitudinem dierum & noctium factum aliter sermone vulgari efferri, & ut formula circa miraculum adhibita opponeretur formulae, qua naturalis rei constitutio exprimitur, quam, si Sol dicatur stetisse, ad designandum, diem miraculose fuisse prolongatum.
units.tr: Reply. But whence will you prove both that Joshua asked for the day to be prolonged by this means, namely by the standing still of the Sun and Moon, and that God did it by this means? You will say from those words: "Sun, stand still," and "the Sun stood still." But in that way you would beg the question and assume as certain what is in dispute. I say, therefore, that since the received formulas about the alternation of day and night speak of "the Sun moving," "the Sun progressing," etc. (which, however, wise men who use them mean nothing other than that alternation and variation in the position of the solar body, although, occupied with prejudices, and from the original institution, they also connote a false cause of this alternation), it could not have been that a miracle concerning the alternation of day and night was expressed in ordinary speech in any other way. And so the formula used of the miracle was set against the formula by which the natural constitution of the thing is expressed; if the Sun is said to have stood still, that is used to signify that the day was miraculously prolonged.

units.la: DCCCXX. Exc. 2. M. p. 127.
units.tr: DCCCXX. Exc. 2. M. p. 127.

units.la: Si ista formula falsa fuisset, tum in ejus locum alia a Josua & facile potuisset & necessario debuisset constitui, potuisset enim eadem opera in hunc modum locutus fuisse: mancat nobis dies.
units.tr: If that expression were false, then Joshua could easily, and indeed necessarily, have chosen another in its place, for he could just as well have spoken in this way: "let the day be lacking to us."

units.la: Resp. Per formulam illam, quatenus a Sp. S. fuit adhibita, nihil salsum fuit expressum, ut saepius dictum, ideoque nulla erit necessitas, quare alia uteretur?
units.tr: Answer: As I have often said, nothing false was expressed through that expression, insofar as the Holy Spirit employed it. So what reason would there be for using another?

units.la: DCCCXXI. Exc. 3. Pergit B. pag. 155.
units.tr: DCCCXXI. Exc. 3. He goes on, p. 155.

units.la: A'πεῳδιόνυσον esse, quod dicam, tunc non fuisse tempus cogitandi de motu corporum, quibus dies efficitur, & considerare, quorum motui ille tribui debeat, atque ita accurate loqui, quia, inquit, considerare quid & quomodo sit loquendum, locum quidem habet in materia controversis, at non in illis de quibus nulla est controversia. De illa autem quaestione nunquam fuisse in populo Dei.
units.tr: I say that it was not then the time to think about the motion of the bodies by which the day is produced, and to consider to which of them that motion ought to be attributed; and so to speak with precision, because, he says, considering what and how one ought to speak has a place in matters of controversy, but not in those about which there is no controversy. And that question was never raised among the people of God.

units.la: Resp. His antea verbis fuerat usus, sed quia video, haec verba cum vel non intellexisse, vel nodum in scirpo quaesivisse, in ipsius gratiam cum clariobus ribus, bus, quantum potui, in Consensu Veritatis commutavi. Nemo vero nisi similis adversario dubitaverit, an etiam illæ res accuratè examinandæ, de quibus nulla est controversia, ut accuratè habeantur cognitæ: potest enim fieri, ut illæ res, quæ sine controversiâ promiscuè à quibusvis tanquam veræ, ex præjudiciis & consuetudine receptâ admittuntur, non minus examen requirant, quàm quæ controversæ sunt.
units.tr: Answer: I had used these words before, but since I see that my opponent either did not understand them or has sought a knot in a bulrush, I have, for his benefit, changed them as clearly as I could in Consensus Veritatis. Yet no one, unless he is like my opponent, would doubt whether those matters too, about which there is no controversy, should be examined with precision so that they are understood accurately. For it can happen that those things which are admitted without controversy by everyone as true, from prejudices and received custom, require no less examination than those which are disputed.

units.la: DCCCXXII. Exc. 4. M. vero p. 127. concedit tum tempus non fuisse, ut quid sit de causis vicissitudinis dierum & noctium, accuratè Josua & examinaret, sed, inquit, non opus fuisse, cum Sp. S. instinctu hanc formulam protulerit.
units.tr: DCCCXXII. Exc. 4. M. indeed p. 127. concedes that there was then no time for Joshua to examine accurately what the causes of the alternation of day and night are, but, he says, there was no need, since he uttered this expression under the impulse of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Resp. Ponamus hoc, quid inde? potuit illa formula ipsi suppeditari à Spiritu Sancto, in quantum formula solita inter homines communiter designat prolongationem diei, quod hic sufficit.
units.tr: Answer: Let us grant this. What follows from it? That expression could have been supplied to him by the Holy Spirit, insofar as the customary expression among men commonly designates the prolongation of a day, which is enough for our purpose here.

units.la: DCCCXXIII. Exc. 5. B. p. 156. Puerile esse quod sequitur (scil. in mea observatione) sciebat Deum intellecturum suam intentionem, quibuscunque verbis eam exprimeret: rationem affert, plane sc. gravem, Josua, inquit, proprie non Deum, sed Solem & Lunam est allocutus.
units.tr: DCCCXXIII. Exc. 5. B. p. 156. That what follows is childish (namely in my observation): he knew that God would understand his intention whatever words he used to express it. He gives a reason, plainly a weighty one: Joshua, he says, did not properly address God, but the Sun and the Moon.

units.la: Resp. Quasi vero dubitari possit, quin verba hæc Josuæ tacitum votum habeant inclusum, quamvis per prosopopœian ad Solem fuerint directa. Quis neget, Apostolorum verba, quibus allocuti fuerunt eos, in quibus miraculum patrandum, in se continuisse precationem, v. g. quando Actor. xiv. 10. Paulus dixit, surge in pedes tuos rectus, ad virum Lystris pedibus captum?
units.tr: Answer: As if it could be doubted that these words of Joshua contain a silent prayer, even though they were directed to the Sun by prosopopoeia. Who would deny that the words of the Apostles, by which they addressed those on whom the miracle was to be performed, contained a prayer? For example, when at Acts 14:10 Paul said to the man at Lystra who was lame in his feet, "Stand upright on your feet."

units.la: DCCCXXIV. Exc. 6. B. p. 156. Quando vero historiographus sacer commemorat miraculum, in eo consistens, quod Sol steterit, non tantum refert diei prolongationem, sed etiam causam, videl. stationem Solis in medio Cœli & quod modo de scriptoribus sacris injiciebamus, hujus historia scriptori etiam est applicandum, vid. quod non aliter scripserit quam secundum rei veritatem in universo Dei populo Prophetis inclusis receptam & creditam.
units.tr: DCCCXXIV. Exc. 6. B. p. 156. When, however, the sacred historian records the miracle, which consists in the Sun's standing still, he relates not only the prolongation of the day but also its cause, namely the Sun's standing in the midst of heaven; and what we have just urged about the sacred writers must also be applied to the writer of this history, namely that he wrote nothing other than according to the truth of the matter, as received and believed among the whole people of God, including the Prophets.

units.la: Resp. Meræ petitiones principii, 1. Miraculum fuisse Solis stationem realem. 2. his verbis ab historiographo referri, hoc est, doceri, testimonio firmari causam prolongationis diei. 3. Solis motum esse veritatem. 4. esse sententiam in universo Dei populo etiam Prophetis receptam, cum de eo non constet; quod tamen, etsi verum esset, nihil nobis incommodaret.
units.tr: Answer: These are mere petitions of the principle: (1) that the miracle was a real standing still of the Sun; (2) that the historian relates these words, that is, teaches and confirms by testimony that the cause of the prolonged day was this; (3) that the motion of the Sun is a truth; (4) that this opinion is held by the whole people of God, including the Prophets, when it is not established that this is so. Yet even if it were true, it would do us no harm.

units.la: DCCCXXV. Exc. 7. M. p. 126. Ideo formulam petitionis Josuæ non mutavit Sp. S. quia per eam rem veram exprimi videbat, adeoque nullam ejus mutanda restare causam, quapropter non iisdem modo verbis &c.
units.tr: DCCCXXV. Exc. 7. M. p. 126. The Holy Spirit therefore did not change the form of Joshua's petition, because he saw that a true thing was expressed by it, and so there was no cause remaining to change it; for this reason he did not use the same words, etc.

units.la: Resp. Ideo non mutavit quia formula erat talis, quâ inter homines debebat exprimi miraculum prolongationis diei, quamvis si ea uteretur aliquis, à præjudiciis nondum liberatus, præter veritatem illam generalem, quam solùm significavit Spiritus Sanctus, etiam præjudicium fuissët consignificaturus.
units.tr: Answer: He did not change it because the form was such that among men the miracle of the prolonged day had to be expressed by it, although if someone used it who was not yet freed from prejudices, he would, besides that general truth which the Holy Spirit alone signified, also be signifying a prejudice along with it.

units.la: DCCCXXVI. Ad Observationem tertiam Exc. 1. B. p. 157. me hac responsione nihil novi adferre.
units.tr: DCCCXXVI. On the Third Observation, Exc. 1. B. p. 157. I bring nothing new in this reply.

units.la: Quod lectoris judicio relinquo, qui facile perspiciet, quantum differant inter se, Historiographum per verba illa tantum significasse prolongationem diei, quæ est prior responsio, & Solem stetisse Josuæ respectu ipsius, nempe situm non variasse, quæ est posterior Keplery & Foscarini, quam non adduco propter auctoritatem, utpote qui nullius hominis auctoritatem tanti putem, ut propterea aliquid in Philosophicis vel Theologicis statuendum vel negandum censeam, sed quod existimem, non incommodè etiam verba illius loci sic posse exponi.
units.tr: I leave it to the judgment of the reader, who will easily see how greatly these differ: that the historian signified by those words only the prolongation of the day, which is the earlier reply, and that the Sun stood still with respect to Joshua, namely that its position did not vary, which is the later reply of Kepler and Foscarini. I do not cite the latter for its authority, since I do not think any man's authority is so great that on its account I would judge something in philosophical or theological matters to be asserted or denied; but because I think that the words of that passage can also be explained in this way without inconvenience.

units.la: DCCCXXVII. Exc. 2. B. D. p. 23. Bona esset responsio, dummodò rem veram esse comprobatum esset, at deficiente illa comprobatione, verba tantum sunt: nec aliquid in specie respondetur, quod non ante in responsione generali productum fuerit; videlicet illa dici secundum apparentiam. Ergo etiam ad retundendam hanc exceptionem sufficere possent vindicia generales. Sed presfius urgebo hunc locum. Verba Jehosuæ facta sunt non tantum ad Solem, sed ad Lunam, & miraculum duabus constabat partibus, videlicet in statione 1. Solis, 2. Luna. Lunæ stationem realem fuisse & non secundum apparentiam Copernicanis fatentibus, certum est; dico ergo & Solis stationem talem fuisse; nulla enim est ratio, cur verba de quiete Solis magis secundum apparentiam debeant exponi, quam verba, quæ Lunæ quietem tribuunt, quaque necessario de intermissione motus sui sumenda sunt. Paria his sunt, quæ in R. St. p. 326. exstant. Quam ineptum est, cum Scriptura & Solem & Lunam miraculo stetisse referat, hoc dictum ita dividere, ut in Sole nihil novi contigerit, ut qui steterit ab initio mundi & semper staturus sit, Luna vero ordinarie quidem moveri, miraculo autem stetisse dicatur. Resp. 1. Bonum factum, quod hactenus adversarius hanc responsionem acceptat, proque bona agnoscit, dummodo rem veram esse comprobatum sit. Id enim cum à nobis abundè in superioribus sit factum, promitteremus nobis eum impositurum veritati magis faventem, nisi contrarium secundo suo scripto fuisset testatus. 2. id quod in genere dictum fuerat de locutionibus vulgaribus, hic applicatur & in specie ostenditur, quomodo haec verba apud Josuam cum veritate nostræ sententiæ non pugnent. Vindicias generales omnes, quascunque afferri vidimus à quibuscunque, superioribus capitibus retudimus. 3. Fateor, verba Josuæ directa esse non tantum ad Solem, sed etiam ad Lunam, & petiisse, ut utraque luminaria starent, hoc est, diem prolongarent, nec noctem adducerent, sed modus standi propterea non utrobique par esse debebat. Utraque ergo hæc luminaria stabant, sed alterum statione vera, alterum apparente, qualis sæpè in Astronomia etiam Ptolemaica locum habet. 4. de utroque luminari Josua loquebatur secundum vulgi præjudicia. Etiamsi enim Luna revera curreret, hoc tamen vulgus non cognoverat per certam demonstrationem, sed æque ac de Sole per sensus apparentiam collegerat, in quo similiter potuisset falli, ac circa Solis motum fuit falsus. Omne enim illud præjudicium vocari debet, quod sine ullâ certâ ratione creditur, & pro vero assumitur, etiamsi casu fiat, ut illud sit verum. 5. Quænam sit ratio, ob quam statio Lunæ debeat attribui in hoc miraculo realis, Soli tantum apparens, patet ex superioribus, unde hæc responsio inepta dici non meretur. Inde tamen non sequitur, Scripturam partim veram, partim falsam esse, nisi ex omnibus locutionibus vulgaribus, quibus Scriptura utitur, ei falsitatis dicam impingere velis, à qua nos illam superius liberavimus.
units.tr: DCCCXXVII. Exc. 2. B. D. p. 23. It would be a good answer, provided that it were proven that the thing is true; but since that proof is lacking, the words are only words, and nothing is answered in particular that was not already put forward in the general answer, namely that those things are said according to appearance. So general defences could also suffice to refute this objection. But I will press this passage more closely. Joshua's words were addressed not only to the Sun but also to the Moon, and the miracle consisted of two parts, namely the standing still of the Sun, first, and of the Moon, second. That the Moon's standing was real and not according to appearance is certain, as the Copernicans admit; I say therefore that the Sun's standing was also of that kind. For there is no reason why the words about the Sun's rest should be explained more according to appearance than the words which ascribe rest to the Moon, and which must necessarily be taken as an interruption of its motion. Things parallel to these are found in R. St. p. 326. How absurd it is, when Scripture reports that both the Sun and the Moon stood still by a miracle, to divide this statement so that nothing new happened to the Sun, which stood still from the beginning of the world and will always stand still, while the Moon is indeed ordinarily moved but is said to have stood still by a miracle. Answer: (1) It is well done that my opponent so far accepts this answer and acknowledges it as good, provided that it is proven that the thing is true. For since we have amply done this above, we would have promised ourselves that he would bring more favour to the truth, had he not testified to the contrary in his second writing. (2) What was said in general about common modes of speech is here applied, and it is shown in particular how these words in Joshua are not at odds with the truth of our view. All the general defences that we have seen put forward by anyone we have refuted in the earlier chapters. (3) I grant that Joshua's words were directed not only to the Sun but also to the Moon, and asked that both lights should stand still, that is, prolong the day and not bring on the night; but the manner of standing need not be the same in both. Both of these lights therefore stood still, but one by a true standing and the other by an apparent one, as is often the case even in Ptolemaic astronomy. (4) Joshua spoke of each light according to the prejudices of the common people. For even if the Moon was really running, the common people had not known this through certain demonstration, but, just as with the Sun, had gathered it from the appearance to the senses, in which they could similarly have been deceived, as they were about the motion of the Sun. For every belief that is held as true without any certain reason should be called a prejudice, even if by chance it turns out to be true. (5) What the reason is why the standing still of the Moon in this miracle should be attributed as real, and that of the Sun only as apparent, is clear from what was said above, so that this reply does not deserve to be called inept. It does not follow from this, however, that Scripture is partly true and partly false, unless you wish to charge it with falsity from all the common modes of speech which Scripture uses, from which charge we freed it above.

units.la: DCCCXXVIII. Idem quod præcedente articulo vidimus concessisse Antagonistam, B. p. 159. repetit inquiens, si argumentis certis & Mathematicis posset probari Terram circa Solem ut in centro quiescentem (quod tamen nos non dicimus, sed circa Solem, in centro motuum Planetarum non Geometrico, sed latè accepto, circa axem suum rotatum) moveri; se ut vi coactum in expositione verborum sacrorum ab eorum proprietate recessurum. Quando verò addit, Imo magis ex concessione loquor quam quod credam talia argumenta unquam invenienda, ostendit animum obfirmatum contra quamvis demonstrationem, quamdiu pro certo habet, argumenta demonstrativa pro nostra sententia nunquam iri repertum. At bene se res habet, quod ipsius judicio non stet cadatve firmitas alicujus demonstrationis, & ex defensione demonstrationis apparere potuit, quàm facile fuerit instantias adversarii refutare.
units.tr: DCCCXXVIII. The Antagonist again repeats what we saw him concede in the previous article (B. p. 159), saying: "If it could be proved by certain and mathematical arguments that the earth moves around the sun as if the sun were fixed at the centre (which we do not say, but rather that the earth turns on its own axis while moving around the sun, which is at the centre of the planets' motions, taken not in the strict geometrical sense but broadly), I would, forced by the force of the argument, depart from the proper sense of the sacred words in their interpretation. But when he adds, 'Indeed I speak more by way of concession than because I believe that such arguments will ever be found,' he shows a mind hardened against any demonstration, so long as he holds for certain that no demonstrative arguments for our view will ever be found. Yet it is well that the firmness of any demonstration does not rest or fall on his judgment, and from the defence of the demonstration it could be seen how easily the adversary's instances could be refuted.

units.la: DCCCXXIX. Inst. 1. B. Rationem sui argumenti esse, quod in eodem loco phrasin eandem diversimode exponere sit contra omnes leges legitimæ expositionis, meque nihil regerere quod istius argumenti vim refringat, sed tantum dicere modum standi simpliciter parem non esse debere.
units.tr: DCCCXXIX. Inst. 1. B. He says that the reason for his argument is that to explain the same phrase in different ways in the same place is contrary to all the laws of legitimate interpretation, and that I have replied nothing that weakens the force of this argument, but have merely said that the manner of standing is not simply to be taken as the same.

units.la: Resp. Ago quod decet respondentem, negando Maj. propositionem argumenti art. 16. adducti, & ratio poterit dari hæc, quia prædicatum debet intelligi pro ratione subjecti, sive, prout admittitur à subjecto. Quod si ergo diversis subjectis idem prædicatum attribuatur, non mirum est, quod illud diversimodè veniat exponendum. Ostendit Dn. Velthusius multis exemplis istius Maj. falsitatem, probavitque, sæpissimè fieri, ut eodem in loco eadem phrasis, pro diversitate subjectorum, de quibus prædicatur, diversimodè debeat exponi, quibus multa alia adhuc possent addi. Sic Psal. cxxxii. 8. Surge Jehova in requiem tuam, tu & arca fœderis tui; ubi sanè τὸ surgere & adire requiem, aliter de Deo, aliter de arcâ est accipiendum. Hag. II. 6, 7. Commoturus sum Cœlum, Terram & Mare & siccum, & commoturus sum omnes gentes, vox commovere alio modo de Cœlis, alio modo de Terrâ, mari & gentibus est accipienda. Matth. V. 25. Ne quando te tradat adversarius judicio, & judex te tradat ministro, ubi prior traditio à posteriori plane differt. Joh. x. 23. si quorum remiseritis peccata, remittuntur eis, remittere peccata alio sensu dicuntur pastores, alio Deus. Verum adversarii hic erat, afferre rationem, quâ probaret, fieri non posse, ut prædicatum diversis subjectis in eodem loco diversimodè attribuatur, quod facere non est ausus.
units.tr: Reply. I do what becomes one who answers: I deny the major premise of the argument adduced in art. 16, and the reason can be given thus: the predicate must be understood according to the nature of the subject, that is, as it is admitted in the subject. If, therefore, the same predicate is attributed to different subjects, it is no wonder that it must be explained in different ways. Mr. Velthusius has shown by many examples the falsity of this major premise, and he has proved that very often the same phrase in the same place must be explained in different ways according to the difference of the subjects of which it is predicated, and many other examples could still be added. Thus in Psalm 132:8, "Arise, O LORD, into thy rest, thou, and the ark of thy covenant": here, surely, the "arising" and "going into rest" must be understood in one way of God and in another way of the ark. Haggai 2:6, 7, "I will yet once shake the heavens, and the earth, and the sea, and the dry land, and I will shake all nations": the word "shake" must be taken in one way of the heavens, in another of the earth, the sea and the nations. Matthew 5:25, "Lest at any time the adversary deliver thee to the judge, and the judge deliver thee to the officer": here the first delivering plainly differs from the later one. John 10:23 (sic), "Whosoever sins ye remit, they are remitted unto them": the ministers are said to remit sins in one sense, God in another. But it was for the adversary here to bring forward a reason by which he might prove that it cannot happen that a predicate is attributed to different subjects in different ways in the same place; this he did not dare to do.

units.la: DCCCXXX. Inst. 2. M. p. 132. Me hic negare conclusionem, me ad incitas redactum &c.
units.tr: DCCCXXX. Inst. 2. M. p. 132. He says that I here deny the conclusion, that I have been reduced to a corner, &c.

units.la: Resp. Remitto te ad præcedentia, ut videas quid negatum, & ob quam rationem.
units.tr: Reply. I refer you to what has gone before, so that you may see what was denied and for what reason.

units.la: DCCCXXXI. Inst. 3. M. p. 133. Sed contradictionem etiam in- venit evidentissimam, si dicam, Solem constitisse, & Solem apparenter tantum constitisse.
units.tr: DCCCXXXI. Inst. 3. M. p. 133. But he also finds a most evident contradiction if I say, that the sun stood still, and that the sun only apparently stood still.

units.la: Resp. Contradictio esset inter has propositiones; Sol stetit revera & Sol stetit apparenter, sive non revera. At non est contradictio inter has; Sol stetit & Sol stetit apparenter. Vides ergo in Adjecto tuo esse contradictionem, non in verbis meis contradictionem esse in adjecto.
units.tr: Reply. There would be a contradiction between these propositions: "The sun stood still in reality" and "The sun stood still apparently, or not in reality." But there is no contradiction between these: "The sun stood still" and "The sun stood still apparently." You see, therefore, that the contradiction lies in your added word, not in my words, and that the contradiction is in the adjective.

units.la: DCCCXXXII. Inst. 4. B. p. 161. Me in Astronomiâ quæsivisse exemplum, cum in Theologiâ non reperirem.
units.tr: DCCCXXXII. Inst. 4. B. p. 161. That I sought an example in astronomy, since I could not find one in theology.

units.la: Resp. Ego ex Astronomiâ non exemplum affero, ubi prædicatum diversis subjectis tributum diversimodè accipiatur, sed dico tantum, stationem non semper denotare stationem veram sive realem, sed etiam apparentem, quomodo etiam in Astronomiâ Ptolemaica locum habeat; inde enim solstitium dictum, non quod revera Solem stare existiment, sed quod tunc stare appareat. Nec erat quod objiceret, me imperitum esse in Phrasibus Astronomorum, quibus Planetarum loca vera & apparentia, ut & motus verus & apparens, idem sint, cum expressissime cap. 5. prioris Edit. hoc est, Dissertationum duarum &c. art. 5. jam annotassem, locum astri verum etiam appellari apparentem; sed ostendit adversarius æruginem suam & arguendi libidinem. Vera sunt loca apparentia, & verus est motus apparens, quia per hæc designatur, quem situm Planetæ respectu visus nostri obtineant, non tamen eo sensu sunt vera, si respectum habeas ad situm, quem inter ipsa corpora cœlestia obtinent. Interea adversarius ipse gravissime impegit, dum motum realem ab apparente non distinxit, prout manifestissime ei ostensum fuit ab Auctore Demonstr. inept. du Bois pag. 24. cui demonstrationi tantum abest, ut quidquam potuerit opponere, ut & publice errorem suum in libello, cui Titulus Den ingetoomde Cartesiaen fuerit confessus. Hanc responsionem Lector applicet ad argumentum, quod verbis diversis significatione idem habet H. p. 44. Tandem quaero &c. quæ videat, cui vacat.
units.tr: Reply. I do not bring forward from astronomy an example where a predicate attributed to different subjects is taken in different ways. I say only that a station does not always denote a true or real station, but also an apparent one, as this also holds in Ptolemaic astronomy; for from this the solstice is so called, not because men think the sun really stands still, but because it then appears to stand still. Nor was there any ground for objecting that I am inexperienced in the phrases of the astronomers, by which the true and apparent places of the planets, and the true and apparent motion, are the same, since in chapter 5 of the earlier edition, in art. 5 of the Two Dissertations, &c., I had most expressly already noted that the true place of a star is also called apparent; but the adversary shows his own spite and his lust for argument. The apparent places are true, and the apparent motion is true, because by these is designated what position the planet holds with respect to our sight; yet they are not true in that sense if you have regard to the position which the heavenly bodies themselves hold among one another. Meanwhile the adversary himself fell most gravely into error, since he did not distinguish real motion from apparent motion, as was very plainly shown to him by the author of the Demonstratio inepta of du Bois, p. 24; so far is he from having been able to oppose anything to that demonstration, that he even publicly confessed his error in the little book with the title Den ingetoomde Cartesiaen. Let the reader apply this reply to the argument which he has with different words but the same meaning (H. p. 44, Tandem quaero, &c.), which let whoever has leisure examine.

units.la: DCCCXXXIII. Inst. 5. M. p. 128. Inane cerebri vestri figmentum, quo Scripturam vobis adversantem eludere nitimini, dicendo motum Solis apparentem tantum imperio Josuæ stetisse &c.
units.tr: DCCCXXXIII. Inst. 5. M. p. 128. An empty figment of your brain, by which you try to evade Scripture, which opposes you, when you say that the apparent motion of the Sun stood still only by Joshua's command, etc.

units.la: Resp. Nos in observatione tertia ad Objectionem Primam verba Scripturæ ita interpretamur, ut dicamus, hæc verba, Sol stà, & Sol stetit, esse intelligenda non simpliciter, sed secundum quid, hoc sensu; Sol sta mihi, & Sol stetit Josuæ, & hoc ipsum non aliud ex illis verbis posse elici. Hæc est nostra hic interpretatio; unde sequitur his verbis non doceri, utrum hoc factum fuerit per Terræ motus inhibitionem realem, Solis vero apparentem, an vero per motus realis, qui in Sole fuerit inhibitionem. Tu vero inaniter oppugnas admodum interpretationem Scripturæ, quam tamen non satis intellexisti, reliqua tibi relinquo tanquam calumniæ valde affinia.
units.tr: Reply. In the third observation on the First Objection, we interpret the words of Scripture as follows: we say that these words, Sun, stand thou still and the Sun stood still, are to be understood not simply but in a certain respect, in this sense: Sun, stand for me, and the Sun stood for Joshua; and that nothing else can be drawn from those words. This is our interpretation here. From it it follows that these words do not teach whether this happened through a real halt of the Earth's motion and an apparent halt of the Sun's, or through a real halt of the Sun's motion. But you futilely attack the interpretation of Scripture, which you have not understood well enough, and I leave the rest to you as calumnies very closely related to one another.

units.la: DCCCXXXIV. Inst. 6. M. p. 128. Solis permansionem supra Horizontem fieri debuisse per veram motus Solis inhibitionem, quia motus Solis apparens non sit motus, adeoque sisti plane non potuerit.
units.tr: DCCCXXXIV. Inst. 6. M. p. 128. The Sun's remaining above the horizon ought to have happened through a true inhibition of the Sun's motion, because the apparent motion of the Sun is not motion, and so it could not be stopped at all.

units.la: Resp. Per verba apud Josuam intelligi posse dico Solis permansionem supra Horizontem, ita ut non determinaretur à Spiritu Sancto, quomodo id sit factum, cum ex verbis illis alius sensus non posset hauriri; an vero id factum sit per inhibitionem motus corporis solaris, an Terræ, aliunde dico inquirendum: motus vero apparens sisti potest non realiter, sed apparenter, prout enim motus est, ita sisti potest: at dico Spiritum Sanctum hic non intendisse plus significare, quam Solis permansionem supra Horizontem, etiamsi formulâ uteretur tali, quali, si usus fuisset infantiæ fantiæ præjudiciis occupatus, præter hoc etiam causam istius falsam consignificassẽt.
units.tr: Reply. I say that by the words in Joshua one can understand the Sun's remaining above the horizon, without the Holy Spirit determining how this was done, since no other sense can be drawn from those words. Whether this happened by an inhibition of the motion of the solar body or of the Earth's, I say must be inquired into from elsewhere. An apparent motion can be stopped not really but apparently; for as it is a motion, so it can be stopped. But I say that the Holy Spirit did not intend here to signify more than the Sun's remaining above the horizon, even though He used a form of words such that, if He had used it while occupied with the prejudices of childhood, He would also have co-signified a false cause of that.

units.la: DCCCXXXV. Inst. 7. M. p. 128. Solis splendor emanat à Sole, Ergo necesse est eum à Sole ita dependere, ut eo moto non possit non moveri, coque stante non possit non stare &c.
units.tr: DCCCXXXV. Inst. 7. M. p. 128. The splendour of the Sun emanates from the Sun; therefore it must depend on the Sun in such a way that, when it moves, it cannot but move, and when it stands still, it cannot but stand still, etc.

units.la: Resp. Ridiculum; quasi verò Solis splendor non possit varios Horizontes subire, etiamsi Sol immotus maneat, dummodo Terra gyret. Quis verò unquam negavit, variationem splendoris Solis super Terra per Terræ gyrationem à Copernicanis optimè posse explicari?
units.tr: Reply. Ridiculous! As if the splendour of the Sun could not pass through various horizons even if the Sun remained motionless, provided the Earth turns. Who ever denied that the variation of the Sun's light over the Earth, through the Earth's rotation, can very well be explained by the Copernicans?

units.la: DCCCXXXVI. Inst. 8. B. p. 162. Si præjudicium vocare libeat, quidquid non cognoscitur per certam demonstrationem &c: se nolle litigare de verbo, talem cognitionem Dialecticos vocare opinionem, quæ tàm Vera quàm falsa esse possit.
units.tr: DCCCXXXVI. Inst. 8. B. p. 162. If it pleases to call prejudice whatever is not known through certain demonstration, etc.: he does not want to quarrel about a word; dialecticians call such knowledge opinion, which can be as true as false.

units.la: Resp. Præjudicium proculdubio, prout constat ex vocis notatione, est judicium quod præveritit perceptionem, quodque proinde est factum sine certâ ratione; si ergo concedat, Josuam de utroque luminari locutum esse secundum præjudicium vulgi, quod fuit factum sine certâ ratione, ergò ex illis locutionibus, quâ talibus, nihil quicquam pro veritate rei colligere licet, sed, ut aliunde cognoscendum, an revera Luna moveatur, ita etiam an Sol, & sic totum argumentum ex illo Scripturæ loco desumtum perit.
units.tr: Reply. Prejudice, undoubtedly, as is clear from the meaning of the word, is a judgment that anticipates perception, and which is therefore made without certain reason. If, then, he concedes that Joshua spoke of both luminaries according to the prejudice of the common people, which was made without certain reason, then from those expressions, as such, nothing at all can be gathered for the truth of the matter; but, as must be known from elsewhere whether the Moon really moves, so also whether the Sun does, and thus the whole argument taken from that passage of Scripture perishes.

units.la: DCCCXXXVII. Exc. 2. Inst. 9. B. p. 163. Si tua præjudicii definitio sit legitima quari posse, an ergo merum præjudicium vocari debeat omnis cognitio rerum naturalium, quæ in prisci Philosophis, quin & in ipso Salomone fuit &c.
units.tr: DCCCXXXVII. Exc. 2. Inst. 9. B. p. 163. If your definition of prejudice is legitimate, one may ask whether every knowledge of natural things should therefore be called mere prejudice, which was in the ancient philosophers, and indeed in Solomon himself, etc.

units.la: Resp. Si Salomon, si prisci Philosophi non cognoverunt res naturales per certam rationem, siquε judicarunt de iis priusquam perceperint, omnino illa cognitio præjudicium dicendum; sin contra non assensi sunt, nisi clarè & distinctè perceptis, ab erroribus & præjudiciis immunes se præservarunt. Eligat quod volet adversarius.
units.tr: Reply. If Solomon and the ancient philosophers did not know natural things through certain reason, and if they judged about them before they perceived them, then that knowledge must certainly be called prejudice. But if on the contrary they assented only to things clearly and distinctly perceived, they kept themselves free from errors and prejudices. Let the adversary choose whichever he wishes.

units.la: Inquit, non usi fuerunt Methodo Cartesianâ, quà solùm secundum vos est certa.
units.tr: He says they did not use the Cartesian method, which alone, according to you, is certain.

units.la: Resp. Methodus Cartesiana est, quâ quis ad innatas notiones communes meditando attendens, æternasque veritates, de quibus nemo, modo rectè attenderit, dubitare queat, indeque sedulâ mente per collectiones & consequentias evidentes procedit ad ea, quæ inde fluunt & dependent, non antea quicquam statuens verum, quàm clare perceptum sit. Hanc Cartesianam dicimus, non quod nemo ante ipsum eâ fuerit usus, sed quod ipse, postquam diu jam esset inter Philosophos abjecta, eam luci dederit, constanterque fuerit secutus & aliis sequendam commendaverit. Hac usum fuisse Salomonem aliosque verè sapientes nulli dubitamus. Qui verò ab illa semita deflexerunt, & obscura ac confusa claris commiscuerunt, illisque non minus, quàm his assensum suum præbuerunt, eos à veritate aberrâsse non est mirum.
units.tr: Reply. The Cartesian method is that by which someone, meditating on the innate common notions and attending to them, and on eternal truths, about which no one who has attended rightly can doubt, proceeds with a careful mind through collections and evident consequences to those things which flow from and depend on them, never holding anything to be true before it has been clearly perceived. We call it Cartesian not because no one before him used it, but because he himself, after it had long been cast aside among philosophers, brought it to light, followed it constantly, and recommended it to others to follow. We do not doubt that Solomon and other truly wise men used it. But that those who turned aside from that path, and mixed the obscure and confused with the clear, and gave their assent to the former no less than to the latter, strayed from the truth is no wonder.

units.la: DCCCXXXVIII. Inst. 10. B. p. 163. Si hac tua præjudicii definitio sit legitima quæro: Annon tota Cartesii Physica merum præjudicium sit dicenda? Quamobrem? quia, inquit, ipse Pp. III. art. 44. Veruntamen, ne etiam nimis arrogantes esse videamur, si de tantis rebus philosophando, genuinam earum veritatem à nobis inventam esse affirmemus, malim hoc in medio relinquere, atque omnia, quæ deinceps scripturus, tanquam hypothesin proponere; quæ quamvis falsa esse existimetur, satis magnum opera pretium me fecisse arbitror, si omnia quæ ex ipsa deducentur cum experimentis consentiant. Et in fine operis: At nihilominus memor meæ tenuitatis, nihil affirmo: sed hæc omnia tum Ecclesiæ Catholicæ auctoritati, tum prudentiorum judiciis submitto; nihilque ab ullo credi velim, nisi quod ipsi evidens & invicta ratio persuadebit. Post quæ Adversarius: Illiusne rationes sunt certa demonstrationes, qui veritatem à se inventam affirmare non audet, & ipse nihil affirmat.
units.tr: DCCCXXXVIII. Inst. 10. B. p. 163. If your definition of prejudice is legitimate, I ask: should not the whole of Descartes' Physics be called mere prejudice? Why? Because, he says, he himself in Principles III, art. 44, says: However, lest we seem too arrogant if, in philosophizing about such great matters, we affirm that we have found their genuine truth, I would rather leave this undecided and propose everything I shall write hereafter as a hypothesis; which, although it be thought false, I think I have done a sufficiently great service if all that is deduced from it agrees with experiments. And at the end of the work: Yet, mindful of my own slightness, I affirm nothing: but I submit all these things both to the authority of the Catholic Church and to the judgments of the more prudent; and I wish nothing to be believed by anyone unless evident and unconquerable reason persuades him of it. After which the adversary says: Are the reasons of a man certain demonstrations, when he does not dare to affirm that the truth was found by himself, and he himself affirms nothing?

units.la: Resp. De Modestia Cartesii in modo loquendi distincta à Dubitatione, egit Cl. Claub. integro cap. Defens. Cartes. atque ita egit, ut ostenderit, malè fieri ab Adversariis, quod fingant absolutè & ex suo judicio Cartesium dicere, quod humanitatis ergò lectorum judicio relinquit; adductis variis similibus loquendi formulis apud alios auctores occurrentibus, ex quibus tamen non inferri possit, quod certam de his rebus, de quibus ita loquuntur, nullam habuerint cognitionem. Quod si citasset B. verba art. 43. & art. penult. Pp. IV. qui supra visos articulos proximè antecedunt, vidisset lector hæc modestiæ causâ à Cart. dicta; proinde in ejus gratiam adscribam: Et certè, si nullis principiis utamur, nisi evidentissime perspectis, si nihil, nisi per Mathematicas consequentias, ex iis deducamus, & interim illa, quæ sic ex ipsis deducemus, cum omnibus naturæ phænomenis accurate consentiant, injuriam Deo facere videremur, si causas rerum hoc pacto à nobis inventas falsas esse suspicaremur, tanquam si nos tàm imperfectos genuisset, ut ratione nostra recte utendo fallamur. Pp. IV. 206. Præterea quædam sunt, etiam in rebus naturalibus, quæ absolute & plus quam moraliter certa existimamus, hoc scilicet innixi Metaphysico fundamento, quod Deus sit summè bonus & minimè fallax, atque ideò facultas, quam nobis dedit ad verum à falso dijudicandum, quoties ea recte utimur, & quid ejus ope distinctè percipimus, ea tatis rare non possit. Tales sunt Mathematica demonstrationes: talis est cognitio, quod res materiales existant; & talia sunt evidentia omnia ratiocinia, quae de ipsis fiunt. In quorum numerum sortassis etiam haec nostra recipientur ab iis, qui considerabunt, quo pacto ex primis & maximè simplicibus cognitionis humanae principiis, continuâ serie deducta sint. Prasertim si satis intelligant, nulla nos objecta externa sentire posse, nisi ab iis aliquis motus localis in nervis nostris excitetur, talemque motum excitari non posse à stellis fixis, longissime hinc distantibus, nisi fiat etiam aliquis motus in illis, & in toto Coelo interjacente: his enim admissis, catera omnia, saltem generaliora, quae de Mundo & Terrâ scripsi, vix aliter quam à me explicata sunt, intelligi posse videntur. Illam autem modestiam usurpavit propter lectores, ut ex ultimis verbis apparet, quia si quis de omnibus à se inventis audacter & pro auctoritate se jactitet, prout in more positum est istis hominibus, videtur privare velle lectorem libertate judicandi, cùm, si modo Philosopho nostro recepto agat, nihil lectoribus credendum praescribat, nisi quod ii accurate perceperint.
units.tr: Reply. Cl. Clauberg, in the whole chapter of his Defence of Descartes, treated of Descartes' modesty in speaking, distinct from doubt, and treated it in such a way as to show that the adversaries do wrong in pretending that Descartes states absolutely, and on his own judgment, what he leaves to the judgment of the readers out of courtesy; adducing various similar forms of speech occurring among other authors, from which, however, it cannot be inferred that they had certain knowledge of those things about which they speak in this way. But if B. had cited the words of article 43 and of the penultimate article of Principles IV, which immediately precede the articles just seen, the reader would have seen that these were said by Descartes for the sake of modesty; therefore, for his sake, I shall add them: And indeed, if we used no principles except those most evidently perceived, and deduced from them nothing except by mathematical consequences, and meanwhile those things which we deduce in this way agreed accurately with all the phenomena of nature, we would seem to do injury to God if we suspected the causes of things found by us in this way to be false, as if He had made us so imperfect that we are deceived while using our reason rightly. Principles IV, 206. Moreover, there are certain things, even in natural matters, which we hold to be absolutely and more than morally certain, relying on this metaphysical foundation, that God is supremely good and least deceptive, and therefore the faculty which He gave us for distinguishing truth from falsehood cannot fail, whenever we use it rightly and perceive something distinctly by its aid. Such are the mathematical demonstrations; such is the knowledge that material things exist; and such are all the evident reasonings that are made about them. Perhaps these things of mine will also be counted among them by those who consider how they have been deduced in a continuous series from the first and most simple principles of human knowledge; especially if they understand well that we can perceive no external objects unless some local motion is excited in our nerves by them, and that such motion cannot be excited by the fixed stars, very far distant from here, unless some motion also takes place in them and in the whole intervening heaven. For granted these things, all the other things I have written, at least the more general ones concerning the World and the Earth, seem to be understood only in the way I have explained them. He used that modesty for the sake of the readers, as appears from the last words, because if anyone boldly boasts of all he has discovered and claims authority for it, as is customary with such men, he seems to want to deprive the reader of the freedom to judge, whereas, if he acts according to our received Philosopher, he prescribes nothing for the readers to believe except what they have accurately perceived.

units.la: DCCCXXXIX. M. p. 134. quærit, quidæsponsio 4. art. 827. data ad argumentum faciat? se enim nolle multum litigare, utrum ea sint præjudicia appellanda, quæ sine certâ ratione cognoscuntur.
units.tr: DCCCXXXIX. At M. p. 134 he asks what the answer given in article 827, paragraph 4, has to do with the argument, since he is unwilling to dispute at length whether those things should be called prejudices which are recognised without any sure reason.

units.la: Resp. Multum vero ad argumentum facit ista responsio; si enim circa utrumque luminare adhibuit sermonem, qui præjudiciis est involutus: ergò non præjudicia voluit significare, sed tantum veritatem generalem, quam etiam Belgæ Interpretes exprimunt, adeoque ex illis verbis neque Solis neque Lunæ statio realis potest colligi, quod intenditur à vestrâ parte.
units.tr: Reply: That answer has a great deal to do with the argument. For if, in speaking of each luminary, he used language that is wrapped in prejudices, then he did not mean to signify prejudices, but only the general truth, which the Belgian translators also express. So from those words no real standing of either the Sun or the Moon can be inferred, which is what your side intends.

units.la: DCCCXL. Tandem M. p. 134. Præter injuriosa verba, quæ lector videat, opponit, unanimem Scripturæ consensum & analogiam Solem moveri asserere.
units.tr: DCCCXL. Finally, at M. p. 134, besides the insulting words that the reader can see, he objects that they assert the Sun is moved, in agreement with the unanimous consent and analogy of Scripture.

units.la: Resp. Illud ipsum esse τὸ ξενούμενον [?], nec de verbis Scripturæ esse quæstionem, sed de ejus legitimo sensu, quem nego esse, per ista verba Solis motum significare, prout ex antecedentibus patet.
units.tr: Reply: That very thing is the matter in question [τὸ ξενούμενον]. The question is not about the words of Scripture but about their proper sense, which I deny signifies the motion of the Sun by these words, as is clear from what precedes.

units.la: DCCCXLI. Ad Observationem quartam Exc. 1. B. p. 165. Me numero responsionum voluisse certare, sed nihil afferre quod alicujus sit momenti. Quid ita? quia, inquit, quod ex Interpretibus Belgis collegit, nihil facit ad rhombum, non enim esse quæstionem, an Josua locutus fuerit locutione vulgari, sed an locutus fuerit secundum apparentiam, non ex rei veritate.
units.tr: DCCCXLI. In answer to our fourth observation, Exc. 1, B. p. 165, he says that I wished to contend by the number of answers but brought forward nothing of any weight. Why so? Because, he says, what I gathered from the Belgian translators has nothing to do with the rhombus; for the question is not whether Joshua spoke in popular language, but whether he spoke according to appearance and not according to the truth of the thing.

units.la: Resp. 1. Quando dicit, me numero responsionum voluisse certare, non me, sed semetipsum notat, cum hoc ipsi valdè sit frequens. Hæc adduxi ex Belgis, ut ostenderem, in quibus nobiscum circa hanc loci interpre-terpreterpretationem sit consensus.
units.tr: Reply 1. When he says that I wished to contend by the number of answers, he refers not to me but to himself, since this is very frequent with him. I cited the Belgians so as to show that in this interpretation of the passage there is agreement between us.

units.la: 2. Quæstio est: An Josua locutus fuerit tali locutione vulgari, quæ non nudam & accuratam rei veritatem, sed ad homines relatam referat? nos affirmamus & probamus hoc exemplo, consensu Belgarum confirmato; nam accuratè loquendo non magis Sol in Gibeone potuit dici consistere, quàm in aliis quibuscunque locis, sub eodem cum Gibeone Horizonte sitis; Itaque hæc locutio non nudam veritatem referebat. Quod si ergo propter rationem evidentem licet colligere, istam esse vulgarem locutionem, licebit & de verbo stare colligere, propter rationem evidentem, illud vulgari sensu accipiendum, quo non nudam veritatem, sed ad homines relatam referat; quibus observatis, reliqua quæ hic addit, nihil nobis obsunt.
units.tr: 2. The question is: Did Joshua speak in such popular language as does not state the bare and exact truth of the thing, but relates it as it is to men? We affirm this and prove it by this example, confirmed by the agreement of the Belgians. For speaking strictly, the Sun could no more be said to stand at Gibeon than in any other place lying under the same horizon as Gibeon. Therefore this expression did not state the bare truth. If, then, on account of this evident reason, we may infer that this is popular language, we may also infer, on account of an evident reason, that the word stand is to be taken in that popular sense, by which it states not the bare truth but the truth as related to men. With these points observed, the rest that he adds here does us no harm.

units.la: DCCCXLII. Exc. 2. B p. 165. Secundum consectarium, inquit, non est majoris momenti. Petebat siquidem heros sanctus, ne Sol sibi occideret, &, ne id fieret ut consisteret è regione Gibeonis. Frustra verò quaritur Emphasis in pronomine SIBI, cum illud non habeatur in verbis Josua nec historiographi &c. Fatemur, ortum & occasum Solis respectum dicere ad loca quibus oritur & occidit: revera tamen illìs oritur, cum sese supra Horizontem conspicuum facit, & occidit, cum sese sub Horizonte occultat.
units.tr: DCCCXLII. Second corollary, Exc. 2, B. p. 165. He says: "It is not of greater weight. The holy hero was asking that the Sun should not set for him, and that this should happen by its standing over Gibeon. And it is in vain that emphasis is sought in the pronoun for him, since it is not found in the words of Joshua or of the historian, etc. We grant that the rising and setting of the Sun refer to the places where it rises and sets. In reality, however, it rises there when it makes itself visible above the horizon, and it sets when it hides itself below the horizon."

units.la: Resp. Imò confirmat meam observationem, uti patet: si enim illa petitio Josuæ de Solis statione est intelligenda, hoc modo, ut Solem peteret sibi non occidere, idque ita factum esse dicat Scriptura, nihil inferetur contra Terræ gyrationem ex hoc loco, quia sive Terra gyret, sive Sol circumferatur circa illam, nihilominus, quamdiu manebat super Horizonte, stabat Josuæ. 2. Etsi autem vox, sibi, non reperiatur in textu, reperitur tamen in Belgis, ex quorum verbis consensum cum meâ interpretatione hîc tantum colligo, neque aliud intendo. 3. Cum ortus & occasus Solis ei conveniat, non minus secundum Copernici sententiam ac Ptolemæi, obtento, per formulam istam apud Josuam nihil aliud denotatum fuisse, quam Solem non occidisse integrum diem, non potest inferri, eum ex moto quiescentem evasisse, cum etiam per Terræ quietem miraculosam potuerit Sol integrum diem non occidisse. Apparet ergo, quanti momenti sit ista observatio, tanti nempe, ut causam antagonistæ plane evertat.
units.tr: Reply: On the contrary, it confirms my observation, as is clear. For if that petition of Joshua about the standing of the Sun is to be understood in this way, that he asked the Sun not to set for him, and Scripture says that this was so done, then nothing can be inferred against the rotation of the Earth from this passage. For whether the Earth turns or the Sun revolves around it, nevertheless, as long as it remained above the horizon, it stood for Joshua. 2. Although the word for him is not found in the text, it is found in the Belgians, and from their words I gather agreement with my interpretation here, and I intend nothing more. 3. Since the rising and setting of the Sun belong to it no less according to Copernicus's opinion than according to Ptolemy's, and since it is granted that by that formula in Joshua nothing else was denoted than that the Sun did not set for a whole day, it cannot be inferred that it has become at rest from being in motion. For by a miraculous rest of the Earth the Sun could likewise not have set for a whole day. It is clear, then, how great the weight of this observation is: great enough, namely, to overturn the opponent's cause entirely.

units.la: DCCCXLIII. Quæ M. p. 129. & 130. objicit, ad ea responsio ex antea notatis facile potest applicari, neque enim operæ pretium est tempus his terere. Auctoritatibus non ducimur humanis in rebus Theologicis, ut propter eas putemus vel aliquid recipiendum vel rejiciendum, sed interim recte contra vos & ad hominem iis utimur, qui semper eas crecrepatis. Belgarum interpretatio hic cum nostrâ convenit, nempe, vulgari hic locutione significatum, Solem Iosuæ non occidisse: ex quo nequicquam colliges, Solem antea fuisse realiter motum; quonam ergo hanc interpretationem adduxerim, vides.
units.tr: DCCCXLIII. As for the objections he raises at M. p. 129 and 130, the answer to them can easily be applied from what was noted before, nor is it worth the time to waste on these matters. We are not led by human authorities in theological questions, so that on account of them we should think either that something must be accepted or rejected. Yet in the meantime we use them rightly against you and ad hominem, against those who always decry them. The Belgian interpretation here agrees with ours, namely, that by popular language it is signified here that the Sun did not set for Joshua. From this you will in vain conclude that the Sun was earlier really moved. Thus you see why I adduced this interpretation.

units.la: DCCCXLIV. Unicum adhuc est, quod posset morari lectorem, quod habet M. p. 132. contra ultima articuli 813. verba: Oriri & occidere, inquit, cum notet actionem haud secus ac το appropinquare, proprie & accurate non potest tribui, nisi ei, in quo est ista actio, non vero alteri ex Diff. 2. cap. 4. §. 48. cum igitur ista actio secundum vos non fit in Sole, nec etiam ortus & occasus proprie & accurate loquendo ei à vobis tribuitur.
units.tr: DCCCXLIV. There is one thing still that might delay the reader, which is found at M. p. 132 against the last words of article 813: "To rise and to set," he says, "since they denote an action, just as to approach does, cannot properly and exactly be attributed except to that in which the action is, and not to another, from Diff. 2, ch. 4, §48. Therefore, since according to you this action is not in the Sun, neither are rising and setting properly and exactly attributed to it by you."

units.la: Resp. Ortus & occasus designat apud Astronomos vel elevationem sive ascensionem supra Horizontem, vel certe apparitionem ejusdem; unde & oriri astra dicunt Ptolemaici ea, quæ conspici incipiunt propter discessum Solis, etiamsi ipsis nullus motus attribuatur; ergo ex ortu & occasu Solis non potest colligi ejus motus: quamvis autem Oriri connotet actionem ex primâ origine, quæ præjudicio vindicari debet, de quo capite 46 videbimus, sufficit, quod in eo sensu à nobis ortus & occasus tribuatur Soli, quomodo secundum omnes Astronomos accipi potest.
units.tr: Reply: Among the astronomers, rising and setting denote either the elevation or ascent above the horizon, or certainly the appearance of the same. Hence the Ptolemaic writers also say that the stars rise which begin to be seen because of the departure of the Sun, even though no motion is attributed to them. Therefore from the rising and setting of the Sun no motion of it can be inferred. Although to rise connotes an action from its first origin, which must be vindicated from prejudice (we shall see this in chapter 46), it is enough that rising and setting are attributed by us to the Sun in that sense in which they can be taken according to all astronomers.

units.la: DCCCXLV. Contra quartam nostram Observationem etiam adduci posset, id quod habet R. St. p. 326. Hoc argumentum eo modo procedit, ac si quis dicat, in historia magorum memoratur casa Bethlemetica, ergo non stella, sed casa Magos ab Oriente est comitata.
units.tr: DCCCXLV. Against our fourth observation there could also be adduced what he has at R. St. p. 326: "This argument proceeds as if someone were to say: in the history of the Magi there is mention of the stable at Bethlehem, therefore it was not the star but the stable that accompanied the Magi from the East."

units.la: Resp. Ex illis Scripturæ verbis, in quibus mentio fit Gibeonis, tantum infertur, esse locutionem hic vulgarem, cum Sol non posset dici proprie Gibeone consistere, etiamsi aliàs de statione vera hæc verba sumenda essent: non enim magis Gibeone poterat dici consistere, quàm alio in loco, qui intra eundem Horizontem comprehenditur, si accurate Scriptura loqui voluisset. Quid autem inde colligatur, ex fine art, 813. est repetendum.
units.tr: Reply: From those words of Scripture in which Gibeon is mentioned, it is inferred only that the language here is popular, since the Sun could not properly be said to stand at Gibeon, even if these words were otherwise to be taken of a true standing. For it could no more be said to stand at Gibeon than in another place included under the same horizon, if Scripture had wished to speak with exact precision. What is inferred from this must be repeated from the end of article 813.
