units.la: DCCCXLVI. Videamus, si quæ præter dicta ex verbis H. habeantur pro ista Objectione Instantiæ. Is pag. 41. urget. 1. verba textus: Sol in Gibhon exspectà & Luna stet super Ajalon; sed tamen præcipue annotat in fine p. 41. Voces imperii hujus cum expendo, quasdam earum ad captum vulgi, quasdam ad rem dici deprehendo: Ad captum & opinionem, quando Sol stare super Gibhon jubetur.
units.tr: DCCCXLVI. Let us see whether there is anything in H.'s words beyond what has been said, which is held for this objection from instance. At p. 41 he presses, first, the words of the text: "Sun, stand thou in Gibeon, and moon, in the valley of Ajalon." But he notes especially at the end of p. 41: "When I weigh the words of this command, I find some of them to be spoken for the understanding of the common people, and some for the thing itself. For the understanding and opinion of the people, when the Sun is bidden to stand over Gibeon."

units.la: Resp. Si hæc dicta sunt ad captum vulgi & opinionem, hoc est, si illa phrasis, super Gibhon, denotat veritatem aliquam præjudiciis involutam & ad homines relatam; Ergo nihil impedit, quo minus etiam phrasis, Sol stà, talem designet.
units.tr: Reply: If these things are said for the understanding and opinion of the common people, that is, if that phrase over Gibeon signifies some truth wrapped in prejudices and related to men, then nothing prevents the phrase the Sun stand from likewise signifying such a truth.

units.la: DCCCXLVII. At, inquit, Josua Solem & Lunam collocavit, quomodo eidem obiter raptim & vix suspiciendo apparebant, & quatenus lumen ipsi in Gabaon utile prabebant: Vere nihilominus Sol super Gabaon fuit physice, licet non Geometrice.
units.tr: DCCCXLVII. "But," he says, "Joshua set the Sun and the Moon in such a way that they appeared to him in passing, hastily and scarcely noticed when he looked up, and insofar as they gave him light useful at Gabaon. Truly, nevertheless, the Sun was physically above Gabaon, though not geometrically."

units.la: Resp. Hoc assumto; Josuam Solem & Lunam collocasse, quomodo ei obiter &c. apparebant, cum non apparuerint ei super Makeda, Bethoron, & alia loca, ergo etiam super iis non collocavit: Attamen non minus erat super iis quam super Gibeon; ergo omnino haec formula veritatem quidem aliquam, sed apparentia sensuum involutam designat, quod est quod intendo.
units.tr: Reply. Granting this assumption, that Joshua set the sun and moon so that they appeared to him in passing, etc., when they did not appear to him over Makkedah, Beth-horon and other places, it follows that he did not set them over these places either. Yet the sun was no less over these places than over Gibeon. So this formula altogether indicates some truth, but one wrapped in the appearances of the senses. This is what I am arguing.

units.la: DCCCXLVIII. 2. Urget verba Historiographi sacri p. 44. & seqq. atque hic tria observat. 1. Vocem stetit & synonymum exspectavit, non festinavit. 2. verba: Et Sol stetit in medio Coeli. 3. Miraculum quod vers. 14. innitur. De primo inquit: Textum hunc emphaticum atque adeo de rei veritate pronunciantem esse arguit. 1. Particula ET, quae est Solis obedientia cum mandato Josua copulativa, similis textus in creatione legitur, ubi Deus dixit, fiat lux ET facta est: Clarior hic & potentior est verborum sensus quam ut hallucinationem admittat. 2. Verba stetit, exspectavit, non festinavit, arguunt Emphasin, quorum vim quis non nisi Scepticus Mercurius sentiat, stetit, id est, a cursu quievit.
units.tr: DCCCXLVIII. 2. He presses the words of the sacred historian, p. 44 and following, and here notes three things. 1. The word "stood" is equivalent to "waited," not "hastened." 2. The words: And the sun stood in the midst of heaven. 3. The miracle, which rests on verse 14. On the first he says: This shows that the text is emphatic and so declares the truth of the matter. 1. The particle AND, which joins the sun's obedience to Joshua's command, is like the text in creation, where God said, "Let there be light," AND there was light. The sense of the words is too clear and powerful to admit a hallucination. 2. The words "stood," "waited," "did not hasten," show emphasis, whose force no one would perceive except a sceptical Mercury: "stood," that is, rested from its course.

units.la: Resp. 1. Quod petiit Josua factum est, licet forte non eo modo quo petiit, suppositio quod modum hujus miraculi putaverit fieri debere per inhibitionem motus corporis solaris. Diem sibi prolongari petiit formula consueta, per quam, an causam istius prolongationis consignificaverit, incertum esse dixi. At quod petiit factum est, &, si quid amplius significavit ex errore & praejudicio ortum, id quia nec necessarium scopo & non nisi ex praejudicio ortum, non opus erat, ut a Deo efficeretur; sufficit, si res petita exhibeatur, etiamsi non secundum eum modum, quo expetimus. 2. quaestio ipsa est, an, quod putat adversarius, per ista verba significetur? id ego non existimo, non magis, ac si ea formula a Copernicano vel Cartesii sententiae defensore usurpata foret. Miraculum per eam formulam significatum existimo a Spiritu Sancto (quod postea recte explicat adversarius) nec quid praeterea. Neque hic ad Emphasin & claritatem verborum provocare licet, quam non nego, sed in sensum adversarii posse trahi pernego.
units.tr: Reply. 1. What Joshua asked was done, though perhaps not in the way he asked it, on the supposition that he thought the manner of this miracle had to be the stopping of the sun's bodily motion. I said that the customary formula by which he asked for the day to be lengthened is uncertain as to whether he meant to signify its cause. But what he asked was done. If he signified anything more, which arose from error and prejudice, then, since it was neither necessary to his purpose nor arose from anything but prejudice, there was no need for God to bring it about. It is enough that the thing asked for is granted, even if not in the way we wanted it. 2. The question itself is whether, as the opponent thinks, what he thinks is signified by these words. I do not think so, any more than if this formula had been used by a Copernican or by a defender of Descartes' opinion. I think the miracle signified by that formula was from the Holy Spirit (which the opponent later explains correctly), and nothing more. Nor here may we appeal to the emphasis and clarity of the words, which I do not deny, but I flatly deny that they can be drawn into the opponent's sense.

units.la: DCCCXLIX. De secundo, inquit, Haec verba: Et Sol stetit in medio Coeli, nihil aliud significare, quam in umbilico Coeli tempore meridiei, id est, nobis hora duodecima. Resp. Sit ita, nihil nobis obest, neque nos ea verba urgemus.
units.tr: DCCCXLIX. As to the second point, he says, these words: "And the sun stood in the midst of heaven," signify nothing other than that at midday the sun was at the centre of the sky, that is, for us at the twelfth hour. Reply. Let it be so; this does us no harm, and we do not press these words.

units.la: DCCCL. Tertium, inquit, expendendum venit, quod familiam hic ducit, miraculum, quod versu 14. innititur, & hinc argumentatur: Quod miraculosum est illud non naturale est; sed Solis Statio illa fuit miraculosa, Ergo.
units.tr: DCCCL. The third point, he says, must be considered, which leads the family here: the miracle, which rests on verse 14, and from this he argues: What is miraculous is not natural; but that stopping of the sun was miraculous. Therefore.

units.la: Resp. facilis est responsio; si miraculum in prolongatione dici constitit, prout explicatur versu 14. & prout hic revera fuit effectus precum Josuæ, omnino ista prolongatio dici non est naturalis existimanda, sed negatur, modum istius miraculi describi in eo loco; nempe factum illud miraculum per inhibitionem cursus Solis realis, quod ipsum quæritur.
units.tr: Reply. The answer is easy. If the miracle is said to consist in the lengthening, as it is explained in verse 14, and as it was in fact the effect of Joshua's prayers, then that lengthening is not to be thought altogether unnatural. But it is denied that the manner of this miracle is described in that place, namely, that the miracle was effected by stopping the real course of the sun, which is itself the very point in question.

units.la: DCCCLI. Tandem generalia quædam proponit quæsita, nempe: An omnia loci istius dicta ad apparentiam & opinionem hominum accipienda sint: an aliqua tantum, an omnino nulla? Ad quæ sine vacillatione respondeo, omnia dicta accipienda esse usu recepto inter homines, qui duplex sæpe est, ut & significent veritatem & consignificent errorem, quo illa veritas est obvoluta: prout autem à Spiritu Sancto adhibentur, censenda sunt tantum veritatem generalem significare secundum ea quæ dicta sunt art. 653, 791. Talia autem esse ea, de quibus est quæstio, assero. Tu, si aliqua sint ita accipienda, dicis, disquisitionem adhuc esse quenam & in quantum taliter dicta sint. Et multorum verborum flatu, fluctus in simpulo inaniter moves. Ego vero respondeo, esse ea, quæ vos frustra contra nos adducitis, idque tuebor, donec contrarium ostenderitis, neque in eo defendendo me quicquam contra Scripturam ponere satis sum certus. Hæc quoad hunc locum dicta sufficiant, quæ enim H. à p. 188. ad 192. habet, ea quantum ad me attinent, abunde refutata sunt.
units.tr: DCCCLI. Finally he sets out certain general questions: Are all the statements of that place to be taken according to appearance and human opinion? Or only some? Or none at all? To these I answer without hesitation that all the statements are to be taken in the common usage of men, which is often double, so that they both signify the truth and co-signify the error in which that truth is wrapped. But when they are used by the Holy Spirit, they are to be judged to signify only a general truth, according to what has been said in articles 653 and 791. I assert that those of which there is question are of this kind. You say that if some are to be taken in this way, the inquiry is still open as to which they are and to what extent they have been so spoken. By blowing many words you stir up waves in a cup to no purpose. I, however, reply that those things which you bring against us in vain are these, and I will maintain this until you show the contrary; nor am I certain that in defending it I set anything against Scripture. Let these things said about this place suffice; as for what H. has from p. 188 to 192, so far as I am concerned, it has been thoroughly refuted.

units.la: CAPUT XLV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XLV.

units.la: Cum sententia dicta conciliatur locus Esaiæ xxxviii. 8.
units.tr: How the passage of Isaiah 38:8 is reconciled with the stated opinion.

units.la: DCCCLII. Secundus locus cum nostra sententia conciliandus est Esaiæ xxxviii. 8. Ecce ego reducturus sum umbram graduum illorum, quæ descendit gradibus Achazi solaribus retrorsum decem gradibus. Et reversus est Sol decem gradibus iisdem, quibus descenderat. Ad quem observo: Per phrases istas, umbram reducturus sum, item, Sol est reversus, nihil aliud designari, quam, variationem quandam situs obvenisse Soli & gnomoni, qui umbram facit, adeoque etiam respectu umbrae ipsius, ita ut Sol eum receperit situm respectu umbrae ipsius gnomonis, quem habuit, antequam gradibus istis decem descenderat: an vero per motum Solis, an Terrae, illa variatio situs contigerit, Scriptura non determinat. Neque phrases hae vulgares, quando a Spiritu Sancto usurpantur, ulterius sunt extendendae, licet iisdem inter homines ortum dederit visus quaedam fallacia & praejudicium sensuum, quod & significatur ab iis, qui eo sunt occupati, sicubi istâ phrasi utantur. Quemadmodum enim nec Ptolemaici nec Tychoniani permittunt, ut quis ex phrasi alterâ hic etiam adhibitâ, Sol descendit, inferat: Solem e sublimiori loco in inferiorem sese dimisisse, quamvis hujus locutionis inventores illud praejudicium consignificaverint, eo quod secundum Ptolemaicos & Tychonianos Sol in circulo moveatur, sed illas phrases explicant tantum respectu nostri, nempe habita ratione nostri Horizontis; ut, quando in Ortu supra nostrum Horizontem se conspiciendum praebet, pergitque, donec ad circulum Meridianum perveniat, dicatur ascendere, descendere vero, quando a circulo Meridiano ad occasum progreditur. Ita & nulla ratio est, quae nos cogat ex phrasi, Sol reversus est, Solis motum realem colligere.
units.tr: 852. The second passage must be reconciled with our opinion, Isaiah 38:8: Behold, I will bring back the shadow of the degrees by which it has gone down on the stairs of Ahaz, ten degrees backward. And the sun returned by the same ten degrees by which it had gone down. On this I observe: by these phrases, I will bring back the shadow and the sun has returned, nothing else is signified than that some variation of position came about between the sun and the gnomon which casts the shadow, and so also with respect to the shadow itself, such that the sun took up with respect to the shadow of the gnomon the position it had held before it went down those ten degrees. Whether this change of position came about by the motion of the sun or of the earth, Scripture does not determine. Nor are these common phrases, when the Holy Spirit uses them, to be extended further, although they have given rise among men to a certain deception and prejudice of the senses, which those who are occupied with it also signify whenever they use that phrase. For just as neither the Ptolemaic nor the Tychonic astronomers allow anyone to infer from the other phrase used here as well, the sun goes down, that the sun has let itself down from a higher place to a lower, although the inventors of this manner of speaking have attached that prejudice to it (since according to the Ptolemaics and Tychonians the sun moves in a circle), yet they explain those phrases only with respect to us, namely with regard to our horizon: so that when at rising it presents itself to be seen above our horizon and continues until it reaches the meridian circle, it is said to ascend, but to descend when it proceeds from the meridian circle to the west. So likewise there is no reason which compels us to gather from the phrase the sun has returned a real motion of the sun.

units.la: DCCCLIII. Videamus nunc, quid contra eam responsionem, clarius nunc aliquanto propositam, ac in Dissertationum editione erat factum, faciant Instantiae Adversariorum. Atque B. hunc locum contra me non urget. H. etiam existimat p. 49. hunc locum posse conferri cum priori, atque ex illius interpretatione pendere. Interim argumentum videtur petere ex Ef. vii. Si, inquit, Achaz signum in superis caelestibus postulasset, factum id dubio procul fuisse, sed ex hypothesi hodiernâ apparenter tantum.
units.tr: 853. Let us now see what the objections of our adversaries do against this answer, now set out somewhat more clearly than it was in the edition of the Dissertations. And B. does not press this passage against me. H. also thinks, on p. 49, that this passage can be compared with the former and depends on its interpretation. Meanwhile he seems to draw an argument from Isaiah 7: If, he says, Ahaz had asked for a sign in the heavenly heights, that would undoubtedly have happened, but on the present hypothesis only apparently.

units.la: Resp. Achaz habebat mandatum divinum, ut peteret sibi signum, vel e profundis vel ex rebus altissimis, id si petiisset, futurum fuisse revera non ambigimus; quod si etiam de Ezechiâ probari posset, cum habuisse facultatem, ut signum peteret, vel ex profundis vel ex rebus altissimis, forte aliquid hoc argumento effectum fuerit. At 2 Reg. xx. 9. optio ei tantum propósita est, utrum velit umbram in solario Achazi abire decem gradibus, an retrocedere, quorum posterius elegit, quod & praestitum est. Nec vero Ezechias determinate id per realem retrogradum motum Solis fieri voluisse legitur, neque per eum factum dicitur, sed per retrogradam mutationem situs corporis solaris, respectu gnomonis, qui umbram projiciebat.
units.tr: Answer: Ahaz had the divine command to ask for a sign for himself, either from the depths or from the highest things; that if he had asked, it would have come about in fact we do not doubt. But if it could also be proved concerning Hezekiah that he had the power to ask for a sign either from the depths or from the highest things, perhaps something might be effected by this argument. But at 2 Kings 20:9 he is offered only the choice whether he wishes the shadow on the dial of Ahaz to go back ten degrees or to go forward, and he chose the latter, which was also done. Nor is it read that Hezekiah wished this to be done by a real retrograde motion of the sun, nor is it said to have been done by that, but by a retrograde change of the position of the solar body with respect to the gnomon which cast the shadow.

units.la: DCCCLIV. Inst. 2. M. p. 135. Duplicem nobis in uno loco fingis locutionem falsam ad captum vulgi compositam 1. quidem, quod Sol dicitur reversus fuisse, cum umbra tantum reversa vere fuerit, sed qua ratione id nobis probaveris? (opponentis enim vices jam sustines, utpote qui haec loca utpote argumenta pro tua sententia citaveris. Differt. 1. cap 4. §. 10.)
units.tr: 854. Objection 2, M. p. 135: You feign in one place a twofold false manner of speaking, composed for the grasp of the common people: first, that the sun is said to have returned, when only the shadow truly returned; but by what reasoning have you proved this to us? (For you already sustain the part of the opponent, since you have cited these passages as arguments for your opinion. Diss. 1, ch. 4, §10.)

units.la: Resp. Tu vero dupliciter falsum committis 1. quod dicis, me locutiones falsas in Scripturam introducere, vel, ut alibi loqueris, me statuere, Scripturam loqui falsum, quod nullibi dixi 2. quod inquis, me hic sustinere partes opponentis citato etiam loco. Diff. 1. cap. 4. qui tamen tibi plane est contrarius. Videat lector, & apparebit, me ibi dicere, quod nolim ad probationem istius sententiae adducere istos locos, quod adhuc sint controversi. Dico itaque, esse hic locutionem vulgarem & receptam, quae ex praejudicio habet ortum, quae tamen, quatenus a Spiritu Sancto adhibetur, verum significet, nempe, Solem mutasse situm suum decem gradibus respectu solarii Achazi, quod aeque fieri potuit per Terrae, quam per corporis solaris retrogradum motum. Quod si a Spiritu Sancto etiam hoc in loco significatum sit, corpus solare realiter retrogressum esse, id ex circumstantiis textus probandum ab adversariis. Ego vero sic ad hominem colligo: Si locutio vulgaris & impropria statuenda in phrasi, Sol descendit, propterea, quia repugnat, Soli in circulo moto ex mente Ptol. competere ascensionem & descensionem proprie, ergo locutio vulgaris & impropria statuenda in phrasi, Sol reversus est, propterea quia repugnat, ut Sol circa Terram singulis diebus obambulet. Quod autem repugnet, a me superius probatum.
units.tr: Answer: You yourself commit a twofold falsehood. First, you say that I introduce false manners of speaking into Scripture, or, as you say elsewhere, that I hold that Scripture speaks falsely, which I have nowhere said. Second, you say that I here sustain the part of the opponent by citing this passage, Diss. 1, ch. 4, which is in fact entirely contrary to you. Let the reader look, and it will appear that I there say that I would not wish to adduce those passages in proof of this opinion, since they are still controverted. I say therefore that there is here a common and received manner of speaking, which arises from prejudice, yet which, insofar as it is used by the Holy Spirit, signifies the truth: namely, that the sun changed its position by ten degrees with respect to the dial of Ahaz, which could as well have happened through the motion of the earth as through a retrograde motion of the solar body. But if the Holy Spirit has signified in this place also that the solar body really went backward, the adversaries must prove this from the circumstances of the text. I, however, reason thus against the man: if a common and improper manner of speaking must be posited in the phrase the sun goes down, because it is incompatible, according to the mind of Ptolemy, that the sun, moving in a circle, should properly have ascent and descent, then a common and improper manner of speaking must likewise be posited in the phrase the sun has returned, because it is incompatible that the sun should walk around the earth every day. That this is incompatible I have proved above.

units.la: DCCCLV. Inst. 3. Pergit M. p. 137. Secunda locutione, quando Sol dicitur descendisse, rem significatam Soli vere competere, me agnoscente, eamque alia tam vulgata loquendi formula exprimi non potuisse; hoc autem non esse loqui falsum ad placitum vulgi.
units.tr: 855. Objection 3, M. p. 137: He goes on. In the second manner of speaking, when the sun is said to have gone down, I acknowledge that the thing signified truly belongs to the sun, and that it could not be expressed by another so common form of speech; but this is not to speak falsely according to the pleasure of the common people.

units.la: Resp. Nullibi dixi, Scripturam loqui falsum ad placitum vulgi, & quamvis antea formulam respondendi a Copernicanis frequentatam adhibuerim, nihil tamen aliud per eam significavi, quam quod saepius explicui, ita ut par sit ratio istius phrasis vulgaris, Sol descendit, quae alterius, Sol regressus est, ut ex dictis patet.
units.tr: Answer: I nowhere said that Scripture speaks falsely according to the pleasure of the common people; and although previously I used the form of answer frequented by the Copernicans, I signified nothing else by it than what I have explained more often, so that the reasoning of this common phrase, the sun goes down, is the same as that of the other, the sun has gone back, as is clear from what has been said.

units.la: DCCCLVI. Inst. 4. Tandem p. 138. Vere imo proprie Soli convenit ascensus & descensus, nempe respectu nostri, si consideratur ut pedes nostros quasi relinquens & versus caput contendens vere & proprie nobis dicitur ascendere & contra.
units.tr: 856. Objection 4, p. 138: Finally, indeed, the rising and setting truly, indeed properly, belong to the sun, namely with respect to us: if it is considered as leaving our feet, as it were, and heading toward the head, it is truly and properly said to us to rise, and conversely.

units.la: Resp. 1. Quod respectu nostri Soli competit, prout hic explicatur, illud Soli proprie & vere non potest competere, neque enim à nobis vel nostris pedibus magis est remotus, quando est in medio Cœli, quam quando est in ortu vel occasu, quoniam lineæ à parte Terræ, cui pedibus insistimus, tanquam centro ad Solem Orientem & Occidentem & in medio Cœli locatum, ductæ sunt æquales; at fi tum proprie descendisset, deberet nobis esse propior. 2. Si consideretur quasi relinquens pedes: ergo non revera, sed fecundum apparentiam. Implicavit ergo & totum sese hic irretivit adversarius.
units.tr: Answer: First, what belongs to the sun with respect to us, as is here explained, cannot belong to it properly and truly; for it is not more remote from us or from our feet when it is in the middle of the heavens than when it is at rising or setting, since the lines drawn from the part of the earth on which we stand, as from a centre, to the sun rising, setting, and located in the middle of the heavens, are equal. But if it truly descended at that time, it ought to be nearer to us. Second, if it is considered as leaving the feet: then not in reality, but according to appearance. The adversary has therefore entangled himself and, in this place, has entangled the whole matter.

units.la: CAPUT XLVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XLVI.

units.la: Proponitur Pfalm. xix. 5, 6, 7. ac cum nostrâ sententiâ conciliatur.
units.tr: Psalm 19:5–7 is set forth and reconciled with our opinion.

units.la: DCCCLVII. Pfal. xix. 2. — 7. sic habent: Cœli enarrant gloriam Dei fortiter, & opus manuum ejus indicat expansum eorum. Dies ad diem eructat sermonem. Et nox ad noctem ostendit scientiam: Non est sermo neque verba eius, & fine his intelligitur vox eorum, simul prodierunt in extremitatem orbis habitabilis sermones eorum, ex quo Soli posuit tentorium in eis. Nam & tanquam sponsus prodiens e thalamo suo, latatur tanquam robustus decursurus viam. Ab extremitate Cœlorum exortus ejus & revolutio ejus ad extremitates eorum est. Quæ verba ut appareat sententiæ, quam defendo, non obesse, sic προφείςω : Gloria sapientiæ, bonitatis, potentiæ altarumque persectionum divinarum in aperto tam clare est posita, ut, si quis oculos & mentem ad Cœlos, & quæ in eis sunt, velit convertere, non possit non inde evidentissime cognoscere; ea aperte sese manifestante in toto expanso, in quo opus manuum Dei excellentissimum & perfectissimum licet intueri. Sed non tantum apertissima est illa Dei gloria ex opere vastissimo Cœlorum, verum etiam est perpetua, singulis diebus & noctibus eam sibi invicem quasi de manu in manum tradentibus, ut nullo unquam tempore desit ejus argumentum. Latissimè quoque ea se extendit, nec impeditur, quo minus cognosci possit à variarum linguarum hominibus, verum liber naturæ & mundi exemplis gloriæ divinæ plenus quibusvis nationibus patet, & à remotissimis terrarum incolis, quocunque oculos vertas, legi potest. Imprimis ea gloria divina agnoscendam se præbet in corpore illo præ aliis in Cœlis conspicuo Sole, qui quasi in iis singulare domicilium habet à Deo paratum, in quo se recondit & occultat, ita tamen ut mane pulcherrimus aspectu sese spectandum exhibeat, vasto admodum corpore, non absimilis giganti robusto, parato tamen ad continuam situs variationem, quae propter celeritatem cum cursu comparari potest; incipiente inde ubi se terminat visus & definente ad oppositos visus terminos. Docet ergo Psalmista in hoc Psalmo, primò generatim gloriam Dei fieri manifestam per Coelos, verf. 2, 3, 4, 5. Dein speciatim per Solem, versus 5. ult. verbis & verf. 6. & 7. Circa primum declarat: 1. quam clarè & manifestè Coeli istam gloriam enarrent verf. 2. 2. quam constanter & perpetuò, versu tertio. 3. tandem, quam late sese ista narratio expandat verf. 4. Secundum quod attinet Soli tribuitur in hoc Psalmo. 1. Occultatio in altera parte hemisphaerii. 2. continua sui corporis lucidissimi singulis diebus super Horizonte exhibitio, ut ab oculis in ista hemisphaerii parte habitantium conspiciatur. 3. continua situs variatio &c.
units.tr: 857. Psalm 19:2–7 reads thus: The heavens declare the glory of God mightily, and the firmament shows the work of his hands. Day unto day utters speech, and night unto night shows knowledge. There is no speech nor words, and their voice is not heard; yet their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the end of the world. In them he has set a tabernacle for the sun, which comes forth like a bridegroom from his chamber and rejoices like a strong man to run his course. Its going forth is from the end of the heavens, and its circuit reaches to the ends of them. That these words do not stand in the way of the opinion I defend, I shall show as follows. The glory of God's wisdom, goodness, power and other perfections is set forth so plainly in the open that whoever turns his eyes and mind to the heavens and the things in them cannot fail to know it most evidently from them. God manifests himself openly in the whole expanse, in which one may behold the most excellent and perfect work of his hands. Yet that glory of God is not only most open from the vast work of the heavens; it is also perpetual, for day and night hand it on, as it were, from hand to hand, so that at no time is there any lack of evidence for it. It also extends very widely, nor is it hindered from being known by men of various tongues. The book of nature and the world, full of examples of the divine glory, lies open to every nation, and can be read by the inhabitants of the most remote lands, wherever you turn your eyes. Above all, the divine glory shows itself to be acknowledged in that sun, which among the heavenly bodies stands out before the others, and which has a singular dwelling in them prepared by God, in which it hides and conceals itself, yet so that in the morning it displays itself most beautifully to be seen. It is a very vast body, not unlike a strong giant, yet ready for continual change of position, which because of its speed may be compared with a race, beginning where the sight ends and ending at the opposite limits of sight. The Psalmist therefore teaches in this psalm: first, in general, that the glory of God is made manifest through the heavens (verses 2, 3, 4, 5); then, in particular, through the sun (the last words of verse 5, and verses 6 and 7). Concerning the first he declares: (1) how clearly and manifestly the heavens declare this glory (verse 2); (2) how constantly and perpetually, in verse 3; (3) finally, how widely this declaration spreads, in verse 4. As for what is ascribed to the sun in this psalm: (1) its hiding in the other half of the hemisphere; (2) its continual display of its most bright body above the horizon every day, so that it is seen by the eyes of those who live in that part of the hemisphere; (3) its continual change of position, and so on.

units.la: DCCCLVIII. Hâc paraphrasi & analysi ita praemissâ, dicimus, in hoc Psalmo occurrere multas locutiones vulgares, praejudiciis innitentes, tum proprias tum etiam Metaphoricas, adhibitas ad significandum veritates generales, ad quas exprimendas communi usu adhiberi solent, quamvis, si usurpentur ab hominibus, quibus velum praejudiciorum non est detractum, etiam praejudicia consignificent. Sic Psalmista 1. per verba illa, Soli disposuit tentorium in Coelo, nihil aliud designat, quàm Solem in Coeli parte oppositâ vesperi sese recondere tanquam in tentorio. 2. per verba, est tanquam sponsus prodiens è thalamo suo, cum mane iterum se conspiciendum praebere. 3. per verba, laetatur tanquam robustus decursurus viam, dispositum esse ad continuam situs mutationem. 4. ab extre-mitate Coelorum exortus ejus & revolutio ejus ad extremitatem eorum, illam variationem situs continuo durare ab uno puncto extremit. visus nostri usque ad punctum oppositum: sed phrases, quibus haec designantur, ortum habent ex praejudiciis, quibus veritates istae, quas dicimus hic significari, sunt obvolutae, quae involucra praejudiciorum ex parte propriis, ex parte metaphoricis phrasibus exprimuntur.
units.tr: 858. With this paraphrase and analysis set forth, we say that in this psalm there occur many common expressions, resting on prejudices, both literal and metaphorical, used to signify general truths, which in common usage are customarily employed to express them. Yet if they are used by men from whom the veil of prejudice has not been removed, they also carry the prejudices along with them. Thus the Psalmist (1) by the words He has set a tabernacle for the sun in the heavens designates nothing other than the sun withdrawing in the evening into the opposite part of the heavens, as if into a tent. (2) By the words it comes forth like a bridegroom from his chamber, he means that in the morning it again presents itself to be seen. (3) By the words it rejoices like a strong man about to run his course, he means that it is disposed to continual change of position. (4) Its going forth is from the end of the heavens, and its circuit is to the ends of them: that this change of position continues without interruption from one point at the limit of our sight to the opposite point. But the phrases by which these things are designated arise from the prejudices by which the truths we say are signified here are wrapped; these wrappings of prejudice are expressed partly in literal and partly in metaphorical phrases.

units.la: DCCCLIX. Praejudicia illa infantiae sunt, quod ubi visus noster terminatur, & Terra Coelum contingere videtur, sunt Coeli extremitates & quasi Solis conditorium, in quo occultetur per totam noctem, ex quo tanquam thalamo mane prodire judicatur tanquam robustus aliquis gigas, cum in ortu longe major appareat quàm in Occidente: De his praejudiciis Tacitus de moribus Germanorum: Trans Suionas aliud mare pigrum ac proprie immotum, quo cingi, cludiqué Terrarum orbem hinc fides, quod extremus cadentis jam Solis fulgor in ortus edurat, adeo clarus ut sidera hebetet. Sonum insuper se mergentis audiri formasque Deorum & radios capitis adspici persuasio adjicit. Ad quae verba Lipsius annotat: Hac persuasio rudis & cascæ plebis fuit. Solem, dum in Oceanum cadit, stridorem edere, non aliter, quam signitum ferrum condatur in aquam, advocata etiam auctoritate Possidonii apud Strabonem & Flori de Decimo Bruto in Hispaniis bellante. Sic Virgil. Georg. 1. hanc vulgi opinionem secutus inquit: Sol quoque & exoriens, & cum se condet in undas Signa dabit. Confer ea, quae supra §. 493. ex Bocharto laudavimus. Fateor quidem, huic praejudicio generali, secundum quod Psalmus sermonem hunc inflexit, alia atque alia esse addita, ut quod Sol undis immergatur, dum occidit &c. est tamen in genere hoc omnium praejudicium, ultra id quod sensus monstrant assurgere non valentium, quod Sol ubi occidit condatur sub Terram quasi, eam fere attingendo, ibique usque ad exortum deses lateat. Unde non mirum est, si propter certissimam rationem etiam circa cursum Solis locutio popularis ex praejudiciis sensuum orta sit agnoscenda.
units.tr: 859. These prejudices belong to infancy: that where our sight ends and the earth seems to touch the heavens, there are the extremities of the heavens and, as it were, the sun's resting-place, in which it lies hidden through the whole night; and from there it is judged to come forth in the morning from its chamber like some strong giant, since at its rising it appears far larger than in the west. Concerning these prejudices Tacitus, in his work on the customs of the Germans, says: Beyond the Suiones there is another sea, sluggish and almost motionless, which is believed to encircle and enclose the whole orb of the lands. The reason for this belief is that the last gleam of the already setting sun lingers toward the east, so bright that it dims the stars. To this is added the belief that the sound of the sun plunging is heard, and the forms of the gods and the rays of their heads are seen. On these words Lipsius remarks: "This belief was that of a rude and foolish common people, that the sun, as it sinks into the ocean, gives off a hissing sound, just as a red-hot iron hisses when plunged into water," appealing also to the authority of Posidonius, as reported by Strabo, and of Florus concerning Decimus Brutus waging war in Spain. So Virgil, in the first Georgic, following this popular opinion, says: The sun too, both rising and when it hides itself in the waves, will give signs. Compare what we cited above from Bochart, §493. I admit that to this general prejudice, according to which the Psalm framed its discourse, other and different things have been added, such as that the sun is plunged into the waves as it sets, and so on. Nevertheless, in general this is the prejudice of all, one which those who cannot rise above what the senses show hold: that the sun, when it sets, is hidden beneath the earth, as it were touching it, and there lies idle until its rising. Hence it is no wonder if, on account of the most certain reason, a popular way of speaking about the course of the sun, arising from the prejudices of the senses, is to be recognised.

units.la: DCCCLX.
units.tr: DCCCLX.

units.la: In quo tanto magis confirmabimur, si consideremus; Ortum etiam, qui in loco allegato Soli tribuitur, proprie loquendo ei non posse convenire, cum ne quidem secundum Ptolemaicum systema Sol proprie possit dici oriri. Quia secundum ipsum Sol movetur in circulo, in quo nulla pars altera humilior est, altiorve: aeque enim omnes a centro sunt remotae: Oriri autem est, e planitie in altum tolli, vel assurgere. Manifestum ergo est, hanc locutionem ad sensuum apparentiam esse accommodatam. His non possum, quin addam verba Zwingeri in Analysi hujus Psalmi; Sol quatenus est vita & mortis & rerum omnium, quae ad vitam necessaria, dator assimilatur sponso: sicut sponsus probe lotus & ornatus de thalamo suo procedit in amplexum sponsae: Ita Sol emergens de Oceano (Poetica phrasi etiam profanis usitata vatibus, Oceani nitidum caput extulit undis) supra Horizontem ascendit, ut inferiorem mundum suo lumine vivificet: Sol quatenus est mortis & eorum quae mortem praecedunt profligator assimilatur gigantis; sicut gigas robore ac celeritate magna occurrit suis hostibus, eos profligat & in fugam conjicit: Ita Sol suo salutari aspectu creaturarum omnium praesertim hominis hostes tum corporeos, tum spirituales sua luce abigit. Quibus verbis etsi non in totum consentio, tamen apparet, quam confinia sint inter responsioni.
units.tr: We will be confirmed in this all the more if we consider that the rising, which is attributed to the Sun in the passage cited, cannot properly belong to it, since even according to the Ptolemaic system the Sun cannot properly be said to rise. For according to that system the Sun moves in a circle in which no part is lower or higher than another, since all are equally distant from the centre. But to rise is to be lifted up on high from a plain, or to rise up. It is therefore clear that this manner of speaking is accommodated to the appearance of the senses. I cannot refrain from adding the words of Zwingerus in his analysis of this Psalm: The Sun, insofar as it is the giver of life and death and of all things necessary to life, is likened to a bridegroom: just as a bridegroom, well washed and adorned, comes out of his bedchamber into the embrace of his bride, so the Sun, rising out of the Ocean (in a poetic phrase used even by profane poets, "the shining head of Ocean lifted itself from the waves"), ascends above the Horizon, so that it may quicken the lower world with its light. The Sun, insofar as it is the destroyer of death and of the things that precede death, is likened to a giant; just as a giant, with great strength and speed, meets his enemies, overthrows them and puts them to flight, so the Sun, by its saving aspect, drives away with its light the enemies of all creatures, especially of man, both bodily and spiritual. Although I do not wholly agree with these words, it nevertheless appears how close the boundaries are between the answers.

units.la: DCCCLXI.
units.tr: DCCCLXI.

units.la: Inst. 1. B. p. 170. Hanc responsionem cum magno impetu aggreditur, atque inquit; Demiror Theologiae Professorem tam debili, ne dicam puerili responsione evasionem tentare, (nota hic sermonem adversarii) nam locutiones vere Metaphoricas vulgares nominat, ut habeat aliquid, e quo errorem vulgi elicere possit.
units.tr: Inst. 1. B. p. 170. He attacks this answer with great vehemence and says: I marvel that a Professor of Theology should attempt an escape with so weak, not to say childish, an answer (note here the adversary's language), for he calls them common expressions that are truly metaphorical, so that he may have something from which he can draw out the error of the common people.

units.la: Resp. Vulgares locutiones sunt, quae veritatem denotant ad homines relatam & praejudiciis obvolutam, quales omnes citatas puto, uti patebit mox plenius. Si tamen Metaphoricas eas velit vocare, dum modo supponat, similitudinem & Metaphoram in sensuum apparentia fundatam, per me id licuerit, saltem tum similiter similitudinem in verbo prodire & decurrere facile potero reperire ad propositum meum plane facientem. Attamen & M. p. 139. eas non vidisse percipio, quod non imputandum, nisi ipsis illis praejudiciis, quibus adhuc est occupatus; ortum enim debere istum sermonem praejudiciis ostendi.
units.tr: Reply. They are common expressions, which denote a truth related to men and wrapped in prejudices, such as all those I have cited, as will become clearer below. If, however, he wishes to call them metaphorical, provided he supposes a likeness and metaphor founded on the appearance to the senses, I am content with that. At least, in the same way, I could easily find in the word prodire and decurrere a likeness that wholly supports my purpose. Yet I perceive that he has not seen these things even at p. 139 of his book, which is not to be imputed to him except to those same prejudices by which he is still occupied; for it must be shown that this manner of speaking arises from prejudices.

units.la: DCCCLXII. Inst. 2. Sed pergit B. p. 170. Soli tentorium competere in Caelo, quia in Caelo versetur ut homo in tentorio suo, 2. Thalamum attribui non Soli, sed sponso, cui Sol comparatur. 3. extremitates Caeli attribui respectu terminationis visus nostri.
units.tr: DCCCLXII. Inst. 2. But B. goes on, p. 170: the tent belongs to the Sun in the heavens, because it moves in the heavens as a man in his tent; 2. the bedchamber is attributed not to the Sun but to the bridegroom, to whom the Sun is compared; 3. the extremities of the heavens are attributed with respect to the limit of our sight.

units.la: Resp. Egregie vero! Quid clarius quam, dum attribuitur tentorium Soli, respectum haberi ad ejus occultationem, quae vesperi contingit, & permansionem sub Terra invariabilem, usque ad matutinum tempus? cum expresse describatur exinde prodire, & dum prodit, ab extremitate coelorum ad extremitatem decurrere. Atsi simpliciter ei tentorium attribueretur, quatenus in Coelo versatur, tum etiam tempore, quo prodit & quo decurrere dicitur ab una extremitate ad alteram, in suo tentorio versari esset dicendus, quod est absonum. Tentorium ergo Soli non poterit competere, nisi respectu habito ad praejudicium ante citatum. 2. Ita sponso tribuitur Thalamus, ut Sol dicatur prodire sicut sponsus prodit e Thalamo: Ergo etiam, saltem per similitudinem, quae tamen non potest non in sensuum apparentia esse fundata: Soli Thalamus attribuitur non minus, quam antea tentorium. 3. Si extremitates Coelis tribuuntur respectu terminationis visus nostri, ergo revera non sunt Coeli, sed visus nostri. At hic tribuuntur Coelo, ergo omnino locutio ista ortum debet praejudicio, quo termini sive extremitates visus nostri ad ipsum Coelum transferuntur.
units.tr: Reply. Excellent indeed! What is clearer than that, when the tent is attributed to the Sun, regard is had to its setting, which happens in the evening, and to its unchanging stay under the Earth until morning? For it is expressly described as coming forth from there, and while it comes forth, as running from one extremity of the heavens to the other. And if the tent were attributed to it simply, insofar as it moves in the heavens, then at the time when it comes forth and when it is said to run from one extremity to the other, it would have to be said to dwell in its tent, which is absurd. The tent therefore cannot belong to the Sun unless regard is had to the prejudice mentioned above. 2. Thus the bedchamber is attributed to the bridegroom, so that the Sun is said to come forth as the bridegroom comes out of his bedchamber. Therefore the bedchamber is also attributed to the Sun, at least by likeness, which nevertheless cannot fail to be founded on the appearance to the senses, no less than the tent was before. 3. If the extremities are attributed to the heavens with respect to the limit of our sight, then they are in truth not extremities of the heavens but of our sight. But here they are attributed to the heavens, so the whole manner of speaking must arise from the prejudice by which the limits or extremities of our sight are transferred to the heavens themselves.

units.la: DCCCLXIII. Inst. 3. Addit B. p. 171. mera esse somnia de praejudi- ciis sensuum & errorem de Sole per totam noctem in quiete manente, ad quem responderit Dial. 25.
units.tr: DCCCLXIII. Inst. 3. B. adds, p. 171, that these are mere dreams from prejudices of the senses, and an error that the Sun remains at rest through the whole night; to which I have replied in Dialogue 25.

units.la: Resp. Ad manus jam non est Dialogus, in quo tamen nihil quicquam ad rem faciens existimo non solutum reperiri in hoc capite, licet forte non praecise in ista solutione mentio Dialogi fuerit facta. Ad præjudicia respeƈtum haberi, satis probavi, quæ refutata oportuit.
units.tr: Reply. The Dialogue is not now at hand, but I think that nothing bearing on the matter has been left unanswered in this chapter, although perhaps the Dialogue was not expressly mentioned in that answer. That regard is had to prejudices I have sufficiently proved, and they had to be refuted.

units.la: DCCLXIV. Inst. 4. B. p. 171. Vocem gigantis in versione quidem vulgata reperiri, sed vocem נָבוֹר in Hebræo, non gigantem, nec hominem quatenus magnus est statura, sed potentem, fortem, robustum designare.
units.tr: DCCLXIV. Inst. 4. B. p. 171. The word giant is indeed found in the Vulgate version, but the Hebrew word gibbor [נָבוֹר] designates not a giant, nor a man great in stature, but one powerful, strong, robust.

units.la: Resp. Vox נָבוֹר fortem, robustum designat non tantum generaliter, sed etiam iu specie de gigante Goliatho usurpatur, 1 Sam. xvii. 52. וַיִּרְאוּ הַפְּלִשְׁתִּים כִּי מֵת גִּבּוֹרָם וַיָּנֻסוּ. Quin ergò hic convenienter reliquis eo sensu usurpetur nihil obstat; cum enim de aliis phænomenis circa Solem loquatur, isque in ortu major appareat, quam in medio Cœli, non inconveniens, si hanc vocem hoc modo interpretemur, uti etiam antea à Zwingero factum vidimus.
units.tr: Reply. The word gibbor [נָבוֹר] designates the strong, the robust, not only in general, but is also used in particular of the giant Goliath, 1 Sam. 17:51: "And when the Philistines saw that their champion was dead, they fled" [וַיִּרְאוּ הַפְּלִשְׁתִּים כִּי מֵת גִּבּוֹרָם וַיָּנֻסוּ]. Why, then, should it not be used here in that sense, agreeing with the rest? Since the passage speaks of other phenomena concerning the Sun, and it appears greater at its rising than in the middle of the heavens, it is not inappropriate to interpret this word in this way, as we have already seen Zwingerus do.

units.la: DCCCLXV. At dicit H. p. 25. Sol gigas dicitur non ob corporis molem, quia scilicet non posset aptus dici ad cursum, sed ratione virtutis.
units.tr: DCCCLXV. But H. says, p. 25: the Sun is called a giant not because of the bulk of its body, since it would not then be fit to be called swift in its course, but by reason of its strength.

units.la: Resp. Major corporis moles, si modo cætera sint paria, majorem virtutem confert, sive robur, si enim sit sufficiens crurum agilitas & copia spiritHuum, quæ musculis crurum celeriter movendis sufficiat, etiam major celeritas ad currendum tali competere potest.
units.tr: Reply. A greater bulk of body, provided the other things are equal, brings greater strength; for if there is sufficient agility of the legs and abundance of spirits to move the leg-muscles quickly, then greater speed in running may also belong to such a body.

units.la: DCCCLXVI. Inst. 5. B. p. 171. Nec ut ad rem loqueretur ipsi probandum erat ex Tacito, qualis fuerit Ethnicorum opinio de finibus orbis Terrarum &c. sed quid creditum fuerit in populo Dei, & quænam super hac materia fuerit fides Prophetarum; & H. pag. 109. negat, hanc tam brutam fuisse Judæorum vulgi opinionem &c. pag. 110, 111.
units.tr: DCCCLXVI. Inst. 5. B. p. 171. Nor was it necessary for him to prove, in order to speak to the point, from Tacitus what the opinion of the heathens was about the limits of the earth's orb, etc., but what was believed among the people of God, and what the faith of the Prophets was on this matter; and H. p. 109 denies that the opinion of the common Jews was so crude, etc., pp. 110, 111.

units.la: Resp. Stupidos credo sibi proponunt lectores, talesque qui non conferunt ipsorum exceptiones cum meis responsionibus (quod quamvis forte in quibusdam fuerint assecuti, tamen non in omnibus, non in iis, qui de hac re accuratè judicare constituerunt) Qui enim inspexerit meam responsionem, videbit debuisse à me probari, locutiones Psalmi xix. quas citavi, ortum habere ex præjudiciis, quibus ab infantia homines promiscuè sive gentiles sive Judæi sive Christiani imbuuntur, quæ locutiones postquam semel fuerint receptæ, etiam ab iis, qui ista præjudicia deposuerint, usurpari possunt ac debent. Istud æque ex Tacito, ac aliunde probare potui, cum præjudiciorum infantiæ & locutionum inde exortarum apud omnes par sit ratio, nisi forte existiment in populo Dei nulla talia fuisse, vel non ortum dedisse locutionibus multis, quod quam frigidum sit nemo non videt. Quamvis autem postea deponantur opiniones multæ à multis, sermo tamen idem manet qui ex præjudiciis habet ortum.
units.tr: Reply. I suppose they propose to their readers stupid people, such as do not compare their exceptions with my replies (which, though perhaps they achieved in some points, did not do so in all, nor with those who have determined to judge this matter accurately). For whoever looks at my reply will see that I had to prove that the expressions of Psalm 19 which I cited arise from prejudices with which men are imbued from infancy, whether Gentiles, Jews or Christians alike; and once these expressions have been received, they can and ought to be used even by those who have laid aside those prejudices. I could prove this from Tacitus as well as from elsewhere, since the reasoning about the prejudices of infancy and the expressions arising from them is the same for all; unless perhaps they think there were no such things among the people of God, or that they gave rise to no expressions, which nobody fails to see is a feeble view. Although many opinions are afterwards laid aside by many, the manner of speaking remains the same, having arisen from prejudices.

units.la: DCCCLXVII. Inst.6. B. p. 172. Oriri, inquit, & occidere tribuitur Soli &c. respectu locorum & Horizontis, oriri quidem, cum se conspicuum exhibet supra Horizontem, occidere vero, cum se occultat sub Horizonte, ita ut utrumque proprie tribuatur Soli &c.
units.tr: DCCCLXVII. Inst. 6. B. p. 172. He says: To rise and to set are attributed to the Sun, etc., with respect to places and the Horizon: it rises when it shows itself visible above the Horizon, and sets when it hides itself below the Horizon, so that each is properly attributed to the Sun, etc.

units.la: Resp. 1. Quod circa proprietatem vocum oriri & occidere observavi non factum esse refragantibus Astronomis discere est ex Keplero, quem ipse Adversarius magnum Astronomum appellat, qui Epit. Astron. Copernicanæ, lib. 3. part 1. p. mihi 206. quærit: Quid sonant voces oriri & occidere? & respondet: Oriri esse e planitie in altum tolli, vel assurgere, adscendere, paulatim magis ac magis emergere, ut montes navigantibus in Oceano videntur ex undis emergere, ut non abs ratione credas vocem ἀνατέλλειν quod montem significat, & ab ὄρος surgere, derivari. Græca vox ἀνατέλλειν affinis est Latini tolli, sonat proprie de plantis, cum se tollunt in auras, ex terra humectâ, quæ φυτὰ dicitur. Occidere & Occumbere est pronum cadere; de cadentibus in acie usurpatur, inde de omnibus intervenientibus. Græca vox δύνειν usurpatur pro receptu in aliquod conclave, subire, intrare, condi, quod sidera post montes in thalamum velut se recipiant. Germanica propositiones auff und niedergang sunt manifestæ, sonant enim sus & de, untergehen est mergi, ut naves in undis. Sic Auctores linguæ Latinæ Festus & Paulus oriri exponunt Nasci vel surgere. Concinit Velius Longus de Orthographia: Talis, inquit, quæstio est inter Cohortes & Coortes, ubi diversam esse significationem voluerunt Grammatici, ut Cohortes sint villarum, unde homines cooriantur pariter: oriri enim apud antiquos surgere frequenter significabat, ut apparet in eo, quod dicitur: Oriens Consul magistrum populi dicat, quod est surgens. Sic & apud Hebræos dicitur Gen. xix. 23. השמש יצא על הארץ, Sol exivit super Terram. Origo ergo vocis est ex præjudiciis. At apud Astronomos vox illa ex præjudiciis ortum habens adhibetur ad designandam veritatem illam generalem, de qua dicit adversarius in instantia proposita, prout & ipsi hanc eandem significationem cap. præcedente art. 844. assignavimus; sed hic quæritur tantum, an is sit sensus istius vocis proprius, & an non circa ipsam hanc impositionem quoddam præjudicium observari possit, quod ei dederit ortum? Ego prius nego, posterius affirmo, eo quod oriri proprie significet e planitie in altum tolli, præjudicium autem sit infantiæ, Terram latissimâ planitie circulariter excurrere in omnes plagas circa spectatorem, à qua etiam originem deduxit Orbis Terrarum appellatio. Non mirum ergo erit, si & oriri dicuntur Astræ ex præjudicio, quod à Terræ planitie in altum assurgere & tolli videantur. Concludo ergo, istam locutionem ad sensuum apparentiam esse accommocommodatam, intellige talem de qua quæstio, nempe quæ cum rei veritate non convenit, ut non meus hic sit soloecismus, sed adversarii, qui conclusiones pro libitu mihi affingit.
units.tr: Reply. 1. That I have not made this observation about the proper sense of the words to rise and to set against the astronomers may be learned from Kepler, whom the adversary himself calls a great astronomer. In the Epitome of Copernican Astronomy, book 3, part 1, p. 206 of my edition, he asks: What do the words to rise and to set mean? and answers: To rise is to be lifted up on high from a plain, or to ascend, gradually emerging more and more, as mountains seem to sailors on the ocean to emerge from the waves; so one may not unreasonably believe that the Greek word anatellein [ἀνατέλλειν], which means a mountain and derives from oros [ὄρος], meaning to rise, is derived from it. The Greek word anatellein is akin to the Latin tolli, and properly refers to plants when they lift themselves into the air out of moist earth, which are called phyta [φυτὰ]. To set and to sink is to fall forward; it is used of those falling in battle, and thence of all who fall. The Greek word dyein [δύνειν] is used for withdrawing into some chamber, to go under, to enter, to be hidden, as if the stars retired behind the mountains into a bedchamber. The German expressions auff and niedergang are plain, for they mean up and down; untergehen means to be submerged, as ships in the waves. Thus the authors of the Latin language, Festus and Paulus, explain oriri as to be born or to rise. Velius Longus in his book on orthography agrees: There is such a question, he says, between cohortes and coortes, where the grammarians wished them to have different meanings, so that cohortes are of farms, whence men rise together; for among the ancients oriri often meant to rise, as appears from the saying: "Oriens consul magistrum populi dicat," which means "rising." So also among the Hebrews it is said in Gen. 19:23: "the sun was risen upon the earth" [השמש יצא על הארץ]. The origin of the word is therefore from prejudices. But among astronomers that word, having its origin in prejudices, is used to designate that general truth of which the adversary speaks in the instance proposed, just as we also assigned this same meaning to it in the preceding chapter, art. 844. But here the question is only whether this is the proper sense of the word, and whether some prejudice cannot be observed in this very imposition, which gave it its origin. I deny the former and affirm the latter, because to rise properly means to be lifted up on high from a plain, whereas the prejudice is of infancy, that the Earth extends in a very broad plain in a circle on all sides around the spectator, from which also the name orbis terrarum was derived. It is therefore no wonder if stars are also said to rise from the prejudice that they seem to ascend and be lifted from the plain of the Earth. I conclude, therefore, that this manner of speaking is accommodated to the appearance of the senses, understood as that kind of thing which is in question, namely that which does not agree with the truth of the matter; so that this is not my solecism but the adversary's, who ascribes conclusions to me at his pleasure.

units.la: DCCCLXVIII. Inst. 7. M. pag. 139. Hic præter scommata in Cartesium conjecta omnia confundit: Præjudicia ipsa, quibus formulæ loquendi sunt involutæ, cum similitudinibus, quibus ratione istorum præjudiciorum illæ formulæ vestiuntur. Præjudicia quænam hic sint, dixi superius eaque probavi; hæc negare oportuisset adversarium & contrarium ostendere. Nam præter præjudicia & Solis cursu & motu reali, & de elevatione è planitie in altum ostendi aliis 3. præjudiciis sermonem Psalmistæ esse obvolutum, quæ tamen non ipse Spiritus Sanctus docet, sed veritatem, quæ iis est obvoluta. Præjudicia illa sunt 1. partem hemisphærii ei oppositam inservire Soli pro tentorio, in quo recondatur & quasi quiescat. 2. Majorem esse, dum exoritur, quam postea. 3. Cœlo competere extremitates, quæ Terram tangant. His præjudiciis dico obvolutum esse sermonem Psalmistæ, sed ab iis qui phrases istas invenerunt; illaque clara sunt & satis à nobis probata. Sed non inter præjudicia pono, quòd Sol non conjugium ineat, quod latetur, & similia ab Adversario inepte adducta. Et quamvis nunc pauci ea præjudicia infantiæ retineant, tamen sufficit, ab infantia nos omnes ita judicasse, illudque judicium inventoribus vocum originem dedisse tales phrases usurpandi.
units.tr: DCCCLXVIII. Inst. 7. M. p. 139. Here, apart from the jests thrown at Descartes, he confuses everything: the prejudices themselves, in which the modes of speech are wrapped, with the similitudes by which those modes of speech are clothed on the basis of those prejudices. I have already said what the prejudices here are, and I have proved them. The opponent should have denied them and shown the contrary. For besides the prejudices about both the course of the Sun and its real motion, I have shown that the Psalmist's language is also wrapped in three other prejudices concerning the rising up and lifting of the Sun from the flatness of the earth. These are not taught by the Holy Spirit himself, but the truth that is wrapped in them is. The prejudices are: (1) that the part of the hemisphere opposite to us serves the Sun as a tent in which it is hidden and as it were rests; (2) that the Sun is larger when it rises than later; (3) that the extremities of the heavens reach down to touch the earth. I say the Psalmist's language is wrapped in these prejudices, but in the sense that those who coined these phrases were wrapped in them. These points are clear and have been adequately proved by us. But I do not count among the prejudices that the Sun does not enter into marriage, that it rejoices, and similar things which the Opponent foolishly brings up. And although few now retain those childish prejudices, it is enough that we all judged this way from infancy, and that this judgment gave the originators of these words the origin of using such phrases.

units.la: DCCCLXIX. H. p. 106. Negat, locutiones dictas à vulgo esse præconceptas, nam, inquit, opinio de Solis tentorio plebejis ingeniis impossibilis erat 1. quia idea talis neque cum sensu rei convenit, neque vulgari captui est apta. 2. Idea quæ Solis, vel in æthere vel in orbis Terra fine &c. concipit tabernaculum, materialis tantum est, non formalis. Ergo non est vera idea, neque possibilis. 3. Idea ista vix ab ingeniosissimis concipi potest, &c.
units.tr: DCCCLXIX. H. p. 106. He denies that the expressions are preconceived by the common people, for, he says, the opinion about the Sun's tent was impossible for plebeian minds: (1) because such an idea neither agrees with the sense of the thing nor is suited to the grasp of ordinary people; (2) the idea which conceives of the Sun's tabernacle in the air or at the edge of the earth, etc., is merely material, not formal. Therefore it is not a true idea, nor a possible one; (3) this idea can hardly be conceived even by the most gifted, etc.

units.la: Resp. Præjudicia infantiæ de Sole multa sunt; ut enim omnes ab infantia putamus Solem motu reali singulis diebus ab una extremitate Cœlorum ad alteram circumvolvi, ita vespreri omnes existimant, Solem sub Terram, quæ infinitis radicibus sit protensa, vel quæ aquis innatet, se recondere, & ibi usque ad sequens matutinum tempus, vel desidem manere, vel novum prodire; quod præjudicium etiam per phrasin metaphoricam, quòd Sol sub Terra sit per noctem tanquam in tentorio, exprimi potest. Probavi id in superioribus, & manifestum erit cuique si attendat ad judicia, quæ ipse ab infantia & prima ætate formaverit; unde patet, talem ideam omnino cum apparentiis sensuum convenire & vulgari captui aptam. 2. veram quidem non esse, sed falsam, imò & contradictoriam, si accuaccuratè examinetur; unde tamen in quantum idea possibilis est, cùm etiam de contradictoriis ideas formare queamus, sed planè confusas.
units.tr: Reply. There are many childish prejudices about the Sun. For just as we all think from infancy that the Sun revolves in real motion each day from one end of the heavens to the other, so everyone supposes in the evening that the Sun hides itself under the earth, which is extended by endless roots or floats on the waters, and there either remains inactive until the following morning or comes forth anew. This prejudice can also be expressed by the metaphorical phrase that the Sun is under the earth through the night as if in a tent. I have proved this above, and it will be plain to anyone who attends to the judgments he himself formed from infancy and early childhood. From this it is clear that such an idea agrees altogether with the appearances to the senses and is suited to the grasp of ordinary people. (2) It is indeed not true but false, and even self-contradictory, if it is examined accurately. Yet insofar as the idea is possible, since we can also form ideas of contradictories, though quite confused ones.

units.la: DCCCLXX. At, inquit, rusticorum aliorumque de plebe non est similitudines formare.
units.tr: DCCCLXX. But, he says, it is not for peasants and others of the common sort to form similitudes.

units.la: Resp. Nihil ad rem, modo quorumvis sit id de Sole præjudicare, quod dixi, idemque formulâ propriâ exprimere, quæ ab aliis facilè in Metaphoricas mutari potest. 2. Nihil obstare video, quo minus quilibet de plebe voces Metaphoricas rebus accommodare possit, etsi formaliter & ex arte Rhetoricâ id præstare nesciat.
units.tr: Reply. This is beside the point, provided that the Sun is prejudged by anyone in the way I have said, and that the same is expressed in its own proper wording, which others can easily turn into metaphors. (2) I see nothing to prevent any common person from applying metaphorical words to things, even if he does not know how to do so formally and by the art of rhetoric.

units.la: DCCCLXXI. Inst. 8. M. p. 140. Maxime mirum, imò absurdum esse, propter aliquas locutiones comparatas, quibus motus Solis describitur, ipsum motum Soli adimere, cum motus sit tertium illud, in quo comparatio constituitur &c. 2. nostram demonstrationem esse ratiunculam &c.
units.tr: DCCCLXXI. Inst. 8. M. p. 140. It is most strange, indeed absurd, to take away motion from the Sun on account of some comparative expressions by which its motion is described, since motion is that third thing in which the comparison is made, etc. (2) that our demonstration is a little argument, etc.

units.la: Resp. Ob rationes manifeste demonstrantes, partem hemisphærii oppositam, non inservire Soli pro tentorio &c. hæc pro præjudiciis habenda, quæ etiam idcirco à Spiritu Sancto non docentur, quamvis sermo ab ipso usurpatus iis ab inventoribus istarum phrasium sit involutus. Ita similiter pro præjudicio habendum censeo Solis motum realem, quod singulis diebus unà cum Cœlo & stellis circa Terram circumvolvatur, ob rationes manifestas omnibus, qui ordine progredi volunt, adeoque eum non doceri à Spiritu Sancto. Nec enim ratiuncula vocari debet à non intelligente Demonstrationem Mathematicam, quæ longiori deductione habet opus, nisi eo ipso suam imperitiam prodere, elit. 2. Falsissimum est, motum hic esse illud tertium, in quo cum cursore Sol comparatur, cum non sit aliud ex mente Sp. S. quam celerrima variatio situs, quæ revera Soli competit.
units.tr: Reply. On account of reasons that clearly demonstrate that the part of the hemisphere opposite us does not serve the Sun as a tent, etc., these are to be counted as prejudices, which for that reason are also not taught by the Holy Spirit, although the speech used by him is wrapped in the prejudices of the originators of those phrases. Likewise I think the real motion of the Sun must be counted a prejudice, namely that it revolves each day around the earth together with the heaven and the stars, for manifest reasons to all who wish to proceed in order; and so it is not taught by the Holy Spirit. Nor should a Mathematical Demonstration, which requires a longer deduction, be called a little argument by one who does not understand it, unless by that very fact he betrays his own inexperience. (2) It is most false that motion is here that third thing in which the Sun is compared with a runner, since according to the mind of the Holy Spirit it is nothing other than the very rapid variation of position, which truly belongs to the Sun.

units.la: DCCCLXXII. Inst. 9. Quoniam verò dixeram, phrasin, qua Sol oriri dicitur, ex præjudicio quoque ortam, atque etiam exinde colligi posse, similiter ut antea, etiam hanc de cursu Solis ex eo ortum habere, objicit M. p. 141. Nihil ergo esse in hoc textu, quod Soli non tribuatur secundum errorem vulgi, nonne igitur, inquit, egregio argumento, ex Solis cursu gloriam Dei celebraverit Propheta?
units.tr: DCCCLXXII. Inst. 9. But since I had said that the phrase by which the Sun is said to rise also arises from a prejudice, and that it can be inferred from this, as before, that this expression about the course of the Sun also has its origin there, he objects at M. p. 141: There is nothing in this text, then, that is not attributed to the Sun according to the error of the common people. Would not, he asks, the Prophet have celebrated God's glory by an excellent argument drawn from the course of the Sun?

units.la: Resp. Quæ formulæ loquendi præjudiciis ortum debeant, quæ non, quidque à Psalte citatis versibus docetur, ex antecedentibus patet, ut &c, quænam argumenta faciant ad gloriam Dei celebrandam. Falsum est, inter alia etiam sumi medium à cursu proprie sic dicto, cum argumentum sufficiens præbeatur à variatione situs, quæ hac phrasi consueta per currere & progredi exprimi solet. Quæ vero de τῶ oriri & occidere habet, ad ea abundè paulo superius est responsum, cum ostensum, quomodo vox Oriri ex quodam præjudicio habeat ortum.
units.tr: Reply. Which modes of speech owe their origin to prejudices, and which do not, is shown by what the Psalmist teaches in the verses he cites, as is plain from the preceding context, and so on; and what arguments serve to celebrate God's glory. It is false that among other things a middle term is taken from the course properly so called, since a sufficient argument is supplied by the variation of position, which is customarily expressed by this phrase through to run and to advance. As for what he says about the τῶ [τῷ] oriri and occidere, a full answer has been given a little above, where it was shown how the word "to rise" has its origin in a certain prejudice.

units.la: DCCCLXXIII. Inst. 10. Fullerus vir doctus in Miscellaneis sacris ita hunc locum urget: lib. 1. cap. 15. in fine pag. 98. Constat, inquit, ipso statim initio Prophetam testari, se non acturum de evanidis hominum imaginationibus, quæ nihili sunt; sed amplissimis operibus manuum Dei ipsius, quæ vera sunt, certa, sincera, solida, ac proinde ad sacrosanctam ejus majestatem celebrandam accommodatissima.
units.tr: DCCCLXXIII. Inst. 10. The learned Fuller urges this passage in his Sacred Miscellanies, book 1, chapter 15, near the end, p. 98: It is established, he says, that from the very beginning the Prophet testifies that he will not treat of the vain imaginations of men, which are nothing; but of the most ample works of God's own hands, which are true, certain, sincere, solid, and therefore most fitting for celebrating his most holy majesty.

units.la: Resp. Nos non dicimus, Solem & Cœlos esse imaginationem evanidam hominum, sed agnoscimus (quis enim non agnosceret?) esse opera Dei maxima, ex quibus potentia ejus, sapientia & bonitas elucet, ut quam maximè; edere etiam effecta realia non diffitemur, qualia sunt influxus in inferiora, Terræ illuminatio, qua fit, ut continua sit vicissitudo dici & noctis, & similia. Tantum quæritur, an opus sit, ut Scriptura modum, quo effecta ista eduntur, explicet ἀπλανεῖα Astronomica, quæ plerisque est ignota, quod vel ipse Fullerus suo exemplo testatur, an vero modo vulgari omnibus perspecto? Hoc disceptatur; utrum ad Terræ illuminationem motus Solis realis requiratur, an sufficiat tantum apparens? quorum posterius nos asserimus & hactenus, ut puto, satis demonstravimus, neque ei Scriptura contradicit.
units.tr: Reply. We do not say that the Sun and the heavens are a vain imagination of men, but we acknowledge (for who would not acknowledge it?) that they are the greatest works of God, from which his power, wisdom and goodness shine forth, as much as possible. Nor do we deny that they produce real effects, such as their influence on lower things, the illumination of the earth, by which there is a continual alternation of day and night, and similar things. The only question is whether it is necessary for Scripture to explain the manner by which these effects are produced by the astronomical fixed-star sphere [ἀπλανεῖα], which is unknown to most people, as Fuller himself shows by his own example, or rather by a common manner perceived by all. This is what is disputed: whether a real motion of the Sun is required for the illumination of the earth, or whether an apparent motion is enough. We assert the latter, and, as I think, have hitherto sufficiently demonstrated it, and Scripture does not contradict it.

units.la: DCCCLXXIV. M. p. 142. Fullero suppetias vult ferre, concedendo, inquit, non agere hic Prophetam de evanidis hominum imaginationibus tacite damnas, quod supra asseruisti: Solis tentorium, Solis thalamum, Cœli extremitates esse falsas opiniones vulgi sive evanidas hominum cogitationes &c.
units.tr: DCCCLXXIV. M. p. 142. He wishes to bring help to Fuller by conceding, he says, that the Prophet does not here treat of the vain imaginations of men, tacitly condemning what you asserted above: that the Sun's tent, the Sun's bridal chamber, and the extremities of the heavens are false opinions of the common people, or vain human thoughts, etc.

units.la: Resp. Quando concedo, agi in hoc Psalmo de operibus Dei maximis, illud ita concedo, ut nihilominus asseram, illa opera Dei maxima describi phrasibus receptis, quæ sæpius ex opinionibus erroneis & præjudiciis habent ortum, quonam ergo quæso modo antecedentia ostendes his damnari? Illud autem inter nos quæri & disceptari debere est satis manifestum, ex statu controversiæ constitutione. In specie autem hic quæri, utrum per phrases prodire, decurrere viam, designetur & attribuatur Soli motus realis, an tantum significent variationem situs Solis respectu Terræ incolarum, quam variationem situs his phrasibus receptis quivis designat, ita ut si præjudiciis sit occupatus eadem consignificet, sin minus, illam ipsam variationem situs significare tantum intendat? Nos prius negamus, posterius affirmamus. Atque hæc sufficiunt etiam ad ea quæ pag. 143. & 144. de statu controversiæ adversarius disceptat.
units.tr: Reply. When I concede that this Psalm treats of God's greatest works, I concede it in such a way that I nonetheless assert that those greatest works of God are described in accepted phrases, which often arise from erroneous opinions and prejudices. How, then, I ask, will you show that the preceding statements are condemned by this? That it must be asked and debated between us, from the very setting of the controversy, is sufficiently plain. But specifically, the question here is whether by the phrases to come forth, to run its course, a real motion is designated and attributed to the Sun, or whether they signify only a variation of the Sun's position with respect to the inhabitants of the earth, which variation anyone designates by these accepted phrases, so that if he is occupied with prejudices he understands the same thing by them, but if not, he intends them to signify only that variation of position itself. We deny the former and affirm the latter. And these things are also sufficient for what the Opponent disputes about the state of the controversy on pages 143 and 144.

units.la: DCCCLXXV. Inst. II. B. D. p. 23. Ergo narrant Cæli Dei gloriam, quia ipsi illi in se continent, & nobis prabent materiam gloriæ divinæ, non apparenter tantum, quoad nostram opinionem, sed revera, ac proinde etiam effecta ac adjuncta idem revera præstant; nam dies enunciat diei, & nox nocti eructat scientiam: Ergo respicit vicissitudinem dierum & noctium: qua cum effectum sit Cælorum, necessario sequitur, Cælum, non autem Terram motu diurno moveri: nam si Terra movetur, non autem Cælum; tum in variatione illa non Cælum, sed Terra narraret gloriam Dei, nam vicissitudo illa non esset originaliter a Cælo, sed a Terra.
units.tr: DCCCLXXV. Inst. II. B. D. p. 23. Therefore the heavens declare the glory of God, because they themselves contain it and furnish us with the matter of God's glory, not merely in appearance, as far as our opinion goes, but in reality. Accordingly, their effects and attributes also truly do this, for day tells day, and night shows knowledge to night. Therefore the psalm refers to the alternation of days and nights. Since this is the effect of the heavens, it follows necessarily that the heaven, and not the earth, is moved by the daily motion. For if the earth moves and not the heaven, then in that alternation it would be not the heaven but the earth that declares the glory of God, since that alternation would not originate from the heaven but from the earth.

units.la: Resp. 1. Quis unquam Copernicanorum dixit, Cœlos præbere materiam gloriæ divinæ apparenter tantum, non revera? imo quænam Philosophia gloriam Dei magis in Cœlis agnoscit? illane, quæ gloriam Dei ex ipsorum pulchritudine, motus directione secundum leges naturæ, eorum immensa magnitudine, nullis terminis, quos non cognitos habet, circumscripta, &c. immensam agnoscit, quod Cartesiana facit, an vero Aristotelica ut vulgo traditur, quæ vix aliquid distincte de iis intelligit? In vicissitudine dierum & noctium distincte consideranda, tum dies ipsæ & noctes, tum earum vicissitudo: dies & noctes debent adscribi Solis præsentiæ vel absentiæ ab hemisphærio nostro; sed vicissitudo variationi situs corporis solaris, quæ vel motui Solis circa Terram (quod quidem dicunt Adversarii, sed ex isto loco probare nequeunt) vel Terræ gyrationi circa axem accepta referenda, quod nos statuimus, moti indubitatis demonstrationibus. Narrari autem gloria Dei in Psalmo dicitur, non præcise & determinate per causam istius vicissitudinis, quam vellent adversarii, sed simpliciter tantum a Psalte per variationem situs & vicissitudinem dierum agnosci dicitur posse. Hæc nunc, ut puto, aliquanto clarius, quam prius explicata sunt, quoniam B. ea non videtur intellexisse; unde & objectiones ejus nequaquam me feriunt, quas, si operæ pretium sit, lector videat pagina 175. & 176.
units.tr: Reply, first. Which of the Copernicans ever said that the heavens furnish the matter of God's glory only in appearance and not in reality? Indeed, what philosophy recognises the glory of God more in the heavens? Is it that which recognises it from their beauty, from the direction of their motion according to the laws of nature, and from their immense greatness, bounded by no limits which it knows, and so on, as the Cartesian philosophy does; or is it the Aristotelian as it is commonly taught, which understands scarcely anything distinctly about them? In the alternation of days and nights, two things must be considered distinctly: the days and nights themselves, and their alternation. Days and nights must be ascribed to the presence or absence of the sun from our hemisphere. The alternation, however, must be referred to the change in the position of the solar body, which is due either to the motion of the sun about the earth (which our opponents assert, but cannot prove from this passage) or to the rotation of the earth about its axis, which we maintain, having been moved by indubitable demonstrations. Moreover, the psalm says that the glory of God is declared, not precisely and definitely through the cause of this alternation, as our opponents would wish, but simply that it can be recognised by the psalmist through the change of position and the alternation of days. These points, as I think, have now been explained somewhat more clearly than before, since the author does not seem to have understood them. Hence his objections do not touch me at all; if it is worth the trouble, let the reader see them on pages 175 and 176.

units.la: DCCCLXXVI. Instantiam suam defendere conatur B. p. 173. dicendo: Id quod nobis tribuit sequi ex nostra doctrina; cum enim, inquit, motum Soli in hoc Psalmo tributum exponant Copernicani (ut & Cartesiani) de motu non reali, sed apparenti, necessario sequitur, Cœlos ih illo motu præbere non realem, sed tantum apparentem materiam gloriæ divinæ. Eadem habet M p. 145.
units.tr: DCCCLXXVI. The author tries to defend his objection on page 173, saying: What follows for us from our doctrine is this: since the Copernicans (and the Cartesians too) explain the motion attributed to the sun in this psalm as a motion not real but apparent, it necessarily follows that the heavens, in that motion, furnish not a real but only an apparent matter of God's glory. He says the same on page 145 of M.

units.la: Resp. Non potest dici, doceri in Psalmo motum apparentem Solis, nisi hac mente, quod usurpetur phrasis, quæ ex apparentia motus Solis, adeoque ex præjudicio habet ortum, qua tamen non illud ipsum præjudicium, quod ei originem dedit, significetur, sed quædam veritas gene-ralis, qualis hic est variatio situs Solis, & hinc orta vicissitudo dierum & noctium. Vicissitudo dierum & noctium vera est, vera est variatio Situs Solis, veræ sunt tempestates veris, æstatis, autumni & hyemis, veræ sunt variationes illæ super Terrâ, quæ ex propinquitate vel remotione Solis à Terrâ, ab ejus luce vel ejus absentiâ oriuntur: hæc omnia non apparentem, sed veram planè præbent gloriæ Dei materiam.
units.tr: Reply. It cannot be said that the psalm teaches an apparent motion of the sun, except in this sense: that a phrase is used which arises from the apparent motion of the sun, and so from prejudice, yet it does not signify that very prejudice which gave rise to it, but some general truth, such as the change of the sun's position and the alternation of days and nights arising from it. The alternation of days and nights is true; the change of the sun's position is true; the seasons of spring, summer, autumn and winter are true; and those variations on the earth which arise from the sun's nearness or remoteness, from its light or its absence, are true. All these furnish the matter of God's glory, not apparent, but altogether real.

units.la: DCCCLXXVII. Pergit B.p.173. atque negat nostram Philosophiam maximè Dei gloriam agnoscere, exinde quia negemus motum Cælorum velocis- simum, & eum ad corpus Physicum nullam proportionem habere, ac per Consequens impossibilem esse statuamus.
