units.tr: DCCCLXXVII. The author goes on, on page 173, and denies that our philosophy especially recognises the glory of God, for the reason that we deny the extremely rapid motion of the heavens, and hold that it has no proportion to a physical body, and consequently is impossible.

units.la: Resq. Quæ de motu isto rapidissimo mea sententia sit, patet ex Dissert. 2. cap. 5. art. 4. & art. 286. cap. 18. hujus libri, quam sententiam meam bene novit adversarius; quare ergo Cartesianis juxta ac Copernicanis eum impossibilem affingit? Non agnoscimus fictitium vestrum raptum firmamenti; non quod impossibilem statuamus istam celeritatem, sed quod nulla ratione demonstretur, & cum constitutione & dispositione corporum cœlestium non conveniat, quæ in vorticibus agitari statuimus, uti ex deductione demonstrationis meæ cap. 18. patet.
units.tr: Reply. What my view of that most rapid motion is appears from Dissertation 2, chapter 5, article 4, and article 286, chapter 18 of this book, a view which my opponent knows well. Why, then, does he impute it as impossible to the Cartesians as well as to the Copernicans? We do not acknowledge your fictitious rapture of the firmament. Not that we hold that speed to be impossible, but because it is not demonstrated by any reasoning, and does not agree with the constitution and arrangement of the heavenly bodies, which we hold are carried along in vortices, as is clear from the deduction of my demonstration in chapter 18.

units.la: DCCCLXXVIII. Addit B. p. 174. Hypothesin Copernicanam maximo laborare incommodo jam probavi Dial. p. 36, 37, 38.
units.tr: DCCCLXXVIII. The author adds, on page 174: I have already proved in the Dialogue, pages 36, 37 and 38, that the Copernican hypothesis labours under very great inconvenience.

units.la: Resp. At etiam diu patefactus est tuus error in Demonstratione Mathematica ignorantiarum & ineptiarum Jac. du Bois &c.
units.tr: Reply. But your error was exposed long ago in the Mathematical Demonstration of the Ignorances and Absurdities of Jacques du Bois, etc.

units.la: DCCCLXXIX. Pergit B. p. 174. Immensam illam stellarum supra sphæram Saturni altitudinem à nobis quidem fingi & supponi, sed non probari, Dial. p. 51. &c. clare se ostendisse.
units.tr: DCCCLXXIX. The author goes on, on page 174: That immense height of the stars above the sphere of Saturn is indeed feigned and supposed by us, but not proved; he has clearly shown this in the Dialogue, page 51, etc.

units.la: Resp. Ad hæc repono Pp. III. art. 7. Cart. Quantum ad fixas, non permittunt quidem phænomena, ut ipsas à Sole aut Terra non magis quam Saturnum distare arbitremur, sed nulla obstant, quo minus ad quarumlibet immensam distantiam remotas esse supponamus: colligiturque ex motibus Cœli infra explicandis, eas à nobis adeo esse distantes, ut Saturnus ad ipsas comparatus videatur admodum propinquus; unde quid de ista immensa altitudine stellarum demonstratum sit, patet.
units.tr: Reply. To this I answer, Principles III, article 7, Cartesius: As far as the fixed stars are concerned, the phenomena do not indeed permit us to think that they are no more distant from the sun or earth than Saturn is; yet nothing prevents us from supposing that they are removed to an immense distance from any point whatever. It is gathered from the motions of the heaven, to be explained below, that they are so distant from us that Saturn, compared with them, appears quite near; whence it is plain what has been demonstrated about that immense height of the stars.

units.la: DCCCLXXX. Tandem inquit pag. 174. Quæ de Philosophia Aristotelica à me dicuntur, ad se nihil facere, cum nunquam professus eam sit. Resp. Quam distincte intelligas opera divina & quam Philosophiam concris coneris defendere apparet manifeste ex inanibus Except. ad meum argumentum, quod cap. 18. vindicavi. Ergo contra te omnino haec facere scias: quod ut melius intelligas consule Caput primum de vulgari & Philosophica notitia.
units.tr: DCCCLXXX. Finally he says, on page 174: What I say about Aristotelian philosophy has nothing to do with him, since he has never professed it. Reply. How distinctly you understand the divine works, and how you try in vain to defend a philosophy against them, appears plainly from the empty exceptions to my argument, which I defended in chapter 18. Know, therefore, that these things apply entirely against you. To understand this better, consult the first chapter, on common and philosophical knowledge.

units.la: DCCCLXXXI. Sed& M. p. 146. hyperaspisten agere vult instantiae undecimae & conatur evincere, ex mea sententia sequi, (Coelos non vere enarrare Dei gloriam, quoniam narrare Coelis non magis competit, quam Soli tentorium, thalamus &c. de quibus dixerim, quod locutione vulgari Soli attribuantur: concludi ergo a paribus vel similibus Coelum ex mea sententia non vere, sed vulgariter tantum enarrare gloriam Dei.
units.tr: DCCCLXXXI. But M., page 146, also wants to carry on a counter-defence against my eleventh objection, and tries to prove that from my opinion it follows that the heavens do not truly declare the glory of God, since the declaring of God's glory belongs to the heavens no more than a tent or a bridal chamber belongs to the sun, of which things I have said that they are attributed to the sun in common speech. It is concluded, therefore, from like or similar things, that the heaven, on my opinion, declares the glory of God not truly but only in common speech.

units.la: Resp. Improprietas non falsitatem infert, nec omnes locutiones impropriae obvolutae sunt praejudiciis, adeoque dispar est ratio phraseos narrare gloriam Dei, & Solem prodire &c. Coeli narrant gloriam Dei vere hoc sensu, quatenus ea, quae in coelis sunt & fiunt, sufficiens suppeditant fundamentum Deum glorificandi creaturis rationalibus. Sed videtur praesupposuisse, me statuere, locutiones illas, quas in Psal. adhiberi dico, ex praejudiciis ortas nullam veritatem, sed falsitatem significare & dicere, quod nego & pernego.
units.tr: Reply. An impropriety does not imply a falsehood, nor are all improper expressions wrapped up in prejudices; so the case of the phrase the heavens declare the glory of God is not the same as that of the sun rises, etc. The heavens do truly declare the glory of God in this sense: that the things which are and happen in the heavens provide a sufficient foundation for rational creatures to glorify God. But he seems to have presupposed that I hold those expressions which I say are used in the psalm, and which arise from prejudices, to signify no truth but falsehood. This I deny, and utterly deny.

units.la: DCCCLXXXII. Tandem digreditur M. p. 174. & seqq. in disquisitionem: Utrum Philosophia Cartesiana sit magis apta ad gloriam divinam, quam Aristotelica, prout vulgo traditur? Ego dixeram, magis aptam esse Cartesianam, quod per eam mundo pulchritudo major attribuatur, motus directio fieri secundum leges naturae doceatur, & mundus maximus concipiatur, talisque, cujus nullos fines possumus cognoscere &c. (si enim collatio instituenda, plura argumenta possent adduci) de quorum posteriori suo loco est actum; de duobus prioribus hic breviter agemus.
units.tr: DCCCLXXXII. Finally, M., page 174 and following, digresses into the inquiry: Whether the Cartesian philosophy is more fitted to the glory of God than the Aristotelian, as it is commonly taught? I had said that the Cartesian is more fitted, because through it greater beauty is ascribed to the world, the direction of motion is taught to happen according to the laws of nature, and the world is conceived as very great, and such that we cannot know its limits, etc. (for if a comparison were to be made, many more arguments could be adduced). Of the latter of these I shall treat in its own place; of the two former, I shall deal briefly here.

units.la: DCCCLXXXIII. Prius autem observo, pulchritudinem generaliter sic definiri posse, quod sit talis rei constitutio, per quam res potest mentem occultaquasi ri ad se rapere & singulari gaudio perfundere: ut autem ea cognoscatur, opus est, ut res prius a mente clare & distincte percipiatur; quo enim clarior & distinctior est perceptio, eo etiam magis ejus pulchritudo in propatulo est. Quae itaque Philosophia clare & distincte explicat naturam coelorum, clare quoque eorum aperit pulchritudinem: At hoc facere Cartesianam ex libris Cartesii certum est, sicut non minus est certum, distincte vix aliquid de iis cognosci posse ex Philosophia Peripatetica, prout vulgo traditur: id autem per partes hic deducere, neque libet neque opus est, cum istius rei disquisitione & comparatione utriusque que Philosophiæ dependeat. Qui utramque Philosophiam habet cognitam, id facile poterit præstare. Quod si quis attendat ad formas substantiales, qualitates occultas & manifestas, ad quæ omnia naturæ secreta Scholastici referunt, & quam parum distincti de iis habeant cognitum consideret, is confiteri necesse habebit, quam parum illa Philosophia ad Cœlorum pulchritudinem possit conferre.
units.tr: DCCCLXXXIII. But first I observe that beauty may be generally defined as such a constitution of a thing by which it can seize the mind, as it were hidden, and fill it with a singular joy. For a thing to be known as beautiful, it must first be clearly and distinctly perceived by the mind; for the clearer and more distinct the perception, the more its beauty lies open. Therefore, whichever philosophy clearly and distinctly explains the nature of the heavens also clearly reveals their beauty. That the Cartesian philosophy does this from the books of Descartes is certain, just as it is no less certain that scarcely anything can be known distinctly about them from the Peripatetic philosophy as it is commonly taught. To deduce this here part by part neither pleases me nor is necessary, since the inquiry into this matter and the comparison of both philosophies depends on it. Whoever has come to know both philosophies can easily do this. But if anyone attends to the substantial forms, the occult and manifest qualities, to which the Scholastics refer all the secrets of nature, and considers how little distinct knowledge they have of them, he will be obliged to confess how little that philosophy can contribute to the beauty of the heavens.

units.la: DCCCLXXXIV. Nec obstat pulchritudini Cœli & mundi, quod indefinitum illum statuamus, hoc est, talem ac tantum ut fines ejus non possimus cognoscere, sed quibuscunque finibus positis semper ultra eos quandam extensionem percipiamus. Nam 1. si non obstat pulchritudini Dei ejus Infinitas, verum eam magis auget, nec mundi & cœlorum pulchritudini oberit Indefinitas, sed augebit potius.
units.tr: DCCCLXXXIV. Nor does it stand in the way of the beauty of heaven and the world that we posit it as indefinite, that is, of such a kind and extent that we cannot know its limits, but whatever limits are set we always perceive some extension beyond them. For (1) if God's infinity does not stand in the way of his beauty but rather increases it, then indefiniteness will not stand in the way of the beauty of the world and the heavens but will rather increase it.

units.la: DCCCLXXXV. 2. Quantum de mundo Philosophia Cartesiana distincte cognoscit, tantum etiam ejus pulchritudinis percipit. De reliquo, quod nempe ultra stellas fixas (excepto Cœlo Beatorum, quod ex sola Scriptura novimus) extenditur, nihil aliud quidem quam extensionem percipit, sed tamen eo ipso majorem mundi & cœlorum pulchritudinem cognoscit, quàm vulgaris, quæ ultra eas nihil vult reperiri. Hæc de priori, quæ si placet lectori conferre cum Objectione M. pag. 147, 148. ei satisfactum videbit.
units.tr: DCCCLXXXV. (2) As far as Cartesian philosophy distinctly knows the world, so far it also perceives its beauty. As for what lies beyond the fixed stars (except the heaven of the blessed, which we know from Scripture alone), it perceives nothing but extension, yet by that very fact it knows the beauty of the world and heavens to be greater than the common view, which holds that nothing is to be found beyond them. As for the former point, if the reader wishes to compare it with the Objection of M., pp. 147, 148, he will see that it has been answered.

units.la: DCCCLXXXVI. Secundum item, nempe quod Philosophia Cartesiana doceat fieri motus directionem secundum leges naturæ, est manifestum ex collatione Pp. II. in quo leges naturæ explicantur, & Pp. III. in quo omnia ex illis deducuntur, demonstratione accurata & evidenti attendentibus, unde non potest non gloria sapientiæ Dei fieri manifesta, qui tam accuratas leges naturæ præscripserit, secundum quas omnia dirigit & gubernat, ut omnium sit accurata convenientia & harmonia. At contra naturæ leges Motum explicat Philosophia scholastica, dum docet; Motum alicujus corporis tendere ad quietem & naturam sua cessare, dum motum affingit corporibus insitum, dum statuit vel cum Ptolemæo orbium & sphærarum sese invicem tanquam pelliculæ cepar-um circumdantium motum inordinatum & impossibilem, vel ex mente Tychonis motum Solis circa Terram, & simultaneum raptum Planetarum, non tamen circumraptâ Terrâ. Vide capitis 18. art. 406. 411.
units.tr: DCCCLXXXVI. The second point, namely that Cartesian philosophy teaches that motion is directed according to the laws of nature, is clear from a comparison of Part II, in which the laws of nature are explained, and Part III, in which everything is deduced from them with accurate and evident demonstration, for anyone who attends to it. Hence the glory of God's wisdom cannot but be made manifest, since he has prescribed such exact laws of nature, by which he directs and governs all things, so that there is exact agreement and harmony among all. But on the contrary, scholastic philosophy explains motion in a way that contradicts the laws of nature, when it teaches that the motion of any body tends to rest and that its nature ceases; when it ascribes to bodies a motion implanted in them; and when it holds either, with Ptolemy, that the spheres and orbs surrounding one another like the skins of an onion have a disordered and impossible motion, or, from the mind of Tycho, that the Sun moves around the Earth and the planets are carried along with it simultaneously, yet without the Earth being carried around. See chapter 18, arts. 406, 411.

units.la: DCCCLXXXVII. Neque hinc infertur, quod motus cœlorum miraculosi & extraordinarii non celebrent vel minus celebrent gloriam Dei; non enim à nobis dicuntur motus secundum leges naturæ gloriam Dei celebrare, oppositè ad motus extraordinarios, & miraculosos, sed oppositè ad motus confusos & inordinatos, nullum fundamentum vel in experientia vel in legibus naturæ habentes, quales sunt motus à Ptolemæo & Tychone confecti, uti ostensum. Itaque & motus miraculosi celebrant gloriam Dei independentiæ & libertatis, quod ut ab ipso leges naturæ pendent, ita eos figere vel refigere pro suo beneplacito possit, & motus naturales celebrant gloriam sapientiæ divinæ, quæ omnia ordine disposuit & constituit sapientissimè & perfectissimè. Atque sic satisfactum iis, quæ à M. p. 149. fuerunt objecta.
units.tr: DCCCLXXXVII. Nor does it follow from this that the miraculous and extraordinary motions of the heavens do not celebrate, or celebrate less, the glory of God. For we do not say that motions according to the laws of nature celebrate God's glory as opposed to extraordinary and miraculous motions, but as opposed to confused and disordered motions, which have no foundation either in experience or in the laws of nature, such as the motions devised by Ptolemy and Tycho, as has been shown. Thus both miraculous motions celebrate the glory of God's independence and freedom, since, although they depend on the laws of nature, he can fix or refix them at his own pleasure; and natural motions celebrate the glory of divine wisdom, which has arranged and established all things in order most wisely and most perfectly. And so the objections made by M. at p. 149 have been answered.

units.la: DCCCLXXXVIII. Sequitur Inft. 12. B. D. p. 424. Hinc porrò suscipio talia argumenta I. Ut sponsu se habet ad gloriam suam non apparenter & ex opinione hominum, sed revera, ita Sol sese habet ad gloriam suam revera, & non ex opinione hominum, apparenter tantum: Totum hoc facile concedent Copernicani. Ergo sic pergo. II. Ut Cursor sese habet ad cursum suum, ita & Sol ad motum suum: At cursor sese habet ad motum realiter, & non secundum apparentiam tantum vel opinionem hominum. Ergo & Sol sese habet ad motum suum realiter, & non secundum apparentiam tantum vel opinionem hominum. III. Prout Sol sese habet ad gloriam suam ipsi in Psalmo tributam; ita etiam sese habet ad suum motum, cum in utraque similitudine nulla diversitatis nota reperiatur: at Sol sese habet ad gloriam revera, & non secundum opinionem hominum apparenter tantum. Ergo habet sese ad motum revera & non apparenter tantum secundum opinionem hominum. Resp. 1. Sufficit convenientia inter Solem & cursorem in variatione situs celerrima, incipiente à quodam termino nobis conspicuo, & in opposita meta nobis itidem conspicua definente, quæ convenientia phrasi, progredi ab extremitate cælorum ad alteram extremitatem, ex præjudicio de motu Solis exortâ, designatur, & quia recepta, à Spiritu Sancto usurpatur, ita tamen ut ab ipso non præjudicium illud, sed veritas generalis, nempe variatio situs Solis designetur. Quemadmodum ergo ex verbis dicentis: Solem sese elevare supra Horizontem & ascendere usque ad medium Cœli, sicut aquila sese elevat à superficie Terra, & usque ad nubes evolat, nemini ne quidem à Ptolemæo permitteretur hæc illatio: ut aquila sese habet ad motum suum, ita Sol ad motum suum; atqui aquila revera è loco inferiori in sublimiorem sese extollit: ergò etiam Sol revera è loco inferiori in sublimiorem sese extollit: ita etiam non licet hic comparationem urgere, ultra illud tertium, in quo fuit instituta. 2. Negamus, quod eodem modo Sol sese habeat ad gloriam suam & ad motum; nam gloria Soli adscribitur à Psalte, non item motus, cum illud ipsum sit, de quaquéquæritur, & quod nos negamus, ut ex dictis satis patet. Quod autem B. p. 177. dicit, in analysi Psalm. 19. se ad oculum ostendisse, inter argumenta, quibus Dei gloria conspicua in cœlis probatur, etiam referri hoc, desumptum à motu Solis, qui comparatur motui cursoris, id nos factum negamus, quum non nisi à variatione situs & hinc orta vicissitudine dierum & noctium argumentum duxisse Psalten superius art. 1. demonstraverimus.
units.tr: DCCCLXXXVIII. There follows Inst. 12, B. D., p. 424: Hence I further draw such arguments. I. As the bridegroom stands in relation to his glory, not apparently and according to the opinion of men but in truth, so the Sun stands in relation to his glory in truth, and not according to the opinion of men, apparently only. The Copernicans will readily grant all this. Therefore I proceed thus. II. As the runner stands in relation to his course, so also the Sun stands in relation to his motion. But the runner stands in relation to his motion really, and not merely according to appearance or the opinion of men. Therefore the Sun also stands in relation to his motion really, and not merely according to appearance or the opinion of men. III. As the Sun stands in relation to the glory ascribed to him in the Psalm, so also he stands in relation to his motion, since in both comparisons no mark of difference is found. But the Sun stands in relation to glory in truth, and not apparently according to the opinion of men. Therefore he stands in relation to motion in truth, and not merely apparently according to the opinion of men. Answer 1. It is enough that there is a likeness between the Sun and the runner in the very rapid change of position, beginning from a certain terminus visible to us and ending at an opposite goal likewise visible to us; this likeness is indicated by the phrase to proceed from one end of the heavens to the other, which arose from the prejudice about the motion of the Sun, and because it is a received phrase, the Holy Spirit uses it, yet in such a way that by it he does not designate that prejudice but a general truth, namely the change of position of the Sun. Therefore, just as from the words of one who says: The Sun raises itself above the Horizon and ascends until it reaches the middle of the heavens, as the eagle raises itself from the surface of the earth and flies up to the clouds, no one, not even Ptolemy, would be permitted this inference: as the eagle stands in relation to its motion, so the Sun stands in relation to its motion; but the eagle really lifts itself from a lower place to a higher; therefore the Sun also really lifts itself from a lower place to a higher; so here too it is not permitted to press the comparison beyond that third point in which it was instituted. 2. We deny that the Sun stands in the same way in relation to his glory and to his motion; for glory is ascribed to the Sun by the Psalmist, but motion is not, since that very thing is what is in question, and what we deny, as is sufficiently clear from what has been said. As for what B. says at p. 177, that in the analysis of Psalm 19 he showed, among the arguments by which God's glory visible in the heavens is proved, that this is also to be referred to the motion of the Sun, which is compared to the motion of a runner, we deny that this was done, since we have demonstrated above, at art. 1, that the Psalmist drew his argument only from the change of position and the consequent alternation of day and night.

units.la: DCCCLXXXIX. Inquit tamen B. p. 177. Sicut gloria cursoris consistit in cursu velocitate, ita etiam gloria solaris sita est in motu ipsius pernicitate &c. Sic H. p. 112. Quemadmodum sponsus ad gloriam & egressum, ita Sol ad pulchritudinem & motum suum sese habet.
units.tr: DCCCLXXXIX. Yet B. says at p. 177: Just as the glory of the runner consists in the swiftness of his course, so also the glory of the sun lies in the speed of its motion, etc. So H. at p. 112: As the bridegroom stands in relation to his glory and his going forth, so the Sun stands in relation to its beauty and its motion.

units.la: Resp. At nego, quod ex textu possit ostendi, gloriam solarem vel in motu vel in motus pernicitate consistere, nego id intendere Spiritum Sanctum phrasi recepta, sed dico, in continua variatione situs & inde orta vicissitudine dierum & noctium comparationis istius tertium constitui. Itaque ut sponsus ad gloriam & egressum, ita Sol ad pulchritudinem & variationem situs sese habet. Et quemadmodum Sol dicitur lætari, quia talis effectus ejus est, qui sequi solet ex lætitia: ita dicitur sese parare ad cursum vel currere, quia talem edit effectum, qualis ex cursu sequi solet.
units.tr: Answer. But I deny that it can be shown from the text that the glory of the Sun consists either in motion or in the swiftness of motion; I deny that the Holy Spirit intends this by the received phrase, but I say that the third term of this comparison is constituted by the continual change of position and the consequent alternation of day and night. Thus, as the bridegroom stands in relation to his glory and going forth, so the Sun stands in relation to its beauty and its change of position. And just as the Sun is said to rejoice because rejoicing is the effect of it that usually follows from joy, so it is said to prepare itself for its course, or to run, because it produces the effect that usually follows from running.

units.la: DCCCXC. Pergit ad meam similitudinem adductam dicendo p. 179. Quis unquam negavit Ptolemaicorum, vel Tychonianorum, Solem revera ascendere supra Horizontem in gradibus Almacantharath? Simile habet H. p. 114. & 115. quod si placet lector videat.
units.tr: DCCCXC. He goes on to my comparison, which he cites, saying at p. 179: Who has ever denied that the Sun, according to the Ptolemaics or the Tychonians, really rises above the Horizon through the degrees of the almacantharath? H. has a similar passage at pp. 114 and 115, which the reader may see if he pleases.

units.la: Resp. Ascendere revera est è Planitie in altum attolli; cum ergo Sol secundum vos in circulo moveatur, cujus centrum est Terra, non potest dici è planitie in altum tolli, adeoque revera ascendere. 2. Nec magis remotus est, à terra cum in medio Cœli conspicitur, quam cum est in ortu, ut supra demonstratum.
units.tr: Answer. To ascend really is to be raised up from a plane into the height. Therefore, since according to you the Sun moves in a circle whose centre is the Earth, it cannot be said to be raised up from a plane into the height, and so it does not really ascend. 2. It is no more remote from the earth when it is seen in mid-heaven than when it is at its rising, as demonstrated above.

units.la: DCCCXCI. Urget adhuc B. p. 180. Hoc est argumenti mei fundamentum. Prout Sol se habet ad suam gloriam præbendo argumentum rei verae, ita etiam Sol sese habet ad suum motum, ita, ut etiam in eo exhibeat argumentum rei verae Dei gloriam manifestantis; Ac proinde in textu non quidem instituitur comparatio inter Solis gloriam & motum, sed referuntur ad eandem rationem argumentandi, in qua cum nulla sit diversitatis nota (vid. quod in priori medium probationis desumeretur à re vera, in posteriori à non vera, sed tantum apparente; necessario sequitur, per motum Solis intelligi debere motum realem.
units.tr: DCCCXCI. B. presses further at p. 180: This is the foundation of my argument. As the Sun stands in relation to its glory by offering the argument of a true thing, so also the Sun stands in relation to its motion, so that in that too it exhibits an argument of a true thing manifesting the glory of God. Accordingly, the text does not indeed institute a comparison between the glory and the motion of the Sun, but they are referred to the same mode of arguing; since in this there is no mark of difference (see that in the former the middle term of the proof is taken from a true thing, in the latter from one not true, but only apparent), it necessarily follows that by the motion of the Sun a real motion must be understood.

units.la: Resp. At ego nego, quod à motu Solis in Psalmo desumitur argumentum ad Dei gloriam manifestandam, imò hoc est ipsum τὸ ζητούμενον, nego enim de Sole motum à Psalte affirmari, sed tantum variationem situs, quae cum vulgo recepta formulâ per cursum exprimatur, dico etiam Spiritum Sanctum eam voluisse adhibere.
units.tr: Reply. But I deny that an argument for displaying the glory of God is drawn from the motion of the Sun in the Psalm. Indeed this is the very point in question [τὸ ζητούμενον]. I deny that the Psalmist affirms motion of the Sun, and say that he speaks only of a change of position, which in the commonly accepted formula is expressed as its "course." I also say that the Holy Spirit wished to use it in that way.

units.la: DCCCXCII. Tandem, inquit B. p. 180. Solem quiescentem non pos- se esse causam vicissitudinis dierum & noctium, jam antea esse probatum.
units.tr: DCCCXCII. Finally, says B. p. 180, that the Sun, being at rest, cannot be the cause of the alternation of days and nights has already been proved before.

units.la: Resp. Nemo negat, quin si & Sol & Terra quiescerent, nulla vicissitudo locum habere queat; sed nego, quòd ea esse nequeat, Sole quiescente, per Terrae motum, prout supra art 875. latius ostendimus. His, quae hactenus diximus, responsum etiam erit ad ea, quae M. objicit pag. 171. & 172. Res enim tota eo redit, an à motu Solis reali desumatur argumentum ad gloriam Dei celebrandam, quod nondum est evictum, cum non nisi phrasi recepta variatio situs Solis & vicissitudo dierum significetur. H. rem hoc argumento conatur evincere p. 25. & 26. Quicquid spectandum nobis hic loci Spiritus Sanctus & admirandum nobis proponit, illud Soli proprie & realiter competit. Atqui motum Solis ab ortu in occasum spectandum nobis Spiritus Sanctus & admirandum proponit. Resp. Min. esse falsam & principii petitionem; neque enim mentem esse Sp. S. ostendi potest, ut ulteriorem hic inter Cursorem & Solem comparationem instituat, quam quoad situs variationem. Verum ut dixi de hoc & reliquis H. à p. 20. usque ad 28. cum conveniant cum instantiis prioribus, jam dictum est satis.
units.tr: Reply. No one denies that if both the Sun and the Earth were at rest, no vicissitude could take place; but I deny that it cannot take place, with the Sun at rest, through the motion of the Earth, as we have shown more fully above in article 875. What we have said so far will also serve as an answer to the objections which M. raises on pages 171 and 172. For the whole matter comes down to this: whether an argument for celebrating the glory of God is drawn from the real motion of the Sun, which has not yet been proved, since the variation of the Sun's position and the alternation of day are signified only by a commonly accepted manner of speaking. H. tries to prove the point by this argument on pages 25 and 26: "Whatever the Holy Spirit here sets before us to contemplate and admire belongs to the Sun properly and really. But the Holy Spirit sets before us to contemplate and admire the motion of the Sun from its rising to its setting." Reply: the minor premise is false and begs the question; for it cannot be shown that the mind of the Holy Spirit is to institute here a comparison between the runner and the Sun any further than as regards the variation of position. But, as I have said about this and the rest of H.'s arguments from page 20 to page 28, since they agree with the earlier instances, enough has already been said.

units.la: DCCCXCII. Inst. 13. B. D. p. 24. in fine, & 25. ab initio. Praeterea cum intenderit Psaltes probare, Coelos narrare gloriam Dei, dicendum erit, Prophetam vel non cognovisse veram rationem, quomodo Coeli enarrent gloriam Dei, apparenterne, an revera; vel eum realem narrationem coelorum probasse argumento quod in se non est verum, sed tantum propter apparentiam verum creditur ab hominibus, qui rei veritatem ignorant. Utrumvis statuatur absurditas omnem modum excedit.
units.tr: DCCCXCII. Inst. 13. B. D. p. 24 at the end, and p. 25 at the beginning. Moreover, since the Psalmist intended to prove that the heavens declare the glory of God, it must be said that the Prophet either did not know the true manner in which the heavens declare the glory of God, whether in appearance or in reality; or else he proved the real declaration of the heavens by an argument which in itself is not true, but is believed true by men who are ignorant of the truth of the matter, only because of its appearance. Whichever alternative is adopted, the absurdity exceeds every measure.

units.la: Resp. Praesupponitur hic, Copernicanos statuere, Coelos gloriam Dei enarrare non revera, sed apparenter, quod supra est eversum. Ostendendum autem fuisset, Psalmum intendisse probare, gloriam Dei enarrari per Solis motum realem, quod est in quaestione. Sol quidem enarrat gloriam Dei, eo ipso, quia est origo vicissitudinis dici & noctis per suam lucem, sed ad id requiri etiam motum ipsius realem est ipsum τὸ ἀμφι-ζητούμενον.
units.tr: Reply. This presupposes that the Copernicans hold that the heavens declare the glory of God not in reality but in appearance, which has been overthrown above. But it would have had to be shown that the Psalm intended to prove that the glory of God is declared through the real motion of the Sun, which is the question at issue. The Sun indeed declares the glory of God simply because it is the source of the alternation of day and night by its light. But that its real motion is also required for this is the very point in dispute [τὸ ἀμφι-ζητούμενον].

units.la: DCCCXCIV. Contra hanc responsionem articuli praecedentis B. p. 181, 182. provocat ad antecedentia, ad quae & ego provoco, cum in iisinanitatem probationis ab Antagonistâ productæ demonstraverim. Quod autem dicit, responsionem suam Dial. p. 24, 26. respicere Keplerum, non obest, quo minus eam, quomodo contra nos potuerit usurpari, spectaremus, & sic eam retunderemus.
units.tr: DCCCXCIV. Against this reply of the preceding article, B. pp. 181 and 182 appeals to what goes before, and I appeal to it too, since in those passages I have demonstrated the emptiness of the proof produced by my opponent. As for his statement that his reply on pages 24 and 26 of the Dialogue looks to Kepler, this does not prevent us from considering how it could be used against us, and so from turning it back.

units.la: DCCCXCV. M. p. 173. Motum Solis esse argumentum principale, ex quo gloriam Dei Psalmista evincat evidentius est, quam ut in dubium quisquam vocare ausit.
units.tr: DCCCXCV. M. p. 173: That the motion of the Sun is the principal argument from which the Psalmist proves the glory of God is more evident than anyone would dare to call into doubt.

units.la: Resp. At nos negamus, id esse evidens, donec clarè probetur, cumsit ipsum quod hîc quæritur.
units.tr: Reply. But we deny that this is evident, until it is clearly proved, since it is itself what is being sought here.

units.la: DCCCXCVI. Tandem cum Jacobus Lansbergius pro se adduceret auctoritatem Calvini, qui ad hunc Psalmum annotat: Itaque satis habuit crasso stylo ingratitudinis arguere totum mundum, nisi de Solis conspectu in pietate proficiat. Hæc ratio est, cur dicat tentorium ei paratum esse: deinde, egredi ipsum ab unâ Cœli extremitate, & transire celeriter in partem oppositam: neque enim argutè inter Philosophos, de integro Cœli circuitu disputat: sed, rudissimis quibusque se accommodans intra ocularem experientiam se continet, ideoque dimidiam cursus partem, quæ sub hemisphærio nostro non cernitur, subticet. Oggerit B. D. p. 26. Dicit quidem Calvinus Sp. Sanctum uti stylo crasso, & non argutè inter Philosophos disputare, sed quid hoc contra nos, vel ad hanc quæstionem? non negamus hoc, non est hæc quæstio nostra, sed, an Spiritus Sanctus ita se esse vulgi sensui attemperet, ut tanquam verum protulerit, quod in se non est verum, sed tantum apparens: id est, an Soli adscribat motum, quia ita apparet, & à vulgo creditur, quamquam revera se esse non moveat, sed quiescat. Hoc verò non dicit Calvinus, sed contrarium asserit, nam Planetis adscribit suos cursus & quasi stadia, & firmamentum stellas omnes fixas in suam revolutionem trahere, dicit.
units.tr: DCCCXCVI. Finally, when Jacob Lansbergius brought forward in his own support the authority of Calvin, who comments on this Psalm: He was content to charge the whole world with ingratitude in a coarse style, unless it profits in piety from the sight of the Sun. This is the reason why he says that a tent has been prepared for it; then, that it goes out from one end of heaven and passes quickly to the opposite part. For he does not dispute subtly among the philosophers about the whole circuit of heaven, but, accommodating himself to the rudest people, keeps within ocular experience, and therefore passes over the half of the course which is not seen under our hemisphere. B. D. objects on p. 26: Calvin indeed says that the Holy Spirit uses a coarse style and does not dispute subtly among the philosophers. But what has this to do with us, or with this question? We do not deny this; it is not our question. Our question is whether the Holy Spirit so accommodates himself to the sense of the common people that he has set forth as true what in itself is not true, but only apparent: that is, whether he ascribes motion to the Sun because it so appears and is believed by the common people, although in reality it does not move but rests. But Calvin does not say this; he asserts the contrary, for he says that he ascribes to the planets their courses and, as it were, their stadia, and that the firmament draws all the fixed stars into its revolution.

units.la: Resp. 1. Lansbergium Calvinum pro se laudare tantum hactenus, ut ostendat, in hoc Psalmo multas esse locutiones vulgares à sensuum apparentiâ derivatas. Nam crassus stylus oppositè ad argutam inter Philosophos disputationem, item, accommodatio ad rudissimos quosque, qui intra oculorum experientiam sese continent, hic infert locutionem à sensuum præjudiciis desumtam, opponiturque semper accutatæ rei veritati, ita ut posito alterutro alterum sit negandum. Et hoc apparet ex Arist. 1. Et hic ad Eud. cap. 6. cui hæc sunt æquipollentia: δοκεῖντα, φαινόμενα, λόγοι κενοί, ἀλόγιστοι, μὴ φιλοσόφως λεγόμενοι. An verò hoc in se est verum, quod Cœlo conveniant extremitates? quod tentorium & thalamum in Cœlis habeat Sol, in quo quiescat? quibus præjudiciis verba Psalmi sunt involuta. 2. Quamvis quoad propositam quæstionem Calvinus à nobis dissentiat, consentit tamen in eo nimis quàm clarè, quod Scriptura formulis circa res naturales accuratam veritatem non sequatur, sed ad præjudicia sensuum eas formulas, ex quibus habent originem, flectat. Quoad propositam verò quæstionem planè nobiscum consensit Cl. Coccejus in Comment. ad Psalmos edito anno hujus seculi LX. Sic ille ad versum 6. hujus Psalmi: Quando Sol supra horizontem incipit apparere, dicitur oriri, exire, prodire (sive revera, sive ita, ut terra, cui appropinquat navis, dicitur ἀνατέλλειν Act. xxvii. 27.) ita, quando à visu nostro occultatur, occidere. Et postea: Solis indefessus & imprapeditus minimeque varians quoad celeritatem, motus est. Cursus Soli attribuitur, quia & ortus & occasus. Motum quendam celerrimum fieri, dum fit dies & nox, oculus ipse testis est. Quod ipsi oculi eâ de re testari possunt, satis argumenti est ad opus Dei indicandum. Ea indicatio etiam cœlo attribuitur, quia sine Sole, qui in cœlo positus est, eum motum non observaremus. Item: Qui motum diurnum hic intelligi volunt, quo efficitur dies & nox ii per fines cœli intelligunt horizontem. Sed non possumus evadere, quin concedamus, phrasin esse de medio sumtam, ad id confusius significandum, quo fit diei & noctis differentia, sive experientiâ vel ratione motus iste, qui in naturâ est, reperiri, servi, demonstrari possit, sive Deus eum velit in arcanis suis retinere. Addam huic Conradum Bergium Professorem Theologum Gymnasii Bremensis & Concionatorem verè pium, qui in Ennœologiæ Theologico-Philosophicæ Parte sextâ, quæ est, Somatologica seu Physica de operibus, Fragmento VI. membro 3. de situ, ordine ac motu cœli & stellarum, quam suis discipulis dictavit, in quorum manibus adhuc sunt, hoc carmine sententiam istam fuit complexus, cujus paraphrasin etiam adjunxit: Quorumvis generum similes densantur in orbe Particulæ proprio, cumque hinc discordia & illinc Terreat, aut æque invitet concordia cunctis Ordine sic maßis oriuntur distantia certo, Motâ acie ut tota stationem singula servent. Nonnulli ad plures affecti æqualiter orbes Cùm calido segnem fugiant agitante quietem, Cuncta & amica petant, per circum sæpe recurrunt. Utque globum impulsu, quo quisque est fortior urgens Temporis in spatio facit & majore moveri, Sic facile est primi motoris ut impetus omnem Afficiat sphaeram durante in sæcula motu, Quem præsertim intus simul & propensio servet.
units.tr: Reply 1. Lansbergius has so far only cited Calvin in his own support to show that in this Psalm there are many common expressions derived from the appearance of the senses. For the "coarse style," set against subtle disputation among the philosophers, and the accommodation to the rudest people, who keep within the experience of their eyes, here introduce an expression taken from the prejudices of the senses. It is always opposed to the accurate truth of the matter, so that if one is affirmed the other must be denied. This is clear from Aristotle, On the Heavens, book 1, and from the Eudemian Ethics, chapter 6, which has these equivalents: opinions, appearances, empty words, irrational, not spoken philosophically [δοκεῖντα, φαινόμενα, λόγοι κενοί, ἀλόγιστοι, μὴ φιλοσόφως λεγόμενοι]. But is it in itself true that the extremities belong to the heavens? That the Sun has a tent and a bridal chamber in the heavens in which it rests? By such prejudices the words of the Psalm are wrapped up. 2. Although Calvin differs from us on the question proposed, he agrees with us far too clearly in this, that Scripture does not follow exact truth in its forms of speech about natural things, but bends those forms, from which they take their origin, to the prejudices of the senses. On the question proposed, the distinguished Coccejus agreed fully with us in his commentary on the Psalms, published in the sixtieth year of this century. Thus he says on verse 6 of this Psalm: When the Sun begins to appear above the horizon, it is said to rise, to go out, to come forth (whether in reality, or as the land toward which a ship approaches is said to rise [ἀνατέλλειν] Acts 27:27), so when it is hidden from our sight, it is said to set. And afterwards: The motion of the Sun is tireless, unhindered, and hardly varies in speed. The course is attributed to the Sun because of both its rising and its setting. That a very swift motion takes place while day and night come about, the eye itself is witness. What the eyes themselves can testify on this matter is sufficient evidence for pointing out the work of God. This indication is also attributed to the heaven, because without the Sun, which is placed in the heaven, we would not observe that motion. Likewise: Those who want the daily motion to be understood here, by which day and night are produced, understand by the boundaries of heaven the horizon. But we cannot escape conceding that the phrase is taken from common usage, to signify more loosely the difference of day and night, whether that motion, which is in nature, can be found, observed, or demonstrated by experience or by reason, or whether God wishes to keep it hidden in his secret counsels. To this I add Conrad Bergius, professor of theology at the Bremen gymnasium and a truly pious preacher, who in the sixth part of his Ennoeologia Theologico-Philosophica, which is the Somatological or Physical part on works, fragment VI, member 3, concerning the position, order and motion of the heaven and the stars, which he dictated to his students (who still have it in their hands), summed up this opinion in the following verse, to which he also added a paraphrase: Particles of each kind are crowded together in their own orbit; when discord arises on one side and fear on the other, or concord equally invites all, thus distances arise in fixed order, so that by the motion of the line each keeps its whole station. Some, equally drawn to several orbits, when the warmth stirs them, flee sluggish rest, and seek all friendly things, and often run back through the circle. And as a globe pressing forward by the impulse of whatever is stronger, makes and is moved in a greater space of time, so easily the impulse of the first mover affects the whole sphere, the motion lasting through the ages, which especially the inner propensity keeps going at the same time.

units.la: Ne placet hæc potius forsan mandare ministris. Unde licet motum stringentia frigora sistant. Impulsu tamen externo terramque moveri Aurasque adjunctas pariter, non cerno repugnans. Nec minus hinc rectè tribuant oracula terræ Fundum, cum cælos fugiens subsidat in imo, Usque & ab his distans nunquam stationc recedat. Aëris at quoties motus impulsio mutat, Sentitur ventus, varias gradibusque locisque &c.
units.tr: Perhaps it is better not to entrust these things to the ministers. Although the stiffening cold halts the motion, I do not see any contradiction in holding that the earth is moved by an external impulse, and the air joined to it likewise. Nor, on this view, do the oracles rightly ascribe to the earth a base, since it, fleeing the heavens, sinks to the lowest point and, standing apart from them, never withdraws from its station. But whenever an impulse changes the motion of the air, wind is felt, varying in its degrees, places and so on.

units.la: Sequitur ejusdem Paraphrasis Exegetica.
units.tr: Follows the same author's Exegetical Paraphrase.

units.la: Sicut igitur plures sunt stellæ, ita etiam plura erunt genera partium similium diverso ab aliis stellis appetitu prædítarum, cumque singulas stellas ab omni parte diversitas & dissensio quædam æquè à se repellat; vel in diversitate similitudo & amicitia attrahat; fit utique ut singulæ stellæ ad plures alias æque invitatæ ad nullas magis movcantur: sed in suo singulæ loco, certo ordine atque distantia ab aliis constanter permaneant, & cum tota stellarum universitas movetur, singula tamen stationem suam atque distantiam in cæteris constanter servent: simili modo atque in exercitu seu acie aliqua singuli milites atque ordines militum motâ tota acie, consentiente discordia suam singuli stationem atque distantiam ab aliis servare solent: intelligitur etiam facile posse fieri, ut nonnulli partium similium orbes, seu stellæ quas planetas vocamus, ad alias plures stellas præ aliis æqualiter affectæ, cum peculiari quodam calore seu appetitu ad motum perpetuo impellantur, eoque tum moveantur, tum ad illarum præcipue propinquitatem moveantur, ad quas æqualiter adfectæ sunt in eundem sæpius circulum, aliæ mense, aliæ alio tempore revolvantur. Cæterum veluti cum rota aliqua aut sphæra super axe aliquo librata, impellitur ad motum, quanto fortior est is qui impellit tanto majori etiam tempore tantoque sæpius sphæra illa in eundem orbem revolvitur: sic etiam intelligitur, facile utique posse fieri, ut ex primo omnipotentis motoris impulsu, sive cœli totius, sive stellarum singularum talis impetus ac motus oriatur, qui in plurima secula durare possit, cum præsertim etiam appetitus forte aliquis nauralis præter hunc impulsum corpori inditus ad motum similiter inclinet ac disponat; nisi forte beneplacitum sit Domini, ut motus hujusmodi mediantibus causis administris cieat, puta Angelis seu intelligentiis, à quibus corpora cœlestia moveri tralatitium est. Quam-
units.tr: Just as there are many stars, so there will also be many kinds of like parts, endowed with an appetite differing from that of the other stars. Since every star is repelled by some difference and disagreement from every side, or else drawn by likeness and friendship in difference, it comes about that each star, equally invited to many others, is moved by none more than the rest. Each remains in its own place, in a fixed order and at a constant distance from the others. When the whole universe of stars is moved, each still keeps its station and distance from the rest, in the same way as in an army or battle line, when the whole line is moved, the individual soldiers and ranks, by a harmony out of discord, usually keep their own station and distance from the others. It is also easily understood that some orbs of like parts, or stars which we call planets, equally disposed toward many other stars, may be perpetually driven to motion by a certain peculiar heat or appetite, and so both move and move especially toward the nearness of those stars toward which they are equally disposed, and revolve more often in the same circle, some in a month, others in another time. Moreover, just as when some wheel or sphere, balanced on an axle, is driven to motion, the stronger the force that drives it, the longer and the more often that sphere turns round in the same orbit, so too it is easily understood that from the first impulse of the almighty mover, whether of the whole heaven or of the individual stars, such an impetus and motion may arise as can endure for very many ages, especially since some natural appetite, placed in the body besides this impulse, similarly inclines and disposes it to motion. Unless perhaps it be the good pleasure of the Lord that such motions be stirred up through intermediate causes as His ministers, for instance Angels or intelligences, by whom the heavenly bodies are commonly said to be moved. As much as

units.la: Quamvis igitur frigoris seu appetitus tenebrosi proprium sit impedire motum, ut tamen etiam orbis ipse terrenus impulsu aliquo à principio externo moveatur, una cum aëre proximo, non video repugnantiam aliquam involvere. Neque propterea minus conveniens fuerit, quod Pf. 104. 5. dicitur, fundavit terram super bases suas, ne moveat se in seculum, & in seculum; eo quod terra distantiam quantam maximam consequi potest ab opposito cœlo appetens, sit infima mundi pars & quasi fundamentum; neque extra illud spatium, in quo à principio forte externo circumvolvitur unquam vel ad dextram, vel ad sinistram, vel ad supernam vel ad infernam partem unquam declinet, sed ab omni parte distantiam suam à cœlo constanter retineat. Cum igitur aëris diurnus una cum terra motus regularis, ex hac hypothesi, sit futurus ab Occidente in Orientem, si hunc motum impulsione aliquâ externâ ex parte variari contingat, dicetur ventus, qui secundum gradus impulsionis, & terminos seu loca ex quibus oritur & ad quæ tendit, varius esse solet. Hactenus Bergius.
units.tr: Although, therefore, it is the nature of cold, or of a dark appetite, to hinder motion, yet that the terrestrial globe itself should be moved by some impulse from an external source, together with the neighbouring air, I do not see that this involves any contradiction. Nor is it therefore less fitting that what is said in Psalm 104:5, He founded the earth upon its bases, that it should not be moved for ever and ever, should hold. For the earth, seeking the greatest possible distance from the opposite heaven, is the lowest part of the world and as it were its foundation; and it never leaves that space within which it is perhaps turned about by an external beginning, nor ever inclines to the right or left, or to the upper or lower part, but constantly keeps its distance from the heaven on every side. Since, then, on this hypothesis, the regular daily motion of the air together with the earth will be from west to east, if it happens that this motion is varied on some side by some external impulse, it will be called wind, which is commonly various according to the degrees of the impulse and the terms or places from which it arises and toward which it tends. Thus far Bergius.

units.la: DCCCXCVII. Contra hanc responsionem insurgit B. p. 185.
units.tr: DCCCXCVII. Against this answer B. rises up, p. 185.

units.la: Calvinum Lansbergio in eo (in quo ab ipso citatur) repugnare clarè evicimus, nam Spiritus Sancti crassum stylum de motu Solis sic intelligit, ut ipsum Solem velocissimè moveri rotundo verbo dicat.
units.tr: We have clearly shown that Calvin contradicts Lansbergius in the passage where he is cited, for he understands the Holy Spirit's crude style about the motion of the Sun in such a way as to say that the Sun itself moves very swiftly in a round course.

units.la: Resp. At ad hoc non citatur Calvinus, ut jam dictum, & mirum quod tàm inaniter repetatur, ad quod jam antea responsum erat. Calvinus utique expresse dicit: Crasso stylo dicere Psalmistam, tentorium Soli paratum esse, egredi ipsum ab una extremitate & transire celeriter in partem oppositam. At crassus stylus opponitur accurato, qui rem ut in se est exprimit & nudam veritatem; ergo crassus designat cum stylum, qui non rem ut in se exprimit, neque nudam veritatem, sed ut ea præjudiciis est involuta, prout etiam hoc est illustratum textu Aristotelis. Nec lubet ulterius de eo disceptare, sed Lectorem ad inspiciendum textum Calvini allegare; quem non dubito perspecturum, quod textus Calvini faciat ad ostendendum, in Psalmo dicto reperiri phrases vulgares, non nudam veritatem, sed præjudiciis involutam exprimentes: etiamsi enim verba eadem non adhibeat, tamen quod illud ipsum, quod dixi, per crassum stylum intelligat, ex exemplis, quæ crassi styli adducit, satis patet.
units.tr: Reply. But Calvin is not cited for this, as has already been said, and it is strange that it should be repeated so idly, when an answer to it had already been given. Calvin indeed expressly says that by a crude style the Psalmist speaks of the tent prepared for the Sun, that it goes forth from one end and passes swiftly to the opposite part. But a crude style is opposed to an accurate one, which expresses the thing as it is in itself and the bare truth; therefore a crude style designates that which does not express the thing as it is in itself, nor the bare truth, but as it is wrapped in prejudices, as this has also been illustrated by the text of Aristotle. Nor is it pleasing to dispute further about this, but I refer the Reader to inspect Calvin's text, which I do not doubt he will see shows that in the Psalm cited there are found common phrases, expressing not the bare truth but truth wrapped in prejudices. For although Calvin does not use the same words, yet that he understands by the crude style the very thing I have said is clear enough from the examples of crude style which he adduces.

units.la: DCCCXCVIII. Prætereo lubens dicteria, quibus adversarii verba scatent, tantum hoc tango, quod dicit p. 187. In Aristotelis citatione, me plane aberrare à Philosophi scopo, qui eo capite tractat modum docendi, cuique Φαινόμενα, δοξῶντα &c. sint, non sententia, quæ dicuntur secundum erroneam
units.tr: DCCCXCVIII. I gladly pass over the taunts with which my opponents' words are full. I touch only on this, which he says on p. 187 about my citation of Aristotle: that I plainly stray from the Philosopher's aim, since in that chapter he treats of the manner of teaching, and that the things called phainomena [Φαινόμενα] and doxounta [δοξοῦντα] are not opinions stated according to the mistaken view of the crowd and not according to the truth of the matter, but probable arguments; and again that things said un-philosophically [μὴ φιλοσόφως λεγόμενα] are not those which are not supported by philosophical reasons, as is clear of itself from a first reading of the text.

units.la: neam opinionem vulgi, & non secundum rei veritatem, sed argumenta probabilia; & rursus μὴ φιλοσόφως λεγόμενα non sint ea, qua non afferuntur Philosophicis rationibus, ut ex primâ textus inspectione per se patet.
units.tr: The crowd's mistaken opinion, and not the truth of the matter, but probable arguments; and again, things said un-philosophically [μὴ φιλοσόφως λεγόμενα] are not those which are not supported by philosophical reasons, as is clear of itself from a first reading of the text.

units.la: Resp. Aristoteles agit dicto loco de rationibus dialecticis oppositè ad analyticas, illas vocando λόγος μὴ φιλοσόφως λεγομένος, quibus æquipollere dicit δοκοῦντα, φαινόμενα, sive vera sint sive falsa. Et sic Neld. Prat. Log. p. 537. Quicquid ἔνδοξον ἐστι, id est, probabile, consentiens cum hominum judicio, licet falsum, id Logicum dicitur. Ibidem: Rationes Logicas contingit esse falsas, si ergo δοκοῦντα, sive vera sint sive falsa, æquipollcant λόγοις μὴ φιλοσόφως λεγομένοις, ergo etiam stylus secundum δόξαν æquipollebit stylo μὴ φιλοσόφως λεγομένῳ, qui est stylus crassus non accuratus: At stylus secundum δόξαν est is, qui innititur notitiæ vulgari, sive vera sive falsa sit. Adde, quod in Dialecticis rationibus explicandis non recedatur à communi & vulgò recepta consuetudine, etiamsi verba non semper ipsis rebus conveniant, teste Neldelio p. 361: manifestum est ergo, Aristotelis verba ei cui adhibentur probando inservire.
units.tr: Reply. In the passage cited, Aristotle is treating of dialectical arguments as opposed to analytic ones, calling them arguments said un-philosophically [λόγοι μὴ φιλοσόφως λεγόμενοι], to which he says the doxounta [δοξοῦντα] and phainomena [φαινόμενα] are equivalent, whether they are true or false. So Neldelius, Prat. Log. p. 537: "Whatever is endoxon [ἔνδοξον], that is, probable and agreeing with human judgment, though false, is called logical." And in the same place: "Logical arguments may happen to be false." If therefore the doxounta, whether true or false, are equivalent to arguments said un-philosophically, then also a style according to opinion will be equivalent to a style said un-philosophically, which is a crude and unrefined style. But a style according to opinion is one that rests on common notions, whether they are true or false. Add that in explaining dialectical arguments one does not depart from common and generally received usage, even if the words do not always fit the things themselves, as Neldelius testifies at p. 361. It is therefore manifest that Aristotle's words serve the purpose for which they are adduced, namely to prove.

units.la: DCCCXCIX. Inquit porrò B. p. 187. dic quæso, quodnam sensuum præjudicium dictat Soli esse thalamum &c. quis ex vulgo qui mentis fuit compos id unquam credidit; an fungos imaginatus es libri tui lectores?
units.tr: DCCCXCIX. Further, B. says at p. 187: Tell me, please, what prejudice of the senses dictates that the Sun is a bridal chamber, &c.? Who among the common people, if he was of sound mind, ever believed this? Or did you imagine mushrooms for the readers of your book?

units.la: Resp. De eo superius art. 859. dixi, quantum satis est, atque ostendi ex Tacito vulgi esse errorem, quod putet, Solem recondi sub altero hemisphærio, indeque oriri istas Metaphoricas locutiones de tentorio & thalamo, quod quia hactenus nec refutavit adversarius, nec ausus est, sed intactum præteriit, magnam ejus insolentiam lector facilè videbit.
units.tr: Reply: About this I said enough above, at art. 859, and showed from Tacitus that it is an error of the common people to think that the Sun is hidden under the other hemisphere, and that from this arise those metaphorical expressions about a tent and a bridal chamber. Since the adversary has not yet refuted this, nor dared to, but has passed it by untouched, the reader will easily see his great impudence.

units.la: CAPUT XLVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XLVII.

units.la: Psalmi xciii. versus 1. & Psal. civ. vers. 5. proponuntur, & cum sententia dicta conciliantur.
units.tr: Psalms 93:1 and 104:5 are set forth and reconciled with the opinion stated.

units.la: DCCCC. Cum sententiâ nostrâ pugnare volunt quidam Psalm. xciii. 1. Etiam stabilitur orbis habitabilis, ne dimoveatur, & Psalm. civ. 5. Fundavit Terram super bases ejus, ne dimoveretur in seculum & perpetuum. Hunc locum posteriorem valde urget Fullerus lib. 1. cap. 15. Miscellan. sacrorum. Summa ipsius rationum huc redit. 1. quia id tantum verè fundatum dicitur, quod locum non mutat, sed in sede suâ immotum quiescit, firmumque ac fixum manet. 2. fundata dicitur super bases suas, Basis autem valet statilimentum, firmam sedem & statum, seu quietem. Imo non super basin, unam videlicet, sed bases, plurimas scilicet aut potius innumeras. 3. Quod postremo sequitur omnem prorsus motum localem vehementius excludit, ne dimoveretur inquit, id est, ne levissimo minimoque motu quoquoversum ferretur.
units.tr: 900. Some men want to set Psalm 93:1 against our view: The world also is stablished, that it cannot be moved, and Psalm 104:5: Who laid the foundations of the earth, that it should not be removed for ever. Fuller, in book 1, chapter 15 of his Miscellanea sacra, presses the latter text hard. The gist of his arguments comes to this. (1) That is said to be truly founded which does not change its place, but rests immovable in its seat and remains firm and fixed. (2) It is said to be founded upon its bases. But a base means a support, a firm seat and standing, or rest. Indeed, it is not upon one base but upon bases, that is, very many or rather countless ones. (3) What follows at the end excludes every local motion most strongly: "that it should not be removed," that is, that it should not be carried about by the slightest motion in any direction.

units.la: Resp. 1. Ad Psal. 93. Vox stabilis, seu stabilire non necessario infert negationem omnis motus: tribuitur enim illa etiam rebus motui quàm maximè obnoxiis. Sic, exempli gratia, stata aetas hominibus tribuitur, sic vocantur stata tempora, quae recurrunt & secum similem actionem introducunt, qualis antea simili tempore fuerat edita; ut quando dicimus: statis temporibus recurrere hyemem, aestatem, &c. Attamen in his motus reperitur, imò ipsum tempus numerus & mensura motus aestimari debet. Sic quoque vocatur ventus stabilis, qui aliquandiu ab eadem parte flatum continuat. Quando ergò de Terrâ dicitur, eam stabiliri, ne dimoveatur, nihil aliud intelligitur, quam eam à seipsa non dissolvi, neque comminui, sed ita firmam manere. Majestatem enim Dei hic Psalmus vult ostendere ex eo, quod ita Terram stabiliverit, cui non repugnat, etiamsi illa tum circa axem volvatur, tum etiam circa Solem deferatur. Quod si verò aliquanto accuratius hunc Psalmum inspiciamus, deprehendemus, Psalmum hunc esse Propheticum, & nequidem de Terrae globo Physicè considerato esse sermonem, sed de Ecclesiâ N. T. Loquitur iste Psalmus de Regno Christi, quod promissum fuerat Jer. xxiii. 5. confer etiam Es. 11. 7. quod ipse Christus in diebus carnis suae praedicabat appropinquâsse, & quod regnum coelorum appellat. Hoc Regnum est Ecclesia N. T. subditi nempe Christi, qui ipsi se totos tradunt gubernandos & regendos. Hoc enim nomine vox הכבד non raro venit, quia Ecclesia est terra frugifera, quae multiplices fructus producit. Opponitur ea Ecclesiae V. T. cui variae obtigerant mutationes: alia enim facies ejus erat tempore Patriarcharum, alia tempore Moisis: haec verò Ecclesia N. T. stabilis erat futura, ut nulla servitus, nulla umbra postquam res ipsa per umbras adumbrata advenit, esset reducenda stabilitâ libertate per Christum.
units.tr: Answer 1. On Psalm 93. The word "stable," or "to establish," does not necessarily imply the denial of all motion, for it is applied even to things most subject to motion. Thus, for example, a "fixed age" is ascribed to men, and "fixed times" are called those which recur and bring with them an action like that which was performed at a similar time before, as when we say that winter and summer return at fixed times, and so on. Yet motion is found in these, and time itself ought to be measured by the number and measure of motion. So too a wind is called "steady" which blows from the same quarter for some time. When therefore it is said of the earth that it is established so that it is not moved, nothing else is meant than that it is not dissolved or broken up by itself, but remains firm in this way. For this Psalm wishes to show the majesty of God from the fact that he has so established the earth, which is not inconsistent with its being turned both about its axis and carried about the sun. But if we examine this Psalm somewhat more carefully, we shall find that it is prophetic, and that it speaks not at all of the globe of the earth considered physically, but of the Church of the New Testament. This Psalm speaks of the kingdom of Christ, which had been promised in Jeremiah 23:5 (compare also Isaiah 11:7), and which Christ himself, in the days of his flesh, preached as having drawn near, and which he calls the kingdom of heaven. This kingdom is the Church of the New Testament, namely the subjects of Christ, who wholly surrender themselves to be governed and ruled by him. For in this sense the word [הכבד] often occurs, because the Church is a fruitful land which produces manifold fruits. It is set against the Church of the Old Testament, which underwent various changes: its appearance was one thing in the time of the Patriarchs and another in the time of Moses; but the Church of the New Testament was to be stable, so that no servitude, no shadow, would need to be restored once the reality itself, shadowed forth by shadows, had come, with liberty established through Christ.

units.la: DCCCCI. 2. Considerandum, quid Psaltes per bases intelligat, & omnis difficultas evanesceet. Psalm. xxiv. verf. 2. dicitur: Nam ipse super maria fundavit eam, scilicet Terram. Hinc aliqui per bases intelligunt aquas subterraneas, alii verò per eas potentiam Dei denotari volunt, quod Terra à potentia Dei sustentetur, quasi esset fundata super fundamenta quaedam. Si enim vellemus nimis urgere vocem basis, deberemus transire in eorum sententiam, qui cum vulgo putant, Terram infinitis radicibus deorsum esse radicatam, ita ut nulli sint Antipodes, (cui sententiae etiam haec phrasis inniti videtur;) quod velle statuere, & esset manifestae experientiae reluctare, & rationibus Astronomicis, quae probant, Terram undique esse rotundâ fluidoAëre circumdatam, quodq; nec ipse Fullerus concessurus esset. Itaq; nihil aliud indicatur his phrasibus, quam Terrae firmitas, quâ fit, ne nutet, concidat & concutiatur, sive, ne vetustate fatiscat aut ruat, ut solent aedificia. Non diinovetur Terra à basibus suis, sed firmiter manet compacta. Digna sunt observatu verba Cl. Cocceji in hunc Psalmum: Fundatio terrae notat partium crassiorum abyssi coagmentationem & collationem in certâ universi parte, tanquam sede, unde nunquam dimoveatur. Qua est veluti exstructio. Cui oppositum בהו ἀκαταστασία in confusione & permixtione partium crassiorum & liquidiorum. Terra significat τὸν ξηρόν. Hoc autem non impedit, quo minus circumferatur Terra una cum basibus suis sive sua firmitate, quemadmodum etiam navis habet sua fundamenta sive bases, nempe inferiores partes, quibus innititur, quae tamen in aquâ una cum suis basibus movetur. Et quemadmodum ex eo, quod Coelo tribuuntur fundamenta in Scripturis, nollent adversae sententiae Patronii inferri, Coelum non moveri; ita & hic vox basis & fundationis nobis obesse non potest. Non male sensum horum verborum expresserunt illi, qui Terram in aequilibrio stabilitam existimant. Cl. Marot id exprimit per contrepoids. Lobwasser per eine gegenwag / & sic Opitius Poematum sacrorum pag. 164. edit. Amstelod. apud Joh. Janssonium anno 1646. in 12. Du hast des himmels fuß / die grosse last der erden Dein weises meisterstück in starcken grund gelegt/ Den baw ihm lassen selbst zur gegenwage werden So daß er weder sincket/ noch auff die seite schlägt.
units.tr: 901. 2. It should be considered what the Psalmist means by the bases, and all difficulty will vanish. In Psalm 24:2 it is said: For he hath founded it upon the seas, namely the earth. Hence some understand by the bases the subterranean waters, while others want the power of God to be denoted by them, namely that the earth is sustained by the power of God, as if it were founded upon certain foundations. For if we pressed the word "base" too much, we should have to go over to the opinion of those who, with the common people, think that the earth is rooted downward by endless roots, so that there are no antipodes (a view which this phrase also seems to rest upon). To maintain this would be to resist plain experience and the astronomical reasons which prove that the earth is everywhere round and surrounded by fluid air, and this Fuller himself would not concede. Therefore nothing else is indicated by these phrases than the firmness of the earth, by which it is kept from wavering, falling and being shaken, or from decaying or collapsing through age, as buildings do. The earth is not moved from its bases, but remains firmly compacted. The words of the distinguished Cocceius on this Psalm are worth noting: The foundation of the earth denotes the joining together of the thicker parts of the abyss and their gathering in a certain part of the universe, as in a seat, from which they are never moved. It is, as it were, a structure. Opposed to this is [בהו] [tohu], disorder [ἀκαταστασία], in the confusion and mixing of the thicker and the liquid parts. Earth signifies the dry land [τὸν ξηρόν]. Yet this does not prevent the earth from being carried around together with its bases, that is, its firmness, just as a ship too has its foundations or bases, namely its lower parts on which it rests, and yet these are moved in the water together with its bases. And just as, because foundations are ascribed to heaven in the Scriptures, the opponents' patrons would not want it to be inferred that heaven does not move, so here too the word "base" and "foundation" cannot harm us. Those who think the earth is established in equilibrium have expressed the sense of these words not badly. The distinguished Marot expresses it by contrepoids (counterweight). Lobwasser expresses it by eine Gegenwag, and so Opitz in his Poemata sacra, p. 164, Amsterdam edition, at the press of Joh. Janssonius, 1646, in 12mo: "Du hast des Himmels Fuß, die grosse Last der Erden, Dein weises Meisterstück, in starcken Grund gelegt; Den Bau ihm lassen selbst zur Gegenwage werden, So daß er weder sincket noch auff die Seite schlägt."

units.la: Concidunt ergo sic tria fulcra Fulleri, quibus nimis firmiter putavit suam sententiam stabilitam fuisse. Similia plane sunt, quae habet B. D. p. 30. ad quae hoc responsum à Lectore poterit applicari. Cum enim nihil novi adferat, quod non in responsione ad instantias Fulleri fuerit sufficiens & sofutum, noluimus in primâ editione, h. e. in Dissertationibus, Lectorem inani repetitione gravare.
units.tr: So the three props of Fuller fall, on which he thought his opinion had been established too firmly. What B. D. says on p. 30 is quite similar, and the reader may apply to it the answer given here. For since he brings nothing new which was not sufficiently and solidly answered in the reply to Fuller's objections, we did not wish, in the first edition, that is in the Dissertations, to burden the reader with empty repetition.

units.la: DCC CCII. Nunc tamen, quia, inquit B. p. 204. & seqq. sua argumenta plane differre ab instantiis Fulleri, ostendamus, quod omnino ipsorum refutatio ex responsionibus Fullero datis sufficienter possit peti. Dicit p. 209. se niti phrasi Hebraicâ, quae propriâ suâ significatione motum negat, quaque non durationem, sed immobilitatem propriè & per se inferat.
units.tr: 902. Now, however, because, as B. says on p. 204 and following, his arguments differ entirely from Fuller's objections, we shall show that their refutation can be sought fully from the answers already given to Fuller. He says on p. 209 that he relies on a Hebrew phrase which by its proper meaning denies motion, and which infers not duration but immobility properly and in itself.

units.la: Resp. Verba Hebraica sic se habent בל המט אף תכון הבל: dixeram autem, ex intentione Spiritus Sancti hujus dicti non alium esse sensum, quàm Terrae partes à se invicem non dissolvi, atque ita eam firmam manere; quae sanè responsio non magis verba Latina quam Hebraea respicit. Si enim is est dicti hujus sensus, non alius erit utique, sive Hebraicâ vel Latinâ vel aliâ linguâ efferatur, ergo ostendere oportuisset Adversarium ex Psalmo, aliud praeterea à Spiritu Sancto intendi & significari, quod nego. Verum ostendamus in ejus gratiam, verba Hebraica immobilitatem Terrae non inferre. Duae sunt, quae hic adhibentur phrases, quarum neutra ad institutum ipsius facit. Neque enim ex voce תכון, neque ex phrasi לא תכוט inferetur, Terram in vortice suo non deferri, cum illa delatione non obstante utrumque de Terrâ dici queat. Verbum הכון in Niphal competere & tribui rebus mobilibus, quibus certo quodam respectu firmitas assignatur, manifestum evadit ex Psalm. LXXXIX. 37. כירח יכון עולם sicut Luna stabilis erit in seculum, & Psal. CXLI. 2. הכון הפלתי קשרת לפניך Statuatur oratio ut suffitus coram te.
units.tr: Answer. The Hebrew words stand thus: Yea, the world is established, that it shall not be moved [אף תכון תבל בל תמוט]. I had said, however, that according to the intention of the Holy Spirit the sense of this saying is nothing other than that the parts of the earth are not dissolved from one another, and so the earth remains firm; and this answer certainly concerns the Latin words no more than the Hebrew ones. For if this is the sense of the saying, it will surely be no different whether it is expressed in Hebrew, Latin or any other language. Therefore the adversary ought to have shown from the Psalm that something else is intended and signified by the Holy Spirit besides this, which I deny. But let us show, for his benefit, that the Hebrew words do not imply the immobility of the earth. There are two phrases used here, and neither serves his purpose. For neither from the word [תכון] nor from the phrase [לא תמוט] will it be inferred that the earth is not carried in its vortex, since both things can be said of the earth despite that carrying. That the verb [הכון] in the Niphal applies to and is ascribed to movable things, to which firmness is assigned in a certain respect, is evident from Psalm 89:37: [כירח יכון עולם], as the moon shall be established for ever, and from Psalm 141:2: [תכון תפלתי קטרת לפניך], let my prayer be set forth as incense before thee.

units.la: Quod si ergo vocibus Hebraicis nitendum, quidni antagonista inferat, etiam Lunam & suffitum non moveri? Ita Psal. VIII. 4. de Lunâ & stellis dicitur: אשר כוננת quae stabilivisti, & tamen Luna movetur, stellae etiam ab adversariis censentur moveri singulis diebus una cum Coelo circa Terram, & revera gyrat quaelibet circa suum axem. Vide Philoponum de Creatione cap. II. ubi haec & similia dicta Scripturae adducta ad probandum ex Scriptura, quod Coelum sit immobile, eodem modo ac nos explicat. Quod vocem טוט attinet, ea adhibetur Psalm. XVII. verf. 5. ubi David rogat Deum: continue gressus meos in orbita tuis בל נמוטו פעמי ne dimoveantur pedes mei; nec tamen licebit inferre, Davidem pedes immobiles petiisse, etiam tum quando gressus instituendi. Nihil ergo praesidii in hoc Psalmo pro oppositâ sententiâ.
units.tr: But if we must rely on the Hebrew words, why should our opponent not infer that the Moon and the incense are also not moved? Thus in Psalm 8:4 it is said of the Moon and the stars: "which thou hast established" [אשר כוננת], and yet the Moon moves; the stars too are held by our opponents to move every day together with the heavens about the earth, and indeed each of them revolves about its own axis. See Philoponus, On the Creation, chapter 2, where he explains these and similar sayings of Scripture, brought forward to prove from Scripture that the heavens are immovable, in the same way as we do. As for the word [טוט], it is used in Psalm 17:5, where David asks God: "Hold up my goings in thy paths" [בל נמוטו פעמי], "that my feet slip not"; yet it will not be permitted to infer that David asked for immovable feet, even when he is setting out his steps. There is therefore no support in this Psalm for the opposite view.

units.la: DCCCCIII. Inst. B. p. 210. Ad Psal. CIV. Argumentum suum non esse fundatum in solâ voce Basis, sed in complexu sententiae, fundavit supra bases, quam dixerit, per similitudinem desumtam esse ab Architectis aedificia sua locantibus in loco solido & immobili, ita ut phraseologia quidem etiam inferat durationem aeternam, sed eâ vi similitudinis, quâ respicit aedificium ideo permanens & durabile, quia in loco solido & immobili est locatum.
units.tr: 903. Institutio, part B, p. 210, on Psalm 104. "His argument is not founded on the word 'bases' alone, but on the whole sense of the sentence. He founded upon bases, which he said were taken by way of comparison from architects who set their buildings on a solid and immovable place, so that the phrase indeed implies eternal duration, but by that force of comparison which regards a building as lasting and durable because it has been placed on a solid and immovable spot."

units.la: Resp. Verba Psal. CIV. sic habent: יסד ארץ על מכוניה בל המוט עולם ועד Fundavit Terram super bases suas ne dimoveatur in seculum & perpetuum, meaq; responsio nō respicit nude vocē bases, sed ipsam phrasin, fundavit super bases; dixi enim, si illa proprie sit sumenda & ad vivum resecanda, debere ex ea colligi, Terram deorsum infinitis radicibus esse radicatam, &c. Ex quibus lectori apparet, jam ad illam instantiam Antagonistæ sufficienter fuisse responsum: si enim Terra est permanens & durabilis, ut ædificium, quod in loco solido & immobili est locatum ergo sub Terrâ debet esse locus solidus & immobilis, quem quidem mihi vellem ostendi: quod enim à nobis concipitur sub Terrâ, id antipodibus nostris est supra Terram & vice versa, at nihil aliud circa Terram reperire licet quàm aërem mobilem, qui sanè non potest esse Terræ locus solidus & immobilis. Comparatio ergo in phrasi ista inter Terram & ædificia est quoad hoc tertium, nempe firmitatem, quâ fit, ne nutet, concidat & concutiatur, sive, ne vetustate fatiscat aut ruat, ut solent ædificia humana: nec illa ulterius debet extendi.
units.tr: Reply. The words of Psalm 104 read thus: "He founded the earth upon its bases, that it should not be moved for ever and ever" [יסד ארץ על מכוניה בל המוט עולם ועד]. My answer does not concern the bare word "bases" but the phrase itself, "founded upon bases." For I said that if this phrase is taken properly and pressed to the letter, it should be inferred from it that the earth is rooted downward by infinite roots, and so on. From this the reader can see that this instance of our opponent has already been sufficiently answered. For if the earth is permanent and durable, like a building that is set on a solid and immovable place, then there must be under the earth a solid and immovable place. I would indeed like to be shown this place: for what we conceive as under the earth is, to our antipodes, above the earth, and vice versa; and nothing else can be found about the earth but the mobile air, which certainly cannot be a solid and immovable place for the earth. The comparison in this phrase, then, between the earth and buildings holds only as to this third point, namely firmness, by which a building is kept from tottering, collapsing and being shaken, or from decaying and falling through age, as human buildings usually do; and the comparison ought not to be extended further.

units.la: DCCCCIV. Quæ M. p. 175, 176. hic profert, ea non sunt tanti, quin ex antea dictis sufficiens haberi possit responsio, & libenter velim me hic æqui lectoris judicio submittere, ut, collatis Adversariorum Objectionibus & nostris responsionibus, censeat, num ex Psalmo xciii, sententia Adversariorum possit probari, dum hoc unum observetur, me sustinere partes Respondentis, cui sufficit inconsequentiam argumentorum ab adversariis allatorum ostendisse. Eadem ratio est eorum, quæ ab ipso afferuntur p.177.&c. cùm enim nihil proponatur, ad quod responsio ex dictis non habeatur, neque operæ est pretium lectorem repetitione molestâ ejusdem responsionis detinere.
units.tr: 904. What M. brings forward here, on pages 175 and 176, is not of such weight that a sufficient answer cannot be had from what has been said before. I would gladly leave this to the fair judgement of the reader, so that, comparing the objections of the opponents with our answers, he may judge whether the opinion of the opponents can be proved from Psalm 93; provided only that it is noted that I am maintaining the part of the respondent, to whom it is enough to have shown the inconsequence of the arguments brought forward by the opponents. The same holds for what is alleged by him on page 177 and following: since nothing is put forward to which an answer cannot be had from what has been said, it is not worth while to detain the reader with a tiresome repetition of the same answer.

units.la: DCCCCV. Iis quæ objicit H. pag. 5, 6, 7. aliquid respondendum est, quærit 1. Cur in sacris literis τὸ fundari non de aliis quoque creaturis prædicetur?
units.tr: 905. Something must be answered to the things which H. objects on pages 5, 6 and 7. He asks, first: "Why is the predicate 'to be founded' not also said in Holy Scripture of other creatures?"

units.la: Resp. Jam ostendimus, prædicari de Lunâ, de suffitu, quibus plura alia loca addi possent.
units.tr: Reply. We have already shown that it is said of the Moon and of the incense, to which many other passages could be added.

units.la: DCCCCVI.
