Addit H p. 7. quòd phrasis, ne dimoveretur in seculum, de integritate & constantia intelligi non posit, arguit vox basis, per quam translative intelligi soliditatem & in integritate constantiam quis non videt? Quòd si phrasis non dimoveri idem significare deberet, tautologia, crassa crambe & inepta locutio Scripturam deformaret, &c.
units.tr: 906. H. adds on page 7: "That the phrase 'that it should not be moved for ever' cannot be understood of integrity and constancy is shown by the word 'bases', through which, by a figure, firmness and constancy in integrity are understood; who does not see this? But if the phrase 'not to be moved' were to mean the same thing, it would be a tautology, a gross cabbage-dish, and an inept expression that would disfigure Scripture, etc."

units.la: Resp. Paraphrasis versf. 5. Psal. civ. hæc est: Deus Terram firmiter compegit, ne nutet & vetustate dehiscat, sicut ædificia solent non firmiter stabilita, in quâ nulla tautologia inanis nec inepta locutio, nisi omnes phrases, quibus una res significatur diversis modis, quales in sacris literis multæ reperiuntur, ad τautologiam referre velis. Neque verò inficior, quin per bases soliditas & in integritate constantia intelligi debeat, sed nego, illam soliditatem & in integritate constantiam, quam Terrae respectu suarum partium inter se invicem cohaerentium, & respectu constantis & sine mutatione motus tribuo, evertere delationem Terrae annuam vel gyrationem diurnam. Cocc. in Gen. p. 84. a. Notandum est, quod fundatio terra non dicatur de toto globo, qui constat ex arida & mari, sed de sola arida. Ideo ex fundatione arida possumus argumentari ad negandum motum totius globi, quia arida fundata supra maria, nihilominus cum mari potest moveri.
units.tr: Reply. The paraphrase of verse 5 of Psalm 104 is this: God firmly put the earth together, so that it should not totter or gape open with age, as buildings that are not firmly established are wont to do. In this there is no empty tautology or inept expression, unless you want to refer to tautology all the phrases by which one thing is signified in different ways, of which many are found in Holy Scripture. Nor do I deny that by "bases" firmness and constancy in integrity must be understood; but I deny that that firmness and constancy in integrity, which I attribute to the earth with respect to its parts cohering with one another, and with respect to a constant motion without change, overturns the earth's yearly motion or its daily rotation. Coccejus on Genesis, p. 84a: "It is to be noted that the foundation of the earth is not said of the whole globe, which consists of dry land and sea, but only of the dry land. Therefore from the foundation of the dry land we can argue to deny motion of the whole globe, because the dry land, founded above the seas, can nevertheless be moved together with the sea."

units.la: CAPUT XLVIII.
units.tr: CAPUT XLVIII.

units.la: Psalmi cIV. versus 19. & Matth. v. versus 45. cum sententia dicta conciliantur.
units.tr: Psalm 104:19 and Matthew 5:45 are reconciled with the statement quoted above.

units.la: DCCCCVII. Psalm. cIV. 19. Fecit Lunam ad statuta tempora, Sol novit occasum suum. Matth. v. 45. Facit enim, ut Sol suus exoriatur super malos ac bonos, & pluit super justos & injustos. Primum locum ita urget B. D. pag. 28. Verum quidem est, hic esse Tropum, cum Soli cognitio tribuitur, quia tantum est facultas viventis; sed & hoc certum est, Soli cognitionem tribui, quia tam certus & ordinatus ejus est cursus, quam bene directa est actio eorum, qui omnia sua scientia & cognitione agunt. Imo & in ipso Tropo argumentum habemus efficax pro motu Solis: nam qualiter ille, qui omnia sua ex cognitione agit, sese habet ad actiones suas, ita & Sol in ordinato suo cursu sese habet ad Occasum suum; datur ergo actio quaedam realis Solis circa Occasum suum, propter quam agenti exratione comparatur: at si Terra mota Sol revera quiesceret, nullum esset fundamentum istius comparationis, ac per consequens invalidum esset argumentum Psalmis, ad probandam Dei gloriam ex luminaris illius ordinato occasu; tum enim non Sol, sed Terra sese movens praeberet medium probationis, cum tamen Psaltes illud non a Terra, sed a Sole desumat. Et quaenam esset in eo probabilitas, quod in exaltatione operum Dei in luminaribus coelestibus, in uno referetur, quod ei revera inest, in altero, quod tantum apparet inesse? nam eo posito sequetur, medium prius revera esse probativum gloriae divinae, posterius tantum apparenter. Ad alterum vero locum haec p. 30. notat: In verbis Domini nostri Jesu Christi hoc notatu dignum est, eum non alio modo loqui de Dei beneficio primo, quod Solem oriri faciat, quam de secundo quod pluat. Atque tò plucre necessario intelligi debet de reali communicatione beneficii & non mere apparenti; Ergo & similiter tò facere oriri oriri de reali & non mere apparenti collatione beneficii exponi debet.
units.tr: DCCCCVII. Psalm 104:19: He appointed the moon for seasons; the sun knoweth his going down. Matthew 5:45: For he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust. B. D. presses the first passage as follows, p. 28: It is true that there is a trope here, when knowledge is attributed to the sun, since it has only the faculty of a living thing. But this also is certain, that knowledge is attributed to the sun because its course is as certain and ordered as the action of those who do everything with knowledge and understanding is well directed. Indeed, in the trope itself we have a strong argument for the sun's motion. For as one who does all his acts from knowledge stands towards his actions, so the sun, in its ordered course, stands towards its setting. There is therefore some real action of the sun about its setting, on account of which it is compared to an agent. But if the earth moved and the sun truly stood still, there would be no foundation for this comparison, and consequently the argument from the psalm would be invalid for proving God's glory from the ordered setting of that luminary. For then it would not be the sun, but the earth moving itself, that would supply the means of proof, whereas the Psalmist takes it not from the earth but from the sun. And what probability would there be in this: that in the exaltation of God's works in the heavenly lights, one thing is referred to what truly belongs to it, and another to what only seems to belong to it? For if that be granted, it will follow that the former means is truly a proof of God's glory, but the latter only apparently. On the second passage he notes this at p. 30: In the words of our Lord Jesus Christ it is worth noting that he does not speak in another way of God's first benefit, that he causes the sun to rise, than of the second, that he sends rain. And the verb "to rain" [τὸ βρέχειν] must necessarily be understood of a real communication of benefit and not a merely apparent one. Therefore the causing to rise must similarly be explained as a real and not merely apparent bestowal of benefit.

units.la: Resp. Ortum & occasum Soli proprie non posse tribui superius vidimus, ibique agnoscendam locutionem vulgarem ostendimus. 2. Argumentum a comparatione Solis cum eo, qui omnia ex sua cognitione agit, est imbecillum. Comparatio enim illa uberius extendi non debet, quam hucusque, quod Soli Occasus obtingat, non aliter, ac si cognitione praeditus omnia ad illum subeundum disposuisset. Ortus autem & Occasus proprie loquendo sonant quid Respectivum & Relativum ad Horizontem, quae, sive Soli contingant per motum proprium realem, sive per Terrae circumvolutionem, stato nihilominus tempore eveniunt, nihilque id instituto Psalmistae obest. Nec si hic convenientia non sit agentis ex cognitione & Solis in reali actione, nullum propterea comparationis fundamentum erit. Tertium enim convenientiae erit in certitudine eventus, quod quemadmodum ex consilio agenti certo quaedam eveniunt, ad quae consilia sua direxit: ita etiam Soli certo obveniat occasus stato tempore & loco pro diversis anni partibus. 3. Psalmistae scopus hic est ostendere, ex operibus sapientiam & providentiam divinam elucere, quod inter alia etiam exemplis Lunae & Solis declarat, quibus statis temporibus occasus & ortus obtingant, & praeterea Lunae variae phases, novilunium, plenilunium &c. Et sic per utraque haec gloria divina revera probatur, quod tam sapienter omnia ordinaverit, ut statis temporibus haec illis contingant. Neque aliquid gloriae Dei detrahitur, si dicatur, Soli occasum suum convenire per motum apparentem; illa enim ex eo elucet, quod Deus per leges naturae Occasum Solis fixum & certum constituerit. 4. Conclusio argumenti ex Matth. V. petiti nobis non obest. Agnosco equidem, Christum hic beneficium utrobique reale Dei Patris praedicare, quod si late loquendo velis ipsum exortum Solis & pluviae casum vocare, sive stricte illuminationem tantum & calefactionem Terrae a Sole exorto, atque irrigationem ejusdem Terrae a pluviae casu, non disceptabo, cum de nomine potius quam de re controversia effet futura. Sed inde non sequitur, quod eodem plane modo & Solis ortus & pluviae lapsus debeant a providentia divina procurari.
units.tr: Reply. First, we have seen above that rising and setting cannot properly be attributed to the sun, and there we showed that this is ordinary language which must be recognised as such. Second, the argument from the comparison of the sun with one who does everything from his knowledge is weak. For that comparison ought not to be extended further than this: that the sun's setting befalls it at a fixed time, just as if it were endowed with knowledge and had arranged everything for its going down. Rising and setting, properly speaking, denote a relation to the horizon, and these happen at a fixed time whether they befall the sun through its own real motion or through the earth's revolution, and this does nothing to hinder the Psalmist's purpose. Nor, if there is no likeness here between an agent acting from knowledge and the sun in real action, will there therefore be no basis for the comparison. For the likeness will lie in the certainty of the outcome: just as certain things happen to an agent acting by plan, toward which he directed his plans, so also the sun's setting certainly befalls it at a fixed time and place for the different parts of the year. Third, the aim of the Psalmist here is to show that God's wisdom and providence shine forth from his works. He declares this among other things by the examples of the moon and the sun, at which fixed times their setting and rising occur, and besides, the varying phases of the moon, new moon, full moon, and so on. Thus by both of these God's glory is truly proved, in that he has so wisely ordered all things that these come to them at set times. Nor is any glory taken from God if it is said that the sun's setting belongs to it through apparent motion; for that glory shines forth from the fact that God, through the laws of nature, has established the sun's setting as fixed and certain. Fourth, the conclusion of the argument drawn from Matthew 5 does not harm us. I admit, indeed, that Christ here proclaims a real benefit of God the Father in both cases. If you wish to call, in a broad sense, the rising of the sun and the falling of rain by these names, or, strictly, the illumination and warming of the earth by the risen sun and its watering by the fall of rain, I will not dispute it, since the controversy would then be about a word rather than a matter. But it does not follow from this that the rising of the sun and the falling of rain must be procured by divine providence in exactly the same way.

units.la: DCCCCVIII. Contra responsionem primam objicit B. pag. 190.
units.tr: 908. Against the first answer, B. objects at p. 190.

units.la: Hanc responsionem non tangere nucleum argumenti sui, se enim a toto complexu sententia argumentatum.
units.tr: This answer does not touch the kernel of his argument, for he argued from the whole complex of the opinion.

units.la: Resp. Etsi haec prima responsio non praecise tangeret argumentum, prout ab ipso urgetur, sufficeret, quod spectaret alios, qui verba Oriri & Occidere urgent. At mox videbimus, vel maximè tangere nucleum argumenti hujus antagonistæ.
units.tr: Reply: Even if this first answer did not hit the argument precisely as he urges it, it would be enough that it looked to others who press the words "to rise" and "to set." But we shall soon see that it touches most of all the kernel of this opponent's argument.

units.la: DCCCCIX. Idem p. 191. contra secundam responsionem instat, ac meis verbis, Soli occasus obtingit non aliter, ac si cognitione praditus omnia ad illum subeundum dispositus esset, hunc affingit sensum: Sol revera quiescens videtur nobis occidere, quasi cognitione praditus dispositus esset Terram circumvolvi, ut ita habitantibus in Terra videretur occasum subire, quam expositionem tropi dicit fore durissimam & plane coactam.
units.tr: 909. The same, at p. 191, presses against my second answer. From my words, "Setting befalls the Sun not otherwise than as if it were endowed with cognition and disposed to undergo it," he draws this sense: "The Sun, really at rest, seems to us to set, as if it were endowed with cognition and disposed so that the Earth revolves, so that to those dwelling on the Earth it would seem to undergo setting." This interpretation of the trope he calls most harsh and plainly forced.

units.la: Resp. Qui sibi imperium sumit in alienas cogitationes, multum fallatur oportet. Quis enim dixit tibi, hic τὸ occidere mihi idem esse quod videri occidere? Unde vero nosti, quod hæc verba mea, ac si cognitione praditus omnia ad eum subeundum dispositus esset, æquivaleant illis, ac si dispositus esset Terram circumvolvi. In utroque misere erras. Atque dum in priori laberis, facto ostendis, quantum prima mea responsio ad rem faciat. Occidere motum inferre nego, sed tantùm occultationem sub Horizonte, idque superius ostendi. Ergo etiamsi Sol occidat & oriatur, inde eum moveri non evincitur. Posterior verborum interpretatio non procedit, nisi apud eum, qui à genere ad speciem argumentari affirmatè sibi licere existimaverit. His etiam satisfactum H. qui pag. 96. art. 16 mihi tribuit, me Ortum Solis apparentem tantùm intelligere.
units.tr: Reply: Whoever takes upon himself authority over other people's thoughts must be much mistaken. For who told you that here I take "to set" to mean the same as "to seem to set"? And how do you know that these words of mine, "as if it were endowed with cognition and disposed to undergo it, are equivalent to those, as if it were disposed to make the Earth revolve"? In both respects you wretchedly err. And while you slip in the former, you show by the very fact how much my first answer bears on the matter. I deny that setting implies motion, but only occultation below the horizon, which I have shown above. Therefore, even if the Sun sets and rises, it is not thereby proved that it moves. The latter interpretation of the words does not follow, except for one who has thought he may freely argue from genus to species. This also answers H., who at p. 96, art. 16, attributes to me that I understand only the apparent rising of the Sun.

units.la: DCCCCX. Pergit B. p. 192. me non ignorasse hanc meæ comparationis absurditatem, ac proinde confugisse ad aliam expositionem his verbis: Nec si hic convenientia non sit agentis ex cognitione & Solis in reali actione, nullum propterea comparationis fundamentum erit. Tertium enim convenientia erit in certitudine eventus &c.
units.tr: 910. B. goes on at p. 192, saying that I was not unaware of the absurdity of my comparison, and therefore had recourse to another explanation in these words: "Nor, if there is no agreement here between an agent acting from cognition and the Sun in real action, will there for that reason be no foundation for the comparison. For the point of agreement will be in the certainty of the event, etc."

units.la: Resp. Somnia hæc sunt mera & inanes ludificationes, quibus nescio quid sibi hic fingit: nec dubito, quin lectori attento pateat, non novam his verbis adductam esse expositionem dicti Christi, sed explicationem & deductionem prioris responsionis.
units.tr: Reply: These are mere dreams and empty mockeries, by which he feigns I know not what for himself. Nor do I doubt that it is plain to an attentive reader that no new explanation of Christ's saying is brought forward in these words, but only an explanation and deduction of my earlier answer.

units.la: DCCCCXI. Addit B. p. 192. Ita quæ ex consilio agenti certo eveniunt, vel respectum habent ad actionem, quæ fit ex consilio & talem effectum certo habet, vel non; si non, ergo non possunt dici ex consilio orta &c. sin vero respectum habent ad actionem consultaneam, tum etiam Soli aliqua actio ordinata est tribuenda, secundùm quam ex consilio agenti comparatur. Simpliciter enim dicere, ita etiam Soli certo obvenit Occasus, nihil dicit relativum ad cognitionem vel actiones ex cognitione, præsertim cùm per τὸ obvenire nihil reale, sed tantùm apparens quid in Sole secundùm Wittichium designetur &c.
units.tr: 911. B. adds at p. 192: "So things that certainly happen to an agent acting by counsel either have regard to an action that is done from counsel and certainly has such an effect, or not. If not, then they cannot be said to arise from counsel, etc. But if they have regard to a deliberate action, then some ordered action must also be attributed to the Sun, by which it is brought about by an agent acting by counsel. For simply to say, 'so too the setting certainly befalls the Sun,' says nothing relative to cognition or to actions from cognition, especially since by 'to befall' nothing real but only something apparent in the Sun is designated, according to Wittich, etc."

units.la: Resp. Ego vero nego & pernego istam sequelam: si illa, quæ ex consilio certo eveniunt, respectum habent ad actionem à consilio imperatam: ergo Soli aliqua actio ordinata est tribuenda; nisi eodem jure velis colligere, Soli actionem aliquam à consilio imperatam tribuendam. Sufficiens enim fundamentum istius comparationis est in certitudine eventus. Falsissimum vero est, quòd certitudo eventus occasus Solis nihil dicat relativum ad cognitionem vel actionem ex cognitione, cujus respectu possit iste eventus ex cognitione dici proficisci. 2. Per τὸ obvenire nihil reale, sed tantum apparens mihi designari, inanis est suspicio antagonistæ, cùm occultatio Solis sub Horizonte, etiamsi non per actionem aliquam Solis ipsi conveniat, nihilominus revera ipsi competat; & verum sit, eum de nocte supra Horizontem nec esse nec posse conspici. Unde iterum cadit absurda comparatio, quam ipse mihi affingit.
units.tr: Reply: I indeed deny, and utterly deny, this inference: if those things which certainly happen by counsel have regard to an action commanded by counsel, then some ordered action must be attributed to the Sun; unless by the same right you wish to conclude that some action commanded by counsel must be attributed to the Sun. For the certainty of the event is a sufficient foundation for this comparison. But it is most false that the certainty of the Sun's setting says nothing relative to cognition, or to action from cognition, with respect to which this event could be said to proceed from cognition. Second, that by "to befall" only something apparent, and not something real, is designated by me, is an empty suspicion of my opponent. For the occultation of the Sun below the horizon, even if it does not belong to the Sun through any action of its own, nonetheless truly belongs to it; and it is true that at night it can neither be nor be seen above the horizon. Whence again falls the absurd comparison which he attributes to me.

units.la: DCCCCXII. Instat B. p. 193. Illa similitudinis applicatio in sola certitudine occasus tollit emphasin verborum propheticorum, quorum scopus est, non simpliciter docere, quod Sol certò occidit; id enim vel pueris & maximè Barbaris notum est, sed in ejus occasu notare admirabilem, constantissimum & ordinatissimum motum talem, qualis in agentibus ex cognitione reperiri solet.
units.tr: 912. B. presses at p. 193: "That application of the likeness, resting only on the certainty of the setting, takes away the emphasis of the prophetic words, whose aim is not simply to teach that the Sun certainly sets. For this is known even to boys and most of all to barbarians, but to note in its setting an admirable, most constant and most orderly motion, of such a kind as is usually found in agents acting from cognition."

units.la: Resp. Hæc ipsa est quæstio, utrum scopus sit Prophetæ, in Solis occasu notare motum talem, qualis in agentibus ex cognitione reperiri solet: id probandum, non pro auctoritate dictandum. Nihil verò video in circumstantis textus, ex quo hic scopus Prophetæ inferri possit. 2. Nec dico simpliciter docere velle prophetam, quod Sol certo occidit, sed quod occasum suum, statis temporibus & locis, diversis anni partibus obtineat; quod si vero pueris & barbaris notum sit, Soli certo obvenire occasum, an ideo dicendum, illud non docere Spiritum Sanctum? annon enim argumenta ad sapientiam & providentiam divinam demonstrandam, ex rebus maximè obviis & pueris barbarisque notis, desumere sæpius solet?
units.tr: Reply: This is precisely the question, whether the prophet's aim is to note in the Sun's setting a motion of such a kind as is usually found in agents acting from cognition. That must be proved, not dictated by authority. Nor do I see anything in the surrounding text from which this aim of the prophet could be inferred. Second, I do not say that the prophet simply wishes to teach that the Sun certainly sets, but that it obtains its setting at fixed times and places in different parts of the year. But if this is known to boys and barbarians, that the setting certainly befalls the Sun, should it therefore be said that the Holy Spirit does not teach it? Does not Scripture often draw its arguments for demonstrating divine wisdom and providence from things most obvious and known even to boys and barbarians?

units.la: DCCCCXII. Contra tertiam responsionem instat B. p. 194. De scopo generali Psalmista non esse quæstionem, sed de medijs quibus probat sapientiam divinam, an desumta sint à rebus veris, an tantùm ab apparentibus? prius à se asseri & respectu luminarium Cœlestium probari eo medio, quòd cum in priori argumentum Prophetæ desumtum sit à motu reali, non nisi inepte dici possit, in posteriori argumentum à merè apparenti elici, cum nulla sit diversitatis nota. H. p. 94. objicit, non tantùm generalem Dei sapientiam hic prædicari, sed etiam specialem &c.
units.tr: 912. Against the third answer, B. presses at p. 194: "The question is not about the general aim of the Psalmist, but about the means by which he proves divine wisdom: are they taken from true things, or only from apparent ones? He asserts beforehand that, with respect to the heavenly luminaries, it is proved by that means. For whereas in the former the prophet's argument is taken from real motion, it can only be said foolishly that in the latter an argument is drawn from what is merely apparent, since there is no mark of difference. H., p. 94, objects that not only the general wisdom of God is proclaimed here, but also the special, etc."

units.la: Resp. Eâdem chordâ oberrat Adversarius, præsupponens, quod ortus & occasus Soli ex meâ sententiâ non reverâ, sed tantùm apparenter conveniat, quod quidem nullibi dictum. Aliud autem est, motum Soli apparenter competere, aliud Occasum, cùm Occasus sine motu proprio sideri ex sententiâ Astronomorum adscribi possit. Non ergo quæstio est, utrum media illa à rebus veris desumta sint, quod non nego, cùm verè Soli occasum certis & statis temporibus certisque locis competere concedam, sed utrum medium illud sit motus Solis, quem ex verbo Occasu elici posse pernego. Quod autem specialem Dei sapientiam agnoscere liceat, ex Solis & Lunæ statô certoque ortu & occasu, non nego, sed libenter confiteor.
units.tr: Reply: The adversary strays on the same string, presupposing that rising and setting belong to the Sun, in my view, not really but only apparently, which is nowhere said. But it is one thing that motion belongs to the Sun apparently, another that setting does, since setting can be ascribed to a star without any motion of its own, according to the opinion of astronomers. So the question is not whether those means are taken from true things, which I do not deny, since I concede that setting truly belongs to the Sun at fixed and set times and places, but whether that means is the motion of the Sun, which I utterly deny can be drawn from the word "setting." That we may acknowledge the special wisdom of God from the fixed and certain rising and setting of the Sun and Moon, I do not deny, but gladly confess.

units.la: At dicit, argumentum prius defumtum est à motu reali Lunæ, ergo & posterius à motu reali Solis erit.
units.tr: But he says: "The former argument is taken from the real motion of the Moon; therefore the latter will also be taken from the real motion of the Sun."

units.la: Resp. Nec prius nec posterius argumentum ad motum istorum corporum cœlestium respicit, sed tantùm ad fixum eorum ordinem, quem Deus iis præfixit, ut statis temporibus & locis oriantur & occidant, qui Ortus & Occasus ipsis revera obtingunt. Ex quo denuo observato cadunt reliqua, quæ contra meam responsionem, quam sibi singit ad suum argumentum, reponit, quæ Lectori si lubeat videre licebit pag. 194. in fine. Nec evadet Wittichius, excipiendo &c.
units.tr: Reply: Neither the former nor the latter argument regards the motion of those heavenly bodies, but only their fixed order, which God prescribed to them, so that they rise and set at set times and places; and this rising and setting truly befall them. From this, observed again, the rest falls, which he objects against my answer, which he feigns for his own argument. The reader may see it, if he pleases, at p. 194, near the end: "Nor will Wittich escape by excepting, etc."

units.la: DCCCCXIV. Videamus nunc Instantias H. si quæ differant ab iis, quæ hactenus fuerunt examinatæ. Exististimat ille primùm p. 91. Soli competere cognitionem naturalem, esseque inter Solem & Intelligentem convenientiam in hoc tertio, nempe in vera rerum cognitione: Ac videtur esse in illorum sententiâ, qui omnibus rebus cognitionem quandam tribuunt, quæ potiùs explosione quàm refutatione digna, cùm sic magno periculo in Theologiâ & Philosophia res materiales cum immaterialibus confundat: ac quid illa sit naturalis Solis cognitio à rationali contradistincta nec intelligi nec explicari possit. Vide hîc Clariss. Claubergium Defens. Cartesianæ p. 585. & seqq. ubi cognitio illa naturalis fusè refutatur.
units.tr: 914. Let us now see H.'s instances, if any differ from those examined so far. He thinks first, at p. 91, that "the Sun has a natural cognition, and there is a convergence between the Sun and an intelligent being in this third point, namely in the true knowledge of things." He seems to be of the opinion of those who attribute to all things a certain cognition, which deserves rejection rather than refutation, since in this way it confuses material things with immaterial ones with great danger in theology and philosophy. Nor can it be understood or explained what that natural cognition of the Sun is, distinguished from rational cognition. See here the most illustrious Clauberg, Defence of Cartesian Philosophy, p. 585 and following, where that natural cognition is refuted at length.

units.la: DCCCCXV. Ait porro p.92. Violatam hic simplicem Scripturæ phrasin & interpretationem & sacra hujus comparationis contractam & violentam esse explicationem &c.
units.tr: 915. Moreover he says, p. 92, that here the simple phrasing and interpretation of Scripture is violated, and the explanation of this comparison is forced and violent, etc.

units.la: Resp. Verba sunt, præterea nihil, & mera principii petitio; quod si violenta, si contracta hæc comparationis explicatio, si pugnans est cum simplice Scripturæ phrasi, ratione aliquâ ex textu allatâ id demonstrandum fuisset, non simpliciter asserendum. Ego verò è contrario offendi, scopum Psalmistæ non requirere amplius, quam quod Soli occasus certo contingat statis temporibus & locis, non aliter ac si cognitione præditus omnia ad istum observandum direxisset.
units.tr: Reply: These are only words, nothing more, and a mere begging of the question. If this explanation of the comparison were forced and violent, if it clashed with the plain phrasing of Scripture, he should have shown this by some reasoning drawn from the text, not simply asserted it. I, on the contrary, have found that the Psalmist's purpose requires no more than that the setting of the sun happens with certainty at fixed times and places, just as if the one who wrote it had directed everything with knowledge towards this.

units.la: DCCCCXVI. Pergit H. p. 93. & inquit, me necessarias & formales corporis naturales operationes contingentes fecisse, imo sic omnino sustulisse; rationes ejus sunt, 1. si Soli occasus obtingit tantum, sequitur quod Sol occasum suum nesciat. 2. si Soli occasus obtingit, sequitur, Solis occasum non esse Solis occasum. Ergo Sol cognoscit tò non suum. pag. 94. repetit illud de Solis necessario, non contingente occasu, deque naturali Solis notitiâ art. 14.
units.tr: 916. He goes on, p. 93, and says that I have made the necessary and formal natural operations of the body contingent, indeed have entirely abolished them. His reasons are: (1) if the setting of the sun happens only contingently, it follows that the sun does not know its setting. (2) If the setting of the sun happens, it follows that the setting of the sun is not the sun's setting. Therefore the sun knows what is not its own. On p. 94 he repeats this about the sun's necessary, not contingent, setting, and about the natural knowledge of the sun, art. 14.

units.la: Resp. 1. Pudere te debebat talium illationum! Quid enim? an contingens est ex meâ sententiâ Solis occasus, quem ei a. certò b. statis temporibus c. per leges naturæ dico convenire? 2. absurdum vero non est, quod Sol proprie loquendo suum occasum nesciat, etiam si improprie recte & verè dicatur Occasum suum nôsse: imo absurda est tua illa, nescio quæ, naturalis cognitio, quam Soli proprie adscribis. 3. quæ vero ista connexio? si Soli occasus obtingit, ergo Solis occasus non est occasus Solis; an licebit inferre? si Christo Passio obtingit; ergo Christi passio non erit passio Christi. A page cum tali illatione! Profecto hæ tuæ ratiocinationes non erant tanti, ut putares, te justam habuisse materiam mecum expostulandi, quod rationibus meis dederim Deum &c. quæ à me sunt plane aliena.
units.tr: Reply: First, you ought to be ashamed of such inferences! For is the setting of the sun, in my view, contingent, when I say that it belongs to the sun (a) certainly, (b) at fixed times, (c) through the laws of nature? Second, it is not absurd that the sun, properly speaking, does not know its own setting, even though it is correctly and truly said, in an improper sense, to know its setting. Indeed your so-called natural knowledge, which you properly ascribe to the sun, is absurd. Third, what kind of connection is this? If the setting happens to the sun, therefore the setting of the sun is not the sun's setting. Could one infer: if the Passion happens to Christ, therefore the Passion of Christ will not be Christ's Passion? What a fine piece of reasoning! Your arguments were certainly not of such weight that you could think you had just cause to complain with me that you have given God to my reasons, etc., which are wholly foreign to me.

units.la: DCCCCXVII. Quæstiones vero, quas H. p. 94. art. 15. proponit cujuscunque sententiæ Philosophis & Mathematicis, tales sunt ut ad eas facile ex antecedentibus haberi responsiones possint. Neque sane operæ pretium est earum repetitione & ad singulas responsione lectorem morari. Videat Adversarius antecedentia, eaque ubi attente consideraverit satisfactum sibi ipse credo autumabit.
units.tr: 917. As for the questions which he (H., p. 94, art. 15) puts to the philosophers and mathematicians of every school, they are such that answers to them can easily be found from what has gone before. Nor is it worth the trouble to repeat them and detain the reader with a reply to each. Let my opponent look at the preceding discussion, and I believe that once he has considered it carefully he will think himself satisfied.

units.la: DCCCCXVIII. Objicit idem p. 96. contra id quod dixi, Soli occasum suum convenire per motum apparentem, neque tamen per id gloriæ Dei quicquam detrahi, inde sequi, 1. me statuere, quod sancti Dei viri Deum laudaverint pro Ortu Lunæ tealj, Solis apparente. 2. Stante meâ responsione sequi, sanctos Dei viros opera Dei erronee percepta falso coram Deo jactitasse, falso Solem & Lunam suos noscere Ortus & Occasus confessos esse, sicque (quod mirandum) gloriam quam Deo reddebant vanam & nullam fuisse, devotionemque Judæorum, qua Solem suum noscere occasum Deo confitebantur, eumque adeo laudabant, purum putum errorem esse. Ratio, quia secundum meam inversionem, inquit, gloria Dei ex eo elucet, quod Deus per leges naturæ Solem fixum & certum constituerit.
units.tr: 918. The same man objects (p. 96) to what I said, that the setting of the sun belongs to it through apparent motion, and that nothing is thereby taken from the glory of God. From this, he says, it follows: (1) that I hold that the holy men of God praised God for the rising of the moon and the sun as it appears. (2) On my answer, it follows that the holy men of God falsely boasted before God of works of God that they had perceived mistakenly, that they falsely confessed that the sun and the moon know their rising and setting, and so (a thing to be wondered at) that the glory they rendered to God was empty and nothing, and that the devotion of the Jews, by which they confessed to God that their sun knew its setting and so praised him, was sheer error. The reason, he says, is that according to my inversion the glory of God shines forth from this, that God by the laws of nature has established the sun as fixed and certain.

units.la: Resp. Ad primum. Distinguere oportuisset adversarium inter motum Solis apparentem & occasum apparentem. Occasum non apparentem, sed verum Soli competere vereque assignatum à Psalmista existimo, sed an per motum Solis realem an apparentem conveniat, significari ab eo nego; ego vero ex ratione, motui ejus apparenti adscribi debere, didici. Ad secundum, me, quod jubet, mirari maximopere, quo artificio tot sequelas ex meis verbis potuerit exprimere. Occultum enim valde esse oportet, & a communi usu remotam. Quis enim haec connectat: Gloria Dei ex eo elucet, quod Deus per leges naturae eum (nempe Solis occasum, non Solem ut ipse autumat) fixum & certum constituerit: ergo Sancti Dei Viri opera Dei erronea perceperunt &c. Scopae dissolutae! Verum dum cogito, video ex hoc solo fonte omnes has sequelas promanasse, quod existimet me sentire, hic falsi quid de Sole Psalterem enunciasse vel docuisse, quam meam sententiam nullibi potuerit monstrare. Solem vere noscere Occasum suum cum Psalmista allero, sed illud noscere proprie intelligi debere nego. Quis ergo sit sensus proprius disquiritur? at quem ego statuam superius sat manifestum factum.
units.tr: Answer. To the first point: my opponent ought to have distinguished between the apparent motion of the sun and its apparent setting. I think the setting that belongs to the sun is not apparent but real, and that it is truly ascribed to it by the Psalmist; but I deny that he means it belongs to the sun through its real motion rather than its apparent motion. I have learned from reason that it must be ascribed to its apparent motion. To the second point: I am to be greatly astonished, as he bids me, by the art with which he has been able to draw so many consequences from my words. For that must be very hidden and remote from common usage. For who would connect these things: "The glory of God shines forth from this, that God by the laws of nature has established it (namely the setting of the sun, not the sun, as he claims) as fixed and certain": therefore the holy men of God perceived the works of God erroneously, and so on? Loose brooms! Yet when I reflect, I see that all these consequences have sprung from this single source: he thinks I have asserted or taught that the Psalmist has pronounced something false about the sun, which he could never show to be my opinion. I agree that the sun truly knows its setting with the Psalmist, but I deny that this "knowing" must be understood in its proper sense. What then is the proper sense? That is being investigated. But the sense I set out above has been made quite plain.

units.la: DCCCCXIX. Per haec etiam sufficienter responsum putem ad ea, quae M. p. 179. & seqq. producit pro loco Psalm. civ. Nam 1. Minor ipsius argumenti negatur una cum probatione ejus, cum ostensum sit, Solem posse dici vere nosse, sed improprie, occasum suum, etiamsi nullus motus ei competat, neque comparatio aliqua in sacris literis est ulterius extendenda, quam circumstantiae & scopus textus requirunt: alias ἰδίᾳ ἐπιλύσει non mentis Spiritus Sancti, de qua hic disquirimus, accepta serenda. 2. quia confitetur antagonista, se non posse assequi, quomodo ex hypothesi Cartesii & Copernici Soli competat Occasus, (quod tam facile est, & nemo, qui vel obiter Astronomiam gustavit, ignorat;) quis non judicabit melius ipsum facturum fuisse, si ab argumento hoc ex parte Astronomico tractando manum abstinuisset? Quod si illud ergo discere cupiat, adeat Gassendi Institut. Astronom. vel Blacu de usu Globorum, vel etiam Keplèri Epit. Astronom. Copernicanae, & clare id ab iis demonstrari percipiet. Videat etiam ea quae ex Keplero supra art. 867. citavi.
units.tr: 919. I think that this is also a sufficient reply to what he brings forward from M. (p. 179 and following) concerning the passage Psalm 104. For: (1) the minor premise of his argument is denied, along with its proof, since it has been shown that the sun can be said to truly know its setting, though improperly, even if no motion belongs to it; nor is any comparison in Holy Scripture to be extended further than the circumstances and the scope of the text require; otherwise one would be bringing in a private interpretation [ἰδίᾳ ἐπιλύσει], not the mind of the Holy Spirit, which is what we are investigating here. (2) Because my opponent confesses that he cannot work out how, on the hypothesis of Descartes and Copernicus, setting belongs to the sun (which is so easy, and which no one who has even briefly tasted astronomy fails to know). Who would not judge that he would have done better to keep his hands off this argument so far as it concerns astronomy? But if he wishes to learn it, let him consult Gassendi's Institutio astronomica, or Blaeu's work on the use of globes, or even Kepler's Epitome of Copernican Astronomy, and he will perceive that these demonstrate it clearly. Let him also look at what I cited from Kepler above, article 867.

units.la: 3. Principii petitio est supra refutata, quando in secundo suo argumento pro confesso assumit, quod motus Solis sit argumentum, quo à Psalmista gloria Dei celebratur. Si cui libet M. pag. 179. & seqq. cum nostris conferre, satisfactum ei abunde percipiet.
units.tr: (3) He has already been refuted above in the matter of begging the question, since in his second argument he takes it for granted that the motion of the sun is the argument by which the glory of God is celebrated by the Psalmist. If anyone cares to compare M. p. 179 and following with our remarks, he will perceive that he has been abundantly satisfied.

units.la: DCCCCXX. Inquit pag. 206. Circa exortum Solis aliò providentia divina sese habet ut circa pluviam. Atqui pluere facit activa influentia tiā in pluviam : Ergo & eadem Solem oriri facit.
units.tr: 920. He says (p. 206): "Concerning the rising of the sun, divine providence stands in the same relation as it does to rain. But the active influence of God brings about rain. Therefore the same active influence makes the sun rise."

units.la: Resp. Christi intentio est docere, & Solis exortum & pluviæ casum providentiæ divinæ esse accepta ferenda, & in eo est tertium convenientiæ, non vero utrumque eodem modo ab eadem pendere, vel æquè Solis exortum fieri per actívam influentiam in Solem ac pluviæ casus per actívam influentiam in aquæ guttas, nisi eodem modo velis inferre, etiam corpus Solis Terram attingere, ut guttæ pluviæ faciunt &c.
units.tr: Answer. Christ's intention is to teach that both the rising of the sun and the falling of rain are to be ascribed to divine providence, and in this lies the third point of comparison. But it does not follow that both depend on the same thing in the same way, or that the rising of the sun happens through active influence on the sun just as the fall of rain happens through active influence on the drops of water, unless you wish to infer in the same way that the body of the sun touches the earth, as raindrops do, and so on.

units.la: DCCCCXXI. Objicit hic etiam H. p. 99. Hoc effatum Christi à me dissectum, alterum ad vulgi errorem, alterum ad veritatem & rem ipsam esse dictum &c. Ad quæ lectoris gratiâ observo, ab Adversario mihi tribui responsionem circa hunc locum, qualis in meâ Dissertatione non appareret, ac proinde ab ipso inaniter verba profundi.
units.tr: 922. In answer to my true reply he objects that I ought to have proved that Christ in those words speaks one way of the rising of the Sun and another way of the falling of rain.

units.la: DCCCCCXXII. Ad veram autem meam responsionem excipit, probandum mihi fuisse, Christum in suis istis verbis aliter de Solis ortu, aliter de pluviæ casu loqui.
units.tr: 922. But against my true answer he objects that I "ought to have proved that Christ, in these words, speaks of the rising of the sun in one way and of the falling of rain in another."

units.la: Resp. At tibi tanquam opponenti ostendendum erat, ex verbis Christi sequi, in omnibus, inter pluviæ casum & exortum Solis esse paritatem, cùm ex verbis Christi non aliud posse colligi, quàm & Solis ortum & pluviæ casum providentiæ divinæ accepta ferenda.
units.tr: Answer. But you, as the opponent, were obliged to show that from Christ's words it follows that in all respects there is a parallel between the fall of rain and the rising of the sun, since from Christ's words nothing else can be gathered than that both the rising of the sun and the falling of rain are to be ascribed to divine providence.

units.la: DCCCCXXIII. Reliqua quæ H. habet à pag. 101. ad 104. quòd ad summam rei nihil faciant, & respiciant tantum verba Dissertationum, quæ hic sunt immutata, clariorque responsio ad hunc locum data sit, non est operæ pretium examinare. Tota enim res eò redit; an ex eo, quòd Christus dicit, Deum facere ut Sol exoriatur super justos & injustos, sequatur, istum Solis ortum ejusdem motui reali esse acceptum ferendum, quod ego nego, donec ab opponentibus, quibus partes probandi incumbunt, clarius fuerit probatum.
units.tr: 923. It is not worth our while to examine the rest of what H. says, from pp. 101 to 104, since it comes to nothing of substance and deals only with the wording of the Dissertations, which has been left unchanged here, and a clearer reply has been given to this point. The whole matter comes down to this: does it follow from Christ's saying that God causes the sun to rise on the just and the unjust that this rising of the sun is to be attributed to its own real motion? I deny it, until the opponents, on whom the burden of proof lies, have proved it more clearly.

units.la: DCCCCXXIV. Tandem quod habet in contrarium M. pag. 184. est mera ignoratio Elenchi. Non enim quæritur, an Soli conveniat Ortus realis, sed an ille ortus realis ei competat ex motu proprio, an ex motu Terræ? Neutrum determinat Scriptura, posterius docet ratio.
units.tr: 924. Finally, what M. says to the contrary at p. 184 is a plain failure to grasp the point at issue. The question is not whether the sun has a real rising, but whether that real rising belongs to it by its own motion, or by the motion of the earth. Scripture decides neither; reason teaches the latter.

units.la: CAPUT XLIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XLIX.

units.la: Adducitur locus Eccles. I. 4, 5. & cum sententia nostra conciliatur.
units.tr: Ecclesiastes 1:4, 5 is cited and reconciled with our view.

units.la: DCCCCXXV. Sequitur Eccles. I. 4, 5. cujus hæc sunt verba: Generatio una abit, & altera advenit, quamvis Terra in seculum permaneat. Oritur Sol & occidit Sol, iterumque ad locum suum adspirat ubi oriatur. Hic Fullerus sese invenisse putat, non quod pueri in fabâ, sed quia ejus verba nonnisi Rhetoricationes continent, ea adscribere nolui; ex responsione verò nostrâ patebit, triumphi hic nullam ei fuisse causam decantandi. B. etiam D. pag. 29. quædam argumenta ex hoc loco sibi videtur exculpere: Hæc argumenta, Ecclesiastæ puta, procul dubio inferunt realem rerum mutationem, variationem, & ad pristinum statum reversionem; ac proinde realem Solis ortum & occasum, & ad locum ortus reversionem, ac per consequens, non ex mera apparentia; nam ineptum esset tale argumentum, Sol movetur oritur & occidit apparenter, secundum hominum opinionem, licet non revera, ergo datur rerum realis vicissitudo: at tum est argumentum optimum, cum verba de motu, ortu & occasu Solis reali intelliguntur. Præterea, cum alia argumenta, primum, tertium & quartum desumantur à rebus in quibus realis & non merè apparens vicissitudo inest, absonum erit statuere, secundum desumtum esse à subjecto, in quo merè apparens & non realu inest vicissitudo. Denique & in ipsa voce adspirare inest vis ad idem probandum. Nam constat, similitudinem esse desumtam ab animalibus, & præsertim equis currentibus, & rursus adspirantibus ad stabula, unde prius exicrant. Hæ ergo sunt partes comparationis, ut animalia sese habent ad reversionem ad stabula, unde prius egressa sunt, ita & Sol sese habet ad reversionem versus locum ortus, unde prius prodierat: At si negemus realem & statuamus merè apparentem Solis motum, inepta erit plane tota similitudo.
units.tr: DCCCCXXV. Next comes Ecclesiastes 1:4, 5, whose words are: One generation passeth away, and another cometh; but the earth abideth for ever. The sun also riseth, and the sun goeth down, and hasteth to his place where he arose. Fuller thinks he has found something here, but I did not wish to set down his words, which contain nothing but rhetorical flourishes, not something a boy would find in a bean. Our reply will show that he has no cause to sing of triumph here. B. also thinks he can extract some arguments from this passage, on p. 29 of D.: These arguments, namely of the Preacher, undoubtedly imply a real change and variation of things, and a return to their former state; and therefore a real rising and setting of the sun, and a return to the place of its rising, and consequently not a mere appearance. For it would be a foolish argument to say: the sun moves, rises and sets apparently, according to human opinion, though not in reality; therefore there is a real succession of things. But the argument is excellent only if the words about the motion, rising and setting of the sun are understood of a real motion. Moreover, since the other arguments, the first, third and fourth, are drawn from things in which a real and not merely apparent change is present, it would be absurd to hold that the second is drawn from a subject in which only an apparent and not a real change is present. Finally, the very word "hasteth" contains a force that proves the same thing. For it is well known that the comparison is taken from animals, especially running horses, which hasten back to the stables from which they came out. These, then, are the parts of the comparison: as animals relate to a return to the stables from which they went out, so the sun relates to a return to the place of its rising from which it had come. But if we deny a real motion and assert that the motion of the sun is merely apparent, the whole comparison will be plainly pointless.

units.la: Resp. 1. Hic locus bene expensus nobis itidem non obest. Scopus Salomonis est, ut ex verf. 2. apparet, ostendere, vanitatem esse in omnibus rebus, nihilque esse consistens firmum & stabile. Id probat ex obviis quibuscunque rebus. Versu tertio demonstrat hoc ex vanis hominum consiliis & laboribus. Dein verf. 4. ex vicissitudine generationis humanæ, quod uno generato alter moriatur & occidat, amplificans hoc à contrario, quod Terra huic vicissitudini non sit obnoxia. Quemadmodum dum enim arborum folia, veteribus decidentibus, nova succrescunt, manente interim eâdem arbore: ita & Terra, quæ est quasi fulcrum omnium ipsi innitentium, eadem manet, mutatis hominibus in eâ viventibus. Quando ergo Terra dicitur, in sæculum permanere, non designatur Terræ situs vel etiam quies, sed duratio & perpetuitas, quod generationibus mutatis illa non ita sit mutationi obnoxia, quod etsi animantibus & hominibus vicissitudines generationis contingant, illa tamen non intereat, aliaque generetur, sed eadem persistat. Versu 5. id porro exemplo ortus & occasus Solis declarat. Sed accommodat hic sese manifestè ad ea, quæ sensibus obvia sunt, eaque exprimit locutionibus & formulis receptis, etiamsi ex præjudiciis habeant ortum. Constat id primo ex eo, quia hic liber est populariter scriptus ἐξωπερικὸς, teste Fayo in Ecclesiastén. Secundo ex ipsis rebus, quibus veritatem probat, quæ sunt obviæ & communes, quemadmodum idem Fayus ad hunc versum expresse docet. Haec à Salomone dicuntur ad vulgi opinionem & sensum paucis verbis. Tertio ex verbis oriri & occidere, quæ ex præjudicio ortum habere declaravimus superius, Unde & Hebraei ponunt Solis ingressum pro occasu, quia sub Terræ labi & condi videtur, Adventum pro ortu, verba sunt Fayi ad versum quartum. Itaque hæc locutio vulgaris, oritur Sol & occidit, qua utitur Salomon, nihil obest veritati nostræ sententiæ. 2. Argumentum Ecclesiastæ tale est, Realis est vicissitudo in eo, quòd Sol nunc supra Terram conspiciatur per ortum, nunc sub illa recondatur per occasum: atque ita situm suum multis modis variet, (sive autem hoc fieret propter Terræ sive propter Cæli motum nihil hic referebat,) Ergo datur rerum vicissitudo. 3. Ecclesiastæ sufficiebat, si probaret vicissitudinem exemplis quibusdam obviis: quod inter alia fecit exemplo Solis ortus & occasus, neque opus erat ut accuratè determinaret, cuinam subjecto inesset ista vicissitudo per motum realem, num Terræ, an vero Soli? Interim nihil vetabat, quin hanc vicissitudinem locutione vulgari exprimeret, quæ ut à vulgo usurpatur eam motui reali Solis adscribit. 4. Ipsa vox adspirare satis ostendit vulgarem locutionem hic adhiberi præjudicio innitentem, ex quâ ut non licet inferre, Soli competere anhelationem, & defatigationem, ita nec ei competere motum. Comparatio ergo in eo consistit, quòd quemadmodum equi adspirent ad stabula, unde fuerunt egressi, ita Sol tam celeriter situm variet, ut similis sit ei, atque ut talis appareat, qui adeo celeriter movetur, ut quasi contentione quadam ad illum locum conetur redire, unde fuerat visus egredi.
units.tr: Answer 1. When this passage is weighed carefully, it does not harm us either. Solomon's aim, as verse 2 shows, is to demonstrate that there is vanity in all things, and that nothing is firm and stable. He proves this from all sorts of ordinary things. In verse 3 he shows it from the vain counsels and labours of men. Then in verse 4, from the succession of human generations, namely that when one is born another dies and passes away, he enlarges the point by contrast: the earth is not subject to this succession. For just as, when the old leaves of trees fall, new ones grow while the same tree remains, so the earth, which is as it were the support of all things resting upon it, remains the same though the men living on it are changed. When, therefore, the earth is said to remain for ever, what is meant is not the earth's position or even its rest, but its duration and perpetuity: that, while generations change, it is not so subject to change; and that, although living creatures and men undergo the succession of generation, it does not perish and another is not produced in its place, but it persists the same. In verse 5 he declares this by the example of the rising and setting of the sun. But here he clearly accommodates himself to what is obvious to the senses, and expresses it in received phrases and formulas, even though these have their origin in prejudice. This is clear, first, from the fact that this book is written in a popular manner, exoterikos [ἐξωτερικός], as Fayus testifies on Ecclesiastes. Second, from the things themselves by which he proves the truth, which are obvious and common, as the same Fayus expressly teaches on this verse: These things are said by Solomon according to the opinion and sense of the common people, in few words. Third, from the words "to rise" and "to set", which, as we have shown above, have their origin in prejudice: Hence also the Hebrews use the entering of the sun for its setting, because it seems to slip and hide under the earth, and its arrival for its rising, are the words of Fayus on verse 4. Therefore this common expression, the sun riseth and goeth down, which Solomon uses, does nothing to hurt the truth of our view. 2. The Preacher's argument is this: There is a real change in that the sun is now seen above the earth at its rising, and now hidden under it at its setting; and so it varies its position in many ways. (Whether this happens because of the motion of the earth or of the heavens makes no difference here.) Therefore there is a change of things. 3. It was enough for the Preacher to prove the change by some obvious examples. Among others he did this by the example of the sun's rising and setting, and there was no need for him to determine precisely in which subject this change inheres through real motion, whether in the earth or in the sun. Nothing prevented him from expressing this change in common speech, which, as the common people use it, ascribes it to the real motion of the sun. 4. The very word hasten sufficiently shows that common speech, resting on prejudice, is used here. Just as it does not follow from this that breathlessness and weariness belong to the sun, so it does not follow that motion does. The comparison therefore consists in this: as horses hasten back to the stables from which they came out, so the sun changes its position so swiftly that it is like, and appears to be, something that moves so fast that it strives, as it were, with some effort to return to the place from which it had been seen to come out.

units.la: DCCCCXXVI. Contra primam responsionem Inst, J. B. p. 198.
units.tr: DCCCCXXVI. Against the first answer, Inst., J. B. p. 198.

units.la: Non dicere Fayum, librum illum ita exotericè scriptum, ut de naturalibus agat secundùm apparentiam, non exactam rei veritatem, verùm ita loquitur &c.
units.tr: Fayus does not say that that book is written so exoterically that it treats of natural things according to appearance, not the exact truth of the thing; but he speaks thus, etc.

units.la: Resp. Argumentum meum primum informâ tale est: In libro ἐξωτεϱικῶν non possunt non occurrere locutiones vulgares ex praejudiciis ortum habentes. At hic liber est ἐξωτεϱικὸς, reste Fayo. Non hic Majori auctoritatem Fayi adjecceram, sed Minori. Major vero suprà probata est. Quod enim non tam limatè & subtiliter est scriptum, quàm ea quae Philosophi aculeatis suis sententiis exprimere solent, in eo reperiri locutiones ex praejudiciis ortum habentes, sed receptas communiter, non est mirum. Adde, quod cum Fayus ita ἐξωτεϱικὸν hunc librum dicat, ut in eo sint dicta ad vulgi opinionem, etiam apparet, Majorem meam ejus auctoritate comprobari.
units.tr: Answer. My first argument, in form, is this: In a book that is exoterikon [ἐξωτερικῶν], common expressions that have their origin in prejudice cannot but occur. But this book is exoterikos [ἐξωτερικός], as Fayus testifies. I did not add Fayus's authority to the major premise here, but to the minor. The major premise, however, was proved above. For it is not surprising that expressions having their origin in prejudice, but commonly received, are found in a work that is not written as closely and subtly as those things which philosophers are accustomed to express in their pointed sentences. Add that, since Fayus calls this book so exoterikos that it contains things said according to the opinion of the common people, it also appears that my major premise is confirmed by his authority.

units.la: Instat M. p. 186. Non sequi Fayus hoc dicit, ergo est verum.
units.tr: M. p. 186 insists: Fayus does not say this, therefore it is true.

units.la: Resp. Non auctoritate Fayi simpliciter nitor, sed adduxi, quatenus Fayus ad rem ipsam provocat, quae probat, hunc librum esse ἐξωτεϱικον.
units.tr: Answer. I do not rest simply on the authority of Fayus, but I cited him in so far as Fayus appeals to the matter itself, which proves that this book is exoterikon.

units.la: DCCCCXXVII. Inst. 2. B. p. 198. Me insigni afficere Fayum injuria, quòd eum citem ut talem, qui in eadem cum Copernicanis & Cartesianis sententiis docuerit & crediderit, Ecclesiasten de Ortu & Occasu Solis agere tantùm secundùm apparentiam & opinionem vulgi, cùm se totum in sententiâ contrariâ prodat &c.
units.tr: DCCCCXXVII. Inst. 2, B. p. 198. He charges me with a gross injustice to Fayus, because I cite him as one who taught and believed, in agreement with the Copernicans and Cartesians, that Ecclesiastes speaks of the rising and setting of the sun only according to appearance and the opinion of the common people, whereas he betrays himself wholly in the contrary view, etc.

units.la: Resp. Ego Fayum cito, quatenus in genere favet illi sententiae, Scripturam quaedam dicere ad vulgi opinionem, hoc est, uti formulis receptis, etiamsi ex opinione erroneâ habeant ortum, & quatenus in citato loco agnoscit tales locutiones, non vero, quod circa hanc specialem quaestionem à parte stet Copernici vel Cartesii, quod mihi nunquam in mentem venit. Audiamus verba Fayi ad versum 4, ex quibus uti patebit (quod nunquam negavi) eum Soli motum, Terrae quietem assignare; ita manifestum erit generali nostrae sententiae patrocinari, pro quâ hic ipsum citavi: Sol oritur & Occidit, nec unquam uno eodemque loco consistit. Hebraei ponunt SOLIS INGRESSVM pro Occasu, quia SOL SVB TERRAS LABI ET CONDI VIDETVR, ADVENTVM pro ortu. Notat autem velocem Solis cursum verbo ענב, quod sorbere vel absorbere significat, quod hauriendi voce Latini denotant, Medium Sol igneus orbem hauserat, ait Virgilius. Significat etiam anhelare, ut Solis cursus citissimus ita denotetur, quod tanquam gigas NB exultat ad currendum viam suam, à summo Coelo egrediens usque ad suum Coelum anhelanti similis Psalm. XIX. quod etiam Poëta dicunt; qui solus circumvolvi ac gyrari cernitur: cùm caeteri Planetae in longum ferri putentur. Tanta autem est celeritas motus solaris, ut una hora Sol conficiat 2884 milliaria, triplicemque habet motum, diurnum, quo 24 horarum tempore nos & Antipodas visit singulis diebus motu primi mobilis: alterum sibi proprium, quo conficit fere singulis diebus gradum unum. Tertium quo spatio 100 annorum gradum unum peragit. Ex quibus motibus dierum, noctium, aequinoctiorum, solstitiorum varietates exsurgunt. Haec autem à Salomone dicuntur AD VUL-GI OPINIONEM ET SENSUM, paucis verbis. Anhelat ad locum suum ex quo ortus est per sua vestigia per Meridiem ad Occasum & Septentrionem decurrens. Neque favent huiusmodi tropi illorum sententiae, qui Solem animatum esse dixerunt. Nam rebus anima expertibus saepissimè attribuuntur ea, quae conveniunt animantibus, sed huiusmodi verbis significatur Solis multiplex vertigo, non ab anima interna (quam non habet) sed à forma sibi à Deo data proprietate profecta. Quod enim omnia audire, videre, lustrare dicitur, id facit non tanquam Dominus, sed tanquam famulus. Unde nomen habet שמש, quod famulari significat. Nunc verò sic argumentor: si eae locutiones sunt vulgares, in quibus Soli tribuuntur ea, quae conveniunt animantibus, propterea quia ex ratione colligitur, Solem non esse animatum; ergo etiam eae locutiones erunt vulgares, in quibus Soli tribuuntur ea, quae convenium rebus, quae è planitie in altum assurgunt, propterea quia ex ratione colligitur, Soli non competere, ut ex planitie in altum assurgat: Sed verum est prius ex mente Fayi; aliam enim rationem afferre non potest, quare haec dicta vulgariter sint accipienda: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: Answer. I cite Fayus in so far as he generally favours that opinion, that Scripture says some things according to the opinion of the common people, that is, uses received formulas even though they have their origin in an erroneous opinion; and in so far as in the passage cited he acknowledges such expressions. I do not cite him because on this particular question he takes the side of Copernicus or Descartes, which never came into my mind. Let us hear the words of Fayus on verse 4, from which it will be plain (what I never denied) that he assigns motion to the sun and rest to the earth; thus it will be clear that he supports our general view, for which I cited him here: The sun riseth and goeth down, and never stays in one and the same place. The Hebrews use the ENTERING OF THE SUN for its setting, because THE SUN SEEMS TO SLIP AND HIDE UNDER THE EARTH, and its ARRIVAL for its rising. He marks the swift course of the sun by the verb [ענב], which means to swallow or absorb, which Latin speakers denote by the word for drinking: The fiery sun had drunk up the middle of the sky, says Virgil. It also means to pant, so that the very swift course of the sun is denoted, as a giant exults with NB to run its course, going out from the highest heaven to its own heaven, like one panting, Psalm 19; which the poets also say, who see only the sun turning and wheeling round, while the other planets are thought to be carried in a straight line. Moreover, the speed of the solar motion is so great that in one hour the sun covers 2884 miles, and it has a threefold motion: the daily motion, by which in the space of 24 hours it visits us and our antipodes every day by the motion of the first mover; another motion proper to itself, by which it covers almost one degree each day; and a third, by which it covers one degree in the space of 100 years. From these motions arise the variations of days, nights, equinoxes and solstices. These things, however, are said by Solomon ACCORDING TO THE OPINION AND SENSE OF THE COMMON PEOPLE, in few words. It pants towards its place from which it rose, running through its own tracks from the south to the west and the north. Nor do figures of this kind favour the view of those who have said that the sun is animate. For things without a soul are very often given what belongs to living beings; but by such words is signified the sun's manifold whirling, proceeding not from an inner soul (which it does not have) but from a property given to it by God. For when it is said that it hears, sees and surveys all things, it does this not as a lord but as a servant. Hence it has its name [שמש], which means to serve. Now I argue thus: if those expressions are common in which the sun is given what belongs to living beings, because from reason it is gathered that the sun is not animate; then those expressions too will be common in which the sun is given what belongs to things that rise from a plain on high, because from reason it is gathered that it does not belong to the sun to rise from a plain on high. But the first is true according to the mind of Fayus, for he cannot give another reason why these things should be taken in a common sense. Therefore the second is true too.

units.la: DCCCCXXVIII. Inst. 3. M. p. 185.
units.tr: DCCCCXXVIII. Inst. 3. M. p. 185.

units.la: Accommodet se per nos quidem ad ea, quae sensibus sunt obvia, dummodo veritatem rei non deserat, & veritatem probandam simul ac suam auctoritatem infalibilitatemque in discrimen non adducat argumentis falsis & in speciem tantum veri, quod fieret, si ex motu apparente tantum verum concluderet.
units.tr: He accommodates himself to us, indeed, to those things which are obvious to the senses, provided he does not depart from the truth of the matter, and does not endanger the truth to be proved, and at the same time his own authority and infallibility, by false arguments which have only the appearance of truth. This would happen if he concluded a truth merely from apparent motion.

units.la: Resp. Concludit Ecclesiastes ex variatione situs, quae Soli obtigit, rerum vicissitudinem, quae situs variatio vera est, verumque argumentum suppeditat, neque quicquam est in nostra sententia, quod veritatem, auctoritatem & infallibilitatem Scripturae in discrimen adducat.
units.tr: Reply. Ecclesiastes concludes from the change of position that the sun undergoes the vicissitude of things. This change of position is real, and it supplies a true argument. Nothing in our view endangers the truth, authority, or infallibility of Scripture.

units.la: DCCCCXXIX. Contra secundam responsionem instat B. p. 201.
units.tr: DCCCCXXIX. He presses again against the second reply. B. p. 201.

units.la: Medium probationis rerum vicissitudinis desumtum à Sole, non à Terra, adeoque à me immutari argumentationem Ecclesiastae, qui argumentetur ab ipso Ortu & Occasu Soli ita competentibus, ut propterea Bestiis anhelantibus ad stabula bula sua possit comparari; qua similitudo nullo modo locum habere poterit, si Sol in sese quiescens propter motum Terra conspiciatur, modo quasi oriens modo quasi occidens &c. Videat Lector, si lubet, plenius p. 201. & 202. quae hic contracte proposui.
units.tr: The middle term of the proof of the vicissitude of things is taken from the Sun, not from the Earth; and so I change the argument of Ecclesiastes, who argues from the very rising and setting of the Sun, which belong to it in such a way that for this reason he may be compared to beasts panting towards their stalls. This likeness could in no way hold if the Sun is seen as resting in itself, because of the motion of the Earth, appearing now as rising, now as setting, and so on. The Reader may, if he likes, see more fully on pages 201 and 202 what I have here set out in brief.

units.la: Resp. 1. Medium probationis Ecclesiastae desumtum esse a Sole non nego, cum expresse dicam, illud ab ortu & occasu Solis petitum, qui ortus & occasus cum denotet apparitionem & occultationem sub Horizonte, non Terrae, sed Soli recte adscribitur. Argumentum itaque Ecclesiastae a me nequaquam immutatur. 2. Tota vis argumenti in similitudine ista consistit, quod Sol comparetur cum bestiis ad stabula sua anhelantibus, quam non inferre motum Solis realem responsione quarta ostendi.
units.tr: Reply 1. I do not deny that the middle term of Ecclesiastes' proof is taken from the Sun, since I expressly say that it is drawn from the rising and setting of the Sun. Since rising and setting denote appearance and disappearance below the horizon, they are rightly ascribed to the Sun, not to the Earth. So the argument of Ecclesiastes is by no means changed by me. 2. The whole force of the argument consists in that likeness, that the Sun is compared with beasts panting towards their stalls. I showed in my fourth reply that this likeness does not imply a real motion of the Sun.

units.la: DCCCCXXX. Sic M. p. 187. Argumentum Ecclesiastae non est tale, ille enim verbis Oriri, Occidere, aspirare, non argumentatur a passione quadam, sive denominatione externa, quae Soli accidat, qualis est tò conspici, sed utitur verbis actionem aliquam in Sole denotantibus.
units.tr: DCCCCXXX. Thus M. p. 187. The argument of Ecclesiastes is not of this kind. For in the words "rises," "sets," and "pants" he does not argue from some passion or external designation which befalls the Sun, such as being seen (τὸ conspici), but he uses words that denote some action in the Sun.

units.la: Resp. Verba ista, ut superius dictum, prout a vulgo inventa sunt & actionem significant, & passionem, cum sint verba non transeuntia, sed immanentia. At a Spiritu Sancto usurpantur tantum ad passionem denotandam, actione & agente non determinatis.
units.tr: Reply. These words, as said above, are used by common speech and signify both action and passion, since they are intransitive, or immanent, verbs. But the Holy Spirit uses them only to denote a passion, without fixing the action or the agent.

units.la: DCCCCXXXI. Inst. B. p. 203. contra responsionem tertiam, Ecclesiastem in exemplo Solis tali uti phraseologia, quae per se notet motum Solis, ita ut non necesse sit hic disputare, an opus fuerit Ecclesiastae ad scopum suum attingendum determinare, cui subjecto proprie insit motus, Soline an vero Terra, sufficere ut ostendatur, eum uti tali modo loquendi, qui per se cogitationes legentium & audientium ducit ad conceptum motus solaris, ita ut vix facilior & commodior occurreret ei, qui expresse intenderet docere motum solarem: saltem in lingua Hebraea phraseologiam aptiorem non dari certum est &c.
units.tr: DCCCCXXXI. He presses, B. p. 203, against the third reply: Ecclesiastes, in the example of the Sun, uses such a phraseology as in itself denotes the motion of the Sun. So it is not necessary to dispute here whether it was needful for Ecclesiastes, in order to reach his aim, to determine to which subject motion properly belongs, the Sun or the Earth. It is enough to show that he uses such a mode of speaking as in itself leads the thoughts of readers and hearers to the concept of solar motion, so that a plainer and more suitable way would scarcely have occurred to one who expressly intended to teach solar motion. At least it is certain that in the Hebrew language no more apt phraseology is available, and so on.

units.la: Resp. 1. Si ex sola phraseologia sit argumentandum non attentis circumstantiis textus & scopo, ergo Soli erit notitia adscribenda, anhelatio & defatigatio, ingressus sub terras, vita & quae non alia, quia secundum hanc instantiam sufficit ostendere; Scripturam uti tali modo loquendi, qui per se cogitationes legentiu & audientium ducit ad conceptum notitia, anhelationis, defatigationis, solaris ingressu sub Terras &c. ita ut vix facilior occurreret ei qui expresse intenderet docere notitiam, vitam & defatigationem solarem &c. 2. Itaque omnino necesse est d.sputare, an opus fuerit Ecclesiasten ad scopum suum attingendum determinare, cuinam subjecto proprie insit motus. Si enim ad scopum nihil attineat, censendumne erit, frustra & extra scopum aliquid determinâsse?
units.tr: Reply 1. If one is to argue from phraseology alone, without attention to the circumstances of the text and its aim, then knowledge, panting, weariness, entering under the earth, life, and whatever else must be ascribed to the Sun. For by this instance it suffices to show that Scripture uses such a mode of speaking as in itself leads the thoughts of readers and hearers to the concept of knowledge, panting, weariness, and the Sun's entering under the earth, and so on, so that a plainer way would scarcely occur to one who expressly intended to teach the knowledge, life, and weariness of the Sun, and so on. 2. Therefore it is altogether necessary to dispute whether it was needful for Ecclesiastes, in order to reach his aim, to determine to which subject motion properly belongs. For if it had nothing to do with his aim, will it not have to be judged that he determined something to no purpose and beside his aim?

units.la: DCCCCXXXII. Inst. ad quartam responsionem B. p. 204. Si vox adspirare spectat ad vulgarem locutionem explicandam, ergo ratio explicationis est quaerenda in apta comparatione partium similitudinis, cumque sit argumentum à similibus, quaerenda est comparatio in qualitate, quæ hic non alia potest dari quàm celeritas, & talis est justa & totalis dispositio argumenti: Qualis est celeritas equi adspirantis ad stabulum, talis est celeritas Solis tendentis in occasum & locum ortus.
units.tr: DCCCCXXXII. On the fourth reply, B. p. 204. If the word "pants" looks to the explanation of common speech, then the ground of the explanation must be sought in an apt comparison of the parts of the likeness. Since the argument is from likenesses, the comparison must be sought in the quality involved, which here can be none other than speed. And such is the just and complete arrangement of the argument: as is the speed of a horse panting towards its stall, so is the speed of the Sun hastening towards its setting and back to the place of its rising.

units.la: Resp. Apta comparatio partium similitudinis consistit in celeritate variationis sitûs, & sic erit hæc julta dispositio; Qualis est celeritas equi adspirantis ad stabulum, talis est celeritas variationis situs in corpore solari, qua fit, ut jam in ortu, postea versus occasum, ac tandem iterum in loco Ortus conspiciatur.
units.tr: Reply. An apt comparison of the parts of the likeness consists in the speed of the change of position. So the just arrangement will be this: as is the speed of a horse panting towards its stall, so is the speed of the change of position in the solar body, by which it comes about that it is now seen at its rising, afterwards towards its setting, and at last again in the place of its rising.

units.la: M. ad tertiam & quartam responsionem nihil habet, p. 187, 184. quod non vel hîc, vel in antecedentibus refutatum inveniat lector.
units.tr: M. has nothing against the third and fourth replies (pp. 187, 184) which the reader will not find refuted either here or in what has gone before.

units.la: DCCCCXXXIII. H. p. 10. Si Ecclesiastes de pluribus corporibus naturalibus proprie realiter & secundùm eorum natura veritatem hic loci agit, sequitur illum de altero quoque, putà de Sole, ejusque ab Ortu in Occasum motu proprie & realiter & secundùm natura ejus veritatem agere; Sed verum est Antecedens. Ergò. Ratio Majoris, cùm hic loci Rex & Physicus post Adamum sapientissimus de multis naturalibus in specie vere & secundum eorum naturam agat, ratio nulla dari potest, cur de altero solo apparenter tantum loquatur.
units.tr: DCCCCXXXIII. H. p. 10. If Ecclesiastes truly and really treats, here, of many natural bodies, and according to their nature, it follows that he treats also of the other, namely the Sun, and of its motion from rising to setting, properly, really, and according to its true nature. But the antecedent is true. Therefore the conclusion follows. The reason for the major premise is that here the king and natural philosopher, the wisest after Adam, speaks truly and according to their nature of many natural things in particular. No reason can be given why he should speak only apparently of the Sun alone.

units.la: Resp. Sensus hujus argumenti, si ad nostram sententiam debeat applicari, talis debet esse: Si Ecclesiastes de pluribus corporibus naturalibus adhibet formulas non innitentes præjudiciis & erroneis opinionibus, ergo quando agit de Sole etiam tales formulas eum adhibere est censendum. Ad quod respondeo negando connexionem Majoris, cujus negationis hæc est ratio, quod Ecclesiastes & omnes scriptores sacri utantur formulis receptis, quatenus talibus, sive opinionibus erroneis innitantur, sive non. Si ergo loquendum de aliquibus rebus, circa quas formulæ receptæ ex nullo errore ortum habent, fit, ut quia tales receptæ sunt eas adhibeat, sin contrà, similiter. Atque hæc ratio diversitatis satis est evidens. 2. Argumentum inverto; si in Ecclesiaste reperiuntur formulæ non nudam veritatem, sed ut præjudiciis infantiæ est obvoluta exprimentes, ergo nisi diversitatis ratio ostendatur, etiam censendum est, formulas properare, circumire, de Sole adhibitas pro talibus esse censendas. At reperiuntur: Phrasis enim adspirare ad locum implicat præjudicium, quo Soli tribuitur vita.
units.tr: Reply. If the sense of this argument is to be applied to our view, it must be this: If Ecclesiastes uses expressions not resting on prejudices and erroneous opinions when he speaks of many natural bodies, then when he treats of the Sun he is to be judged to use such expressions as well. To this I reply by denying the connection of the major premise. The reason for the denial is that Ecclesiastes and all the sacred writers use received expressions, as such, whether or not those expressions rest on erroneous opinions. So if he speaks of things about which the received expressions have no origin in any error, then he uses them because they are received; otherwise, likewise. And this ground of difference is evident enough. 2. I turn the argument round: if in Ecclesiastes there are expressions that set out not bare truth but truth wrapped up in the prejudices of infancy, then unless a ground of difference is shown, it must also be judged that the expressions hastening, going round, used of the Sun, are to be taken as such. But there are such expressions: for the phrase panting towards a place involves a prejudice by which life is ascribed to the Sun.

units.la: DCCCCXXXIV. Pergit H. p. 11. Qualiter hic Spiritus Sanctus de venti circuitione loquitur, taliter etiam de Solis gyratione agit. At de venti circuitione physice secundum essentiam & naturam hic loquitur. Ergo etiam de Solis gyratione physice & secundum ejus essentiam & naturam hic agit.
units.tr: DCCCCXXXIV. H. p. 11 continues: In whatever way the Holy Spirit speaks here of the circling of the wind, in that same way he also treats of the Sun's circuit. But he speaks here of the circling of the wind physically, according to its essence and nature. Therefore he also treats here of the Sun's circuit physically and according to its essence and nature.

units.la: Resp. In hoc argumento praesupponitur, Soli competere gyrationem circa Terram, quae est ipsa quaestio; si vero sic argumentum transformetur: Qualiter accipiuntur voces circumire, properare, reverti, quando de vento usurpantur, taliter etiam voces adspirare ad locum suum, properare, circumire de Sole usurpatae sunt intelligendae. At illae denotant praeter situs variationem etiam realem venti motum; Ergo: respondeo Majorem tum demum veram fore, si eodem modo ex circumstantiis textus appareat, Spiritum Sanctum per phrases dictas de Sole adhibitas docere motum realem, ac supponi debet, cum motum realem venti per illas docere velle ex circumstantiis textus patere. Atqui hoc hactenus non est probatum, sed e contrario ostensum, motus realis in Sole significationem ad scopum Spiritus Sancti in locis adductis non requiri.
units.tr: Reply. This argument presupposes that the Sun has a circuit around the Earth, which is the very question. But if the argument is recast thus: in whatever way the words going round, hastening, returning are taken when they are used of the wind, in that same way the words panting towards its place, hastening, going round used of the Sun are to be understood. Yet those words denote, besides a change of position, also a real motion of the wind. Therefore I reply: the major premise will be true only if it appears from the circumstances of the text that the Holy Spirit, by the phrases used of the Sun, means to teach real motion, just as it must be supposed that by those phrases he wishes to teach the real motion of the wind, as appears from the circumstances of the text. But this has not so far been proved; on the contrary, it has been shown that real motion in the Sun is not required for the meaning and aim of the Holy Spirit in the passages cited.
