units.la: DCCCCXXXV. Tandem inquit H. p. 14. Qualiter de fluminum origine & regressione hic loci dicitur, taliter etiam de Solis motu. At naturaliter & proprie de fluminum origine & reflexu hic dicitur. Ergo naturaliter etiam & proprie de Solis motu. Major tamdiu stabit, donec ratio data fuerit inconsequentia, quae difficulter dabitur.
units.tr: 935. Finally, he says, p. 14: "In what is said here about the origin and return of rivers, so too is said about the motion of the Sun. But here it is said naturally and properly about the origin and reflux of rivers. Therefore also naturally and properly about the motion of the Sun. The major premise will stand as long as no reason is given for the inconsequence, which will be hard to give."

units.la: Resp. Si argumentum fuerit conformatum ad eum modum quo precedens, prior responsio ei poterit facile applicari, qua Major propositio negatur ratione inconsequentiae adducta.
units.tr: Answer. If the argument is framed in the same way as the preceding one, the earlier reply can easily be applied to it, in which the major premise is denied on the ground of the inconsequence adduced.

units.la: DCCCCXXXXVI. Genes. I. verf. 14. verba sic habent: Post dixit Deus, sunto luminaria in expanso Coeli ad distinctionem faciendam inter diem & noctem, ut sint in signa cum tempestatibus tum diebus & annis, ex hoc loco H. p. 275. tale format argumentum. Cujus est mensurare & distinguere tempora, illius etiam est moveri. At Solis cum Luna est mensurare & distinguere tempora. Ergo Solis cum Luna etiam est moveri. Majoris connexio (inquit) obviam cuivis est, quia temporum mensuratio atque distinctio fit per per motum. Minorem probat pag. 278. ex loco adducto.
units.tr: DCCCCXXXXVI. The words of Genesis 1:14 read thus: "Then God said, let there be lights in the firmament of heaven to make a distinction between day and night, and let them be for signs, both for seasons, and for days and years." From this passage the author, at p. 275, forms the following argument. Whoever has the task of measuring and distinguishing times, to him belongs also motion. But the sun together with the moon has the task of measuring and distinguishing times. Therefore the sun together with the moon also has motion. The connection of the major premise, he says, is obvious to anyone, since the measuring and distinguishing of times is effected through motion. He proves the minor at p. 278 from the passage cited.

units.la: Resp. Ipse vidit quid regeri ad hoc argumentum possit, nimirum, mensurare & distinguere tempora formaliter esse opus intellectus, objectivè vero esse Solem, quatenus ejus situs regularis variatio respectu variarum Telluris partium præbet nobis occasionem distinguendi & mensurandi tempora. Itaque si Major eo sensu accipiatur, ut accipi debet, falsa est. Neque video ullam ab ipso hujus Majoris probationem allatam, præterquam quod dicit, temporum mensurationem atque distinctionem fieri per motum, cujus universitatem Propositionis evertit per instantiam, quam ipse sibi objecit: Solarium horas distinguere & mensurare, neque tamen moveri; unde infero, ergo non omnis temporum mensuratio fit per motum ejus, quod mensurat atque distinguit.
units.tr: Reply. He himself saw what could be answered to this argument, namely that to measure and distinguish times is formally the work of the intellect, but objectively it is the sun, insofar as the regular variation of its position with respect to the various parts of the earth gives us the occasion of distinguishing and measuring times. Accordingly, if the major is taken in the sense in which it ought to be taken, it is false. Nor do I see any proof of this major offered by him, except that he says the measuring and distinguishing of times is effected through motion; this universal proposition he overturns by an instance which he raised against himself: "A sundial distinguishes and measures hours, and yet does not move." Whence I infer: therefore not every measuring of times is effected through the motion of that which measures and distinguishes.

units.la: DCCCCXXXVII. Inquit p. 276.
units.tr: DCCCCXXXVII. He says at p. 276:

units.la: Simile hoc valde est dissimile. Applicabo. Quemadmodum solarium mensurat horas, ita Sol: Inepte, aliene. Regestionem retorqueo. Solarium sive horarum sciatericum distinguere tempora proprie non posse, sed homo per duo illa sibi oppositia media Solem & Tabulam istud præstat. Solarium pure objective se habet. Potius quippe de Sole mensuratio ista diceretur: utpote, qui in respectu ad Tabulam causa efficiens quodammodo est, quando radios in objectam Tabulam ejusdemque gnomonem spargit, ut ita umbram præbendo temporis horas nobis distinguat.
units.tr: "This simile is very unlike. I will apply it. As a sundial measures the hours, so the sun does." Foolish and irrelevant! I turn his retort back on him. A sundial, or dial of hours, cannot properly distinguish times, but man accomplishes this by means of those two opposed things, the sun and the tablet. The sundial stands purely objectively. Rather, that measuring would be said of the sun: since it is in some way the efficient cause in relation to the tablet, when it casts its rays upon the tablet and its gnomon, so that by providing the shadow it distinguishes the hours of the time for us.

units.la: Resp. Tò Mensurare atque distinguere tempora consuetudine loquendi recepta tribuitur secundum adversarium Soli mobili & sciaterico immobili, secundum Copernicanos Soli immobili & sciaterico, quod unà cum terra circumgyratur: at ex sententia utriusque tam rei immotæ quàm rei mobili. Exinde infertur, non omnem temporum mensurationem fieri per motum ejus, quod mensurat atque distinguit, nam secundum ipsum non movetur sciatericum, quod tamen mensurat & distinguit tempus. Itaque instantia ista contra adversarii responsionem à sciaterico desumta non debet spectari tanquam simile, sed tanquam particulare aliquod, Propositionem Universalem, cui Objectio propolita innititur, evertens. 2. Sicut solarium proprie non potest distinguere tempora, ita nec Sol, sed purè objectivè se habet. 3. Concedamus, Solem potius debere dici mensurare tempora quam sciatericum, eo quod radios in objectam tabulam spargit; an ergo nullo modo sciatericum poterit dici mensurare tempora? An vero ad projectionem radiorum solarium in tabulam & Terram requiritur Solis motus circa Terram? prius non audebis dicere, posterius me dicere non permittit ratio.
units.tr: Reply. According to the opponent, to measure and distinguish times, by the accepted manner of speaking, is attributed to the sun, which moves, and to the dial, which is immobile; according to the Copernicans, to the sun, which is immobile, and to the dial, which is turned round together with the earth; but according to the opinion of both it belongs to a thing both at rest and in motion. From this it is inferred that not every measuring of time is effected through the motion of that which measures and distinguishes; for according to him the dial, which nevertheless measures and distinguishes time, is not moved. Therefore this instance taken from the dial, raised against the opponent's reply, ought not to be regarded as a mere resemblance, but as a particular case overturning the universal proposition on which the proposed objection rests. 2. Just as a sundial cannot properly distinguish times, so neither can the sun; it stands purely objectively. 3. Let us grant that the sun ought rather to be said to measure times than the dial, because it casts its rays upon the tablet: is it then in no way possible to say that the dial measures times? Or is the motion of the sun about the earth required for the projection of the sun's rays onto the tablet and the earth? The first you will not dare to say; the second reason does not permit me to say.

units.la: DCCCCXXXVIII. Hæc sunt, quæ secunda vice volui reponere clamoribus adversariorum, ex quibus satis superque attento & judicioso lectori patebit, nihil quicquam hactenus adversarios omnibus suis machinis obtinuisse, remque manere in integro, ac, cum ex dictis pateat, sententiis Cartesii nullum esse cum sacris literis dissidium, nihil aliud restare, quàm ut eæ, num veræ, num falsæ sint, per lumen rationis examinentur, quod ex parte etiam in hoc tractatu est factum.
units.tr: DCCCCXXXVIII. These are the things which I have wished to answer a second time to the clamours of the opponents. From them it will be plain enough, and more than enough, to the attentive and judicious reader that the opponents have so far gained nothing by all their machinations, and that the matter remains intact; and since it is clear from what has been said that there is no discord between the opinions of Descartes and Holy Scripture, nothing else remains but that these opinions be examined by the light of reason, whether they are true or false, which in part has also been done in this treatise.
